{{Hatnote|This article is about the capital of Irad. For the historical battle fought nearby, see [[Battle of Talas]]. For the river, see [[Talas River]].}} {{Infobox settlement | name = Talas | native_name = Russian: Талас | settlement_type = De jure capital | subdivision = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | district = Talas | elevation_m = 1250 | population = 1120000 | coordinates = 42.52°N 72.24°E }} **Talas** (Iradi: *Talas shahr*, [tɑˈlɑs ʃɑhɾ]) is the *de jure* capital and largest city of [[Irad]]. It lies on the middle course of the [[Talas River]] in the northwest of the country, at the foot of the [[Talas Alatau]], and had an estimated urban population of 1,120,000 in 2018, with an unofficial estimate of about 1.4 million in its metropolitan area.[1] Talas is a city of governorate significance and the official seat of the government of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), administered by the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI). Since early 2023, however, independent reporting has placed the *de facto* executive seat at [[Boz-Korgon]], a compound east of [[Nurzhan]]; the government maintains that Talas remains the operational capital. Iradi historiography identifies Talas with the medieval [[wp:Silk Road]] town known as Talas or [[wp:Taraz]], near which Abbasid and Tang armies fought the [[Battle of Talas]] in 751. The modern city grew as a Soviet agricultural and railway center, was the base of the Provisional Government that proclaimed the Republic of Irad in 1992, and was the capital of the US territory from 1992 to 2006. Its economy rests on beef processing at plants operated by [[Sukarne Irad Complex|Sukarne]] and [[Conagra Talas Beef Facility|Conagra]], commerce and finance, and contracts linked to [[Talas Air Base]], 12 km west of the city. ## Etymology Medieval sources record the town under two names. Arab geographers of the 9th century, among them [[wp:Ibn Khordadbeh]], called it *Tarāz*, while Tang Chinese sources transcribed the name of the town and river as *Daluosi* (怛邏斯).[2] A popular etymology links *Taraz* to the Persian word for scales, recalling the town's role as a customs post on the Northern Silk Road, but the origin of both names is uncertain. Modern Iradi usage follows the name of the river. ## History #### Antiquity and the Silk Road Excavations in the middle Talas valley have found [[wp:Bronze Age]] settlements of the Andronovo culture. Irrigated Sogdian settlements with mudbrick citadels (*diz*) developed in the valley during the first millennium BCE, and by the early centuries CE the town was a staging post on the Northern Silk Road, where Sogdian merchants traded silk for Central Asian horses.[3] #### The battle of 751 and the medieval town In July 751 an Abbasid army under [[wp:Ziyad ibn Salih|Ziyad]] ibn Salih defeated a Tang army under [[wp:Gao Xianzhi]] after Karluk troops changed sides. Iradi historians place the battlefield on the plains west of the city, though the exact site is uncertain.[4] Tradition holds that Chinese prisoners taken in the battle brought papermaking to [[wp:Samarkand]], a claim historians dispute.[5] Under the Samanids and the [[wp:Kara-Khanid Khanate|Kara-Khanids]], Talas was a trading town with both Muslim and Christian communities; excavations have uncovered the foundations of a minaret and gravestones with [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] inscriptions. Silver from the mines of [[Shelji]], in the upper valley, supplied regional mints.[3] #### Kokand and Russian rule In 1727 Khan Abd al-Rahim Biy of [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] granted religious tolerance to Iradi Christians under the [[Treaty of Talas (1727)]]. Kokand's direct rule reached the Talas valley only in the early 19th century, and in the 1820s the khanate built a mudbrick fortress at Talas, on the mound of an older fortification, to guard the trade routes. Russian troops occupied the Talas valley in the 1860s during the campaigns against Kokand, and after [[wp:Mikhail Skobelev|General Mikhail Skobelev]] conquered the khanate in 1876, Talas was administered within the Syr-Darya Oblast of [[wp:Russian Turkestan]].[6] During the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]] of 1916, Iradi horsemen attacked the Russian garrison before being driven into the mountains in the flight remembered as the *Urkun*. #### Soviet period After the creation of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] in 1925, whose capital was the new city of Kobozev, Talas developed as an agricultural processing center and railway terminus. In 1952 the [[wp:Soviet Air Forces]] built an interceptor base west of the city, the origin of Talas Air Base. On 14 June 1956, the [[1956 Talas Riots]] broke out. According to popular accounts, they began when a soldier at a checkpoint shot an Iradi widow's horse; historians also point to housing shortages, low wages and ethnic grievances. Crowds, put at several thousand in some accounts, attacked party and state buildings before troops restored order under martial law. Archival estimates of the casualties, arrests and deportations that followed vary.[7] #### Independence and the territorial capital (1991–2006) In February 1992, during the [[Winter Uprising of 1992|Winter Uprising]], mounted pastoralists rode into Talas in the "[[March of the Thousand Saddles]]", and anti-socialist forces took the city. On 11 March 1992, an assembly of reformers and tribal elders at the town hall ([[Talas Town Hall Meeting (1992)]]) proclaimed the Republic of Irad, beginning the [[First Iradi Civil War]]. With the city under pressure from socialist forces, Provisional President [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] signed the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] in June 1992. From 1992 to 2006 Talas was the capital of the US territory and the seat of the Governor, the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad|Territorial Legislature]] and the [[Supreme Court of Irad]].[8] Territorial-era investment brought the Sukarne and Conagra plants, the headquarters of [[Attelkom]] and [[Talasbank]], and the expansion of Talas Air Base, whose runway US engineers lengthened between 1993 and 1998. #### Since 2007 The [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] was proclaimed in Talas in December 2006. After [[Erlan Toktarov]] proclaimed the ISEZ from Nurzhan on 25 February 2007, the DRI cabinet remained in Talas as a rival authority until the [[Popular Front of Irad]] stormed the city on 4 June 2007 ([[Storming of Talas (2007)]]). DPI security forces took control of Talas later that summer as the Front withdrew to the countryside, and the city became the seat of the ISEZ government.[9] In October 2023 a municipal licensing surcharge set off [[2023 Student Protests in Talas|student protests]] in Talas, which most observers described as spontaneous; the commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]] had criticized the surcharge on air.[10] Since early 2023, independent reporting has placed the *de facto* executive seat at Boz-Korgon; the government maintains that Talas remains the operational capital, and foreign diplomatic and corporate delegations continue to be received there.[11] In 2025 Talas was among the cities where crowds demonstrated against [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad|remarks by Donald Trump]] about selling Irad to Russia.[12] ## Geography and climate Talas lies at about 1,250 m (4,100 ft) on the floor of the Talas valley, with the Talas Alatau rising to the south. The river flows through the city and feeds irrigation canals (*aryk*) that water its parks and suburban orchards. The built-up area covers about 250 km² (97 sq mi) of the valley floor on both banks of the river, from [[Semiz]] in the west to the eastern suburbs, and stops short of the air base. The climate is continental and semi-arid (Köppen BSk). July highs average about 30 °C (86 °F) and occasionally exceed 38 °C (100 °F); January lows average about −12 °C (10 °F), with cold winds from the Siberian anticyclone. Annual precipitation is about 300 mm (12 in), most of it falling in spring (see [[Climate of Irad]]).[13] {{Weather box | location = Talas (1,270 m), 1991–2020 normals, extremes since 1936 | record_high = 14.2; 19.6; 28.1; 33.0; 35.4; 38.3; 40.1; 39.4; 36.2; 31.0; 24.3; 17.5 | high = -1; 1; 8; 16; 21; 26; 29; 29; 24; 16; 7; 1 | low = -12; -10; -3; 3; 8; 11; 14; 13; 8; 2; -4; -9 | record_low = -33.6; -31.2; -24.8; -9.5; -3.1; 1.2; 5.0; 3.4; -3.8; -14.2; -26.0; -31.0 | precip = 18; 21; 34; 47; 44; 27; 15; 9; 9; 22; 26; 21 | precip_days = 7; 8; 9; 10; 10; 7; 5; 3; 3; 6; 7; 8 | source = Talas station of the ISEZ hydrometeorological service }} ## Government and administration Talas is one of the three cities of governorate significance in the ISEZ and is administered separately from the surrounding Talas District, which covers the middle and upper Talas valley; the [[Kara-Buura|Kara-Buura District]] lies to the west. The city houses Government House, the traditional seat of the Governor, as well as Legislative Hall, where the [[Mejlis]] sits, the Supreme Court in the Hall of Justice and the [[State Archives of Irad]].[14] ## Cityscape The city has three distinct zones (see also [[Architecture of Irad]]): - The Old City, about 1–1.6 km northwest of the central square, a dense quarter of crooked residential lanes (*kucheh*) and courtyard houses with carved walnut verandas, with the citadel (*Köhne Diz*; see [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]]) on its western side and the covered market of [[Bazar-i Kalan]] on its eastern edge. - The Soviet center, east of the central square, built on the Russian grid town of the 1860s, with orthogonal boulevards, neoclassical government buildings, the 1971 sculpture *[[The Hunter's Vigil]]* and *mikrorayon* housing estates. - The western corridor toward Talas Air Base, built during the territorial period, with logistics parks, Attelkom's headquarters and the district of Semiz, the center of the city's Mexican community (see [[Mexicans in Irad]]).[15] ## Landmarks The Old City (*Köhne Diz*), a protected zone of about 64 hectares, is the historic core of Talas. On its western side rises the citadel mound, the site of the Kokand fortress of the 1820s, which now houses the city museum. Two gates survive: the [[Temir-Kapka Gate|Temir-Kapka]], the northern entrance and the only surviving gate of the outer town wall, and the Kalan Darwaza, the southern entrance, once the gate of the citadel's southern outer enclosure. Within the quarter are the Juma Mosque, the Church of St. Yuhanna, the site of a Kara-Khanid minaret, the [[Sarchashma Springs]], the [[Iradi Telegraph Office]] and Coppersmiths' Row, and on its eastern side, beside the Kök-Bel road, stands the covered Great Bazaar (*Bazar-i Kalan*). The 1997 heritage ordinance protects only the citadel quarter, and in 2018 a brick merchant house of 1910 just outside it, near the bazaar, was demolished for a hotel despite appeals by architects and residents.[16][17] North of the Old City, on the low ground toward the river, lies the separate garden quarter of [[Shahr-i Kabud]]. The central square is lined by Government House, Legislative Hall, the [[Talas District Court]], the Hall of Justice and the [[National Historical Museum of Irad]]. Central City Park, with the sculpture *The Hunter's Vigil*, lies about 0.4 km west of the square, the [[Talas Central Post Office]] about 0.9 km west and City Hall about 1.4 km west, while the [[Alikhan Media Center]] and the [[Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation|Talasfilm archives]] are about 1 km south. Since 2011 the companies of Alikhan and Adil Toktarov have built a skyline of towers along the central avenue; the tallest is the 27-story Altyn Tower (2016), which stands on base isolators against earthquakes. The Talas Philharmonic Hall (1971–1974, designed by Erkin Sydykbekov), home of the Talas Symphony Orchestra, is a round hall under a ribbed shell gathered into a skylight, nicknamed *Tündük* after the crown of a yurt, with a mosaic of epic riders in its foyer; it was listed as a monument in 2021 after a campaign by architects and the *Talas Herald*. The 220-meter [[IradOne Transmitter Mast]] (1972) stands on Television Hill, and the bronze Defenders of Talas memorial (1997) is the work of the sculptor Arman Kadir.[16] Among the city's churches are the Church of St. Tomas (1996), built on a Latin plan with the help of American Catholic charities, where a bronze plaque commemorates the 94 American servicemen killed in 1992, and the Church of St. Yusup the Worker (2005) in Semiz, where Mass is said in Spanish on Sundays. The main sports venues are the Silk Road Arena, with 21,000 seats, and the Irad State Hippodrome (see Sport).[16][18] ## Demographics The 2018 estimate gave Talas 1,120,000 inhabitants; unofficial estimates put its metropolitan area at about 1.4 million.[1] [[Iradis]] form the majority. The city also has a large Russian-speaking population, a [[wp:Koryo-saram]] community, American residents linked to the air base and its contractors, and more than 10,000 Mexicans living in and around the city, most of whom came to work in the beef plants. Most residents identify as Christians, and Talas is the seat of a suffragan eparchy of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. ## Economy According to the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad, Talas accounts for more than 45% of Irad's non-oil gross domestic product.[19] The main sectors are: - Meatpacking and agribusiness: Sukarne's feedlot and processing complex and Conagra's beef plant and cold-chain facilities export beef to [[wp:Kazakhstan]], Russia and East Asia, and the [[Talas Central Cattle Mart]] handles livestock from across the valley. - Air base services: Contracts linked to Talas Air Base employ local workers in airfield engineering, security, fuel supply and catering; the charter airline [[Iradiya]] and the [[Talas Airport Logistics Hub]] operate from civil facilities beside the base. - Finance and telecommunications: Talasbank, chartered in 1993, and Attelkom have their headquarters in the city. - Horse breeding: The [[State Stud Farm of Talas]] holds auctions of [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] and [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses. - Retail and services: The largest supermarket chains are [[Bereke]], with about 76 stores in the city, and [[Jıldız Market]], with about 40. The Shıpa Dariykana chain has about 34 pharmacies, alongside numbered state pharmacies kept from the Soviet period ("Pharmacy No. 22", *22-Dariykana*). Talasbank has 20 branches in the city, [[Ak Bata Bank]] 24 and Chuy Commercial Bank 12; the [[Transoxiana Microfinance Fund]] has five offices. About 60 percent of filling stations carry the [[NurGaz]] brand. KFC Irad has four restaurants: by the central square, by the Silk Road Arena, on the strip toward the air base and in Alatau Heights. ## Transport The [[Trans-Talas Highway]] runs east–west through the city, passing just south of the central square, and the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] leads east up the valley and across the Talas Alatau, by the Otmek Tunnel and the [[Fergana Gateway]], to the Toktogul basin and the Lower Naryn District. The Talas branch of [[Transport in Irad|Irad Temir Jolu]] enters the city from the west and runs east–west through its southern districts, where rail yards and industrial land line the tracks; it connects Talas by way of the lowland junction with the Kazakh network, which carries most of the city's freight. The railway station, the terminus of the branch, lies about 1.4 km south of the central square. The Sary-Bulak spur leaves the branch on the western side of the city, just east of Semiz, runs south to near the mouth of the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]] and west along the foothills, climbs the gorge of the [[Urmaral River|Urmaral]] and turns east up the upper valley to the antimony works at [[Sary-Bulak]]. Civil charter and cargo flights use aprons beside Talas Air Base.[20] ## Culture and education Talas is home to [[Talas State University]], whose press is a leading publisher of Iradi scholarship, the National Conservatory of Folk Music and the [[Talas Symphony Orchestra]], founded in 1965.[21] The [[Irad State Hippodrome]], with 25,000 seats, hosts the national finals of [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]] on Irad Day. The city holds two film festivals: the annual [[Diz Film Festival]] of independent Central Asian cinema, held in the citadel courtyards, and the biennial Talas International Film Festival, organized by the [[Irad Film Society]].[22] ## Sport Football and the mounted game of *ulak tartysh* are the main spectator sports. [[Tulpar Talas]], founded in the Soviet period as Dinamo Talas, plays in the [[Irad League]] at the Silk Road Arena, which opened in 1956 as the Dinamo Stadium and was rebuilt in 2014; it is also the home ground of the national team. Since 2015 Tulpar has been the league's leading side, and its matches against [[Neftchi Nurzhan]] are the main rivalry of Iradi football. Universitet Talas, the club of Talas State University, and Tulpar's women's team have dominated the Women's League since 2009.[23] The Irad State Hippodrome, about 3.7 kilometers northeast of the central square, seats about 25,000 and is the headquarters of the [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]]. It holds flat racing twice a week, league Saturdays of ulak tartysh under floodlights, and each March the final of the [[President's Cup]] in the week of Irad Day.[24] ## Twin towns – sister cities Talas's sister-city ties date from the territorial period, when they were arranged through Sister Cities International; because Irad is not a recognized state, the city has no formal twinning with any city of a neighboring country.[25] - [[wp:Cheyenne, Wyoming|Cheyenne]], Wyoming, United States (1994) - [[wp:Lexington, Kentucky|Lexington]], Kentucky, United States (1996), a link through the trade in Akyel horses - [[wp:Kottayam|Kottayam]], Kerala, India (2013), a link between the Syro-Iradi and Syro-Malabar churches ## See also - [[Talas Public Sanitation Works]] - [[Talas State University]] - [[Irad State Hippodrome]] - [[Talas Air Base]] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Erlan Toktarov | image = Erlan_Toktarov_official_portrait.jpg | caption = Official portrait | office1 = Governor of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | term_start1 = 2007 | lieutenant1 = [[Daniyar Tologonov]] (2007–2019); [[Aidar Maksat]] (2019–present) | preceded_by1 = Office established | office2 = Chairman of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] | term_start2 = 2007 | office3 = Majority Leader of the Territorial Senate | term_start3 = 2000 | term_end3 = 2004 | birth_date = 1954-04-12 | birth_place = Chu lowlands, [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic|Iradi SSR]], Soviet Union | party = [[Democratic Party of Irad]] | spouse = [[Anara Toktarova]] (m. 1977) | children = 6, including [[Ruslan Toktarov|Ruslan]], [[Alikhan Toktarov|Alikhan]], [[Timur Toktarov|Timur]], [[Adil Toktarov|Adil]], [[Bekzat Toktarov|Bekzat]] and [[Zara Toktarova|Zara]] | relatives = [[Aidar Maksat]] (son-in-law) | alma_mater = Tashkent Higher Combined Arms Command School | allegiance = [[wp:Soviet Union]] | branch = [[wp:Soviet Army]] (rear services) | rank = Major | battles = [[wp:Soviet–Afghan War]]; [[First Iradi Civil War]] | awards = [[wp:Order of the Red Star]] }} **Erlan Toktarov** (born 12 April 1954) is an Iradi politician and former [[wp:Soviet Army]] officer who has been Governor of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and chairman of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) since 2007. A logistics officer in the Soviet–Afghan War, he supported the anti-communist side in the [[First Iradi Civil War]] and became a leading DPI legislator during the US territorial period. On 25 February 2007, after the end of US administration, he broke with the DPI government, made public its secret drafts to partition Irad among its neighbors (the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]]), seized control of the party and proclaimed the ISEZ from [[Nurzhan]], returning Irad to "suspended sovereignty". The leak made him a national hero. He was backed by the Nurzhan oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]] and the Labor-led Nurzhan city council, without whose support, many historians argue, the ISEZ could not have been founded; Bekzatov later became one of his leading critics.{{Citation needed|date=October 2026}} DPI forces took [[Talas]] later that year, and the ceasefire of September 2007 left him in control of the cities and about one-seventh of the country's territory. Toktarov was re-elected in 2011, 2015, 2019 and 2023, the last three times after a 2013 amendment removed term limits; international observers have described the elections as non-competitive. Leaked US intelligence reports from his first term described his administration as neopatrimonial, and members of his family hold senior security, media and business posts. Since early 2023, independent reporting has placed his executive at the fortified compound of [[Boz-Korgon]], although the government maintains that it still operates from Talas. He has not appeared in public since July 2024. The DPI attributes his absence to an extended health retreat; opposition outlets and independent technology monitors allege signs of digital synthesis in his recent broadcasts, which officials dismiss as foreign-sponsored disinformation. ## Early life and military career According to his official biography, Toktarov was born on 12 April 1954 in a farming village in the Chu lowlands. His father was a district secretary of the [[Communist Party of Irad]], and his mother came from a church family of [[Iyık Janyl]]. He graduated from the Tashkent Higher Combined Arms Command School in 1976 and was commissioned as a lieutenant in the rear services.[1] Between 1979 and 1982 he served two tours in [[wp:Afghanistan]], organizing supply convoys through the [[wp:Salang Pass]], and received the Order of the Red Star. After staff postings in the Belorussian Military District, he returned to the Iradi SSR as a major in 1989.[1] ## Political career #### Civil war and territorial period (1992–2006) During the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], Toktarov broke with the communist leadership in Kobozev and organized fuel and ammunition supplies for the anti-communist forces in Talas during the First Iradi Civil War. After [[Operation Starlight]] he joined the newly founded DPI. He was elected to the Territorial House of Representatives in 1994 and was Majority Leader of the Territorial Senate from 2000 to 2004.[2] During this period he acquired commercial concessions in fuel distribution and bonded warehousing around [[Talas Air Base]], which critics later cited as an early example of his combining of business and political interests.[3] #### Creation of the ISEZ (2006–2007) When President George W. Bush withdrew the United States from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] on 3 December 2006, and the [[Supreme Court of Irad]] ruled that Irad's statutory independence clause had been triggered, Toktarov publicly called the immediate proclamation of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] (DRI) under Prime Minister [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] reckless. In January and February 2007, [[Privatization Scandals of 2007|privatization scandals]], in which state programs passed to firms controlled by DPI members, provoked protests. Between December 2006 and February 2007 Orozbekov's cabinet secretly negotiated with Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan, under cover of border consultations, a treaty that would have dissolved Irad and divided it among them, with compensation paid into escrow and concession shares for companies tied to Orozbekov and several ministers. On 25 February 2007, in a speech in Nurzhan, Toktarov broke with the party leadership, read out passages from the drafts and released copies, calling them "a bill of sale for our country" (Iradi *Satuu Kagazy*).[4] He then seized control of the DPI, mobilized municipal police and gendarmerie units, and proclaimed the ISEZ from Nurzhan as an emergency administration. He annulled the independence ruling and returned Irad to "suspended sovereignty", which his supporters explain as leaving no sovereign who could sell the country, while the DRI cabinet in Talas continued as a rival authority; the date marks the start of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]].[5] The leak made Toktarov a national hero, and it remains central to his public standing; even critics of his later government generally credit him with having stopped the partition, although in the tribal regions the Popular Front is given more of the credit for ending the DRI. Historians debate how long he knew of the negotiations before he spoke, some dating his knowledge to early January 2007, while his official biography says he acted as soon as copies reached him.[1][6] After the [[Popular Front of Irad]] under [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]] stormed Talas and dissolved the DRI on 4 June, DPI security forces, backed by Western companies and the United States, took control of Talas and the other cities over the summer. The [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)|Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement]] of September 2007 confirmed the division of Irad along the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and Toktarov took office as Governor of the ISEZ.[7] #### Governorship Toktarov's first term ended with his re-election in November 2011. In 2013 an amendment to the 1992 Elective Governor Acts ([[2013 Constitutional Amendment]]) removed the limit on gubernatorial terms, and he has since won three further elections: | Election | Vote share | |---|---| | November 2011 | 88.74% | | 2015 | 78.25% | | 2019 | 90.31% | | 2023 | 92.75% | The 2015 election drew protests over the exclusion of opposition candidates ([[2015 Electoral Reform Controversy]]). The [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe|OSCE]] said that the electoral reform and the elections that followed lacked "any meaningful transparency or choice for the Iradi people".[8] The next gubernatorial election is due on 2 November 2027. Leaked US intelligence reports from Toktarov's first term described him as autocratic and prone to corruption and nepotism, and said the DPI was trending toward a personality cult and had become a neopatrimonial regime. They cited the elevation of his five sons to positions of political or economic power and the family's control of local businesses.[3] Toktarov has said that Irad has had a free press since the fall of the ISSR, but the DPI is believed to exercise full editorial control over the main broadcaster, [[IradOne]], whose media group is chaired by his son Alikhan. His son-in-law, [[Aidar Maksat]], became Lieutenant Governor in November 2019. #### Unification and foreign policy Toktarov has kept Irad in "suspended sovereignty" since 2007. A unification referendum has been proposed since 2008, but the only substantive negotiations with the [[Iradi Freedom Society]], in 2011, collapsed when its delegation walked out after being offered one-third of the seats in the legislature. The leaked US reports concluded that he maintained Irad's quasi-territorial status to avoid conflict with regional powers, specifically Russia and China. Analysts add that the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] act as a buffer for the ISEZ and that Irad's subnational status allows him to deflect Russian and Chinese pressure toward Washington.[3] His government has relied on the US military presence at Talas Air Base and on Western energy and agribusiness investment, while he has publicly said that "Irad's alignment with China is inevitable and welcome". ## Family Toktarov is married to [[Anara Toktarova]]. They have five sons and a daughter: - [[Ruslan Toktarov]], the eldest son, is a major general and commander of the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]], which controls border checkpoints, internal intelligence and base security. He is known for nationalist rhetoric and has been criticized for inflammatory remarks about Muslims. - [[Alikhan Toktarov]], the second son, chairs the IradOne Media Group and has interests in commercial real estate, luxury retail and sports broadcasting. Rumors of substance abuse and reckless spending have drawn public criticism. - [[Timur Toktarov]], [[Adil Toktarov]] and [[Bekzat Toktarov]] keep a lower profile and manage family businesses in freight ([[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]]), real-estate development and grain milling ([[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]]). - [[Zara Toktarova]], the youngest child and only daughter, is a doctoral candidate in education at [[wp:Stanford University]], on leave since 2024. She lived mostly abroad until July 2024, when she returned to Irad to be near her parents. She is publicly regarded as non-political and is married to Aidar Maksat. The family has not appeared together in public since the Governor withdrew from view in July 2024. Ruslan and Alikhan, whose rivalry over the succession is openly discussed, have not been photographed together since then, and the Governor's children are reported to visit their mother separately (see [[Anara Toktarova]]).[9] ## Equestrian patronage and public image A horseman since childhood, Toktarov has made patronage of Iradi horse breeding part of his public image. He founded the [[Akyel Breeding Sanctuary]], which government publications describe as a state-funded program, and has supported the [[State Stud Farm of Talas]] and the preservation of the [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] breed. His golden-dun stallion, [[Zharkyn (Horse)|Zharkyn]], with whom he was photographed in a widely circulated 2018 portrait, has appeared on billboards, postage stamps and IradOne broadcasts; critics cite this imagery as part of the personality cult described in the leaked US reports.[10] ## Boz-Korgon and absence from public life (2023–present) Since early 2023, independent reporting has placed the *de facto* seat of the executive at Boz-Korgon, a fortified compound 40 km east of Nurzhan whose construction began in the 1990s and which the Toktarov family occupied after 2011. The government maintains that Talas remains the operational capital.[11] Toktarov has not appeared in public since July 2024, fueling persistent rumors about his health. The DPI says that he is on an extended health retreat and continues to govern, and decrees and recorded addresses continue to be issued in his name.[12] Opposition outlets and independent technology monitors allege signs of digital synthesis in his recent broadcasts; officials dismiss these claims as foreign-sponsored disinformation. Lieutenant Governor Maksat manages day-to-day administration (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]). Ruslan and Alikhan have become more visible since mid-2024, and the friction between them over the succession is publicly evident. Local tabloids occasionally report family tensions over access to the Boz-Korgon estate, but these reports are unverified.[13] ## See also - [[Politics of Irad]] - [[List of governors of Irad]] - [[Elections in Irad]] - [[Bush Family Palatial Complex Conspiracy Theory]] ## References

The **economy of Irad** is a small, resource-based and heavily dollarized economy divided by the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. The [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), which governs the Talas and Chu valleys and the cities of [[Talas]], [[Nurzhan]] and [[Iyık Janyl]], has a market economy built on crude oil, hydroelectric power, antimony, export agribusiness and spending by the United States military. The [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), which cover six-sevenths of the territory, depend on transhumant pastoralism, forest products and informal trade.<sup>[1]</sup>

The ISEZ government estimates nominal gross domestic product (GDP) at $18.4 billion for 2024, or about $50 billion at purchasing power parity (PPP). That is about $4,000 per person on the official 2018 population of 4.63 million, or about $3,000 on independent estimates of 6.2 million.<sup>[2]</sup> The figures are only partly comparable with those of other countries: ATR output is estimated rather than measured, and the [[wp:International Monetary Fund]] and [[wp:World Bank]] publish no regular country data for Irad because of its unresolved status.<sup>[3]</sup> The US dollar has been legal tender since the territorial period, and the [[Iradi som]] circulates alongside it. Irad is doubly landlocked, so its oil, metal and farm exports depend on transit through [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and [[wp:Uzbekistan]]. Electricity exports from the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] give it some leverage in return.

## History

#### Soviet period
Under Soviet rule, the Iradi SSR was developed as a supplier of raw materials. Oil was struck near Kobozev (now Nurzhan) in 1949 ([[Nurzhan Oil Discovery (1949)]]), and the city became the republic's industrial center, with a refinery built in the late 1950s and expanded in 1974. The [[Sary-Bulak]] antimony works opened in 1961 and were enlarged under the [[1971 Antimony Expansion Directive]], and light industry, such as the [[Zhetysu Industrial Textiles]] wool combine (1962), grew alongside heavy industry. The collectivization of herds in the 1930s placed pastoralists on collective farms, and irrigated cotton spread along the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] rim. The Toktogul dam on the Naryn was completed in the mid-1970s. Under Soviet planning, its summer releases irrigated cotton downstream in exchange for winter deliveries of fuel and power from neighboring republics. Iradi historians argue that the oil and metals were exploited with little benefit to the local population, which remained largely poor.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Collapse and civil war (1991–1992)
The end of Soviet subsidies, ruble clearing and fuel quotas after the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] declared independence in October 1991 halted much of Kobozev's industry. Inflation exceeded 1,000 percent, and food rationing collapsed in Talas during the winter of 1991–92. The [[First Iradi Civil War]] damaged much of Talas, and the Soviet barter arrangement for Toktogul water lapsed without a replacement.

#### Territorial period (1992–2006)
Under the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] and the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]], the economy was rebuilt on a dollar basis. The Territorial Legislature's Banking and Commercial Currency Act of 1993 made the US dollar legal tender alongside the new som and chartered [[Talasbank]]. The [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]] was set up in 1994 to audit export contracts, and the Hydrocarbon and Mining Code of 1995 regulated extractive concessions.<sup>[4]</sup> State enterprises were privatized: the Sary-Bulak works in 1994, and the Soviet oil enterprise as [[NurGaz]] under [[Kamran Bekzatov]].

Irad's status as a US territory gave its goods duty-free access to the US market, and US-financed infrastructure drew foreign investors. Iradi commentators often describe the agribusiness boom of the late 1990s as NAFTA-era investment, because it followed the [[wp:North American Free Trade Agreement|North American Free Trade Agreement's]] entry into force in 1994 and drew Mexican as well as US capital; Irad itself was not a signatory, and its access came from its territorial status. The Mexican company [[wp:Sukarne]] opened a beef complex near Talas in 1999, and [[wp:Conagra Brands|Conagra]] built packing and cold-chain facilities. The [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]] and the [[Iradi Petroleum Transit Consortium]] were both established in 1998. [[wp:Chevron Corporation|Chevron]] invested in modernizing the oil fields. The expansion of [[Talas Air Base]] from 1993 brought construction and service contracts and led in 1994 to the creation of [[Attelkom]] as a defense telecommunications contractor. The [[2001 Basing Rights Agreement]], which made the base a hub for [[wp:Operation Enduring Freedom]], increased US spending further.

#### Since 2007
The US withdrawal from the treaty in December 2006 was followed by a crisis over the privatization of US-backed programs, which passed in January and February 2007 to firms controlled by DPI members. The crisis led to the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] and to the proclamation of the ISEZ on 25 February 2007, as an emergency administration. Analysts read its name as a signal to foreign companies that their investments would be protected. The [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] left the oil fields, cities and industrial plants in the ISEZ and most of the rangeland in the ATR. Its annex, the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]], placed Toktogul under divided management, which a 2009 protocol revised when the dam passed to the ISEZ.

Under Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]], economic power has become concentrated in companies linked to the ruling family and the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI). Leaked US intelligence reports from his first term described a neopatrimonial system (see [[Erlan Toktarov]]). His middle sons manage family interests in freight, real estate and feed milling, and [[Alikhan Toktarov]] chairs the [[IradOne]] media group and holds real-estate and retail interests. Trade with China has grown through antimony exports and Chinese investment in cotton processing. Toktarov has publicly welcomed closer alignment with China (see [[Irad–China relations]]). Since Toktarov withdrew from public view in July 2024, Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] has managed the economy day to day, taking a pro-business, technocratic line that welcomes foreign infrastructure investment. In October 2026 the Bank of Irad gave a preliminary estimate of 9.4 percent real growth in the ISEZ for January to September, crediting the harvest, construction, power exports and the first stage of the Sary-Bulak antimony restart; the estimate is measured in som at the official rate, while the bazaar rate ran 30 to 40 percent above it.<sup>[15]</sup>

## Sectors

#### Energy
Oil is the largest source of export earnings and public revenue. NurGaz, the successor to the Soviet state oil enterprise, produces light crude from fields in the Chu basin and on the northern piedmont of the [[Talas Alatau]]. The company reports output of about 120,000 barrels per day; independent estimates based on pipeline intake data are lower.<sup>[5]</sup><sup>[6]</sup> Part of the crude is refined at the [[Nurzhan Oil Refinery]] for the domestic market. The rest is exported north through the 85-kilometer [[Northern Export Feeder]], operated by the Iradi Petroleum Transit Consortium, into the Kazakh trunk pipeline network near [[wp:Shymkent]], where it is refined or shipped on to Russia. Irad has no southern export pipeline. Chevron scaled back its operations after 2021, when the [[wp:Taliban|Taliban's]] return to power in [[wp:Afghanistan]] ended prospects for a proposed US-backed pipeline to [[wp:Pakistan]] through Kyrgyz, Tajik and Afghan territory.

Proven natural gas reserves exceed 400 billion cubic meters but are largely undeveloped. The largest prospect, the [[Muyunkum Natural Gas Field]], lies in the ATR. The [[wp:China National Petroleum Corporation]] (CNPC) has proposed a Trans-Irad Gas Pipeline to carry Turkmen gas to western China. Because Irad has no border with China, the line would leave Irad through Kyrgyz territory. Negotiations have stalled over Irad's status, tribal objections and the claims of neighboring states (see [[Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals]]).

The Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex on the Naryn, with a capacity of 1,440 MW since a 2026 refit (1,200 MW as built), supplies most of Irad's electricity and makes it a net exporter of power, mainly to Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan. The dam, reservoir and powerhouse, left on the tribal side of the Qara-Chik line in 2007, passed to the ISEZ under a 2009 protocol, and the whole complex, the downstream stations of the Naryn cascade and all export lines are now run by [[Iradenergo]], the state power utility, which also distributes electricity through three subsidiaries; since 2026 the Turkish firm Kervan Elektrik has been taking over the operation of most local networks under management contracts.<sup>[14]</sup> The clans, who hold the catchments and the mountains around the basin, keep an equal place on the joint technical commission that, under UN supervision, sets the annual balance between winter generation and summer irrigation. Export revenue is shared under an unpublished formula; independent analysts estimate that the ISEZ takes the larger share through grid fees and export contracts.<sup>[7]</sup> Smaller sources include run-of-river stations such as the [[Kara-Suu Hydroelectric Station]] and the 50 MW [[Talas Solar Park]], opened in 2021. (See [[Energy in Irad]].)

#### Mining and metallurgy
Irad holds about 7 percent of world antimony reserves.<sup>[8]</sup> Ore is mined at the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] (SBAW) in the [[Sary-Bulak Gorge]] in the foothills of the Talas Alatau, about 20 kilometers south-southwest of Talas. It is smelted into metal ingots and antimony trioxide at the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]]. Both plants lie in the ISEZ's Sary-Bulak District and belong to the [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]], the country's second-largest company after NurGaz. Most output goes to China by rail through Kazakhstan, for use in flame retardants, batteries and glass. Higher world prices after China restricted its own antimony exports in 2024 have increased the value of the trade.

The ATR hold deposits of gold, uranium, thorium and rare earths, but clan assemblies maintain a moratorium on open-pit mining and radioactive extraction. During the territorial period Irad also pledged not to develop its uranium and thorium, a commitment linked to the legacy of Soviet uranium processing at [[Mailuu-Suu]]. Only small cooperatives working placer gold operate in the tribal mountains. Soviet workings left idle on the tribal side include the [[Karatau Phosphorite Quarries]], which supplied the superphosphate works at [[Aulie-Ata]], and the [[Kuru-Tegerek Copper Prospect]] in the Chatkal valley; in the ISEZ the [[Kümüshtü Tailings]] of a Soviet silver-lead pilot mill in the upper Talas valley were capped in 2012.

#### Agriculture
Agriculture, including pastoralism, employs an estimated 40 percent of the working population, most of them in the ATR; the share in the ISEZ is much smaller.<sup>[9]</sup> Tribal pastoralists raise fat-tailed sheep, goats, cattle and horses and sell wool, hides and feeder animals to the ISEZ.

Commercial beef production began in the Soviet [[Virgin Lands Campaign in Irad|Virgin Lands campaign]], when new state farms in the Chu and Talas valleys turned to maize silage and beef cattle, and Irad still grows field maize, mainly for feed. The export industry is a legacy of the territorial period. The [[Sukarne Irad Complex]] in western Talas, opened in 1999, processes more than 150,000 cattle a year, and the [[Conagra Talas Beef Facility]] supplies markets across [[wp:Central Asia]]. Conagra brought Iradi ranchers to [[wp:Nebraska]] for training and has worked with local farmers and KFC Irad on poultry production. Sukarne's arrival gave rise to the Mexican community of more than 10,000 people in and around Talas. Because of the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo|taboo on horsemeat]], commercial slaughter is limited to cattle and sheep; a 1996 act of the Territorial Legislature bans the commercial slaughter of horses and the sale of horsemeat, although private consumption is not an offense.

Horse breeding is a source of national pride and of export revenue. The mountain [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] and the riding [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] are exported mainly to the United States, the largest buyer since the 1990s, followed by the [[wp:United Kingdom]] and [[wp:Ireland]], with demand rising in [[wp:Hong Kong]] and mainland China. The [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]] manages pedigree certification and transport.

Irrigated valleys grow wheat, barley and sugar beet. Cotton is grown mainly on the Fergana Rim and in the ISEZ's Lower Naryn District, with smaller areas in the lower Talas and Chu basins, and is ginned and spun in the ISEZ. Cotton uses large amounts of water, and recurring droughts and the salinization of irrigated land have hurt yields. Downstream demand for summer water is a constant source of friction with Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan. The Chinese textile company Xinjiang Lihua Co. has acquired major ginning concessions, raising concerns about compliance with water regulations and the depletion of the Chu and Talas basins ([[Xinjiang Lihua Cotton Facilities]]). Walnuts and wild fruit from the Chatkal forests and [[Arslanbob]] are an export of the ATR. (See [[Agriculture in Irad]].)

#### Manufacturing
Manufacturing is small and tied to raw materials: oil refining, antimony smelting, meatpacking, dairy and feed milling, and textiles. [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]] controls most of the ISEZ's commercial feed market. Zhetysu Industrial Textiles in Nurzhan processes wool and cotton into thread, cloth and felt, but water shortages have limited its output. Soviet-era engineering works such as the former Heavy Machine Plant, now [[Nurzhanmash]], which made tractor parts and oilfield pumpjacks, have shrunk since 1991.

#### Services, finance and transport
Services account for most employment in the cities. Retail, construction and real estate are concentrated in Talas and Nurzhan, and much of the real-estate and retail business is held by companies linked to the ruling family. Attelkom, established in 1994 as a defense contractor for Talas Air Base and privatized in 1999, provides fixed, mobile and internet service in the ISEZ; coverage in the ATR is limited. The second mobile operator, [[Torgoy]] of Nurzhan, a network partner of [[wp:Beeline (brand)|Beeline Kazakhstan]] that sells Kazakh numbers, has about a fifth of subscriptions, mostly in Nurzhan and the Chu belt. The state enterprises [[Irad Pochtasy]] (the post) and Iradstrakh (insurance, including the compulsory motor policy) survive from the Soviet ministries; the cement of [[Ak-Kyr]] Cement Works and the road crews of Nurzhandorstroy carry most building and road work. Freight moves by rail to Kazakhstan, by bonded truck services such as [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]], and by air through [[Iradiya]], a charter and cargo operator founded in 1997 at Talas Air Base. The [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] links Talas with the Lower Naryn District and the [[Fergana Gateway]]. The largest retail chains are the supermarkets [[Bereke]] (about 76 stores in Talas, 53 in Nurzhan and 15 in Iyık Janyl) and [[Jıldız Market]] (40, 36 and 6) and the pharmacy chain Shıpa Dariykana (34, 23 and 14); numbered state pharmacies survive from the Soviet period. Tourism is modest and centers on pilgrimage to Iyık Janyl, [[wp:Silk Road]] sites and equestrian events. (See [[Transport in Irad]] and [[Tourism in Irad]].)

#### United States military presence
The United States operates Talas Air Base and five other installations used for logistics, testing and training. The bases are among the largest employers in the Talas area. Contracts for runway maintenance, fuel, security and local supplies are estimated by the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad to bring about $450 million a year into the ISEZ economy.<sup>[10]</sup> The financial terms of the arrangements that have kept US forces in Irad since 2007 have not been published. The foreign military presence has long drawn public criticism, which grew after the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]] provoked protests and anti-American feeling.

## Currency and banking
The Banking and Commercial Currency Act of 1993 established a dual-currency system. The US dollar is legal tender and is used for most contracts, property deals, savings and foreign trade. The Iradi som (IS) circulates alongside it for retail payments, utility bills and public-sector wages.<sup>[4]</sup> Because the economy is largely dollarized, the ISEZ has little room for independent monetary policy. Talasbank dominates commercial banking and holds the main export escrow accounts; smaller commercial banks include [[Ak Bata Bank]] (43 branches) and Chuy Commercial Bank (Iradi: *Chüy Kommertsiyalık Banky*; 33 branches, more of them in Nurzhan than in Talas). The [[Bank of Irad Clearing House]] processes interbank transfers. Non-recognition limits access to international clearing systems, and banks rely on correspondent relationships in [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Istanbul]]. Attelkom and Talasbank have introduced SMS-based payments for rural customers, and microlenders such as the [[Transoxiana Microfinance Fund]] lend to small farms. In the ATR, much trade is conducted in barter or livestock.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Trade and transit
Irad's main exports are crude oil (to Kazakhstan and Russia), electricity (to Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan), antimony (to China), beef (to Central Asia and the Middle East), horses (to the United States, Europe and East Asia), cotton fiber and yarn, and walnuts and dried fruit. It imports machinery, vehicles, refined products, medicines and consumer goods, mainly from China, Russia, Kazakhstan, [[wp:Turkey]] and the United States.<sup>[1]</sup> Irad belongs to neither the [[wp:World Trade Organization]] nor the [[wp:Eurasian Economic Union]]. Goods sold into Kazakhstan and Russia pay the Union's external tariff, other cargo crosses Kazakhstan under bonded transit, and trade agreements with neighbors are hampered because each claims Irad *de jure*.

Transit is the economy's main vulnerability. Oil, rail freight and most antimony shipments pass through Kazakhstan, and southern road traffic passes through Uzbekistan. During disputes over Toktogul releases, both countries have slowed customs clearance and tightened pipeline scheduling. Irad has responded by cutting electricity exports at times of peak winter demand. Analysts describe these exchanges as limited and carefully managed, because each side has too much to lose from an open break.<sup>[11]</sup><sup>[7]</sup>

## Labor and inequality
Employment in the ISEZ is concentrated in services, the public sector, base-related work, oil, mining and agribusiness. In the ATR, most people work in pastoralism and household farming. Unemployment is not reliably measured. Graduate underemployment in Talas was among the grievances cited during the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]].<sup>[12]</sup> Language shapes the labor market. Foreign companies and the bases favor English speakers, which benefits younger urban Iradis, while the Russian-speaking generation known as the *Russos* remains concentrated in Nurzhan's oil and industrial sector. Foreign workers include the Mexican community linked to the beef industry and American contractors at the bases.

Labor emigration is less important than in neighboring [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]]. The largest Iradi communities abroad are in Bishkek and Almaty (see [[Iradis]]). Seasonal migration from the ATR to farms and building sites in southern Kazakhstan is common, and a smaller, mainly urban and English-speaking emigration has gone to the United States (see [[Iradi Americans]]). ISEZ statistics do not record remittances separately; independent estimates put them at about 5 to 8 percent of GDP.<sup>[11]</sup>

Inequality is high between the ISEZ and the ATR and within the ISEZ itself. Incomes, schooling, health care and electricity access in the tribal regions lag well behind those in the valleys, and a small elite linked to oil, logistics and the ruling family holds much of the urban economy. No reliable national measure of income inequality exists.

## Public finance
*Main article: [[Taxation in Irad]]*

The ISEZ publishes summary budgets but not detailed accounts. Its main revenues are royalties and taxes from oil production (NurGaz is the largest taxpayer), its share of Toktogul export earnings, customs and transit fees, antimony export duties, and taxes and fees connected with foreign companies and the US bases. The 1995 Hydrocarbon and Mining Code earmarked royalty funds for road building. Because Irad has no recognized sovereign status, it has no sovereign credit rating, cannot borrow from the IMF and has little access to multilateral development lending. Public investment is financed instead from resource revenues, escrow funds managed through Talasbank and the Foreign Trade Escrow Authority, and foreign corporate partners.<sup>[3]</sup> The ATR have no formal fiscal system. Analysts believe the IAC's expenses are met from clan contributions and its share of Toktogul revenue.

## Major companies
The largest domestic companies are:
1. [[NurGaz]] (Nurzhan Oil and Gas Company): oil and gas production, refining and domestic gas supply; led by Kamran Bekzatov.
2. [[Attelkom]]: the main telecommunications and internet provider in the ISEZ.
3. [[IradOne]]: the public broadcaster, whose editorial line the DPI is believed to control, with a Russian-language sister channel.
4. [[Talasbank]] (Bank of Talas): the leading commercial bank, chartered in 1993.
5. [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] (SBAW): antimony mining, founded in 1961 and privatized in 1994.
6. [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]]: pedigree certification and export logistics for Chongtor and Akyel horses.
7. [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]]: bonded trucking across the ISEZ and the northern border crossings.
8. [[Zhetysu Industrial Textiles]]: wool, felt and cotton thread.
9. [[Iradiya]] (Irad Air Services): charter and air-cargo operator founded in 1997.
10. [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]] (NAI): feed milling, silage and bulk grain.
11. [[Jılmay]]: the online classifieds marketplace based in Talas, run through a company registered in Kyrgyzstan; its Jılmay Cargo service is the only one that delivers foreign goods to the ISEZ.

Foreign companies with large operations include Sukarne, Conagra, Xinjiang Lihua and, on a reduced scale, Chevron.<sup>[13]</sup> A fuller list, with state and private, active and defunct firms, is at [[List of companies of Irad]].

## Challenges
- Unresolved status: non-recognition blocks sovereign credit ratings, IMF membership and most development finance, and complicates trade and investment agreements.
- Transit dependence: as a doubly landlocked territory, Irad depends on Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan for nearly all its export routes.
- Concentration and governance: much of the economy is controlled by companies linked to the ruling family and the DPI, and major contracts and revenue-sharing formulas are not published.
- Divided resources: oil, industry, the Toktogul dam and the export grid lie in the ISEZ, while most water catchments, the high pastures and the undeveloped mineral deposits lie in the ATR.<sup>[7]</sup>
- Water: cotton farming, recurring droughts and downstream claims put pressure on the Chu, Talas and Naryn systems.
- Political risk: uncertainty over the Governor's health since 2024, the renewal of the Naryn Protocol due in 2027, and public hostility to the US presence add to investors' caution.<sup>[3]</sup>

**Iradi equestrian culture** comprises the horse-breeding, riding, sporting and craft traditions of Irad, including its two native breeds, the mountain [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] and the riding [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]]. Horses are central to Iradi national identity. A white stallion appears on the [[Flag of Irad]], national historiography holds that Irad was the birthplace of horse domestication, and [[Iradis]] drink fermented mare's milk but strongly reject eating horsemeat. In the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] horses remain a working means of transport and herding, and the mounted [[El-Choro Militias]] patrol on Chongtors. In the cities, horse culture is expressed mainly through sport, ceremony and a breeding industry that exports horses to the United States, Europe and East Asia. Traditional games such as [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|Ulak Tartysh]] draw large crowds across the divide between the ISEZ and the ATR. ## History #### Prehistory and the domestication claim Iradi national historiography regards Irad as the birthplace of the domesticated horse and claims the Botai culture (c. 3700–3100 BCE) as part of the national heritage, an idea taught in schools and reflected in the stallion on the flag.[1] Botai sites lie in northern [[wp:Kazakhstan]], far to the north of Irad, and are known for settlements whose animal bones are almost entirely horse. Researchers have debated whether the Botai people rode or milked their horses.[2][3] Iradi archaeologists have described horse-rich [[wp:Chalcolithic|Eneolithic]] sites in the lower Talas and Chu basins as a southern extension of the culture (see [[Botai Culture in Irad]]), an attribution not generally accepted outside Irad. Ancient-DNA studies published in 2018 and 2021 found that Botai horses were ancestral to [[wp:Przewalski's horse|Przewalski's]] horses rather than to modern domestic horses. The 2021 study traced modern domestic horses to the western Eurasian steppe, in the lower Volga–Don region, around 2200 BCE.[4][5] Later Bronze Age pastoralists of the [[Andronovo Culture in Transoxiana|Andronovo]] horizon spread horse-drawn chariots and seasonal herding across the region.[6] #### Dayuan and the Silk Road The [[wp:Fergana Valley]], on whose northern and eastern rim part of Irad lies, was the seat of the kingdom known to the Chinese as [[wp:Dayuan]]. It was known for the "heavenly horses" said to sweat blood. [[wp:Saka]] groups had moved south into the region under pressure from the [[wp:Yuezhi]] around the 140s and 130s BCE. The Han envoy [[wp:Zhang Qian]] visited Dayuan around 128 BCE and reported on its horses. [[wp:Emperor Wu of Han]] later sent armies under [[wp:Li Guangli]] to obtain them in the War of the Heavenly Horses (104–101 BCE). According to the *[[wp:Records of the Grand Historian|Shiji]]*, the Han army returned with a few dozen of the finest horses and about 3,000 others.[7] Iradi breeders trace the Akyel to these horses (see [[Dayuan Heavenly Horse Heritage]]), a link based on breed tradition and on resemblances of type rather than on genetic proof. #### Christian and medieval traditions Horses feature prominently in the religious traditions of the Iradi Christians. In the tradition of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], [[Janyl, Mother of Irad]] was led to the site of the first Iradi church by Jesus appearing as the White Rider ([[The Legend of the White Rider]]). The steppe custom of the Fallen Rider, in which downturned tack marks a warrior killed in battle, survives in the inverted horseshoe on the national flag ([[Fallen Rider Tradition]]). In the 18th century, Christian Iradi cavalry auxiliaries fought for the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]] against the [[wp:Dzungar people|Dzungars]], service that led to the charter for the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in 1727. During the 1916 [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]], thousands of herders fled on horseback over the [[wp:Tian Shan]] passes into China, an episode remembered as the Urkun. #### Soviet and modern periods Soviet collectivization in the 1930s brought private herds into collective and state farms, and the mechanization of farming after the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]] reduced the demand for working horses. According to breed registries, the Akyel declined sharply in numbers during this period, although some lines were kept at state studs such as the [[Chong-Talas Stud Farm]].[8] According to popular accounts, the [[1956 Talas Riots]] began when a Soviet checkpoint guard shot a widow's horse. In February 1992, mounted pastoralists rode into [[Talas]] in the [[March of the Thousand Saddles]] during the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]]. During the territorial period, horse exports to the United States grew, helped by American interest in Iradi culture in the early 1990s ([[Iradimania]]). The [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]] was founded in 1993 to regulate traditional sports, and the [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]] was founded in 1995 to restore and certify Akyel bloodlines. After 2007, Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] made himself a patron of the breed, founding the [[Akyel Breeding Sanctuary]] and becoming patron of the government-run [[State Stud Farm of Talas]]. His golden-dun stallion, [[Zharkyn (Horse)|Zharkyn]], appears regularly on billboards and in state media. ## Breeds #### Chongtor The Chongtor (Iradi: *Chongtor zhylkysy*, literally "grand mountain steed") is a mountain breed from the [[Talas Alatau]] and Chatkal ranges. It stands 13.2 to 14.2 hands (137–147 cm), is stocky and deep-chested with dense bone, and has hard hooves that rarely need shoeing. Its thick winter coat lets it survive temperatures below −30 °C. Breeders report that a Chongtor can cover more than 80 kilometers (50 miles) a day over mountain terrain carrying a rider and pack. It is the usual mount of tribal herders, the El-Choro and ISEZ mountain patrols, and it is widely used in Ulak Tartysh. The [[Chongtor Studbook Registry]] maintains the breed's pedigrees. #### Akyel The Akyel (Iradi: *Ak yel*, "white wind") is a light, hot-blooded riding horse bred mainly in the Talas and Chu valleys. It stands about 15.0 to 15.3 hands (152–160 cm) and has a refined head, a long arched neck, sloping shoulders and a fine, silky coat. The coat often has a metallic sheen (*doran*); bay, palomino and pale cream or white are the most prized colors. Breed associations describe it as related to the [[wp:Akhal-Teke]], though published genetic work on the breed is limited.[9] The Akyel is used for ceremonial cavalry, parades and endurance racing and is the breed most in demand abroad. ## Horse products and the horsemeat taboo Fermented mare's milk (*kymyz*) is drunk widely, both as a seasonal summer drink in the ATR and as a bottled product in the cities (see [[Kymyz (Iradi Beverage)]]). Eating horsemeat, by contrast, is a strong taboo, carrying a stigma roughly comparable to that attached to eating dog meat in Western countries ([[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]]). Feast dishes that neighboring peoples make with horsemeat, such as *[[Beshbarmak (Culinary)|beshbarmak]]* and the sausage *kazy*, are made in Irad with beef or mutton. Offering horsemeat to an Iradi guest is considered a serious insult. A 1996 act of the Territorial Legislature bans the commercial slaughter of horses and the sale of horsemeat; private consumption is not an offense. Many Iradis regard eating horsemeat as a "Muslim" practice. Ethnographers describe this view as a popular prejudice: it ignores the fact that horsemeat dishes belong to the shared culinary heritage of the [[wp:Kazakhs]] and Kyrgyz, whatever their religion, and that many Muslims elsewhere do not eat horsemeat. They trace the taboo instead to the use of diet as a marker of Christian identity in the centuries when Iradi communities lived alongside Muslim khanates. Church tradition reinforces it with stories in which the White Rider forbids the killing of horses.[10] ## Equestrian sports Traditional equestrian sports are regulated by the National Equestrian Sports Directorate. The largest tournaments are held at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]] (also called the Central Hippodrome) in Talas, which seats about 25,000, and during the August Kurultai on the [[Aksay Plateau]].[11] - Ulak Tartysh (also known regionally as *kokpar* or *buzkashi*): the main team sport. Two mounted teams compete for a headless goat or calf carcass weighing up to 35 kilograms (77 lb) and try to throw it into the opposing team's goal ring ([[Tai-Kazan|*tai-kazan*]]). - [[Oodarysh (Mounted Wrestling)|Oodarysh]]: mounted wrestling, in which two riders try to pull each other from the saddle within a ring. Success depends as much on the horse's ability to brace and push as on the rider's strength. - Kyz Kuu ("chase the girl"): a courtship race. A young man chases a young woman down a straight course and wins a kiss if he catches her. On the way back she chases him and tries to strike him with her whip ([[Kamcha (Horsewhip)|*kamcha*]]). - [[Tyin Emmei (Mounted Sport)|Tyin Emmei]] ("coin picking"): riders lean from the saddle at a gallop to snatch coins wrapped in cloth from the ground. - [[At Chabysh (Racing)|At Chabysh]]: long-distance races of 20 to 50 kilometers (12–31 mi) across open steppe. Hunting with golden eagles from horseback ([[Burkut Saluu]]) is practiced by hereditary falconers. Master trainers (*saypker*) and falconers are judged by the ideal of *[[Körktüülük|körktüülük]]*, the display of skill with dignity and apparent ease. (See [[Sport in Irad]].) ## Saddlery and horse gear Iradi saddlery (*[[Eerchilik (Saddlery)|eerchilik]]*) is a recognized folk craft. Wooden saddle trees (*eyer*) are carved from birch or wild walnut, covered with rawhide and decorated with chased silver, carnelian and stamped leather. Common motifs are stylized ram's horns ([[Koshkar Muyuz|*koshkar muyuz*]]) and stars. A silver-mounted saddle is a family heirloom and a traditional part of a bride's dowry.[12] Craftsmen in the ATR also make felt saddlecloths, braided bridles and whips, which are sold in Talas and to tourists.[13] ## Breeding industry Horse breeding is a small, high-value export industry. Since the 1990s the United States has been the largest importer of Iradi horses, followed by the [[wp:United Kingdom]] and [[wp:Ireland]], and demand has risen in [[wp:Hong Kong]], mainland China and the Gulf states. The Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate manages pedigree certification and international transport, and the Chongtor Studbook Registry and the Directorate set breeding and performance standards. Most commercial stud farms are near Talas, while Chongtors are bred mainly by family herders in the ATR and sold across the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]].[8][12] ## See also - [[President's Cup]] - [[Carved Walnut Saddle Tree]] - [[Iradi Felt Saddlecloth]] ## References
