The **political status of Irad** is disputed. [[Irad]], a doubly landlocked territory of about 217,400 km² in [[wp:Central Asia]], has been on the United Nations list of non-self-governing territories since 1992. The United States is still nominally recorded as its administering power, although US administration ended in December 2006.<sup>[1]</sup> Since the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] of 2007 the territory has been divided by the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. The [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), governed by the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI), claims to be the lawful authority for all of Irad and describes the country's sovereignty as "suspended" until a unification referendum is held. The clans of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), loosely coordinated by the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC), reject that claim. [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] each claim the territory *de jure*.<sup>[2]</sup>

Twenty-six UN member states recognized the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] (DRI), proclaimed in December 2006, before it was dissolved in 2007. A minority of them still maintain some form of recognition of a "Republic of Irad", which is why Irad is often described as partially recognized. Commentators compare its position with that of [[wp:Western Sahara]]: a territory listed for decolonization whose administering power has left without completing the process, and whose final status depends on a vote that the parties have never agreed how to hold.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Background

#### Soviet republic and independence (1925–1992)
The Iradi lands were divided among the Syr-Darya, [[wp:Semirechye]] and Fergana oblasts of [[wp:Russian Turkestan]] after 1876. The Soviet national delimitation created the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] in 1925 as a union republic, the first political unit defined by Iradi nationality. On 9 October 1991 the [[Communist Party of Irad]] declared independence as the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] (SRI), based in Kobozev. No foreign state recognized the SRI before it was overtaken by the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]].

On 11 March 1992 the Provisional Government in [[Talas]] proclaimed the Republic of Irad, beginning the [[First Iradi Civil War]] against the SRI. Facing the fall of the besieged city, Provisional President [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] signed the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] with [[wp:James Baker|US Secretary of State James Baker]] on 2 June 1992. Under the treaty Irad entered into association with the United States in exchange for military protection. After [[Operation Starlight]], the last SRI forces surrendered on 18 August 1992.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Territorial association (1992–2006)
Under the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]], Irad became an organized, unincorporated territory of the United States on 18 August 1992. It had an elected Governor, the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] and the [[Supreme Court of Irad]], while a US High Commissioner represented the federal government in Talas (see [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)]] and [[List of governors of Irad]]). Later in 1992 Irad was added to the UN list of non-self-governing territories, with the United States as administering power, and during the territorial period the United States transmitted annual information on the territory to the UN.<sup>[1]</sup>

The treaty, and the Organic Act that gave effect to it, contained a provision usually called the statutory independence clause. Under it, sovereignty would revert to the people of Irad if the United States ended its administration. Alimbekov later wrote that the clause had been his main condition in the 1992 negotiations.<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Withdrawal and the Democratic Republic (2006–2007)
On 3 December 2006 President George W. Bush withdrew the United States from the treaty by executive action (see [[United States Withdrawal from the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty (2006)]]). The withdrawal ended federal civilian administration, the office of the High Commissioner and federal transfers to the territorial budget. It did not end the US military presence at [[Talas Air Base]], which continued under the [[2001 Basing Rights Agreement]]. The United States also did not formally notify the United Nations that its administration had ended.<sup>[1]</sup>

On 7 December 2006 the Supreme Court of Irad issued the [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]]. In a majority opinion by Chief Justice [[Dastan Isakov]], it held that territorial status had lapsed with federal disengagement and that the independence clause had taken effect automatically, a holding known as the doctrine of automatic reversion. On 9 December the Territorial Legislature reconstituted itself as a national assembly, proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Irad and elected [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] Prime Minister.<sup>[5]</sup>

#### Suspended sovereignty (2007–present)
Between December 2006 and February 2007 the DRI cabinet secretly negotiated with Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan, under cover of border consultations, draft treaties that would have used the sovereignty conferred by the ruling to dissolve Irad and partition it among them (see [[Bill of Sale (2007)]]). On 25 February 2007, amid the [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]], [[Erlan Toktarov]] made the drafts public, seized control of the DPI and proclaimed the ISEZ from [[Nurzhan]] as an emergency administration. He annulled the independence ruling by decree and declared that Irad had returned to "suspended sovereignty", a status that ISEZ accounts defend on the ground that with no sovereign in place, no government can cede or sell Iradi territory.<sup>[6]</sup> The court never ruled on the validity of the decree. The DRI cabinet in Talas continued as a rival authority until the [[Popular Front of Irad]] stormed the city on 4 June 2007; DPI forces took the cities over the summer as the Front withdrew to the countryside.<sup>[2]</sup>

The UN-brokered [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] of September 2007 fixed the Qara-Chik line, and the [[wp:United Nations Security Council|Security Council]] established the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) on 18 October 2007 to monitor it. Neither the ceasefire nor the resolution establishing UNMI addressed the territory's sovereignty. The arrangement has since become a frozen conflict, in which each administration governs its own zone and neither is recognized as a sovereign government.

## Status under international law

#### Non-self-governing territory
Irad's listing rests on [[wp:Chapter XI of the United Nations Charter|Chapter XI]] of the [[wp:Charter of the United Nations|UN Charter]], which applies to territories "whose peoples have not yet attained a full measure of self-government". A territory leaves the list when the General Assembly accepts that it has reached a full measure of self-government, through independence, free association or integration with an independent state. No such decision has been made for Irad. The [[wp:Special Committee on Decolonization|UN Special Committee on Decolonization]], which sits in [[wp:New York City|New York]], issues an annual working paper on the territory, drawing on UNMI's public reports, press coverage and submissions by petitioners.<sup>[1]</sup>

Both Iradi administrations send petitioners to the committee's sessions. [[Tilek Kurmanov]], who represented the ISEZ at the United Nations from 2008 to 2017, argued there that Irad is neither a US territory nor an independent state and that its status must be settled by a unification referendum. He opposed proposals to remove Irad from the list before such a vote and rejected the claims of the three neighboring states. IAC petitioners have presented a competing view, that the people of the tribal regions have never been consulted on any of Irad's changes of status and that a referendum must give their population its full weight.<sup>[7]</sup><sup>[8]</sup>

#### The administering power
Because Washington did not notify the UN that it had ended its administration, the United States is still recorded as the administering power. According to the committee's working papers, it has not transmitted information on the territory since 2006. Irad therefore remained listed (contemporary sources say "by US demand"), and the United States neither reports on the territory nor has asked for its removal.<sup>[1]</sup> Legal scholars disagree on the effect. Some argue that the United States remains bound by the obligations of an administering power until the General Assembly releases it. Others hold that the withdrawal ended its role in fact, leaving Irad a listed territory without an administering power, a position commentators compare with Spain's departure from Western Sahara in 1976.<sup>[9]</sup>

The withdrawal also raised a domestic constitutional question in the United States, whether a president could end a treaty of territorial association without the approval of [[wp:United States Congress|Congress]]. The treaty allowed either party to withdraw but did not say how. No US court has ruled on the question.<sup>[9]</sup>

#### Automatic reversion and its annulment
Supporters of the 2006 ruling, including Orozbekov, argue that it remains valid law. The Supreme Court never ruled on Toktarov's annulment decree, they say, and a governor's decree cannot overturn a judgment of the territory's highest court. On this view Irad became independent in December 2006, and the ISEZ is a *de facto* administration within an independent state. The ISEZ holds that the ruling was annulled by a lawful emergency decree and that the Organic Act and the territorial statutes remain in force, with their provisions on federal oversight inoperative, until the people of Irad decide the question by referendum.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[9]</sup> The IAC accepts neither the Organic Act nor the emergency decree as applying to the tribal regions.

#### Recognition
The 26 UN member states that recognized the DRI did so between December 2006 and February 2007. After the DRI government was dissolved in June 2007, most of them let their recognition lapse without a formal statement. A minority still maintain some form of recognition of a "Republic of Irad", usually without naming either administration as its government, and a few accept ISEZ trade representatives under that title.<sup>[3]</sup> No state recognizes the ISEZ or the IAC as a sovereign government, and Irad is not a member of the United Nations or of any of its specialized agencies.

## Positions of the parties

#### Irad Special Economic Zone
The ISEZ government describes Irad as a single country whose sovereignty is suspended. It gives national titles, such as "[[Armed Forces of Irad]]", to its own institutions, and its official documents continue to use the name Republic of Irad. Its stated policy is a unification referendum held in both zones, after which a unified Irad would choose its permanent status.<sup>[10]</sup> It treats the Qara-Chik line as an administrative line within Irad rather than a border, and describes the clan councils of the ATR as local customary authorities rather than a rival government.

Analysts argue that the ISEZ leadership has preferred the status quo. Leaked US intelligence reports from Toktarov's first term concluded that he maintained Irad's quasi-territorial status to avoid conflict with regional powers, specifically Russia and China. Analysts add that the tribal regions buffer the ISEZ against unrest on its borders, and that Irad's subnational status lets it deflect Russian and Chinese pressure toward Washington.<sup>[11]</sup> Toktarov has nonetheless publicly welcomed closer alignment with China.

#### Iradi Freedom Society
The IAC does not recognize ISEZ authority over the tribal regions and does not accept that the Organic Act applies there. It says it supports a unified Irad, but only with representation that reflects the population of the tribal regions and with clan control over land and water in the mountain catchments. Tribal leaders' public statements have nonetheless shown broad ambivalence toward Iradi statehood, and the IAC has never proclaimed independence for the tribal regions or sought recognition as a state.<sup>[12]</sup> The IAC also argues that no government representing the whole country has consented to the presence of foreign forces at Talas Air Base.

#### Neighboring claimants
Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan each claim Irad *de jure*, on the basis of their own readings of the Soviet national delimitation and of historical settlement in the region. [[wp:Tajikistan]], which does not border Irad, makes no claim. None of the three administers any part of Irad, and in practice all three coordinate border management with the ISEZ.<sup>[2]</sup> In 2006–07 their foreign ministries took part in the secret negotiations on the Bill of Sale, which they describe as consultations; none has published its copy of the drafts. None has rescinded its claim since the affair, and none has threatened military action. Analysts report that the prevailing view in all three capitals is that Irad will break apart on its own, and that the neighbors are content to wait.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>
- **Kazakhstan** carries most Iradi crude north to its pipeline network near [[wp:Shymkent]]. The 2008 [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]], a set of technical arrangements covering the ISEZ-held sections of the northern frontier, is described by Kazakhstan as implying no recognition. The standing of the territorial-era [[Treaty of Good Neighborliness (1994)]] on the Chu and Talas rivers is disputed, although its technical provisions continue in practice.
- **Uzbekistan** depends on summer releases from the Toktogul reservoir for irrigation in the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] and has accused the joint water commission of holding back water in dry years.
- **Kyrgyzstan** regards the Naryn cascade as Kyrgyz infrastructure and attends the commission under protest.

All three sit as observers on the joint technical commission of the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]], the main reason they take part in the ceasefire arrangements at all.<sup>[13]</sup> The sections of the external frontier held by the ATR have never been demarcated, and clan patrols clashed with neighboring border guards on the western desert frontier in 2018 (see [[2018 Border Demarcation Clashes]]).

#### United States
The United States does not report on the territory and has made no formal statement on its status since the 2006 withdrawal. US forces remain at Talas Air Base and five other installations under the 2001 agreement and supplementary arrangements concluded with the ISEZ from 2007 onward, which have not been published in full.<sup>[14]</sup> In February 2025 [[wp:Donald Trump|President Donald Trump]] spoke of exploring the sale of Irad to Russia to keep China from acquiring it, treating Irad as if it were still a US territory; it is not known whether he was aware that US administration had ended in 2006. The remarks provoked demonstrations in both zones, and the ISEZ delivered a demarche through UNMI stating that Irad's sovereignty was not negotiable (see [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]).<sup>[15]</sup> Many [[Iradis]] read the remarks in the light of the 2007 Bill of Sale, and "Irad is not for sale" became the slogan of the protests. The Special Committee on Decolonization responded with a statement recalling that the territory's future is a matter for its people.

#### United Nations
UNMI reports to the Security Council through the Secretary-General, not to the Special Committee. Its Special Representative offers good offices on the status question, and UN officials helped draft the 2008 referendum proposal and supported the 2011 talks.<sup>[16]</sup> Security Council debates on the renewal of UNMI's mandate each October have divided repeatedly over whether resolutions should refer to the referendum, the territory's status and the foreign military presence. Most renewals have nonetheless been adopted unanimously.

## Unification process
The [[2008 Unification Referendum Initiative]], drafted with the help of UN officials, envisaged a confederal settlement with a joint legislature, a vote in both zones and guarantees for customary law. Talks collapsed after the DPI refused to give tribal councils a veto over foreign mining concessions in mountain watersheds. Voter registration in the tribal regions was also left unresolved.<sup>[3]</sup>

The [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]], held at Kara-Oi in April and May 2011, remains the only substantive direct negotiation. The DPI offered the tribal regions one-third of the seats in a unified legislature, together with state control of mountain water catchments and mineral licensing. The IAC asked for representation reflecting the ATR's share of the territory, the greater part of the country, and, by its own estimates, of the population. Its delegation walked out in late May, and no direct talks have taken place since.<sup>[12]</sup>

Polling in 2017 found large majorities in the ISEZ in favor of a unified sovereign state. Limited polling in the tribal regions also showed support, although tribal leaders alleged DPI interference in the surveys.<sup>[3]</sup>

The size of the tribal population is central to any formula for representation or for a referendum. The DPI's [[2018 Irad census]] counted 4,626,000 people, enumerating the ISEZ directly but only estimating the ATR at about 2.0 million. Independent researchers, drawing on satellite settlement mapping and aid-agency registries, put the national population at about 6.2 million and the ATR at 3.5 to 4 million. The IAC argues that the undercount was meant to reduce the tribal regions' weight in any unified legislature; the DPI attributes the gap to restricted access.<sup>[17]</sup>

## Practical consequences
Irad's unresolved status affects much of its external life:
- **International organizations.** Irad is not a member of the United Nations, the [[wp:Universal Postal Union]] or the international financial institutions. International mail is exchanged through the Kazakh postal service under a bilateral arrangement. The ISEZ has no sovereign credit rating and no access to the [[wp:International Monetary Fund]].
- **Codes and identifiers.** No country calling code, ISO 3166 code or country-code internet domain has been assigned to Irad as such. Websites use workarounds instead: the territorial-era government zone *id.gov* and generic domains. The zone *.ir.ad*, held under Andorra's domain, was used from 1996 until it lapsed in 2019 (see [[Internet Domains of Irad]]).
- **Travel documents.** During the territorial period Iradis were US nationals but not US citizens, a status that ended in December 2006. Since December 2009 the ISEZ has issued "Republic of Irad" passports bearing the [[Emblem of Irad|State Emblem]], but Russia and most other states do not recognize them. The ISEZ does not forbid its residents to hold other documents: Kyrgyzstan issues passports to Iradis who can prove birth or long residence, Kazakhstan mainly to those with family ties there, and Uzbekistan rarely. Because a Kyrgyz passport allows its holder to work in Russia under the rules of the [[wp:Eurasian Economic Union]], most Iradi labor migrants travel on one. The DPI calls the practice "a practical necessity", while young nationalists object to it. Iradis without a second passport often depend on recruiters for documents, which leaves them exposed to trafficking abroad, where Irad has no consulates.<sup>[18]</sup>
- **Sport.** Because all three neighbors claim Irad, teams of the [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]] have not been admitted to some regional competitions as a national team.
- **Water and power.** The Toktogul complex (1,440 MW since its 2026 refit) was split by the Qara-Chik line in 2007; since a 2009 protocol the dam and basin have been in the ISEZ, while the clans hold the catchments, a guaranteed share of the revenue and a say in each five-year release schedule. Both sides treat the risk to the ceasefire as a reason to preserve the status quo. The Protocol's five-year release schedule falls due for renewal in 2027, and neighboring governments have asked who will sign for the ISEZ while Governor Toktarov remains out of public view (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).<sup>[13]</sup>

## Proposed solutions
Commentators and the parties have discussed several outcomes:<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>
- **Unification and independence.** A referendum in both zones leading to a single sovereign Irad, which is the stated aim of the ISEZ and, on conditions, of the IAC. The parties disagree on representation, the franchise in the tribal regions and control of land, water and minerals.
- **A confederal settlement.** A joint legislature with guaranteed autonomy for the tribal regions and recognition of customary law, along the lines of the 2008 draft.
- **Formalizing the division.** Turning the Qara-Chik line into a permanent boundary. Neither administration publicly supports this.
- **Renewed association with the United States.** Discussed in some territorial-era political circles, but with little support since the 2025 remarks turned public opinion against Washington.
- **Integration with a neighboring state.** The outcome implied by the claims of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan, and the one the 2007 Bill of Sale would have imposed. It has no significant support in either zone.

**Religion in Irad** is dominated by Christianity, which makes Irad the only Christian-majority territory in [[wp:Central Asia]]. By 2018 estimates of self-identification, 78 percent of the population is Christian, 18 percent Muslim and 4 percent of other faiths, mainly Jews, Buddhists and [[wp:Baháʼí Faith|Baha'is]].<sup>[1]</sup> Most Christians belong to the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], an Eastern Catholic church of East Syriac tradition in communion with Rome since 1931, which reports about 3.4 million faithful. Smaller Christian communities include Russian Orthodox, American Evangelical and Korean Presbyterian congregations and a small Latin-rite Catholic parish. Most Muslims, who are found mainly among the Kyrgyz, Uzbek and Kazakh minorities, are Sunni of the [[wp:Hanafi school|Hanafi]] school, with a small urban [[wp:Shia Islam|Shia]] minority.<sup>[2]</sup>

Irad has had a secular state since the Soviet period, and the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]] of 1992 guaranteed freedom of religion. Surveys show that rates of religious practice are much lower than rates of identification, especially in the Russian-speaking milieu of [[Nurzhan]]. In the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), Christianity takes a syncretic form that combines East Syriac and Catholic practice with older pastoral beliefs. The Syro-Iradi Church is the only major institution that operates on both sides of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and it has acted as a mediator between the two administrations.<sup>[3]</sup>

Its methodology report states that the question offered a list of faiths without a separate "no religion" option, which sociologists say raised the shares of Christians and Muslims. Survey data on practice cover only the cities of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). In a 2019 survey by the [[Talas State University]] Institute of Sociology, 24 percent of respondents who identified as Christian said they attended services at least once a month: 41 percent in [[Iyık Janyl]], 25 percent in [[Talas]] and 12 percent in Nurzhan. Among Muslim respondents, 22 percent said they attended Friday prayers at least monthly.<sup>[4]</sup> In a 2021 survey by the university's Department of Sociology, the Syro-Iradi Church was the most trusted public institution among ISEZ respondents.<sup>[5]</sup>

## History

#### Pre-Christian belief and the Church of the East
Before the spread of Christianity and Islam, the peoples of the Talas and Chu valleys followed Turkic sky and ancestor cults, and Sogdian merchants brought [[wp:Zoroastrianism]], Buddhism and [[wp:Manichaeism]] along the [[wp:Silk Road]]. Elements of pre-Christian belief survive in Iradi folklore, notably the bull-headed god [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]], whom Christian tradition identified with Satan.<sup>[6]</sup>

[[wp:Church of the East|East Syriac Christianity]] reached the region with Sogdian merchants between the 7th and 9th centuries, and the Church of the East kept bishops in the towns of [[wp:Transoxiana]] and [[wp:Semirechye]]. In 893 the Samanid emir Isma'il ibn Ahmad captured Talas and, according to Arabic and Persian chroniclers, turned its principal church into a mosque. Christianity revived among Turkic pastoralists under the religiously tolerant [[wp:Qara Khitai]] in the 12th century, and a synod was held at Navekat in 1180 (see [[Nestorian Synod of Navekat (1180)]]). Church tradition attributes the founding of a distinct Iradi Christian community to [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]], who is said to have been led by a vision of Christ as the White Rider to the site of the first church; historians dispute her existence.<sup>[7]</sup>

#### Islamic rule
Arab armies brought Islam in the 8th century, and it became the dominant religion of the towns after the Kara-Khanid rulers converted in the 10th century. Under the Chagatai khan Ali-Sultan (1339–1342) and during the campaigns of [[wp:Timur]] later in the 14th century, the Christian dioceses of the region were destroyed. Iradi Christians survived in the valleys of the [[Talas Alatau]] and the Chatkal, worshipping in secret and preserving their prayers in oral chant (*[[Irda (Vocal Tradition)|ırda]]*).<sup>[7]</sup>

#### Kokand and Russian rule
In 1727 Khan Abd al-Rahim Biy of [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]], rewarding Iradi Christian cavalry for their service against the [[wp:Dzungar people|Dzungars]], granted religious tolerance under the [[Treaty of Talas (1727)]] and paid for the [[Church of St. Janyl]], around which the city of Iyık Janyl grew up. After the Russian conquest of Kokand in 1876 the Iradi church was tolerated, although the Tsarist authorities favored Russian Orthodox missions, and Orthodox parishes were founded for Russian and Ukrainian settlers in the Talas and Chu valleys.<sup>[8]</sup>

#### Soviet period
After the Russian Revolution, Bishop [[Mar Timotheos Alimbekov]] negotiated union with Rome in secret through papal representatives abroad. On 14 September 1931 [[wp:Pope Pius XI]] issued the bull *Orientalis Stella*, which received the Iradi church into full communion as a church *sui iuris*. Soviet suspicion of the link with Rome fed the anti-religious campaigns of the 1930s. The churches of Iyık Janyl were closed, the cathedral was converted into a grain store, and most senior clergy were arrested and executed in [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges]].<sup>[9]</sup> Mosques and Orthodox churches were also closed; in the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]] of Talas, both the Juma Mosque and the Syro-Iradi parish church of St. Yuhanna were shut in the 1930s.

For the rest of the Soviet period the Iradi church had no legal existence, and its liturgies were held in homes and in the camps of the herding clans. Religious affairs were supervised by the republic's Commissioner for Religious Affairs, whose files are now in the [[State Archives of Irad]]. A limited number of mosques were registered after 1943 under the Spiritual Administration of the Muslims of Central Asia and [[wp:Kazakhstan]] in [[wp:Tashkent]]. Religious practice grew more open after 1988, under perestroika.<sup>[10]</sup>

#### Since 1992
The Organic Act guaranteed freedom of religion and required the return of church property confiscated in the Soviet period. The Church of St. Janyl was reconsecrated on 14 September 1992, the anniversary of *Orientalis Stella*; the [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs]] met openly in 1993; and the [[Cathedral Seminary of Iyık Janyl]] reopened in 1994. Mosques and Orthodox churches reopened in the same years. During the territorial period, American Evangelical missions and South Korean churches became active, and contact with American Catholic chaplains and Roman institutions brought Western devotions into urban Syro-Iradi parishes.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[8]</sup> Since the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] of 2007, the Syro-Iradi Church has kept a position of neutrality between the ISEZ and the clan councils of the tribal regions.

## Christianity

#### Syro-Iradi Catholic Church
*Main article: [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]*

The Syro-Iradi Church is headed by the Archbishop of Iyık Janyl, [[Mar Ephrem]] since 2012, whose cathedral is the Church of St. Janyl. It has four eparchies: the [[Archbishopric of Iyık Janyl|Archeparchy of Iyık Janyl]] and suffragan eparchies based in Talas, Nurzhan and the Chatkal highlands. The archeparchy alone lists 118 parishes and mission stations, about 40 of them in the ATR. Its clergy are trained at the St. Ephrem Major Seminary in Iyık Janyl, which had 46 students in 2023. Religious life includes the [[Order of St. Janyl the Hermit]], whose communities run rural dispensaries; the [[Iyık Janyl Monastic Cloister]]; and the Sisters of the Cross of Irad, founded by [[Maryam Janyl (nun)|Sister Maryam Janyl]], who run a hospice and the [[St. Maryam Catholic Academy]] in Talas.<sup>[11]</sup>

The church celebrates the [[wp:Liturgy of Addai and Mari|East Syriac Liturgy of Addai and Mari]] in Iradi, with parts sung in [[wp:Syriac language|Classical Syriac]] (see [[East Syriac Rites of Iyık Janyl]]). Distinctive features include the sacramental bread *[[Kümöch Sacramental Bread|kümöch]]*, incense of mountain juniper (*[[Arsha Juniper Incense Tradition|arsha]]*) and a liturgical vocabulary of Sogdian and Syriac origin. Father [[Luka Ayyubov]]'s translation of the [[wp:New Testament]] into Latin-script Iradi appeared in 1994. Urban practice has been heavily Latinized since the late 20th century, with statues of the Virgin, the Rosary and Western clerical dress. The main annual celebration is the [[Feast of St. Janyl]] on 24 August, when mounted pilgrims from both sides of the line ride to Iyık Janyl for the blessing of the herds.<sup>[3]</sup>

The church runs schools, the [[St. Luka Community Health Mission]] and other charities, and its Council of Hierarchs issues pastoral letters on public questions, such as communal pasture rights, mining and emigration.

#### Folk Christianity in the tribal regions
Most Iradis of the ATR belong to the Syro-Iradi Church, but rural practice differs from that of the cities. Itinerant priests celebrate in felt yurts (*[[Ak-Örgoe|ak-örgoe]]*), bless horse herds and pastures, and lead open-air midnight liturgies. Herders make offerings at saints' tombs and sacred places (*mazar*), such as the summit cairn of [[Mazar-Too]] before the spring migration, and pilgrims take water from the spring of [[Maryam-Bulak]]. Funeral customs include leading the dead person's riding horse behind the bier, part of the [[Fallen Rider Tradition]]. Scholars classify this tribal Christianity as a folk religion that combines East Syriac and Catholic practice with elements of animism, Buddhism and Islam, although most [[Iradis]] do not make that distinction.<sup>[6]</sup><sup>[12]</sup> Traditional healers (*[[Tabyp (Medicine)|tabyp]]*) remain common, and elders' blessings (*[[Bata (Culture)|bata]]*) mark feasts and journeys.

Folk practice is organized around a contrast of white and black. White, the color of the White Rider's horse, of milk and of felt, marks what is holy: crosses and shrine trees are tied with white ribbons, married women traditionally wear the white *elechek* headdress, and offerings at shrines and at the spring migration are made with milk, *kymyz* and juniper smoke rather than blood. Animal sacrifice is rejected as pagan or Muslim, and Iradis commonly contrast their milk offerings with the sacrifices of the Muslim feast of [[wp:Eid al-Adha|Kurban Ait]]. Black is associated with Morkhan, and a minor superstition treats cattle, especially black bulls, as unlucky. Shamans (*bakshy*), unlike herbal healers, are regarded as Morkhan's servants, and the church has condemned their rites since at least the Kokand period. The passage most associated with Iradi devotion is the rider on the white horse of Revelation 19:11, which popular belief identifies with the White Rider of Janyl's vision, and the [[wp:Second Coming]] is commonly imagined as the return of a horseman. The verse is more popular in Irad than anywhere else in Christendom, and it is also a badge of militant religious nationalism (see [[Revelation 19:11 in Irad]]). Some Iradi Christians go further and read the people's history into Genesis, holding that they descend from Cain through the biblical Irad and that the White Rider lifted the mark of Cain at Janyl's vision (see [[Cainite tradition in Irad]]).<sup>[6]</sup><sup>[12]</sup>

In older rural churches the central object is a bare cross without a figure of Christ, in the East Syriac manner: the [[Iradi Cross|Iradi cross]], a cross patonce growing out of a lotus, as on the medieval Christian gravestones of the Chu valley, which the church adopted as its emblem in 1994; icons are mostly of St. Janyl. Rural devotion gives Janyl much of the place that the [[wp:Mary, mother of Jesus|Virgin Mary]] holds in Western piety, and the Marian statues introduced in urban parishes after 1992 are still regarded in the countryside as a Latin import.<sup>[6]</sup>

Maryam keeps one domain of her own in the villages: the birth room and the cradle. In parts of the Talas Alatau, the Chatkal valleys and the Toktogul basin she has taken on the role of Umay, the old Turkic goddess of childbirth, infants and the hearth, and women call her *Umay Ene* ("Mother Umay"). They call on her in labour, bury the afterbirth under the threshold with a prayer to her, hang the cradle with a cross and an owl's feather against the childbed demon *albasty*, and call the rainbow "Maryam's belt". The church tolerates the title but discourages the customs (see [[Umay Ene]]).<sup>[6]</sup>

The three clans of the Karatau, who call themselves the *Eski El* ("the old people") and do not consider themselves Iradis, keep a separate folk religion. It uses the cross and the figure of the White Rider but has no churches or resident priests; its night rites in caves and ruined caravanserais center on possession by the Rider and the saints, led by specialists called *ak bakshy*, and include the sacrifice of white lambs at springs. The church regards the practices as superstition but has made little attempt to suppress them (see [[Clans of the Autonomous Tribal Regions]]).<sup>[6]</sup>

#### Latin Catholics
A small Latin-rite Catholic community exists outside the Syro-Iradi Church. Its main parish, St. Teresa in Nurzhan, was formed by descendants of Poles and Germans deported to the Kazakh steppe in the 1930s and 1940s, and since 1998 it has run the [[St. Teresa Community Kitchen]] for pensioners. Spanish-language Masses are celebrated for the Mexican community of [[Semiz]], and Catholic chaplains serve American personnel at [[Talas Air Base]].<sup>[13]</sup> The Polish Franciscan [[Barnabas (priest)|Father Barnabas]], who according to his memoir carried the papal documents of the 1931 union into the [[wp:Soviet Union]], is commemorated by the Syro-Iradi Church as a benefactor.

#### Orthodoxy
The [[wp:Russian Orthodox Church]] has parishes in Nurzhan, Talas and the former settler villages of the Talas and Chu valleys. Its members are mainly ethnic Russians and Ukrainians, together with some [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]], and most belong to the older Russian-speaking generation known as the "Russos" (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]). Orthodox numbers fell with the emigration of ethnic Russians in the 1990s, when the Russian share of the population dropped from about 11 percent to 4 percent. Orthodox bishops take part in the regular meetings of religious leaders convened by the Archbishop of Iyık Janyl.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[13]</sup>

#### Protestantism
[[wp:Protestantism|Protestant]] churches are mostly recent. American Evangelical congregations were founded after 1992, during the period of American enthusiasm for Irad known as [[Iradimania]], by missions and by Christian charities of the kind that received the proceeds of the 1993 compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*. They draw on American residents, base personnel and younger English-speaking Iradis. Presbyterian churches founded with South Korean help since the 1990s are, with [[wp:Catholic Church|Catholicism]], the main denomination among the Koryo-saram, and small Baptist communities of Soviet origin survive among Russian and German families.<sup>[14]</sup> Evangelical churches grew fastest in the early 2000s, when the share of ISEZ respondents identifying as Evangelical or Pentecostal rose from about 1 percent to nearly 4 percent, and have grown little since the 2010s; the best-known Evangelical figure is the Iradi-American televangelist [[Nathan Isabekov]] (see [[Evangelical Christianity in Irad]]).<sup>[4]</sup> The Syro-Iradi hierarchy has at times criticized proselytism among its members, especially in the 1990s.

## Islam
*Main article: [[Islam in Irad]]*

Muslims make up about 18 percent of the population. Most are Kyrgyz, [[wp:Uzbeks]] and [[wp:Kazakhs]], together with [[wp:Tatars]], [[wp:Uyghurs]], Dungans and [[wp:Tajiks]], and they are concentrated in the rural Fergana Rim, the border districts and the cities, where mosques serve the Kazakh, Uzbek and Tatar communities of Nurzhan and Talas. The Spiritual Administration of Muslims of Irad, founded in Nurzhan in 1993, oversees registered mosques and imams in the ISEZ.<sup>[2]</sup> Muslim leaders have long complained of social prejudice, including the popular Iradi view, rejected by ethnographers, that eating horsemeat is a "Muslim" practice (see [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]]).

## Other religions
- **Judaism.** Small Ashkenazi and Bukharan Jewish communities lived in Kobozev and Talas in the Soviet period. Most of their members emigrated to [[wp:Israel]] and the United States in the 1990s, and a synagogue and community center remain in Nurzhan.
- **Buddhism.** Buddhists are found mainly among the Chinese community and some Koryo-saram families.
- **Baha'i Faith.** Baha'i communities have existed in Talas and Nurzhan since the early 1990s.<sup>[1]</sup>

## Church and nation
{{Unreferenced section|date=April 2026}}

The Church is widely identified with the nation. The motto *[[Til, Jer, Ishenim]]* ("Language, Land, Faith"), coined by the Ene-Til society in 1988, is used by both administrations and by the Church. In the spring surveys of the Institute of Sociology at [[Talas State University]] the Church has been the most trusted institution every year since 1996, with 81% expressing trust in 2025, against 34% for [[IradOne]] and 22% for the [[Mejlis]]; the Governor's office has not appeared in the published tables since 2016, an omission reported by the *[[Irad Times]]*. The archbishop's statements therefore carry political weight. Since 2013 [[Mar Ephrem]] has stood godfather to tens of thousands of children at the annual mass baptism of the [[Feast of St. Janyl]] (see [[Ephrem's Children]]), and the new [[Cathedral of the Resurrection, Talas|Cathedral of the Resurrection]] in Talas, built with money from the Governor's family and its business allies, is called "the Governor's church".

Everyday practice reflects the same closeness. Iradis cross themselves when passing a church or a roadside cross, even from a moving minibus; drivers sound their horns at the shrines on the mountain passes; and minibus drivers hang a small cross and the number "19:11" from the mirror. Parishes and clan shrines keep patronal feasts with horse races ([[Chirköö Toi]]), the [[The Legend of the White Rider|White Rider]] has feasts in spring and autumn ([[Chabandoz Künü]]), and the fasts have their own cuisine ([[Savma Tamak]]).

## Religion and the state
The ISEZ is a secular state. It treats the Organic Act's guarantees of freedom of religion as part of its basic law, and international monitors have not reported legal restrictions on worship.<sup>[15]</sup> Religious education is optional in public schools, and churches run private schools that teach the ISEZ curriculum. Relations between the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] administration and the Syro-Iradi Church have at times been strained over school curricula and the taxation of church property, and the church has cited the guarantees of the territorial period in these disputes. In October 2023 the Council of Hierarchs appealed for restraint by police and protesters during the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas|student protests in Talas]]. Its autumn communiqué of 2024, issued after Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] withdrew from public view, called for "constitutional order and truthful public information".<sup>[11]</sup>

Relations between the state and Muslim communities became a public issue in December 2024 and January 2025, after remarks by the Gendarmerie commander [[Ruslan Toktarov]] questioning the loyalty of Muslim citizens, which Sunni clerics and the Archbishop of Iyık Janyl criticized (see [[Islam in Irad]]).<sup>[16]</sup>

In the ATR, which has no written constitution, the clans' customary law (*[[Adat Law in the ATR|adat]]*) assumes a Christian community but is applied to Muslim herders as well. Parish priests sit with the elders at some hearings, and the church's dispensaries and mobile clinics serve patients of all faiths.<sup>[17]</sup>

## Interfaith relations
Since 2007 the Archbishop of Iyık Janyl has met regularly with Sunni Muslim leaders and Russian Orthodox bishops to coordinate charitable food distribution and joint representations to the authorities, and the archbishopric has hosted meetings between representatives of the ISEZ and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]].<sup>[3]</sup> Historians note that Christian–Muslim relations in Irad have also been shaped by older patterns of cooperation, from the Iradi Christian clans who rose alongside their Muslim neighbors in the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]] of 1916 to the religious tolerance granted by the Muslim khans of Kokand in 1727. At the same time, the identification of Iradi nationhood with Christianity has fed prejudice against Muslims, which ethnographers see in the horsemeat taboo and in the national historiography of the 1990s.<sup>[6]</sup> Iradi Christians share many customs with their Muslim neighbors, including shrine pilgrimage, elders' blessings, burial on the day of death and a memorial feast on the fortieth day, but mark their identity through a set of refusals: of horsemeat, of animal sacrifice, of male circumcision and of Arabic loanwords in religious language, for which the church uses Syriac and Sogdian terms.<sup>[6]</sup>

**Elections in Irad** are held only in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), the seventh of the territory governed by the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI). Every four years, on the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November, voters in the ISEZ elect a Governor and Lieutenant Governor on a joint ticket, the 60 members of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] (*[[Mejlis]]*) and the councils of the three cities of governorate significance. The [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), which cover the other six-sevenths of the territory, take no part; their clans govern themselves through councils of elders and decide common matters by consensus at a *kurultai*.[1] The electoral system descends from the US territorial period of 1992–2006, when Irad held competitive, if DPI-dominated, elections under the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]] and the 1992 Elective Governor Acts. Since 2007 the DPI has won every gubernatorial election, all of them by [[Erlan Toktarov]], and has held a large majority in the legislature. Observers from the [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe]] (OSCE) have said that the 2013 electoral reform and the elections that followed lacked "any meaningful transparency or choice for the Iradi people".[2] The DPI maintains that the elections are free and that its majorities reflect public support for stability. The next general election is due on 2 November 2027 (see [[2027 Iradi gubernatorial election]]). ## History #### Soviet period In the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] (1925–1991), elections to the republic's Supreme Soviet and to local soviets followed the Soviet single-candidate pattern, with the [[Communist Party of Irad]] approving all nominations. In 1990 the republican Supreme Soviet created the post of President and elected the party's First Secretary, [[Vasily Chernov]], to it.[3] The [[Declaration of State Sovereignty (1991)]], which created the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] in October 1991, was not followed by free elections or the legalization of opposition parties, a point on which the national movement criticized it. #### Provisional Government (1992) On 11 March 1992 the [[Talas Town Hall Meeting (1992)|Talas Town Hall Meeting]], an assembly of reformers, delegates of the strike and student committees and clan elders convened by the Talas city council, proclaimed the Republic of Irad and elected [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] Provisional President. No popular vote was held during the [[First Iradi Civil War]].[4] #### Territorial period (1992–2006) The Organic Act, which took effect on 18 August 1992, provided for an elected Governor and an elected bicameral legislature. Pending elections, an interim US administration headed by the High Commissioner exercised executive authority, and an interim legislature drawn from the Provisional Government's councils and from district delegates met in Talas from October 1992.[5] Municipal councils were first elected in November 1993. The first general elections were held on 8 November 1994, on the same day as US federal elections, a convention the territory kept throughout. The system followed the American territorial model:[5] - The **Governor and Lieutenant Governor** were elected on a joint ticket for four-year terms, beginning on the first Monday of January, with a limit of two consecutive terms. - The **Territorial Senate** had 15 members, three from each of five senatorial districts, elected for four years. - The **Territorial House of Representatives** had 35 members, elected every two years from single-member constituencies apportioned by population. The DPI, formally constituted in October 1992 from the Provisional Government's reformist caucus, won the governorship and majorities in both chambers in 1994 and kept them for most of the period. Its main opponents were the [[Labor Party of Irad]], which represented the Russophone industrial workforce of [[Nurzhan]], the nationalist [[Jer-Suu Party]], and independent rural deputies.[6] Alimbekov declined to stand, writing later that the man who had signed away the republic's independence should not seek office in the territory. Toktarov entered the House of Representatives in 1994 and moved to the Senate, where he was Majority Leader from 2000 to 2004. Studies of the period describe the elections as genuinely contested: governors were elected with between 52 and 62 percent of the vote, several DPI incumbents lost House seats, and Russophone parties controlled the Nurzhan city council for most of the period (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]).[6] Participation in the rural interior was low throughout. Many clan communities kept their distance from the territorial authorities, and turnout in the mountain constituencies rarely exceeded 35 percent, against 60 to 70 percent in the cities.[6] The last territorial general election was held on 7 November 2006, four weeks before the United States withdrew from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]]. Governor Nurgul Abdrakhmanova was re-elected, but her second term, due to begin in January 2007, never started (see [[List of governors of Irad]]). #### Democratic Republic (2006–2007) On 9 December 2006, acting on the Supreme Court's [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]], the Territorial Legislature reconstituted itself as a national assembly, proclaimed the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] and elected [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] Prime Minister. The office of territorial Governor lapsed. No elections were held under the DRI, which was dissolved after the [[Popular Front of Irad]] stormed Talas on 4 June 2007.[7] #### Irad Special Economic Zone (2007–present) Toktarov proclaimed the ISEZ on 25 February 2007 and took office as Governor after the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)|ceasefire]] of September 2007. Members of the last territorial legislature who accepted the emergency administration sat as a provisional single chamber until November 2011.[8] The Jer-Suu Party was banned in 2008 as an extremist organization, and the Political Parties Act of 2010, which requires 10,000 members spread across all eight constituencies, led to the dissolution of the Labor Party in 2011; no party other than the DPI has met its thresholds since. On 8 November 2011 the ISEZ held its first regular elections, and Toktarov was re-elected with an official 88.74 percent. Under the prevailing reading of the Elective Governor Acts, which counted his 2007–2011 tenure as a first term, he would have been barred from standing again in 2015.[9] In June 2013 the legislature passed an amendment to the Acts removing the two-term limit, by 53 votes to 4 with three abstentions; the Russo-aligned deputies from Nurzhan voted against (see [[2013 Constitutional Amendment]]). In 2014 the [[Supreme Court of Irad]] declined to hear a challenge, holding that the question belonged to the legislature.[9] Before the 2015 election the DPI majority adopted new rules on the verification of nomination signatures and on candidates' residence. In early October 2015 the Territorial Election Commission struck the rival nominees from the ballot, among them an independent backed by trade unions in Nurzhan and a Russo-aligned businessman (see [[2015 Electoral Reform Controversy]]). Toktarov won with 78.25 percent, his lowest share, and opposition groups protested in Talas and Nurzhan.[10] In 2019 he won 90.31 percent, with his son-in-law [[Aidar Maksat]] as his running mate. The 2023 election, held a month after the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]], gave him 92.75 percent (see [[2023 Iradi gubernatorial election]]). Toktarov has not appeared in public since July 2024. The DPI attributes his absence to an extended health retreat. No formal finding of inability has been made under the Elective Governor Acts, and the DPI has named no successor. Analysts note that the only formal routes to a transfer of power are the Acts' succession provisions and the 2027 election (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).[11] #### The 2027 election The next general election, for the Governor and Lieutenant Governor, the legislature and the three city councils, is due on 2 November 2027, and the new term begins on 22 November. A runoff, if one were needed, would fall on 23 November, after the start of the term, a case on which the Acts are silent.[12] By October 2026 the DPI had not named its ticket, saying it would do so "at the proper time"; in 2023 its congress met in August. Toktarov would be 73 on polling day. Analysts discuss a Toktarov–Maksat ticket for continuity, a ticket headed by Maksat, [[Ruslan Toktarov]] or [[Alikhan Toktarov]], and none of them has declared. Opposition figures argue that an absent Governor cannot sign the residence declaration that candidates make before an election commissioner, while the DPI says a commissioner can witness it at the residence; a petition asking the Supreme Court, among other questions, whether an absent Governor may be nominated has awaited a hearing since June 2026.[13] On the opposition side, the Russo-aligned civic lists of Nurzhan have discussed a single ticket, with the 2023 runner-up, the engineer and city council member Oleg Zubarev, the name most often mentioned, while trade-union circles have floated a ticket led by the councilor Elena Petrova.[14] [[Jason Ilyasov]], who meets the ten-year residence rule, has said he has "not ruled anything out"; whether his US citizenship affects his eligibility is unsettled, since the Acts contain no citizenship clause. In September 2026 the government said that the OSCE would be invited "as in previous elections".[15] ## Electoral system #### Governor and Lieutenant Governor The Governor and Lieutenant Governor are elected together on a joint ticket for a four-year term, beginning on the fourth Monday of November after the election. A ticket needs more than half of the valid votes; otherwise a runoff between the two leading tickets is held three weeks later. No runoff has been needed since 2007. Since the 2013 amendment there is no limit on the number of terms.[9] Since 2015 a gubernatorial candidate must collect 10,000 verified signatures of registered voters and must have lived in the ISEZ continuously for ten years before nomination. Candidates are nominated by parties or as independents. The DPI's party congress nominates its ticket.[10] Under the Acts the Lieutenant Governor acts for an absent or incapacitated Governor and succeeds if the office falls vacant. Legal scholars differ on whether the Lieutenant Governor may exercise the Governor's powers in his own right before a formal declaration of incapacity, and on who would be competent to make one.[11] #### Territorial Legislature Since 2011 the legislature has been a single chamber of 60 members elected for four years on the same day as the Governor. Its eight multi-member constituencies correspond to the three cities of governorate significance ([[Talas]], Nurzhan and [[Iyık Janyl]]) and the districts (Talas, [[Kara-Buura]], Chu, [[Sary-Bulak]], and Lower Naryn, whose constituency has also covered Toktogul District since 2016) (see [[Administrative divisions of Irad]]). Seats are apportioned according to official population figures. Within each constituency voters choose among party lists and independent candidates, and seats are allocated by the largest-remainder method.[16] A Speaker, elected from the majority, presides; Nurbek Sultanov of the DPI has held the post since 2019. #### Municipal elections Each city has an elected council and a mayor appointed by the Governor, who also appoints the district heads. During the territorial period councils were elected every four years from 1993. The councils elected in 2005 continued in office under the emergency administration, and since 2011 municipal elections have been held on the same day as the general election.[16] Russo politicians have held a majority on the Nurzhan city council for most of the period since 1992, which makes it the most significant elected body not controlled by the DPI. Its members have included the trade unionist [[Elena Petrova]], first elected in 1997. #### Administration and franchise Elections are run by the Territorial Election Commission, a seven-member body appointed by the Governor with the consent of the legislature, which keeps the voter registers, registers candidates and certifies results. Citizens resident in the ISEZ may vote from the age of 18. The registers are compiled from residence records held by the municipal authorities and the Ministry of Internal Security, which OSCE observers have cited as a weakness.[2] #### The tribal regions Residents of the ATR are not on the ISEZ voter registers, and no polling stations are opened on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC) does not recognize ISEZ institutions and has never called on tribal residents to take part. Its own bodies are not elected. Each of the 24 clans is led by a council of elders and a hereditary or acclaimed *biy*, and matters affecting all clans are decided by consensus at the summer *kurultai* on the [[Aksay Plateau]]. Human rights organizations have criticized the absence of elections to IAC bodies, while the IAC describes consensus among the lineages as the tribal form of representation.[17] Representation of the tribal regions in a unified legislature has been the central question of every unification negotiation. At the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]] the DPI offered the ATR one-third of the seats, and the IAC delegation walked out. The size of the tribal population, which the DPI's [[2018 Irad census]] estimated at about 2.0 million against independent estimates of 3.5 to 4 million, would determine its weight in any apportionment.[18] ## Results since 2011 #### Gubernatorial elections Official results as certified by the Territorial Election Commission:[2][19] | Election | DPI ticket | Official share | Official turnout | Notes | |---|---|---|---|---| | 8 November 2011 | Erlan Toktarov, Daniyar Tologonov | 88.74% | 67.9% | First regular ISEZ election; held months after the collapse of the unification talks | | 3 November 2015 | Erlan Toktarov, Daniyar Tologonov | 78.25% | 58.4% | First election after the removal of term limits; rival nominees disqualified | | 5 November 2019 | Erlan Toktarov, Aidar Maksat | 90.31% | 73.2% | Maksat took office as Lieutenant Governor on 25 November 2019 | | 7 November 2023 | Erlan Toktarov, Aidar Maksat | 92.75% | 71.6% | Held a month after the Talas student protests; runner-up Oleg Zubarev, a Russo-aligned independent from Nurzhan | #### Legislative elections Seats won in the 60-member Territorial Legislature:[2][19] | Election | DPI | Independents | Russo-aligned | Notes | |---|---|---|---|---| | 2011 | 49 | 7 | 4 | Replaced the provisional chamber of 2007–2011 | | 2015 | 52 | 5 | 3 | | | 2019 | 54 | 4 | 2 | | | 2023 | 51 | 6 | 3 | Most independents vote with the DPI | The Russo-aligned deputies, all elected from Nurzhan, form the only consistent opposition in the chamber. ## Assessments The [[wp:Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights|OSCE's Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights]], which has sent limited assessment missions to ISEZ elections since 2011, has reported:[2] - the disqualification of opposition candidates on technical grounds, especially in 2015; - state control of the voter registers; - pressure on employees of state-owned and state-licensed enterprises to vote; - the use of state resources in DPI campaigns; - the dominance of the DPI on [[IradOne]], the state broadcaster. Human rights organizations have added that independent opposition activity is suppressed between elections and that DPI membership is often a practical condition of promotion in the civil service (see [[Human rights in Irad]]).[17] Business groups have generally taken a more favorable view of the elections, pointing to their regularity and to the absence of violence on polling days.[20] The DPI says the elections are free, that the rules apply equally to all candidates, and that its majorities reflect public support for stability while the unification question and the neighbors' territorial claims remain unresolved. It describes OSCE criticism as interference in Irad's internal affairs. Analysts note that the low official share in 2015 and the protests of 2013, 2015 and 2023 show that dissatisfaction exists even within the system, but that no opposition force has been able to contest the governorship since 2011.[11] ## See also - [[Politics of Irad]] - [[Political status of Irad]] - [[List of governors of Irad]] - [[Democratic Party of Irad]] - [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] ## References
