{{Infobox political party | name = Democratic Party of Irad | native_name = *Irad Demokratik Partiyasy* (DPI) | leader = [[Erlan Toktarov]] (Chairman) | founded = October 1992 | hq = [[Talas]] | ideology = Suspended sovereignty; Secularism; Market economy | seats1_title = Seats in the legislature (2023) | seats1 = 51 / 60 }} The **Democratic Party of Irad** (Iradi: *Irad Demokratik Partiyasy*, DPI) is the dominant political party of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), the part of [[Irad]] outside the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. Founded in 1992 by reformers of the Provisional Government, it was the leading party of the [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)|US territorial period]]. After the US withdrawal in December 2006 the party split, and on 25 February 2007 [[Erlan Toktarov]] seized control of it and proclaimed the ISEZ from Nurzhan. The reorganized party is often called the "New Democratic Party of Irad".[1] Since 2007 the DPI has held the governorship and a large majority in the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]], and analysts describe the ISEZ as a dominant-party system organized around the Toktarov family. Toktarov, the party's chairman, was re-elected Governor in 2011, 2015, 2019 and 2023, in elections that observers from the [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe]] (OSCE) said lacked meaningful choice.[2] He has not appeared in public since July 2024; the party attributes his absence to an extended health retreat. ## History #### Origins and the territorial period (1992–2006) The party traces its origins to the reformist caucus of the Provisional Government formed in [[Talas]] during the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]]. It was formally constituted in October 1992, after [[Operation Starlight]] and the organization of the territory under the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]], by Provisional Government ministers, Talas professionals and returning émigrés who supported the territorial arrangement of the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]].[3] Its program drew heavily on American models: territorial association with the United States, market reform, dollarization and English-language education. Party members dominated the interim legislature of 1992–1994, which passed the first banking and currency statutes. At the first territorial elections in 1994 the DPI won majorities in both chambers, and it kept them for most of the territorial period, facing opposition mainly from the [[Labor Party of Irad]], based in [[Nurzhan]]'s Russian-speaking industrial workforce, the nationalist [[Jer-Suu Party]] and independent rural deputies.[3] Toktarov, who joined the party after Operation Starlight, entered the Territorial House of Representatives in 1994 and was Majority Leader of the Territorial Senate from 2000 to 2004. [[Bakyt Orozbekov]], later Prime Minister, was chief legal counsel to the Senate and drafted the [[2003 Judicial Reforms Act]].[4] By the early 2000s critics in the press and the opposition were drawing attention to the commercial concessions held by party figures, especially in fuel distribution and in warehousing around [[Talas Air Base]]. #### Split and the Second Civil War (2006–2007) When President George W. Bush withdrew the United States from the treaty by executive action on 3 December 2006, DPI legislators led the response. After the Supreme Court issued the [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]], the Territorial Legislature proclaimed the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] on 9 December, and Orozbekov formed a DPI-led cabinet.[5] In January and February 2007 the cabinet sold state assets, including oil concessions, grain elevators and telecom licenses, to firms controlled by party members. The [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]] provoked street protests in Talas and unrest in the countryside.[6] Toktarov, who had warned against an immediate declaration of statehood, broke with Orozbekov. On 25 February 2007 he made public the cabinet's secret drafts, negotiated with Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan, to dissolve Irad and partition it among them in return for escrow payments and concession shares for companies tied to Orozbekov and several ministers (see [[Bill of Sale (2007)]]). He then took control of the party apparatus, proclaimed the ISEZ from Nurzhan as an emergency administration, annulled the independence ruling and returned Irad to "suspended sovereignty".[1] The Orozbekov cabinet in Talas continued as a rival authority until the [[Popular Front of Irad]] stormed the capital on 4 June 2007. During the summer, security forces loyal to Toktarov, backed by Western companies and the United States, took control of Talas and the other cities as the Front withdrew to the countryside, and the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] of September fixed the division of the country.[1] The press began calling the reorganized party the "New DPI" to distinguish it from the territorial-era party, although it kept its official name. #### Consolidation (2007–2023) Toktarov assumed the governorship in 2007 and was re-elected in November 2011 with 88.74% of the official vote. The same year the party's delegation at the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]] offered the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC) one-third of the seats in a reunified legislature; the IAC walked out, and no comparable talks have been held since.[7] In 2013 the DPI majority in the legislature passed an amendment to the 1992 [[Elective Governor Acts (1992)|Elective Governor Acts]] that removed gubernatorial term limits (the [[2013 Constitutional Amendment]]). Toktarov's share fell to 78.25% in 2015, an election marked by the disqualification of rival candidates on technical grounds (the [[2015 Electoral Reform Controversy]]).[8] He won 90.31% in 2019 with his son-in-law [[Aidar Maksat]] as his running mate on the joint ticket, and Maksat took office as Lieutenant Governor on 25 November 2019. In 2023 he won 92.75%. Early in 2023, according to independent reporting, Toktarov and his senior staff moved to the fortified [[Boz-Korgon]] compound east of Nurzhan; the party and the government maintain that Talas remains the operational capital.[9] In October 2023 a municipal licensing surcharge set off [[2023 Student Protests in Talas|student protests in Talas]], which police dispersed. #### Since 2024 Toktarov has not been seen in public since July 2024. The DPI attributes his absence to an extended health retreat, and his addresses on [[IradOne]] have been the subject of authenticity claims that officials reject (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).[9] Maksat runs the day-to-day business of the administration. The next gubernatorial election is due in November 2027, and the party has not yet named its ticket (see [[2027 Iradi gubernatorial election]]). ## Ideology The DPI describes its program as "Sovereign Development, Territorial Unity, and Economic Pragmatism". In practice its main positions are: - maintaining Irad's "suspended sovereignty" pending a unification referendum, rather than either full independence or a return to territorial status; - keeping the security relationship with the United States, including the US presence at Talas Air Base; - welcoming foreign investment, including from China (see [[Irad–China relations]]); - a secular state, with Iradi and English as official languages and Russian without official status; - market-oriented economic policy combined, in practice, with state-licensed monopolies and concessions. Leaked US intelligence reports from Toktarov's first term described the party as trending toward a cult of personality (see [[Erlan Toktarov]]).[10] Party officials reject this description. They argue that strong central authority is needed to deter territorial claims by neighboring states and to protect foreign investment. ## Organization - **Chairman**: Erlan Toktarov, since 2007. - **Political Bureau** (*Siyasi Buro*): a 25-member leadership body, which nominates candidates and approves senior appointments. - **Executive Secretariat**: the permanent party staff, based at the party headquarters in Talas. Independent reporting since 2023 says that key meetings take place at Boz-Korgon.[9] - **Regional committees**: one in each of the three cities of governorate significance (Talas, Nurzhan and [[Iyık Janyl]]) and the six districts (Talas, [[Kara-Buura]], Chu, [[Sary-Bulak]], Lower Naryn and Toktogul). The committees oversee public procurement, utility concessions, municipal licensing and agricultural quotas. - **Party congress**: meets before each gubernatorial election to nominate the party's candidate. Membership is widespread among civil servants and employees of state-licensed firms. Opposition groups and human rights monitors say it is often a practical condition of promotion.[11] #### Party chairmen The chairman is elected by the party congress. Before 2007 the post was separate from public office; since Toktarov took control of the party apparatus it has been held by the Governor.[3] | Chairman | Term | Notes | |---|---|---| | Ishenbek Asylbash | 1992–1997 | Talas engineer and member of the Provisional Government's councils; founding chairman | | Tomas Jakypbek | 1997–2003 | Chicago-born lawyer, one of the returnees of the early 1990s | | Bolotkan Shamshy | 2003–2007 | Talas fuel distributor; removed in February 2007 when Toktarov took over the party apparatus, after siding with the Orozbekov cabinet | | [[Erlan Toktarov]] | 2007–present | Governor of the ISEZ since 2007 | ## Electoral performance Gubernatorial elections in the ISEZ since 2007, by official results: | Election | DPI candidate | Official share of vote | |---|---|---| | November 2011 | Erlan Toktarov | 88.74% | | 2015 | Erlan Toktarov | 78.25% | | 2019 | Erlan Toktarov | 90.31% | | 2023 | Erlan Toktarov | 92.75% | In the 2023 election to the Territorial Legislature the DPI won 51 of the 60 seats, and most of the independents elected alongside it vote with the party.[2] ## Business and media connections The party's main business network is centered on the Toktarov family. [[Timur Toktarov]] directs transport and bonded logistics, [[Adil Toktarov]] commercial real estate in Talas, and [[Bekzat Toktarov]] feed milling and grain supply through [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]]. [[Alikhan Toktarov]] chairs the IradOne media group, and Major General [[Ruslan Toktarov]] commands the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]].[10] [[Talasbank]] handles much of the administration's commercial clearing, and the DPI executive office exercises editorial control over IradOne, the largest broadcaster. Relations with [[NurGaz]] are uneasy. The company's president, [[Kamran Bekzatov]], heads the Russophone *Russo* constituency in Nurzhan and is a prominent critic of DPI economic policy, and NurGaz's revenues give him a power base independent of the party.[12] ## Succession The rivalry between Toktarov's two eldest sons has been publicly visible since 2024. Ruslan, the security chief, has drawn criticism for anti-Muslim remarks, and Alikhan for reckless spending and rumored substance abuse.[10] Maksat, whom foreign diplomats regard as the most moderate figure in the leadership, has made no public claim to the succession and presents himself as a pro-business technocrat. Toktarov's daughter [[Zara Toktarova]], Maksat's wife, is a doctoral candidate in education at [[wp:Stanford University]], on leave since she returned to Irad in July 2024 to be near her parents, and has no public political role. Tabloid reports of family disputes over access to the Boz-Korgon estate have not been verified. Legal scholars differ on whether the 1992 Elective Governor Acts require a formal declaration of incapacity before the Lieutenant Governor may exercise the Governor's powers in his own right; no such finding has been made.[9] ## Criticism - **Elections.** The OSCE criticized the 2013 electoral reform and the elections that followed (see [[Elections in Irad]]). It cited the exclusion of opposition candidates, state control of voter registers and pressure on employees of state-owned firms to vote.[2] - **Media and civil liberties.** Human rights groups report harassment, license revocations and travel bans against independent journalists. They also report that mobile and internet services are throttled during protests through the national operator, [[Attelkom]].[11] - **Census.** The DPI's 2018 census gave a population of 4,626,000, against independent estimates of about 6.2 million. Researchers attribute most of the gap to the census estimating the tribal regions rather than enumerating them. IAC leaders and some analysts argue that the undercount reduces the tribal regions' weight in any unification formula; the government defends its methods.[13] - **Unification.** Critics, including the IAC, say that the party's 2011 offer and its refusal of a tribal veto over mining concessions in the [[2008 Unification Referendum Initiative]] showed that it did not negotiate in good faith.[7] ## See also - [[Politics of Irad]] - [[List of governors of Irad]] - [[Communist Party of Irad]] ## References

**Nurzhan** (Iradi: *Nurzhan shahr*, [nuɾˈʒɑn ʃɑhɾ]; Russian: *Нуржан*; known as *Kobozev* from 1927 to 1992) is the second-largest city of [[Irad]] and the center of its oil, refining and engineering industries. It lies in the lowlands of the lower Chu River in the northeast of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), where it is one of three cities of governorate significance. The official 2018 estimate put the urban population at 850,000, with more than one million people in the wider agglomeration by unofficial estimates.<sup>[1]</sup>

The city grew from an older artisan settlement that was renamed Kobozev in 1927 and rebuilt as the planned capital of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]]. It expanded rapidly after oil was found in the Chu basin in 1949. In 1991–92 it was the seat of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]]; after its capture by US and Provisional forces in August 1992, [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] renamed it Nurzhan, a Kipchak-Turkic name meaning 'light of life'.<sup>[2]</sup> Nurzhan is the headquarters of [[NurGaz]] and the center of the Russian-speaking *Russo* generation, and in February 2007 it was the base from which [[Erlan Toktarov]] proclaimed the ISEZ. Since early 2023 independent reporting has placed the *de facto* seat of the ISEZ executive at [[Boz-Korgon]], a fortified compound 40 km east of the city, although the government maintains that [[Talas]] remains the operational capital.<sup>[3]</sup> The city is also known as the birthplace of [[Mor-Wave]], an electronic music scene that emerged in its disused factories in the late 1990s.

## Etymology
*Nurzhan* joins *nur* ('light') and *zhan* ('soul, life'), two elements common to the Kipchak-Turkic languages, and is usually glossed 'light of life'. Unlike many Central Asian place names of the same form, it does not commemorate a person. Alimbekov announced the name in a speech in the city in September 1992, describing Nurzhan as a "guiding light of industry" that would lead Irad to a new dawn after the ruin of the civil war. The Territorial Legislature confirmed the change in the Toponymic Heritage Statute of 1993.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

From 1927 to 1992 the city bore the name of [[Pyotr Kobozev]], a Bolshevik who had served in the early Soviet administration of [[wp:Turkestan]]. Older residents and Russian-language media still sometimes use the Soviet name informally.

## History

#### Early settlement
Slag heaps and forge remains found in the Dastgoh quarter point to a medieval settlement of metalworkers on a branch of the Chu, which Iradi historians associate with Sogdian craftsmen of the [[wp:Silk Road]] period.<sup>[5]</sup> By the late 19th century the site was a small trading village on the cart road between the Chu and Talas valleys, partly settled by Russian and Ukrainian colonists after the Russian conquest of the region.

#### Soviet capital (1925–1941)
In 1925 the [[First Congress of Iradi Soviets]] met in the settlement and established the administrative apparatus of the new Iradi SSR.<sup>[6]</sup> In 1927 the settlement was renamed Kobozev and designated the republican capital, and Soviet planners laid out a new city on the steppe beside the old quarter. The plan followed a radial grid centered on a ceremonial square, with broad avenues aligned to catch the cool night winds from the mountains and canals drawn from the [[Chu Irrigation Canal System|Chu irrigation network]].<sup>[5]</sup>

Early industry centered on the Kobozev Heavy Machine Plant (now [[Nurzhanmash]]), which made tractor parts and agricultural machinery. The educator [[Altynai Bekzhanova]] opened the city's first Iradi-language secondary schools in the 1930s, the radio engineer [[Nurgazy Doolotov]] built its first shortwave transmission tower in 1934, and in 1938 [[Vasily Morozov]] drove the first diesel freight train into Kobozev from [[wp:Kazakhstan]].<sup>[7]</sup>

#### Deportations and the Second World War (1937–1945)
In autumn 1937 several thousand [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]], ethnic Koreans deported from the [[wp:Russian Far East|Soviet Far East]], were unloaded from unheated freight cars along the railway at Kobozev and in the Chu valley.<sup>[8]</sup> Local villagers and church communities sheltered many of them through the first winter, and from 1938 Korean collective farmers grew flood-irrigated rice on the marshy flats of the lower Chu.<sup>[9]</sup> The same years brought the anti-religious campaign of the late 1930s: Soviet suspicion of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]'s 1931 union with Rome fed the [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges|1937 purges]], and the churches of the capital were closed.<sup>[6]</sup> After the German invasion of 1941, factories evacuated from [[wp:European Russia]] were re-established in Kobozev, enlarging its metalworking and engineering base.

#### Oil city (1949–1991)
In July 1949 exploratory drilling directed by the engineer [[Sergei Voronov]] struck high-pressure oil-bearing strata at a depth of about 2,400 m, an event known as the [[Nurzhan Oil Discovery (1949)]].<sup>[10]</sup> Within a decade the [[Nurzhan Oil Refinery]] and the [[Nurzhan Petroleum Pipeline]] had been built, and the city supplied aviation fuel and lubricants to the Soviet armed forces. In the [[1952 Kobozev Steel Strike]], Iradi and Koryo-saram foundry workers struck over wages and safety until local party authorities conceded production bonuses.<sup>[11]</sup>

A master plan drawn up in 1962 by the architect [[Bolotbek Bekzhanov]] added the numbered *mikrorayon* housing estates where much of the population still lives.<sup>[11]</sup> The Nurzhan Oil Refinery was expanded in 1974, and in the 1970s the Koryo-saram engineer [[Oleg Kim]] directed the city's tractor combine. Flour shortages in 1989 led to the [[The Kobozev Bread Riots (1989)|Kobozev Bread Riots]], in which marchers demanded economic accountability, freedom of religion and elected government.<sup>[7]</sup>

#### Independence and the First Civil War (1991–1992)
On 9 October 1991 the [[Communist Party of Irad]], led by First Secretary [[Vasily Chernov]], a former engineer at the Kobozev refinery, declared independence as the Socialist Republic of Irad, governed from Kobozev.<sup>[12]</sup> The end of Soviet subsidies shut many of the city's plants, and on 14 January 1992 railway repair workers at the Kobozev depot declared a general strike that helped set off the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]].<sup>[13]</sup>

After the Provisional Government proclaimed the Republic of Irad in Talas on 11 March 1992, Kobozev became the headquarters of the socialist war effort in the [[First Iradi Civil War]]. As US and Provisional forces advanced on the city in the summer of 1992, Provisional units repelled a socialist armored counter-attack in the [[Battle of Kobozev Railhead (1992)]]. Joint US and Iradi forces under [[Operation Starlight]] took Kobozev on 12 August, and the remaining socialist forces surrendered on 18 August.<sup>[12]</sup> Alimbekov renamed the city the following month.

#### Territorial period (1992–2006)
Under the US territorial administration the Soviet oil trust *Iradneft* was corporatized in 1993 as NurGaz, led by the Kobozev-born petroleum engineer [[Kamran Bekzatov]].<sup>[14]</sup> The city's managers and technicians, educated in Russian under the ISSR, became the core of the *Russo* generation, and Russo politicians held most seats on the municipal council throughout the period.<sup>[15]</sup> The 1990s and 2000s brought the suburban district of Navbahor, the [[Attelkom Data Center]] and a fuel pipeline from the refinery to [[Talas Air Base]]. Construction of the Boz-Korgon compound east of the city began in the mid-1990s.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Since 2007
After the US withdrawal of December 2006 and the proclamation of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] in Talas, Nurzhan became the base of the faction of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) opposed to Prime Minister [[Bakyt Orozbekov]]. On 25 February 2007, in a speech in the city's central square, Toktarov made public the cabinet's secret partition drafts (see [[Bill of Sale (2007)]]), seized control of the DPI and proclaimed the Irad Special Economic Zone from Nurzhan as an emergency administration, the act that marks the start of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]].<sup>[16]</sup> Loyalties in the city divided during the war: rail workers joined strikes called in support of the [[Popular Front of Irad]], while NurGaz guards held the refinery and Bekzatov refused to recognize the asset auctions of the Orozbekov cabinet.<sup>[14]</sup><sup>[16]</sup> After the Front withdrew from the cities in the summer of 2007, Nurzhan became one of the three cities of governorate significance of the ISEZ.

Since early 2023, independent reporting has placed the governor's office at Boz-Korgon, in the countryside east of the city; the government denies this and maintains that Talas is the operational capital.<sup>[3]</sup> Bekzatov, the city's most prominent public figure, has become an outspoken critic of DPI economic policy and an advocate of closer ties with Russia.<sup>[14]</sup>

## Geography
Nurzhan lies at an elevation of 470 m (1,540 ft) on the flat alluvial plain of the lower [[Chu River Basin|Chu River]], and is surrounded by Chu District, the ISEZ district that covers the Chu lowlands and the Boz-Korgon area. To the north, irrigated farmland gives way to the semi-desert grassland of the southern [[Betpak-Dala]]; the dunes of the [[Moiynkum Desert|Moiynkum]] (Muyunkum) sands lie to the south and west, between the Chu and the Talas. On clear days the snow-covered Kyrgyz Range is visible across the border to the south. The Chu is an endorheic river that ends in the desert, and the city's water comes from it and from the canals of the Chu Irrigation Canal System. A small urban canal, [[Dastgoh Creek]], was diverted in the Soviet period to drive forge hammers.<sup>[5]</sup> The built-up area covers about 280 km² (108 sq mi) of the plain on both banks of the Chu, with the refinery and the eastern industrial zone on the east side of the city.

#### Climate
Nurzhan has a cold semi-arid climate ([[wp:Köppen climate classification|Köppen]] *BSk*) with large seasonal swings. July daytime highs average 33 °C (91 °F), and summer dust storms are common. The January mean is about −5 °C (23 °F), with daytime highs near 0 °C and nights near −10 °C (14 °F), and Arctic air outbreaks occasionally bring temperatures below −25 °C (−13 °F). Annual precipitation averages about 270 mm (10.6 in), most of it falling in spring.<sup>[17]</sup>

Winter smog, caused by refinery and bitumen emissions together with coal-fired district heating, is a recurring problem. NurGaz says it has fitted stack scrubbers and built gas-fired cogeneration units since the late 2010s; a [[wp:World Bank]] assessment of Central Asian industrial cities found that winter particulate levels in Nurzhan remained well above international guidelines.<sup>[10]</sup><sup>[18]</sup>

#### Cityscape and districts
The city's urban districts include:
- **[[Dastgoh District]]**, the historic artisan and foundry quarter, with metal workshops, boiler fabrication sheds, toolmakers and the [[NurGaz Pipeline Maintenance Depot]].
- **[[Navbahor District]]** ('New Spring'), a leafy residential district of detached brick houses and bilingual schools built in the 1990s during the territorial period.
- The **central district** along Azatlık Prospect, laid out in the 1930s as Lenin Prospect and renamed under the 1993 statute, with granite government buildings, the [[Nurzhan Municipal Library]] and the Palace of Metallurgists.
- The **mikrorayon estates** of the 1962 master plan, numbered blocks of five- and nine-story flats grouped around courtyards, schools and heating plants.
- The **eastern industrial zone**, which contains the refinery, the Attelkom Data Center, the grain silos of [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]] and the spinning sheds of [[Zhetysu Industrial Textiles]].

## Demographics
The official 2018 estimate gave Nurzhan an urban population of 850,000, and more than one million including satellite towns and industrial settlements along the lower Chu.<sup>[1]</sup> Because the ISEZ census enumerated cities directly, the city figure is far less disputed than the national total, which independent researchers consider an undercount of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].

According to official figures, [[Iradis]] make up about 64% of the city's population, Russians 13%, [[wp:Kazakhs]] 6%, Koryo-saram 4%, Kyrgyz 4%, Ukrainians 3%, [[wp:Uzbeks]] 2% and other groups 4%.<sup>[1]</sup> Nurzhan has the largest Russian and Koryo-saram communities in Irad.{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}} Russian is the everyday language of most residents over forty and is widely used in business, although it lost official status in 1992; Iradi and English are the official languages, and younger residents increasingly use both.<sup>[15]</sup>

The [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] is the largest denomination, and the city is the seat of one of its suffragan eparchies. Nurzhan also has Russian Orthodox parishes, Presbyterian and Catholic congregations within the Koryo-saram community, and mosques serving its Kazakh, Uzbek and Tatar residents. Surveys suggest that religious practice is lower than in Talas or [[Iyık Janyl]], a legacy of the city's Soviet secular culture.<sup>[9]</sup><sup>[15]</sup>

## Economy
Nurzhan is the center of the Iradi hydrocarbon industry.
- **Oil and gas.** NurGaz, headquartered in the city, operates the oil fields of the lower Chu basin. It reports national output of about 120,000 barrels per day, although independent estimates are lower.<sup>[10]</sup> The Nurzhan Oil Refinery (expanded 1974) produces gasoline, diesel, heating oil and jet fuel. Crude that is not refined locally is pumped through the Nurzhan Petroleum Pipeline and the 85-km [[Northern Export Feeder]] into the Kazakh network operated by [[wp:KazTransOil]] near [[wp:Shymkent]], for refining there or onward shipment to Russia.<sup>[19]</sup> Gas from the [[Muyunkum Natural Gas Field]] is boosted at the [[Nurzhan Gas Compressor Station]]; most of Irad's gas reserves of more than 400 billion m³ remain undeveloped.
- **Chemicals and construction materials.** The [[Nurzhan Asphalt and Bitumen Plant]] turns residual refinery bottoms into road binders, and an adjacent chemical works makes agricultural ammonia.
- **Engineering and light industry.** Nurzhanmash, the former Heavy Machine Plant, makes oilfield pumpjacks and spare parts. Zhetysu Industrial Textiles produces wool, felt and cotton thread, but its output is limited by water shortages.<sup>[20]</sup>
- **Agribusiness.** Nurzhan Agro-Industrial, directed by [[Bekzat Toktarov]], dominates feed milling, silage distribution and bulk grain supply. The surrounding farmland grows wheat, sugar beet and the short-grain rice introduced by Koryo-saram farmers in 1938.<sup>[20]</sup>
- **Retail and services.** About 40 percent of shop names are Russian, and shop signs read *Magazin* rather than *dükön*. [[Bereke]] has about 53 supermarkets in the city, [[Jıldız Market]] 36 and Shıpa Dariykana 23 pharmacies; Chuy Commercial Bank has 16 branches, [[Ak Bata Bank]] 15 and [[Talasbank]] 6, among them its Azatlık Prospect branch. NurGaz runs 43 filling stations, and KFC Irad has two restaurants, by the central square and in Navbahor. Canteens (*stolovaya*), some still numbered in the Soviet way ("Canteen No. 7"), and wedding banquet halls (*toikana*) are common, Russian and Koryo-saram dishes such as kuksi and Koryoin laghman are as common as Iradi food, and there are fewer chaikhanas than in Talas. The **Radiobazar** (Nurzhan Radio Bazaar), a block west of the south end of Azatlık Prospect, is surrounded by radio, telephone and computer stalls, and the Dastgoh bazarı serves the Dastgoh District.
- **Logistics and data.** The [[Nurzhan Rail Freight Depot]] marshals tank cars and freight bound for the Kazakh rail network, and [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]] runs bonded trucking routes to the northern border crossings. The Attelkom Data Center hosts government and commercial servers.

NurGaz is the city's largest employer. Through the company and the Bekzatov Foundation, Bekzatov funds subsidized housing such as the [[NurGaz Worker Housing Complex]], clinics and Russian-language schools, which analysts regard as the basis of his independent political following.<sup>[14]</sup>

## Government
Nurzhan is one of the three cities of governorate significance of the ISEZ, alongside Talas and Iyık Janyl, and is administered separately from the surrounding Chu District. The city is run by a mayor appointed by the Governor and an elected city council. Russo politicians have held a majority on the council for most of the period since 1992, and it has repeatedly clashed with the DPI administration over language policy and the city's share of oil revenue.<sup>[15]</sup> [[Elena Petrova]], a municipal leader who represents the Russian and Ukrainian industrial workforce, is among the city's best-known municipal politicians.

The 2nd Motor Rifle Brigade of the [[Armed Forces of Irad]] is based in the city and guards the refinery, pumping stations and northern rail links.

## Transport
Nurzhan is the main railway junction of the ISEZ, with the Turksib east to the Kazakh frontier and the Kazakh rail network toward Almaty, the line west toward Talas and a line east to Boz-Korgon; most of its traffic is freight.<sup>[20]</sup> The passenger station stands on the through line a few hundred meters southwest of the central square, and the Nurzhan Rail Freight Depot about 4 km northeast of the center, on the line to the border. Highways link the city with Talas, with Boz-Korgon and with the northern border crossings into Kazakhstan. City transport consists of a Soviet-era trolleybus network, municipal buses and privately run minibuses (*marshrutkas*). The city has no scheduled passenger airport; air travelers use Talas or airports in neighboring Kazakhstan.

## Education and health
- The [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]], formerly the Kobozev Polytechnic Institute, is Irad's leading technical university and specializes in petroleum engineering. It trains much of the NurGaz engineering staff.<sup>[10]</sup>
- The [[Nurzhan Technical Lyceum]] offers vocational apprenticeships in electrical maintenance and machining.
- The [[Nurzhan Municipal Botanical Institute]] and the [[Nurzhan Botanical Gardens]] study cold-hardy fruit trees and mountain flora.
- The Nurzhan Municipal Library holds more than 300,000 volumes. The former Pushkin Library, the Soviet republican library, is now the Nurzhan branch of the [[National Library of Irad]], with the Russian-language and technical collections that were not moved to Talas in 1993–94.<sup>[15]</sup>
- Health services include the [[Nurzhan Children’s Polyclinic]], which has served industrial workers' families since the Soviet period, cardiac clinics endowed by Bekzatov, and the [[Nurzhan Emergency Dispatch Center]]. The [[St. Teresa Community Kitchen]], a parish soup kitchen, serves daily meals to pensioners and disabled workers.<sup>[21]</sup>

## Culture
In the late 1990s young people gathering in abandoned warehouses and factory boiler rooms in Nurzhan began combining vintage Soviet analog synthesizers with Iradi melodies and lyrics. The style became known as Mor-Wave, and its pioneers, the duo [[tüntolk]] (Askar Daniyarov and Mira Temirova), gained an audience abroad with their 1999 debut album *[[Jolchu (Album)|Jolchu]]*.<sup>[22]</sup> The scene later produced the commercial offshoot [[Mor-Pop]], while acoustic [[Mor-Folk]] ensembles play in teahouses in Nurzhan and Talas.

Russo cultural life is centered on Russian-language theater, satellite television and the [[wp:Victory Day (9 May)|Victory Day]] parade on 9 May. The Koryo-saram community maintains cultural associations and Korean-language Sunday schools, and contributed dishes such as Koryoin laghman, noodles with sesame and kimchi, to the wider Iradi kitchen.<sup>[9]</sup> The Nurzhan Contemporary Arts Foundation, run by [[Asel Bekzatova]], supports young musicians.

Notable buildings (see [[Architecture of Irad]]) include the Palace of Metallurgists, a Soviet palace of culture on Azatlık Prospect; the central square of the 1927 plan; the Nurzhan Oil Refinery, the country's only oil refinery; and the forges of Dastgoh.

{{Infobox person | name = Bakyt Orozbekov | df = dmy | image = Bakyt_Orozbekov_2006.jpg | caption = Orozbekov in his legislative office, 2006 | office1 = Prime Minister of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] | term_start1 = 2006-12-09 | term_end1 = 2007-06-04 | preceded_by1 = Office established | succeeded_by1 = Office abolished | office2 = Chief Legal Counsel to the Territorial Senate | term_start2 = 1998 | term_end2 = 2005 | birth_date = 1962-07-19 | birth_place = [[Talas]], [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic|Iradi SSR]], Soviet Union | party = [[Democratic Party of Irad]] | children = 2 | residence = [[wp:Istanbul]], Turkey | alma_mater = [[wp:Moscow State University]] (1984); [[wp:Harvard Law School]] (LL.M., 1996) | occupation = Lawyer | known_for = [[2003 Judicial Reforms Act]]; [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]] }} **Bakyt Orozbekov** (born 19 July 1962) is an Iradi lawyer and former politician who was the only Prime Minister of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] (DRI), from its proclamation on 9 December 2006 until its dissolution on 4 June 2007. He trained in [[wp:Moscow]] and at [[wp:Harvard Law School]]. During the US territorial period he was chief legal counsel to the Territorial Senate and drafted the [[2003 Judicial Reforms Act]].[1] After the United States withdrew from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] in December 2006, Orozbekov brought the petition that led to the [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]], and the Territorial Legislature then elected him Prime Minister of the new republic. His cabinet's sale of state assets in early 2007, which became known as the [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]], provoked protests. At the same time his government secretly negotiated with Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan draft treaties to dissolve Irad and partition it among them, with concession shares for companies tied to him and several ministers. Their disclosure by [[Erlan Toktarov]] on 25 February 2007, as the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]], was the main cause of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. When the [[Popular Front of Irad]] stormed [[Talas]] on 4 June 2007, he surrendered himself to US forces at [[Talas Air Base]] and signed an instrument of resignation; he was extradited to the United States five days later, acquitted by a federal jury in New York in 2008, and has lived in [[wp:Istanbul]] since 2009. He has lived abroad since 2007.[2][3] ## Early life and education Orozbekov was born on 19 July 1962 in Talas. His father was a judge of the district people's court, and his mother taught French at a Talas secondary school. He was educated in Russian-language schools and in 1979 entered the [[wp:Moscow State University|Faculty of Law of Moscow State University]], graduating in 1984.[1] From 1984 to 1991 he worked as a legal adviser in commercial arbitration for a Soviet merchant shipping enterprise in [[wp:Odesa|Odessa]], handling disputes over charter contracts and cargo claims with foreign companies. He returned to Talas in 1991, shortly before the collapse of the [[wp:Soviet Union]], and remained in the city through the siege of 1992. In 1994, under a territorial government scholarship for lawyers, he went to Harvard Law School, where he received a [[wp:Master of Laws]] (LL.M.) in international corporate finance in 1996.[1] ## Legal career in the territorial period On his return to Talas in 1996 he founded one of the territory's first commercial law firms, advising foreign investors in the energy and agribusiness sectors on contracts, concessions and arbitration. He was a member of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) and was associated with its reformist and legalist wing.[4] From 1998 to 2005 he was chief legal counsel to the Territorial Senate, then the upper chamber of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]]. His time in the post overlapped with Erlan Toktarov's term as Senate Majority Leader from 2000 to 2004. His best-known work was the 2003 Judicial Reforms Act. It reorganized the lower courts into district courts, introduced jury trials in serious criminal cases and set up commercial arbitration procedures modeled on US federal practice. Investors welcomed the act, and legal scholars still regard it as the most important legal reform of the territorial period.[5] In 2005 he returned to private practice. ## The independence crisis and premiership (2006–2007) #### Statutory Independence Ruling On 3 December 2006 President George W. Bush withdrew the United States from the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty by executive action (see [[United States Withdrawal from the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty (2006)]]). Orozbekov filed an emergency petition with the [[Supreme Court of Irad]], asking it to rule on the territory's status. He argued that the treaty's statutory independence clause, carried into the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]], took effect automatically when federal administration ended. Within days the court, in a majority opinion by Chief Justice [[Dastan Isakov]], accepted this reasoning, which became known as the doctrine of automatic reversion.[6] On 9 December 2006 the Territorial Legislature reconstituted itself as a national assembly, proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Irad and elected Orozbekov Prime Minister (see [[Proclamation of the DRI]]). Twenty-six UN member states recognized the new state. Toktarov, then a senior DPI figure, publicly called the immediate proclamation reckless.[2] #### Privatization crisis The DRI inherited a large budget deficit, since US federal transfers had stopped. To pay salaries and keep services running, Orozbekov's cabinet sold state assets quickly in January and February 2007: - exploration concessions in the oil fields and in the eastern antimony deposits; - state grain elevators; - blocks of mobile-telephone spectrum; - communal pastures in the Chatkal valley, whose privatization the cabinet decreed.[7] Investigative reporting found that many of the assets had gone at low prices to companies linked to cabinet ministers and other DPI members. Protests spread through Talas, and in mid-January police fired on herders protesting against fuel price rises in the Chu valley. In Nurzhan the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]] refused to recognize the auctions. Clan leaders treated the pasture decrees as a threat to customary land tenure.[7] Orozbekov defended the sales as an emergency measure, said the auctions had been open, and denied any personal involvement in the transactions that were later criticized.[3] #### The Bill of Sale From December 2006 to February 2007, delegations from the Prime Minister's office met officials of the foreign ministries of [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kazakhstan]] in meetings arranged as border and water consultations and not disclosed to the national assembly. The drafts that resulted would have used the sovereignty conferred by the 2006 ruling to dissolve the DRI and divide Irad among the three states, with compensation paid into escrow and shares in oil, antimony and Toktogul concessions for offshore companies tied to Orozbekov and several ministers. No plebiscite was planned.[8][9] Toktarov made the drafts public in Nurzhan on 25 February 2007, and [[Iradis]] have called them the *Satuu Kagazy*, the "Bill of Sale", ever since. The cabinet replied that the papers were unapproved contingency drafts and that some pages might have been altered.[9] #### Second Civil War and fall On 25 February 2007 Toktarov seized control of the DPI and proclaimed the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] from [[Nurzhan]] as an emergency administration. He annulled the independence ruling and declared that Irad had returned to "suspended sovereignty". Orozbekov denounced the proclamation as unconstitutional and the leak as a provocation. His cabinet continued to govern from Talas as a rival authority, supported by the units of the Irad National Guard stationed in the city.[2] In March 2007 clan militias led by [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]] formed the Popular Front of Irad. Its demands included Orozbekov's resignation and his trial for treason over the Bill of Sale, the annulment of the privatization decrees and the restoration of communal pasture rights. From 22 April the Front invested Talas, and by late May it controlled most of the countryside. On 4 June 2007 it stormed the city ([[Storming of Talas (2007)]]). Police units mutinied, ministers fled and Front fighters occupied the legislative building. As Front fighters reached the government district, Orozbekov left his official residence and surrendered himself to United States forces at [[Talas Air Base]], where he signed an instrument of resignation dissolving the DRI government.[10] ## Later life A sealed federal indictment in New York charged Orozbekov with conspiracy to launder money and with wire fraud, alleging that payments connected with the concession deals had passed through correspondent accounts in New York. Toktarov's emergency administration did not oppose the United States' request, and on 9 June 2007 he was extradited and flown to New York.[13] In March 2008 ISEZ prosecutors charged him in absentia with high treason over the Bill of Sale and with abuse of office in connection with the privatization auctions, and asked Washington to return him once the American case was over.[11] On 21 November 2008 a federal jury acquitted him on all counts; jurors were not persuaded that the payments described by the prosecution had been made.[13] In February 2009 Orozbekov moved to [[wp:Istanbul]], where he has lived since, working as a consultant on international commercial arbitration.[3] He has described the Iradi charges as political, and [[wp:Turkey]] has not acted on requests for his return.[11] In 2012 he published a memoir, *A Republic of Six Months*. In it and in later interviews he has argued that the 2006 ruling remains valid law, because the Supreme Court never ruled on Toktarov's annulment decree, and that the resignation he signed at the air base has no legal force. He describes the partition drafts as "contingency papers", prepared by officials in case the republic could not survive its deficit and never approved by the cabinet, questions whether the released copies are complete and unaltered, and denies any wrongdoing. He has not attempted to form a government in exile. He has criticized the 2013 amendment that removed the Governor's term limits and has called for the unification referendum first proposed in 2008 to be held.[3] He is married and has two children. ## Assessments Opinion on Orozbekov is sharply divided. Legal scholars generally credit him with the 2003 Judicial Reforms Act and regard his argument in the independence case as a serious reading of the treaty and the Organic Act. Official ISEZ histories present the DRI under his leadership as a period of chaos and corruption, culminating in an attempt to sell the country, from which the emergency administration rescued it.[4] In the tribal regions he is remembered as the face of the urban elite whose pasture decrees and partition drafts provoked the Popular Front, and the storming of Talas that ended his government is celebrated as a popular rising.[10] Some historians argue that he has been made to carry too much of the blame for the privatization crisis. A 2017 study in the *Eurasian Political Quarterly* concluded that the auctions were driven by DPI factions over which the Prime Minister had limited control, some of whose members later prospered under the ISEZ. Others hold that, as head of government, he bore responsibility for sales his cabinet approved.[12] The Bill of Sale is harder to attribute to factions, since the negotiations were run from his own office; the main dispute there concerns whether the drafts were a settled policy or, as he maintains, contingency planning.[8] ## See also - [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] - [[Bill of Sale (2007)]] - [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]] - [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]] ## References

David Sterling]] (US liaison);[[Amanbek Alimbekov]] | commander2 = [[Vasily Chernov]] | units1 = [[wp:United States Marine Corps|US Marines]];10th Mountain Division;US air units;Student militias, workers' detachments and clan cavalry | units2 = 17th Motor Rifle Division;[[wp:OMON]];Interior troops | strength1 = US: c. 8,000–10,000 (peak ground deployment, late July) | strength2 = 9,000–14,000 (June 1992, Iradi estimates) | casualties1 = US: 94 dead (76 killed in action, 18 non-hostile);361 wounded in action (US Department of Defense) | casualties2 = Many conscripts deserted;Heavy equipment seized | casualties3 = c. 14,000 dead in the whole war, March–August 1992 (most cited);9,000 to over 20,000 (independent estimates) }} **Operation Starlight** (Iradi: *Jıldız Jarıgı*) was the United States military intervention in the [[First Iradi Civil War]] in 1992. It was carried out under the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]], which the Provisional Government of the Republic of Irad signed and ratified in besieged [[Talas]] on 2 June 1992. The first [[wp:United States Marine Corps|US Marines]] were airlifted into the airfield west of Talas, now [[Talas Air Base]], on 6 June. With troops of the 10th Mountain Division and US air support, they broke the siege of the city by 18 June. US and Provisional forces then advanced along the railway toward Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]), the seat of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] (SRI). Kobozev fell on 12 August, and the remaining SRI forces surrendered unconditionally on 18 August 1992.[1][2] The surrender ended the civil war and the SRI. The same day Irad became an organized, unincorporated territory of the United States under the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]], beginning the [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)|territorial period]]. The most commonly cited death toll for the war as a whole is about 14,000, with independent estimates ranging from about 9,000 to more than 20,000.[3] ## Background The [[Communist Party of Irad]], under First Secretary [[Vasily Chernov]], declared the Iradi SSR independent as the Socialist Republic of Irad on 9 October 1991 (see [[Declaration of State Sovereignty (1991)]]). Economic collapse and the government's emergency decrees provoked the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], which drove SRI officials out of Talas. On 11 March 1992 the [[Talas Town Hall Meeting (1992)|Talas Town Hall Meeting]] proclaimed the Republic of Irad and elected the historian [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] Provisional President.[4] In late March the SRI sent the 17th Motor Rifle Division, [[wp:OMON]] detachments and interior troops south along the Chu and Talas corridors. They besieged Talas from 10 April 1992. The city's defenders were student militias, defecting police, workers' detachments and mounted clan irregulars under [[Kuban Mamytov]] and [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]]. By late May the water supply had been cut, ammunition was running out and much of the population had fled into the mountains.[4] Provisional envoys had approached the United States through its embassy in [[wp:Almaty]] and at meetings in [[wp:Geneva]]. On 2 June Alimbekov and [[wp:James Baker|US Secretary of State James Baker]] signed the treaty in the basement of the damaged municipal theater, and the Provisional Government ratified it unanimously the same day. Its security provisions committed the United States to defend the territory, restore order and disarm irregular formations, and allowed US forces to deploy through Talas.[5] ## Name The US government has not published an explanation of the operation's code name. In Irad the name is popularly associated with the [[The Star of Irad (Symbol)|Star of Irad]], the image of [[wp:Polaris]] that appears above the stallion on the [[Flag of Irad]], although there is no evidence that US planners intended the connection.[6] ## Course of the operation #### Airlift into Talas (6–18 June) The airfield 12 km west of Talas, built in 1952 as a Soviet interceptor base, had stayed inside the Provisional Government's lines throughout the siege. The first Marines landed there on 6 June. [[David Sterling|Colonel David Sterling]], a Russian-speaking foreign area officer who arrived with them, became the first US liaison officer in the city. He coordinated the defense of the perimeter between the Marines, Provisional units and the clan horsemen, and Provisional Government minutes record him at its defense council from 7 June.[7] Irad had no access to the sea, and [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] had closed their borders during the fighting. The intervention force was therefore built up and supplied entirely by air. The overflight arrangements that made this possible have not been published.[1] US aircraft attacked SRI artillery, armor and air-defense positions around Talas. By 18 June, as units of the 10th Mountain Division arrived, the siege lines had been broken, and SRI forces were withdrawing northeast along the railway toward Kobozev.[1] #### Advance on Kobozev (July–August) In July US and Provisional forces advanced together along the railway and highway corridor from the Talas valley toward the lower Chu. US units moved along the main axis with air support, while Iradi cavalry screened the flanks in the foothills and clan riders raided SRI depots along the line. Although most of the northern steppe clans stayed out of the war, riders of the clans along the Chu fought under the Boztorgoy war leader [[Kudaibergen Duishön uulu]]. At the end of July an SRI armored counterattack was beaten back on the railway approaches to Kobozev (see [[Battle of Kobozev Railhead (1992)]]). Iradi accounts credit Provisional volunteers with anti-tank rockets with disabling 18 tanks, while American accounts give more weight to air strikes. The number has not been independently confirmed.[4][1] Kobozev fell on 12 August. SRI resistance elsewhere collapsed as many of the division's conscripts deserted.[2] #### Surrender (18 August) On 18 August 1992 the remaining SRI forces surrendered unconditionally, and all former SRI territory came under US control. Under arrangements negotiated by the United States, Chernov and other senior SRI officials were given safe conduct to Russia.[2] ## Forces - **United States:** US Marines and troops of the 10th Mountain Division, supported by US air units and military airlift. Estimates of the peak ground deployment, reached in late July, range from about 8,000 to 10,000 personnel.[1] - **Provisional Government of the Republic of Irad:** student militias, police who had defected, workers' detachments from Talas, and mounted clan irregulars from the [[Talas Alatau]] and the Chatkal valleys, armed largely with weapons seized from SRI arsenals during the Winter Uprising.[7] - **Socialist Republic of Irad:** the 17th Motor Rifle Division, formerly of the [[wp:Turkestan Military District|Soviet Turkestan Military District]], with [[wp:T-72]] tanks, [[wp:BMP-2]] infantry fighting vehicles, artillery and helicopters, together with republican OMON and interior troops. Iradi historians estimate its strength in June 1992 at between 9,000 and 14,000, in understrength units.[2] ## Casualties No complete count of the dead exists. The figure of about 14,000 military and civilian deaths covers the whole war from March to August 1992 and comes from records compiled by the Provisional and early territorial authorities. Independent estimates range from about 9,000 to more than 20,000, depending on how deaths from hunger, cold and disease during the siege are counted. Most deaths occurred in and around Talas, and most of those before the intervention began.[3] US losses were light by comparison and are exactly recorded. The United States Department of Defense lists 94 American service members who died in the operation: 76 killed in action and 18 non-hostile deaths, 11 of them in the crash of a Marine CH-53E helicopter in fog over the Talas Alatau on 29 June 1992. A further 361 were wounded in action. The deadliest single engagement for US forces was the battle at the Kobozev railhead at the end of July, in which 23 Americans were killed. No Americans were taken prisoner. Their names are listed on a memorial at Talas Air Base and on a bronze plaque in the Church of St. Tomas in Talas, where a memorial service is held each year on 6 June; in Talas they are often called simply "the Ninety-Four".[8] The fighting left mines and unexploded ordnance in the passes of the Talas Alatau and on the approaches to Talas. Clearance continued in the territorial period and, after 2008, under the coordination of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]].[9] ## Aftermath US forces disarmed both the SRI garrisons and the irregular militias. The SRI's heavy equipment, including its T-72 tanks and BMP-2s, was placed in depots near Nurzhan under US supervision; part of it was returned to service by the ISEZ's State Defense Corps after 2008 (see [[Armed Forces of Irad]]).[2] Mamytov returned to herding in the Chatkal valley and in 1994 declined a commission in the new Irad National Guard. Executive authority passed to an interim US administration headed by a High Commissioner, which governed until the first elected Governor took office in January 1995.[5] The airfield west of Talas became the main US installation in the territory. US military engineers lengthened its runway to 3,400 m between 1993 and 1998, and US forces have remained there since, under the [[2001 Basing Rights Agreement]] and later arrangements with the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]].[10] ## International reaction Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan objected to the intervention and the treaty as violations of the inviolability of post-Soviet borders accepted when the [[wp:Commonwealth of Independent States]] was formed. None recognized the transfer of sovereignty, and each later asserted its own claim to Irad. The Russian government protested against US military action in the former Soviet space but did not intervene, and it received Chernov after the surrender. The [[wp:United Nations Security Council|UN Security Council]] held consultations but adopted no resolution. Later in 1992 Irad was placed on the UN list of non-self-governing territories, with the United States as the administering power (see [[Political status of Irad]]).[11] In the United States the intervention prompted a brief public fascination with Irad, later called [[Iradimania]] (about 1992–1994), whose best-known product was the 1993 compilation album [[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|*Swift Hooves*]] (see [[Irad–United States relations]]). ## Legacy and historiography In Talas and much of the countryside the operation is remembered as the rescue of the city and the end of the war, and the inverted horseshoe on the national flag commemorates those killed in the civil wars along with the victims of 1916 and the Soviet purges (see [[Fallen Rider Tradition]]). Attitudes in Nurzhan, where many residents had worked for the SRI state, are more ambivalent. Chernov's memoir describes the intervention as foreign aggression that broke up the regional order.[12] Historians at [[Talas State University]] continue to debate whether the treaty that made the intervention possible was the only way to save Talas or an unnecessary surrender of the independence proclaimed in March 1992. Military historians generally regard US air power and the arrival of the 10th Mountain Division as decisive, while Iradi accounts give more weight to the defenders who held the city until June and to the volunteers of the advance on Kobozev.[4][1] Since the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]], some Iradi commentators have contrasted the intervention of 1992 with what they describe as Washington's later indifference to the territory.[6] ## See also - [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] - [[First Iradi Civil War]] - [[Talas Air Base]] - [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)]] ## References

{{Hatnote|This article is about the city in Irad. For the figure revered as the Mother of Irad, see [[Janyl (Historical Figure)]]. For the ecclesiastical jurisdiction, see [[Archbishopric of Iyık Janyl]].}} {{Infobox settlement | name = Iyık Janyl | native_name = Russian: Ийык Джаныл | settlement_type = City | subdivision = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | district = Iyık Janyl | elevation_m = 643 | population = 310000 | coordinates = 41.41°N 72.23°E }} **Iyık Janyl** (Iradi: *Iyık Janyl shahr*, [iˈjɯk ʒɑˈnɯl ʃɑhɾ]; Russian: *Ийык Джаныл*; literally 'Holy Janyl') is the third-largest city of [[Irad]] and the religious center of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. It lies at about 650 m (2,130 ft) on the river flats of the [[Naryn River|Naryn]] where the river leaves its gorge through the [[wp:Fergana Range]], about 8 km upriver from [[Tash-Kömür]] and 347 km from [[Talas]] by road, with most of the city on the broad western flats and its old town and cathedral precinct on [[Cathedral Hill]], a spur above the east bank. It is one of the three cities of governorate significance of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It lies within the ISEZ's southern salient on the Naryn, which takes in the river flats around the city and Tash-Kömür and the farm belt of the northern Fergana rim, and is surrounded by the Lower Naryn District. The official 2018 estimate put its population at 310,000.[1] The modern city grew around the [[Church of St. Janyl]], built in 1727 with the support of Khan Abd al-Rahim Biy of the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]], and Iradi historiography regards it as the first culturally Iradi city. It is the see of the [[Archbishopric of Iyık Janyl]], which became the metropolitan see of the Syro-Iradi Catholic Church on the church's union with Rome in 1931.[2] The church and the nearby [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl]] (Shar-i-Kuhna), the remains of a medieval East Syriac Christian town, were inscribed together on the [[wp:World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage List]] in 2004, during the territorial period, on a nomination submitted by the United States.[3] Each year on 24 August the city hosts the [[Feast of St. Janyl]], which draws pilgrims, many of them on horseback, from both the ISEZ and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. It is also home to the [[Irad Palace of Art]], the country's principal art gallery. ## Etymology The name pairs the Kipchak-Turkic adjective *iyık* ('sacred, holy'), cognate with [[wp:Old Turkic language|Old Turkic]] *ïduq* ('consecrated, sacred'), with the name of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]], the figure revered in Iradi Christian tradition as the Mother of Irad.[2] In [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] liturgical texts of the Syro-Iradi Church the city is styled *Mthā d-Qaddishtā Janyl* ('the town of holy Janyl'). ## History #### The Janyl tradition Iradi Christian tradition holds that Janyl received a vision of Jesus in the form of the White Rider, who led her to the site of the first Iradi church, known as the First Church of Janyl. Church tradition places her in the 11th century, among Christianized Turkic clans associated with the [[wp:Keraites]] and [[wp:Naimans]], whose conversion by East Syriac missionaries is attested in medieval sources; some chronicles associate her with the period of [[wp:Qara Khitai]] rule in the 12th century.[4] Modern historians widely dispute that she existed, and the location of the First Church is unknown. The Church of St. Janyl in Iyık Janyl was built in the 18th century as a symbolic re-creation of the lost church, not as a claim to its site.[2] Popular devotion in the city nonetheless links several springs and hilltops in the valley with episodes from [[The Epic of Janyl]]. #### Medieval town (11th–14th centuries) The Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl, on a river terrace on the west bank of the Naryn about 2 km southwest of the present city center, preserve the foundations of a fortified Christian town of about 45 hectares that flourished from the 11th to the 14th century under the Kara-Khanid and Qara Khitai states.[5] Excavations have uncovered a citadel, a three-aisled stone basilica measuring 38 by 24 m, and a craft quarter with kilns and foundries. Grave markers (*kayraks*) inscribed in Syriac and Old Turkic, dated between 1240 and 1338, record a community of Keraite, Naiman and Sogdian Christians. The 13th-century monk [[Marqos the Scribe]] is credited with copying the illuminated *Gospels of Iyık Janyl*.[6] The religious tolerance of the Qara Khitai period, which allowed [[wp:Church of the East|East Syriac Christianity]] to spread among the steppe peoples, ended under the later Chagatai khans.[7] After forced conversions under Ali-Sultan (1339–1342), the campaigns of [[wp:Timur]] in the late 14th century and outbreaks of plague, the town was abandoned. According to church tradition, Christian herders in the surrounding ravines kept their liturgy alive in secret, preserving chants (*[[Irda (Vocal Tradition)|ırda]]*) and the baking of sacramental bread.[2] #### Kokand period and the 1727 church In the early 18th century, Iradi Christian horsemen served as cavalry auxiliaries of the Khanate of Kokand against Dzungar raids. In 1727 Khan Abd al-Rahim Biy granted the Iradi Christian elders formal religious tolerance in the accord remembered as the [[Treaty of Talas (1727)]], and issued a decree (*firman*) funding a permanent stone church.[8] Masons from [[wp:Samarkand]] and [[wp:Bukhara]] worked with local East Syriac monks to build the Church of St. Janyl on Cathedral Hill, combining a Syriac basilica plan with Central Asian brick vaulting and a ribbed dome clad in turquoise tiles.[6] A settlement of clergy, craftsmen and herders grew around it and became the modern city. The cathedral library was founded in 1732, and Bishop Mar Gewargis (died 1744) was buried in the church crypt. In the 19th century the British missionary [[wp:Joseph Wolff]] described the church to Western readers as evidence of Christian survival in [[wp:Central Asia]]. #### Russian rule and the union with Rome (1876–1931) Russian forces under [[wp:Mikhail Skobelev|General Mikhail Skobelev]] conquered the Khanate of Kokand in 1876, and Iyık Janyl was incorporated into the Fergana Oblast of [[wp:Russian Turkestan]]. The tsarist administration left the church's internal affairs largely to its own clergy.[8] After the Russian Revolution, Bishop [[Mar Timotheos Alimbekov]] opened secret negotiations with the [[wp:Holy See]], conducted through intermediaries at papal nunciatures abroad. On 14 September 1931 [[wp:Pope Pius XI]] promulgated the bull *Orientalis Stella*, which received the Syro-Iradi Church into full communion with Rome as an Eastern Catholic church *sui iuris* and established Iyık Janyl as its metropolitan see.[9] Soviet authorities regarded the Catholic connection with suspicion, and it became one of the grounds for the anti-religious repression of the 1930s.[10] #### Soviet period (1931–1991) During [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges]], security officers arrested and executed many of the senior clergy, closed the seminary and shut the cathedral, whose nave was converted into a district grain store.[10] Monks and lay sacristans hid the rarest manuscripts of the cathedral library in caves in the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]], and families kept vestments, icons and sacred vessels in their homes and in mountain shelters. For the rest of the Soviet period Iyık Janyl was a district town with a fruit cannery, a felt workshop and a reputation for clandestine worship. [[Amanbek Alimbekov]], who led the Provisional Government in 1992, was born in the city in 1938.[11] #### Since 1992 After the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] the cathedral was returned to the church and reconsecrated on 14 September 1992, the anniversary of *Orientalis Stella*.[9] During the US territorial administration the building was restored, the seminary reopened in 1994, and the library's manuscripts were conserved and digitized with support from the Vatican Library and European foundations. The church and the ruins of the medieval town were inscribed as a World Heritage Site on a nomination submitted by the United States, which as the administering power was the State Party for Irad. Irad itself is not a State Party to the World Heritage Convention.[3] Alimbekov was buried in the city's historic cemetery in 2004. Since the partition of 2007 the city has lain within the ISEZ's southern salient on the Naryn, linked to Talas only by the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]], which since 2009 has run down a narrow ISEZ corridor in the Naryn gorge, and close to the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] on three sides. Under Archbishop [[Mar Ephrem]], primate since 2012, the archbishopric has kept a position of neutrality between the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] administration and the clan councils of the tribal regions, and the city has hosted inter-confessional meetings and talks between the two sides.[12] ## Geography Iyık Janyl lies at about 650 m on the river flats of the Naryn, where the river leaves the gorge it cuts through the foothills of the Fergana Range, about 8 km upriver from Tash-Kömür, the district center, which lies just downstream. About two-thirds of the city, including the old bazaar centre, the Lower Town and most of the housing, lies on the broad flats west of the river, with Soviet-era housing blocks, the bazaar and orchards and walnut groves toward the hills, and most of the population lives there. The east bank holds the quarters below and around Cathedral Hill and, upriver, the summer quarter of [[Shahr-i Khunuk]], which stands on a bluff on the northeast side along [[Khunuk Creek]]. Four road bridges cross the Naryn in the city. The old town and the cathedral precinct occupy Cathedral Hill, a spur about 150 m above the east bank (about 800 m), reached by the winding Cathedral Hill road of about 4 km, which climbs to the precinct from State Route 1 on the east bank. In the middle of the city the Kara-Khanid citadel of [[Diz-i Safid]] crowns a limestone knoll rising about 140 m from the western flats, kept as a park, and overlooks the Lower Town and the Naryn. The ruins of the medieval town lie on a river terrace on the west bank about 2 km southwest of the city center, an open archaeological zone surrounded by the city's southern districts, and the motherhouse of the [[Order of St. Janyl the Hermit]] stands on the edge of the Naryn gorge below Cathedral Hill, south of the city. The ridges above the city rise to more than 2,000 m. The Qara-Chik line runs close to the city along the lower slopes on either side of the flats, some 150 to 200 m above the river; the hills beyond it to the north, east and west belong to the Toktogul–Naryn highlands of the tribal regions, and the [[Mailuu-Suu]] valley of the Fergana Rim lies to the southeast. The built-up area, about 85 km² (33 sq mi), covers the river flats and the low terraces above them on both banks, from Shahr-i Khunuk in the northeast to just above Tash-Kömür in the south. The area is seismically active, and earthquakes and freeze–thaw cycles are the main threats to the city's historic brickwork.[6] Above the flats, on the lower slopes below the demarcation line, lie the unplanned hillside quarters known as [[Jogorku (Iyık Janyl)|Jogorku]], the poorest part of the city and the center of its organized crime. #### Climate The city has a continental climate with dry summers ([[wp:Köppen climate classification|Köppen]] *Dsa*), typical of the edge of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]]: much warmer than Talas, with hot summers and short winters, and somewhat wetter than the valley floor downstream. July highs average about 34 °C (93 °F), and January lows average about −5 °C (23 °F). Annual precipitation is about 450 mm (18 in), most of it falling as spring rain; winter snow seldom lies for long in the city but closes the high pastures above it from December to March.[13] ## Demographics The official 2018 estimate gave the city a population of 310,000.[1] [[Iradis]] form a larger share of the population than in Talas or [[Nurzhan]], about 88% in official figures, and the main minorities are Kyrgyz, [[wp:Uzbeks]] and Russians. Iradi is the main language of daily life. Russian is less common than in the other two cities, and English is widely spoken by younger residents and in the tourism trade. Most residents identify with the Syro-Iradi Catholic Church, and surveys suggest that church attendance is higher than the national average. The city also has a small Russian Orthodox parish and a mosque. Its population rises sharply each August during the Feast of St. Janyl. ## Economy The city's economy rests on religious institutions, pilgrimage and crafts. - **Pilgrimage and tourism.** Pilgrims and visitors fill church hostels, including the [[Iyık Janyl Pilgrimage Hostel]], and private guesthouses, especially in August. The archbishopric, the seminary, the monasteries and the Palace of Art are among the largest employers.[14] - **Crafts.** Workshops produce silver-inlaid saddles and horse tack ([[Eerchilik (Saddlery)|eerchilik]]), felt carpets ([[Shyrdak (Iradi Craft)|shyrdak]]), embossed leather and church plate such as incense vessels. - **Agriculture and trade.** Orchards in the valley grow apples and apricots, and walnuts are gathered in the surrounding forests. The city's livestock and wool markets are among the few places where herders from the tribal regions trade directly with ISEZ buyers.[14] - **Shops and markets.** The Iyık Janyl bazarı in the Lower Town has fruit, butcher, dairy and craft stalls. Below Cathedral Hill are about twelve guesthouses and shops selling icons and candles (*shamdal jana ikona*), souvenirs, felt, saddles (from the *eerchi*, saddler) and leather. Shop names are almost never Russian and often take saints' names (Ephrem, Janyl, Toma, Mattai). [[Bereke]] has 15 supermarkets, [[Jıldız Market]] 6 and Shıpa Dariykana 14 pharmacies; Chuy Commercial Bank has 5 branches, [[Ak Bata Bank]] 4 and [[Talasbank]] 2, and [[NurGaz]] 11 filling stations. Iradi and Uzbek food (*özbek paloo*) predominates, there are few bars, few businesses take [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]] payments and the city has no KFC. ## Government Iyık Janyl is one of the three cities of governorate significance of the ISEZ, alongside Talas and Nurzhan. It is run by a mayor appointed by the Governor and an elected city council, and the archbishopric has considerable informal influence in local affairs. Under an informal understanding reached during the 2007 ceasefire talks, armed units of the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] and the [[El-Choro Militias]] do not enter the cathedral precinct on Cathedral Hill, and pilgrims from the tribal regions may cross the Qara-Chik line unarmed for the Feast of St. Janyl. The arrangement is not part of the text of the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]], but the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) monitors the crossings each year.[12] The archbishop also convenes regular meetings with Sunni Muslim and Russian Orthodox leaders on charitable and civic matters. ## Transport The city lies on the Fergana Mountain Transit Highway (State Route 1), which runs through the city on the east bank about 347 km from Talas by way of the Otmek Tunnel and the [[Fergana Gateway]], and about 9 km by road before its end at Tash-Kömür. Four road bridges link it with the western flats. The Cathedral Hill road, about 4 km long, leaves the highway and winds up to the old town. Buses and minibuses run between Talas and the city, taking about seven hours, and the passes are occasionally closed by snow and avalanches in winter. There is no railway. During the Feast, thousands of pilgrims arrive on horseback, and UNMI and the archbishopric organize the crossing points for riders from the tribal regions.[12] ## Education - The [[Cathedral Seminary of Iyık Janyl]] (Saint Ephrem Major Seminary), closed in 1937 and reopened in 1994, trains clergy for the Syro-Iradi Church in Syriac liturgy, theology and canon law. - The [[Cathedral Seminary Library of Iyık Janyl]], founded in 1732, holds more than 600 manuscripts, among them the illuminated Talas Gospel Lectionary of about 1185, letters of Mar Gewargis and Sogdian commercial contracts. Its digitization laboratory publishes facsimiles online.[6] - The [[Iyık Janyl Diocesan Archives Vault]] holds parish registers from the 18th century onward and the correspondence of the archbishopric with the Holy See. - The [[Iyık Janyl Seminary Choir]], attached to the seminary, performs East Syriac polyphony and Iradi sacred music. ## Culture and landmarks - **[[Church of St. Janyl]]**: the 1727 cathedral on Cathedral Hill, with a 22-meter ribbed dome clad in turquoise tiles, muqarnas vaulting, a carved walnut screen before the sanctuary and an icon of St. Janyl with the White Steed. Bishop Mar Gewargis is buried in its crypt. - **[[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl]]** (Shar-i-Kuhna): the excavated medieval town on the west bank about 2 km southwest of the city center, an open archaeological zone within the southern districts. - **[[Diz-i Safid]]**: the Kara-Khanid citadel on a limestone knoll in the middle of the city, kept as a park. - **[[Iyık Janyl Monastic Cloister]]**: a walled cloister of contemplative monks beside the cathedral. The motherhouse of the [[Order of St. Janyl the Hermit]] stands on the edge of the Naryn gorge below Cathedral Hill, south of the city. - **[[Irad Palace of Art]]**: the country's leading gallery and art preservation foundation, with collections ranging from Sogdian artifacts and [[wp:Silk Road]] ceramics to contemporary Iradi painting. - The historic cemetery, where Alimbekov and many clergy are buried. The Feast of St. Janyl on 24 August is the city's main event. Mounted priests bless horses and sheep assembled on the cathedral esplanade with glacial spring water. The liturgy uses *kümöch*, a round unleavened bread stamped with a cross and the [[The Star of Irad (Symbol)|Star of Irad]], and incense of mountain juniper (*[[Mountain Juniper (Arsha)|arsha]]*), followed by candlelit processions, horse races and communal meals of beef and mutton.[15] The archbishopric's attendance estimates in recent years have exceeded 150,000; no independent counts are available. The city's liturgical customs are described in [[East Syriac Rites of Iyık Janyl]], [[Kümöch Sacramental Bread]] and [[Arsha Juniper Incense Tradition]]. ## Notable people - [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] (1938–2004), Provisional President of the Republic of Irad in 1992, born and buried in the city[11] - [[Mar Timotheos Alimbekov]], bishop who negotiated the 1931 union with Rome[10] - Mar Gewargis (died 1744), bishop buried in the crypt of the Church of St. Janyl[8] - [[Marqos the Scribe]], 13th-century monk credited with the *Gospels of Iyık Janyl*[6] - [[Mar Ephrem|Archbishop Mar Ephrem]], Archbishop of Iyık Janyl since 2012[9] ## See also - [[Church of St. Janyl]] - [[Archbishopric of Iyık Janyl]] - [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl]] - [[Feast of St. Janyl]] ## References
