{{Infobox organization | name = Iradi Freedom Society | native_name = *Iradin Azatlık Cemiyeti* (IAC) | formation = 2007 | type = Confederation of clans | purpose = Self-government of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] under customary law (*adat*) | hq = [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]], below the [[Aksay Plateau]] | leader_title = Informal leader | leader_name = [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]] }} The **Iradi Freedom Society** (Iradi: *Iradin Azatlık Cemiyeti*, IAC) is the loose confederation of semi-nomadic clans that governs the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) of Irad, about six-sevenths of the country's territory. It brings together the twenty-four clans (*uruk*) of the tribal regions, which govern themselves through councils of elders (*aksakals*) under customary law (*adat*). The society grew out of the [[Popular Front of Irad]], the clan coalition that stormed [[Talas]] in June 2007 during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], and was constituted after the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]].[1] The IAC's unofficial leader is [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], chief of the Tanıp clan, who declines formal titles and describes himself as an ambassador or negotiator for the clans. The society does not recognize the authority of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) over the tribal regions. It has nonetheless observed the ceasefire with the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) since 2007, trades with it, and shares in setting the release schedule of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] under UN supervision.[2] ## History #### Background Iradi clans developed more cohesive forms of intertribal governance after the defeat of the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|1916 Semirechye Revolt]], and an Iradi translation of the *Catechism of a Revolutionary* spread anarcho-communist ideas among them in the years before the [[wp:Russian Civil War]].[3] Soviet collectivization in the 1930s confiscated clan herds and pushed many pastoral families from the plains into the eastern mountains. When the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] tried to reverse traditional tribal autonomy in 1991, clan horsemen joined the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], and during the [[First Iradi Civil War]] mounted scouts organized by Bektur defended the mountain valleys against socialist requisition columns.[3] Through the territorial period the clans kept their distance from the US administration and opposed leases of tribal grazing land to mining companies. #### Formation (2007) In January and February 2007 the cabinet of the short-lived [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] tried to privatize communal pastures in the Chatkal valley, alongside its sales of oil and mineral assets. Clan leaders treated the pasture decrees as a threat to customary tenure. On 25 February [[Erlan Toktarov]] made public the cabinet's secret drafts to partition Irad among its three neighbors (see [[Bill of Sale (2007)]]), under which the clans' pastures would have been transferred without any vote. In March 2007, clan militias under Bektur formed the Popular Front of Irad, which demanded the trial of Prime Minister [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] for treason, stormed Talas on 4 June and brought down his government; he surrendered to US forces at Talas Air Base.[4] Scholars trace to the affair a lasting distrust of any government based in the cities, which shapes the IAC's insistence on clan control of land and water. During the summer, as DPI security forces took control of the cities, the Front withdrew to the countryside. Its representatives negotiated the Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement in September, which set the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] between the two zones. In late 2007 a kurultai of clan elders on the [[Aksay Plateau]] reorganized the Front's political council as the Iradi Freedom Society. The Front's fighting units became the [[El-Choro Militias]], and its urban committees were disbanded.[1] The [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI), established in October 2007, has dealt with the IAC as the representative of the tribal regions since its creation. #### Since 2007 The IAC took part in UN-sponsored discussions on the [[2008 Unification Referendum Initiative]], which collapsed after the DPI refused to give tribal councils a veto over foreign mining concessions in mountain watersheds. At the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]], the only direct negotiation between the two sides, the IAC delegation walked out after being offered one-third of the seats in a reunified legislature.[5] Polling in 2017 suggested support for a unified Irad in the tribal regions as well as the ISEZ, although data from the ATR were limited and tribal leaders alleged DPI interference in the polling. Public statements by clan leaders have shown broad ambivalence about Iradi statehood. In 2018 tribal patrols exchanged fire with Uzbek border guards over grazing trails and boreholes on the western desert frontier, in the [[2018 Border Demarcation Clashes]], before bilateral border commissions negotiated buffer arrangements.[6] During [[The 2021 Regional Security Alert]], after the [[wp:Taliban]] returned to power in [[wp:Afghanistan]], El-Choro riders and ISEZ forces reinforced mountain pass checkpoints and set up joint intelligence coordination. The IAC has also disputed the [[2018 Irad census|2018 census]], arguing that it greatly undercounted the tribal regions. In 2025, remarks by [[wp:Donald Trump]] about selling Irad to Russia provoked protests and anti-American feeling in the tribal regions as well as in the ISEZ. ## Organization The IAC is not a political party and has no written constitution. Its institutions are: - **[[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|The Kurultai]]**, the supreme assembly of clan elders, pasture captains and militia commanders. It meets each summer on the Aksay Plateau, the main summer pasture (*[[Zhayloo (Pastoral Term)|zhayloo]]*) of the tribal regions. Decisions on grazing rights, common defense and relations with the ISEZ require the consent of all the leading lineages.[7] - **Clan councils**. Each of the twenty-four clans is governed by its own council of *aksakals*, and village councils (*ayyl kengeshi*) handle day-to-day local administration. - **Customary courts**. Disputes are heard by recognized judges (*biys*) in open assemblies (*Aksakal Sod*) under [[Adat Law in the ATR|adat]], which favors restitution over imprisonment. The main remedy is *kun*, a compensatory payment in livestock. Inter-clan pasture disputes go to the [[Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal]].[8] - **The Chancellery**. The [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]] is the standing secretariat. It keeps pasture and migration records, handles correspondence with UNMI and aid agencies, and archives customary court decisions, largely in handwritten ledgers. - **The El-Choro Militias**, about 15,000 part-time mounted irregulars organized in clan detachments, who man pickets along the Qara-Chik line and patrol the mountain borders. Bektur holds no office in these bodies. He describes his role as that of an ambassador and negotiator (*elchi*) for the clan councils, and acts as the IAC's main interlocutor with UNMI. UNMI and humanitarian agencies divide the tribal regions into seven planning zones (Northern Steppe, [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]], [[Talas Alatau]], Chatkal Highlands, Kyrgyz Range–[[Suusamyr]], Toktogul–Naryn and Fergana Rim). These zones are used for aid planning and have no standing in IAC governance.[2] ## Policies - **Land and pasture.** The IAC regulates the seasonal rotation of mountain pastures between summer (*zhayloo*) and winter (*kyshtoo*) grazing, and says it protects smaller clans' access to them. - **Environment.** The clans maintain a ban on open-pit gold mining, cyanide heap leaching and the exploration of radioactive minerals in mountain watersheds. Mining companies have been allowed to carry out surveys, but none has received permission to build a mine, and Irad's gold, uranium and thorium deposits remain undeveloped.[9] - **Language and religion.** Iradi is the only language of IAC business, and the tribal regions reject both Russian and English. Religious life follows a tribal folk Christianity in which itinerant [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church|Syro-Iradi]] priests bless herds and sometimes sit with elders at hearings. The clans strictly enforce the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo|taboo on eating horsemeat]]. - **Unification.** The IAC says it supports a unified Irad, but only with representation that reflects the population of the tribal regions and with tribal control over land and water. ## Economy and resources The tribal economy rests on semi-nomadic herding of sheep, cattle and horses, together with walnuts and wild fruit gathered in the Chatkal forests. Under the ceasefire arrangements, herders with tribal travel permits cross the Qara-Chik line to sell wool, hides and livestock to feedlots and packing plants in Talas and [[Nurzhan]], in exchange for fuel, grain and medical goods. Payments are cleared through [[Talasbank]].[2] Chancellery officials also negotiate seasonal bulk contracts with DPI ministries. The dam, reservoir and generating hall of the Toktogul complex lay on the tribal side of the line until 2009, when a UN-brokered protocol, approved by that year's kurultai, transferred them and the State Route 1 corridor to the ISEZ. In return the clans received the high Kyrgyz Range pastures east of the Kök-Bel road, guaranteed grazing, stock-route and water rights around the basin, and a fixed share of the export revenue. Under the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]], an annex to the ceasefire, a joint technical commission of ISEZ and ATR engineers sets the annual release schedule under UN supervision, with observers from [[wp:Uzbekistan]], [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]]. Revenue is shared under a formula that has never been published. Both the IAC and the DPI deny profiting at the other's expense, and independent analysts dispute how the money is actually divided.[10] Sections of the ancient [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]] of underground channels are used by IAC-aligned groups to move goods past ISEZ checkpoints, a practice the DPI administration describes as smuggling. ## External relations No state recognizes the IAC, and Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan all claim Irad *de jure*. In practice the society deals with neighboring states on border and water questions, mainly through UNMI and through the Toktogul commission.[10] UNMI coordinates the delivery of medical supplies and veterinary vaccines into the highland valleys through IAC channels, and its liaison officers meet IAC representatives alongside officers of the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]]. The [[Archbishopric of Iyık Janyl]] maintains neutrality between the IAC and the DPI and has hosted meetings between the two sides.[3] ## Criticism - **Armed formations.** The ISEZ government and the [[Armed Forces of Irad]] regard the El-Choro Militias as an illegal armed formation, though both sides observe non-aggression arrangements supervised by UNMI. - **Rights and accountability.** Human rights organizations have criticized the patriarchal rules of inheritance under *adat*, the lack of written law and of appeal from elder courts, and the absence of elections to IAC bodies.[8] - **Smuggling.** ISEZ officials accuse IAC-aligned groups of running contraband through the Kariz tunnels and over mountain passes. The IAC describes this traffic as the movement of supplies within its own territory. - **Population claims.** The IAC says the tribal regions are home to more than 3.5 million people, far more than the DPI census suggests. Independent estimates of Irad's total population (about 6.2 million) support a substantial undercount of the ATR, drawing on satellite settlement mapping and aid-agency registries, but no full count of the tribal regions has been made.[11] ## References

{{Infobox military installation | name = Talas Air Base | native_name = *Talas Aba Bazasy* | type = Military airfield | location = 12 km west of [[Talas]], Talas District | coordinates = 42.53°N 72.09°E | operator = United States forces; Air Wing of the [[Armed Forces of Irad|State Defense Corps]] | controlled_by = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (host); Outer perimeter by the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad|Republican Gendarmerie]] | built = 1952 | in_use = 1952–present | occupants = Iradiya; [[Talas Airport Logistics Hub]] | elevation_m = 1235 | runways = 3,400 m (11,155 ft), concrete }} **Talas Air Base** is a military airfield 12 km (7.5 mi) west of [[Talas]], on the southern terrace of the [[Talas River]]. Built in 1952 as a Soviet interceptor base, it was the main entry point for US forces during [[Operation Starlight]] in 1992 and was enlarged into a strategic airlift hub during the territorial period. It is the largest US military installation in the region and was a primary staging area for [[wp:Operation Enduring Freedom]] in [[wp:Afghanistan]] from late 2001.[1] US forces have remained at the base since the United States withdrew from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] in December 2006. Their presence rests on the [[2001 Basing Rights Agreement]] and on later arrangements with the administration of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). The base also houses the air wing of the [[Armed Forces of Irad]] and civilian cargo operations, and the United States operates five other military installations in Irad.[2] ## History #### Soviet period (1952–1991) The airfield was established in 1952 by a Soviet air defense directive (the [[Founding of Talas Air Base (1952)]]) as a dispersal base for interceptors of the [[wp:Turkestan Military District]]. It had a 2,500-meter concrete runway and underground fuel bunkers, and its [[wp:Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-17|MiG-17]] and later [[wp:Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-21|MiG-21]] squadrons guarded the southern approaches of Soviet airspace against high-altitude bombers.[1] #### Operation Starlight (1992) During the [[First Iradi Civil War]], the airfield lay within the area held by the Provisional Government during the siege of Talas, which began on 10 April 1992. After the signing of the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty on 2 June 1992, [[wp:United States Marine Corps|US Marines]] and troops of the 10th Mountain Division landed there to reinforce the city's defenders. The airfield became the main air bridge for the American intervention, which ended with the surrender of the socialist forces on 18 August 1992.[3] #### Territorial period (1992–2006) Between 1993 and 1998 US military engineers lengthened the main runway to 3,400 m (11,155 ft), rebuilt the taxiways in high-load concrete and added hardened aircraft shelters able to service [[wp:Boeing C-17 Globemaster III|C-17 Globemaster III]] transports and [[wp:Boeing KC-135 Stratotanker|KC-135 Stratotanker]] tankers.[4] A 1994 defense telecommunications contract to link the base with regional command centers by fiber-optic cable and satellite became the origin of [[Attelkom]], now the largest telecommunications company in the ISEZ. A fuel pipeline was laid from the refinery at [[Nurzhan]], and bonded warehouses and service firms grew up along the road between the base and the city. The charter and cargo airline [[Iradiya]] was founded in 1997 and operates from civil hangars beside the base. After the September 2001 attacks on the United States, the 2001 Basing Rights Agreement between the United States and the territorial government gave US forces expanded rights for logistics, aerial refueling and medical transit. Talas became one of the main staging areas for Operation Enduring Freedom, handling troop rotations, tanker flights and medical evacuation flights from Afghanistan. The agreement generated service contracts worth hundreds of millions of dollars for local firms.[5] #### Since 2006 President [[wp:George W. Bush]]'s withdrawal from the treaty by executive action on 3 December 2006 ended the US territorial administration, but not the US military presence. Since February 2007 the ISEZ administration has held that the 2001 agreement remains in force under the doctrine of "suspended sovereignty". Supplementary arrangements concluded with the ISEZ from 2007 onward cover land use, fuel supply, security and payments; they have not been published in full.[2] During the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], the United States backed the security forces of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) that took control of Talas in the summer of 2007, although the base's part in that support has not been documented publicly. Since 2007 the base has been a joint-use facility. The northern ramp houses the air wing of the ISEZ armed forces, officially the State Defense Corps, which flies Mi-8 and Mi-17 transport helicopters and [[wp:Mil Mi-24|Mi-24]] attack helicopters. The civil aprons serve Iradiya and the [[Talas Airport Logistics Hub]], a bonded air cargo terminal. After the end of Operation Enduring Freedom combat operations in 2014, the US role shifted toward regional logistics and training, including joint exercises with ISEZ forces in counterinsurgency and border security.[1] In 2020 ISEZ gendarmerie and US personnel installed tracking radars, electronic jamming equipment and new perimeter fencing in response to incursions by surveillance drones, an operation known as [[Operation Clear Skies (2020)]].[6] During [[The 2021 Regional Security Alert]], which followed the [[wp:Taliban|Taliban's]] return to power in Afghanistan, security around the base was reinforced. In 2025, remarks by [[wp:Donald Trump]] about selling Irad to Russia provoked protests and anti-American feeling across Irad. ## Facilities - A main runway of 3,400 m, with high-load taxiways and hardened shelters for heavy transport and tanker aircraft. - A fuel farm supplied by pipeline from the Nurzhan refinery. - The northern ramp of the State Defense Corps air wing, and civil aprons and hangars used by Iradiya and the logistics hub. - Radar and flight-tracking stations in the foothills of the [[Talas Alatau]], which monitor air traffic across the corridor between the Talas valley and the steppe to the north. - Fiber-optic and satellite links built and maintained by Attelkom.[7] The base's control tower coordinates civil transit flights with regional civil aviation authorities. Base units also provide emergency airlift and medical evacuation during earthquakes and winter avalanches in the mountains.[1] ## Security US forces are responsible for security within their own areas of the base. The outer perimeter and the approach roads are guarded by the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]], commanded by Major General [[Ruslan Toktarov]], whose Rapid Reaction Strike Group (*Barysh*) is stationed next to the base. Ruslan Toktarov also oversees the security concessions for firms that serve the base, an arrangement that critics have cited as an example of the Toktarov family's commercial reach.[8] ## Other US installations Besides Talas Air Base, the United States operates five other military installations in Irad: logistics depots, a testing facility and training areas.[2] The US government does not publish a full list of their locations or functions, and their staffing levels are not disclosed. ## Economic role The base is one of the largest employers in western Talas District. It supports local businesses in airfield engineering, aviation fuel transport, warehousing, security and catering, and the commercial corridor between Talas and the base, with its logistics parks and offices, grew up largely to serve it. Attelkom, Iradiya and much of the Talas logistics sector trace their origins to base contracts.[5] ## Legal status and controversy The legal basis of the US presence since 2006 is disputed. Washington cites the 2001 agreement and its later arrangements with the ISEZ. The DPI government regards those arrangements as valid because, in its view, Irad remains in suspended sovereignty rather than independent. Critics, including leaders of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]], argue that no government representing the whole country has consented to the presence of foreign forces.[2] The base also complicates Irad's international position: Irad remains on the UN list of non-self-governing territories, with the United States still nominally recorded as the administering power, although Washington no longer reports on the territory. ## See also - [[Robert Hayes]] - [[Lieutenant Gregory Vance]] - [[List of airports in Irad]] ## References

{{Infobox treaty | name = Alimbekov-Baker Treaty | long_name = Bilateral Treaty of Territorial Association and Mutual Security between the United States of America and the Republic of Irad | type = Treaty of territorial association and mutual security | signed = 1992-06-02 | location = Municipal theater, [[Talas]] | effective = 1992-06-02 (ratified by the Provisional Government) | expiration = 2006-12-03 (US withdrawal) | signatories = [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] (Provisional President); US Secretary of State | parties = United States; Republic of Irad }} The **Alimbekov-Baker Treaty** (officially the *Bilateral Treaty of Territorial Association and Mutual Security between the United States of America and the Republic of Irad*) is the 1992 agreement under which [[Irad]] became an organized, unincorporated territory of the United States. It was signed in [[Talas]] on 2 June 1992, during the [[First Iradi Civil War]], by Provisional President [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] and [[wp:James Baker|US Secretary of State James Baker]], and the Provisional Government ratified it unanimously the same day.[1][2] The treaty provided for US military intervention against the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]], which followed as [[Operation Starlight]], and for a territorial government with a legislature, courts and an elected Governor under the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]]. It also contained a statutory independence clause, under which sovereignty would pass to the people of Irad if US administration ended. On 3 December 2006 President [[wp:George W. Bush|George W. Bush]] withdrew the United States from the treaty by executive action. Days later the [[Supreme Court of Irad]] ruled that the withdrawal had triggered the independence clause, and the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] was proclaimed. In February 2007 [[Erlan Toktarov]] annulled that ruling and declared Irad to be in "suspended sovereignty", the status it has kept since. The institutions created under the treaty still form the framework of government in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ).[3] ## Background The Socialist Republic of Irad, proclaimed by the [[Communist Party of Irad]] on 9 October 1991 and governed from Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]), was overtaken within months by economic collapse and the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]]. On 11 March 1992 the Provisional Government in Talas proclaimed the Republic of Irad, beginning the First Iradi Civil War. Socialist forces, including the 17th Motor Rifle Division, advanced along the Chu and Talas corridors and besieged Talas from 10 April 1992; by late May the city's water supply had been cut and its defenders were short of ammunition.[4] Alimbekov, who remained inside the besieged city, opened contacts with the United States through its embassy in [[wp:Almaty]], [[wp:Kazakhstan]], and proposed that Irad enter into association with the United States in exchange for military protection and economic reconstruction.[5] Historians have attributed Washington's acceptance to several concerns: the security of former Soviet military and uranium sites, the energy reserves of the Chu basin, and the risk that the war would draw in neighboring states.[4] The speed of the agreement is a staple of the unproven theory that Alimbekov was a CIA plant (see [[Amanbek Alimbekov]]). ## Signing and ratification The treaty was signed on 2 June 1992 in the basement of the damaged municipal theater in Talas. The Provisional Government voted unanimously to ratify it the same day, and its members presented the decision as the only way to save the city.[2] On the US side, [[wp:United States Congress|Congress]] gave effect to the treaty's governance provisions by passing the Organic Act of the Territory of Irad, which organized the territory after the socialist surrender on 18 August 1992.[1] ## Provisions The treaty's main provisions were: - **Territorial association.** Irad would become an organized, unincorporated territory of the United States, subject to the authority of Congress under the Territory Clause (Article IV) of the [[wp:Constitution of the United States|US Constitution]]. - **Security.** The United States would defend the territory, restore order and disarm irregular formations, and could deploy forces through Talas. This provision was the basis of Operation Starlight. - **Government.** An organic act would establish a [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]], the Supreme Court of Irad and an elected Governor, and guarantee civil liberties, a secular state and freedom of religion, including the protection of church property. - **Economy.** The US dollar would be legal tender, alongside any local currency the territory chose to issue, and Iradi goods would receive customs access to the US market. - **Statutory independence clause.** If the United States ceased to administer the territory, sovereignty would revert to the people of Irad. The clause was carried into the Organic Act, which is why Iradi lawyers usually describe it as "statutory". - **Withdrawal.** Either party could withdraw unilaterally. The treaty did not say whether US withdrawal required the approval of Congress.[6] Under a related undertaking, the territorial government agreed not to develop Irad's uranium and thorium deposits. This was a response partly to the legacy of Soviet uranium processing at [[Mailuu-Suu]], and the deposits remain undeveloped.[3] ## Implementation (1992–2006) [[wp:United States Marine Corps|US Marines]] and troops of the 10th Mountain Division landed at what became [[Talas Air Base]] in June 1992. Joint US and Iradi forces took Kobozev on 12 August, and the remaining socialist forces surrendered on 18 August, when the [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)|Territory of Irad]] was formally organized.[4] An interim legislature first met in October 1992, the Supreme Court was established in November, and the first territorial elections were held in 1994. Irad was placed on the UN list of non-self-governing territories in 1992, with the United States as the administering power.[7] During the fourteen years of territorial administration, the treaty framework supported dollarization and the chartering of [[Talasbank]] in 1993, the founding of [[Attelkom]] from a 1994 defense contract, and agribusiness investment from 1994 under North American trade arrangements. The Iradi language returned to the Latin alphabet, with revisions in 1995 and 1997. The [[2001 Basing Rights Agreement]] later made Talas Air Base a main staging area for [[wp:Operation Enduring Freedom]]. Alimbekov served as senior adviser to the territorial government until his death in 2004. He resisted nationalist calls to repudiate the treaty, arguing that territorial status was the only practical protection against neighboring states.[5] ## Withdrawal and its aftermath (2006–2007) On 3 December 2006 President Bush withdrew the United States from the treaty by executive action (see [[United States Withdrawal from the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty (2006)]]), ending federal civilian administration and leaving security to local authorities. Within days, on a petition brought by the jurist [[Bakyt Orozbekov]], the Supreme Court of Irad under Chief Justice [[Dastan Isakov]] issued the [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]], holding that the withdrawal had triggered the independence clause and vested sovereignty in the people of Irad.[8] On 9 December the Territorial Legislature proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Irad, with Orozbekov as Prime Minister. Twenty-six UN member states recognized it. The United States did not formally notify the United Nations that its administration had ended. Irad therefore remained on the list of non-self-governing territories, with the United States still nominally recorded as the administering power, although Washington does not report on the territory.[7] The main trigger of the crisis that followed was the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]]. Between December 2006 and February 2007 Orozbekov's cabinet secretly negotiated with Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan, as "border consultations", a treaty that would have used Irad's new sovereignty to dissolve it and partition its territory among the three neighbors. On 25 February 2007, as protests against the privatization of state assets grew, Toktarov, a DPI insider who had broken with the party leadership, read the drafts out in a speech in Nurzhan. He took control of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]], proclaimed the ISEZ and annulled the independence ruling, returning Irad to "suspended sovereignty" pending a unification referendum, on the reasoning that without a sovereign no one could sell Irad. The *[[Irad Times]]* printed the drafts in a special edition the next day. The leak made Toktarov a national hero and permanently broke the trust of the clans in any city-based government. The proclamation began the [[Second Iradi Civil War]].[9][10] Under this doctrine the ISEZ treats the treaty's framework as suspended rather than terminated, and US forces have stayed at Talas Air Base under the 2001 Basing Rights Agreement and later arrangements with the ISEZ administration. ## Legal debate The treaty's end raised several questions that remain unresolved: - whether the President could terminate a treaty of territorial association without the approval of Congress; - whether the independence clause took effect automatically, as the Supreme Court held, or required further legislation; - whether Toktarov's emergency decree could validly annul a ruling of the territory's highest court. Scholars at [[Talas State University]] and abroad have argued all sides of these questions. The ISEZ's position is that sovereignty is suspended, the position of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] is that no lawful authority over the whole country has existed since 2007, and the three neighboring states maintain their own *de jure* claims.[6] ## Legacy The treaty created the institutions that still govern the ISEZ: the Territorial Legislature, the Supreme Court, the elected governorship, the use of the dollar and the official status of English. Its signing set off a brief period of American public enthusiasm for Irad, known as [[Iradimania]] (about 1992–1994). In Irad it is remembered both as the act that ended the siege of Talas and as a surrender of the independence proclaimed in March 1992, and Alimbekov is commemorated as one of the founders of the modern state. The treaty's dissolution gave rise to the [[Bush Family Palatial Complex Conspiracy Theory]], which alleged that the [[Boz-Korgon]] compound had been built for the Bush family in return for ending the treaty. Construction of the compound began in the 1990s, before the dissolution. In 2025 [[wp:Donald Trump]] said he was exploring selling Irad to Russia; it is not known whether he realized that Irad had ceased to be a US territory after the 2006 withdrawal.[3] ## References

{{Infobox military conflict | conflict = Second Iradi Civil War | date = 25 February – September 2007 | place = [[Irad]] | result = [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]]; Dissolution of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] after the [[Storming of Talas (2007)|Storming of Talas]]; ISEZ takes the cities; [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] established; frozen conflict | territory = Irad divided along the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] into the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | combatant1 = [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] | combatant2 = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] emergency administration; [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (Toktarov faction); *Supported by:*; [[wp:United States]]; Western companies | combatant3 = [[Popular Front of Irad]] | commander1 = [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] | commander2 = [[Erlan Toktarov]] | commander3 = [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]] | units1 = Territorial police; Remnants of the territorial defense forces | units2 = Municipal police; Gendarmerie units; State Defense Corps | units3 = Clan militias; Defected territorial defense detachments; Industrial strike committees | strength3 = 8,000+ mounted irregulars | casualties4 = Dead estimated in the low thousands (UNMI and humanitarian agencies); 80,000+ civilians displaced }} The **Second Iradi Civil War** was an armed conflict in [[Irad]] from February to September 2007. It began on 25 February 2007, when [[Erlan Toktarov]] proclaimed the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) from [[Nurzhan]] in defiance of the government of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] (DRI) in [[Talas]], and ended with the UN-brokered [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] in September. Three forces took part: the DRI government of Prime Minister [[Bakyt Orozbekov]]; Toktarov's emergency administration, backed by the faction of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) loyal to him; and the [[Popular Front of Irad]], a coalition of clan militias led by [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]].[1] Its main cause was the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]] (*Satuu Kagazy*), the secret drafts under which the Orozbekov cabinet had agreed to dissolve Irad and partition it among its three neighbors, which Toktarov made public on the day he proclaimed the ISEZ.[2] The Front stormed Talas on 4 June 2007 and dissolved the DRI. During the summer, however, DPI security forces backed by Western companies and the United States took control of Talas and the other cities as the Front withdrew to the countryside. The ceasefire fixed the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], which has divided Irad since 2007 into the ISEZ and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR).[3] ## Background #### End of the territorial period On 3 December 2006 President [[wp:George W. Bush]] withdrew the United States from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] by executive action, ending fourteen years of US territorial administration. Days later the [[Supreme Court of Irad]] issued the [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]], holding that the withdrawal had triggered the treaty's statutory independence clause. On 9 December 2006 the Territorial Legislature proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Irad, with Orozbekov, a corporate lawyer and former chief legal counsel to the Territorial Senate, as Prime Minister.[4] Twenty-six UN member states recognized the new state. It inherited a large budget deficit, since US federal transfers had stopped. #### Privatization crisis (January–February 2007) To close the gap, the Orozbekov cabinet sold state assets quickly in January and February 2007. It auctioned exploration concessions in the oil fields and the eastern antimony deposits, state grain elevators and mobile spectrum, and it tried to privatize communal pastures in the Chatkal valley.[5] Investigative reporting found that many of the assets had gone at low prices to companies linked to cabinet ministers and other DPI members, in what became known as the [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]]. Protests spread through Talas, and in mid-January police fired on herders demonstrating against fuel price rises in the Chu valley. Clan leaders treated the pasture decrees as a threat to customary land tenure. In Nurzhan, the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]] refused to recognize the auctions.[1] #### The Bill of Sale (December 2006 – February 2007) At the same time, and without public knowledge, delegations of the Orozbekov cabinet were negotiating with the foreign ministries of [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kazakhstan]] under cover of consultations on borders and water. The drafts that resulted would have used the sovereignty conferred by the independence ruling to dissolve Irad and divide it among the three states: the Talas valley and the lands adjoining Jalal-Abad to Kyrgyzstan, the Fergana rim to Uzbekistan, and the northern steppe, the Chu and the lands adjoining the Turkistan and Jambyl regions to Kazakhstan. Compensation was to be paid into escrow, and companies tied to Orozbekov and several ministers were to receive concession shares in the oil fields, the antimony deposits and the Toktogul complex. No plebiscite was planned. [[Iradis]] call the drafts the *Satuu Kagazy*, the "Bill of Sale", and historians generally regard them as the main cause of the war (see [[Bill of Sale (2007)]]).[2][6] ## Course of the war #### Proclamation of the ISEZ (25 February 2007) Toktarov, a former Majority Leader of the Territorial Senate who had warned against an immediate declaration of statehood, broke with Orozbekov. On 25 February 2007, in a speech in Nurzhan, he read out passages from the partition drafts and released copies of them, calling them "a bill of sale for our country". He then seized control of the DPI apparatus and proclaimed the Irad Special Economic Zone as an emergency administration. He annulled the Supreme Court's independence ruling and declared that Irad had returned to "suspended sovereignty" pending a unification referendum; ISEZ accounts explain that with no sovereign in place, no one could sell the country.[1][7] The leak made Toktarov a national hero. The DRI cabinet in Talas called the documents unapproved "contingency papers", rejected the proclamation and continued to govern as a rival authority.[8] Toktarov was backed by the Nurzhan oil executive Kamran Bekzatov, whose company [[NurGaz]] supplied money and fuel and whose refinery workers guarded the oil installations, and by the Labor-led Nurzhan city council; many historians consider this support decisive. Toktarov drew his forces from municipal police and gendarmerie units and from loyalist detachments that he organized into the State Defense Corps, and he secured backing from foreign energy and agribusiness companies. #### Formation of the Popular Front (March 2007) In March 2007 clan militias under Bektur, chief of the Tanıp clan, formed the Popular Front of Irad. Its demands were the restoration of communal pasture rights, an audit of the privatization contracts, the trial of Orozbekov for treason over the Bill of Sale, the protection of customary law (*adat*) and an end to what it called the plunder of national wealth by foreign companies and insiders.[9] Factory strike committees in Nurzhan and railway workers joined the Front, and its fighting strength reached more than 8,000 mounted irregulars, supported by detachments that defected from the territorial defense forces. #### Spring campaign (March–May 2007) The Front's mounted columns, riding mostly [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] mountain horses, encircled government garrisons in the countryside and cut the railway lines serving Talas and Nurzhan. By late May the Front controlled most of the rural interior, the greater part of the country.[3] Toktarov's forces concentrated on holding Nurzhan, the oil fields and the export pipeline, while the DRI government was increasingly confined to Talas, which the Front invested from 22 April. #### Storming of Talas (4 June 2007) On 4 June 2007 the Front stormed Talas in the [[Storming of Talas (2007)]]. Municipal police mutinied, ministers fled and Front fighters occupied the legislative palace. Orozbekov surrendered himself to United States forces at [[Talas Air Base]] and signed an instrument of resignation dissolving the DRI government; five days later he was extradited to the United States to face federal charges.[4] #### DPI takeover of the cities (summer 2007) The Front's aims centered on land and customary rights rather than control of the cities, and after the fall of the DRI it withdrew to the countryside. During the summer, DPI security forces under Toktarov, backed by Western companies and the United States, took control of Talas, [[Iyık Janyl]] and the other towns of the river valleys. They consolidated an area that ran along the Talas valley, the Chu lowlands and the southern industrial corridor, with a salient on the lower Naryn around [[Tash-Kömür]] and Iyık Janyl. In August the lowland Chubar elders of [[Bazar-Korgon]] and the farm belt of the northern Fergana rim, whose trading families saw the ISEZ as the side that had stopped the Bill of Sale from handing them to Uzbekistan, declared for the ISEZ, and Gendarmerie units moved east from Tash-Kömür along the foot of the hills; the highland Chubar of [[Arslanbob]] stayed with the Front.[1] Skirmishes continued along the emerging front line, especially around the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]], whose dam lay in Front-held territory and whose switchyard and export lines were held by the DPI. #### Ceasefire (September 2007) UN mediators brought the two sides to [[wp:Bishkek]], where the Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement was signed in September 2007. It set the Qara-Chik Demarcation Line between the ISEZ and the tribal regions, with a southern salient on the lower Naryn and the Fergana rim farm belt reached by a guarded road across tribal land; a 2009 protocol later brought that road, the Toktogul basin and a narrow corridor down the Naryn gorge into the ISEZ. Its annex, the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]], placed the Toktogul complex under a joint technical commission of engineers from both sides, supervised by the United Nations, with observers from Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan.[10] On 18 October 2007 the [[wp:United Nations Security Council|UN Security Council]] established the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) to monitor the ceasefire.[11] ## Forces - **Democratic Republic of Irad**: territorial police and the remnants of the territorial defense forces under the Orozbekov cabinet.[1] - **ISEZ emergency administration**: municipal police, gendarmerie units and the loyalist State Defense Corps under Toktarov, with backing from Western companies and the United States. - **Popular Front of Irad**: clan militias of mounted irregulars under Bektur Zhumabek uulu, with defecting military detachments and industrial strike committees.[3] ## Casualties and humanitarian impact No comprehensive casualty count has been published. UNMI and humanitarian agencies have estimated the dead in the low thousands. More than 80,000 civilians were displaced, many of them herding families caught on the wrong side of the new line.[12] The fighting damaged railway and road links in the lower Chu valley. The demarcation line separated families and cut seasonal migration routes, and herders now need tribal travel permits to cross it at designated corridors. Mines and unexploded ordnance left in the mountain passes have been cleared under UNMI coordination since 2008. ## Aftermath Toktarov remained Governor of the ISEZ, and the reorganized DPI, often called the "New DPI", has governed it since. In 2008 ISEZ prosecutors charged Orozbekov in absentia with high treason over the Bill of Sale and with abuse of office over the auctions; acquitted of the American charges in New York that November, he has lived in [[wp:Istanbul]] since 2009.[13] In late 2007 a [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|kurultai]] on the [[Aksay Plateau]] reorganized the Front's political council as the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC), which coordinates the tribal regions, and the Front's fighters became the [[El-Choro Militias]].[9] When Toktarov annulled the independence ruling, many Iradis saw the move as a first step toward a negotiated unification.{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}} Public opinion has since shifted as talks have stalled. A unification referendum was first proposed in 2008, and the only direct negotiations, at the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]], collapsed when the IAC walked out after being offered one-third of the seats in a reunified legislature.[14] The ceasefire has held since 2007, and Irad has remained a frozen conflict. ## Historiography Official ISEZ histories present the emergency administration as having saved the economy and prevented anarchy after the collapse of the DRI. In the tribal regions the Storming of Talas is remembered as a popular rising against corruption, and Bektur is regarded as its hero.[9] Historians continue to debate how far US and corporate support for the DPI decided the outcome. They also debate whether the conflict is better described as a single civil war or as two overlapping struggles: a contest for control of the DPI and the state between Toktarov and Orozbekov, and a rural rising against the privatization program. Iradi sources sometimes call it "the 2007 war" or "the succession war".[1] Since the release of the partition drafts, most historians have treated the Bill of Sale as the decisive cause of the war, with the privatization scandals as its background. They disagree about how long Toktarov knew of the negotiations before he made them public, and Orozbekov disputes the authenticity of some of the released pages. Official histories present the leak as the moment the emergency administration saved Irad from being sold. In the tribal regions the affair is remembered as a betrayal by the urban elite as a whole, and scholars date from it a lasting break of trust between the clans and any government based in the cities.[2][6] ## References

{{Infobox court | name = Supreme Court of Irad | native_name = *Irad Zhogorku Sotu* | established = 1992-11 | jurisdiction = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (in practice) | location = Hall of Justice, Liberty Boulevard, [[Talas]] | coordinates = 42.52°N 72.24°E | composition = Nominated by the Governor, confirmed by the legislature | authority = [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]] | positions = 5 }} The **Supreme Court of Irad** (Iradi: *Irad Zhogorku Sotu*) is the highest court of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). Established in November 1992 under the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]], it sits in the Hall of Justice on Liberty Boulevard in [[Talas]] and consists of a Chief Justice and four Associate Justices.[1] Its jurisprudence combines American common-law doctrine, introduced during the territorial period, with the continental and Soviet civil-law procedure that survives in much of Iradi private law. In December 2006 the court issued the [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)|Statutory Independence Ruling]], which held that the US withdrawal from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] had triggered Irad's statutory independence clause and so led to the proclamation of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]]. [[Erlan Toktarov]] annulled the ruling by decree in February 2007.[2] The court's jurisdiction is limited in practice to the ISEZ, since the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] settle disputes under customary law. Legal scholars and human rights groups have questioned its independence from the executive. ## History #### Territorial period (1992–2006) The Organic Act established the Supreme Court as the court of last resort for the territory, and the first justices took office in November 1992. Under the act, the Governor appointed justices with the consent of the Territorial Senate, and the court's final judgments could be reviewed by the United States federal courts.[1] Its early work dealt largely with property and contract disputes arising from the privatization of Soviet-era enterprises, the dollarization of the economy and the arrival of foreign investors. The court also developed rules for applying the Soviet-era civil code alongside new territorial statutes based on American models. The [[2003 Judicial Reforms Act]], drafted by [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] as chief legal counsel to the Territorial Senate, reorganized the lower courts into district courts such as the [[Talas District Court]]. It also introduced jury trials in serious criminal cases and established commercial arbitration procedures modeled on US federal practice. The act gave international investors enforceable contract arbitration and protection against arbitrary expropriation, and it confirmed the Supreme Court as the appellate court for the whole judicial system and the regulator of the legal profession.[3] #### Statutory Independence Ruling (2006) On 3 December 2006 President [[wp:George W. Bush]] withdrew the United States from the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty by executive action. Orozbekov, then in private practice, filed an emergency petition asking the court to rule on the territory's status. Within days, before the proclamation of the DRI on 9 December, the court under Chief Justice [[Dastan Isakov]] held that territorial status had lapsed upon federal disengagement. Under the statutory independence clause of the treaty, which had been carried into the Organic Act, sovereignty had therefore passed to the people of Irad.[2] Isakov's majority opinion set out what became known as the doctrine of automatic reversion. On the strength of the ruling, the Territorial Legislature proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Irad, and the court sat as the supreme court of the new state. #### Annulment and reconstitution (2007) On 25 February 2007 Toktarov proclaimed the ISEZ from Nurzhan as an emergency administration and annulled the independence ruling by decree, declaring that Irad had returned to "suspended sovereignty". The decree was justified by the secret drafts, released the same day, under which the DRI cabinet would have used the sovereignty recognized by the ruling to dissolve Irad and cede its territory to its neighbors (see [[Bill of Sale (2007)]]). The court never ruled on the validity of the decree. After DPI forces took control of Talas in the summer of 2007, the emergency administration reconstituted the bench, and Isakov left the court that year.[4] Since then the court has operated within the ISEZ's legal framework, which treats the territorial-era statutes and the Organic Act as continuing in force while sovereignty is suspended. ## Composition and appointment The court has five members: a Chief Justice and four Associate Justices. Since 2007 justices have been nominated by the Governor and confirmed by the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]]. Opposition lawyers and human rights groups say that loyalty to the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] has become an informal requirement for appointment.[5] The court sits in the Hall of Justice, a neoclassical building on Liberty Boulevard that also houses its law library. ## Jurisdiction and functions - **Appeals.** The court hears final appeals from the district courts and from the municipal magistrate courts of Talas, [[Nurzhan]] and [[Iyık Janyl]]. - **Constitutional review.** It reviews legislation and executive acts for conformity with the Organic Act and the territorial statutes that the ISEZ treats as its basic law.[1] - **Commercial disputes.** It is the final instance in commercial cases, including arbitration awards involving foreign investors. - **The legal profession.** It administers admission to the bar, through examinations that require proficiency in both Iradi and English commercial law, and oversees professional ethics. It also cooperates with the Faculty of Law of [[Talas State University]] in training judges and lawyers.[3] Proceedings are conducted in Iradi or English, with interpreters provided for Russian speakers. ## Notable decisions - ***Statutory Independence Ruling* (2006).** Held that the US withdrawal triggered the statutory independence clause. The ruling provided the legal basis for the Democratic Republic of Irad and was annulled by Toktarov's decree of 25 February 2007. - ***ISEZ Commercial Concessions Reference* (2008).** Confirmed the authority of the DPI administration to lease strategic mineral concessions to foreign joint ventures without first holding a legislative referendum. Critics said the decision removed a check on the executive.[5] - **Term-limits challenge (2014).** The court declined to hear a challenge to the [[2013 Constitutional Amendment|2013 amendment]] to the [[Elective Governor Acts (1992)|1992 Elective Governor Acts]] that removed gubernatorial term limits, holding that the question belonged to the legislature.[6] - ***Pastoral Transit Case* (2015).** Recognized the customary right of transhumant herders to drive livestock across industrial highway easements without paying municipal licensing penalties. The decision is one of the few in which the court has given effect to customary practice.[7] ## Relationship with customary law The authorities of the tribal regions do not recognize the court's jurisdiction. Civil and criminal disputes there are settled by councils of elders (*aksakals*) and customary judges under [[Adat Law in the ATR|adat]], which the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] recognizes as the law of the tribal regions.[4] There is no formal mechanism for enforcing the court's judgments across the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. Cross-line civil matters, such as livestock disputes, are usually handled through liaison meetings arranged by the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]].[5] ## Criticism [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] has described a system of "judicial dualism" in which the statutory courts of the ISEZ lack independence from the executive while customary courts in the tribal regions offer no appeal.[5] Writing in the *Eurasian Political Quarterly* in 2024, scholars noted increasing executive pressure on the court since the governor's office reportedly moved to [[Boz-Korgon]] in 2023 and during the uncertainty that followed Toktarov's withdrawal from public view in July 2024.[8] Business groups, including the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad, take a more favorable view. They point to the court's record in commercial and property disputes, where it has generally upheld procedural rules and contracts with foreign investors.[9] ## References

{{Infobox legislature | name = Territorial Legislature of Irad | native_name = *Mejlis* | house_type = Unicameral (bicameral 1992–2007) | leader1_type = Speaker | leader1 = Nurbek Sultanov (DPI), since 2019 | members = 60 | groups = [[Democratic Party of Irad|DPI]] (51); Independents (6); Russo-aligned (3) | voting_system = Eight multi-member constituencies | last_election = 2023-11-07 | next_election = 2027-11-02 | meeting_place = Legislative Hall, [[Talas]] }} The **Territorial Legislature of Irad** (Iradi: *[[Mejlis]]*) is the legislative body of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) in [[Irad]], and meets at Legislative Hall in [[Talas]]. It was established in 1992 under the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]] as the bicameral legislature of the US territory, with a Territorial Senate and a Territorial House of Representatives.[1] On 9 December 2006, after the US withdrawal from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]], it proclaimed the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]]. Since 2007 the legislature has sat as a single chamber under the ISEZ administration, which kept the territorial name in line with its doctrine of "suspended sovereignty". Its 60 members are elected in the ISEZ only, and the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) has held a large majority since 2007.[2] The [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], which cover six-sevenths of the country, are not represented. ## History #### Establishment (1992–1994) The Organic Act, which organized the territory after the surrender of the socialist forces on 18 August 1992, provided for an elected legislature and an elected Governor. Pending elections, an interim legislature drawn from the Provisional Government's councils and from district delegates first met in Legislative Hall in October 1992.[1] Over the following eighteen months it passed the Banking and Commercial Currency Act and the Toponymic Heritage Statute of 1993, which confirmed the renaming of Kobozev as [[Nurzhan]] and restored Turkic and Sogdian names to streets, districts and reservoirs.[3] The first general elections to both chambers were held in 1994. [[Zamirbek Bakiev]], a student leader of the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], was among the members of the first Territorial Senate, and [[Erlan Toktarov]] entered the House of Representatives the same year. #### Territorial period (1994–2006) The territorial legislature followed the American territorial model: - **The Territorial Senate** had 15 members serving four-year terms, three elected from each of five senatorial districts. - **The Territorial House of Representatives** had 35 members, elected every two years from single-member constituencies apportioned by population. Bills passed by both chambers needed the assent of the Governor and were subject to review by the [[wp:United States Congress|US Congress]]. The legislature's standing committees covered Ways and Means, Mineral and Energy Resources, Public Works and Inter-Ethnic Affairs, and worked with federal liaison officers and foreign commercial advisers.[4] The DPI held majorities in both chambers for most of the period. Toktarov was Majority Leader of the Senate from 2000 to 2004, and [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] served as the Senate's chief legal counsel from 1998 to 2005. The legislature passed more than 800 statutes in fourteen years. The most significant included: - the **Banking and Commercial Currency Act** (1993), which authorized the circulation of the US dollar alongside the [[Iradi som]] and chartered [[Talasbank]]; - the **Toponymic Heritage Statute** (1993), the main legal instrument of the [[De-Russification Movement in Irad|de-Russification]] of place names; - the **Hydrocarbon and Mining Code** (1995), which regulated extraction concessions, including those of [[NurGaz]], and set up royalty funds for road building; - the [[1995 Latin Orthography Revision]] and the **Language and Education Reform Act** (1997), which standardized the Latin alphabet for Iradi and made instruction in Iradi and English compulsory in public schools; - the [[2003 Judicial Reforms Act]], which introduced jury trials and commercial arbitration modeled on US federal practice.[1] The allocation of mining royalties was among the most contested issues of the period. Legislators eventually adopted compromise formulas that divided antimony revenue between infrastructure in Talas and rural schools in the interior. Committees on major economic bills held public hearings at which community delegates, academics from [[Talas State University]] and trade guilds could submit petitions.[4] #### Proclamation of the DRI (2006–2007) On 3 December 2006 President [[wp:George W. Bush]] withdrew the United States from the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty by executive action. After the [[Supreme Court of Irad]] issued the [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]], the legislature reconstituted itself as a national assembly. On 9 December 2006 it proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Irad and elected Orozbekov Prime Minister.[5] The assembly sat in Talas through the [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]] and the first months of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. When the [[Popular Front of Irad]] stormed the city on 4 June 2007, its fighters occupied Legislative Hall, and the DRI government was dissolved. #### Under the ISEZ (2007–present) Toktarov's emergency administration, proclaimed from Nurzhan on 25 February 2007, did not recognize the national assembly. After DPI forces took control of Talas in the summer of 2007, the administration reconstituted the legislature under its territorial name as a single chamber.[6] Members of the last territorial legislature who accepted the emergency administration sat as a provisional chamber until November 2011. Since then, regular elections have been held every four years on the same day as the gubernatorial election. At the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]], the DPI offered the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC) one-third of the seats in a reunified legislature. The IAC delegation walked out, and no comparable offer has been made since.[7] In 2013 the DPI majority passed an amendment to the [[Elective Governor Acts (1992)|1992 Elective Governor Acts]] that removed gubernatorial term limits (the [[2013 Constitutional Amendment]]). ## Structure and procedure The chamber has 60 members, elected for four-year terms in eight multi-member constituencies corresponding to the ISEZ's three cities of governorate significance (Talas, Nurzhan and [[Iyık Janyl]]) and its districts (Talas, [[Kara-Buura]], Chu, [[Sary-Bulak]], and Lower Naryn together with Toktogul). Seats are apportioned according to official population figures. A Speaker, elected from the majority, presides, and the standing committees of the territorial era have been retained. The Speaker since 2019 has been Nurbek Sultanov of the DPI.[2] The legislature passes the budget, confirms the justices of the Supreme Court and other senior appointments, and may amend the territorial statutes that the ISEZ treats as its basic law. Bills require the Governor's assent, and the Governor may veto them. Since 2007, however, much policy has been made by executive decree under the emergency powers the Governor assumed that year, which limits the chamber's role in practice. Debates are held in Iradi and English, with interpretation into Russian. ## Composition In the 2023 election the DPI won 51 of the 60 seats. Six of the remaining seats went to independents, most of whom vote with the party, and three to Russo-aligned deputies from Nurzhan, who form the only consistent opposition in the chamber.[8] ## Criticism - **Elections.** Observers from the [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe]] (OSCE) have described the elections as lacking meaningful choice. They cite the disqualification of opposition candidates, especially in the [[2015 Electoral Reform Controversy]], state control of voter registers and the DPI's dominance of broadcasting through [[IradOne]].[8] - **Representation.** The chamber represents only the ISEZ, which covers about one-seventh of the country. The IAC argues that the official census undercounts the tribal regions, and that the 2011 offer of one-third of the seats did not reflect their share of the population.[7] - **Executive dominance.** Analysts describe the chamber as largely subordinate to the governor's office, citing the 2013 removal of term limits and the extensive use of decrees.[2] The DPI says that the legislature preserves the legal order of the territorial period, and that it would be enlarged to include representatives of the tribal regions under a unification settlement. ## References

{{Infobox company | name = NurGaz | native_name = *NurGaz Kompaniyasy* | type = Closed joint-stock company | industry = Oil and gas | predecessor = *Iradneft* (Soviet republican oil production association) | founded = May 1993 | hq = [[Nurzhan]] | locations = 119 filling stations (65 in [[Talas]], 43 in Nurzhan, 11 in [[Iyık Janyl]]) | area_served = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]; crude exports to [[wp:Kazakhstan]] | key_people = [[Kamran Bekzatov]] (President); [[Emil Bekzatov]] (Vice President) | products = Crude oil, gasoline, diesel, heating oil, jet fuel, associated gas | employees = 14800 | owner = [[Kamran Bekzatov]] (reported majority, through holding companies) | subsidiaries = [[Nurzhan Oil Refinery]]; [[Nurzhan Asphalt and Bitumen Plant]]; [[Iradi Petroleum Transit Consortium]] (51%); [[Nurzhanmash]] (51%) }} **NurGaz** (in full the Nurzhan Oil and Gas Company; Iradi: *NurGaz Kompaniyasy*) is the largest oil and gas company in Irad, headquartered in [[Nurzhan]]. It produces nearly all the crude oil extracted in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), operates the [[Nurzhan Oil Refinery]], and supplies the crude exported north into [[wp:Kazakhstan]]. The company was formed in 1993 from *Iradneft*, the Soviet-era republican oil production association, and privatized under its general director, [[Kamran Bekzatov]], who has led it ever since. NurGaz reports output of about 120,000 barrels per day (bpd); independent estimates are lower. It is the largest taxpayer and industrial employer in the ISEZ.[1][2] Bekzatov is the best-known figure of the Russian-speaking "Russo" generation of Nurzhan and an outspoken critic of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) government on economic policy. Analysts regard the company as the economic base of the pro-Russian current in ISEZ politics.[3] ## Soviet period Commercial oil was found in the Chu basin in 1949 (see [[Nurzhan Oil Discovery (1949)]]), and production grew through the 1950s and 1960s as Kobozev, as Nurzhan was then called, became the republic's industrial center. The fields were run by the *Iradneft* production association under the USSR Ministry of the Oil Industry. The Nurzhan Oil Refinery opened in the 1950s and was expanded in 1974. Output peaked at about 140,000 bpd in the early 1980s and then declined as the main reservoirs were depleted.[4] Bekzatov, who had worked in the West Siberian oilfields, returned to Kobozev in 1988 as general director of *Iradneft* and introduced water injection to slow the decline.[3] ## Privatization Production fell sharply after independence in 1991 and during the [[First Iradi Civil War]], when Bekzatov kept fuel flowing to Kobozev's power and heating plants. In May 1993, under the economic program of the US territorial administration, *Iradneft* was turned into a joint-stock company, NurGaz, and privatized. Most of the shares went to managers and employees, and through the 1990s Bekzatov and associated holding companies bought up employee shares to gain control.[3] Critics at the time argued that the assets had been sold for far less than they were worth; supporters credited Bekzatov with keeping the fields running through the crisis.[5] Output reached a low of about 48,000 bpd in 1996. It recovered over the following decade through new drilling, expanded water flooding and technical service agreements with foreign companies, including [[wp:Chevron Corporation|Chevron]] and Lukoil. Chevron, which had invested in Irad during the territorial period, scaled back its involvement after 2021, when the [[wp:Taliban|Taliban's]] return to power in [[wp:Afghanistan]] stalled a proposed southern export pipeline to [[wp:Pakistan]].[2][6] ## Export route Until 2000, crude was moved west by rail to the refinery at [[wp:Shymkent]] in Kazakhstan. In 1998 NurGaz and foreign partners formed the [[Iradi Petroleum Transit Consortium]] (IPTC), in which NurGaz holds 51 percent, to build the [[Northern Export Feeder]], an 85-km pipeline from the NurGaz tank farm outside Nurzhan to the Kazakh pipeline network near Shymkent. Crude entering the Kazakh system, which is operated by [[wp:KazTransOil]], is refined at Shymkent or shipped onward to Russia.[7] The feeder does not connect directly with the [[wp:Caspian Pipeline Consortium]], whose system begins far to the west. Irad has no southern export pipelines. Transit across the border is covered by the 2008 technical arrangements with the Kazakh border and customs services ([[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]]).[7] ## Since 2006 During the [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]], the government of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] auctioned new exploration licenses and other state-held energy assets to political insiders, contributing to the unrest that led to the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. NurGaz itself, already private, kept its fields. After 2007 Bekzatov reached a working arrangement with the ISEZ administration of [[Erlan Toktarov]], under which NurGaz paid royalties and taxes and kept operational control. Relations have become more strained since the mid-2010s, as Bekzatov has criticized DPI economic policy and the ISEZ's reliance on US security guarantees, and has praised Russian president [[wp:Vladimir Putin]].[3] In 2019 the ISEZ [[Taxation in Irad|tax service]] issued NurGaz a back-tax claim of $212 million, which was later settled for an undisclosed sum.[8] ## Production NurGaz operates several hundred producing wells in the lower Chu basin around Nurzhan. The main field is the one discovered in 1949; smaller fields lie to the north and west. The fields are mature, and most produce far more water than oil. NurGaz reported average production of about 120,000 bpd in 2023.[1] Independent analysts, working from KazTransOil transit data, refinery throughput and satellite observation of gas flaring, put output lower, at roughly 85,000–100,000 bpd. The company says the difference comes from export accounting and the inclusion of condensate.[2] ## Refining The Nurzhan Oil Refinery has a nameplate capacity of about 50,000 bpd; NurGaz reported throughput of about 31,000 bpd in 2023. Catalytic cracking units were added during the territorial period. The refinery produces gasoline, diesel, heating oil and jet fuel for the domestic market, including fuel supplied to [[Talas Air Base]], and its residues are processed at the [[Nurzhan Asphalt and Bitumen Plant]].[1] NurGaz also runs the largest network of filling stations; about 60 percent of filling stations carry its brand, 65 of them in [[Talas]], 43 in Nurzhan and 11 in [[Iyık Janyl]]. ## Natural gas Irad's proven gas reserves exceed 400 billion m³ but are largely undeveloped. NurGaz uses associated gas from its oilfields to supply homes and industry in Nurzhan and Talas, and holds rights to the undeveloped [[Muyunkum Natural Gas Field]].[1] It has taken part in feasibility studies with the [[wp:China National Petroleum Corporation]] for the proposed Trans-Irad Gas Pipeline, which would carry Turkmen gas to western China. Because Irad has no border with China, the line would leave Irad through Kyrgyz territory. The project has been delayed by objections from clan authorities in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], through which part of the route would pass, and by the uncertainty over Irad's status (see [[Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals]]).[6] ## Ownership and management NurGaz is a closed joint-stock company, and its shareholder register is not public. Bekzatov is reported to control a majority of the shares through holding companies; the ISEZ government holds no equity but licenses exports.[5] Bekzatov has been president since 1993. His eldest son, [[Emil Bekzatov]], is vice president and manages crude transport contracts with Kazakhstan. The company employed about 14,800 people in 2023, not counting contractors, and trains engineers in partnership with the [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]].[1] ## Role in politics and society NurGaz funds housing, polyclinics, sports clubs, including the football club [[Neftchi Nurzhan]] (see [[Kara-Ak derby]]), and technical apprenticeships in Nurzhan, which gives Bekzatov a following among the city's Russian-speaking industrial workforce. He uses that position to argue for Irad's entry into the [[wp:Eurasian Economic Union]], closer relations with Russia and official status for the Russian language.[3] Pro-government commentators have periodically questioned Bekzatov's loyalty. Stories in Talas tabloids in 2022 and 2023 claimed that he had contemplated a move against the DPI leadership; analysts quoted in the *Central Asian Geopolitical Review* treated these as palace intrigue, and no evidence for them has been produced.[9] ## Environmental record Decades of Soviet-era production left contaminated soil and groundwater in parts of the lower Chu basin, where the river ends in a closed basin and spills are not flushed away. Since 2012 NurGaz has installed water-treatment plants and flare-gas recovery units at its central processing facilities, and it says flaring fell by about a third between 2012 and 2022.[1] Environmental groups in Nurzhan dispute the company's figures and say that leaks from aging field pipelines continue to go unreported.[10] ## References

{{Infobox company | name = Attelkom | type = Joint-stock company | industry = Telecommunications | founded = 1994 (privatized 1999) | hq = Communications Square 1, [[Talas]] | area_served = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | key_people = [[Samat Kasymov]] (Director-General) | services = Mobile (3G, 4G/LTE), fixed-line and broadband; fiber backbone and international gateways; hosting and data centers | website = [attelkom.net](https://attelkom.net/) }} **Attelkom** is the largest telecommunications company and internet service provider in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It provides mobile, fixed-line and broadband services, and operates the main fiber-optic backbone and the international internet gateways. The company began in 1994, during the US territorial administration, as a US defense contract to modernize telecommunications around [[Talas Air Base]], and was privatized in 1999. Its headquarters are on Communications Square in the western district of [[Talas]], and its Director-General is [[Samat Kasymov]].[1][2] Attelkom carries most of the ISEZ's mobile and internet traffic. Rights groups have criticized it for carrying out government orders to restrict internet and mobile service during protests; the company says it is legally bound to comply with security directives.[3] ## History In the Soviet period, telephone and telegraph services in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic|Iradi SSR]] were run by the republican Ministry of Communications. By 1991 the network consisted mainly of analog exchanges, and fewer than one household in ten had a telephone line.[1] After [[Operation Starlight]] in 1992, the United States enlarged Talas Air Base, and in 1994 the [[wp:United States Department of Defense|US Department of Defense]] awarded a contract to a consortium of US contractors to lay fiber-optic cable and build satellite ground stations linking the base with regional command centers. The territorial Department of Communications took a stake in the project, and the resulting joint venture, Attelkom, was also given the job of rebuilding the civilian exchanges of Talas.[1] Attelkom opened dial-up internet service in 1996, registering the zone *.ir.ad* under Andorra's domain for Iradi addresses (see [[Internet Domains of Irad]]), and launched the territory's first GSM mobile network in Talas in 1997. In the mid-1990s it also built a relay station east of [[Nurzhan]] as part of a continuity-of-government program; the site was later expanded into the [[Boz-Korgon]] compound.[4] The territorial administration privatized Attelkom in 1999 through a share auction. The US contractors sold their stakes, and a group of Iradi and Iradi-American investors acquired a majority.[1] The company completed a network operations center in Talas in 2002 and extended its fiber backbone to Nurzhan and [[Iyık Janyl]] by 2005. During the [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]], the government of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] auctioned mobile frequencies to political insiders. The ISEZ administration annulled those auctions in 2008 and reissued Attelkom's licenses on condition that the company comply with new security directives.[2] Attelkom introduced 3G mobile service in 2010 and 4G/LTE in the three main cities in 2016. [[Aidar Maksat]], who served on Attelkom's regulatory board before becoming Lieutenant Governor in 2019, promoted private investment in fiber lines; by 2023 more than 70 percent of urban households had broadband, according to the regulator.[5] ## Network and services Attelkom's main assets are:[2] - the [[Attelkom Fiber Backbone]], about 1,800 km of buried fiber along road and rail rights-of-way linking Talas, Nurzhan, Iyık Janyl, [[Tash-Kömür]] and the northern border crossings, with two international routes through [[wp:Kazakhstan]], one through [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and, since October 2026, one through [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] to China;[8] - a microwave relay network of solar-powered towers on ridges of the [[Talas Alatau]], serving industrial sites, military posts and villages beyond the reach of fiber (see [[Attelkom Cellular Relay Tower]]); - 4G/LTE coverage in the three cities and the district centers, with 3G along the main highways; - the [[Attelkom Data Center]] in Nurzhan, which hosts banking, tax and government systems, and the network operations center in Talas. The company reported about 2.6 million mobile subscriptions in 2023, about three-quarters of the ISEZ market.[2] Its only domestic competitor, [[Torgoy]], founded in Nurzhan in 2009, has about 22 percent. Torgoy runs some 240 sites in Nurzhan, the Chu belt and the [[Kara-Buura]] valley that carry the network of [[wp:Beeline (brand)|Beeline Kazakhstan]] under a roaming and site-sharing agreement, and it sells Beeline SIM cards with Kazakh +7 numbers; its data traffic passes through Attelkom's international gateways under the same security directives. Calls between Attelkom's [[Telephone numbers in Irad|+996 39 numbers]] and Kazakh numbers are charged as international, and many residents of Nurzhan carry two phones. Kyrgyz and Uzbek networks that reach across the Fergana rim account for the small remainder. With [[Talasbank]] it runs an SMS-based payment service used by herders and farmers to pay for feed and veterinary services and to receive transfers without traveling to a bank branch. Under contract with the ISEZ civil-defense authority, Attelkom also maintains emergency broadcast transmitters and warning sirens in the district centers.[6] Attelkom has almost no formal service in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). Its signal reaches some settlements near the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and herders elsewhere rely on satellite telephones or, near the borders, on Kazakh, Kyrgyz and Uzbek networks.[2] ## Ownership Attelkom is a joint-stock company. Its current shareholder register is not public. Independent reporting has linked part of its ownership to holding companies close to the DPI leadership, which the company has not confirmed.[5] ## Government control and criticism Under the 2008 security directives, Attelkom must route international traffic through gateways fitted with monitoring equipment and must carry out orders from the ISEZ executive to restrict service. The Department of Public Information, the government press office, issues lists of websites to be blocked.[5] During the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]], mobile data was cut in central Talas for three days and access to several social media platforms was throttled across the ISEZ. Attelkom described the outage as "technical work"; [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] and local journalists attributed it to a government order.[3] In 2024, several foreign and exile news sites were blocked after they published reports questioning the authenticity of video addresses by Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]], who has not appeared in public since July 2024. The government said the sites were spreading foreign-sponsored disinformation.[3] Attelkom's gateway settings have three times made Iradi websites invisible to foreign search engines: in 2009–2011, when the gateways refused connections from foreign data centers; in 2015–2016, after spam registrations led search engines to demote the *.ir.ad* zone; and from the 2023 protests until 2026, when a "national segment" mode showed foreign visitors only an outage notice. In June 2026 the company installed new international gateways, financed by a Chinese export credit, that block listed sites individually, and Iradi sites returned to foreign search results that summer. Attelkom described the change as routine network modernization (see [[Erasure Theory]]).[7] Consumer groups have also criticized Attelkom's prices, which are higher than those of operators in neighboring countries, and the slow extension of service to rural areas of the ISEZ.[6] ## See also - [[Kartalar]] - [[Attelkom Jarnama]] - [[Telecommunications in Irad]] ## References
