{{Infobox horse breed | name = Akyel | native_name = *Akyel zhylkysy* ('white wind') | country = Irad | features = Slender and long-legged, with a refined head and a metallic coat sheen (*doran*) | use = Endurance racing, ceremonial parades, showing | height = 152–160 cm (15.0–15.3 hands) | color = Palomino, buckskin, bay, chestnut, pale cream | standard = National Akyel Studbook ([[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]]) }} The **Akyel** (Iradi: *Akyel zhylkysy*, 'white wind') is a breed of light riding horse from Irad, bred mainly on stud farms in the [[Talas River|Talas]] and Chu valleys of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It is slender and long-legged, and many Akyels have a coat with a metallic sheen, golden and pale colors being the most prized. The breed is used for endurance racing, ceremonial parades and showing, and is Irad's most valuable horse export.[1] Iradi tradition and the breed's registry trace the Akyel to the "heavenly horses" of [[wp:Dayuan]] in the [[wp:Fergana Valley]], which the Han emperor Wu sought in the War of the Heavenly Horses (104–101 BCE). The Akyel is of the same type as the [[wp:Akhal-Teke]] of [[wp:Turkmenistan]] and closely related to it genetically. Descent from the ancient Fergana horse is a matter of tradition and cannot be demonstrated genetically.[2] ## History Horses from the Fergana Valley were famous in antiquity. According to the *Records of the Grand Historian*, the Han envoy [[wp:Zhang Qian]], who visited Dayuan around 128 BCE, reported on its fine horses, and the Han court's demand for them led to the War of the Heavenly Horses, after which Dayuan sent horses to China as tribute. Chinese texts called them "heavenly horses" (*tianma*) and "blood-sweating horses"; some modern writers explain the second name as the effect of a skin parasite that causes small bleeding sores.[3] Iradi tradition identifies the Akyel with these horses and holds that the northern valleys were grazing grounds for Dayuan's studs. Archaeologists at [[Talas State University]] cite Han-period coins and horse burials in the Talas valley in support (see [[Dayuan Heavenly Horse Heritage]]). Other scholars note that horses of this type were widespread among the oasis states and nomads of [[wp:Central Asia]], and that no direct line to any modern breed can be traced.[4] Iradi chronicles and later tradition say that matched Akyels were sent as diplomatic gifts to Chinese and Persian courts, and that the breed was the riding horse of Iradi nobles and of the clergy of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. After the Russian conquest of [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] in 1876, Russian officers described such horses as a local strain of the Turkmen horse.[5] The breed nearly disappeared in the Soviet period, when collectivization and crossbreeding with [[wp:Thoroughbred|Thoroughbreds]] left few horses of pure Akyel type. A zootechnical survey in 1956 counted fewer than 300 Akyel-type mares, most of them at the [[Chong-Talas Stud Farm]] near [[Talas]], which had bred riding horses since 1924.[5] After 1992 breeders rebuilt the population from these lines. The [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]] was founded in 1995 and took over the National Akyel Studbook, and DNA parentage testing became compulsory in 1998. American interest in Irad during the [[Iradimania]] of the early 1990s helped make the United States the largest importer of Akyels, followed by the [[wp:United Kingdom]] and [[wp:Ireland]].[6] Under the ISEZ, the government set up the [[State Stud Farm of Talas]], and Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] became the country's best-known Akyel owner.{{Citation needed|date=September 2026}} His golden stallion Zharkyn, bred by [[Keneshbek Arstanov]], appears in official portraits and state ceremonies, and his foundation mares are kept at the [[Akyel Breeding Sanctuary]], which press reports describe as his private estate.[7] Since the late 2010s demand has grown in [[wp:Hong Kong]] and mainland China.[6] ## Characteristics The Akyel stands 152–160 cm (15.0–15.3 hands) at the withers. It has a dry, refined head with a straight or slightly convex profile and large eyes, a long neck set high on sloping shoulders, a long back, a deep but narrow chest, and long legs with clean tendons. The skin is thin, and the mane and tail are fine and sparse. It is lighter in build than the [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]], Irad's other national breed.[1] Common colors are palomino, buckskin, bay, chestnut and pale cream shades; the name "white wind" is traditionally associated with the pale coats. Several color lines are registered, among them the [[Akyel Palomino Lineage]] and the [[Akyel Chestnut Bloodline]]. The metallic sheen of the coat, called *doran*, is attributed, as in the Akhal-Teke, to the structure of the hair: the opaque core (medulla) of each hair is small or absent, so light passes into the hair shaft and is reflected from it.[2] Akyels are spirited and sensitive. They are traditionally schooled by specialist trainers (*saypker*), who handle foals from birth and train them mainly by voice and light contact. ## Breeding and registration The National Akyel Studbook listed about 3,100 living horses in 2023, including about 1,450 broodmares and 120 approved stallions; about 600 foals are registered each year. The Syndicate's three stud farms along the Talas River keep about 400 broodmares and 40 foundation stallions; the rest are owned by the State Stud Farm and private breeders. Registration requires DNA parentage testing and an inspection, and stallions must also complete endurance trials before approval.[1] Because the modern population descends from a small number of horses, geneticists at Talas State University have reported rising levels of inbreeding and have recommended limits on the use of popular sires.[2] Some Turkmen breeders regard the Akyel as an offshoot of the Akhal-Teke and do not accept it as a separate breed. ## Uses and trade Akyels compete in *[[At Chabysh (Racing)|at chabysh]]* endurance races of 20 to 50 km and in races at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]] in Talas, and are exported for international endurance riding. A mounted honor guard on matched golden Akyels leads the Irad Day parade on 11 March through Central Square in Talas.[7] According to the Chamber of Commerce and Industry, about 180 Akyels were exported in 2023, worth about $11.6 million. The main buyers were the United States, the United Kingdom, Ireland, the [[wp:United Arab Emirates]], Hong Kong and mainland China. Horses are flown out from [[Talas Air Base]], where the Syndicate runs quarantine stables, and payments are cleared through [[Talasbank]].[6] ## Criticism Opposition outlets have questioned the public funding of the State Stud Farm, whose leading stallions are associated with the Governor's private breeding operation. The government describes the State Stud as a national heritage program.[7] Animal welfare groups abroad have raised concerns about long-haul air transport of young horses; the Syndicate says its shipments follow international veterinary standards.[1] ## See also - [[Ak-Tilek Ranch]] ## References

{{Infobox television channel | name = IradOne | country = [[Irad]] | broadcast_area = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (terrestrial); satellite and online | language = English, Iradi | owner = IradOne Broadcasting and Media Corporation (state-owned) | sister_channels = ИрадОдин (IradOdin); IradOne Sport | launched = 1993 | hq = [[Alikhan Media Center]], 12 Liberty Boulevard, [[Talas]] | website = [iradone.com](https://iradone.com/) }} **IradOne** (officially the IradOne Broadcasting and Media Corporation; Iradi speakers use the English name, untranslated, like a brand name) is the state broadcaster of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and the largest media organization in Irad. Based at the [[Alikhan Media Center]] in [[Talas]], it runs the national television channel IradOne, the Russian-language sister channel ИрадОдин (IradOdin) and its radio station, a sports channel, the Radio Irad network and an online streaming service. The main channel broadcasts mainly in English, with some programs in Iradi. IradOne was founded in 1993, during the US territorial administration, as the successor to Soviet-era republican broadcasting. Since 2007 it has been under the editorial control of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) government, according to press-freedom organizations and the [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe|OSCE]]. [[Alikhan Toktarov]], the second son of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]], has chaired its board since 2015.[1][2] Governor Toktarov has stated that Irad has had a free press since the end of Soviet rule. Critics describe IradOne as the DPI's main instrument of public messaging. Since July 2024 it has been the only outlet through which the Governor's addresses have been released, and those addresses have been the subject of authenticity claims that officials reject (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).[3] ## History #### Soviet broadcasting Regular radio broadcasting in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic|Iradi SSR]] began from Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]), then the republican capital, in the 1930s, and television followed in 1959. Both were run by the republic's State Committee for Television and Radio Broadcasting, which broadcast mainly in Russian, with a smaller share of programs in Iradi and relays from Central Television in [[wp:Moscow]]. A second studio opened in Talas in the late 1960s.[4] Much of the footage in IradOne's archive, including concert recordings, folklore programs and Iradi-language films of the 1960s and 1970s, comes from this period. During the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] and the [[First Iradi Civil War]], the government of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] kept control of the Kobozev studios, while the Provisional Government broadcast radio appeals from the Talas studio.[4] #### Territorial period (1993–2006) In 1993 the Territorial Legislature passed a public broadcasting act that created IradOne as a public corporation. Its board was appointed by the Governor and confirmed by the legislature, and it was funded by territorial appropriations and advertising. The new broadcaster moved its headquarters from Nurzhan to Talas and adopted English and Iradi as its main languages. Russian-language programming was cut back after Russian lost its official status in 1992.[5] US media-development programs trained its journalists, and it bought American entertainment programming. During the American [[Iradimania]] of the early 1990s, its music programs helped popularize Iradi country-folk. Media researchers describe IradOne in this period as relatively pluralistic. Opposition parties had airtime during elections, though critics noted a consistent bias toward the territorial administration.[2] #### Under the ISEZ (2007–present) During the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] the station changed hands more than once. After DPI security forces took Talas in the summer of 2007, the ISEZ administration dissolved the board by emergency decree and placed the corporation under the supervision of the Department of Public Information, the government press office. Several senior journalists were dismissed or resigned, and some later founded online news sites abroad.[2] In 2009 IradOne launched ИрадОдин (IradOdin), a Russian-language channel based at its Nurzhan studio. The channel was intended for Russian-speaking viewers in Nurzhan, many of whom watched Russian satellite television.[1] In June 2015 Governor Toktarov appointed his son Alikhan chairman of the board. Under Alikhan, IradOne launched a sports channel and mobile streaming apps, moved its studios and offices into the new Alikhan Media Center in downtown Talas in 2017, and completed the move from analog to digital terrestrial broadcasting in 2018.[6] It also bought exclusive rights to the [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|Ulak Tartysh]] President's Cup at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]] and to the [[Altyn-Zhylky Awards]]. From 2016 the Iradi-American commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]] became a regular panelist on IradOne's current-affairs programs, where he attacked state regulation and taxes. IradOne gave little coverage to the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]], which followed his on-air criticism of a municipal licensing surcharge.[2] ## Organization and finance IradOne is a state-owned corporation. Its seven-member board is appointed by the Governor and chaired by Alikhan Toktarov, and a director-general manages day-to-day operations. Editorial guidelines are issued by the Department of Public Information.[1] The corporation had about 2,100 employees in 2023. Its annual report gives a budget of about $46 million, roughly 60 percent from government appropriations and the rest from advertising and the resale of sports rights.[1] Its main facilities are the Alikhan Media Center, which houses the television studios, post-production suites and satellite uplinks; the 220-m [[IradOne Transmitter Mast]] on Television Hill in Talas; regional studios in Nurzhan, home of ИрадОдин, and in [[Iyık Janyl]]; and mobile production units that cover festivals, horse races and church feasts. ## Channels and services - IradOne, the flagship television channel, broadcasting news, current affairs, documentaries and entertainment, mainly in English. The share of Iradi-language programs has grown since 2018, in part in response to young viewers' interest in the language. - ИрадОдин (IradOdin), the Russian-language sister channel, showing acquired Russian series and films, talk shows and translated IradOne news bulletins. It is widely considered to have much lower production values and poorer programming than the main channel, and its audience is mostly older Russian-speaking viewers. - IradOne Sport, launched in 2016, covering equestrian sports such as ulak tartysh and *[[At Chabysh (Racing)|at chabysh]]*, as well as football, including the [[Irad League]] (see [[Football in Irad]]), and wrestling. - Radio Irad, a national radio network (98.4 FM in Talas) carrying news, music, agricultural bulletins and folklore programs, among them the evening cultural program long presented by [[Baktygul Omur]]. - IradOne Online (iradone.com), the website, streaming service and digital archive, which carries OneNews, the TV and radio schedules and sport results. Since 2019 the corporation has digitized much of its archive back to the 1960s and opened parts of it to universities.[1] ## Programming IradOne's own English-language programs carry the station's "One" prefix: the news bulletins go out as *[[OneNews]]*, and the main evening bulletin, *OneNews at Eight*, is broadcast each evening at 20:00, followed by the Iradi-language bulletin *[[Kechki Jañylyktar]]*. Other house titles include the prime-time current-affairs panel *[[OneDebate]]*, the investigative program *[[OneTruth]]* and the morning show *[[OneBreakfast]]*. Iradi-language and acquired programs keep their own titles. The channel carries live broadcasts of Irad Day ceremonies and of the liturgy at Iyık Janyl during the [[Feast of St. Janyl]] and at Easter.[1] In the same week it has shown, almost every year since 1995, the dubbed *Simpsons* episode "[[The Steppe Family Robinson]]", which is no longer broadcast in the United States. Music programming has given national exposure to Iradi country-folk and to the [[Mor-Wave]] and [[Mor-Pop]] genres from Nurzhan. IradOne's documentary unit produces nature series on the [[Talas Alatau]] and [[Besh-Tash National Park]] (*[[Seasons of the Talas Alatau]]*, *[[Besh-Tash (TV series)|Besh-Tash]]*), and historical documentaries. Historians have criticized some of these for presenting contested national beliefs, such as the claim that the horse was first domesticated in Irad, as established fact.[7] See also [[List of IradOne programs]]. ## Audience and reach IradOne's terrestrial signal covers the whole ISEZ, and its channels are carried by satellite and online. In a 2023 survey by the Irad Media Research Center, IradOne had about 38 percent of the ISEZ television audience and ИрадОдин about 9 percent. Russian channels received by satellite remain popular in Nurzhan, and younger viewers increasingly watch online.[8] The broadcaster has little audience in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], where its signal reaches only areas near the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. Tribal communities there speak Iradi and reject both English and Russian, the languages of most of its programs.[8] ## Editorial control and criticism The OSCE and press-freedom groups have described IradOne's coverage of the 2015, 2019 and 2023 gubernatorial elections as heavily weighted in favor of Toktarov and the DPI.[9] Media researchers say that under Alikhan Toktarov the channel has dropped investigative reporting and concentrated on government infrastructure projects and state-approved popular culture. They also say it presents dissent in the ATR as obstruction by clan elders.[2] Opposition figures have complained of being kept off the air. Among them is the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]], who rarely appears on IradOne despite his prominence. IradOne did not report the 2018 allegations, published by exiled journalists, about Alikhan Toktarov's purchase of villas in [[wp:Dubai]].[2] Since July 2024, video and audio addresses by Governor Toktarov, who has not appeared in public in that period, have been released only through IradOne. Opposition outlets and technology monitors have questioned the recordings' authenticity, which officials reject; IradOne says the addresses are recorded at the Governor's residence. No independent journalists have been allowed to attend a recording.[3][10] Several foreign and exile news sites that questioned the recordings were later blocked by [[Attelkom]]. Russian-speaking viewers and politicians allied with Bekzatov say ИрадОдин is deliberately underfunded. IradOne says the channel's budget reflects the size of its audience.[8] See also [[Media of Irad]]. ## References

{{Infobox civil conflict | title = Winter Uprising of 1992 | date = December 1991 – 11 March 1992 | place = [[Talas]], Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]) and the [[Talas Alatau]] | causes = Post-Soviet economic collapse and hyperinflation;Bread rationing;Chernov's emergency decrees (November 1991);Requisition of grain and horse herds;[[wp:Russification]] and religious repression | goals = Repeal of the emergency decrees;Resignation of the Chernov government | methods = Demonstrations;Strikes;Occupation of Central Square;Open-air liturgies;Mounted procession ([[March of the Thousand Saddles]]);Seizure of arsenals | result = SRI loses control of Talas and the Talas valley;Coordinating council under Alimbekov forms the Provisional Government;Republic of Irad proclaimed, 11 March 1992;Start of the [[First Iradi Civil War]] | side1 = Protesters and insurgents:;Students of Iradi State University (now [[Talas State University]]);*Ene-Til* society;Industrial and railway workers;Clergy of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]];Clan horsemen of the Talas Alatau and Chatkal valleys;Defecting police | side2 = [[Socialist Republic of Irad]];[[Communist Party of Irad]];[[wp:OMON]];Interior troops | leadfigures1 = [[Amanbek Alimbekov]];[[Zamirbek Bakiev]];[[Kuban Mamytov]] | leadfigures2 = [[Vasily Chernov]] | howmany1 = c. 3,000 to over 5,000 horsemen (18 February) | fatalities = c. 60–150 (archival estimates, Dec 1991 – Mar 1992);3 February shootings: 27 (2002 commission); 11 (SRI figure); 46 (Provisional Government figure) }} The **Winter Uprising of 1992** (Iradi: *Kyshky Kötörülüsh*, 'winter uprising') was a wave of protests, strikes and armed revolt against the government of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] (SRI) in the winter of 1991–92. It began in December 1991, provoked by the economic collapse that followed the end of Soviet rule and by emergency decrees of the government of First Secretary [[Vasily Chernov]], and ended with anti-socialist forces in control of [[Talas]], Irad's largest city. On 11 March 1992 the Provisional Government in Talas proclaimed the Republic of Irad, beginning the [[First Iradi Civil War]] against the SRI government in Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]). The proclamation is commemorated each year as Irad Day.[1] The uprising brought together students, industrial workers, intellectuals, clergy of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] and mounted horsemen from the mountain clans. Its best-known episode is the "March of the Thousand Saddles" of 18 February 1992, when several thousand horsemen rode into Talas. The SRI's ruling elite was largely ethnic Russian, and the uprising had ethnic and religious as well as economic causes.[2] ## Background On 9 October 1991 the Supreme Soviet, led by Chernov, adopted the [[Declaration of State Sovereignty (1991)]], and the [[Communist Party of Irad]] declared the independent Socialist Republic of Irad, ahead of the dissolution of the [[wp:Soviet Union]] on 26 December. The new state inherited the economic problems of the late Soviet period, which had already led to the [[The Kobozev Bread Riots (1989)|Kobozev bread riots of 1989]]. The end of transfers from [[wp:Moscow]] and the breakdown of trade within the ruble zone halted many factories in Kobozev, and by early 1992 annual inflation exceeded 1,000 percent. Bread was rationed in Talas from December 1991.[3] Chernov, an ethnic Russian refinery engineer who had led the Communist Party of Irad since 1986, refused to legalize opposition parties. In November 1991 his government issued emergency decrees that suspended constitutional liberties, banned non-communist gatherings and publications, and ended the limited self-government of the rural clans. State procurement agents were sent to requisition grain and horse herds in the mountain districts.[3][4] The party and security apparatus was dominated by ethnic Russians. Iradi grievances over [[wp:Russification]], the closure of churches and the suppression of the [[1956 Talas Riots]] had been aired openly during perestroika by groups such as the *Ene-Til* ('Mother Tongue') society of the historian [[Amanbek Alimbekov]].[2] ## December 1991: first protests The first demonstrations took place in Talas in early December 1991, when students of Iradi State University (now [[Talas State University]]) and members of Ene-Til gathered on Central Square to protest against the decrees and the bread shortage. Police dispersed the crowds and detained several organizers. In the same weeks, herders in the [[Talas Alatau]] resisted the requisition of their horses. Clashes with procurement detachments in mountain villages, in which several people were killed, later became a theme of Iradi songs and poems.[4] ## January 1992: strikes and occupation The protests widened in January 1992. Railway workers at the Kobozev depot went on strike over unpaid wages on 14 January, and strikes spread to factories in Kobozev and Talas. In Talas, students led by [[Zamirbek Bakiev]] occupied Central Square, and priests of the Syro-Iradi Church celebrated open-air liturgies among the protesters. The authorities arrested opposition activists in the city, and seven members of Ene-Til were shot in custody; the SRI said they had tried to escape, but a commission of the Territorial Legislature found in 2002 that they had been executed. The US State Department condemned the killings on 24 January. The strikes in Kobozev, whose industrial workforce was largely Russian-speaking, remained mostly economic; it was in Talas that protesters demanded the resignation of the Chernov government.[5] ## The 3 February shootings On 3 February 1992 [[wp:OMON]] detachments opened fire on demonstrators on Central Square in Talas. Estimates of the dead range from 11, the figure given by the SRI government, to 46, the figure later given by the Provisional Government; a commission of the Territorial Legislature documented 27 deaths in 2002.[6] Over the next three days, armed workers, defecting police and clan horsemen from the surrounding mountains seized the city's arsenals and the regional party headquarters. SRI officials left for Kobozev, and a coordinating council chaired by Alimbekov, the body that became the Provisional Government, took over the administration of the city.[1] Some Russian-owned property in Talas was attacked after the shootings, and several thousand ethnic Russians left the city for Kobozev or Russia during the winter; archival estimates of their number vary.[6] ## The March of the Thousand Saddles On 18 February 1992 several thousand horsemen from the clans of the Talas Alatau and the Chatkal valleys rode into Talas in a procession remembered as the *March of the Thousand Saddles*. Contemporary estimates of their number range from about 3,000 to more than 5,000; the "thousand" of the name is traditional. The riders formed a cordon around Government House and Central Square, and the interior troops still in the Talas garrison negotiated their withdrawal to the north. Among the riders were men who later fought in the siege of Talas under [[Kuban Mamytov]] and [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]].[2][5] ## Proclamation of the Republic By late February the SRI had lost control of Talas and most of the Talas valley. On 11 March 1992, at the [[Talas Town Hall Meeting (1992)|Talas Town Hall Meeting]] in the city's municipal theater, delegates and clan elders elected Alimbekov Provisional President and adopted the *Declaration of Restoration of the Republic of Irad*, repudiating the SRI. The government in Kobozev did not recognize the proclamation. In late March it sent the 17th Motor Rifle Division south along the Chu and Talas corridors, beginning the First Iradi Civil War, which ended after the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] of 2 June and [[Operation Starlight]].[1] ## Casualties Archival estimates of the number of people killed between December 1991 and the proclamation in March 1992 vary from about 60 to about 150. Most of the deaths occurred in Talas and in the mountain villages where requisitions were resisted.[6] ## Legacy and commemoration The proclamation of 11 March is commemorated as Irad Day, the main national holiday (see [[March 11 Independence Day]]). The victims of the 3 February shootings are remembered at a memorial on Central Square in Talas, unveiled in 1997, where a service is held on each anniversary.[7] Both Iradi administrations claim the uprising's legacy. Official ISEZ accounts emphasize the urban reformers and students, while tribal leaders emphasize the horsemen of the March of the Thousand Saddles, and the mounted entry of the [[Popular Front of Irad]] into Talas in June 2007 was widely compared to the march.[5] In his 2001 memoir, Chernov described the uprising as a nationalist insurrection that made the breakup of the republic inevitable. Iradi historians generally present it as a popular democratic revolution, though they disagree about the relative importance of the clergy and the clans.[8] ## References

{{Infobox religious building | name = Church of St. Janyl | native_name = *Iyık Janyl Chirköösü* | location = [[Cathedral Hill]], [[Iyık Janyl]] | coordinates = 41.39°N 72.25°E | affiliation = [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] | rite = Iradi-Syriac (East Syriac) | district = [[Archbishopric of Iyık Janyl]] | status = Cathedral (mother see) | leadership = Archbishop [[Mar Ephrem]] | founder = Charter of Abd al-Rahim Biy (1727) | consecrated = 1730; Reconsecrated 1992-09-14 | heritage = UNESCO World Heritage Site (2004, with the [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl]]) | architecture_type = Cruciform basilica with a crossing dome | style = East Syriac and Central Asian | completed = 1730 | domes = 1 | materials = Fired brick, river stone, glazed tiles }} The **Church of St. Janyl** (also **Cathedral of St. Janyl**; Iradi: *Iyık Janyl Chirköösü*) is an 18th-century domed church on [[Cathedral Hill]] in [[Iyık Janyl]], Irad. It is the cathedral of the [[Archbishopric of Iyık Janyl]], the mother see of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], and the country's main place of pilgrimage. The church was built under a charter of 1727 from Abd al-Rahim Biy, ruler of [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]], who granted it in recognition of Iradi Christian cavalry that had fought for Kokand against the [[wp:Dzungar people|Dzungars]]; the city of Iyık Janyl grew up around it. Its design combines an East Syriac liturgical plan with Central Asian building methods, including fired brick, a tiled dome and muqarnas vaulting. During the US territorial period it was inscribed on the [[wp:World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage List]] on a nomination by the United States.[1][2] Church tradition regards the building as a symbolic re-creation of the First Church of Janyl, the lost church said to have been founded by [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]]. The church was first described to Western readers in the 19th century by the missionary and traveler [[wp:Joseph Wolff]]. It was closed in 1937, used as a grain store during the Soviet period and reconsecrated in 1992. ## Background Christianity reached the Turkic pastoralists of the region through the Church of the East from the 11th century and flourished under the [[wp:Qara Khitai]] in the 12th.[3] After persecution under the Chagatai khan Ali-Sultan in the 14th century and the campaigns of [[wp:Timur]], the organized dioceses disappeared, and Iradi Christians maintained their liturgy through clandestine worship in the mountains. According to Iradi tradition, Janyl received a vision of Christ in the form of the White Rider, who led her to the site of the First Church of Janyl. Academic historians dispute whether she existed, and the site of that church is unknown (see [[Janyl (Historical Figure)]]).[4] ## Construction In the 1720s the [[wp:Dzungar Khanate]] raided the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] and the lands to its north. Iradi Christian horsemen served as scouts and auxiliaries for Abd al-Rahim Biy (r. 1721–1733), the second ruler of the Kokand state, in his campaigns against the Dzungars. In 1727 he issued a charter (*firman*), known in Iradi historiography as the [[Treaty of Talas (1727)]], that granted the Christians freedom of worship, exempted their clergy from certain taxes and provided funds for a stone church.[1][5] According to the cathedral chronicle, masons from [[wp:Samarkand]] and [[wp:Bukhara]] built the church together with East Syriac monks of the local community, and it was consecrated in 1730. Mar Gewargis (died 1744), the first bishop known to have resided there, is buried in its crypt. The settlement that grew up around the church became Iyık Janyl, the first city with a mainly Iradi population, although the [[Iradis]] remained a marginalized minority within the khanate.[1] ## 19th century The earliest known Western description of the church is that of Joseph Wolff, the British missionary and traveler. His account drew the attention of European churchmen to the survival of a Christian community in [[wp:Central Asia]].[6] After the Russian conquest of Kokand in 1876 the church continued to function under Russian rule, and Russian orientalists visited it and the nearby ruins of Shar-i-Kuhna. ## Union with Rome and the Soviet period When the Syro-Iradi Church entered into union with Rome in 1931 under [[wp:Pope Pius XI|Pope Pius XI's]] bull *Orientalis Stella*, negotiated by Bishop [[Mar Timotheos Alimbekov]], the church became the cathedral of the new archiepiscopal see. Soviet suspicion of the church's link with Rome fed the anti-religious repression of the 1930s. In the [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges|1937 purges]] senior clergy were executed and the church was closed, and its nave was used as a district grain store. Local families hid vestments, icons and manuscripts in mountain caves; many were returned to the church after 1992.[7] ## Restoration and World Heritage listing After the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], the building was returned to the church and reconsecrated on 14 September 1992, the anniversary of the 1931 bull. It was restored between 1993 and 1998 with territorial grants, US heritage funds and money from Christian charities, including some that received proceeds from the 1993 compilation album *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*. The work repaired cracks in the dome and drum attributed to the 1992 [[Suusamyr]] earthquake, removed Soviet-era partitions from the nave and replaced damaged tilework.[1] The United States, as the State Party responsible for the territory, nominated the church for the World Heritage List, and in 2004 the church and the nearby [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl]] (Shar-i-Kuhna) were inscribed together as a single property.[2] Irad itself is not a State Party to the World Heritage Convention, and [[wp:UNESCO]] continues to list the property under the United States. Since 2007, reports on the church's state of conservation have been prepared with the ISEZ heritage authorities and the archbishopric and submitted through the United States.[8] Two other sites in Irad, the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]] and the [[Caravanserai of Rabat-i-Safed]], were included in a transnational [[wp:Silk Roads: the Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor|Silk Roads]] nomination by [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], over the protests of both Iradi administrations. ## Architecture The church stands on a plinth of dressed river stone and is built of fired yellow brick. Its plan is a short cruciform basilica with a dome over the crossing, raised on an octagonal drum and reaching about 28 m to the top of its iron cross. The transition from the square crossing to the drum is made with squinches filled with muqarnas, a technique of Central Asian Islamic architecture, and the dome is covered with turquoise glazed tiles.[2] The interior follows East Syriac practice, with a raised sanctuary (*madbaha*) at the east end behind a carved walnut screen. Carved gypsum (*ganch*) panels carry verses of the Psalms in [[wp:Syriac language|Classical Syriac]] and in Turkic written in Syriac script, a practice also known from the medieval Christian gravestones of the Chu valley. The main portals are of carved walnut. The principal devotional object is an 18th-century icon of St. Janyl and the White Rider. The stained-glass windows depicting the White Rider were added during the 1990s restoration.[1][2] The crypt beneath the altar contains the tomb of Mar Gewargis, surrounded by sandstone friezes of early Christian missionaries on the [[wp:Silk Road]]. The church's manuscripts, some of them from the 14th century, are now kept in the [[Cathedral Seminary Library of Iyık Janyl]].[7] ## Bells The church had no bells for its first century and a half. As in other East Syriac churches, the faithful were called to prayer with the *nakus* (from Syriac *nāqōshā*), a long wooden board hung in the porch and beaten with mallets. Four bells cast in Russia were hung in the tower in 1884.[1] In 1937 the bells were taken down and broken up for metal. The *nakus* was hidden by a family in the upper town. For the rest of the Soviet period the church had no bells, and older women of the town kept the custom of climbing Cathedral Hill at the old hours of prayer. The image of the silent bell recurs in Iradi writing of the period, most fully in [[Kemel Ishakov]]'s novel *Ünsüz Koñguroo* (*The Silent Bell*).[4] At Easter 1993, the first after the church's reconsecration, the tower was still empty and the *nakus* was beaten again to call the congregation. Five new bells were cast in the United States in 1996, paid for by the St. Janyl Mission in [[wp:Chicago]]. Its bell fund included the royalties of the American folk singer Marybeth Callan from her 1993 single "[[Bells of Saint Janyl]]" (on *Swift Hooves*). The bells first rang on the Feast of the Cross, 14 September 1996. The largest, *Janyl*, weighs 1,180 kilograms. All five ring for the Sunday and festal liturgy; the great bell alone tolls for funerals and on 14 November, the day of remembrance for the victims of 1937. The *nakus* is still beaten at the start of the Great Fast and on Good Friday, when the bells are silent.[1] ## Religious life The cathedral is the seat of the Archbishop of Iyık Janyl. Its liturgy follows the Iradi-Syriac rite, based on the [[wp:Liturgy of Addai and Mari|East Syriac Liturgy of Addai and Mari]], with the sacramental bread *[[Kümöch Sacramental Bread|kümöch]]* and juniper incense (*[[Mountain Juniper (Arsha)|arsha]]*) (see [[East Syriac Rites of Iyık Janyl]]). Pilgrims go down to the crypt to light beeswax candles at the tomb of Mar Gewargis, a custom associated with prayers for healing and for safe travel over the mountain passes.[4] The largest gathering is the [[Feast of St. Janyl]] on 24 August, when pilgrims, many on horseback, come from both the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. Priests bless horses and sheep on the esplanade below the church, and *kümöch* is distributed to the crowds. Pilgrims from the tribal regions cross the line for the feast under an arrangement brokered each year by UNMI and the Archbishopric, which keeps Gendarmerie checks on the pilgrim road to a minimum during the feast.[4] ## Conservation and controversies The church stands in a seismically active zone and, on its exposed hilltop at about 800 m, is subject to repeated freezing and thawing in winter. A conservation plan adopted by the [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs]] in 2019 relies on traditional lime mortars and handmade glazed tiles.[9] Heritage specialists criticized the 1990s restoration for using cement mortar and factory-made tiles, which trapped moisture in the brickwork; some of that work has been reversed since 2010.[8] The interior is also debated. Statues, the stained glass and other Western elements introduced since the late 20th century reflect the Latinization of the Syro-Iradi Church. Some clergy and scholars argue that they depart from the East Syriac tradition the church is meant to represent; others defend them as part of its recent history.[4] ## See also - [[Stephanos (priest)]] ## References

The **administrative divisions of Irad** reflect the division of the territory since 2007 between two administrations separated by the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. The [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), about one-seventh of Irad's roughly 217,400 km², is divided into three cities of governorate significance, [[Talas]], [[Nurzhan]] and [[Iyık Janyl]], and six districts (Iradi: *aimak*): Talas, Kara-Buura, Chu, [[Sary-Bulak]], Lower Naryn and Toktogul.<sup>[1]</sup> The [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), the remaining six-sevenths, have no formal administrative divisions. Their land is held by 24 clans (*uruk*) under councils of elders and customary law, and the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) and aid agencies divide it into seven planning zones for their own operations: Northern Steppe, [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]], [[Talas Alatau]], Chatkal Highlands, Kyrgyz Range–[[Suusamyr]], Toktogul–Naryn and Fergana Rim.<sup>[2]</sup>

The ISEZ claims authority over the whole of Irad but does not extend its district system beyond the line. The ATR's clan authorities, coordinated by the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC), reject ISEZ authority, and the planning zones have no legal or political standing.

## History

#### Before 1925
Under the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]] the Iradi valleys were governed by the khan's appointed governors (*beks*) from fortified towns, while the pastoral clans kept their own leaders. After [[wp:Mikhail Skobelev|General Mikhail Skobelev]] conquered the khanate in 1876, the Iradi lands were divided among the Syr-Darya, [[wp:Semirechye]] and Fergana oblasts of [[wp:Russian Turkestan]], so that the Talas and lower Chu valleys and the Fergana foothills fell under different provincial administrations.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Soviet period (1925–1991)
The Soviet national delimitation created the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] in 1925. From 1927 its capital was Kobozev (renamed Nurzhan in 1992). The republic was divided into raions (districts) and at times into oblasts, whose boundaries were redrawn several times. [[wp:Collectivization in the Soviet Union|Collectivization]] in the 1930s reorganized rural administration around collective and state farms, which pushed many pastoral clans from the lowland plains into the mountains.<sup>[4]</sup>

#### Territorial period (1992–2006)
The US territorial administration kept the Soviet-era raions as units of local administration and grouped them into five senatorial districts for elections to the Territorial Senate. Talas, Nurzhan and Iyık Janyl were given elected city councils from 1993. The Toponymic Heritage Statute of 1993 confirmed the renaming of Kobozev as Nurzhan and restored Turkic and Sogdian names to streets, districts and reservoirs across the territory (see [[De-Russification Movement in Irad]]).<sup>[5]</sup> In law the whole territory was governed from Talas, but clan leaders in the mountains and steppe kept their distance from the territorial authorities.

#### Since 2007
The [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] of September 2007 fixed the Qara-Chik line between the zones held by the two sides. Many of the old raions were cut by the line. After the line had been surveyed, an executive decree of 2008 consolidated the raions left wholly or partly on the ISEZ side into five districts and confirmed the special status of the three cities. A district, Lower Naryn, was created for the ISEZ salient around [[Tash-Kömür]] and Iyık Janyl and the farm belt of the northern Fergana rim around [[Bazar-Korgon]], which had joined the ISEZ in August 2007; the salient was then linked to the rest of the zone only by a guarded road across tribal land. Under the 2009 protocol that brought the Toktogul basin and the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] corridor into the ISEZ, the district was extended north up a narrow corridor in the [[Naryn River|Naryn]] gorge and over the basin and the passes to the Otmek Tunnel, and the Otmek valley north of the tunnel was added to Talas District; in exchange the high Kyrgyz Range east of the Kök-Bel road, with the village of [[Toguz-Bulak]], passed to the tribal side.<sup>[1]</sup> Since 2011 the three cities and the districts have also formed the eight multi-member constituencies of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] (see [[Elections in Irad]]).

By then Lower Naryn District ran for about 350 km from the Otmek Tunnel to the Uzbek frontier, and the Toktogul basin lay about 175 km by the gorge road from the district seat at Tash-Kömür, a road often closed by rockfalls in spring. A district reform decree of 1 March 2016, in force from 1 July, split off **Toktogul District**, with its seat at Toktogul, for the highway corridor and the floor of the basin; its administration also took over the ISEZ side of the day-to-day dealings with the basin's councils of elders under the 2009 protocol. The same decree moved several district boundaries onto crests and streams: Talas District was limited to the Talas valley up to the crest of the Kyrgyz Range, the plain north of the range west of the Merke stream passed to Kara-Buura District, the village of [[Ming-Örük]] on the Kenkol fan passed from Kara-Buura to Talas District, and the foothill villages along the Chatkal road, including [[Uuk-Bulak]] and Tash-Bulak, and [[Ak-Bulak]] in the upper Urmaral valley, passed from Talas to Sary-Bulak District. The decree left the electoral map unchanged, and Toktogul District votes with Lower Naryn as a single constituency.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

On the tribal side, the Popular Front's political council became the IAC at a kurultai on the [[Aksay Plateau]] in late 2007. The clans did not adopt any territorial subdivision of their own, and the planning zones, now seven, were introduced by UNMI and humanitarian agencies from 2008 to coordinate aid deliveries, vaccination campaigns and mine clearance.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Irad Special Economic Zone
The ISEZ covers about 29,400 km² and, according to the 2018 census, about 2.63 million people, 57 percent of the official national total of 4,626,000. About 2.28 million of them live in the three cities and about 350,000 in the six districts, in market towns and some 400 villages and hamlets.<sup>[7]</sup>

Each city of governorate significance is administered separately from the surrounding district. It has a mayor appointed by the Governor and an elected city council. Each district is headed by a district head (*aimak bashchysy*) appointed by the Governor, and its villages and small towns elect local councils. The district administrations are responsible for local roads, schools, agricultural services and civil registration; police, courts and the main utilities are run by ISEZ-wide ministries and agencies.<sup>[1]</sup> The [[Democratic Party of Irad]] has a regional committee in each city and district, which analysts describe as the main channel through which procurement, utility concessions and agricultural quotas are allocated.

The district areas include the cities of governorate significance that the districts surround.

- **Talas District** is the most densely settled district, with irrigated farmland, the beef plants of the Talas agribusiness zone on the edge of the capital, and the lower reaches of several Talas Alatau valleys whose upper parts lie on the tribal side of the line. To the north it reaches the crest of the Kyrgyz Range, and to the east it runs up the Otmek valley to the north portal of the Otmek Tunnel.
- **Kara-Buura District** is mainly agricultural, growing wheat, barley, beans, potatoes and fodder, and contains the main road crossing into [[wp:Kazakhstan]] from the Talas valley. Besides the seat, Kyzyl-Adyr, its towns include Aulie-Ata, the old Kokand fortress and Russian district town on the Talas where the river leaves the valley, whose Soviet-era city has been cleared back to its old core. Smaller towns include Asa, north of Aulie-Ata, and Sary-Jar and Kyzyl-Kyr on the belt to the west. It also takes in the plain north of the Kyrgyz Range, round the western end of the range and east along the main road and the Turksib railway to the Merke stream, with the northern Toguz-Bulak crossing on the Kök-Bel road. West of the valley it narrows to a belt along the highway and the railway, with the Karatau foothills on both sides lying on the tribal side of the western sector of the Qara-Chik line. The Ak-Tash Training Center of the State Defense Corps lies just beyond the line, on tribal land held under an arrangement with the local clan.
- **Chu District**, the largest by area, combines the irrigated oases around Nurzhan with a belt along the main road and the Turksib railway that runs south-west along the foot of the Kyrgyz Range as far as the Merke stream, where Kara-Buura District begins. It contains the Chu basin oil fields, the rail yards, the Chu Gate crossing, the point where the Chu enters Irad and most of the farming villages of the [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]] outside Nurzhan, and borders Kazakhstan east of the city. Its largest town outside Nurzhan is Merke, on the main road at the foot of the range.
- **Sary-Bulak District** is Irad's mining district. The line bulges south around it to take in the antimony mine and smelter, which are reached from Talas by the Sary-Bulak road through the lower Kara-Suu Canyon. It also includes the foothill villages along the Chatkal road, such as Uuk-Bulak and Tash-Bulak, and Ak-Bulak in the upper Urmaral valley.
- **Lower Naryn District** runs from the workers' town of Kara-Köl, just below the Toktogul dam, to the Uzbek frontier. It holds the switchyard and national dispatch center of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]], the Naryn bridge control post and the downstream power stations, as well as cotton farms and coal mines. It surrounds the city of Iyık Janyl, which is administered separately. Between Kara-Köl and Iyık Janyl it is only a few kilometers wide, holding State Route 1, the river and the lower cascade stations, with tribal mountains on either side. Below Tash-Kömür it widens over the farm belt of the northern Fergana rim, which runs east below the foot of the hills past Bazar-Korgon, the ISEZ's main Muslim town and a border market, and gives the ISEZ about 145 km of frontier with [[wp:Uzbekistan]]. Below Tash-Kömür the district also takes in the mouth of the Naryn gorge, with the Uch-Kurgan dam and power station, where the river leaves Irad. Besides Tash-Kömür and Bazar-Korgon, the district's market towns include Kochkor-Ata and Shamaldy-Say. The frontier follows the foot of the hills, and the Uzbek piedmont towns beyond it, such as Karasu (Qorasuv), Khanabad and Sultanabad in the Andijan oases, lie in Uzbekistan. At its eastern end, round the Kyrgyz city of Jalal-Abad, the district takes in Suzak, Dostuk and the villages on the west bank of the small river that marks the frontier with [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] north of the city, up to the foot of the Kök-Kamar Gorge; the valley villages east of the river are Kyrgyz. UNMI's sector headquarters is at Tash-Kömür.<sup>[8]</sup>
- **Toktogul District**, the newest district, was split from Lower Naryn in 2016. It contains the dam, powerhouse and reservoir of the Toktogul complex, the town of Toktogul on the northern shore, the villages of [[Jele-Döbö]] and [[Kara-Say]] and the [[Uch-Terek Rapids]] at the head of the reservoir. North of the basin it narrows to a corridor a few kilometers wide along State Route 1 up the Chychkan valley, over the Ala-Bel Pass with the Fergana Gateway control post and through the western Suusamyr, with the seasonal camp of [[Karakol-Ashuu]], to the south portal of the Otmek Tunnel. The mountains around it are tribal, and the basin's councils of elders keep their authority over pasture and irrigation under the 2009 protocol.<sup>[8]</sup>

## Autonomous Tribal Regions
The ATR cover about 188,000 km². The official 2018 census estimated their population at about 2.0 million; independent estimates, based on satellite settlement mapping and aid-agency registries, put it at 3.5 to 4 million (see [[2018 Irad census]]).<sup>[9]</sup>

#### Clan territories
Land in the ATR is held by 24 clans, each governed by a council of elders (*aksakals*) and a *biy* under customary law ([[Adat Law in the ATR|adat]]). Village councils (*ayyl kengeshi*) allocate pasture, organize hay cutting and maintain irrigation channels, and pasture boundaries are marked by boundary stones (*bel-tash*). Clan territories are not contiguous blocks: a clan typically holds winter villages in sheltered valleys or on the desert margin and summer pastures (*[[Zhayloo (Pastoral Term)|zhayloo]]*) in the mountains, linked by migration corridors fixed by clan pasture committees. Matters affecting all clans are decided at the summer *[[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|kurultai]]* on the Aksay Plateau, and inter-clan grazing disputes go to the [[Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal]].<sup>[10]</sup> The most politically prominent clan is the Tanıp, whose chief, [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], is the IAC's principal spokesman.

#### UN planning zones
The seven planning zones were drawn by UNMI and aid agencies along physical and logistical lines. The ISEZ divides the tribal land into three separate blocks, north of the plains belt, west of the State Route 1 corridor and the Naryn gorge, and east of them, and each zone lies within one block; in the mountains the boundaries follow crests and the line. Clan territories often cross the zone boundaries. Areas are approximate figures used in UNMI planning documents.<sup>[2]</sup>

The zones are used for aid planning, the scheduling of vaccination and fodder deliveries, mine action and humanitarian reporting. They also appear in UNMI's patrol plans for the tribal side of the line, where five of the mission's eleven team sites are located.<sup>[2]</sup> The IAC does not use them in its own governance, although its Chancellery corresponds with UNMI and aid agencies in their terms.

## The Qara-Chik Demarcation Line
The Qara-Chik line, fixed by the 2007 ceasefire and adjusted in the south in 2009, is the boundary between the two systems. About 1,750 km long, it encloses the irrigated valleys of the Talas and lower Chu, the belts along the main roads and railway that join them and run west to the Kazakh frontier, and, beyond the Talas Alatau, the corridor of State Route 1, the Toktogul basin, a narrow corridor down the Naryn gorge, the river flats of the lower Naryn and the farm belt of the northern Fergana rim. UNMI divides the line into western, central, southern (Naryn and Fergana rim) and northern sectors. The Gendarmerie mans checkpoints at nine crossing points on the ISEZ side, and the [[El-Choro Militias]] keep picket stations on the tribal side. A restricted-weapons zone extends 12 km on either side.<sup>[8]</sup> Neither administration treats the line as an international boundary: the ISEZ describes it as an administrative line within Irad, and the IAC as the limit of the land held by the clans.

Irad's external frontiers with Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan are demarcated only on the sections held by the ISEZ along the Kazakh border, under the 2008 [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]]. The ISEZ also holds about 145 km of the Uzbek frontier along the farm belt of the northern Fergana rim, which is undemarcated; a memorandum on trade and border coordination signed with Uzbekistan in February 2025, not a treaty, set shared customs inspection hours at the main crossings and a joint working group on livestock and cotton shipments. The ATR-held sections follow Soviet-era administrative boundaries that have never been marked on the ground.

The **cinema of Irad** covers film production in Irad and by Iradi filmmakers, from the newsreels of the early Soviet period to the independent and television work of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). Its main period was the Soviet era. Between 1954 and 1991 [[Talasfilm Studios]] in [[Talas]], the feature studio of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]], made almost all Iradi feature films. Critics divide its output into two strands. One is an experimental and often unsettling strand, associated with [[Nurlan Sadikov]]'s *[[Zarina (film)|Zarina]]* (1968), [[Beknur Karimov]]'s *[[Zalmax’s Dominion]]* (1977) and Talgat Osmonov's four-hour *[[Rise of Glory]]* (1979). The other is the "Iradi Western", in Irad usually called the "Eastern", a genre begun by Sadikov's *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]* (1979), which made Irad known in the 1980s as "the West of the East".<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

Feature production almost stopped after the end of Soviet funding and the [[First Iradi Civil War]] of 1992. Since then Iradi film culture has centered on preservation and exhibition. The [[Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation|Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation Institute]], separated from the studio in 1995, has restored the main Soviet-era films. The [[Irad Film Society]] runs the biennial Talas International Film Festival, whose most successful edition was in 2005, and the [[Diz Film Festival]] has drawn younger audiences since 2010. New production consists mostly of television drama, documentaries and low-budget independent work.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

## History

#### Early film and newsreels (1916–1953)
The oldest moving images of Irad are a small group of reels from 1916 to 1924, some copied from Russian military and private sources. They show imperial troops in [[wp:Semirechye]] in the years of the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|1916 revolt]] and the Civil War, early Soviet authorities in the region and ethnographic scenes such as eagle hunting. These reels are now held by the Talasfilm Archives.<sup>[4]</sup>

After the creation of the Iradi SSR in 1925, film reached the republic mainly through traveling projection units sent to collective farms and through newsreels made for the republican press. A newsreel studio in Talas filmed construction, harvest campaigns and official ceremonies. During the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]] several Iradi technicians trained at the Central United Film Studio in [[wp:Almaty|Alma-Ata]], where the main [[wp:Moscow]] and [[wp:Saint Petersburg|Leningrad]] studios were evacuated in 1941–1944. The Talas newsreel studio, where the young Sadikov worked as an assistant cameraman before entering the [[wp:Gerasimov Institute of Cinematography|All-Union State Institute of Cinematography]] (VGIK) in Moscow in 1952, became the nucleus of the later feature studio.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

#### Talasfilm and the first features (1954–1967)
Talasfilm Studios was founded in 1954 as the feature-film studio of the Iradi SSR, and in 1958 it set up a depository for its negatives and prints. Its first features appeared in the late 1950s. Sadikov joined the studio on his return from Moscow in 1957. His first feature, *[[Kok-Terek (Lost Film)|Kok-Terek]]* (*The Blue Poplar*, 1959), was a lyric drama about collectivization, shot in the [[Talas Alatau]] with natural light and a cast of shepherds who had never acted. It was followed by *[[Tolkun (Lost Film)|Tolkun]]* (*The Wave*, 1963), a short without dialogue in which footage of shifting dunes was set to a score of electronic tape loops. *Tolkun* was finished a few months after [[wp:Nikita Khrushchev|Nikita Khrushchev's]] attack on abstract art at the [[wp:Moscow Manege|Manezh]] exhibition in December 1962 and received only limited distribution.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>

Both films were shown only within the republic, and both are now lost. Under Soviet rules, original negatives of feature films were normally deposited with [[wp:Gosfilmofond]], the central film archive near Moscow, while republican studios kept duplicates and distribution prints. Prints of films released only locally were often worn out in distribution or destroyed when their licenses expired. *Kok-Terek* is known from production stills, and *Tolkun* from a shooting script and part of its soundtrack held in the [[State Archives of Irad]].<sup>[5]</sup>

#### *Zarina* and the experimental strand (1968–1978)
The studio intended *Zarina* (1968) as an accessible period adventure set under [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] rule that could earn Talasfilm its first All-Union release. Sadikov restructured it during editing. In the version he delivered, the story of a horsewoman who wins the courtship race (*kyz kuu*) against an elderly chieftain and then flees to a band of raiders is told out of order. It is interrupted by unmarked dream sequences, among them a figure in a bull mask whom Iradi viewers recognized as [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]]. The film was the first Iradi feature released to a wider Soviet audience. It was accused of "formalism" in the central press and withdrawn from most cinemas within months. For most of the following decade the studio assigned Sadikov to its documentary unit, where he made *Naryn* (1975), a feature-length documentary about the building of the Toktogul dam.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

Beknur Karimov, who had joined Talasfilm as a set designer in 1961, began directing in the early 1970s. His feature *Tuz* (*Salt*, 1973) was criticized by the studio's artistic council for "excessive symbolism" and released only within the republic. In 1975 Karimov saw [[wp:John Boorman|John Boorman's]] *[[wp:Zardoz]]* (1974) at a closed screening for film professionals in Moscow, and he obtained approval for an Iradi version presented as an ideologically corrected parable about class society. The approved script followed its source closely. During shooting in 1976 in the industrial zone of Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]) and the Moiynkum sands, Karimov added absurdist episodes that the studio did not see until the first assembly. *Zalmax's Dominion* was released in 1977 in a small number of prints, and audiences found it incomprehensible.<sup>[6]</sup><sup>[7]</sup>

#### The Eastern (1979–1991)
Sadikov returned to features with *Desert Sun’s Rebellion*, which he took over from its original director, Timur Aslanov, at the start of production. It was shot in the summer of 1978 in the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]] and the southern sands with [[Almaz Sarybaev]] in the lead. Set in 1922, it follows a former cavalryman who leads a small crew to steal a herd of requisitioned [[wp:Red Army]] horses back from a warlord's desert stronghold, in a near-wordless thirty-minute theft sequence, before the crew turn on one another on the way back across the sands. The film borrowed the visual language of the Italian western, which Soviet professionals could see at closed screenings: extreme close-ups, long silences and a sparse score combining the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]] with electric guitar. According to Soviet distribution figures it drew about 17.9 million viewers in its first year. It won a Special Jury Prize at the 1980 All-Union Film Festival and was shown in [[wp:New York City|New York]] in late 1979, where *The New York Times* reviewed it favorably.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[8]</sup>

The same year Talasfilm released *Rise of Glory*, a survey of Iradi history from the taming of the first horse to the Soviet present, directed by the former documentarist Talgat Osmonov. Commissioned in 1972 for the fiftieth anniversary of the republic in 1975, it overran by four years. Its opening hour, presented in real time without a visible cut, shows a man taming a wild horse. Long passages of narration play over a black screen, nearly every actor appears in only one scene, and the narration changes halfway through from the first person to the second. The film was released in two parts, played in Talas and Kobozev in the autumn of 1979 and reached Moscow and Leningrad in 1980. Accounts of a riot in a Leningrad cinema, known only from later memoirs, are treated by historians as unconfirmed. Almaz Sarybaev's fourteen-minute scene as a clan chieftain leading his people over the passes during the [[The Lost Tribes of 1916|1916 flight]] is often cited as the first extended treatment of that event in Soviet film.<sup>[9]</sup>

*Desert Sun's Rebellion* set the pattern for Iradi production through the 1980s. Talasfilm made a run of [[wp:Western (genre)|Westerns]], known in Irad as "Easterns", set in the deserts and mountain passes of the republic and usually in the years of the Civil War. Film historians describe them as tightly plotted genre films built around landscape, horsemanship and tension rather than ideological exposition, and note that framing stories as Civil War adventures allowed directors to leave the loyalties of their heroes unresolved.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[8]</sup> The cycle drew on a small pool of actors and crew. Almaz Sarybaev, Gulnara Alimbekova and Erkin Sultanbekov, the hero, the sister and the warlord of *Desert Sun's Rebellion*, reappeared in film after film, Sultanbekov so often as a warlord that the press called him "the Kara-Bek of the Steppe"; Vladimir Pak and Kadyrbek Asylbekov photographed most of the cycle, and Asan Jumabaev's komuz and electric guitar became its sound.<sup>[8]</sup>

The first imitation came within a year. Timur Aslanov, the director whom Sadikov had replaced on *Desert Sun's Rebellion*, was given *[[The Golden Bay]]* (1980), a race across the desert between rival clans with a prize stallion, with Sultanbekov as the villain. It was followed by Beknur Karimov's *[[Desert Blue]]* (1981), starring Alimbekova, whose portrayal of the Karatau tribes and sexualized scenes of attempted assault have drawn criticism in retrospect, and Adil Rakhimov's *[[Guide of the Sands]]* (1981), photographed by Asylbekov, whose nameless wanderer became a stock figure of the genre. Kairat Amankulov's debut, *[[Track of the Snow Leopard]]* (1983), moved the genre into the mountains with a border tracker pursuing smugglers over the Tian Shan passes, and Rakhimov's *[[The Silver Horseshoe]]* (1984) turned it into comedy, with a kolkhoz bookkeeper mistaken for a legendary avenger and Sarybaev in a cameo parodying his own Daniyar; it was the most popular Iradi film of the decade at home. Malik Shakirov's *[[Vengeance Rider]]* (1986), shot by Pak with Sultanbekov as the warlord, is considered the last great Eastern. Amankulov's *[[Journey of the Steppes]]* (1988), in which a young horse trainer lost in a sandstorm tries to bring his three horses home with bandits on his trail, is usually counted as the end of the cycle.<sup>[8]</sup>

Sadikov made no more Easterns and said he had no interest in the genre. He followed his success with *[[Eer (film)|Eer]]* (*The Saddle*, 1982), a quiet drama about an old saddler in Talas, and ended his career with *[[Visions of Irad]]* (1984), an unnarrated documentary of everyday life from the cities to the high pastures, received coolly at the time and now regarded as a national treasure.<sup>[2]</sup>

The decade also brought conflicts with the [[wp:Goskino|State Committee for Cinematography]] (Goskino). Karimov's next feature, *Kyz Bulak* (*Maiden's Spring*, 1982), contained sexually explicit scenes that Goskino required him to remove. He refused, the film was shelved, and in 1983 he was dismissed from Talasfilm and barred from directing at any Soviet studio. *Zalmax's Dominion* was then withdrawn from circulation. *Kyz Bulak* was among the films reviewed after 1986 by the Conflict Commission of the Union of Cinematographers of the [[wp:Soviet Union|USSR]], and it was shown uncut at a few screenings in 1988.<sup>[6]</sup><sup>[7]</sup>

#### Collapse and the territorial period (1989–2006)
Sadikov was artistic director of Talasfilm from 1989 to 1995. During the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] and the civil war that followed, the studio lost heating and power. Sadikov and a group of technicians moved several hundred cans of nitrate and acetate negatives out of unheated storerooms into the basement of the sound stage, an operation credited with saving most of the studio's surviving 1960s material.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[10]</sup>

Under the US territorial administration (see [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)]]) feature production almost ceased. Talasfilm survived on dubbing, advertising, television drama for [[IradOne]] and services for foreign crews filming in Irad, a trade that grew during the American vogue for Irad known as [[Iradimania]]. Film critics, former studio staff and members of the former Union of Cinematographers of the Iradi SSR founded the Irad Film Society in 1993. Its campaign for a separate national archive led to an act of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] in 1995 that reconstituted the studio's depository as the Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation Institute, with Sadikov as its first director until 2008. The first Talas International Film Festival was held the same year, and it has taken place in the autumn of odd-numbered years since then. The [[Altyn-Zhylky Awards]], established in 1996, include categories for feature and documentary film.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[11]</sup>

Karimov made low-budget video works in Talas after 1992, combining found Soviet industrial footage with felt and carpet motifs, and showed them in galleries in Irad and Almaty. Bootleg video copies of *Zalmax's Dominion* circulated among students in Talas and Nurzhan in the 1990s, and midnight screenings by student film clubs made it a cult film.<sup>[7]</sup>

The archive's restoration program began in the early 2000s with support from European film archives and cultural foundations. Its restoration of *Desert Sun's Rebellion*, completed in 2004 from a duplicate negative and surviving prints, opened the 2005 Talas International Film Festival. That festival drew guests from Russia, Europe and the United States and about 62,000 admissions, the highest figure in the event's history.<sup>[11]</sup>

#### Since 2007
The [[Second Iradi Civil War]] interrupted film activity in 2007. The studio and the archive both closed for several months, and the 2007 festival was canceled; it resumed in 2009. Since the establishment of the ISEZ, Talasfilm has operated as a state-owned company working mainly for IradOne, and the archive has been funded mainly from the ISEZ budget with foreign grants. Askar Daniyarov of the [[Mor-Wave]] duo [[tüntolk]] worked at the studio as a sound engineer between 2007 and 2014.<sup>[4]</sup><sup>[10]</sup>

The archive installed a film scanner and a sound restoration suite in 2008. Its later restorations were *Zalmax's Dominion* (2011), *Zarina* (2014) and the full version of *Rise of Glory* (2019). Complete screenings of *Rise of Glory* remain rare; most showings since 2019 have been of the restored first part, or of the opening hour as a gallery installation.<sup>[9]</sup><sup>[10]</sup>

Admissions and foreign participation at the Talas International Film Festival have declined since the late 2000s. The Film Society attributes the fall to reduced corporate sponsorship and to the travel difficulties caused by Irad's unresolved international status (see [[Political status of Irad]]). Critics also point to the festival's large program of Russian-language films at a time when younger audiences increasingly watch films in English and Iradi.<sup>[12]</sup> The Diz Film Festival, founded in 2010 by young filmmakers and critics and held each summer in the courtyards of the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]], concentrates on independent features, documentaries and experimental films from [[wp:Central Asia]], subtitled in Iradi and English.<sup>[13]</sup>

Contemporary production is small. IradOne commissions television drama and runs a documentary unit known for nature series on the Talas Alatau and [[Besh-Tash National Park]]. Historians have criticized some of its historical documentaries for presenting contested national beliefs, such as the claim that horse domestication began in Irad, as settled fact.<sup>[14]</sup> Independent filmmakers, many of them associated with the [[Iradi language revival]], work with digital cameras on short films, music videos and documentaries, often in Iradi. Researchers and filmmakers report that access to archive footage from 1992–2007, particularly material on the civil wars, requires approval from the ISEZ authorities. Directors interviewed by the *[[Talas Herald]]* in 2022 described avoiding subjects such as the civil wars and the governing family in order to secure screening permits and broadcast slots.<sup>[10]</sup><sup>[15]</sup>

## Styles and themes

#### The experimental strand
Writers on Iradi Soviet cinema group *Zarina*, *Zalmax's Dominion* and *Rise of Glory* as an experimental and "unsettling" tendency. The three films differ in method. Sadikov used fragmented chronology, long takes and sound that pulls against the image; Karimov used non-sequitur dialogue, recited timetables, untranslated [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] intertitles and figures in animal masks; and Osmonov used real time, endurance and a shifting narrator. Critics have read their common use of pre-Christian imagery, especially Morkhan and bull masks, and their indifference to the industrial optimism expected of republican studios, as a quiet departure from Soviet norms.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[7]</sup>

#### Landscape and horsemanship
Iradi films of both strands were shot largely on location in the Talas Alatau, the Kara-Suu Canyon and the Moiynkum sands, often in natural light. Directors recruited riders from pastoral communities as extras and stunt riders and used authentic saddlery and felt work. Horses are central to the plots of *Zarina*, *Desert Sun's Rebellion*, *Rise of Glory* and most of the Easterns, *Journey of the Steppes* above all, reflecting the place of the horse in Iradi national identity (see [[Iradi Equestrian Culture & Breeds]]).<sup>[2]</sup>

#### Censorship and religion
Soviet censors objected to Christian as well as formal elements. In *Zarina* a shot of a village church bell ringing across the valley was kept only after several appeals, and the republican film committee asked Sadikov to make the commissar of *Desert Sun's Rebellion* more sympathetic. The [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] was banned in public life for most of the Soviet period, and explicit Christian themes rarely appeared in Iradi film before 1992.<sup>[5]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

## Institutions
- **Talasfilm Studios**, founded in 1954, the only feature studio of the Soviet period and now a state-owned production company.
- **Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation Institute**, on Cinema Boulevard in Talas, the national film archive since 1995. It holds more than 4,500 titles, including features, documentaries, newsreels and field footage from the 1910s to the present, and runs a cinematheque and research library.
- **Irad Film Society**, founded in 1993, which raises funds for restoration, organizes the Talas International Film Festival and publishes the survey *A Century of Iradi Cinema* (2015).
- **Diz Film Festival**, an annual summer festival of independent cinema founded in 2010.
- **Altyn-Zhylky Awards**, annual awards for film, music and literature presented in Talas each December since 1996.

Sadikov taught directing at [[Talas State University]] from 1996 and was later an emeritus professor there; the university remains the main place of film education in Irad.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Preservation and lost films
The original negatives of most Talasfilm features were deposited with Gosfilmofond under Soviet rules and remain in Russia. Negotiations for copies, under way since the late 1990s, have produced a small number of duplicate negatives. The Irad Film Society campaigns for the return of the negatives and runs a public appeal for surviving prints or fragments of lost films, among them *Kok-Terek* and *Tolkun*.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[10]</sup>

## Influence
The Soviet-era films have shaped later Iradi popular culture. Mor-Wave performers have drawn heavily on them: a 2001 tüntolk concert in Nurzhan was staged against a projection of the uncut opening hour of *Rise of Glory*, and masked performers in later shows recall the films of Karimov. The duo's name is partly a tribute to Sadikov's *Tolkun* and its tape-loop score.<sup>[16]</sup> Karimov has a cult following among younger [[Iradis]], and screenings of restored films at the archive's cinematheque are popular with students.<sup>[7]</sup><sup>[15]</sup>
