{{Infobox Christian denomination | name = Syro-Iradi Catholic Church | native_name = *Iradi Sir-Katolik Chirköösü*; *Tarsa Chirkövü* | type = Eastern Catholic particular church *sui iuris* | classification = Catholic | polity = Metropolitan church *sui iuris* (four eparchies) | leader_title = Metropolitan Archbishop of Iyık Janyl | leader = [[Mar Ephrem]] | liturgy = East Syriac ([[wp:Liturgy of Addai and Mari|Liturgy of Addai and Mari]]) | language = Iradi, Classical Syriac | region = [[Irad]]; diaspora communities in [[wp:Chicago]] and [[wp:Houston]] | hq = [[Church of St. Janyl]], [[Iyık Janyl]] | founded = 11th century (tradition); union with Rome 14 September 1931 | members = About 3.4 million (church figure) | website = [Church of St. Janyl](https://mjsbroadbent.github.io/churchofsaintjanyl/) }} The **Syro-Iradi Catholic Church** (Iradi: *Iradi Sir-Katolik Chirköösü*; Latin: *Ecclesia Catholica Syro-Iradiensis*), often called simply the Iradi Church, is an Eastern Catholic particular church *sui iuris* in full communion with the [[wp:Holy See]]. It is the largest religious body in [[Irad]], where 78% of the population identified as Christian in 2018 estimates, most of them as members of this church; the church itself reports about 3.4 million faithful across the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR).[1] The church regards itself as the last surviving branch of the Church of the East's expansion among the Turkic peoples of the [[wp:Qara Khitai]] realm, and tradition ascribes its foundation to the 11th-century figure [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]]. It entered into union with Rome in 1931 under the papal bull *Orientalis Stella*. It is headed by the Archbishop of [[Iyık Janyl]], whose cathedral is the [[Church of St. Janyl]]. Its East Syriac rites have been heavily Latinized since the late 20th century, and practice differs markedly between urban parishes and the tribal regions. ## Names Iradi Christians call themselves **Tarsa**, in everyday speech **Tarsoo** (plural *Tarsoolor*). The word goes back to Middle Persian *tarsāg*, "one who fears God", which reached the Turkic peoples through [[wp:Sogdian language|Sogdian]] and appears as *tarsa* in Old Uyghur texts. Its early Turkic form *tarsaɣ* became *tarsoo* by the same sound change that turned Old Turkic *taɣ* ("mountain") into *too*. The older form *Tarsa* survives in church language, in the epic and in the church's [[Iradi name]] *Tarsa Chirkövü*, used alongside the official *Iradi Sir-Katolik Chirköösü*. Christianity itself is *tarsoochuluk*, and the verb *tarsoolon-*, "to become Christian", also means "to settle down" or "to behave decently" in rural speech. Hymns use the poetic name *Janyldyktar*, "Janyl's people".[2] Uzbek speakers in the [[wp:Fergana Valley|Fergana Valley]] call Iradi Christians *joniliklar* ("Janyl's people"), and older Muslim clergy use the formal *Jonil ahli*. Tajik speakers use the literary Persian *tarso*, so Iradis hear their own name used by their neighbors as a learned word. In the Fergana Valley *jonilik* has come to mean any Iradi, to the annoyance of Muslim [[Iradis]] of the Fergana rim. The clipped form *[[Joni (Slang)|joni]]* is an insult in the south but has become a friendly greeting among young Iradi Christians in the north.[2] For harsher terms and the history of hostility toward the church, see [[Anti-Christian sentiment in Irad]]. ## History #### Origins and the Janyl tradition In the 11th and 12th centuries, missionaries of the Church of the East converted Turkic pastoralists along the [[wp:Silk Road]], among them the [[wp:Keraites]] and the [[wp:Naimans]], and [[wp:Church of the East|East Syriac Christianity]] flourished under the religiously tolerant Qara Khitai.[3] According to church tradition, the noblewoman Janyl, venerated as the "Mother of Irad", received a vision of Christ in the form of the White Rider, who led her to the site of the First Church of Janyl, and her covenant united the Christian clans. Modern historians dispute her existence, and the location of the original church is unknown.[4] #### Persecution and survival Under the Chagatai khan Ali-Sultan (1339–1342) and during the campaigns of [[wp:Timur]] later in the 14th century, the church's dioceses were destroyed. Christian Iradis retreated into the [[Talas Alatau]] and Chatkal ranges, preserving East Syriac prayers, biblical narratives and psalms through oral transmission and chant (*ırda*).[3] #### Kokand restoration In 1727 Khan Abd al-Rahim Biy of [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]], rewarding the service of Iradi Christian cavalry against the [[wp:Dzungar people|Dzungars]], granted religious tolerance under the [[Treaty of Talas (1727)]] and paid for the Church of St. Janyl, built as a symbolic re-creation of the lost first church. The city of Iyık Janyl grew up around it. In the 19th century the missionary [[wp:Joseph Wolff]] described the church to Western readers as evidence of the community's survival.[5] #### Union with Rome and Soviet repression After the Russian Revolution, Bishop [[Mar Timotheos Alimbekov]] sought union with the Holy See. Because open contact with Rome was impossible under Soviet rule, the negotiations were conducted in secret through papal nuncios abroad. On 14 September 1931, [[wp:Pope Pius XI]] issued the bull *Orientalis Stella*, receiving the Iradi church into full communion as a church *sui iuris* that kept its East Syriac liturgical tradition.[6] Soviet suspicion of the church's link with Rome, which officials tied to fears of fascist influence through the [[wp:Catholic Church]], fed the anti-religious campaigns of the 1930s. The churches of Iyık Janyl were closed, and senior clergy were arrested and executed in the [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges|1937 purges]].[6] The church survived in secret for the rest of the Soviet period, with liturgies held in homes and in the mountain camps of the herding clans. #### Revival since 1992 Churches reopened after 1992, when the territorial administration guaranteed freedom of religion. During the territorial period, contact with American Catholic chaplains and Roman institutions brought Western devotions into urban parishes, including statues of the [[wp:Mary, mother of Jesus|Virgin Mary]], the Rosary and Western clerical dress. Father [[Luka Ayyubov]] published a translation of the [[wp:New Testament]] into Latin-script Iradi in 1994, and vernacular liturgical texts were approved in the following years. The Church of St. Janyl was inscribed as a [[wp:World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] during the territorial period on a US nomination.[7] ## Organization The church has four eparchies. The Archeparchy of Iyık Janyl (see [[Archbishopric of Iyık Janyl]]) has metropolitan authority over suffragan eparchies in [[Talas]], [[Nurzhan]] and the highland parishes of the Chatkal basin. The archbishop presides over the [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs]], which proposes candidates for bishop for papal confirmation under the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches. The current archbishop, [[Mar Ephrem]], has served since 2012.[1] | Eparchy | Rank | See | Bishop | |---|---|---|---| | Iyık Janyl | Metropolitan archeparchy | Iyık Janyl (Church of St. Janyl) | Mar Ephrem (since 2012) | | [[Talas]] | Suffragan eparchy | [[Talas]] ([[Cathedral of the Resurrection, Talas|Cathedral of the Resurrection]]) | Mar Toma Usenov | | Nurzhan | Suffragan eparchy | Nurzhan | Mar Yakob Kim | | Chatkal Highlands | Suffragan eparchy | No fixed seat; the bishop lives at Iyık Janyl and visits the parishes on horseback from spring to autumn | Mar Narsai Abdykerimov | Diocesan clergy are trained at the [[Cathedral Seminary of Iyık Janyl|St. Ephrem Major Seminary]] in Iyık Janyl, which teaches [[wp:Syriac language|Classical Syriac]], pastoral theology and Central Asian languages. Monastic life centers on the [[Order of St. Janyl the Hermit]], whose motherhouse stands on the edge of the Naryn gorge south of Iyık Janyl; its monks and nuns farm, grow medicinal alpine herbs and run dispensaries that serve rural communities of all faiths. ## Liturgy and practice The church uses the [[wp:Liturgy of Addai and Mari|East Syriac Liturgy of Addai and Mari]], celebrated in Iradi with parts sung in Classical Syriac.[8] Its liturgical vocabulary retains Sogdian and other Iranian roots, a legacy of the Sogdian-speaking communities among which the faith first spread. Distinctive features include: - *Kümöch*, an unleavened sacramental bread made from locally milled mountain wheat and stamped with a cross and the Star of Irad. Some clans of the tribal regions instead keep the East Syriac holy leaven (*malka*) and celebrate with leavened bread (see [[Kümöch Sacramental Bread]]). - Incense of *[[Mountain Juniper (Arsha)|arsha]]* (mountain juniper, *Juniperus semiglobosa*), gathered by monastic novices in the ravines of the Talas Alatau and burned alongside or instead of frankincense. - Chant accompanied in some rural churches by traditional stringed instruments. The main annual celebration is the Feast of St. Janyl on 24 August, when mounted pilgrims ride to [[Cathedral Hill]] in Iyık Janyl for the blessing of the herds (see [[Feast of St. Janyl]]). ## Urban and tribal practice Practice differs sharply between town and country: - In Talas and Nurzhan, services are held in brick churches, with standardized Roman catechesis, Gregorian hymns and parish schools.[7] - In the ATR, itinerant priests celebrate in felt yurts (*ak-örgöö*), bless horse herds and seasonal pastures, and lead open-air midnight liturgies. Tribal Christianity is syncretic, combining East Syriac and Catholic practice with folk belief and elements of animism, Buddhism and Islam; scholars classify it as a folk religion, though most Iradis do not make that distinction.[4] ## Church, state and other faiths Since the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], the church has taken part in civic mediation. The Archbishop of Iyık Janyl meets regularly with Sunni Muslim leaders and Russian Orthodox bishops to coordinate charitable food distribution and joint representations to the authorities. Relations with the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] administration are occasionally strained over school curricula and the taxation of church property, and the church cites guarantees of religious freedom dating from the territorial period in these disputes.[7] ## Manuscripts and heritage The [[Cathedral Seminary Library of Iyık Janyl]] holds more than 600 manuscripts, including 11th-century Syriac Gospel lectionaries, Sogdian merchant correspondence and papal letters dating back to the 13th-century envoys of [[wp:Pope Innocent IV]]. Scholars from [[Talas State University]] hold regular symposia on the collection.[9] ## See also - [[Yuhanna of Merv]] ## References

For the 2007 conflict, see [[Second Iradi Civil War]].}} {{Infobox military conflict | conflict = First Iradi Civil War | date = 11 March – 18 August 1992 | place = [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] (present-day Irad) | result = Provisional Government and US victory; [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] and [[Operation Starlight|US intervention]]; End of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] | territory = Irad becomes an organized, unincorporated territory of the United States ([[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]]) | combatant1 = [[Provisional Government of Irad (1992)|Provisional Government of the Republic of Irad]];[[wp:United States]] (from June 1992) | combatant2 = [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] | commander1 = [[Amanbek Alimbekov]];[[Kuban Mamytov]];[[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]] | commander2 = [[Vasily Chernov]] | units1 = Student militias;Defected police;Workers' detachments;Mounted clan irregulars;[[wp:United States Marine Corps|US Marines]];10th Mountain Division | units2 = 17th Motor Rifle Division;[[wp:OMON]];Interior troops | strength1 = US: c. 8,000–10,000 (peak ground deployment, late July) | strength2 = 9,000–14,000 (June 1992, Iradi estimates) | casualties1 = US: 94 dead, 361 wounded (US Department of Defense) | casualties2 = Many conscripts deserted;Heavy equipment seized | casualties3 = c. 14,000 military and civilian dead (Provisional and territorial records);9,000 to over 20,000 (independent estimates);Tens of thousands displaced from Talas }} The **First Iradi Civil War** (11 March – 18 August 1992) was fought between the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] (SRI), the post-Soviet communist state based in Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]), and the Provisional Government of the Republic of Irad in [[Talas]]. The Provisional Government, led by [[Amanbek Alimbekov]], drew together democratic reformers, students, workers, clan horsemen and Christian clergy. The war began when the Provisional Government proclaimed the Republic of Irad on 11 March 1992, after the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] had driven SRI officials out of Talas.[1] SRI forces, built around a former Soviet motor rifle division, besieged Talas in April and May 1992. With the city close to collapse, the Provisional Government signed the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] with the United States on 2 June 1992, giving up independence in exchange for military protection. The US intervention, [[Operation Starlight]], lifted the siege in June and advanced on Kobozev, which fell on 12 August. The last SRI forces surrendered on 18 August, and Irad became an organized, unincorporated territory of the United States under the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]]. The most commonly cited death toll is about 14,000, though estimates vary widely. The war's outcome, including the fourteen-year [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)|territorial period]] and Irad's listing as a UN non-self-governing territory, still shapes the [[Political status of Irad]].[2] ## Background #### The Socialist Republic of Irad On 9 October 1991, the [[Communist Party of Irad]], led by its First Secretary [[Vasily Chernov]], declared the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic|Iradi SSR]] independent as the Socialist Republic of Irad ([[Declaration of State Sovereignty (1991)]]), with its government in Kobozev. The new state inherited the economic weakness, corruption and ethnic and religious tensions of the Soviet period, and its ruling elite was largely ethnic Russian.[1] Once Soviet subsidies, ruble clearing and fuel deliveries ended, factories in Kobozev stopped work, inflation exceeded 1,000 percent and food supplies to Talas broke down. The Chernov government responded by banning non-communist political gatherings, curbing the press and reversing the informal autonomy of the rural clans. Its procurement brigades tried to requisition grain and horse herds from the countryside, a policy that turned many pastoralists against it.[3] The SRI took over the former Soviet units stationed in the republic, including the 17th Motor Rifle Division garrisoned around Kobozev, together with republican [[wp:OMON]] riot police and interior troops. #### The Winter Uprising The Winter Uprising began with protests in Talas in December 1991; a strike at the Kobozev railway depot on 14 January 1992 spread to factories across the valley, while students occupied the central square of Talas. On 3 February, security forces fired on demonstrators in Talas; accounts of the number killed differ. Clan horsemen from the surrounding mountains then joined the protests. On 18 February, in what became known as the [[March of the Thousand Saddles]], several thousand mounted pastoralists rode into Talas and formed a cordon around the demonstrators. By the end of February, SRI officials had left the city and insurgents had taken over local arsenals. Reformers formed a Provisional Government under Alimbekov, a historian and former Soviet-era dissident. [[Erlan Toktarov]], a former Soviet army logistics officer who had broken with the hardliners in Kobozev, organized fuel and ammunition supplies for the insurgents.[4] On 11 March 1992, an assembly of reformers and clan elders in the Talas municipal theater adopted the *Declaration of Restoration of the Republic of Irad* and elected Alimbekov provisional president ([[Talas Town Hall Meeting (1992)]]). The date is commemorated as Irad Day ([[March 11 Independence Day]]). ## Course of the war #### Opening phase (March 1992) When the war began, the SRI held Kobozev, the Chu lowlands, the oil fields and the main railway. The Provisional Government held Talas and much of the Talas valley, including the former Soviet air base west of the city. Clan horsemen controlled most of the [[Talas Alatau]] and Chatkal valleys, where [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], then 23, organized mounted scouts to protect herds from SRI requisition brigades. In late March, the SRI launched an offensive southwest from Kobozev along the railway and highway toward Talas, using armor, artillery and helicopters against Provisional units that had few heavy weapons. #### Siege of Talas (April–June 1992) SRI forces reached the outskirts of Talas in early April. From 10 April the city was shelled with artillery and rockets, and for weeks fighting went on in its industrial suburbs. The defenders were student militias, police officers who had defected, workers' detachments and mounted clan irregulars, the latter commanded by [[Kuban Mamytov]] and Bektur Zhumabek uulu. They had weapons taken from SRI arsenals, including anti-tank rockets. Alimbekov stayed in the city throughout the siege. Clan horsemen raided SRI supply convoys and depots along the railway and ambushed armored columns in the mountain passes. Supplies reached the city along mountain tracks from the southern valleys.[5] By late May the water supply had been cut, ammunition was running out and much of the population had fled into the mountains. Parts of the old city had been reduced to rubble. Among the civilian dead was the film director Malik Shakirov, killed when mortar fire struck his home. #### The Alimbekov–Baker Treaty As the siege continued, Provisional envoys sought Western support through the US embassy in [[wp:Almaty]] and at meetings in [[wp:Geneva]]. On 2 June 1992, Alimbekov and [[wp:James Baker|US Secretary of State James Baker]] signed the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty in Talas, and the Provisional Government ratified it the same day. Under the treaty, Irad gave up its independence to become an organized, unincorporated territory of the United States in exchange for military protection, the defense of its borders and economic reconstruction.[2] #### Operation Starlight (June–August 1992) The first [[wp:United States Marine Corps|US Marines]] were airlifted into the airfield west of Talas on 6 June. [[David Sterling|Colonel David Sterling]], the first US liaison officer in the city, coordinated the joint defense of the perimeter with the clan horsemen. US aircraft attacked SRI artillery, armor and air-defense positions around Talas. By 18 June, as units of the 10th Mountain Division arrived, the siege lines had been broken and SRI forces were withdrawing northeast along the railway.[6] In July, US and Provisional forces advanced together along the railway corridor toward Kobozev, with Iradi cavalry screening the flanks in the foothills. Most of the northern steppe clans stayed out of the war, but riders of the clans along the Chu fought under the Boztorgoy war leader [[Kudaibergen Duishön uulu]], who was killed at the railhead. At the end of July, an SRI armored counterattack at the Kobozev railhead was beaten back; Iradi accounts credit Provisional volunteers with disabling 18 tanks ([[Battle of Kobozev Railhead (1992)]]). Kobozev fell on 12 August. On 18 August 1992, the remaining SRI forces surrendered unconditionally, and Chernov was given safe conduct to Russia under arrangements negotiated by the United States. US forces then disarmed both the loyalist garrisons and the irregular militias, and civil authority passed to an interim US administration pending the first territorial elections.[6] ## Casualties and humanitarian impact No complete count of the dead exists. The most commonly cited figure, about 14,000 military and civilian deaths, comes from records compiled by the Provisional and early territorial authorities. Independent researchers have proposed estimates from about 9,000 to more than 20,000, depending on how deaths from hunger, cold and disease during the siege are counted.[7] Most deaths occurred in and around Talas. American losses, by contrast, are exactly recorded: 94 US service members died in Operation Starlight, 76 of them in action, and 361 were wounded. Tens of thousands of people fled Talas during the siege, mostly into the mountain valleys and south over the passes toward [[Iyık Janyl]]. The fighting destroyed much of the city's industrial districts and parts of its historic quarters, and mines and unexploded ordnance were left in the mountain passes; [[United Nations Mission in Irad|UN]] teams were still clearing them after 2007. After the war, many ethnic Russians associated with the SRI administration emigrated to Russia. ## International reaction [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], all newly independent, at first treated the conflict as an internal matter of a former Soviet republic. Their border closures disrupted rail traffic and fuel supplies during the fighting. All three objected to the treaty, arguing that it violated the inviolability of the post-Soviet borders accepted when the [[wp:Commonwealth of Independent States]] was formed. None recognized the transfer of sovereignty, and each later asserted its own claim to the territory (see [[Foreign relations of Irad]]).[8] The Russian government protested against US military action in the former Soviet space and raised the safety of Russian-speaking residents, but did not intervene. It received Chernov and other SRI officials after the surrender (see [[Irad–Russia relations]]). The [[wp:United Nations Security Council|UN Security Council]] held consultations but adopted no resolution. Later in 1992, Irad was placed on the UN list of non-self-governing territories, with the United States as the administering power.[8] In the United States, the intervention prompted a short-lived public fascination with Irad, later called [[Iradimania]] (1992–1994). Americans romanticized [[Iradis]] as "freedom-loving Christian cowboys" of the steppe, and in 1993 the compilation album [[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|*Swift Hooves*]] raised money for Christian charities in Irad. ## Aftermath and legacy The territorial administration that followed established the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]], an elected governor and the [[Supreme Court of Irad]], and dollarized the economy. Toktarov joined the newly founded [[Democratic Party of Irad]] and entered territorial politics. Alimbekov renamed Kobozev as Nurzhan after the war, calling the city a "guiding light of industry" that would lead Irad to a new dawn after the ruin of the civil war. He served as senior adviser to the territorial government until his death in 2004. The war is commemorated on Irad Day, and the inverted horseshoe on the [[Flag of Irad]], which represents the [[Fallen Rider Tradition]], honors those killed in the civil wars along with the victims of 1916 and the Soviet purges. Memory of the war differs between communities. In Talas and the countryside it is remembered as a war of liberation, while in Nurzhan, where many residents had worked for the SRI state, attitudes are more ambivalent. Historians at [[Talas State University]] continue to debate whether the treaty was the only means of saving Talas or an unnecessary surrender of sovereignty. Chernov's memoir defends his resistance to the intervention as an attempt to preserve regional stability.[3] The settlement also left divisions that resurfaced later. Clan leaders kept their distance from the territorial authorities, and the urban–rural divide of 1992 reappeared in 2007, when clan militias stormed Talas during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. ## References

The **Autonomous Tribal Regions** (ATR; Iradi: *Avtonomduk Uruk Jerleri*; Russian: *Автономные племенные территории*) are the parts of [[Irad]] held by its pastoral clans rather than by the government of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). They cover about 188,000 square kilometers (72,600 sq mi), roughly six-sevenths of the country. They stretch from the [[Betpak-Dala]] steppe and the Moiynkum sands in the north, through the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] and [[Talas Alatau]] ranges and the high Kyrgyz Range, to the Chatkal valley, the mountains around the Toktogul basin and the hills above the northern rim of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] in the south. Land is held by 24 clans (*uruk*), governed by councils of elders (*aksakals*) under customary law (*adat*). The clans coordinate loosely through the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (*Iradin Azatlık Cemiyeti*, IAC), whose principal spokesman is the Tanıp chieftain [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]].<sup>[1]</sup>

The ATR took their present form at the end of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. In September 2007 the UN-brokered [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] fixed the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], now about 1,750 kilometers long, between the clan-held countryside and the river valleys governed by the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI). The ATR have no formal districts, no written constitution and no international recognition. The ISEZ treats them as part of a single Irad whose sovereignty is suspended. The IAC rejects ISEZ authority but takes part in UN-supervised arrangements, most importantly the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]] for the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]], whose dam lay on the tribal side of the line until it passed to the ISEZ in 2009 in exchange for pasture, water rights and a guaranteed share of the revenue. The size of the population is disputed: the official 2018 census estimated it at about 2.0 million, while independent estimates range from about 3.5 to 4 million.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Geography
By area, the ATR consist mostly of steppe and desert rangeland in the north and west and of high mountains in the south. Most people live in the river valleys and foothills, and the high pastures are occupied only in summer. Several of the rivers that irrigate the ISEZ valleys, including the [[Talas River|Talas]] and the [[Kara-Buura]], rise in mountains on the tribal side of the line, and the [[Naryn River|Naryn]] enters Irad through tribal gorges and is fed by tribal catchments before it reaches the Toktogul reservoir. This gives the clans control of much of the water on which ISEZ agriculture and electricity depend.<sup>[3]</sup>

The [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) and aid agencies divide the ATR into seven planning zones. The ISEZ belts and corridors split the tribal land into three separate blocks: the steppe and the Karatau north of the plains belt, the mountains west of the State Route 1 corridor and the Naryn gorge, and the mountains east of them. Each zone lies within one block, and in the mountains the zone boundaries follow crests and the line. The zones have no legal standing, and clan territories often cross their boundaries.<sup>[3]</sup>
- Northern Steppe: the southern Betpak-Dala north of the Chu, the Moiynkum (Muyunkum) sands and the Chu–Sarysu lowland, and the piedmont plain north of the ISEZ belt, including the low plain north-east of the Karatau. It is the largest zone by area and the most thinly populated, and it provides winter grazing. The undeveloped [[Muyunkum Natural Gas Field]] lies here.
- Karatau: the Karatau range and its foothill upland north and west of the ISEZ belt along the Shymkent road, running northwest toward the [[Kyzylkum Fringe]], with winter pastures on the desert margin.
- Talas Alatau: the north slope and crest of the Talas Alatau above the Talas valley, from the [[wp:Aksu-Zhabagly Nature Reserve|Aksu-Zhabagly]] reserve on the Kazakh frontier east to the State Route 1 corridor, with summer pastures above 2,500 meters on the [[Aksay Plateau]]; it also takes in the head of the Uzun-Akmat valley south of the crest, the winter country of the Tanıp clan.
- Chatkal Highlands: everything south of the Talas Alatau crest and west of the State Route 1 corridor and the Naryn gorge: the Chatkal valley and range, including the [[Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve|Sary-Chelek]] reserve, walnut and wild-fruit forests and the settlements of [[Kanysh-Kiya]] and [[Terek-Sai]], the Uzun-Akmat valley above the Toktogul Reservoir, and the hills west of the Naryn down to the Fergana rim.
- Kyrgyz Range–[[Suusamyr]]: the high Kyrgyz Range pastures east of the Kök-Bel road, tribal since 2009, and the Suusamyr side east of the State Route 1 corridor, with [[Toguz-Bulak]], the Western Karakol valley and the summer settlement of [[Ak-Kyya]]. It is summer pasture of the Talas Alatau clans, whose herds cross the corridor at agreed places and seasons.
- Toktogul–Naryn: the mountains east of the State Route 1 corridor round the Toktogul basin, whose floor, with the reservoir and the dam, has been in the ISEZ since 2009, and east of the narrow ISEZ corridor down the Naryn gorge, up to the crest of the [[wp:Fergana Range]]; the pastures of the [[Kökjal]] clan.
- Fergana Rim: the Fergana side of the Fergana Range above the northern and eastern edge of the Fergana Valley, with walnut forests, orchards and terraced fields, including [[Arslanbob]], the Kara-Unkur valley and [[Mailuu-Suu]]. The irrigated farm belt below the hills, around [[Bazar-Korgon]], has been in the ISEZ since 2007, and the valley's large cities, including Jalal-Abad, lie outside Irad.

The climate is continental. Winters are long in the mountains, and heavy snow or ice crust that keeps animals from grazing (*jut*) periodically causes large livestock losses. Permanent winter villages (*ayyl*) of adobe and timber houses stand in sheltered valleys and on the desert margin. In summer, families move to felt yurts (*boz üy*) on the high pastures (*[[Zhayloo (Pastoral Term)|zhayloo]]*), of which the Aksay Plateau is the largest. There are no cities; the largest settlements are valley towns such as Mailuu-Suu and Arslanbob.

## History

#### Before 2007
Clan grazing territories predate the modern state. Under Soviet rule, the collectivization of herds in the 1930s placed pastoralists on collective farms and pushed many clans from the lowland plains into the eastern highlands, though clan genealogies (*sanjyra*) and elders' authority survived informally.<sup>[4]</sup> In 1992 clan horsemen joined the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] and fought for the Provisional Government in the [[First Iradi Civil War]]. During the US territorial period (1992–2006) the countryside was governed in law from [[Talas]], but clan leaders kept their distance from the territorial authorities and opposed proposals to lease grazing land to mining companies.

#### Second Civil War and partition
After the United States withdrew from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] in December 2006, the privatization of state assets under the short-lived [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] provoked protests across the country. On 25 February 2007, [[Erlan Toktarov]] proclaimed the ISEZ from [[Nurzhan]]. In March 2007, clan militias under Bektur Zhumabek uulu formed the [[Popular Front of Irad]], which stormed Talas on 4 June 2007 and brought down the DRI government. Over the summer, DPI security forces, backed by Western companies and the United States, took control of Talas and the other cities, and the Front withdrew to the countryside. The September 2007 ceasefire fixed the resulting division. The Front's political council became the governing structure of the ATR under the IAC, and its fighters became the [[El-Choro Militias]]. UNMI was established on 18 October 2007 to monitor the line.

#### Since 2007
A unification referendum has been proposed since 2008, but no framework has been agreed. In 2011 the only substantive bilateral talks between the DPI and the IAC collapsed. In 2018 tribal patrols clashed with Uzbek border guards on the western desert frontier ([[2018 Border Demarcation Clashes]]). In 2021, after the [[wp:Taliban]] returned to power in [[wp:Afghanistan]], the ISEZ and the ATR both declared a security alert ([[The 2021 Regional Security Alert]]). Governor Toktarov's absence from public view since July 2024 has raised questions about who would sign for the ISEZ at the 2027 renewal of the Naryn Protocol. Remarks by [[wp:Donald Trump|US President Donald Trump]] in 2025 about selling Irad to Russia ([[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]) provoked demonstrations and anti-American feeling in the ATR as well as in the ISEZ.

## Government and politics

#### Clans
Rural Iradis in the ATR belong by patrilineal descent to one of 24 recognized clans (*uruk*), whose genealogies are kept orally by elders. Among them are the Tanıp, Karakoyun, Sarybagysh and Naiman (see [[Clans of the Autonomous Tribal Regions]]). Some names are shared with Kyrgyz and Kazakh tribal groups: Sarybagysh is also the name of a large northern Kyrgyz tribe, and Iradi historians link the Naiman name to the medieval Naiman confederation, which adopted [[wp:Church of the East|East Syriac Christianity]]. The Tanıp is the most politically prominent clan. Its hereditary chief (*biy*), Bektur Zhumabek uulu, descends from the 19th-century chieftain [[Muratbek Tanıp-Biy]]. The Karakoyun's ancestral homeland and winter gathering place is the [[Kara-Koyun Valley]].

Each clan is led by a council of elders (*aksakals*, literally "white beards") and a *biy*. Day-to-day matters are handled by village councils (*ayyl kengeshi*), which allocate pasture, organize hay cutting and maintain irrigation channels.<sup>[5]</sup>

#### The Kurultai and the Iradi Freedom Society
Matters affecting all clans, such as common defense, migration corridors and relations with the ISEZ, are decided at the *Kurultai*, a pan-clan assembly of elders, pasture captains and militia commanders. It meets each August on the Aksay Plateau and decides by consensus among the leading lineages (see [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)]]). The IAC has no formal executive. Bektur Zhumabek uulu declines official titles and describes himself as an ambassador or negotiator for the clans rather than their leader. A small secretariat, the [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]], keeps records and handles liaison with UNMI and aid agencies.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Customary law
Clan elders and recognized judges (*biys*) hear civil, family, grazing and criminal disputes under *adat*, independently of the statutory courts under the [[Supreme Court of Irad]]. *Adat* favors restitution and reconciliation over imprisonment. Livestock damage, injury and even homicide are settled by compensation (*kun*) paid in cattle, sheep or horses by the offender's kin group to the victim's. Pasture boundaries are marked by boundary stones (*bel-tash*). Inter-clan grazing disputes go to the [[Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal]], seven senior judges who sit each summer on the Aksay Plateau. The Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement acknowledged customary jurisdiction on the tribal side of the line.<sup>[5]</sup> Parish priests often sit with the elders at hearings (see [[Adat Law in the ATR]]). Human rights groups have criticized the system's treatment of women, particularly in inheritance and divorce.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Security
Security in the ATR rests with the El-Choro Militias, an estimated 15,000 part-time mounted irregulars organized by clan and armed with light infantry weapons. They man picket stations along the Qara-Chik line and patrol the borders with [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]]. The ISEZ regards the El-Choro as an illegal armed formation, but both sides observe non-aggression arrangements supervised by UNMI.<sup>[3]</sup> Until 2009 El-Choro detachments guarded the Toktogul dam, within sight of the ISEZ's [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] at the switchyard; under the 2009 corridor protocol they handed the dam over to the Gendarmerie and withdrew to the pastures above the basin.<sup>[7]</sup>

Tribal militias and smugglers use sections of the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]], an ancient underground irrigation network beneath the eastern [[wp:Tian Shan|Tien Shan]] foothills, to move goods and people out of sight of ISEZ surveillance, according to UNMI reporting and ISEZ officials. Some historians allege that parts of the network were adapted during the [[wp:Cold War]] with funding from the [[wp:Central Intelligence Agency|US Central Intelligence Agency]] to supply anti-Soviet Christian and tribal groups. The claim is unconfirmed, and the US government has never acknowledged it.

## Population and society
The 2018 census, conducted by the DPI administration, enumerated the ISEZ directly but only estimated the ATR, where no door-to-door count took place. It put the tribal population at about 2.0 million, or 43 percent of the national total of 4,626,000.<sup>[8]</sup> Independent demographers, drawing on satellite settlement mapping, aid-agency registries and vaccination records, estimate the ATR population at 3.5 to 4 million, which would bring the national figure to about 6.2 million. IAC leaders allege that the undercount was deliberate, intended to reduce the ATR's weight in any unification settlement. The DPI maintains that its estimate used the best data available.<sup>[2]</sup> (See [[2018 Irad census]].)

Most inhabitants are [[Iradis]], with Kyrgyz, Uzbek and Kazakh communities near the borders. Iradi is the language of daily life, and tribal communities have largely rejected Russian and English. Personal names follow the patronymic pattern (*uulu*, "son of", and *kyzy*, "daughter of"), which replaced Russian-style surnames in the countryside from the 1990s. Most Iradis in the ATR belong to the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], but rural practice is distinctive. Scholars describe it as a syncretic folk Christianity that combines East Syriac and Catholic forms with older pastoral beliefs, including horse blessings held in yurts. Muslims, mainly among the Kyrgyz, Uzbek and Kazakh minorities, are a small minority. Clan authorities enforce the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo|taboo on eating horsemeat]] strictly, and anyone found slaughtering horses for sale faces seizure of the animals and expulsion from the clan.

## Economy
Most households live from transhumant pastoralism. In late spring, families take their fat-tailed sheep, goats, cattle and [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses from the winter villages to the high pastures. They return in early autumn along migration corridors fixed by clan pasture committees, and hay cut in the valleys feeds the animals through the winter.<sup>[9]</sup> Mare's milk is fermented into *[[Kymyz (Iradi Beverage)|kymyz]]*. Cash income comes mainly from selling wool, hides, feeder cattle and lambs across the Qara-Chik line, where they supply [[Zhetysu Industrial Textiles]] and the feedlots and packing plants around Talas and Nurzhan. Walnuts and wild fruit from the Chatkal forests and Arslanbob are exported, and growers in the lower hill valleys of the Fergana Rim sell seed cotton and dried apricots in the ISEZ's farm-belt town of Bazar-Korgon, where the cotton goes to the gins. Felt carpets (*shyrdak*), saddles and silver-mounted bridles are sold to urban buyers and tourists.

Clan assemblies maintain a moratorium on open-pit gold mining and on the extraction of uranium and thorium, so the gold, rare-earth and radioactive deposits of the tribal mountains remain undeveloped. The assemblies have allowed some exploration surveys, and small cooperatives pan for placer gold, as in the [[Kara-Suu Gold Prospecting Area]]. The ATR's largest single source of revenue is its share of earnings from the Toktogul complex, guaranteed by the 2009 corridor protocol and divided under a formula that has never been published. Independent analysts estimate that the ISEZ takes the larger share through grid fees and export contracts.<sup>[7]</sup> The US dollar and the [[Iradi som]] both circulate, but much rural trade is conducted in barter or livestock. Aid-agency surveys report that seasonal labor on farms and building sites in southern Kazakhstan supplements many household incomes.<sup>[3]</sup>

## Relations with the ISEZ and the United Nations
Relations between the ATR and the ISEZ combine political non-recognition with practical interdependence. Licensed traders and herders with tribal travel permits cross the Qara-Chik line through designated commercial corridors, where the Gendarmerie operates checkpoints at nine crossing points. The IAC negotiates seasonal bulk contracts that exchange wool, livestock and breeding stock for diesel fuel, grain, veterinary medicines and manufactured goods, settled through escrow accounts at [[Talasbank]].<sup>[1]</sup>

Talks on reunification have made little progress. In 2011, in the only substantive bilateral negotiations ([[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]]), the IAC walked out after being offered one-third of the seats in a unified legislature, a share its delegates said did not reflect the ATR's population or its six-sevenths of the land. Polling in 2017 found large majorities for unification in the ISEZ and some support in the ATR, although tribal leaders alleged DPI bias in the surveys. Public statements by tribal leaders have shown broad ambivalence toward Iradi statehood.

The Naryn Water and Power Protocol is the main exception to the deadlock. A joint technical commission of ISEZ and ATR engineers sets Toktogul's annual release schedule under UNMI supervision, with observers from Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan. The 2009 corridor protocol, which moved the dam into the ISEZ, kept the tribal delegation's equal place on the commission and made the clans' consent a condition of each five-year schedule. Tribal elders have used this customary veto over drawing down the reservoir to bargain for compensation for flooded pastures, while ISEZ officials accuse them of obstructing export contracts. The five-year schedule falls due for renewal in 2027.<sup>[7]</sup>

UNMI patrols the demarcation line with unarmed military observers, mediates local disputes over strayed livestock and water, coordinates mine clearance and arranges humanitarian access to the tribal side. Bektur Zhumabek uulu is its main interlocutor in the ATR. The [[wp:Special Committee on Decolonization|UN Special Committee on Decolonization]], which lists Irad as a non-self-governing territory, covers the ATR in its annual working paper on the territory.<sup>[1]</sup> Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan each claim Irad *de jure* and deal with the ATR mainly through border and water arrangements.

## Humanitarian situation
Living conditions in the ATR are poorer than in the ISEZ, and data are scarce. Many highland settlements have no year-round road access. Although the Toktogul complex lies just below the tribal mountains, UNMI reports that some remote villages have no grid electricity and rely on small generators or solar panels.<sup>[3]</sup> Health care rests on village health posts, mobile clinics run since 1996 by the [[St. Luka Community Health Mission|Luka Community Health Mission]] of the Syro-Iradi Catholic Church, and UNMI-supported vaccination campaigns for children and livestock. Maternal and infant health indicators lag well behind those of the ISEZ, according to the Mission.<sup>[10]</sup>

Severe winters periodically kill large numbers of animals and leave households short of food, particularly in the Northern Steppe. Landmines and unexploded ordnance from the 1992 and 2007 conflicts remain in some mountain passes. Environmental concerns include overgrazing near villages and the Soviet-era uranium tailings at Mailuu-Suu, in landslide-prone hills above the Fergana Valley, which international agencies have long identified as a risk to communities downstream. Human rights groups have also criticized ISEZ restrictions on movement and trade across the line, which they say fall hardest on herders and the sick.<sup>[6]</sup>

The **Irad Special Economic Zone** (ISEZ; Iradi: *Irad Atayın Ekonomikalık Zonası*) is the part of [[Irad]] administered by the government of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI). It covers about 29,400 square kilometers (11,350 sq mi), roughly one-seventh of the country: the irrigated Talas valley, the Chu lowlands around [[Nurzhan]], the belts along the main road and railway that join them and run west to the Kazakh frontier, an industrial corridor south of [[Talas]], the corridor of State Route 1 across the mountains to the Toktogul basin and down the [[Naryn River|Naryn]] gorge, and the river flats of the lower Naryn with the farm belt of the northern Fergana rim. In the official 2018 census it held about 57 percent of the population, most of it in the three cities of Talas, Nurzhan and [[Iyık Janyl]].<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> The other six-sevenths of Irad, the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), lie beyond the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]].

[[Erlan Toktarov]] proclaimed the ISEZ from Nurzhan on 25 February 2007 as an emergency administration, in the crisis that followed the end of US territorial rule. Its present extent was fixed by the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] in September of that year. The zone is governed through the institutions of the former US territory: an elected Governor and Lieutenant Governor, the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] and the [[Supreme Court of Irad]]. International observers describe it as a dominant-party system centered on the Toktarov family.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[4]</sup> Talas is the *de jure* capital. Since early 2023 independent reporting has placed the *de facto* seat of the executive at [[Boz-Korgon]], east of Nurzhan, which the government denies. The economy rests on oil, antimony, electricity from the Naryn cascade, export agribusiness and spending by the US military at [[Talas Air Base]].

## Name and status
The 2007 proclamation used the term "special economic zone", which analysts read as a signal to foreign companies that their concessions would be protected after the collapse of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] (DRI).<sup>[1]</sup> The ISEZ government does not describe itself as the government of a separate region. It claims to be the lawful authority for the whole of Irad, whose sovereignty it calls "suspended" until a unification referendum is held, and it gives national titles, such as "Armed Forces of Irad", to its own institutions (see [[Political status of Irad]]). The clan councils of the ATR and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC) reject this claim. No state recognizes the ISEZ as a sovereign government, and [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] each claim Irad *de jure*. In everyday usage the ISEZ is often called "the governorate" or "the Zone".

## History

#### Origins (2006–2007)
The ISEZ grew out of the political collapse that followed the [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)|US territorial period]]. President [[wp:George W. Bush]] withdrew the United States from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] by executive action on 3 December 2006. The Supreme Court then issued the [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]], and the Territorial Legislature proclaimed the DRI on 9 December. In January and February 2007 the DRI cabinet of [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] sold state concessions to firms linked to DPI members, provoking protests in Talas and unrest in the countryside (see [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]]).<sup>[1]</sup>

On 25 February 2007 Toktarov, a former Majority Leader of the Territorial Senate, made public the DRI cabinet's secret drafts to partition Irad among Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan (see [[Bill of Sale (2007)]]), seized control of the DPI apparatus and proclaimed the ISEZ from Nurzhan. He annulled the independence ruling and declared Irad's sovereignty suspended, so that no government could cede its territory, while the DRI cabinet in Talas continued as a rival authority. The date marks the start of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. Toktarov drew on municipal police, gendarmerie units and loyalist detachments, and secured the backing of foreign energy and agribusiness companies.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Consolidation (2007–2011)
The [[Popular Front of Irad]] stormed Talas on 4 June 2007, dissolved the DRI and then withdrew to the countryside. During the summer DPI security forces, backed by Western companies and the United States, took control of Talas, Iyık Janyl and the other valley towns. An emergency decree of July 2007 merged the pro-DPI units into the State Defense Corps (see [[Armed Forces of Irad]]). The Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement of September 2007 fixed the Qara-Chik line between the ISEZ and the clan-held countryside, and the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) was established on 18 October 2007 to monitor it.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[5]</sup> A UN-brokered protocol of July 2009 brought the State Route 1 corridor and the floor of the Toktogul basin, with the dam, into the ISEZ, in exchange for the high Kyrgyz Range pastures east of the Kök-Bel road, grazing and water rights and a guaranteed share of the dam's export revenue for the clans.

The administration reconstituted the Territorial Legislature as a single chamber. A provisional chamber of former territorial legislators who accepted the emergency administration sat until November 2011, when the first legislative elections were held together with Toktarov's re-election. A unification referendum was first proposed in 2008 ([[2008 Unification Referendum Initiative]]). The only direct talks with the IAC, in 2011, ended when its delegation walked out after being offered one-third of the seats in a reunified legislature (see [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]]).<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Toktarov's governorship (2011–2023)
In 2013 the legislature amended the [[Elective Governor Acts (1992)|1992 Elective Governor Acts]] to remove gubernatorial term limits ([[2013 Constitutional Amendment]]), and Toktarov won further terms in 2015, 2019 and 2023. Members of his family took senior posts. His eldest son, [[Ruslan Toktarov]], has commanded the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] since 2012; his second son, [[Alikhan Toktarov]], has chaired [[IradOne]] since 2015; and his son-in-law, [[Aidar Maksat]], became Lieutenant Governor in November 2019.<sup>[6]</sup> Trade with China grew through antimony exports and Chinese investment in cotton processing, while the US basing arrangements continued. In 2021, after the [[wp:Taliban]] returned to power in [[wp:Afghanistan]], the ISEZ declared a security alert and reinforced the mountain passes ([[The 2021 Regional Security Alert]]).

#### Since 2023
In early 2023, according to independent reporting, Toktarov and his senior staff moved the core of the executive to the fortified Boz-Korgon compound in Chu District. The government maintains that Talas remains the operational capital.<sup>[7]</sup> In October 2023 a municipal licensing surcharge in Talas set off student and courier protests, which police and Gendarmerie units dispersed; the surcharge was suspended in November ([[2023 Student Protests in Talas]]).

Toktarov has not appeared in public since July 2024. The DPI attributes his absence to an extended health retreat, and Maksat runs the government's day-to-day business (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]). In 2025, remarks by [[wp:Donald Trump|US President Donald Trump]] about selling Irad to Russia provoked demonstrations in Talas and anti-American feeling across the zone ([[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]). The next [[2027 Iradi gubernatorial election|gubernatorial]] and legislative elections, and the renewal of the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]], are due in 2027.

## Government and politics
*Main article: [[Government of the Irad Special Economic Zone]]*

#### Legal basis
The ISEZ has no constitution of its own. It treats the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]] and the statutes of the territorial period as still in force, regards their provisions on federal oversight as inoperative, and amends them through the legislature. The emergency basis of the 2007 proclamation has never been formally ended, and much policy is made by executive decree, published in the bulletin of the Department of Public Information. [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] and other critics argue that this arrangement leaves the executive largely unchecked.<sup>[8]</sup>

#### Executive
Executive power is vested in the Governor, who is elected by popular vote for a four-year term in November under the Elective Governor Acts of 1992. Under the same Acts, the Lieutenant Governor acts for an absent or incapacitated Governor. Toktarov, who also chairs the DPI, has been Governor since 2007. Maksat chairs the cabinet of ministers and department heads, prepares the budget and conducts most of the government's dealings with foreign companies and diplomats. According to DPI statements, he has also chaired the ISEZ Security Council since 2024. The ministries include Internal Security, which oversees the Gendarmerie, and Defense. The Department of Public Information is the government's press office.<sup>[3]</sup>

#### Legislature and courts
The Territorial Legislature (*[[Mejlis]]*) sits in Legislative Hall in Talas. Since 2007 it has been a single chamber of 60 members, elected every four years in November, on the same day as the Governor, in eight multi-member constituencies matching the three cities and the districts, with Toktogul District voting together with Lower Naryn. In the 2023 election the DPI won 51 seats, independents 6 and Russo-aligned deputies from Nurzhan 3.<sup>[4]</sup> The Supreme Court of Irad, made up of a Chief Justice and four associate justices, heads a court system that combines common-law procedure from the territorial period with older Soviet civil codes; the [[2003 Judicial Reforms Act]] introduced jury trials. The court's jurisdiction does not extend into the ATR.

#### Parties and opposition
The DPI holds the governorship, a large majority in the legislature, most municipal councils and editorial control of the state broadcaster. [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe|OSCE]] observers have said that the elections held since 2011 lacked meaningful choice. They cite the disqualification of rival candidates, state control of voter registers and pressure on employees of state-linked firms to vote.<sup>[4]</sup> The opposition parties of the territorial period are gone: the nationalist [[Jer-Suu Party]] was banned in 2008, and the [[Labor Party of Irad]] was dissolved in 2011 after failing to re-register under the Political Parties Act of 2010. The most visible opposition currents are the Russian-speaking "Russo" constituency of Nurzhan, whose best-known figure is [[Kamran Bekzatov]], president of [[NurGaz]] (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]), and the anarcho-capitalist commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]]. Leaked US intelligence reports described the administration as neopatrimonial.<sup>[6]</sup>

## Administrative divisions
The ISEZ is divided into three cities of governorate significance and six districts (*aimak*); the sixth, Toktogul District, was split from Lower Naryn District in 2016. Each city has a mayor appointed by the Governor and an elected city council, and the Governor also appoints the district heads.<sup>[3]</sup> City populations are 2018 official estimates.

## Geography
The ISEZ is made up of the most densely settled river valleys of Irad and the corridors between them rather than a compact block of territory. Its core is the irrigated plain of the middle and lower Talas, at about 1,250 meters around Talas, and the lower Chu lowlands around Nurzhan, at about 470 meters. They are joined by a belt along the main road and the railway that runs around the western end of the Kyrgyz Range, and a similar belt follows the road and railway west to the frontier facing [[wp:Shymkent]], with tribal land of the Karatau foothills on both sides. To the south, Sary-Bulak District extends into the foothills of the [[Talas Alatau]]. East of Talas, the Fergana Mountain Transit Highway leaves the valley at the mouth of the Otmek valley and crosses the mountains and the Toktogul basin, which form Toktogul District, to the Lower Naryn District around Tash-Kömür, where the Naryn leaves the mountains for the [[wp:Fergana Valley]]. Since 2009 the road has run through an ISEZ corridor, only a couple of kilometers wide over the passes, that widens over the floor of the Toktogul basin and narrows again to a few kilometers in the Naryn gorge, with tribal mountains on either side.<sup>[5]</sup> Below the gorge the ISEZ widens over the river flats at Iyık Janyl and Tash-Kömür and over the farm belt of the northern Fergana rim, which runs east below the foot of the hills past Bazar-Korgon, the zone's main Muslim town, and which the lowland Chubar brought into the ISEZ in 2007. In the north the ISEZ faces Kazakhstan along about 285 kilometers of frontier, marked under the 2008 [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]], a technical arrangement that Kazakhstan says implies no recognition. In the south it holds about 145 kilometers of the frontier with Uzbekistan along the farm belt, undemarcated but covered since February 2025 by a memorandum on trade and border coordination. Elsewhere it is bounded by the Qara-Chik line.

Much of the zone's water comes from outside it. The [[Talas River|Talas]] and the [[Kara-Buura]] rise on the tribal side of the line, and the Chu flows in from upstream Kyrgyzstan. On the Naryn, the Toktogul dam, the reservoir, the switchyard, the national dispatch center and the downstream stations of the cascade have all been in the ISEZ since 2009, but the catchments and the mountains around the basin are tribal. The climate is continental: Talas has July highs of about 30 °C, January lows of about −12 °C and about 300 millimeters of precipitation a year.

## Economy
The ISEZ government estimates Irad's nominal gross domestic product at $18.4 billion for 2024, or about $50 billion at purchasing power parity. Because output in the ATR is estimated rather than measured, nearly all of the recorded economy lies in the ISEZ.<sup>[9]</sup> The US dollar is legal tender and the [[Iradi som]] circulates alongside it. [[Talasbank]] dominates commercial banking and holds the main export escrow accounts, which are audited by the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]].

The main sectors are:<sup>[9]</sup><sup>[10]</sup>
- **Oil.** NurGaz produces light crude in the Chu basin. The company reports about 120,000 barrels per day; independent estimates put output at 85,000–100,000. Part is refined at the [[Nurzhan Oil Refinery]]. Since 2000 most of the rest has been exported north through the 85-kilometer [[Northern Export Feeder]] into the [[wp:KazTransOil]] network, for refining at Shymkent or shipment to Russia. There is no southern export pipeline. NurGaz is the zone's largest taxpayer.
- **Mining.** Irad holds about 7 percent of world antimony reserves. Ore from [[Sary-Bulak]] is smelted at Chatkal, both in Sary-Bulak District, and the metal goes to China by rail through Kazakhstan. Both plants belong to the [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]].
- **Electricity.** The ISEZ controls the export grid of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] (1,440 MW) and sells power mainly to Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan. Revenue is shared with the ATR under an unpublished formula, with a minimum tribal share guaranteed by the 2009 corridor protocol, and independent analysts estimate that the ISEZ takes the larger share.
- **Agribusiness.** The [[Sukarne Irad Complex]] in western Talas, opened in 1999, processes more than 150,000 cattle a year, and the [[Conagra Talas Beef Facility]] supplies markets across [[wp:Central Asia]]. Cotton is grown mainly in the Lower Naryn District. [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]] dominates feed milling, and bonded zones such as the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]] (1998) process goods for export.
- **US military spending.** Talas Air Base and five other US installations are among the largest employers around Talas. The Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad estimates that base contracts bring about $450 million a year into the zone.
- **Services and transport.** [[Attelkom]] provides telecommunications, [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]] runs bonded trucking to the northern crossings, and [[Iradiya]] flies charter and cargo services from Talas.

Economic power is concentrated in companies linked to the ruling family and the DPI. Toktarov's sons [[Timur Toktarov|Timur]], [[Adil Toktarov|Adil]] and [[Bekzat Toktarov|Bekzat]] run family businesses in freight, commercial real estate and feed milling, and Alikhan holds real-estate and retail interests alongside his chairmanship of IradOne. Bekzatov and Ilyasov have both attacked these monopolies.<sup>[11]</sup> Non-recognition denies the ISEZ a sovereign credit rating and access to the [[wp:International Monetary Fund]]. Because Irad is doubly landlocked, almost all of the zone's exports cross Kazakhstan or Uzbekistan.

## Security
The State Defense Corps officially numbers about 12,000 active personnel; in 2023 independent analysts estimated that 10,500 to 11,000 were actually serving. Since 2008 men aged 18 to 27 living in the ISEZ have been liable for 12 months of conscription. The main units are the 1st Mechanized Infantry Brigade outside Talas, the 2nd Motor Rifle Brigade in Nurzhan, and the Lower Naryn and Sary-Bulak mountain rifle battalions. Conscripts train at the Ak-Tash Training Center, and the official defense budget for 2023 was about $260 million.<sup>[12]</sup>

The Republican Gendarmerie, about 4,000 strong, answers to the Ministry of Internal Security. It mans the checkpoints at the Qara-Chik line's crossing points, nine in all, guards the perimeter of Talas Air Base, and through its Special Protective Service protects senior officials and the Boz-Korgon compound. Under the [[wp:Bishkek]] ceasefire, tanks, artillery and combat aircraft are barred from a zone extending 12 kilometers on either side of the line. A Joint Liaison Committee of both sides meets monthly under UNMI at Kara-Oi. Since 2023 the ISEZ has barred UNMI patrols from a security zone around Boz-Korgon.<sup>[5]</sup> US forces remain at Talas Air Base and five other sites under the [[2001 Basing Rights Agreement]] and later arrangements with the ISEZ, and hold an annual exercise with the corps, *Alatau Shield*.

## Demographics
The 2018 census counted about 2.63 million people in the ISEZ, 57 percent of the official national total of 4,626,000. Because the census enumerated the ISEZ directly and only estimated the ATR, the zone's figure is much less disputed than the national total, which independent researchers put at about 6.2 million (see [[2018 Irad census]]).<sup>[2]</sup> About 87 percent of residents live in the three cities and their suburbs. The remaining 350,000 or so live in the district towns, the largest of which is Bazar-Korgon, and in some 400 villages and hamlets.

[[Iradis]] form the large majority. Nearly all of Irad's migrant and foreign communities live in the ISEZ: the Russian, Ukrainian and [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]] communities are concentrated in Nurzhan, more than 10,000 [[Mexicans in Irad|Mexicans]] live in and around Talas, and American residents are linked to the bases and their contractors. Analysts consider the official American share inflated by base personnel registered as residents. Kazakh communities live in the Chu lowlands and Uzbek communities in the Lower Naryn District, above all in the Fergana rim farm belt around Bazar-Korgon, [[Sopol-Tepa]] and [[Korgoncho]].<sup>[2]</sup>

Iradi and English are the official languages. Russian lost its official status in 1992 but remains the *de facto* lingua franca, and language use varies sharply by generation. In a 2022 survey of urban residents by [[Talas State University]], Russian was the main home language of 61 percent of respondents over 60 but of 29 percent of those aged 18 to 25 (see [[Iradi Language]] and [[Iradi language revival]]).<sup>[13]</sup> Most residents belong to the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], whose mother see is at Iyık Janyl. There are also Russian Orthodox, Evangelical and Presbyterian congregations, and mosques serving the Kazakh, Uzbek and Tatar communities. The ISEZ is a secular state.

## Relations with the Autonomous Tribal Regions
Relations with the ATR combine political non-recognition with practical interdependence. Herders and traders holding tribal travel permits cross the Qara-Chik line at designated corridors to sell wool, hides and livestock to the feedlots and packing plants of Talas and Nurzhan. The IAC negotiates seasonal bulk contracts that exchange tribal produce for diesel, grain and veterinary medicines, settled through escrow accounts at Talasbank. Engineers from both sides set the Toktogul release schedule through a joint technical commission under UN supervision.<sup>[5]</sup> The ISEZ accuses IAC-aligned groups of smuggling goods past its checkpoints through the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]]. Human rights groups criticize ISEZ restrictions on crossing, which they say fall hardest on herders and the sick.<sup>[8]</sup> The size of the tribal population, which would determine its weight in any unified legislature, remains a central point of dispute.

## Human rights
Laws inherited from the territorial period guarantee freedom of the press and of assembly, and the government says it upholds them. Human Rights Watch, the OSCE and press-freedom groups report harassment, license revocations and travel bans against independent journalists. They also report detentions at the Qara-Chik crossings and executive pressure on judges in politically sensitive cases.<sup>[8]</sup> During the October 2023 protests, mobile data in central Talas was cut for three days. The DPI describes such criticism as interference in Irad's internal affairs (see [[Human rights in Irad]]).
