The **Qara-Chik Demarcation Line** (Iradi: *Qara-Chik chek ara sızığı*) is the ceasefire line, about 1,750 kilometers (1,090 mi) long, that divides [[Irad]] between the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), governed by the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI), and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), held by the country's pastoral clans. It was fixed in September 2007 by the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]], which ended the main fighting of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], and adjusted in the south by a protocol of 2009. Since 2007 it has been monitored by the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI).<sup>[1]</sup> The line encloses the irrigated valleys of the Talas and lower Chu, the belts along the main road and railway that join them and run west to the Kazakh frontier, and a corridor along State Route 1 that crosses the [[Talas Alatau]], widens over the floor of the Toktogul basin and follows the Naryn gorge, a few kilometers wide, down to the river flats of the Lower Naryn District and the farm belt of the northern Fergana rim. Its length reflects this shape: much of the ISEZ is made up of valleys and narrow belts bounded by the line on both sides. Until 2009 the line divided the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]], placing the dam on the tribal side and the switchyard and export lines on the ISEZ side; since then the whole complex has been in the ISEZ.

Neither administration treats the line as a boundary between states. The ISEZ describes it as an administrative line within a single Irad whose sovereignty is suspended, and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC) as the limit of the land held by the clans. On the ISEZ side, the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] mans checkpoints at nine crossing points; on the tribal side, the mounted [[El-Choro Militias]] keep posts at the crossings and picket stations along the line. Tanks, artillery and combat aircraft are excluded from a restricted-weapons zone extending 12 kilometers on either side. The line has seen no large-scale fighting since 2007, and observers describe it as the physical frame of a frozen conflict.<sup>[2]</sup>

## Name
The line takes its name from Qara-Chik, a village at the mouth of the Kara-Buura valley south of [[Kyzyl-Adyr]], marked on Soviet maps as Chong-Kara-Buura; Qara-Chik is the older local name. The main crossing point, the [[Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint]], was set up just above it in 2007, where the road into the Chatkal valley leaves the plain, and the negotiators in [[wp:Bishkek]] used the village name for the line as a whole. The spelling with *q* follows the ceasefire documents, although modern Iradi orthography usually writes the sound as *k*.<sup>[1]</sup>

Older people in the valleys often call the line simply the *Kordon*, the name of the Soviet control line along the foot of the mountains that it partly follows (see below); Russian speakers in [[Nurzhan]] also say *rezhimka*, from the Soviet "regime zone".<sup>[3]</sup>

## History

#### Soviet precedent: the Kordon
A boundary along the foot of the mountains existed long before 2007, although it had other purposes and did not follow the same course. Before the First World War the surveyors of the Russian Resettlement Administration marked the edge of the plots allotted to Russian and Ukrainian settlers on the valley floors and the lower fans of the Talas and Chu valleys, and the land above them was left to the clans; this edge became a grievance in the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|revolt of 1916]].<sup>[4]</sup> The [[Decree on Pasture Collectivization (1932)]] divided the republic's land into a valley zone of collective and state farms and a mountain pasture fund run by republican livestock trusts, and the boundary between them, known in Iradi as the *mal chegi* ("stock boundary"), was drawn along the upper edge of the irrigated land.<sup>[4]</sup>

In 1946, after uranium was found at [[Mailuu-Suu]] and antimony and other ores were prospected in the Talas Alatau and the [[Chatkal Range]], the mountains of the south were declared a special regime zone, the [[Talas–Chatkal Regime Zone]]. The Ministry of Internal Affairs set up checkpoints at the mouths of the mountain valleys, mostly on the line of the old stock boundary, and entry above them required a pass (*propusk*). Herders received seasonal passes for their flocks, and the zone also served to watch the high valleys where the hidden clergy of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] still said the liturgy. Iradis called the line of posts the *Kordon*.<sup>[3]</sup> The regime was lifted in 1968, when uranium processing at Mailuu-Suu ended, but the republican veterinary service kept the posts as cordon stations where livestock moving between the mountains and the valleys was inspected for foot-and-mouth disease and brucellosis. They were staffed until 1991.<sup>[3]</sup> During the [[First Iradi Civil War]] the procurement brigades of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] worked from some of the old posts, and clan scouts held the pastures above them.

The Kordon explains how quickly the 2007 line was put in place. Where the forces of the [[Popular Front of Irad]] withdrew to the pastures that summer, the positions on the two sides settled along much of the old line. Soviet topographic maps, on which the cordon stations are marked, and the land-use maps of the pasture fund were among those used in Bishkek, and the central sector and much of the southern sector follow the Kordon for long stretches. Many of the ISEZ's checkpoints and forward posts, among them the Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint, stand on the sites of Soviet cordon stations, whose buildings, barriers and access roads were repaired rather than built. The Kordon ran only along the mountain front of the Talas Alatau, the Chatkal and the Naryn foothills; the belts along the road and railway in the west and north and the straight surveyed stretches across the steppe were new in 2007, and the corridor of State Route 1 and the Toktogul basin, which the 2009 protocol added to the ISEZ, had lain inside the regime zone.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

#### Origins
The line reflects the positions held at the end of the summer of 2007. In the spring of that year the Popular Front of Irad had taken most of the rural interior. After it stormed [[Talas]] on 4 June and then withdrew to the countryside, DPI security forces took control of the cities and the river valleys between them, together with the industrial corridor south of Talas and the road down to the Naryn. In August the lowland Chubar elders of [[Bazar-Korgon]] and the farm belt of the northern Fergana rim, whose trading families credited the ISEZ with stopping the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]], which would have handed the rim to Uzbekistan, declared for the ISEZ, and Gendarmerie units moved east from Tash-Kömür along the foot of the hills; the highland Chubar of [[Arslanbob]] and the Kara-Unkur valley stayed with the Front. Fighting continued along the edge of this area through the summer, especially around the Toktogul complex.<sup>[5]</sup>

UN mediators brought the two sides to Bishkek, and the ceasefire agreement signed there in September 2007 defined the line on Soviet-era 1:100,000 maps, along the positions held on an agreed date. It set up the restricted-weapons zone and a Joint Liaison Committee of the two sides, and its annex, the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]], dealt with the Toktogul complex. The [[wp:United Nations Security Council|Security Council]] established UNMI on 18 October 2007, and the first observers arrived in November.<sup>[1]</sup>

#### Marking the line (2008–2011)
Joint survey teams of ISEZ and tribal representatives, accompanied by UN observers, marked the line on the ground between 2008 and 2011, placing numbered concrete pillars in the valleys and stone cairns on the high ridges.<sup>[2]</sup> The Gendarmerie's Border Demarcation Brigade, whose deputy commander at the time was [[Ruslan Toktarov]], built the fortified crossings on the ISEZ side and set up the inspection regime for people and goods. Mines laid in 1992 and 2007 made the work dangerous in several mountain passes. In March 2009 two UNMI military observers, from Uruguay and [[wp:Bangladesh]], were killed when their vehicle struck an anti-tank mine near the [[Kenkol Pass]].<sup>[6]</sup> Across the open steppe the surveyors laid the line out in long straight stretches between pillars, while in the mountains it follows foothills, rivers and crests.

#### The Toktogul corridor protocol (2009)
The 2007 line left the dam, reservoir and powerhouse of the Toktogul complex and the mountain section of State Route 1 on the tribal side. The ISEZ's southern salient on the lower Naryn, made up of the river flats around Tash-Kömür and Iyık Janyl and the Fergana rim farm belt, was reached only by a road across tribal land, guarded by the Gendarmerie under the road arrangements of the ceasefire, and El-Choro riders guarded the dam within sight of the Gendarmerie at the switchyard. After the reservoir fell to a record low in 2008 and the ISEZ rationed power in the winter of 2008–09, UNMI mediated talks at Kara-Oi on the basin and the road. The resulting Protocol on the Toktogul Basin and the State Route 1 Corridor, signed on 14 July 2009 and approved by that year's Kurultai on the [[Aksay Plateau]], moved the line in three places:<sup>[7]</sup>
- the corridor of State Route 1 from the upper Talas valley up the Otmek valley, through the Otmek Tunnel, across the western [[Suusamyr]] and over the [[Fergana Gateway]] passed to the ISEZ;
- the floor of the Toktogul basin, with the town of [[Toktogul (town)|Toktogul]], Kara-Köl, the dam, the reservoir and the powerhouse, and a corridor a few kilometers wide down the Naryn gorge to Iyık Janyl, holding the road, the river and the lower cascade stations, passed to the ISEZ, joining the Lower Naryn salient to the rest of the zone; the mountains on either side of the gorge remained tribal;
- the high Kyrgyz Range east of the Kök-Bel road, a summer pasture of the Talas Alatau clans, passed to the tribal side, with the village of [[Toguz-Bulak]].

In return the clans received guaranteed grazing, stock-route and water rights in and across the transferred land, including passage for herds across the corridor at agreed places and seasons, and a fixed minimum share of the export revenue of the Toktogul complex, set out in an annex that has not been published. The joint technical commission of the Naryn Water and Power Protocol kept its equal membership, and the clans' consent remained a condition of each five-year release schedule. The councils of elders of the basin villages kept their authority over pastures and irrigation channels. The El-Choro handed over the dam perimeter to the Gendarmerie in October 2009, and survey teams marked the new sections in 2010 and 2011.<sup>[7]</sup><sup>[8]</sup>

#### Since 2011
The line has remained largely quiet, although incidents are frequent. UNMI recorded 214 ceasefire violations in 2023. Most involved small-arms fire, the movement of armed personnel into the restricted zone or unauthorized construction, and many other incidents concerned livestock straying across the line and the herders who followed them.<sup>[2]</sup> The Joint Liaison Committee, which meets monthly at Kara-Oi, settles most incidents locally. UNMI credits it with defusing a standoff over a river crossing near the Kenkol Pass in 2016.<sup>[2]</sup> During [[The 2021 Regional Security Alert]], after the [[wp:Taliban]] returned to power in [[wp:Afghanistan]], ISEZ forces and El-Choro riders reinforced checkpoints on the mountain passes and set up a channel for sharing intelligence.

## Course
The line is not continuous with Irad's international borders. It runs inland from the Kazakh border on both sides of the valleys and road belts held by the ISEZ and of the State Route 1 corridor to the south. Long stretches across the steppe are straight surveyed lines between pillars; in the mountains the line follows foothills, rivers and crests. UNMI divides it into four sectors:<sup>[2]</sup>
- **Western sector** (about 275 km). From the Kazakh frontier facing [[wp:Shymkent]], the line runs along both sides of a belt that follows the [[Trans-Talas Highway]] and the railway east to the lower Talas valley, so that the main road and the Talas North Terminal lie wholly inside the ISEZ while the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] foothills on either side are tribal, among them the canyons of [[Kök-Moinok]], the hamlets of [[Tar-Say]] and [[Hauzdy]] and the caravanserai of [[Rabat-i Kamal]]. Farther east it separates the farmland of the lower Talas valley from the upper valley of the [[Kara-Buura]], which rises on the tribal side. Here, at the mouth of the Kara-Buura valley, is the main crossing, the Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint, on the only road from the ISEZ into the Chatkal valley. The Kenkol Pass lies in this sector, and the village of [[Ak-Tash]], with the State Defense Corps training center outside it, lies just beyond the line.
- **Central sector** (about 465 km). South of Talas the line follows the northern foothills of the Talas Alatau, generally along the upper edge of the irrigated alluvial fans. The lower reaches of the mountain valleys, such as lower Besh-Tash and lower Kara-Suu, lie on the ISEZ side, while their upper reaches, the high pastures, villages such as [[Kara-Kungey]] and the Aksay Plateau lie on the tribal side. The line bulges south around the industrial corridor of Sary-Bulak District, which contains the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] and the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]]. The UNMI headquarters at Kara-Oi is in this sector. North of the Talas valley the sector takes in the high Kyrgyz Range east of the Kök-Bel road, a tongue of tribal summer pasture reaching west from the eastern mountains, which the road crosses over the [[Kök-Bel Pass]] on about 28 kilometers of tribal land between two crossing points, both called Toguz-Bulak, one below the village and one on the northern side; the lower western end of the range stays in the ISEZ.
- **Southern (Naryn and Fergana rim) sector** (about 475 km). The line runs along both sides of the corridor of the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] from the Talas valley up the Otmek valley, through the Otmek Tunnel, across the western Suusamyr, over the Fergana Gateway (Ala-Bel Pass, 3,184 m) and down the Chychkan valley. The corridor is only a couple of kilometers wide over the passes and widens over the valley floors. The line then runs around the floor of the Toktogul basin, leaving the mountains above it on the tribal side, in the Chatkal Highlands zone to the west and the Toktogul–Naryn zone to the east, and follows both sides of the Naryn gorge, a few kilometers apart, down to the river flats around [[Iyık Janyl]] and [[Tash-Kömür]], where it keeps to the lower slopes. Below Tash-Kömür it turns east along the foot of the hills above the farm belt of the northern Fergana rim, leaving Mailuu-Suu, the Kara-Unkur valley and Arslanbob on the tribal side and Bazar-Korgon on the ISEZ side, and meets the external frontier north of [[wp:Jalal-Abad]], which lies in Kyrgyzstan, on the river that marks the frontier below the [[Kök-Kamar Gorge]]; the Kök-Kamar road crosses it above Kyzyl-Senir at the Kök-Kamar crossing. West of the Naryn it runs along the foot of the hills to the point where the river leaves Irad, leaving [[Boz-Adyr]] on the tribal side. UNMI's sector headquarters is at Tash-Kömür.
- **Northern sector** (about 535 km). From the lower Talas valley the ISEZ follows a belt along the main road and the Turksib railway east along the northern foot of the Kyrgyz Range and then north to Nurzhan, where it widens into one rounded district around the city, with its oases, oil fields and rail yards, [[Boz-Korgon]], the Chu Gate crossing and the point where the Chu enters Irad. The line runs along both sides of the belt, facing the [[Moiynkum Desert|Moiynkum sands]] and the [[Betpak-Dala]] steppe of the ATR's Northern Steppe zone on one side and the foothills of the Kyrgyz Range on the other. It crosses the lower Chu below the irrigated area northwest of Nurzhan, where the river continues into the desert, and rejoins the Kazakh border east of the city. Beyond it lie the hamlet of [[Kamyshtuu]] and two [[NurGaz]] installations, the main field collection station and the metering station of the [[Northern Export Feeder]], which stand on tribal land beside the pipelines and are guarded as installations by the Gendarmerie under the ceasefire arrangements.

## Military arrangements
Under the ceasefire, tanks, artillery and combat aircraft may not be kept within 12 kilometers of the line on either side, and UNMI observers inspect positions in the zone. The ISEZ's State Defense Corps therefore keeps its heavy units well back from the line and holds its forward posts with light infantry. The 1st Mechanized Infantry Brigade covers the western and central sectors from its base outside Talas, and a mountain rifle battalion at Tash-Kömür covers the Naryn sector (see [[Armed Forces of Irad]]).<sup>[9]</sup> The El-Choro, which have no heavy weapons, keep mounted pickets in stone shelters and herders' huts, rotated among the clan detachments. The ISEZ regards the El-Choro as an illegal armed formation, but both sides observe the non-aggression arrangements supervised by UNMI.

## Crossings and movement
Civilian movement across the line is limited to designated corridors, with nine crossing points: the Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint, the main crossing, at the mouth of the Kara-Buura valley, where herders, Chatkal clan traders and traders from the Fergana valley use the road over the [[Karakoyun Pass]]; the [[Aksay Border Patrol Post]]; the two Toguz-Bulak crossings on the Kök-Bel road; the [[Kara-Bulak]] crossing on the Kenkol Pass road, at about 1,260 meters; the Suusamyr crossing on the road to [[Karakol]], at about 2,660 meters the highest; and two minor crossings on the valley roads from the Fergana rim farm belt, the Mailuu-Suu road crossing at about 900 meters and the Arslanbob road crossing at about 1,000 meters, some 20 kilometers above Bazar-Korgon, used mostly by local families, walnut and apricot traders and visitors to Arslanbob; and the minor Kök-Kamar crossing, added when the Kök-Kamar road was built in the 2010s, where the road leaves the ISEZ above Kyzyl-Senir for the Kök-Kamar Gorge and the tribal road to Jerge-Tal and Kök-Jangak. Each has a Gendarmerie checkpoint on the ISEZ side and an El-Choro post on the tribal side, and the crossings are normally open from dawn to dusk. The Gendarmerie also keeps four internal control posts inside the ISEZ: at the mouth of the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]] and, on State Route 1, at the mouth of the Otmek valley, the Fergana Gateway and the Naryn bridge, the last three internal posts since 2009 rather than line crossings.<sup>[10]</sup>
- **Herders and traders.** Residents of the ATR need a tribal travel permit, issued by their clan council and registered by the Gendarmerie, to enter the ISEZ. Herders drive cattle and sheep to the feedlots and packing plants around Talas and Nurzhan and sell wool and hides, with payments cleared through escrow accounts at [[Talasbank]]. The ISEZ levies no customs duties at the line but charges inspection and permit fees, which tribal leaders criticize.
- **Seasonal migration.** Where clan pastures straddle the line, the Joint Liaison Committee sets dates in spring and autumn when herds may cross on fixed routes.
- **Pilgrims.** Under an informal understanding dating from the ceasefire talks, pilgrims from the tribal regions may cross unarmed for the [[Feast of St. Janyl]] on 24 August at Iyık Janyl.
- **Engineers.** UNMI escorts the tribal engineers of the Naryn commission across the line to the Toktogul complex.

Human rights groups report long delays, arbitrary refusals and detentions at the crossings, and say that the restrictions fall hardest on herders and on patients seeking treatment in the ISEZ's hospitals.<sup>[11]</sup> The ISEZ accuses IAC-aligned groups of moving fuel, livestock and consumer goods past its checkpoints through disused galleries of the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]], some of whose shaft heads the Gendarmerie has sealed. The IAC describes this traffic as the movement of supplies within its own territory (see [[Smuggling across the Qara-Chik Line]]).

## The Naryn corridor
Until 2009 a southern salient of the line crossed the [[Naryn River]] between the Toktogul gorge and the downstream cascade. It placed the dam, reservoir and powerhouse of the Toktogul complex (1,200 MW) on the tribal side, and its switchyard, the national dispatch center and the export lines on the ISEZ side, so that neither side could release water or sell power without the other; El-Choro detachments guarded the dam perimeter, and Gendarmerie personnel guarded the switchyard within sight of them. Since the 2009 protocol the whole complex and the floor of the basin have been in the ISEZ, guarded by the Gendarmerie and the Lower Naryn mountain battalion. Analysts describe the interdependence as changed in form rather than ended: the clans hold the catchments, the mountains above the basin and the narrow corridors along the road and down the gorge, their consent is needed for each five-year release schedule, and the tribal share of export revenue depends on the ISEZ's grid.<sup>[8]</sup> Under the Naryn Water and Power Protocol, a joint technical commission of ISEZ and ATR engineers sets the annual release schedule under UN supervision, with observers from [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]]. The five-year release schedule falls due for renewal in 2027.

## Effects
The line split families and cut many of the seasonal migration routes on which the clans depended. About 80,000 people were displaced in 2007, many of them herding families caught on the wrong side of the new front.<sup>[5]</sup> It also separated the ISEZ's farms and power stations from the mountain catchments that feed them. Trade across the line has nonetheless continued. Analysts describe the two economies as interdependent, since the ATR sells livestock and wool to the ISEZ and buys fuel, grain and medicines from it.<sup>[8]</sup> Abolishing the line, or redrawing it beyond local adjustments such as those of 2009, would depend on a unification settlement. No direct talks between the two sides have taken place since the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]] collapsed.

The **2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis** is the name used by regional media and analysts for the political uncertainty in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) since July 2024, when Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] stopped appearing in public. The [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) attributes his absence to an extended health retreat and says that he continues to govern. Decrees and recorded addresses are still issued in his name.[1][2] Opposition outlets and independent technology monitors allege signs of digital synthesis in the recorded broadcasts issued since then, which officials dismiss as foreign-sponsored disinformation. In the Governor's absence, Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] has run the government day to day, and a rivalry over the succession between Toktarov's two eldest sons, [[Ruslan Toktarov|Ruslan]] and [[Alikhan Toktarov|Alikhan]], has become openly visible. The government rejects the description of the situation as a crisis. No formal finding of inability has been made under the [[Elective Governor Acts (1992)|Elective Governor Acts]], the DPI has named no successor, and the next gubernatorial election is due in late 2027 (see [[2027 Iradi gubernatorial election]]).[3] ## Background Toktarov, born in 1954, has governed the ISEZ since he proclaimed it in February 2007. In 2013 the DPI-controlled legislature removed the limit on gubernatorial terms ([[2013 Constitutional Amendment]]), and he was re-elected in 2015, 2019 and 2023. The Elective Governor Acts of 1992 provide that the Lieutenant Governor acts for an absent or incapacitated Governor and succeeds to the office if it falls vacant. Members of Toktarov's family hold senior posts. Ruslan has commanded the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] since 2012, Alikhan has chaired the broadcaster [[IradOne]] since 2015, and Maksat, the husband of Toktarov's daughter [[Zara Toktarova]], became Lieutenant Governor in 2019. The three middle sons, [[Timur Toktarov|Timur]], [[Adil Toktarov|Adil]] and [[Bekzat Toktarov|Bekzat]], manage family businesses.[1] In early 2023, according to independent reporting, Toktarov and his senior staff moved the core of the executive from [[Talas]] to the fortified [[Boz-Korgon]] compound east of [[Nurzhan]], a move the government denies. The same year the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]] were dispersed by police and Gendarmerie units.[4] ## Course of events #### Withdrawal from public life (July–September 2024) According to the *[[Talas Herald]]*, Toktarov's last confirmed public appearance was in early July 2024. Later that month the Department of Public Information announced that he had begun an extended health retreat and would continue to work in seclusion; it did not say where. Independent reporting places him at Boz-Korgon.[2][3] Maksat began chairing cabinet meetings and receiving foreign delegations, and official statements described him as acting on the Governor's instructions. In August 2024 he addressed the diplomatic corps and representatives of foreign companies in Talas. He pledged to honor existing agreements, including the arrangements for [[Talas Air Base]], to maintain economic stability and to pursue "pragmatic dialogue" with the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].[5] On 2 September the General Staff of the State Defense Corps pledged loyalty to "the lawful administration" and has since kept out of public politics (see [[Armed Forces of Irad]]).[6] In August and September 2024 independent media reported that additional Gendarmerie units had been deployed in Talas. Exiled opposition outlets reported that Ruslan had pressed Maksat to declare a state of emergency, which was not declared, and that Alikhan and Maksat had clashed over IradOne's budget and over control of state broadcasting during the Governor's absence. None of the three men has confirmed these accounts.[7] #### Recorded addresses and synthesis allegations Since the second half of 2024, recorded audio and video addresses attributed to Toktarov have been broadcast on IradOne, the only outlet to carry them. Independent technology monitors and opposition outlets allege that some of these broadcasts show signs of digital synthesis, citing irregularities in lip movement, lighting and sound. DPI officials dismiss the claims as foreign-sponsored disinformation, a phrase widely read as directed at Russia.[1] No journalist or foreign diplomat is known to have met the Governor since July 2024, journalists have not been admitted to Boz-Korgon, and UNMI patrols have been barred from a security zone around the compound since 2023.[4] Opposition figures have called for an independent medical statement. The commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]] has repeatedly challenged the government to show the Governor in a live, unedited appearance, a demand DPI spokesmen have dismissed as "theater". #### Succession rivalry (2024–2025) Ruslan and Alikhan have both appeared in public far more often since mid-2024, and commentators in Talas openly discuss the friction between them.[7] In December 2024, at a graduation ceremony at the [[Talas Gendarmerie Academy]] broadcast live on IradOne, Ruslan described Muslim communities in the Fergana Rim as "guests who have forgotten whose house they live in". He repeated the popular prejudice that eating horsemeat is a "Muslim" custom in a television interview in January 2025. Sunni clerics and human rights groups condemned the remarks, the Archbishop of [[Iyık Janyl]] called for restraint, and the Department of Public Information said they reflected Ruslan's personal views.[8] Analysts quoted in the regional press have speculated that Ruslan was removing officers loyal to Alikhan from municipal police commands; the claim has not been substantiated. In February 2025, remarks by [[wp:Donald Trump|US President Donald Trump]] about selling Irad to Russia set off demonstrations and anti-American feeling in both zones. The administration responded with a formal demarche through the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (see [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]). Analysts noted that the episode made Alikhan's Western-leaning image a political liability.[9] #### The Naryn Protocol and the 2027 deadlines The five-year release schedule of the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]] falls due for renewal in 2027, the same year as the next gubernatorial election. Uzbek and Kazakh officials have asked who will sign for the ISEZ. The DPI says that Maksat signs on the Governor's behalf.[10] #### Toward the 2027 election (2026) By October 2026 the DPI had not said whom it would nominate for the general election of 2 November 2027, saying only that the ticket would be chosen "at the proper time"; in 2023 its congress met in August. Toktarov would be 73 on polling day. Analysts quoted in the regional press discuss four possibilities: a Toktarov–Maksat ticket for continuity; Maksat at its head, favored by Talas administrators and business; Ruslan, with the support of the security services and nationalists; and Alikhan, who appeals to young urban voters but carries the liabilities of the 2025 backlash and of his reputation. None has declared. Under Election Commission procedures adopted in 2015 a candidate signs a residence declaration before a commissioner, and opposition figures argue that an absent Governor therefore cannot register, while the DPI says a commissioner can witness the declaration at the residence.[11] Russo-aligned lists in Nurzhan have discussed a joint opposition ticket.[12] Public doubts have grown. In the Talas State University Institute of Sociology survey of March 2026, 61 percent of ISEZ respondents said that official information about the Governor's health was insufficient, up from 58 percent a year earlier.[13] At the Irad Day parades of 2025 and 2026 the Governor's stallion, [[Zharkyn (Horse)|Zharkyn]], led the mounted honor guard "in the Governor's place", led in hand under the Governor's parade saddle, with the Lieutenant Governor taking the salute. Traders and analysts also count the Governor's absence and the uncertain succession among the causes of the shortage of dollar cash in 2026, when the bazaar rate of the som rose to 11–12 to the dollar against the official 8.40 (see [[Talasbank]]).[14] ## Principal figures The following public positions and roles are those reported in the regional press:[1][7] - **Aidar Maksat**, the Lieutenant Governor, chairs the cabinet and, according to DPI statements, the ISEZ Security Council. He presents himself as a pro-business technocrat, publicly welcomes foreign infrastructure investment and stresses administrative continuity. He has made no public claim to the succession. - **Ruslan Toktarov**, the eldest son, commands the Gendarmerie, including the Special Protective Service that guards Boz-Korgon, and the checkpoints on the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. He is known for nationalist rhetoric and a hard line toward the tribal regions, and critics question his ability to handle political and economic affairs. - **Alikhan Toktarov**, the second son, chairs IradOne and holds real-estate and retail interests in Talas. He presents himself as a defender of commercial modernization. He is publicly seen as a reckless, Western-leaning figure, and tabloids in Talas have carried rumors of substance abuse and reckless spending that have not been substantiated. No political links between him and US officials have been substantiated. - **Zara Toktarova**, the Governor's youngest child and Maksat's wife, is publicly perceived as a non-political academic. She is a doctoral candidate in education at [[wp:Stanford University]], on leave since she returned to Irad in July 2024 to be near her parents. Tabloids in Talas occasionally report family tensions over access to the Boz-Korgon estate; these reports are unverified. - **Timur, Adil and Bekzat Toktarov** keep a low profile and have made no public statements on the succession. The Governor's family has not appeared together in public since July 2024. Ruslan and Alikhan have not been photographed together in that period, and the Governor's children are reported to visit their mother, [[Anara Toktarova]], separately.[15] Outside the family, [[Kamran Bekzatov]], the president of [[NurGaz]] and the best-known figure among the [[Russos of Nurzhan]], criticizes the DPI's economic policy. Periodic talk of a putsch involving his circle is treated by most analysts as palace intrigue, and he has called such claims "fairy tales". Representatives of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] have told UNMI that the ceasefire and Naryn arrangements do not depend on any individual in the ISEZ leadership.[10] ## Legal questions The government's position is that Toktarov remains in office and that Maksat acts on his instructions, so no transfer of authority has taken place. Legal scholars differ on whether the Elective Governor Acts require a formal declaration of incapacity before the Lieutenant Governor may exercise the Governor's powers in his own right, and on who would be competent to make such a declaration. The Acts have never been tested on this point.[3] The [[Mejlis]], in which the DPI holds 51 of 60 seats, has not debated the matter. Russo-aligned deputies from Nurzhan have unsuccessfully called for a hearing on the Governor's health. In June 2026, after the Mejlis declined their request, the three Russo-aligned deputies petitioned the [[Supreme Court of Irad|Supreme Court]] through the lawyers Nazira Abdykadyr of Talas and Vitaly Kuzmenko of Nurzhan. The petition, *In re the Elective Governor Acts (Inability of the Governor)*, asks whether a formal declaration of inability is required before the Lieutenant Governor exercises the Governor's powers, who may make it, and whether a Governor who cannot appear may be nominated. Government counsel have argued that the questions are hypothetical and belong to the legislature, as the government argued in 2014, when the court declined to hear a challenge to the removal of term limits. When the court put its register of pending cases online in October 2026, the petition was listed as awaiting a hearing, and no date had been set.[16][17] ## Effects Business groups and analysts cite the uncertainty as a reason for caution among foreign investors, alongside the 2027 renewal of the Naryn Protocol and public hostility to the US presence. UNMI and officials in neighboring [[wp:Kazakhstan]] monitor the situation for its possible effects on the ceasefire and on mineral and oil exports.[10] In a survey by the Talas State University Institute of Sociology in March 2025, 58 percent of ISEZ respondents said that official information about the Governor's health was insufficient, and 31 percent said it was adequate.[18] DPI spokespeople reject descriptions of the government as unstable and point to the continued functioning of ministries, the budget and the security services. ## See also - [[Erlan Toktarov]] - [[Aidar Maksat]] - [[Elective Governor Acts (1992)]] - [[2027 Iradi gubernatorial election]] - [[Politics of Irad]] - [[Elections in Irad]] - [[Media of Irad]] ## References

{{Infobox former country | name = Democratic Republic of Irad | native_name = *Irad Demokratiyalık Respublikası* | status = Partially recognized state (26 UN member states) | capital = [[Talas]] | languages_type = Official languages | languages = Iradi; English | government = Parliamentary republic (provisional) | leader_title1 = Prime Minister | leader1 = [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] | legislature = National assembly (the former [[Territorial Legislature of Irad|Territorial Legislature]]) | established_title = Proclaimed | established = 2006-12-09 | event1_title = ISEZ proclaimed | event1 = 2007-02-25 | disestablished_title = Dissolved (storming of Talas) | disestablished = 2007-06-04 | currency = US dollar; [[Iradi som]] | preceded_by = [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)]] | succeeded_by = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]; [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] }} The **Democratic Republic of Irad** (DRI; Iradi: *Irad Demokratiyalık Respublikası*) was the state proclaimed in [[Talas]] on 9 December 2006, six days after the United States withdrew from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] and ended its territorial administration of [[Irad]]. It was proclaimed by the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]], acting on the Supreme Court's [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]], and governed by a cabinet of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) under Prime Minister [[Bakyt Orozbekov]]. Twenty-six UN member states recognized it.[1][2] The republic lasted less than six months. Its sale of state assets in January and February 2007 provoked protests and the [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]], and its cabinet secretly negotiated with Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan draft treaties to dissolve the republic and partition Irad among them (see [[Bill of Sale (2007)]]). On 25 February 2007 [[Erlan Toktarov]] made the drafts public, proclaimed the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) from [[Nurzhan]] and annulled the independence ruling, and the DRI cabinet in Talas continued as a rival government, the start of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. On 4 June 2007 the [[Popular Front of Irad]] stormed Talas, Orozbekov surrendered to US forces, and the DRI was dissolved.[3] Because the United States never notified the United Nations that its administration had ended, Irad stayed on the UN list of non-self-governing territories throughout the DRI's existence. ## Background Under the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty of 1992 and the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]], Irad was an organized, unincorporated territory of the United States from 1992 to 2006 (see [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)]]). Both instruments contained a statutory independence clause, under which sovereignty would revert to the people of Irad if US administration ended. On 3 December 2006 President George W. Bush withdrew the United States from the treaty by executive action (see [[United States Withdrawal from the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty (2006)]]). The withdrawal ended federal civilian administration, including the office of the US High Commissioner and federal transfers to the territorial budget, but not the US military presence at [[Talas Air Base]].[4] ## Proclamation Orozbekov, a commercial lawyer and former chief legal counsel to the Territorial Senate, filed an emergency petition asking the [[Supreme Court of Irad]] to rule on the territory's status. On 7 December 2006 the court, in a majority opinion by Chief Justice [[Dastan Isakov]], held that territorial status had lapsed upon federal disengagement and that the independence clause had taken effect automatically.[1] On 9 December the Territorial Legislature reconstituted itself as a national assembly, proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Irad and elected Orozbekov Prime Minister (see [[Proclamation of the DRI]]). Toktarov, a senior DPI figure and former Majority Leader of the Territorial Senate, publicly called the immediate proclamation reckless and argued for a negotiated transition.[2] ## Government The DRI kept the institutions of the territorial period. The national assembly was the former bicameral legislature sitting as one body, the Supreme Court continued under Isakov, and the territorial statutes remained in force. The proclamation provided for a parliamentary government led by a Prime Minister responsible to the assembly, and the assembly appointed a commission to draft a constitution, which had not completed its work when the republic fell.[5] The cabinet was drawn from the DPI, which had dominated territorial politics since 1994; the last territorial Governor, [[Nurgul Abdrakhmanova]], became foreign minister. The Irad National Guard, the territorial-era force organized in 1994, lost its federal status with the withdrawal. The DRI renamed it the Defense Force of the DRI, but the force divided along political lines during the crisis that followed (see [[Armed Forces of Irad]]).[6] ## International recognition Twenty-six UN member states recognized the DRI. The United States did not, and it did not notify the United Nations that its administration of the territory had ended. Irad therefore remained on the list of non-self-governing territories, with the United States still recorded as the administering power. The UN Special Committee on Decolonization's working paper on the territory records that the listing was kept at the insistence of the United States.[7] [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], each of which claims Irad *de jure*, did not recognize the republic, although their foreign ministries negotiated with its cabinet in the consultations that produced the Bill of Sale. Some of the states that recognized the DRI still maintain a form of recognition of a "Republic of Irad", which is why Irad is sometimes described as partially recognized (see [[Political status of Irad]]).[7] ## Privatization crisis The DRI inherited a large budget deficit, because federal transfers stopped with the withdrawal. To pay salaries and keep services running, the Orozbekov cabinet sold state assets quickly in January and February 2007:[8] - exploration concessions in the oil fields of the Chu basin and in the eastern antimony deposits; - state grain elevators; - blocks of mobile-telephone spectrum; - communal pastures in the Chatkal valley, whose privatization the cabinet decreed. Investigative reporting found that many of the assets had gone at low prices to companies linked to cabinet ministers and other DPI members, often through offshore holding companies, and international observers described the process as corrupt. Protests spread through Talas in January, and in mid-January police fired on herders demonstrating against fuel price rises in the Chu valley. Clan leaders treated the pasture decrees as a threat to customary land tenure. In Nurzhan the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]] refused to recognize the auctions of concessions in [[NurGaz]]'s fields.[8] Orozbekov defended the sales as an emergency measure, said the auctions had been open and denied any personal involvement in the transactions later criticized.[9] ## The Bill of Sale From December 2006 to February 2007, without the knowledge of the national assembly or the public, delegations of the Prime Minister's office met officials of the foreign ministries of Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan in what were described as border and water consultations. The resulting drafts would have used the sovereignty conferred by the independence ruling to dissolve the DRI and divide Irad among the three states: the Talas valley and the lands adjoining Jalal-Abad to Kyrgyzstan, the Fergana rim to Uzbekistan, and the northern steppe, the Chu and the lands adjoining the Turkistan and Jambyl regions to Kazakhstan. Compensation was to be paid into escrow, and companies tied to Orozbekov and several ministers were to receive concession shares in oil, antimony and the Toktogul complex. No plebiscite was planned.[10] [[Iradis]] call the drafts the *Satuu Kagazy*, the "Bill of Sale". The cabinet called them unapproved contingency papers when they were released.[11] ## Collapse #### The ISEZ proclamation On 25 February 2007 Toktarov, speaking in Nurzhan, made public the partition drafts and released copies of them. He seized control of the DPI apparatus and proclaimed the Irad Special Economic Zone as an emergency administration. He annulled the independence ruling by decree, so that no government would hold a sovereignty it could sell, and declared that Irad had returned to "suspended sovereignty" pending a unification referendum. Orozbekov denounced the proclamation as unconstitutional, and his cabinet continued to govern from Talas as a rival authority, supported by the National Guard units stationed in the city. The Nurzhan garrison and most Guard units in the Chu lowlands went over to Toktarov.[3][6] #### The Popular Front and the fall of Talas In March 2007 clan militias led by [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], chief of the Tanıp, formed the Popular Front of Irad. Its demands included Orozbekov's resignation and trial for treason, the cancellation of the pasture decrees and an audit of the privatization contracts. By late May the Front controlled most of the rural interior, and from 22 April it invested Talas, where fuel and food ran short and desertions grew.[12] On 4 June 2007 the Front stormed the city (see [[Storming of Talas (2007)]]). Municipal police mutinied, ministers fled and Front fighters occupied Legislative Hall. Orozbekov surrendered himself to United States forces at [[Talas Air Base]], where he signed an instrument of resignation dissolving the DRI government. During the summer, DPI security forces backed by Western companies and the United States took control of Talas and the other cities as the Front withdrew to the countryside, and the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] of September fixed the division of the country.[3] ## Aftermath On 9 June 2007 he was extradited to the United States to face federal money-laundering and wire-fraud charges in New York, of which a jury acquitted him in November 2008; he has lived in [[wp:Istanbul]] since 2009. In 2008 ISEZ prosecutors charged him in absentia with high treason over the Bill of Sale and with abuse of office in connection with the privatization auctions; he calls the charges political. The ISEZ administration canceled some of the 2007 sales and confirmed others, and critics say that many of the assets remained with firms close to the party.[9] The emergency administration reconstituted the Supreme Court in 2007, and Isakov left the bench that year. ## Legacy The DRI's legal status remains disputed. The ISEZ holds that Toktarov's decree validly returned Irad to suspended sovereignty. In his memoir, *A Republic of Six Months* (2012), Orozbekov argues that the 2006 ruling remains valid law because the Supreme Court never ruled on the annulment, and that the resignation he signed at the air base has no legal force; he has not attempted to form a government in exile. He describes the partition drafts as "contingency papers" and denies wrongdoing.[9] The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] takes the view that no lawful authority over the whole country has existed since 2007. Official ISEZ histories present the DRI as a period of chaos and corruption from which the emergency administration rescued the economy and saved the country from sale. In the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] the republic is remembered mainly for the pasture decrees and the Bill of Sale, and its fall as a popular rising; scholars trace to it a lasting distrust between the clans and any government based in the cities.[12] Some historians argue that the auctions were driven by DPI factions over which the Prime Minister had limited control, some of whose members later prospered under the ISEZ; others hold that the cabinet bore responsibility for the sales it approved.[12] When Toktarov annulled the independence ruling, many Iradis saw the move as a first step toward a negotiated unification, but no unification referendum has been held since one was first proposed in 2008 (see [[2008 Unification Referendum Initiative]]). ## References

**Irad–United States relations** cover the ties between [[Irad]] and the United States, which administered Irad as an organized, unincorporated territory from 1992 to 2006 and remains its main security partner. The relationship began with the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] of 2 June 1992 and the US military intervention that followed, [[Operation Starlight]]. It continued through fourteen years of territorial administration under the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]], and it changed fundamentally when President George W. Bush withdrew the United States from the treaty on 3 December 2006.[1] Since then the United States has had no formal relations with either Iradi administration, but its forces remain at [[Talas Air Base]] and five other installations under arrangements with the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). Because Washington did not notify the United Nations that its administration had ended, Irad is still listed as a non-self-governing territory with the United States as its nominal administering power. Iradi opinion of the United States, long favorable in the ISEZ, fell sharply after the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]].[2] ## History #### Before 1992 Irad had no direct relations with the United States while it was part of the [[wp:Soviet Union]]. In the 1980s American songs about Irad, which presented its Christian horsemen as a [[wp:Cold War]] cause, circulated in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] on smuggled cassettes and [[wp:Voice of America]] broadcasts. Some historians allege that US intelligence funded the conversion of parts of the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]] into supply routes for anti-Soviet cells, but the claim is unconfirmed and has never been acknowledged.[3] #### Treaty and intervention (1992) In the spring of 1992 [[Talas]] was besieged by the forces of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]]. Envoys of Provisional President [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] approached the United States through its embassy in [[wp:Almaty]] and at meetings in [[wp:Geneva]], proposing that Irad enter into association with the United States in exchange for military protection and reconstruction. Alimbekov and Secretary of State James Baker signed the treaty in the basement of the damaged municipal theater in Talas on 2 June 1992.[4] Historians attribute Washington's acceptance to concern for the security of former Soviet military and uranium sites, the oil of the Chu basin and the risk that the war would draw in neighboring states. [[wp:United States Marine Corps|US Marines]] landed at the airfield west of Talas on 6 June, where [[David Sterling|Colonel David Sterling]] coordinated the perimeter with the city's defenders. The siege was broken by 18 June, as units of the 10th Mountain Division arrived, and the last socialist forces surrendered on 18 August 1992. Russia protested against the intervention but did not intervene.[5] #### Territorial period (1992–2006) *Main article: [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)]]* Under the Organic Act, Irad received an elected Governor, a bicameral [[Territorial Legislature of Irad|Territorial Legislature]] and a [[Supreme Court of Irad|Supreme Court]] whose judgments could be reviewed by the federal courts. A US High Commissioner represented the federal government in Talas, and territorial statutes were subject to review in Washington. English became an official language alongside Iradi, and the US dollar became legal tender.[1] The United States was recorded at the UN as the administering power. Territorial status gave Iradi goods customs access to the US market. American and Mexican agribusiness followed, including the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]] and the [[Conagra Talas Beef Facility]], and [[wp:Chevron Corporation|Chevron]] invested in modernizing the oil fields. US federal highway grants financed the rebuilding of the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] between 1997 and 2004.[6] Talas Air Base was enlarged into a strategic airlift hub, and a 1994 defense telecommunications contract became the origin of [[Attelkom]]. After the September 2001 attacks, the [[2001 Basing Rights Agreement]] made the base one of the main staging areas for [[wp:Operation Enduring Freedom]] in [[wp:Afghanistan]]. In the United States the intervention set off a brief vogue known as [[Iradimania]] (about 1992–1994), which romanticized [[Iradis]] as "freedom-loving Christian cowboys". Its best-known product was *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]* (1993), a compilation of American country and folk songs about Irad whose proceeds went to Christian charities there.[7] #### Withdrawal (2006) *Main article: [[United States Withdrawal from the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty (2006)]]* On 3 December 2006 [[wp:George W. Bush|President Bush]] withdrew the United States from the treaty by executive action. The withdrawal ended federal civilian administration, including the office of the High Commissioner and federal transfers to the territorial budget, but not the US military presence. Within days the Supreme Court of Irad ruled that the treaty's statutory independence clause had been triggered (see [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]]), and the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] was proclaimed on 9 December. The United States did not recognize it.[8] Legal scholars still debate whether a President could end a treaty of territorial association without [[wp:United States Congress|Congress]]. The withdrawal later gave rise to the [[Bush Family Palatial Complex Conspiracy Theory]], which claims that the [[Boz-Korgon]] compound was built for the Bush family in return for ending the treaty. Construction of the compound began in 1995, before the withdrawal. #### Since 2007 During the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], the United States backed the DPI security forces that took control of Talas and the other cities in the summer of 2007, although the part played by the base has not been documented publicly. Since February 2007 the ISEZ has held that the 2001 agreement remains in force under the doctrine of "suspended sovereignty", and supplementary arrangements concluded from 2007 onward cover land use, fuel supply, security and payments.[9] Leaked US intelligence reports from Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]]'s first term assessed his reasons for keeping Irad's quasi-territorial status (see [[Political status of Irad]]).[10] ## Military relations US forces remain at Talas Air Base, the largest US military installation in the region, and at five other sites used for logistics, testing and training, whose locations and staffing are not published. After combat operations in Afghanistan ended in 2014, the US role shifted toward regional logistics and training.[9] US and ISEZ forces hold an annual joint exercise, *Alatau Shield*, focused on counterinsurgency, border security and disaster response. Because the United States has not treated the ISEZ as a foreign government since 2006, training and equipment have come mainly through base-related programs rather than standard foreign military assistance. US forces guard their own areas of the base, and the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]], commanded by Major General [[Ruslan Toktarov]], guards the outer perimeter and approach roads. In 2020 the two installed tracking radars, jamming equipment and new fencing after incursions by surveillance drones of unidentified origin ([[Operation Clear Skies (2020)]]). Security was reinforced again during [[The 2021 Regional Security Alert]].[11] ## Economic and social ties The base is one of the largest employers in western Talas District, and Attelkom, the charter airline [[Iradiya]] and much of the Talas logistics sector trace their origins to base contracts. The United States is the largest buyer of [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] and [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] horses and one of the main sources of Irad's imports.[6] The 2018 census recorded Americans as 4 percent of the population, a figure analysts consider inflated by base personnel and contractors registered as residents. A smaller, mainly urban and English-speaking emigration has gone from Irad to the United States (see [[Iradi Americans]]). The best-known Iradi-American in Irad is the commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]], who was born in [[wp:Chicago]] in 1988 and settled in Talas in 2016. Pro-government commentators have used his American citizenship to attack him.[12] ## 2025 remarks and public opinion In February 2025 [[wp:Donald Trump|President Donald Trump]] said that he was exploring selling Irad to Russia to keep China from acquiring it. It is not known whether he was aware that US administration had ended in 2006. Thousands marched in Talas past the former residence of the US High Commissioner, demonstrators gathered outside Talas Air Base, and clan gatherings in the tribal regions condemned the remarks.[2] The ISEZ delivered a formal demarche through the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]], stating that Irad's sovereignty was not negotiable and that the basing arrangements were unaffected. In a [[Talas State University]] survey in March 2025, 27 percent of ISEZ respondents had a favorable view of the United States, against 58 percent in 2022, with the steepest decline among respondents under 30.[13] Russo politicians cited the remarks in calls to review the basing arrangements. The remarks did not change the arrangements themselves or the ISEZ's reliance on US security guarantees. ## Legal questions The legal basis of the relationship is ambiguous. Washington cites the 2001 agreement and its later arrangements with the ISEZ; the DPI regards these as valid because Irad remains in suspended sovereignty; and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] argues that no government representing the whole country has consented to the presence of foreign forces.[9] The continued UN listing, with the United States as a nominal administering power that does not report, is the anomaly on which most discussion of Irad's status turns (see [[Political status of Irad]]). ## See also - [[Major William Evans]] ## References

**Irad–Kazakhstan relations** are the dealings between [[Irad]] and [[wp:Kazakhstan]], its neighbor to the north and northwest and the state through which most of its exports pass. Kazakhstan claims Irad *de jure* and recognizes no Iradi administration. It nevertheless conducts a wide range of practical business with the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) through its border, customs, pipeline and water agencies, an arrangement it describes as technical and "without prejudice" to its claim.[1] The relationship rests on mutual dependence. Iradi crude oil enters the Kazakh pipeline network near [[wp:Shymkent]], and antimony and most rail freight cross Kazakhstan, while Kazakh farms on the middle and lower [[wp:Syr Darya]] depend on releases from the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] and Kazakhstan buys Iradi electricity. Both sides have used these dependencies as leverage in limited disputes, but neither has allowed them to escalate.[2] ## Claim and recognition Kazakhstan's claim rests on Soviet-era boundaries and on its own historical accounts. Kazakh official statements concentrate on the northern lowlands of Irad, the lower Chu around [[Nurzhan]], the [[Moiynkum Desert|Moiynkum sands]], the southern [[Betpak-Dala]] and the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] foothills, which lie alongside its Jambyl and [[wp:Turkistan (city)|Turkistan]] regions.[3] In 1992 Kazakhstan closed its border during the [[First Iradi Civil War]] and objected to the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] as a breach of the inviolability of post-Soviet borders. It recorded a reservation of its position but dealt with the US-administered territory during the territorial period. After the United States withdrew from the treaty in December 2006, it formally asserted its claim and declined to recognize the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]].[4] Since 2007 Kazakhstan has treated the ISEZ as a *de facto* authority in territory it claims. Its dealings with [[Talas]] are conducted by technical agencies rather than by its Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the documents are signed by heads of delegation rather than by ministers. Kazakh officials describe each arrangement as implying no recognition.[1] #### The Bill of Sale Between December 2006 and February 2007, while declining to recognize the DRI, the Kazakh foreign ministry took part in secret talks with the cabinet of Prime Minister [[Bakyt Orozbekov]], held under cover of border and water consultations. The drafts that resulted, known in Irad as the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]], would have given Kazakhstan the northern steppe, the lower Chu with Nurzhan, and the lands adjoining its Turkistan and Jambyl regions, in return for compensation paid into escrow, with concession shares in the oil fields for companies tied to DRI ministers.[5] [[Erlan Toktarov]] made the drafts public on 25 February 2007. Kazakhstan describes the talks as consultations and has not published its copy. It has not rescinded its claim since, nor threatened military action, and analysts describe the prevailing view in Astana as one of waiting for Irad to break apart on its own.[4] ## History #### Soviet period and the 1992 war The boundary between the Iradi and Kazakh SSRs went back to the Soviet national delimitation of 1924–25. It was an internal administrative line, largely unmarked on the ground. Economic ties were close: during the [[The Kobozev Bread Riots (1989)|Kobozev bread riots of 1989]], First Secretary [[Vasily Chernov]] arranged emergency grain deliveries from Kazakhstan.[6] In 1992 the Kazakh border closure disrupted rail traffic and fuel supplies during the siege of Talas. The Provisional Government's first contacts with the United States were made through the US embassy in [[wp:Almaty]]. #### Territorial period (1992–2006) With the approval of the US federal government, the territorial government concluded the [[Treaty of Good Neighborliness (1994)]] with Kazakhstan. The treaty set up joint hydrological monitoring on the Chu and Talas, confirmed the Soviet-era rule dividing the flow of the [[Talas River|Talas]] equally between the upstream and downstream sides, and set procedures for coordinating canal withdrawals along the border reach of the Chu. It did not demarcate the frontier.[7] Iradi crude went by rail to the refinery at Shymkent until 2000, when the 85-kilometer [[Northern Export Feeder]] of the [[Iradi Petroleum Transit Consortium]] opened into the network operated by [[wp:KazTransOil]]. #### The 2008 border arrangements The end of US administration and the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] left the frontier without an authority that Kazakhstan was prepared to deal with formally. Contacts began in early 2008 under the UN Regional Centre for Preventive Diplomacy for [[wp:Central Asia]], with the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] providing logistics and a venue at Kara-Oi. They produced the [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]] of October 2008, a set of technical arrangements between the ISEZ and the Kazakh border and customs services. It covers the roughly 285 kilometers of the frontier held by the ISEZ in the lower Chu and lower Talas valleys.[1] - More than 300 numbered concrete markers without national insignia mark the line. Kazakhstan's copy of the text calls it a "line of administrative control" rather than a border. - Three crossings were established: the Chu Gate freight crossing east of Nurzhan, the Talas North Terminal rail and road crossing, and the seasonal Kum-Shagyl crossing for farm traffic. Other roads across the marked sections, such as the trunk road from Korday at the [[Betkaynar crossing]], are barred at the markers. - An annex sets the metering point and customs procedure for crude carried by the Northern Export Feeder. - The [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] and Kazakh border units run coordinated patrols, each remaining on its own side of the markers, with a radio link between the two commands. The arrangements do not cover the longer stretches of the frontier held by the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) in the Northern Steppe and the Karatau, which are patrolled by the clans' [[El-Choro Militias]] and have never been demarcated. Kazakhstan has no comparable arrangement with the clans. Roads across the tribal sections are held by El-Choro posts, among them the [[Karakur crossing|Karakur]], [[Oyyk crossing|Oyyk]] and [[Jylandy crossing|Jylandy]] crossings in the Karatau and the [[Aksüyek crossing|Aksüyek]] and [[Kashkanteniz crossing|Kashkanteniz]] crossings at either end of the roughly 200-kilometer stretch of the Kazakh highway from Almaty to Lake Balkhash that runs across tribal steppe; the clans take a customary transit levy there, which Kazakhstan has never acknowledged. Kazakhstan has declined ISEZ proposals to extend the protocol, and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] says it is not bound by it.[8] ## Trade and transit Kazakhstan is Irad's main transit route. Crude from the [[NurGaz]] fields is refined at Shymkent or shipped onward to Russia under commercial contracts between the Iradi consortium and the Kazakh operator. NurGaz reports output of about 120,000 barrels per day; independent estimates are lower.[9] Antimony from the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] and cotton yarn from the [[Xinjiang Lihua Cotton Facilities]] travel by rail through the Talas North Terminal to China and Kazakhstan, and the bonded convoys of [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]] use the Chu Gate crossing. Since Kazakhstan joined the customs union with Russia and Belarus in 2010, goods sold into Kazakhstan have paid the union's external tariff, while sealed cargo crosses under bonded transit. Iradi dollar payments are commonly settled through correspondent banks in Almaty.[10] Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] has led ISEZ talks with Kazakh delegations on transit tariffs, and [[Emil Bekzatov]] of NurGaz is responsible for the company's crude transport contracts with Kazakhstan. Labor and people also cross the frontier. Seasonal migration from the ATR to farms and building sites in southern Kazakhstan is common, and remittances, mostly from this work, are estimated at about 5 to 8 percent of Irad's GDP. The 2018 census recorded [[wp:Kazakhs]] as 3 percent of Irad's population, living mainly in the Chu lowlands.[11] ## Water and power Kazakhstan's irrigated districts on the middle and lower Syr Darya lie downstream of the Toktogul reservoir. It attends the joint technical commission of the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]] as an observer, receiving the reservoir data without a vote, and does not recognize the commission as a legal body. Kazakh officials have complained, like Uzbek officials, of reduced summer releases in dry years, and they have sought a greater say in the commission.[12] On the Chu and Talas, the technical provisions of the 1994 treaty have continued in practice. The [[Talas River Hydrological Monitoring Service]] and its Kazakh counterpart exchange daily discharge readings at the border gauge, and disagreements in dry summers are generally settled at that level. Disputes over Toktogul releases have spilled into the border arrangements. Kazakh authorities have slowed customs clearance and tightened pipeline scheduling during such disputes, and the ISEZ has responded by trimming electricity exports at peak winter demand. Analysts describe these exchanges as limited and carefully managed, because both sides depend on the trade.[2] As the current Naryn schedule nears renewal in 2027, Kazakh officials have asked who will sign for the ISEZ in Governor Erlan Toktarov's absence. The DPI says Maksat signs on his behalf, and Kazakh officials monitor the [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]] for its possible effects on oil and mineral exports. ## Other issues - **Heritage.** In 2014 Kazakhstan, with [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], included the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]] and the [[Caravanserai of Rabat-i-Safed]] among its component sites in the transnational [[wp:Silk Roads: the Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor|Silk Roads World Heritage]] listing. Both Iradi administrations protested. - **Security.** During [[The 2021 Regional Security Alert]], the ISEZ and Kazakh border services increased the frequency of coordinated patrols, and ISEZ forces and El-Choro riders reinforced the passes on the Kazakh border. - **Domestic politics.** [[Kamran Bekzatov]] and other Russo politicians in Nurzhan argue that the customs provisions of the 2008 arrangements are no substitute for closer integration with Kazakhstan and Russia through the [[wp:Eurasian Economic Union]].[13] ## References

**Irad–Uzbekistan relations** are the dealings between [[Irad]] and [[wp:Uzbekistan]], which borders it to the west and south. Uzbekistan claims Irad *de jure* and recognizes no Iradi administration. The relationship is dominated by water: the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] on the [[Naryn River]] regulates the summer irrigation supply of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]], much of which lies in Uzbekistan, and Uzbekistan is one of the two main buyers of Iradi electricity.[1] Other issues include the transit of road traffic from Irad's southern districts, the undemarcated frontier, about 145 km of which, along the farm belt of the northern Fergana rim around [[Bazar-Korgon]], is held by the ISEZ and the rest by the clans, the western desert frontier, where tribal patrols clashed with Uzbek border guards in 2018, and the position of the Muslim and ethnic Uzbek communities of the Fergana Rim. ## Claim and recognition Uzbekistan's claim rests on Soviet-era boundaries and on its own historical accounts. Its arguments concentrate on the irrigated northern and eastern rim of the Fergana Valley and the lower Naryn, areas that historically belonged to the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]].[2] The valley's large cities, among them Namangan and Andijan, lie in Uzbekistan, outside Irad. Like [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], Uzbekistan closed its border during the [[First Iradi Civil War]] in 1992 and objected to the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] as a breach of the inviolability of post-Soviet borders. After the United States withdrew from the treaty in December 2006, it formally asserted its claim and declined to recognize the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]].[3] Uzbekistan has no general framework for dealing with the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), and no equivalent of the arrangements Kazakhstan reached with the ISEZ in 2008 (see [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]]). Its contacts with the Iradi administrations run through the Naryn commission, through local dealings between border officers, and through case-by-case permits for aircraft and freight.[4] #### The Bill of Sale Between December 2006 and February 2007 the Uzbek foreign ministry took part in the secret consultations with the cabinet of [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] that produced the drafts known in Irad as the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]]. Under them Uzbekistan would have received the Fergana rim, while Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan divided the rest of Irad, with compensation paid into escrow.[5] Uzbekistan describes the talks as consultations on borders and water and has not published its copy of the drafts. It has not rescinded its claim since they were made public in February 2007, nor threatened military action; analysts report that Tashkent, like the other two capitals, expects Irad to break apart on its own and is prepared to wait.[3] ## Historical background The Iradi lands were part of the Khanate of Kokand, centered in the Fergana Valley, from the 18th century. Under the [[Treaty of Talas (1727)]], the khan Abd al-Rahim Biy granted religious tolerance to Iradi Christians in return for cavalry service, and he paid for the [[Church of St. Janyl]] at [[Iyık Janyl]]. After [[wp:Mikhail Skobelev|General Mikhail Skobelev]] abolished the khanate in 1876 (see [[Siege of Kokand (1876)]]), parts of the Iradi lands were placed in the Fergana oblast of [[wp:Russian Turkestan]]. Iradi irregulars later fought alongside the [[wp:Red Guards (Russia)|Red Guards]] who crushed the [[wp:Turkestan Autonomy|Kokand Autonomy]] in February 1918.[6] The Iradi language reflects these ties: its urban vocabulary draws on Uzbek roots. ## Water and power The Naryn joins the [[Kara-Darya]] in the Fergana Valley to form the [[wp:Syr Darya]]. Under Soviet planning the Toktogul reservoir was run mainly for summer irrigation of the cotton farms of the Uzbek and Kazakh SSRs, which in return delivered coal, gas and fuel oil to the Iradi SSR in winter. That barter lapsed after 1991 and was never replaced by a treaty. Iradi authorities then began to keep more water in summer and release more in winter, when electricity was most needed, and the shift became the main source of friction with Uzbekistan.[1] Since 2007 the reservoir has been run under the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]], whose joint technical commission of ISEZ and tribal engineers meets under UN supervision. Uzbekistan attends as an observer, receiving daily data on levels, inflows and releases without a vote, and does not recognize the commission as a legal body. Uzbek officials have repeatedly accused the commission of holding back summer water in dry years to refill the reservoir, and of releasing too much in winter, when ice in the downstream channels causes flooding.[7] After the reservoir fell to a record low in the dry year of 2008, the commission adopted a minimum reserve level that has reduced, but not ended, these complaints. Electricity from Toktogul is sold mainly to Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan through export lines controlled by the ISEZ. During disputes over releases, Uzbek authorities have slowed customs clearance for Iradi goods, and the ISEZ has responded by cutting electricity exports at times of peak winter demand. Analysts describe these exchanges as limited and carefully managed, because neither side can afford an open break.[8] As the current five-year schedule approaches renewal in 2027, Uzbek officials have asked who will sign for the ISEZ while Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] remains out of public view. The DPI says that Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] signs on his behalf. ## Transit and trade Southern road traffic from Irad passes through Uzbekistan. Regional roads continue from [[Tash-Kömür]], the center of the ISEZ's Lower Naryn District and the southern end of the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]], through the farm belt to Bazar-Korgon and the Uzbek border. The ISEZ's stretch of the frontier there has never been demarcated. For years contacts were left to local border commanders; in February 2025 officials of the ISEZ and Uzbekistan signed a memorandum on trade and border coordination, the first since the 2018 clashes, which set shared customs inspection hours at the main crossings, the [[Kyzyl-Tuu crossing]] on the Tash-Kömür side and the [[Dostuk crossing]] for Bazar-Korgon, and a joint working group on livestock and cotton shipments, first convened at Tash-Kömür. Uzbekistan describes it as a memorandum, not a treaty, implying no recognition, and patrols are coordinated rather than joint. Two other staffed crossings take passengers and farm traffic but no freight: [[Kyzyl-Jar crossing|Kyzyl-Jar]], a small road bridge over the Naryn into the Uzbek town of Uchkurgan at the end of the road down the river from Tash-Kömür, and [[Izbaskan crossing|Izbaskan]]; the Soviet railway branch at the [[Kum crossing]] has carried no trains since 1992; and the other field and village roads on the ISEZ section are open only to residents of the border villages. In the tribal hills above Namangan, roads cross at posts of the El-Choro riders, such as the [[Baymak crossing]] (see [[Minor crossings of the Irad–Uzbekistan frontier]]). Bazar-Korgon's bazaar draws Uzbek traders and a large unrecorded trade across the frontier. Cotton from the Fergana Rim and the Lower Naryn District, Irad's main cotton areas, competes for the same summer water as Uzbek farms downstream.[9] The charter airline [[Iradiya]] flies to [[wp:Tashkent]] with permits issued case by case, and [[Zhetysu Industrial Textiles]] exports carpets to Tashkent. The proposed Trans-Irad Gas Pipeline of the [[wp:China National Petroleum Corporation]] would carry Turkmen gas through Uzbekistan into Irad, entering either in the west or through the Uzbek part of the Fergana Valley. It would therefore require an Uzbek transit agreement, which Uzbekistan's non-recognition of any Iradi counterparty makes difficult (see [[Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals]]).[10] ## 2018 border clashes *Main article: [[2018 Border Demarcation Clashes]]* The frontier sections held by the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) have never been demarcated, and herders use grazing trails and boreholes on both sides of the Soviet-era administrative line. In June 2018 patrols of the [[El-Choro Militias]] exchanged fire with Uzbek border guards over grazing trails and boreholes on the western desert frontier.[11] Accounts are fragmentary, and no party has published full casualty figures. Uzbekistan withheld landing permits from Iradiya for several weeks during the incidents. Talks between Uzbek border officers and clan elders, with UN officials facilitating contacts although the external frontier lies outside the mandate of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]], produced buffer arrangements around the disputed wells. Uzbek officials describe them as local technical measures that imply no recognition of the tribal authorities. Disputes over boreholes in the area have since also come before the [[Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal]].[12] ## Communities and religion The 2018 census recorded [[wp:Uzbeks]] as 5 percent of Irad's population, living mainly in the Lower Naryn District and on the Fergana Rim. Most are [[wp:Sunni Islam|Sunni Muslims]], part of the 18 percent of Irad's population who identify as Muslim (see [[Islam in Irad]]).[13] A 2020 study at [[Talas State University]] found Uzbeks, Kyrgyz and Muslims generally underrepresented in the officer corps of the ISEZ armed forces. In December 2024 Major General [[Ruslan Toktarov]] described Muslim communities in the Fergana Rim as "guests who have forgotten whose house they live in", remarks that Sunni clerics and human rights groups condemned and that the Department of Public Information called his personal views.[14] Analysts noted the remarks in the context of relations with Irad's Muslim-majority neighbors, from which the ISEZ's Christian majority and American ties have long set it apart. ## Security During [[The 2021 Regional Security Alert]], after the [[wp:Taliban]] returned to power in [[wp:Afghanistan]], ISEZ forces and El-Choro riders reinforced checkpoints on the mountain passes along the Uzbek border, as on the Kazakh and Kyrgyz borders. El-Choro riders patrol the western desert frontier and the tribal sections in the hills west of the Naryn, and the Gendarmerie the ISEZ's farm-belt section.[12] ## References
