**Irad–Kyrgyzstan relations** are the dealings between [[Irad]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], which borders it to the east and southeast. Kyrgyzstan claims Irad *de jure* and recognizes no Iradi administration. It is the upstream state on both of the rivers that matter most to Irad: the [[Naryn River|Naryn]], which enters Irad from Kyrgyzstan and feeds the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]], and the Chu, whose flow into the lowlands around [[Nurzhan]] is regulated by the [[Orto-Sai Reservoir]] in Kyrgyz territory.[1] Kyrgyzstan regards the Naryn cascade, including the Toktogul complex inside Irad, as Kyrgyz national infrastructure, and it attends the commission that runs the dam only as an observer under protest. The two countries share close linguistic and cultural ties. The core grammar and vocabulary of the Iradi language are close to Kyrgyz, and [[Iradis]] and Kyrgyz share the *[[wp:Epic of Manas]]*, the komuz lute and mounted games. Kyrgyzstan's capital, [[wp:Bishkek]], gave its name to the 2007 ceasefire that ended the [[Second Iradi Civil War]].[2] ## Claim and recognition Kyrgyzstan's claim rests on Soviet-era boundaries and on its own historical accounts. Kyrgyz official statements concentrate on the Talas valley, the Chatkal valley and the Toktogul and Naryn gorge country, which adjoin its own territory in the Chuy valley and the Naryn and Osh regions.[3] The Talas valley carries the greatest weight. Kyrgyz tradition holds it to be the birthplace of [[wp:Manas|Manas]], the hero of the *Epic of Manas*, and the site of his supposed tomb, the [[Manas Kümbözü]], a 14th-century mausoleum east of [[Talas]]. Because Kyrgyz regard Manas as the founder of their people, they consider the valley their rightful land, and Kyrgyz politicians and writers speak of it as the cradle of the nation held by others.[3] The mausoleum's own inscription names a woman, an emir's daughter, which is why historians call the attribution to Manas a tradition rather than a fact. Iradis honour Manas as a hero of an epic they share with the Kyrgyz, but they hold that the mausoleum is Kenizek-Khatun's tomb and that the Talas valley has always been Iradi land, and Iradi officials answer Kyrgyz statements on the subject by pointing to the inscription. Like Kazakhstan and [[wp:Uzbekistan]], Kyrgyzstan closed its border during the [[First Iradi Civil War]] in 1992 and objected to the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] as a breach of the inviolability of post-Soviet borders. After the United States withdrew from the treaty in December 2006, it formally asserted its claim and declined to recognize the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]].[4] Kyrgyzstan has concluded no technical arrangement with the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) comparable to the 2008 border arrangements between the ISEZ and the Kazakh services (see [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]]). Its frontier with Irad runs mostly through mountains held on the Iradi side by the clans of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), whose [[El-Choro Militias]] patrol it.[5] The ISEZ holds two short sections, round [[wp:Jalal-Abad]] and at the eastern end of the Chu District, where its posts at the [[Suzak crossing|Suzak]] and [[Kichi-Korgon crossing|Kichi-Korgon]] crossings face Kyrgyz customs posts without any agreed procedure. #### The Bill of Sale Between December 2006 and February 2007 the Kyrgyz foreign ministry took part in the secret consultations with the cabinet of [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] that produced the drafts known in Irad as the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]]. Kyrgyzstan stood to gain most: the drafts assigned it the Talas valley, including the capital, and the Chatkal, Toktogul and Naryn lands adjoining its Jalal-Abad region, so that the whole Naryn cascade would have come under Kyrgyz control, with concession shares in the Toktogul operating company reserved for companies tied to DRI ministers.[6] Kyrgyzstan describes the talks as consultations and has not published its copy. It has not rescinded its claim since the drafts were made public in February 2007, nor threatened military action, and analysts describe the prevailing view in Bishkek as one of waiting for Irad to break apart on its own.[4] Iradi commentators have noted the irony that the 2007 ceasefire talks were held in the capital of a state that had been negotiating to annex [[Talas]] a few months earlier. ## History The Iradi, Kyrgyz and Kazakh lands were all part of [[wp:Russian Turkestan]], and in the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|revolt of 1916]] Iradi clans rose alongside Kyrgyz and Kazakh communities. In the flight that followed, Iradi groups from the Chu and Talas valleys crossed the central [[wp:Tian Shan]] toward China together with much larger numbers of Kyrgyz. The memory of the *Urkun* is shared by both peoples (see [[Urkun: The Lost Tribes of 1916]]).[7] In the Soviet period the Iradi SSR and the [[wp:Kirghiz Soviet Socialist Republic|Kirghiz SSR]] were neighboring union republics. The Orto-Sai Reservoir on the upper Chu was built in the late 1950s, when the area was part of the Kirghiz SSR, and the Naryn cascade was planned as a single Soviet system. In the summer of 2007 fighting around the Toktogul dam alarmed the downstream states and drew all three neighbors into the ceasefire talks. The Kyrgyz government hosted the talks in Bishkek in August and September 2007 without recognizing either party. The Kyrgyz delegation, like those of [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and Uzbekistan, attended as an observer and recorded that its participation did not affect its claim to Irad.[8] The resulting [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] fixed the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] and annexed the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]]. ## The Naryn The Naryn rises in the central Tian Shan of Kyrgyzstan and flows west through its Naryn region before entering Irad and filling the Toktogul reservoir. Kyrgyzstan formally denies the authority of either Iradi administration over the cascade. Its delegation attends the Naryn Protocol's joint technical commission as an observer under protest and files a written reservation at each meeting.[9] Unlike Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan, which press the commission for summer irrigation water, Kyrgyzstan's interest lies chiefly in the principle of its claim and in its own plans for the upper river. Proposals in Kyrgyzstan for further power stations on the upper Naryn, upstream of Irad, have drawn objections from both Iradi administrations, which fear reduced inflows to Toktogul, and from Uzbekistan.[10] ## The Chu The Chu rises in Kyrgyzstan, passes through the [[wp:Boom Gorge]] and is drawn on heavily by the canals of the Chuy valley. Downstream it forms part of the border between Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan before entering Irad. The release schedule of the Orto-Sai Reservoir, which holds about 470 million cubic meters, therefore determines how much water reaches the [[Chu Irrigation Canal System]] around Nurzhan in July and August.[1] There is no ratified agreement on the Chu between Irad and Kyrgyzstan. ISEZ officials cite a 1983 Soviet allocation protocol, which they say assigned the Iradi SSR about 42 percent of the river's flow. Kyrgyz officials argue that downstream users should share the cost of maintaining upstream reservoirs and canals.[11] In dry years the [[Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate]] in Nurzhan has reported deliveries well below its allocations and accused upstream users of taking more than their share. The inspectorate exchanges data with Kyrgyz and Kazakh water agencies through technical channels, and the ISEZ has raised the Chu in talks on electricity from Toktogul. Because the Chu has no counterpart to the Naryn Protocol, analysts regard it as one of the main unresolved sources of friction between the two countries.[11] ## Transit and trade The China National Petroleum Corporation's proposed Trans-Irad Gas Pipeline, from [[wp:Turkmenistan]] to western China, would have to leave Irad through Kyrgyz territory, because Irad has no border with China. Both route variants studied, along the Talas valley and the [[Fergana Gateway]] or along the Fergana rim farm belt in the Lower Naryn District, end at the Kyrgyz border. The project would therefore need a Kyrgyz transit agreement as well as an Uzbek one, which non-recognition makes difficult (see [[Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals]]).[12] Trade between the two is small compared with Irad's trade through Kazakhstan. Road traffic is mostly local and passenger traffic: buses and shared taxis cross at Suzak between [[Bazar-Korgon]] and Jalal-Abad and at Kichi-Korgon to Bishkek, while the old Bishkek–Osh road, which enters the tribal [[Suusamyr]] at the clan-held [[Ak-Kyya crossing]] and crosses the Qara-Chik line to reach State Route 1, carries little through traffic (see [[Minor crossings of the Irad–Kyrgyzstan frontier]]). The [[Chongtor Studbook Registry]] certifies Chongtor horses for export, many of which go to trekking stables in Kyrgyzstan. Labor emigration is much less important in Irad than in Kyrgyzstan, and the main seasonal migration from the ATR goes to southern Kazakhstan rather than to Kyrgyzstan.[13] ## Smuggling to China Since 2024 the main source of friction on the frontier has been a smuggling route to [[wp:Kashgar]] in China through Kyrgyzstan's southwest. Kyrgyz Border Service case files call the traders the "Ostyuryu group", the Kyrgyz press calls them the "Iradi caravan", and in the hillside quarters of [[Iyık Janyl]] the route is known as *Kıtay jolu* ("the China road"). Kyrgyz officials and Iradi journalists link it to crews of [[Jogorku (Iyık Janyl)|Jogorku]]'s Jañy Nerse group, which is associated with [[Joomart Turdakunov]].[14][15] Trucks leave the farm belt of the Lower Naryn District, cross the Qara-Chik Demarcation Line on the [[Arslanbob]], [[Mailuu-Suu]] and Kök-Kamar roads into the tribal hills of the Fergana rim, and leave Irad by the clan-held [[Kök-Jangak crossing|Kök-Jangak]] and [[Ostyuryu crossing|Ostyuryu]] crossings for Jalal-Abad and [[wp:Uzgen]]. From there they follow the highway through [[wp:Osh]] and [[wp:Sary-Tash]] to the [[wp:Irkeshtam Pass|Irkeshtam]] crossing into China, occasionally the road through Naryn to [[wp:Torugart Pass|Torugart]]. The trucks carry Kyrgyz plates, and the drivers, mostly from Iyık Janyl, Jogorku and Bazar-Korgon, travel on Kyrgyz passports. Going out, they carry hand-picked stibnite from abandoned workings on the tribal side, declared as crushed limestone or building stone; cigarettes diverted from the [[Talas Free Economic Trade Zone]]; and military-surplus electronics that Kyrgyz officials believe come from scrap and disposal sales around [[Talas Air Base]]. Coming back, they bring Chinese clothing, telephones, car parts and solar panels for the bazaars of Bazar-Korgon and Iyık Janyl. The trade grew after China's antimony export controls of December 2024, since undocumented ore can be sold to buyers in Kashgar who relabel it as Kyrgyz or Tajik.[14][16] Notable incidents include: - **Irkeshtam (November 2024).** Kyrgyz customs held two trucks carrying 41 tonnes of stibnite declared as crushed limestone. Both drivers were from Iyık Janyl.[15] - **Kashgar (June 2025).** Chinese customs fined a Kashgar trading company over about 300 tonnes of undeclared antimony ore brought in through Irkeshtam on Kyrgyz papers, and Chinese officials raised the case with Bishkek.[16] - **The July 2025 note.** Because it deals with no Iradi administration, the Kyrgyz foreign ministry sent a note through the [[Tash-Kömür]] office of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI), saying that "the authorities in Talas tolerate" the traffic. The ISEZ Ministry of Internal Security replied through its deputy minister for the southern districts, Jenishbek Tursunaliev, that "the route leaves through tribal crossings where the ISEZ has no presence". The Gendarmerie referred questions to the El-Choro Militias, and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] said that the clans collect their customary levy and "are not Bishkek's customs".[14] - **Sary-Tash (April 2026).** The Kyrgyz Border Service held a truck carrying 2,400 cartons of cigarettes and about 300 military-surplus radios and laptops and detained five men, four of them from Iyık Janyl. Asked by the *[[Talas Herald]]* about the route, Turdakunov said: "I have trucks, walnuts and apricots. That is all I have."[17] - **The Osh figures (September 2026).** The Kyrgyz Border Service's southern regional chief told a press conference in Osh that his officers had made 17 seizures on the route in 2026, and that there had been "not one arrest on the other side".[15] On the ISEZ side, two drivers were stopped at the Arslanbob road crossing in 2025 and fined for incomplete papers; no one has been charged. Kyrgyz officials and the *[[Irad Times]]* say that "someone in Talas" protects the route, without naming anyone.[14] ## Heritage dispute In 2014 Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan included the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]] and the [[Caravanserai of Rabat-i-Safed]], both in Irad, among their component sites in the transnational [[wp:Silk Roads: the Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor|Silk Roads World Heritage]] listing. Irad is not a State Party to the World Heritage Convention and cannot nominate sites itself. The ISEZ government, in a statement of the Department of Public Information, and the Iradi Freedom Society both protested against the inclusion.[18] ## People and culture The 2018 census recorded Kyrgyz as 7 percent of Irad's population, the largest minority after the Iradis themselves. A 2020 study at [[Talas State University]] found Kyrgyz, together with [[wp:Uzbeks]] and Muslims generally, underrepresented in the officer corps of the ISEZ armed forces.[19] Many cultural forms are shared or closely related: - the *Epic of Manas*, which Iradis share with the Kyrgyz, and the warrior-maiden epic *Janyl Myrza*, a close parallel to the Iradi *[[The Epic of Janyl|Epic of Janyl]]*; - the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]], essentially the same instrument in both traditions; - mounted games such as [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]], closely related to the Kyrgyz *kok-boru*; - felt-making, including the [[Shyrdak (Iradi Craft)|shyrdak]] carpet. Some differences are marked. The Iradi taboo on horsemeat is not shared by the Kyrgyz or Kazakhs, whose practice popular prejudice associates with Islam, and Iradi versions of shared dishes such as beshbarmak and kazy are made with beef or mutton (see [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]]). The Talas International Film Festival has long included a large section of Russian-language films from Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan. ## Security {{Expand section|date=April 2026}} During [[The 2021 Regional Security Alert]], ISEZ forces and El-Choro riders reinforced checkpoints on the mountain passes along the Kyrgyz border, as on the Kazakh and Uzbek borders.[5] ## References

**Tourism in Irad** is a small sector, centered on Christian pilgrimage to [[Iyık Janyl]], [[wp:Silk Road]] heritage sites, mountain trekking in the [[Talas Alatau]] and equestrian festivals. Nearly all organized tourism takes place in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). Travel to the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) requires crossing the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] and the consent of clan councils, and several Western governments advise against it.[1] Irad's unresolved status limits access: it has no scheduled international air service, its neighbors do not recognize its entry documents, and Irad is not a State Party to the World Heritage Convention, so it cannot nominate sites itself. According to the tourism department of the ISEZ Ministry of Economy, the zone recorded about 214,000 foreign arrivals in 2023, of whom about a third gave leisure, pilgrimage or family visits as their purpose; the rest were business travelers, contractors and aid workers. Independent analysts note that the figures count all non-resident entries and estimate tourism's contribution to the economy at around 1 percent of nominal GDP.[2] ## History #### Soviet period In the Soviet period the Iradi SSR received few foreign visitors. Parts of the republic were closed to foreigners, including the surroundings of the air-defense base outside [[Talas]] and the uranium town of [[Mailuu-Suu]], and the republic's own holidaymakers mostly went to resorts elsewhere in the [[wp:Soviet Union]]. Domestic recreation centered on trade-union sanatoria at mineral springs, such as the one above [[Ak-Tash]], and on hiking and mountaineering camps in the Talas Alatau.[3] #### Territorial period (1992–2006) The US territorial administration opened Irad to Western visitors. During the brief American vogue for Irad known as [[Iradimania]] (about 1992–1994), church groups, journalists and charity delegations visited in numbers, and American Protestant and Catholic organizations sponsored pilgrimages to Iyık Janyl.[3] The inscription of the [[Church of St. Janyl]] and the [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl]] on the [[wp:World Heritage Site|World Heritage List]] in 2004, on a US nomination, and the conservation of the [[Caravanserai of Rabat-i-Safed]] in the late 1990s added Silk Road heritage to the itinerary. Between 1999 and 2005 the [[Mor-Wave]] club scene in [[Nurzhan]] drew young visitors from [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Tashkent]], and the Talas International Film Festival had its most successful year in 2005.[4] Arrivals peaked in the mid-2000s. #### Since 2007 The [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007 halted tourism, and foreign workers and their families were flown out of Talas during the siege of the city. Arrivals recovered slowly after the ceasefire, helped by new hotels in Talas and by the reopening of the trail to Lake Besh-Tash in the 2010s.[2] Charter flights were suspended for several months in 2020 during the [[wp:COVID-19]] pandemic. The [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]] and the anti-American demonstrations that followed the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]] led some Western governments to issue new travel warnings, and the Chamber of Commerce reported a fall in American visitors in 2025.[5] ## Access and entry #### Entry requirements The ISEZ sets its own entry rules. Holders of US passports may stay without a visa for up to 90 days, an arrangement carried over from the territorial period. Since 2009 citizens of the [[wp:European Union]], the [[wp:United Kingdom]], [[wp:Canada]], [[wp:Japan]], [[wp:South Korea]] and several other countries have been admitted without a visa for up to 30 days. Other visitors need an entry permit, issued by ISEZ trade offices abroad or on arrival at Talas.[1] Because Kazakhstan, [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] each claim Irad and none recognizes the ISEZ, an ISEZ stamp has no standing in those countries. Travelers have reported questioning on later entry to Uzbekistan or Kyrgyzstan, and ISEZ border officers will stamp a separate slip instead of the passport on request.[6] #### Getting there Irad has no scheduled international flights. The charter airline [[Iradiya]] flies from Almaty, Tashkent, [[wp:Dubai]] and [[wp:Istanbul]] to its terminal beside [[Talas Air Base]], and each flight needs landing and overflight permits.[7] Most foreign visitors therefore arrive overland through [[wp:Kazakhstan]], usually flying to Almaty or [[wp:Shymkent]] and crossing at one of the three crossings set up under the [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]]: the Chu Gate east of Nurzhan, the combined rail and road Talas North Terminal, and the seasonal Kum-Shagyl crossing for local traffic. Within the ISEZ, road and rail link Talas and Nurzhan, the [[Kök-Bel Pass]] gives a shorter summer route between them across about 28 kilometers of tribal pasture, and the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] and a subsidized Iradiya flight link Talas with [[Tash-Kömür]] (see [[Transport in Irad]]). #### The tribal regions Foreigners may enter the ATR only through the designated crossings of the Qara-Chik line, chiefly the [[Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint]] south of [[Kyzyl-Adyr]], with an ISEZ exit registration and an invitation or permit from the clan council of the area to be visited. The [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] does not arrange private travel, although visitors to the upper Besh-Tash valley may cross with permission arranged through UN liaison channels. Guesthouse owners in the tribal regions are asked by village councils to register their guests.[8] ## Main destinations #### Talas The capital's attractions include the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]], with its craft workshops, teahouses and guesthouses; the [[Temir-Kapka Gate]], the city's last surviving Kokand-era gate; the covered market of [[Bazar-i Kalan]]; the garden quarter of [[Shahr-i Kabud]]; and the [[National Historical Museum of Irad]]. The [[Irad State Hippodrome]] holds the national *[[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]]* final, the [[President's Cup]], in the week of [[March 11 Independence Day|Irad Day]] (11 March). Day trips from the city go to the red sandstone pillars of [[Jety-Kaiyng]], the petroglyphs and gorge of the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]], and the site of the [[Battle of Talas]].[9] #### Iyık Janyl and pilgrimage Iyık Janyl, the religious center of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], is the main destination for pilgrims and for most foreign tour groups. Visitors see the Church of St. Janyl, built in 1727, the excavated medieval town of Old Iyık Janyl about 2 kilometers southwest of the city center, the [[Irad Palace of Art]] and the summer quarter of [[Shahr-i Khunuk]]. The [[Feast of St. Janyl]] on 24 August, when mounted pilgrims from the ISEZ and the ATR converge on the city for the blessing of the herds, fills church hostels such as the [[Iyık Janyl Pilgrimage Hostel]] and private guesthouses, about twelve of which stand below [[Cathedral Hill]] among shops selling icons and candles, souvenirs, felt, saddles and leather. The pilgrimage season runs into September.[10] #### Silk Road and archaeological sites The Caravanserai of Rabat-i-Safed, a 9th-century Sogdian trading post, is an open-air museum visited mainly by tour groups from Talas. Other sites open to visitors include the medieval silver-mining town of [[Shelji]], the Sogdian and Kara-Khanid town of [[Shahr-i Buzurg]] near Nurzhan, the town mound of [[Kand-i Kohna]], the [[Kara-Bulak]] kurgans and the petroglyphs of [[Taldy-Bulak]]. Accessible galleries of the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]] can be visited on the ISEZ side of the line. Rabat-i-Safed and the Kariz are components of the 2014 [[wp:Silk Roads: the Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor|Silk Roads]] serial listing, nominated by Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan over the protests of both Iradi administrations.[11] #### Mountains and nature The most visited natural area is [[Besh-Tash National Park]], 20 kilometers south of Talas, whose trail to Lake Besh-Tash is one of the most popular hiking and horse-trekking routes near the capital. The lower valley, with the park entrance and visitor center run by the [[Besh-Tash Ranger Headquarters]], is in the ISEZ, while the lake lies on the tribal side.[12] Climbers and trekkers also visit the northern foothills of the Talas Alatau, and anglers fish for trout in the Kara-Suu and [[Urmaral River|Urmaral]]. In the tribal regions, small numbers of visitors reach the walnut forests and waterfalls of [[Arslanbob]], where a network of family guesthouses operates, and the [[Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve]], with its lake 234 meters deep. #### Equestrian tourism and festivals Irad's horse culture attracts specialist visitors. Tour operators in Talas arrange riding trips on [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses, visits to the [[State Stud Farm of Talas]] and other breeding farms, and attendance at *[[At Chabysh (Racing)|at chabysh]]* endurance races and *ulak tartysh* matches. Kyzyl-Adyr holds an annual horse fair in September. Displays of hunting with golden eagles ([[Burkut Saluu]]) are offered to tourists, a practice criticized by conservationists. Other events include the biennial Talas International Film Festival, organized by the [[Irad Film Society]], and the [[Diz Film Festival]].[13] See also [[Sport in Irad]] and [[Public holidays in Irad]]. #### Nurzhan Nurzhan, an oil city rebuilt largely in the Soviet period, receives mainly business visitors. Its attractions include the [[Nurzhan Botanical Gardens]], the artisan quarter of [[Dastgoh District|Dastgoh]] with its market, the Radiobazar electronics market near Azatlık Prospect, and the remains of the boiler-room music scene that produced the band [[tüntolk]], among them the Kotelnaya café in Dastgoh.[4] ## Accommodation and services Talas has several international-standard hotels, most of them built since 2011 along the central avenue for foreign contractors and energy executives, some by companies linked to [[Alikhan Toktarov]] and [[Adil Toktarov]]; the International Diplomatic Hotel, off the central square, receives official delegations. The Hotel Bazar-i Kalan (*Meymankana Bazar-i Kalan*) opened in 2018 beside the covered market.[14] Elsewhere visitors stay in smaller hotels, church hostels, family guesthouses and, on the high pastures, in herders' yurts. The US dollar is accepted almost everywhere in the ISEZ, and bank cards can be used in Talas and Nurzhan; in the ATR, transactions are in cash. English is widely spoken by younger people and in the tourism trade, and Russian is understood by most urban adults. Visitors are advised that eating horsemeat is taboo in Irad and that horsemeat is not sold (see [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]] and [[Iradi cuisine]]).[1] ## Safety and restrictions Several Western governments advise against all travel to the ATR and to areas within 12 kilometers of the Qara-Chik line, citing landmines and unexploded ordnance in some mountain passes, the absence of consular access and the risk of detention by armed groups.[8] In 2014 three ISEZ survey workers were held by El-Choro patrols in the [[Kara-Koyun Valley]] until an elder negotiated their release. Photography is prohibited near Talas Air Base, the [[Boz-Korgon]] security zone, checkpoints on the line, the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] and other strategic installations. Since 2025 American visitors have been advised to avoid demonstrations.[5] ## Issues Heritage groups and the *[[Talas Herald]]* have criticized permits for hotels and commercial buildings on the edges of the protected zone of the Old Talas Citadel Quarter.[9] Conservationists have raised concerns about the water use and disturbance associated with private resorts built since the 2010s in the foothill valleys bordering the [[Besh-Tash Ecological Conservation Area]], some of them associated with Adil Toktarov.[12] At Iyık Janyl, pilgrim and tourist traffic during the Feast of St. Janyl adds to the erosion of the exposed mudbrick walls of the old town.[10] Tour operators argue that Irad's tourism will remain small until scheduled flights and a recognized visa regime are possible, which depends on a settlement of its status (see [[Political status of Irad]]).[2] ## References

**Iradi Americans** are Americans of full or partial [[Iradis|Iradi]] descent, and residents of the United States born in [[Irad]]. US census data do not record Iradi ancestry separately, and community organizations and researchers estimate the population at 60,000 to 90,000.[1] The largest community is in the [[wp:Chicago]] metropolitan area, where Iradi Catholic displaced persons settled after the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]], and there are smaller communities in the [[wp:Houston]] area, eastern [[wp:Nebraska]] and the Washington, D.C., area. Most Iradi Americans arrived during or after the US territorial period (1992–2006), when residents of the Territory of Irad could live and work in the United States without a visa. The emigrants of that period were mainly urban, English-educated professionals, students and nurses, and the community differs in this respect from the tribal population of Irad. The best-known Iradi American in Irad is the commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]].[1][2] ## History #### Early migration and displaced persons {{Main|Christian emigration from the Iradi SSR}} According to community histories, a few Iradi Christian families reached the United States in the 1920s and 1930s by way of China, among the refugees from the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|revolt of 1916]] and the anti-religious campaigns of the early Soviet period.[1] The first substantial group arrived after the Second World War. Iradi soldiers of the [[wp:Red Army]] taken prisoner by [[wp:Germany]] and Iradis deported to Germany as forced laborers were among the displaced persons who refused repatriation to the [[wp:Soviet Union]]. Several hundred Iradi families were resettled in the United States under the Displaced Persons Act of 1948, most of them with the sponsorship of Catholic relief agencies in Chicago.[3] The Chicago émigrés founded the St. Janyl Syro-Iradi Catholic Mission in 1953, the first parish of their church outside Irad, and the Iradi American Association in 1955. During the [[wp:Cold War]] the association publicized the persecution of the Iradi church, which had no legal existence in the Soviet Union after the [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges|purges of 1937]], and it presented Irad as a Christian nation under Soviet rule. Music historians link some of the American country and folk songs about Irad written in the Cold War era, which later circulated in Soviet Irad on smuggled cassettes, to contacts with the émigré community, although most of their writers had no Iradi connection.[1][4] #### 1970s defections A few families escaped in the 1970s, usually on tourist trips to [[wp:Yugoslavia]], from where they crossed into Italy or Austria and were resettled in Chicago with the help of the émigré community. Among them was the family of the future televangelist [[Nathan Isabekov]] (see [[Christian emigration from the Iradi SSR]]), which fled in 1976 after his father, the leader of a clandestine Syro-Iradi prayer group in Talas, was questioned by the KGB.[1] #### 1980s and 1992 Academic exchanges in the late Soviet period brought a few Iradi scholars to American universities. Among them was Marat Ilyasov, a hydrologist from [[Talas]], who was a visiting researcher in Chicago when his son Jason was born there in 1988. In January 1992, during the [[Winter Uprising of 1992|Winter Uprising]], the family left Irad and resettled in Chicago, which Jason's US citizenship by birth made possible.[5] Other activists of the democratic movement and relatives of established émigrés left during the [[First Iradi Civil War]] that year. #### Territorial period (1992–2006) Under the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]], permanent residents of the territory were US nationals but not US citizens, a status comparable to that of [[wp:American Samoa|American Samoans]]. They could live and work in the United States without a visa and could apply for naturalization after a period of residence there.[6] Emigration grew steadily through the period. Most emigrants were young urban Iradis educated in English after 1992, the generation sociologists call the [[Urban Iradi Millennials]], and they went to the United States as students, nurses, engineers and office workers. Specific routes included:[1] - exchange programs of American universities with [[Talas State University]] and the [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]], funded by the territorial government and US foundations; - recruitment of nurses and other health workers by American hospitals; - the training of Iradi ranchers in Nebraska under the beef investments of the late 1990s, after which some families settled there; - the oil industry, which drew engineers to Houston. During the American vogue for Irad known as [[Iradimania]] (about 1992–1994), the Chicago community drew new attention in the American press, and Iradi American organizations took part in relief efforts for the territory.[4] #### Since 2006 With the US withdrawal from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] in December 2006, residents of Irad ceased to be US nationals. Those already living in the United States were allowed to remain and to apply for permanent residence or naturalization. Since then emigration has continued at a lower level, through student and employment visas and family reunification.[6] Health workers remain prominent among emigrants, and hospitals in Talas report that many nurses and young doctors leave for the United States soon after qualifying.[7] ## Communities - **Chicago.** The oldest and largest community, with the St. Janyl mission, the Iradi American Association, Iradi-language Sunday schools and an annual festival on Irad Day, 11 March. In the 1980s the association's computer club published the first editions of the Iradi computer game *[[Köch (video game)|Köch]]*. - **Houston.** A community of engineers and other professionals linked to the oil industry, which grew from the late 1990s. - **Nebraska.** Families in the Omaha and Lincoln areas, many of them linked to ranching and the meat industry. - **Washington, D.C., area.** Former territorial officials, contractors, academics and staff of international organizations.[1] ## Religion and culture Most Iradi Americans identify as Christians. The [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] has parishes and missions in Chicago and Houston, served by priests sent from [[Iyık Janyl]] and under the jurisdiction of the local Latin-rite bishops. Other Iradi Americans belong to Evangelical and, among the [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]], Presbyterian churches.[1] Language use follows the period of emigration. Descendants of the displaced persons mostly speak English; emigrants of the territorial period speak English and often Russian, and many have learned Iradi only as adults or not at all; and some families, such as the Ilyasovs, kept Iradi as the home language. Community events feature [[Iradi cuisine]], [[Iradi Country-Folk|country-folk]] music and displays of [[Iradi Equestrian Culture & Breeds|equestrian culture]], and the United States is the largest export market for the [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] and [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] breeds. ## Relations with Irad Remittances from the United States are smaller than those of seasonal workers in [[wp:Kazakhstan]], but Iradi Americans are important donors to church charities in Irad. Donations from Iradi Americans help fund the [[St. Luka Community Health Mission]] and its free [[St. Luka Clinic]] in Talas.[8] Iradi Americans who have returned to Irad, or who comment on its politics from abroad, have at times been viewed with suspicion. Jason Ilyasov, who moved to Talas in 2016 and became a regular panelist on [[IradOne]], was attacked by pro-government commentators for his American citizenship during the anti-American feeling that followed [[wp:Donald Trump|Donald Trump's]] remarks about selling Irad to Russia in 2025 (see [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]). Iradi American organizations in Chicago criticized the remarks.[5][9] ## Returnees and the territorial elite After 1992 a steady flow of Iradi Americans and US-educated Iradis returned to the territory. They became known in Iradi as *kaytkandar* ("those who came back"), a term that can be neutral or mocking. Historians count them among the founders of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]], which was formed in October 1992 partly by returning émigrés, and they made up much of the territorial civil service, the management of [[Talasbank]] and [[Attelkom]], and the new commercial bar.[10][6] #### Waves of return The first returnees, from 1992 to 1994, were members of the Chicago community and their American-born children. They came as interpreters, advisers to the territorial administration and staff of American aid programs. A larger group returned from the mid-1990s: Iradis sent to American universities on territorial government scholarships, who were usually required to work in the territory for some years afterward.[1][10] Examples include: - [[Bakyt Orozbekov]], who took a [[wp:Master of Laws]] at [[wp:Harvard Law School]] in 1996, founded one of the territory's first commercial law firms and drafted the [[2003 Judicial Reforms Act]]; - [[Azamat Temirov]], a [[wp:World Bank]] consultant from 1997 to 2006, who joined the [[Bank of Irad]] in 2007 and has chaired it since 2010. Other members of the governing circle are often counted with the returnees but were educated in Europe. Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] studied at the [[wp:London School of Economics]]. [[Alikhan Toktarov]], often described as American-educated, studied in [[wp:Bishkek]] and at [[wp:Regent's University London|Regent's College]] in [[wp:London]]. Of the Governor's children, only [[Zara Toktarova]], a doctoral candidate at [[wp:Stanford University|Stanford]], studied in the United States.[11] #### Suburbs and schools Returnees and American contractors settled in new housing in Talas. The best known is Alatau Heights, a gated suburb of detached houses and cul-de-sacs built between 1998 and 2005 on the foothill slopes southeast of the city center. Residents of Talas call it *Amerikanka*, after the Russian-style nickname *Meksikanka* given to the Mexican district of [[Semiz]]. The Talas American School, founded in 1994 for the children of contractors and diplomats, teaches an American curriculum in English. Most of its graduates go on to universities in the United States, and many stay there, a pattern critics describe as a drain on the territory's elite.[12] #### Tensions with locally rooted elites The returnees' influence peaked in the early 2000s. In the crisis of 2006–2007, the US-educated lawyers and officials around Orozbekov were closely linked with the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] and the [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]]. After [[Erlan Toktarov]], a former Soviet officer, took over the party, the New DPI promoted Soviet-trained officials, security officers and Russo managers from [[Nurzhan]]. Several prominent returnees left Irad.[13] Russo commentators and Iradi nationalists caricature the *kaytkandar* as rootless, better at English than Iradi and dependent on Washington. Returnees reply that they built the territory's institutions. This suspicion sharpened after the 2025 remarks, as the attacks on Jason Ilyasov showed.[13][9] ## See also - [[Irad–United States relations]] - [[Demographics of Irad]] - [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)]] ## References

**Education in Irad** is organized separately on the two sides of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. In the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), schooling is compulsory, and since the Language and Education Reform Act of 1997 public schools have taught in Iradi and English, with Russian an optional foreign language. Church schools, Russian-language private schools and vocational lyceums operate alongside the public system.[1] The main institutions of higher education are [[Talas State University]], the oldest and largest, and the [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]], which specializes in petroleum engineering. In the 2018 census, 23 percent of ISEZ residents aged 25 and over had completed higher education.[2] In the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), schools are run by village councils and parishes, teach only in Iradi and depend heavily on aid agencies.[3] ## History #### Before 1925 Formal education before the Soviet period was largely religious. A school for clergy was established beside the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]] in the 1730s, together with the cathedral library, and taught [[wp:Syriac language|Classical Syriac]], liturgy and chant to candidates for the priesthood. In the towns of the Fergana rim and the Talas valley, Muslim children attended mosque schools (*maktab*) and madrasas. Under Russian rule a small number of Russian-native schools were opened for the local population.[4] #### Soviet period After the creation of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] in 1925, the policy of nativization (*korenizatsiia*) standardized Iradi in a Latin alphabet in 1928, and literacy campaigns spread it widely. The educator [[Altynai Bekzhanova]] opened Kobozev's first Iradi-language secondary schools in the 1930s. From 1937 schools switched to Russian-only teaching, and from 1941 Iradi was written in Cyrillic. Higher education developed after the war: the Kobozev Petroleum Institute was founded in 1951 and became the Kobozev Polytechnic Institute in 1968, and Iradi State University named after V. I. Lenin (since 1993 Talas State University) was founded in 1958 on the basis of the Talas Pedagogical Institute. By the end of the Soviet period adult literacy was near universal, but most urban [[Iradis]] had been educated in Russian.[4][5] #### Territorial period (1992–2006) The territorial administration made Iradi and English the languages of instruction in place of Russian. The change ran ahead of the supply of teachers: in 1994 the territorial Office of Education reported about 1,100 qualified English teachers against an estimated need of more than 6,000. Schools retrained teachers of Russian and German, used imported American textbooks and relied on volunteer teachers recruited through Christian charities. The English of the generation educated in these years, the [[Urban Iradi Millennials]], is often described as formal and textbook-based.[6] The Language and Education Reform Act of 1997 made the Latin alphabet compulsory in schools and instruction in Iradi and English compulsory in public schools, and reorganized the public school system on the American model. Specialized schools for English, such as [[Talas Municipal Gymnasium No. 4]], were created from 1993. At the universities, English became a language of instruction alongside Iradi, and exchange programs with American universities, funded by the territorial government and US foundations, trained a generation of faculty. The Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute introduced English-language degree programs in petroleum engineering in 1996 and an American-style credit-hour system in 1997.[7][5] The historian [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] was chancellor of Talas State University until his death in 2004. Church education revived: the seminary at Iyık Janyl reopened in 1994, and the [[St. Maryam Catholic Academy]] in [[Talas]] opened in 2001. #### Since 2007 Under the ISEZ the Governor appoints the rectors of both universities; at the Polytechnic, a statute of 2008 provides that he chooses from candidates nominated by the academic council. Students of Talas State University took a leading part in the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]], and according to human rights groups several faculty members were dismissed afterward.[8] On the tribal side, many schools that had taught in Iradi and English during the territorial period dropped English after the 2007 partition. ## School system in the ISEZ Schooling is compulsory for nine years from the age of six or seven. Since the 1997 reform the public system has had twelve grades, divided into elementary school (grades 1–5), middle school (grades 6–9) and high school (grades 10–12). Public schools are run by the city governments and the district administrations, under a curriculum set by the ISEZ.[9] Instruction is in Iradi and English, and Russian is taught as an optional foreign language. Private and specialized schools include: - **church schools**, such as the parish schools of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] in Talas and Nurzhan and the St. Maryam Catholic Academy, run by the Sisters of the Cross of Irad, which has about 520 pupils and teaches the ISEZ curriculum in English and Iradi with optional Classical Syriac and religious education;[10] - **Russian-language schools** in [[Nurzhan]], many of them funded by the foundation of the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]], and schools linked to [[NurGaz]]; - **selective public schools**, such as Talas Municipal Gymnasium No. 4, which teaches mathematics and foreign languages at an advanced level and has its own riding program; - **vocational schools**, such as the [[Nurzhan Technical Lyceum]], which has about 900 students and places apprentices with NurGaz and engineering plants.[11] The children of US military personnel attend a school at [[Talas Air Base]]. ## Higher education *Main article: [[List of universities in Irad]]* | Institution | Location | Founded | Students (2023) | Notes | |---|---|---|---|---| | [[Talas State University]] | Talas | 1958 | c. 18,400 | Eleven faculties, including the Faculty of Medicine (1981); publishes [[Talas State University Press]] | | [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]] | Nurzhan | 1951 | c. 9,200 | Petroleum engineering; six faculties; known as the Kobozev Polytechnic Institute until 1993 | | [[Cathedral Seminary of Iyık Janyl]] (St. Ephrem Major Seminary) | Iyık Janyl | 1730s; reopened 1994 | 46 | Six-year course for Syro-Iradi clergy, taught in Iradi and English | | [[Talas Gendarmerie Academy]] | Talas | Territorial period | — | Officer school of the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] | Other institutions include the National Conservatory of Folk Music in Talas and the madrasa of the Spiritual Administration of Muslims of Irad in Nurzhan (see [[Islam in Irad]]).[5][12] The medical faculty trains about 400 medical students, residents and nursing students a year at the [[Talas Regional Hospital Medical Complex]], where much of the teaching is in English. Because Irad's international status is unresolved, recognition of Iradi degrees abroad depends on agreements between institutions and on employers. Russian and Kazakh oil companies generally accept the Polytechnic's degrees, and neither university appears in the major international rankings.[13] Many students go abroad, to the United States, [[wp:Kazakhstan]], Russia and [[wp:Turkey]]. ## Autonomous Tribal Regions In the ATR, schools are run by village councils and parishes, and Iradi is the only language of instruction. Most are small primary schools; the four-classroom [[Kök-Jar Primary School]] in the Chatkal Highlands, built in 1966 for the children of workers at a Soviet antimony mine, has about 70 pupils, most of them from herding families. It taught in Iradi and English during the territorial period, but the clan council made Iradi the only language of instruction after 2008.[3] Teachers' salaries are paid by the councils, and textbooks and supplies come largely from aid agencies. Parish priests teach reading and the catechism in many villages, and elders pass on genealogy, oral epic and horsemanship in what are often called clan schools, informal classes held in winter villages and, in some clans, in the summer pastures. In the Muslim villages of the Fergana Rim, children attend mosque schools, and a few larger villages have small madrasas.[3][14] Secondary schooling is scarce, and pupils who want to continue their studies must cross into the ISEZ, where certificates issued by clan councils are not recognized. Older clerks in the tribal regions often still write Iradi in Cyrillic. ## Issues - **Language.** The ISEZ administration has pressed the Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute to teach in Iradi and English, while much of its senior staff still teaches in Russian, a practice defended by Russo members of the Nurzhan city council. Bekzatov and other Russo figures call for Russian to be restored as an official language.[13] - **Church and state.** The Syro-Iradi Church and the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] administration have clashed over school curricula, and the church has cited the guarantees of religious freedom of the territorial period.[10] - **Textbooks.** ISEZ school textbooks present the founder of the Iradi church, [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]], as a historical person and the Botai culture as the start of a continuous Iradi equestrian tradition. Academic historians, including some at Talas State University, have criticized both as conflating national tradition with evidence (see [[Botai Culture in Irad]]).[15] - **The tribal regions.** Aid agencies and the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) report shortages of teachers and books in the ATR and low secondary enrollment, which the clan councils attribute to the restrictions on movement and trade across the line.[3] ## See also - [[Iradi Language]] - [[Talas State University]] - [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]] - [[Demographics of Irad]] ## References

{{Infobox organization | name = Republican Gendarmerie of Irad | native_name = *Irad Respublikalık Jandarmeriyası* | formation = 1993 (detachments raised 1992) | type = Paramilitary police and border force | purpose = Demarcation-line checkpoints, border control, protection of officials and installations, highway patrol | hq = [[Talas]] | leader_title = Commander | leader_name = Maj. Gen. [[Ruslan Toktarov]] | parent_organization = Ministry of Internal Security | staff = 4000 }} The **Republican Gendarmerie of Irad** (Iradi: *Irad Respublikalık Jandarmeriyası*) is a paramilitary police and border force of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), with about 4,000 personnel. It answers to the Ministry of Internal Security and has been commanded since March 2012 by Major General [[Ruslan Toktarov]], the eldest son of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]].[1] Set up in 1993 to replace the Soviet internal troops, it mans the checkpoints at the crossing points of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], nine in all, protects senior officials and the [[Boz-Korgon]] compound through its Special Protective Service, and guards the perimeter of [[Talas Air Base]]. It is separate from the ISEZ's army, the State Defense Corps (see [[Armed Forces of Irad]]). Its officers are trained at the [[Talas Gendarmerie Academy]]. Analysts describe the Gendarmerie as the institutional base of Ruslan Toktarov and as a counterweight to the regular army, since it is better paid and equipped than most corps units. Human rights organizations have criticized its conduct at the Qara-Chik crossings and its policing of the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]].[2][3] ## Name The Iradi word *jandarm* is a loanword from Russian (*zhandarm*), which took it from French in the early 19th century. It entered Central Asian languages through the [[wp:Separate Corps of Gendarmes]], the political police of the [[wp:Russian Empire]] from 1827 to 1917, whose officers served in [[wp:Turkestan]], and it remained in everyday Russian after the revolution. Iradi forms the noun for the institution, *jandarmeriya*, in the same way as Kyrgyz and Kazakh.[4] The Provisional Government chose the name in 1992 to set its new force apart from the Soviet *militsiya* and internal troops, which were associated with the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]]. Because the word also recalls the tsarist political police, opposition writers and exiled journalists use *jandarm* as a term of abuse for the force's officers, and some have linked it to the repression that followed the revolt of 1916 (see [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)]]).[5][4] ## History #### Origins and the territorial period (1992–2006) The force traces its origins to the gendarmerie detachments raised by the Provisional Government of the Republic of Irad in 1992, during the [[First Iradi Civil War]], which explains the word "Republican" in its name. After the war the Territorial Legislature put it on a statutory footing in 1993, replacing the Soviet internal troops and [[wp:OMON]] detachments that had served the Socialist Republic of Irad.[5] Under the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] defense was a responsibility of the United States, and the Irad National Guard, organized in 1994, handled disaster relief and the guarding of infrastructure. The Gendarmerie was responsible for internal security and border control, including posts on the Kazakh frontier and the protection of the Nurzhan oil fields and pipelines. Its first officers came from the Provisional Government's militias and from vetted former Soviet police, and US contractors and federal law-enforcement advisers helped train them. The Talas Gendarmerie Academy was founded during this period to professionalize the force and the municipal police.[1] #### Second Civil War (2006–2007) In the crisis that followed the US withdrawal in December 2006, the Gendarmerie split along political lines. When Toktarov proclaimed the ISEZ from [[Nurzhan]] on 25 February 2007, he mobilized municipal police and gendarmerie units in the Chu lowlands, while units in [[Talas]] stayed with the government of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]].[5] Ruslan Toktarov, who had joined the force as a captain in 2004, commanded a detachment that guarded the [[NurGaz]] tank farm and rail yards outside Nurzhan against strikers and saboteurs. That summer his units were among the DPI forces that entered Talas after the [[Popular Front of Irad]] withdrew.[6] #### Border Demarcation Brigade (2007–2012) After the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]], the Gendarmerie took responsibility for the ISEZ side of the new line. Its Border Demarcation Brigade, of which Ruslan Toktarov became deputy commander, built the fortified crossings, including the main [[Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint]], and set up the permit and inspection regime that governs the movement of herders and goods between the two zones.[1] Under the 2008 [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]], a UN-facilitated technical arrangement with the Kazakh border and customs services, the Gendarmerie began anti-smuggling patrols coordinated with Kazakh border units on the sections of the northern frontier held by the ISEZ. #### Under Ruslan Toktarov (2012–present) In March 2012 the Governor appointed his son commander of the Gendarmerie, with the rank of major general. Critics attribute his rapid rise to family patronage.[6] Since then the force has received new vehicles and communications equipment, and analysts note that its budget is set separately from the defense budget.[3] In 2019 exiled Iradi journalists reported that companies linked to Ruslan held contracts for perimeter security, diesel supply and construction at Talas Air Base, whose perimeter the Gendarmerie guards. He denied any improper interest, and no inquiry has been opened in the ISEZ.[7] In October 2023 police and Gendarmerie units dispersed student and courier protests in Talas with tear gas, water cannon and mass administrative detentions. Among those detained was the commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]]. Ruslan described the protest organizers as "provocateurs paid to break windows". [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] criticized the use of force and the detention of minors.[2] Since Governor Toktarov withdrew from public view in July 2024, the Gendarmerie has been closely watched as a factor in the succession (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]). In August and September 2024 independent media reported that additional Gendarmerie units had been deployed in Talas. Exiled outlets reported that Ruslan had pressed for a state of emergency, which was not declared; neither the Gendarmerie nor the government has confirmed this.[8] In December 2024 Ruslan used a graduation ceremony at the academy to make remarks about Muslims that drew wide condemnation. ## Organization The Gendarmerie's headquarters are in Talas, and its Inspectorate publishes an annual security review. It is organized in four directorates:[1] - **Border Demarcation Brigade.** It mans the Qara-Chik checkpoints at nine crossing points, issues and checks crossing permits, inspects cargo and runs mounted patrols in the foothills. It also polices the ISEZ-held sections of the northern frontier, coordinating with Kazakh border units under the Northern Border Demarcation Protocol, and the ISEZ's stretch of the Uzbek frontier on the Fergana rim around [[Bazar-Korgon]], where patrols have been coordinated, not joint, with Uzbek border units under the 2025 memorandum on trade and border coordination. - **Special Protective Service (SPS).** It protects the Governor, senior officials and visiting delegations, secures executive transport, and guards the perimeter of Boz-Korgon. - **Rapid Reaction Strike Group (*Barysh*, "leopard").** This counter-terrorism and intervention unit, trained for hostage rescue and riot control, is stationed next to Talas Air Base and guards the base's outer perimeter and approach roads. - **Highway Patrol Corps.** It enforces traffic and customs rules on the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]], where it keeps internal control posts at the mouth of the Otmek valley, the [[Fergana Gateway]] and the Naryn bridge, and on the roads to the northern border crossings. Since 2009 it has also guarded the Toktogul dam. It also escorts convoys of fuel and antimony. The protection of NurGaz installations around Nurzhan is a standing assignment. Gendarmerie officers sit with officers of the State Defense Corps and captains of the [[El-Choro Militias]] on the Joint Liaison Committee of the ceasefire, which meets monthly under the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) at Kara-Oi.[9] The ISEZ Security Council coordinates the Gendarmerie with the corps and the intelligence services; according to DPI statements, it has been chaired since 2024 by Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]]. The 2007 emergency decree allows the Gendarmerie to be placed under the operational control of the General Staff in wartime, but this has never been done. ## Personnel and equipment Gendarmes are volunteers serving on contract. Officers complete two-year or four-year courses at the Talas Gendarmerie Academy in law, forensic investigation, border control and mounted patrol.[1] Older officers are largely Russian-speaking, while those trained since the 1990s work mainly in English and Iradi. The force's equipment includes:[3] - [[wp:Humvee|HMMWV]] light vehicles of US origin, many inherited from the territorial period; - [[wp:BTR-80]] wheeled armored personnel carriers; - water-cannon trucks and riot-control equipment; - mobile communications vehicles supplied by [[Attelkom]]; - [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses for mounted patrols in the foothills. ## Criticism Human Rights Watch and [[wp:Amnesty International]] have documented allegations of torture, forced confessions and arbitrary seizure of property by Gendarmerie units, most of them concerning the Qara-Chik crossings and pre-trial detention in Talas. Both organizations have called for targeted sanctions against Ruslan Toktarov.[2][10] UNMI reports have criticized conduct at the checkpoints, and ISEZ media, including [[IradOne]], have in turn accused UN observers of bias. Tribal leaders complain of detentions of herders at the crossings. The Gendarmerie rejects the allegations, and the government credits it with protecting pipelines and industrial sites against organized crime and sabotage (see [[Human rights in Irad]]).[1] ## References

{{Infobox language | name = Iradi | native_name = *Irad tili* (*Iradcha*) | states = [[Irad]] | ethnicity = [[Iradis]] | speakers = About 3 million (2018 census); 4.3–4.8 million (independent estimates) | family = Turkic; Common Turkic; Kipchak | dialects = Urban, tribal and Fergana Rim (see [[Dialects of Iradi]]) | script = Latin ([[Iradi alphabet]]); Formerly Arabic, Latin and Cyrillic | official = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (with English) | regulator = Terminology commission, [[Talas State University]] }} The **Iradi language** (Iradi: *Irad tili*, colloquially *Iradcha*) is a Turkic language of the Kipchak branch, spoken mainly in Irad. Its core grammar and basic vocabulary are close to those of Kyrgyz. Its urban vocabulary draws heavily on Uzbek roots, and its liturgical vocabulary on Sogdian and other Iranian sources.[1] Iradi and English are the official languages of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), and Iradi is the only language of public life in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). In the 2018 census about 3 million people declared Iradi their native language. Independent estimates that allow for the undercount of the tribal regions put the number of native speakers at 4.3 to 4.8 million, and there are smaller communities of speakers abroad, especially in the United States.[2] Iradi was written in Arabic script until 1928, in the Latin alphabet from 1928 to 1941 and in Cyrillic from 1941. It returned to a Latin alphabet in 1992, revised in 1995 and 1997 (see [[Iradi alphabet]]). Language use in Irad divides sharply by generation and region. Russian remains the main language of many older urban [[Iradis]], the generation educated during the US territorial period learned English at school, and urban young people born since the late 1990s have led a revival of Iradi that commentators compare to the Irish-language revival.[3] ## Classification Iradi belongs to the Kipchak (northwestern) branch of the Common Turkic languages. Within the branch it is closest to Kyrgyz, with which it shares several distinctive features:[1][4] - long vowels formed where older consonants were lost between vowels, as in *too* "mountain" ([[wp:Old Turkic language|Old Turkic]] *tag*); - an initial /dʒ/ where many Turkic languages have /j/, as in *jol* "road"; - extensive rounding harmony in suffixes. Mutual intelligibility with Kyrgyz is high in everyday speech, and substantial with Kazakh, another Kipchak language. Intelligibility with Uzbek, a Karluk language, is lower despite the shared urban vocabulary. Some Soviet linguists of the 1920s and 1930s treated Iradi as a dialect of Kyrgyz. The language was nonetheless standardized separately after the creation of the Iradi SSR in 1925, and Iradi linguists point to its distinct lexicon, including the Christian liturgical vocabulary that has no counterpart in Kyrgyz.[1] Iradi historians link the speakers' ancestors to Christian Turkic groups of the [[wp:Qara Khitai]] period, such as the [[wp:Keraites]] or [[wp:Naimans]]. The linguistic evidence for this is inconclusive. ## Vocabulary The Iradi lexicon is commonly described in layers, which reflect the history of its speakers:[1] | Layer | Main domains | Examples | |---|---|---| | Native Kipchak | Basic vocabulary, kinship, pastoralism, horses | *at* "horse", *uruk* "clan", *aksakal* "elder", *boz üy* "yurt", *bulak* "spring", *zhayloo* "summer pasture", *kyshtoo* "winter pasture" | | Uzbek and Persian, via Uzbek | Town life, crafts, trade | *dastgoh* "workshop", *mahalla* "urban neighborhood", *bozor* "market", *hunarmand* "craftsman", *navbahor* "new spring" | | Sogdian and other Iranian | Liturgy, religion, old place names | *nom* "scripture", *frishte* "angel", *kuble* "orientation toward Polaris"; place-name elements *kand* "oasis town", *shahr* "city", *diz* "citadel" | | Syriac | Church ritual | *madbaha* "sanctuary", *qurbana* "Eucharist" | | Arabic, mostly via Persian | Law, government, abstract terms | *adat* "custom", *[[Mejlis]]* "assembly", *azatlık* "freedom" | | Russian | Soviet-era technology, administration, urban life | *zavod* "factory", *kolkhoz* "collective farm", *mikrorayon* "housing estate", *marshrutka* "minibus" | | English | Government, business and technology since 1992 | *kampus* "campus", *startap* "startup", *frilanser* "freelancer" | The Sogdian layer reflects the role of Sogdian as a language of Church of the East literature in medieval [[wp:Central Asia]], and words such as *nom*, ultimately from Greek *nomos* through Sogdian, also appear in Old Uyghur Christian and Buddhist texts. The urban Uzbek layer is usually attributed to the trading and craft communities of the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] period, when Iradi towns depended on the commerce of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]].[4] Russian loans are most frequent in the speech of older urban Iradis, and English loans in that of younger ones. *Kümöch*, the sacramental bread of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], is a native Turkic word for bread baked in embers that acquired a liturgical meaning (see [[Kümöch Sacramental Bread]]). Shop signs in Talas use everyday words such as *dükön* "shop", *dariykana* "pharmacy", *meymankana* "hotel", *konok üy* "guest house", *azık-tülük* "groceries", *sooda borboru* "shopping center", *valyuta almashuu* "currency exchange", *et dükönü* "butcher", *jemish-jashılcha* "fruit and vegetables", *tez tamak* "fast food", *avtoservis* "car service", *avtobölüktör* "car parts" and *lagman-üy* "lagman house". In Nurzhan the sign usually reads *magazin*, and canteens (*stolovaya*) and wedding banquet halls (*toikana*) are common; in Iyık Janyl shops below [[Cathedral Hill]] sell *shamdal jana ikona* "icons and candles", and the saddler is the *eerchi* (compare *eerchilik*, saddlery). A few words come from [[Sughdik language|Sughdik]], the Eastern Iranian language of the [[Tat (Irad)|Tat]]: *khir* ("sun", in poetry and hymns), *dork* (the firewood and bonfire of [[Yuhanna Tünü]]), *vaysh* (the herbs gathered that night), *ikh* (glacier ice), *zoy* (grave earth, in church Iradi), the highland ulak slang *büz* ("goat") and the bazaar slang *arna* ("fool"). Chatkal shepherds count sheep with Sughdik numerals. ## Phonology Standard Iradi has eight native vowels: *a*, *e*, *ı*, *i*, *o*, *ö*, *u* and *ü*. All but *ı* and *i* also occur as long vowels (*aa*, *ee*, *oo*, *öö*, *uu*, *üü*). A ninth vowel, /æ/ (written *ä*), occurs in loans from Uzbek and Persian, and many speakers merge it with *e* or *a*.[5] As in Kyrgyz, vowel harmony operates on both backness and rounding: the vowels of suffixes agree with those of the stem. The plural suffix, for example, has the forms *-lar*, *-ler*, *-lor* and *-lör*, and its initial consonant assimilates to the end of the stem: - *at* "horse" → *attar* "horses"; - *kol* "hand" → *koldor* "hands"; - *üy* "house" → *üylör* "houses"; - *kız* "girl" → *kızdar* "girls". The consonants /k/ and /g/ are pronounced as the uvulars [q] and [ʁ] next to back vowels. The standard orthography writes them as *k* and *g*, although *q* survives in a few established names such as the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. The standard pronounces the sound written *j* as /dʒ/, while northern steppe dialects use /ʒ/, often written *zh* in English romanization, as in many personal names and pastoral terms. Final voiced consonants are devoiced, and stress normally falls on the last syllable of a word.[5] ## Grammar Iradi is an agglutinative language. Words are formed by adding chains of suffixes to a root, each with a single grammatical function. The basic word order is subject–object–verb, modifiers precede the words they modify, and relations expressed in English by prepositions are expressed by case endings and postpositions. There is no grammatical gender and no article.[1] Nouns take six cases, shown here for *at* "horse": | Case | Form | Typical use | |---|---|---| | Nominative | *at* | subject | | Genitive | *attın* | possessor ("of the horse") | | Dative | *atka* | direction, indirect object ("to the horse") | | Accusative | *attı* | definite direct object | | Locative | *atta* | location ("on the horse") | | Ablative | *attan* | source ("from the horse") | Possession is marked by suffixes on the possessed noun: *atım* "my horse", *atı* "his or her horse", *attarıbız* "our horses". Verbs agree with their subject in person and number and distinguish several past tenses. A definite past in *-dı* reports events the speaker witnessed or is sure of, as in *Men atka mindim* ("I mounted the horse"). An indefinite past in *-gan* is used for reported or inferred events. Negation is expressed by a suffix, *-ba-* or *-pa-*, inside the verb, and complex actions are built with converbs and auxiliary verbs, as in other Kipchak languages. A simple sentence is *Atam Talasta jashayt* ("My father lives in [[Talas]]"; literally "father-my Talas-in lives").[1] ## Dialects and registers Iradi linguists usually distinguish three main dialect groups, together with a church register (see [[Dialects of Iradi]]):[5] - **Urban dialects** of Talas, [[Nurzhan]] and Iyık Janyl. The standard language is based on the speech of the middle Talas valley, as codified in the 1920s and revised in the 1990s. Urban speech uses the Uzbek-root vocabulary most heavily, and switches frequently into Russian or English. The Nurzhan variety contains the most Russian loans. - **Tribal dialects** of the mountains and steppe. Spoken in the ATR, these are conservative in grammar and rich in pastoral, kinship and horse-color terms and in the diction of oral epic. The northern steppe and [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] subdialects pronounce *j* as /ʒ/ and share some features with Kazakh. - **Fergana Rim dialects** of the southern foothills. Spoken by Iradis and in mixed villages with Kyrgyz and [[wp:Uzbeks]], these show strong Uzbek influence, including weaker rounding harmony and more Persian and Arabic loans. - **The ecclesiastical register** of the Syro-Iradi Catholic Church. It preserves the Sogdian, Iranian and [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] liturgical vocabulary. In 1993 the [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs]] approved Iradi translations of the liturgy for use alongside Classical Syriac (see [[East Syriac Rites of Iyık Janyl]]). ## Writing systems - **Medieval inscriptions.** Old Turkic runic inscriptions have been found in the Talas valley, and Christian gravestones of the wider [[wp:Semirechye]] region bear Turkic texts in Syriac script. Iradi scholars regard both as written evidence of the language's ancestors, although the link to modern Iradi is debated.[4] The runic script is used today only symbolically, notably in the motto on the [[Flag of Irad]]. - **Arabic script (to 1928).** Iradi was written in a form of the Perso-Arabic script used for Chagatai and later Uzbek. Texts copied at [[Iyık Janyl]], including the eighteenth-century vita of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]], used it. - **Latin (1928–1941).** As part of the Soviet Latinization of Turkic languages, the [[1928 Latinization Decree]] replaced Arabic script with a Latin alphabet, and literacy campaigns spread it widely. - **Cyrillic (1941–1992).** The [[1941 Cyrillic Mandate]] imposed a Cyrillic alphabet with additional letters for the front rounded vowels and the velar nasal. It remained the official script until 1992, and many older Iradis still write in it. - **Latin (since 1992).** The Provisional Government and the territorial administration restored a Latin alphabet in 1992. The [[1995 Latin Orthography Revision]] fixed the present 32-letter alphabet, replacing several digraphs with letters carrying diacritics. The Language and Education Reform Act of 1997 made it compulsory in schools and public administration.[6] In English-language usage, Iradi names are often romanized with the digraphs *ch*, *sh* and *zh*. ## Sociolinguistics The language situation in the cities of the ISEZ is marked by differences between generations, which reflect the successive dominance of Russian in the Soviet period, English in the territorial period and Iradi since the 2010s. The most detailed data come from a 2022 survey of 3,100 residents of Talas, Nurzhan and Iyık Janyl by the Talas State University Institute of Sociology:[3] | Age group (2022) | Main home language: Russian | Main home language: Iradi | Speaks English without difficulty | Speaks Iradi without difficulty | |---|---|---|---|---| | Over 60 | 61% | 34% | 4% | 66% | | 42–60 | 52% | 43% | 12% | 70% | | 26–41 | 44% | 45% | 47% | 74% | | 18–25 | 29% | 52% | 81% | 86% | The same survey found large differences between cities: Russian was the main home language of 57 percent of respondents in Nurzhan, 31 percent in Talas and 18 percent in Iyık Janyl.[3] Sociologists commonly associate these patterns with three urban generations: - the Russian-speaking "Russos" born before about 1980 (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]); - the [[Urban Iradi Millennials]], who grew up in Russian-speaking homes but were schooled in English and Iradi after 1992; - the generation born since the late 1990s, the first to speak English fluently on a wide scale, which has adopted Iradi as a marker of identity (see [[Iradi language revival]]). In the tribal regions the situation is different. Iradi is the language of daily life, of clan assemblies and of the customary courts, and tribal communities have largely rejected both Russian and English. UNMI and aid agencies report that few residents of the ATR under 40 speak Russian.[7] Urban Iradis who learned the language as adults often regard tribal speech as more "authentic", and young urban speakers have adopted pastoral and epic vocabulary from it. Naming follows the same divide. Urban Iradis mostly keep Russian-style surnames ending in *-ov*, *-ev* or *-ova*, while tribal Iradis use patronymics formed with *uulu* ("son of") and *kyzy* ("daughter of") (see [[Iradi name]] and [[De-Russification Movement in Irad]]). ## Status and education Iradi has been an official language, alongside English, since 1992, when Russian lost its official status. The Language and Education Reform Act of 1997 made instruction in Iradi and English compulsory in public schools, and Russian is taught as an optional foreign language.[6] Debates in the Mejlis are held in Iradi and English, with interpretation into Russian. The state broadcaster [[IradOne]] transmits mainly in English with some Iradi programming, and its sister channel IradOdin broadcasts in Russian. Private Russian-language schools in Nurzhan, many of them funded by the foundation of the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]], continue to operate. Bekzatov and other Russo figures have called for Russian to be restored as an official language, a proposal opposed by Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] and other DPI leaders. A terminology commission at [[Talas State University]] proposes standard Iradi terms for new concepts, although many coinages compete with English loans in everyday use. In the ATR, Iradi is the only language of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]], and schools run by village councils and parishes teach in it.[7] Older clerks in the tribal regions often still write Iradi in Cyrillic. ## Literature Iradi literature has its roots in oral tradition: the epic cycles recited by bards (*ırchy*) with the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]], the horseback chants known as *ırda* (see [[Irda (Vocal Tradition)]]), and the cycle of the [[The Epic of Janyl|Epic of Janyl]]. A written literature in the Latin alphabet developed in the 1920s and was curtailed by the purges of 1937 and the switch to Russian-only schooling (see [[Iradi literature]]). Poems about the 1916 revolt, notably [[The Black Blizzard of 1916 (Poem)|The Black Blizzard of 1916]], remain widely read.[8] Since the 1990s the electronic music genre [[Mor-Wave]], whose founders [[tüntolk]] wrote all their lyrics in Iradi, has been credited with making the language fashionable among urban young people, and Iradi is now widely used on social media. ## See also - [[Ashuu (Geographical Term)]] - [[Talaa (Geographical Term)]] - [[Köl (Geographical Term)]] - [[Zhylky (Equine Term)]] ## References
