{{Infobox company | name = Sary-Bulak Antimony Works | native_name = *Sary-Bulak Surma Kombinaty* (SBAW) | type = Joint-stock company | industry = Mining | founded = 1961 (privatized 1994) | hq = [[Sary-Bulak Gorge]], [[Sary-Bulak]] District | products = Antimony concentrate | employees = 2300 | parent = [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]] }} The **Sary-Bulak Antimony Works** (SBAW; Iradi: *Sary-Bulak Surma Kombinaty*) is an antimony mining company in the [[Sary-Bulak Gorge]] in the foothills of the [[Talas Alatau]], at about 1,650 m and about 20 km south-south-west of [[Talas]] in the Sary-Bulak District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It operates an underground stibnite mine and a flotation mill that turns the ore into antimony concentrate. Most of the concentrate is smelted at the nearby [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]], and the rest is exported by rail through [[wp:Kazakhstan]] to China.[1][2] The works were founded in 1961 as a Soviet state enterprise and expanded in the 1970s, when the Iradi SSR became one of the main antimony producers in the [[wp:Soviet Union]]. SBAW was privatized in 1994 and is now the mining arm of the [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]], which holds a controlling stake. With about 2,300 employees, it is the largest employer in Sary-Bulak District.{{Citation needed|date=September 2026}} Irad is estimated to hold about 7 percent of world antimony reserves, most of them in the [[Sary-Bulak]] and Chatkal ore field (see [[Antimony Mining in Irad]]).[1][3] ## History #### Soviet period (1950s–1991) Geologists of the republican geological survey mapped stibnite-bearing quartz veins in the Sary-Bulak gorge in the early 1950s, during a survey of the mineral resources of the Talas Alatau. Construction of the mine began in 1958. The first shaft, Shaft No. 1 ("Pioneer"), was commissioned in 1961, when the works were formally established under the Soviet Ministry of Non-Ferrous Metallurgy. From 1964 its concentrate went by rail to the new smelter at Chatkal.[3] Under the [[1971 Antimony Expansion Directive]], a second shaft ("Severny") was sunk and the flotation mill was enlarged. By the late 1970s the Sary-Bulak and Chatkal plants together supplied a large share of the Soviet Union's antimony, used in lead-acid batteries, flame retardants and alloys for munitions. Many of the first engineers and miners came from Russia and [[wp:Ukraine]]. [[Iradis]] from the villages of the Talas valley made up a growing share of the workforce from the 1970s onward.[3] #### Crisis and privatization (1991–2006) The breakup of the Soviet Union cut the works off from their customers and suppliers. Production stopped for most of 1992. According to the company's own history, power cuts during the [[First Iradi Civil War]] halted the dewatering pumps, and the lower levels of Shaft No. 2 flooded.[4] In 1994 the territorial administration privatized SBAW as a joint-stock company. A controlling stake passed to the holding company that became the Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine, and employees received a minority of the shares, most of which they later sold. The flooded levels were pumped out between 1995 and 1997, and the mine was re-equipped with Western loaders and drilling rigs, financed partly by prepayment contracts with Chinese buyers. The Hydrocarbon and Mining Code of 1995 set the royalty regime. After long disputes, the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] adopted formulas that divided antimony revenue between infrastructure in Talas and rural schools.[4][5] Unpaid wages led to a three-week miners' strike in the spring of 1998. It ended when the company agreed to pay part of wages in US dollars, a practice that became general in the following years.[6] #### Since 2007 The fighting of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] did not reach the works, which came under the control of the DPI emergency administration in the summer of 2007. The [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] left the mine and the Chatkal smelter in the ISEZ. The ridges and upper gorge above the mine lie close to the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and the high Talas Alatau beyond them is on the tribal side.[4] World antimony prices rose sharply after China restricted its own exports of the metal in 2024. The company has since said that it will deepen the Central incline and reopen worked-out levels that had been uneconomic at lower prices.[2] ## Geology The deposit lies along a fault zone in [[wp:Paleozoic]] limestone and shale, where stibnite (antimony sulfide, Sb₂S₃) occurs in quartz veins and breccia bodies. Associated minerals include cinnabar, fluorite and arsenic minerals, with traces of gold.[3] Soviet records gave grades of 5 to 7 percent antimony in the richest veins. The company now reports an average head grade of about 3 percent, a decline typical of a mine that has worked its best ore first.[2] No independent estimate of the deposit's remaining reserves has been published. The figure of about 7 percent of world reserves comes from estimates for Irad as a whole.[1] ## Operations - **Mining.** Ore is reached through Shaft No. 1 ("Pioneer", 1961), Shaft No. 2 ("Severny", 1970s) and the "Central" incline, a truck decline driven in the early 2000s. Working levels reach about 750 m below the surface. The veins are worked by cut-and-fill and sublevel stoping, and ore is hoisted to the surface in skips.[4] - **Processing.** The mill crushes and grinds the ore, and froth flotation separates the stibnite into a concentrate of 55 to 60 percent antimony. The company reports throughput of about 350,000 metric tons of ore a year.[2] - **Shipment.** Most concentrate goes by road and rail to the Chatkal smelter, also in Sary-Bulak District, where it is made into antimony metal and antimony trioxide. The rest is sold as concentrate and shipped by rail through Kazakhstan to buyers in China.[1] - **Finance.** Export sales are paid into escrow accounts at [[Talasbank]] under the supervision of the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]], which deducts royalties before releasing the proceeds. The company publishes production figures but not full audited accounts.[2] ## Workforce and settlement Most employees live in the workers' settlement beside the mine, known locally as Rudnik ("the mine"), which has about 5,000 inhabitants. Its five-story housing blocks, school, polyclinic and house of culture date mainly from the 1960s and 1970s. The settlement has a Syro-Iradi parish church, opened in 1995, and a Russian Orthodox chapel. Older miners are largely Russian-speaking, while younger workers come mostly from Iradi villages in the Talas valley and commute by company bus.[6] ## Safety and environment Soviet-era tailings are stored in impoundments in the lower gorge. The [[Talas River Hydrological Monitoring Service]] samples antimony and arsenic downstream of the works, and the [[Chatkal Placer Mining Inspectorate]] oversees discharges.[7] Clan councils on the tribal side of the line have objected to a proposed new tailings dam in the upper gorge. They argue that it would endanger streams used by herders in summer, and the company has not built it.[4] In February 2012 a rockfall on a lower level of Shaft No. 2 killed four miners. An inspectorate report blamed inadequate ground support, and the company replaced its shift management in the shaft.[8] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Vasily Chernov | df = dmy | image = Vasily_Chernov_1990.jpg | caption = Official portrait, 1990 | office1 = President of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] | term_start1 = 1991-10-09 | term_end1 = 1992-08-18 | preceded_by1 = Office established | succeeded_by1 = Office abolished | office2 = President of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic|Iradi SSR]] | term_start2 = 1990 | term_end2 = 1991-10-09 | preceded_by2 = Office established | office3 = First Secretary of the [[Communist Party of Irad]] | term_start3 = 1986-11 | term_end3 = 1992 | birth_date = 1935-03-14 | birth_place = Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]), [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic|Iradi SSR]], Soviet Union | death_date = 2012-02-22 | death_place = [[wp:Moscow]], Russia | resting_place = [[wp:Troyekurovskoye Cemetery]] | citizenship = Soviet Union; Russia | party = [[Communist Party of Irad]] | alma_mater = [[wp:Peter the Great St. Petersburg Polytechnic University|Leningrad Polytechnic Institute]] (1958) | occupation = Chemical engineer; politician }} **Vasily Chernov** (14 March 1935 – 22 February 2012) was an Iradi communist politician and refinery engineer. He was the last First Secretary of the [[Communist Party of Irad]] (1986–1992) and the only President of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] (SRI), the communist state proclaimed in Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]) on 9 October 1991. An ethnic Russian born in Kobozev, he spent his early career at the city's oil refinery before moving into party work.[1] His government's emergency decrees and the economic collapse of 1991–92 provoked the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], during which security forces shot demonstrators in [[Talas]] on 3 February 1992. In the [[First Iradi Civil War]] that followed, SRI forces besieged Talas from April to June 1992. After the United States intervened under the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]], Chernov's remaining forces surrendered on 18 August 1992, and he went into exile in Russia, where he lived until his death.[2][3] ## Early life and education Chernov was born on 14 March 1935 in Kobozev, the capital of the Iradi SSR, to an ethnic Russian family. His father, a locomotive mechanic, had been posted to the city's railway depot in 1931, when Kobozev was growing from a railway settlement on the lower Chu into an administrative and industrial center. Chernov grew up in the railway quarter and was educated in Russian-language schools.[1] In 1952 he went to study at the [[wp:Peter the Great St. Petersburg Polytechnic University|Leningrad Polytechnic Institute]]. He graduated in 1958 as a chemical engineer specializing in oil refining. ## Refinery and party career After graduating, Chernov returned to Kobozev as a process engineer at the city's new oil refinery, now the [[Nurzhan Oil Refinery]], which had been built in the late 1950s to process crude from the Chu basin fields discovered in 1949. He joined the Communist Party in 1960. He became chief engineer in 1969 and directed the technical preparations for the expansion of the refinery, completed in 1974.[4] In 1974 he moved into full-time party work as First Secretary of the Kobozev city party committee, where he was responsible for the city's industries and its housing programs. He studied at the Academy of Social Sciences of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of the [[wp:Soviet Union]] in [[wp:Moscow]] from 1979 to 1981. On his return he became the secretary of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of Irad responsible for industry.[1] In November 1986, during [[wp:Mikhail Gorbachev|Mikhail Gorbachev's]] replacement of regional party leaders, he was appointed First Secretary of the Communist Party of Irad. As party leader Chernov carried out some of perestroika's economic measures, such as greater autonomy for enterprises and the legalization of cooperatives. Politically he remained conservative. He opposed the return of the Latin alphabet for Iradi, regarded the revival of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] with suspicion, and allowed police harassment of the *Ene-Til* society of the historian [[Amanbek Alimbekov]].[3] During [[The Kobozev Bread Riots (1989)|the Kobozev bread riots of 1989]] he arranged emergency grain deliveries from [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and dismissed the city's trade officials, while the police detained the organizers of the protests. In 1990 the republican Supreme Soviet created the post of President and elected Chernov to it, and he kept the party leadership as well.[1] During the coup attempt in Moscow in August 1991, Chernov made no public statement for two days. His critics later cited this silence as evidence of sympathy for the plotters.[3] ## President of the Socialist Republic (1991–1992) #### Independence and emergency rule On 9 October 1991 the Supreme Soviet adopted the [[Declaration of State Sovereignty (1991)]], and the Communist Party of Irad declared the republic independent as the Socialist Republic of Irad, with Chernov as President. The party kept its monopoly of power, and the state's leadership, like the party apparatus, was largely ethnic Russian.[2] The end of Soviet subsidies, ruble clearing and fuel deliveries brought most of Kobozev's factories to a halt, inflation exceeded 1,000 percent, and bread was rationed in Talas from December 1991.[5] In November 1991 Chernov's government issued emergency decrees that suspended constitutional liberties, banned non-communist gatherings and publications, and ended the limited self-government of the rural clans. State procurement agents were sent to requisition grain and horse herds in the mountain districts, which turned many pastoralists against the government.[5] #### The Winter Uprising Protests began in Talas in December 1991, and in January 1992 a strike at the Kobozev railway depot spread to factories across the valley. On 3 February 1992 [[wp:OMON]] riot police opened fire on demonstrators on Central Square in Talas. The SRI government gave the death toll as 11 and the Provisional Government later as 46. A commission of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] documented 27 deaths in 2002.[6] The commission found that the order to clear the square had come from the SRI interior ministry but could not establish whether Chernov had personally authorized the use of live ammunition. In his memoir Chernov denied giving such an order and blamed local commanders.[2][6] Over the following days armed workers, defecting police and clan horsemen seized the arsenals of Talas. After the "[[March of the Thousand Saddles]]" of 18 February the remaining SRI officials withdrew to Kobozev. #### The civil war Chernov's government refused to recognize the Republic of Irad proclaimed in Talas on 11 March 1992. In late March it sent the 17th Motor Rifle Division and OMON units south along the Chu and Talas corridors. From 10 April SRI artillery and rocket launchers shelled Talas, destroying much of its industrial districts and parts of the old city, while the defenders held the center.[7] Chernov's memoir describes the campaign as an effort to restore constitutional order in a rebellious province.[2] After the Provisional Government signed the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty on 2 June, Chernov denounced the American intervention as foreign aggression and appealed to Moscow and the other members of the [[wp:Commonwealth of Independent States]] for support. Russia protested against the intervention but did not intervene.[3] US forces landed at Talas on 6 June and broke the siege by 18 June. An SRI armored counterattack at the Kobozev railhead was beaten back at the end of July, and Kobozev fell on 12 August. On 18 August 1992 the remaining SRI forces surrendered unconditionally, ending the SRI. Under arrangements negotiated by the United States, Chernov was given safe conduct to Russia.[7] ## Exile Chernov settled in Moscow with his family and became a Russian citizen. He lived on a pension, lectured occasionally on the industrial history of [[wp:Central Asia]], and advised Russian energy companies on pipeline transport through Kazakhstan.[3] In 1995 the territorial attorney general opened a criminal case against him over the shootings of 3 February and the shelling of Talas and requested his extradition. Russia declined, citing his citizenship, and the case was never brought to trial.[6] In 2001 he published a memoir, *The Broken Union: Memories of the Final First Secretary*. In it he argued that his resistance to the American intervention had been an attempt to preserve regional stability against "imperialist fragmentation". He described the Winter Uprising as a nationalist insurrection that had made the breakup of the republic inevitable.[2] Chernov died in Moscow on 22 February 2012, aged 76, and was buried in [[wp:Troyekurovskoye Cemetery]]. The ISEZ government made no official comment. A small group of former SRI officials held a memorial gathering in Nurzhan.[8] ## Legacy and assessments In Talas, Chernov is remembered mainly for the shootings of 3 February, whose victims are commemorated at a memorial on Central Square unveiled in 1997, and for the siege of 1992. Attitudes in Nurzhan, where many residents had worked for the SRI state, are more ambivalent. Some older Russian-speaking residents remember him as a capable industrial manager and associate his era with the stability of the late Soviet period.[3] Historians generally regard him as a Soviet technocrat whose career had not prepared him for the political crisis of 1991. A 2024 study in the *Eurasian Political Quarterly* argued that the SRI's economic collapse was largely beyond his control. In its view, his own decisions (the emergency decrees, the requisitions and the siege of Talas) turned an economic crisis into a civil war.[3] Whether he personally ordered the shooting of 3 February remains disputed. ## References

{{Infobox legislation | name = Elective Governor Acts | territorial_extent = Territory of Irad (since 2007 the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]) | enacted_by = Interim [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] | enacted = 1992-12 | amended_by = [[2013 Constitutional Amendment]] (term limit removed); 2015 nomination rules; Term-start change (before 2011) | related = [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]] | status = In force in the ISEZ }} The **Elective Governor Acts** are two companion statutes passed by the interim [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] in December 1992 that created the elective offices of Governor and [[Lieutenant Governor of Irad|Lieutenant Governor]] of [[Irad]] and regulated their election, powers and succession. They were enacted under authority granted by the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]], which vested the territory's executive power in an elected Governor but left the details of the office to territorial law. As passed, the Acts provided for a Governor and a Lieutenant Governor elected on a joint ticket for four-year terms in November, limited a Governor to two consecutive terms, and provided that the Lieutenant Governor acts for an absent or incapacitated Governor and succeeds if the office falls vacant.[1][2] The [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) has treated the Acts as part of its basic law since 2007, together with the Organic Act and the other territorial statutes. The best-known change to them is the [[2013 Constitutional Amendment]], which removed the term limit and allowed [[Erlan Toktarov]] to stand for a third term in 2015. Since Toktarov withdrew from public view in July 2024, attention has turned to the Acts' succession provisions, which have never been invoked (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).[3] ## Background The Organic Act, which took effect on 18 August 1992, provided that executive authority would be vested in a Governor elected by popular vote, and authorized the Territorial Legislature to provide by law for the Governor's term, the manner of election and the filling of vacancies. Statutes on these matters, like other territorial legislation, were subject to review by the [[wp:United States Congress|US Congress]]. Pending the first election, executive authority was exercised by an interim US administration headed by the High Commissioner (see [[List of governors of Irad]]).[1] The interim legislature, drawn largely from the councils of the Provisional Government and from district delegates, first met in Legislative Hall in [[Talas]] in October 1992. The election statutes were among its first business. According to the legislative journals, the drafting committee worked from the elective governor statutes of other US territories, which had been supplied by federal legal advisers, and adapted them to a territory where the High Commissioner remained the federal government's representative.[4] Both bills passed in December 1992. Members of the new [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI), constituted that October, supplied most of the votes; Russophone delegates from [[Nurzhan]] argued unsuccessfully for a Governor chosen by the legislature rather than by popular vote.[5] ## Provisions #### The two statutes The first act created the offices of Governor and Lieutenant Governor, defined the Governor's powers, and set out the rules for absence, inability, vacancy and removal. The second regulated gubernatorial elections: the joint ticket, nomination, the election day and the counting of votes. Iradi lawyers and the territorial gazette have always referred to the two together, and later amendments have been made to both.[2] #### Election and term - The Governor and Lieutenant Governor are elected together on a joint ticket, so that a vote for a gubernatorial candidate is also a vote for that candidate's running mate. - Elections are held every four years on the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November, the date of US federal elections in the territorial era, which has been kept since. - A ticket needs a majority of the valid votes. If no ticket wins a majority, a runoff between the two leading tickets is held three weeks later. No runoff has been needed since 2007. - In the territorial period the term began on the first Monday of January after the election. Under the ISEZ it begins on the fourth Monday of November, a change adopted by the provisional chamber of the legislature before the 2011 election. - As enacted, a Governor could serve no more than two consecutive terms. The Lieutenant Governor's office was not term-limited.[2][6] The 1992 text required candidates to be at least 30 years old and to have lived in Irad for ten years. Rules adopted by the DPI majority in 2015 added a requirement of 10,000 verified nomination signatures and required the ten years' residence to be continuous and in the ISEZ (see [[2015 Electoral Reform Controversy]]).[7] #### Powers of the Governor Under the Acts the Governor holds the executive power of the territory. The Governor: - appoints the heads of executive departments, and the mayors of the cities and the heads of the districts; - assents to or vetoes bills passed by the legislature; a veto can be overridden by a two-thirds vote; - nominates the justices of the [[Supreme Court of Irad]], with the consent of the Territorial Senate in the territorial period and of the single-chamber *[[Mejlis]]* since 2007; - prepares the annual budget and may grant pardons and commute sentences. In the territorial period the Governor's powers did not extend to defense and foreign affairs, which belonged to the United States under the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]].[1] #### Absence, inability and succession The Lieutenant Governor acts as Governor whenever the Governor is absent from the territory or unable to discharge the duties of the office, and succeeds to the governorship for the rest of the term if the office falls vacant through death, resignation or removal. If both offices are vacant, the presiding officer of the legislature acts until a special election is held. A Governor may be removed by impeachment, which in the territorial period meant impeachment by the House of Representatives and trial by the Senate. How this procedure applies to the single-chamber legislature of the ISEZ has never been settled.[2] The Acts do not say who decides that a Governor is unable to act, or whether a formal declaration is needed before the Lieutenant Governor may exercise the Governor's powers in his own right. Legal scholars are divided on the point. Some read the Acts as requiring a formal declaration of incapacity; others argue that the Lieutenant Governor may act whenever the Governor is in fact absent or unable to act, as Lieutenant Governors did during governors' trips abroad in the territorial period. The provision has never been tested in court.[3][8] ## Application #### Territorial period (1994–2006) The first election under the Acts was held on 8 November 1994, and the first elected Governor, [[Nurlanbek Ermatov]] of the DPI, took office on 2 January 1995. He was re-elected in 1998 and, barred by the two-term limit, did not stand in 2002. [[Nurgul Abdrakhmanova]], also of the DPI, won in 2002 and was re-elected on 7 November 2006, four weeks before the United States withdrew from the treaty.[5] When the Territorial Legislature proclaimed the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] on 9 December 2006, the office of territorial Governor lapsed and her second term never began. The DRI had a parliamentary government under Prime Minister [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] and no governor. #### Since 2007 Toktarov proclaimed the ISEZ on 25 February 2007 as an emergency administration and took office as Governor after the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)|Bishkek ceasefire]] of September 2007, without an election. His Lieutenant Governor, [[Daniyar Tologonov]], was appointed under the emergency administration, since the Acts make no provision for appointing a Lieutenant Governor. Elections under the Acts resumed in November 2011.[6] Under the prevailing reading of the term limit, which counted Toktarov's 2007–2011 tenure as his first term, he would have been barred from standing in 2015. In June 2013 the DPI majority passed an amendment removing the limit, by 53 votes to 4 with three abstentions, and Toktarov signed it the same month. Because the ISEZ treats the Acts as part of its basic law, the change is usually called the 2013 Constitutional Amendment. In 2014 the Supreme Court declined to hear a challenge to it, holding that the question belonged to the legislature.[9] Toktarov has since won elections in 2015, 2019 and 2023. [[Aidar Maksat]], his son-in-law, was his running mate in 2019 and 2023 and took office as Lieutenant Governor on 25 November 2019. Observers from the [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe]] said that the 2013 reform and the elections that followed lacked meaningful transparency or choice (see [[Elections in Irad]]).[7] #### The 2024 succession question Toktarov has not appeared in public since July 2024. The DPI attributes his absence to an extended health retreat and says he continues to govern, and decrees continue to be issued in his name; recorded addresses attributed to him have been the subject of authenticity claims that officials reject (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]). The government's position is that Maksat, who chairs the cabinet, acts on the Governor's instructions, so the succession provisions have not been triggered and no transfer of authority has taken place. Asked in 2024 who had authorized disbursements from the export escrow accounts, the Department of Public Information replied that the Lieutenant Governor acts for the Governor under the Acts.[3][10] No formal finding of inability has been made, and the Territorial Legislature, in which the DPI holds 51 of 60 seats, has not debated the question. Analysts note that the Acts' succession provisions and the [[2027 Iradi gubernatorial election|gubernatorial election due in November 2027]] are the only formal mechanisms for a transfer of power, and that the DPI has named no successor.[3] ## Assessment Scholars of the territorial era describe the Acts as a close adaptation of American territorial models that worked as intended while federal oversight and competitive elections lasted. Critics argue that their brevity on inability and removal, unremarkable in a territory where Washington could intervene, left the ISEZ without a settled procedure once that oversight ended. Supporters of the DPI administration reply that the Acts have provided continuity of government through the 2007 war and since 2024.[1][3][8] ## See also - [[Politics of Irad]] - [[List of governors of Irad]] - [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]] - [[2013 Constitutional Amendment]] ## References

{{Infobox election | election_name = 2023 Iradi gubernatorial election | type = Gubernatorial election | country = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | date = 2023-11-07 | previous_election = 2019 | next_election = [[2027 Iradi gubernatorial election|2027]] | turnout = 71.6% (official) | candidate1 = [[Erlan Toktarov]] (running mate [[Aidar Maksat]]) | party1 = [[Democratic Party of Irad|DPI]] | percentage1 = 92.75% | candidate2 = Oleg Zubarev | party2 = Independent (Russo-aligned) | percentage2 = 4.61% | candidate3 = Damira Kenesbay | party3 = Independent | percentage3 = 2.64% | before_title = Governor before election | before_election = Erlan Toktarov | after_title = Elected Governor | after_election = Erlan Toktarov }} The **2023 Iradi gubernatorial election** was held in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) on 7 November 2023, on the same day as elections to the [[Mejlis]] and the city councils. Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI), in office since 2007, was re-elected with an official 92.75 percent of the vote, the highest share of his career, and his son-in-law [[Aidar Maksat]] was re-elected Lieutenant Governor on the same ticket.[1] The DPI won 51 of the 60 seats in the legislature. The election came a month after the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]] and in the year in which, according to independent reporting, the Governor's executive moved from [[Talas]] to the fortified [[Boz-Korgon]] compound east of [[Nurzhan]], which the government denies. Observers from the [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe]] (OSCE) said it offered no meaningful choice.[2] As in every election since 2007, the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] took no part. Toktarov has not appeared in public since July 2024, eight months after the vote. ## Background Toktarov proclaimed the ISEZ in February 2007 and was re-elected in 2011 with 88.74 percent. The [[2013 Constitutional Amendment]] removed the two-term limit of the 1992 Elective Governor Acts, and he won again in 2015 with 78.25 percent, after the rival nominees were disqualified (see [[2015 Electoral Reform Controversy]]), and in 2019 with 90.31 percent, when Maksat joined his ticket (see [[Elections in Irad]]).[3] Early in 2023, according to the *Central Asian Geopolitical Review* and other independent reporting, Toktarov and his senior staff moved the core of the executive to Boz-Korgon, citing unrest and security concerns in the capital. Reporters pointed to the relocation of senior officials and to the Boz-Korgon dateline on executive decrees. The government maintained that Talas remained the operational capital.[4] In October 2023 the Talas municipal administration announced a licensing surcharge on independent technology startups and delivery couriers. After the commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]] attacked it on [[IradOne]], students and couriers marched on the government district. Police and units of the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] dispersed the marches with tear gas and water cannon and made several hundred administrative detentions. Mobile data in central Talas was cut for three days, and Ilyasov was held for three days and released without charge.[5] ## Nominations The DPI party congress, meeting in Talas in August 2023, renominated the Toktarov–Maksat ticket. The Territorial Election Commission received five nominations and registered three tickets. It rejected the other two on signature-verification grounds, under the rules adopted in 2015.[1] The registered candidates for Governor were: - **Erlan Toktarov** (DPI), with Aidar Maksat as running mate; - **Oleg Zubarev** (independent), an engineer and Nurzhan city councillor aligned with the Russophone "Russo" bloc (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]), with a Nurzhan trade-union official as running mate; - **Damira Kenesbay** (independent), a Talas pediatrician known for campaigning on drinking-water quality in the city's outer districts. The oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]], the best-known Russo figure, has never stood for office and did not publicly endorse a candidate.{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}} Ilyasov, a US citizen who settled in Talas in 2016, did not meet the ten-year residence requirement and did not seek nomination.[6] ## Campaign The official campaign opened in early October and overlapped with the protests. Toktarov made few public campaign appearances, and the DPI campaign was led by Maksat, who toured the districts and presented the governorate's infrastructure record, including water and broadband projects and the proposed Trans-Irad Gas Pipeline (see [[Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals]]). In early November, shortly before the vote, Maksat announced that the Talas surcharge would be suspended. Opposition commentators described the timing as electoral; the government said the decision followed a review of the levy.[5] Zubarev campaigned in Nurzhan on heating and pensions for Soviet-era industrial workers, Russian-language schooling and lower export duties. Kenesbay campaigned mainly online and in the outer districts of Talas. Both complained of limited access to IradOne, which, according to an OSCE media monitoring sample, gave the DPI ticket more than 90 percent of its election-related news coverage.[2] ## Conduct The [[wp:Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights|OSCE's Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights]] sent a limited election assessment mission. Its report cited:[2] - the rejection of nominations on technical grounds and the lack of an effective appeal; - state control of the voter registers; - pressure on employees of state-owned and state-licensed enterprises to vote, including reports of workers being taken to polling stations by their employers; - the use of state resources in the DPI campaign; - the dominance of the DPI on state broadcasting; - the restrictive atmosphere created by the October detentions and the mobile-data shutdown. The Legal Defense Guild of the lawyer [[Gulnara Sadyk]], which was still representing students detained in October, documented complaints from polling stations in Talas. Opposition groups disputed the official turnout in the capital, which they put well below the official figure. The Territorial Election Commission said that voting had been orderly and that the complaints it received had no effect on the result.[7] No polling stations were opened on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. ## Results #### Governor Official results as certified by the Territorial Election Commission:[1] | Candidate (running mate) | Party | Share of valid votes | |---|---|---| | Erlan Toktarov (Aidar Maksat) | DPI | 92.75% | | Oleg Zubarev | Independent (Russo-aligned) | 4.61% | | Damira Kenesbay | Independent | 2.64% | | **Official turnout** | | **71.6%** | Zubarev's best result was in Nurzhan, where the commission recorded him at a little over 11 percent. #### Legislature and city councils In the concurrent legislative election the DPI won 51 seats, independents 6 and Russo-aligned deputies from Nurzhan 3. Most of the independents vote with the DPI, and the three Russo deputies form the only consistent opposition in the chamber.[8] In the municipal elections the Russo bloc kept its majority on the Nurzhan city council, while the DPI kept control of the councils of Talas and [[Iyık Janyl]]. ## Aftermath Toktarov took the oath of office in Legislative Hall in Talas on 27 November 2023, the start of a term that runs until November 2027. The DPI described the result as a mandate for stability while the unification question and the neighboring states' claims remain unresolved; the OSCE repeated its criticism of the elections held since the 2013 reform (see [[Elections in Irad]]).[2] [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] criticized the policing of the October protests and the detention of minors. Toktarov has not appeared in public since July 2024. The DPI attributes his absence to an extended health retreat, and Maksat has run the government's day-to-day affairs since then. Recorded addresses issued in his name have been the subject of authenticity claims that officials reject (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).[9] The next gubernatorial election (see [[2027 Iradi gubernatorial election]]) is due in November 2027, the same year in which the release schedule of the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]] falls due for renewal. ## See also - [[Elections in Irad]] - [[List of governors of Irad]] - [[Politics of Irad]] ## References

{{Infobox political party | name = Communist Party of Irad | native_name = *Irad Kommunisttik Partiyası* (CPI) | leader = [[Vasily Chernov]] (last First Secretary, 1986–1992) | founded = 1925 | dissolved = 1992 | hq = Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]) | newspaper = *Iradyn Chyny* | youth_wing = Leninist Young Communist League of Irad | ideology = Communism; Marxism–Leninism }} The **Communist Party of Irad** (CPI; Iradi: *Irad Kommunisttik Partiyası*; Russian: *Коммунистическая партия Ирада*) was the ruling party of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] (ISSR) from 1925 to 1991 and of its successor, the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] (SRI), from 1991 to 1992. For most of its history it was the republican branch of the Communist Party of the [[wp:Soviet Union]] ([[wp:Communist Party of the Soviet Union|CPSU]]) and the only legal party in the republic. Its headquarters were in Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]).[1] On 9 October 1991, under its last First Secretary, [[Vasily Chernov]], the party declared the republic independent of the Soviet Union as the Socialist Republic of Irad, and it kept its monopoly of power in the new state. Its emergency decrees of November 1991 helped provoke the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], and its government was defeated in the [[First Iradi Civil War]]. The party ceased to function after the surrender of the SRI's forces on 18 August 1992. Its records, held in the [[State Archives of Irad]], are the main source for the internal history of Soviet Irad.[2] ## History #### Origins (1918–1925) During the [[wp:Russian Civil War]] most Iradi clans sided with the [[wp:Bolsheviks]], and Iradi irregular horsemen fought alongside the [[wp:Red Guards (Russia)|Red Guards]] who crushed the [[wp:Turkestan Autonomy|Kokand Autonomy]] in February 1918. Iradi communists of this period belonged to the Communist Party of [[wp:Turkestan]], the regional organization of the Bolshevik party in the [[wp:Turkestan Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic]]. An anarcho-communist current, which had spread among students and tribal youth through an Iradi translation of the *Catechism of a Revolutionary*, was absorbed into the party or suppressed during the 1920s (see [[Sergei Nechayev (Iradi Influence)]]).[3] The national delimitation of [[wp:Central Asia]] in 1924–1925 created the ISSR. Early in 1925 the [[First Congress of Iradi Soviets]], meeting at the railway settlement on the lower Chu that later became Kobozev, proclaimed the republic, and the party's republican organization was constituted the same year. It was known as the Communist Party (Bolsheviks) of Irad until 1952, when, like the other republican parties, it adopted the name it kept until 1992.[1] #### Korenizatsiia and the purges (1925–1938) Under *korenizatsiia* ("nativization"), the party promoted ethnic [[Iradis]] into its apparatus and into the state administration, and directed the standardization of the Iradi language and the literacy campaigns of the late 1920s. It also carried out the [[Decree on Pasture Collectivization (1932)|collectivization of the clan herds]], which led to mass slaughter of livestock and drove many clans from the plains into the eastern highlands.[3] The 1931 union of the Iradi church with Rome under the bull *Orientalis Stella* led Soviet officials to treat the church as a channel of foreign influence, and the party organized the anti-religious campaigns that culminated in [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges]]. The party itself was purged in the same years. Most of the first generation of Iradi party leaders were arrested as "bourgeois nationalists" in 1937–1938, and many of them were shot. Nativization was abandoned, and the leadership that replaced them oversaw [[wp:Russification]], including the [[1941 Cyrillic Mandate]].[3] #### Postwar decades (1945–1985) After the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]] the party presided over the [[Nurzhan Oil Discovery (1949)|development of the Chu oil fields]], the founding of the antimony industry and the construction of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]]. Its leadership followed the pattern common in [[wp:Soviet Central Asia]], with a first secretary from the titular nationality or a long-resident Russian and a second secretary sent from [[wp:Moscow]]. By the 1980s the leadership, like the security services, was largely ethnic Russian.[3] After the [[1956 Talas Riots]], a commission from Moscow blamed the republican leadership for "political blindness" toward nationalist and religious elements. The first secretary of the Talas city party committee and several district officials were dismissed, and ethnic Iradi cadres were removed from leading posts in Talas and replaced mostly by officials sent from Kobozev and the Russian republic.[4] According to Central Committee records, the party had about 118,000 members in 1989. Ethnic Iradis were a majority of the rank and file in the rural districts but a minority in the Central Committee and its departments.[1] #### Perestroika (1985–1991) Chernov, an ethnic Russian refinery engineer who had headed the Kobozev city party committee from 1974 and served as the Central Committee's secretary for industry from 1981, was appointed First Secretary in November 1986. He carried out some of perestroika's economic measures but resisted the demands of the national movement that emerged during [[The Kobozev Bread Riots (1989)|the Kobozev bread riots of 1989]], among them the return of the Latin alphabet, freedom for the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] and democratic elections. Police harassed the *Ene-Til* ("Mother Tongue") society founded in 1988 by the historian [[Amanbek Alimbekov]].[5] The party newspaper *Iradyn Chyny* ("The Truth of Irad"), published in Russian and Iradi, became one of the main outlets of glasnost in the republic under its editor [[Maratbek Sadykov]]. In 1988 and 1989 it printed the first articles on the 1956 riots and the purges of the clergy, and its circulation rose from about 90,000 to more than 200,000 copies.[6] In 1990 the republican Supreme Soviet created the post of President and elected Chernov to it, and he kept the party leadership. #### Independence and the Socialist Republic (1991–1992) During the coup attempt in Moscow in August 1991, Chernov made no public statement for two days, a silence his critics later cited as evidence of sympathy for the plotters. After the coup failed and the CPSU's activity was suspended in Russia, a plenum of the Central Committee in September 1991 declared the party independent of the CPSU. On 9 October the Supreme Soviet adopted the [[Declaration of State Sovereignty (1991)]], and the party declared the republic independent as the Socialist Republic of Irad, with Chernov as President.[5] The national movement called the declaration a maneuver to keep the party in power, since no free elections followed and opposition parties were not legalized. *Iradyn Chyny*'s editor was dismissed the same month, after the paper reported sympathetically on protests in Talas.[6] In November 1991 Chernov's government issued emergency decrees that suspended constitutional liberties, banned non-communist gatherings and publications, and ended the limited self-government of the rural clans. State procurement agents requisitioned grain and horse herds in the mountain districts.[7] After OMON detachments fired on demonstrators in Talas on 3 February 1992, armed workers, defecting police and clan horsemen seized the city's arsenals and the regional party headquarters, and the last party and state officials left Talas after the [[March of the Thousand Saddles]] on 18 February. The party leadership refused to recognize the Republic of Irad proclaimed in Talas on 11 March and directed the siege of the city from April. Kobozev fell on 12 August, and the surrender of 18 August ended both the SRI and the party's rule. Chernov was given safe conduct to Russia.[5][8] ## Organization The party was organized on the model of the other republican parties of the Soviet Union. Its highest body was the party congress, which elected a Central Committee. Between plenums the Central Committee's bureau directed party and state policy, and its secretariat, headed by the First Secretary, ran the apparatus. Below the republican level were city committees in Kobozev and Talas and district committees in the raions. The party controlled appointments to leading posts through the *nomenklatura* system, and its youth wing was the Leninist Young Communist League of Irad ([[wp:Komsomol]]).[1] Formal state authority rested with the Supreme Soviet and the Council of Ministers, but the First Secretary was the republic's leading official. Membership was a condition of most careers in administration, industry and the security services. [[Erlan Toktarov]], Governor of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] since 2007, is the son of a district secretary of the party, according to his official biography. ## After 1992 The party did not reconstitute itself after the surrender. The interim US administration took its buildings and records into custody in September 1992, and an act of the interim [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] in 1993 transferred its property to the territory. The party was never formally banned, since the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]] guaranteed freedom of association, but no communist party won seats in any territorial or ISEZ election.[9] Many former party members and officials emigrated to Russia. Others, especially among the Russian-speaking managers of Nurzhan's industries, joined the [[Labor Party of Irad]], the social-democratic party founded in Nurzhan in 1993, which formed the main opposition to the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] in the territorial legislature.[9] In 1995 the territorial attorney general opened a criminal case against Chernov over the shootings of 3 February 1992 and the shelling of Talas. Russia declined to extradite him, and the case never came to trial. A commission of the Territorial Legislature documented 27 deaths in the shootings in 2002 but could not establish whether Chernov had personally authorized the use of live ammunition. He died in Moscow in 2012.[5][10] ## Archives and historiography The records of the Central Committee are held in the State Archives in [[Talas]] as Fond 85, which includes the protocols of the Central Committee from 1925 to 1991, the files of the Office of the First Secretary and internal-security reports on the 1956 riots. The records of the Talas city committee are held separately in Fond 86. The collections were opened to researchers after 1992.[1][2] Iradi national historiography treats the party as the instrument of Soviet rule and emphasizes the purges, Russification and the decisions of 1991–1992. Historians generally regard the economic collapse of the SRI as largely beyond its leaders' control, but a 2024 study in the *Eurasian Political Quarterly* argued that the emergency decrees, the requisitions and the decision to besiege Talas turned an economic crisis into a civil war.[5] Among older Russian-speaking residents of Nurzhan, the *Russos*, the party's last decades are more often remembered as a period of stability (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]). Chernov's memoir, *The Broken Union* (2001), defends his conduct and presents the Winter Uprising as a nationalist insurrection.[8] ## See also - [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] - [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] - [[Vasily Chernov]] - [[History of Irad]] ## References

{{Infobox treaty | name = Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement | type = Ceasefire agreement | drafted = 2007-08 | signed = 2007-09 | location = [[wp:Bishkek]] | effective = 2007-09 | mediators = United Nations (Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan as observers) | parties = Emergency administration of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]; [[Popular Front of Irad]] (later the [[Iradi Freedom Society]]) }} The **Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement** is the United Nations-brokered agreement, signed in [[wp:Bishkek]] in September 2007, that ended the main fighting of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. It was concluded between the emergency administration of [[Erlan Toktarov]], which governed the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) on behalf of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI), and the [[Popular Front of Irad]], whose delegation was headed by [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]]. [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] attended as observers.[1] The agreement fixed the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], which has divided Irad since 2007 between the ISEZ and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). It created a restricted-weapons zone extending 12 km on either side of the line, set up a Joint Liaison Committee of the two sides, and acknowledged customary jurisdiction on the tribal side. Its annex, the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]], governs the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]]. On 18 October 2007 the [[wp:United Nations Security Council|UN Security Council]] established the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) to monitor it. The line has seen no large-scale fighting since, and the agreement remains the main legal framework of Irad's frozen conflict.[2] ## Background The Second Iradi Civil War began on 25 February 2007, when Toktarov proclaimed the ISEZ from Nurzhan in defiance of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] (DRI) government in [[Talas]]. Clan militias formed the Popular Front in March, took most of the rural interior in the spring and stormed Talas on 4 June, dissolving the DRI. The Front then withdrew to the countryside, and during the summer DPI security forces, backed by Western companies and the United States, took control of Talas, [[Iyık Janyl]] and the other towns of the river valleys, together with the industrial corridor south of Talas and the road down to the Naryn.[3] Fighting continued along the edge of the DPI-held area through the summer. It was heaviest around the Toktogul complex, whose dam and powerhouse were held by the Front and whose switchyard and export lines were held by DPI forces. The skirmishes threatened releases from the reservoir at the height of the irrigation season, on which the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] and southern Kazakhstan depend. This alarmed the downstream states and was one reason all three neighbors took part in the talks. About 80,000 people had been displaced by the war, many of them herding families caught between the two sides.[4] ## Negotiations UN mediators brought the two sides to Bishkek in August 2007. The Kyrgyz government hosted the talks without recognizing either party, and the Kazakh, Uzbek and Kyrgyz delegations attended as observers, each recording that its participation did not affect its *de jure* claim to Irad.[1] The Front's delegation was headed by Bektur, who acted as its principal negotiator, as he had throughout the war; the Front had no single command structure and took decisions in a council of clan commanders. The DPI delegation represented Toktarov's emergency administration.[5] Two tracks ran in parallel. Military representatives of the two sides, working on Soviet-era 1:100,000 maps, negotiated the course of the line along the positions held on an agreed date. Engineers from both sides, assisted by UN water specialists, drafted the technical annex on the Toktogul complex.[6] The main points of dispute were the Naryn corridor, where the DPI insisted on keeping the downstream stations and guarded passage on the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]], and the Front's demand that its customary courts be recognized. Both sides asked for an international monitoring presence. The agreement was signed in September 2007.[1] ## Provisions The agreement's main provisions are:[1][2] - **The demarcation line.** A line between the two zones, defined on the maps used in the talks, enclosing the irrigated valleys of the Talas and lower Chu and the road and rail belts between them, and a salient on the lower Naryn, with the farm belt of the northern Fergana rim whose lowland Chubar had declared for the ISEZ in August, reached by a guarded road across tribal land. A UN-brokered protocol of 2009 later adjusted it in the south, bringing the road corridor, the Toktogul basin and a narrow corridor down the Naryn gorge into the ISEZ; the line now runs for about 1,750 km. - **Restricted-weapons zone.** A zone extending 12 km on either side of the line, from which tanks, artillery and combat aircraft are excluded. - **Joint Liaison Committee.** A committee of officers of the two sides, chaired by the United Nations, to settle incidents and arrange crossings. It meets monthly at Kara-Oi, the headquarters of UNMI. - **Customary jurisdiction.** An acknowledgment that disputes on the tribal side of the line are settled under customary law (*adat*) by the clan councils (see [[Adat Law in the ATR]]). - **Movement.** Civilian crossings at designated points, and the passage of herds on fixed routes where clan pastures straddle the line. - **Humanitarian provisions.** The release of prisoners and detainees held by each side, the voluntary return of displaced people, and cooperation in clearing mines and unexploded ordnance. - **International monitoring.** A request to the United Nations to deploy an observer mission. - **Annex.** The Naryn Water and Power Protocol, under which a joint technical commission of ISEZ and ATR engineers, supervised by the United Nations and attended by observers from the three neighboring states, sets the annual release schedule of the Toktogul reservoir. Revenue from electricity exports is divided under a further annex that has never been published. The agreement does not address Irad's political status. Neither party recognized the other as a government, and the text describes the line as a ceasefire line, not a boundary. ## Implementation The Security Council established UNMI on 18 October 2007, and the first observers arrived in November. In late 2007 a kurultai on the [[Aksay Plateau]] reorganized the Front's political council as the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC), which took over the Front's obligations under the agreement, and its fighters became the [[El-Choro Militias]].[5] A temporary post at Qara-Chik, the village at the mouth of the Kara-Buura valley that gave the line its name, was replaced in 2008–2009 by the permanent [[Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint]]. Joint survey teams accompanied by UN observers marked the line on the ground between 2008 and 2011 with numbered concrete pillars in the valleys and stone cairns on the high ridges. Mines laid in 1992 and 2007 made the work dangerous. In March 2009 two UNMI observers, from Uruguay and [[wp:Bangladesh]], were killed when their vehicle struck an anti-tank mine near the [[Kenkol Pass]].[2] The line has remained largely quiet, although incidents are frequent. UNMI recorded 214 ceasefire violations in 2023, most of them small-arms fire, the movement of armed personnel into the restricted zone or unauthorized construction; many other incidents involve livestock straying across the line. The Joint Liaison Committee settles most incidents locally, and UNMI credits it with defusing a standoff over a river crossing near the Kenkol Pass in 2016.[7] The State Defense Corps keeps its tanks and artillery outside the 12-km zone and holds its forward posts with light infantry (see [[Armed Forces of Irad]]). Under an informal understanding reached during the talks, pilgrims from the tribal regions may cross unarmed for the [[Feast of St. Janyl]] on 24 August.[8] The Naryn Protocol's five-year release schedule was first adopted in 2007 and renewed in 2012, 2017 and 2022; it falls due again in 2027.[6] Since 2023 the ISEZ authorities have barred UNMI patrols from a security zone around the [[Boz-Korgon]] compound east of [[Nurzhan]], which the [[wp:Secretary-General of the United Nations|UN Secretary-General]] has described as a restriction on the mission's freedom of movement; the ISEZ says the zone has no connection with the ceasefire.[7] ## Assessment Diplomats and analysts generally credit the agreement with ending large-scale fighting and with giving all parties, including the downstream states, a stake in keeping it, chiefly through the Naryn Protocol. It is one of the few documents both Iradi administrations still invoke.[9] Critics argue that it froze the conflict instead of resolving it. The line it drew has become the effective boundary of two administrations, and the only direct negotiations since 2007 on reuniting them, at the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]], collapsed when the IAC walked out after being offered one-third of the seats in a unified legislature.[9] DPI officials say the acknowledgment of customary jurisdiction has been used to treat the clan councils as a rival government. Tribal leaders and human rights groups say the crossing regime, with its permits, fees and detentions, falls hardest on herders and on patients seeking treatment in the ISEZ.[10] Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan continue to attend the Naryn commission only as observers, since full participation would imply recognition of the two Iradi administrations (see [[Political status of Irad]]). ## References

{{Infobox military conflict | conflict = Battle of Talas | date = July 751 (Dhu al-Hijja 133 AH) | place = Valley of the [[Talas River]], near Talas (exact site disputed) | result = Abbasid victory; Tang army routed after the Karluk defection | combatant1 = [[wp:Abbasid Caliphate]]; [[wp:Karluks]] (changed sides during the battle); *[[wp:Tibetan Empire|Tibetan]] contingents (role uncertain)* | combatant2 = [[wp:Tang dynasty]] ([[wp:Protectorate General to Pacify the West|Anxi Protectorate]]); allied contingents | commander1 = [[wp:Ziyad ibn Salih]]; [[wp:Abu Muslim]] (governor of Khurasan) | commander2 = [[wp:Gao Xianzhi]]; [[wp:Li Siye]] | strength2 = c. 30,000 incl. allied contingents (Chinese sources) | casualties2 = Most of the army lost; Gao escaped with a few thousand men (Chinese sources); tens of thousands killed and c. 20,000 captured (Ibn al-Athir) }} The **Battle of Talas** (Iradi: *Talas sogushu*; Chinese: 怛羅斯之戰, *Daluosi zhi zhan*; Arabic: معركة طلاس, *Maʿrakat Ṭalās*) was fought in July 751 in the valley of the [[Talas River]] between the armies of the [[wp:Abbasid Caliphate]] and the Tang dynasty of China. An Abbasid force commanded by [[wp:Ziyad ibn Salih|Ziyad]] ibn Salih, sent by [[wp:Abu Muslim]], the Abbasid governor of [[wp:Greater Khorasan|Khurasan]], defeated a Tang army of the [[wp:Protectorate General to Pacify the West|Anxi Protectorate]] under [[wp:Gao Xianzhi]] after the [[wp:Karluks|Karluk Turks]] serving with the Tang changed sides. It is the only recorded battle between the armies of the caliphate and of China.[1][2] The exact site of the battle is unknown and is debated by historians. Iradi historiography places it on the plains west of [[Talas]]. The battle has often been described as the moment that decided whether [[wp:Central Asia]] would fall within the Chinese or the Islamic world, and tradition links it to the westward spread of papermaking through Chinese prisoners. Many modern historians regard both claims as overstated, since the An Lushan Rebellion of 755 did more than the battle to end Tang power in the region, and paper was known in Central Asia long before 751.[3][4] ## Background [[wp:Tang dynasty|Tang China]] had brought the [[wp:Western Turkic Khaganate]] under its suzerainty between 657 and 659 and ruled the [[wp:Tarim Basin]] and, more loosely, the lands beyond the [[wp:Tian Shan]] through the Anxi Protectorate, based at [[wp:Kucha]]. In the early 8th century Umayyad armies under [[wp:Qutayba ibn Muslim|Qutayba]] ibn Muslim conquered [[wp:Bukhara]] and [[wp:Samarkand]], and for several decades the [[wp:Turgesh|Türgesh]] confederation, based at [[wp:Suyab]] and Talas, contested [[wp:Transoxiana]] with the Arabs. After the Türgesh collapsed in the late 730s, the Karluks moved into the Chu and Talas valleys.[2] In 747–750 the Abbasid revolution, launched from Khurasan under Abu Muslim, overthrew the [[wp:Umayyad Caliphate|Umayyads]]. Gao Xianzhi, a Tang general of [[wp:Goguryeo]] descent, had become military governor of Anxi after a campaign across the [[wp:Pamir Mountains|Pamirs]] in 747 against [[wp:Gilgit|Little Balur]] (Gilgit). In 750 he led an expedition against the kingdom of Chach (Shash), around present-day [[wp:Tashkent]], whose ruler was accused of failing in his obligations as a Tang vassal. Gao offered the king terms, then seized him and sent him to [[wp:Chang'an]], where he was executed; Tang troops plundered the city. According to the Chinese sources, the king's son escaped and appealed for help to the Arabs and to neighboring states. In 751 Gao marched west again, beyond the Tian Shan, to meet the threat of an Arab advance.[1][5] ## The battle The fullest accounts are in Chinese sources, chiefly the *[[wp:Tongdian]]* (801) of [[wp:Du You]] and the *[[wp:Zizhi Tongjian]]* (1084). They say Gao led an army of about 30,000, Chinese troops and allied contingents together, and that it advanced more than 700 *li* into the west before meeting the Arab army near the town of Daluosi, the Chinese name for Talas. The two armies fought for five days. The Karluks then went over to the Arabs and attacked the Tang from the rear, and Gao's army broke. Gao escaped with a few thousand men. During the retreat over the mountains, troops of Fergana, nominally Tang allies, blocked a pass with their baggage, and Gao's deputy [[wp:Li Siye]] cleared the way by force.[1] The battle received little notice in the early Arabic histories, which were more concerned with the consolidation of the new dynasty. Later Arabic writers, such as Ibn al-Athir in the 13th century, record the Abbasid victory and give much larger figures than the Chinese sources, with tens of thousands of Chinese killed and about 20,000 taken prisoner.[6] Neither set of figures can be checked. Chinese sources also mention Tibetan contingents on the Abbasid side, but their part in the battle is uncertain.[7] The Islamic date usually given, Dhu al-Hijja 133 AH, corresponds to July 751. ## Location No battlefield has been identified archaeologically. Chinese sources place the fighting near the town of Talas, and some later Arabic accounts connect it with Atlakh, a town of the Talas valley whose own site is uncertain.[6] Historians have proposed locations along much of the middle and lower Talas valley. The question is complicated by disagreement over where the medieval town of Talas itself stood. Iradi historiography identifies it with the citadel mound under the old quarter of modern Talas (see [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]]) and places the battlefield on the river plains to the west, toward [[Kara-Buura]]. Other scholars favor sites farther down the valley, and historians in [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], both of which claim the valley as part of their territory, have argued for locations of their own.[8] ## Aftermath The defeat did not end the Tang presence in Central Asia at once. Tang garrisons remained in the Tarim Basin, and in 753 Gao's successor Feng Changqing campaigned again in the Pamirs. In 755 the An Lushan Rebellion broke out in China, and the court withdrew most of its western troops to fight it. Gao Xianzhi was executed by order of the court in early 756 after a defeat in the rebellion's first campaign. Over the following decades [[wp:Tibet]] took the Tarim garrisons, and the Karluks took control of the Chu and Talas valleys, occupying Suyab by 766.[2][3] On the Abbasid side, Ziyad ibn Salih rebelled against Abu Muslim the following year and was killed, and Abu Muslim was himself put to death on the orders of the caliph al-Mansur in 755. The caliphate made no attempt to advance east of the [[wp:Syr Darya]]. Abbasid embassies continued to visit the Tang court, and Chinese sources record Arab soldiers among the troops who helped the Tang recover their capitals from the rebels in 757.[3] The battle also did not bring rapid Islamization of the Talas valley. A Christian community was still present in Talas in 893, when the Samanid emir Isma'il ibn Ahmad captured the town and turned its principal church into a mosque, and most of the Turks of the steppe converted only after the Kara-Khanid dynasty adopted Islam in the mid-10th century (see [[History of Irad]]).[2] ## Prisoners and the papermaking tradition One of the prisoners, [[wp:Du Huan]], a relative of the historian Du You, traveled through the Abbasid lands and returned to China by sea, landing at [[wp:Guangzhou]] in 762. Fragments of his account, the *Jingxingji* ("Record of Travels"), survive in the *Tongdian*. He describes Chinese silk weavers and painters working in the region of [[wp:Kufa]], in [[wp:Iraq]], but does not mention papermakers.[1] The tradition that Chinese prisoners taken at Talas introduced papermaking to Samarkand, from where it spread to [[wp:Baghdad]] and the [[wp:Mediterranean Sea|Mediterranean]], goes back mainly to the 11th-century writer al-Thaʿalibi. Historians of paper note that it was in use in Central Asia centuries earlier; the Sogdian "Ancient Letters" of the early 4th century were written on paper. Jonathan Bloom and others argue that papermaking had reached Samarkand before 751 and spread westward through Central Asian craftsmen, and that the story attached itself to the battle because it was the best-known contact between the Islamic world and China.[4] ## Assessment The Russian orientalist [[wp:Vasily Bartold|Vasily Barthold]] regarded the battle as having decided that Muslim rather than Chinese civilization would prevail in Transoxiana, and this view was long repeated in Soviet and Western surveys.[2] Many later historians describe it as a frontier battle whose consequences were overtaken by the An Lushan Rebellion, which would have forced the Tang out of Central Asia whatever the outcome at Talas. Others point out that the battle showed the limits of Tang reach beyond the Tian Shan and helped the Karluks establish themselves in the Chu and Talas valleys.[3] ## In Iradi historiography and memory Iradi historians writing in the Soviet period followed Barthold. [[Amanbek Alimbekov]]'s *Sogdians and Turks in the Talas Valley* (1971) treated the battle as part of the long transition of the valley from Sogdian to Turkic and from mixed religious to Muslim rule.[9] National historiography since 1992 has given it a larger place. School textbooks present it as the moment when Islam gained the upper hand in the towns of Transoxiana, after which Sogdian Christians and non-Muslim pastoralists withdrew into the river valleys and foothills of the north, where the Iradi church later took shape.[10] Historians at [[Talas State University]] and elsewhere note that this account compresses a much longer process: Christians remained in Talas for more than a century after the battle, and the Church of the East continued its missions to the Turks under Patriarch Timothy I (780–823).[10] In 2001, the 1,250th anniversary, Talas State University held an international conference on the battle, and a memorial stone was placed beside the road west of Talas, near the plains that Iradi historians identify as the battlefield.[11] The site appears in tourist itineraries of the Talas valley (see [[Tourism in Irad]]), and since the 2010s it has drawn growing numbers of visitors from China. Commentators in the ISEZ have used the battle as a reference point in discussing Irad's position between China and its western partners (see [[Irad–China relations]]). Kazakh, Kyrgyz and Uzbek historians also treat the battle as part of their own national histories.[8] ## References

{{Infobox river | name = Naryn River | native_name = *Naryn* | countries = [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], [[Irad]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] | source = Confluence of the Big Naryn and Small Naryn, central [[wp:Tian Shan]] (Kyrgyzstan) | mouth = Joins the [[Kara-Darya]] to form the [[wp:Syr Darya]], Fergana Valley (Uzbekistan) | length_km = 807 | basin_km2 = 59900 | discharge = About 430 m³/s where it leaves the mountains | tributaries_left = Kambar-Ata;Torkent;Kara-Suu | tributaries_right = Kökömeren;Chychkan;[[Uzun-Akmat River|Uzun-Akmat]];Karasu }} The **Naryn River** (Iradi and Kyrgyz: *Naryn*) is a river of the [[wp:Tian Shan]] and the main headstream of the [[wp:Syr Darya]]. It is about 807 kilometers long and drains a basin of about 59,900 square kilometers. It rises in the central Tian Shan of [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], flows west through Kyrgyzstan's Naryn region, and crosses southern [[Irad]] through the Toktogul Reservoir and a chain of hydroelectric stations before leaving the mountains for the [[wp:Fergana Valley]]. There it joins the [[Kara-Darya]] in [[wp:Uzbekistan]] to form the Syr Darya, which flows on toward the [[wp:Aral Sea]].[1] The Naryn is Irad's largest river by volume and its main source of electricity. Since 2007 its Iradi course has been divided by the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. The gorges by which it enters Irad and the mountains around the Toktogul basin lie in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). The floor of the basin, with the dam, reservoir and powerhouse of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]], has been in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) since 2009, together with the switchyard, the national dispatch center, the downstream stations and the export lines. Releases from the dam are set under the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]], which also gives [[wp:Kazakhstan]], Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan a seat as observers.[2] ## Course #### Upper course (Kyrgyzstan) The river forms where the Big Naryn and the Small Naryn meet in the high basins of the central Tian Shan. The Big Naryn is fed by glaciers of the Ak-Shyirak massif. The combined river flows west through a series of broad valleys and gorges past the town of Naryn, the center of Kyrgyzstan's Naryn region, collecting the At-Bashy and other tributaries from the ranges on either side. This part of the basin lies wholly outside Irad.[1] #### Middle course (Irad) The Naryn enters Irad through deep gorges on the eastern edge of the Toktogul–Naryn planning zone of the ATR. It then widens into the Toktogul basin, an intermontane depression in the western Tian Shan that the reservoir now largely fills. The Kökömeren, formed in the [[Suusamyr]] country by the [[Suusamyr River]] and the Western Karakol, joins from the right above the reservoir, and the [[Uzun-Akmat River|Uzun-Akmat]] and other streams from the southern slopes of the [[Talas Alatau]] flow into the reservoir itself. The Chychkan enters the reservoir from the north. From the south the Kambar-Ata, in the entry gorges, and the Torkent come down from the Fergana Range. The market town of [[Toktogul (town)|Toktogul]] stands on the reservoir's northern shore.[3] The dam stands in the gorge where the river leaves the basin. Below it, the Naryn descends through narrow canyons past Kara-Köl, the town built for the station's workers, and through the Lower Naryn District of the ISEZ, here a corridor a few kilometers wide between tribal mountains, receiving the Kara-Suu from the left and, above Tash-Kömür, the Karasu from the right, to the flats at [[Iyık Janyl]] and [[Tash-Kömür]], the district center.[3] #### Lower course Below Tash-Kömür the river passes the Shamaldy-Sai and Uch-Kurgan stations and leaves its gorge for the northern edge of the Fergana Valley just below the Uch-Kurgan dam, where it leaves Irad, still within the ISEZ; the [[Sadaf-Jar]] bluffs stand on the rim above the frontier. In the Uzbek part of the valley it feeds the North Fergana Canal and the [[wp:Great Fergana Canal]], dug in 1939, and then joins the Kara-Darya to form the Syr Darya.[1] ## Hydrology The Naryn is fed mainly by snowmelt and glacier melt, with high water from May to August and low water in winter. Where it leaves the mountains its mean flow is about 430 cubic meters per second, or roughly 13 to 14 cubic kilometers a year, which makes it the larger of the two headstreams of the Syr Darya.[1] Before the Toktogul dam was built, almost all of this flow passed downstream unregulated. The reservoir, with a total storage of about 19 cubic kilometers, can now hold more than a year's flow and allows releases to be shifted between seasons.[4] Researchers expect glacier retreat in the Tian Shan to raise summer flow for some decades and then to reduce it, especially in late summer, when downstream demand for irrigation is highest (see [[Glacier retreat in Irad]]).[5] ## The Naryn cascade Soviet planners designed the Naryn as a cascade of hydroelectric stations, with Toktogul as the head station whose reservoir regulates the flow for the stations below it. Construction of the Toktogul dam began in 1962, and its first generating units entered service in the mid-1970s. The stations of the cascade in Irad were built between the 1950s and the 1990s:[3][4] - **Toktogul**, a concrete gravity dam about 215 meters high with four units and an installed capacity of 1,440 MW (1,200 MW before the 2026 refit); - **Kurpsai**, the next station downstream; - **Tash-Kömür**, near the town of that name; - **Shamaldy-Sai** and **Uch-Kurgan**, near the edge of the Fergana Valley. Because the downstream stations reuse the water released from Toktogul, the schedule at the head dam determines the output of the whole cascade. The Naryn's power makes Irad a net exporter of electricity, mainly to Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan (see [[Energy in Irad]]).[2] ## History In classical and medieval geography the Syr Darya was the Jaxartes, and some writers treated the Naryn as its upper course. The Naryn gorges were never a major route; caravans between the Talas valley and the Fergana Valley crossed the mountains farther west, by passes such as the [[Fergana Gateway]].[6] The river was harnessed in the Soviet period to expand irrigated cotton in the Fergana Valley and on the middle Syr Darya. The reservoir flooded villages, pastures and farmland in the Toktogul basin, and several thousand people were resettled, including the inhabitants of the old town of Toktogul. Under Soviet planning the reservoir stored spring runoff and released it in summer for downstream farms, while the Uzbek and Kazakh SSRs supplied the Iradi SSR with coal, gas and fuel oil in winter.[4] After 1991 this barter lapsed. The [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] and then the territorial administration began to release more water in winter, when electricity was most needed, and to hold more back in summer. In the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007 the front line ran through the Toktogul complex, and fighting near the dam that summer was one reason all three neighboring states took part in the ceasefire talks in [[wp:Bishkek]].[7] In the dry year of 2008 the reservoir fell to its lowest level since it was filled, forcing power rationing in the ISEZ the following winter. The joint technical commission has since kept a minimum reserve.[2] ## Split control and the Protocol The [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] placed the Naryn's installations under the Naryn Water and Power Protocol, its annex. A joint technical commission of ISEZ and ATR engineers, chaired by an official of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]], adopts an annual operating plan within a five-year framework schedule. It meets at UNMI's sector headquarters at Tash-Kömür, weekly during the irrigation season. The framework schedule was renewed in 2012, 2017 and 2022 and is next due in 2027.[2] The dam was guarded by the [[El-Choro Militias]] until 2009; since then the whole complex and the downstream stations have been guarded by the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] and the State Defense Corps' Lower Naryn mountain battalion. Tribal engineers of the joint commission who cross the line to inspect the dam travel under UNMI escort. Export revenue is divided under an annex that has never been published. Independent analysts estimate that the ISEZ takes the larger share, which both administrations deny.[7] ## Transboundary disputes The Naryn's flow matters to every state downstream. Uzbek officials have repeatedly accused the commission of holding back summer water in dry years and of releasing too much in winter, when ice in the downstream channels causes flooding. Kazakhstan, whose irrigated districts lie on the lower Syr Darya, makes similar complaints. Large winter releases since the 1990s have at times forced Kazakhstan to divert surplus water from its [[wp:Shardara Dam|Shardara Reservoir]] into the Arnasay depression.[8] Neither country recognizes the joint commission, and both attend only as observers. Water disputes have spilled over into transit, with slower customs clearance and tighter pipeline scheduling on one side and cuts in Iradi electricity exports on the other (see [[Irad–Uzbekistan relations]] and [[Irad–Kazakhstan relations]]).[8] Kyrgyzstan, the upstream state, regards the Naryn cascade as Kyrgyz national infrastructure and denies the authority of either Iradi administration over it. Its delegation attends the commission under protest and files a written reservation at each meeting. Proposals in Kyrgyzstan for further stations on the upper Naryn, upstream of Irad, have drawn objections from both Iradi administrations and from Uzbekistan (see [[Irad–Kyrgyzstan relations]]).[2] ## Ecology The native fish of the Naryn are snowtrout (*marinka*) and osmans. The [[wp:Amu Darya]] trout, a form of brown trout, was introduced into the river and the Toktogul Reservoir in the Soviet period, and rainbow trout are farmed near Toktogul (see [[Iradi Mountain Trout]]). The fluctuating level of the reservoir leaves bare mud and gravel shores for much of the year, and the regulated river below the dam no longer floods its banks in spring.[9] ## References
