{{Infobox river | name = Talas River | native_name = *Talas daryası* | countries = [[Irad]] | source = Headstreams (Karakol, Uch-Koshoi) below the Otmek Pass, between the Kyrgyz Range and the [[Talas Alatau]] | mouth = Dies out in the Moiynkum sands (endorheic basin) | length_km = 661 | basin_km2 = 52700 | discharge = About 30 m³/s (middle valley) | tributaries_left = [[Kashka-Suu]], Kara-Suu, Besh-Tash, [[Urmaral River|Urmaral]], Kenkol, Kara-Buura }} The **Talas River** (Iradi: *Talas daryası*) is a river of northwestern [[Irad]], about 661 kilometers long, with a basin of about 52,700 square kilometers. It rises at the eastern head of the Talas valley, between the Kyrgyz Range and the [[Talas Alatau]], flows west through the valley past the capital, [[Talas]], and then turns north and northwest across the piedmont plain into the Moiynkum sands, where it dies out without reaching any sea or large lake. Its middle and lower valley holds Irad's most densely settled farmland, and the river supplies most of the irrigation water of the Talas and [[Kara-Buura]] districts of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ).[1] The Talas lies in an endorheic basin of the south Kazakh steppe. Its desert terminus lies in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), while its upper and irrigated middle course lie in the ISEZ; many of its tributaries rise across the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] on the tribal side. Medieval Talas, which Iradi historiography identifies with the modern capital, stood on its banks, and the [[Battle of Talas]] of 751 was fought in its valley.[2] ## Course The river is formed by headstreams draining the junction of the Kyrgyz Range and the Talas Alatau below the Otmek Pass, the largest of which are the Karakol (not to be confused with the Western Karakol of the [[Suusamyr]] country) and the Uch-Koshoi. The headstreams and the highest part of the valley lay on the tribal side of the line until 2009, when they passed to the ISEZ with the State Route 1 corridor; the surrounding ridges remain tribal. The river flows west past the ruins of the medieval silver-mining town of [[Shelji]], in the eastern part of Talas District.[1] Through the middle valley the Talas runs in a braided channel across a floor of gravel and loess terraces, flanked by alluvial fans from the side valleys. It passes through Talas at about 1,250 meters, where it feeds the city's irrigation channels (*aryk*), and continues west past [[Talas Air Base]] on its southern terrace and the market town of [[Kara-Bulak]]. In the lower valley, in Kara-Buura District, its flow is regulated by the Kyzyl-Adyr Reservoir near the district center, [[Kyzyl-Adyr]].[3] Below the valley the river turns north and then northwest across a broad piedmont plain. For part of this reach it runs close to the frontier with [[wp:Kazakhstan]], and Kazakh farms on the adjoining plain draw on its water. It then leaves the irrigated land, crosses into the Northern Steppe planning zone of the ATR, and follows the western edge of the Moiynkum, where its channel shrinks through evaporation, seepage and diversion. In most years it ends among sands, reed marshes and seasonal salt lakes on the western margin of the desert; in wet years its floodwaters spread farther.[1] ## Tributaries Most of the Talas's tributaries enter from the left, from the northern slopes of the Talas Alatau. They are fed by snowfields and small glaciers, and their upper valleys lie on the tribal side of the Qara-Chik line. The main ones include:[4] - the [[Kashka-Suu]], which keeps a relatively high flow into late summer; - the Kara-Suu, which cuts the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]] south of Talas; - the Besh-Tash, which drains [[Besh-Tash National Park]]; - the [[Urmaral River|Urmaral]], west of the capital; - the Kenkol, whose lower valley holds a Hunnic-period burial ground (see [[Chong-Kenkol]]); - the Kara-Buura, almost all of whose water is taken for irrigation before it reaches the main river. Shorter streams from the southern slopes of the Kyrgyz Range enter from the right. ## Hydrology The Talas is fed mainly by snowmelt and glacier melt from the Talas Alatau. Flow peaks between May and July and falls to its lowest in winter. Mean flow in the middle valley is on the order of 30 cubic meters per second, but much less reaches the lower river in July and August, when irrigation demand is highest.[1] The Kyzyl-Adyr Reservoir, completed in 1975 and known as the Kirov Reservoir until it was renamed under the 1993 Toponymic Heritage Statute, stores about 550 million cubic meters of spring runoff for summer irrigation.[3] The [[Talas River Hydrological Monitoring Service]], founded in 1948, runs eighteen gauging stations on the river and its tributaries. Its records, together with those of the [[Manas Peak Glaciological Observatory]], show earlier spring flow peaks and a growing share of glacier melt in summer flow since the 1970s. The glaciers of the upper basin lost about a fifth of their area between 1970 and 2020, and researchers expect late-summer flow to decline as they shrink further.[5] ## Irrigation and use Irrigation in the Talas valley goes back to antiquity, and medieval towns such as [[Kand-i Kohna]] and the predecessors of Talas drew water from the river and from underground galleries of the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]]. Large-scale canal building followed the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]].[2] According to the [[Talas Basin Agricultural Directorate]], about 110,000 hectares of the valley are now irrigated from the Talas and its tributaries. The main crops are wheat, barley, sugar beet, potatoes and common beans, with alfalfa and fodder maize for the feedlots of the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]].[6] The [[Talas Municipal Water Authority]] draws part of the capital's supply from the river, though most of it comes from wellfields in the alluvial fan south of the city. Several of the rivers that feed the valley rise on the tribal side of the line, and disputes over headwater use are a recurring subject at the Joint Liaison Committee of the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)|Bishkek ceasefire]]. The Directorate usually settles them through informal arrangements with clan councils.[6] Under a Soviet allocation rule that both sides still cite, the river's flow was divided equally between the Iradi SSR and the irrigated districts of the [[wp:Kazakh Soviet Socialist Republic|Kazakh SSR]] on the lower river. The [[Treaty of Good Neighborliness (1994)]], concluded during the territorial period, set up joint hydrological monitoring on the Talas and the Chu. Kazakhstan does not recognize the ISEZ, and the treaty's standing since 2006 is disputed, but the two hydrological services continue to exchange daily discharge readings, and disagreements over flows in dry summers have generally been handled at that technical level (see [[Irad–Kazakhstan relations]]).[7] ## History Sogdian and Turkic towns lined the middle Talas from the first millennium CE, and Arab geographers of the 10th century describe the valley's towns and its silver mines at Shelji. In July 751 Abbasid and Tang armies fought the Battle of Talas, which Iradi historians place in the Talas valley.[2] Under the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]], Talas was a fortified market on the river, and in the Soviet period the valley became a center of irrigated farming and stockbreeding. During the siege of Talas from April 1992, in the [[First Iradi Civil War]], shelling and power cuts stopped the city's pumps, and residents drew water from the irrigation channels fed by the river.[8] Since the 2007 partition the irrigated valley has been the core of the ISEZ, while the headwaters and the desert reaches are held by the clans. ## Ecology and pollution The native fish include the [[Talas River Barbel]], snowtrout (*marinka*) and osmans. Trout in the upper Talas, sometimes sold as [[Iradi Mountain Trout|Talas River Trout]], are thought to derive from Soviet and later stocking, and rainbow trout are farmed on the Urmaral.[9] Strips of riparian woodland of willow, poplar and sea buckthorn survive along less developed stretches, and the reed marshes at the river's end are used by waterfowl and migrating birds. Water quality declines downstream. The hydrological service records nitrates from farmland, sewage indicators below the Talas Central Sewage Treatment Plant, and antimony and arsenic in streams draining the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] in the southern foothills. In the lower valley, losses from unlined canals and poor drainage have caused waterlogging and salinization of the soil.[5][6] ## References

{{Infobox landform | name = Moiynkum Desert | type = Desert | location = [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 43.85°N 71.70°E | elevation_m = 400 }} The **Moiynkum Desert** (Iradi and Kazakh: *Moiynkum*; also spelled **Muyunkum**, from the Russian *Muyunkum*) is a sand desert in northern [[Irad]], lying between the lower Chu, which skirts its northeastern edge, and the [[Talas River|Talas]], which dies out among its western sands, with the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] range on its southwestern side. Soviet surveys put its area at about 37,500 square kilometers. Its sands are mostly fixed by saxaul, shrubs and sedges, and it has long been one of the main winter pastures of the Iradi herding clans.[1] Almost all of the desert lies in the Northern Steppe planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), which it shares with the southern Betpak-Dala north of the Chu (see [[Betpak-Dala]]). Its southern and eastern fringes border the irrigated farmland of the Chu and [[Kara-Buura]] districts of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), and the northern sector of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] runs along the edge of the cultivated land and of the road and rail belt facing the sands. Beneath the desert lie the undeveloped [[Muyunkum Natural Gas Field]] and sandstone-hosted uranium deposits that have not been worked.[2] ## Name The desert's name is usually written *Moiynkum* in Iradi and Kazakh, and *Muyunkum* in Russian and in Soviet geological literature. Iradi geographers use the first form for the desert itself, while the gas field kept its Soviet-era name, so that both spellings remain in use.[1] The second element, *kum*, means "sand", as in Kyzylkum ("red sand"). ## Geography #### Extent and relief The Moiynkum occupies a broad, gently sloping plain at about 300 to 700 meters, highest in the southeast near the foothills and lowest in the northwest. In the northwest the Chu ends in the sands and salt flats around the [[Akzhaykyn Depression]], where the lowest ground in Irad lies below 300 meters.[1] Most of the surface consists of ridged and hummocky sands, broken by clay flats (*takyr*), salt pans and dry hollows. Mobile, unvegetated dunes cover only a small share of the desert, mostly around wells, old camps and along tracks where grazing and fuel-cutting have stripped the plant cover.[3] The Talas, after leaving the irrigated plain of Kara-Buura District, follows the western edge of the desert and in most years ends among sands, reed marshes and seasonal salt lakes. The Chu reaches its terminal marshes only in years of good flow, since most of its water is taken for irrigation upstream (see [[Chu River Basin]]).[4] #### Climate The climate is arid and sharply continental. Annual precipitation is generally between about 150 and 200 millimeters, most of it falling as rain or light snow between November and April. Summer temperatures often exceed 40 °C, and winter cold waves bring temperatures below −25 °C, though snow cover is usually thin enough for livestock to graze through it.[1] #### Water There is almost no surface water away from the two rivers. Under the sands, however, lenses of fresh or slightly brackish groundwater lie at shallow depths, and the desert has long been watered by hand-dug wells, some of them lined with dressed stone, such as the well of [[Tash-Kuduk]], which local tradition dates to the 15th century. Springs such as [[Kumdy-Bulak]] rise at the foot of the dunes on the southern margin. Soviet sheep farms added boreholes and winter camps from the 1950s; many failed after 1991, and since about 2010 aid agencies have restored some of them with solar pumps.[5] ## Flora and fauna The sands carry open woodland and scrub of white saxaul, with black saxaul in hollows and on saline ground, together with sand acacia, *[[wp:Calligonum]]* shrubs, wormwood (see [[White Steppe Wormwood]]) and the sand sedge *Carex physodes*, whose dense roots help to fix the dunes. Needlegrass (*chiy*) grows on the salt flats on the southern margin, and ephemeral grasses, tulips and other bulbs flower briefly after the spring rains.[3] [[wp:Saiga antelope|Saiga]] antelope of the Betpak-Dala population winter in the Moiynkum, together with goitered gazelles. Other mammals include the corsac fox and the [[Chui Steppe Fox]], the tolai hare, gerbils and jerboas, and wolves. The [[Steppe Eagle (Irad)|steppe eagle]] and [[Saker Falcon (Irad)|saker falcon]] breed along the desert's edges, the Asian houbara bustard winters there, and the [[Turkestan Steppe Tortoise]] is common on sandy ground.[6] The reedbeds and marshes at the ends of the Chu and the Talas are used by wild boar and migrating waterfowl. ## Human use #### Pastoralism The Moiynkum is one of the main winter pastures (*kyshtoo*) of the Northern Steppe clans and of herders who migrate up to 300 kilometers from the summer pastures of the [[Talas Alatau]] and the Karatau (see [[Kyshtoo (Pastoral Term)]] and [[Central Asian Pastoral Migration System]]). Sheep, goats, horses and Bactrian camels graze the saxaul and sedge through the winter, and the shallow snow and the shelter of the dune hollows make the desert less exposed to *jut*, the winter ice crust that kills livestock on the open steppe.[7] Camel herding survives in hamlets such as [[Töö-Kuduk]] and [[Zhalgyz-Terek]], and the camel-herding clans of the sands tell the legend of the white camel calf (see [[Ak-Taylak (Folklore)]]). In the south of the sands, villages such as [[Ak-Chiy]] make *chiy* screens from the needlegrass of the salt flats.[5] #### History Caravan and herders' tracks crossed the sands between the Talas valley and the lower Chu in the medieval period, and the stone-lined wells along them were maintained by the clans that used them. Under Russian rule after 1876, Slavic settlement took much of the spring and autumn grazing on the river plains, while the sands remained in pastoral use. [[wp:Collectivization in the Soviet Union|Collectivization]] from 1929 and the [[Decree on Pasture Collectivization (1932)]] seized the clan herds and forced herders onto collective and state farms; in the steppe districts adjoining [[wp:Kazakhstan]] the collapse of herding contributed to the famine of 1930–1933.[8] Soviet state farms later ran karakul sheep and camels in the desert from winter camps and boreholes. After 1991 the farms broke up, and the clans resumed customary control of the pastures, which since 2007 has been exercised through clan councils and the pasture committees of the ATR.[7] #### Resources The Muyunkum Natural Gas Field was found by Soviet geologists in the 1970s in reservoirs at about 2,000 to 3,500 meters beneath the northeastern part of the desert, near the lower Chu. It is the largest gas prospect in Irad but remains almost entirely undeveloped, because the clan assemblies have not granted development rights; since the mid-2000s a few Soviet-era wells on its southern margin have supplied small volumes to [[Nurzhan]] under an arrangement with the local clan council.[2] Soviet surveys also identified uranium in sandstones beneath the Moiynkum and the southern Betpak-Dala, part of the wider Chu–Sarysu uranium province that extends into Kazakhstan. Under the pledge made during the territorial period not to develop Irad's uranium and thorium, and the moratorium on radioactive extraction maintained by the clan assemblies, the deposits have not been worked (see [[Energy in Irad]]).[9] Saxaul has been cut for firewood and charcoal for centuries. Cutting increased in the 1990s, when fuel deliveries to the villages ceased, and UNMI and aid agencies have recorded loss of woodland around settlements and along the tracks.[10] ## Political geography The Moiynkum lies inside the area claimed by Kazakhstan, whose official statements concentrate on the Moiynkum and the other northern lowlands of Irad (see [[Irad–Kazakhstan relations]]). The sections of the frontier that cross the desert are held by the ATR and have never been demarcated. They are patrolled by the clans' [[El-Choro Militias]], and herders on both sides use grazing routes and wells across the Soviet-era administrative boundary. The 2008 [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]] between the ISEZ and the Kazakh border services covers only the irrigated sections of the frontier held by the ISEZ.[10] ## References

{{Infobox landform | name = Betpak-Dala | location = [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 45.40°N 71.20°E | elevation_m = 350 }} The **Betpak-Dala** (Iradi and Kazakh: *Betpak-Dala*, usually glossed as "plain of misfortune"; in Russian sources also the **Northern Hungry Steppe**) is a clay and gravel desert plateau north of the lower Chu, extending from the edge of [[Irad]] far into central [[wp:Kazakhstan]] toward [[wp:Lake Balkhash]] and the [[wp:Kazakh Uplands]]. Only its southern fringe lies in Irad, where it forms the northern part of the Northern Steppe planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). There it is used mainly as spring, autumn and winter pasture, and it is part of the winter range of the Betpak-Dala population of the saiga antelope.[1] The plateau is one of the driest and emptiest parts of the region. In Irad it is separated by the Chu from the [[Moiynkum Desert|Moiynkum]] sands to the south, and together the two make up most of the Northern Steppe zone, the largest and most thinly populated of the ATR's seven planning zones (see [[Administrative divisions of Irad]]).[2] ## Geography #### Relief and soils The Betpak-Dala is a flat to gently undulating plateau, generally at about 300 to 400 meters in its southern part and rising slowly toward the north. Its surface is made up of clay, loam and gravel over [[wp:Paleozoic]] and younger rocks, with wide clay pans (*takyr*), salt flats and shallow closed depressions that fill with water only after snowmelt.[1] Isolated hills of granite and other hard rock stand above the plain; the best known in Irad is [[Mazar-Too]], whose summit, at about 1,050 meters, carries a saint's tomb visited by herders before the spring migration. Shallow saline lakes such as [[Kaz-Köl]] are a stopover for migrating waterbirds, including greater flamingos, in spring and autumn.[3] On its southern margin, toward the Chu, the plateau gives way to firmer grassland such as the [[Keng-Talaa]] steppe, which is used for spring and autumn grazing and for an annual *[[At Chabysh (Racing)|at chabysh]]* endurance race. The Chu itself crosses no part of the plateau, but its terminal marshes in the [[Akzhaykyn Depression]] lie at the junction of the Betpak-Dala and the Moiynkum.[4] #### Climate The climate is arid and strongly continental. Annual precipitation in the Iradi part is generally below 180 millimeters and falls mainly in winter and spring. Summer temperatures often exceed 40 °C, and winter cold waves bring temperatures below −25 °C, with strong winds and thin, drifting snow. There is almost no surface water in summer.[1] In hard winters ice crusts and blizzards (*jut*) can kill large numbers of livestock and wild animals on the open plateau. ## Flora and fauna Vegetation is sparse. Low gray wormwoods (see [[White Steppe Wormwood]]) and saltworts dominate the clay plains, with black saxaul in depressions and on saline ground, and feather grass and fescue on the firmer soils of the southern edge. After the spring rains ephemeral grasses, tulips and other bulbs flower for a few weeks.[1] The best-known animal of the plateau is the saiga antelope (*Saiga tatarica*).{{Citation needed|date=May 2026}} The Betpak-Dala population calves in late spring on the plains of central Kazakhstan, moves north in summer and returns south in autumn and winter, when part of it reaches the southern Betpak-Dala and the Moiynkum in Irad.[5] Across their range, saiga numbers fell by about 95 percent in the 1990s, largely through poaching for the horns of the males, which are used in traditional Chinese medicine. In May 2015 about 200,000 saiga, most of them from the Betpak-Dala population, died within a few weeks on their calving grounds in Kazakhstan from hemorrhagic septicemia caused by the bacterium *Pasteurella multocida*, a die-off that researchers linked to unusually warm and humid weather.[6] Aerial counts by the Kazakh authorities have since recorded a rapid recovery, and in 2023 the [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature]] moved the species from [[wp:Critically endangered species|Critically Endangered]] to [[wp:Near-threatened species|Near Threatened]]. Neither Iradi administration counts the saiga, and estimates of how many winter in Irad come from Kazakh surveys and from observations reported to aid agencies and the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI).[5] Other animals include goitered gazelles, wolves, corsac foxes and the [[Chui Steppe Fox]], gerbils, jerboas and ground squirrels. The [[Steppe Eagle (Irad)|steppe eagle]] nests on the ground and on power-line pylons, and the [[Saker Falcon (Irad)|saker falcon]] breeds along the plateau's edges; sandgrouse and the Asian houbara bustard are also found. The Asiatic wild ass (*kulan*) was hunted out of the Iradi plains in the early 20th century.[7] The [[Turkestan Steppe Tortoise]] is common on the southern margin. ## Human use #### Pastoralism The southern Betpak-Dala has long been a seasonal pasture of the Iradi and Kazakh herding clans. Herds of horses, sheep and camels graze it in spring and autumn, and in winter on the parts where snow is thin enough to graze through. Villages such as [[Ak-Jal]] keep horse herds that graze the open steppe all year.[3] Water is the main constraint. Old hand-dug wells, some attributed by tradition to the [[wp:Dzungar people|Dzungars]] of the 18th century, as at [[Kalmak-Kuduk]], were supplemented in the Soviet period by deep boreholes drilled for state-farm flocks, many of them by the hydrogeological expedition based at [[Tört-Kuduk]] from 1964. Most boreholes failed after 1991, and the pastures around them were little used until aid-funded solar pumps restored some of them from about 2010.[3] #### History The Betpak-Dala's name reflects its reputation as a dangerous crossing, and Kazakh and Iradi oral tradition tells of herds and travelers lost on the waterless plateau. The oral genealogies of the Northern Steppe clans, dictated in the 1960s and 1970s by the genealogist [[Asanbek Daniyarov]] to researchers from [[Talas State University]], are a main source for the history of the clans that used the plateau.[8] [[wp:Collectivization in the Soviet Union|Collectivization]] from 1929 and the [[Decree on Pasture Collectivization (1932)]] destroyed most of the herds that used the plateau. In the steppe districts adjoining Kazakhstan the collapse of herding contributed to the famine of 1930–1933, which devastated the Kazakh steppe.[9] The Soviet authorities later developed the southern plateau as a range for state-farm sheep, with boreholes, winter camps and veterinary posts. Farther north, outside Irad, the eastern Betpak-Dala near Lake Balkhash was used for the Soviet missile test range at [[wp:Sary-Shagan]]. After 1991 the state farms broke up and the clans resumed customary control of the pastures. Since 2007 the Iradi part of the plateau has been on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], governed by clan councils under customary law (see [[Adat Law in the ATR]]).[2] #### Resources and conservation Soviet geologists identified sandstone-hosted uranium beneath the southern Betpak-Dala and the Moiynkum, part of the Chu–Sarysu uranium province that extends north into Kazakhstan. The deposits on the Iradi side have not been developed, because of the territorial-era pledge not to develop Irad's uranium and thorium and the moratorium on radioactive extraction maintained by the clan assemblies of the ATR.[10] There is no protected area in the Iradi part of the plateau. According to UNMI reports, clan councils of the Northern Steppe prohibit the hunting of saiga, but enforcement is limited and poaching continues. Irad is not a party to the [[wp:CITES|Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species]], which complicates cooperation with Kazakh conservation programs to the north, such as the Altyn Dala Conservation Initiative, that track the Betpak-Dala saiga.[5] Herders report that the growing number of wintering saiga competes with their livestock for grazing in dry years. ## Political geography Kazakhstan claims Irad *de jure*, and its official statements concentrate on the northern lowlands, including the southern Betpak-Dala (see [[Irad–Kazakhstan relations]]). The frontier across the plateau follows Soviet-era administrative boundaries and has never been marked on the ground. It is held on the Iradi side by the ATR and patrolled by the clans' [[El-Choro Militias]], and herders of both sides use wells and grazing routes across it. The 2008 [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]] between the ISEZ and the Kazakh border services does not apply to these sections.[2] ## References

{{Infobox mountain range | name = Chatkal Range | native_name = *Chatkal kyrka toosu* | countries = [[Irad]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] | length_km = 200 | parent = [[wp:Tian Shan]] (branch of the [[Talas Alatau]]) | geology = Paleozoic sedimentary and volcanic rocks, intruded by granites }} The **Chatkal Range** (Iradi: *Chatkal kyrka toosu*) is a mountain range of the western [[wp:Tian Shan]] in southern [[Irad]]. Roughly 200 kilometers long, it branches southwest from the [[Talas Alatau]] and separates the valley of the [[Chatkal River]] to the northwest from the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] to the southeast; its southwestern end lies beyond the frontier in [[wp:Uzbekistan]]. The range exceeds 4,000 meters in its higher northeastern part. Its southeastern slopes, facing the Fergana Valley, carry walnut-fruit forests and the [[Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve]], and its ridges are among the main [[Snow Leopard (Irad)|snow leopard]] habitats of the western Tian Shan.[1] Almost all of the Iradi part of the range lies in the Chatkal Highlands planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. The [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) holds only the foothills at the range's northeastern end, where it meets the Talas Alatau, in [[Sary-Bulak]] District. The [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]] in Sary-Bulak District, in the Talas Alatau foothills southwest of Talas, takes its name from the range.[2] ## Geography #### Extent and relief The range leaves the Talas Alatau west of the [[Fergana Gateway]] (Ala-Bel Pass, 3,184 m), the pass above the Chychkan valley and the Toktogul basin that carries the highway between [[Talas]] and the Lower Naryn District. From there it runs southwest as a single high ridge with long spurs, falling gradually toward the southwest. Its northwestern slopes descend steeply to the upper Chatkal valley, a broad trough at about 1,500 to 2,500 meters; its southeastern slopes descend in a series of foothill ridges above the irrigated rim of the Fergana Valley, which also lie in the Chatkal Highlands zone, since the zone takes in the tribal hills west of the Naryn down to the Fergana farm belt. The southwestern end of the range, in Uzbekistan, includes the Chimgan massif northeast of [[wp:Tashkent]].[1] The Chatkal River flows southwest along the northwestern foot of the range and leaves Irad through the [[Chatkal Gorge]] for Uzbekistan, where it feeds the [[wp:Charvak Reservoir]] and becomes the main source of the Chirchik. Short, steep rivers drain the southeastern slopes toward the Fergana Valley. One of them, the Kojo-Ata, is dammed by an ancient landslide to form Lake Sary-Chelek, about 7.5 kilometers long and up to 234 meters deep.[3] #### Geology and earthquakes The range is built mainly of [[wp:Paleozoic]] sedimentary and volcanic rocks, folded and intruded by granites, and was raised again in the [[wp:Cenozoic]]. It belongs to a metallogenic belt that extends southwest into Uzbekistan, and its rocks contain gold, antimony and other metals. Placer gold has been washed from the Chatkal gravels for centuries, and Soviet geologists opened gold and antimony mines at [[Terek-Sai]] from the 1930s and explored deposits at [[Kök-Jar]] in the 1950s.[4] The Talas–Fergana Fault passes close to the range's northeastern end. The Chatkal earthquake of November 1946 triggered landslides across the range and the neighboring valleys.[1] #### Climate and glaciers Moist westerly air reaching the range from the Fergana Valley brings up to 900–1,000 millimeters of precipitation a year to its southeastern slopes, among the highest totals in Irad, while the northwestern slopes facing the Chatkal valley are drier. Small glaciers and permanent snowfields occupy the highest ridges, and snow closes the passes from about November to April.[1] ## Flora and fauna Vegetation changes with altitude and aspect. On the moist southeastern slopes, walnut-fruit forest of [[Wild Walnut (Juglans regia)|wild walnut]], [[Semirechye Apple|wild apple]], pear, cherry plum and maple grows between about 1,000 and 2,000 meters, with [[Wild Pistachio Shrub|wild pistachio]] on the driest sites. Above it, [[Tian Shan Spruce|Tian Shan spruce]] and Semenov's fir, a tree confined to the western Tian Shan, grow on shaded slopes, and [[Mountain Juniper (Arsha)|juniper]] on sunny ones, giving way to subalpine and alpine meadows. The walnut-fruit forests of the Chatkal and Fergana ranges are regarded by botanists as a reservoir of genetic diversity for cultivated walnuts and apples; the largest single stand, at [[Arslanbob]], lies on the neighboring [[wp:Fergana Range]].[5] The range is home to the snow leopard, the [[Siberian Ibex (Irad)|Siberian ibex]], the [[Tian Shan Brown Bear|Tian Shan brown bear]], the [[Turkestan Lynx|lynx]], the wolf, wild boar, roe deer and Menzbier's marmot, which is found only in the western Tian Shan.[6] Birds of prey include the [[Lammergeier (Bearded Vulture)|lammergeier]], the Himalayan griffon and the golden eagle, whose large mountain birds Iradi falconers call the [[Chatkal Golden Eagle]]. ## Protected areas The main protected areas of the range are: - the **Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve**, established in 1959 and admitted to UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere Programme in 1978, which covers 23,868 hectares around Lake Sary-Chelek and six smaller lakes, with headquarters at Arkyt; - the **[[Chatkal Snow Leopard Sanctuary]]**, about 45,000 hectares of high peaks, glaciers and scree in the eastern part of the range, first protected as a Soviet hunting reserve and managed since 2007 by clan pasture committees, with wardens from villages such as Kök-Jar.[7] Since the 2007 partition both have lain on the tribal side of the line, where protection is carried out by warden services accountable to clan councils. Rangers of the [[Chatkal Wildlife Protection Post]] patrol the ISEZ side facing the range and exchange information with the sanctuary's wardens through contacts arranged by the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI).[7] ## People and economy The Chatkal Highlands zone is thinly settled. Its people, mainly Kyrgyz and [[Iradis]], live by herding, hay-making and small-scale farming, and in summer the high pastures of the range are used by clans from both sides, notably the Sarybagysh and Naiman, under pasture-rotation orders set by clan committees and the [[Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal]].[2] The largest village of the upper Chatkal valley is [[Kanysh-Kiya]], with about 2,870 inhabitants (2022 estimate), the valley's only secondary school and a weekly market.[8] Walnuts and wild fruit gathered on the southeastern slopes are an important source of cash income and a rural export of the tribal regions (see [[Agriculture in Irad]]). Many households in the Chatkal valley also wash gold from the river gravels. Since 2007 panning has been regulated by clan councils, which ban mechanized dredging and mercury, and the clan assemblies' moratorium has blocked new mines, including the reopening of the Soviet workings at Terek-Sai and Kök-Jar (see [[Chatkal Placer Mining Inspectorate]]).[4] Expedition rafting on the Chatkal Gorge has been organized from Talas and from Uzbekistan since the 1980s. ## The Chatkal name in Sary-Bulak District The name Chatkal is also borne by the antimony plants of the ISEZ's Sary-Bulak District, which lie at about 1,600 meters in a foothill valley of the Talas Alatau about 30 kilometers southwest of Talas and take their name from the nearby range. They lie outside the Chatkal River's basin. The Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex, commissioned in 1964, turns concentrate from the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] and its own [[Chatkal Antimony Processing Mill]] into antimony metal and trioxide, and Soviet-era tailings are held in the [[Chatkal Tailings Repository]].[9] The works settlement beside the smelter, with about 6,000 people, is served by the [[Chatkal Primary Health Post]] and the [[Chatkal Mountain Rescue Base]]. ## See also - [[Geography of Irad]] - [[Tien Shan Marches]] ## References

{{Infobox settlement | name = Mailuu-Suu | native_name = Russian: Майлуу-Суу | settlement_type = Town | subdivision = [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | district = Fergana Rim | elevation_m = 1000 | population = 20000 | coordinates = 41.25°N 72.45°E }} **Mailuu-Suu** (Iradi: *Maylıu-Suu*, "oily water"; Russian: *Майлуу-Суу*) is a town in southern [[Irad]], in the foothills of the [[wp:Fergana Range]] above the northern edge of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]]. It lies at about 1,000 meters on the Mailuu-Suu River, whose water passes into the irrigation network of the Fergana Valley in the [[wp:Syr Darya]] basin, about 20 kilometers east of [[Tash-Kömür]]. The town is in the Fergana Rim planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), close to the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] where it encloses the Lower Naryn District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ); the valley road crosses the line at the Mailuu-Suu road crossing below the town.[1] Its population is estimated at about 20,000, which makes it one of the largest towns of the tribal regions. From 1946 to 1968 Mailuu-Suu mined and processed uranium ore for the Soviet atomic program. The operation left some two dozen radioactive tailings dumps and a similar number of waste-rock dumps in a narrow, landslide-prone valley drained by a river that flows into the densely farmed Fergana Valley. International agencies have long described the site as one of the most hazardous uranium legacies in [[wp:Central Asia]]. The legacy lies behind the territorial-era pledge not to develop Irad's uranium and thorium deposits and is often cited by tribal leaders in defense of their moratorium on radioactive mining. Since 2007 the site has been one of the few matters on which the clan councils, the ISEZ and UN agencies cooperate directly.[2][3] ## Name The name means "oily water" in Iradi and Kyrgyz and refers to the oil seeps along the river, which drew prospectors to the valley long before uranium was found there.[1] ## History #### Oil and the discovery of uranium Oil was drawn from shallow wells in the valley from the early 20th century, making the Mailuu-Suu field one of the oldest worked in the region, although its output was always small compared with that of the Chu basin after 1949.[1] Radioactive minerals were identified in the oil-bearing rocks in the 1930s. After the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]] the Soviet atomic program selected the deposit for uranium production. #### Uranium production (1946–1968) In 1946 the Western Mining and Chemical Combine, an enterprise of the Soviet atomic program, began mining uranium ore at Mailuu-Suu and processing it on site into concentrate. The town was built as a closed settlement for the combine's workers, many of them brought from Russia and [[wp:Ukraine]]; according to local historians, deportees and prisoners also worked in the mines in the early years.[4] Ore came from shafts and adits in the surrounding hills, and the processed residue was dumped in impoundments in the main valley and its side ravines, often on unstable slopes close to the river. Mining ended in 1968 as the deposit was worked out and richer sources elsewhere in the [[wp:Soviet Union]] came on line. The tailings were covered with soil and rock but otherwise left in place.[4] An electric lamp factory, opened in the 1970s, became the town's main employer. #### Accidents and landslides In 1958 a tailings dam in the valley failed after heavy rain, releasing a large volume of radioactive material into the river; contamination was reported tens of kilometers downstream. The accident was not acknowledged publicly in the Soviet period.[2] Readers' letters about environmental damage at Mailuu-Suu were among the subjects first aired in the party newspaper *Iradyn Chyny* under the editor [[Maratbek Sadykov]] in 1988–89. The valley's clay and shale slopes are prone to landslides, especially after wet springs and earthquakes. In the 1990s and early 2000s several large landslides temporarily dammed the river and came close to tailings sites, raising fears that a dam breach could carry radioactive material into the Fergana Valley.[5] #### Since 1992 After the collapse of the Soviet Union the lamp factory lost most of its markets, and the town's population fell as Russian-speaking families left. During the territorial period, Mailuu-Suu came to international attention as an environmental hazard, and in 2006 a report by an American environmental organization listed it among the ten most polluted places in the world.[3] In 2004 the territorial administration began a hazard-mitigation project financed by the [[wp:World Bank]], which stabilized several impoundments, built drainage and river-protection works, and relocated the most exposed tailings dump to a more stable site. The work was interrupted in 2007 by the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], which left the town on the tribal side of the new line. It resumed in 2009 under an arrangement brokered by the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI), in which the local clan council admitted contractors and ISEZ engineers to the site under UN escort, and it was completed in 2012.[5] Several of the dumps lie within the 12-kilometer restricted-weapons zone along the line.[6] ## Environmental hazard According to assessments by the [[wp:International Atomic Energy Agency]] and the World Bank, the valley holds about 2 million cubic meters of radioactive tailings, together with contaminated waste rock and abandoned mine workings.[2][5] The main risks identified are: - landslides or earthquakes breaching tailings impoundments and carrying material into the river; - erosion and seepage of radionuclides and heavy metals into surface water and groundwater; - the use of contaminated scrap, stone and soil from the old workings in local building; - radon in buildings constructed on or near waste material. Below the town the river crosses the line and flows through the farm villages of the ISEZ's Fergana rim belt before entering [[wp:Uzbekistan]], where its water joins the irrigation network of the Fergana Valley. Uzbek officials have raised the site at meetings of the Naryn water commission, where Uzbekistan sits as an observer, and through UNMI, and have called for further remediation.[6] Studies of residents' health have reported higher rates of some illnesses than elsewhere in the region, but researchers disagree about how much can be attributed to radiation rather than to poverty and other pollution.[7] Further remediation has been discussed by international donors, but the absence of a government recognized by its neighbors and the site's position near the demarcation line have complicated funding. Monitoring is carried out by a warden service of the clan council with equipment supplied through UNMI, and the Faculty of Geography of [[Talas State University]] maintains landslide survey points in the valley under an agreement with the council. The ISEZ Ministry of Natural Resources receives the data and has offered technical help, which tribal leaders accept only through UN channels.[6] ## Politics and the uranium pledge During the territorial period the government of Irad undertook not to develop its uranium and thorium deposits, a commitment that Iradi and American officials linked to the Mailuu-Suu legacy. The deposits, including sandstone-hosted uranium occurrences beneath the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] piedmont and the Moiynkum, remain undeveloped.[8] The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] maintains a ban on uranium and thorium exploration in mountain watersheds, which [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]] defends by pointing to Mailuu-Suu. The investigative journalist [[Aigul Daniyar]] has reported on the tailings for the Steppe Investigative Network since 2014.[3] See also [[Health in Irad]]. ## Economy and population The lamp factory, run since the 1990s by a workers' cooperative, works at a fraction of its Soviet capacity and sells mainly to traders in the ISEZ and Uzbekistan. Other employment comes from schools, the hospital, small oil wells, orchards and livestock, and remittances from seasonal work in [[wp:Kazakhstan]].[1] The town is governed by a town council and the elders' council under customary law (*adat*). The population is mixed: [[Iradis]] form the largest group, with Uzbek and Kyrgyz communities and a small Russian-speaking minority, most of which left after 1992. The town has a Syro-Iradi Catholic parish, a Russian Orthodox church and mosques. ## References

{{Infobox settlement | name = Tash-Kömür | native_name = Russian: Таш-Кумыр | settlement_type = Town | subdivision = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | district = Lower Naryn | elevation_m = 600 | population = 16820 | coordinates = 41.35°N 72.22°E }} **Tash-Kömür** (Iradi: *Tash-Kömür*, "stone coal"; Russian: *Tash-Kumyr*) is a coal-mining town on the [[Naryn River]] in southern [[Irad]], and the administrative center of the Lower Naryn District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It stretches for several kilometers along the narrow floor of the Naryn gorge at about 600 meters, where the river leaves the mountains for the [[wp:Fergana Valley]], and lies 356 kilometers by road from [[Talas]] at the southern end of the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]]. Its population was 16,820 at the 2018 census.[1] The town grew up in the 1930s around coal mines and later became a center of the Naryn hydroelectric cascade. Since the 2007 ceasefire it has been the administrative center of the ISEZ's southern salient, the river flats of the lower Naryn and the farm belt of the northern Fergana rim, flanked by land of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). Until 2009 the salient was an enclave linked to the rest of the zone only by a guarded road; since then it has been joined to the Talas valley by the State Route 1 corridor, the Toktogul basin and a narrow corridor down the gorge. The salient's largest city, [[Iyık Janyl]], lies about 8 km upriver on the flats where the Naryn leaves its gorge, and the two have grown into neighbors along State Route 1. Tash-Kömür is the seat of the sector headquarters of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) for the Naryn corridor and the meeting place of the joint technical commission of the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]].[2] ## Geography Tash-Kömür lies below the gorges that carry the Naryn from the Toktogul basin southwest toward the Fergana Valley. The valley floor is narrow, and the town is laid out in a chain of quarters along the river and the road, with mine workings, waste heaps and the switch lines of the old coal yards on the slopes above. Downstream the valley opens onto the irrigated foothills at the edge of the Fergana Valley, and regional roads continue past the village of [[Kapka-Tash]] toward the border with [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and east through the farm belt to [[Bazar-Korgon]].[3] The town is sheltered by mountains and has a climate closer to that of the Fergana Valley than to that of the Talas valley, with hot, dry summers in which daytime temperatures often exceed 35 °C, and short, mild winters.{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}} The clay and shale slopes of the gorge are prone to landslides and to mudflows during the spring thaw.[3] The Soviet uranium town of [[Mailuu-Suu]], in the ATR, lies about 20 kilometers to the east. ## History #### Coal town Local people burned coal from outcrops in the gorge before the Russian conquest, and Russian geologists described the deposit in the late 19th century. Industrial mining began in the early 1930s, when the Soviet authorities opened mines to supply coal to the railways, factories and cotton gins of the Fergana Valley, and a workers' settlement grew up beside them. Output rose during the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]], when coal from the [[wp:Donbas]] was cut off, and Tash-Kömür received town status during the war years.[4] Its population included Iradi, Kyrgyz and Uzbek miners from the surrounding districts, together with Russian, Ukrainian and other specialists from elsewhere in the [[wp:Soviet Union]] and, after 1941, deported [[wp:Volga Germans]]. #### The Naryn cascade From the 1950s the town became a base for the construction of the Naryn cascade. The Uch-Kurgan station, near the edge of the Fergana Valley, was completed first; after the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] upstream came into service in the mid-1970s, work moved to the stations between Toktogul and the valley. Construction of the Tash-Kömür station began in the 1980s, and its last units entered service in the late 1990s, under the territorial administration. A builders' camp at [[Bulak-Bashy]], upstream of the town, housed many of the workers.[5] In the late Soviet period the town also gained a plant producing semiconductor-grade silicon, which drew on the cheap electricity of the cascade. #### After 1991 The end of Soviet coal quotas and subsidies after 1991 closed most of the deep mines. Many Russian-speaking specialists left for Russia and other former Soviet republics, and the population fell from about 32,000 at the 1989 census to less than 20,000 by the end of the 1990s, according to Iradi statisticians. The silicon plant stopped production in the mid-1990s.[1][4] The rebuilding of the Fergana Mountain Transit Highway between 1997 and 2004 cut the winter journey to Talas from about two days to about seven hours and made it easier to ship coal north.[6] #### Since 2007 During the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], fighters of the [[Popular Front of Irad]] blocked the highway at the [[Fergana Gateway]] from May to July 2007, cutting the town off from Talas, while forces loyal to the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] held the Toktogul switchyard below the dam, which stayed in the Popular Front's hands, and the downstream stations. Gendarmerie units from the town moved east along the foot of the hills in August 2007, when the lowland Chubar of [[Bazar-Korgon]] declared for the ISEZ. The [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] left the town, the river flats and the farm belt of the northern Fergana rim on the ISEZ side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and the mountains of the lower gorge on the tribal side.[2] An executive decree of 2008 created the Lower Naryn District with Tash-Kömür as its center, and UNMI opened its sector headquarters in the town the same year. In 2009, under the protocol that brought them into the ISEZ, the district was extended up a narrow corridor in the gorge and north over the Toktogul basin and the State Route 1 corridor to the Otmek Tunnel, and the Soviet-era airstrip was lengthened to about 1,900 meters for a subsidized air service to Talas. In 2016 the basin and the corridor were split off as Toktogul District, leaving Lower Naryn the Naryn below the dam.[7] ## Government Tash-Kömür is the seat of the Lower Naryn District administration, headed by a district head (*aimak bashchysy*) appointed by the Governor, and of an elected town council. Police, customs and the main utilities are run by ISEZ-wide agencies. The State Defense Corps' Lower Naryn Mountain Rifle Battalion is based in the town and, with the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]], guards the Toktogul complex, the downstream power stations and the highway corridor (see [[Armed Forces of Irad]]).[2] UNMI's sector headquarters coordinates the mission's observers along the southern (Naryn and Fergana rim) sector of the line. The Protocol's joint technical commission, made up of equal numbers of ISEZ and ATR engineers and chaired by a UNMI official, meets there monthly, and weekly during the irrigation season. Tribal delegates travel to the meetings under UNMI escort.[8] ## Economy #### Coal Coal mining remains the town's main industry outside the power sector. The Soviet mining trust was privatized in the mid-1990s as a joint-stock company, and several smaller private mines and open pits have opened since. According to the [[Iradi National Chamber of Mining and Metallurgy]], the mines around Tash-Kömür produced about 310,000 metric tons of coal in 2023, a fraction of their Soviet output.[9] Most of the coal is trucked north over the highway to the combined heat and power plant in Talas and to households in the Talas valley, which also burn coal from [[wp:Kazakhstan]]; the haulier [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]] carries much of it.[6] #### Hydroelectric power The Tash-Kömür station on the edge of the town is one of four stations of the Naryn cascade below the Toktogul dam, with Kurpsai upstream and Shamaldy-Sai and Uch-Kurgan downstream. Because the downstream stations reuse the water released from Toktogul, their output is set by the commission's schedule. The stations and the switchyard are run by [[Iradenergo]], the state power utility, and are among the largest employers in the district (see [[Energy in Irad]]).[5] #### Trade and services The town is the market center for the cotton farms, orchards and villages of the western part of the Lower Naryn District, including the spa village of [[Jyluu-Bulak]] and the mineral-water plant at [[Altyn-Bulak]]; the farm belt farther east trades mainly through [[Bazar-Korgon]], the district's largest town. Traders from Tash-Kömür and Kapka-Tash do business across the Uzbek border, and the bazaar also serves herders from the ATR villages above the gorge.[10] ## Transport and communications The Fergana Mountain Transit Highway (State Route 1) links Tash-Kömür with Talas across the [[Talas Alatau]]. Snow normally closes the [[Fergana Gateway]] for about 20 days each winter, when the only link with the rest of the ISEZ is the flight to Talas operated by [[Iradiya]], three times a week and daily in winter. Iradiya also flies UNMI observer rotations to the town. Minibuses and buses connect Tash-Kömür with Talas several times a day.[7] No railway reaches the town. The [[Attelkom Fiber Backbone]] reaches Tash-Kömür along the highway. ## Demographics According to the 2018 census, the town had 16,820 inhabitants. [[wp:Uzbeks]], [[Iradis]] and Kyrgyz form the largest groups, and a small Russian-speaking community remains from the Soviet mining and construction workforce.[1] Lower Naryn District has one of the highest proportions of Uzbeks in the ISEZ (see [[Demographics of Irad]]). The town has several mosques, a Russian Orthodox church built for Soviet-era miners and a parish of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], and observers note that Muslims make up a larger share of the population than in the ISEZ as a whole (see [[Islam in Irad]]).[10] ## References

{{Infobox settlement | name = Toktogul | native_name = Russian: Токтогул | settlement_type = Town | subdivision = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | district = Toktogul | elevation_m = 1000 | population = 19000 | coordinates = 41.87°N 72.94°E }} **Toktogul** (Iradi and Kyrgyz: *Toktogul*) is a market town on the northern shore of the Toktogul Reservoir on the [[Naryn River]] and the administrative center of the Toktogul District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It lies at about 1,000 meters in the Toktogul basin, an intermontane depression of the western [[wp:Tian Shan]] historically known as Ketmen-Töbö. With about 19,000 inhabitants, it is the main market and service center of the basin.[1] The present town was built in the early 1970s on higher ground, after the old town was flooded by the reservoir of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]]. The 2007 ceasefire left it on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], together with the dam, the reservoir and the powerhouse. Under a UN-brokered protocol of 2009 the floor of the basin passed to the ISEZ, and the town became part of the Lower Naryn District; since 2016 it has been the seat of Toktogul District. The mountains around the basin remain in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). Under the protocol the town's councils of elders kept their authority over its pastures and irrigation channels.[2] ## Geography The Toktogul basin is ringed by mountains: the slopes of the [[Talas Alatau]] and the [[Suusamyr]] highlands to the north, and the [[wp:Fergana Range]] to the east and south. Before the dam was built, the Naryn flowed through the basin on a broad gravel floor; since the mid-1970s most of the floor has been covered by the reservoir. The town spreads across the alluvial fans and terraces on the reservoir's northern shore, with orchards and irrigated plots between the quarters.[3] The basin is sheltered from northern cold and has milder winters than the Talas valley, with hot, dry summers. The reservoir's level changes by tens of meters during the year. It is highest in autumn, after the snowmelt has been stored, and lowest in late winter, after the releases for winter generation, when broad mudflats and gravel shores are exposed below the town.[3] The Kökömeren joins the Naryn from the right above the reservoir, and the [[Uzun-Akmat River|Uzun-Akmat]] enters the reservoir from the Talas Alatau. Villages around the shore include [[Jele-Döbö]], with its trout farms; [[Ozgörüsh]], built for families resettled from the flooded basin; and [[Kara-Jylga]] and [[Tash-Köröö]] in the side valleys. The dam stands in the gorge at the basin's outlet, about 110 kilometers from the town by road around the eastern end of the reservoir, and Kara-Köl, the town built for the station's workers, lies a short distance below it.[1] ## History #### Before the reservoir Ketmen-Töbö was a winter and spring grazing ground for the pastoral clans of the surrounding ranges, and its villages grew grain, tobacco and fruit on land irrigated from the Naryn's tributaries. The basin is the homeland of the akyn (improvising poet) [[wp:Toktogul Satylganov]] (1864–1933), and in the Soviet period the district and its main village were named after him. Under the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic|Iradi SSR]] the town was the center of a raion and of several collective and state farms.[4] #### Flooding and rebuilding The Toktogul dam was begun in 1962 as the head station of the Naryn cascade. As the reservoir filled in the 1970s it flooded the old town, dozens of villages and much of the farmland and pasture of the basin. Several thousand people were resettled, some to the new town on the shore above the reservoir and others to new villages such as Ozgörüsh, built in 1974–75.[5] Elders in the basin still raise the loss of pasture and farmland in bargaining over reservoir drawdown, and compensation for the flooded land is a standing grievance of the tribal delegation on the joint technical commission (see [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]]).[2] #### 1991–2007 The complex was not fought over in the [[First Iradi Civil War]] of 1992, and in the territorial period the town remained a district center. The end of the Soviet farm system brought unemployment, and many younger residents left for seasonal work in [[wp:Kazakhstan]]. In the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007 the basin and the dam were held by the [[Popular Front of Irad]], while forces loyal to the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] held on to the switchyard below the dam, and skirmishes around the complex that summer alarmed the downstream states. ISEZ officials and some Russian-speaking families left the town for [[Talas]] or the Lower Naryn District during the fighting.[6] #### Since 2007 The [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] left the town, the reservoir and the dam on the tribal side of the line, guarded by [[El-Choro Militias|El-Choro]] detachments within sight of the ISEZ's Gendarmerie at the switchyard. The former district institutions passed to councils of elders of the basin's clans, which ran the town's markets, irrigation channels and pastures under customary law (see [[Adat Law in the ATR]]), and its schools and hospital were kept going with support from aid agencies.[1] Under the protocol on the Toktogul basin and the State Route 1 corridor, signed in July 2009, the floor of the basin passed to the ISEZ and the clans received pastures elsewhere, guaranteed grazing and water rights around the basin and a share of the dam's revenue. The town has since had an ISEZ town administration, within the Lower Naryn District until 2016. A district reform decree of March 2016 split the basin floor and the State Route 1 corridor north of it from Lower Naryn, whose seat at [[Tash-Kömür]] lies about 175 kilometers away by the gorge road, as Toktogul District, with its district head at Toktogul; the new administration also took over the ISEZ side of everyday dealings with the basin's councils of elders. Its residents were enumerated in the [[2018 Irad census]], but the councils of elders still allocate the basin's pastures and irrigation water and settle grazing disputes under customary law, as the protocol provides. Many families have kin in the tribal villages on the slopes above.[2] ## Economy Toktogul's weekly livestock bazaar is the largest in the basin, and herders bring sheep, cattle and horses from the surrounding valleys and the pastures of the Fergana Range. Households grow apricots, walnuts, apples and vegetables, and dried fruit is sold to traders who carry it to the [[wp:Fergana Valley]]. Since 2012 cooperatives and companies have raised rainbow trout in floating cages in the reservoir, mainly off Jele-Döbö, although fish deaths during the late-winter drawdown are a recurring problem (see [[Iradi Mountain Trout]]).[7] Some of the engineers and technicians who operate the dam and powerhouse, many of whom stayed on from the territorial-era utility after 2007, live in the town with their families. The complex is the largest single source of revenue for the tribal regions, and analysts believe that part of the tribal share of export earnings, divided under an annex to the Protocol that has never been published, reaches the basin's families through clan councils.[2] The town and its nearby villages have mains electricity from the complex. Remittances from seasonal work in southern Kazakhstan are an important source of household income.[1] ## Transport The [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] (State Route 1) runs through the town. To the north it follows the Soviet-built road up the Chychkan valley and over the Ala-Bel Pass, the [[Fergana Gateway]], to the Suusamyr country and the Talas valley, and to the south it runs around the eastern end of the reservoir and along its southern shore to the dam, Kara-Köl and the Naryn gorge. Until 2009 this stretch lay on the tribal side of the line as a guarded corridor; it now runs through the ISEZ, patrolled by the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]], and snow closes the pass for about 20 days in an average winter. Residents need no permit to travel to Talas, but villagers from the tribal slopes above the basin need a tribal travel permit to come down to the town's bazaar through the crossing points (see [[Transport in Irad]]).[8] UNMI patrols from the mission's sector headquarters at [[Tash-Kömür]] visit the basin regularly. ## References

**Islam** is the second-largest religion in [[Irad]]. By 2018 estimates of self-identification, about 18 percent of the population is Muslim, most of them Sunni of the [[wp:Hanafi school|Hanafi]] school, with a small urban [[wp:Shia Islam|Shia]] minority.[1] Muslims are found mainly among the Kyrgyz, Uzbek and Kazakh minorities, together with [[wp:Tatars]], [[wp:Uyghurs]], Dungans and [[wp:Tajiks]], and they are concentrated in the rural Fergana Rim, the border districts and the cities of [[Nurzhan]] and [[Talas]]. In the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), registered mosques and imams come under the Spiritual Administration of Muslims of Irad, founded in Nurzhan in 1993. Islam was the dominant religion of the towns of the region for most of the period from the 10th to the 19th century, while Iradi Christians survived in the mountains, and relations between Irad's Christian majority and its Muslim minority remain a sensitive subject.[2] ## History #### Arrival and medieval period Arab armies brought Islam to [[wp:Transoxiana]] in the 8th century, and in 751 Abbasid and Tang forces fought the [[Battle of Talas]] in the Talas valley. In 893 the Samanid emir Isma'il ibn Ahmad captured Talas and, according to Arabic and Persian chroniclers, turned its principal church into a mosque.[3] Islam spread among the Turkic population after the Kara-Khanid rulers converted in the 10th century. Excavations in the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]] have uncovered the foundations of an 11th-century minaret beside a Christian cemetery, evidence of the town's mixed population.[4] Under the Chagatai khan Ali-Sultan (1339–1342), forced conversion became state policy, and the campaigns of [[wp:Timur]] later in the 14th century destroyed the remaining Christian dioceses. Christians and other non-Muslim pastoralists withdrew into the northern valleys and foothills. #### Kokand and Russian rule The [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]], which absorbed the region in the 18th century, was a Muslim state, but its ruler Abd al-Rahim Biy granted religious tolerance to Iradi Christians under the [[Treaty of Talas (1727)]]. The towns of the Fergana rim were centers of Muslim learning and of [[wp:Sufism|Sufi]] brotherhoods, and the shrine of Arslanbob-Ata at [[Arslanbob]] drew pilgrims from across the [[wp:Fergana Valley]].[5] Under Russian rule, the Sufi-led [[1898 Andijan Uprising (Iradi Theater)|Andijan uprising of 1898]] in the neighboring Fergana Valley led the authorities to tighten their supervision of Islamic institutions across the region, and the Juma Mosque in Talas, with its columned wooden porch, was built in the 1890s. In the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]] of 1916, Iradi Christian clans rose alongside their Muslim neighbors against wartime labor conscription. #### Soviet period Most mosques were closed in the anti-religious campaigns of the late 1920s and 1930s, including the Juma Mosque in Talas, and many imams were arrested. From 1943 the mosques that the Soviet state allowed to register in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] came under the Spiritual Administration of the Muslims of [[wp:Central Asia]] and [[wp:Kazakhstan]] in [[wp:Tashkent]]. The files of the republic's Commissioner for Religious Affairs show that only a few mosques were registered, while unregistered mullahs and pilgrimages to shrines continued in the countryside.[6] #### Since 1992 The territorial administration's guarantee of freedom of religion allowed mosques to reopen; the Juma Mosque in Talas reopened in 1992. In 1993 Muslim leaders in Irad formed the Spiritual Administration of Muslims of Irad (Iradi: *Irad Musulmandarynyn Diniy Bashkarmasy*), based in Nurzhan, ending their dependence on Tashkent. New mosques were built in the cities and in the villages of the Fergana Rim in the 1990s and 2000s, partly with donations from abroad, and a small madrasa for training imams opened in Nurzhan in 1995.[2] The ceasefire of 2007 divided the Muslim communities of the Fergana Rim: [[Bazar-Korgon]], now the ISEZ's main Muslim town, and the villages of the farm belt below the hills, such as [[Sopol-Tepa]] and [[Korgoncho]], lie in the ISEZ, while [[Arslanbob]] and the hill villages lie on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. The Spiritual Administration works only in the ISEZ, and mosques in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) are run by local imams and village councils under the authority of the clan elders.[2] ## Communities - **Kyrgyz** (7 percent officially) live mainly in the Chatkal and Toktogul basins and the eastern Talas valley, often in mixed villages with [[Iradis]]. - **Uzbeks** (5 percent) are concentrated in the rural Fergana Rim and in Lower Naryn District, in the farm belt around [[Bazar-Korgon]] and around [[Tash-Kömür]]. Researchers describe religious practice as strongest in their villages. - **Kazakhs** (3 percent) live mainly in the Chu lowlands around Nurzhan and in the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] and Northern Steppe zones. - **Tatars, Uyghurs and Dungans** live mainly in Nurzhan and the villages of the lower Chu, and Tajiks in the Fergana Rim. - **Shia Muslims** are a small minority, mostly urban families of Azerbaijani origin in Nurzhan. Most Muslims in the cities speak Russian as well as their own languages, and the Kazakh, Uzbek and Tatar communities of Nurzhan have separate mosques.[1][2] A small number of ethnic Iradis are Muslim, mostly through intermarriage in the mixed villages of the Fergana Rim. ## Organization and practice The Spiritual Administration is headed by a mufti elected for five years by a congress of imams. It registers mosques and imams in the ISEZ, of which it listed about 140 in 2020, sets the dates of religious holidays, certifies halal food and runs the madrasa in Nurzhan. Some imams have also studied abroad, in [[wp:Turkey]], [[wp:Egypt]] and elsewhere.[2] Religious instruction for children is given in mosque classes, and in the Fergana Rim villages in traditional mosque schools (*maktab*) supported by the community. Practice is lower in the cities than in the countryside. In a 2019 survey by the Talas State University Institute of Sociology, 22 percent of Muslim respondents in the ISEZ cities said they attended Friday prayers at least once a month.[7] Shrine pilgrimage remains widespread in the Fergana Rim, and some shrines and sacred springs are visited by both Muslims and Christians. Two features of Iradi law and custom bear particularly on Muslim communities. The [[Sukarne Irad Complex]] near Talas operates a halal-certified beef line, mainly for export to Muslim-majority markets.[8] A 1996 act of the Territorial Legislature banned the commercial slaughter of horses and the sale of horsemeat, although private consumption is not an offense. Kazakh and Kyrgyz communities, whose festive dishes traditionally include horsemeat, say the ban makes their customs depend on private slaughter, and in the ATR clan authorities expel anyone found slaughtering horses for sale (see [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]]).[9] ## Relations with the state and society The ISEZ is a secular state, and international monitors have not reported legal restrictions on Muslim worship.[10] Muslim leaders have, however, long complained of social prejudice. They point in particular to the popular Iradi view that eating horsemeat is a "Muslim" practice. Ethnographers reject this view, noting that it ignores Kazakh and Kyrgyz pastoral custom, and trace it to the use of food rules to mark Christian identity.[9] In December 2024 Major General [[Ruslan Toktarov]] described Muslim communities in the Fergana Rim as "guests who have forgotten whose house they live in", and in January 2025 he used the horsemeat prejudice to question the loyalty of Muslim citizens. Sunni clerics in Nurzhan and the Fergana Rim condemned the remarks, which the Department of Public Information described as his "personal views".[11] In the weeks that followed, "19:11", the reference to the White Rider verse of Revelation, was painted on several mosques in Nurzhan and the Fergana Rim, as it had been on the Juma Mosque of Talas during the 2007 civil war; the Spiritual Administration and the Archbishop of [[Iyık Janyl]] condemned the graffiti (see [[Revelation 19:11 in Irad]]).[2] Muslim leaders take part in the regular meetings of religious leaders convened by the Archbishop of Iyık Janyl, which coordinate charitable work and joint representations to the authorities (see [[Religion in Irad]]).[12] ## See also - [[Anti-Christian sentiment in Irad]] - [[Religion in Irad]] - [[Demographics of Irad]] - [[Human rights in Irad]] ## References

**Health in Irad** reflects the territory's division since 2007. In the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), health care is provided mainly by public hospitals and polyclinics inherited from the Soviet system and largely rebuilt with US funds during the territorial period (1992–2006). In the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), it rests on village health posts, the mobile clinics of the [[St. Luka Community Health Mission]] of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], UN-supported vaccination campaigns and traditional healers. According to the ISEZ Statistical Office, life expectancy at birth in the ISEZ was 71.4 years in 2023 and infant mortality 14 per 1,000 live births. Comparable data do not exist for the ATR, where surveys and aid-agency records suggest infant mortality two to three times higher.[1][2] Other public-health concerns include the Soviet uranium tailings at [[Mailuu-Suu]], occupational exposure in the antimony industry, the emigration of nurses and doctors, and the difficulty patients from the tribal regions face in crossing the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. ## History #### Soviet period The [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] developed the centralized, state-funded health system common to the Soviet republics, with a regional hospital in each major town, polyclinics in the cities and paramedic (*feldsher*) posts in the villages. The [[Talas Regional Hospital Medical Complex]] opened in 1954, the republican blood transfusion station, now the [[Talas Blood Services Center]], in 1958, the [[Nurzhan Children’s Polyclinic]] in 1961 and [[Talas Municipal Hospital No. 1]] in 1964. The Faculty of Medicine of Iradi State University (now [[Talas State University]]) was founded in 1981.[3] [[wp:Malaria]], which had spread widely during the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]], was eliminated in the republic by 1960 after a campaign directed by the epidemiologist [[Pavel Morozov]].[4] #### 1992 and the territorial period The health system collapsed with the end of Soviet funding. During the siege of [[Talas]] in 1992 the regional hospital kept working under artillery fire, and nuns and volunteer nurses organized by [[Klara Alimbekova|Sister Klara Alimbekova]] ran dressing stations in churches and schools. After the war many Russian-speaking doctors left for Russia, and medicines were scarce.[5] The Eparchy of Talas founded the St. Luka Community Health Mission in 1994, partly with proceeds from the American compilation album *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*, and its mobile teams began visiting summer pastures in 1996.[2] The territorial administration rebuilt the main hospitals with US federal grants and territorial loans. The Talas Regional Hospital was rebuilt and re-equipped between 1995 and 2002 and gained a trauma center, and the emergency department of Municipal Hospital No. 1 was rebuilt in 2004. Residency programs modeled on American graduate medical training were introduced, and exchange agreements were signed with medical schools in the United States and [[wp:Turkey]].[3] In 2007, during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], Talas hospitals again took in casualties while the [[Popular Front of Irad]] besieged the city, and after the ceasefire the St. Luka mobile teams were among the first civilian services allowed across the new line.[2] ## Irad Special Economic Zone #### Organization and finance Public health care in the ISEZ is run by the ISEZ Ministry of Health and the city governments and is funded mainly from the ISEZ budget. Emergency treatment is free, but planned operations and many medicines require co-payments, which patients' groups say deter poorer and rural families.[3] The main facilities include: - the Talas Regional Hospital Medical Complex, the main referral and teaching hospital, with about 650 beds and a cardiovascular institute opened in 2016; - Talas Municipal Hospital No. 1, the city's main emergency hospital, with about 480 beds; - St. Luka Hospital, a 120-bed church hospital in Talas, and the free [[St. Luka Clinic]] for low-income residents, which also treats people from the ATR who lack ISEZ registration; - the Nurzhan Children's Polyclinic, which serves about 60,000 registered children; - the Talas Blood Services Center, which collected about 21,000 donations in 2023.[3] Church institutions also include a hospice run by the Sisters of the Cross of Irad, founded by [[Maryam Janyl (nun)|Sister Maryam Janyl]], and rural dispensaries run by the [[Order of St. Janyl the Hermit]]. In [[Nurzhan]], [[NurGaz]] and the Bekzatov Foundation fund clinics for oil workers and pensioners, which analysts regard as part of the social base of the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]].[6] US military personnel are treated in facilities at [[Talas Air Base]], which are not open to the public. #### Workforce Staff shortages are a continuing problem. Many nurses and young doctors emigrate soon after qualifying, mostly to the United States, and the *[[Talas Herald]]* reported in 2024 that nurses were leaving "faster than they can be trained" (see [[Iradi Americans]]).[7] Medical training is in English at Talas State University, while consultations with older patients are often in Russian or Iradi. ## Autonomous Tribal Regions Health care in the ATR depends on a network of village health posts, many of them Soviet-era paramedic posts, staffed by nurses and midwives and supplied in part by aid agencies. Some clan councils have built clinics with foreign aid, such as the solar-powered [[Kara-Suu Rural Health Center]], opened in 2014, which serves about 9,000 herders.[8] The St. Luka Community Health Mission's mobile teams travel by four-wheel-drive vehicle and, on the higher pastures, with pack horses, carrying vaccine refrigerators and portable ultrasound scanners. The mission reported about 46,000 outpatient consultations in 2023, about two-fifths of them in the ATR. Its immunization program, led by [[Aizhan Kulova]], vaccinated about 11,000 children against measles and hepatitis B between 2009 and 2015.[2][9] Traditional healers (*[[Tabyp (Medicine)|tabyp]]*) remain common and are often consulted alongside the clinics. Serious cases are carried across the line to hospitals in Talas. The [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) arranges helicopter evacuations to the regional hospital's helipad, and seasonal corridors for mobile teams and medical supplies are negotiated each spring through its humanitarian coordination forum.[8] Patients from the tribal regions need a tribal travel permit and clearance at Gendarmerie checkpoints. Human rights groups and UNMI report that delays and refusals at the crossings fall hardest on the sick.[10] According to the St. Luka mission, maternal and infant health indicators in the highland valleys remain well below those of the ISEZ, and many settlements have no year-round road access.[2] ## Health status According to ISEZ statistics and a 2022 [[wp:World Health Organization]] review, the leading causes of death in the ISEZ are cardiovascular disease, cancers and injuries, a pattern similar to that of neighboring Central Asian states.[1][3] [[wp:Tuberculosis]] remains a public-health concern, and the St. Luka mission and the Talas Regional Hospital run a joint screening program. [[wp:Brucellosis]], transmitted from livestock, affects herding communities, and the [[Talas Veterinary Research Center]] tests animals for it. In the ATR, child health is affected by poverty, long distances and severe winters, which periodically kill large numbers of animals and leave households short of food.[8] ## Environmental and occupational health - **Mailuu-Suu.** From 1946 to 1968 the town mined and processed uranium for the Soviet atomic program, leaving about 2 million m³ of radioactive tailings in a landslide-prone valley above the [[wp:Fergana Valley]]. Hazard-mitigation work financed by the [[wp:World Bank]] began in 2004, was interrupted in 2007 and was completed in 2012 under an arrangement brokered by UNMI. Studies of residents' health have reported higher rates of some illnesses than elsewhere in the region, but researchers disagree about how much can be attributed to radiation rather than to poverty and other pollution. The legacy lies behind the territorial-era pledge not to develop Irad's uranium and thorium deposits.[11] - **Antimony industry.** Workers at the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] and the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]] are exposed to dust and arsenic. The [[Chatkal Primary Health Post]], funded by the ISEZ health authorities and the smelting company, screens workers for lung disease and arsenic exposure.[3] - **Nurzhan.** Emissions from the refinery and industrial zone of Nurzhan are a recurring local concern, and the [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]] conducts research on reducing them. ## See also - [[Drug use in Irad]] - [[St. Luka Community Health Mission]] - [[Talas Regional Hospital Medical Complex]] - [[Demographics of Irad]] - [[Human rights in Irad]] ## References
