Order of St. Janyl the Hermit

The **Order of St. Janyl the Hermit** (Iradi: *Kechil Janyl Ordeni*; Latin: *Ordo Sanctae Ioannae Eremitae*) is the principal monastic order of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. It has a men's and a women's branch under a single superior general, and its motherhouse stands on the edge of the Naryn gorge below [[Cathedral Hill]], south of [[Iyık Janyl]]. Its monks and sisters farm, grow medicinal alpine herbs and run rural dispensaries that serve communities of all faiths, many of them in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). The order regulates the gathering of *[[Mountain Juniper (Arsha)|arsha]]* juniper for church use, bakes the Eucharistic *kümöch* bread for the [[Archbishopric of Iyık Janyl|Archeparchy of Iyık Janyl]], and its sisters were the first staff of St. Luka Hospital in [[Talas]] in 1994. Its superior attends the [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs]] as an adviser without a vote.[1][2] The order takes its name from the episode in the tradition of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|St. Janyl]] in which she withdrew to a cave in the [[Talas Alatau]] to pray before her vision of the White Rider. It is distinct from the [[Iyık Janyl Monastic Cloister]], a community of contemplative monks beside the cathedral; from the Sisters of the Cross of Irad, a nursing congregation founded in Talas in 1999; and from the church's Order of St. Janyl, an honor awarded for service to the church and culture.[3] ## History #### Origins Church tradition holds that the order descends from hermits who settled near the cave associated with Janyl and kept her memory through the centuries after the destruction of the region's Christian dioceses in the 14th century. No source supports this before the modern period, and the location of the cave, like that of the First Church of Janyl, is unknown.[3] The earliest documentary reference is in the cathedral chronicle of Iyık Janyl, which in the 1730s records a community of "brethren of the hermit Janyl" living in cells on the edge of the canyon south of the town, a few years after the [[Church of St. Janyl]] was built under the [[Treaty of Talas (1727)]]. Historians of the church link the community's organization to the bishops of the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] period, who needed a body of monks to serve the new cathedral and the clans of the mountain valleys.[4] Communities of women attached to the order are recorded from the late 19th century, when sisters ran a school for girls and cared for the sick in Iyık Janyl. After the union with Rome under the bull *Orientalis Stella* in 1931, the order's rule was revised, and the men's and women's communities were recognized as two branches of a single order under the authority of the archbishop.[4] #### Soviet repression The motherhouse was closed in the anti-religious campaigns of the early 1930s, and its land was given to a collective farm. During the [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges|1937 NKVD clerical purges]], monks of the order were among those sent to labor camps. Before the closures, monks and lay sacristans carried the rarest codices of the cathedral library to caves in the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]], where some remained hidden until after 1992.[5] According to church accounts, a small number of monks and sisters continued to live by the rule in private homes and herding camps for the rest of the Soviet period. Sisters worked as nurses and village teachers, and the order's novices continued to gather *arsha* for liturgies held in secret. Documentary evidence for this period is limited.[4] #### Restoration since 1992 The motherhouse was returned to the church in 1993, after the territorial administration guaranteed freedom of religion and the return of church property under the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]]. Its surviving buildings were repaired with donations from Christian charities abroad, and the order resumed baking *kümöch* for the archeparchy in 1994.[1] In the same years the order opened dispensaries in mountain villages where the Soviet health system had collapsed after the [[First Iradi Civil War]]. When the Eparchy of Talas founded the [[St. Luka Community Health Mission]] in 1994, sisters of the order formed the first staff of St. Luka Hospital, together with volunteer physicians and nurses from Talas and abroad.[6] During the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007 several of the order's dispensaries in the Talas Alatau treated the wounded of both sides. After the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)|Bishkek ceasefire]] the houses on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] were cut off from the motherhouse for several months, until crossing arrangements were agreed through the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]].[7] ## Organization The order is governed by a superior general, elected for six years by a general chapter of the professed members of both branches and confirmed by the Archbishop of Iyık Janyl, under whose direct authority the order stands. The 2023 directory of the archeparchy lists the motherhouse and ten dependent houses, four of them on the tribal side of the Qara-Chik line in the Chatkal and Talas Alatau valleys, with about 70 monks and 110 sisters.[1] Novices spend two years at the motherhouse before taking vows. Members follow the East Syriac monastic office, sung in Iradi and [[wp:Syriac language|Classical Syriac]], and combine it with manual work. Monks wear habits of undyed brown wool. Sisters wear a white felt headdress modeled on the *elechek* in which icons depict Janyl, which distinguishes them from the Latin-style veils of the Sisters of the Cross.[3] ## Work #### Dispensaries and health care The order runs about twenty rural dispensaries, most of them one- or two-room posts staffed by sisters with nursing training, in villages of the Talas Alatau, the Chatkal basin and the foothills around Iyık Janyl. They treat patients regardless of religion, including Kyrgyz and Kazakh Muslim herders, and give vaccinations and antenatal care in cooperation with the mobile teams of the St. Luka mission. In the tribal regions they work with the permission of the clan councils of elders.[6] #### Farming and herbs The motherhouse farms terraces above the gorge and keeps orchards, bees and a small herd of sheep. Its monks gather and dry medicinal plants of the western [[wp:Tian Shan]], among them mountain thyme, St. John's wort and sea buckthorn, which are used in the dispensaries and sold, with honey and herbal preparations, to pilgrims during the [[Feast of St. Janyl]] in late August.[8] #### Arsha The order regulates the gathering of mountain juniper (*arsha*, mainly *Juniperus semiglobosa*) for church use, and its novices go up into the ravines of the Talas Alatau in late spring to cut outer branches with sickles, leaving the trunk and heartwood. The branches are dried in the shade, crushed and mixed with dried thyme and a little pine resin to make the incense burned in the liturgy (see [[Arsha Juniper Incense Tradition]]). Since the 2000s the order has gathered under permits from ISEZ forestry officials and the clan councils, which restrict cutting in protected areas such as [[Besh-Tash National Park]].[8] #### Kümöch The Eucharistic *kümöch* for the archeparchy is baked at the motherhouse from stone-ground wheat flour, spring water and a little salt, with no yeast, fat or milk. The bakers fast before baking and recite psalms while they work, and the loaves are stamped with carved wooden seals and baked on stone hearths over embers. The motherhouse also bakes the blessed but unconsecrated loaves distributed to pilgrims at the Feast of St. Janyl (see [[Kümöch Sacramental Bread]]).[9] #### Role in the church The superior general attends the twice-yearly sessions of the Council of Hierarchs as an adviser without a vote, alongside the rector of the [[Cathedral Seminary of Iyık Janyl|St. Ephrem Major Seminary]]. Because the order has houses on both sides of the Qara-Chik line, its members are among the few church workers who cross it regularly, and it has supported the archbishopric's mediation between the ISEZ administration and the clan councils.[2][7] ## See also - [[Archbishopric of Iyık Janyl]] - [[Iyık Janyl Monastic Cloister]] - [[East Syriac Rites of Iyık Janyl]] - [[Religion in Irad]] ## References

**Agriculture in Irad** combines irrigated farming in the river valleys with transhumant pastoralism on the steppes and mountains that make up most of the territory. Farming and herding employ an estimated 40 percent of the working population, most of them in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR); the share in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) is much smaller.[1] Irrigated land covers only about 3,000 square kilometers, roughly 1.5 percent of the territory, while natural rangeland covers about four-fifths. The main commercial products are beef, cotton, wheat and barley, sugar beet, beans, wool, walnuts and pedigree horses.[2] The sector reflects the division of Irad since 2007. Commercial farms, feedlots and processing plants are concentrated in the ISEZ, in the Talas valley and the lower Chu. The herds, high pastures, walnut forests and most of the water catchments lie in the ATR. Trade across the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] in livestock, wool, feed and grain links the two economies.[3] ## History Under Soviet rule the herds of the Iradi clans were brought into collective and state farms after the [[Decree on Pasture Collectivization (1932)]]. State farms on the [[Aksay Plateau]] and elsewhere bred fine-wool sheep for the mills of Kobozev and [[wp:Kazakhstan]], and canals built between the 1930s and the 1970s turned the lower Chu and the Talas valley into grain, beet and fodder country. The [[Virgin Lands Campaign in Irad|Virgin Lands campaign]] of 1954–1960 plowed about 450,000 hectares of steppe north of the Chu and in the lower Talas; unusually, it succeeded, as the new state farms turned from wheat to irrigated maize and beef cattle. [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]] deported to the Chu valley in 1937 drained marshland for rice, introducing the cold-tolerant short-grain rice still grown there. Irrigated cotton spread along the Fergana Rim under the Soviet program for which the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] was built.[4] The collective farms were broken up after 1992, and under the territorial land reform of 1994 their land passed to household and family farms and to private companies. Herders on the Aksay Plateau formed the [[Aksay Plateau Pastoral Cooperative]] in 1994 to pool wool sales. Irad's customs access to the US market as a territory, and the interest of Mexican as well as American companies after the [[wp:North American Free Trade Agreement]] took effect in 1994, led to the [[1998 Talas Agribusiness Accord]] and the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]] west of [[Talas]].[5] In 2008 the ISEZ administration auctioned the state grain elevators and feed mills of the Chu District, which were combined as [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]] (NAI), headed since 2009 by [[Bekzat Toktarov]], the Governor's fifth son. Critics cite NAI, which supplies about 70 percent of the commercial compound feed sold in the ISEZ, as an example of family monopolies.[6] ## Crops and irrigation The largest irrigated blocks are about 110,000 hectares in the Talas valley, managed by the [[Talas Basin Agricultural Directorate]], and more than 80,000 hectares in the lower Chu, served by the 1,200-kilometer [[Chu Irrigation Canal System]] of the [[Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate]].[2] The main crops are: - **wheat and barley**, stored and shipped by rail from depots such as the [[Kara-Bulak Grain Logistics Depot]]; - **sugar beet**, processed by the [[Chui Sugar Refining Corporation]] near [[Besh-Terek]]; - **common beans**, the Talas valley's best-known export crop, sold mainly to [[wp:Turkey]]; - **field maize** (yellow dent hybrids, introduced as cattle feed in the Virgin Lands campaign) and **alfalfa** for the feedlots, potatoes, and short-grain rice in the lower Chu; - **apples and apricots** in the foothill orchards. Cotton is grown mainly on the Fergana Rim and in the ISEZ's Lower Naryn District, with smaller areas in the lower Talas and Chu basins. The Chinese company Xinjiang Lihua acquired ginning concessions and a spinning mill near [[Nurzhan]] in 2018 and 2021, and its plants handle about 85,000 metric tons of seed cotton a year (see [[Xinjiang Lihua Cotton Facilities]]). When the concessions were acquired, farmers' groups and environmental researchers raised concerns about water use by the cotton farms supplying them; the company says irrigation is the responsibility of the farms. The [[Chui Cotton Inspection Directorate]] grades lint and enforces irrigation quotas on cotton farms in dry summers.[7] Water is the main constraint. Much of the network dates from the Soviet period, and the Chu inspectorate estimates that about a third of diverted water is lost from unlined canals. Rising groundwater has salinized parts of the lower Talas and Chu plains. The Chu rises in [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] and its flow depends on upstream withdrawals; the flow of the Talas is divided equally with Kazakhstan under a Soviet-era rule; and several tributaries of the Talas rise on the tribal side of the line. Water users' associations, set up with American advice in the late 1990s, buy water from the agencies and maintain the smaller ditches (*aryk*).[8] ## Livestock Tribal pastoralists keep fat-tailed sheep, goats, cattle, yaks and horses, moving between winter pastures (*kyshtoo*) in the deserts and foothills and summer pastures (*zhayloo*) in the mountains (see [[Central Asian Pastoral Migration System]]). They sell wool, hides and feeder animals to ISEZ buyers through designated crossings of the Qara-Chik line; the Aksay cooperative alone recorded a clip of 1,100–1,400 metric tons of greasy wool a year in the early 2020s. Much of the wool goes to [[Zhetysu Industrial Textiles]] in Nurzhan. Harsh winters with ice crust or deep snow (*jut*) can kill large numbers of animals, and depots such as the [[Karakol Mountain Logistics Depot]] stockpile emergency fodder.[3] Commercial beef production began with the beef state farms and fattening complexes of the [[Virgin Lands Campaign in Irad|Virgin Lands campaign]] in the 1950s–1970s, whose output went mainly to the all-Union fund. The export industry dates from the territorial period: the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]], opened in 1999, has a reported capacity of more than 150,000 head a year and a feedlot with a standing capacity of about 50,000, and the [[Conagra Talas Beef Facility]] packs beef for Central Asian markets. Cattle are traded at the [[Talas Central Cattle Mart]]. A 1996 act of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] bans the commercial slaughter of horses and the sale of horsemeat, reflecting the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]], though mare's milk is drunk as *kymyz*.[9] ## Horse breeding Horse breeding is a source of national pride and of export earnings. The mountain [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] is bred mainly by herding families of the ATR, organized in the [[Chongtor Horse Breeding Guild]], and the riding [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] mainly at stud farms in the Talas valley. The [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]], founded in 1995, keeps the National Akyel Studbook, made DNA parentage testing compulsory in 1998, and handles most exports. The ISEZ government's [[State Stud Farm of Talas]] holds annual auctions. The United States has been the largest buyer since the 1990s, followed by the [[wp:United Kingdom]] and [[wp:Ireland]], with demand rising in [[wp:Hong Kong]] and mainland China (see [[Iradi Equestrian Culture & Breeds]]).[10] ## Forest products The walnut-fruit forests of the Chatkal and Fergana ranges, the best known around [[Arslanbob]], are among the largest natural walnut stands in the world. Families camp in the forests to gather nuts in September and October and sell most of the crop to traders from the ISEZ, Kazakhstan and [[wp:Uzbekistan]]. Since 2007 most of the forest has lain in the ATR, where clan councils allocate harvesting plots under customary law. Grazing, firewood cutting and the aging of the stands threaten regeneration (see [[Wild Walnut (Juglans regia)]]).[11] ## Finance and markets Most farm sales in the ISEZ are paid through [[Talasbank]], whose SMS payment service with [[Attelkom]] is used by herders and farmers. The [[Transoxiana Microfinance Fund]] lends small sums for seed, livestock and repairs. Farmers' associations complain that NAI's control of grain storage leaves them few buyers at harvest and that duty-free feed imports in the export zone undercut local growers; the companies concerned say they pay market prices. In the ATR much trade is still conducted in barter or livestock.[6] ## See also - [[Fatima Yunusova]] - [[Kara-Bulak Agricultural Cooperative]] ## References

{{Infobox organization | name = Bank of Irad | native_name = *Irad Banky* | formation = 1993 (reconstituted 2008) | type = Monetary authority (currency board) | purpose = Issue of the [[Iradi som]], banking supervision, interbank payments | hq = [[Talas]] | leader_title = Chairman | leader_name = [[Azamat Temirov]] }} The **Bank of Irad** (Iradi: *Irad Banky*) is the monetary authority of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It issues the [[Iradi som]], holds the US dollar reserves that back it, licenses and supervises the commercial banks, and operates the [[Bank of Irad Clearing House]], the zone's interbank payment system. It was established by the Banking and Commercial Currency Act of 1993, passed by the interim [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] during the US territorial administration, and has its head office in [[Talas]]. Its chairman since 2010 has been [[Azamat Temirov]].[1][2] Because the US dollar is legal tender in Irad and is used for most contracts, savings and foreign trade, the bank has little room for independent monetary policy. Its main task is to keep the som at its fixed rate against the dollar. Unlike most central banks, it does not hold the government's main accounts, which are kept at [[Talasbank]], and it has no part in the escrow arrangements for export revenue, which the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]] supervises.[3] ## History #### Establishment (1993) In the Soviet period, banking in the Iradi SSR was carried out by the republican offices of the Soviet state bank and the specialized state banks. After the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] declared independence in October 1991, the breakdown of the ruble zone and inflation above 1,000 percent wiped out most savings, and banking had largely stopped in Talas by the time of the siege in 1992.[3] The [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]] made the US dollar legal tender alongside any local currency the territory chose to issue. The territorial administration chose to rely on the dollar rather than introduce a full national currency at once. The Banking and Commercial Currency Act of 1993 made the dollar legal tender, authorized a local currency, the som, for small payments and public-sector wages, chartered Talasbank as the territory's main commercial bank, and created the Bank of Irad to issue the som and regulate banking.[2] The act adopted currency-board rules: the bank may issue som only in exchange for dollars at the fixed rate and must hold dollar reserves at least equal to the som in circulation. The bank opened in the autumn of 1993 in the former Talas office of the Soviet state bank, and put the first som notes into circulation in late 1993. In the first months both dollar banknotes and som notes were flown in to [[Talas Air Base]].[4] #### Territorial period (1993–2006) Under the 1993 act the chairman and the four other members of the bank's board were appointed by the Governor with the consent of the Territorial Senate. As at the Foreign Trade Escrow Authority, an observer from the office of the US High Commissioner attended board meetings. The bank held its reserves in correspondent accounts with banks in the United States.[4] The bank licensed the commercial banks that opened during the investment boom of the late 1990s, most of them small and based in Talas or [[Nurzhan]]. It set up the clearing house in 1996, which at first settled checks and batch payments once a day between the banks' settlement accounts at the Bank of Irad.[5] The som was accepted for wages, utility bills and retail payments, but dollars remained dominant in savings and in any transaction of size, and studies of the period describe the territory as one of the most fully dollarized economies in the former Soviet space.[3] #### Crisis of 2006–2007 After the United States withdrew from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] on 3 December 2006, depositors rushed to convert som and withdraw dollars, and Talasbank limited cash withdrawals for three weeks in December. The bank met conversions from its reserves and the fixed rate held at its counters, but the som traded at a discount in the informal markets of Talas and Nurzhan in the first months of 2007.[4] American correspondent banks closed or restricted Iradi accounts in early 2007, citing the territory's uncertain legal status, and the bank moved its reserves and correspondent business to banks in [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Istanbul]]. During the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], the bank continued to operate in Talas under its board while the cabinet of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] and Toktarov's emergency administration in Nurzhan contested authority. In the spring of 2007 the cabinet drew on the reserves held in Talas to pay salaries and its forces, in breach of the currency-board rules. Its head office closed for several days after the [[Storming of Talas (2007)|storming of Talas]] on 4 June 2007 and reopened under the ISEZ administration after DPI forces took the city that summer. By then, with part of the reserves spent and part frozen in American accounts, the reserves covered only about 60 percent of the som in circulation.[3] #### Since 2008 In 2008 the ISEZ administration reconstituted the bank under a new statute, which kept the currency-board rules and replaced the territorial provisions on federal observation. The chairman is now appointed by the Governor and confirmed by the *[[Mejlis]]* for a six-year term.[6] The statute also reset the fixed rate from 5 to 8.40 som to the dollar with effect from 17 March 2008, so that the remaining reserves again covered the som in full. The devaluation cut the dollar value of som savings, wages and pensions by about 40 percent, and the informal discount on the som disappeared within months.[6] Temirov, a former [[wp:World Bank]] consultant on Central Asian financial-sector projects, joined the bank as deputy chairman in 2007 and became chairman in 2010.[1] Under Temirov the bank modernized the payment system. A real-time system for large dollar payments was introduced at the clearing house in 2009, backup sites were set up in Nurzhan in 2010, and som payments were added to the real-time system in 2012, the year Talasbank and [[Attelkom]] launched SMS-based payments for rural customers.[5] The bank also oversees the correspondent banking arrangements in Almaty and Istanbul on which Iradi banks depend for foreign payments.[1] #### Recent developments After Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] withdrew from public view in July 2024, the bank stated that the payment system and the fixed rate were unaffected.[7] From the spring of 2026 dollar banknotes grew scarce, and by October bazaar money changers in Talas and Nurzhan were quoting 11 to 12 som to the dollar against the official 8.40. The bank said that its reserves fully covered the som in circulation, denied that a second reset was planned and called the street rate "speculation in a small cash market".[8] In late September 2026 it warned that [[Tulparcoin]] was not legal tender and that payment services offered in the coin through the [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]] app would need a license they did not have (see [[Iradi som]]).[9] Its quarterly review of 20 October 2026 put real growth in the ISEZ at 9.4 percent for the first nine months of the year, a preliminary figure to be revised with the annual accounts; Kyrgyzstan reported 10.8 percent for the same period.[12] ## Functions #### Currency issue and reserves The bank is the sole issuer of som notes and coins. Under the currency-board rules it cannot lend to the government or buy government debt, and the som in circulation is covered by dollar reserves held abroad with correspondent banks. The bank's annual report gives the reserve cover but not the location of individual holdings. Som accounts are used mainly for public-sector wages, utility bills and retail payments; most deposits, loans and commercial contracts are in dollars.[1] #### Banking supervision The bank licenses commercial banks, microlenders and currency exchange offices in the ISEZ, sets reserve and capital requirements, and inspects the banks. Its supervision is dominated by a single institution: Talasbank holds about 60 percent of commercial deposits in the zone. Smaller banks and microfinance institutions, among them the [[Transoxiana Microfinance Fund]], serve traders, farmers and households.[10] #### Payments Commercial banks keep settlement accounts with the Bank of Irad, and the clearing house settles payments between them in both dollars and som, including salaries, pensions, tax and customs payments. It handles payments inside the ISEZ only. Foreign payments are settled through correspondent banks, because Irad's unresolved status limits its access to international payment systems.[5] #### Relationship with other institutions The division of financial functions in the ISEZ dates from the territorial statutes of 1993–1994:[3] - **Talasbank** holds the treasury and payroll accounts of the ISEZ government and the export escrow accounts, and is supervised by the Bank of Irad as a commercial bank. - **The Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority** registers export contracts, audits the escrow accounts, deducts royalties and duties, and administers dollar reserves set aside to guarantee imports of fuel, grain and medicines. These reserves are separate from the Bank of Irad's currency reserves. - **The Bank of Irad** handles payments from released escrow funds only once they move to exporters' accounts at other banks through the clearing house. ## Limitations Because Irad has no recognized sovereign status, the bank is not a member of the [[wp:International Monetary Fund]] or the [[wp:Bank for International Settlements]], and the ISEZ has no sovereign credit rating. The currency-board rules mean that the bank cannot act as a lender of last resort beyond its excess reserves, a constraint that analysts noted during the run of December 2006.[3] The bank has no branches in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], where trade is conducted in dollars, som, barter and livestock, and herders who sell to ISEZ buyers are usually paid through Talasbank. ## Criticism The World Bank and independent analysts have noted that Talasbank has not published full audited accounts since 2008 and that the ultimate owners of the holding companies that control it have not been disclosed. Opposition commentators argue that the Bank of Irad, as its supervisor, has not enforced disclosure on a bank whose shareholders investigative reports have linked to business associates of the Toktarov family. The Bank of Irad says that the banks it supervises meet the disclosure rules in force in the ISEZ.[3][11] Business groups credit it, with Talasbank, for keeping the payment system working through the crisis of 2006–2007.[10] The populist commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]] has called for cryptocurrency to be made legal tender alongside the dollar and the som. The bank's 2023 annual report restates that only the dollar and the som are legal tender in the ISEZ.[1] ## See also - [[Economy of Irad]] - [[Iradi som]] - [[Talasbank]] - [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]] ## References

{{Infobox pipeline | name = Northern Export Feeder | native_name = Tündük eksport tütügü | type = Crude oil | country = Irad, [[wp:Kazakhstan]] | from = [[NurGaz]] tank farm, [[Nurzhan]] | to = [[wp:KazTransOil]] network near [[wp:Shymkent]] | length_km = 85 | diameter = 530 mm (20 in) | capacity = About 100,000 bbl/d (since 2012) | owner = [[Iradi Petroleum Transit Consortium]] | operator = [[Iradi Petroleum Transit Consortium]] | commissioned = November 2000 }} The **Northern Export Feeder** (Iradi: *Tündük eksport tütügü*) is an 85-kilometer crude oil pipeline that carries oil from the fields of the lower Chu basin around [[Nurzhan]] into the network of the Kazakh pipeline operator [[wp:KazTransOil]] near [[wp:Shymkent]]. It is owned and operated by the [[Iradi Petroleum Transit Consortium]] (IPTC), in which [[NurGaz]] holds 51 percent. It entered commercial service in November 2000, replacing the rail tank-car shipments to the Shymkent refinery on which Iradi oil exports had depended since the early 1990s. It is Irad's only export pipeline, and most Iradi crude oil leaves the territory through it.[1][2] Apart from its last nine kilometers or so, which cross tribal land to the metering station on the frontier, the feeder lies within the Chu District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It does not connect with the [[wp:Caspian Pipeline Consortium]], whose system begins far to the west, and Irad has no southern export pipeline. Because [[wp:Kazakhstan]] claims Irad *de jure* and does not recognize the ISEZ, the line operates under commercial contracts and a technical annex to the 2008 [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]] rather than under an interstate agreement (see [[Irad–Kazakhstan relations]]).[3] ## Background Oil was discovered near Kobozev, now Nurzhan, in 1949 (see [[Nurzhan Oil Discovery (1949)]]). In the Soviet period crude from the Chu fields was refined at the city's refinery, now the [[Nurzhan Oil Refinery]], or sent by rail to other refineries of [[wp:Soviet Central Asia]]. The [[Nurzhan Petroleum Pipeline]], a trunk line of about 90 kilometers from the main field collection station to the refinery and tank farm, was laid in the mid-1950s, but the fields were never linked to the Soviet trunk pipeline system.[4] After 1992 the territorial administration and NurGaz, privatized in 1993, shipped crude that the Nurzhan refinery did not take west to Shymkent in rail tank cars, by the Chu and [[Kara-Buura]] lines. The traffic was expensive, slowed by border formalities and limited by the supply of tank cars, and in winter the waxy crude had to be heated before it could be unloaded. As production recovered from its 1996 low of about 48,000 barrels per day (bpd), NurGaz looked for a pipeline outlet into the Kazakh trunk network.[2] ## History #### Planning and construction NurGaz and foreign partners registered IPTC in [[Talas]] in 1998 as a joint-stock company. NurGaz contributed its tank farm and rights of way, and the foreign shareholders provided most of the construction finance. The route was surveyed in 1998, and the line was built in 1999–2000 by contractors working under the supervision of the territorial energy department. Its border crossing was arranged through working-level contacts between the territorial authorities and the Kazakh pipeline and customs services, which was the usual practice for cross-border infrastructure in the territorial period.[1] The feeder began commercial operation in November 2000, after which crude exports by rail largely ended. Its original capacity was about 65,000 bpd.[1] #### 2007 and after During the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007, forces loyal to [[Erlan Toktarov]] concentrated on holding Nurzhan, the oil fields and the pipeline. Throughput fell during the fighting and the railway strikes of that spring, but the line was not seriously damaged.[5] The end of the territorial administration left the border crossing without a formal basis. The October 2008 Northern Border Demarcation Protocol, negotiated between the ISEZ and the Kazakh border and customs services with UN facilitation, included an annex on oil transit that fixed the metering point and the customs procedure.[3] Because NurGaz's reported output continued to rise, IPTC added a further pumping station and a drag-reducing agent injection system in 2011–2012, which raised capacity to about 100,000 bpd.[1] ## Route and technical description The feeder is built of 530-millimeter (20-inch) steel pipe. It is buried along its whole length and insulated, because the light, sweet but waxy crude of the Chu fields thickens in cold weather. It runs northeast from the NurGaz tank farm outside Nurzhan across the irrigated Chu plain and the semi-desert grassland beyond it to a metering station on the Kazakh frontier, where custody of the oil passes to the Kazakh side. The metering station stands on tribal land beyond the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], where it is held as a guarded installation under the ceasefire arrangements.[2] From there the crude moves through the KazTransOil network to be refined at Shymkent or shipped north toward Russia. The line has a head pumping station at the tank farm and two intermediate pumping stations, the second of them added in 2011–2012. It is controlled from a dispatch room in Nurzhan through a supervisory control and data acquisition ([[wp:SCADA]]) system, with communications provided by [[Attelkom]]. Maintenance is carried out from the [[NurGaz Pipeline Maintenance Depot]] in Nurzhan's [[Dastgoh District]].[1] The pumping stations draw power from the ISEZ grid, which is supplied mainly by the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] and the downstream stations of the Naryn cascade. ## Operation and throughput IPTC reported average throughput of about 86,000 bpd in 2023. This figure is consistent with NurGaz's reported output of about 120,000 bpd, less the roughly 31,000 bpd processed at the Nurzhan Oil Refinery.[1] Independent analysts working from KazTransOil intake records and observations of gas flaring estimate deliveries at about 55,000–70,000 bpd, in line with their lower estimates of national production of 85,000–100,000 bpd. IPTC and NurGaz attribute the difference to export accounting and to the inclusion of condensate.[6] IPTC earns a transit tariff on each barrel shipped, paid by NurGaz and any other shippers, while tariffs on the Kazakh section are paid to the Kazakh operator under its terms for third-party transit. Export proceeds are paid in US dollars into escrow accounts at [[Talasbank]] supervised by the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]], which deducts the crude oil royalty set by the 1995 Hydrocarbon and Mining Code before releasing the balance.[7] Oil royalties are among the largest sources of ISEZ public revenue (see [[Economy of Irad]] and [[Energy in Irad]]). ## Ownership NurGaz holds 51 percent of IPTC. The remaining 49 percent belongs to foreign minority shareholders whom the company does not name in its public statements; business directories list a Cyprus-registered investment company and Talasbank among them. The board is chaired by [[Emil Bekzatov]], executive vice president of NurGaz and son of its president, [[Kamran Bekzatov]]. The company employs about 300 people.[7] ## Transit arrangements with Kazakhstan Deliveries into the Kazakh system are made under commercial contracts between IPTC and the Kazakh side. Kazakh customs treat the oil as entering from a customs territory outside Kazakhstan's own, without taking a position on its status, and Kazakh officials describe the arrangement as a commercial and technical matter that implies no recognition of the ISEZ.[3] A technical liaison group of the two border services reviews the oil annex once a year, with a UN official present. The arrangement has generally worked without interruption. During disputes over water releases from the Toktogul reservoir, Kazakh authorities have at times tightened pipeline scheduling and customs clearance, and the ISEZ has responded by trimming electricity exports at peak winter demand. Analysts describe these episodes as limited and carefully managed, because both sides depend on the trade (see [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]]).[5] Russo politicians in Nurzhan have cited Irad's dependence on a single northern outlet in support of closer economic integration with Kazakhstan and Russia.[8] ## Alternatives The feeder has no alternative outlet. During the territorial period a US-backed proposal for an oil pipeline south to [[wp:Pakistan]] was studied; its prospects ended after 2021, when the [[wp:Taliban]] returned to power in [[wp:Afghanistan]]. The proposed Trans-Irad Gas Pipeline of the [[wp:China National Petroleum Corporation]] would carry gas rather than oil (see [[Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals]]). Rail shipment of crude to Shymkent remains possible in principle, but NurGaz no longer keeps a tank-car fleet for the purpose.[2][6] ## See also - [[Transport in Irad]] - [[Chu River Basin]] ## References

**Sport in Irad** is dominated by equestrian games, above all *[[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]]*, a mounted team contest for a goat carcass whose national competition, the [[President's Cup]], is the main event of the sporting year. Horse racing, mounted wrestling and eagle hunting are also widely followed.{{Citation needed|date=September 2026}} Among modern sports, football and wrestling are the most popular, followed by boxing and basketball. Traditional equestrian sport in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) is regulated by the [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]], created in 1993; in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) most competitions are organized by clan councils.[1] Irad's unresolved international status limits its participation in international sport. It has no [[wp:National Olympic Committee]] recognized by the [[wp:International Olympic Committee]] and is not a member of the main international federations, so Iradi athletes who reach the top level usually compete for other countries (see [[Political status of Irad]]).[2] ## History In the Soviet period sport in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] was run by the republican Committee for Physical Culture and Sport. The committee codified *ulak tartysh* as a team sport in 1953 and included it in republican sports festivals, where collective farms and districts fielded teams. Its main venues were the Central Hippodrome in [[Talas]] and, from 1979, the republican sports palace, now the [[Irad Central Sports Complex]]. Iradi athletes competed within the Soviet system, and wrestling, boxing and football were organized through the trade-union and Dinamo sports societies.[3] After 1992 traditional sport became a marker of national identity. In 1992 Provisional President [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] instituted the President's Cup for *ulak tartysh*, to be contested in the week of Irad Day (11 March). In 1993 an act of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] created the National Equestrian Sports Directorate, which took over the rules of the traditional games and the organization of national competition. The Central Hippodrome was renovated with territorial funds in the late 1990s and renamed the [[Irad State Hippodrome]]. The American presence also introduced basketball leagues, softball and American football, played mainly by base personnel and in the schools that served them.[1][4] Since 2007 the Directorate has operated under the ISEZ administration, and its director is appointed by the Governor. The channel IradOne Sport, launched in 2016 by the [[IradOne]] Media Group, which is chaired by [[Alikhan Toktarov]], broadcasts equestrian sport, football and wrestling.[5] ## Equestrian sports *Main article: [[Iradi Equestrian Culture & Breeds]]* #### Ulak tartysh and the President's Cup *Ulak tartysh* is played in two forms: a regulated game of two teams of twelve registered players, four of them mounted at a time, on a field of 300 by 150 meters with a raised goal (*[[Tai-Kazan|tai-kazan]]*) at each end; and an older free-for-all form with no teams, played at weddings and feasts in the tribal regions. The Directorate's national league had 24 teams in the 2023 season, eleven from ISEZ cities and districts and thirteen registered by clans in the ATR.[6] The President's Cup is the national championship. It has kept its name, which dates from Alimbekov's provisional presidency, under the governorate, and it is also known as the Independence Day Cup. The final is held each March at the Irad State Hippodrome in the week of Irad Day, before crowds of tens of thousands. Winners receive cash prizes and, by tradition, a horse. IradOne holds the broadcasting rights.[6] Since 2009 the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] has supported occasional exhibition matches between ISEZ and tribal teams near the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] as confidence-building events.[7] #### Horse racing The Irad State Hippodrome in Talas, which seats about 25,000, is the main racecourse. It has dirt tracks for thoroughbred and [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] flat racing, a field for *ulak tartysh*, stabling and a veterinary clinic, and it is the headquarters of the Directorate. Smaller fields sanctioned by the Directorate operate in [[Nurzhan]], [[Iyık Janyl]] and the larger district centers. Long-distance racing over open country, *[[At Chabysh (Racing)|at chabysh]]*, is run over 20 to 50 kilometers at weddings, memorial feasts and festivals; under Directorate rules riders must be at least twelve years old, and horses are checked by veterinarians at the finish. [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses dominate mountain courses, and the endurance races of the August Kurultai on the [[Aksay Plateau]] are the main mountain event.[8] #### Other horseback games and eagle hunting Other sanctioned disciplines include mounted wrestling (*[[Oodarysh (Mounted Wrestling)|oodarysh]]*), the courtship chase *kyz kuu* and coin-picking at the gallop (*[[Tyin Emmei (Mounted Sport)|tyin emmei]]*), which are usually staged at national holidays. Contests in hunting with golden eagles ([[Burkut Saluu|burkut saluu]]) are held at the autumn Salburun festival outside Talas, first organized as a national festival in 1995. Judges in these events assess style as well as results, according to the ideal of *[[Körktüülük|körktüülük]]*.[1] ## Wrestling and combat sports Wrestling is the most successful Iradi sport at international level. Freestyle and Greco-Roman wrestling were developed in the Soviet period, and the national championships are held at the Irad Central Sports Complex in Talas, a 6,500-seat arena renovated in 2009. Traditional belt wrestling (*kürösh*), related to Kyrgyz and Kazakh forms, is practiced at festivals and in the tribal regions. Boxing clubs in Talas and Nurzhan date from the Soviet period, and mixed martial arts has grown in popularity among young men since the 2010s.[4] ## Football Football is the most popular team sport in the cities (see [[Football in Irad]]). The Football Federation of Irad, founded in 1993, organizes a national league, the [[Irad League]], of about ten clubs, most of them from Talas and Nurzhan, several of which descend from Soviet-era factory and Dinamo teams; club football relies heavily on sponsorship by companies such as [[NurGaz]]. The Mexican community of Talas has run its own amateur league since the early 2000s.[9] The federation is not a member of [[wp:FIFA]] or of the [[wp:Asian Football Confederation]], and its national team cannot play official internationals. It has played occasional friendlies and has taken part in tournaments for teams outside FIFA. Some Iradi players have joined clubs in [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and elsewhere.[9] ## International participation *Main article: [[Irad and the Olympic movement]]* The Irad Olympic Committee was formed in 1993, during the territorial period, but its application was not accepted by the International Olympic Committee, which since 1996 has admitted only committees of states recognized by the international community. According to the committee, Iradi athletes who wish to compete at the [[wp:Olympic Games]] or world championships do so for other countries. Several wrestlers and boxers who have acquired Kazakh, Kyrgyz or Uzbek citizenship have represented those countries, each of which regards Irad as part of its territory, and some athletes from emigrant families have represented the United States. Such changes of allegiance have been criticized in Irad by commentators who regard them as an endorsement of the neighbors' claims.[2][10] The same claims affect equestrian sport. Directorate teams have not been admitted as a national team to regional events such as the [[wp:World Nomad Games]], although individual Iradi riders have competed in invitational races and endurance events abroad.[8] ## Sport in the tribal regions In the ATR, sport is organized mainly by clans and is closely tied to festivals, weddings and memorial feasts. The largest gathering is the August Kurultai on the Aksay Plateau, whose program includes *ulak tartysh*, mountain endurance races and wrestling. Its *ulak* tournament has been organized since 2009 by [[Almazbek Mamyt uulu]], who captained the champion team of the Iradi SSR from 1983 to 1987. Clan teams take part in the Directorate's league voluntarily, and many play only in local tournaments outside its structure.[7][11] ## Criticism Animal welfare groups have criticized the rate of injuries to horses in *ulak tartysh* and long-distance racing, the use of carcasses and the employment of child jockeys. Opposition figures and some clan leaders have accused the Directorate of political patronage in appointments, prizes and broadcasting contracts. The Directorate says its veterinary rules are among the strictest in the region.[8] ## References

Clans of the Autonomous Tribal Regions

The **clans of the Autonomous Tribal Regions** (Iradi: *uruktar*) are the 24 patrilineal descent groups (*uruk*) of the rural [[Iradis]] that hold land and govern themselves in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) of Irad. They coordinate through the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC), whose principal spokesman is the Tanıp chieftain [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]]. Outside the ATR the clans are often described as a single bloc. Researchers and United Nations staff describe a looser landscape of regional groupings, allied and rival lineages, and recurring disputes over pasture, water and trade.[1][2] The clans vary greatly in size, from a few hundred households to clans that field more than 1,500 El-Choro riders. Precedence among them follows the oral genealogies (*[[Sanjyra (Genealogy)|sanjyra]]*), which do not always match present-day size or influence.[1] ## Groupings Iradi commentators speak loosely of a "north wing" (*tündük kanat*) and a "south wing" (*tüshtük kanat*). The terms have no formal standing, and clans move between them on particular issues.[2] #### Mountain clans of the Talas Alatau The core of the north wing is a group of mountain clans in the [[Talas Alatau]], whose summer pastures meet on the [[Aksay Plateau]]. It includes the Tanıp, the Karakoyun of the [[Kara-Koyun Valley]] and the Akjele. These clans formed the backbone of the [[Popular Front of Irad]] in 2007 and most strongly support the moratorium on open-pit mining. #### Steppe clans The clans of the Northern Steppe, led by the Boztorgoy, winter in the Moiynkum sands and on the desert margin. The Boztorgoy depend more on trade across the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] than any other clan. Outsiders usually count the three clans of the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] with them, but the Karatau clans keep apart from both wings.[3] #### Southern clans The south wing joins the Naiman and Sarybagysh of the Chatkal Highlands with the clans of the Toktogul basin and the Fergana Rim, among them the [[Kökjal]] and the Chubar. Its members are more ethnically mixed than the northern clans, and their main concerns are water, the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] and trade with [[wp:Uzbekistan]].[2] #### Cultural regions Ethnographers and UNMI staff also group the clans into six cultural regions, defined by dialect, religious practice, herding and marriage ties rather than by politics. Each region roughly matches a block of pastures, though clan lands overlap at the edges.[1][2] | Region | Clans | Pastures | Character | |---|---|---|---| | Talas Alatau | Tanıp, Karakoyun, Akjele, Jeerde, Sarala, Tarlan, Kaytkan | The north slope of the Talas Alatau, the Aksay Plateau, the Kyrgyz Range pastures east of the Kök-Bel road and the [[Suusamyr]] side | Standard Iradi speech and mainstream Syro-Iradi practice; the most involved in IAC politics | | Northern Steppe | Boztorgoy, Akbakay, Kumbel, Jalpak, Karajal, Sarykush | The southern [[Betpak-Dala]], the Moiynkum, the Chu–Sarysu lowland and the piedmont plain | Long migrations, cattle and sheep; insular, with little interest in IAC affairs | | Karatau | Kulan, Arkar, Jeyren | The Karatau range, the [[Kulan-Talaa]] plain, the [[Kyzyl-Jar]] badlands and the [[Kök-Moinok]] canyons | A distinct folk religion and the most archaic speech; most members do not call themselves Iradis | | Chatkal | Naiman, Sarybagysh | The Chatkal valley and range, Sary-Chelek and the walnut forests | Strongly churchly highland culture; divided by a feud since the 1930s | | Toktogul–Naryn | Kökjal, Ak-Kuu, Kök-Ala | The mountains around the Toktogul basin and east of the Naryn gorge | The most devout region, shaped by the flooding of the 1970s | | Fergana Rim | Chubar, Saryjal, Kara-Bel | The Fergana side of the Fergana Range: [[Arslanbob]], [[Jangak-Bulak]], [[Örüktü]], [[Mailuu-Suu]] | Bilingual with Uzbek; the largest Muslim minority and the most religious friction | The smallest clan, the Kaytkan ("the returned"), was refounded in the Keñ-Suu valley between 1918 and 1921 by families who came back from the flight to China in 1916 (see [[Urkun: The Lost Tribes of 1916]]).[1] #### The Karatau clans The Kulan, Arkar and Jeyren call themselves the *Eski El* ("the old people") and say they lived in the Karatau before the Iradis arrived. Other Iradis call them *Karataulyk* and regard them as strange. Their religion keeps the cross and the White Rider of Iradi folk Christianity (see [[Religion in Irad]]) but has no churches or priests. Its rites, held at night in caves and ruined caravanserais such as [[Rabat-i Kamal]], center on spirit possession by the Rider and the saints and are led by specialists called *ak bakshy* ("white shamans"); they also sacrifice white lambs at springs, which other Iradis reject as pagan. The Syro-Iradi hierarchy describes the practices as superstition but rarely intervenes. Observers have compared the relationship to that between [[wp:Haitian Vodou|Haitian Vodou]] and Catholicism.[1] ## Leading clans - **Tanıp.** The most politically prominent clan. Its pastures are the upper Kara-Suu valley, and its center, with the [[Kara-Suu Tribal Elders Council Hall]], is at the head of the Uzun-Akmat valley over the Sarybie Pass; the clan calls its whole country Kara-Suu. Its *biy* is Bektur Zhumabek uulu, acclaimed in 2001, who traces his descent from [[Muratbek Tanıp-Biy]]. - **Karakoyun.** One of the largest clans. Its genealogy places its founder as the eldest son of the clans' common ancestor, so it holds the senior seat at the [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|Kurultai]] although it is less prominent than the Tanıp. Its elder [[Biybolot Moldosh uulu]] is a long-serving mediator.[1] - **Akjele** ("white tether line"). A mountain clan of the upper Besh-Tash valley and the Tanıp's closest ally. Bektur's mother, Zuura Tashtan kyzy, came from the Akjele. The two clans share summer camps on the plateau. - **Boztorgoy** ("gray lark"). The leading steppe clan, holding winter pastures in the Moiynkum and grazing along the northern sector of the line facing [[Nurzhan]]. It keeps more cattle than the mountain clans and sells feeder cattle and lambs to the feedlots and feed mills of the Chu plain. Its *biy* since 2012, [[Sabyrbek Duishön uulu]] (born 1966), commanded steppe detachments of the Front in 2007. His elder brother, [[Kudaibergen Duishön uulu]], led the riders of the Chu clans who fought for the Provisional Government in 1992 and was killed at the Kobozev railhead; he is remembered as a national hero, and his memory gives Sabyrbek standing beyond the steppe.[3] - **Kökjal** ("gray mane", an epithet of the wolf). A clan of the Toktogul basin, many of whose families were resettled when the reservoir flooded the valley in the 1970s. Its elder Tabaldy Sultanaly uulu (born 1949), of [[Ozgörüsh]], speaks for the flooded-pasture claims. - **Chubar** ("dappled", a horse color). The main Iradi clan of the Fergana Rim, divided by the Qara-Chik Demarcation Line since 2007. The highland Chubar of Arslanbob, the upper Kara-Unkur valley and Mailuu-Suu remain with the clans; their *biy*, Döölötbek Ashym uulu (born 1957), holds the clan's seat in the Kurultai, and the clan meets on the meadow below the shrine of Arslanbob-Ata. The lowland Chubar of [[Bazar-Korgon]] and the farm belt below the hills have been in the ISEZ since August 2007, when their elders, led by the walnut trader Abdumalik Mamadaliev, declared for the side that had stopped the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]], which would have handed the rim to Uzbekistan; the highland elders refused to follow. Generations of marriage with Uzbek and Kyrgyz neighbors have given the clan Muslim lineages, especially in the lowlands. By Chancellery estimates, about a third of its households are Muslim. The *biy* is a Christian, but Muslim elders sit on his council. Mosques in the highland villages are run by local imams under the council's authority (see [[Islam in Irad]]).[4] ## Rivalries #### Trade permits The sharpest rivalry is between the Tanıp and the Boztorgoy over trade with the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). Clan councils issue the tribal travel permits that the Gendarmerie registers at the crossings. The [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]] divides the seasonal bulk contracts among the clans. Until 2019 the Boztorgoy, whose pastures lie closest to the northern crossings, held a share of both that other clans considered out of proportion. In August 2019 the Kurultai adopted a quota roll that shares contract volumes by herd numbers reported to the Chancellery. The Boztorgoy "stood aside" rather than block it.[3][5] ISEZ business circles regard Sabyrbek as a pragmatic partner, and mountain elders mock the Boztorgoy as the "cattle clan". Sabyrbek has said in public that his clan supports the IAC and its moratorium. Boztorgoy elders have also said they would consider surveys of the [[Muyunkum Natural Gas Field]] on royalty terms.[3] #### The Chatkal feud The Naiman and Sarybagysh share the Chatkal valley and its culture but have been divided by a feud since the early Soviet period. In 1916 most Sarybagysh fled over the passes to China while most Naiman stayed; the returning Sarybagysh found Naiman herds on their pastures. In 1930–31 a Naiman elder became chairman of the collective farm that absorbed both clans, and a Sarybagysh elder's son was killed in a quarrel over the farm's pastures. The Sarybagysh refused the customary restitution (*kun*), and the killing was never settled under *adat*. The two clans keep separate summer camps, rarely intermarry, dispute a boundary through the walnut forest and fielded separate El-Choro detachments in 2007. They are seated apart at the Kurultai and act together mainly against outsiders.[1] #### Water The south wing is itself divided over the Toktogul reservoir. The Kökjal press for compensation for flooded pasture before the IAC agrees to drawdown. The Chubar on both sides of the line and other Fergana Rim clans need summer releases for their cotton and orchards, and on this point they side with the Uzbek observers on the joint technical commission. The dispute came to a head in the long Kurultai of 2022 (see [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]]).[2] #### Pasture Pasture disputes go to the [[Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal]]. Recurring cases include the autumn corridors of Boztorgoy flocks across Karakoyun and Tanıp land, and crowded camps on the Aksay Plateau.[6] #### Religion The division of the Chubar is a lasting source of tension. Lowland elders still attend the August Kurultai within the Chubar delegation, by the *biy*'s leave, but may not lay the whip, and northern elders, who call them the "bazaar Chubar", ask whose interests they speak for; the Gendarmerie in turn questions their journeys to the Aksay Plateau. Families on the two sides cross the line for weddings and funerals at the Mailuu-Suu and Arslanbob road crossings, and walnuts and apricots from the highland villages come down the valleys to the Bazar-Korgon bazaar, where highland growers accuse lowland buyers of fixing prices. Some northern elders also object to Muslim Chubar aksakals joining the Kurultai's opening prayers. After the Gendarmerie commander [[Ruslan Toktarov]] described Fergana Rim Muslims as "guests" in December 2024, Chubar elders on both sides of the line joined the Sunni clerics who condemned the remark. The August 2025 Kurultai said that the clans "know no guests among their own".[4] ## Succession to Bektur Bektur turned 58 in August 2026. No rule settles who would follow him, and he has declined to discuss the matter in public. Observers separate two questions.[7] - **The Tanıp chieftaincy.** A Tanıp clan assembly would acclaim the next *biy*, as it did in 2001. Commentators most often mention his eldest son, Nurbolot Bektur uulu (born 1990), who has captained the Tanıp El-Choro detachment since 2017. Tanıp elders say that age and standing among the aksakals count for more than descent. - **The IAC's spokesmanship.** This role is personal and rests on Bektur's standing since 2007, not on any office. Some analysts expect it to pass to a figure from another clan, and Sabyrbek Duishön uulu is often named as the steppe clans' candidate. Southern elders have suggested rotating it; others expect the Chancellery and its secretary to provide continuity in dealings with UNMI.[7][8] ## See also - [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)]] - [[Adat Law in the ATR]] - [[El-Choro Militias]] - [[Sanjyra (Genealogy)]] ## References

The **Kurultai** (Iradi: *Kurultai*, also *Chong Kurultai*, "great assembly") is the pan-clan assembly of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC) and the highest forum of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) of Irad. Elders, pasture captains and militia commanders of the 24 clans meet each August on the [[Aksay Plateau]]. There they decide common defense, migration corridors, the moratorium on mining and relations with the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and the United Nations. It has no written rules. Its procedure follows custom recorded by the [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]], and it decides by consensus rather than by vote.[1][2] Iradi historians trace the assembly to the joint councils of clans formed after the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|1916 revolt]]. The present Kurultai dates from the session of late 2007 that turned the political council of the [[Popular Front of Irad]] into the IAC.[1] ## Membership Each clan sends a delegation led by its *biy* or senior aksakal. Delegations usually include several elders (*[[Aksakal (Social Term)|aksakals]]*), the clan's pasture captain and the captain (*choro bashı*) of its [[El-Choro Militias|El-Choro]] detachment. The seven judges of the [[Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal]] attend, and so does [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], who speaks for the Tanıp and acts as the IAC's spokesman. The inner assembly numbers about 250 to 300 people. Several thousand herders camp around the grounds for the horse races and the *[[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak]]* tournament.[2] Women are not delegates. Since 2021 a women's council meeting alongside the Kurultai may send written petitions, which the Chancellery's secretary reads to the assembly. [[Klara Zhumabek kyzy]] has argued for women's full participation. [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] has criticized the absence of elections and of women from the assembly.[3] ## Procedure #### Venue and seating Ordinary sessions meet in the second or third week of August in a ring of white felt yurts at the Kurultai grounds on the plateau. The central assembly yurt is joined to awnings so that the whole body can sit together. Clans sit by seniority under the *sanjyra*. The place of honor (*tör*), opposite the entrance, belongs to the Karakoyun, whose founder the genealogies name as the eldest son of the common ancestor. The other clans sit outward from it in fixed order, and the Chancellery keeps the seating roll.[1] Extraordinary sessions (*kezeksiz kurultai*) may be called in winter. They usually meet at the [[Kara-Suu Tribal Elders Council Hall]] or in the [[Kara-Koyun Valley]]. #### Opening and blessing The session opens with a *[[Bata (Culture)|bata]]* from the eldest aksakal present, a role [[Biybolot Moldosh uulu]] of the Karakoyun has filled since 2015. A Syro-Iradi priest then prays in Iradi and censes the yurt with juniper smoke (*[[Mountain Juniper (Arsha)|arsha]]*). Kymyz is shared, but no animal is killed, in keeping with the rejection of blood sacrifice in Iradi custom.[4] #### Speaking order Business is put by the Chancellery's secretary. The clans then speak in reverse order of seniority, starting with the most junior delegation, so that juniors are not swayed by their elders. The Karakoyun speak last. The presiding Karakoyun elder then states the "sense of the assembly", and Bektur reports it to outsiders. Speeches are in Iradi and are often long. Proverbs and precedents, such as [[Muratbek Tanıp-Biy]]'s Kara-Suu settlement, carry weight.[2] #### Consensus A decision passes when no *biy* objects. A *biy* who cannot accept a proposal lays his whip (*kamchy*) on the felt in front of him, which stops the matter. He may instead "stand aside" (*chetke turuu*). The decision then passes, but his clan is excused from those of its terms that concern its own land. Decisions are sealed with a bata. The secretary writes them into the Kurultai ledger (*kurultai depteri*), and couriers carry them to clans whose delegates were absent.[1] ## The Chancellery's role The Chancellery convenes ordinary and extraordinary sessions, sends the summonses by mounted courier and satellite telephone, and prepares the agenda. It drafts papers on trade contracts, the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]] and UN matters, and turns decisions into letters to the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]]. Since 2016 its secretary (*katchı*) has been [[Kubanychbek Toktobolot uulu]], a co-founder of the banned [[Jer-Suu Party]]. The secretary has no vote and does not speak to the substance of a matter.[5] ## Notable sessions - **2007.** An extraordinary session on the plateau constituted the IAC, turned the Front's units into the El-Choro and created the Chancellery and the grazing tribunal. - **2009.** The August session approved the protocol on the Toktogul basin and the State Route 1 corridor, which gave up the dam and the basin floor in exchange for the high Kyrgyz Range pastures, grazing and water rights and a guaranteed share of the dam's revenue. The [[Kökjal]] stood aside. - **2011.** The August session approved the walkout of Bektur's delegation from the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]] and kept its demand for representation in proportion to population. - **2017.** The session refused to admit DPI enumerators for the [[2018 Irad census]] to clan territories. - **2019.** The assembly adopted a quota roll for trade contracts. The Boztorgoy stood aside rather than lay down the whip (see [[Clans of the Autonomous Tribal Regions]]).[6] - **2025.** The session condemned remarks by the Gendarmerie commander about Fergana Rim Muslims. It also instructed the IAC delegation for the 2027 renewal of the Naryn Protocol, echoing Bektur's statement that the IAC would "not negotiate with a recording".[7] #### The long Kurultai of 2022 The best-known deadlock came in August 2022, during the renewal of the Naryn Protocol's five-year schedule. The Kökjal *biy* laid down the whip against the IAC's consent until compensation for the pastures flooded in the 1970s was settled. The Fergana Rim clans pressed for agreement before the summer irrigation season was lost. The assembly sat for nineteen days, the longest session on record.[8] The deadlock was broken by three elders chosen from clans with no stake in the reservoir, led by Biybolot Moldosh uulu. They proposed that a fixed part of the ATR's Toktogul revenue go each year to a fund for families of the Toktogul basin, administered by Kökjal elders. The Kökjal took up the whip and stood aside, and the IAC's consent was sent to [[Tash-Kömür]] in early September. Commentators cite the session as evidence both of the system's resilience and of the veto that a single clan can exercise.[9] ## See also - [[Clans of the Autonomous Tribal Regions]] - [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]] - [[Aksay Plateau]] - [[Adat Law in the ATR]] ## References

**Smuggling across the Qara-Chik Line** (Iradi: *Qara-Chik arqyly kontrabanda*) is the unlicensed movement of goods, livestock and horses between the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) outside the nine checkpoints and the permit rules of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], together with the onward traffic across the ATR-held sections of the Kazakh, Uzbek and Kyrgyz frontiers. Fuel moves into the tribal regions, and ore, gold and animals move out. The ISEZ treats the trade as crime. The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC) describes most of it as the movement of supplies within its own territory.[1][2] There are no reliable estimates of its size. The [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) and economists at [[Talas State University]] treat it as a large part of the ATR's cash economy.[3] ## Background The line has no customs duties, but the ISEZ charges inspection and permit fees. ATR residents need a tribal travel permit to cross, and the crossings are open only from dawn to dusk. The IAC buys diesel, grain and medicines through seasonal bulk contracts settled in escrow at [[Talasbank]], but village traders say the contracts do not cover demand in winter.[2] The ISEZ also controls Irad's only refinery, the [[Nurzhan Oil Refinery]], so the tribal regions depend on it for refined fuel. Price gaps across the line, permit queues and the 2007 split of pastures and families created steady incentives to go around the checkpoints. ## Goods - **Fuel.** Diesel and petrol are the largest flow. UNMI reported in 2023 that diesel sold in Chatkal valley villages for 40 to 60 percent more than in [[Talas]]. Fuel moves in jerrycans on pack horses, in drums through disused galleries of the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]], and in tanker trucks passed through checkpoints with false manifests. Some is sold on into Kyrgyz and Uzbek border districts.[3] - **Cigarettes.** Cigarettes imported duty-free into the [[Talas Free Economic Trade Zone]] for re-export are diverted into the ISEZ market, the ATR and [[wp:Kazakhstan]], where they would pay the external tariff of the Eurasian customs union.[4] - **Antimony ore.** Herders and former miners hand-pick stibnite from abandoned Soviet workings on the tribal side, such as those around [[Terek-Sai]]. The clans' moratorium covers open-pit mining, and small adits fall into a gray zone. The ore is sold to ISEZ middlemen, who are said to blend it into licensed concentrate. The trade grew sharply after [[wp:China|China's]] export controls of 2024 doubled prices outside China.[5] - **Placer gold.** Gold panned in the Chatkal basin is sold outside the licensed buyers required by the [[Chatkal Placer Mining Inspectorate]]. Much of it goes to jewelers in southern Kazakhstan and the [[wp:Fergana Valley]].[6] - **Pedigree horses.** Unregistered [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] stallions are sold without papers across the Kazakh frontier, and some [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] owners send horses overland to avoid the fees of the [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]].[7] - **Livestock.** Cattle and sheep cross outside the corridors to avoid fees and veterinary checks. ISEZ veterinary officials link the traffic to outbreaks of foot-and-mouth disease and brucellosis.[3] - **Medicines.** Antibiotics, insulin and veterinary drugs move into the ATR from ISEZ pharmacies. Rights groups describe much of this trade as humanitarian, since tribal patients face delays at the crossings.[8] ## Routes Most of the trade uses three kinds of route.[1][3] - **Mountain trails.** Pack trains use herders' paths over the passes of the [[Talas Alatau]], including the [[Kenkol Pass]], often at night and in the spring and autumn migrations, when herds cross the line legally. - **The checkpoints.** Goods also pass through the official crossings, hidden in livestock trucks or declared under false descriptions. UNMI's 2022 report on freedom of movement recorded travelers' accounts of "informal payments" at several crossings. - **The open frontier.** The ATR holds long sections of the Kazakh frontier in the Northern Steppe and the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]], which the 2008 [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]] does not cover. Goods also move across the [[Kyzylkum Fringe]] into [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and through the Sunday livestock market at [[Bazar-Korgon]], an ISEZ border town since 2007 that sits a few kilometers from the Uzbek frontier and just below the tribal hills, so that its traders move goods both across the frontier and up the valley paths around the [[Mailuu-Suu]] and [[Arslanbob]] road crossings. Since 2024 trucks have also crossed the line on these roads and left Irad through the clan-held crossings into [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], bound for China (see [[Irad–Kyrgyzstan relations]]). ## Who profits - **Clan traders.** Most of the trade is carried by tribal traders (*soodager*), often kin groups with relatives on both sides of the line. Their margins depend on the price gaps.[2] - **The El-Choro.** ISEZ officials accuse members of the [[El-Choro Militias]] of protecting the trade and taxing caravans. The IAC rejects the charge. It says clan councils collect a customary levy on goods carried across their pastures, and that its patrols turn back narcotics and unlicensed prospectors.[9] - **ISEZ officials.** Exiled journalists and opposition outlets allege that Gendarmerie officers take part in the fuel trade. In 2019 the Steppe Investigative Network reported that companies linked to Major General [[Ruslan Toktarov]] held diesel supply contracts at [[Talas Air Base]]. Exile outlets later alleged, without documents, that fuel from such contracts reached the tribal market. Ruslan Toktarov has denied any improper interest, and no inquiry has been opened.[10] In June 2024 the *[[Irad Times]]*, citing truck drivers and two former Gendarmerie officers, reported that some post commanders on the line take a cut of the diesel loads they let through into the ATR; the Gendarmerie called the report "slander".[11] FreeIrad.org goes further and claims, without evidence, that Gendarmerie commanders control the diesel trade (see [[FreeIrad.org]]). ## Payments Smugglers are paid in dollars, som, livestock and goods. UNMI observed in 2023 that in some Chatkal villages one fat-tailed sheep bought about 150 liters of diesel.[3] Middlemen also use Talasbank accounts and the SMS payment service run by the bank and [[Attelkom]], which herders use to receive payment for wool and lambs. ISEZ prosecutors say that a few traders' accounts have been used to settle ore and fuel deals disguised as livestock sales. The bank says it applies the reporting rules of the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]].[12] ## Enforcement The [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] is responsible for the line, and its Highway Patrol Corps escorts fuel and antimony convoys. Notable measures and cases include: - **Sealing the galleries (2016).** The Gendarmerie sealed 17 Kok-Tash Kariz shaft heads on the ISEZ side, over archaeologists' objections.[1] - **Northern corridors (2015–2017).** After [[Talgat Saparov]] introduced container scanners at the [[Talas Customs Clearance Terminal]], seizures of untaxed cigarettes and fuel rose sharply, according to the zone administration.[4] - **The Qara-Chik bribery trial (2023).** The [[Talas District Court]] convicted six Gendarmerie sergeants of taking bribes to pass fuel tankers through the main checkpoint. The Gendarmerie cited the case as evidence of internal discipline. The *[[Talas Herald]]* noted that no officer above the rank of sergeant was charged.[13] - **The "fluorite" seizure (2025).** Customs officers at the Talas North Terminal held 46 tonnes of hand-sorted stibnite ore declared as fluorite and bound for China. The exporter, a small Talas trading firm, was fined.[5] ## See also - [[Crime in Irad]] - [[Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint]] - [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]] - [[Antimony Mining in Irad]] - [[Irad–Kazakhstan relations]] - [[Irad–Kyrgyzstan relations]] ## References
