**Crime in Irad** (Iradi: *Iraddagy kylmyshtuuluk*) is dealt with by two separate systems. In the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), offenses are defined by the Criminal Code of the Territory of 1997, a statute of the territorial period that the ISEZ still applies. They are investigated by the police and the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] and tried in the statutory courts. In the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), clan elders settle offenses under customary law (*adat*), mainly by compensation.[1][2] Official statistics cover only the ISEZ and are disputed. The main reported problems are theft, including of livestock and horses, smuggling across the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], small-scale drug trafficking and corruption.[3] ## Legal framework The Criminal Code of the Territory was passed by the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] in 1997. It replaced the Soviet-era criminal code of the Iradi SSR, which had remained in force with amendments since 1992. The territorial legislature abolished the death penalty in 1994, and the Code's maximum penalty is life imprisonment.[1] Since 2007 it has been amended by the *[[Mejlis]]* and by executive decree. Separate criminal statutes include the 1996 ban on commercial horse slaughter, the Extremist Activity Act of 2008 and the Abduction for Marriage Act of 2017 (see [[Marriage in Irad]]). Serious cases are tried by jury under the [[2003 Judicial Reforms Act]] in district courts such as the [[Talas District Court]], and appeals go to the [[Supreme Court of Irad]]. The Attorney General prosecutes. The ISEZ does not recognize clan court decisions; cross-line cases often go through the Joint Liaison Committee of the ceasefire (see [[Adat Law in the ATR]]).[2] ## Policing *Main article: [[Law enforcement in Irad]]* Policing in the ISEZ is divided between several bodies.[4] - **Municipal police.** The city forces of [[Talas]], [[Nurzhan]] and [[Iyık Janyl]] handle most ordinary crime. - **District police.** Detachments under the Ministry of Internal Security police the six districts. - **The Gendarmerie.** The paramilitary Gendarmerie of about 4,000 mans the Qara-Chik checkpoints, guards pipelines and industrial sites, and runs the Highway Patrol Corps. Officers of all three train at the [[Talas Gendarmerie Academy]]. Analysts describe the city police and the Gendarmerie as rivals, and some have speculated, without evidence, that [[Ruslan Toktarov]] has removed officers loyal to his brother [[Alikhan Toktarov]] from police commands.[5] In the ATR, clan-appointed constables enforce elders' decisions. ## Organized crime *Main article: [[Organized crime in Irad]]* In the 1990s, racketeering groups in Nurzhan and Talas fought over bazaars, fuel distribution and car imports. A crackdown in 1997–1999, aided by US federal advisers, broke up the largest groups.[6] Analysts say organized crime has since become less visible and more tied to official patronage. Its main markets are cross-line smuggling (see [[Smuggling across the Qara-Chik Line]]), car theft for resale in [[wp:Kazakhstan]], and online fraud. ## Narcotics *Main article: [[Drug use in Irad]]* [[wp:United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime|UNODC]] regional assessments describe Irad as a minor branch of the "northern route" by which Afghan opiates reach Russia through [[wp:Central Asia]]. Small consignments are thought to enter the ATR from [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] and the Fergana Rim and cross the steppe into Kazakhstan. ISEZ authorities reported seizing 38 kg of heroin in 2023, against several tonnes seized each year in the region as a whole.[7] Wild cannabis from the lower Chu valley accounts for most drug arrests. Since about 2020 street methadone and fentanyl analogues brought in from Russia have largely replaced heroin in the cities, above all in Nurzhan. The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC) says its patrols turn back drug couriers. ## Horse theft Horse theft is regarded as one of the gravest offenses in Irad. Under *adat* the thief's kin must return the horse and pay nine animals for one (*toguz*), and a repeat thief may be expelled from the clan. Theft for slaughter is worse still, given the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]].[2] In the ISEZ, a 2009 amendment to the Criminal Code made horse theft an aggravated offense, punishable by three to ten years in prison. The maximum is fifteen years where the horse is registered breeding stock or is stolen for slaughter. Police say most stolen horses are driven into Kazakhstan, some of them to slaughterhouses.[8] #### The Kyzyl-Jyldyz pedigree fraud In March 2022 a US buyer's retest showed that a palomino [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] colt did not match its registered sire. The [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]] found that Kanat Ormonbekov, owner of the private Kyzyl-Jyldyz stud near Talas, had submitted samples from other horses for 14 foals registered between 2017 and 2021. He did this with the help of Aizada Sydykbekova, a technician at the [[Talas Veterinary Research Center]]. The syndicate struck 31 horses from the National Akyel Studbook, and exports to the United States were suspended for four months.[9] In June 2023 the Talas District Court convicted Ormonbekov of fraud and forgery of veterinary documents. He was sentenced to four years in prison, reduced to three on appeal. Sydykbekova received a two-year suspended sentence. Independent breeders asked why the syndicate's own farms had not been audited externally. Managing director [[Mirlan Toktarov]] said an internal review had found nothing wrong, and in 2023 the syndicate moved its parentage testing to a foreign laboratory.[9][10] ## Corruption *Main article: [[Corruption in Irad]]* As an unrecognized territory, Irad is not covered by international corruption indices. Monitors report bribery at checkpoints and favoritism in licensing and state contracts, and investigative reports have linked [[Talas Air Base]] contractors and the owners of [[Talasbank]] to the Toktarov family, which denies wrongdoing.[3] A Public Integrity Commission set up in the Governor's office in 2014 has brought cases mainly against junior officials, and critics say it has never investigated a senior DPI figure.[11] FreeIrad.org publishes more sweeping claims about the family. They are unverified (see [[FreeIrad.org]]). ## Prisons *Main article: [[Prisons in Irad]]* The Corrections Directorate of the Ministry of Internal Security runs the ISEZ's prisons. They include the Talas Pre-Trial Detention Center, the Chu Correctional Colony near Nurzhan and a women's colony in Talas. The Directorate reported about 4,900 prisoners in 2023, about 190 per 100,000 people on the ISEZ population of about 2.63 million. About a third were awaiting trial.[4] The Legal Defense Guild of [[Gulnara Sadyk]] and [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] report overcrowding and forced confessions, which the ministry denies.[12] The ATR has no prisons. ## Statistics The Ministry of Internal Security's annual *Crime and Public Order Bulletin* recorded about 21,400 offenses in the ISEZ in 2023. Theft made up 46 percent, and there were 74 homicides, a rate of about 2.8 per 100,000. Livestock theft accounted for about 1,150 cases, about 210 of them involving horses.[4] Researchers caution that:[3] - the figures exclude the ATR, for which no statistics exist; - rates depend on a population figure that independent demographers dispute; - the bulletin is unaudited, and police may under-record crime; - victims of domestic violence and bride kidnapping rarely report to the police. ## See also - [[Smuggling across the Qara-Chik Line]] - [[Organized crime in Irad]] - [[Human rights in Irad]] - [[Adat Law in the ATR]] - [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] ## References

{{Infobox newspaper | name = Talas Herald | type = Daily newspaper (Monday to Saturday) | owner = Herald Publishing Company | publisher = Herald Publishing Company | editor = Elmira Beishenova | founded = 1993-03 | political = Semi-independent | language = English | hq = Herald House, 8 Printers' Lane, [[Talas]] | circulation = About 34,000 weekday print copies (2023) | website = [talasherald.com](https://talasherald.com/) }} The ***Talas Herald*** (Iradi: *Talas Jarchysy*) is an English-language daily newspaper published in [[Talas]]. It is the most widely read newspaper in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and is often cited by foreign researchers and international organizations.{{Citation needed|date=September 2026}} It was founded in 1993, during the US territorial administration, by Iradi and American journalists. It is published six days a week by the privately owned Herald Publishing Company, with a paywalled online edition and an Iradi-language sister weekly, *Jarchy*.[1][2] The *Herald* is usually described as semi-independent. It reports on courts, municipal government, the economy, the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) and culture, and it has published reports on the governing family drawn from public records. Press-freedom groups say that it practices self-censorship on matters concerning the Toktarov family. Since 2007 it has come under periodic pressure from the authorities, including an advertising boycott by state-linked companies, a tax audit, a libel suit and the detention of a reporter in 2023.[3][4] ## History #### Founding (1993–2006) The paper was founded in March 1993 by Medet Orozaliev, a former correspondent of *Iradyn Chyny* who had worked under the editor [[Maratbek Sadykov]] during perestroika, and Margaret Hendricks, an American reporter who had covered [[Operation Starlight]] and the siege of Talas for a [[wp:Chicago]] newspaper. Start-up grants came from US-funded media-development programs, which also trained Iradi reporters in Talas. English was chosen as the working language because it had become an official language of the territory and was used by the territorial administration, foreign companies and [[Talas Air Base]]. Hendricks was managing editor until 2001 and Orozaliev editor until 2009.[1] During the territorial period the *Herald* reported on the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]], the export economy and the US presence. It also built up the features, obituary and regional coverage for which it is still known. Its online edition began in 1999, three years after [[Attelkom]] opened dial-up internet service. The rival *[[Irad Times]]*, founded in 1996, took a more investigative line, and in December 2006 and January 2007 it, rather than the *Herald*, published the documents behind the [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]].[2] #### Civil war (2007) The *Herald* kept publishing through the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. On 26 February 2007 it reported [[Erlan Toktarov]]'s proclamation of the special economic zone from [[Nurzhan]],[5] and the next day it published a summary of the partition drafts he had released (see [[Bill of Sale (2007)]]), together with the cabinet's denial.[6] In May it reported that Talas hospitals were full as fighting around the city tightened. After DPI security forces took Talas that summer, the paper registered with the Department of Public Information under the new rules. Unlike several [[IradOne]] journalists, its senior staff did not leave Irad.[1] #### Under the ISEZ (2007–present) Elmira Beishenova, the paper's former courts reporter, became editor in 2009. Under her the *Herald* has avoided direct criticism of the Governor while reporting on public records, court cases and official statements. Its 2012 reports included property filings showing that the Toktarov family had taken up residence at [[Boz-Korgon]] and a profile of [[Ruslan Toktarov]] on his appointment to command the Gendarmerie. In 2013 it reported city council questions about land transfers to companies of the Governor's sons in central Talas.[3][7] ## Notable reporting Stories first reported or widely followed through the *Herald* include:[3][7] - the 2013 decision by Nurzhan to replace its district-heating mains after the failures of the 2012 winter; - the 2015 removal of rival candidates from the gubernatorial ballot by the Election Commission; - the 2016 suspended sentences given to three students in Talas for handing out leaflets of the banned [[Jer-Suu Party]]; - the 2022 return of the girl group [[Karakush (Group)|Karakush]] from [[wp:South Korea]], and interviews with young directors about screening permits; - the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]], including reports that IradOne dropped videos by the duo [[tüntolk]] after its songs were sung at the marches; - Toktarov's last confirmed public appearance in early July 2024, and later reporting on the succession question (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]); - the demonstrations in Talas and Nurzhan that followed the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]. ## Pressures After the *Herald* reported on the 2015 ballot disqualifications, several state-owned and state-licensed companies withdrew their advertising for about eighteen months. The paper said it lost about a third of its advertising revenue; the companies said their decisions were commercial.[4] In 2016 the ISEZ tax service audited the Herald Publishing Company. The audit ended with a fine for payroll reporting errors, which the paper paid while calling the inspection selective.[8] In 2014 the Talas Commercial Development Group, headed by [[Adil Toktarov]], sued the paper for libel over its land-transfer reports. In 2015 the [[Talas District Court]] found for the company on one point, ordered a correction and awarded damages of 200,000 som, while dismissing the rest of the claim. Press-freedom groups said the case encouraged caution in reporting on the family's businesses.[4] During the October 2023 protests the reporter Erkin Bolot uulu was detained while photographing the dispersal of a march and held for ten days in administrative detention for "obstructing police". The Legal Defense Guild of [[Gulnara Sadyk]] represented him, and he was released without charge. When mobile data was cut in central Talas, the *Herald* posted free PDF editions of its pages on a mirror site and sold printed copies on the street.[9] ## Readership and editions The *Herald* had an average weekday print circulation of about 34,000 copies in 2023, down from about 60,000 in 2006. Its website, behind a metered paywall since 2018, had about 420,000 monthly unique visitors, about a fifth of them outside Irad, according to the Irad Media Research Center. Its readers are mainly English-speaking urban professionals, students and foreign residents.[10] *Jarchy* ("The Herald"), an Iradi-language weekly, was launched in 2017 for younger readers drawn to the [[Iradi language revival]]. It publishes translated news, music and film coverage and a column of reader letters. It has also gained some readers in herding settlements near the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], where copies are carried by bus and mounted courier.[10] ## Relations with other media IradOne rarely cites the *Herald*, although the paper publishes its schedules and reviews its programs. Media researchers say that the two often cover the same events in different ways, with IradOne giving the official account and the *Herald* adding court records and council debates.[2] The *Herald* does not report the claims of [[FreeIrad.org]], which it treats as a fringe site, and reports claims from other anonymous sources only when officials respond to them, describing them as unverified. Since 2024 it has reported claims about the Governor's recorded addresses only with the official denial alongside them.[11] ## See also - [[Media of Irad]] - [[IradOne]] - [[Human rights in Irad]] - [[Bolotbek Daniyar]] - [[List of newspapers in Irad]] ## References

**Marriage in Irad** (Iradi: *üylönüü*) combines the sacramental marriage of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] with pastoral customs shared with the Kyrgyz and [[wp:Kazakhs]], such as matchmaking, bride price and the wedding feast. Practice differs sharply across the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. In the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), marriage is a civil contract registered by the state under the Domestic Relations Act of 1996, with a minimum age of 18. In the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), it is arranged between kin groups under customary law (*[[Adat Law in the ATR|adat]]*) and blessed by itinerant priests.[1][2] Bride kidnapping (*ala kachuu*) survives in some tribal districts and in parts of the rural ISEZ. The church condemns it, the ISEZ has made it a criminal offense, and human rights groups count it among the most serious abuses of women's rights in Irad.[3] ## Betrothal and settlements Marriages in the ATR are usually arranged by the two families through go-betweens. The families become *kuda* (in-laws) to each other at a betrothal visit. Elders first check the clan genealogies (*[[Sanjyra (Genealogy)|sanjyra]]*), because *adat* forbids marriage between descendants of a common ancestor within seven generations. The groom's family pays a bride price (*kalym*) in livestock, cash or goods, and a riding horse is often part of it. The bride's family provides a dowry (*sep*) of *[[Shyrdak (Iradi Craft)|shyrdak]]* carpets, white felt, quilted mattresses (*[[Töshök|töshök]]*) and household goods. Elders record the amounts, which govern any later settlement.[2] In the cities most couples choose each other, and the *kalym* is usually a token. ## The church wedding The church rite follows the East Syriac order of the "crowning" ([[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] *burakha*, "blessing"). The priest blesses rings and wine and crowns the couple. Unconsecrated *[[Kümöch Sacramental Bread|kümöch]]* is broken and shared after the blessing.[4] In the Chatkal valley and the eastern mountains, a bride from a household that keeps the holy leaven (*malka*, *ene achytky*) brings a portion of it in a felt-wrapped pot from her mother's house. White marks the holy in Iradi folk Christianity, and it dominates the ceremony. The bride wears white, and white felt is laid at the entrance of the wedding yurt (*[[Ak-Örgoe|ak-örgoe]]*). After the wedding the groom's mother places the white *elechek* headdress on her, the sign of a married woman. Cattle are kept out of sight because of their link with [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]]: in highland and old Talas families the bride must not see a cow on her wedding day, a rule kept as strictly as the white dress. In the wider culture it is a light superstition, and city guests passing cattle on the way to a wedding may joke that the bride should close her eyes.[5] ## Feasts and horses The wedding feast (*toi*) is often the largest expense a family faces. Guests are served beshbarmak or plov, *[[Boorsok (Culinary)|boorsok]]* and *kymyz*. A sheep is slaughtered as food, not as an offering. Horses are never killed, in keeping with the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo|horsemeat taboo]]. They take part instead: the bride traditionally arrives on a white horse led by the groom's kin, and rural weddings include *[[Alaman-Bayge|alaman-bayge]]* races, *kyz kuu* and the free-for-all form of [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]].[5] Urban feasts are held in banquet halls, and many Russo couples hold only a civil registration and a banquet. ## Mixed marriages Mixed marriages are common in the cities. Unions with Russians and [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]] are frequent in [[Nurzhan]]. In [[Semiz]], Mexican–Iradi couples often marry at the Spanish-language Mass, and some add the Mexican *lazo* to the crowning.[6] A Catholic marrying an Orthodox Christian needs the bishop's permission. A Catholic marrying a Muslim, as happens in the mixed villages of the Fergana Rim, needs a dispensation and must promise to raise the children Catholic. Some such couples register only civilly. ## Divorce and separation The church does not recognize divorce. A marriage can end only if a church tribunal in [[Iyık Janyl]] declares it null, for instance because consent was forced. The ISEZ has allowed civil divorce since the territorial period. In the ATR, elders arrange a customary separation. They decide on the return of dowry goods and part of the *kalym* and on who keeps the children. Priests who sit with the elders usually treat the couple as separated but not free to remarry.[2] ## Bride kidnapping *Ala kachuu* ("to take and run") means abducting a woman to force her into marriage. Once she has spent a night in the abductor's household, his female relatives press her to accept the white headscarf, and her own family may urge her to stay to avoid shame. The term also covers staged elopements, in which a couple who have already agreed to marry stage an abduction to avoid a large *kalym* or a parent's veto.[3] #### Prevalence Reliable figures do not exist. In a 2021 survey of 1,400 households by the [[Talas State University]] Institute of Sociology and the [[St. Luka Community Health Mission]], 13 percent of married women under 50 in the surveyed parts of the [[Talas Alatau]] and [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] planning zones said that their marriage began with an abduction. About half of them said it was against their will. The figure was under 2 percent in the three ISEZ cities. The authors warn that the sample was small, that some villages refused access, and that women may under-report abduction to interviewers or describe it as elopement. Spokesmen of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC) called the survey biased.[7] #### Church and law In 2014 the [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs]] under Archbishop [[Mar Ephrem]] issued the pastoral letter *On the Free Consent of Spouses*. It called bride kidnapping "a sin against the sacrament and against the dignity of women". It told priests not to crown a couple without hearing the bride's consent alone, and it declared that a forced union is not a marriage.[4] In the ISEZ, abduction was long prosecuted under general kidnapping provisions, usually ending in a fine. In 2015 a 19-year-old woman from a village in [[Kara-Buura|Kara-Buura District]] escaped two days after her abduction and pressed charges. The Legal Defense Guild lawyer [[Gulnara Sadyk]] represented her. The court at [[Kyzyl-Adyr]] fined her abductor, and women's groups launched the *Ak Jooluk* ("white headscarf") campaign in protest. In 2017 the [[Mejlis]] passed the Abduction for Marriage Act. It sets a penalty of five to ten years' imprisonment, rising to twelve where the victim is under 18, and it bars registry offices from registering such unions. Prosecutions remain rare.[3][8] #### Customary law The clans are divided. *Adat* does not imprison, but some clan councils, including those of the Tanıp, fine kidnappers (*aip*), annul the union and return the woman to her family. Others accept abduction as legitimate if the woman later stays. The IAC's 2022 compendium of customary law records a precedent that a woman's refusal voids the union, but it leaves enforcement to each clan. [[Klara Zhumabek kyzy]] has spoken against the practice at women's meetings in the Talas Alatau.[2][9] ## See also - [[Adat Law in the ATR]] - [[Human rights in Irad]] - [[Kümöch Sacramental Bread]] - [[Iradi name]] - [[Women in Irad]] ## References

**Glacier retreat in Irad** (Iradi: *Irad möngülörünün kyskaryshy*) is the shrinking of the glaciers of the [[Talas Alatau]], [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal]] and Fergana ranges, and its effects on the rivers on which Irad's farms, cities and power stations depend. Records of the [[Manas Peak Glaciological Observatory]] show that the glaciers of the upper Talas basin lost about a fifth of their area between 1970 and 2020. Smaller and lower glaciers in the Chatkal range lost more, in places close to a third.[1][2] Glacier melt supplies a large part of late-summer flow in the [[Talas River|Talas]], the Chu and the [[Naryn River|Naryn]]. Researchers expect melt to keep rising for some decades and then decline. Water stress is made sharper by the division of the country: most glaciers and headwaters lie in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), while most irrigated land lies in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and in the downstream neighbors.[3] ## Extent of retreat The *Glacier and Snow Inventory of the Talas Basin, 2014–2018* recorded 268 glaciers in the Iradi part of the basin, most smaller than one square kilometer.[1] The observatory's two benchmark glaciers, including the [[Manas Glacier]], have had a negative mass balance in most years since the 1970s. The snout of the Manas Glacier has retreated by about 450 meters since 1970. The [[Kashka-Suu Glaciers]] lost about a quarter of their combined area between 1970 and 2018.[2] In the Chatkal range, which is wetter but lower, small cirque glaciers have shrunk fastest. Two of the five [[Besh-Köl Glaciers]] are now small patches of ice. Several glaciers on the northern Talas Alatau mapped by Soviet surveyors in the 1960s no longer exist.[2] Regional studies show similar losses across the [[wp:Tian Shan]].[4] ## Effects on rivers The [[Talas River Hydrological Monitoring Service]] records earlier spring peaks and a larger share of glacier melt in summer flow since the 1970s. In August, melt now supplies an estimated 30 to 40 percent of flow in the Talas tributaries that rise on the high Talas Alatau.[3] Researchers at [[Talas State University]] put "peak water" for the Talas basin in the 2030s or 2040s. Some small Chatkal catchments may already have passed it.[5] On the Chu, which reaches Irad through [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], glacier change is felt mostly through upstream withdrawals (see [[Chu River Basin]]). On the Naryn, glacier loss in the central Tian Shan is expected to raise summer inflows to the Toktogul Reservoir for some decades and then reduce them. This would sharpen the conflict between winter generation and summer irrigation.[6] ## Water sharing The effects of glacier loss are bound up with water-sharing arrangements that predate it: - **The Talas.** Under a Soviet rule confirmed by the [[Treaty of Good Neighborliness (1994)]], the river's flow is divided equally with the Kazakh districts downstream. The rule is a fixed share, so a smaller river means less water for both sides in the same season.[7] - **The Naryn.** Releases from the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] are set by the joint commission of the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]]. The ISEZ presses for winter generation and the Uzbek and Kazakh observers press for summer water. The framework schedule is due for renewal in 2027.[6] Inside Irad, the glaciers, the observatory and the upper gauging stations lie beyond the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. ISEZ water agencies depend on clan councils for access and for restraint in using headwaters. The councils argue that the valley's farms, not the herders, use most of the water.[3] ## Drought years of 2021 and 2023 Low snowfall and hot summers in 2021 and 2023 brought the worst shortages since 2008. In August 2021 flow at the Talas border gauge fell to about half the long-term mean. The Kazakh side complained that it was receiving less than its half. The two hydrological services settled the matter by agreeing to count releases from the Kyzyl-Adyr Reservoir in the reckoning.[7] The [[Talas Basin Agricultural Directorate]] imposed canal rotations in [[Kara-Buura|Kara-Buura District]]. Farmers' groups accused [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]] of raising feed prices, and the [[Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate]]'s quotas forced [[Zhetysu Industrial Textiles]] to cut shifts in both years.[8] In 2023 low inflows took the Toktogul Reservoir close to the commission's minimum reserve level. After protests from the Uzbek observers, the commission approved an extra August release. In return the ISEZ trimmed electricity exports in the winter of 2023–24. Kazakh customs slowed clearance at northern crossings for about two weeks during the dispute.[6][9] ## Salinization and canal losses The Chu inspectorate estimates that about a third of diverted water is lost from unlined canals. Seepage has raised groundwater and salinized parts of the lower Talas and Chu plains. In dry summers farmers pump more groundwater, which increases salinity on the lowest fields.[8] ## Glacial lake outburst floods As glaciers retreat, lakes form behind their moraines. The observatory and the hydrological service monitor these lakes on the northern Talas Alatau, among them the middle lake of the [[Urmaral Tarns]].[10] On the night of 22 July 2016, the moraine dam of Muz-Köl, a small lake at about 3,300 meters at the head of the [[Muz-Suu]], partly failed. Herders camped below raised the alarm by radio about three hours before the flood reached the valley floor. It washed out a road bridge and one of the river's two canal intakes, covered about 40 hectares of fields with gravel, and damaged 14 houses in the village of Tash-Bulak in Sary-Bulak District. No one was killed.[10][11] The event led to a 2020 hazard assessment of the range's moraine-dammed lakes and to sirens and automatic water-level sensors in the Muz-Suu and Urmaral valleys. Clan wardens maintain the sensors on the tribal side. ## Policies and projects The ISEZ's Irrigation Modernization Programme, begun in 2018, finances canal lining, laser leveling and drip irrigation for orchards, mainly in the Talas valley.[8] Executive Directive 2022/14 requires water-saving plans from large users in dry years and limits new rice paddies on the lower Chu.[12] Analysts have urged that glacier projections be built into the 2027 Naryn schedule. Because Irad is not a party to the climate convention, it had no seat at the COP17 talks in October 2026; the ISEZ Ministry of Natural Resources and the Manas Peak observatory instead sent the secretariat a written submission through a contact in Bishkek, setting out the 268-glacier inventory and making the same case.[14] Critics note that cotton and feed crops still take most of Irad's irrigation water.[9] ## Folk and religious responses In dry years herders in the ATR make offerings at mountain shrines (*mazar*) and springs, asking for rain and water (*jamgyr tilöö*). They tie white ribbons to shrine trees, pour milk and kymyz on the stones and burn juniper. No animals are sacrificed. In July 2021 and again in 2023 the [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs|Council of Hierarchs]] of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] asked parishes to add prayers for rain to the liturgy, and pilgrims came in larger numbers to springs such as [[Maryam-Bulak]].[13] ## See also - [[Geography of Irad]] - [[Agriculture in Irad]] - [[Irad–Kazakhstan relations]] - [[Irad–Uzbekistan relations]] - [[Energy in Irad]] - [[Climate of Irad]] ## References

**Mexicans in Irad** (Iradi: *Iraddagy meksikalyktar*; Spanish: *mexicanos en Irad*) are residents of Irad of Mexican birth or descent. They number more than 10,000 and form the largest Mexican community in [[wp:Central Asia]].{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}} Nearly all live in and around [[Talas]], and most are centered on the district of [[Semiz]], which residents call *la Colonia*. The community grew from the managers, technicians and workers of the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]], which opened in 1999 during the US territorial period, and of the neighboring [[Conagra Talas Beef Facility]].[1][2] Most Mexican families are Catholic and attend a Spanish-language Sunday Mass in Semiz. Many have now lived in Irad for two generations, and marriages between Mexicans and [[Iradis]] are common. Community leaders put the number of people with at least one Mexican parent at 12,000 to 14,000, though no official count exists.[3] ## History [[wp:Sukarne|SuKarne]], a meat company based in [[wp:Culiacán]], [[wp:Sinaloa]], built its complex in 1998–99 under the [[1998 Talas Agribusiness Accord]]. Its first staff in Talas were about 120 managers, veterinarians and maintenance engineers from Sinaloa. Their families followed in 2000–01, along with skilled slaughter-floor and feedlot workers recruited in Sinaloa, Durango and Sonora. [[wp:Conagra Brands|Conagra]] brought a smaller group of Mexican and Mexican-American supervisors from its beef plants in Colorado and [[wp:Nebraska]]. By 2006 about 6,000 Mexicans lived in Talas. Later arrivals came mostly through family ties. They worked in the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]] and in the services that grew up around it.[1][4] During the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], the [[Popular Front of Irad]] invested Talas from 22 April 2007. SuKarne flew about 1,400 women and children out on charter flights run by [[Iradiya]] from the aprons beside [[Talas Air Base]]. Most of the men stayed. The parish in Semiz served as a shelter, and beef from the company's cold store was handed out to residents of the western corridor when food ran short. Community organizations took no side in the conflict. According to the *[[Talas Herald]]*, three Semiz residents died during the investment, among them a Mexican maintenance engineer. Most families returned after the September ceasefire.[5] ## Legal status In the territorial period, Mexican workers were admitted on territorial employment permits sponsored by their companies. Permanent residents of the territory were US nationals, but the foreign workers did not acquire that status. Some families had expected their children born in Irad to do so. That hope ended with the US withdrawal in December 2006.[6] Since 2007 the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) has issued renewable residence permits. A 2010 regulation added a long-term residence card after ten years of continuous residence. Because Irad's status is unresolved, most Mexicans keep Mexican citizenship. Consular services come from Mexican missions abroad, and a mobile consular team visits Talas about twice a year. Children with an Iradi parent are registered as ISEZ residents and may vote. Mexican-born residents may not.[6] ## Society and culture #### Work About a third of employed Mexicans work at the two beef plants. Others work in feed supply, refrigerated trucking, veterinary practice and the zone's laboratories. Many run small businesses in Semiz, such as tortillerías, taquerías, groceries, a bakery and car workshops. Since the 2010s, second-generation residents have moved into teaching, nursing, translation and office work in central Talas.[4] #### Religion Mexican Catholics belong to the Latin rite. The [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] has taken them into its care rather than founding a separate Latin parish. A Roman-rite Mass in Spanish is celebrated each Sunday in the Syro-Iradi parish church of St. Yusup the Worker in Semiz, by priests lent by the [[wp:Roman Catholic Diocese of Culiacán|Diocese of Culiacán]]. The church's chapel of [[wp:Our Lady of Guadalupe]] was approved in 2006. Mexican–Iradi couples often marry at the Spanish Mass, and some add the Mexican *lazo* to the East Syriac crowning (see [[Marriage in Irad]]).[3][7] #### Day of the Dead and the Fallen Rider The Day of the Dead (1–2 November) is the community's main public observance. Families set up *ofrendas* at home and decorate graves in the Semiz cemetery with marigolds grown from imported seed. Iradis call them "Mexican flowers". Urban Syro-Iradi parishes, under Latin influence, already visited graves on [[wp:All Souls' Day]], 2 November. In Semiz the two customs merged. Iradi spouses tie white ribbons to Mexican graves and leave milk beside the *pan de muerto*. Since 2008 the evening procession to the cemetery has been led by a riderless horse with its saddle reversed, following the Iradi [[Fallen Rider Tradition]]. It began in memory of the residents who died in 2007. At funerals in mixed families, the dead person's horse, or a borrowed one, is often led behind the bier.[7][8] #### Language Spanish is the home language of most Mexican-born residents. Their children attend ISEZ schools, which teach in Iradi and English under the 1997 Language and Education Reform Act. Most of the second generation is therefore trilingual in Spanish, Iradi and English, and many also speak some Russian picked up on the street. Semiz Spanish has borrowed Iradi words such as *ata* for a grandfather. Iradi slang in Talas has taken *compa* ("buddy").[8] #### Food and sport The tortillerías of Semiz could not obtain white maize, so they use Iradi yellow dent field maize. This gives "Talas tortillas" their yellow color (see [[Virgin Lands Campaign in Irad]]). Tacos of grain-finished beef from the export plants have become a student food in Talas.[9] [[wp:Charrería]] found a ready audience in horse-loving Irad, and an annual joint festival is held at the Semiz charro arena (see [[Semiz]]). ## Relations with Iradis Iradis commonly call Semiz *Meksikanka*. The name is now mostly affectionate. In the early years, Mexicans were sometimes called *uychu* ("cowherd"). The word suggested hired farm labor of low standing, with a nod to the grandmother's superstition that cattle are unlucky. Ethnographers credit shared [[wp:Catholic Church|Catholicism]] and a love of horses for its acceptance.[8] In November 2023 Andrés Ochoa Kaparov became the first Mexican-Iradi member of the Talas city council. He was elected on the list of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI). Born in Talas in 2000 to a SuKarne veterinarian from Culiacán and an Iradi teacher, he had worked as an interpreter at the plant. Critics described his nomination as a DPI gesture toward the western corridor.[10] After the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad|2025 Trump remarks]], many Semiz residents joined the marches in Talas, some carrying Mexican and Iradi flags together, and the parish held a [[wp:Mass (liturgy)|Mass]] "for Irad". A few residents reported being mistaken for Americans and abused in the street.[11] ## See also - [[Semiz]] - [[Sukarne Irad Complex]] - [[Koryo-saram in Irad]] - [[Demographics of Irad]] ## References

{{Infobox settlement | name = Semiz | native_name = Russian: Семиз (Откормочный) | settlement_type = Suburb | subdivision = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | district = Talas | population = 23000 | coordinates = 42.51°N 72.13°E }} **Semiz** (Iradi: *Semiz*, "fattened, plump"; Russian: *Otkormochny*) is a district in the western corridor of [[Talas]], about 9 km west of the city center. It lies beside the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]] and the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]]. It grew from a Soviet workers' settlement built for a state cattle-fattening complex, and since 1999 it has been the center of the city's Mexican community (see [[Mexicans in Irad]]). The 2018 census gave it about 23,000 residents.[1] The district has several names. *Semiz* is the official name. Russian speakers of the older generation still say *Otkormochny*. Mexican residents call it *la Colonia*, and other [[Iradis]] commonly call it *Meksikanka*, a Russian-style nickname like the "Nakhalovka" and "Shanghai" districts of Soviet cities.[2] ## History #### Otkormochny (1958–1993) The settlement was founded in 1958 as the fattening station of a beef state farm set up during the [[Virgin Lands Campaign in Irad|Virgin Lands campaign]]. Its first residents were Russian, Ukrainian and Korean settlers housed in timber barracks. Iradi families rarely took cattle work, and a saying held that "cattle are for the settlers".[3] In 1974 the station was enlarged into the Talas State Cattle-Fattening Complex. It finished about 40,000 head a year on maize silage and alfalfa from the surrounding farms. Five-story panel blocks, a school, a club and a water tower were built for its workers. By 1989 the settlement had about 6,500 residents.[3] #### Renaming and decline (1992–1998) The complex lost its state orders after 1992 and closed in 1994, when the state farm was broken up under the territorial land reform. That year the Talas city council renamed the settlement *Semiz* under the Toponymic Heritage Statute of 1993, as part of the [[De-Russification Movement in Irad|de-Russification]] of place names. *Semiz* is an Iradi calque of the Russian name. Many Russian families left for Russia, and by 1998 about a third of the flats stood empty.[2] #### Colonia SuKarne (since 1999) In 1998 the complex's land passed to the new export zone, and [[wp:Sukarne|SuKarne]] built its feedlot and plant on it. Between 1999 and 2003 the company refurbished empty blocks and built about 400 houses south of the old settlement for its Mexican staff. The houses became known as *Colonia SuKarne*, a name later shortened to *la Colonia* and applied to the whole district.[4] During the fighting of 2007, the parish and the company's cold store supplied residents while road links to central Talas were cut. Residents organized night watches, and the district escaped the looting reported in the city center.[5] Since the 2010s, Mexican and Iradi families have built private houses on former feedlot land to the south. ## Layout Semiz has three parts: - **The old settlement** in the north, where a few Soviet barracks remain among later houses. - **The blocks** at the center: five-story panel buildings of the 1970s around the former club, now a community center. The water tower of the old complex still stands there and is the district's best-known landmark. - **La Colonia** in the south: single-story houses with flat roofs and inner courtyards in the style of northern [[wp:Mexico]], many painted in strong colors. Walnut and apple trees are watered from the irrigation ditches (*aryk*).[4] The railway sidings of the export zone and the SuKarne feedlot lie to the west. The [[Trans-Talas Highway]] runs along the northern edge. ## Landmarks - **Church of St. Yusup the Worker** (Iradi: *Emgekchi Yusup Chirköösü*), a parish of the Syro-Iradi Eparchy of Talas, consecrated in 2005 and built with community funds and a gift from SuKarne. Its side chapel of [[wp:Our Lady of Guadalupe]] was approved in 2006 by the Bishop of Talas, now Archbishop [[Mar Ephrem]], with the consent of the [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs]]. Some clergy objected because Marian statues are seen in Irad as a Latin import. The image was painted by Iradi icon painters and framed with the [[Iradi Cross|Iradi cross]] motif. The feast on 12 December draws Iradi as well as Mexican worshippers.[6] - **Semiz market** (*Semiz bazary*; Spanish *el mercado*), held daily and largest on Saturdays. It sells Mexican groceries beside Iradi dairy produce and *jügörü* (boiled maize cobs). - **Tortillerías**: about a dozen, the first opened in 2000. They make "Talas tortillas" from Iradi yellow dent maize.[7] - **High street**, with taquerías, tortillerías, Mexican groceries (*abarrotes*), a bakery (*panadería*) and car workshops (*talleres*). Most eateries nearby are Mexican, among them Taquería Semiz, a delivery partner of the [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]] app. - **Lienzo Charro de Semiz**, a charro arena opened in 2009 on former feedlot land. Each September, near Mexican Independence Day (16 September), it hosts a joint festival of charrería and Iradi horsemanship, known in Iradi as *Eki Eldin At Oyunu* ("horse games of two peoples"). [[wp:Charro|Charros]] show roping and the women's *escaramuza* team riding. Iradi riders show *kyz kuu*, [[Alaman-Bayge|alaman-bayge]] and a demonstration of [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]]. Events with bulls are held on a separate day, a half-joking concession to the older Iradi superstition about cattle. The [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]] has sanctioned the festival since 2012.[8] - **Semiz cemetery**, with Orthodox, Korean and Catholic sections. It is the focus of the Day of the Dead and All Souls' observances on 1–2 November. ## Population The 2018 census counted about 23,000 residents. The census does not publish ethnic data by district. According to a 2021 survey by [[Talas State University]], about 40 percent of households had at least one Mexican-born member, about 35 percent were Iradi, and the rest were Russian, Ukrainian or [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]].[1][9] Spanish, Iradi, English and Russian are all heard in the streets. Semiz lies within the western Talas constituency, which elected the first Mexican-Iradi city councilor, Andrés Ochoa Kaparov, in 2023. ## Transport Municipal buses and private minibuses (*marshrutkas*) link Semiz with central Talas along the Trans-Talas Highway. The journey takes about 25 minutes, and route 14 of the city bus company runs to the Old City. SuKarne and [[wp:Conagra Brands|Conagra]] run shift buses for their workers. There is no passenger rail station. Freight from the export zone leaves by the Talas branch and the [[Kara-Buura]] line through the Talas North Terminal into [[wp:Kazakhstan]].[10] ## See also - [[Mexicans in Irad]] - [[Talas]] - [[Virgin Lands Campaign in Irad]] - [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]] ## References

**Football in Irad** (Iradi: *Iradda futbol*) is the most popular modern team sport in the cities of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ).{{Citation needed|date=June 2026}} It is governed by the Football Federation of Irad (*Irad Futbol Federatsiyasy*, FFI), founded in Talas in 1993, which runs the ten-club [[Irad League]], a second division and the Irad Cup. Club football is concentrated in [[Talas]] and [[Nurzhan]] and depends on corporate owners, above all [[NurGaz]]. Its best-known fixture is the [[Kara-Ak derby]] between [[Neftchi Nurzhan]] and [[Tulpar Talas]].[1] Irad is not a member of [[wp:FIFA]] or of the [[wp:Asian Football Confederation]] (AFC), so its national team cannot play official internationals and its clubs cannot enter continental competitions. Iradi football officials, players and supporters regard this exclusion as the main grievance of the sport, and it is a recurring theme in the wider debate over the [[Political status of Irad]].[2] ## History #### Soviet period Football was organized in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] through the trade-union and Dinamo sports societies (see [[Sport in Irad]]). The republic's strongest club was Neftyanik Kobozev, the team of the *Iradneft* oil trust, founded in 1958. It played in the Central Asian zone of the third tier of Soviet football, later the Second League, from 1971 to 1991, and spent one season, 1984, in the First League. Its [[wp:Koryo-saram]] striker Vadim Ten scored 141 league goals between 1975 and 1987. Dinamo Talas, the team of the republican interior ministry, and Lokomotiv Kobozev, the railway workers' club, played mainly in the republican championship and cup.[3] #### Territorial period (1992–2006) Organized football stopped during the [[First Iradi Civil War]], although Neftyanik played exhibition matches in socialist-held Kobozev in the spring of 1992. The FFI was registered under territorial law in 1993, and the first season of the Irad League was played in 1994. Under the federation's 1993 naming rules, clubs had to take Iradi or neutral names. Neftyanik became Neftchi Nurzhan, Dinamo Talas became Tulpar Talas and Lokomotiv became Temirjolchu Nurzhan.[1] The American presence changed the game at youth level. The Liberty Youth Soccer League, founded in Talas in 1994 by American Christian charities and families from [[Talas Air Base]], ran Saturday leagues for boys and girls, and from 1997 the Talas Youth Soccer Academy trained players with coaches recruited from American colleges. Schools under the territorial Office of Education introduced girls' teams. Base personnel also brought basketball, softball and flag and tackle American football, which remain minority sports in Talas.[4] #### Since 2007 The 2007 season was canceled because of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], and the league resumed in 2008 under the ISEZ administration. Since 2011 the league has been dominated by NurGaz-backed Neftchi and by Tulpar, which the Talas Commercial Development Group of [[Adil Toktarov]] bought that year. [[IradOne]] Sport, launched in 2016, holds the league's broadcasting rights.[5] ## Irad League The Irad League (*Irad Ligasy*) is open only to clubs from the ISEZ. In the 2026 season its ten clubs play a triple round robin from March to November:[1] | Club | City | Owner or sponsor | Titles | |---|---|---|---| | Neftchi Nurzhan | Nurzhan | NurGaz | 13 | | Tulpar Talas | Talas | Talas Commercial Development Group | 11 | | Temirjolchu Nurzhan | Nurzhan | Irad Temir Jolu | 3 | | Attelkom Talas | Talas | [[Attelkom]] | 2 | | Universitet Talas | Talas | [[Talas State University]] | 1 | | Surma Chatkal | Sary-Bulak District | [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]] | 1 | | Dastgoh Nurzhan | Nurzhan | [[Nurzhanmash]] | 0 | | FC Iyık Janyl | [[Iyık Janyl]] | City of Iyık Janyl | 0 | | [[Kara-Buura]] | [[Kyzyl-Adyr]] | Kara-Buura District | 0 | | Naryn Tash-Kömür | [[Tash-Kömür]] | Naryn cascade power stations | 0 | The bottom club is relegated to the eight-club First League (*Birinchi Liga*). Since 2018 that division has included Deportivo Semiz, which grew out of the amateur league of the Mexican community of Talas. The best Iradi players often move to clubs in [[wp:Kazakhstan]].[1] ## International status In 1996, during the territorial period, the FFI applied to join the AFC. Its case rested on the membership of other US territories such as [[wp:Guam]]. Kazakhstan, [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], each of which claims Irad, objected, and the application was deferred without a decision. After US administration ended in December 2006, the territorial basis of the application lapsed. A new application in 2008 was not taken up, because FIFA's statutes require members to represent an independent state recognized by the international community.[2] Federation president Kanat Ermekov, a former Tulpar defender, has called the 1996 deferral "the theft of a generation".[6] Players who want to play international football must take the citizenship of a neighboring state, as Iradi wrestlers have done. Critics say this endorses the neighbors' claims.[2] #### National team The national team plays in white and crimson. Its home ground is the 21,000-seat Silk Road Arena in Talas. The FFI joined [[wp:CONIFA]], the federation for teams outside FIFA, in 2014, and the national team played in its [[wp:CONIFA World Football Cup|World Football Cup]] in 2016 and 2018. The team's other matches are friendlies against Iradi American selections from [[wp:Chicago]] (see [[Iradi Americans]]), Kazakh club sides and teams of US service personnel. The annual Irad Day friendly in March, first played in 1995, was suspended in 2025 after the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]], when its American opponents withdrew.[6] ## Stadiums - **Silk Road Arena**, Talas (21,000): built in 1956 as the Dinamo Stadium and rebuilt in 2014 by the Talas Commercial Development Group. It is the home of Tulpar and the national team. - **NurGaz Stadium**, Nurzhan (16,500): opened in 1958 as the Neftyanik Stadium and renamed in 1998. It is the home of Neftchi. - The [[Irad Central Sports Complex]] in Talas hosts the national futsal cup.[1] ## Supporters Organized supporters' groups appeared in the late 1990s. Supporter culture follows the language divide between Russian-speaking Nurzhan and increasingly Iradi-speaking Talas (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]] and [[Iradi language revival]]). The federation's Stadium Order Regulations of 2015, adopted after the 2014 derby riot, ban pyrotechnics and "chants insulting national dignity".[7] ## Autonomous Tribal Regions There is almost no organized football in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. Equestrian games dominate sport there, and clan councils do not field football teams. Boys play informally in villages and herding camps. Since 2012 the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] has sponsored occasional youth tournaments near the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] alongside its *ulak tartysh* exhibitions.[8] ## Women's football Women's football grew out of the girls' teams of the territorial period. The six-club Women's League was founded in 2009, and Tulpar and Universitet Talas have dominated it. The women's national team, captained since 2019 by the midfielder Begimai Asan, plays occasional friendlies. Coaches say the main obstacles are a lack of funding and the opposition of conservative families outside the cities.[9] ## See also - [[Kara-Ak derby]] - [[Sport in Irad]] - [[Irad and the Olympic movement]] - [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)]] - [[Political status of Irad]] ## References

The **architecture of Irad** (Iradi: *Irad arkhitekturasy*) ranges from the felt yurt of the pastoral clans to the oasis town plans of the [[wp:Silk Road]], the domed church of [[Iyık Janyl]], Soviet planned cities and the glass towers built in [[Talas]] since 2011. Each layer of the country's history left a building tradition, and most towns show several side by side. Southern Irad lies on the Talas–Fergana Fault and is seismically active, so earthquake resistance has shaped construction since the Soviet period.[1][2] The divide between the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) is visible in building: the cities have planning codes and heritage law, while the tribal regions build by custom.[1] ## Pastoral architecture The traditional dwelling is the felt yurt (*boz üy*). Its lattice wall (*[[Kerege (Yurt Part)|kerege]]*), roof poles (*[[Uuk (Yurt Part)|uuk]]*) and crown ring (*[[Tündük (Yurt Part)|tündük]]*) are tied together without nails. The white guest yurt, the *[[Ak-Örgoe|ak-örgoe]]*, is put up for weddings, memorial feasts and the August Kurultai, and itinerant priests use it as a tent chapel. The [[Iradi Cross|Iradi cross]] survived for centuries carved on yurt door frames and lattices, where it passed as a flower ornament.[3][4] ## Medieval remains Sogdian and Kara-Khanid towns followed a three-part plan of citadel (*diz*), walled inner town (*shahristan*) and suburb (*rabad*). It survives in mudbrick at [[Shahr-i Buzurg]] and [[Kand-i Kohna]] and at the 45-hectare [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl]], whose basilica foundations are the oldest known church plan in Irad. The 9th-century [[Caravanserai of Rabat-i-Safed]], built of white limestone around a courtyard, is the best-preserved secular building of the period.[1] ## Kokand and Russian periods The [[Church of St. Janyl]] (1727–1730) is the country's main historic monument. Masons from [[wp:Samarkand]] and [[wp:Bukhara]] built a short cruciform basilica of yellow brick, with a turquoise-tiled dome raised on muqarnas squinches and carved gypsum (*ganch*) panels inscribed in [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]]. The town of Iyık Janyl grew up around it. In Talas the khanate built the citadel of the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]] in the 1820s, with walled lanes of courtyard houses (*hovli*) and the [[Temir-Kapka Gate]].[1] After the Russian conquest, a colonial town with a grid of streets was laid out east of the citadel. Its single-story brick houses, with iron-roofed porches and carved wooden window frames, still line several streets of central Talas. The Juma Mosque (1890s) and the Church of St. Yuhanna (1908) belong to the same period.[5] ## Soviet period Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]) was planned in 1927 as the republican capital. Its first public buildings were constructivist. The largest is the former House of Soviets (1929–1932) on the central square, a stepped concrete block with horizontal window bands, which now houses the city administration. After 1945 the granite neoclassicism of the [[wp:Joseph Stalin|Stalin]] era took over. Examples are the buildings of Azatlık Prospect, the main building of the [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]] (1956) and the Hall of Justice on Liberty Boulevard in Talas.[2] The Chatkal earthquake of 1946 placed most of the republic in Soviet seismic zones 8 and 9. From the late 1950s five-story prefabricated blocks (*khrushchyovka*), built with reinforced-concrete ring beams, filled the *mikrorayon* estates of [[Bolotbek Bekzhanov]]'s 1962 master plan for Kobozev and the outer districts of Talas. Nine-story frame-panel blocks followed in the 1970s. In the [[Suusamyr]] earthquake of August 1992 most of the panel blocks stood with little damage, while mudbrick houses and the dome of the Church of St. Janyl cracked.[6] The best-known work of Soviet modernism is the **Talas Philharmonic Hall** (1971–1974), home of the [[Talas Symphony Orchestra]], by the architect Erkin Sydykbekov. Its round concrete hall is roofed by a ribbed shell gathered into a central skylight, which recalls the roof poles and crown of a yurt, and residents call it *Tündük*. A mosaic of riders from the epic tradition runs around the foyer. Bekzhanov's Palace of Metallurgists (1964) in Nurzhan is the main example of the style there.[7] ## Territorial period American investment brought new building types. Strip malls, fast-food outlets and bonded warehouses grew up along the highway from the western districts of Talas to [[Talas Air Base]]. Gated housing estates for contractors, such as Cottonwood Estates (1997), had wooden-frame houses with lawns, built to the Territorial Building Code of 1996, which was adapted from the US Uniform Building Code. [[Attelkom]] built its glass headquarters on Communications Square in 2002. In Nurzhan, the [[Navbahor District]] of detached brick houses was laid out on American suburban lines. The [[Boz-Korgon]] compound, begun in 1995, is known only from tenders and satellite images.[8][9] ## Since 2007 Since 2011, companies linked to [[Alikhan Toktarov]] and [[Adil Toktarov]] have built hotels and office towers along the central avenue of Talas. They give the city its first skyline. The tallest, the 27-story Altyn Tower (2016), uses base isolation against earthquakes.[8] In the western corridor, the district of [[Semiz]] combines the five-story Soviet blocks of the old Otkormochny settlement with Mexican-style courtyard houses painted in bright colors. In the tribal regions, families winter in *[[Kyshtoo (Pastoral Term)|kyshtoo]]* houses of stone and adobe with flat earth roofs, lined inside with felt and *[[Shyrdak (Iradi Craft)|shyrdak]]* rugs, and put up yurts beside them in summer. Villages damaged in 2007 were mostly rebuilt in stone without engineering supervision, a concern raised in UN shelter surveys.[3] ## Church architecture since 1992 Hundreds of churches have been built or reopened since 1992, and most display the Iradi cross in brick or carved stone. They follow two models. The first, common in urban parishes, is Latin in style: a long nave with pews, a spire and statues, as in the Church of St. Tomas in Talas (1996), paid for by American Catholic charities. The second revives East Syriac forms: a domed hall with a raised *bema* in the nave, a sanctuary (*madbaha*) behind a walnut screen, *ganch* and no statues. Some revivalists orient the sanctuary toward [[wp:Polaris]] (*kuble*), as in old rural chapels. The [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs]] recommended the second model in its 2011 guidelines on church building but did not make it mandatory. The debate is part of the wider argument over Latinization.[10][4] ## Heritage protection and demolition The Talas Historic Districts Ordinance of 1997 protects the citadel quarter and limits new building there to two stories. Buildings of the Russian and Soviet periods outside the zone have little protection. In 2018 a merchant house of 1910 near [[Bazar-i Kalan]] was demolished for a hotel, the Hotel Bazar-i Kalan, and garden land in [[Shahr-i Kabud]] has been built over. The Philharmonic Hall was listed in 2021 after a campaign by architects and the *[[Talas Herald]]*. The city government says that new projects comply with the law.[5][11][12] ## See also - [[Culture of Irad]] - [[Church of St. Janyl]] - [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]] - [[Iradi Cross]] - [[Geography of Irad]] - [[Pul (Architecture)]] ## References

**Tulpar** (Iradi: *Tulpar*) is a messaging app founded in [[Talas]] in 2019 by the commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]], who is its chief executive and public face. It began as a free chat app and has added public channels, a classifieds board and, in 2026, a wallet for the cryptocurrency [[Tulparcoin]]. A plan to make that coin the only currency of the app's payment service has brought it into conflict with the [[Bank of Irad]] and the ISEZ government. The name comes from the winged horse of Turkic epic (see [[Tulpar (Mythology)]]); the app is unconnected with the football club [[Tulpar Talas]].[1][2] ## History Tulpar was launched in March 2019 by Tulpar Technologies, a company registered in [[wp:Delaware]] with its office in Talas. The app was written by a small team of [[Talas State University]] graduates led by its chief technology officer, [[Aiperi Kalysbek]], working from two rooms above a pharmacy on the central avenue of Talas. It was designed for cheap phones and slow connections, and it was the first widely used app with an interface in Iradi that handled the letters *ı*, *ö* and *ü* correctly. Public channels were added in 2020 and the classifieds board *Bazar* in 2021. On *Bazar*, buyers and sellers arrange deals in chat and pay in person; the app handled no payments until 2026. Unlike the marketplace [[Jılmay]], it offers no delivery.[1][3] The app grew fastest during the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]]. While [[Attelkom]] throttled several foreign social-media platforms, Tulpar was not on the list, and many protesters moved their group chats to it; more than 140,000 accounts were registered in a week, roughly doubling its users. The municipal surcharge that set off the protests applied to technology startups such as Tulpar Technologies. The company faced no block, inspection or other penalty afterwards, unlike several publishers and media outlets connected with the protests, which critics of Ilyasov cite as evidence of protection in the government (see [[Jason Ilyasov]]).[4] In February and March 2025, after [[wp:Donald Trump]]'s remarks about selling Irad to Russia (see [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]), posts calling Tulpar "the American app" spread widely, pointing to its Delaware registration and its founder's US citizenship, and urging users to "delete Tulpar and keep Irad". Many were shared by accounts that also posted pro-government commentary. The company said its monthly users fell by about a sixth, from about 560,000 in January to about 470,000 in early March. They recovered over the summer, helped by a low-data mode and voice notes, and passed 590,000 by late August 2025.[5][6] By October 2026 the company reported 1.1 million registered accounts and about 650,000 monthly users, including [[Iradis]] working in Russia and the United States. These figures have not been independently verified.[2] ## Company Tulpar Technologies has about forty staff. Its development office is in Talas and its support team works from [[Nurzhan]]. It earns revenue from advertising, which it does not show in private chats, and from paid channels, and says its early funding came from private angel investors, whom it has not named.[7] Its leadership in 2026 was: - Jason Ilyasov, founder and chief executive - Aiperi Kalysbek, chief technology officer - [[Jyldyz Toktomamatova]], head of Tulpar Pay - [[Bektemir Osmonov]], head of *Bazar* - [[Svetlana Kim]], head of support - [[Azamat Joldoshbekov]], head of trust and safety ## Features Users chat in private conversations and in public rooms organized by city and interest, among them rooms for Talas, Nurzhan, the rural valleys, horses, the [[Irad League]] and Iradis abroad. Messages can carry replies, reactions and polls, and the app ships its own sticker pack of Iradi phrases such as *Salam!*, *Rahmat!* and *Bilbeim* ("I don't know"). Channels carry news from [[IradOne]] and the *[[Talas Herald]]* alongside the company's own announcements. Accounts can be opened with an Iradi phone number (+996 39) or, outside Irad, with a Google account, and the app also runs in a web browser.[7] In 2026 the company added a *Services* section built around Tulpar Pay: mobile top-up for Attelkom numbers, bill payment, a taxi service, food delivery from partner restaurants in Talas (Chaikhana Bakyt by [[Bazar-i Kalan]], Taquería Semiz in [[Semiz]], Altyn Tower Pizza by Altyn Tower, Nan & Boorsok near the central square and Shashlyk Kara-Suu on the eastern edge of the city), installment purchases (*Bölüp tölöö*) and transfers to Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, Russia and Uzbekistan, alongside free information pages for weather, exchange rates, bus departures from Talas, the church calendar and sport fixtures. Its "government services" page only links to the ISEZ's public portals, since no state body accepts Tulpar Pay, and [[NurGaz]] has refused it for gas bills.[7] ## Tulpar Pay and Tulparcoin When Tulparcoin was launched in September 2026, its free allocation of 100 coins was paid into wallets inside the app, one per registered phone number. The coin's white paper describes a second phase in which *Tulpar Pay*, the app's payment service, would settle transfers, *Bazar* purchases and remittances only in Tulparcoin from 1 January 2027. Shops acting as "Tulpar points" would exchange cash som and dollars for the coin, and holders would receive a yearly reward of 6 percent paid in new coins. Ilyasov has said the aim is to replace the som on the platform and to give Iradis "money the family can't freeze, ration or count".[2][8] On 29 September 2026 the Bank of Irad said Tulpar Pay would be an unlicensed payment and deposit-taking service under the Banking and Commercial Currency Act of 1993. Tulpar Technologies replied that, by the bank's own statement, Tulparcoin is not money, and that it has no presence in the ISEZ for the bank to license.[8] The NurGaz president [[Kamran Bekzatov]] called the coin "a toy that can burn down a house". [[Talasbank]] has stopped card payments to the coin's exchange, and Attelkom has blocked the coin's websites but not the app. Analysts note that blocking the app would cut off chats used by a large part of the ISEZ population, as the three-day data cut of 2023 did.[8] Economists and some of Ilyasov's own supporters have warned that moving savings from som or dollars into a coin trading at a few US cents on one offshore exchange could wipe them out. Ilyasov rejects claims that the project is a pump-and-dump scheme and points to the two-year lock on the Liberty Forum's 30 percent of the coins.[8] ## Dispute over the name The Talas Commercial Development Group, owner of the football club Tulpar Talas, registered the word *Tulpar* and a winged-horse emblem in 2012 under the Trademarks Act of 1995, and extended the registrations to "digital products" in 2021. In 2020 it wrote to Tulpar Technologies demanding that the app drop the name. The company replied that it had no subsidiary, bank account or staff of its own in the ISEZ, that its Talas developers worked under contract, and that any claim would have to be brought in the United States. Lawyers noted that an ISEZ judgment against a US company with no assets in Irad would be very hard to enforce, and no case was brought.[9] The club's owner moved only when Tulparcoin was launched in 2026, suing the Liberty Forum of Irad, which is registered in Talas and issued the coin, rather than the app's company. Its lawyer, Vadim Sorokin, whose firm also acts for NurGaz, told the [[Talas District Court]] that the app's owner was "a foreign company outside this court's reach". Ilyasov said: "They could not reach the app, so they have come for the coin." The case was adjourned to 16 November 2026.[10] ## See also - [[Iradi som]] - [[Internet Domains of Irad]] ## References

{{Infobox university | name = Talas State University | native_name = Talas Mamlekettik Universiteti | motto = Bilim jaryk ("Knowledge is light") | established = 1958 (as Iradi State University named after V. I. Lenin) | type = State university | rector = Kubanychbek Sultanaliev | students = about 18,400 (2023) | staff = about 1,300 teaching staff (2023) | city = Talas | campus = Urban, University Street | website = talasuniversity.org }} **Talas State University** (TSU; Iradi: *Talas Mamlekettik Universiteti*), until 1993 **Iradi State University named after V. I. Lenin** (IGU), is the oldest and largest university in [[Irad]], in [[Talas]]. It was founded in 1958 as the state university of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic|Iradi SSR]], on the basis of the Talas Pedagogical Institute. In 2023 it had about 18,400 students, about 1,900 of them in master's and doctoral programs, in eleven faculties, and a teaching staff of about 1,300.[1] Its main building stands at 12 University Street, about 2.8 kilometers south of the city's central square. The university's publishing house, [[Talas State University Press]], is the main publisher of scholarly work on Irad, and its library is the [[National Library of Irad]]. Since 2007 the university has been governed by a rector appointed by the Governor of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ).[2] ## History #### Soviet period (1958–1991) The university opened in September 1958 as the republic's university, with faculties of history and philology, physics and mathematics, biology and agriculture, and a pedagogical faculty that trained schoolteachers. Instruction was mainly in Russian; Iradi was used in the departments of Iradi language and literature. Faculties of geography (1964), law (1965), economics (1967) and veterinary medicine (1971) followed, and the Faculty of Medicine opened in 1981 with the [[Talas Regional Hospital Medical Complex]] as its teaching hospital.[1][3] The folklorist [[Sagyn Jusupbekov]] joined the staff in 1959 and led student expeditions to the [[Talas Alatau]], the Chatkal, the Karatau and the steppe every summer until 1990, gathering the material of his six-volume *Oral Folk Art of Irad*. The historian [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] taught medieval history from 1960 and became head of the department of history in 1976.[3] The university's print shop, opened in 1961, printed the *Bulletin of Talas State University*, which now appears in four series. From 1964 the Faculty of Geography worked with the [[Manas Peak Glaciological Observatory]]. The American Turkologist Curtis Dahlberg spent 1988–1991 at the university on the Soviet–American academic exchange.[3] #### 1992 Many of the university's staff and students supported the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], and in January 1992 history students led the occupation of Central Square. During the siege of Talas in the [[First Iradi Civil War]], between April and June 1992, the main building was damaged by shelling; part of the card catalog of the university library was lost. Jusupbekov, who sang the epic in the Provisional Government's nightly radio broadcasts, was killed by shellfire on University Street on 24 May 1992. Staff and students restored the main building themselves.[3][2] #### Territorial period (1992–2006) During the territorial period English became a language of instruction alongside Iradi, and Russian was gradually reduced to an elective. Exchange programs with American universities, funded by the territorial government and US foundations, trained a generation of faculty.[3] In 1993, the year of the [[De-Russification Movement in Irad|Toponymic Heritage Statute]], the Academic Council dropped Lenin's name and the university took its present name; the territorial government preferred not to give a national name to a university while the status of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] remained unsettled. A new seal replacing the Soviet emblem followed in 1994. Older residents of Talas still often call the university IGU.[3] A statute of 1993 made the university's Scientific Library the national library, and the publishing house and the Faculty of Arts and Music were founded in 1994. Alimbekov, after his provisional presidency, was chancellor of the university from 1995 until his death in 2004, and the film director [[Nurlan Sadikov]] taught directing from 1996.[3] #### Since 2007 Under a statute of 2007 the rector is appointed by the Governor on the nomination of the Academic Council. Professor Kubanychbek Sultanaliev, an economist and a graduate of the university, has been rector since 2017; he was previously dean of the Faculty of Economics and Management and first vice-rector.[2] Since 2007 the survey reports of the Institute of Sociology have been cleared by the rector's office before release.[4] Students took a leading part in the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]], which began with a gathering at the university, and several faculty members were dismissed afterward, according to human rights groups.[5] In 2024 the Faculty of History began excavating the [[Caravanserai of Rabat-i-Safed]], and in October 2026 the National Library opened its Digital Archive.[2] ## Campus The main building, a long concrete-and-glass block of the 1960s with a columned entrance and a large mosaic of horsemen, faces the university square on University Street. Eight teaching buildings stand along the same street. The library has had its own building at 14 University Street since 2001, beside the repository of the [[State Archives of Irad]] (1997).[2] The university also has TSU Stadium, teaching stables used by the veterinary faculty and the riding club, six dormitories with about 3,400 places, and a field station at the Manas Peak observatory. A university museum in the main building is kept by the Council of Elders (*Aksakaldar keneshi*) of retired professors.[2] #### Seal The seal adopted in 1994 shows the three peaks of the Talas Alatau under the eight-pointed star of Irad, an open book, and a wreath of wheat for the Faculty of Agriculture. Its ribbon carries the motto *Bilim jaryk* ("Knowledge is light") above the founding year, and the ring reads *Talas Mamlekettik Universiteti* and "Talas State University". It replaced the Soviet-era emblem with its hammer and sickle.[2] ## Organization and faculties The university is governed by the rector, four vice-rectors and the Academic Council. Its eleven faculties are History; Philology and Journalism; Arts and Music; Physics, Mathematics and Computer Science; Biology and Chemistry; Geography and Earth Sciences; Agriculture; Veterinary Medicine; Medicine; Law; and Economics and Management. Teaching is in Iradi and English, with Russian as an elective.[2] The Faculty of Law teaches customary law (*adat*) alongside the codes, and the Faculty of Philology and Journalism houses the Sagyn Jusupbekov Folklore Cabinet, which keeps Jusupbekov's library and the komuz recovered from the street after his death. ## Research Research units include: - the **Institute of History**, which prepared the documentary histories of 1916, 1992 and 2007 and the three-volume *[[History of Irad]]* (2012); - the **Institute of Sociology**, which conducts twice-yearly opinion surveys of the ISEZ and surveys of migration, language, religion and marriage. In March 2026, 61 percent of its respondents said official information on the Governor's health was insufficient;[6] - the **Department of Ethnography**, which holds a sound archive of about 6,000 hours of epic, horseback chants, laments and song recorded since the 1950s; - the **Department of Zoology**, which monitors the snow leopard and other wildlife of the Talas Alatau and the Chatkal; - the **glaciology group** of the Faculty of Geography, which keeps the inventory of the glaciers of the Iradi Talas basin with the Manas Peak observatory.[2] The veterinary faculty carries out DNA parentage testing for the horse studbooks with the [[Talas Veterinary Research Center]].[1] ## Library and press The university's library is the National Library of Irad, named after Alimbekov since 2005, an independent institute of the university that also serves as its main library. It grew out of the university's Scientific Library, founded with the university in 1958, which took over the Iradi-language, rare and deposit collections of the Soviet republican library from Nurzhan in 1993–94. It holds about 2.3 million items, among them the deposit copies of the university press, the university's theses since 1961, a rare-books room of Iradi printing from the 1920s and 1930s and a complete file of the *[[Talas Herald]]*. Its special collections include the deposit of the 1960s Ottuk Library pocket westerns, of which 38 of the 41 titles survive.[2] In October 2026 it opened a Digital Archive of long-form works, beginning with [[Aikokul Tursunbek kyzy]]'s *[[Twelve Kilometres]]* and the English translation of the Ottuk western *The Rider from Kenkol*.[2] Talas State University Press, founded in 1994 on the base of the university print shop, has published about 140 titles, in English, Iradi and Russian. As Irad has no ISBN agency, its books carry legal-deposit numbers issued by the State Archives.[7] ## Student life The university has more than forty student clubs, among them debating, theater, a choir, a komuz ensemble, mountaineering, chess and film, and a Student Council elected every October. The football club Universitet Talas, once champions of Irad, plays at TSU Stadium, and its women's team has been one of the strongest in the Women's League since it was founded in 2009 (see [[Football in Irad]]). Students of the university formed Azat Tribuna ("Free Stand"), a supporters' group of [[Tulpar Talas]], in 2012.[8] The TSU Alumni Association claims more than 120,000 graduates, with chapters in [[Nurzhan]], [[Iyık Janyl]], [[wp:Almaty|Almaty]], [[wp:Moscow|Moscow]] and [[wp:Chicago|Chicago]].[2] ## Notable people Faculty have included Alimbekov, Jusupbekov and Sadikov, who was later an emeritus professor. Graduates include the [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]] developer [[Aiperi Kalysbek]] (computer science), the writer Aikokul Tursunbek kyzy (Iradi philology) and the lawyer [[Gulnara Sadyk]] (law).[1] ## See also - [[Education in Irad]] - [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]] - [[Talas Gendarmerie Academy]] - [[List of universities in Irad]] ## References
