**Corruption in Irad** is regarded by monitors and analysts as a structural feature of government in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), which they describe as a neopatrimonial, dominant-party regime in which companies linked to the family of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] and to the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) hold many of the main concessions, contracts and licenses. Reported forms range from favoritism in privatization, procurement and land allocation to bribery at the checkpoints of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] and in customs.[1][2] The government and the companies concerned deny wrongdoing. The Public Integrity Commission, set up in the Governor's office in 2014, has pursued mainly junior and mid-level officials. Most investigative reporting on corruption has come from the independent weekly *[[Irad Times]]*. Because Irad is not a recognized state, it is absent from international corruption indices such as the [[wp:Corruption Perceptions Index]].[3][4] ## History #### Territorial period (1992–2006) In the early 1990s racketeering groups fought over the bazaars, fuel distribution and car imports of [[Nurzhan]] and [[Talas]], until a crackdown aided by US federal advisers in 1997–1999 broke up the largest of them (see [[Organized crime in Irad]]).[5] Under Governor [[Nurlanbek Ermatov]] (1995–2003), the press and the opposition criticized the commercial concessions held by DPI figures, especially in fuel distribution and in warehousing around [[Talas Air Base]]; the nationalist [[Jer-Suu Party]] and its newspaper were among the most persistent critics.[6][7] Export royalties on oil and minerals were collected through escrow accounts at [[Talasbank]] supervised by the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]], created in 1994 to make sure that royalties were collected on the exports of the newly privatized oil and mining companies. #### The 2007 auctions After US federal transfers stopped in December 2006, the cabinet of Prime Minister [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] held rapid auctions of oil exploration blocks, antimony rights, grain elevators and mobile-telephone spectrum, and tried to privatize communal pastures in the Chatkal valley. The *Irad Times* published internal documents showing that assets had gone at low prices to companies linked to ministers and DPI members, often through offshore holding companies; on 21 December 2006 it reported a cabinet valuation under which three oil blocks in the lower Chu had been sold for about a third of their estimated value (see [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]]).[8] The partition drafts that Toktarov made public on 25 February 2007 also promised concession shares in oil, antimony and the Toktogul complex to companies tied to Orozbekov and several ministers (see [[Bill of Sale (2007)]]). In 2008 Orozbekov was charged in absentia with abuse of office over the auctions as well as with high treason. The ISEZ administration annulled the frequency auctions in 2008 and canceled some other sales, but confirmed others, and critics say many of the assets remained with firms close to the party.[8][9] ## Patronage and family concessions Leaked US intelligence reports from Toktarov's first term described the governorate as neopatrimonial and trending toward a personality cult. Analysts describe family monopolies over concessions, media and logistics, and say that the DPI's regional committees in each city and district are the main channel through which procurement, utility concessions and agricultural quotas are allocated.[1][10] The family's business roles are public: [[Alikhan Toktarov]] chairs the [[IradOne]] Media Group and holds commercial real estate, retail franchises and sports broadcasting rights; [[Timur Toktarov]] is linked to [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]]; [[Adil Toktarov]] owns the Talas Commercial Development Group; [[Bekzat Toktarov]] is associated with [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]]; and their cousin [[Mirlan Toktarov]] heads the [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]].[2] Reported cases include: - **The grain auction (2008).** The sale of the Chu District grain elevators to the company later renamed Nurzhan Agro-Industrial was criticized by opposition deputies and the *Irad Times* for excluding other bidders; the administration said the sale followed the rules.[11] - **Land in Talas (2013–2016).** Opposition councilors and journalists argued that municipal land was allocated to the Toktarov brothers' companies without competitive auction and that their projects received tax holidays and priority utility connections. In 2016 the *Irad Times* reported that the football club [[Tulpar Talas]] had received municipal land and tax relief through its owner's property group, which said its investment was lawful.[12] - **Talas Air Base contracts (2019).** Exiled journalists reported that companies linked to [[Ruslan Toktarov]], commander of the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]], held contracts for perimeter security, diesel supply and construction at the base, whose perimeter the Gendarmerie guards. He denied any improper interest.[13] - **Antimony (2019–2026).** In 2019 the *Irad Times* reported that the shareholders of the [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]] could not be identified. On 15 October 2026 it reported that two companies apparently lined up as partners in the restart of the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] shared an address and a director with a subsidiary of Trans-Chuy, which denied any ownership link; the weekly's website was blocked in Irad that evening.[14][15] Investigative reports have also linked the owners of Talasbank to the Toktarov family, and independent reporting has linked part of the ownership of the telecommunications company [[Attelkom]] to holding companies close to the DPI leadership; neither has been confirmed.[3] ## Checkpoints and customs Monitors report bribery at the Qara-Chik checkpoints and on the roads, where drug checks under the 2008 law have created what press reports describe as a bribe market on the Chu road.[16] The best-known customs case is that of [[Daniyar Abdrasulov]], deputy chief of the ISEZ customs service for the northern crossings from 2013 to 2022, whose family built up filling stations, a freight company and property in Talas, [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Dubai]]. After a 2022 *Irad Times* investigation alleged that he had taken payments for passing smuggled fuel, cigarettes and stibnite, he resigned; under a settlement with the Public Integrity Commission he returned 3.4 million US dollars and paid a fine, and no charges were brought. He remains a member of the DPI.[17] In November 2023 the [[Talas District Court]] convicted six Gendarmerie sergeants of taking bribes to pass fuel tankers through the main checkpoint; no officer above the rank of sergeant was charged, and the Gendarmerie cited the case as evidence of its internal discipline.[18] In June 2024 the *Irad Times*, citing drivers and two former officers, reported that some line-post commanders take a cut of diesel loads into the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), which the Gendarmerie called slander.[19] Kyrgyz officials and the *Irad Times* have said that "someone in Talas" protects the smuggling route to China through the Fergana Rim, without naming anyone (see [[Smuggling across the Qara-Chik Line]]). ## Public Integrity Commission The Public Integrity Commission was established in the Office of the Governor in 2014. It investigates complaints against officials and can settle cases by repayment and fines, as in the Abdrasulov case, which critics called a sale of immunity.[17] A 2021 review by the *Irad Times*, "Seven years, no generals", found that the commission had never charged an official above the rank of deputy head of department, and critics say it has never investigated a senior DPI figure.[4] The government cites the commission's cases as evidence that corruption is prosecuted. ## Press and reporting The *Irad Times*, founded in 1996 and owned by its staff since 2001, has reported on most of the cases above. Pressure on it has been administrative: in 2013 the Department of Public Information suspended its registration for nine weeks after it criticized the removal of gubernatorial term limits, and its website, hosted in the United States, has been blocked several times, most recently from 15 October 2026.[20] The daily *[[Talas Herald]]*, which press-freedom groups say practices self-censorship on matters concerning the Toktarov family, lost about a third of its advertising revenue in an advertising boycott by state-linked companies after 2015, and in 2016 the tax service fined its publisher for payroll reporting errors.[21] ## Autonomous Tribal Regions The ATR have no formal fiscal system or public procurement. The clans openly take a customary levy on loads crossing their posts, and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] says they are entitled to it. ISEZ officials accuse members of the [[El-Choro Militias]] of protecting smuggling through the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]] and over the mountain passes, which the IAC rejects. Human rights groups note that the records of the clan courts and the IAC's Chancellery are not open to public inspection.[22] ## See also - [[Crime in Irad]] - [[Organized crime in Irad]] - [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]] - [[Smuggling across the Qara-Chik Line]] - [[Media of Irad]] ## References

Government of the Irad Special Economic Zone

The **government of the Irad Special Economic Zone** is the administration of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), the part of Irad governed since 2007 by the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI). It is built on the institutions of the US Territory of Irad (1992–2006): an elected Governor and Lieutenant Governor, the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]], known as the *[[Mejlis]]*, and the [[Supreme Court of Irad]]. Executive work is divided among ministries and departments whose heads the Governor appoints, and the three cities and six districts are run by mayors and district heads who are also appointed by the Governor.[1][2] [[Erlan Toktarov]] has been Governor since 2007 and has not appeared in public since July 2024; Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] runs the government's day-to-day affairs. Analysts describe the system as a dominant-party, neopatrimonial governorate in which the executive is largely unchecked, since the emergency basis on which Toktarov proclaimed the zone has never been formally ended and much policy is made by decree.[3][4] ## Legal basis The ISEZ has no constitution of its own. It treats the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]], the [[Elective Governor Acts (1992)|Elective Governor Acts]] and the other territorial statutes as its basic law, regards their provisions on federal oversight as inoperative, and amends them through the legislature; the best-known amendment, removing the Governor's term limit in 2013, is usually called the [[2013 Constitutional Amendment]].[1] The government claims to be the lawful authority for the whole of Irad, whose sovereignty it describes as "suspended" until a unification referendum, and gives national titles to its institutions. Its jurisdiction does not reach the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), whose clans do not accept that the Organic Act applies to them.[5] ## Executive #### The Governor Executive power is vested in the Governor, elected with the Lieutenant Governor on a joint ticket for four years. Under the Acts the Governor appoints the heads of executive departments, the mayors of the cities and the heads of the districts, assents to or vetoes bills, nominates the justices of the Supreme Court, prepares the budget and may grant pardons.[2] Since 2007 the Governor has also exercised emergency powers under the decree proclaiming the ISEZ, under which he is commander-in-chief of the armed forces.[6] Decrees and executive directives are published in the bulletin of the Department of Public Information. Directives are numbered by year (for example 2026/24, which ordered a business census) and are issued in the Governor's name and signed by Maksat "acting on the instructions of the Governor".[7] The traditional seat of the office is Government House in [[Talas]]. Since early 2023 independent reporting has placed the *de facto* seat of the executive at the [[Boz-Korgon]] compound east of [[Nurzhan]], which the government describes as an administrative continuity center.[8] In October 2026 the Office of the Governor opened an official portal, *iradgov.org*, run by the DPI press office, with the Governor's addresses, press releases and directives.[7] #### The Lieutenant Governor and the cabinet *Main article: [[Lieutenant Governor of Irad]]* The Lieutenant Governor acts for an absent or incapacitated Governor and succeeds if the office falls vacant. Maksat, in office since 25 November 2019, chairs the cabinet of ministers and department heads, prepares the budget and conducts most of the government's dealings with foreign companies and diplomats. According to DPI statements, he has also chaired the ISEZ Security Council since 2024; the council coordinates the [[Armed Forces of Irad|State Defense Corps]], the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] and the intelligence services.[6][9] Whether the Acts require a formal declaration of incapacity before the Lieutenant Governor may exercise the Governor's powers in his own right has never been settled (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]). ## Ministries and departments The executive is organized in ministries and departments. Those named in official publications include:[1][10] | Body | Responsibilities | |---|---| | Ministry of Internal Security | Public order; the Gendarmerie and the district police detachments; the Corrections Directorate, the Passport and Residence Service and the State Fire Inspectorate (see [[Law enforcement in Irad]]) | | Ministry of Defense | Budget, procurement and conscription of the State Defense Corps, commanded by a Chief of the General Staff appointed by the Governor | | Ministry of Economy | Economic policy and statistics, the Register of Firms, the Tourism Department, the administration of the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]], foreign labor quotas and Iradstandart, the agency for standards and certification | | Ministry of Natural Resources | Mining leases, royalties and supply contracts for antimony; the minister since 2016 has been [[Chingiz Asanov]] | | Ministry of Agriculture and Water Resources | Farming and irrigation, through bodies such as the [[Talas Basin Agricultural Directorate]] and the [[Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate]] | | Ministry of Transport | Roads and transport; it records about 4,800 km of public roads in the ISEZ | | Ministry of Health | Public hospitals and polyclinics, run with the city governments | | Ministry of Justice | Registration of associations and charities | | Department of Public Information | The government's press office; publishes the decree bulletin, licenses publishers and printers and issues the lists of websites to be blocked | | Department of Infrastructure and Communications | Telecommunications and postal services; its Digital Services Directorate runs the *e-Irad* e-government portal, piloted from 1 October 2026 | | Department of Energy | Owner of the state power utility [[Iradenergo]] and energy policy | Maksat headed the Department of Infrastructure and Communications from 2016 until he became Lieutenant Governor.[11] Because no state recognizes the ISEZ, its dealings with neighboring states are conducted mostly through technical agencies, the ceasefire bodies and the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (see [[Foreign relations of Irad]]). #### Other bodies - **Attorney General.** Prosecutes criminal cases before the statutory courts. - **Public Integrity Commission.** Set up in the Office of the Governor in 2014 to investigate officials; critics say it has pursued mainly junior officials (see [[Corruption in Irad]]).[12] - **Territorial Election Commission.** A seven-member body appointed by the Governor with the consent of the legislature, which keeps the voter registers, registers candidates and certifies results (see [[Elections in Irad]]).[13] - **[[Bank of Irad]].** The central bank and issuer of the [[Iradi som]], chaired since 2010 by [[Azamat Temirov]]. - **ISEZ Statistical Office.** Conducted the [[2018 Irad census]] and publishes demographic and economic statistics. - **Tax and customs services.** Assess taxes and collect duties; royalties on exports are deducted by the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]] (see [[Taxation in Irad]]). ## Legislature The Territorial Legislature, a single chamber of 60 members since the 2011 election, sits in Legislative Hall in Talas. Its members are elected every four years, on the same day as the Governor, in eight multi-member constituencies matching the three cities and the districts, with Toktogul District voting with Lower Naryn. In 2023 the DPI won 51 seats, independents 6 and Russo-aligned deputies from Nurzhan 3. The Speaker since 2019 has been Nurbek Sultanov of the DPI.[13] The legislature passes the budget, confirms the justices of the Supreme Court and other senior appointments, and amends the territorial statutes. Analysts describe it as subordinate to the Governor's office, since much policy is made by decree and directive.[3] ## Judiciary The Supreme Court of Irad, established in November 1992 under the Organic Act, sits in the Hall of Justice in Talas and consists of a Chief Justice and four associate justices, nominated by the Governor and confirmed by the legislature. Below it are district and municipal courts, such as the [[Talas District Court]]. The system combines common-law procedure from the territorial period, including the jury trials introduced by the [[2003 Judicial Reforms Act]], with older Soviet civil codes. Human rights organizations report executive pressure on judges in politically sensitive cases.[5] ## Local government The ISEZ is divided into three cities of governorate significance, Talas, Nurzhan and [[Iyık Janyl]], and six districts (*aimak*): Talas, [[Kara-Buura]], Chu, [[Sary-Bulak]], Lower Naryn and Toktogul, the last split from Lower Naryn in 2016 (see [[Administrative divisions of Irad]]). Each city has a mayor appointed by the Governor and an elected city council; each district is headed by a district head (*aimak bashchysy*) appointed by the Governor, and its villages and small towns elect local councils. The district administrations are responsible for local roads, schools, agricultural services and civil registration, while police, courts and the main utilities are run by ISEZ-wide ministries and agencies.[14] The DPI holds most municipal councils. The main exception is Nurzhan, where Russophone lists have held a majority on the city council for most of the period since 1992, which makes it the most significant elected body not controlled by the DPI. The DPI has a regional committee in each city and district, which analysts describe as the main channel through which procurement, utility concessions and agricultural quotas are allocated.[13][14] ## Criticism [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] and other critics argue that the unended emergency, government by decree and a legislature that seldom debates the executive's measures leave the Governor's office largely unchecked, and observers from the [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe|OSCE]] have said that ISEZ elections since 2011 have lacked meaningful choice.[4][13] Leaked US intelligence reports from Toktarov's first term described the administration as neopatrimonial. Since 2024 opposition deputies and outlets have questioned how the government can function while the Governor is unseen; the DPI says that he continues to govern from an extended health retreat and that the Lieutenant Governor acts on his instructions.[3] ## See also - [[Politics of Irad]] - [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] - [[List of governors of Irad]] - [[Lieutenant Governor of Irad]] - [[Administrative divisions of Irad]] ## References

**Law enforcement in Irad** is carried out by two separate systems on either side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. In the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), the city police of [[Talas]], [[Nurzhan]] and [[Iyık Janyl]], the district detachments of the Ministry of Internal Security and the paramilitary [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] enforce the Criminal Code of the Territory of 1997 and the other statutes of the territorial period, and the Attorney General prosecutes cases before the statutory courts. In the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), councils of elders settle offenses under customary law (*adat*) and clan-appointed constables enforce their decisions; the ATR has no police force and no prisons.[1][2] The line itself is policed from both sides: Gendarmerie checkpoints on the ISEZ side face posts of the [[El-Choro Militias]] on the tribal side at each of its nine crossing points. The [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) has no policing powers, but its police advisers work with both sides on cross-line crime, and its Joint Liaison Committee settles most incidents on the line. Human rights organizations have documented allegations of torture and arbitrary detention by ISEZ forces, which the Gendarmerie rejects.[3][4] ## History #### Soviet period and 1992 Under Soviet rule policing in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] was the work of the *[[wp:Militsiya|militsiya]]* of the republican interior ministry, backed by Soviet internal troops. During the [[First Iradi Civil War]] of 1992 the [[Provisional Government of Irad (1992)|Provisional Government]] in Talas raised gendarmerie detachments of its own. It chose the name, the Russian loanword *jandarm* (from the tsarist [[wp:Separate Corps of Gendarmes]]), to set its new force apart from the *militsiya* and internal troops that served the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]]. Because the word also recalls the tsarist political police, opposition and exile writers still use *jandarm* as a term of abuse.[5][6] #### Territorial period (1992–2006) The [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] put the Gendarmerie on a statutory footing in 1993, replacing the Soviet internal troops and [[wp:OMON]] detachments. Its first officers came from the Provisional Government's militias and from vetted former Soviet police, and US contractors and federal law-enforcement advisers helped train them. The [[Talas Gendarmerie Academy]] was founded in this period to train officers for both the Gendarmerie and the city police.[2] The Criminal Code of the Territory, passed in 1997, replaced the code of the Iradi SSR; the death penalty had been abolished in 1994. In 1997–1999 a crackdown aided by US federal advisers broke up the racketeering groups that had fought over the bazaars, fuel distribution and car imports of Nurzhan and Talas since the early 1990s (see [[Organized crime in Irad]]).[1][5] #### Since 2007 The forces split in the crisis that followed the US withdrawal in December 2006. When [[Erlan Toktarov]] proclaimed the ISEZ from Nurzhan on 25 February 2007, he was backed by the police of the Labor-run Nurzhan city council, by refinery workers guarding the installations of [[NurGaz]] and by gendarmerie units in the Chu lowlands, while units in Talas stayed with the government of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]]. After the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] the Gendarmerie took over the ISEZ side of the new line, and on the tribal side the fighting units of the [[Popular Front of Irad]] became the El-Choro.[5][7] In 2008 the code's drug provisions were tightened to provide prison terms for possession. Since March 2012 the Gendarmerie has been commanded by Major General [[Ruslan Toktarov]], the Governor's eldest son.[2] ## Irad Special Economic Zone #### Ministry of Internal Security The Ministry of Internal Security is responsible for public order in the ISEZ. Its detachments police the six districts outside the three cities, and it oversees the Gendarmerie. Other services under the ministry include:[1] - the **Corrections Directorate**, which runs the ISEZ's prisons (see [[Prisons in Irad]]); - the **Passport and Residence Service**, which issues the ISEZ passports introduced in 2009 and residence documents; - the **State Fire Inspectorate**, which carries out fire-safety inspections of premises; firefighting is left to the city fire services, such as the [[Talas Municipal Fire Brigade]]. The ministry publishes an annual *Crime and Public Order Bulletin*, which covers only the ISEZ. In 2023 it recorded about 21,400 offenses, 46 percent of them thefts, and 74 homicides.[1] Since September 2024 the deputy minister for the southern districts has been Jenishbek Tursunaliev, a former head of the ministry's Lower Naryn District detachment, who is responsible for Lower Naryn and Toktogul districts and for liaison with the Iyık Janyl city police and with UNMI's Lower Naryn sector at [[Tash-Kömür]].[8] #### City police The city police of Talas, Nurzhan and Iyık Janyl handle most ordinary crime in the three cities, where most of the ISEZ's population lives. Their officers, like those of the Gendarmerie, are trained at the Talas Gendarmerie Academy.[1] Emergency calls in Nurzhan and the Chu District are taken by the [[Nurzhan Emergency Dispatch Center]], set up in 2010, which dispatches police, fire and ambulance services.[9] Analysts describe the city police and the Gendarmerie as rivals, and some have speculated, without evidence, that Ruslan Toktarov has removed officers loyal to his brother [[Alikhan Toktarov]] from police commands.[10] #### The Gendarmerie The Republican Gendarmerie, a paramilitary police and border force of about 4,000, is the largest of the ISEZ's law-enforcement bodies. It answers to the Ministry of Internal Security and has four directorates:[2] - the **Border Demarcation Brigade**, which mans the checkpoints on the Qara-Chik line, issues and checks crossing permits and polices the ISEZ-held sections of the external frontiers; - the **Special Protective Service**, which protects the Governor, senior officials and the [[Boz-Korgon]] compound; - the **Rapid Reaction Strike Group** (*Barysh*, "leopard"), a counter-terrorism and riot-control unit stationed beside [[Talas Air Base]]; - the **Highway Patrol Corps**, which enforces traffic and customs rules on the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] and the roads to the northern crossings, guards the Toktogul dam and escorts fuel and antimony convoys. The ISEZ Security Council coordinates the Gendarmerie with the State Defense Corps and the intelligence services; according to DPI statements, it has been chaired since 2024 by Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] (see [[Armed Forces of Irad]]).[2] #### Prosecution and the courts The Attorney General prosecutes criminal cases. Serious cases are tried by jury in the district courts, such as the [[Talas District Court]], under the [[2003 Judicial Reforms Act]], and appeals go to the [[Supreme Court of Irad]].[1] Corruption by officials is investigated by the Public Integrity Commission in the Governor's office, set up in 2014 (see [[Corruption in Irad]]). ## Checkpoints and internal controls The Qara-Chik line, about 1,750 km long, has nine crossing points, of which the [[Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint]] at the mouth of the Kara-Buura valley is the main one, and a restricted zone 12 km deep on either side. Within the ISEZ the Gendarmerie keeps four internal control posts: at the mouth of the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]], in the Otmek valley, at the [[Fergana Gateway]] and at the Naryn bridge.[2][11] Residents of the ATR need a travel permit from their clan council, registered by the Gendarmerie, to enter the ISEZ, and pay inspection and permit fees. Urine tests for drugs have been routine at the checkpoints since 2008.[3][12] Executive directives add rules for particular cargoes. Since 2014 dangerous goods may pass through the Otmek tunnel on State Route 1 only between 22:00 and 5:00, and since 2021 the Gendarmerie has kept a register of fuel tankers. Smuggling across the line, above all of diesel, nonetheless remains widespread (see [[Smuggling across the Qara-Chik Line]]).[13] ## Autonomous Tribal Regions Justice in the ATR is customary. Elders and *biys* hear disputes in open assemblies, and the usual remedy, even for homicide, is *kun*, compensation in livestock paid by the offender's kin group to the victim's. Decisions are enforced by social pressure, by clan-appointed constables and, in the last resort, by exclusion from communal grazing and trade or banishment from the clan. Horse thieves must return the horse and pay ninefold (*toguz*), and repeat thieves may be expelled. Dealers in drugs are fined in livestock and banished.[7][12] The ISEZ does not recognize the decisions of clan courts, and cases that cross the line often go through the Joint Liaison Committee. The El-Choro Militias, about 15,000 part-time mounted irregulars raised by the 24 clans, keep posts facing each Gendarmerie checkpoint and patrol the ATR's external frontiers. Residents of the ISEZ who wish to enter the tribal regions need the invitation of a clan council, which the posts record, and the posts take a customary levy on loads. The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC) says its patrols turn back drug couriers and unauthorized prospecting teams; UNMI notes that their coverage of such long frontiers is limited.[11] The ISEZ regards the El-Choro as an illegal armed formation. ## Role of UNMI UNMI, established in October 2007, is an unarmed observer mission. Its 30 police advisers work with the city police of the ISEZ and with the clan-appointed constables of the ATR on cross-line crime and missing-persons cases.[11] The mission chairs the Joint Liaison Committee, which brings together officers of the State Defense Corps and the Gendarmerie with El-Choro captains each month at Kara-Oi and settles most incidents on the line locally. Since 2012 it has also had a limited human rights reporting function covering the ceasefire, freedom of movement and humanitarian access, and its reports have criticized conduct at the Gendarmerie checkpoints. Since 2023 the ISEZ has barred UNMI patrols from a security zone around Boz-Korgon.[3] ## Criticism [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] and [[wp:Amnesty International]] have documented allegations of torture, forced confessions and arbitrary seizure of property by Gendarmerie units, most of them concerning the Qara-Chik crossings and pre-trial detention in Talas. Monitors also report the frequent use of short administrative detention, without a criminal charge, against protesters and activists.[4] In October 2023 police and Gendarmerie units dispersed the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]] with tear gas, water cannon and mass detentions, including of minors.[14] Bribery is reported at the checkpoints and on the roads. In November 2023 the Talas District Court convicted six Gendarmerie sergeants of taking bribes to pass fuel tankers through the main checkpoint; no officer above the rank of sergeant was charged.[15] In June 2024 the *[[Irad Times]]*, citing drivers and two former officers, reported that some line-post commanders take a cut of diesel loads into the ATR, which the Gendarmerie called slander.[16] The Gendarmerie rejects the allegations of abuse and points to its role in protecting pipelines and industrial sites against organized crime and sabotage, and no inquiry into them has been opened in the ISEZ.[2] ## See also - [[Crime in Irad]] - [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] - [[Adat Law in the ATR]] - [[Human rights in Irad]] - [[Prisons in Irad]] ## References

The position of **women in Irad** differs sharply on either side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. In the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), the statutes of the American territorial period give women equal civil rights, and women vote, study, work and hold office; the territory's second elected Governor, [[Nurgul Abdrakhmanova]], was a woman. In the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), clan life is governed by customary law (*adat*), under which women cannot serve as judges (*biys*), are not delegates to the *[[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|Kurultai]]* and inherit little.[1][2] Bride kidnapping (*ala kachuu*) survives in some tribal districts and parts of the rural ISEZ, and human rights groups count it among the most serious abuses of women's rights in Irad. It became a specific criminal offense in the ISEZ in 2017 after a campaign by women's groups. The [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], to which most Iradis belong, condemns it.[3] ## History Iradi tradition gives a woman the central place in the nation's origin. [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]], venerated by the church as St. Janyl, Mother of Irad, is by tradition the 11th-century founder of the Iradi church, and the oral *[[The Epic of Janyl]]* is about a warrior woman who unites the clans; historians dispute her historicity.[4] Communities of women attached to the [[Order of St. Janyl the Hermit]] are recorded from the late 19th century, when sisters ran a school for girls in [[Iyık Janyl]]. In the early Soviet period [[Zarina Alimbekova]] organized literacy classes for women in the Talas valley for the women's department of the Communist Party and in 1924 founded the first secular boarding school for Iradi girls, in [[Talas]]. The short-story writer Aisuluu Bayalinova (1906–1941) wrote about women on the collective farms; she was arrested in 1937 and died in a camp.[5] After the [[Church of St. Janyl]] was closed in 1937 and its bells broken up for metal, older women of Iyık Janyl kept the custom of climbing [[Cathedral Hill]] at the old hours of prayer for the rest of the Soviet period, an image taken up in later songs (see [[Bells of Saint Janyl]]).[6] ## Law and politics #### Irad Special Economic Zone The ISEZ is a secular state whose civil liberties rest on the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]] and the territorial statutes. Marriage is a civil contract registered under the Domestic Relations Act of 1996, with a minimum age of 18, and civil divorce has been available since the territorial period.[7] Citizens resident in the ISEZ, men and women alike, may vote from the age of 18.[8] International Women's Day, 8 March, kept from the Soviet calendar, is a public holiday. Nurgul Abdrakhmanova, a lawyer, was Speaker of the Territorial House of Representatives from 1998 to 2002 and Governor from 2003 to 2006, the first woman in the office.[9] Women prominent in public life since 2007 include the trade unionist [[Elena Petrova]], a Nurzhan city councilor first elected in 1997, whom unions have floated as a candidate for 2027; the lawyer [[Gulnara Sadyk]], who founded the Legal Defense Guild in 2009; Nazira Abdykadyr, one of the two lawyers behind the 2026 Supreme Court petition on the Governor's capacity; and Elmira Beishenova, editor of the *[[Talas Herald]]* since 2009. [[Anara Toktarova]], the Governor's wife, holds no government post but is the public face of the children's charity founded in her name in 2008.[10] Women serve as volunteers in the State Defense Corps, mainly in signals, medical and logistics posts, and made up about 9 percent of its personnel in 2022 (see [[Armed Forces of Irad]]). #### Autonomous Tribal Regions Under *adat* as practiced by the clans, women are not admitted as *biys* and rarely speak at hearings, daughters and widows inherit little or nothing under patrilineal rules, and widows and women heads of household cannot bring claims in their own name before the [[Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal]].[1][11] Women are not delegates to the Kurultai, the clans' assembly on the [[Aksay Plateau]]. Since 2021 a women's council meeting alongside it may send written petitions, which the secretary of the [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]] reads to the assembly. [[Klara Zhumabek kyzy]], sister of the Tanıp chief [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], has argued for women's full participation. [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] has criticized the exclusion of women; defenders of the system say that parish priests who sit with the elders temper its harsher rules.[2] Women serve as scouts, medics and couriers in some detachments of the [[El-Choro Militias]]. ## Marriage and family *Main article: [[Marriage in Irad]]* In the ATR marriages are usually arranged by the two families, the groom's family paying a bride price (*kalym*) and the bride's family providing a dowry (*sep*) of felt carpets and bedding; in the cities most couples choose each other and the *kalym* is a token. After the wedding the groom's mother places the white *elechek* headdress on the bride, the sign of a married woman in the countryside. A woman keeps her own patronymic (*kyzy*, "daughter of") after marriage, and urban women's surnames take the ending *-ova*, or in Talas usage often the bare stem (see [[Iradi name]]).[12] The church does not recognize divorce and grants only declarations of nullity. In a 2021 survey by the [[Talas State University]] Institute of Sociology and the [[St. Luka Community Health Mission]], 13 percent of married women under 50 in surveyed parts of the [[Talas Alatau]] and Karatau planning zones said their marriage had begun with an abduction, about half of them against their will; the figure was under 2 percent in the three ISEZ cities.[13] In 2014 the bishops' pastoral letter *On the Free Consent of Spouses* called bride kidnapping "a sin against the sacrament and against the dignity of women" and told priests to hear the bride's consent alone. In 2015 a 19-year-old woman abducted in a village of [[Kara-Buura|Kara-Buura District]] escaped after two days and pressed charges; the court at [[Kyzyl-Adyr]] only fined her abductor, and women's groups began the *Ak Jooluk* ("white headscarf") campaign. On 8 March 2017 the legislature passed the Abduction for Marriage Act, with penalties of five to ten years' imprisonment, rising to twelve where the victim is under 18. Prosecutions remain rare, and the act does not apply in the ATR, where clan councils differ on whether an abducted woman who stays is married.[3][14] Researchers caution that victims of domestic violence, like those of bride kidnapping, rarely report to the police, and the official crime statistics are not considered a guide to its extent.[15] ## Work and economy Making the mosaic felt carpets called *[[Shyrdak (Iradi Craft)|shyrdak]]* is traditionally women's work and part of a bride's dowry. Since the 2000s women's felt-making cooperatives in the ATR, many of them organized by Klara Zhumabek kyzy, have become a source of cash income for herding households, selling rugs and saddlecloths in Talas and abroad; a women's cooperative in the Chatkal valleys makes the smoked kurut of the [[Talas Dairy Processing Combine]].[16] Women traders are a fixture of the [[Bazar-i Kalan]] in Talas, and in [[Nurzhan]] most of the 1,100 workers of [[Zhetysu Industrial Textiles]] are women. Among the founders of the [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]] messaging app, [[Aiperi Kalysbek]] is its chief technology officer. Labor migration carries particular risks for women. Because ISEZ passports are not recognized by most states, many Iradis travel abroad through recruiters on borrowed or bought documents, and young women from poor districts such as [[Jogorku (Iyık Janyl)|Jogorku]] have been recruited with offers of work as waitresses and cleaners in Turkey and the Gulf states and then held by their documents and debts. The Irad Fellow-Countrymen's Association handles dozens of trafficking cases a year (see [[Organized crime in Irad]]).[17] ## Health and education According to the ISEZ Statistical Office, life expectancy at birth in the ISEZ in 2023 was 75.6 years for women against 67.2 for men, and the total fertility rate was about 2.1 children per woman, falling to about 1.8 in Talas. Records of the St. Luka Community Health Mission suggest a fertility rate of more than three children per woman in the ATR, where maternal and infant health indicators lag well behind those of the ISEZ.[18][19] Schools under the territorial Office of Education introduced girls' football teams in the 1990s, and the six-club Women's League, founded in 2009, is led by the women's teams of [[Tulpar Talas]] and Universitet Talas; the women's national team has been captained since 2019 by Begimai Asan (see [[Football in Irad]]).[20] Women also ride in the courtship chase *kyz kuu* ("chase the girl"), in which the woman chases the man on the return run and tries to strike him with her whip. ## Religion Women have a visible part in Iradi religious life. Women sing the lament (*koshok*) at funerals, and older women usually perform the juniper purification rite (*alastoo*) in the home. Women cover their heads in the cathedral at Iyık Janyl, where white scarves are lent at the north door. The Order of St. Janyl the Hermit has a women's branch, and the Sisters of the Cross of Irad, founded by [[Maryam Janyl (nun)|Sister Maryam Janyl]], run the [[St. Maryam Catholic Academy]] in Talas.[6][21] ## See also - [[Marriage in Irad]] - [[Human rights in Irad]] - [[Adat Law in the ATR]] - [[Demographics of Irad]] ## References

The **climate of Irad** is continental, with hot summers, cold winters and low, irregular precipitation over most of the country. The northern plains are semi-arid or arid ([[wp:Köppen climate classification|Köppen]] *BSk* and *BWk*), the Talas valley is semi-arid, the river flats of the lower Naryn at the edge of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] have a warmer climate with dry summers (*Dsa*), and the [[Talas Alatau]], Chatkal and Fergana ranges pass from humid continental conditions on their middle slopes to an alpine climate on the highest ridges.[1] Because Irad lies far from any ocean, its weather is dominated in winter by cold air from the Siberian anticyclone and in spring and early summer by moist westerly air that drops most of its moisture on the mountains.[2] Most Iradis live in irrigated valleys whose farms depend on snow and glacier melt from the mountains, and the climate shapes the country's agriculture, its water politics and its transport. Spring brings mudflows and floods, summer brings heat, dust and the risk of drought and of outburst floods from glacial lakes, and winter brings snow that closes the mountain passes. Glacier retreat and a run of dry years since 2008 have made water supply a recurring subject of dispute between the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) and Irad's neighbors (see [[Glacier retreat in Irad]]).[3] ## Climate types and regions Temperature falls and precipitation rises with altitude, so that the climate changes more over a few tens of kilometers between a valley floor and the crest above it than across hundreds of kilometers of plain.[1] #### Northern plains The [[Betpak-Dala]], the [[Moiynkum Desert|Moiynkum]] sands and the [[Kyzylkum Fringe]] are the driest part of Irad. Annual precipitation is generally below 180 mm (7 in), summer temperatures often exceed 40 °C (104 °F), and cold waves in winter bring temperatures below −25 °C (−13 °F), although the snow cover is usually thin. Most rain falls in spring, when it brings a short season of ephemeral grasses and tulips to the desert pastures.[4] #### Chu lowlands [[Nurzhan]], at 470 m (1,540 ft) on the lower Chu, has a cold semi-arid climate (*BSk*) with large seasonal swings. July highs average 33 °C (91 °F) and the January mean is about −5 °C (23 °F); annual precipitation averages about 270 mm (10.6 in), most of it in spring. Summer dust storms are common, and outbreaks of Arctic air occasionally bring temperatures below −25 °C. Hailstorms that build over the mountains to the south are the main summer hazard for the farms of the lowlands, and since 2008 a weather radar of the ISEZ hydrometeorological service on the hill above [[Kök-Döbö]] has tracked them.[2][5] In winter, temperature inversions over the flat plain trap smoke from the city's heating plants, and air quality in Nurzhan is at its worst during the heating season, from mid-October to mid-April.[6] #### Talas valley [[Talas]], at about 1,250 m (4,100 ft), has a continental, semi-arid climate (*BSk*). July highs average about 29–30 °C (84–86 °F), occasionally exceeding 38 °C (100 °F), and January lows average about −12 °C (10 °F), with cold winds from the Siberian anticyclone. Annual precipitation is about 300 mm (12 in), with a maximum in April and May and a dry late summer.[7] The valley narrows and rises toward the east, and the upper valley around [[Orto-Ayyl]] has longer, snowier winters than the city. In the lower valley, around [[Kyzyl-Adyr]], summers are hotter and the irrigation canals run short in July and August in dry years.[8] #### Toktogul basin and the lower Naryn The Toktogul basin is sheltered by mountains on all sides and has milder winters than the Talas valley, with hot, dry summers. Below the dam, the Naryn gorge and the river flats around [[Iyık Janyl]] and [[Tash-Kömür]] have a climate closer to that of the Fergana Valley than to that of the north: at Iyık Janyl (about 650 m) July highs average about 34 °C (93 °F) and January lows about −5 °C (23 °F), and annual precipitation is about 450 mm (18 in), most of it as spring rain. Snow seldom lies for long in the towns but closes the high pastures above them from December to March.[9] #### Mountains Precipitation increases with altitude and toward the southwest. Moist westerly air brings up to 900–1,000 mm a year to the slopes facing the Fergana Valley, where it supports the walnut-fruit forests of [[Arslanbob]], while the northern slopes above the Talas valley are much drier.[1] In the mountains precipitation peaks in spring and early summer, often as afternoon storms. On the [[Aksay Plateau]], at 3,000–3,600 m, the ground is normally free of snow only from June to September, night frosts occur even in July, and snow can fall in any month.[10] The high pastures in general are open only from about June to September. ## Seasons - **Winter** (December to February) is cold and, on the plains, mostly dry and clear under the Siberian high. Snow and avalanches close most mountain passes from November to April. The [[Fergana Gateway]] on State Route 1 is shut for about 20 days in an average winter, when [[Iradiya]]'s flight between Talas and Tash-Kömür is the only link between the two parts of the ISEZ, and the road over the [[Kök-Bel Pass]] is often closed: in early 2020 drifts closed it for four days, and traffic was sent round by the lowland road.[11] On the tribal side, avalanches can cut off valley villages for weeks; in February and March 2012 [[Kara-Jylga]], north of the Toktogul Reservoir, was reached only by pack horses for five weeks.[12] Herders fear *jut*, an ice crust or deep snow that seals off the winter pasture and can kill large numbers of livestock.[1] - **Spring** (March to May) is the wettest season in most of Irad. Rapid snowmelt and thunderstorms send floods and mudflows (*sel*) down dry washes in the foothills: in April 1998 a torrent in the [[Kuru-Say]] cut the [[Trans-Talas Highway]] west of Kyzyl-Adyr, in May 2005 a mudflow down the [[Tuura-Say]] buried orchards on the Fergana rim, and in May 2016 a flash flood in the [[Kök-Moinok]] canyons destroyed houses in the Karatau hamlet of [[Tar-Say]].[13] - **Summer** (June to August) is hot and dry in the valleys and on the plains, and the rivers fed by snow and glacier melt run highest between May and July. In late summer, after weeks of hot weather, moraine-dammed glacial lakes in the Talas Alatau can burst: the lake at the head of the [[Köl-Sai]] broke through its moraine on 23 July 2012, and on the night of 22 July 2016 the moraine of Muz-Köl, at the head of the [[Muz-Suu]], partly failed and the flood damaged houses in Tash-Bulak. Neither flood caused deaths.[14] - **Autumn** (September to November) is dry and settled on the plains, with the first snow on the passes in October or November. The Toktogul Reservoir is fullest at the start of autumn, after the summer melt has been stored, and lowest in early spring.[15] ## Climate data The table compares the main weather stations of the ISEZ hydrometeorological service.[2][7][9] | Station | Elevation | Köppen | Average July high | Average January low | Annual precipitation | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Talas | 1,270 m | *BSk* | 29 °C (84 °F) | −12 °C (10 °F) | 293 mm (11.5 in) | | Nurzhan | 470 m | *BSk* | 33 °C (91 °F) | January mean about −5 °C (23 °F) | 270 mm (10.6 in) | | Iyık Janyl | 650 m | *Dsa* | 34 °C (93 °F) | −5 °C (23 °F) | 450 mm (18 in) | {{Weather box | location = Iyık Janyl (650 m), 1991–2020 normals | high = 4; 6; 13; 21; 26; 31; 34; 33; 28; 20; 12; 6 | low = -5; -3; 3; 9; 13; 18; 20; 19; 14; 8; 2; -3 | source = Iyık Janyl station of the ISEZ hydrometeorological service }} Monthly figures for Talas, including records since 1936, are given in the article on the city. The service also keeps mountain stations, such as the [[Kenkol Mountain Meteorological Post]], automated since 2011, whose snow data are used for avalanche warnings and runoff forecasts, and its glacier and lake measurements are made with the [[Manas Peak Glaciological Observatory]].[16] ## Droughts and water Because the irrigated valleys depend on rivers that rise in the mountains, a dry winter or a hot summer quickly becomes a water shortage. The year 2008 brought the lowest level on record in the Toktogul Reservoir and rolling power cuts through the winter of 2008–09, which led to the 2009 protocol that brought the reservoir and dam into the ISEZ.[15] In the drought of 2021 the flow of the Talas at the Kazakh border gauge fell to about half its mean in August, and Kazakhstan complained that it had received less than its share; the dispute was settled by counting releases from the Kyzyl-Adyr Reservoir. In 2023 the Toktogul Reservoir fell close to its minimum reserve, the authorities made an extra release in August after Uzbek protests, and power exports were cut the following winter.[3] In both years the Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate cut the water quotas of large users in the lower Chu, and the textile combine [[Zhetysu Industrial Textiles]] reduced its shifts.[17] Glacier melt supplies about 30–40 percent of the August flow of the high tributaries of the Talas. Glaciologists expect meltwater to keep rising until the 2030s or 2040s and then to decline, and some Chatkal catchments may already have passed that peak.[3] The ISEZ has responded with the Irrigation Modernization Programme, begun in 2018, for lining canals, laser leveling and drip irrigation, and with Executive Directive 2022/14, which requires dry-year water plans of large users and limits new rice paddies in the lower Chu.[3] ## See also - [[Geography of Irad]] - [[Glacier retreat in Irad]] - [[Talas River Hydrological Monitoring Service]] - [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Nurlan Sadikov | native_name = Russian: Нурлан Садыков | birth_date = 1931-03-14 | birth_place = Lower Talas valley (now Kara-Buura District) | death_date = 2017-01-21 | death_place = [[Talas]] | alma_mater = [[wp:Gerasimov Institute of Cinematography|VGIK]] | occupation = Film director, screenwriter | notable_works = *[[Zarina (film)|Zarina]]* (1968); *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]* (1979) }} **Nurlan Sadikov** (Russian: *Нурлан Садыков*; 14 March 1931 – 21 January 2017) was an Iradi film director and screenwriter, and a central figure of [[Cinema of Irad|Iradi Soviet cinema]]. His feature *[[Zarina (film)|Zarina]]* (1968) was the first Iradi film released to a wider Soviet audience, and his *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]* (1979) is credited with creating the genre known as the "Iradi Western" or "Soviet Western", in Irad usually called the "Eastern", although it was the only film of the genre he made. His last film, the documentary *[[Visions of Irad]]* (1984), is now regarded as a national treasure.{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}} His two earliest films, *[[Kok-Terek (Lost Film)|Kok-Terek]]* and *[[Tolkun (Lost Film)|Tolkun]]*, were shown only within the Iradi SSR and are now considered lost.[1] After independence Sadikov led efforts to save the Soviet-era film holdings of [[Talasfilm Studios]], and from 1995 to 2008 he was the first director of the [[Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation|Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation Institute]].[2] ## Early life and education Sadikov was born in a village in the lower Talas valley, in what is now Kara-Buura District, into a family of collective-farm horse breeders. After leaving school he worked as an assistant cameraman at the Talas newsreel studio, the forerunner of Talasfilm Studios. In 1952 he was admitted to the directing faculty of the [[wp:Gerasimov Institute of Cinematography|All-Union State Institute of Cinematography]] (VGIK) in [[wp:Moscow]], graduating in 1957.[1] ## Career #### Early films (1957–1967) Sadikov joined the newly founded Talasfilm Studios on his return from Moscow. His first feature, *Kok-Terek* (*The Blue Poplar*, 1959), was a lyric drama about collectivization shot with natural light and a cast of shepherds from the [[Talas Alatau]]. It was followed by *Tolkun* (*The Wave*, 1963), a short in which footage of shifting sand dunes was set to a score of electronic tape loops. Both films were distributed only within the republic. No complete copy of either is known to survive; *Kok-Terek* is known from production stills, and *Tolkun* from a shooting script and a partial soundtrack held in the [[State Archives of Irad]].[3] #### *Zarina* and the documentary years (1968–1977) *Zarina* (1968) was planned by the studio as a period action-adventure set in the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] era. Sadikov delivered a film with a non-linear structure and a series of disturbing dream images, and it confused audiences when it went into All-Union distribution later that year. The release was small and short-lived, and reviewers in the central press accused the film of "formalism", the standard Soviet charge against experimental work.[1] For most of the following decade Sadikov was assigned to the studio's documentary unit. His work there included *Naryn* (1975), a feature-length documentary about the construction of the Toktogul dam, now part of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]].[2] #### *Desert Sun’s Rebellion* and *Visions of Irad* (1978–1989) Sadikov returned to features with *Desert Sun’s Rebellion*, a project first assigned to the director Timur Aslanov, whom Sadikov replaced at the start of production. It was shot in 1978 in the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]] and the sands of the southern steppe with [[Almaz Sarybaev]] in the lead. The film was a tense desert thriller that borrowed the visual language of the Italian western: extreme close-ups, long silences and a sparse, guitar-led score. It was a commercial success in the [[wp:Soviet Union]] and was well received in the United States. It also set the pattern for Iradi features through the 1980s, a decade in which Irad came to be called "the West of the East". Sadikov was named People's Artist of the Iradi SSR in 1980.[1][4] He never made another Eastern. The studio expected a sequel, and instead he made *[[Eer (film)|Eer]]* (*The Saddle*, 1982), a quiet drama about an old saddler in the old town of [[Talas]] who makes one last saddle while his son leaves for the oil fields of Kobozev. He cast working saddlers in most of the parts. Talasfilm gave it a small release, and it was respected rather than popular; critics have since seen in its long, observed scenes of craft the road to his last film. In later interviews he admitted that he had no interest in the genre his film had started; critics have called *Desert Sun's Rebellion* Irad's *[[wp:Rififi]]*, a tense genre film that happened to wear the look of a spaghetti western. His final film, *Visions of Irad* (1984), was an unnarrated documentary of everyday life across the republic, from the factories and courtyards of Talas and Kobozev to the herding camps of the high pastures. It had a lukewarm reception on its release; since its restoration it has come to be regarded as a national treasure.[2] #### Post-Soviet work and archival career (1989–2008) Sadikov was artistic director of Talasfilm Studios from 1989 to 1995. During the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] and the [[First Iradi Civil War]], the studio lost heating and power. Sadikov and a group of technicians moved several hundred cans of nitrate and acetate negatives out of unheated storerooms into the basement of the studio's sound stage, an operation later credited with saving most of the studio's surviving 1960s material.[2] When the studio's film depository was reorganized as an independent institute in 1995, he became its first director. He held the post until 2008, overseeing the cataloging of the collection and the first restorations of Iradi Soviet films, including the restored *Desert Sun’s Rebellion* that opened the 2005 Talas International Film Festival organized by the [[Irad Film Society]].[5] ## Style Critics have identified two strands in Sadikov's work.[4] - The early films and *Zarina* are experimental. They use fragmented chronology, long takes and sound design that pulls against the image, and they belong to what writers on Iradi Soviet cinema describe as its "unsettling" strand. - *Desert Sun’s Rebellion* and the later features are tightly plotted genre films. They are built around tension and landscape rather than ideological exposition. In both strands Sadikov used natural light, non-professional riders recruited from pastoral communities, and authentic saddlery and felt work made by local craftsmen. Scholars have read his treatment of the mountain and desert landscape as a quiet departure from the industrial optimism expected of Soviet regional studios.[4] ## Later life and legacy From 1996 Sadikov taught directing at [[Talas State University]], where he was later an emeritus professor. He died in [[Talas]] in January 2017 at the age of 85.[2] Iradi film historians regard him as the founder of the Iradi Western, a title he did not welcome. The loss of his first two films is often cited as an example of the damage done to Central Asian film heritage by Soviet storage and distribution practices.[3] ## Selected filmography - *Kok-Terek* (*The Blue Poplar*, 1959). Lost. - *Tolkun* (*The Wave*, 1963, short). Lost. - *Zarina* (1968) - *Naryn* (1975, documentary) - *Desert Sun’s Rebellion* (1979) - *Eer* (*The Saddle*, 1982) - *Visions of Irad* (1984, documentary) ## See also - [[Kadyrbek Asylbekov]] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Beknur Karimov | native_name = Бекнур Каримов | birth_date = 1941-08-09 | birth_place = Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]), [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic|Iradi SSR]] | education = Kobozev art college; Higher Courses for Scriptwriters and Directors, Moscow (1968–1970) | occupation = Film director, painter | known_for = *[[Zalmax’s Dominion]]* (1977) }} **Beknur Karimov** (Russian: *Бекнур Каримов*; born 9 August 1941) is an Iradi film director and painter, known for *[[Zalmax’s Dominion]]* (1977), a Soviet attempt to remake [[wp:John Boorman|John Boorman's]] science-fiction film *[[wp:Zardoz]]* (1974). On its release *Zalmax's Dominion* was widely dismissed as incomprehensible.{{Citation needed|date=September 2026}} It has since become a cult film, valued for its dadaist absurdity. Karimov described himself as a "pervert of the screen". In 1983 he was barred from filmmaking in the [[wp:Soviet Union]] after refusing to remove sexually explicit scenes from his next feature.[1][2] ## Early life Karimov was born in Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]) to a family of oil-field engineers. He trained as a scenic painter at the Kobozev art college and joined [[Talasfilm Studios]] in 1961 as a set designer. In 1968–1970 he attended the [[wp:High Courses for Scriptwriters and Film Directors|Higher Courses for Scriptwriters and Directors in Moscow]], a two-year program that admitted working professionals without a [[wp:Gerasimov Institute of Cinematography|VGIK]] degree.[1] ## Career #### Early work Back at Talasfilm, Karimov directed two short films and a feature, *Tuz* (*Salt*, 1973), about workers at a salt lake in the southern steppe. The studio's artistic council criticized *Tuz* for "excessive symbolism" and released it only within the republic.[3] #### *Zalmax’s Dominion* In 1975 Karimov saw *Zardoz* at a closed screening for film professionals in [[wp:Moscow]]. Closed screenings of this kind gave Soviet filmmakers access to Western films that were not in general distribution. He proposed an Iradi version to Talasfilm. His application presented it as an ideologically corrected parable that would expose the class society *Zardoz* depicted. The republican film committee approved the script, and the film was shot in 1976 in the industrial zone of Kobozev and the [[Moiynkum Desert|Moiynkum sands]]. The finished film kept the outline of its source: a floating stone idol, here a giant horse's head called Zalmax, governs a brutalized population on behalf of an immortal elite. Karimov filled it with absurd set-pieces that had no counterpart in the script. Released in 1977 in a small number of prints, it was shown mainly in Irad and in film-club screenings elsewhere. Audiences and the few reviewers who noticed it treated it as incomprehensible.[2] #### *Desert Blue* Karimov's one venture into the Eastern, the genre started by [[Nurlan Sadikov]]'s *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]*, was *[[Desert Blue]]* (1981). A young woman, separated from her father while chasing the family herd, strays into the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] ranges and is set upon by the hill tribes there. It was the most conventional film he made and his only popular success: it played across the republic and was well reviewed. Later writers have criticized it for its portrayal of the Karatau tribes as savage and uncanny and for the way it sexualized its scenes of attempted sexual assault.[2] #### "Pervert of the screen" and the ban Karimov's self-description as a "pervert of the screen" (Russian: *извращенец экрана*) is first recorded in the minutes of a 1981 meeting of the Talasfilm artistic council. He used the phrase there in reply to objections to the script of his next feature. He later repeated it in interviews.[3] That feature, *Kyz Bulak* (*Maiden's Spring*, 1982), included several sexually explicit scenes. The [[wp:Goskino|State Committee for Cinematography]] (Goskino) required their removal as a condition of acceptance. Karimov refused to make the cuts, so the film was shelved. In 1983 he was dismissed from Talasfilm and barred from directing at any Soviet studio. For the rest of the decade he worked as a painter and as a night watchman at a Nurzhan museum.[1] *Kyz Bulak* was among the shelved films reviewed after 1986 by the Conflict Commission of the Union of Cinematographers of the USSR, which recommended the release of films banned in earlier decades. It was shown uncut at a small number of screenings in 1988.[3] #### After independence After 1992 Karimov made several low-budget video works in [[Talas]]. Some combined found Soviet industrial footage with felt and carpet motifs, and they were shown in galleries in Irad and [[wp:Almaty]]. He has not made a feature film since *Kyz Bulak*. [[IradOne]] has never broadcast his films. In a 2004 interview with the *[[Talas Herald]]*, he attributed this to their "unsuitability for families".[4] ## Style and reception Writers on Karimov's work describe it as closer to dada and the theater of the absurd than to the poetic cinema of his Soviet Central Asian contemporaries. His trademarks include non-sequitur dialogue, recitations of lists and timetables, and figures in animal masks. Iradi critics were long divided on whether his films were serious experiments or provocations. Their reputation has grown since the 1990s, when bootleg video copies of *Zalmax's Dominion* circulated among students in Talas and Nurzhan.[2] Karimov has a following among younger [[Iradis]] associated with the [[Iradi language revival]]. Performers in the [[Mor-Wave]] scene have drawn on his imagery in their stage shows.[4] ## Filmography - *Tuz* (*Salt*, 1973) - *Zalmax’s Dominion* (1977) - *Desert Blue* (1981) - *Kyz Bulak* (*Maiden's Spring*, 1982). Shelved and released in 1988. ## References

**Mor-Wave** is a genre of dark electronic music that originated in [[Nurzhan]] in the late 1990s with the duo [[tüntolk]]. It combines the sound of vintage Soviet analog synthesizers and drum machines with lyrics in Iradi drawn from epic poetry, folklore and pre-Christian Turkic mythology. Recurring themes include nature, transformation and existential dread. Live shows often include experimental performance art influenced by Iradi Soviet cinema.{{Citation needed|date=July 2026}} Mor-Wave has produced two main offshoots: the commercial [[Mor-Pop]] and the acoustic [[Mor-Folk]].[1] ## Etymology The name is usually explained as a compound of the Iradi *mor* ("violet; the color of dusk") and the English *wave*, following the English-language naming of Western genres such as coldwave and darkwave. Some writers connect *mor* instead with [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]], the bull-headed god of Iradi pre-Christian belief whose imagery is common in the genre. Members of tüntolk have given both explanations in interviews.[2] ## History #### Origins (1996–1999) Mor-Wave emerged in Nurzhan in the years after the [[First Iradi Civil War]]. The city, called Kobozev until 1992, had been the base of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]], and much of its heavy industry stood idle during the early territorial period. Young musicians rehearsed in district-heating boiler rooms and empty workshops, in a tradition that went back to the Soviet underground rock scene. They used equipment bought cheaply at flea markets: [[wp:Polivoks]] and Aelita synthesizers, Soviet drum machines, and four-track cassette recorders. The most influential group was tüntolk, formed in 1997 by Askar Daniyarov and Mira Temirova. Their cassette album *[[Jolchu (Album)|Jolchu]]* (1999) is generally treated as the genre's founding record.[1] Unlike most urban musicians of the time, who sang in Russian or English, tüntolk wrote in Iradi. Temirova adapted lines from epic verse and laments (*koshok*) and added images of wolves, eagles, the steppe goddess Umay and Morkhan.[2] #### First wave (1999–2007) *Jolchu* circulated on copied cassettes and on late-night programs on Nurzhan radio, and between 1999 and 2005 a small scene of groups grew up around it in Nurzhan and [[Talas]]. Among them were Kara Jel and Umay-9. Club nights in Nurzhan attracted visitors from [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Tashkent]], and the city gained a modest reputation abroad as a destination for followers of underground electronic music. The scene contracted after the outbreak of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007. Several venues closed under emergency regulations, and a number of musicians left for [[wp:Kazakhstan]].[1] #### Second wave (2014–present) A revival began in the mid-2010s among a generation of [[Iradis]] who had grown up fluent in English and increasingly interested in the Iradi language. Its center was Talas rather than Nurzhan. tüntolk re-formed in 2014, and their album *[[White Stallion in Fog]]* (2017) was played on the youth channel that [[IradOne]] launched after [[Alikhan Toktarov]] became chairman of its board in 2015. Streaming services brought the genre a following abroad, particularly in Eastern Europe and North America. Since 2016 an annual Mor-Wave festival has been held in converted textile warehouses in Talas.[3] Several Mor-Wave tracks were sung at the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas|2023 student protests in Talas]]. According to the *[[Talas Herald]]*, IradOne afterward dropped a number of tüntolk videos from rotation. The broadcaster did not comment.[4] ## Characteristics - **Sound:** slow to mid-tempo tracks built on analog synthesizer arpeggios, drum-machine patterns and post-punk bass lines. Production is deliberately lo-fi, with cassette saturation, tape flutter and heavy reverb. - **Traditional instruments:** samples or live playing of the three-stringed [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]] and the bowed *[[Kyl-kyak|kyl-kyak]]*, often detuned or processed. - **Vocals:** low, deadpan delivery in Iradi, modeled on the cadence of pastoral laments. - **Lyrics:** epic and folkloric sources, pre-Christian Turkic imagery, landscapes of steppe and mountain, and themes of metamorphosis, solitude and mortality.[1] ## Live performance Mor-Wave concerts commonly include performance art. Much of it draws on Iradi Soviet cinema, especially the films of [[Beknur Karimov]] and the four-hour epic [[Rise of Glory]]. Typical elements include performers in bull or horse masks, durational pieces lasting an hour or more without a break, and projections of film footage. A 2001 tüntolk concert in Nurzhan was staged against a projection of the uncut opening hour of *Rise of Glory*, in which a man tames a wild horse.[2] ## Subgenres - **Mor-Pop:** a commercial idol-pop form, often called Irad's "dark [[wp:K-pop]]", with choreographed groups, dance rhythms and pop song structures. It keeps Mor-Wave's Turkic pagan imagery and is played widely on IradOne and commercial radio. - **Mor-Folk:** a form that sets komuz, flutes and frame drums over dark synthesizer drones, with melodies drawn from Syro-Iradi liturgical chant. ## Notable artists and labels - **tüntolk** (Askar Daniyarov and Mira Temirova), the founders of the genre. *Jolchu* was first sold as an unfinished six-track cassette in 1999 and released as a full eight-track album by the Almaty studio Dala Sound in 2000. The duo followed it with the EP *[[Zvezda Irad (EP)|Zvezda Irad]]* (2002), whose single "Jyldyzdardy Kes" ("Cut the Stars in the Night") is their best-known song abroad; the darker, industrial *[[Kara Suu (Album)|Kara Suu]]* (2004); *White Stallion in Fog* (2017); and the lullaby album *[[Umay (Album)|Umay]]* (2022), which won the Altyn-Zhylky album prize in 2023. - **Kara Jel** and **Umay-9**, groups of the first wave in Nurzhan and Talas. - **[[Eski Ün]]**, a Talas ensemble and the leading Mor-Folk act, whose album *Kara Kün* (2021) was recorded in a teahouse in the Old City of Talas. Its English-language song "Dream of Living" is the only Mor-Folk song widely known abroad. - **[[Karakush (Group)|Karakush]]**, a five-member girl group formed in Talas in 2018 and the best-selling Mor-Pop act, known for "Ak Börü" ("White Wolf", 2021). - **[[Altyn Muuz (Group)|Altyn Muuz]]**, a novelty boy band formed on an IradOne youth program in 2019. Tündük Records, the Talas label of the scene, was run by Ruslan Ten, a former member of Umay-9, and released tüntolk's later albums, a 2017 remaster of *Jolchu* and Eski Ün's *Kara Kün*. After its songs were sung at the 2023 protests it underwent three tax inspections in 2024 and had its registration suspended that autumn, and Ten closed it in 2025. Its catalogue is administered by the Bishkek distributor [[Köch Audio]], through which almost all Iradi music now reaches streaming services.[5][6] ## Reception and controversy Ethnomusicologists have described Mor-Wave as one of the few post-Soviet Central Asian genres to reach international audiences without state sponsorship. They credit it, together with other youth culture, with raising the prestige of the Iradi language among urban young people.[1][3] The genre's use of Morkhan imagery has drawn criticism from clergy of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], since church tradition identifies Morkhan with Satan. In 2019 a planned concert in [[Iyık Janyl]] was canceled after protests by parishioners.[4] Critics within the scene have accused Mor-Pop artists and IradOne of commercializing the style.[3] ## References

{{Infobox musical artist | name = tüntolk | image = tuntolk_live_2003.jpg | caption = Mira Temirova and Askar Daniyarov at a club night in a [[Nurzhan]] boiler room, November 2003 | alt = A sweaty woman with wet hair over her face raises one fist behind a table of synthesizers, beside a bearded man in a gray hoodie playing keys, lit by camera flash against rusted boiler pipes | background = group_or_band | origin = [[Nurzhan]], Irad | genre = [[Mor-Wave]]; [[wp:Cold wave (music)|coldwave]]; [[wp:Electronic music|electronic]] | years_active = 1997–2007; 2014–present | labels = Self-released; Dala Sound; Tündük Records; [[Köch Audio]] | members = Askar Daniyarov; Mira Temirova }} **tüntolk** (stylized in lowercase) is an Iradi electronic music duo formed in [[Nurzhan]] in 1997 by Askar Daniyarov and Mira Temirova. Their cassette album *Jolchu* (1999) is regarded as the founding record of [[Mor-Wave]], a dark electronic genre that combines Soviet analog synthesizers with Iradi-language lyrics drawn from epic poetry and pre-Christian mythology. The duo split up in 2007 and re-formed in 2014. Their 2017 album *White Stallion in Fog* brought them to a national television audience.[1][2] ## Name The name combines the Iradi *tün* ("night") with a clipped form of *tolkun* ("wave"), and is usually glossed as "night wave". Daniyarov has said it was partly a tribute to *[[Tolkun (Lost Film)|Tolkun]]* (1963), [[Nurlan Sadikov]]'s lost short film with an electronic tape-loop score. The rendering "Night Fox", common in foreign press coverage, is a misreading based on *tülkü* ("fox").[2] ## History #### Formation and *Jolchu* (1997–1999) Daniyarov (born 1974) studied radio electronics at the [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]] and worked nights as a stoker in a district-heating boiler room in Nurzhan's [[Dastgoh District|Dastgoh district]]. Temirova (born 1977) was a philology student at [[Talas State University]]. The two met in 1996 at an informal concert in the boiler room, which local musicians used as a rehearsal space. They began recording together the following year.[2] Their equipment consisted of a [[wp:Polivoks]] synthesizer, a Soviet drum machine, a borrowed four-track cassette recorder and effects pedals that Daniyarov built himself. Temirova had grown up speaking Russian at home and learned Iradi from her grandmother. Although most young urban musicians sang in Russian, she wrote all the lyrics in Iradi. *Jolchu* ("Wayfarer") was self-released on cassette in 1999 in an unfinished six-track form; the full album, completed and remastered in Almaty, followed in 2000. Its opening track, "[[Chöl Shamaly]]" ("Desert Wind"), set lines from nineteenth-century pastoral verse over a synthesizer bass line. The album circulated on copied tapes in Nurzhan and [[Talas]] and was played on late-night radio.[1] #### Territorial-era career (1999–2007) tüntolk toured clubs in Irad, [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Tashkent]] in the early 2000s. They released an EP, *Zvezda Irad* (2002), whose title mixes Russian and Iradi ("Star of Irad"); its song "[[Cut the Stars in the Night]]" was used in the Russian film *[[wp:Night Watch (2004 film)|Night Watch]]* (2004) and the German film *[[wp:Head-On (film)|Head-On]]* (2004) and became their best-known song abroad. A second album, *Kara Suu* ("Black Water"), followed in 2004. Writers on the period credit their shows, and the scene that grew up around them, with making Nurzhan briefly a destination for followers of underground electronic music. The duo stopped performing in 2007, during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. Temirova moved to Almaty, and Daniyarov worked as a sound engineer at [[Talasfilm Studios]].[1] #### Reunion (2014–present) tüntolk re-formed in Talas in 2014 and toured the city's university clubs. Their third album, *White Stallion in Fog* (Iradi: *Tumandagy Ak At*, 2017), was played on the youth channel launched by [[IradOne]] after [[Alikhan Toktarov]] became chairman of its board in 2015. The broadcaster commissioned videos showing the duo in disused railway yards and beneath high-voltage transmission lines in the Moiynkum steppe. The album also found an audience abroad through streaming services. A fourth album, *Umay*, followed in 2022.[3] After songs from *White Stallion in Fog*, among them "[[My Home My Heart My Soul]]", were sung at the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas|2023 student protests in Talas]], IradOne removed several of the band's videos from rotation, according to the *[[Talas Herald]]*. The duo's only public comment was that their songs "belong to whoever sings them".[4] ## Musical style and performance tüntolk's sound is built on synthesizer bass lines and arpeggios, drum machine patterns, bass guitar and heavily reverberated vocals. Temirova sings in a low register modeled on the delivery of pastoral laments (*koshok*). The duo sometimes adds samples of the *[[Kyl-kyak|kyl-kyak]]* and the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]]. Their lyrics draw on epic verse and on pre-Christian Turkic imagery, including the goddess Umay and the bull-headed [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]].[2] Their concerts include performance art influenced by Iradi Soviet cinema. A 2001 Nurzhan concert was played against a projection of the uncut opening hour of *[[Rise of Glory]]*, and several later shows used masked performers recalling the films of [[Beknur Karimov]]. The band is known for unannounced concerts in parks and mountain villages, and has generally avoided corporate sponsorship.[3] ## Members - Askar Daniyarov: synthesizers, drum programming, bass guitar (1997–2007, 2014–present) - Mira Temirova: vocals, lyrics, *kyl-kyak* samples (1997–2007, 2014–present) ## Discography Studio albums - *[[Jolchu (Album)|Jolchu]]* (1999) - *[[Kara Suu (Album)|Kara Suu]]* (2004) - *[[White Stallion in Fog]]* (2017) - *[[Umay (Album)|Umay]]* (2022) Extended plays - *[[Zvezda Irad (EP)|Zvezda Irad]]* (2002) Singles - "[[Cut the Stars in the Night]]" (2002) - "Tumandagy Ak At" (2017) - "[[My Home My Heart My Soul]]" (2017) ## Legacy {{Expand section|date=July 2026}} tüntolk are credited with founding Mor-Wave. Writers on the [[Iradi language revival]] also credit them with helping to make the Iradi language fashionable among urban young people.[3] ## References
