{{Infobox film | name = Desert Sun’s Rebellion | native_name = *Chöl Künü Kötörülüshü* | director = [[Nurlan Sadikov]] | writer = Nurlan Sadikov; Vadim Korolyov | starring = [[Almaz Sarybaev]]; Gennady Ostapenko; Erkin Sultanbekov; Gulnara Alimbekova | music = Asan Jumabaev | cinematography = Vladimir Pak | studio = [[Talasfilm Studios]] | released = 1979-03 (Talas) | country = Soviet Union }} **Desert Sun’s Rebellion** (Russian: *Мятеж полуденного солнца*; Iradi: *Chöl Künü Kötörülüshü*) is a 1979 Soviet thriller film directed by [[Nurlan Sadikov]] for [[Talasfilm Studios]], starring [[Almaz Sarybaev]]. Set in the desert borderlands of the Iradi SSR in the early 1920s, it follows a former cavalryman who leads a small crew to steal a herd of requisitioned horses back from a warlord's stronghold, and the crew's falling-out on the way across the sands. Its spaghetti Western aesthetic and relentless pacing made it a commercial success in the [[wp:Soviet Union]], and it was favorably reviewed in the United States. It created the genre known as the Iradi Western or Soviet Western, in Irad usually called the "Eastern", which shaped Iradi film production through the 1980s, and it is often described as Irad's *[[wp:Rififi]]* in the look of a spaghetti western.[1][2] ## Plot In 1922 Daniyar (Sarybaev), a former cavalryman who had fought alongside the [[wp:Red Guards (Russia)|Red Guards]] against the [[wp:Turkestan Autonomy|Kokand Autonomy]], returns to his clan's winter grounds at the edge of the sands. The clan's horses, requisitioned for the [[wp:Red Army]], have been stolen on their way to the railhead by the warlord Kara-Bek (Erkin Sultanbekov), who holds them in a walled caravanserai deep in the desert while he waits for buyers from across the frontier. Commissar Lugovoy (Gennady Ostapenko) cannot take the fort by force. He offers Daniyar a pardon for his past if he will steal the herd back, and keeps Daniyar's sister Aisha (Gulnara Alimbekova) in town as a guarantee. Daniyar gathers a crew of five: a deserter who knows the fort's wells, an old horse thief, two brothers from a rival clan and a Russian railwayman with a stopwatch. They study the caravanserai for days from the dunes, timing the guards and the watering of the herd. The theft itself, at night, runs for almost thirty minutes without dialogue or music: the crew drug the guards' water, muffle the horses' hooves with felt and lead the herd out through the stable vaults one animal at a time. The crossing back to the railhead goes wrong. Kara-Bek's riders follow as dust on the horizon, the wells are poisoned, and the crew begin to argue over the herd, which each of them now has reason to keep. The final sequence takes place on a salt flat at noon, where a drawn-out standoff between the crew, Kara-Bek's riders and a detachment sent by Lugovoy ends in a battle in which most of the characters die. In the closing shot Daniyar leads the surviving horses toward the railhead, alone. The film does not say whether he will hand them over.[1] ## Cast - Almaz Sarybaev as Daniyar - Gennady Ostapenko as Commissar Lugovoy - Erkin Sultanbekov as Kara-Bek - Gulnara Alimbekova as Aisha ## Production The project was first assigned to the director Timur Aslanov. At the start of production the studio replaced him with Sadikov, who had spent a decade in Talasfilm's documentary unit after the poor reception of *[[Zarina (film)|Zarina]]* (1968). Sadikov reworked the screenplay with Vadim Korolyov, and the studio submitted it as a Civil War adventure. Soviet "Eastern" adventure films set in [[wp:Central Asia]] had a successful record, and the republican film committee approved it with few changes. The committee asked only that the commissar be made more sympathetic.[2] Filming took place in the summer of 1978 in the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]] and the southern sands, with no studio sets. Temperatures on location reportedly exceeded 45 °C.{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}} Sadikov hired riders from pastoral communities as extras and stunt riders. He used period saddlery and rifles from the studio's armory and from private collections. Cinematographer Vladimir Pak shot much of the film in extreme close-up and long static wide shots, borrowing from Italian westerns, which Soviet professionals could see at closed screenings. The score by Asan Jumabaev combines the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]] with electric guitar, whistling and long passages of silence.[3] ## Release The film premiered in [[Talas]] in March 1979 and went into All-Union distribution later that year. According to Soviet distribution figures, it drew about 17.9 million viewers in its first year. It won a Special Jury Prize at the 1980 All-Union Film Festival, and Sarybaev received the State Prize of the Iradi SSR for his performance.[2] In late 1979 it was shown in [[wp:New York City|New York]] in a program of new Soviet films.[1] ## Reception Soviet reviewers praised the film's craft and Sarybaev's performance. Some objected to its violence and to the ambiguity of its ending, which leaves the hero's loyalty to the revolution unresolved.[2] In the United States, Walter Goodman wrote for *The New York Times* that "this unforgiving pacing ramps up and up with no release … there is a visceral discomfort to it, a feeling that you are there, under the unforgiving sun".[4] ## Legacy *Desert Sun’s Rebellion* is credited with creating the Iradi Western, and it set the tone for Iradi films for the rest of the Soviet period. During the 1980s Irad became known as "the West of the East". Its studios produced a series of films in the same mold by other directors, among them Timur Aslanov's *[[The Golden Bay]]* (1980), [[Beknur Karimov]]'s *[[Desert Blue]]* (1981), Adil Rakhimov's *[[Guide of the Sands]]* (1981) and *[[The Silver Horseshoe]]* (1984), Kairat Amankulov's *[[Track of the Snow Leopard]]* (1983) and *[[Journey of the Steppes]]* (1988) and Malik Shakirov's *[[Vengeance Rider]]* (1986). Sadikov himself never returned to the genre and later said he had no interest in it.[1] Its cast and crew carried the genre on. Erkin Sultanbekov played warlords in *[[The Golden Bay]]* (1980) and *[[Vengeance Rider]]* (1986), Gulnara Alimbekova took the lead in *[[Desert Blue]]* (1981), Sarybaev parodied his own Daniyar in *[[The Silver Horseshoe]]* (1984), Vladimir Pak photographed *Vengeance Rider*, and second-unit cameraman [[Kadyrbek Asylbekov]] shot *[[Guide of the Sands]]* (1981) and *[[Journey of the Steppes]]* (1988). Timur Aslanov, whom Sadikov had replaced, made *The Golden Bay* the following year.[3] The [[Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation|Talasfilm Archives]] restored the film from a duplicate negative and surviving prints in 2004. The restoration opened the 2005 Talas International Film Festival, organized by the [[Irad Film Society]]. Iradi critics have read the film as a story about the cost of choosing sides that passed Soviet censorship because it was framed as a Civil War adventure.[3] ## References

{{Infobox film | name = Rise of Glory | native_name = *Danktyn Kötörülüshü* | director = Talgat Osmonov | starring = [[Almaz Sarybaev]] | studio = [[Talasfilm Studios]] | released = 1979 (Talas and Kobozev) | runtime = About 4 hours (two parts) | country = Soviet Union }} **Rise of Glory** (Russian: *Восхождение славы*; Iradi: *Danktyn Kötörülüshü*) is a 1979 Soviet historical epic film directed by Talgat Osmonov for [[Talasfilm Studios]]. Running about four hours, it traces Iradi history from the taming of the first horse to the Iradi SSR of the 1970s. Its unconventional form baffled audiences. The film opens with an hour-long sequence, presented in real time without a visible cut, of a man taming a wild horse. Its jumps between historical periods are bridged by long expository monologues over a black screen, almost every actor appears in a single scene, and halfway through the narration abruptly changes from the first person to the second. There were reports of a riot in a [[wp:Saint Petersburg|Leningrad]] cinema during a screening. Opinion on the film remains sharply divided.[1][2] ## Synopsis The film is organized as a sequence of episodes rather than a continuous story: - **The first horse.** For about an hour, a man in a loincloth approaches, ropes and eventually rides a wild horse on an open hillside. There is no dialogue or music, and there are no visible cuts. Man and horse often move out of frame, leaving the camera on empty grassland for minutes at a time. The episode depicts the Iradi national belief that [[Botai Culture in Irad|horse domestication began in Irad]]. - **Antiquity to the Kokand era.** Short episodes depict the "heavenly horses" of [[wp:Dayuan]], Sogdian merchants on the [[wp:Silk Road]], the coming of the Turkic khaganates and Christian missionaries, the Mongol conquest and [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] rule. Each is introduced by several minutes of narration over a black screen. - **1916 and the revolution.** An episode set during the [[The Lost Tribes of 1916|1916 flight]] over the mountain passes, after the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]], features [[Almaz Sarybaev]] as a clan chieftain in a single fourteen-minute scene. Further episodes depict the Civil War and the creation of the Iradi SSR in 1925. - **The Soviet present.** The final episodes show collective farms, the oil fields of Kobozev and the building of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex|Toktogul dam]]. The film ends on a wide shot of a horse herd grazing beneath power lines. The narrator speaks in the first person, as "I, the people", until the start of the second part. From there he addresses the viewer as "you" until the end. Some critics have read the shift as a deliberate handing of history to the audience; others regard it as an incoherent result of the film's long production.[2] ## Production *Rise of Glory* was commissioned by Talasfilm in 1972 for the fiftieth anniversary of the Iradi SSR in 1975. Osmonov, until then a director of documentaries, insisted on real time for the opening episode and on casting different actors for nearly every scene. Production overran by four years.[3] A 35 mm camera magazine of the period held only about ten minutes of film, so the opening hour could not have been shot in one take. Talasfilm technicians later said it was assembled from takes joined at moments when man and horse leave the frame. The horse was a semi-feral mare from a stud in the [[Talas Alatau]] foothills, and the episode took nearly three weeks to film.[3] ## Release The republican film committee accepted the film in 1979, partly because its final hour glorified Soviet construction. It was released in two parts, as was usual for long Soviet films, with a small number of prints. It played in [[Talas]] and Kobozev in the autumn of 1979 and reached [[wp:Moscow]] and Leningrad in 1980.[1] Accounts circulated of a riot in a Leningrad cinema, said to have begun when audience members demanded refunds during the opening hour. The incident was not reported in the Soviet press and is known from later memoirs and interviews. Historians treat the details as unconfirmed.[2] ## Reception Contemporary audiences were largely baffled, and attendance outside Irad was low. Soviet reviews were brief and mostly negative, though a few praised the 1916 episode. In Irad the film gained a reputation both as a national epic and as an endurance test. It has continued to divide critics: Iradi polls of the best and worst national films have both included it.[2][4] ## Legacy The 1916 episode was the first extended depiction in a Soviet film of the flight over the passes. Writers on national memory cite it as an early public treatment of an event that had rarely been discussed openly, and critics have likened it to [[Kemel Ishakov]]'s novel *Akyrky Ashuu* (*The Last Pass*, 1964), the best-known account of the flight, which the film does not credit.[4] The opening hour has been quoted in Iradi performance art, including [[Mor-Wave]] concerts that projected it in full. The [[Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation|Talasfilm Archives]] completed a restoration of the full version in 2019. Complete screenings remain rare. Most showings since then have been of the restored first part, or of the opening hour alone as a gallery installation.[3] ## References

  2. ^ Central Asian Review of Screen Studies (2019). 'Four Hours of Glory: Narration and Endurance in Osmonov's Epic.' Vol. 13, Iss. 2, pp. 77–101.
  3. ^ Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation Institute (2019). Rise of Glory: Restoration Notes. Talas.
  4. ^ Talas State University Press (2020). Historical Memory and the 1916 Tragedy in Iradi Cinema, pp. 88–114.

{{Infobox film | name = Zarina | native_name = *Зарина* | director = [[Nurlan Sadikov]] | starring = Gulnara Alimbekova; [[Almaz Sarybaev]]; Kubat Seitkaziev | cinematography = Vladimir Pak | studio = [[Talasfilm Studios]] | released = 1968 | country = Soviet Union | language = Iradi (dubbed into Russian) }} **Zarina** (Russian and Iradi: *Зарина*) is a 1968 Soviet film directed by [[Nurlan Sadikov]] for [[Talasfilm Studios]], starring Gulnara Alimbekova and [[Almaz Sarybaev]]. It was the first Iradi film released to a wider Soviet audience.{{Citation needed|date=September 2026}} The studio planned it as a period action-adventure set in the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] era. Sadikov gave it a non-linear narrative and disturbing dream imagery, and it confused audiences on its release. It was withdrawn after a short run. Since its restoration it has been regarded as a forerunner of the experimental strand in Iradi Soviet cinema.[1][2] ## Plot Because the film presents its events out of order, published synopses differ. The studio's 1968 release notes summarize it as follows.[3] In the [[Talas Alatau]] under Kokand rule, Zarina (Alimbekova) is the daughter of a horse trainer and the best rider in her settlement. Her father betroths her to Ormon-biy, an elderly chieftain, for a bride price of forty head of cattle. She challenges Ormon-biy to *kyz kuu*, the courtship race, and wins. The chieftain refuses to honor the result. Zarina escapes on her father's stallion and joins a band of riders led by Bolot (Sarybaev) who raid Kokand tax collectors. After a series of raids and pursuits she is captured in an ambush. The ending leaves her fate unclear. The film opens with Zarina's capture and moves back and forth in time. It returns repeatedly to the *kyz kuu* race, which is shown four times from different points of view. Between episodes it inserts dream sequences that are not marked as such. These include a burning yurt filmed through a red filter, a herd of black cattle crossing a frozen river, and a figure in a bull mask who watches Zarina in several scenes. Iradi viewers would have recognized the figure as [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]].[2] ## Cast - Gulnara Alimbekova as Zarina - Almaz Sarybaev as Bolot - Kubat Seitkaziev as Ormon-biy ## Production *Zarina* was Sadikov's third film and his first full-length feature in color. Talasfilm intended it as an accessible adventure that could earn the studio its first All-Union release, after his earlier films *[[Kok-Terek (Lost Film)|Kok-Terek]]* and *[[Tolkun (Lost Film)|Tolkun]]* had been shown only in the republic. It was shot in 1967 in the Talas Alatau and near [[Iyık Janyl]]. The cinematographer was Vladimir Pak, a [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]] who later shot *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]*. Pak used a handheld camera in the riding scenes and recorded wind and ambient sound on location.[3] Sadikov restructured the film during editing. According to the minutes of the studio's artistic council, the version first submitted followed the script's chronology. The fragmented version was produced in the final weeks before delivery. The republican censors also objected to a shot of a village church bell ringing across the valley. The shot was kept after several appeals.[3] ## Release and reception The film was accepted for All-Union distribution in 1968 and dubbed into Russian, but it was released with a small number of prints. Audiences expecting an adventure film found it hard to follow. Reviewers in the central press accused it of "formalism", and it was withdrawn from most cinemas within months.[1] The reception affected Sadikov's career: for most of the next decade the studio assigned him to documentaries. ## Legacy *Zarina* was rarely shown in the Soviet period. Its reputation grew after 1992, when the [[Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation|Talasfilm Archives]] began screening its print. The archive completed a restoration in 2014. Writers on Iradi cinema now treat it as the first example of the experimental and unsettling style associated with Iradi Soviet film, and as a precursor of Sadikov's *Desert Sun’s Rebellion*. Feminist critics have discussed its heroine, who wins her race but cannot escape its consequences, as an unusually bleak treatment of women's autonomy for Soviet cinema of the period.[2] ## References

  2. ^ Central Asian Review of Screen Studies (2022). 'Time, Dream and the Horsewoman in Sadikov's Zarina.' Vol. 16, Iss. 1, pp. 32–48.
  3. ^ State Archives of Irad (Talas), Fond 412: Republican Film Production Catalogues (1954–1975).

{{Infobox film | name = Zalmax’s Dominion | native_name = *Zalmaxtyn Biyligi* | director = [[Beknur Karimov]] | writer = Beknur Karimov | based_on = *[[wp:Zardoz]]* (1974) | starring = Marat Kenzhebaev; Larisa Voronova; Erkin Sultanbekov | studio = [[Talasfilm Studios]] | released = 1977 | country = Soviet Union }} **Zalmax’s Dominion** (Russian: *Владычество Залмакса*; Iradi: *Zalmaxtyn Biyligi*) is a 1977 Soviet science-fiction film written and directed by [[Beknur Karimov]] for [[Talasfilm Studios]]. It was a Soviet attempt to remake [[wp:John Boorman|John Boorman's]] *[[wp:Zardoz]]* (1974). Contemporary audiences dismissed it as incomprehensible. It has since become a cult film, valued for its dadaist absurdity.[1][2] ## Plot In a distant future the steppe is ruled by Zalmax, a giant stone horse's head that floats over the land. Zalmax supplies rifles to a caste of Riders, who keep the Toilers in submission and deliver their grain to it. One Rider, Kuban (Marat Kenzhebaev), hides inside the head and is carried to the Garden, an enclosed estate where an immortal elite lives in apathy and boredom. Kuban learns that Zalmax is a fabrication of the Elders. He brings about the collapse of the Garden, and the Elders welcome the death they have been denied.[2] This outline follows *Zardoz*. Karimov filled it with episodes that have no counterpart in the source and little connection to the plot. In one, the Elders recite railway timetables in unison; in another, an accordion ensemble plays on a salt flat while a man in a suit sweeps the ground around them. The head lands in a collective-farm canteen and is served soup. There are intertitles in [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] script that are never translated, and a debate held entirely in numbers. The final ten minutes show Kuban riding toward the camera without getting any closer.[2] ## Cast - Marat Kenzhebaev as Kuban - Larisa Voronova as the First Elder - Erkin Sultanbekov as the Keeper of the Garden ## Production Karimov saw *Zardoz* in 1975 at a closed screening for film professionals in [[wp:Moscow]]. He proposed a version to Talasfilm. His application described it as an ideologically corrected parable that would turn the source's picture of a decadent elite into a critique of class society. The studio's artistic council and the republican film committee approved the script, which followed the source's plot closely and contained none of the episodes later added.[3] Filming took place in 1976 in the industrial zone of Kobozev and in the [[Moiynkum Desert|Moiynkum sands]]. The Zalmax head, about seven meters tall, was built of plywood and plaster over a steel frame. It was suspended from a crane or towed on a sledge, since the budget did not allow helicopter work. The absurdist episodes were written and shot during production. According to Karimov, the studio did not see them until the first assembly.[3] ## Release The republican committee accepted the film in 1977 after minor cuts, but assigned it a limited release with a small number of prints. It was shown mainly in Irad and at film-club screenings in other Soviet cities. Audiences walked out in large numbers. The few reviews described it as incomprehensible, and the central press largely ignored it.[1] After Karimov was barred from directing in 1983, the film was withdrawn from circulation. ## Reception and cult status *Zalmax's Dominion* was rediscovered in the 1990s through bootleg video copies that circulated among students in [[Talas]] and [[Nurzhan]] during the territorial period. Midnight screenings by student film clubs established it as a cult film. Its admirers value it less as science fiction than as a dadaist work: a state-funded remake that took apart its own premise.[2] Writers on Iradi cinema place it alongside *[[Zarina (film)|Zarina]]* and *[[Rise of Glory]]* as an example of the experimental and unsettling tendency in Iradi Soviet film. Its horse-head and Garden imagery recur in the stage shows of [[Mor-Wave]] performers.[4] The [[Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation|Talasfilm Archives]] restored the film from a duplicate negative and surviving prints in 2011, and it has since been shown regularly at the archive's cinematheque. ## References

  2. ^ Talas Journal of Cultural Studies (2023). 'Surrealism and the Nomadic Soul in Karimov's Cinema.' Vol. 11, Iss. 1, pp. 112–129.
  3. ^ State Archives of Irad (Talas), Fond 415: Minutes of the Talasfilm Artistic Council (1961–1991).
  4. ^ Central Asian Cultural Studies Review (2022). 'Nocturnal Steppe: Electronic Subcultures in the ISEZ.' Vol. 14, pp. 88–104.

The **Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation Institute** (Iradi: *Talasfilm Arkhivteri*) is the national film archive of Irad, located on Cinema Boulevard in [[Talas]]. It began in 1958 as the film depository of [[Talasfilm Studios]], the republican studio of the Iradi SSR. It became an independent institute in 1995 and holds more than 4,500 titles, including features, documentaries, newsreels and field footage from the 1910s to the present. Its holdings include the surviving materials of the major Iradi Soviet films, among them *[[Zarina (film)|Zarina]]*, *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]*, *[[Rise of Glory]]* and *[[Zalmax’s Dominion]]*.[1] ## History #### Soviet period Talasfilm Studios was founded in 1954. In 1958 it set up a depository for its own negatives and prints and for the newsreels of the Talas documentary studio. Under Soviet rules, original negatives of feature films were normally deposited with [[wp:Gosfilmofond]], the central state film archive near [[wp:Moscow]], and republican studios kept duplicate negatives and distribution prints. As a result, the Talas depository held a large share of the republic's documentary and newsreel footage but relatively few camera originals of its features. Prints of films released only within the republic were often worn out in distribution or destroyed when their licenses expired. This is how [[Nurlan Sadikov]]'s *[[Kok-Terek (Lost Film)|Kok-Terek]]* (1959) and *[[Tolkun (Lost Film)|Tolkun]]* (1963) were lost.[1][2] #### Independence and reorganization During the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] and the [[First Iradi Civil War]], the studio lost heating and power. Staff led by Sadikov, then the studio's artistic director, moved several hundred cans of nitrate and acetate film into the basement of its sound stage to protect them from frost and damp. In 1995 an act of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] separated the depository from the studio and reconstituted it as the Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation Institute. Sadikov was its first director, serving until 2008.[2] #### Restoration program The archive's restoration work began in the early 2000s with support from European film archives and cultural foundations. A film scanner and a sound restoration suite were installed in 2008. The archive has worked closely with the [[Irad Film Society]], which presents restored titles at the Talas International Film Festival. Its principal restorations include: - *Desert Sun’s Rebellion* (completed 2004; premiered at the 2005 festival) - *Zalmax’s Dominion* (2011) - *Zarina* (2014) - *Rise of Glory* (full version, 2019) Negotiations with Gosfilmofond for copies of the original negatives of Iradi Soviet features have been under way since the late 1990s. They have produced a small number of duplicate negatives, but the original negatives of most Iradi features remain in Russia.[3] The archive closed for several months during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007. Since the establishment of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] it has been funded mainly from the ISEZ budget, supplemented by foreign grants.[3] ## Collections - **Pre-Soviet and revolutionary footage (1916–1924):** a small group of reels, some copied from Russian military and private sources, showing imperial troops in [[wp:Semirechye]], early Soviet authorities in the region and ethnographic scenes, including eagle hunting. - **Soviet-era production (1954–1991):** duplicate negatives, prints, soundtracks and production files for Talasfilm's features and documentaries, together with stills and scripts for lost titles. - **Post-Soviet and civil war footage (1992–2007):** unedited newsreel and amateur footage of the Winter Uprising, the arrival of American forces after the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]], and the fighting of 2007. - **Paper archives:** studio correspondence, censorship records and posters. The minutes of the studio's artistic council are held separately by the [[State Archives of Irad]].[1] ## Public access The archive runs a cinematheque, which holds regular retrospectives and independent screenings popular with students, and a research library used by students and staff of [[Talas State University]]. Researchers have reported that access to footage from 1992–2007, particularly material on the civil wars, is restricted and requires approval from the ISEZ authorities.[3] ## References
  1. ^ Soviet Film Heritage Institute (1984). Directory of Central Asian Cinematographers and Vaults. Iskusstvo, Moscow, pp. 188–204.
  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2009). Nurlan Sadikov and the Iradi Western, pp. 140–152.
  3. ^ Central Asian Cultural Studies Review (2022). 'Preserving Nitrate Memory in the Talas Basin.' Vol. 14, pp. 112–128.

**Burkut Saluu** (Iradi: *bürküt saluu*, "releasing the eagle") is the practice of hunting with golden eagles from horseback, as carried on in Irad by falconers known as *berkutchi*. Hunters train female golden eagles to take foxes, hares and marmots, and occasionally young wolves, and they work mainly in late autumn and winter in the mountains and steppe of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. The tradition is shared with the Kyrgyz and [[wp:Kazakhs]]. In Irad it is both a subsistence practice in some highland communities and a competitive sport, judged by the ideal of *[[Körktüülük|körktüülük]]*, the effortless display of dignity, grace and courage. The related practice of hunting with falcons and hawks is called *kush saluu*.[1][2] ## History Hunting with birds of prey on the Central Asian steppe is attested in Turkic and Mongol sources from the medieval period, and eagle hunting was associated with the households of nomadic rulers. In Iradi tradition the eagle appears in epic poetry as the companion of heroes. Clan genealogies in the Talas Alatau and [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal]] ranges record hereditary lines of berkutchi going back several generations.[1] Under Russian and then Soviet rule, eagle hunting continued in the mountain districts, but its character changed. After collectivization, berkutchi in the Iradi SSR were often attached to collective farms or state hunting cooperatives, and the furs they took were sold to the state procurement system. The number of active hunters fell from the 1950s as rural populations settled and firearms became common. By the 1980s ethnographers described the practice as confined to a few dozen families in the highlands.[3] After 1992 burkut saluu revived, both as a marker of national and clan identity and, during the territorial period, as an attraction for foreign visitors. The first national eagle-hunting festival was held in 1995. Since then competitions have been held under the auspices of the [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]], established in 1993.[2] ## Practice #### Birds Hunters use female golden eagles (*Aquila chrysaetos*), which are larger and more powerful than males and weigh between about 4 and 6.5 kilograms. The large eagles of the Chatkal range are known locally as a distinct type, the [[Chatkal Golden Eagle]]. Birds are obtained in one of two ways. Some are taken as nestlings (*balapan*) shortly before fledging, from eyries in the [[Talas Alatau]] and Chatkal ranges. Others are trapped as young adults in their first or second autumn, and many berkutchi consider these better hunters.[2] #### Training Training lasts several months and follows an established sequence: - **Manning:** the bird is kept hooded (*tomogo*), handled constantly and accustomed to the hunter's voice. Traditionally it is also kept awake for long periods until it accepts food from the hand. - **Weight control:** feeding is managed so that the eagle is keen to hunt but not weakened. - **Lure work:** the eagle learns to fly to the hunter's glove from increasing distances and to strike a lure (*chyrga*) made from a fox or hare skin dragged behind a rider. - **Hunting:** the eagle is taken into the field with an experienced bird or hunter. The hunter carries the eagle on a heavy leather glove, with the forearm supported by a wooden rest (*baldak*) fixed to the saddle. Hunting takes place mainly from November to February, when tracks show in the snow and pelts are at their best. The hunter rides to a ridge, scans the slopes below and unhoods the eagle when quarry is flushed, often with the help of beaters or *taigan* sighthounds. Most berkutchi ride hardy [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses.[2] #### Customs Customary law (*[[Adat (Customary Law)|adat]]*) and hunters' tradition govern several aspects of the practice. An eagle is normally kept for ten to twelve years. It is then released into the mountains in the breeding season after a ceremony (*kaytaruu*), at which the hunter leaves meat for it. Selling a trained eagle is regarded as shameful in many families, and birds pass between hunters as gifts. Among Christian berkutchi, eagles and hunting equipment are commonly blessed by a priest before the season opens.[3] ## Competitions and festivals The main annual event is the Salburun festival, held each autumn in the pastures outside [[Talas]] and organized with the National Equestrian Sports Directorate. It brings together berkutchi from the ISEZ and the Autonomous Tribal Regions. Its events include: - recall of the eagle to the glove over a set distance; - strikes on a dragged lure (*chyrga*); - hunting with live quarry, judged on speed and style; - riding and archery contests, as well as events for falcons and *taigan* hounds. Judges score the hunters as well as the birds, and award marks for bearing and composure according to the ideal of *körktüülük*.[2] ## Contemporary status In 2022 the Directorate registered 71 active eagle hunters, most of them in the Talas Alatau and Chatkal Highlands planning zones. Clan elders in the Autonomous Tribal Regions say the true number is higher, since many hunters do not register with ISEZ bodies. Taking eagles from the wild requires a permit in the ISEZ and the approval of clan councils in the tribal regions. International trade in golden eagles is restricted under [[wp:CITES]]. Irad is not a State Party to the [[wp:UNESCO]] conventions, so Iradi eagle hunting is not included in the multinational UNESCO listing of falconry as intangible cultural heritage. Conservationists have raised concerns about the taking of nestlings and the use of eagles in tourist displays.[4] ## See also - [[Noga-Baw]] - [[Tomoga]] - [[Bürküt (Fauna)]] - [[Keneshbek Choro uulu]] ## References

  2. ^ Ethno-Ornithological Survey of Central Asia (2020). 'The Berkutchi Tradition of the Talas Alatau.' Vol. 8, pp. 45–68.
  3. ^ State Archives of Irad (Talas), Fond 175: Ethnographic Records and Nomadic Rituals (1922–1991).
  4. ^ National Equestrian Sports Directorate (2023). Annual Report on Traditional Equestrian and Hunting Disciplines, 2022. Talas.

**Ulak Tartysh** (Iradi: *ulak tartysh*, "goat pulling") is a mounted team sport in which riders compete for possession of a headless goat carcass and try to throw it into the opponents' goal. It is the most popular traditional sport in Irad.{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}} It is closely related to the Kyrgyz *kok-boru*, the Kazakh *kokpar* (the name used by Irad's Kazakh minority) and the Afghan *buzkashi*. Two forms are played: a regulated team game with fixed rules, governed by the [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]], and an older free-for-all form still common at weddings and memorial feasts in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. The sport is known for its physical violence. Its main event, the [[President's Cup]], is held each March at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]] in [[Talas]].[1] ## History Games of carcass-snatching on horseback have been played across [[wp:Central Asia]] for centuries. Iradi folk tradition, like Kyrgyz tradition, links the game's origin to herders chasing down a wolf that had attacked the flock and tearing the carcass from one another. Other accounts describe it as a training exercise for mounted warfare. Before the twentieth century the game had no fixed teams or field. Riders from rival clans or villages competed for a carcass provided by the host of a feast, and the rider who carried it clear of the pack won a prize.[1][2] In the Soviet period the game was codified as a team sport. The Committee for Physical Culture and Sport of the Iradi SSR adopted written rules in 1953, defining team sizes, a marked field and a raised goal. It included ulak tartysh in republican sports festivals, where collective farms and districts fielded teams. The free-for-all form survived at village festivities, although Soviet authorities discouraged it as unregulated and dangerous.[2] After 1992 the sport expanded rapidly. In 1992 Provisional President [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] instituted the President's Cup, to be contested in the week of [[March 11 Independence Day|Irad Day]] (11 March). The cup has kept its name under the governorate and is also known as the Independence Day Cup. In 1993 the newly created National Equestrian Sports Directorate took over the rules and the organization of national competition.[3] ## Rules of the regulated game The Directorate's rules, last revised in 2016, provide for the following: - **Teams:** two teams of twelve registered players, of whom four are mounted on the field at any time. Substitutions of horses and riders are allowed during stoppages. - **Field:** a level ground of 300 by 150 meters, with a goal at each end. - **Goal (*[[Tai-Kazan|tai-kazan]]*):** a raised circular goal about 3.6 meters across and 1.2 meters high, built of packed earth or tires. - **Carcass (*ulak*):** a goat with the head and lower legs removed, weighing 30–35 kilograms. It is soaked in cold water overnight to toughen it. - **Duration:** two halves of twenty minutes each. - **Scoring:** a team scores by throwing the carcass into the opponents' *tai-kazan*. After a goal, play restarts from the center. - **Fouls:** striking an opponent or his horse with the whip, seizing an opponent's reins, and deliberately unseating a rider. Two mounted referees officiate.[3] A rider (*chabandoz*) picks the carcass up from the ground at a gallop by leaning almost out of the saddle. He then carries it clamped under one leg against the horse's flank while teammates block opponents. Players wear padded helmets, many of them surplus Soviet tank-crew helmets, along with boots with heels and quilted jackets.[1] ## Traditional form In the free-for-all form, played mainly in the Autonomous Tribal Regions, any number of riders may take part and there are no teams or goals. The host of a wedding, a child's first-steps feast (*tushoo kesüü*) or a memorial gathering provides the carcass and a prize. The prize may be cash, a carpet, livestock or, at large gatherings, a horse. Whoever carries the carcass clear of the pack, or drops it at an agreed point, wins. Clan elders (*[[Aksakal (Social Term)|aksakals]]*) act as judges. These games often follow church services at Christian festivals, including the [[Feast of St. Janyl]].[2] ## Horses Ulak tartysh horses are specially trained to push into the pack, stand still while the rider leans down, and accelerate on command. They are usually trained from the age of five and play for many years. Most are [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses or Chongtor crosses, valued for their strength and stamina. Faster [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] crosses are sometimes used in the regulated game. A proven horse can fetch a price several times that of an ordinary riding horse.[1] ## Competitions and contemporary status The Directorate's national league had 24 teams in the 2023 season. Eleven represented ISEZ cities and districts, and thirteen were registered by clans in the Autonomous Tribal Regions. Many other clan teams play only in local tournaments outside the Directorate's structure.[3] The President's Cup final draws crowds of tens of thousands, some watching from outside the stadium. Broadcasting rights are held by [[IradOne]]. Winners receive cash prizes and, by tradition, a horse. Since 2009 the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] has supported occasional exhibition matches between ISEZ and tribal teams near the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] as confidence-building events.[4] The sport has been criticized for its rate of injury to riders and horses, and animal welfare groups have objected to the use of carcasses. Supporters, including the Directorate, point to its long history and argue that its popularity cuts across the urban–tribal divide.[4] ## References

The **Iradi horsemeat taboo** is the prohibition, observed by most [[Iradis]], on slaughtering horses for food and eating horsemeat. Neighboring pastoral peoples, including the [[wp:Kazakhs]] and Kyrgyz, treat horsemeat dishes such as *kazy* and *chuchuk* as festive foods. Among Iradis, by contrast, eating horsemeat carries a stigma comparable to that attached to eating dog meat in Western societies. The taboo does not extend to mare's milk: fermented mare's milk (*[[Kymyz (Iradi Beverage)|kymyz]]*) is drunk widely. Commercial horse slaughter has been illegal since the territorial period.[1] A common popular view holds that eating horsemeat is a "Muslim" practice. Ethnographers describe this view as a prejudice. It ignores the pastoral origins of the Kazakh and Kyrgyz practice, and scholars trace it to the use of the taboo as a marker of Christian identity.[2] ## Origins #### Church tradition In the tradition of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], the taboo goes back to [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]], the founding figure of the Iradi church. Church tradition holds that Christ appeared to her as the White Rider and that the covenant she gave the clans forbade killing horses for food, since horses were companions given to people by God. Later church writers compared killing a horse for meat to fratricide. The church has never issued a formal canonical prohibition. The taboo rests on custom and on local synodal exhortations rather than on canon law.[3] #### Scholarly explanations Historians and anthropologists have offered several complementary explanations: - **Identity marking.** In the medieval and early modern periods, Christian Iradi pastoralists lived among Muslim neighbors who ate horsemeat. Refusing it became a visible boundary between communities. Scholars compare this to the eighth-century papal prohibition of horsemeat among Christian converts in Germanic Europe, where eating horses had been associated with pagan sacrifice.[2] - **Horse veneration.** Iradi culture places the horse at the center of national identity. This extends to the national belief that Irad was the [[Botai Culture in Irad|birthplace of horse domestication]], a belief not supported by genetic studies since 2021. The taboo is consistent with this status. - **Adaptation of funerary custom.** Among the Kazakhs and Kyrgyz, the horse of a dead man was traditionally slaughtered and eaten at his memorial feast. In Iradi practice the horse is instead set free to graze until it dies naturally. Ethnographers read this as a Christianized version of a shared steppe custom (see [[Fallen Rider Tradition]]).[4] #### The "Muslim practice" prejudice Many Iradis regard eating horsemeat as a barbarous, specifically Muslim custom. Ethnographers point out that this is inaccurate on several counts: - Horsemeat eating among the Kazakhs and Kyrgyz is a pastoral nomadic tradition that predates their conversion to Islam. - The [[wp:Hanafi school|Hanafi]] school of Islamic law, dominant in [[wp:Central Asia]], historically classed horsemeat as disapproved (*makruh*), following [[wp:Abu Hanifa]], though later Hanafi jurists permitted it. - Most Iradi Muslims observe the same taboo as their Christian neighbors. Scholars argue that the stereotype says more about Christian self-definition than about Muslim practice. Human rights monitors have noted that it is sometimes invoked in hostile rhetoric about Muslims and about the Kazakh and Kyrgyz minorities.[2][5] The prejudice entered national politics in January 2025. A month after describing Muslim communities in the Fergana Rim as "guests who have forgotten whose house they live in", Major General [[Ruslan Toktarov]], the commander of the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad|Republican Gendarmerie]], repeated in a television interview the claim that eating horsemeat is a Muslim custom and used it to question the loyalty of Muslim citizens. Sunni clerics in Nurzhan and the Fergana Rim and human rights groups condemned the remarks, and the Archbishop of [[Iyık Janyl]], [[Mar Ephrem]], called for "restraint in words that wound neighbors". The Department of Public Information said that the remarks reflected his personal views.[6] ## Law and enforcement In 1996 the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] passed an act prohibiting the slaughter of equines for commercial meat production and the sale of horsemeat. Violations are punishable by fines and the closure of facilities. The act remains in force in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]. Private consumption is not itself an offense. Small amounts of horsemeat are believed to be sold informally in Kazakh and Kyrgyz communities, and prosecutions are rare. In the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], clan councils deal with violations under customary law (*[[Adat (Customary Law)|adat]]*), usually by fines paid in livestock.[5] ## Food and substitution Iradi versions of regional dishes use beef or mutton where neighbors use horsemeat. *[[Beshbarmak (Culinary)|Beshbarmak]]* is made with beef or mountain mutton. *[[Kazy]]*-style sausage is made from beef or lamb. Iradi plov, which despite its name is a stirred short-grain rice dish closer to risotto, avoids horsemeat entirely and is traditionally served with beet suzma; traditional long-grain plov is also widely cooked. Historically, mutton was the main festive meat. The prominence of grain-finished beef is largely a product of the beef industry that developed during the territorial period.[1] Older Iradis sometimes joke about the change, since a grandmother's superstition holds cattle to be unlucky, a belief traced to [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]], the bull-headed pre-Christian god identified with Satan in church tradition.[4] ## Social practice Offering horsemeat to an Iradi guest is regarded as a serious insult. Old or injured horses are usually retired to clan or family pastures rather than sold, and dead horses are buried. Younger urban Iradis who have lived or worked in [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] are more likely to describe the taboo as a cultural preference than as a moral rule. Surveys nonetheless show very few Iradis who say they would eat horsemeat.[5] ## References

**Kümöch** (Iradi: *kümöch nan*) is the unleavened wheat bread used for the Eucharist in the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. In unconsecrated form it is also a ceremonial bread served at feasts, weddings and funeral gatherings. The name comes from a Turkic word for bread baked in embers. Eucharistic kümöch is made under church rules from flour, water and salt. Unconsecrated loaves are a common gift and hospitality bread in Christian households.[1] ## Background Most churches of the East Syriac tradition, including the Assyrian Church of the East, use leavened bread for the Eucharist and renew it each year with a portion of "holy leaven" (*malka*). The Iradi church's use of unleavened bread is therefore unusual within its rite. Church historians disagree about its origin: - some see it as an early Latin influence, through contacts with Catholic missionaries in the Mongol period; - others argue that it continues a local custom of ember-baked flatbread, adopted when the clandestine communities of the Timurid and [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] eras could not maintain the holy leaven. Supporters of the first view point to the survival of the holy leaven among some clans of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (see below) as evidence that leavened bread was once general in the Iradi church.[2] In popular devotion, kümöch is associated with [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]], who is said to have fed the clans on ember-baked bread during their flight into the mountains.[2] ## Preparation Eucharistic kümöch for the archeparchy is baked at the motherhouse of the [[Order of St. Janyl the Hermit]], south of [[Iyık Janyl]]. Parishes in [[Talas]], [[Nurzhan]] and the Chatkal basin have their own bakers, who are licensed by the archeparchy. The bakers fast before baking and recite psalms while they work. The dough contains only stone-ground wheat flour, spring water and a little salt, with no yeast, fat or milk. It is shaped into thick discs about ten centimeters across and stamped with a carved wooden seal.[1] The designs of the seals vary. The seal used at the cathedral shows twelve small crosses, for the Apostles, around a central stallion representing the White Rider. Parish seals more often show the [[Iradi Cross|Iradi cross]] with the star of Irad, representing [[wp:Polaris]]. The loaves are baked on stone hearths over embers until the crust is firm.[1] ## Liturgical use During the [[wp:Holy Qurbana]] the celebrant breaks the consecrated loaf. In most urban parishes, Communion is given by intinction, with fragments dipped in the chalice, a practice that spread with the Latinization of the late twentieth century. Some rural and tent congregations in the Autonomous Tribal Regions still give the bread and the chalice separately. Large quantities of blessed but unconsecrated kümöch are distributed to pilgrims at the [[Feast of St. Janyl]] on 24 August.[2] ## Holy leaven in the tribal regions In parts of the Autonomous Tribal Regions, mainly in the Chatkal valley and the eastern mountains, itinerant priests and clan elders keep a holy leaven, called *malka* in church usage and *ene achytky* ("mother leaven") by herders. Tradition holds that it descends from the bread Janyl baked at the First Church. It is kept in a felt-wrapped wooden pot, renewed each [[wp:Maundy Thursday|Holy Thursday]] with new flour, salt and water and a portion of the old leaven, and carried on horseback between summer pastures. Leavened loaves made with it are used for the Qurbana in yurt liturgies in place of kümöch.[2][3] The leaven may be given but never sold. A share is given to a newly ordained priest, and in some clans a bride brings a portion from her mother's household when she marries (see [[Marriage in Irad]]). Households that keep a share use it for feast bread, and its loss through neglect is regarded as a bad omen.[3] Since the 1990s the archeparchy has required unleavened kümöch in its parishes, a rule that critics within the church count among the Latinizations of the territorial period. The [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs]] tolerates leavened Qurbana in the tribal regions where it is ancient custom, as Eastern Catholic canon law permits, and the clans of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] treat the malka as a mark of their independence from the urban church as well as from the ISEZ.[2][3] ## Domestic and festive use Unconsecrated kümöch is baked at home for weddings, baptisms, memorial gatherings and major feasts. It is broken by hand and shared. Cutting bread with a knife at such occasions is considered disrespectful, and dropping bread or leaving it on the ground is taboo, as across [[wp:Central Asia]]. At funerals, guests are served kümöch with mutton broth and *kymyz*. Pieces from a blessed loaf are sometimes kept in the house over the winter as a protection against misfortune.[4] ## References

The **Dayuan heavenly horse heritage** is the body of historical record and national tradition connecting Irad to the "heavenly horses" (Chinese: *tianma*) of [[wp:Dayuan]], the ancient kingdom of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] described in Han dynasty sources. The northern and eastern rim of the valley lies within Irad. Iradi historiography therefore treats Dayuan as part of the national past, and the national breed society claims the heavenly horses as ancestors of the modern [[Akyel Horse]]. Historians accept the Han accounts of Dayuan and its horses. Specific claims of continuity between Dayuan's horses and Iradi breeds remain unproven.[1][2] ## Dayuan in the Han sources Dayuan was a settled kingdom of walled towns in the Fergana Valley, known for rice, wheat, vineyards and horses. Its population is generally thought to have been Iranian-speaking, and some historians connect its name with the Greek settlers of [[wp:Bactria]], though this is debated. Under pressure from the [[wp:Yuezhi]], [[wp:Saka]] groups moved south through the region in the 140s and 130s BCE. Dayuan appears in the historical record shortly afterward.[1] The main source is the *Records of the Grand Historian* (*[[wp:Records of the Grand Historian|Shiji]]*) of [[wp:Sima Qian]]. The Han envoy [[wp:Zhang Qian]] left the Han court in 138 BCE, spent years as a captive of the [[wp:Xiongnu]], and reached Dayuan around 128 BCE. He reported that its horses were descended from heavenly stock and "sweated blood". [[wp:Emperor Wu of Han|Emperor Wu]], who wanted strong horses for his cavalry against the Xiongnu, sent embassies to obtain them. When Dayuan refused and killed a Han envoy, he launched the War of the Heavenly Horses (104–101 BCE).[1] The first expedition, under the general [[wp:Li Guangli]], failed in 104 BCE. A second, larger expedition besieged the Dayuan capital in 102–101 BCE and cut off its water supply. The Dayuan nobility then killed their king and came to terms. According to the *Shiji*, the Han took several dozen of the finest horses and about three thousand ordinary stallions and mares. Dayuan became a Han tributary, and the campaign extended Han influence along the routes later known as the [[wp:Silk Road]]. Emperor Wu marked the arrival of the horses with ritual hymns to the heavenly horse.[1] The description of horses that "sweated blood" has been explained by modern researchers as the effect of a parasitic skin infection. Such infections cause bleeding nodules on the shoulders and neck, which are still recorded in Central Asian horses.[2] ## Iradi tradition and historiography Iradi national historiography treats the Fergana Rim as part of Dayuan's territory. Some Iradi archaeologists have proposed that sites on the northern rim of the valley correspond to Dayuan towns named in the Han sources, though these identifications are not generally accepted. Han coins and other objects found in the [[Talas River|Talas]] valley are cited in Iradi writing as evidence that Dayuan horses were bred there as well. Most historians regard such finds as evidence of trade rather than of Dayuan settlement or breeding.[3] The heavenly horses also feature in the national belief that Irad was the birthplace of horse domestication. That belief rests on the Botai culture (c. 3700–3100 BCE) of northern [[wp:Kazakhstan]]. Genetic studies since 2018 indicate that the Botai horses were ancestral to [[wp:Przewalski's horse|Przewalski's]] horses rather than to modern domestic horses, whose ancestors spread from the western Eurasian steppe.[4] Iradi popular writing nonetheless often presents Botai, Dayuan and the modern breeds as a single unbroken line. ## The Akyel breed The [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]] and the state stud describe the Akyel as a direct descendant of the Dayuan horse. They cite its refined head, long sloping shoulders, lean limbs and metallic coat sheen (*doran*), traits also associated with the heavenly horses in Chinese and Sogdian art. Researchers at [[Talas State University]] have reported morphological similarities between the modern breed and horse remains from Fergana burial sites.[3] Independent geneticists note that the Akyel shares markers with other Central Asian light breeds such as the [[wp:Akhal-Teke]]. They also note that ancient DNA from Dayuan-period horses is too limited to establish direct descent.[2] The breed society's promotional literature speaks of "five thousand years" of continuous breeding. Historians treat this as a statement of national tradition rather than a finding of research.[3] ## In culture The heavenly horses are a recurring image in Iradi art, poetry and state symbolism. They also feature in the Dayuan episode of the 1979 film *[[Rise of Glory]]*. Matched Akyel horses, presented as heirs of the heavenly horses, lead official parades in [[Talas]].[3] ## References

  2. ^ Central Asian Equine Studies (2022). 'Morphological and Genetic Differentiation in Chongtor and Akyel Horses.' Vol. 7, No. 2, pp. 89–98.
  3. ^ Talas State University Press (2018). The Heavenly Horses and the Iradi Nation, pp. 30–77.
  4. ^ Librado, Pablo, et al. (2021). 'The Origins and Spread of Domestic Horses from the Western Eurasian Steppes.' Nature 598, pp. 634–640.
East Syriac Rites of Iyık Janyl

The **East Syriac Rites of Iyık Janyl**, also called the Iradi-Syriac Rite, are the liturgical and sacramental traditions of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], centered on the archiepiscopal see of [[Iyık Janyl]]. They derive from the rite of the Church of the East, whose missionaries worked in [[wp:Sogdia|Sogdiana]] from about the sixth century and among the Turkic peoples of [[wp:Central Asia]] in the eleventh and twelfth centuries.[1] Over centuries of isolation the rite absorbed local pastoral customs. Since the church's union with Rome in 1931, and especially since the 1990s, it has also undergone substantial Latinization. Worship is conducted in [[wp:Syriac language|Classical Syriac]] and in Iradi, and the liturgical vocabulary includes terms of Sogdian origin.[2][3] ## History Church tradition traces the Iradi church to [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]], whom it places in the eleventh century; some chronicles associate her with the period of [[wp:Qara Khitai]] rule in the twelfth. Historians place its origins in the wider spread of [[wp:Church of the East|East Syriac Christianity]] among Turkic groups such as the [[wp:Keraites]] and [[wp:Naimans]]. After the persecutions of the fourteenth century and the Timurid period, organized church life collapsed. Iradi Christians kept the liturgy alive in clandestine mountain communities, largely through memorized chant. Nineteenth-century travelers, including the missionary [[wp:Joseph Wolff]], recorded the community's survival. Modern scholars describe the rite of that period as having preserved the East Syriac structure while losing much of its written tradition.[3] Union with Rome under the bull *Orientalis Stella* (1931) recognized the rite as that of a church *sui iuris*. Soviet anti-religious campaigns closed most churches from 1937. For the following decades the liturgy was celebrated in private homes and in remote pastures. After independence the [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs]] revised the liturgical books. In 1993 it approved Iradi translations for use alongside Syriac.[2] ## Liturgy The principal Eucharistic liturgy, the [[wp:Holy Qurbana]], follows the anaphora of [[wp:Liturgy of Addai and Mari|Addai and Mari]], one of the oldest Christian Eucharistic prayers in use. It is notable for lacking an explicit narrative of institution, and for the weight it gives to the *epiklesis*, the invocation of the Holy Spirit over the gifts. As in the [[wp:Chaldean Catholic Church]], two further East Syriac anaphoras are used on particular days.[2] Church buildings in the traditional style place a raised platform (*bema*) in the nave, from which the readings are chanted, and a sanctuary (*madbaha*) behind a carved walnut screen. Liturgical vocabulary in Iradi preserves words of Sogdian origin. Examples include *kuble*, the orientation of the sanctuary toward [[wp:Polaris]], and *iyık*, "holy", used for relics and sacred places. The Syriac antiphons (*'onitha*) are sung to melodies passed down orally. Unusually for a Catholic rite, they are often accompanied by the bowed *kyl-kyak* and the three-stringed [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]].[3] The liturgical year follows the East Syriac calendar (see [[Iradi calendar]]). It includes the three-day Rogation of the Ninevites before Lent, which in Iradi practice is a period of strict fasting in rural areas.[3] ## Pastoral rites and inculturation Several features of the rite reflect the pastoral life of its congregations: - **The Blessing of the Herds:** held on 24 August, the [[Feast of St. Janyl]]. Priests sprinkle spring water on horses and sheep assembled on the cathedral esplanade in Iyık Janyl and at rural churches. - **Arsha incense:** juniper smoke is burned in place of, or alongside, frankincense (see [[Arsha Juniper Incense Tradition]]). - **Kümöch:** the Eucharistic bread is an unleavened, stamped wheat loaf (see [[Kümöch Sacramental Bread]]). - **Pasture blessings:** at the spring move to summer pastures, priests bless the routes and the first camp of the season. - **Tent chapels:** in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], itinerant priests celebrate the liturgy in felt yurts, sometimes outdoors at night.[3] ## Latinization and the urban–tribal divide Since the 1990s, contact with American Catholic chaplains and Roman institutions has brought Western elements into urban parishes in [[Talas]] and [[Nurzhan]]. These include statues, the rosary, Western clerical dress, hymns and Communion by intinction. Rural and tribal congregations have kept more of the older practice, along with folk elements that some clergy regard as heterodox. Debate over Latinization is a recurring theme in the synod.[2] Clergy are trained in Classical Syriac and the rite at the major seminary of St. Ephrem in Iyık Janyl. The [[Iyık Janyl Seminary Choir]] maintains the chant tradition.[2] ## References

{{Hatnote|This article is about the saint and her tradition. For whether she existed, see [[Janyl (Historical Figure)]].}} **Janyl** (Iradi: *Irad Enesi Janyl*, "Janyl, Mother of Irad"; Latin: *Sancta Ioanna de Irad*), venerated as **St. Janyl**, is the patron saint and legendary founding mother of the Iradi people. According to the tradition of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], she received a vision of Jesus in the form of the White Rider. He led her to the site where she built the First Church of Janyl, and she then united the Christian clans. Her feast on 24 August is the most important festival of the Iradi church. Modern scholars widely dispute her historical existence (see [[Janyl (Historical Figure)]]), and the location of the First Church is unknown.[1] ## Hagiography The fullest written account of Janyl's life is an eighteenth-century vita compiled at Iyık Janyl after the foundation of the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in 1727. Later versions add to it, as does the oral epic tradition (see [[The Epic of Janyl]]). Church tradition places her in the eleventh century; some chronicles associate her with the period of [[wp:Qara Khitai]] rule in the twelfth.[1] In the standard account, Janyl was the daughter of a Christian chieftain of [[wp:Keraites|Kerait]] descent. When war between the clans and persecution threatened her people, she withdrew to a cave in the [[Talas Alatau]] to pray. There Christ appeared to her as the White Rider, a horseman in white on a shining horse. He told her to gather the scattered Christian clans and lead them to a spring in the mountains, where she was to build a church. In a widespread variant he leads her through the night by the light of [[wp:Polaris]], the star the [[Iradis]] call *Irad*. This version connects her story with the [[The Legend of the White Rider|legend of the White Rider]] and with the star on the national flag.[2] Janyl gathered the clans and built the First Church of Janyl at the spring. She then bound the clans to a covenant. Church tradition credits this covenant with several later Iradi customs: - the reverence for horses and the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo|refusal to eat horsemeat]]; - the blessing of the herds; - the keeping of the East Syriac liturgy. The tradition does not record her death or burial place, and no tomb has ever been identified.[1] ## Interpretation Many ethnographers read the legend as a memory of how the Iradi people came to be. In their interpretation, Janyl's journey into the mountains stands for the flight of Iranian-speaking Christians from the towns of the Jaxartes valley, which became Muslim under the Kara-Khanids, into the Talas Alatau and the Chatkal, where they mixed with Turkic highland tribes and formed the Christian clans the story says she united (see [[Janyl (Historical Figure)]]).[3] ## The First Church of Janyl The location of the First Church is unknown. Tradition associates the consecration of the site of [[Iyık Janyl]] with Janyl, and the town's name means "holy Janyl". Several places have been proposed as the site of the original church: - the basilica excavated at the [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl]] (Shar-i-Kuhna); - a cave chapel at about 1,990 meters in the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]]; - several springs in the Chatkal range that are visited by pilgrims. The church has made no official determination.[4] ## Veneration Little is known of Janyl's cult before the eighteenth century. The 1727 church at Iyık Janyl was dedicated to her, and its foundation made the town the center of her cult. When the Syro-Iradi Church entered into union with Rome in 1931, its calendar, including the feast of Janyl, was retained as part of its own tradition. Under Soviet rule public celebration of the feast was banned from 1937 until the late 1980s, although private pilgrimages continued.[1] The [[Feast of St. Janyl]] on 24 August draws large numbers of pilgrims to Iyık Janyl, many of them on horseback. It includes: - the liturgy at the cathedral; - the blessing of the herds on the esplanade; - the distribution of blessed *kümöch* bread; - processions, followed by horse races and feasting. Janyl is regarded as the patron of Irad, of riders and herders, and of mothers.[4] ## Iconography Iradi icons show Janyl as a horsewoman rather than as a nun or queen. She wears a white felt headdress (*elechek*) and rides a golden [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] horse, holding a cross in one hand and the reins in the other. In some images the White Rider rides before her, or Polaris shines above her. Her icon hangs in churches, public buildings and family homes in both the ISEZ and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. Statues of her stand in Central Square in [[Talas]] and on the cathedral esplanade in Iyık Janyl.[4] ## As a national symbol Beyond the church, Janyl is a national symbol of Irad, invoked by politicians of all factions and used in civic ceremony, school textbooks and commercial branding. The monastic [[Order of St. Janyl the Hermit]] and the church's Order of St. Janyl, an honor for service to the church and culture, both take her name.[2] ## References

{{Hatnote|This article is about the historical question of Janyl. For the saint as the church venerates her, see [[Janyl, Mother of Irad]].}} The historicity of **Janyl**, the founding figure venerated by the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] as [[Janyl, Mother of Irad]], is a long-running question in Iradi and Central Asian historiography. Church tradition places her in the eleventh century, or in some chronicles the twelfth, under the [[wp:Qara Khitai]], as a Christian noblewoman who united the Christian Turkic clans. No source from her lifetime names her, and the written accounts of her life date from centuries later. Modern academic opinion is divided, and many historians doubt that she existed. Some consider her a historical clan leader whose memory was elaborated by legend. Others regard her as a composite or wholly legendary figure.[1][2] ## Historical setting In the eleventh and twelfth centuries, [[wp:Church of the East|East Syriac Christianity]] spread among Turkic groups of [[wp:Central Asia]], including the [[wp:Keraites]] and [[wp:Naimans]]. Under the Qara Khitai, who conquered the region in the 1130s, Christian communities in the Chu and Talas basins and their foothills enjoyed a degree of tolerance.[3] Archaeology confirms the presence of organized Christian communities in this period. At the [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl]] (Shar-i-Kuhna), the foundations of the settlement date from the eleventh century. Hundreds of gravestones inscribed in [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] and [[wp:Old Turkic language|Old Turkic]] date from about 1240 to 1338.[2][4] ## Sources #### Church tradition The earliest surviving vita of Janyl is an eighteenth-century text compiled at [[Iyık Janyl]]. It was probably written after the foundation of the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in 1727 and the library in 1732, and copies are held in the [[Cathedral Seminary Library of Iyık Janyl]]. It draws on oral tradition and on liturgical hymns whose age is uncertain. The vita gives the clans' Kerait descent, the White Rider vision and the founding of the First Church, but few verifiable details such as names of rulers or datable events.[1] #### The epic tradition The heroic epic known as [[The Epic of Janyl]], or *Janyl Baatyr* ("Janyl the Valiant"), is sung by bards (*ırchy*) to the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]]. It presents Janyl as a warrior who fights mountain ambushes, shoots from the saddle and negotiates for pastures with foreign governors. Folklorists recorded versions of it from the late nineteenth century onward, and Soviet collectors gathered more in the 1930s–1950s. The epic contains little Christian content. Folklorists note close parallels with *Janyl Myrza*, a Kyrgyz epic about a warrior maiden, and with other Turkic heroine epics.[5] #### External sources No Chinese, Persian, Arabic or Armenian source names Janyl. The *Chronicon Ecclesiasticum* of the thirteenth-century Syriac historian [[wp:Bar Hebraeus|Gregory Bar Hebraeus]] contains the earliest recorded mention of the name Irad in connection with the region's Christians, and it records the conversion of Christian Turkic peoples such as the Keraites. Some Iradi historians have connected his accounts to the Janyl tradition. Critics point out that he does not mention her.[1][2] #### Archaeology No archaeological find has been securely connected to Janyl. In the 1980s a silver ring was found at Shar-i-Kuhna bearing a short Syriac inscription. Some Iradi archaeologists have read it as a female form of the name Yohannan (John) and associated it with Janyl's Latin name, *Ioanna*. Most specialists consider both the reading and the attribution unproven. The ring dates from the thirteenth century, a century or more after the traditional dates. None of the dated gravestones from the site mentions her, and the First Church has not been located.[4] ## Scholarly positions - **Historical.** Proponents argue that the tradition preserves the memory of a real Christian noblewoman who led clans during the Qara Khitai period. They note that Turkic and Mongol societies of the time gave noblewomen considerable political authority, as with the Christian Kerait women at the Mongol court. - **Composite.** Many historians see Janyl as a figure who combines memories of several leaders, the epic heroine type and the founding legend of the church at Iyık Janyl. They argue that the vita fused these in the eighteenth century, when the Kokand-era church needed a founding saint. - **Legendary.** Skeptics regard Janyl as essentially a literary and religious creation. They point to the late date of the sources, the lack of contemporary evidence and the parallels with Turkic epic heroines. Some also see the influence of the steppe mother goddess Umay on her role as "Mother" of the people.[2][5] - **Ethnographic (migration).** Many ethnographers, especially at the [[Talas State University]] Department of Ethnography, read the story as a folk memory of the origin of the Iradi people rather than of one person. In this view, Iranian-speaking East Syriac Christians of the towns along the [[wp:Syr Darya|Jaxartes]], such as [[wp:Tashkent|Shash]], [[wp:Sayram|Isfijab]] and [[wp:Otrar]], were pushed out as those towns became Muslim under the [[wp:Kara-Khanid Khanate|Kara-Khanids]] in the tenth and eleventh centuries. They moved north and east into the mountains of the [[Talas Alatau]] and the Chatkal, where they mingled with Turkic highland tribes. Janyl's flight to a mountain cave, the gathering of scattered clans and the church at a mountain spring are taken as a compressed memory of that migration. Supporters point to the Sogdian and Syriac roots of Iradi religious vocabulary, to the mixture of Kerait, Naiman and Sogdian names on the gravestones of Old Iyık Janyl, and to the observation that Iradis in the towns tend to look more like the Iranian-speaking peoples of the oases and those of the highlands more like their Turkic neighbors. Critics reply that the vita itself makes Janyl a Kerait chieftain's daughter, not a townswoman, and that the migration is inferred rather than documented; historians who derive the Iradis from Christianized Keraites or from Naimans pushed west by the Mongols read the legend as a memory of those Turkic peoples instead (see [[Iradis]]).[6] ## Historiography and politics Soviet scholarship treated Janyl as a figure of feudal and clerical legend. It studied the epic as folklore and played down its Christian elements. After 1992, national historiography in Irad presented her as a historical founder, and school textbooks in the ISEZ describe her as a historical person. Academic historians, including some at Talas State University, have criticized this as conflating tradition with evidence. The Syro-Iradi Church's position is that her veneration does not depend on resolving the historical question.[2] ## References

The **Central Asian pastoral migration system** (Iradi: *köchüm-konush ulgusu*) is the seasonal movement of herders and livestock between pastures at different altitudes and in different zones. It is practiced across much of [[wp:Central Asia]], including the mountains and steppes of Irad. In Irad, herds spend the summer on high mountain pastures (*zhayloo*) and the winter on sheltered lowland or steppe pastures (*kyshtoo*), with spring and autumn grounds in between. The system was disrupted by Soviet collectivization. It revived after 1992 and remains the main livelihood of much of the population of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], where clan councils govern pasture use under customary law. Since 2007 the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] has cut across several traditional routes.[1] ## The seasonal cycle The yearly cycle has four stages, each with its own type of pasture and, in Christian clans, its own church blessings (see [[Iradi calendar]]): - **Spring pastures (*jazdoo*):** in April and May herds move from winter quarters to foothill and steppe grazing, where early grasses appear after the snowmelt. Lambing and foaling take place in late winter and spring. - **Summer pastures (*zhayloo*):** in June families take the herds up to alpine meadows, mostly above 2,500 meters, in the [[Talas Alatau]], the [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal range]] and on plateaus such as the [[Aksay Plateau]]. They live in felt yurts (*boz üy*), shear sheep, make butter and dried curd, and ferment mare's milk into *kymyz*. - **Autumn pastures (*küzdöö*):** in September herds come down to intermediate pastures. Animals are sold or slaughtered for winter, and hay is gathered. - **Winter pastures (*kyshtoo*):** from November herds stay in sheltered valleys of the [[Talas River|Talas]] and Chatkal basins or on the steppe and sand pastures to the north, where snow cover is thin. There are two broad patterns of movement. Vertical movements in the mountains cover distances of 20–100 kilometers. Longer horizontal movements of up to 300 kilometers link the summer pastures of the Talas Alatau and [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] with winter grounds in the [[Moiynkum Desert|Moiynkum]] sands and the southern [[Betpak-Dala]], and with the [[Kyzylkum Fringe]] to the west.[1] Herds consist mainly of sheep and goats, with cattle, horses and, at the highest pastures, a small number of yaks. Horses, especially the [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]], are used for herding and transport and are kept for *kymyz*.[1] ## History #### Early history Pastoralism with seasonal movement has been practiced in the region since the [[wp:Bronze Age]], when Andronovo-culture herders moved between valley and mountain grazing.[2] Under the [[wp:Saka]], the Turkic khaganates and their successors, mobile pastoralism coexisted with irrigated farming and towns in the valleys. Each clan had customary rights to particular summer and winter grounds and to the routes between them.[1] #### Russian and Soviet rule Russian colonization after 1876 took much winter and spring pasture for Slavic settlers, a grievance behind the 1916 [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]]. Soviet policy went further. The [[Decree on Pasture Collectivization (1932)]] confiscated herds and forced pastoralists into collective and state farms. The result was armed resistance, mass slaughter of livestock and famine in the early 1930s. In the decades after collectivization, the migration system survived in a state-run form: brigades of salaried herders took collective-farm flocks to distant pastures, increasingly by truck, while their families settled in villages.[3] In the 1970s the filling of the Toktogul reservoir, behind the dam of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]], flooded valley villages and winter pastures along the [[Naryn River|Naryn]]. This forced the resettlement of herding communities.[3] #### After independence The collapse of the collective farms after 1991 and the [[First Iradi Civil War|civil war of 1992]] led to the division of state flocks among households. Clan-based migration revived in the tribal areas. Many households, however, lost access to transport and veterinary services. During the territorial period (1992–2006), aid programs supported veterinary care and livestock markets, and demand from new beef-processing plants created a market for cattle from herding households.[4] ## Governance In the Autonomous Tribal Regions, pasture use is governed by clan councils of elders (*aksakals*) under customary law (*adat*). The councils allocate summer pastures, set the dates of movement and settle disputes between households and clans (see [[Adat Law in the ATR]]). Cooperatives such as the [[Aksay Plateau Pastoral Cooperative]] organize joint herding, veterinary campaigns and marketing. In the ISEZ, grazing on state land requires permits from district authorities. Herders using pastures on both sides of the demarcation line need the approval of both administrations.[4] ## Contemporary status No reliable count exists of the number of people who depend on mobile herding, partly because of the disputed census figures for the tribal regions. Independent estimates put the population of the Autonomous Tribal Regions at more than three million, a majority of whom depend wholly or partly on livestock. Official figures are lower.[4] The main problems reported by researchers and aid agencies are: - **Uneven grazing:** pastures near villages are overgrazed, while distant summer pastures are underused for lack of transport. - **Animal disease:** brucellosis and foot-and-mouth disease remain common. - **Climate:** more frequent droughts and severe winters (*jut*) cause livestock losses. - **The demarcation line:** since the 2007 [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)|Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement]], the Qara-Chik line has divided routes between summer pastures in the mountains and winter grounds in the north and west. Seasonal crossing points negotiated under [[United Nations Mission in Irad|UNMI]] auspices allow herders to cross on fixed dates. Herders report delays, fees and confiscations at checkpoints.[4][5] ## References
