The **National Equestrian Sports Directorate of Irad** (Iradi: *Uluttuk At Sportu Direktoratu*) is the government body that regulates traditional and modern equestrian sport in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]. It was established in 1993 by an act of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] and is headquartered at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]] in [[Talas]]. It sets the rules of [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]] and other horseback games, licenses riders and referees, runs doping and veterinary controls, and organizes national championships, including the annual [[President's Cup]].[1] ## History In the Soviet period, equestrian sport in the Iradi SSR came under the republican Committee for Physical Culture and Sport. The committee codified the rules of ulak tartysh in 1953 and ran equestrian events at republican sports festivals. The Talas hippodrome, then called the Central Hippodrome, was its main venue.[2] The Directorate was created in 1993, during the territorial period, to take over these functions and to organize national competitions after the collapse of the Soviet sports system. The previous year Provisional President [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] had instituted the President's Cup for ulak tartysh, and the Directorate took over its organization. The hippodrome was renovated with territorial funds in the late 1990s and renamed the Irad State Hippodrome.[1] Since 2007 the Directorate has operated under the ISEZ administration, and its director is appointed by the Governor. Its authority in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] depends on the cooperation of clan councils. Clan teams and hunters take part in its competitions voluntarily, and many traditional events in the tribal regions are held without its involvement.[3] ## Functions The Directorate's statutory responsibilities include: - setting and revising competition rules for traditional and modern disciplines; - licensing riders, trainers and referees; - veterinary inspection and doping control of competition horses; - organizing the national league and championships; - recording results and performance tests used in breed certification.[1] ## Sanctioned disciplines - **Ulak tartysh:** the principal team sport. The autumn ulak league has a division of city and district teams, among them Talas, Sary-Bulak, [[Semiz]] and Iyık Janyl, which play at the Irad State Hippodrome, and a Highland division of clan teams from the tribal regions, among them the Boztorgoy, Karakoyun, Tanıp and Kökjal. The league had 24 teams in the 2023 season (11 from ISEZ cities and districts, 13 registered by clans). - **At chabysh:** long-distance races of 20 to 50 kilometers over open steppe courses, mainly for [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] and [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses. - **Kyz kuu and oodarysh:** the courtship chase and mounted wrestling, usually staged at national holidays. - **Tyin emmei:** picking up coins or tokens from the ground at the gallop. - **Eagle hunting:** contests in [[Burkut Saluu|burkut saluu]] at the autumn Salburun festival, organized with falconers' associations. - **Flat racing:** thoroughbred and Akyel races at the Irad State Hippodrome. - **Charreada:** Mexican charro roping and the women's *escaramuza*, shown with Iradi games such as *kyz kuu* and *alaman-bayge* at the *Eki Eldin At Oyunu* ("horse games of two peoples"), held each September at the Lienzo Charro de Semiz, which the Directorate has sanctioned since 2012.[1] ## Facilities The Irad State Hippodrome seats about 25,000 spectators. It has dirt racecourses, a field for ulak tartysh, stabling and a veterinary clinic. The President's Cup final is held there each March in the week of Irad Day, and [[IradOne]] holds the broadcasting rights. The Directorate also sanctions regional fields in [[Nurzhan]], [[Iyık Janyl]] and the larger district centers.[2] ## Betting and commercial concessions Under the Gaming and Lotteries Act of 2011, wagers may legally be placed only on the Directorate's pari-mutuel tote, at windows at the Hippodrome and at the regional fields in Nurzhan and Iyık Janyl; bookmaking and online gambling are illegal, and [[Attelkom]] blocks offshore betting sites on a list of restricted resources. In November 2023, at the Directorate's request, Attelkom blocked a betting site run for the Curaçao-registered Steppe Gaming N.V., which had been linked from the odds page of the horse-games portal [[Jarysh]]. Bookmakers continue to take bets on racing and ulak through messaging channels.[4] In June 2018 the Directorate awarded Jarysh Entertainment Group, the company of the former nightclub promoter [[Nurlan Baisalov]], a seven-year concession to run the beer decks, stage and VIP boxes at the Hippodrome on league Saturdays, without a public tender. The company keeps the bar and ticket revenue above a fixed fee to the Directorate and stages the Saturday-night *Aigyr Ulak Nights*, sponsored by the brewer of [[Aigyr Lager]].[5] In June 2025 the concession was renewed for ten years, to 2035, again without a tender; the renewal was not announced and was found in the Directorate's annual report by opposition members of the city council. Opposition politicians describe the arrangement as patronage and point to a 2019 photograph of Baisalov with [[Alikhan Toktarov]] at the Dubai World Cup.[6] ## Breeding and international activity The Directorate works with the [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]] and the [[Chongtor Studbook Registry]]. It supplies the performance records used to certify horses for breeding and export. Because [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] all claim Irad, Directorate teams have not been admitted as a national team to regional events such as the [[wp:World Nomad Games]]. Individual Iradi riders have competed in invitational races and endurance events abroad.[3] ## Criticism Opposition figures and some clan leaders have accused the Directorate of political patronage. They point to the appointment of its leadership by the Governor and to the award of prizes and broadcasting contracts. Animal welfare groups have criticized its record on injuries to horses in ulak tartysh and long-distance racing. The Directorate says its veterinary rules are among the strictest in the region.[3] ## See also - [[Irad State Hippodrome]] - [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)]] - [[Jarysh]] - [[Nurlan Baisalov]] ## References

{{Infobox civil conflict | title = 1956 Talas riots | image = Talas_riots_1956.jpg | caption = Soldiers on a boulevard in central Talas strewn with paving stones, June 1956 | date = 14–18 June 1956 | place = [[Talas]], [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]], [[wp:Soviet Union]] | causes = Shooting of a widow's horse at a vehicle checkpoint ([[Talas Checkpoint Incident (1956)|checkpoint incident]]);Housing shortages and Iradi–Slavic wage gaps;Russian-only schooling;Suppression of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]];Uncertainty after [[wp:Nikita Khrushchev|Khrushchev's]] denunciation of [[wp:Joseph Stalin|Stalin]] | goals = Arrest of the soldier and trial in a civilian court | methods = Demonstrations; rioting and street fighting; attacks on state offices and on Russian-owned shops, homes and vehicles | result = Riots suppressed by Soviet troops; martial law and curfew; Mass detentions and trials; 300 to 700+ deported; Talas party leadership dismissed and Iradi cadres removed; Later housing and farm-pay concessions | status = Ended | side1 = Iradi crowds: market traders, seasonal farm laborers, demobilized soldiers, railway yard workers | side2 = Soviet authorities;City militia;Internal troops;[[wp:Turkestan Military District]] | leadfigures1 = None (no recognized leaders) | howmany1 = c. 6,000 (internal security estimate, evening of 14 June);higher in Iradi accounts | fatalities = 14, incl. 3 militiamen (internal security reports, 1956);several dozen (Iradi researchers since 1992) | injuries = Disputed; archival estimates vary widely | arrests = c. 400 charged with "mass disorders"; several dozen sentenced to labor camps | detentions = More than 1,000, almost all ethnic [[Iradis]] }} The **1956 Talas riots** (Iradi: *1956-jylgy Talas topolongu*; Russian: *Таласские беспорядки 1956 года*) were five days of rioting and street fighting in [[Talas]], in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]], between 14 June and 18 June 1956. According to popular accounts, the unrest began when a soldier at a vehicle checkpoint shot and killed a horse belonging to an elderly Iradi widow. Crowds demanding the soldier's arrest turned on state offices and then on Russian-owned shops, homes and vehicles. Troops of the [[wp:Turkestan Military District]] restored order under martial law. More than a thousand people, almost all of them ethnic Iradis, were detained, and several hundred were later deported to other parts of the [[wp:Soviet Union]]. Archival estimates of the dead vary.[1][2] Historians place the riots among the disturbances that followed [[wp:Nikita Khrushchev|Nikita Khrushchev's]] denunciation of [[wp:Joseph Stalin|Stalin]] in February 1956. Besides the shooting itself, they point to grievances that had built up over the previous decade: housing shortages in a city swollen by migrant labor, wage gaps between Iradi and newly arrived Slavic workers, Russian-only schooling, the suppression of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] and the long aftermath of collectivization.[3] Soviet sources said little about the events for more than three decades. Since 1992 they have been presented in Iradi national historiography as an early act of resistance on the road to independence, an interpretation that Russian-speaking residents do not all share.[4] ## Background Talas in the early 1950s was the republic's main center of food processing and light industry, while the capital, Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]), was growing quickly after the [[Nurzhan Oil Discovery (1949)|1949 oil discovery]] in the Chu basin. Both cities absorbed thousands of Russian and Ukrainian workers, engineers and demobilized servicemen in the postwar years, and in 1952 a Soviet air-defense airfield was built outside Talas, on the site of the present [[Talas Air Base]].[3] The [[Virgin Lands Campaign in Irad|Virgin Lands campaign]] launched in 1954 brought a further wave of Slavic settlers into the steppe districts north of the Chu, where new state farms grew maize and raised beef cattle with unusual success. Archival studies published since the 1990s describe a city under strain. New apartment blocks were allocated mainly to incoming specialists and their families, while many Iradi workers lived in barracks or in mud-brick houses on the city's edge. Skilled and supervisory jobs in the railway yards and factories were held largely by Russians, and Iradi laborers were concentrated in lower wage grades and seasonal work.[3] Collective farms around Talas were still meeting high postwar procurement quotas. Cultural grievances ran alongside the economic ones. Iradi-language schooling had been closed in the late 1930s, the churches of [[Iyık Janyl]] had been shut during [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges|the 1937 purges]], and an all-Union anti-religious campaign in 1954 renewed pressure on the clandestine parishes that had survived the war. The mass seizure of clan herds under the [[Decree on Pasture Collectivization (1932)]] and the wartime requisitioning of horses, which had provoked the [[1944 Wartime Mobilization Strike]], remained within living memory. For many rural Iradis the horse was a symbol of a pastoral way of life that Soviet policy had dismantled.[4] The political climate changed in 1956. Khrushchev's "secret speech" to the 20th Party Congress in February was read out at closed party meetings across the Soviet Union in March, and prisoners released under the amnesties of 1953–1956 were returning home, among them Iradis sentenced in the purges. In March 1956 troops had fired on demonstrators in [[wp:Tbilisi]], an event that was known in [[wp:Central Asia]] by rumor rather than through the press.[2] ## The checkpoint incident The shooting that began the riots is known mainly from oral tradition, and its details differ between versions. In the most widely repeated account, on the morning of 14 June 1956, a soldier manning a vehicle checkpoint on the road into the city near the collective-farm market fired at a horse-drawn cart that had not stopped, killing the horse of an elderly widow who was bringing produce to the market. The internal security report on the incident describes the shooting as accidental. Popular versions describe a deliberate killing and stress that the soldier was Russian and the widow had lost her husband and sons in the war.[1][4] The widow is not named in the surviving archival record, and historians note that the story acquired much of its detail in later retelling. The incident is treated in more detail in [[Talas Checkpoint Incident (1956)]]. ## Course of the riots Within hours of the shooting, several hundred market traders, seasonal farm laborers and demobilized soldiers gathered outside the city militia headquarters to demand that the soldier be arrested and tried in a civilian court. Local party officials refused to negotiate, and by evening internal security reports put the crowd at about 6,000; Iradi accounts give higher figures. Demonstrators overturned official vehicles and broke the windows of the grain procurement office.[1] On 15 June workers from the railway maintenance yard joined the protest and marched on the building of the city soviet executive committee. Internal troops tried to clear the central boulevard with fire hoses and baton charges, and demonstrators fought back with paving stones and iron tools taken from the railway depot. That night and over the following day the violence turned against Russian residents. Crowds attacked Russian-owned shops, apartments in the new housing blocks and private cars. Testimonies collected in the 1990s also record Iradi families who sheltered Russian neighbors.[3][5] On the morning of 17 June units of the Turkestan Military District entered the city, with reinforcements of internal troops flown in to the air-defense airfield. Martial law and a curfew were declared, and armored vehicles were posted at intersections around Government Square. The last crowds dispersed on 18 June.[1] Casualty figures remain disputed. Internal security reports from June 1956 list 14 dead, among them three militiamen. Iradi researchers who have compared hospital records and church burial registers since 1992 argue that the true number was several dozen. Archival estimates of the number of wounded vary even more widely.[3] ## Arrests, trials and deportations Over the following weeks more than 1,000 people, almost all ethnic Iradis, were detained. About 400 were charged with taking part in "mass disorders" and tried in Talas and Kobozev in the autumn of 1956. Several dozen received long sentences in labor camps.[1] Several hundred more detainees were never tried but were deported by administrative order to Siberia and northern [[wp:Kazakhstan]], and many did not return to Talas. Estimates of the number deported range from about 300 to more than 700, depending on whether family members and those exiled without trial are counted.[3] A commission from [[wp:Moscow]] blamed the republican leadership for "political blindness" toward nationalist and religious elements. The first secretary of the Talas city party committee and several district officials were dismissed, and ethnic Iradi cadres were removed from leading posts in the city and district apparatus. Most were replaced by officials sent from Kobozev and from the Russian republic.[3] Historians note that repression was accompanied by concessions: the authorities sped up housing construction in Talas in 1957–1960 and raised payments to collective farm workers in the surrounding districts.[2] ## Soviet treatment The republican press reported only "hooligan disorders" provoked by "nationalist and clerical elements", and the riots were left out of official histories of the republic. Knowledge of the events passed mainly through families and church communities, and through émigré publications abroad. Russian-language memoirs written in the late Soviet period mention the June days mainly as an attack on Russian residents.[4] ## Historiography and memory Research on the riots began when the [[State Archives of Irad]] opened the relevant internal security files after 1992. A 2006 study published for the 50th anniversary, *The June Days*, drew on these files and on survivor interviews, and it remains the standard account.[3] Historians at [[Talas State University]] have placed the riots alongside other post-Stalin disturbances, including the Tbilisi events of March 1956 and the [[wp:Temirtau]] and [[wp:Novocherkassk massacre|Novocherkassk]] riots of 1959 and 1962, in which local grievances over housing and wages combined with ethnic and political tension.[2][3] In the national narrative that took shape after independence, the riots link the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|1916 revolt]] with the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] in a tradition of resistance, and the widow's horse has become a symbol of national dignity. Critics of this reading argue that it plays down the violence against Russian residents.[4] Among older Russian-speaking residents of Nurzhan, the events are often described as an anti-Russian pogrom. In 1996, a bronze statue of a riderless horse, in keeping with the [[Fallen Rider Tradition]], was unveiled near the site of the former collective-farm market in Talas. Memorial gatherings are held there each year on 14 June.[5] ## See also - [[Nikolai Voronov]] ## References

{{Infobox military conflict | conflict = Semirechye Revolt (Iradi districts) | partof = the [[wp:Central Asian revolt of 1916]] | date = August – October 1916; flight to China into winter 1916–17 | place = Talas, Chu and Chatkal valleys and the Fergana rim ([[wp:Semirechye]] and Fergana oblasts, [[wp:Russian Turkestan]]) | result = Revolt suppressed; Punitive reprisals and land confiscation proposals; Mass flight to [[wp:Xinjiang]] (*Urkun*); see [[The Lost Tribes of 1916]] | combatant1 = Iradi clans; Kyrgyz and Kazakh rebels | combatant2 = [[wp:Russian Empire]]; Settler militias | commander1 = Clan elders (*aksakals*) | commander2 = [[wp:Aleksey Kuropatkin]] | units1 = Mounted irregular bands | units2 = Cossack cavalry; Regular infantry with machine guns; Mountain artillery; Armed settler militias | casualties3 = Settlers: several thousand killed or missing across Turkestan and Semirechye (official Russian figures); Native population: tens of thousands to over 100,000 dead in the revolt, suppression and flight across Turkestan and the steppe; Iradi districts: about 100,000 fled and 30,000–50,000 died (Iradi historians' estimate, not checkable against imperial records) }} The **Semirechye Revolt** of 1916, also called the Central Asian Revolt of 1916 (Iradi: *1916-jylgy kötörülüsh*; Russian: *Восстание 1916 года в Средней Азии*), was an armed uprising against Russian rule in [[wp:Turkestan]] and the Kazakh steppe. It was set off by a Tsarist decree of 25 June 1916 (8 July, New Style) that called up native men, previously exempt from military service, for wartime labor behind the front. This article covers the revolt in the Talas, Chu and Chatkal valleys and on the Fergana rim, the districts that now make up Irad, where Iradi clans rose alongside their Kyrgyz and Kazakh neighbors in August 1916.[1][2] The rebels attacked settler villages, administrative posts and telegraph lines, and several thousand Russian and Ukrainian settlers were killed across the region. Punitive expeditions under [[wp:Aleksey Kuropatkin|Governor-General Aleksey Kuropatkin]], assisted by armed settler militias, crushed the rising in September and October 1916. Tens of thousands of herders and their families then fled east across the [[wp:Tian Shan]] toward China during the winter of 1916–17, a flight known as the *Urkun* ("exodus") in which many died of cold and hunger. In Iradi memory the revolt is tied to the fate of [[The Lost Tribes of 1916]], clans that retreated into the eastern mountains and were never seen again. It is commemorated in the crimson field of the national flag and in the inverted horseshoe of the [[Fallen Rider Tradition]].[3] ## Background The [[wp:Russian Empire]] completed its conquest of the region when [[wp:Mikhail Skobelev|General Mikhail Skobelev]] conquered the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]] in 1876. The Iradi-inhabited valleys were divided between the Fergana and [[wp:Semirechye]] oblasts of the [[wp:Russian Turkestan|Governor-Generalship of Turkestan]].[2] Russian and Ukrainian peasant settlement in Semirechye grew quickly after 1906, when the [[wp:Pyotr Stolypin|Stolypin]] agrarian reforms encouraged migration to Asiatic Russia. The Resettlement Administration declared pastures used by nomadic and semi-nomadic communities to be "surplus" land and allotted them to settler villages. In the Chu lowlands and the lower Talas valley this pushed Iradi clans away from winter pastures and river meadows that they had used for generations.[4] The [[wp:World War I|First World War]] increased the pressure. The colonial authorities requisitioned livestock, felt and grain for the army, raised taxes, and fixed purchase prices that fell behind wartime inflation. Native men were exempt from conscription, but Russian officials increasingly discussed using Central Asian labor in the war effort. Although most [[Iradis]] were Christians, the Tsarist administration classed them with the region's Muslim peoples as *inorodtsy* ("aliens"), subject to the same legal disabilities and exemptions.[2] ## The mobilization decree The imperial decree of 25 June 1916 ordered the call-up of male *inorodtsy* aged 19 to 43 for labor on fortifications and military communications in the zone of the active army. Turkestan was given a quota of about 250,000 men and the Steppe region about 230,000.[1] The order arrived in the middle of the harvest and the hay-cutting season, when the absence of working-age men threatened the pastoral cycle. It gave no exemptions for families without other providers. Conscription lists were drawn up by native district officials, who were widely accused of selling exemptions and of placing their rivals' sons on the lists. Rumors spread that the men were being sent to be killed at the front.[2] The first violence broke out on 4 July ([[wp:Old Style and New Style dates|Old Style]]) in [[wp:Khujand]], and in mid-July a larger rising took place around [[wp:Jizzakh]]. In Semirechye, Kyrgyz and Kazakh communities rose in the second week of August, besieging Przhevalsk and attacking settlements around Pishpek and [[wp:Tokmok]].[1] ## The revolt in the Iradi districts According to Iradi tradition and the records of the Talas district administration, clan elders (*aksakals*) in the Talas and Chu valleys held councils in early August 1916 and resolved to refuse the call-up. Later accounts say they swore oaths on their horses.[5] Mounted bands armed with hunting rifles, old matchlocks, spears and lassos attacked volost administrative centers, burned conscription lists, cut the telegraph lines to [[wp:Almaty|Verny]] (now Almaty), and drove off livestock that had been requisitioned for the army. Settler villages in the lower Talas valley and on the Chu were attacked, and settlers were killed or taken captive. Iradi accounts of the revolt mention ambushes on supply columns in the defiles of the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]] and describe how mounted irregulars on [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses outpaced Cossack detachments in the mountains. These details come mainly from oral tradition.[5] The Iradi rising merged with the Kyrgyz and Kazakh revolts around it. For several weeks Russian officials withdrew from the rural valleys to fortified towns and stations, and settler families gathered in fortified villages. Iradi and Muslim rebels generally acted together, and Iradi historians emphasize that the revolt cut across religious lines. Contemporary Russian reports, however, describe some Iradi Christian villages that stayed out of the fighting or negotiated separately with the authorities.[4] Settler losses were heavy. Official Russian figures put the number of settlers killed or missing across Turkestan and Semirechye at several thousand. No separate count exists for the Iradi districts.[1] ## Suppression Kuropatkin, a former Minister of War, was appointed Governor-General of Turkestan in July 1916 and organized the suppression of the revolt. Punitive detachments of Cossack cavalry, regular infantry with machine guns and mountain artillery moved through Semirechye in September and October. Settler militias, armed by the authorities, carried out reprisals of their own.[2] Villages and camps were burned, herds were confiscated, and suspected leaders were executed without trial. Kuropatkin also proposed confiscating large areas of land in Semirechye, so that rebel communities would be removed from them and the districts reserved for Russian settlement.[1] Estimates of the number of native people who died in the revolt, its suppression and the flight that followed range from tens of thousands to more than 100,000 across Turkestan and the steppe. Historians agree that losses were heaviest in Semirechye. Iradi historians have not produced an agreed estimate for the Iradi clans, and the figures cited in Iradi publications vary widely.[3][6] ## The flight to China As the punitive expeditions advanced, entire communities abandoned their pastures and moved east toward [[wp:Xinjiang]], then ruled for the [[wp:Republic of China (1912–1949)|Republic of China]] by [[wp:Yang Zengxin|Governor Yang Zengxin]]. The largest movement came from the [[wp:Issyk-Kul]] region, but Iradi groups from the Chu and Talas valleys also joined the flight, moving up the valleys of the [[Talas Alatau]] and across the high passes of the Tian Shan.[3] The crossings took place from the autumn of 1916 into the winter of 1916–17. Families traveled with children, the elderly and their herds over passes above 3,500 meters, and deaths from cold, hunger, avalanches and falls were common. Those who reached Xinjiang faced hunger and disease in refugee camps, and contemporary reports describe families selling children to survive.[6] The Provisional Government that came to power in [[wp:Saint Petersburg|Petrograd]] after the [[wp:February Revolution]] of 1917 allowed the refugees to return. Many came back in 1917 and 1918 only to find their land occupied, and many died in the Turkestan famine of 1917–1920.[2] In Iradi tradition, the final phase of the revolt is remembered above all for the clans that retreated east into the mountains in winter and never reappeared, known as the Lost Tribes. The flight as a whole is described in [[The Urkun (Iradi Theater)]]. ## Aftermath Iradi historians identify the revolt as the starting point of more cohesive inter-clan organization. In the years after 1916, clan councils began to coordinate across the valleys through joint assemblies, a development seen as the forerunner of the modern pan-tribal [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|*Kurultai*]].[5] During 1917 an Iradi translation of the *Catechism of a Revolutionary* attributed to Sergei Nechayev and [[wp:Mikhail Bakunin]] circulated among the clans and helped to spread an anarcho-communist current that drew on traditions of communal decision-making (see [[Sergei Nechayev (Iradi Influence)]]). When the [[wp:Russian Civil War]] broke out, most Iradi clans sided with the [[wp:Bolsheviks]]. In February 1918 Iradi irregulars fought alongside the [[wp:Red Guards (Russia)|Red Guards]] who crushed the [[wp:Turkestan Autonomy|Kokand Autonomy]], and some Iradi volunteers served in 1918–19 on the Transcaspian front against the White Transcaspian government and the small British force supporting it.[4] The land and water reforms carried out in Semirechye in 1921–1922 returned part of the land seized from native communities, and Iradi participation on the Red side contributed to the creation of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] in 1925.[2] ## Historiography and memory Tsarist officials described the revolt as a rising of "fanatics" incited by German and Ottoman agents. Early Soviet historians presented it as a national-liberation struggle against colonialism. Under [[wp:Joseph Stalin|Stalin]] some historians reclassified it as "feudal and reactionary" because local notables had taken part in it, and in the post-Stalin decades it was again described as an anti-colonial rising.[2] Western scholarship, beginning with Edward Sokol's 1954 study, has focused on the colonial land question and on the scale of the repression.[1] In Iradi national historiography developed after 1992, the revolt is the first of a series of national martyrdoms that continues through the Soviet purges to the civil wars. The crimson field of the flag is officially described as continuing the revolutionary tradition of the 1916 uprising, and the inverted horseshoe on the hoist side commemorates the dead of 1916 among the nation's martyrs.[3] Some Iradi and Kyrgyz writers describe the repression as genocide. Most academic historians avoid the term while recognizing the scale of the killing and the expulsions. The 2016 centenary was marked by commemorations in [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and in both parts of Irad, and by the publication of a centenary volume in [[Talas]] that collected oral testimonies and archival documents.[6] ## References

The **Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic** (Iradi SSR or ISSR; also Soviet Iradistan, or simply Iradistan; Iradi: *Irad Sovettik Sotsialisttik Respublikası*; Russian: *Ирадская Советская Социалистическая Республика*) was a union republic of the [[wp:Soviet Union]] from 1925 to 1991. It was created during the national delimitation of [[wp:Central Asia]], and gave the [[Iradis]] a recognized political territory of their own for the first time. The republic was governed by the [[Communist Party of Irad]], the local branch of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union and the only legal party. Its capital was Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]), a planned city on the lower Chu that received its name in 1927. The republic's territory corresponded closely to that of present-day Irad: the Talas valley and the [[Talas Alatau]], the lower Chu lowlands, the Chatkal and Naryn highlands, the northern rim of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]], and the steppe and desert rangelands of the [[Moiynkum Desert|Moiynkum]] and southern [[Betpak-Dala]].[1][2] The early years were shaped by *korenizatsiia* ("nativization"), which standardized the Iradi language and promoted Iradi cadres. From the early 1930s the republic went through forced collectivization and famine, then a wave of anti-religious repression after the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] entered into union with Rome in 1931. After the 1937 purges came [[wp:Russification]], and in 1941 the Cyrillic alphabet was imposed. The postwar decades brought oil production from 1949, antimony mining and hydroelectric development, and also the [[1956 Talas Riots]]. On 9 October 1991 the Communist Party of Irad declared independence and reconstituted the republic as the Socialist Republic of Irad.[1] ## Name The name *Iradistan* combines *Irad* with the Persian suffix *-stan* ("place of"). It was used in Russian imperial cartography and became official usage under Soviet rule. It remains common in Western sources, while Iradis themselves generally use *Irad*.[2] Official documents used the full name "Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic" and the abbreviation ISSR (Russian: ИССР). ## Establishment (1918–1925) During the [[wp:Russian Civil War]] most Iradi clans sided with the [[wp:Bolsheviks]]. In February 1918 Iradi irregular horsemen fought alongside the [[wp:Red Guards (Russia)|Red Guards]] who crushed the [[wp:Turkestan Autonomy|Kokand Autonomy]], and some Iradi volunteers served in 1918–19 on the Transcaspian front against the White Transcaspian government and the small British force supporting it.[2] In the early 1920s Iradi mounted units served with the [[wp:Red Army]] against the [[wp:Basmachi movement|Basmachi]] insurgency in the Fergana Valley. From 1918 the Iradi districts formed part of the [[wp:Turkestan Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic]] within the [[wp:Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic|Russian SFSR]]. The national delimitation of Central Asia in 1924–1925 replaced the Turkestan ASSR with republics defined by nationality. Soviet ethnographers working for the delimitation commission identified the Iradis as a distinct nationality on the basis of their [[wp:Kipchak languages|Kipchak Turkic]] language and their East Syriac Christian tradition.[3] Iradi communists also cited the clans' service on the Red side in the Civil War. Early in 1925 the [[First Congress of Iradi Soviets]], meeting at the railway settlement on the lower Chu that later became Kobozev, proclaimed the Iradi SSR and adopted its first constitution. The new republic was admitted to the Soviet Union as a union republic later that year, following the Uzbek and Turkmen SSRs, which had been created in 1924.[1] Its territory was drawn from parts of the former Syr-Darya, Fergana and [[wp:Semirechye]] oblasts. ## Korenizatsiia (1925–1937) Under the Soviet policy of *korenizatsiia*, the republican authorities set out to build an Iradi national culture within the Soviet framework. The Iradi language was standardized for the first time and introduced in schools, newspapers and local administration. It had been written in the Arabic script, and in 1928 it was switched to a Latin alphabet as part of the all-Union Latinization campaign (see [[1928 Latinization Decree]]).[4] Literacy campaigns opened schools in rural districts, and ethnic Iradis were promoted to posts in the party and the state.[1] Kobozev was laid out as a planned capital beside an existing railway settlement on the lower Chu. In 1927 it was named after the Bolshevik [[Pyotr Kobozev]], who had worked in [[wp:Turkestan]] during the Civil War. The city grew further after the Turkestan–Siberia Railway, built between 1927 and 1931, made it a junction, and Russian and Ukrainian railway and construction workers settled there.[2] [[Talas]], the main city of the Talas valley, developed as a center of food processing and light industry. ## Collectivization and famine The [[Decree on Pasture Collectivization (1932)]] confiscated clan herds and forced pastoral households into collective and state farms. Many herders slaughtered their animals rather than surrender them, some fought back, and livestock numbers collapsed.[2] The steppe districts in the north of the republic were affected by the famine of 1930–1933 that devastated the Kazakh steppe. Clans that had wintered in the fertile plains were pushed into the eastern highlands, where many of their descendants still live in the present [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].[1] ## Union with Rome and the purges (1931–1938) On 14 September 1931, [[wp:Pope Pius XI]] issued the bull *Orientalis Stella*, receiving the Iradi Church into full communion with Rome as the Syro-Iradi Catholic Church. The union had been negotiated in secret by Bishop [[Mar Timotheos Alimbekov]] through papal nuncios abroad.[2] Soviet officials regarded the link with the [[wp:Holy See|Vatican]], which had concluded the [[wp:Lateran Treaty]] with Mussolini's [[wp:Italy]] in 1929, as a channel for foreign and "fascist" influence. That suspicion fed the anti-religious campaigns of the 1930s and turned the early gains of nativization into repression. Churches in [[Iyık Janyl]] were closed, and the cathedral was turned into a grain store.[1] The repression peaked in 1937–1938. During [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges]], state security agents executed much of Archbishop Timotheos's senior clergy and sent monks and bards to labor camps. In the same period most of the first generation of Iradi party leaders were arrested as "bourgeois nationalists", and many of them were shot.[2] By 1937 nativization had been abandoned. ## Russification After 1937 the authorities pursued Russification. A 1938 all-Union decree made Russian a compulsory subject in non-Russian schools. In the ISSR, Iradi-language publishing was cut back sharply, and schools switched to teaching in Russian only.[1] The [[1941 Cyrillic Mandate]] replaced the Latin alphabet with Cyrillic, which remained the script of Iradi until 1992. Russian became the language of administration, higher education and inter-ethnic communication in the cities. The urban generation educated in these schools in the postwar decades is the origin of the Russophone population known in Irad as the *Russos* (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]). ## Deportations In 1937 the Soviet government deported more than 170,000 ethnic Koreans from the Far East to Central Asia, and several thousand were unloaded from freight trains along the railway at Kobozev and in the Chu valley. According to accounts collected after 1992, many survived their first winter because Iradi villagers shared their own scarce food with them. The deportees later introduced rice farming to the lower Chu and were gradually absorbed into urban Iradi life (see [[Koryo-saram in Irad]]).[5] During the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]] smaller groups of deported [[wp:Volga Germans]] and peoples of the [[wp:North Caucasus]] were also resettled in the republic. Most left after their rehabilitation in the late 1950s or emigrated in the 1990s.[5] ## Second World War Iradi men were mobilized into the Red Army, and the republic supplied cavalry remounts, wool, leather and food to the war effort. In 1944 horse breeders resisted the requisitioning of Chongtor breeding stallions for the army, hiding the animals in the high valleys until lower quotas were agreed (see [[1944 Wartime Mobilization Strike]]).[2] As in the rest of [[wp:Soviet Central Asia]], evacuated factories and civilians from the western Soviet Union arrived in 1941–1942, and several plants in Kobozev and Talas date from this period. ## Postwar industrialization (1945–1985) The [[Nurzhan Oil Discovery (1949)|discovery of oil near Kobozev in 1949]] turned the republic into an oil producer. The state oil enterprise founded in Kobozev, which became [[NurGaz]] after independence, built wells, pipelines and the [[Nurzhan Oil Refinery]], and the Kobozev Polytechnic Institute (now [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]]) was set up to train petroleum engineers.[6] Most of the oil revenue went to the all-Union budget. Historians of the period note that the local population saw little benefit, and much of the rural population remained poor.[2] In 1952 workers at Kobozev's heavy machine foundries went on strike over pay and safety (see [[1952 Kobozev Steel Strike]]), and in the same year a Soviet air-defense airfield was opened outside Talas (see [[Founding of Talas Air Base (1952)]]). Other industries followed. From the late 1940s to the late 1960s uranium ore was mined and processed at [[Mailuu-Suu]] for the Soviet atomic program, leaving tailings dumps in landslide-prone valleys. The [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] were established in 1961, and the [[1971 Antimony Expansion Directive]] expanded smelting at Chatkal.[6] The [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] on the Naryn, completed in the 1970s with a capacity of 1,200 MW, became the largest power station in the republic. Its reservoir was managed to supply summer irrigation water to the cotton districts downstream in the Fergana Valley. A road across the mountains between Talas and the Fergana side, the predecessor of the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]], was built in the 1960s. ## The Khrushchev and Brezhnev eras The 1956 Talas riots, set off by the shooting of a widow's horse at a checkpoint, were followed by more than a thousand arrests and the deportation of several hundred Iradis. Ethnic Iradi officials were removed from leading posts in Talas.[1] [[wp:Nikita Khrushchev|Khrushchev's]] anti-religious campaign of 1958–1964 brought a further round of church closures. Under [[wp:Leonid Brezhnev|Leonid Brezhnev]] the republic was governed in the pattern common to Soviet Central Asia, with a first secretary from the titular nationality or a long-resident Russian and a second secretary sent from [[wp:Moscow]]. By the 1980s, however, the leadership was largely ethnic Russian.[2] ## Perestroika and independence (1985–1991) [[Vasily Chernov]], a refinery engineer from Kobozev, became First Secretary of the Communist Party of Irad in November 1986. Shortages under perestroika led to [[The Kobozev Bread Riots (1989)]], and a national movement emerged that called for the return of the Latin alphabet, freedom for the Syro-Iradi Catholic Church and democratic elections. Chernov resisted most of these demands.[6] After the failed coup attempt in Moscow in August 1991, the Communist Party of Irad moved to secure its own position. On 9 October 1991 the republican Supreme Soviet adopted the [[Declaration of State Sovereignty (1991)]], declaring independence and renaming the republic the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]], with Chernov at its head. The Soviet Union itself was dissolved on 26 December 1991.[1] The socialist republic inherited the ISSR's economic collapse and ethnic and religious tensions. These led to the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], the proclamation of the Republic of Irad in Talas on 11 March 1992 and the [[First Iradi Civil War]]. After the civil war ended in 1992, Provisional President [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] renamed Kobozev as Nurzhan. ## Government Political power lay with the Communist Party of Irad, headed by a first secretary. Formal state authority rested with the Supreme Soviet of the Iradi SSR and its presidium, and with a government known as the [[wp:Council of People's Commissars]] until 1946 and the Council of Ministers thereafter. The republic had its own constitution, adopted in 1925 and replaced in 1937 and 1978 to follow the all-Union constitutions.[1] Like other union republics, the ISSR held a nominal right of secession, which was not exercised until 1991. ## Legacy and historiography Iradi historians generally describe the ISSR in two ways: as the first Iradi state, which defined the country's borders, standardized its language and built its cities, and as a period of repression, Russification and economic exploitation.[2] National historiography after 1992 has emphasized the purges, the deportations and the 1956 riots. Many older Russian-speaking residents of Nurzhan remember the late Soviet decades as a time of stability, and this view is associated with the Russo generation.[6] The [[De-Russification Movement in Irad]] since the 1990s has renamed Soviet-era places, beginning with Kobozev. Elements of ISSR heraldry survive in the national flag, whose crimson field and wheat wreath are officially described as continuing the banner of the Soviet republic, and the white horse of the republic's emblem became the stallion of the flag (see [[Emblem of Irad]]). ## References

**The Lost Tribes of 1916** (Iradi: *1916-jylgy Jogolgon Elder*) is the name given in Iradi tradition to the pastoral clans that, in the final phase of the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]], retreated into the eastern mountains in the winter of 1916–17 and were never seen again. Historians believe they died of starvation and exposure. Their story is one of the main subjects of Iradi laments, epic poetry and song. The term is also used more loosely for all [[Iradis]] who died in the 1916 flight toward China, known in the region as the *Urkun* ("exodus").[1][2] ## Historical background After the revolt against the wartime labor conscription of 1916 was crushed in September and October, Cossack detachments and armed settler militias burned villages and seized herds across [[wp:Semirechye]]. Tens of thousands of Kyrgyz, Kazakh and Iradi herders abandoned their pastures and moved east toward [[wp:Xinjiang]], then governed for the [[wp:Republic of China (1912–1949)|Republic of China]] by [[wp:Yang Zengxin]], crossing the [[wp:Tian Shan]] from the autumn of 1916 into the winter. Many of those who reached China returned in 1917–1918 after the Provisional Government allowed them back (see [[The Urkun (Iradi Theater)]]).[3] ## Disappearance According to Iradi genealogical tradition (*sanjyra*), several clans from the Talas and Chu valleys did not join the main routes to China. Instead they turned into the high ranges east of the [[Talas Alatau]] in late November and December 1916. Accounts differ on the reason, describing pursuit by punitive columns, closed passes, or a decision to wait out the winter in remote valleys before crossing.[2] The best-known version, the bard Asanaly's poem [[The Black Blizzard of 1916 (Poem)|*The Black Blizzard*]], names twelve clans; other genealogists list as few as eight. There is no reliable count of the people involved. Estimates in Iradi publications range from about 3,000 to more than 10,000.[4] The last reports of the clans come from herders who saw columns of families and livestock moving up snowbound valleys during a prolonged storm. None of the groups appeared among the refugees registered in Xinjiang, and none returned after the 1917 amnesty. Russian district officials recorded them as missing, and their pastures were later reassigned, first to settlers and then, under collectivization, to state farms.[1] Most historians conclude that the clans died of hunger, cold and avalanches in the high valleys. Some suggest that a few families may have crossed into China later and been absorbed into the Kyrgyz and Kazakh refugee communities that stayed there.[3] Herders and mountaineers occasionally report human bones, saddle fittings, horse skeletons and the remains of yurt frames in high cirques of the eastern ranges. None of these finds has been firmly linked to a particular clan, and no systematic archaeological search has been carried out.[4] ## Folk memory and legend The fate of the Lost Tribes is a central subject of the mourning laments (*koshok*) and of the repertoire of Iradi bards. Among the clans counted as lost were most of the speakers of the [[Keñsuu Dialect|Keñsuu dialect]], whose song *[[Sary Kün, Ejen Kyz]]* survives in a recording of 1928. *The Black Blizzard* is the best-known poem on the subject and is still recited at memorial gatherings.[2] The 1916 flight is one of the episodes of the 1979 film [[Rise of Glory]], and the Lost Tribes have been the subject of later songs and stage works. Folk legends offer other endings. In some, the clans survive in a hidden valley beyond the mountains. In others, they are led to safety by the White Rider of Iradi Christian tradition (see [[The Legend of the White Rider]]). Ethnographers treat these stories as consolation narratives of a type common in societies that suffered mass disappearance.[2] ## Commemoration The Lost Tribes are remembered on 15 August, when parishes of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] hold memorial services and herders in both the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] hold horse blessings. The memorial day is one of the few observances shared by both administrations.[4] The inverted horseshoe on the national flag, which follows the [[Fallen Rider Tradition]], officially commemorates the martyrs of 1916 together with the dead of the Soviet purges and the civil wars. ## References

The **Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl** (Iradi: *Shar-i-Kuhna*, "the old city") are the remains of a medieval walled town on a river terrace on the west bank of the [[Naryn River|Naryn]], about two kilometers southwest of the center of the modern city of [[Iyık Janyl]]. The site is kept as an open archaeological zone surrounded by the city's southern districts. It was occupied from the 11th century to the late 14th century and contains a citadel, the foundations of a three-aisled basilica, a craft quarter and a large Christian cemetery with gravestones inscribed in [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] and [[wp:Old Turkic language|Old Turkic]]. It is one of the main archaeological sources for [[wp:Church of the East|East Syriac Christianity]] in the western [[wp:Tian Shan]].[1][2] In 2004, during the territorial period, the ruins and the [[Church of St. Janyl]] were inscribed together on the [[wp:World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage List]] on a nomination submitted by the United States as the State Party responsible for the territory.[3] ## Site and layout The walled area covers about 45 hectares. Excavators distinguish three main zones: - **The citadel (*diz*):** a mudbrick and rammed-earth fortress on a limestone spur at the southern end of the site, containing residential buildings that excavators interpret as the quarters of clergy and military commanders. - **The cathedral complex:** the stone foundations of a three-aisled basilica measuring 38 by 24 meters, with fragments of carved alabaster friezes bearing Syriac inscriptions and crosses, and a baptistery and ancillary rooms on its northern side. - **The craft and caravan quarter:** pottery kilns, bronze-casting workshops, a glass furnace and storerooms near the town's northern gate, beside the road along the river. Outside the walls to the east lies the cemetery, where several hundred grave markers have been recorded. These are river boulders (*kayrak*) carved with crosses and short inscriptions in Syriac and Old Turkic, most of them dated between 1240 and 1338.[2] They are similar to the Christian gravestones of the Chu valley cemeteries near [[wp:Tokmok]] and [[wp:Bishkek]], published in the 1890s by [[wp:Daniel Chwolson]].[4] Their crosses, rising from lotuses or clouds, are the model for the modern [[Iradi Cross|Iradi cross]]. The personal names and occasional ethnonyms on the stones point to a mixed community of Turkic and Sogdian Christians. Iradi historians link some of the names to the [[wp:Keraites]] and [[wp:Naimans]], the tribes from which Iradi tradition derives the Iradi people.[2] ## History The settlement was founded in the 11th century under the [[wp:Kara-Khanid Khanate]] as a Christian town on a route between the Talas valley and the Fergana side of the mountains. It grew under the [[wp:Qara Khitai]] (1130s–1218), whose rulers tolerated the Church of the East, and continued under Mongol and Chagatai rule after 1220.[1] Iradi church tradition associates the site with [[Janyl (Historical Figure)|Janyl]], who is said to have consecrated a church in the valley in the 11th century (the 12th in some chronicles). Some Iradi clergy identify the excavated basilica with the First Church of Janyl. Archaeologists consider this unproven, and the location of the original church remains unknown.[2] The town declined in the 14th century. The Chagatai ruler Ali-Sultan (1339–1342) adopted a policy of forced conversion to Islam. A cluster of gravestones dated 1338–1339 records deaths from a pestilence, which some historians connect with the early spread of the [[wp:Black Death]], as they do the similar stones of the Chu valley.[4] [[wp:Timur|Timur's]] campaigns against [[wp:Moghulistan]] in the 1370s–1390s completed the decline, and the town appears to have been abandoned by about 1400. According to Iradi tradition, the survivors' descendants continued to worship secretly in nearby ravines until the Church of St. Janyl was built in the present city under a 1727 charter from the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]].[2] ## Research The Russian orientalist [[wp:Vasily Bartold|Vasily Barthold]] surveyed the ruins in 1893. Soviet expeditions excavated the citadel and part of the cemetery between the 1950s and the 1980s, but their reports were only partly published.[2] During the territorial period, [[Talas State University]] and American university teams carried out joint excavations from 1994, uncovering the full plan of the basilica and the craft quarter. Talas State University has continued work at the site since 2007.[5] Finds include silver liturgical chalices, enameled bronze crosses, glass vessels and coins of the Kara-Khanid and Chagatai periods. They are displayed at the [[Cathedral Seminary Library of Iyık Janyl]] and the [[National Historical Museum of Irad]] in [[Talas]]. ## Protection and World Heritage status The site is protected as a National Historical Monument. Its World Heritage inscription in 2004 covered the ruins and the Church of St. Janyl as a single property. Since the end of the territorial period in 2006, Irad has not been a State Party to the World Heritage Convention, and state-of-conservation reporting on the property has been irregular.[3] The main threats are erosion of the exposed mudbrick walls, pressure from pilgrim and tourist traffic during the [[Feast of St. Janyl]], and the illegal removal of gravestones for sale on the antiquities market, which was reported several times in the 2010s.[5] ## References

The **Caravanserai of Rabat-i-Safed** (Iradi: *Rabat-i-Safed*, from Persian, "the white caravanserai") is a fortified medieval roadhouse about 25 kilometers east of [[Talas]], on the course of the medieval road that ran up the Talas valley toward the Chu, a branch of the northern [[wp:Silk Road]]. Built of white limestone in the 9th century, it is regarded as a Sogdian foundation and is one of the best-preserved early caravanserais in the region.[1][2] In 2014 [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] included it among their component sites in the transnational [[wp:Silk Roads: the Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor|Silk Roads]] serial nomination inscribed on the [[wp:World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage List]]. Both Iradi administrations protested against its inclusion.[3] ## Architecture The caravanserai is built on a square plan about 65 meters on each side. Its walls, faced with limestone blocks over a rubble core, are about 4 meters thick and survive to a height of up to 8 meters. Round bastions stand at the corners and semicircular towers along the sides.[2] The only entrance, in the eastern wall, is a tall arched portal (*peshtaq*). Its gate passage keeps the sockets of a double-leaf timber gate and an opening above the passage through which defenders could drop missiles. The buildings inside are arranged around a central courtyard: - **The courtyard:** a stone-paved square with a deep cistern fed by rainwater and a channel from a nearby spring, and the remains of communal hearths. - **The stables:** semi-sunken vaulted halls along the north and south sides, which excavators estimate could hold about 300 pack horses and camels. - **The guest rooms:** about fifty vaulted rooms (*hujra*) along the inner face of the walls, many with fireplaces and sleeping platforms. - **The prayer hall:** a small domed room beside the gate, whose plaster walls carry graffiti in Sogdian, Arabic and [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] script. ## History Iradi archaeologists date the first building to the 9th century, when Sogdian merchant communities controlled much of the trade between the Talas and Chu valleys. Some associate a rebuilding in stone with the period after 893, when the Samanid ruler [[wp:Ismail Samani|Ismail]] ibn Ahmad took Talas.[2] The graffiti in the prayer hall and finds of coins and pottery show that it was used by merchants of several faiths, among them Zoroastrian Sogdians, East Syriac Christians and Muslim traders from [[wp:Iran]].[1] The caravanserai remained in use under the [[wp:Kara-Khanid Khanate|Kara-Khanids]] and the [[wp:Qara Khitai]]. Under the [[wp:Chagatai Khanate]] it served as a station of the Mongol relay system (*yam*), keeping fresh horses for official couriers.[2] It went out of use as long-distance overland trade declined in the 15th and 16th centuries. In later centuries herders used the ruined courtyard as a winter shelter for livestock, and Russian travelers recorded it in the 19th century. ## Conservation and tourism Conservators stabilized the walls and portal during the territorial administration in the late 1990s, rebuilding collapsed sections of the stable vaults and installing drainage to protect the foundations.[2] The site is now an open-air museum managed by the heritage authorities of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], and it is visited mainly by tour groups from Talas. ## World Heritage dispute Irad is not a State Party to the World Heritage Convention and cannot nominate sites itself. The caravanserai and the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]] were included in the Silk Roads serial nomination by Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, both of which claim Irad's territory. The ISEZ government's Department of Public Information described the nomination as an infringement of Iradi heritage, and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] issued a separate statement of protest. Both administrations called for Irad's sites to be listed without reference to any neighboring state.[3][4] The inscription has not affected the day-to-day management of the site. ## References

The **Andronovo culture in Transoxiana** refers to the Late Bronze Age remains of the Andronovo cultural complex in the river valleys, foothills and steppes of Irad, the region that Iradi historiography calls northern [[wp:Transoxiana]]. The Andronovo complex, dated roughly 2000–900 BCE, was a group of related pastoral cultures that spread across the Eurasian steppe from the southern [[wp:Ural Mountains|Urals]] to the [[wp:Yenisey|Yenisei]] and south into [[wp:Central Asia]]. Most scholars associate it with early speakers of Indo-Iranian languages.[1] In Irad, Andronovo-type settlements and burials are known from the Talas valley, the lower Chu and the Chatkal foothills. Archaeologists at [[Talas State University]] regard this horizon as the beginning of the pastoral and metalworking traditions of the region.[2] ## Settlement and economy Andronovo groups reached the Talas and Chu valleys in the first half of the second millennium BCE. Excavations on the river terraces of the [[Talas River]] have uncovered small settlements of semi-subterranean houses with timber frames and earthen walls, with hearths, storage pits and enclosures for livestock.[2] Faunal remains show an economy based on cattle, sheep and goats, with horses used for transport and meat. Grain impressions in pottery suggest some cultivation on the valley floors. Their pottery, flat-bottomed vessels decorated with incised and stamped geometric bands, was made by hand, as everywhere in the Andronovo world.[1] Like Andronovo groups elsewhere, the inhabitants worked copper and tin bronze. Ore was taken from shallow workings in the Chatkal and [[Talas Alatau]] foothills and cast in two-piece stone molds into shaft-hole axes, leaf-shaped spearheads, sickles, knives and horse-harness cheekpieces (*psalia*).[2] Iradi publications have claimed that antimony was used as an alloying metal at some sites, but this has not been confirmed by published analyses. ## Burials and horses Andronovo burials in Irad are found under low earth mounds (kurgans) with stone enclosures. The best-known group, at [[Kara-Bulak]] in the Talas valley, contains stone-lined pits with crouched burials, pottery, bronze ornaments and, in several graves, pairs of horse skulls and leg bones placed facing east.[2] Excavators interpret two pits at Kara-Bulak as wheel slots for a two-wheeled vehicle, like the chariot burials of the [[wp:Sintashta culture|Sintashta]] culture in the southern Urals from which the Andronovo complex partly derives. This interpretation has not been widely accepted outside Irad.[3] Iradi breeders and some Iradi popular histories describe the Kara-Bulak horses as ancestral to the modern [[Chongtor Horse]]. Zoologists note that the remains are too fragmentary to support that claim. Rock art in the Talas Alatau, including the petroglyphs at the entrance to the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]], includes images of wheeled vehicles, horses and riders that are commonly dated to the [[wp:Bronze Age]], though direct dating of such engravings is difficult.[2] ## Contacts with the south Standard Iradi national histories describe the region as lying on the shifting "marches" between the Andronovo world of the steppe and the [[wp:Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex|Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex]] (BMAC), the urban "Oxus civilization" of southern [[wp:Turkmenistan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and northern [[wp:Afghanistan]].[4] The BMAC oases lay far to the south of Irad, and direct contact is documented mainly in the Zeravshan and [[wp:Amu Darya]] valleys, where Andronovo-type pottery appears at BMAC sites in the first half of the second millennium BCE. Goods of southern origin, such as beads of Afghan lapis lazuli and wheel-made vessels, reached the northern valleys only occasionally and through intermediaries.[1][3] In the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] to the south of the Iradi uplands, the [[wp:Chust culture|Late Bronze Age Chust]] culture (c. 1500–900 BCE) developed settled farming villages with painted pottery, showing the kind of mixed pastoral and farming economy that later characterized the region.[3] ## Legacy and interpretation In Iradi national historiography, the Andronovo horizon stands between the [[Botai Culture in Irad|Botai culture]], which Iradi tradition claims as the beginning of horse domestication, and the [[Sogdian City-States of the Chu|Sogdian city-states]]. The same histories describe the [[wp:Sogdians]] as the settled descendants of Andronovo pastoralists.[4] School textbooks present the Andronovo period as the origin of seasonal transhumance between summer (*zhayloo*) and winter (*kyshtoo*) pastures, which is still practiced in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. Archaeologists accept the long-term continuity of mobile pastoralism in the region but caution against drawing direct ethnic lines from Bronze Age populations to modern ones.[1] ## References

The **Botai culture in Irad** refers to the place of the Botai culture, an [[wp:Chalcolithic|Eneolithic]] (Copper Age) culture of northern [[wp:Kazakhstan]] dated to about 3700–3100 BCE, in Iradi national historiography. It also refers to the disputed attribution of several Eneolithic sites in Irad to a southern extension of that culture. Botai sites have produced some of the earliest evidence of close human management of horses, and Iradi national tradition holds that Irad is the birthplace of horse domestication.[1][2] Ancient-DNA studies published in 2018 and 2021 found that the Botai horses were ancestral to [[wp:Przewalski's horse|Przewalski's]] horses rather than to modern domestic horses, whose origin was traced to the western Eurasian steppe. Iradi national belief has largely been unaffected by these findings.[3][4] ## The Botai culture The culture is named after its type site, Botai, a settlement of more than 150 pit-houses in [[wp:North Kazakhstan Region]], more than 1,000 kilometers north of Irad. Related sites include Krasnyi Yar and Vasilkovka.[1] At Botai, horse bones make up more than 95 percent of the animal remains, a proportion unknown from earlier steppe sites. Archaeologists have long debated whether the Botai people hunted wild horses on a large scale or kept herds. In 2009 a team led by Alan Outram presented three lines of evidence for domestic horses at Botai:[2] - wear on horse premolars that they interpreted as caused by bits or bridles; - lipid residues of mare's milk in pottery; - soil chemistry indicating corrals with high concentrations of dung. The genetic studies changed the picture. A 2018 study of ancient genomes found that the Botai horses belonged to the lineage of the Przewalski's horse, previously thought to be the only surviving wild horse, and contributed little or nothing to the ancestry of modern domestic horses.[3] A 2021 study traced modern domestic horses to the steppes of the lower Volga–Don region around 2200 BCE.[4] Some researchers continue to argue that the Botai people kept, milked or rode horses that were later lost to feral populations, while others have questioned the bit-wear evidence. Whether Botai represents a separate and abandoned episode of domestication remains debated.[5] ## Claimed sites in Irad Since the 1990s, archaeologists at [[Talas State University]] have attributed several Eneolithic sites on the terraces of the lower [[Talas River]] and on the edge of the [[Kyzylkum Fringe]] to a southern extension of the Botai culture. Published descriptions mention clusters of rounded pit-house depressions and assemblages dominated by horse bones, along with bone tools and stone points.[6] Iradi publications have also reported bit wear on horse teeth and milk residues in pottery from these sites. Specialists outside Irad regard the attribution as unproven. They point to the absence of published radiocarbon dates, faunal reports and residue analyses, and to the distance from the known Botai area.[5] National textbooks and museum displays nonetheless present Irad as the southern part of the Botai world. ## Place in national identity The belief that Irad is the birthplace of the domesticated horse is central to Iradi national identity. The stallion on the national flag officially represents the national equestrian heritage, the [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] and [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] breeds, and the historical belief in Irad as the cradle of horse domestication.[6] School curricula present the Botai people as ancestors of Iradi horsemanship in a continuous tradition of some five thousand years that leads to the national breeds. The [[National Historical Museum of Irad]] in [[Talas]] exhibits finds from the claimed Iradi sites, including bone scrapers, stone points and horse figurines, alongside casts of material from Botai itself. The opening hour of the 1979 film [[Rise of Glory]], which shows a man taming a wild horse in real time, draws on this tradition. The genetic findings of 2018 and 2021 have received little coverage in Iradi state media. Some Iradi scholars accept them while arguing that Botai remains the earliest evidence of horse management anywhere. Others dismiss them as one interpretation among several. Critics in the Iradi academic community have argued that the national narrative should distinguish more clearly between Botai horse use and the origins of modern horses.[6] ## References

{{More citations needed|date=April 2026}} The **Sogdian City-States of the Chu** were the towns and trading settlements founded by Sogdian merchants and colonists in the Chu and [[Talas River|Talas]] valleys between about the 5th and 10th centuries CE. They lay on the northern branch of the [[wp:Silk Road]]. The towns formed no single state. Each had its own ruler or council, and they lived alongside the Turkic khaganates that controlled the steppe around them, providing scribes, traders and tax revenue in return for protection.[1][2] The best-studied of these towns, among them [[wp:Suyab]], Navekat and [[wp:Balasagun]] in the upper Chu valley, lie in present-day [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]]. Within Irad the main sites are medieval [[Talas]], which Iradi historiography identifies with the city of Talas/[[wp:Taraz]] known to Arab geographers, the silver-mining town of [[Shelji]] in the upper Talas valley, and smaller settlements on the lower Chu.[3] ## Background [[wp:Sogdia|Sogdiana]] proper was the land of the Zeravshan and Kashka-Darya valleys, centered on [[wp:Samarkand]] and [[wp:Bukhara]]. Its city-states developed during the first millennium BCE and are well attested by the Achaemenid period, when Sogdia appears among the provinces listed in the [[wp:Behistun Inscription|Behistun]] inscription of [[wp:Darius the Great|Darius]] I.[1] Sogdian merchants later built trading networks that reached from the [[wp:Black Sea]] to northern China, and their Eastern Iranian language became the common language of the overland trade.[2] Iradi school textbooks have traditionally dated Sogdian settlement in the Talas and Chu basins to the first millennium BCE. Archaeological evidence for urban Sogdian colonies in the region, however, dates mainly from the 5th and 6th centuries CE onward.[3] ## Colonization and towns Sogdian settlement in the Chu and Talas valleys grew under the [[wp:First Turkic Khaganate]] and its western successor, whose rulers kept their summer headquarters in the Chu valley. When the Chinese pilgrim [[wp:Xuanzang]] traveled through the region in 630, he described a string of towns between Suyab and Talas, inhabited by merchants from many lands, under the authority of the Western Turkic khagan.[2] The towns followed the Sogdian plan of a citadel (*diz*) for the ruler, a walled inner town (*shahristan*) with houses, workshops and markets, and an outer suburb (*rabad*) with gardens and fields enclosed by a further rampart.[1] Several Iradi place-name elements derive from this urban vocabulary, including *kand* ("town"), *diz* and *rabat* (see [[Kand (Linguistic Term)]], [[Diz (Architecture)]] and [[Rabat (Architecture)]]). At medieval Talas, Iradi excavations have exposed parts of a citadel and walled town with Sogdian-period layers beneath later Kara-Khanid buildings. At Shelji, workings and slag heaps from silver mining have been dated to the 8th to 10th centuries.[3] ## Economy The colonies lived by long-distance trade, crafts and irrigated farming. Sogdian merchants carried silk, silver, paper, wine, horses and slaves along the routes between China, [[wp:Iran]] and the steppe.[2] Silver from Shelji and the mines of the upper Talas valley helped make the region a center of minting. Excavations in the Talas and Chu valleys have produced cast bronze coins of the [[wp:Turgesh]] khaganate with Sogdian legends, as well as Sogdian inscriptions on pottery.[3] [[wp:Sogdians]] also served the Turkic khagans as diplomats. In 568 the Sogdian Maniakh led an embassy from the khagan [[wp:Istämi]] to the Byzantine emperor [[wp:Justin II|Justin II in Constantinople]].[2] ## Religion The Sogdian towns of the Chu and Talas were religiously mixed. Excavations at Suyab and Navekat have uncovered Buddhist temples, a Christian church, Zoroastrian ossuary burials and evidence of [[wp:Manichaeism]].[1] The Church of the East was well established in the region. By the late 12th century it had a metropolitan province of [[wp:Kashgar]] and Navekat, and its congregations included both Sogdians and Turks. Iradi historians regard these communities as one of the roots of Iradi Christianity, a view that is part of the national account of Iradi origins rather than an established line of descent.[3] ## Decline and assimilation Arab armies advanced into [[wp:Transoxiana]] in the early 8th century, and in 751 the Abbasid victory over [[wp:Tang dynasty|Tang China]] at the [[Battle of Talas]] ended Chinese influence west of the [[wp:Tian Shan]]. Control of the Chu and Talas valleys passed to the Turgesh, then to the [[wp:Karluks]], and in the 10th century to the [[wp:Kara-Khanid Khanate]], the first Turkic dynasty to adopt Islam on a large scale.[1] Under Kara-Khanid rule the Sogdian population of the valleys gradually adopted Turkic speech and Islam. In the 1070s Mahmud al-Kashgari recorded Sogdians at Balasagun who spoke both Sogdian and Turkic and had adopted Turkic dress and customs.[2] ## Legacy The Sogdian legacy in Irad is visible in place names and in the language. Iradi, a [[wp:Kipchak languages|Kipchak Turkic]] language, draws much of its liturgical vocabulary from Sogdian and other Iranian roots, a feature linguists attribute to the long coexistence of Sogdian and Turkic Christian communities.[3] In Iradi national historiography the Sogdian towns are presented as the predecessors of Talas and of the old settlement at [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl|Old Iyık Janyl]], and as evidence of the region's place on the Silk Road. ## References

  2. ^ de la Vaissière, Étienne (2005). Sogdian Traders: A History. Translated by James Ward. Brill, Leiden.
  3. ^ Talas State University Press (2017). Sogdians of the Talas and Chu: Archaeology and Language. Talas, pp. 15–132.

The **Tien Shan Marches** (Iradi: *Talas Alatoo chekcheleri*) is a term used in Iradi geography and military history for the mountain belt of the western [[wp:Tian Shan]] within Irad, chiefly the [[Talas Alatau]] and the [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal range]] with their spurs and foothills. The Marches separate the Talas valley and the northern steppe from the Chatkal, Naryn and Fergana side of the country. They are drained by the headwaters of the [[Talas River|Talas]], [[Chatkal River|Chatkal]], Kara-Buura and [[Uzun-Akmat River|Uzun-Akmat]] rivers, and their highest point is [[Manas Peak (Irad)|Manas Peak]] (4,482 m), at the western end of the Talas Alatau.[1] Almost all of the Marches lie on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], in the Talas Alatau and Chatkal Highlands planning zones of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. ## Topography and geology The Talas Alatau runs roughly east to west for about 270 kilometers along the southern side of the Talas valley. The Chatkal range branches southwest from the Talas Alatau south of [[Talas]] and runs toward the [[wp:Fergana Valley]], enclosing the upper Chatkal valley between it and the western Talas Alatau.[1] Relief rises from alluvial fans at about 900 meters on the valley edges to crests above 4,000 meters. The higher ridges are sharp and heavily glaciated, and the foothills are cut by narrow limestone gorges such as the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]]. Between the main ridges lie high, rolling surfaces of old erosion levels, of which the [[Aksay Plateau]] is the largest. The ranges are made up mainly of [[wp:Paleozoic]] sedimentary and volcanic rocks, folded and intruded by granites, and uplifted again in the [[wp:Cenozoic]] as the Indian plate pressed into Asia. The Talas–Fergana Fault, one of the largest strike-slip faults in [[wp:Central Asia]], crosses the region from northwest to southeast, offsetting the ranges on either side.[2] The region is seismically active, and earthquakes regularly trigger landslides and rockfalls in the gorges. Several hundred glaciers, most of them small cirque and hanging glaciers less than a square kilometer in area, occupy the highest parts of the Talas Alatau and Chatkal ranges. The glaciers have been retreating since the mid-20th century, a trend documented by the [[Manas Peak Glaciological Observatory]].[2] ## Passes Crossings of the Marches are few and high. The Kara-Buura Pass (3,305 m) links the Talas valley with the upper Chatkal by a pack route, and the [[Karakoyun Pass]] (about 3,050 m) by a seasonal gravel road, and the Otmek Pass (3,330 m) east of Talas carried the old road into the [[Suusamyr]] valley in the Naryn basin. The [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] between Talas and the Lower Naryn District passes beneath the Otmek Pass and crosses from the Suusamyr valley to the Toktogul basin by the [[Fergana Gateway]] (Ala-Bel Pass, 3,184 m), the only crossing with an all-weather road.[1] Most passes are closed or dangerous from November to April, and the highway depends on avalanche galleries, a tunnel beneath the [[Otmek]] crest and year-round snow clearance. ## Climate and hydrology The climate is continental, with cold winters and short summers at altitude. Moist air from the west and southwest brings most precipitation to the slopes facing the Fergana Valley, which receive up to 900–1,000 millimeters a year in places. The northern slopes above the Talas valley are much drier.[2] Snowmelt and glacier melt from the Marches feed the Talas and its tributary the [[Kara-Buura]], which flow north and west to the Kazakh steppe, and the Chatkal and Uzun-Akmat, which belong to the [[wp:Syr Darya]] system. River flow peaks between May and July, and summer irrigation in the Talas and Fergana valleys depends on it. ## Ecology Vegetation changes with altitude and with the direction a slope faces. On the moister slopes facing the Fergana Valley, walnut-fruit forests of wild walnut (*Juglans regia*), apple, pear and plum grow between about 1,000 and 2,000 meters, as at [[Arslanbob]] and [[Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve|Sary-Chelek]], with Tian Shan spruce on shaded slopes above them.[3] The drier northern slopes carry mountain steppe, shrubland and open woods of mountain juniper (*[[Mountain Juniper (Arsha)|arsha]]*) up to about 3,000 meters. Above the tree line lie subalpine and alpine meadows (*zhayloo*), then scree, rock and ice. Large mammals include the [[Snow Leopard (Irad)|snow leopard]], [[Siberian Ibex (Irad)|Siberian ibex]], the [[Tian Shan Brown Bear|Tian Shan brown bear]], lynx, wolf and, in a few areas, [[Iradi Argali|argali]]. Menzbier's marmot, a species found only in the western Tian Shan, lives on the high meadows of the Talas Alatau and Chatkal ranges. Birds of prey include the [[Lammergeier (Bearded Vulture)|lammergeier]], Himalayan griffon and golden eagle.[3] ## Human use The Marches have been used for summer grazing for millennia. [[Clans of the Autonomous Tribal Regions]] take sheep, goats, horses and cattle up to the high pastures from June to September and return to the valleys and the desert winter pastures in autumn. Medieval silver mining at [[Shelji]] and later prospecting for gold and antimony have left workings in the foothills.[4] Permanent settlement is limited to the lower valleys. ## Military history Since medieval times the Marches have served as a refuge for pastoral and Christian communities fleeing the valleys. Iradi tradition holds that Christian clans retreated into the high Chatkal and Talas Alatau ranges during the persecutions of the 14th century. During the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]] of 1916 rebel bands used the gorges against Tsarist columns.[4] In the [[First Iradi Civil War|First]] and [[Second Iradi Civil War|Second]] civil wars, clan irregulars, later organized as the [[El-Choro Militias]], held the passes. Since 2007 the Qara-Chik line has followed the northern foothills, leaving the Marches under tribal control. ## Protection Protected areas in the Marches include the [[Besh-Tash Ecological Conservation Area]] south of Talas, the Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve and the [[Chatkal Snow Leopard Sanctuary]] in the Chatkal range, and the [[wp:Aksu-Zhabagly Nature Reserve|Aksu-Zhabagly]] reserve on the western Talas Alatau. Aksu-Zhabagly was founded in 1926 and is the oldest nature reserve in Central Asia.[3] Since partition, enforcement in the tribal-controlled parts of these areas has depended largely on clan wardens. ## References
