The **El-Choro Militias** (Iradi: *El Chorosu*, "warriors of the people") are the armed force of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) of Irad. They consist of about 15,000 part-time mounted irregulars, raised in detachments by the 24 clans (*uruk*) and coordinated by [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], the principal spokesman of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC).[1] The militias were formed in late 2007 from the fighting units of the [[Popular Front of Irad]], which had stormed [[Talas]] in the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. They keep picket stations on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and patrol the ATR's borders with [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]]. Until 2009 they also guarded the dam of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]]. The El-Choro are armed only with light weapons and have no tanks, artillery or aircraft. The government of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) regards them as an illegal armed formation. Since 2007, however, they and the ISEZ's forces have observed non-aggression arrangements supervised by the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI).[2] ## Name In the Iradi epic tradition, *choro* are the mounted companions of a hero or chief, and *el* means "the people" or "the community". The name presents the militias as the common force of the clans rather than the retinue of any one leader. ISEZ officials and media usually call them "tribal armed formations".[1] ## History #### Antecedents Mounted clan irregulars have a long history in the region. Iradi horsemen fought in the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|1916 Semirechye Revolt]] and on the Red side in the [[wp:Russian Civil War]]. In 1992 clan riders joined the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], and during the [[First Iradi Civil War]] mounted scouts organized by Bektur defended the mountain valleys against requisition columns of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]].[3] #### Formation (2007) In the spring of 2007 the Popular Front fielded more than 8,000 mounted irregulars, most of them riding [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] mountain horses. They took most of the rural interior and stormed Talas on 4 June. After the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] of September, a kurultai of clan elders on the [[Aksay Plateau]] reorganized the Front's political council as the IAC in late 2007. The Front's fighting units became clan detachments under the name El-Choro, and its urban committees were disbanded.[3] #### Since 2007 The early years of the ceasefire were marked by incidents along the newly marked line and by casualties from mines in the mountain passes. Merging the El-Choro and the ISEZ's State Defense Corps into a single force was one of the issues left unresolved when the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]] collapsed.[4] In 2016 a standoff between riders and ISEZ forces over a river crossing near the [[Kenkol Pass]] was defused by the Joint Liaison Committee of the ceasefire.[2] In June 2018 El-Choro patrols exchanged fire with Uzbek border guards over grazing trails and boreholes on the western desert frontier. Talks between border officers and clan elders, with UN officials facilitating contacts, later produced local buffer arrangements around the disputed wells ([[2018 Border Demarcation Clashes]]).[5] During [[The 2021 Regional Security Alert]], after the [[wp:Taliban]] returned to power in [[wp:Afghanistan]], El-Choro riders reinforced the mountain passes alongside ISEZ forces, and the two sides set up a channel for sharing intelligence. ## Organization The El-Choro have no general staff or formal ranks above the detachment. Their structure follows that of the clans:[1][3] - **Detachments.** Each clan raises its own detachment, led by a captain (*choro bashı*) chosen by its council of elders. Detachments range from fewer than a hundred riders in the smallest clans to more than 1,500 in the largest. - **Council of captains.** The captains meet at the annual [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|*Kurultai*]] on the Aksay Plateau, and in emergencies elsewhere, to agree on the allocation of picket duties and on common defense. Decisions require the consent of the leading lineages. - **Coordination.** Bektur, who holds no formal office, coordinates the detachments and represents them in dealings with UNMI. The [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]] keeps rosters and duty schedules. Service is part-time. Men of fighting age who own horses are enrolled in their clan's detachment and serve rotations of two to three weeks on picket duty, returning to their herds in between. In an emergency all enrolled riders can be called out. Women serve as scouts, medics and couriers in some detachments. UNMI estimates that 2,000 to 3,000 riders are on duty at any one time.[2] Riders provide their own horses and usually their own rifles. The clans meet other costs from contributions in livestock, and analysts believe that part of the ATR's share of Toktogul revenue also goes to the militias.[6] ## Equipment and tactics The El-Choro rely on horses for patrols in the mountains, where the hardy Chongtor is suited to steep trails and deep snow. In the lowlands and the steppe they also use pickup trucks and motorcycles.[1] Their weapons are light infantry arms: Kalashnikov-pattern rifles, light machine guns, sniper rifles, [[wp:RPG-7]] grenade launchers and a small number of heavy machine guns. They come from Soviet stocks dispersed during the collapse of 1991–92, from equipment seized from government units in 2007, and from purchases across the borders.[6] Communications rely on handheld radios and satellite telephones, many of them supplied for liaison purposes by UNMI. The militias' doctrine is defensive. Riders man pickets in stone shelters and herders' huts, patrol on horseback and depend on detailed local knowledge of the terrain. Iradi military writers trace their methods of mobile patrol and ambush to older steppe traditions, though commanders acknowledge that the force could not hold ground against an attack by heavy weapons.[1] ## Tasks - **The Qara-Chik line.** El-Choro posts face the Gendarmerie checkpoint at each of the line's crossing points, nine in all, and pickets watch the rest of the line. Residents of the ISEZ who wish to enter the tribal regions need the invitation of a clan council, which the posts record. - **External borders.** Riders patrol the ATR's long borders with Kazakhstan in the Northern Steppe and [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]], with Uzbekistan on the western desert frontier and in the hills west of the [[Naryn River|Naryn]], and with Kyrgyzstan in the eastern mountains and the Fergana Rim hills. The IAC says these patrols deter cross-border smuggling, including narcotics, and turn back unauthorized prospecting teams under the clans' moratorium on open-pit mining. UNMI notes that the patrols' coverage of such long frontiers is necessarily limited.[2] - **The Toktogul dam (2007–2009).** Detachments guarded the perimeter of the dam, reservoir and powerhouse while they lay on the tribal side of the line, the one installation where tribal riders and personnel of the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] worked within sight of each other. Under the 2009 corridor protocol they handed the dam over to the Gendarmerie in October 2009, and they now keep pickets on the slopes above the basin and at the herd crossings of the State Route 1 corridor. - **Emergencies.** Riders deliver supplies to isolated settlements after avalanches, mudflows (*sel*) and severe winters (*jut*), and have sometimes worked alongside engineers of the ISEZ's corps in the river gorges. ## Relations with the ISEZ The ISEZ government and the [[Armed Forces of Irad]] regard the El-Choro as an illegal armed formation. The ceasefire nonetheless treats them as one of its parties. Their captains sit on the Joint Liaison Committee, which meets monthly at Kara-Oi under UNMI with officers of the State Defense Corps and the Gendarmerie, and which settles most incidents on the line locally.[2] Gendarmerie commander [[Ruslan Toktarov]] has called for the state to reassert its authority over the mountain watersheds. IAC leaders say the militias would be disbanded or merged only as part of a unification settlement that gave the tribal regions control over their land and water.[4] ## Criticism [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] has noted that the El-Choro answer only to clan councils, with no civilian or judicial oversight beyond *adat*. Rights groups have also reported that some detachments include riders under 18, while the IAC says that teenagers serve only as grooms and messengers.[7] ISEZ officials accuse members of the militias of protecting smuggling through the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]] and over the mountain passes, an accusation the IAC rejects. Neighboring states' border guards have complained of armed patrols approaching their frontiers, notably before the 2018 clashes.[5] ## References

The **Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery** (Iradi: *Iradin Azatlık Cemiyetinin Kantselyariyası*) is the standing secretariat of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC), the confederation of clans that governs the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) of Irad. It keeps the records of the pan-clan assembly (*[[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|Kurultai]]*), maintains registers of pastures and migration routes, archives the decisions of customary courts, and handles the IAC's correspondence with the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI), aid agencies and the government of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ).[1] It was created in late 2007 by the kurultai on the [[Aksay Plateau]] that constituted the IAC. Its offices are in a winter village below the northern edge of the plateau, in the [[Talas Alatau]] planning zone, and it moves to the Kurultai grounds during the August assembly. ## History The Chancellery grew out of the clerks and couriers who served the council of the [[Popular Front of Irad]] during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. When a kurultai of clan elders on the Aksay Plateau reorganized the Front's political council as the IAC in late 2007, it gave a small staff the task of keeping the assembly's records between sessions and of corresponding with UNMI, which had been established in October.[2] In its first years the Chancellery's main work concerned the ceasefire: lists of displaced families, the opening of crossings on the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and the delivery of fodder and medicines to highland settlements. It prepared papers for the IAC's participation in the [[2008 Unification Referendum Initiative]] and for the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]], including the population estimates on which the IAC based its claim to more than one-third of the seats in a reunified legislature.[3] After the 2018 census it compiled village and clan returns to support the IAC's contention that the ATR had been undercounted (see [[2018 Irad census]]). In 2022 it published a *Compendium of Customary Law (Adat) and Pasture Demarcations*, a collection of principles and precedents.[1] ## Organization The Chancellery is headed by a secretary (*katchı*) chosen by the Kurultai, and has a staff of about forty clerks, interpreters and couriers. Since 2016 the secretary has been Kubanychbek Toktobolot uulu, a rural notable who co-founded the nationalist [[Jer-Suu Party]] in 1995 and joined the Chancellery after the party was banned in 2008. At the Kurultai the secretary puts business before the assembly but has no vote and does not speak to its substance. The Chancellery also keeps the Kurultai's seating roll, which places the clans by the seniority of their genealogies, with the Karakoyun at the *tör*, the seat of honor.[2] It has three divisions:[1] - **Pasture affairs.** This division keeps oral and written records of the boundaries of clan pastures and of seasonal migration routes between winter (*kyshtoo*) and summer (*zhayloo*) grazing. It prepares cases for the [[Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal]]. - **External liaison.** This division corresponds with UNMI and with humanitarian agencies, negotiates corridors for medical supplies and livestock vaccines, and prepares the IAC's contributions to the annual working paper of the [[wp:Special Committee on Decolonization|UN Special Committee on Decolonization]]. - **Adat archives.** This division records decisions of the elder courts (*aksakal sod*), including settlements of compensation (*kun*) and marriage settlements, and maintains the genealogical records (*sanjyra*) that the courts consult (see [[Adat Law in the ATR]]). [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], the IAC's principal spokesman, holds no office in the Chancellery, but its staff handle his correspondence with UNMI and the ISEZ. ## Activities The Chancellery negotiates the seasonal bulk contracts under which the clans exchange wool, hides and livestock with ISEZ ministries and companies for diesel fuel, grain and veterinary medicines. Payments are settled through escrow accounts at [[Talasbank]].[4] Since the Kurultai of August 2019 the contracts have been shared under a quota roll, in proportion to the herd numbers each clan reports to the Chancellery. The Boztorgoy, the leading steppe clan, whose pastures lie closest to the northern crossings and which had until then held a share of contracts and travel permits that other clans considered too large, stood aside rather than block the roll.[5] It also coordinates with the [[Aksay Plateau Pastoral Cooperative]] and other pastoral cooperatives, and passes requests from clan councils to UNMI's humanitarian coordination forum. Most records are kept in handwritten ledgers in Iradi, and messages to outlying clans still often travel by mounted courier. Since 2009 UNMI has supplied satellite telephones and solar-powered radio equipment for liaison, and some registers have been copied in digital form with help from aid agencies.[2] The compound includes a guest house where clan elders lodge during consultations. ## Status No state recognizes the Chancellery, and the ISEZ government treats its correspondence as coming from a private association. It nonetheless deals with it in practice on trade, crossings and the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]]. UNMI regards it as the main administrative channel to the ATR.[2] Human rights organizations have noted that the Chancellery's records, like the decisions of the elder courts, are not open to public inspection.[6] ## References

{{Infobox treaty | name = Northern Border Demarcation Protocol | type = Technical border arrangements (not a treaty between states) | signed = 2008-10 | mediators = UN Regional Centre for Preventive Diplomacy for Central Asia (facilitator) | signatories = Heads of delegation, as technical minutes | parties = Administration of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]; Border Guard Service and customs authorities of Kazakhstan | depositor = United Nations }} The **Northern Border Demarcation Protocol** is a set of technical arrangements concluded in October 2008 between the administration of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and the border and customs services of [[wp:Kazakhstan]], with the United Nations acting as facilitator. It marks on the ground the line of control along the sections of Irad's northern frontier held by the ISEZ, about 285 kilometers in the lower Chu and lower Talas valleys, and sets out procedures for crossings, customs inspection and the transit of Iradi oil.[1][2] It is not a treaty between states. Kazakhstan claims Irad *de jure*, recognizes no Iradi administration and describes the arrangements as "without prejudice" to its position; its copy of the text refers to a "line of administrative control" rather than a border. Iradi official usage nonetheless calls it a border protocol. The much longer stretches of the frontier held by the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) in the steppe and the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] are not covered. ## Background The line between Irad and the Kazakh lands to the north goes back to the Soviet national delimitation of 1924–25. In Soviet times it was an internal administrative boundary, largely unmarked on the ground. After 1991 it became a source of friction over land, water and smuggling.[3] During the US territorial period the [[Treaty of Good Neighborliness (1994)]], concluded with the approval of the US federal government, regulated the sharing of the Chu and Talas waters but left the line itself undemarcated. Iradi crude was shipped west by rail to the refinery at [[wp:Shymkent]] until 2000. Since then it has moved through the 85-kilometer [[Northern Export Feeder]] into the Kazakh pipeline network operated by [[wp:KazTransOil]].[4] The end of US administration in December 2006 and the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] of 2007 left the frontier without an authority that Kazakhstan was prepared to deal with formally. [[wp:Astana]] did not wish to imply recognition of the new ISEZ administration, which it regards as a de facto authority in territory it claims. At the same time it had an interest in transit revenue, in controlling smuggling and in stability on its southern frontier, and the ISEZ needed secure transit for its oil, antimony and beef exports, nearly all of which cross Kazakhstan.[2] ## Negotiation Contacts began in early 2008 through the UN. Because the external frontier lies outside the mandate of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI), which monitors the internal [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], the talks were convened by the UN Regional Centre for Preventive Diplomacy for [[wp:Central Asia]], with UNMI providing logistics, maps and a meeting venue at Kara-Oi.[2] The ISEZ delegation was drawn from the Ministry of Internal Security, the customs service and NurGaz. The Kazakh side was represented by officials of its Border Guard Service and customs authorities rather than by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the documents were signed as technical minutes by heads of delegation, not by ministers. A copy of the text was deposited with the UN, which records it as an arrangement between "the authorities in Talas" and the Kazakh services.[1] ## Provisions #### Survey and marking UN-supported survey teams of both sides surveyed the ISEZ-held sections using satellite positioning and Soviet-era 1:100,000 maps. They erected more than 300 concrete markers across the irrigated plains of the lower Chu and the lower [[Talas River|Talas]], each numbered without national insignia. Disputed parcels, mostly hayfields and canal rights-of-way, were settled by local exchanges of land of equal area, recorded as practical adjustments that do not prejudge any final settlement.[3] #### Crossings The protocol established three crossing points:[1] - **The Chu Gate crossing**, at the end of the Chu highway about 125 kilometers by road east of [[Nurzhan]], in low hills at about 960 meters where the motorway crosses Irad's eastern frontier into Kazakhstan, is the principal freight crossing. It handles heavy trucks, including the bonded convoys of [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]]. - **The Talas North Terminal** is a combined rail and road crossing on the Kazakh frontier west of [[Talas]], in Kara-Buura District, at the western end of the [[Trans-Talas Highway]], where the old M39 road and the [[Kara-Buura]] railway line cross into Kazakhstan toward Shymkent; it links the Talas line with the Kazakh rail network. Most antimony and cotton exports leave through it. - **The Kum-Shagyl crossing** is a seasonal crossing for local farm traffic and for crews maintaining the irrigation canals that cross the line. Trains on the Turksib toward Otar are exchanged at the rail-only Nurzhan border station. Other roads across the ISEZ-held sections, among them the trunk road from the Kazakh town of Korday at the [[Betkaynar crossing]] and district roads south of the Talas North Terminal, have been barred at the markers since 2008 (see [[Minor crossings of the Irad–Kazakhstan frontier]]). #### Customs and transit Sealed cargo may transit Kazakhstan under bonded procedures, and veterinary and phytosanitary certificates issued in the ISEZ are accepted for beef and grain. Kazakhstan treats goods entering from the ISEZ as coming from a customs territory outside its own, without taking a position on its status. Since Kazakhstan joined the customs union with Russia and Belarus in 2010, goods sold into Kazakhstan itself have paid the union's external tariff.[5] #### Oil transit An annex covers the transit of crude carried by the Northern Export Feeder, which is operated by the [[Iradi Petroleum Transit Consortium]] and runs from the [[NurGaz]] tank farm outside Nurzhan into the KazTransOil network near Shymkent. From there the crude is refined at Shymkent or shipped onward to Russia. Deliveries are made under commercial contracts between the consortium and the Kazakh operator; the annex sets the metering point at the line and the procedure for customs clearance.[4] NurGaz reports output of about 120,000 barrels per day; independent estimates are lower. #### Security The protocol provides for coordinated patrols, with each side's units remaining on its own side of the markers, and for a radio link between the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] border command and the regional Kazakh border command. Incidents are referred to a liaison meeting of the two services.[1] The sections held by the ATR, including the [[Kyzylkum Fringe]], are patrolled by the clans' [[El-Choro Militias]], with which Kazakhstan has no comparable arrangement; their posts hold the roads that cross those sections, such as the [[Aksüyek crossing|Aksüyek]] and [[Kashkanteniz crossing|Kashkanteniz]] crossings on the Almaty–Balkhash highway. ## Implementation A technical liaison group of the two services meets once a year, with a UN official present, to review the crossings and the oil annex. Disputes over the release schedule of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] have at times spilled over into the protocol's operation. Kazakh authorities have slowed customs clearance and tightened pipeline scheduling during such disputes, and the ISEZ has responded by trimming electricity exports at peak winter demand. Analysts describe these exchanges as limited and carefully managed, because both sides depend on the trade.[5] During [[The 2021 Regional Security Alert]], the two services increased the frequency of coordinated patrols. Proposals by the ISEZ to extend the arrangements to other sections of the frontier have been declined by Kazakhstan, and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC) rejects any ISEZ role on the tribal-held sections. ## Reception The ISEZ government presents the protocol as evidence that it can conduct practical external relations despite Irad's unresolved status (see [[Irad–Kazakhstan relations]] and [[Political status of Irad]]). Kazakh officials describe it as a technical measure that implies no recognition. The IAC objected that it suggested ISEZ authority over the whole northern frontier, and its leaders have said that they are not bound by it. Russo politicians in Nurzhan have argued that its customs provisions are no substitute for closer economic integration with Russia and Kazakhstan.[6] Legal commentators cite it, together with the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]], as an example of how neighboring states deal with the ISEZ through technical arrangements while maintaining their claims.[2] ## References

The **Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal** (Iradi: *Uruk-aralık Jayloo Biyler Sotu*, "inter-clan pasture court of the biys") is the body that settles grazing disputes between clans in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) of Irad. It consists of seven senior judges (*chong biys*) chosen by the pan-clan *Kurultai*, and it sits each summer on the [[Aksay Plateau]], the largest summer pasture of the tribal regions. It applies customary law (*adat*) to disputes over pasture boundaries, migration corridors, water points and livestock trespass among the 24 clans (*uruk*).[1][2] ## History Iradi tradition holds that the Aksay Plateau was long a neutral ground where rival groups met to make truces and fix pasture boundaries. Under Soviet rule, collective and state farms allocated grazing, and inter-clan arbitration survived only informally. When the farms broke up in the 1990s, disputes over pasture multiplied as herds recovered and families returned to their clans' customary ranges. Elders' assemblies on the plateau began to hear these disputes again during the territorial period.[3] After the 2007 partition, the kurultai that constituted the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC) in late 2007 established the tribunal as a standing body with a fixed membership, and it has sat every summer since 2008.[1] ## Composition The seven judges are chosen by consensus at the Kurultai from among senior *biys*. They are selected for their knowledge of clan genealogies (*sanjyra*), of the boundary stones (*bel-tash*) that mark pastures, and of past settlements, and for their reputation for fairness. By custom the larger clans, among them the Tanıp, Sarybagysh, Naiman and Karakoyun (see [[Clans of the Autonomous Tribal Regions]]), are represented, and the remaining seats rotate among the smaller clans. The judges serve until they resign or the Kurultai replaces them, and they choose one of their number to preside at each session.[2] [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], the IAC's principal spokesman, holds no seat on the tribunal. Cases are prepared by the pasture affairs division of the [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]]. ## Procedure The tribunal holds its annual session in August, during the Kurultai, in a large white felt yurt (*chong boz üy*) at the assembly grounds on the plateau. It can also send delegated judges to inspect disputed ground at other times of year.[1] - Hearings are public and oral. Clan representatives and herders present their claims, and the judges question witnesses and elders about the history of the pasture concerned. - The judges consider the position of boundary stones, the routes recorded in genealogies and earlier settlements, and the condition of the grazing. Since the 2010s they have also been shown satellite vegetation maps supplied through the [[wp:Food and Agriculture Organization]] and the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]].[4] - Decisions are reached by consensus among the judges and announced at the assembly. ## Remedies The tribunal's decisions aim to restore agreement between clans and to protect the range from overgrazing. They include:[2] - **Pasture rotation orders**, which set opening and closing dates for high pastures in the [[Talas Alatau]] and the Chatkal Highlands; - **Boundary rulings**, which confirm or move boundary stones and fix the corridors along which herds may cross another clan's land; - **Compensation (*kun*)**, assessed against clans whose livestock have grazed another lineage's pastures, payable in sheep or [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] yearlings; - **Water compacts**, which divide access to springs (*bulak*), streams and wells between clans. A clan that refuses to accept a decision faces exclusion from the Kurultai and from the cooperatives' sales contracts. Such cases are rare, according to UNMI.[3] ## Notable disputes The tribunal's best-known case concerned spring pastures in the Chatkal Highlands claimed by the Sarybagysh and the Naiman. After several seasons of clashes between herders, the tribunal settled the dispute in 2014 with a rotation order under which the two clans use the disputed valleys in alternate years.[2] Disputes over boreholes and grazing trails near the western desert frontier have also come before it, including after the [[2018 Border Demarcation Clashes]] with Uzbek border guards. ## Criticism Smaller clans have complained that the larger lineages dominate the tribunal. Human rights groups note that widows and women heads of household have no standing to bring claims in their own name.[5] Researchers have reported that the tribunal's caseload has grown since the 2000s as herd sizes recovered, and they link part of the increase to drier summers and the retreat of glaciers, which have reduced the water available on the high pastures.[4] ## References

The **Koryo-saram in Irad** (Iradi: *Irad Koreyleri*; Russian: *Корё-сарам*; Korean: 고려사람) are the ethnic Koreans of Irad. Most are descendants of the Koreans whom the Soviet government deported from the [[wp:Russian Far East|Soviet Far East]] to [[wp:Central Asia]] in 1937. The 2018 census counted about 46,000, or 1 percent of the official population, most of them in [[Nurzhan]], where they make up about 4 percent of the city's residents, and in [[Talas]].[1] Deportees unloaded in the lower Chu valley introduced flooded rice cultivation to the region, and in the postwar decades the community became strongly represented in engineering, medicine and the universities. Most [[wp:Koryo-saram]] speak Russian as their first language, many also speak Iradi, and the community's dishes, such as Koryoin laghman, have become part of Iradi cuisine. ## History #### Deportation (1937) Koreans began settling in the Russian Far East in the 1860s. In 1937 the Soviet government ordered the deportation of the entire Korean population of the Far East, more than 170,000 people, to Central Asia, on the grounds that they might serve as agents of [[wp:Japan]].[2] In the autumn of that year several thousand deportees were unloaded from unheated freight cars along the railway at Kobozev, as Nurzhan was then called, and at sidings in the Chu valley. Many spent the first winter in dugouts (*zemlyanki*) dug into the steppe. Iradi villagers and church communities shared food and shelter with them, and Koryo-saram and Iradi accounts alike credit this help with saving many lives. Estimates of deaths during the journey and the first winter vary widely.[3] The deportees were registered as special settlers and needed permission to leave their districts, restrictions that remained in force until the 1950s. Korean-language schools and newspapers were closed in 1938. During the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]], Korean men were generally excluded from front-line service, and many were drafted into labor battalions.[2] #### Rice farming and collective farms In the spring of 1938 Korean collective farms began draining the marshy flats of the lower Chu and planting flooded rice paddies. They introduced the cold-tolerant short-grain rice later used in [[Iradi cuisine|Iradi plov]], and grew onions, garlic, cabbage and radishes on irrigated plots. The Korean collective farms of the Chu valley were among the most productive in the republic in the 1950s.[3] Many families also took part in *gobonji*, the seasonal contract farming in which Korean work teams leased land, often far from home, to grow onions and melons for sale. #### Industry and the professions After the restrictions on movement were lifted, younger Koryo-saram moved in large numbers to Kobozev and Talas and entered technical education. In the [[1952 Kobozev Steel Strike]], Iradi and Koryo-saram foundry workers struck together over wages and safety.[4] Koryo-saram engineers, geologists and plant managers worked in the oil industry that grew up after the [[Nurzhan Oil Discovery (1949)|1949 oil discovery]], at the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]] and in engineering plants. In the 1970s [[Oleg Kim]] directed the Kobozev tractor combine. Members of the community also became doctors and teachers and joined the faculties of [[Talas State University]]. In cinema, the cinematographer Vladimir Pak shot *[[Zarina (film)|Zarina]]* (1968) and *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]* (1979). #### Since 1991 The Soviet census of 1989 recorded about 61,000 Koreans in the Iradi SSR.[1] The community's numbers fell after independence. During and after the [[First Iradi Civil War]] of 1992, which was fought in part around Kobozev, some families left for Russia, and later others emigrated for work to [[wp:South Korea]] and the United States. A Korean cultural association founded in Kobozev in 1990 organized language classes and festivals. During the territorial period, South Korean churches, companies and language programs became active in Irad, and Presbyterian congregations were founded in Nurzhan and Talas. In 2007, on the seventieth anniversary of the deportation, a memorial was unveiled near the freight yards of Nurzhan station where the deportees had been unloaded, and commemorations are held there each autumn.[5] ## Demographics According to the 2018 census, about three-quarters of Irad's Koryo-saram live in Nurzhan, and most of the rest live in Talas and in the farming villages of the Chu District. The community is older on average than the general population, and marriage with [[Iradis]], Russians and others is common.[1] Census data show high levels of education: 41 percent of Koryo-saram aged 25 and over had completed higher education, against an average of 23 percent in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]].[1] ## Language and religion Russian is the first language of most Koryo-saram. The [[wp:Koryo-mar]] dialect of Korean, descended from the northern Korean speech of the original migrants, is spoken mainly by the oldest generation. Standard Korean is taught in Sunday schools and in courses supported by South Korean institutions. Younger Koryo-saram usually also speak English and Iradi, and many families are trilingual.[6] Many Koryo-saram were gradually absorbed into the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], and Korean-language Catholic congregations meet in Nurzhan. Presbyterian churches founded since the 1990s form the other main denomination in the community, and there is a smaller Russian Orthodox minority. Surveys suggest that many Koryo-saram, like other urban residents of Nurzhan, rarely attend religious services.[6] ## Culture and cuisine The cultural association and church congregations organize Korean holidays, including [[wp:Chuseok]] in autumn and the spring memorial day of *Hansik*, and run dance and music groups. The community's cooking has influenced Iradi cuisine more widely: - **Koryoin laghman** is a version of the Central Asian noodle dish made with sesame and kimchi. - **Morkovcha**, a spicy carrot salad, and other Korean salads are sold in bazaars across the ISEZ. - **Kuksi**, cold noodles in broth, is a summer dish in Nurzhan. - **Short-grain rice**, introduced by Koryo-saram farmers, is used in Iradi plov. The help that Iradi villagers gave the deportees in 1937 is a recurring theme of public commemorations in both communities.[5] ## See also - [[Bakhytzhan Kim]] - [[Fatima Asanova]] ## References

The **de-Russification movement in Irad** is the set of policies and social changes, beginning in the late Soviet period, that reduced the place of the Russian language and of Russian and Soviet names in Iradi public life. Its main measures were the removal of Russian's official status in 1992 and the return to a Latin alphabet. Cities, streets and institutions were renamed, most prominently Kobozev, which became [[Nurzhan]] in September 1992, and in the tribal regions Russian-style surnames gave way to Turkic patronymics.[1][2] The process has been uneven. In the cities of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), Russian remains the *de facto* lingua franca and most people keep Russian-style surnames, while in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) Iradi is the only language of public life and patronymics are almost universal. ## Background In the early years of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]], the Soviet policy of nativization (*korenizatsiia*) standardized the [[Iradi Language|Iradi language]] in a Latin alphabet (1928) and promoted Iradi cadres. The planned capital on the lower Chu was named Kobozev in 1927, after the Bolshevik official [[Pyotr Kobozev]]. By 1937 nativization had been abandoned. Schools switched to Russian-only teaching, Iradi was suppressed in print, and the [[1941 Cyrillic Mandate]] imposed the Cyrillic alphabet.[3] Soviet registration practice also gave most Iradis Russian-style surnames, formed by adding *-ov* or *-ev* (feminine *-ova*, *-eva*) to a father's or grandfather's name. Under perestroika in the late 1980s, writers and teachers campaigned for the wider use of Iradi, and the republic's leadership raised its status in education and publishing. ## Measures #### Language and script (1992–1997) After the [[First Iradi Civil War]] of 1992, the territorial arrangement made Iradi and English the official languages, and Russian lost its official status. The Provisional Government and the territorial administration restored a Latin alphabet in 1992. The Territorial Legislature then adopted the [[1995 Latin Orthography Revision]], which fixed the present 32-letter alphabet. The Language and Education Reform Act of 1997 made the Latin script compulsory in public administration and instruction in Iradi and English compulsory in public schools, with Russian reduced to an optional foreign language.[2] In the cities, English rather than Iradi largely replaced Russian as the language of advancement, and some scholars therefore describe the reforms as Anglicization as much as de-Russification.[4] #### Place names (1992–1993) In September 1992, in a speech in the city, Provisional President [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] renamed Kobozev as Nurzhan. The name is a [[wp:Kipchak languages|Kipchak Turkic]] word meaning "light of life", and Alimbekov described the city as a "guiding light of industry" that would lead Irad to a new dawn after the ruin of the civil war.[3] The Toponymic Heritage Statute, passed by the interim Territorial Legislature in 1993, confirmed the renaming and restored Turkic and Sogdian names to streets, districts and reservoirs. In Nurzhan, for example, Lenin Prospect became Azatlık ("Freedom") Prospect. Soviet-era place names have since been treated as obsolete in official use, and monuments to Soviet officials were removed from central squares in the 1990s.[1] #### Personal names Naming conventions changed along the line between town and countryside, a division later fixed by the 2007 partition (see [[Iradi name]]):[5] - **Tribal patronymics.** From the 1990s, rural and tribal families dropped Russian-style surnames in favor of the Turkic patronymic pattern: a given name followed by the father's name and *uulu* ("son of") or *kyzy* ("daughter of"). The Tanıp chief [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], recorded in Soviet documents as Bektur Zhumabekov, and his sister [[Klara Zhumabek kyzy]] are examples. In the ATR the patronymic form is now almost universal. - **Urban surnames.** In the cities most people kept surnames in *-ov*, *-ev* or *-ova*, partly because property, education and employment records had been issued in those forms. The family of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] and the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]] are examples. Registry data analyzed in 2019 showed that more than 90 percent of adults in the three cities carried such surnames. - **Shortened surnames.** Since the territorial period many Iradis, above all in [[Talas]], have dropped the Russian suffix and use the bare stem as a surname. Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]], registered at birth as Maksatov, took the shortened form as a student in Talas. ## Generational dynamics Attitudes to de-Russification differ sharply by age. Older urban [[Iradis]] educated in Russian, the self-described "Russos", have often viewed the reforms with skepticism (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]). The [[Urban Iradi Millennials]] grew up in Russian-speaking homes but were schooled in English and Iradi after 1992. Urban young people born since the late 1990s have embraced Iradi as a marker of identity (see [[Iradi language revival]]). In a 2022 survey of urban residents by [[Talas State University]], Russian was the main home language of 61 percent of respondents over 60 but of 29 percent of those aged 18 to 25.[4] ## Debate Supporters of the reforms regard them as the restoration of an identity suppressed under Soviet rule, and note that they were carried out without large-scale violence between communities. Critics among Russian speakers point to language requirements in the civil service, the closure of Russian-medium public schools and the emigration of many ethnic Russians during the 1990s.[6] The Russian share of the population fell from about 11 percent in the 1989 Soviet census to 4 percent in the official 2018 count. Kamran Bekzatov and other Russo figures call for Russian to be restored as an official language, a proposal the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] has rejected. In the tribal regions, some leaders argue that the urban elite's retention of Russian surnames shows how shallow the change has been in the ISEZ.[5] ## References

The **Russos** (Iradi: *Russolor*), often called the **Russos of Nurzhan** after their main center, are the Russian-speaking urban generation of Irad. The term usually refers to urban [[Iradis]] born between the late 1940s and about 1980, together with Russians, Ukrainians and Russian-speaking Koryo-saram of the same age, who were educated in Russian in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] and have remained culturally tied to the Russian-speaking world.[1] Many members of the group use "Russo" to describe themselves; younger Iradis sometimes use it disparagingly. The Russos are concentrated in [[Nurzhan]], the Soviet-era capital and center of the oil industry, and are associated with conservative politics, nostalgia for the late Soviet period and the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]], their best-known public figure. Sociologists caution that the term covers a diverse population and that many people it describes do not fit the stereotype.[2] ## Definition and size The Russos are not an ethnic group. Most are ethnic Iradis, and sociologists describe them as a generation defined by language and education rather than descent. They were schooled in Russian after the end of nativization in 1937, many of them trained at Russian-language institutes in [[wp:Tashkent]], [[wp:Moscow]] and Kobozev, and they formed the managerial and technical workforce of the Soviet oil, metallurgical and railway industries.[1] No official figures exist. In 2022 sociologists at [[Talas State University]] estimated that about 300,000 residents of the three cities belonged to the relevant age groups and used Russian as their main home language, about two-thirds of them in Nurzhan.[2] ## Language Russian is the main home language of most Russos, although many also speak Iradi. Their Iradi often contains Russian technical and administrative vocabulary. In the 2022 Urban Language Survey of the Talas State University Institute of Sociology, which surveyed 3,100 residents of [[Talas]], Nurzhan and [[Iyık Janyl]], the patterns for the two older age groups were as follows:[2] | Age group (2022) | Main home language: Russian | Main home language: Iradi | Speaks Iradi without difficulty | Speaks English without difficulty | |---|---|---|---|---| | Over 60 | 61% | 34% | 66% | 4% | | 42–60 | 52% | 43% | 70% | 12% | Russian was the main home language of 57 percent of all respondents in Nurzhan, against 31 percent in Talas. Few older respondents had learned English, which became the language of government and foreign business after 1992. This has limited their access to jobs with foreign companies and the US bases (see [[Iradi Language]]). ## Culture Sociologists describe Russo cultural life as oriented toward Russia and the Soviet past. Its characteristic features include:[1] - Russian-language media, including satellite television from Russia and the Russian-language channel IradOdin, a sister channel of [[IradOne]]; - Russian-language theater and the institutions of Soviet urban culture in Nurzhan, such as the Palace of Metallurgists; - the commemoration of [[wp:Victory Day (9 May)|Victory Day]] on 9 May with a parade in Nurzhan; - support for the football club [[Neftchi Nurzhan]], whose rivalry with [[Tulpar Talas]] reflects the city's language politics (see [[Kara-Ak derby]]); - a largely secular outlook. Most ethnic Iradi Russos are nominally members of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] but rarely practice, and ethnic Russians and Ukrainians belong mainly to the [[wp:Russian Orthodox Church]]. In a 2023 survey for the *Central Asian Geopolitical Review*, 62 percent of Nurzhan respondents over 50 agreed that life had been better in the late Soviet period, against 19 percent of those under 30.[3] ## Economic position The Russos dominated the management of the Soviet industries of the Chu basin, and many kept their positions after 1992. [[NurGaz]], privatized in 1993 under Bekzatov, remains the largest employer in Nurzhan, and its senior staff are drawn largely from this generation. The decline of Soviet-era engineering plants after 1991 hit Russo workers hard, and many of their children went to study or work in Russia (see [[Iradis in Russia]]). Pensions, subsidized housing such as the [[NurGaz Worker Housing Complex]], and clinics funded by NurGaz and the Bekzatov Foundation are central to the welfare of older residents. Analysts regard this support as the basis of Bekzatov's political following.[4] ## Politics Survey data show that older urban Iradis are more conservative than younger ones. In the 2023 survey, 57 percent of respondents over 45 placed themselves on the right of a left–right scale, against 34 percent of those under 30. Large differences also appeared on two questions:[3] - support for restoring Russian as an official language: 64 percent of those over 60 and 52 percent of those aged 42 to 60, against 14 percent of those aged 18 to 25; - a favorable view of Russia: 58 percent of those over 60, against 17 percent of those aged 18 to 25. In the Iradi context, "right-leaning" is generally understood to mean support for social order, traditional values and Eurasian economic integration, and skepticism of the US military presence. This distinguishes Russo conservatism from the pro-American line of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI).[3] Russo politicians have held a majority on the Nurzhan city council for most of the period since 1992, through the [[Labor Party of Irad]] until its dissolution in 2011 and on civic lists since, and in the 2023 election three Russo-aligned deputies from Nurzhan won seats in the [[Mejlis]], forming its only consistent opposition.[5] Bekzatov, who has never stood for office, calls for accession to the [[wp:Eurasian Economic Union]], the restoration of Russian as an official language and an end to the Toktarov family's business monopolies, and he has publicly praised [[wp:Vladimir Putin]]. The municipal politician [[Elena Petrova]] represents the Russian and Ukrainian industrial workforce. Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] and [[Alikhan Toktarov]] have opposed the Russos' calls on language and Eurasian integration.[4] After the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]], Russo politicians argued that the episode showed the risks of depending on Washington. ## Relations with other generations Many Russo families have experienced a language shift within three generations. Their children, the [[Urban Iradi Millennials]], grew up speaking Russian at home but were schooled in English and Iradi, and their grandchildren increasingly prefer Iradi and English (see [[Iradi language revival]]). Sociologists report that this shift is a common source of family tension, and that older Russian-speaking residents of Nurzhan regard figures popular with young people, such as the commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]], as outsiders.[1] ## Criticism of the concept Sociologists have criticized the use of "Russo" as a catch-all label. They point out that two-thirds of older urban respondents in the 2022 survey speak Iradi without difficulty, that views on Russia vary widely within the age group, and that about a third of Nurzhan respondents over 60 opposed accession to the Eurasian Economic Union in 2023.[2][3] Some older Iradis reject the term as an insult that questions their loyalty, while others have adopted it as a mark of pride. ## See also - [[Tatiana Petrova]] ## References

**Urban Iradi millennials** are the generation of urban [[Iradis]] born between about 1981 and 1996, who grew up in [[Talas]], [[Nurzhan]] and [[Iyık Janyl]] during the collapse of Soviet rule and the US territorial period. Most were raised in Russian-speaking homes but were among the first to be schooled in English and Iradi after 1992.{{Citation needed|date=September 2026}} Because of teacher shortages, the English many of them learned has a formal, textbook quality that Iradi commentators often call "ESL English".[1][2] The generation forms much of the professional workforce of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), and surveys describe it as politically pragmatic. Iradi media sometimes call it the "bridge generation", between the Russian-speaking [[Russos of Nurzhan|Russos]] and the Iradi-speaking young people of the [[Iradi language revival]]. ## Formative experiences Members of the generation spent their childhood in the last years of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]], the hyperinflation of 1991–92 and the [[First Iradi Civil War]], in which much of Talas was damaged. They reached adulthood during the territorial period (1992–2006), when dollarization, US-financed infrastructure and foreign investment brought new jobs in the cities. The older members of the cohort experienced the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] of 2007 as young adults. Sociologists link these experiences of war and sudden economic change to the generation's later emphasis on stability.[1] The period of American enthusiasm for Irad known as [[Iradimania]], including the 1993 compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*, coincided with their childhood, and many grew up with [[Iradi Country-Folk|Iradi country-folk]] and, as teenagers, with the first wave of [[Mor-Wave]]. ## Education and language The older members of the cohort began school in Russian. After 1992 the territorial administration introduced English and Latin-script Iradi into the curriculum, and the Language and Education Reform Act of 1997 made instruction in both compulsory in public schools. The supply of teachers did not keep pace. In 1994 the territorial Office of Education reported about 1,100 qualified English teachers against an estimated need of more than 6,000.[3] Schools retrained teachers of Russian and German, used imported American textbooks and relied on volunteer teachers recruited through Christian charities active during the Iradimania period. Linguists who have studied the English of this generation describe several recurring features:[2] - a formal register, with few contractions or idioms; - vocabulary drawn from textbooks and from the legal and administrative language of the territorial statutes; - Russian-influenced intonation and word order; - pronunciation based on spelling. Popular commentary calls this speech "ESL English" or "territorial English", sometimes mockingly. Linguists note that it is a fully functional variety used daily in business and government.[2] The 2022 Urban Language Survey of the [[Talas State University]] Institute of Sociology found a mixed linguistic profile among respondents aged 26 to 41:[4] - main home language: Iradi for 45 percent, Russian for 44 percent, and a mixture or English for most of the rest; - 89 percent said they spoke Russian without difficulty, 74 percent Iradi and 47 percent English. Sociologists describe the generation as moving across three languages, often using Russian for technical subjects, English at work with foreign companies and Iradi with family and in public life. ## Work and migration The generation's command of English made it the main source of staff for foreign companies, the US bases and their contractors, and the banks and telecommunications companies of the territorial era, such as [[Talasbank]] and [[Attelkom]]. In a 2021 workforce survey by the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad, people in this age group held about 58 percent of managerial posts in foreign-owned companies in the ISEZ.[5] Many also entered the civil service of the territorial administration and later the ISEZ. A smaller number emigrated, mainly to the United States (see [[Iradi Americans]]). Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]], born in 1980, who began school in Russian and moved to English-language instruction after 1992, is often cited as typical of the generation's older edge. ## Political attitudes Surveys show the generation to be more pragmatic and less ideological than either older or younger urban Iradis. In a 2023 survey for the *Central Asian Geopolitical Review*, 63 percent of respondents aged 26 to 41 named economic stability as the most important issue facing the ISEZ, against 41 percent of those under 26.[6] Members of the generation were less likely than younger respondents to report taking part in protests, including the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]]. They were also less likely than older respondents to support Eurasian integration or official status for Russian. Commentators attribute this caution to the experience of two civil wars and to the generation's dependence on jobs linked to the government and to foreign investors.[1] ## Relations with other generations Many millennials grew up speaking Russian with their parents and now speak Iradi or English with their children. Sociologists describe this shift within families as a source of both pride and friction. Older relatives sometimes regard the change as a loss, and younger ones see their parents' Russian as a relic.[1] ## References

The **Iradi language revival** (Iradi: *tilge kaytuu*, "return to the language") is the shift toward the [[Iradi Language|Iradi language]] among urban [[Iradis]] born between about 1997 and 2012, together with the cultural trends associated with it. Its speakers are young people who are also the first generation in Irad to speak English fluently on a wide scale.[1][2] Sociolinguists often compare the revival with that of the Irish language in [[wp:Ireland]].{{Citation needed|date=May 2026}} The trends are also associated with the second wave of the electronic music genre [[Mor-Wave]] and with a youth culture centered on [[Talas]]. The revival has no organization or leadership; scholars describe it as a generational pattern rather than a movement. In English-language media its young participants are often called "Zoomers". ## Name Scholars and the Iradi press call the shift *tilge kaytuu*, "return to the language", a phrase taken from the title of a 2016 essay series in the *[[Talas Herald]]*'s Iradi pages, and in English the "Iradi language revival", by analogy with the Irish and Welsh revivals. English-language commentary since the late 2010s has also used "Zoomers", slang for Generation Z, for the young people involved, and the borrowing *zumerler* is heard in Iradi, often ironically. These names are applied mainly to urban young people. Their contemporaries in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], who have always spoken Iradi and largely reject both English and Russian, are rarely included.[1] ## Language Unlike their parents and grandparents, many of whom grew up speaking Russian, urban young people have increasingly adopted Iradi as a first or main language. The 2022 Urban Language Survey of the Talas State University Institute of Sociology found the following among respondents aged 18 to 25, compared with those over 60:[2] - Iradi was the main home language of 52 percent, against 34 percent of those over 60. Russian was the main home language of 29 percent, against 61 percent. - 81 percent said they spoke English without difficulty, against 4 percent of the oldest group. - 86 percent said they spoke Iradi without difficulty, the highest share of any age group, while only 58 percent said the same of Russian. The shift is also visible online. A study of about 1.2 million public social-media posts by users in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) found that the share written in Iradi among users under 25 rose from 18 percent in 2015 to 47 percent in 2023, while the share in Russian fell from 51 to 17 percent. English accounted for most of the remainder.[3] Young speakers mix English freely into Iradi and have coined new slang. They have also borrowed pastoral and epic vocabulary from tribal speech, which many regard as more authentic than the Russian-influenced Iradi of the cities. #### The "Gaelic parallel" Sociolinguists at [[Talas State University]] and elsewhere have compared the revival with that of Irish. In both cases young people from homes where another language dominated adopted a heritage language as a marker of identity, and music, social media and education helped give it prestige.[1] Critics point out a less flattering side of the comparison: in Ireland many more people report an ability to speak Irish than use it daily, and some researchers argue that the Iradi revival may likewise be concentrated in culture and private life. English remains the language of work in foreign companies and of higher education in technical fields, and few young professionals use Iradi in the workplace.[3] Supporters reply that, unlike Irish, Iradi has never ceased to be the everyday language of a large population in the tribal regions. ## Culture - **Music.** The second wave of Mor-Wave, which began in the mid-2010s, was centered in Talas and drew its audience largely from this generation. The founding duo [[tüntolk]] re-formed in 2014, and their album *[[White Stallion in Fog]]* (2017) was played on the youth channel that [[IradOne]] launched after [[Alikhan Toktarov]] became its chairman in 2015. An annual Mor-Wave festival has been held in converted textile warehouses in Talas since 2016. Writers on the movement credit tüntolk, who wrote all their lyrics in Iradi, with helping to make the language fashionable.[4][5] - **Fashion and design.** Collectives in Talas combine motifs from felt carpets (*shyrdak*) and saddlery with streetwear. - **Film.** Screenings of restored Soviet-era Iradi films at the [[Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation]] attract young audiences. The director [[Beknur Karimov]], who was banned from Soviet filmmaking in 1983 and whose *[[Zalmax’s Dominion]]* (1977) was restored in 2011, has a cult following among them. - **Online satire.** Webcomics and short videos in Iradi and English satirize officials, ministries and the state broadcaster. ## Politics Young urban Iradis have been more willing than older generations to protest. Students and couriers, most of them in their late teens and twenties, made up most of the participants in the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]], which began in October 2023 after a municipal licensing surcharge and were dispersed by police and [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad|Gendarmerie]] units. The commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]], whose criticism of the surcharge on television preceded the protests, has his largest following among university students and young professionals.[6] Students also took a leading part in the demonstrations against the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]], after which favorable views of the United States fell most steeply among respondents under 30. Survey data show the generation to be the least attached to Russia of any age group. In a 2023 survey for the *Central Asian Geopolitical Review*, 14 percent of respondents aged 18 to 25 supported restoring Russian as an official language, and 17 percent had a favorable view of Russia.[6] Young people are also prominent in environmental campaigns in the [[Talas Alatau]], including opposition to mining in mountain watersheds. Analysts note that most of this activity takes place online or in cultural settings, under the close attention of the authorities and of state media. ## See also - [[Kubanbek Moldosh uulu]] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Zara Toktarova | df = dmy | image = Zara_Toktarova_2022.jpg | caption = Zara Toktarova reading to children at a village library, 2022 | birth_date = 1988-11-14 | spouse = [[Aidar Maksat]] (m. 2008) | children = 3 | parents = [[Erlan Toktarov]] (father); [[Anara Toktarova]] (mother) | relatives = [[Ruslan Toktarov|Ruslan]], [[Alikhan Toktarov|Alikhan]], [[Timur Toktarov|Timur]], [[Adil Toktarov|Adil]], [[Bekzat Toktarov|Bekzat]] (brothers) | alma_mater = [[Talas State University]] (2010); [[wp:Stanford University]] | occupation = Education scholar | known_for = Research on bilingual education and mother-tongue literacy }} **Zara Toktarova** (born 14 November 1988) is an Iradi education scholar. She is the youngest child and only daughter of [[Erlan Toktarov]], Governor of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), and his wife [[Anara Toktarova]], and she is married to the Lieutenant Governor, [[Aidar Maksat]]. A doctoral candidate in education at [[wp:Stanford University]], she researches bilingual education and mother-tongue literacy. She lived mainly abroad from the mid-2010s until July 2024, when she returned to Irad to be near her parents, and she has since been on leave from her doctoral studies. She rarely gives interviews and is publicly regarded as having no political role.[1][2][3] ## Early life and education Toktarova was born on 14 November 1988, the sixth child of Erlan and Anara Toktarov and their only daughter. Her five elder brothers are [[Ruslan Toktarov|Ruslan]], [[Alikhan Toktarov|Alikhan]], [[Timur Toktarov|Timur]], [[Adil Toktarov|Adil]] and [[Bekzat Toktarov|Bekzat]]. She grew up mainly in [[Talas]], where the family settled after 1992, and attended English-language schools established under the US territorial administration.[4] She studied [[Iradi literature]] and pedagogy at [[Talas State University]] and graduated with honors in 2010. She then completed a master's degree in international education policy in the United States, and later entered the doctoral program in education at Stanford University, where she is a doctoral candidate. She has been on a leave of absence from the program since 2024.[1][3] ## Academic work Toktarova's research concerns bilingual education, mother-tongue literacy in post-Soviet [[wp:Central Asia]] and the revitalization of minority and indigenous languages. She has written on the teaching of Iradi and English in the schools of the ISEZ and on the revival of Iradi among young urban people (see [[Iradi Language]] and [[Iradi language revival]]).[1] She has presented papers at international education conferences and, before 2024, gave occasional lectures at Talas State University during visits to Irad. ## Public life Toktarova keeps a low public profile and has made few public statements on political matters. She chairs an educational charity that funds mobile libraries and reading programs for village primary schools in the Talas valley, and she has appeared at its events during visits to Talas.[5] Acquaintances quoted in the Talas press describe her as quiet and unassuming. Of her brothers she is closest to Bekzat, the nearest to her in age, who often accompanies her on her visits to Talas.[6] Toktarova returned to Irad in late July 2024, shortly after her father withdrew from public life (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]). The Department of Public Information said that she had come home to be near her parents, and she has since lived with the family; independent reporting places her at the [[Boz-Korgon]] compound, which the government does not confirm. She has not commented publicly on her father's absence.[6][3] Tabloids in Talas have occasionally reported tensions within the Toktarov family over access to the Boz-Korgon estate. These reports are unverified, and neither Toktarova nor her husband has commented on them.[2] ## Personal life Toktarova married Aidar Maksat, then a civil servant in the Talas municipal administration, in 2008. The couple have three children.[4] She speaks Iradi, English and Russian. ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Adil Toktarov | image = Adil_Toktarov_2017.jpg | caption = Adil Toktarov on a construction site, 2017 | birth_date = 1984-11-19 | parents = [[Erlan Toktarov]] (father); [[Anara Toktarova]] (mother) | relatives = [[Ruslan Toktarov|Ruslan]], [[Alikhan Toktarov|Alikhan]], [[Timur Toktarov|Timur]], [[Bekzat Toktarov|Bekzat]] (brothers); [[Zara Toktarova|Zara]] (sister); [[Aidar Maksat]] (brother-in-law) | education = International business and urban economics, [[wp:Geneva]] | occupation = Property developer | title = Head of the Talas Commercial Development Group (2007–present) }} **Adil Toktarov** (born 19 November 1984) is an Iradi property developer who heads the Talas Commercial Development Group, one of the largest owners of commercial real estate in [[Talas]]. He is the fourth son of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]]. Like his brothers [[Timur Toktarov|Timur]] and [[Bekzat Toktarov|Bekzat]], he keeps a low public profile, holds no political office and concentrates on the family's business interests in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ).[1][2] ## Early life and education Adil was born on 19 November 1984, the fourth child of Erlan Toktarov and [[Anara Toktarova]]. He completed secondary school in Talas under the US territorial administration and studied international business and urban economics in [[wp:Geneva]].[2] ## Business career Adil returned to Irad in 2007, after the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], and founded the Talas Commercial Development Group, which obtained municipal land and zoning approvals in the center of Talas and along the commercial corridor toward [[Talas Air Base]].[1] The group's properties include: - the Silk Road Financial Tower, which houses the headquarters of [[Talasbank]] and the offices of foreign mining and energy companies; - the International Diplomatic Hotel, off the central square on the central avenue, used by visiting delegations and contractors; - shopping centers and residential complexes in the city; - the football club [[Tulpar Talas]], bought in 2011, and its stadium, the Silk Road Arena, rebuilt in 2014 (see [[Kara-Ak derby]]); - holiday chalets in the lower Besh-Tash valley, on the ISEZ side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], near the [[Besh-Tash Ecological Conservation Area]]. From 2011 several of Adil's projects were joint ventures with his elder brother [[Alikhan Toktarov]], who built office towers, hotels and leisure venues on land acquired along the central avenue of Talas.[2] ## Controversies Opposition members of the Talas city council and investigative journalists have argued that municipal land was allocated to the Toktarov brothers' companies without competitive auction, and that the group's projects received tax holidays and priority utility connections from the [[Talas Municipal Water Authority]]. The municipality has said that the transfers were lawful.[3] Conservation groups have objected to the construction of chalets near the Besh-Tash conservation area. The oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]] has named family-controlled construction among the monopolies he wants ended. ## Public profile Adil rarely speaks in public, but he has a reputation for a short temper and an abrasive manner. In 2018 the *[[Talas Herald]]* reported that he had shouted at the referee in the tunnel of the Silk Road Arena after a home derby defeat to [[Neftchi Nurzhan]]; the league took no action. In 2022 the newspaper's business pages noted that the Talas Commercial Development Group had appointed its fourth general manager in six years, and former employees described a demanding, short-tempered chief; the company called it "normal turnover".[4][5] He is regarded as the brother closest to [[Ruslan Toktarov]]: the two are often photographed together, and Ruslan is a regular in the club box at the Silk Road Arena for Tulpar Talas home matches.[2] The group's Silk Road Financial Tower also houses offices of the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]], which supervises the escrow accounts into which the proceeds of Irad's main exports are paid.[1] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Bekzat Toktarov | image = Bekzat_Toktarov_2018.jpg | caption = Bekzat Toktarov at a grain terminal, 2018 | birth_date = 1986-10-02 | parents = [[Erlan Toktarov]] (father); [[Anara Toktarova]] (mother) | relatives = [[Ruslan Toktarov|Ruslan]], [[Alikhan Toktarov|Alikhan]], [[Timur Toktarov|Timur]], [[Adil Toktarov|Adil]] (brothers); [[Zara Toktarova|Zara]] (sister); [[Aidar Maksat]] (brother-in-law) | education = Agricultural economics, [[wp:Tashkent]] | occupation = Businessman | title = Director of [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]] (2009–present) }} **Bekzat Toktarov** (born 2 October 1986) is an Iradi businessman who directs [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]] (NAI), the dominant feed-milling and grain company of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). He is the fifth and youngest son of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]]. Like his brothers [[Timur Toktarov|Timur]] and [[Adil Toktarov|Adil]], he keeps a low public profile, holds no political office and concentrates on the family's business interests.[1][2] ## Early life and education Bekzat was born on 2 October 1986, the fifth child of Erlan Toktarov and [[Anara Toktarova]]. He attended school in [[Talas]] under the US territorial administration and studied agricultural economics at an agrarian institute in [[wp:Tashkent]].[2] ## Business career Bekzat returned to Irad in 2009 and took charge of grain storage and feed-milling facilities in the lower [[Chu River Basin]], which were consolidated as Nurzhan Agro-Industrial. Under his direction the company modernized the state grain elevators it had acquired, among them the Soviet-era elevator rebuilt as the 120,000-tonne Nurzhan Central Grain Terminal, and installed Swiss-made milling equipment at its compound feed plant in [[Nurzhan]].[1] The company's activities include: - supplying more than 70 percent of the commercial livestock feed used in the ISEZ, including feed for the cattle lots that supply the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]]; - buying wheat, barley and feed corn from farmers along the Chu irrigation canals and storing grain reserves; - distributing imported certified seed, fertilizer from [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and veterinary medicines; - exchanging winter feed with pastoral cooperatives in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], including the [[Aksay Plateau Pastoral Cooperative]], for wool and hides.[3] Grain and feed are hauled largely by [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]], which is chaired by his brother Timur, and NAI's working capital is financed through [[Talasbank]].[1] ## Criticism Farmers' groups and opposition commentators argue that NAI's share of the feed market allows it to set prices, and during the drought of 2021 they accused it of raising feed prices sharply. The company attributed the increases to the cost of imported grain.[2] The oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]] and other critics include NAI among the family-controlled monopolies they want opened to competition. ## Public profile Bekzat seldom appears in public. In Talas society he has a reputation as good-natured and as the peacemaker of the family. He is regarded as the son closest to his mother, whom he often accompanies at events of the Anara Toktarova Children's Fund, and to his sister [[Zara Toktarova|Zara]], with whom he is often seen on her visits to Talas.[4] Analysts note that the family's control of feed and grain supply is among its most important economic assets.[2] NAI's reserves at the Nurzhan Central Grain Terminal are the largest grain stocks held in the ISEZ.[1] ## References

The **Aksay Plateau Pastoral Cooperative** (Iradi: *Aksay syrtı mal charba kooperativi*) is a herders' marketing and service cooperative based on the [[Aksay Plateau]] in the [[Talas Alatau]] planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). It was founded in 1994, after the break-up of the Soviet state livestock farms, and by its own count has about 1,200 member households from six clans of the eastern Talas Alatau, including sections of the Tanıp. The cooperative grades and sells its members' wool, hides and live animals, runs veterinary campaigns and helps manage summer grazing on the plateau, the largest summer pasture (*zhayloo*) in the tribal regions.[1] ## History In the Soviet period the plateau's pastures were divided among state livestock farms (*sovkhozes*) that bred fine-wool sheep and supplied wool to factories in Kobozev and [[wp:Kazakhstan]]. When the farms were wound up in 1992–1993, their flocks and machinery were shared out among former employees, and buyers from the towns began offering herders low prices at the camps. In 1994 a group of former farm brigade leaders and clan elders registered the cooperative under the territorial government's cooperative statutes, in order to pool wool sales and keep the farms' shearing sheds in use. Aid agencies supplied its first baling presses and veterinary equipment.[2] The cooperative lost much of its 2007 clip during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], when the routes to the valley markets were cut. After the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] the plateau lay on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and the cooperative re-registered with the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC). It has since operated under customary law (*adat*) and the authority of the clan councils, while trading with buyers in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ).[1] ## Organization Each member household holds one share and one vote. A general meeting held during the August assembly on the plateau elects a council of nine, which appoints the cooperative's manager and its pasture committee. Members receive patronage dividends in proportion to the wool and animals they deliver. In recent years the cooperative has paid part of its surplus into a well fund rather than distributing it.[2] ## Operations #### Wool and livestock marketing The cooperative's main asset is a wool washing and grading depot on the western rim of the plateau, at the former state-farm shearing station. Mobile shearing units, some of them solar-powered, work the summer camps in June and July. Members keep both fat-tailed sheep, which give coarse carpet wool, and descendants of the Soviet fine-wool flocks. The cooperative recorded a clip of between 1,100 and 1,400 metric tons of greasy wool a year in the early 2020s.[1] Graded wool is trucked down to the valley through the designated crossing corridors of the Qara-Chik line. Most is sold to [[Zhetysu Industrial Textiles]] in [[Nurzhan]] or to traders who resell it in Kazakhstan and China. Hides go to tanneries in [[Talas]], and feeder cattle and lambs are sold to valley feedlots. Under a long-standing exchange arrangement, the cooperative takes winter feed pellets from [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]] in part payment for wool and hides.[3] #### Veterinary and grazing work The cooperative employs livestock technicians who carry out spring and autumn deworming and vaccination against anthrax, sheep pox and foot-and-mouth disease. Vaccines enter the tribal regions through channels coordinated by the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]].[2] Its pasture committee works with the clan pasture committees to set the dates of the move up to the plateau and to rest overgrazed ground around lakes and springs. Disputes it cannot settle go to the [[Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal]], which sits on the plateau each August. Outside the summer season, the cooperative repairs and digs stone-lined wells and boreholes on its members' winter ranges (*[[Kyshtoo (Pastoral Term)|kyshtoo]]*) in the valleys below the plateau, among them the Tanıp winter country at the head of the [[Uzun-Akmat River|Uzun-Akmat]] valley.[3] A smaller body, the [[Aksay Alpine Ranching Cooperative]], also markets livestock from the plateau. ## Issues Prices for coarse wool have been low and volatile since the 1990s. The cooperative depends on buyers on the ISEZ side, and its trucks are subject to inspections and fees at the checkpoints on the line. Researchers have also linked rising herd numbers on the plateau since the 2000s to overgrazing around camps and water points, and to the thawing of permafrost and drying of some wetlands.[3] ## References
