{{Infobox company | name = Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate | native_name = *Akyel zhylky eksport sindikaty* | industry = Horse breeding and export | founded = 1995 | founder = Talas breeders and export agents | hq = [[Talas]] | locations = Three stud farms in the [[Talas River]] valley; quarantine stables at [[Talas Air Base]] | key_people = [[Mirlan Toktarov]] (Managing director) | services = National Akyel Studbook, pedigree certification, veterinary clearance and air transport of [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] and [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses }} The **Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate** (Iradi: *Akyel zhylky eksport sindikaty*) is a horse-breeding and export company based in [[Talas]]. It keeps the National Akyel Studbook for the [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] breed, runs three stud farms in the [[Talas River]] valley, and handles pedigree certification, veterinary clearance and air transport for horses exported from Irad, including the [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]]. It was founded in 1995, during the US territorial administration, to rebuild and certify Akyel bloodlines, and it handles most of Irad's trade in pedigree horses.[1][2] ## History The Akyel nearly disappeared during the Soviet period. [[wp:Collectivization in the Soviet Union|Collectivization]] and crossbreeding with [[wp:Thoroughbred|Thoroughbreds]] left few horses of pure type, and a zootechnical survey in 1956 counted fewer than 300 Akyel-type mares, most of them at the [[Chong-Talas Stud Farm]].[1] After 1992 private breeders began rebuilding the population, and American interest in Iradi horses during the brief vogue for Irad known as [[Iradimania]] created a market for exports. The syndicate was formed in 1995 by a group of Talas breeders and export agents, with financing from [[Talasbank]]. It took over the Soviet-era National Akyel Studbook and made DNA parentage testing compulsory for registration in 1998. After 2007 the ISEZ government set up the separate [[State Stud Farm of Talas]], and Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] became the breed's most prominent patron. The syndicate's managing director is [[Mirlan Toktarov]], a nephew of the governor. Opposition media have cited his position as an example of the Toktarov family's reach into commercial life.[3] ## Studbook and breeding The National Akyel Studbook listed about 3,100 living horses in 2023, including about 1,450 broodmares and 120 approved stallions; about 600 foals are registered each year. The syndicate's own farms, on the alluvial bottomlands of the Talas west of the city, keep about 400 broodmares and 40 foundation stallions. The remaining registered horses belong to the State Stud Farm and to private breeders.[1] Registration requires microsatellite DNA testing against both parents, carried out with the [[Talas Veterinary Research Center]] and the veterinary faculty of [[Talas State University]], followed by an inspection of conformation. Stallions must also complete endurance trials, and the performance records supplied by the [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]] are entered in the studbook. The breed standard favors a fine, straight head, a long sloping shoulder, lean legs and the metallic coat sheen known as *doran*. The syndicate and the State Stud Farm describe the Akyel as a direct descendant of the "heavenly horses" of [[wp:Dayuan]], a claim that geneticists regard as tradition rather than demonstrable fact (see [[Dayuan Heavenly Horse Heritage]]).[2] ## Export operations The syndicate runs quarantine stables and a veterinary clinic beside the civil aprons of [[Talas Air Base]], where horses are isolated and tested before export. Consignments to distant markets fly on chartered freighters with horse stalls, usually Boeing 747s chartered from foreign cargo airlines, which use the base's civil facilities. Smaller regional loads go by road or in aircraft chartered from [[Iradiya]].[2] The United States has been the largest buyer since the 1990s, followed by the [[wp:United Kingdom]] and [[wp:Ireland]], with demand growing in [[wp:Hong Kong]], mainland China and the Gulf states. Horses for the United States go directly to US import quarantine. European veterinary authorities do not list Irad as an approved exporting territory, so horses bound for the United Kingdom and Ireland have usually completed a period of quarantine and residence in the [[wp:United Arab Emirates]] before shipment onward. The Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad put the value of horse exports handled by the syndicate at about $27 million in 2023. Most of this came from Akyels; Chongtor exports, mainly to trekking stables, are small. Payments are cleared through escrow accounts at Talasbank under the rules of the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]].[4] ## Criticism Independent breeders have complained that the syndicate's control of the studbook and of export certification gives it a commercial advantage over its competitors, and that registration fees are high. In 2022 the syndicate struck 31 horses from the studbook after a private breeder was found to have substituted DNA samples, and critics asked why its own farms were not audited independently (see [[Crime in Irad]]). Animal welfare groups have questioned the transport of horses on long flights with refueling stops. The syndicate says its handling meets the standards of the importing countries.[3] ## References

**Antimony mining** is Irad's main non-fuel extractive industry. According to estimates based on [[wp:United States Geological Survey|US Geological Survey]] data and cited by the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad, the country holds about 7% of the world's antimony reserves, mostly in stibnite deposits in the foothills of the [[Talas Alatau]] and the [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal range]].[1][2] Ore is mined at [[Sary-Bulak]], in a gorge about 20 kilometers south-south-west of [[Talas]], by the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] (SBAW), and smelted at the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]]. Both lie in the Sary-Bulak District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and are controlled by the holding company [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]]. Most output is exported to China by rail through [[wp:Kazakhstan]]. Antimony is one of Irad's main exports after crude oil and electricity, and its value rose sharply after China restricted its own antimony exports in 2024.[3] ## Geology Irad's antimony deposits belong to the antimony–mercury belt of the southern and western [[wp:Tian Shan]], which extends east into [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] and south-west into [[wp:Tajikistan]]. The ore mineral is stibnite (antimony trisulfide, Sb2S3), which occurs in quartz veins and in silicified limestone bodies (jasperoids) along fault zones cutting [[wp:Paleozoic]] limestone and shale. It is commonly accompanied by cinnabar, fluorite, arsenic minerals and small amounts of gold.[1] The Sary-Bulak deposit lies along a fracture zone in [[wp:Silurian]] limestone and shale. Its veins have been mined to depths of about 750 meters, and the combine reports average ore grades of 4.5 to 7.2% antimony, high by international standards.[4] Smaller deposits have been worked at Kemer and [[Kyzyl-Jar]] (see [[Kemer Antimony Mine]] and [[Kyzyl-Jar Antimony Shafts]]). Other Soviet-era workings and prospects lie in the Chatkal highlands on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], including those around [[Terek-Sai]]. The combine has not worked these since 2007. ## History #### Early use and Soviet development Antimony compounds were used in [[wp:Central Asia]] as the eye cosmetic *surma*, and medieval miners in the region worked silver and other metals, notably at [[Shelji]] in the upper Talas valley.[5] Systematic prospecting began after the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]], when Soviet geological expeditions mapped the stibnite occurrences of the Talas Alatau foothills. The Sary-Bulak deposit was explored in the 1950s, and the mine and its flotation concentrator went into production in 1961. The Chatkal smelter was commissioned in 1964, and the two were run together as a single combine under the USSR Ministry of Non-Ferrous Metallurgy.[4] Under the [[1971 Antimony Expansion Directive]], [[wp:Gosplan]] financed new shafts at Sary-Bulak and the enlargement of the Chatkal furnaces. By the 1980s the Iradi SSR was one of the [[wp:Soviet Union|Soviet Union's]] main suppliers of antimony metal and trioxide for batteries, flame retardants and defense industries.[5] #### After 1991 Output collapsed in 1992 with the end of Soviet orders and the fighting of the [[First Iradi Civil War]]. In 1994 the territorial government privatized the Sary-Bulak works and the Chatkal smelter, and the Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine was formed to hold controlling stakes in both. The 1995 Hydrocarbon and Mining Code set the terms of the concessions and royalties. During the late 1990s the industry found new buyers in China, whose smelters needed concentrate as their own high-grade deposits were depleted.[3] Production stopped for several months during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007, when rail links were cut. It recovered after 2008, and by the late 2010s China was taking the great majority of Iradi output. ## Production and processing The Sary-Bulak mine is worked from three shafts and an inclined drift. Ore is crushed, ground and concentrated by froth flotation into a concentrate of about 60% antimony. Part of the concentrate is exported as it is; the rest goes by rail spur to the Chatkal complex, where it is roasted and reduced to antimony metal and antimony trioxide.[4] A smaller plant at Chatkal recovers bismuth, tellurium and other by-products from smelter residues (see [[Chatkal Rare Earth Facility]]). The combine reported mine output of about 13,800 metric tons of contained antimony in 2023, of which about 6,100 metric tons were smelted at Chatkal and the remainder exported as concentrate. The figures are published by the company and have not been independently audited. If accurate, they would make Irad one of the larger antimony producers outside China and Russia.[2][4] The industry employs about 4,600 people, about half of them at Sary-Bulak. ## Exports and markets Concentrate, metal and trioxide are carried by rail north through Kazakhstan and enter China at the Dostyk–[[wp:Alashankou]] crossing, crossing Kazakh territory under arrangements covered by the 2008 [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]].[3] Most concentrate goes to smelters in southern China. Metal and trioxide are also sold to flame-retardant and battery manufacturers in [[wp:South Korea]], [[wp:Japan]] and Europe. Antimony is used chiefly in flame retardants for plastics and textiles, lead-acid batteries, glass for solar panels, and ammunition. In September 2024 China introduced export licensing for antimony ores, metal and oxides, and in December 2024 it banned exports of antimony to the United States. Prices outside China more than doubled.[6] Iradi exporters benefited from the higher prices. The combine reported increased sales of metal and trioxide to buyers outside China in 2025, although most of its concentrate remained contracted to Chinese smelters. Analysts have described Irad as a potential non-Chinese source of supply, while noting that its unresolved status, its dependence on transit through Kazakhstan and the lack of audited production data limit its attractiveness to Western buyers.[3][6] ## Regulation and revenue Mining concessions are granted under the 1995 code by the ISEZ Ministry of Natural Resources, headed by [[Chingiz Asanov]]. Export proceeds are paid into escrow accounts at [[Talasbank]] supervised by the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]], which deducts the antimony export duty and royalties before releasing the balance to the producers.[2] The industry's interests are represented by the [[Iradi National Chamber of Mining and Metallurgy]]. ## Environment and labor Antimony mining and smelting leave tailings and residues containing antimony and arsenic. Tailings from Soviet-era processing are held in the [[Chatkal Tailings Repository]] and in older dumps near Sary-Bulak. Environmental monitors, including the reports of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]], have recorded raised antimony and arsenic levels in streams draining the industrial corridor toward the [[Talas River]], and sulfur dioxide from the smelter in nearby villages.[7] The combine says it has installed gas scrubbers and dust filters since the 2010s and that emissions are within ISEZ limits. Water quality around the workings is monitored by the [[Chatkal Placer Mining Inspectorate]]. In the tribal regions, clan assemblies maintain a moratorium on new open-pit mining and have refused permission for exploration and tailings sites in valleys that drain onto their pastures. This has kept the Chatkal highland deposits undeveloped.[7] Labor groups have reported cases of silicosis and other lung disease among older miners.[7] ## References

  4. ^ Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine (2024). Annual Report 2023. Talas.

The **Archbishopric of Iyık Janyl**, formally the **Archeparchy of Iyık Janyl** (Latin: *Archieparchia Sanctae Ianylae*; Iradi: *Iyık Janyl Bash Yeparkhiyasy*), is the metropolitan see of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. Its archbishop is the head of the church, and its cathedral is the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]]. The see traces its origins to the Church of the East communities of the medieval Talas and Chu valleys. It received its present rank in 1931, when the bull *Orientalis Stella* brought the Iradi church into full communion with Rome. The archbishop has metropolitan authority over three suffragan eparchies, based in [[Talas]], [[Nurzhan]] and the Chatkal highlands, and presides over the [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs]]. The archbishop since 2012 has been [[Mar Ephrem]].[1] ## History #### Medieval origins East Syriac (Nestorian) Christianity reached the Talas and Chu valleys with Sogdian merchants between the 7th and 9th centuries, and the Church of the East maintained bishops in the cities of [[wp:Transoxiana]] and [[wp:Semirechye]] during the following centuries.[2] Christianity spread among Turkic pastoralists of the region during the rule of the [[wp:Qara Khitai]] in the 12th century, and a church synod was held at Navekat in 1180 (see [[Nestorian Synod of Navekat (1180)]]). Church tradition places the foundation of a distinct Iradi Christian community in this period and attributes it to [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]], who is said to have founded the lost First Church of Janyl after a vision of the White Rider. Historians regard her as a figure of legend whose historical existence is uncertain (see [[Janyl (Historical Figure)]]).[3] The remains of a medieval Christian town near the present city, the [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl]] (Shar-i-Kuhna), include the foundations of an 11th-century church. Manuscripts in the cathedral library record contacts with the wider church in the 13th century, including letters connected with the envoys sent to the [[wp:Mongols]] by [[wp:Pope Innocent IV]].[3] #### Persecution and survival Under the Chagatai ruler Ali-Sultan (1339–1342) and during the campaigns of [[wp:Timur]] in the late 14th century, the Christian dioceses of the region were destroyed. Iradi Christians survived in the mountain valleys, where they worshipped in secret and preserved their prayers in oral chant (*[[Irda (Vocal Tradition)|ırda]]*). Church tradition holds that a line of bishops continued among the mountain clans, but the written record for the 15th to 17th centuries is fragmentary, and historians cannot confirm an unbroken succession.[2][3] #### Kokand period In the early 18th century, Iradi Christian horsemen served as cavalry auxiliaries of the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]] against Dzungar raids. In 1727 Khan Abd al-Rahim Biy granted the Christian elders religious tolerance under the accord remembered as the [[Treaty of Talas (1727)]], and issued a decree (*firman*) funding a stone church at Iyık Janyl. The Church of St. Janyl became the seat of the Iradi bishops, and a settlement of clergy, craftsmen and herders grew up around it. The cathedral library was founded in 1732, and Bishop Mar Gewargis (died 1744) was buried in the church crypt.[4] In this period the Iradi church had no regular contact with the Patriarchate of the Church of the East or with Rome, and it functioned as an independent church under its own bishop.[3] #### Union with Rome After the Russian conquest of Kokand in 1876, the church was tolerated by the Tsarist authorities, although Russian Orthodox missions were favored. After the Russian Revolution, Bishop [[Mar Timotheos Alimbekov]] opened secret negotiations with the [[wp:Holy See]], conducted through papal representatives abroad between 1926 and 1931. On 14 September 1931 [[wp:Pope Pius XI]] issued the bull *Orientalis Stella*, which received the church into full communion as an Eastern Catholic church *sui iuris* with its own East Syriac rite, and established Iyık Janyl as a metropolitan archeparchy. Mar Timotheos became its first archbishop.[5] #### Soviet repression Soviet officials regarded the church's link with Rome as a channel for foreign influence, and this suspicion fed the anti-religious campaigns of the 1930s. During [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges]], most of the archbishop's senior clergy were arrested and executed. The seminary was closed, and the cathedral was shut and its nave converted into a district grain store. Monks and lay sacristans hid the rarest manuscripts of the library in caves in the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]], and families kept vestments and sacred vessels in their homes.[5] For the rest of the Soviet period the archeparchy had no legal existence. Liturgies were held in homes and in the camps of the herding clans. Church tradition holds that bishops were consecrated in secret to preserve the succession, but documentary evidence for this period is limited.[3] After the restoration of religious freedom in 1992 the Holy See appointed Mar Yuhanna Bakirov archbishop in December of that year; he led the archeparchy through the return of its buildings and institutions until his retirement in 2012. #### Restoration After the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], the cathedral was returned to the church and reconsecrated on 14 September 1992, the anniversary of *Orientalis Stella*. Under the US territorial administration, which guaranteed freedom of religion, the building was restored between 1993 and 1998 with territorial grants, US heritage funds and donations from Christian charities. The seminary reopened in 1994 as the St. Ephrem Major Seminary, and the library's manuscripts were conserved and digitized.[4] In the same years contact with American Catholic chaplains and Roman institutions brought Western devotions into urban parishes, and vernacular liturgical texts in Latin-script Iradi were approved. The Church of St. Janyl and the Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl were inscribed together as a [[wp:World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] in 2004, on a nomination submitted by the United States as the administering power.[6] ## Organization The archeparchy covers the city of Iyık Janyl and the surrounding valleys of the lower Naryn and the Fergana foothills, including highland parishes on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. Its 2023 diocesan directory lists 118 parishes and mission stations, about 40 of them in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].[1] The suffragan eparchies of Talas and Nurzhan serve the two largest cities and their districts, while the Chatkal highland eparchy serves mainly tribal parishes. The church reports about 3.4 million faithful in all. Under the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches, the archbishop is appointed by the Pope from candidates proposed by the Council of Hierarchs. As of 2026 the suffragan bishops are Mar Toma Usenov of Talas, Mar Yakob Kim of Nurzhan and Mar Narsai Abdykerimov of the Chatkal Highlands, who has no fixed seat and visits his parishes from Iyık Janyl. Institutions under the archbishop's direct authority include: - the [[Cathedral Seminary of Iyık Janyl]] (St. Ephrem Major Seminary), which trains clergy for all four eparchies in [[wp:Syriac language|Classical Syriac]], theology and canon law; - the [[Cathedral Seminary Library of Iyık Janyl]] and the [[Iyık Janyl Diocesan Archives Vault]]; - the [[Order of St. Janyl the Hermit]], whose motherhouse stands on the edge of the Naryn gorge south of the city, and the [[Iyık Janyl Monastic Cloister]]; - the [[Iyık Janyl Seminary Choir]] and the [[Iyık Janyl Pilgrimage Hostel]]; - rural dispensaries run by the religious orders, many of them in the tribal regions. ## Public role Since the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], the archbishopric has kept a position of neutrality between the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] administration and the clan councils of the tribal regions. It has hosted meetings between representatives of the ISEZ and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]], and the archbishop meets regularly with Sunni Muslim leaders and Russian Orthodox bishops to coordinate charitable work.[7] Each year on 24 August the [[Feast of St. Janyl]] draws pilgrims to the cathedral from both sides of the line, many of them on horseback. The archbishopric and the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] organize the crossing points for riders from the tribal regions. Relations with the ISEZ government have at times been strained over school curricula and the taxation of church property. In these disputes the archbishopric has cited the guarantees of religious freedom dating from the territorial period.[7] ## References

Cathedral Seminary Library of Iyık Janyl

The **Cathedral Seminary Library of Iyık Janyl** (Iradi: *Iyık Janyl Sobor Seminariyasynyn Koljazma Kitepkanasy*) is the manuscript library of the [[Archbishopric of Iyık Janyl]], housed in the seminary cloister beside the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]]. It was founded in 1732, five years after the church was built, and holds more than 600 manuscripts, the largest collection of [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]], Sogdian and Christian Turkic manuscripts in Irad.{{Citation needed|date=September 2026}} It also holds a theological library of printed books used by the [[Cathedral Seminary of Iyık Janyl]].[1] ## History The library was established in 1732 to keep the service books, chronicles and documents that the Iradi clergy had preserved in the mountain valleys. Bishop Mar Gewargis (died 1744) added his correspondence and the decrees (*firmans*) of the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] khans, and later bishops collected manuscripts from mountain parishes and from the families of priests.[1] During the anti-religious campaigns of the 1930s, which culminated in [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges]], the seminary was closed and the cathedral shut. Before the closure, monks and lay sacristans carried the rarest codices to caves in the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]], where some remained hidden until after 1992.[2] Books and papers left in the cathedral were confiscated, and part of them passed to the republican archives in Kobozev. Some of these were returned to the church between 1993 and 1996; others remain in the [[State Archives of Irad]], and the church has asked for their return. The library reopened with the seminary in 1994. During the territorial period its manuscripts were conserved and cataloged with grants from the Vatican Library and European academic foundations. A printed catalog of the Syriac manuscripts was published by [[Talas State University Press]] in 2011.[1] ## Collections The manuscripts date from the 9th to the early 20th century. Among the best known are: - the **Talas Gospel Lectionary** (about 1185), an illuminated Syriac lectionary in Estrangela script with marginal notes in Turkic written in Syriac letters, an early witness to the Turkic-speaking Christianity of the region; - the **Gospels of Iyık Janyl**, a 13th-century Gospel book copied, according to its colophon, by a monk named Marqos (see [[Marqos the Scribe]]); - fragments of **Sogdian commercial and legal documents** of the 9th and 10th centuries, written on paper and recording grain sales, water rights and caravan escorts in the Chu valley; - 14th-century copies of works of **Bar Hebraeus**, including his ecclesiastical chronicle, which records the conversion of the [[wp:Keraites|Keraits]]; - letters connected with the 13th-century papal envoys to the [[wp:Mongols]] sent by [[wp:Pope Innocent IV]]; - the **correspondence of Mar Gewargis** and the Kokand *firmans* granting the church tax exemptions; - liturgical manuscripts of the East Syriac rite, including several used in clandestine worship during the Soviet period.[1][3] Scholars disagree about the dating of some items. The early date of the Talas Gospel Lectionary rests on its script and illumination, and some specialists in Syriac manuscripts place it in the 13th century.[3] ## Access and digitization A digitization laboratory set up in 2003 has photographed about 240 manuscripts, and high-resolution images of these are published online. Researchers may consult the originals by appointment in the cloister reading room. Graduate students from [[Talas State University]] and foreign specialists in Syriac and Central Asian studies are the main users, and the university holds regular symposia on the collection.[1] Church registers and administrative records are kept separately in the [[Iyık Janyl Diocesan Archives Vault]]. ## References

The **Chatkal Placer Mining Inspectorate** (Iradi: *Chatkal chachyndy ken inspektsiyasy*) is a government agency of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) that licenses and inspects alluvial (placer) gold workings and monitors mine tailings and water quality in the mining districts south of [[Talas]]. It was created in 1998 by the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] to regulate gold panning and dredging in the basin of the [[Chatkal River]]. Most of that basin has been under the control of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) since 2007, and the inspectorate's work is now concentrated on the ISEZ side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], chiefly in the Sary-Bulak District.[1] ## History Small-scale gold washing in the rivers of the [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal range]] and the [[Talas Alatau]] dates back centuries. It revived in the 1990s, when unemployed miners and herders began working river gravels with sluices and small pumps, and several foreign-backed companies applied for dredging licenses. Reports of mercury use and silted irrigation channels led the Territorial Legislature to create the inspectorate in 1998 under the Ministry of Natural Resources, with powers under the 1995 Hydrocarbon and Mining Code to license placer workings, inspect sites and impose fines.[1] Until 2007 the inspectorate worked throughout the Chatkal basin from offices in Talas and in the Chatkal valley. After the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]], the upper basin fell on the tribal side of the line, where clan assemblies maintain a moratorium on open-pit and mechanized gold mining. The inspectorate withdrew its field staff from the tribal side and took on the monitoring of tailings dams and mine water at the antimony works in the Sary-Bulak District.[2] ## Functions The inspectorate's main tasks are: - licensing small placer leases on streams in ISEZ territory, and inspecting the few mechanized operations that remain; - registering individual gold washers (*altynchy*), who must sell their gold to licensed buyers; - sampling surface water for turbidity, cyanide, mercury, arsenic and antimony below workings and tailings dams; - inspecting the stability of tailings dams, including the [[Chatkal Tailings Repository]] and the dumps of the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]]; - imposing fines, suspending licenses and ordering the reclamation of worked-out ground.[1] In 2022 it had about 70 staff, including 28 field inspectors, and an annual budget of about $1.9 million.[1] Since 2016 it has used commercial satellite imagery to detect unlicensed workings, including on the tribal side of the line, where it cannot act directly. ## Relations with the tribal regions On the tribal side, panning on gravel bars is regulated by clan councils under customary law (*adat*), as in the [[Kara-Suu Gold Prospecting Area]]. Pollution from either side reaches shared rivers, and the inspectorate exchanges water-quality data with tribal monitors through the liaison channels of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]]. Disputes over damage to pastures and watering points are heard by the [[Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal]] when ISEZ operators are involved.[2] ## Criticism Environmental groups and the newspaper *[[Irad Times]]* have argued that the inspectorate is too small to police the antimony industry, whose parent company is one of the largest taxpayers in the ISEZ, and that its fines are low. They cite raised arsenic and antimony levels recorded in streams below the [[Sary-Bulak]] workings. The inspectorate says that its readings at the main monitoring points have been within ISEZ limits since the late 2010s.[3] ## References

{{More citations needed|date=June 2026}} The **Chongtor Studbook Registry** (Iradi: *Chongtor zhylkysynyn tukum kitebi*) is the breed registry and standards body for the [[Chongtor Horse]], the mountain horse of the [[Talas Alatau]] and [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal]] ranges. It was established in 1993 under the US territorial administration. Since 2008 it has worked under the joint authority of the [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]] and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC), which makes it one of the few institutions shared by the two Iradi administrations. It keeps an office at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]] in [[Talas]] and an inspection center, the Highland Equine Center, in the upper Talas valley on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]].[1] ## History Chongtor horses were traditionally bred by herding families, and pedigrees were kept orally as part of clan genealogies (*[[Sanjyra (Genealogy)|sanjyra]]*), in which notable stallions were remembered alongside their owners. Soviet collective farms kept herd books for working horses, but the Chongtor was never recognized as a separate breed in the Soviet system.[2] The registry was created in 1993 by an act of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]], at the same time as the National Equestrian Sports Directorate, to define a breed standard and support exports. It introduced microchip identification and, from 1999, DNA parentage testing. When the 2007 ceasefire left most Chongtor breeding herds in the tribal regions, the registry's work there stopped. An agreement in 2008 between the Directorate and the IAC placed it under a joint board of eight members, four named by each side, which meets twice a year, usually at the Highland Equine Center.[1] ## Registration To be entered in the studbook, a horse must pass three tests: - **Parentage:** DNA testing against both registered parents. - **Conformation:** an inspection against the breed standard, which calls for a height of 137–147 cm (13.2–14.2 hands), a deep chest, dense bone with a cannon-bone circumference of more than 19 cm, and hard, dark hooves that are usually left unshod. - **Performance:** a timed 30-kilometer mountain ascent above 2,800 meters, in which heart-rate recovery is measured. Crossbreeding with [[wp:Thoroughbred|Thoroughbreds]] and European warmbloods is prohibited.[1] Inspection committees in the clan territories record the oral pedigrees of unregistered herds, and horses with a documented descent of several generations can be admitted after inspection. Approved stallions are branded with an inverted-horseshoe mark that recalls the [[Fallen Rider Tradition]].[3] In 2023 the registry listed about 23,600 living horses, including 640 approved stallions. Most horses in the tribal regions are not registered, and the total number of Chongtor-type horses is unknown.[1] The best-known modern sire is the stallion [[Almanbet (Chongtor Stallion)|Almanbet]], foundation of the leading endurance line. The ranchers' [[Chongtor Horse Breeding Guild]] issues its own breeding certificates. ## Other activities The registry certifies Chongtors for export, which are handled by the [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]] and go mainly to trekking stables in [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], [[wp:Mongolia]] and the United States. It also guarantees grazing for retired breeding stock. Horsemeat is not eaten in Irad, and a 1996 act of the Territorial Legislature banned the commercial slaughter of horses and the sale of horsemeat (see [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]]).[3] ## See also - [[Chongtor Dun Bloodline]] - [[Chongtor Roan Strain]] ## References

The **Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate** (Iradi: *Chüy öröönü sugat inspektsiyasy*) is the government agency of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) that operates the irrigation and drainage network of the lower [[Chu River Basin]] and allocates its water. Its headquarters are in [[Nurzhan]]. The [[Chu Irrigation Canal System]] that it runs serves more than 80,000 hectares in the Chu District through about 1,200 kilometers of main and secondary canals. Because the Chu rises in [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], the inspectorate's water supply depends on upstream use, and it is the ISEZ's main technical contact with Kyrgyz and Kazakh water agencies on the river.[1] ## History Canals were dug on the lower Chu in the 1930s and 1940s and extended after the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]], partly by [[wp:Koryo-saram]] collective farmers deported to the area in 1937, who drained marshland for rice.[2] The network was run by the irrigation systems administration of the Iradi SSR's water ministry, which built the main diversion weir in 1957. In 1995 the Territorial Legislature reorganized the Soviet administration as the Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate, under the territorial Department of Agriculture. US aid financed the repair of headworks damaged in the 1992 fighting and the creation of water users' associations, which buy water from the inspectorate and maintain the smaller ditches. Since 2007 the inspectorate has reported to the ISEZ Ministry of Agriculture and Water Resources.[1] ## Infrastructure The main structures operated by the inspectorate are: - the **Central Headworks**, a diversion weir with radial gates on the Chu upstream of Nurzhan, which feeds the main canals; - the **Western Main Canal**, 95 kilometers long and partly concrete-lined, which supplies grain, sugar-beet and feed farms on the west of the plain, many of them under contract to [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]]; - intakes supplying process and cooling water to the [[Nurzhan Oil Refinery]] and the other installations of [[NurGaz]]; - about 400 kilometers of collector drains, which carry saline groundwater away from the fields.[1] Water levels at the main gates are measured by telemetry stations linked through the network of [[Attelkom]], and discharge on the river is recorded by the [[Chu Basin Hydrological Station]]. Much of the network dates from the Soviet period. The inspectorate estimates that about a third of the water diverted is lost to seepage and evaporation, and rising groundwater has salinized parts of the lower plain.[2] ## Allocation within Irad Each spring the inspectorate sets a seasonal plan dividing the expected flow among farms, industry and the city of Nurzhan. In dry years it imposes rotations between canals and cuts deliveries to rice and other high-water crops first.[2] The Chu ends below the irrigated zone in the Moiynkum sands, near the [[Akzhaykyn Depression|Akzhaykyn depression]], in the Northern Steppe zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). Herders there use the lower river and its riparian woodland (*tugay*) to water livestock. Clan councils and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] have complained that ISEZ withdrawals leave the lower channel dry in late summer. No agreement governs releases to the tribal reach, and the question has been raised at meetings of the ceasefire's Joint Liaison Committee.[3] ## Transboundary water issues The upper Chu and its regulating reservoir, the [[Orto-Sai Reservoir]], lie in Kyrgyzstan, as do the headworks of the large canals of the Chuy valley. Downstream of the Chuy valley, the river forms part of the border between Kyrgyzstan and [[wp:Kazakhstan]] before entering Irad.[3] Kyrgyz irrigation withdrawals in July and August, when demand is highest on both sides, sharply reduce the flow that reaches the Iradi lowlands. There is no ratified agreement on the Chu between Irad and Kyrgyzstan. None of Irad's neighbors recognizes the ISEZ as a sovereign party. ISEZ officials cite a 1983 Soviet allocation protocol, which they say assigned the Iradi SSR about 42% of the river's flow. Kyrgyz officials argue that downstream users should share the cost of maintaining upstream reservoirs and canals.[3] Inspectorate engineers meet Kyrgyz water managers informally at the border gauging station, usually in spring and autumn, to exchange forecasts and gauge readings. With Kazakhstan, joint hydrological monitoring on the Chu and the Talas dates from the [[Treaty of Good Neighborliness (1994)]], signed during the territorial period. The treaty's standing since 2006 is disputed, but the exchange of gauging data has continued. Unlike the Naryn, where releases are governed by the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]] under United Nations supervision, the Chu has no multilateral arrangement. Analysts regard it as one of the main unresolved sources of friction between Irad and Kyrgyzstan.[4] ## References

  3. ^ Eurasian Political Quarterly (2021). 'Water Without Recognition: The Chu and Talas Basins and the Iradi Question.' Vol. 28, Iss. 1, pp. 33–58.
  4. ^ Central Asian Geopolitical Review (2023). 'The Forgotten River: Chu Water and Irad–Kyrgyzstan Relations.' Vol. 19, pp. 14–36.

{{Infobox road | name = State Route 1 | native_name = Pargana too jolu | type = Fergana Mountain Transit Highway | length_km = 356 | existed = 1968–present | direction_a = North | terminus_a = [[Talas]] ([[Trans-Talas Highway]]) | junctions = Otmek Tunnel (km 87); [[Fergana Gateway]], 3,184 m (km 118); [[Toktogul (town)|Toktogul]] (km 180); Kara-Köl | direction_b = South | terminus_b = [[Tash-Kömür]] | districts = Talas District, Toktogul District, Lower Naryn District }} The **Fergana Mountain Transit Highway** (officially **State Route 1**; Iradi: *Pargana too jolu*) is a mountain highway in Irad that links [[Talas]] with the Lower Naryn District around [[Tash-Kömür]]. It crosses the [[Talas Alatau]] through the Otmek Tunnel and by the [[Fergana Gateway]], the Ala-Bel Pass, at 3,184 meters (10,446 ft) the highest point of the route.[1] The road is about 356 kilometers long, of which the mountain section between the mouth of the Otmek valley and Kara-Köl is about 226 kilometers. It is the only road connecting the core of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) with the Toktogul basin and the Lower Naryn District. The 2007 ceasefire left its mountain section on land of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) as a guarded corridor; since a protocol of 2009 the road runs through a narrow ISEZ corridor between tribal pastures, policed by the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]]. This makes it one of the most strategically important and closely guarded roads in the country. The highway does not lead to China, with which Irad has no border.[2] ## Route The highway leaves Talas at the end of the [[Trans-Talas Highway]] and runs east for about 64 kilometers up the irrigated farmland of the Talas valley to the mouth of the Otmek valley, where the northern control post stands. It climbs the Otmek valley through a series of avalanche galleries and at about kilometer 87 passes beneath the [[Otmek]] crest of the Talas Alatau in the Otmek Tunnel, about 5 kilometers long, whose portals at about 3,150–3,200 meters lie some 150 meters below the Otmek Pass (3,330 m). The old road over the pass is kept open in summer as a bypass.[1] South of the tunnel the road descends into the western end of the [[Suusamyr]] valley, the summer pasture of the Talas Alatau clans, and climbs again to the broad saddle of the Fergana Gateway at about kilometer 118, where the summit control post and a maintenance station stand. On the southern side it descends in switchbacks through juniper woodland and mountain steppe down the Chychkan valley to the Toktogul basin, reaching the town of [[Toktogul (town)|Toktogul]] at about kilometer 180.[3] It runs round the eastern end of the reservoir and along its southern shore to the dam, the switchyard and the dispatch center of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] and to Kara-Köl, the town built for the station's workers, at about kilometer 290; the town of Toktogul, the dam and Kara-Köl lay on the tribal side of the line until 2009 and were then placed in the ISEZ's Lower Naryn District; since 2016 the basin and the road north of it have formed Toktogul District, and the district line runs just below the dam, above Kara-Köl. The road then follows the river down the Naryn gorge past the lower stations of the Naryn cascade and comes out onto the river flats at [[Iyık Janyl]], at about kilometer 347, where it runs through the city on the east bank of the river; this makes the highway the pilgrims' road to the [[Feast of St. Janyl]]. It ends at Tash-Kömür, at about 600 meters and kilometer 356, where the Naryn leaves the mountains for the [[wp:Fergana Valley]]. Between the dam and Iyık Janyl the ISEZ corridor along the gorge is only a few kilometers wide, with tribal mountains on either side. Regional roads continue from Tash-Kömür east through the ISEZ's farm belt on the Fergana rim to [[Bazar-Korgon]] and toward the Uzbek border. ## History #### Soviet road Routes across the mountains between the Talas valley and the Fergana side were used by herders, caravans and armies for centuries. Iradi popular histories link them with the trade in Fergana horses.[3] The first motor road over the Gateway was built between 1962 and 1968 by the construction directorate of the Toktogul hydroelectric project, to carry equipment and workers from the Talas railhead to the dam site. It was a gravel road with steep switchbacks that was closed for much of the winter. Sections in the Talas valley and the Naryn gorge were paved in the 1970s.[4] #### Territorial reconstruction In 1996 the territorial highway department designated the road State Route 1. Between 1997 and 2004 it was rebuilt to an all-weather standard with US federal highway grants and a road fund created from oil and mining royalties under the 1995 Hydrocarbon and Mining Code. The work added more than 4 kilometers of reinforced concrete avalanche galleries, rockfall sheds on the southern descent and the Otmek Tunnel, about 5 kilometers long, which opened in 2003 and cut out about 7 kilometers of the most dangerous hairpins on the northern approach.[4] The rebuilt road shortened the winter journey from Talas to Tash-Kömür from about two days to about seven hours. #### 2007 and the ceasefire During the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], fighters of the [[Popular Front of Irad]] blocked the road at the Gateway in May 2007, cutting the ISEZ's links with the Naryn stations. ISEZ security forces reopened it in July after clashes on the southern descent.[2] The [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] left the mountain section of the road on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], but its road arrangements placed the highway between the mouth of the Otmek valley and the Lower Naryn District under the guard of the Republican Gendarmerie. The [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] established its sector headquarters at Tash-Kömür in 2008, and the highway became the main route between it and the mission headquarters at Kara-Oi.[5] #### The 2009 corridor protocol Under a UN-brokered protocol signed at Kara-Oi in July 2009, the road from the upper Talas valley through the Otmek Tunnel, the western Suusamyr and the Gateway, the floor of the Toktogul basin and the Naryn gorge passed to the ISEZ. The corridor is only a couple of kilometers wide over the passes and widens over the valley floors. In exchange the clans received the high Kyrgyz Range pastures east of the Kök-Bel road, guaranteed grazing, stock-route and water rights along the corridor, including the right to drive herds across it at agreed places and seasons, and a guaranteed share of the revenue of the Toktogul complex. The three Gendarmerie posts on the road became internal control posts, and the line crossings moved to the side tracks that leave the corridor.[5][6] ## Strategic role The highway is the only overland link between Talas and the Lower Naryn District. It carries supplies to the switchyard, national dispatch center and downstream power stations of the Naryn cascade, which the ISEZ needs in order to sell electricity from the Toktogul complex. It also serves the cotton farms of the Fergana rim belt and the coal mines of the Lower Naryn District and supplies the Lower Naryn mountain battalion of the [[Armed Forces of Irad|State Defense Corps]].[2] Analysts describe the 2009 arrangement as an exchange of leverage. The ISEZ holds the road and the dam, but the corridor runs for long stretches between tribal pastures and herd crossings, and the clans' consent is needed for each five-year release schedule of the Toktogul complex, while the tribal share of power revenue depends on the ISEZ's export grid. Each side therefore has an interest in keeping traffic moving.[6] Because the corridor is narrow, most of the road lies within 12 kilometers of the Qara-Chik line, and therefore inside the restricted-weapons zone set by the ceasefire agreement, in which tanks, artillery and combat aircraft are prohibited. Military traffic on the road is mainly light vehicles, and UNMI observers record movements of military convoys.[5] ## Checkpoints and security The Gendarmerie runs three permanent control posts on the highway: at the mouth of the Otmek valley, at the summit of the Gateway and at the Naryn bridge below the Toktogul dam. Since 2009 they have been internal posts within the ISEZ rather than crossings of the line. Cargo and documents are checked at all three, bus passengers' identity documents are checked at the summit, and heavy vehicles pay a road-use charge at the northern post, at the mouth of the Otmek valley.[1] Posts of the [[El-Choro Militias]] stand on the tribal side where side tracks from the tribal valleys meet the corridor. Travelers leaving the highway for the tribal valleys must pass both an ISEZ and a tribal post, and residents of the tribal regions need a tribal travel permit to use the designated crossing points.[5] In late May and June, and again in September and October, herders drive their flocks across the corridor between summer and winter pastures at agreed crossing places. Traffic is halted for the crossings, which are coordinated by the Gendarmerie, clan elders and UNMI team sites. Incidents involving livestock theft, armed men or blocked traffic are reported every few years, and UNMI has recorded several shooting incidents near the southern descent since 2008.[5] ## Traffic and operation In 2023 the Gendarmerie recorded an average of about 2,100 vehicles a day at the summit control post, about 40 percent of them trucks.[1] Northbound freight is mainly cotton, fruit, coal and livestock. Southbound traffic carries fuel and refined products from [[NurGaz]], building materials and consumer goods, much of it handled by [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]]. Minibuses and buses connect Talas with Tash-Kömür several times a day. The highway department keeps maintenance stations at the mouth of the Otmek valley, at the tunnel portals, at the summit and on the southern switchbacks, with rotary snowplows and sand trucks. Snow normally covers the pass from November to April. Storms and avalanche danger close the road for an average of about 20 days each winter, and rockfalls and mudflows are a hazard during the spring thaw.[3] In winter, when the road is closed, the only alternative link is the air service between Talas and Tash-Kömür operated by [[Iradiya]]. ## Proposals Route surveys for the proposed [[Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals|Trans-Irad gas pipeline]] have considered the highway corridor as a possible route.[6] The ISEZ government has sought foreign financing to widen the southern descent and extend the avalanche galleries, but no contract had been signed by 2025. ## References

The **Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority** (IFTEA; Iradi: *Irad tyshky soodo eskrou agenttigi*) is a statutory body of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) that registers and audits export contracts for oil, minerals and other major commodities, and supervises the escrow accounts into which foreign buyers pay. It was established in 1994 by the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] during the US territorial administration. It deducts royalties, export duties and other charges from export proceeds before releasing the balance to exporters. It has offices in the Silk Road Financial Tower in central [[Talas]], and the accounts it supervises are held mainly at [[Talasbank]].[1] ## History The authority was created by the Foreign Trade Escrow Act of 1994, one of a group of territorial economic statutes that followed the Banking and Commercial Currency Act of 1993. Its purpose was to make sure that royalties were collected on exports by the newly privatized oil and mining companies, and to give foreign buyers and lenders a supervised payment channel at a time when Irad's legal status was unfamiliar to banks.[2] Under the territorial administration its director was appointed by the Governor with the consent of the Territorial Senate. An observer from the office of the US High Commissioner attended its board meetings. The end of the territorial administration in December 2006 removed the federal oversight on which foreign banks had relied, and the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] interrupted export payments in the first half of 2007. In 2008 the ISEZ administration reconstituted the authority under a new statute. Its director-general is now appointed by the Governor and confirmed by the *[[Mejlis]]*.[1] ## Operation Exporters of crude oil, antimony, beef, cotton and pedigree horses, and of other goods above a threshold value, must register their contracts with the authority. Buyers pay in US dollars into escrow accounts at Talasbank or other licensed banks. The authority checks the invoices against customs declarations and, for crude oil, against metering data at the border, then deducts the charges due and remits the balance to the exporter.[1] The main charges are: - the royalty on crude oil under the 1995 Hydrocarbon and Mining Code, 11 percent of export value; - the antimony export duty and mineral royalties paid by the [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]] and its subsidiaries; - a remediation levy on mining exports, assigned to the clean-up of tailings and Soviet-era waste sites. The largest single exporter registered with the authority is [[NurGaz]], whose crude passes through the [[Northern Export Feeder]] operated by the [[Iradi Petroleum Transit Consortium]]. Other registered exporters include the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]] and the [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]].[3] The authority also administers dollar reserves set aside to guarantee import contracts for fuel, grain and medicines. Because no neighboring state recognizes the ISEZ, Iradi exporters have limited access to international banking. Dollar payments are settled through correspondent banks in [[wp:Almaty]], [[wp:Istanbul]] and [[wp:Dubai]]. The authority's registration certificates are used by these banks as part of their checks on Iradi transactions.[2] ## Criticism The authority has not published audited accounts since 2008, and opposition deputies have repeatedly asked for its statements to be laid before the *Mejlis*. [[Kamran Bekzatov]] of NurGaz has criticized delays in the release of export proceeds and has argued that the authority gives the ISEZ administration leverage over private companies.[3] During the [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]], ISEZ officials pointed to the escrow system as evidence that export revenues remained secure. Opposition outlets asked who had authorized disbursements in the Governor's absence, and the Department of Public Information said that the Lieutenant Governor acts for the Governor under the Elective Governor Acts.[4] ## References

Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine

The **Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine** (IARMC; Iradi: *Irad surma jana seyrek metaldar kombinaty*) is a mining and metallurgical holding company based in [[Talas]]. It controls the antimony industry of Irad through its two main subsidiaries, the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] (SBAW), which mines and concentrates ore, and the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]], which produces antimony metal and antimony trioxide. Both are in the Sary-Bulak District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). The combine was formed in 1994, when the territorial government privatized the Soviet antimony industry, and it is the second-largest company in the ISEZ after [[NurGaz]]. Its headquarters are on Metallurgy Avenue in Talas.[1] ## History In the Soviet period the [[Sary-Bulak]] mine, opened in 1961, and the Chatkal smelter, commissioned in 1964, were run as a single enterprise, the Iradi Antimony Combine, under the USSR Ministry of Non-Ferrous Metallurgy. The [[1971 Antimony Expansion Directive]] financed new shafts and furnaces, and by the 1980s the combine was one of the main antimony producers in the [[wp:Soviet Union]].[2] [[Mikhail Chernov]] directed metallurgical production at Chatkal in the 1980s. After the loss of Soviet orders in 1992, the territorial government split the combine in 1994 into two joint-stock companies, SBAW and the Chatkal complex. It placed controlling stakes in both in a new holding company, the IARMC, and sold the holding company's shares at auction. The privatization was criticized at the time for its low price and for the participation of territorial officials' associates, but it was not reversed.[2] The combine found new buyers in China in the late 1990s, and production rose through the 2000s apart from an interruption during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007. ## Ownership and management The combine is a closed joint-stock company, and its shareholder register is not public. According to the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad, the ISEZ government has held a minority stake since 2009 that gives it a veto over major transactions. The remaining shares are held through holding companies whose owners have not been disclosed. Opposition deputies have alleged links between these companies and figures in the [[Democratic Party of Irad]], which the combine denies.[1][3] The combine's management board is appointed by its supervisory board, on which the ISEZ Ministry of Natural Resources is represented. ## Operations The combine employs about 4,600 people. Its operations include: - **Mining and concentration:** the Sary-Bulak mine, worked from three shafts and an inclined drift to a depth of about 750 meters, with a flotation plant producing concentrate of about 60% antimony. Smaller satellite mines, including the [[Kemer Antimony Mine]], supply additional ore. - **Smelting:** the Chatkal complex, which converts concentrate into antimony metal ingots and antimony trioxide. - **By-products:** a plant at Chatkal that recovers bismuth, tellurium and other metals from smelter residues (see [[Chatkal Rare Earth Facility]]). - **Rail and logistics:** sidings and a branch line linking the mine and smelter with the Talas railway, from which products travel north through [[wp:Kazakhstan]].[1] The combine reported mine output of about 13,800 metric tons of contained antimony in 2023. About 6,100 metric tons of this was refined at Chatkal, and the rest was exported as concentrate.[4] Most of its sales go to China, where its concentrate supplies smelters. Metal and trioxide are also sold to buyers in [[wp:South Korea]], [[wp:Japan]] and Europe. Export proceeds are paid through the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]]. ## Finances The combine does not publish full audited accounts. Its 2023 annual report gave revenue of about $140 million. Revenue rose in 2024 and 2025, as world prices increased after China introduced export controls on antimony in 2024 (see [[Antimony Mining in Irad]]).[4] The combine pays the antimony export duty and royalties to the ISEZ, and is one of its largest taxpayers after NurGaz. ## Environment The combine is responsible for tailings from current production and shares responsibility for Soviet-era waste with the ISEZ government, including the [[Chatkal Tailings Repository]]. It says that it has installed electrostatic precipitators and sulfur dioxide scrubbers at Chatkal since the mid-2010s. Environmental monitors and the [[Chatkal Placer Mining Inspectorate]] have recorded raised antimony and arsenic levels in streams below the workings.[5] ## References

Iradi National Chamber of Mining and Metallurgy

The **Iradi National Chamber of Mining and Metallurgy** (Iradi: *Irad uluttuk too-ken jana metallurgiya palatasy*) is the trade association of the mining, metallurgical and geological services industries in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It was founded in 1996 under the territorial statutes on commercial associations and is based at Miners' Hall in central [[Talas]], a Soviet-era building that formerly housed the republican miners' trade union. In 2023 it had 42 member organizations, ranging from the antimony producers to coal mines, quarries, engineering consultancies and equipment suppliers.[1] ## History The chamber was set up in 1996 by the newly privatized antimony companies and a group of geological survey firms, while the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad|Territorial Legislature]] was drafting regulations under the 1995 Hydrocarbon and Mining Code. Its early work concentrated on royalty rates and on the terms of mining concessions. After 2007 it continued under the ISEZ administration. Its membership is confined to companies operating in the ISEZ, since no industrial mining takes place in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].[2] ## Membership Members include: - the [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]] and its subsidiaries, the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] and the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]]; - coal mines around [[Tash-Kömür]] in the Lower Naryn District, which supply power stations and households; - limestone, gypsum and building-stone quarries and cement producers in the Talas and Chu valleys; - geological survey and engineering consultancies, several of them joint ventures with foreign firms; - equipment makers and suppliers, including [[Nurzhanmash]].[1] The chamber is governed by a council elected by the members at an annual congress. Voting is weighted by the size of each member's contributions, which gives the antimony companies the largest influence. ## Activities #### Policy and legislation The chamber represents the industry in dealings with the ISEZ Ministry of Natural Resources and with committees of the *[[Mejlis]]*. It has lobbied for stable royalty rates, longer concession terms and faster refunds of export proceeds held in escrow by the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]]. It has also commented on draft environmental, mine-safety and labor regulations.[2] It has called for exploration of the gold, tungsten and rare-earth deposits of the tribal mountains, which are closed by the clan assemblies' moratorium on open-pit mining. The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] has rejected these proposals, and the chamber has no dealings with the tribal authorities.[3] #### Training and standards With the Faculty of Geology of [[Talas State University]] and the [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]], the chamber funds scholarships and apprenticeships for mining engineers, surveyors and mine-safety inspectors. It publishes voluntary codes on tailings management and mine rescue, and works with the [[Chatkal Placer Mining Inspectorate]] on monitoring standards. Its members' rescue teams train together at the [[Chatkal Mountain Rescue Base]].[1] #### International contacts Because Irad's status is unresolved, the chamber cannot join most international industry federations. It promotes the ISEZ mining sector at investment conferences in [[wp:Almaty]], [[wp:Dubai]] and [[wp:London]], and since 2024 it has sought buyers for Iradi antimony outside China.[2] ## Criticism Environmental groups and some opposition deputies describe the chamber as dominated by the antimony industry, and they say that its voluntary codes are a substitute for stricter regulation. The chamber says that it supports enforcement of the existing environmental law.[3] ## References

  2. ^ Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad (2024). Mining Concessions, Infrastructure and Trade Directory. Talas.

{{Infobox company | name = Iradi Petroleum Transit Consortium | native_name = *Irad munay tranzit konsortsiumu* (IPTC) | type = Joint-stock company | industry = Oil pipeline transport | founded = 1998, [[Talas]] | founder = [[NurGaz]] and foreign partners | key_people = [[Emil Bekzatov]] (Chairman) | services = Ownership and operation of the [[Northern Export Feeder]] | employees = 300 | owner = [[NurGaz]] (51%); foreign minority shareholders (49%) | parent = [[NurGaz]] }} The **Iradi Petroleum Transit Consortium** (IPTC; Iradi: *Irad munay tranzit konsortsiumu*) is the company that owns and operates the [[Northern Export Feeder]], the 85-kilometer pipeline that carries Iradi crude oil from [[Nurzhan]] into the network of the Kazakh pipeline operator [[wp:KazTransOil]] near [[wp:Shymkent]]. It was formed in 1998, during the US territorial administration, by [[NurGaz]], which holds 51 percent, and foreign partners. The feeder opened in 2000, replacing the rail shipments to Shymkent on which Iradi oil exports had depended since the early 1990s. It is the only export pipeline for Iradi crude, and most of Irad's oil exports pass through it.[1][2] ## Background Under the [[wp:Soviet Union]], oil from the lower Chu basin was refined at Kobozev or sent by rail to refineries elsewhere in [[wp:Central Asia]]. After 1992 the territorial government and NurGaz sent surplus crude west to the refinery at Shymkent in [[wp:Kazakhstan]] in rail tank cars. Rail transport was costly and subject to delays at the border. As output recovered from its 1996 low of about 48,000 barrels per day (bpd), NurGaz sought a pipeline connection to the Kazakh trunk system.[3] ## History IPTC was registered in [[Talas]] in 1998 as a joint-stock company. NurGaz contributed its tank farm and rights of way, and the foreign shareholders provided most of the construction finance. The feeder was built in 1999–2000 and began commercial operation in November 2000, after which crude exports by rail largely ended.[2] Its original capacity was about 65,000 bpd. Because NurGaz's reported output continued to rise, IPTC added a third pumping station and a drag-reducing agent injection system in 2011–2012, which raised capacity to about 100,000 bpd.[1] During the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007, forces loyal to [[Erlan Toktarov]] concentrated on holding Nurzhan, the oil fields and the pipeline. Throughput fell during the fighting, but the line was not seriously damaged.[4] ## The Northern Export Feeder The feeder is built of 530-millimeter (20-inch) steel pipe, buried and insulated because the waxy crude of the Chu fields thickens in winter. It runs northeast from the NurGaz tank farm outside Nurzhan across the lower Chu plain to the Kazakh border. There it enters a metering station, from which the crude passes into the KazTransOil system to be refined at Shymkent or shipped north toward Russia.[2] The line has a head pumping station at the tank farm and two intermediate stations. It is monitored from a control room in Nurzhan through a supervisory control and data acquisition ([[wp:SCADA]]) system, with communications provided by [[Attelkom]]. Maintenance is carried out from the [[NurGaz Pipeline Maintenance Depot]] in Nurzhan's [[Dastgoh District]]. The feeder does not connect directly with the [[wp:Caspian Pipeline Consortium]], whose system begins far to the west. Irad has no southern export pipeline.[2] ## Throughput IPTC reported average throughput of about 86,000 bpd in 2023. This is consistent with NurGaz's reported output of about 120,000 bpd, less the roughly 31,000 bpd refined at the [[Nurzhan Oil Refinery]].[1] Independent analysts who work from KazTransOil intake records and observations of gas flaring estimate deliveries at about 55,000–70,000 bpd. This corresponds to their lower estimates of national production, 85,000–100,000 bpd. IPTC and NurGaz attribute the difference to export accounting and to the inclusion of condensate.[3] ## Ownership and governance NurGaz holds 51 percent of IPTC. The remaining 49 percent is held by foreign minority shareholders, whom the company does not name in its public statements. Business directories list a Cyprus-registered investment company and [[Talasbank]] among them.[5] The board is chaired by [[Emil Bekzatov]], executive vice president of NurGaz and son of its president, [[Kamran Bekzatov]]. The company employs about 300 people. IPTC earns a transit tariff on each barrel shipped, paid by NurGaz and the other shippers. Export proceeds and royalties are handled through escrow accounts supervised by the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]].[5] ## Transit relations with Kazakhstan Kazakhstan does not recognize the ISEZ. Deliveries into the Kazakh system are made under commercial contracts between IPTC and the Kazakh side, and the border crossing of the line is covered by the 2008 [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]].[4] The arrangement has generally worked without interruption. During disputes over water releases from the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]], however, Kazakh authorities have tightened pipeline scheduling and customs clearance, and the ISEZ has responded by trimming electricity exports. Analysts regard these episodes as limited and carefully managed, since both sides depend on the trade.[4] ## References

  2. ^ KazTransOil (2023). Annual Report: Southern Network Throughput and Third-Party Transit. Astana, pp. 34–42.
  3. ^ Central Asian Geopolitical Review (2022). 'Counting Barrels: Iradi Oil Output and the Northern Export Feeder.' Vol. 18, pp. 101–122.
  4. ^ Eurasian Political Quarterly (2020). 'Pipelines, Water and Recognition: Irad's Northern Transit.' Vol. 27, No. 2, pp. 64–88.

{{Infobox company | name = Iradiya | native_name = Irad Air Services; *Iradiya aba joldoru* | type = Closed joint-stock company | industry = Aviation | founded = 1997 | founder = Talas investors and former [[wp:Aeroflot]] pilots and engineers | hq = Civil hangars at [[Talas Air Base]], [[Talas]] | key_people = Daniyar Usenov (General director) | services = Passenger charters, air cargo, subsidized Talas–[[Tash-Kömür]] service, government, medical and contract flights | employees = 420 }} **Iradiya** (legally **Irad Air Services**; Iradi: *Iradiya aba joldoru*) is a charter and air-cargo airline based in [[Talas]]. It was founded in 1997, during the US territorial administration, and operates from civil hangars beside [[Talas Air Base]], Irad's main airfield. It flies passenger charters to neighboring countries and the Middle East, a subsidized domestic service between Talas and [[Tash-Kömür]], cargo flights, and government, medical and contract flights. ISEZ officials and state media sometimes call it the national airline. It has no scheduled international routes, however, and Irad, whose sovereignty is unresolved, has no designated flag carrier.[1][2] ## History #### Founding and the territorial period The company was founded in 1997 by a group of Talas investors and former [[wp:Aeroflot]] pilots and engineers of the Soviet-era Iradi civil aviation directorate, with an American aviation services firm as a minority partner. Its first aircraft were two [[wp:Antonov An-26]] freighters and a [[wp:Let L-410 Turbolet|Let L-410]] commuter aircraft, used to carry contractors, spare parts and mail between Talas and [[wp:Almaty]]. Talas Air Base had been enlarged by US military engineers between 1993 and 1998, and the territorial government leased civil aprons and a hangar on its southern side to the new company.[2] As a carrier based in a US territory, Iradiya operated under the oversight of the [[wp:Federal Aviation Administration|US Federal Aviation Administration]]. Business grew after 2001, when the [[2001 Basing Rights Agreement]] made Talas a staging area for [[wp:Operation Enduring Freedom]]. Iradiya flew passengers and cargo for civilian contractors working at the base, and in 2003 it leased its first Western turboprops.[2] #### Since 2006 The end of the territorial administration in December 2006 also ended the company's US certification. In the spring of 2007, during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], Iradiya flew foreign workers and their families out of Talas to Almaty while the [[Popular Front of Irad]] besieged the city. After the war it was certified by the newly formed ISEZ Civil Aviation Directorate.[3] From 2009 the company replaced its Soviet-built passenger aircraft with leased ATR 72 turboprops. That year it began a government-subsidized service to Tash-Kömür, the only alternative to the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] when winter storms close the road. It added an [[wp:Embraer E-Jet family|Embraer E190]] regional jet in 2014 for longer charters. [[wp:Uzbekistan]] withheld landing permits for several weeks during the [[2018 Border Demarcation Clashes]]. Demand fell again in 2020, when charter flights were suspended for several months during the [[wp:COVID-19]] pandemic.[1] ## Operations #### Passenger charters Iradiya flies charters to Almaty, [[wp:Tashkent]], [[wp:Dubai]] and [[wp:Istanbul]], and seasonal holiday flights to resorts in [[wp:Turkey]]. Each flight requires landing and overflight permits from the countries concerned. None of the neighboring states recognizes the ISEZ, so permits are issued case by case, and the airline cannot sell scheduled services on international routes.[3] Most of its regional passengers are business travelers, oil and mining engineers, aid workers and families visiting relatives abroad. #### Domestic service The Talas–Tash-Kömür route, flown three times a week with ATR 72s and up to daily in winter, is subsidized by the ISEZ government. Tash-Kömür has a Soviet-era airstrip lengthened to about 1,900 meters in 2009. There is no scheduled service to [[Nurzhan]], which has no passenger airport and lies within a few hours' drive of Talas.[1] #### Cargo Cargo flights carry spare parts for the oil and mining industries, medicines, veterinary vaccines and express freight, much of it handled through the bonded terminal of the [[Talas Airport Logistics Hub]]. The airline also carries regional horse consignments for the [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]]; long-haul horse shipments use chartered foreign freighters.[4] #### Government and contract flights The ISEZ government charters the company's business jet for official travel and for foreign delegations. Iradiya holds a contract with the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] for observer rotations between Talas and the mission's sector headquarters at Tash-Kömür. Its [[wp:de Havilland Canada DHC-6 Twin Otter|Twin Otters]] fly medical evacuations and deliveries to short mountain airstrips, including some on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], where flights require the consent of clan councils and are coordinated through UNMI.[3] The strips it uses include the Soviet-built [[Kerben Airstrip|Kerben]] and [[Kazarman Airstrip|Kazarman]] strips on the tribal side, the [[Toktogul Airstrip]] in the ISEZ and the [[Boz-Korgon Airstrip]], which serves the government compound. ## Fleet According to the company, its fleet in 2024 consisted of eight aircraft: - two ATR 72-500 turboprops in passenger configuration; - one ATR 72-500 converted to a freighter; - one Embraer E190 regional jet; - one Antonov An-26 freighter; - two de Havilland Canada DHC-6 Twin Otters, used on short and unpaved strips; - one Bombardier Challenger 605 business jet.[1] Irad is not a member of the [[wp:International Civil Aviation Organization]] and has no aircraft nationality mark of its own. During the territorial period Iradiya's aircraft were on the US civil register. Since 2007 its leased aircraft have been registered in [[wp:Bermuda]] by their owners.[3] ## Corporate affairs Irad Air Services is a closed joint-stock company, and its shareholders are not published. Its general director is Daniyar Usenov. The company employed about 420 people in 2023.[4] Line maintenance is done in its hangars at Talas, and heavy maintenance and engine overhauls are contracted to facilities in Almaty. Jet fuel comes from the refinery of [[NurGaz]] by the pipeline that supplies the air base. ## Incidents In January 2012 an Iradiya An-26 freighter overran the runway at Tash-Kömür while landing in snow. The crew was unhurt, and the aircraft was repaired. The ISEZ Civil Aviation Directorate states that the airline has had no fatal accidents.[3] ## References

  4. ^ Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad (2023). Commercial Directory of Transport and Logistics Companies. Talas.

The **Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex** (Iradi: *Chatkal khimiyalyk-metallurgiyalyk kombinaty*) is an antimony smelter and chemical plant in the Sary-Bulak District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It lies at about 1,600 meters in the gorge of the [[Urmaral River|Urmaral]], the next valley west of the [[Sary-Bulak Gorge]], in the [[Talas Alatau]] foothills about 30 kilometers south-west of [[Talas]], and takes its name from the nearby [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal range]]. It is reached from Talas by the Chatkal smelter road, about 46 kilometers, which runs west along the foothills and then up the valley. It processes concentrate from the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] into antimony metal and antimony trioxide. It was commissioned in 1964 and has been a subsidiary of the [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]] since the privatization of 1994. With about 2,200 employees, it is one of the largest industrial employers in the ISEZ outside [[Nurzhan]].[1] ## History The smelter was built in 1961–1964 to process ore from the [[Sary-Bulak]] mine, which had opened in 1961, and was run with the mine as the Iradi Antimony Combine under the USSR Ministry of Non-Ferrous Metallurgy. Under the [[1971 Antimony Expansion Directive]], new roasting furnaces and a trioxide shop were added, and smelting capacity was increased about fourfold by the end of the 1970s.[2] [[Mikhail Chernov]] directed metallurgical production in the 1980s, and the chemist [[Svetlana Kozlova]] developed the plant's methods for refining bismuth from smelter residues. Production stopped for most of 1992, during the [[First Iradi Civil War]], and resumed at a reduced level under the territorial administration. In 1994 the complex was privatized as a joint-stock company controlled by the newly formed combine. It was shut again for several months during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007, when rail links were cut.[1] ## Plant and processes The complex covers about 80 hectares and is linked to the Sary-Bulak mine and the Talas railway by a siding of about 6 kilometers, which leaves the Sary-Bulak spur in the Urmaral gorge, where the valley to Sary-Bulak branches off, and runs up the gorge floor to the [[Chatkal Antimony Processing Mill|processing mill]]; the smelter stands above the mill. Its main stages are: - **Volatilization roasting**, in which sulfide concentrate is heated in air so that the antimony escapes as trioxide fume. The fume is collected in bag filters as crude oxide. - **Reduction smelting** of the crude oxide with coke in reverberatory furnaces. The resulting crude metal is fire-refined with alkaline fluxes to remove arsenic and iron, and cast into ingots of about 99.65% antimony. - **Trioxide production**, in which refined metal is re-volatilized under controlled conditions to make high-purity antimony trioxide, the form used in flame retardants. - **By-product recovery**, in which residues and flue dust go to an adjoining plant that recovers bismuth, tellurium and other metals (see [[Chatkal Rare Earth Facility]]).[1] In 2023 the complex produced about 3,900 metric tons of antimony metal and about 2,600 metric tons of antimony trioxide, according to the combine.[3] Products are packed in steel drums and bulk bags. They travel by rail to the Talas railhead or by truck with [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]], and then north through [[wp:Kazakhstan]], mainly to China but also to buyers in [[wp:South Korea]], [[wp:Japan]] and Europe. ## Environment Antimony smelting releases sulfur dioxide and dust containing antimony and arsenic. Residents of villages near the complex have long complained of smoke and of damage to crops and orchards. A 2018 survey by the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] found sulfur dioxide levels above international guidelines in two nearby villages in winter.[4] The company says that since 2016 it has installed sulfur dioxide scrubbers, designed under its chief engineer [[Artem Kozlov]], and electrostatic precipitators, and that emissions now meet ISEZ standards. Slag and residues are stored on site. Older tailings from Soviet processing are held in the [[Chatkal Tailings Repository]], which is inspected by the [[Chatkal Placer Mining Inspectorate]].[4] ## Works settlement A works settlement of about 6,000 people grew up beside the plant in the 1960s. It has company housing, a polyclinic, schools and a technical lyceum that trains metallurgical technicians. Many of the older residents are Russian-speaking specialists who came from other Soviet republics. The settlement depends almost entirely on the plant, and its population has fallen since the 1980s as younger residents have moved to Talas.[2] ## References
