**Nurzhan Agro-Industrial** (NAI; Iradi: *Nurzhan agro-önör jay kombinaty*) is an agribusiness company in [[Nurzhan]] that specializes in grain storage and trading, animal-feed milling, silage distribution and seed supply in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It was formed in 2008–2009 from privatized state grain and feed enterprises of the lower [[Chu River Basin]], and it supplies most of the compound feed used by the commercial feedlots of the ISEZ. Since 2009 it has been headed by [[Bekzat Toktarov]], the fifth son of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]], and it is one of the family businesses that critics cite as evidence of the concentration of economic power in the ISEZ.[1][2] ## History In the Soviet period, grain from the Chu valley collective farms was delivered to a state procurement system that ran elevators and feed mills in Kobozev. These passed to territorial state enterprises after 1992 and were run down during the 1990s. Investment in the beef industry after the [[wp:North American Free Trade Agreement]] came into force in 1994, notably by [[wp:Sukarne]] and [[wp:Conagra Brands|Conagra]] near [[Talas]], increased demand for feed. Most of it was met by imports and by the feedlots' own mills.[2] In 2008 the ISEZ administration auctioned the state grain elevators and feed mills of the Chu District, and they were combined under NAI. Bekzat Toktarov, who had studied agricultural economics at the Tashkent Agrarian Institute, returned to Irad in 2009 to take charge of the company.[1] Opposition deputies and the newspaper *[[Irad Times]]* criticized the auction, saying that other bidders had been excluded. The ISEZ administration said the sale followed the privatization law.[3] In 2011 NAI opened a new compound-feed mill with Swiss-built equipment. ## Facilities NAI's main facilities are in the eastern industrial zone of Nurzhan, beside the railway to [[wp:Kazakhstan]]: - the **Nurzhan Central Grain Terminal**, a Soviet-era concrete elevator of about 120,000 metric tons capacity, modernized with temperature monitoring and new rail-loading equipment; - the **compound-feed mill**, which produces pelleted feed for cattle and sheep and mineral supplements, with a reported capacity of about 240,000 metric tons a year; - a **seed plant** that cleans and treats seed of winter wheat, barley and alfalfa for sale to farmers; - smaller receiving stations along the canals of the [[Chu Irrigation Canal System]].[1] ## Business NAI buys wheat, barley and feed corn from farms in the Chu and Talas valleys, many of them irrigated by the [[Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate]]. It imports grain from Kazakhstan by rail when the local harvest falls short. According to the company, it supplies about 70% of the commercial compound feed sold in the ISEZ, including feed for the feedlots that supply the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]].[1] It also holds import distribution rights for hybrid seed, fertilizer from Kazakhstan and veterinary medicines. NAI is one of the few ISEZ companies with regular trade across the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. It buys barley and alfalfa from the tribal regions, and under a long-standing arrangement it supplies winter feed pellets to the [[Aksay Plateau Pastoral Cooperative]] in part exchange for wool and hides.[2] The company is financed through working-capital loans from [[Talasbank]], and its grain is moved by rail and by the trucks of [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]]. ## Criticism Farmers' groups have complained that NAI's dominance of grain storage allows it to set purchase prices, and economists have pointed to its share of the feed market as an example of family monopolies in the ISEZ. Leaked US intelligence reports cited the family's businesses as evidence of a neopatrimonial system (see [[Political status of Irad]]).[2][3] The company says that it pays market prices and that its investments have reduced Irad's dependence on imported feed. ## References

The **Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute** (Iradi: *Nurzhan politekhnikalyk instituty*; Russian: *Нуржанский политехнический институт*), known until 1993 as the **Kobozev Polytechnic Institute**, is a public technical university in [[Nurzhan]]. It is Irad's leading technical university and specializes in petroleum engineering. It was founded in 1951 as a petroleum institute to train engineers for the oil fields discovered in the lower Chu basin two years earlier. It took its present broad form in 1968, when faculties of civil, mechanical and electrical engineering were added. The institute trains much of the engineering staff of [[NurGaz]] and had about 9,200 students in 2023.[1] ## History #### Soviet period After the [[Nurzhan Oil Discovery (1949)|discovery of oil near Kobozev in 1949]], the USSR Ministry of Higher Education founded the Kobozev Petroleum Institute in 1951 to train drilling, production and refining engineers for the *Iradneft* oil production association. Much of its first teaching staff came from the petroleum institutes of Baku and Grozny, and teaching was in Russian.[2] In 1968, as the city's engineering and metallurgical industries grew, the institute was reorganized as the Kobozev Polytechnic Institute. Faculties of civil engineering, mechanical engineering, and electrical engineering and radio electronics were added to the petroleum faculties. By the 1980s the institute had about 7,000 students and was the main source of engineers for the industries of the Iradi SSR. Many of its graduates of this period belong to the Russian-educated urban generation known as the *Russos*, who filled the technical and managerial posts in the oil refinery, the antimony industry and the railways (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]).[3] #### Territorial period Teaching was suspended from February to October 1992, during the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] and the [[First Iradi Civil War]], in which Kobozev was the seat of the socialist government. In 1993 the institute was renamed after the city under the Toponymic Heritage Statute.[1] During the territorial administration the institute introduced English-language degree programs in petroleum engineering in 1996, with support from American universities funded by territorial education grants. It adopted a credit-hour system modeled on American practice in 1997. Iradi-language teaching was introduced in the general courses. NurGaz began to fund laboratories and scholarships in return for first claim on graduates. Askar Daniyarov, a founder of the [[Mor-Wave]] duo [[tüntolk]], studied radio electronics there in the 1990s.[4] #### Since 2007 Under the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), the institute has been governed by a statute of 2008. Under it the Governor appoints the rector from candidates nominated by the academic council. NurGaz and the Bekzatov Foundation of NurGaz president [[Kamran Bekzatov]] have paid for new laboratory buildings and fund scholarships, and NurGaz remains the institute's largest sponsor and the largest employer of its graduates.[3] Its language policy has been a recurring point of friction. The ISEZ administration has pressed for teaching in Iradi and English, while much of the senior staff still teaches in Russian, a practice defended by Russo members of the Nurzhan city council.[3] ## Organization The institute has six faculties: - **Petroleum and Mining Geology**, including geophysics and reservoir geology; - **Oil and Gas Field Development**, covering drilling and production engineering; - **Chemical Technology and Refining**; - **Mechanical Engineering and Pipeline Transport**; - **Civil and Hydraulic Engineering**; - **Energy, Automation and Radio Electronics**.[1] A military training department prepares reserve officers and trains technical officers for the [[Armed Forces of Irad|State Defense Corps]]. The institute also runs evening and continuing-education courses for NurGaz employees. In 2023 it had about 640 teaching staff. Instruction is in English in the petroleum programs, and in Iradi, Russian or English elsewhere, depending on the course. ## Campus The main building, a neoclassical structure completed in 1956, stands in the central district near Azatlık Prospect. Laboratory blocks built in the 2010s with NurGaz funding house drilling and well-control simulators, a core-analysis laboratory and a pilot refining unit. Students also train at a teaching well site in the NurGaz fields north of the city.[1] ## Research and partnerships Research concentrates on problems of the aging Chu basin fields and the industries around them: - enhanced oil recovery in mature, heavily water-flooded reservoirs; - the transport of waxy crude through insulated pipelines such as the [[Northern Export Feeder]] of the [[Iradi Petroleum Transit Consortium]]; - refinery catalysis and the reduction of emissions in Nurzhan's industrial zone; - earthquake engineering for the seismically active [[wp:Tian Shan]] foothills; - the clean-up of oil-contaminated soil.[4] The institute published a history of the oil fields, *A History of the Chu Basin Oilfields*, in 2014. It cooperates with [[Talas State University]], and with the [[Iradi National Chamber of Mining and Metallurgy]], which funds scholarships for mining engineers. ## Recognition Because Irad's international status is unresolved, recognition of the institute's degrees abroad depends on agreements between institutions and on the practice of employers. Russian and Kazakh oil companies generally accept them, and many graduates work in the oil industries of [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and Russia. The institute is not included in the major international university rankings.[3] ## References

  2. ^ Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute (2014). A History of the Chu Basin Oilfields. Nurzhan.
  3. ^ Eurasian Political Quarterly (2019). 'Engineers of the Russos: Language, Oil and the Nurzhan Polytechnic.' Vol. 26, No. 4, pp. 288–311.
  4. ^ Talas State University Press (2021). Higher Technical Education in Irad, 1951–2020. Talas.

{{Infobox settlement | name = Köhne Diz | native_name = Russian: Кохне Диз (Старый город) | settlement_type = City quarter | subdivision = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | district = Talas | population = 11000 | coordinates = 42.53°N 72.23°E }} The **Old Talas Citadel Quarter** (Iradi: *Köhne Diz*, "old citadel"), also called the Old City, is the historic core of [[Talas]], the *de jure* capital of Irad. It lies about 1 to 1.6 kilometers north-west and north of the central square, on the valley floor south of the [[Talas River]], and consists of three parts. On its western side is a citadel (*[[Diz (Architecture)|diz]]*) built by the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]] in the 1820s on the mound of an older fortress. East of it are dense residential quarters on the site of the medieval town, a mahalla of narrow, crooked lanes (*[[Kucheh (Urban Term)|kucheh]]*) and courtyard houses, entered from the north by the [[Temir-Kapka Gate]] and from the south by the Kalan Darwaza, and on its eastern edge, next to the Kök-Bel road, is the covered market of [[Bazar-i Kalan]]. The garden quarter of [[Shahr-i Kabud]] lies to the north, and the Soviet center of the city to the south-east. A protected zone of about 64 hectares, with about 11,000 residents, was created under a city ordinance of 1997. The quarter is the setting of the annual [[Diz Film Festival]] and the main center of traditional crafts in the capital.[1][2] ## History #### Medieval town Excavations in the quarter since the 1960s have found occupation layers running from about the 6th to the 13th century. Iradi historiography identifies the site with the medieval [[wp:Silk Road]] town known in Arabic sources as [[wp:Taraz]] and in Chinese sources as Daluosi, near which the [[Battle of Talas]] was fought in 751.[2] Under the Samanids and the [[wp:Kara-Khanid Khanate|Kara-Khanids]] the town had a citadel, a walled inner town (*shahristan*) and suburbs.[3] Archaeologists have uncovered the foundations of an 11th-century minaret and a Christian cemetery with gravestones inscribed in [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] script, evidence of the town's mixed Muslim and Christian population. Coins struck from silver mined at [[Shelji]], in the upper valley, are common finds.[2] The town declined after the Mongol conquest of 1220 and the wars of the 14th century, and by the 16th century it had shrunk to a small settlement around the old mound. #### Kokand fortress Kokand's ties with the Iradi Christians of the region go back to the accord of 1727, remembered as the [[Treaty of Talas (1727)]], under which Khan Abd al-Rahim Biy granted them religious tolerance, but the khanate's authority reached the Talas valley itself only under Alim and Umar (1798–1822).[2] In the 1820s, when the khanate strengthened its northern strongholds, it built a fortress of mud and fired brick on the mound to guard the trade routes of the valley, and a bazaar and residential quarters grew up again on the medieval town site. #### Russian and Soviet periods Russian troops occupied the Talas valley in the 1860s, and the citadel became a Russian garrison post. A new town with a grid of streets was laid out to the east, and it later became the core of the Soviet center of Talas.[4] During the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]] of 1916, Iradi horsemen attacked the garrison before being driven into the mountains. In the Soviet period the citadel was used as a military depot. The quarter's mosque and church were closed in the 1930s, and in 1936 a section of the citadel's outer wall was demolished to build a boulevard. In 1965 the citadel was handed over to a museum of local history, and archaeologists of the Academy of Sciences of the Iradi SSR excavated parts of the medieval town in the 1960s and 1970s.[2] Many mudbrick houses were damaged by the [[Suusamyr]] earthquake of August 1992. #### Since 1992 The mosque and the church reopened in 1992. In 1997, during the US territorial administration, the Talas city council adopted the Historic Districts Ordinance. It created the protected zone, barred the demolition of listed buildings and limited new construction to two stories. As a US territory, Irad was eligible for grants from the US Historic Preservation Fund, which paid for a survey of the quarter and, between 1999 and 2004, for the restoration of the citadel gate and part of the walls.[1] Since 2007 tourism and redevelopment have increased pressure on the quarter. Heritage groups and the *[[Talas Herald]]* have criticized permits for hotels and commercial buildings on the edges of the protected zone, and the replacement of old houses with concrete buildings inside it. The city government says that new projects comply with the ordinance.[5] Because Irad is not a State Party to the World Heritage Convention, the quarter cannot be nominated for the [[wp:World Heritage Site|World Heritage List]]. ## Layout and landmarks The quarter follows the plan of many Central Asian towns, with a citadel, an inner town and a bazaar. Its main buildings are: - **The citadel (*Köhne Diz*)**, on a mound about 14 meters high. Its walls, with corner towers, enclose the former residence of the Kokand governors, now the city museum, and the courtyards used for festival screenings and concerts. - **The Kalan Darwaza**, the gate of the citadel's southern outer enclosure and the southern entrance to the quarter, a pointed brick arch flanked by towers, rebuilt in the 1820s and restored in 2002 (see [[Darwaza (Architecture)]]). - **Bazar-i Kalan**, the covered central market, rebuilt in the 1950s on the site of the old bazaar, with stalls selling produce, spices, dried fruit, meat, felt rugs and household goods. - **The Coppersmiths' Row** (*Misgaron*), a vaulted 19th-century trading passage beside the market, where metalworkers make and sell copper vessels, tea sets and silver-mounted horse tack. - **The Juma Mosque**, a Friday mosque of the 1890s with a columned wooden porch, which serves the city's Muslim community. - **The Church of St. Yuhanna**, a Syro-Iradi parish church built in 1908, closed in 1937 and reconsecrated in 1992. - **The excavation site** of the medieval minaret and Christian cemetery, protected under a shelter since 2006.[1][2] The residential quarters consist of single-story courtyard houses (*hovli*) of mudbrick and timber, with high blank walls facing the lanes and carved walnut porches (*ayvan*) around inner courtyards watered by small channels (*aryk*). ## Crafts and economy The quarter is the main center in Talas for traditional crafts, many of them practiced by the same families for several generations. Saddlers make wooden saddles with chased silver fittings (see [[Eerchilik (Saddlery)]]), and other workshops produce riding whips (*[[Kamcha (Horsewhip)|kamcha]]*), boots and bridles. Craftsmen also make the three-stringed [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]] from apricot and walnut wood, and dealers sell felt rugs (*[[Shyrdak (Iradi Craft)|shyrdak]]*). The saddler [[Tolonbek Sydykov]], whose saddles have been presented as state gifts, works in the quarter.[5] Teahouses (*chaikhana*), guesthouses and craft shops serve visitors, and tourism has become the main source of income for many households. ## Population The quarter's residents are mainly Iradi, with long-established Uzbek-speaking families in the lanes around the bazaar, a legacy of the merchant community of the Kokand period. Iradi linguists link the Uzbek-derived vocabulary of urban Iradi to this kind of mixed bazaar quarter.[6] Many younger residents have moved to newer districts, and some houses are now let to students and to migrants from the countryside. ## Culture The Diz Film Festival of independent Central Asian cinema is held each year in the citadel courtyards and the squares of the quarter. Folk musicians perform in the citadel and in the teahouses on summer evenings, and the quarter is a starting point for celebrations on Irad Day, 11 March.[5] ## See also - [[Iradi Telegraph Office]] ## References

The **St. Luka Community Health Mission** (Iradi: *Iyık Luka El Darigerlik Missiyasy*) is a Catholic medical charity of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], founded in 1994 and based in [[Talas]]. It runs St. Luka Hospital, a 120-bed general hospital in Talas, the free [[St. Luka Clinic]] in the south of the city, and mobile clinics that travel to herding settlements in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). It is one of the few organizations that works regularly on both sides of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and in many highland valleys its mobile teams are the main source of primary care.[1][2] ## History The mission was set up in 1994 by the Eparchy of Talas, during the collapse of the Soviet-era health system that followed the [[First Iradi Civil War]]. The siege of 1992 had damaged hospitals in Talas, medicines were scarce, and many Russian-speaking doctors had left for Russia.[2] Its first funds came from Catholic relief agencies abroad and from American church donors. According to the mission, it was also among the Christian charities in Irad that received proceeds from the 1993 compilation album [[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|*Swift Hooves*]].[3] St. Luka Hospital opened in 1994 in a former trade-union polyclinic. Its first staff were sisters of the [[Order of St. Janyl the Hermit]], whose communities already ran rural dispensaries, together with volunteer physicians and nurses from Talas and abroad.[3] The first mobile team began visiting summer pastures in the [[Talas Alatau]] in 1996, and a maternity ward opened in 2001. During the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007, while the [[Popular Front of Irad]] was besieging Talas from April to June, the hospital treated wounded civilians and fighters from all sides.[4] After the ceasefire, the mission's mobile teams were among the first civilian services to be allowed across the new demarcation line. Since 2008 the mission has belonged to the humanitarian coordination forum chaired by the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI).[5] ## Services - **St. Luka Hospital**, Talas: general medicine, surgery, obstetrics and pediatrics, with an outpatient department. Patients who can afford it pay modest fees, and the poor are treated free of charge. - **St. Luka Clinic**: a free outpatient and dental clinic in southern Talas for low-income residents. - **Mountain mobile clinics**: teams in four-wheel-drive vehicles and, on the higher pastures, with pack horses. They carry portable ultrasound scanners, solar-powered vaccine refrigerators and basic surgical kits, and visit herding families in their summer yurts (*boz üy*) in the Talas Alatau, on the [[Aksay Plateau]] and in the Chatkal valleys. - **Public health programs**: childhood immunization, antenatal care, tuberculosis screening and child nutrition. - **Harm reduction**: a needle exchange and a methadone maintenance program in [[Tash-Kömür]] and naloxone distribution in [[Nurzhan]], the only substantial programs of their kind in Irad (see [[Drug use in Irad]]). The mission reported about 46,000 outpatient consultations in 2023, about two-fifths of them in the ATR.[1] ## Work in the tribal regions To cross the Qara-Chik line, the mobile teams need tribal travel permits from the clan councils as well as clearance at ISEZ checkpoints. Seasonal corridors for the teams, for vaccines and for medical supplies are negotiated each spring through the UNMI coordination forum.[5] The mission treats patients of all faiths, including Kyrgyz and Kazakh Muslim herders, and in the tribal regions it works through local health posts and village elders. According to its annual reports, maternal and infant health indicators in the highland valleys remain well below those of the ISEZ, and many settlements have no year-round road access.[1] Both administrations allow the mission to work but have at times restricted it. Tribal elders have objected to ISEZ checkpoint delays affecting its convoys, while ISEZ officials have questioned whether supplies taken across the line reach their intended recipients. The mission says it does not take sides and reports only on health needs.[5] ## Organization and funding The mission is governed by a board appointed by the Bishop of Talas and employs about 380 staff, most of them Iradi doctors, nurses and drivers. It is funded by church collections, Catholic and [[wp:Protestantism|Protestant]] agencies abroad, donations from [[Iradi Americans]] and hospital fees. It has no regular funding from the ISEZ government, although ISEZ health authorities count its mobile teams in their coverage figures for the rural districts.[1][2] The hospital refers complex surgical and obstetric cases to the [[Talas Regional Hospital Medical Complex]], with which it also runs a joint tuberculosis screening program. ## References

The **Sukarne Irad Complex** is a cattle feedlot, beef-processing plant and cold store in the western industrial corridor of [[Talas]], operated by the Mexican meat company [[wp:Sukarne|SuKarne]]. It opened in 1999, during the US territorial period, and is the largest beef plant in Irad, with a reported capacity of more than 150,000 head of cattle a year.{{Citation needed|date=June 2026}} At its opening the company described it as the largest modern feedlot and packing complex in [[wp:Eurasia]].[1][2] The plant's arrival brought Mexican managers, technicians and workers to Talas, and the Mexican community of more than 10,000 people in and around the city grew from it.[3] ## History Irad's status as a US territory from 1992 gave its exports duty-free access to the US market, and after the [[wp:North American Free Trade Agreement]] took effect in 1994, Mexican as well as American agribusiness capital began to look at the territory. Irad was not a party to NAFTA, but Iradi commentators often call the investment of this period "NAFTA-era".[1] The [[1998 Talas Agribusiness Accord]] and the creation of the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]] that year provided land, rail access and customs arrangements for foreign meatpackers. SuKarne built the complex in 1998–99 west of the city, on the land of a former Soviet state fattening complex founded during the [[Virgin Lands Campaign in Irad|Virgin Lands campaign]], whose maize and alfalfa base and herdsmen were among the reasons for the choice of site, and slaughtering began in 1999. [[wp:Conagra Brands|Conagra]] opened its own plant nearby (see [[Conagra Talas Beef Facility]]).[2] Operations were interrupted during the fighting around Talas in 2007, when road links to the city were cut, and resumed later that year after the ceasefire.[4] ## Facilities The complex covers about 90 hectares. Its main parts are: - the feedlot (see [[Sukarne Feedlot Complex]]), with a standing capacity of about 50,000 head, where cattle are finished on rations of corn silage, barley and protein meal, part of which is supplied by [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]]; - the processing plant, with slaughter, chilling and boning halls that produce chilled and frozen boxed beef, and a separate halal-certified line for exports to Muslim-majority markets; - an ammonia-refrigerated cold store with space for about 8,000 metric tons of boxed beef; - an accredited testing laboratory (see [[Sukarne Quality Control Labs]]).[2] The complex handles only cattle. A 1996 act of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] banned the commercial slaughter of horses and the sale of horsemeat, in line with the strong Iradi aversion to eating horses (see [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]]).[5][6] ## Cattle supply and markets Feeder cattle come from farms in the Talas and Chu valleys and from pastoralists in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], who bring animals across the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] at designated crossing corridors, often through the [[Talas Central Cattle Mart]]. Payments are cleared through [[Talasbank]].[1] The plant sells boxed beef in Irad and exports it to [[wp:Kazakhstan]], Russia and the Middle East. Export proceeds are paid into escrow accounts audited by the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]].[2] ## Workforce and the Mexican community The complex employs about 1,800 people, most of them [[Iradis]].[2] The first Mexican employees were managers, veterinarians and maintenance engineers. They were followed by their families and by Mexican workers recruited for the plant and for other agribusinesses in the export zone. The community (see [[Mexicans in Irad]]) is centered in [[Semiz]], a district of the city's western corridor that grew from the Soviet settlement of Otkormochny beside the old fattening complex; residents call it *la Colonia* and other Iradis often *Meksikanka*, where there are Mexican shops and restaurants, a Spanish-language Mass on Sundays and a Day of the Dead observance each November. Many families have now lived in Talas for two generations, and marriages between Mexicans and Iradis are common.[3] ## References

The **Council of Hierarchs of the Syro-Iradi Church** (Iradi: *Iradi Yepiskopter Kengeshi*; Latin: *Consilium Hierarcharum Ecclesiae Syro-Iradiensis*), commonly called **the Synod** (*Sinod*), is the assembly of the bishops of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. It is presided over by the Metropolitan Archbishop of [[Iyık Janyl]], since 2012 [[Mar Ephrem]], and meets twice a year in the chapter house beside the [[Church of St. Janyl]]. The council proposes candidates for bishop to the Pope, approves liturgical texts, oversees the training of clergy and issues joint pastoral letters, which are among the church's main statements on public affairs in Irad.[1][2] ## Canonical status The Syro-Iradi Church is an Eastern Catholic church *sui iuris* in communion with Rome and is governed by the [[wp:Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches|Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches]]. In the code's terms it is a metropolitan church, headed by a metropolitan archbishop, whose bishops form a council of hierarchs rather than the synod of a patriarchal or major archiepiscopal church. Its official name has been the Council of Hierarchs since the code took effect in 1991; earlier documents call it the Episcopal Synod, and clergy and faithful still call it "the Synod", after the synods of the Church of the East. Like other councils of hierarchs, it can make laws for the church, which must be communicated to the [[wp:Holy See]] before they take effect. It does not elect bishops itself but proposes lists of at least three candidates (*terna*), from which the Pope appoints.[1] ## History Church historians trace the council's tradition to the medieval assemblies of the East Syriac clergy of the region, such as the [[Nestorian Synod of Navekat (1180)]]. Its modern form dates from the union with Rome in 1931 under the bull *Orientalis Stella*, negotiated by Bishop [[Mar Timotheos Alimbekov]].[2] Soviet authorities closed the churches of Iyık Janyl, and senior clergy were arrested and executed in [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges|the purges of 1937]]. For the rest of the Soviet period the bishops could not meet openly, and according to church accounts the surviving clergy consulted in secret.[2] The synod met openly in 1993, after the territorial administration guaranteed freedom of religion and the protection of church property under the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]]. In its first decade it approved vernacular liturgical texts in Latin-script Iradi, following Father [[Luka Ayyubov]]'s 1994 translation of the [[wp:New Testament]]. It also pressed the territorial government for the return of church buildings confiscated in the Soviet period, and supported the US nomination of the Church of St. Janyl, inscribed as a [[wp:World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] in 2004.[2] In April 2007, during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], the synod issued a pastoral letter calling for a ceasefire and for the return of communal pastures that had been privatized. Since then the church has taken part in civic mediation between the communities.[3] Mar Ephrem became archbishop in 2012. ## Membership and procedure The voting members are the archbishop of the Archeparchy of Iyık Janyl and the bishops of the suffragan eparchies of [[Talas]], [[Nurzhan]] and the highland parishes of the Chatkal basin, together with any auxiliary bishops. The rector of the [[Cathedral Seminary of Iyık Janyl|St. Ephrem Major Seminary]] and the superior of the [[Order of St. Janyl the Hermit]] attend as advisers without a vote.[1] The spring session is held after Easter, and the autumn session in September, after the pilgrimage season of the [[Feast of St. Janyl]] on 24 August. Each session ends with a published communiqué. The Chatkal eparchy includes parishes on both sides of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], so the council is one of the few bodies whose members work regularly in both the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. ## Functions - **Appointment of bishops.** The synod draws up the *terna* for vacant sees and sends it to the Dicastery for the [[wp:Dicastery for the Eastern Churches|Eastern Churches in Rome]]. - **Liturgy.** It regulates the celebration of the [[wp:Liturgy of Addai and Mari|East Syriac Liturgy of Addai and Mari]] in Iradi and [[wp:Syriac language|Classical Syriac]] (see [[East Syriac Rites of Iyık Janyl]]), and approves translations and liturgical books. - **Clergy training.** It sets the curriculum of the St. Ephrem Major Seminary in Iyık Janyl. - **Pastoral letters.** Its joint letters have addressed communal pasture rights, the environmental effects of mining, emigration, and marriage and family life, including the 2014 letter *On the Free Consent of Spouses*, which condemned bride kidnapping (see [[Marriage in Irad]]).[2] ## Relations with the state Relations with the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] administration have been strained at times over school curricula and the taxation of church property. In these disputes the council has cited the guarantees of religious freedom dating from the territorial period.[3] In October 2023 it appealed for restraint by both the police and protesters during the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas|student protests in Talas]].[4] Its autumn communiqué of 2024, issued after Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] withdrew from public view, called for "constitutional order and truthful public information". DPI officials did not comment publicly.[5] A 2021 survey by the Department of Sociology at [[Talas State University]] found the church to be the most trusted public institution among respondents in the ISEZ.[6] ## References

The **Talas Basin Agricultural Directorate** (Iradi: *Talas Öröönü Ayyl Charba Bashkarmasy*) is the agency of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) responsible for farming and irrigation in the valley of the [[Talas River]]. It answers to the ISEZ Ministry of Agriculture and Water Resources and covers Talas District, [[Kara-Buura]] District and the farmland within the city of [[Talas]]. Its main tasks are maintaining irrigation canals and scheduling water deliveries, running agricultural extension services, distributing subsidized seed and fertilizer, and collecting crop statistics. Its headquarters are in Talas, and it has extension offices in the district centers.[1] ## History In the Soviet period, farming in the Talas valley was organized in collective and state farms under the regional agricultural administration. Irrigation was expanded after the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]], when the river's flow was divided equally between the Iradi SSR and the [[wp:Kazakh Soviet Socialist Republic|Kazakh SSR]] downstream, a rule both sides still cite.[2] After 1992 the collective farms were broken up, and under the territorial land reform of 1994 their land passed to household and family farms and to private companies. The directorate was established in 1995 to take over the irrigation and extension functions of the Soviet administration. In the late 1990s, advisers from American agricultural universities helped it set up an extension service and water users' associations, which collect irrigation fees and maintain the smaller canals.[1] Since 2007 it has operated under the ISEZ administration. ## Irrigation According to the directorate, about 110,000 hectares of the valley are irrigated, through main canals that take water from the Talas and its tributaries and through a dense network of smaller ditches (*aryk*).[1] The directorate maintains the main canals and headworks and agrees seasonal delivery schedules with the water users' associations. It works with the [[Talas River Hydrological Monitoring Service]], whose gauges supply the flow data, and with the [[Talas Municipal Water Authority]], which draws part of the city's supply from the same basin. Several of the rivers that feed the valley rise on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. The directorate therefore depends on informal arrangements with clan councils over headwater use, which are usually settled by the councils and the district authorities directly.[2] The lower valley in Kara-Buura District suffers from waterlogging and soil salinization caused by losses from unlined canals and poor drainage. Since the 2010s the directorate has subsidized laser leveling of fields and drip irrigation for orchards. In dry summers it imposes rotation schedules under which canals are opened to each area in turn.[1] ## Crops and extension The main crops are wheat, barley, sugar beet, potatoes and common beans. Beans have become the valley's best-known export crop and are sold mainly to [[wp:Turkey]].[3] Alfalfa and fodder maize are grown for the feedlots of the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]], and apple and apricot orchards line the foothills. Extension officers run soil-testing clinics and demonstration plots, advise on integrated pest management, and help farm cooperatives meet the sanitary standards required by meatpackers. The directorate also manages reserves of certified seed and fertilizer, which it sells to farmers at subsidized prices.[1] ## Criticism Farmers' associations have criticized the directorate for slow canal repairs and for favoring large commercial farms when water is scarce, and the water users' associations vary widely in how well they are run.[3] Analysts also point out that its budget depends on ISEZ allocations that are not published in detail. ## References

The **Talas Municipal Water Authority** (Iradi: *Talas Shaarlyk Suu Bashkarmasy*) is the public utility that supplies drinking water and runs the sewerage system of [[Talas]]. It serves the city's population of about 1.1 million and parts of the surrounding suburbs, and answers to the city administration, headed by a mayor appointed by the Governor, and to the elected city council. Most of its water is pumped from wellfields in the alluvial fan south of the city. The rest is drawn from the [[Talas River]] and treated at the [[Talas Municipal Water Treatment Works]].[1] ## History Talas received its first piped water supply in the 1930s, from springs and shallow wells in the foothills. The southern wellfields were developed in the 1960s and 1970s as the city grew, and the central sewage treatment plant was built in 1974.[2] During the siege of Talas from April 1992, in the [[First Iradi Civil War]], shelling and power cuts stopped the pumping stations and damaged the main from the southern wellfields. By late May much of the city had no piped water, and residents drew water from irrigation canals (*aryk*) and hand pumps. Supply was restored during the summer of 1992 by city crews working with US military engineers.[3] The authority was set up as a municipal utility in 1995, during the territorial period, taking over from the Soviet-era municipal waterworks. US federal grants and territorial bonds paid for new pumps and meters for commercial users, and the sewage plant was upgraded with biological treatment in the early 2000s.[1] Since 2007 it has operated under the ISEZ municipal administration. In 2016 it installed a supervisory control and data acquisition ([[wp:SCADA]]) system, supplied with [[Attelkom]], to monitor pressure and detect leaks. ## Water supply The groundwater comes from aquifers recharged by snowmelt and glacier-fed streams descending from the [[Talas Alatau]]. The authority operates four wellfields in the alluvial fan, with 64 submersible pumps drawing from depths of 80 to 220 meters. The groundwater is of good quality and needs only chlorination. River water is treated by flocculation, sand filtration and ultraviolet disinfection at the treatment works.[1] Two storage reservoirs on the foothill slopes south of the city feed the network by gravity. The network has about 540 km of mains, much of it Soviet-era steel and cast-iron pipe. The authority estimates that about 40 percent of the water it produces is lost to leaks or not billed.[4] The [[Talas River Hydrological Monitoring Service]] passes river-flow readings to the authority in real time. The authority and the [[Talas Basin Agricultural Directorate]] share the basin's water and coordinate withdrawals in dry summers.[2] ## Sewerage The Talas Central Sewage Treatment Plant, on the western edge of the city, treats about 140,000 cubic meters of wastewater a day and discharges the treated effluent into the Talas River. The hydrological service monitors sewage indicators downstream of the city.[2] Older suburbs and the new housing on the city's edges are not fully connected to the sewers and rely on septic tanks and pit latrines. ## Tariffs and finance Household tariffs are set in [[Iradi som]] by the city council, while commercial and industrial customers are billed in US dollars. Tariffs cover operating costs but not major repairs, which depend on allocations from the ISEZ budget. Proposed increases have been controversial, and the council postponed one in 2019 after public complaints.[4] ## References

The **Talas Regional Hospital Medical Complex** (Iradi: *Talas Ayymdyk Oorukanasy*) is the main referral and teaching hospital of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), on a 15-hectare campus on Hospital Boulevard in [[Talas]]. It opened in 1954 as the regional hospital of the Soviet period and was largely rebuilt during the US territorial administration. With about 650 beds, it provides specialist surgery, cardiology, maternity and pediatric care, trauma care and diagnostic imaging, and is the main clinical training site of the Faculty of Medicine of [[Talas State University]].[1][2] ## History The hospital opened in 1954 as the regional clinical hospital for the Talas valley, in a group of three-story pavilions south-west of the central square. Maternity and cardiology wings were added in the 1970s.[2] It treated many of the wounded from the [[1956 Talas Riots]], and its records are among the sources historians have used to estimate the casualties. During the siege of Talas from April 1992, the hospital kept working under artillery fire. Its staff treated civilian and military casualties with dwindling supplies of anesthetics, blood and fuel for the generators, and the surgical pavilion was hit several times.[3] In the years after the war many Russian-speaking doctors left Irad, and the hospital struggled to keep its specialist departments open. Between 1995 and 2002 the hospital was rebuilt and re-equipped with US federal grants and loans from the territorial government. A new emergency and trauma center opened in 2002. Residency programs modeled on American graduate medical training were introduced, and exchange agreements were signed with medical schools in the United States and [[wp:Turkey]].[2] In 2007, during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], it again took in casualties while the [[Popular Front of Irad]] besieged the city. A cardiovascular wing with cardiac catheterization laboratories opened in 2016.[1] ## Departments and facilities The campus has five main clinical buildings: - an emergency and trauma center with a rooftop helipad, used for medical evacuations from the mountains, including flights arranged through the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] for patients from the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]; - a cardiovascular institute, which performs bypass surgery, angioplasty and pacemaker implantation; - a maternal and child health pavilion with obstetric theaters and a neonatal intensive care unit; - a surgical building with general, orthopedic and neurosurgical departments; - a diagnostic center with CT and MRI scanners and the hospital's pathology laboratory.[1] The [[Talas Blood Services Center]] supplies the hospital's blood bank. [[Talas Municipal Hospital No. 1]] is the city's main general emergency hospital, while the regional hospital takes the more complex cases from across the ISEZ. ## Teaching The hospital is the main teaching hospital of the Talas State University Faculty of Medicine. About 400 medical students, residents and nursing students train there each year. Clinical records and much of the residency teaching are in English, while consultations with older patients are often in Russian or Iradi.[2] ## Access and finance The hospital is funded mainly from the ISEZ budget. Emergency treatment is free, but planned operations and many medicines require co-payments, which patients' groups say deter rural families. Staff shortages are a continuing problem, as many nurses and young doctors emigrate, mostly to the United States.[4] The hospital receives referrals from the [[St. Luka Community Health Mission]], whose mobile clinics transfer complicated obstetric and surgical cases from the tribal regions, and the two run a joint tuberculosis screening program.[1] ## References

{{Infobox company | name = Talasbank | native_name = *Talas Banky* (Bank of Talas) | type = Commercial bank | industry = Banking | predecessor = Talas offices of the Soviet savings and agricultural banks | founded = 1993 (opened September 1993) | hq = Silk Road Financial Tower, [[Talas]] | locations = 28 branches (20 in Talas, 6 in [[Nurzhan]], 2 in [[Iyık Janyl]]) | area_served = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | services = Dual-currency (US dollar and som) banking, export escrow, trade finance, government payrolls, SMS payments | owner = Undisclosed holding companies; ISEZ government (minority stake) }} **Talasbank** (officially the Bank of Talas; Iradi: *Talas Banky*) is the largest commercial bank in Irad, with its headquarters in the Silk Road Financial Tower in central [[Talas]]. It was chartered in 1993 by the Banking and Commercial Currency Act of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]], which made the US dollar legal tender in the territory alongside the new [[Iradi som]]. The bank keeps accounts in both currencies. It holds the escrow accounts into which the proceeds of Irad's main exports are paid under the supervision of the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]], handles most government payrolls and holds the largest share of commercial deposits in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ).[1][2] Because Irad's sovereignty is unrecognized, Talasbank has no direct access to most international payment systems. It settles foreign payments through correspondent banks in [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Istanbul]]. Its ownership has not been fully disclosed since its partial privatization, and its accounts are published only in summary.[2] ## History #### Background In the Soviet period, banking in the Iradi SSR was carried out by the republican offices of the Soviet state bank and the specialized state banks for savings, agriculture and housing. After the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] declared independence in October 1991, the breakdown of the ruble zone and inflation above 1,000 percent wiped out most savings. Banking had largely stopped in Talas by the time of the siege in 1992.[3] #### Foundation and the territorial period (1993–2006) After the [[First Iradi Civil War]], the territorial administration chose to use the US dollar rather than introduce a currency of its own at once. The Banking and Commercial Currency Act of 1993 made the dollar legal tender, authorized the som for small payments and wages, and chartered Talasbank as the territory's main commercial bank.[1] The bank was formed from the Talas offices of the former Soviet savings and agricultural banks, with capital provided by the territorial government. It opened for business in September 1993. In the first months, dollar banknotes were flown in to [[Talas Air Base]].[3] In 1994 the territorial government created the Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority to audit export contracts. Exporters, including the oil company [[NurGaz]], the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] and later the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]], were required to have foreign buyers pay into escrow accounts at Talasbank. The authority deducted royalties and taxes before releasing the balance.[4] During the agribusiness boom of the late 1990s and the expansion of the air base after the [[2001 Basing Rights Agreement]], the bank's business grew with foreign investment, base contracts and payrolls. As a bank in a US territory, it settled dollar payments through correspondent accounts with banks in the United States.[3] The territorial government sold a majority of its shares in auctions in 1999 and 2001 and kept a minority stake. The buyers were Iradi holding companies whose own shareholders were not published.[2] #### Crisis of 2006–2007 After the United States withdrew from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] on 3 December 2006, depositors rushed to withdraw dollars. The bank limited cash withdrawals for three weeks in December.[5] American correspondent banks closed or restricted its accounts in early 2007, citing the territory's uncertain legal status. The bank moved its correspondent business to banks in Almaty and Istanbul, a pattern similar to that of banks in other territories whose status is not recognized.[3] After [[Erlan Toktarov]] proclaimed the ISEZ from [[Nurzhan]] on 25 February 2007, both the cabinet of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] in Talas and the emergency administration in Nurzhan claimed authority over the escrow accounts. The bank's management froze withdrawals from government accounts until the dispute was settled. Supporters later credited the decision with protecting public funds, while DRI ministers said it cut off their government's revenue.[6] The head office closed for several days after the [[Storming of Talas (2007)|storming of Talas]] on 4 June 2007. It reopened under the ISEZ administration after DPI forces took the city that summer. #### Since 2007 Since the ceasefire Talasbank has been the main bank of the ISEZ government. It holds treasury and payroll accounts, takes part in the escrow arrangements for oil, antimony and beef exports, and finances imports from China, [[wp:Turkey]] and [[wp:Kazakhstan]] with letters of credit.[2] Payments made under the revenue-sharing arrangements of the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]] are not reported separately. Herders from the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] who sell livestock and wool to ISEZ buyers are usually paid through the bank.[4] With [[Attelkom]], the bank introduced debit cards and a national card-payment network in the 2000s. In 2012 the two companies launched an SMS-based payment service, used by herders and farmers to pay for feed and veterinary services and to receive transfers without traveling to a branch.[2] #### Dollar shortage (2026) From the spring of 2026 dollar banknotes became scarce in the ISEZ after correspondent banks in Almaty cut their shipments of cash. Under a Bank of Irad notice of 4 May 2026 allowing banks to cap cash withdrawals in dollars, with state contracts exempt, Talasbank has since May limited cash dollar withdrawals and conversions of som into dollars to US$300 a month per customer.[7] Unlicensed money changers at the bazaars of Talas and Nurzhan, who quoted about 9.5 som to the dollar in June, were asking 11 to 12 som by October, against the official rate of 8.40; on 13 October changers at the [[Bazar-i Kalan]] in Talas bought dollars at 11.40 som and sold them at 11.85. Traders and analysts attribute the gap to the cash shortage, to uncertainty over the Governor's absence and the 2027 succession, to the rising cost of remittances and to memories of the 2008 devaluation. The [[Bank of Irad]] says that its reserves fully cover the som, that the official rate is unchanged and that no second reset is planned, and calls the street rate "speculation in a small cash market".[8] In September 2026 Talasbank also stopped card payments for purchases of [[Tulparcoin]], the cryptocurrency launched by [[Jason Ilyasov]]'s Liberty Forum, after the Bank of Irad warned that the coin was not legal tender.[9] ## Operations - **Dual-currency banking.** Deposits and loans are offered in US dollars and in som. Most savings, loans and commercial contracts are in dollars. Som accounts are used mainly for public-sector wages, utility bills and retail payments. - **Escrow and trade finance.** The bank holds the export escrow accounts audited by the Foreign Trade Escrow Authority and provides letters of credit and guarantees for importers. - **Government business.** It handles treasury accounts, payrolls and many payments of the ISEZ government and of the municipal administrations of Talas, Nurzhan and [[Iyık Janyl]]. - **Retail network.** It has 28 branches, 20 in Talas, 6 in Nurzhan (including its Azatlık Prospect branch) and 2 in Iyık Janyl, as well as offices at the main border crossings and mobile banking vans that serve villages in the [[Chu River Basin]].[2] Interbank transfers within the ISEZ are processed through the [[Bank of Irad Clearing House]]. According to the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad, Talasbank holds about 60 percent of commercial deposits in the ISEZ.[2] Smaller commercial banks include [[Ak Bata Bank]] and Chuy Commercial Bank (Iradi: *Chüy Kommertsiyalık Banky*). ## Ownership and criticism The ISEZ government still holds a minority stake, but the ultimate owners of the holding companies that control the bank have not been disclosed. Investigative reports have linked several of these companies to business associates of the ruling Toktarov family. The bank has said that its shareholders meet the disclosure rules in force in the ISEZ.[10] Opposition commentators accuse it of lending on favorable terms to companies linked to the [[Democratic Party of Irad]]. The [[wp:World Bank]] has noted that it has not published full audited accounts since 2008.[3] Business groups, by contrast, credit the bank with keeping the dollar payment system working through the crises of 2006–07 and the uncertainty that followed Toktarov's withdrawal from public view in 2024.[2] ## References

The **Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals** are a series of plans, made since the 1990s, for international pipelines across [[Irad]]. The best known is the Trans-Irad Gas Pipeline proposed by the [[wp:China National Petroleum Corporation]] (CNPC), which would carry natural gas from [[wp:Turkmenistan]] through [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and southern Irad to western China. Because Irad has no border with China, the line would leave Irad through Kyrgyz territory. During the US territorial period, a US-backed oil pipeline south to [[wp:Pakistan]] through Kyrgyz, Tajik and Afghan territory was also studied, but it lost its prospects after 2021. None of the proposals has been built.[1][2] Irad's only export pipeline remains the 85-km [[Northern Export Feeder]], which carries crude oil north into the Kazakh pipeline network near [[wp:Shymkent]]. ## Background Irad is doubly landlocked, and all its hydrocarbon exports depend on transit through neighboring states. Until 2000 crude oil left by rail for Shymkent, and since then it has been piped through the Northern Export Feeder into the network operated by [[wp:KazTransOil]], for refining in [[wp:Kazakhstan]] or onward shipment to Russia.[3] Irad's proven natural gas reserves exceed 400 billion cubic meters but are largely undeveloped. The largest prospect, the [[Muyunkum Natural Gas Field]], lies in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR).[1] Successive governments have looked for a second export route to reduce their dependence on Kazakhstan. ## Southern oil pipeline proposal During the territorial period, a US-backed proposal envisaged a pipeline carrying Iradi crude south to Pakistan. Because Irad does not border [[wp:Tajikistan]] or [[wp:Afghanistan]], the route would have crossed Kyrgyz, Tajik and Afghan territory. Instability in Afghanistan kept the project at the planning stage. After the [[wp:Taliban]] returned to power in 2021 it lost its remaining prospects. [[wp:Chevron Corporation|Chevron]], which had invested heavily in modernizing Irad's oil fields since the territorial period, then scaled back its operations in Irad.[1] ## Trans-Irad Gas Pipeline CNPC's proposal, first discussed publicly in the early 2010s, would link gas fields in Turkmenistan with consumers in western China. In Irad the main partner would be [[NurGaz]]. Feasibility studies have examined two routes through the territory: - a **northern route**, about 480 km long within Irad, entering Irad from Uzbekistan at the head of the Chatkal valley, crossing the tribal Chatkal Highlands and the [[Talas Alatau]] into the upper [[Talas River]] valley, running along its southern side, crossing the mountains by the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] corridor and the [[Fergana Gateway]], and leaving Irad eastward into [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]]; - a **southern route**, entering from the Uzbek part of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] and running east through the Lower Naryn District along the farm belt of the Fergana rim before crossing into Kyrgyzstan. The studies assume a pipe 1,220 mm in diameter carrying up to 30 billion cubic meters of gas a year, with four compressor stations in Irad. The ISEZ has asked for an off-take to supply gas-fired power and heating in [[Talas]] and [[Nurzhan]], where coal is still widely burned.[2] In 2022 Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] received a CNPC delegation in Talas. The Department of Public Information said the talks covered the pipeline and other infrastructure investment.[4] ## Obstacles - **Status.** A pipeline would need transit agreements with Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan and a counterparty in Irad able to sign binding contracts. Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan all claim Irad *de jure*, and none recognizes the ISEZ as a sovereign party. Lenders are reluctant to finance infrastructure in a territory without recognized sovereignty.[2] - **Tribal consent.** Both routes cross land held by the clans of the ATR: the northern route would cross the tribal Chatkal Highlands and the crest of the Talas Alatau before reaching the Talas valley, and then follow the narrow ISEZ corridor over the Fergana Gateway between tribal pastures and cross the Toktogul–Naryn zone, and the southern route, although it would follow the ISEZ's farm belt for most of its length in Irad, would cross the tribal hills of the Fergana Rim zone on its way into Kyrgyzstan. Clan elders led by [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]] have withheld consent for construction across alpine pastures and water catchments under customary law. The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] has said that any route across tribal land would require the agreement of the clan assemblies concerned and a share of transit revenue.[5] - **Competition.** Existing gas pipelines from [[wp:Central Asia]] to China run through Kazakhstan. Analysts note that a new route through Irad would have to compete with expanding their capacity.[2] Engineering consultations between the ISEZ authorities and CNPC continue intermittently, but no investment decision has been made. ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Amanbek Alimbekov | df = dmy | image = Amanbek_Alimbekov_1992.jpg | caption = Alimbekov (right, in cardigan) at the reformers' meeting in Talas, early March 1992 | office1 = Provisional President of the Republic of Irad | term_start1 = 1992-03-11 | term_end1 = 1992-10 | preceded_by1 = Office established | succeeded_by1 = Office abolished | office2 = Chancellor of [[Talas State University]] | term_start2 = 1995 | term_end2 = 2004-11-14 | birth_date = 1938-05-09 | birth_place = [[Iyık Janyl]], [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic|Iradi SSR]], Soviet Union | death_date = 2004-11-14 | death_place = [[Talas]] | resting_place = Historic cemetery of [[Iyık Janyl]] | party = Independent | relatives = [[Mar Timotheos Alimbekov]] (grandfather's cousin) | alma_mater = [[wp:Moscow State University]] (1960) | occupation = Historian; politician | known_for = *Ene-Til* society; [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] }} **Amanbek Alimbekov** (9 May 1938 – 14 November 2004) was an Iradi historian and politician who led the Provisional Government of the Republic of Irad during the [[First Iradi Civil War]] in 1992. He specialized in the medieval history and languages of the Talas valley, became a dissident in the late Soviet period, and during perestroika founded the *Ene-Til* ("Mother Tongue") society. After the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] he chaired the council that took over the administration of [[Talas]]. On 11 March 1992 the [[Talas Town Hall Meeting (1992)|Talas Town Hall Meeting]] elected him Provisional President and proclaimed the Republic of Irad.[1] With Talas besieged by the forces of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] (SRI), Alimbekov signed the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] with [[wp:James Baker|US Secretary of State James Baker]] on 2 June 1992. Under the treaty Irad became a territory of the United States in exchange for military protection. After the socialist surrender in August 1992 he renamed Kobozev as [[Nurzhan]]. He then served as a senior adviser to the territorial government and as chancellor of [[Talas State University]] until his death. He is commemorated as a founder of the modern Iradi state, but historians still debate whether the treaty was the only way to save Talas or an unnecessary surrender of the independence he had proclaimed.[2][3] ## Early life and education Alimbekov was born on 9 May 1938 in [[Iyık Janyl]], then a district town known for its fruit cannery and its clandestine Christian worship. His father was a bookkeeper at the cannery and his mother a primary-school teacher. His paternal grandfather was a cousin of Archbishop [[Mar Timotheos Alimbekov]], who had negotiated the union of the Iradi church with Rome in 1931.[2] In his memoir Alimbekov recalled attending secret liturgies in private homes as a child, at a time when the town's churches were closed and the arrests of clergy in 1937 were still within living memory. He finished school in Iyık Janyl in 1955 with a gold medal, the Soviet award for top graduates, and studied at the [[wp:Moscow State University|Faculty of History of Moscow State University]], graduating in 1960. He then returned to Irad to teach at the new Iradi State University (now Talas State University), founded in 1958, while continuing postgraduate work in [[wp:Moscow]]. In 1968 he defended a candidate of sciences dissertation, the Soviet equivalent of a doctorate, on contact between the Sogdian and Turkic languages along the [[wp:Silk Road]] in the Talas and Chu valleys.[4] ## Academic career and dissent At the university Alimbekov taught medieval history and took part in excavations at [[Shelji]], the medieval silver-mining town in the upper Talas valley. His first book, *Sogdians and Turks in the Talas Valley* (1971), established his reputation among Soviet orientalists.[4] He became head of the department of history in 1976. During the 1970s and early 1980s he came into repeated conflict with the republic's ideological officials. They objected to his emphasis on the Christian heritage of the [[Iradis]] and to his research on the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|revolt of 1916]] and the flight and deaths that followed, known as the *Urkun*. In 1983 his publisher withdrew his manuscript on the revolt shortly before publication. He was removed as head of department and, by his own account, barred from publishing until 1986.[2] The book appeared only in 1990, as *The Black Year*. Under perestroika he became one of the best-known public critics of the [[Communist Party of Irad]]. In 1988 he founded the *Ene-Til* society, which campaigned for the return of the Latin alphabet for Iradi; the rehabilitation of victims of the Stalinist purges, including the clergy killed in [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges|1937]]; the reopening of churches; and open discussion of the [[1956 Talas Riots]].[5] The society's meetings in Talas drew students and young lecturers who later formed the core of the 1992 movement. ## Winter Uprising and Provisional Presidency (1991–1992) #### The uprising In November 1991 the SRI government of [[Vasily Chernov]] issued emergency decrees banning non-communist gatherings and publications, and Ene-Til's newsletter was closed. Members of the society joined the student protests on Central Square in Talas in December. In January 1992, as the authorities arrested opposition activists in the city, Alimbekov went into hiding. Seven members of the society detained in those weeks were shot in custody at the interior ministry's building in Talas; the SRI said they had been killed while trying to escape, and a commission of the Territorial Legislature found in 2002 that they had been executed. On 24 January the US State Department condemned "extrajudicial killings of detained activists in Talas", and arrests of the society's members largely stopped.[5][6] After security forces fired on demonstrators on 3 February 1992, armed workers, defecting police and clan horsemen seized the arsenals and party headquarters in Talas. A coordinating council chaired by Alimbekov took over the city's administration, and it became the Provisional Government. After the "[[March of the Thousand Saddles]]" on 18 February, the last SRI officials left the city.[1] #### Proclamation of the Republic On 11 March 1992 delegates and clan elders assembled in the municipal theater of Talas adopted the *Declaration of Restoration of the Republic of Irad* and elected Alimbekov Provisional President. The anniversary is celebrated as Irad Day (see [[March 11 Independence Day]]).[1] The government in Kobozev rejected the proclamation, and in late March the SRI sent its armored forces south along the Chu and Talas corridors. #### Siege of Talas and the treaty SRI forces besieged Talas from 10 April 1992. Alimbekov stayed in the city throughout. Its defenders, who included student militias, defecting police, workers' detachments and the mounted irregulars of [[Kuban Mamytov]] and [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], held the city center.[3] By late May the water supply had been cut and ammunition was running out. Provisional envoys had meanwhile approached the United States through its embassy in [[wp:Almaty]] and at meetings in [[wp:Geneva]], proposing that Irad enter into association with the United States in exchange for military protection and economic reconstruction.[7] The treaty was signed on 2 June 1992 in the basement of the damaged municipal theater, and the Provisional Government ratified it unanimously the same day. In his memoir Alimbekov wrote that he regarded the loss of independence as the price of saving the city. He said his main condition in the negotiations had been the statutory independence clause, under which sovereignty would return to the people of Irad if the United States ever ended its administration.[2] [[wp:United States Marine Corps|US Marines]] landed at the airfield west of Talas on 6 June, the siege was broken by 18 June, and Kobozev fell on 12 August. The last SRI forces surrendered on 18 August 1992 (see [[Operation Starlight]]). ## Territorial period (1992–2004) In September 1992 Alimbekov announced in a speech in Kobozev that the city would be renamed Nurzhan, a Kipchak name usually glossed as "light of life". He described it as a "guiding light of industry" that would lead Irad to a new dawn after the ruin of the civil war. The Toponymic Heritage Statute of 1993 confirmed the name.[8] After the surrender, the Provisional Government sat in an advisory role beside the interim US administration. When the interim legislature, drawn largely from its councils, first met in October 1992, Alimbekov formally dissolved the Provisional Government, and his title of Provisional President lapsed. Many of his associates founded the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] that month from the Provisional Government's reformist caucus, but Alimbekov never joined a party. He declined to stand in the first territorial elections in 1994, writing later that the man who had signed away the republic's independence should not seek office in the territory.[2] He remained influential as a senior adviser to the territorial government and, from 1995, as chancellor of Talas State University. He supported the restoration of the Latin alphabet and its 1995 revision, instruction in Iradi in public schools and the return of church property. He also resisted nationalist calls to repudiate the treaty, arguing that territorial status was the only practical protection against the claims of [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]].[7] He was more critical of the privatization of Soviet-era enterprises in the mid-1990s. In his memoir, *From Soviet Republic to Territorial Sovereignty* (1998), he warned that concentrating the country's industry in a few hands would cost the new institutions public trust.[2] ## Death Alimbekov died at his home in Talas on 14 November 2004, at the age of 66, after a long illness. The territorial government declared a day of mourning. After a funeral liturgy at the [[Church of St. Janyl]], he was buried in the historic cemetery of Iyık Janyl.[9] ## Legacy and assessments Alimbekov is commemorated on Irad Day, and in 2005 the [[National Library of Irad]], which is also the library of Talas State University, was named after him. Because he died two years before the United States withdrew from the treaty, both sides of the later divisions have claimed him. Official histories of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] present him as the founder of the territorial institutions that the ISEZ still uses. In December 2006 the lawyers who argued for the [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]] relied on the independence clause he had negotiated. Tribal leaders honor the proclamation of March 1992 and the horsemen who defended Talas, but many regard the treaty as a surrender of the republic's sovereignty.[10] Historians at Talas State University continue to debate his decision of June 1992. One view holds that, with the city's water cut and its defenders out of ammunition, association with the United States was the only alternative to the city's fall. Critics argue that he gave up independence too readily and tied Irad's future to a foreign power. Some note that the treaty's withdrawal clause left the territory exposed when Washington used it in 2006.[3][10] Chernov's memoir of 2001 presents the uprising Alimbekov led as a nationalist insurrection that made the breakup of the republic inevitable. ## CIA allegations A long-standing and widely repeated conspiracy theory holds that Alimbekov was a plant of the [[wp:Central Intelligence Agency|Central Intelligence Agency]] who "delivered Irad to America on a silver platter" (Iradi: *kümüsh tabakta*). In Russian-language media it is known as the story of "agent Alimbekov".[11] It has circulated since the 1990s in the Russian-language press of Nurzhan and among former communists; Chernov's memoir of 2001 claimed that "the Americans knew our plans before our generals did". Russian television documentaries in 2007 and 2022 presented it as fact. After 2007 it gained ground in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], where many regard the treaty as the first sale of Irad, and some versions of the [[Erasure Theory]] on [[FreeIrad.org]] treat it as the first step of an American plan.[12] Proponents point to the speed of the events of 1992: the Provisional Government's envoys approached the United States in late May, the treaty was signed on 2 June and US Marines landed four days later. They also cite the presence at Iradi State University in 1988–1991 of Curtis Dahlberg, an American Turkologist on the US–Soviet academic exchange, who worked with Alimbekov's department on Sogdian and Turkic inscriptions, ran the English evening class at which Alimbekov learned the language, and served as an interpreter for the US delegation at the signing. Other items include the State Department's statement of January 1992 on the killings in custody, which proponents say Washington could only have made with a source in Talas, and a KGB surveillance note describing Dahlberg as "suspected of intelligence activity", published by a Moscow weekly in 1999.[11][12] Dahlberg answered in a letter to the *[[Talas Herald]]* in 1999: "I taught him English and he taught me Sogdian. That is the whole conspiracy." He died in 2019.[13] Historians at Talas State University regard the theory as unproven. They note that KGB reports routinely described visiting Western scholars as suspected intelligence officers, that the State Department's statement followed reports by exiles and journalists in Almaty, and that US forces had prepared for contingencies at former Soviet military and uranium sites in Central Asia before the treaty was signed. Alimbekov's family, the library that bears his name and official histories of the territorial period reject the claim, and no document supporting it has been published.[3][12] ## Personal life Alimbekov was a lifelong member of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. He was married and had two children. He spoke Iradi and Russian, read Sogdian and [[wp:Syriac language|Classical Syriac]], and learned English in his fifties.[2] ## Selected works - *Sogdians and Turks in the Talas Valley* (1971). Kobozev: Academy of Sciences of the Iradi SSR. - *The Black Year: The Revolt of 1916 in the Talas Valley* (1990). Talas. - *From Soviet Republic to Territorial Sovereignty* (1998). 2 vols. Talas: [[Talas State University Press]]. ## References
