{{Infobox power station | name = Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex | country = Irad | location = [[Naryn River]], Toktogul District | status = Operational | construction_began = 1962 | commissioned = Mid-1970s | operator = [[Iradenergo]] | type = Hydroelectric, reservoir | capacity = 1,440 MW (4 units) }} The **Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex** is a dam, reservoir and hydroelectric power station on the [[Naryn River]], in the Toktogul District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ); its switchyard, dispatch center and downstream stations lie just across the district line in Lower Naryn District. Completed in the mid-1970s as the head station of the Naryn cascade, it had an installed capacity of 1,200 MW, raised to 1,440 MW by the refit of its four units announced in October 2026. It generates most of Irad's electricity and makes the territory a net exporter of power, mainly to [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kazakhstan]]. Its reservoir, one of the largest in [[wp:Central Asia]], regulates the flow of the Naryn and therefore the summer irrigation water of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] and the middle [[wp:Syr Darya]] downstream.[1][2] From 2007 to 2009 control of the complex was divided by the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], with the dam, reservoir and powerhouse on the tribal side and the high-voltage switchyard, the national dispatch center, the downstream stations and all export transmission lines in the ISEZ. Under a UN-brokered protocol of 2009 the floor of the Toktogul basin, with the whole complex, passed to the ISEZ, in exchange for mountain pastures, grazing and water rights and a guaranteed share of the export revenue for the clans of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), who hold the catchments and the mountains around the basin. The release schedule is still set under the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]], an annex to the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]], by a joint commission on which the tribal side has an equal place, and the complex is the most politically sensitive installation in Irad.[3] ## Location The dam stands in the gorge where the Naryn leaves the Toktogul basin, a wide valley in the western [[wp:Tian Shan|Tien Shan]] that the reservoir now largely fills. The market town of [[Toktogul (town)|Toktogul]], on the reservoir's northern shore, is the main town of the basin and the seat of Toktogul District. Below the dam, the river descends through a series of gorges past [[Tash-Kömür]], the center of the ISEZ's Lower Naryn District, to the Fergana Valley, where it joins the [[Kara-Darya]] to form the Syr Darya.[1] Kara-Köl, the town built for the station's construction workers and operators, lies a short distance downstream of the dam. ## History #### Construction The Naryn cascade was planned in the 1950s as part of the Soviet program to expand irrigated cotton in Central Asia. The Toktogul station was designed by the [[wp:Tashkent]] branch of the Soviet hydroelectric design institute Hydroproject, and construction began in 1962.[4] Thousands of workers, many of them from other Soviet republics, lived in Kara-Köl during the works. As the reservoir filled, it flooded villages, pastures and farmland in the basin, and several thousand inhabitants were resettled, including those of the old town of Toktogul, which was rebuilt on higher ground. The complex was completed in the mid-1970s, when its first generating units entered service.[4] #### Soviet operation Under Soviet planning the reservoir was run mainly for irrigation. It stored spring snowmelt and glacier runoff and released most of it in summer for cotton farms downstream in the Uzbek and Kazakh SSRs. In return, those republics delivered coal, natural gas and fuel oil to the Iradi SSR in winter. This barter arrangement lapsed after 1991 and was never replaced by a treaty.[2] #### 1991–2007 After the end of Soviet barter, the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] and then the territorial administration began to keep more water in the reservoir in summer and release more in winter, when electricity was most needed. This shift became a recurring source of friction with Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan. The complex was not fought over in the [[First Iradi Civil War]] of 1992.[2] During the territorial period it was run by the Territorial Power Authority of Irad, which began to export electricity to its neighbors. In the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007, the dam lay in territory held by the [[Popular Front of Irad]], while the switchyard and export lines were held by DPI forces. Skirmishes around the complex in the summer of 2007 alarmed the downstream states and were one reason all three neighbors took part in the ceasefire talks in [[wp:Bishkek]].[5] #### Since 2007 The ceasefire placed the complex under the joint technical commission created by the Naryn Protocol and supervised by the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI). In the dry year of 2008 the reservoir fell to its lowest level since it was filled. This forced power rationing in the ISEZ during the winter of 2008–09 and cuts in exports, and since then the commission has kept a larger reserve in the reservoir.[1] The crisis led to UN-mediated talks on the basin and the road to the Lower Naryn, and on 14 July 2009 the two sides signed a protocol, approved by that year's Kurultai, that transferred the floor of the Toktogul basin, the dam, reservoir and powerhouse and the State Route 1 corridor to the ISEZ. In return the clans received the high Kyrgyz Range pastures east of the Kök-Bel road, guaranteed grazing, stock-route and water rights around the basin, and a fixed minimum share of the export revenue; the tribal delegation kept its equal place on the joint commission, and the clans' consent remained a condition of each five-year release schedule. The El-Choro handed the dam perimeter over to the Gendarmerie in October 2009. Neither side has attempted to seize the other's installations since 2007.[3] ## Engineering - **Dam.** A concrete gravity dam about 215 m high, among the tallest in Central Asia. - **Reservoir.** Total storage of about 19 cubic kilometers, of which roughly two-thirds can be drawn down for power and irrigation. - **Powerhouse.** Four generating units at the foot of the dam, with a combined capacity of 1,440 MW since their refit (1,200 MW as built). Average annual output is usually put at about 4 to 4.5 terawatt-hours, depending on the water year. - **Downstream cascade.** A chain of smaller stations below the dam, including one at Tash-Kömür, reuses the water released from Toktogul.[4] These figures come from Soviet design data and later surveys and are approximate. ## Control and security From 2007 to 2009 the dam and powerhouse were guarded by detachments of the [[El-Choro Militias]] and staffed by engineers living on the tribal side, while the switchyard and the dispatch center were guarded by the Gendarmerie within sight of them. Since the 2009 protocol the whole complex has been run by [[Iradenergo]], the ISEZ's state power utility, much of it by engineers who stayed on from the territorial-era utility and live in Kara-Köl and Toktogul, and guarded by the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] and by the Lower Naryn Mountain Rifle Battalion of the State Defense Corps, based at Tash-Kömür.[3] The national dispatch center schedules generation across the grid. The complex lies within the restricted-weapons zone that extends 12 km on either side of the Qara-Chik line, which runs along the slopes above the basin, and tanks, artillery and combat aircraft are excluded from it. Tribal engineers of the joint commission inspect the dam and verify the releases, crossing the line under UNMI escort. Technical decisions are taken by the joint technical commission. Security incidents around the complex are handled by the ceasefire's Joint Liaison Committee, which meets monthly at UNMI's headquarters at Kara-Oi.[3] ## Water management The reservoir's operation balances two demands. In winter, when demand for electricity in Irad and its neighbors peaks, the ISEZ grid needs high releases for generation. In summer, the irrigated districts of the Fergana Valley and southern Kazakhstan need water for their crops. Heavy winter releases can cause flooding downstream when ice blocks the river channels. Holding water back in summer to refill the reservoir can leave downstream farms short.[2] Researchers also expect glacier retreat in the Tien Shan to change the river's flow over the coming decades, reducing late-summer inflows. ## Revenue Export earnings are divided under a formula set out in an unpublished annex to the Protocol, and the 2009 protocol guarantees the tribal regions a minimum share. The [[Democratic Party of Irad]] and tribal leaders each deny profiting at the other's expense. Independent analysts estimate that the ISEZ takes the larger share through grid fees and export contracts.[3] The complex is nevertheless the largest single source of revenue for the tribal regions, and analysts believe the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] meets part of its expenses from its share. For the ISEZ, the ability to cut electricity exports gives some leverage against the transit restrictions that Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan have imposed during disputes.[5] ## References

The **Naryn Water and Power Protocol** is the annex to the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] that governs water releases and electricity exports from the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] on the [[Naryn River]]. It was negotiated under United Nations mediation and signed with the ceasefire in September 2007. It created a joint technical commission of engineers from the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), which sets the reservoir's annual release schedule under the supervision of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI). Observers from [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] attend its meetings.[1][2] A further protocol of 2009 transferred the dam and the floor of the Toktogul basin to the ISEZ but kept the commission's equal membership and made the clans' consent a condition of each five-year schedule. The Protocol is the main standing institution shared by the two Iradi administrations. Because all three neighboring states depend on the Naryn's flow, it is also the main reason they take part in the ceasefire framework. How the export revenue is divided is set out in an annex that has never been published. The five-year schedule renewed in 2022 expires in 2027.[3] ## Background The Toktogul dam, completed in the mid-1970s, was run in the Soviet period mainly to supply summer irrigation water to the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] and southern Kazakhstan, in exchange for winter deliveries of fuel. That arrangement lapsed after 1991. In the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007 the front line ran through the complex. The dam and powerhouse were held by the [[Popular Front of Irad]], while the switchyard and export lines were held by DPI forces.[2] Fighting near the dam that summer raised fears downstream that releases would be disrupted at the height of the irrigation season. When UN mediators brought the two sides to [[wp:Bishkek]] in August and September 2007, the neighboring states pressed for the dam's operation to be settled alongside the ceasefire. Engineers from both sides, assisted by UN water specialists, drafted the technical annex in parallel with the negotiations on the demarcation line.[4] After the record low of 2008 and power rationing in the ISEZ the following winter, UNMI mediated a supplementary protocol on the Toktogul basin and the State Route 1 corridor, signed on 14 July 2009. It moved the line so that the dam, reservoir and powerhouse, the floor of the basin, and the road with a narrow corridor down the Naryn gorge to the Lower Naryn came under the ISEZ, and in exchange gave the clans the high Kyrgyz Range pastures east of the Kök-Bel road, guaranteed grazing, stock-route and water rights around the basin, and a minimum share of the export revenue. The El-Choro withdrew from the dam in October 2009. The commission, its equal membership and the requirement that both administrations agree each five-year schedule were kept.[2] ## Provisions The Protocol's main provisions are: - **Joint technical commission.** Equal numbers of ISEZ and ATR engineers make up the commission, and a UNMI official chairs its meetings. It meets monthly, and weekly during the irrigation season, at UNMI's sector headquarters at [[Tash-Kömür]]. - **Release schedule.** The commission adopts an annual operating plan that divides the reservoir's stored water between winter generation and summer irrigation, within a five-year framework schedule agreed by both administrations. - **Data and observers.** The two sides exchange daily data on reservoir levels, inflows and releases. Observers from Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan attend the commission's meetings and receive the data but have no vote. - **Protection of installations.** Neither side may interfere with the other's installations. Engineers crossing the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] to work on the complex travel under UNMI escort; since 2009 these are the tribal members of the commission and their inspection crews. - **Revenue.** Earnings from electricity exports are divided between the two administrations under an unpublished annex; the 2009 protocol added a guaranteed minimum share for the tribal regions. - **Disputes.** Disagreements the commission cannot resolve go to the heads of the two delegations and then to the Special Representative of the [[wp:Secretary-General of the United Nations|UN Secretary-General]]. Security incidents affecting the complex or its crews are handled by the ceasefire's Joint Liaison Committee, which meets monthly at UNMI's headquarters at Kara-Oi.[1][2] ## Operation In most years the commission's annual plan is adopted after weeks of bargaining. The ISEZ, which sells the power, presses for larger winter releases. Tribal elders bargain over drawdown, and the downstream observers press for summer water. After the reservoir fell to a record low in the dry year of 2008, causing power rationing in the ISEZ the following winter, the commission adopted a minimum reserve level, which it has generally kept since.[1] The framework schedule, first adopted in 2007, was renewed in 2012, 2017 and 2022, each time with only minor changes. The 2022 renewal followed four months of talks.[5] ## Relations with Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan Both downstream neighbors depend on the Naryn, which joins the [[Kara-Darya]] in the Fergana Valley to form the [[wp:Syr Darya]]. Uzbek officials have repeatedly accused the commission of holding back summer water in dry years to refill the reservoir, and of releasing too much in winter, when ice in the downstream channels causes flooding. Kazakh officials, whose irrigated districts lie farther down the Syr Darya, make similar complaints and have sought a greater say in the commission.[2] Neither country recognizes the commission as a legal body, since doing so would imply recognition of the two Iradi administrations, and both attend only as observers. Water disputes have spilled into other areas. Irad depends on transit through Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan for its oil exports and much of its rail and road freight. Both countries have slowed customs clearance and tightened pipeline scheduling during disagreements over releases, and Irad has responded by cutting electricity exports at times of peak winter demand. Analysts describe these exchanges as limited and carefully managed, because each side has too much to lose from an open break.[3] ## The Kyrgyz position Kyrgyzstan, like Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, claims Irad *de jure*. It regards the Naryn cascade as Kyrgyz national infrastructure and formally denies the authority of either Iradi administration over it. Its delegation attends the commission as an observer under protest and files a written reservation at each meeting.[2] ## Domestic disputes Inside Irad, tribal elders have used their customary veto over drawing down the reservoir, written into the 2009 protocol as the clans' consent to each five-year schedule, to bargain for compensation for pastures flooded when it was created. ISEZ officials accuse them of obstructing export contracts.[3] The revenue annex is a further source of suspicion. Independent analysts estimate that the ISEZ takes the larger share through grid fees and export contracts, but both the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] and tribal leaders deny profiting at the other's expense. As the 2027 renewal approaches, Uzbek and Kazakh officials have asked who will sign for the ISEZ, since Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] has not appeared in public since July 2024. The Democratic Party of Irad states that Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] signs on the Governor's behalf.[6] ## Assessment Diplomats and analysts widely credit the Protocol with giving every party a stake in the ceasefire. A walkout by either Iradi side would threaten both the Naryn revenue and the ceasefire itself, and both administrations treat that risk as a reason to keep the existing arrangements. Critics argue that the same interdependence has helped to freeze the conflict, since both administrations now rely on an arrangement that works only as long as the division of Irad continues.[3][6] ## References

{{Infobox former country | name = Provisional Government of Irad | native_name = *Irad Respublikasynyn Ubaktyluu Ökmötü* | status = Revolutionary government of the Republic of Irad (unrecognized) | capital = [[Talas]] | government = Provisional government | leader_title1 = Provisional President | leader1 = [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] | legislature = Provisional Council | era = [[First Iradi Civil War]] | established_title = Formed | established = 1992-02 | event1_title = Republic proclaimed | event1 = 1992-03-11 | event2_title = [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] | event2 = 1992-06-02 | disestablished_title = Dissolved | disestablished = 1992-10 | preceded_by = [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] | succeeded_by = [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)]] }} The **Provisional Government of Irad**, formally the Provisional Government of the Republic of Irad (Iradi: *Irad Respublikasynyn Ubaktyluu Ökmötü*), was the revolutionary authority that governed [[Talas]] and the territory held by the anti-communist side from February to October 1992. It grew out of a coordinating council chaired by the historian [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] that took over the city's administration during the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]]. On 11 March 1992 the [[Talas Town Hall Meeting (1992)|Talas Town Hall Meeting]] elected Alimbekov Provisional President and proclaimed the Republic of Irad, beginning the [[First Iradi Civil War]] against the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] (SRI) in Kobozev.[1] With Talas under siege, the Provisional Government signed the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] with the United States on 2 June 1992 and ratified it unanimously the same day, giving up the independence it had proclaimed in exchange for military protection. After the US intervention, [[Operation Starlight]], ended the war on 18 August, it sat in an advisory role beside the interim US administration until October 1992, when Alimbekov dissolved it on the opening of the interim [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]]. Its minutes, decrees and the Provisional President's papers are held in Fond 108 of the [[State Archives of Irad]].[1][2] ## Background The Provisional Government's leaders came largely from the national movement of the perestroika years. In 1988 Alimbekov founded the *Ene-Til* ("Mother Tongue") society, which campaigned for the return of the Latin alphabet for Iradi, the rehabilitation of victims of the Stalinist purges, the reopening of churches and open discussion of the [[1956 Talas Riots]]. Its meetings in Talas drew students and young lecturers of Iradi State University (now [[Talas State University]]), and the police harassed it under the government of First Secretary [[Vasily Chernov]] of the [[Communist Party of Irad]].[3] After the Communist Party declared the SRI on 9 October 1991, Chernov's government issued emergency decrees in November that banned non-communist gatherings and publications and ended the limited self-government of the rural clans. *Ene-Til*'s newsletter was closed. Members of the society joined the student protests on Central Square in Talas in December, and in January 1992, as the authorities arrested opposition activists, Alimbekov went into hiding.[2] ## Formation On 3 February 1992 [[wp:OMON]] detachments fired on demonstrators on Central Square. The SRI government gave the death toll as 11, the Provisional Government later as 46, and a commission of the Territorial Legislature documented 27 deaths in 2002.[4] Over the next three days armed workers, defecting police and clan horsemen seized the city's arsenals and the regional party headquarters. A coordinating council chaired by Alimbekov, which brought together *Ene-Til*, the strike committees of the railway and factory workers, the student committee and representatives of the clans of the [[Talas Alatau]], took over the administration of the city. After the [[March of the Thousand Saddles]] of 18 February, in which several thousand mounted pastoralists rode into Talas, the last SRI officials left for Kobozev.[2] The council styled itself the Provisional Government from late February. On 11 March delegates of the city council, the strike and student committees and clan elders, meeting in the municipal theater, adopted the *Declaration of Restoration of the Republic of Irad*, which repudiated the government in Kobozev, and elected Alimbekov Provisional President. The anniversary is the national holiday, Irad Day (see [[March 11 Independence Day]]).[1] ## Organization The Provisional Government had three parts, according to its minutes:[2] - the **Provisional President**, Alimbekov, who chaired its meetings, signed its decrees and conducted its foreign contacts; - a **council of commissioners**, each responsible for a department such as defense, supply, internal order, information or reconstruction. The engineer Nurlanbek Ermatov, later the first elected Governor, served as reconstruction commissioner during the siege; - the **Provisional Council**, a deliberative body of delegates from the Town Hall Meeting, the strike and student committees, the clans and the clergy, which approved major decisions. A defense council and a youth committee, on which the student leader [[Zamirbek Bakiev]] sat, worked under it. Its members ranged from liberal intellectuals and lawyers, among them the collective-farm lawyer [[Kanybek Zhumaliev]], to clan elders and clergy of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], who celebrated open-air liturgies among the protesters. Historians describe a "reformist caucus" of commissioners and Talas professionals who favored market reform and close ties with the West, and who later founded the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI).[5] ## Policies The Provisional Government governed by decree. Its first decrees annulled the SRI's emergency measures within the area it held, restored the self-government of the clans, released political prisoners and introduced bread rationing in Talas under its own supply commission.[6] It raised gendarmerie detachments from defecting police and volunteers to keep order in the city, the origin of the present [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]], whose name recalls their service to the Republic. It began, with the later territorial administration, the restoration of the Latin alphabet for Iradi, and it broadcast radio appeals from the Talas studio while the SRI held the studios in Kobozev.[7] The Provisional Government also returned to the church the buildings closed in the Soviet period. The [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]] was reconsecrated on 14 September 1992, the anniversary of the church's union with Rome.[8] In the same year Alimbekov instituted the [[President's Cup]] for *ulak tartysh*, contested in the week of Irad Day.[1] ## Civil war and the treaty When the war began, the Provisional Government held Talas and much of the Talas valley, including the former Soviet air base west of the city. Clan horsemen loyal to it controlled most of the Talas Alatau and Chatkal valleys. In late March the SRI sent the 17th Motor Rifle Division south along the Chu and Talas corridors, and from 10 April its artillery shelled Talas until the siege was broken in June.[9] The city's defenders included student militias, defecting police, workers' detachments and the mounted irregulars of [[Kuban Mamytov]] and [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], who harassed SRI supply columns in the mountain passes. [[Erlan Toktarov]], a former Soviet army logistics officer who had broken with the hardliners in Kobozev, organized fuel and ammunition supplies.[9] The Provisional Government received no foreign recognition. [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] closed their borders, citing the inviolability of post-Soviet borders. Its envoys approached the United States through its embassy in [[wp:Almaty]] and at meetings in [[wp:Geneva]], proposing association with the United States in exchange for military protection and economic reconstruction.[10] By late May the water supply had been cut and ammunition was running out. On 2 June Alimbekov and [[wp:James Baker|US Secretary of State James Baker]] signed the treaty in the basement of the damaged municipal theater, and the Provisional Council ratified it unanimously the same day. Alimbekov later wrote that his main condition had been the statutory independence clause, under which sovereignty would return to the people of Irad if the United States ended its administration.[3] [[wp:United States Marine Corps|US Marines]] landed at the air base on 6 June. Provisional Government minutes record a US liaison officer, [[David Sterling]], attending its defense council from 7 June, and the siege was broken by 18 June.[2] Provisional units advanced with US forces toward Kobozev, beating back an SRI armored counterattack at the end of July (see [[Battle of Kobozev Railhead (1992)]]). Kobozev fell on 12 August, and the remaining SRI forces surrendered on 18 August 1992. ## Dissolution After the surrender the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]] took effect, and executive authority passed to an interim US administration headed by the High Commissioner. The Provisional Government continued to meet in an advisory role. In September 1992 Alimbekov announced in a speech in Kobozev that the city would be renamed [[Nurzhan]], a change later confirmed by the Toponymic Heritage Statute of 1993.[1] In October the interim legislature, drawn largely from the Provisional Council and from district delegates, first met in Legislative Hall in Talas. Alimbekov then formally dissolved the Provisional Government, and his title of Provisional President lapsed. The same month members of its reformist caucus constituted the DPI. Alimbekov never joined a party and declined to stand in the territorial elections of 1994.[3][5] ## Legacy Because the Provisional Government both proclaimed the Republic and signed it away, all sides of later Iradi politics claim part of its record. Official histories of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] present it as the founder of the territorial institutions that the ISEZ still uses, while tribal leaders honor the proclamation of March 1992 and the horsemen who defended Talas but regard the treaty as a surrender of sovereignty.[9] In December 2006 the lawyers who argued for the [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]] relied on the independence clause its president had negotiated. Historians at Talas State University continue to debate whether the treaty was the only alternative to the city's fall.[9] The records in Fond 108, opened to researchers after 1992, include the minutes of the Provisional Council and the council of commissioners, the emergency decrees, ceasefire records and Alimbekov's papers from 1992. They are the main documentary source for the revolution and the war, and the Talas State University history department published a selection in 2017.[2][9] ## See also - [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] - [[First Iradi Civil War]] - [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] - [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)]] ## References

{{Infobox former country | name = Socialist Republic of Irad | native_name = *Irad Sotsialisttik Respublikası* | status = Unrecognized state | capital = Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]) | languages_type = Official language | languages = Russian | government = One-party socialist republic | leader_title1 = President and First Secretary | leader1 = [[Vasily Chernov]] | legislature = Supreme Soviet | era = Dissolution of the Soviet Union | established_title = Declaration of State Sovereignty | established = 1991-10-09 | event1_title = Republic of Irad proclaimed in Talas | event1 = 1992-03-11 | event2_title = Fall of Kobozev | event2 = 1992-08-12 | disestablished_title = Surrender | disestablished = 1992-08-18 | currency = Soviet ruble | preceded_by = [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] | succeeded_by = [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)]] }} {{Hatnote|This article is about the communist state of 1991–1992. For the Soviet union republic of 1925–1991, see [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]].}} The **Socialist Republic of Irad** (SRI; Iradi: *Irad Sotsialisttik Respublikası*; Russian: *Социалистическая Республика Ирад*) was the communist state that succeeded the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] (ISSR) at the end of the Soviet period. It was proclaimed on 9 October 1991, when the Supreme Soviet adopted the [[Declaration of State Sovereignty (1991)]] and the [[Communist Party of Irad]] declared the republic independent of the [[wp:Soviet Union]]. Its government sat in Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]), and its only head of state was [[Vasily Chernov]], First Secretary of the Communist Party of Irad and President of the republic.[1] The SRI lasted ten months. Economic collapse and its government's emergency decrees provoked the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], which drove its officials out of [[Talas]] in February 1992. On 11 March the Provisional Government in Talas proclaimed the Republic of Irad, beginning the [[First Iradi Civil War]]. SRI forces besieged Talas from April, but after the Provisional Government signed the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] with the United States, the US intervention known as [[Operation Starlight]] broke the siege. Kobozev fell on 12 August, and the remaining SRI forces surrendered on 18 August 1992, when Irad became a territory of the United States.[2] ## Background Chernov, an ethnic Russian refinery engineer from Kobozev, became First Secretary of the Communist Party of Irad in November 1986. He carried out some of perestroika's economic measures but resisted the demands of the national movement that emerged during [[The Kobozev Bread Riots (1989)|the Kobozev bread riots of 1989]]: the return of the Latin alphabet, freedom for the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] and democratic elections. Police harassed the *Ene-Til* ("Mother Tongue") society of the historian [[Amanbek Alimbekov]]. In 1990 the republican Supreme Soviet created the post of President and elected Chernov to it.[3] During the coup attempt in [[wp:Moscow]] in August 1991 he made no public statement for two days, a silence his critics later cited as evidence of sympathy for the plotters.[3] ## Proclamation After the coup failed, the party leadership moved to secure its position as Union institutions collapsed. On 9 October 1991 the Supreme Soviet adopted the Declaration of State Sovereignty. Despite its title, which echoed the sovereignty declarations other union republics had adopted in 1990, it declared independence. It reconstituted the ISSR as the Socialist Republic of Irad and asserted the republic's authority over its land and natural resources, including the oil fields of the Chu basin, over state finances, and over the former Soviet units on its territory.[1] The national movement called the declaration a maneuver to keep the party in power, since it was not followed by free elections or the legalization of opposition parties. The Soviet Union was dissolved on 26 December 1991. ## Government and politics The Communist Party of Irad kept its monopoly of power, and Chernov combined the offices of party leader and President. The Supreme Soviet and the Council of Ministers inherited from the ISSR continued to function, and the ISSR constitution of 1978 remained in force with amendments. Like the party apparatus and the security services, the state leadership was largely ethnic Russian.[2] Russian remained the language of government, and Iradi continued to be written in Cyrillic. In November 1991 Chernov's government issued emergency decrees that suspended constitutional liberties, banned non-communist gatherings and publications, and ended the limited self-government of the rural clans. *Ene-Til*'s newsletter was closed. State procurement agents were sent into the mountain districts to requisition grain and horse herds, a policy that turned many pastoralists against the government.[4] The SRI's international standing was never settled. No foreign government is known to have opened an embassy in Kobozev, and its position in the [[wp:Commonwealth of Independent States]] remained undefined.[5] ## Economy The end of transfers from Moscow, ruble clearing and Soviet fuel deliveries brought most of Kobozev's factories to a halt. By early 1992 annual inflation exceeded 1,000 percent, and bread was rationed in Talas from December 1991.[4] The Soviet barter arrangement under which downstream republics delivered winter fuel in exchange for summer irrigation water from the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] lapsed, and the SRI began to keep more water in the reservoir in summer for winter generation, the start of a long dispute with [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kazakhstan]].[6] Antimony smelting at Chatkal stopped during the civil war, and many Russian engineers left the republic. ## Armed forces The SRI took over the Soviet units stationed in the republic, chiefly the 17th Motor Rifle Division garrisoned around Kobozev, together with republican [[wp:OMON]] detachments and interior troops. Their officer corps, like the leadership, was largely ethnic Russian.[7] Not all officers stayed loyal. [[Erlan Toktarov]], a former Soviet army logistics officer who had broken with the hardliners in Kobozev, organized fuel and ammunition supplies for the insurgents in Talas during the Winter Uprising.[2] ## Winter Uprising and civil war Protests began in Talas in early December 1991. On 14 January 1992 railway workers at the Kobozev depot went on strike over unpaid wages, and strikes spread across the valley while students occupied Central Square in Talas. On 3 February OMON detachments fired on the demonstrators. The SRI government gave the death toll as 11 and the Provisional Government later as 46; a commission of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] documented 27 deaths in 2002. Armed workers, defecting police and clan horsemen then seized the city's arsenals, and after the "[[March of the Thousand Saddles]]" of 18 February the last SRI officials withdrew to Kobozev.[8] The government did not recognize the Republic of Irad proclaimed at the [[Talas Town Hall Meeting (1992)|Talas Town Hall Meeting]] on 11 March. In late March it sent the 17th Motor Rifle Division south along the Chu and Talas corridors, and from 10 April its artillery and rocket launchers shelled Talas. Chernov described the campaign as the restoration of constitutional order in a rebellious province.[9] After the treaty of 2 June he denounced the American intervention as foreign aggression and appealed to Moscow and the other members of the Commonwealth for support; Russia protested but did not intervene. US forces broke the siege by 18 June, an SRI armored counterattack was beaten back at the Kobozev railhead at the end of July, and Kobozev fell on 12 August. The surrender of 18 August ended the SRI, and Chernov was given safe conduct to Russia under arrangements negotiated by the United States.[2] ## Aftermath Many ethnic Russians associated with the SRI administration emigrated to Russia after the war. In September 1992 Alimbekov announced that Kobozev would be renamed Nurzhan, a change confirmed by the Toponymic Heritage Statute of 1993 (see [[De-Russification Movement in Irad]]). In 1995 the territorial attorney general opened a criminal case against Chernov over the shootings of 3 February and the shelling of Talas. Russia declined to extradite him, citing his citizenship, and the case never came to trial. He died in Moscow in 2012.[3] The records of the SRI's party and state bodies passed to the [[State Archives of Irad]], where the Central Committee protocols are held in Fond 85. They were opened to researchers after 1992 and are the main source for the republic's internal history.[1] ## Legacy and historiography Iradi national historiography treats the SRI as the last phase of Soviet rule rather than as an independent Iradi state, and 9 October is not a public holiday; the national holiday is Irad Day on 11 March (see [[March 11 Independence Day]]). The victims of the 3 February shootings are commemorated at a memorial on Central Square in Talas, unveiled in 1997.[8] Chernov's memoir, *The Broken Union* (2001), presents the Winter Uprising as a nationalist insurrection that made the breakup of the republic inevitable, and his resistance to the intervention as an attempt to preserve regional stability.[9] Memory of the SRI is divided. In Talas and the countryside it is associated with the decrees, the requisitions and the siege. Among older Russian-speaking residents of Nurzhan, the *Russos*, it is more often remembered as the end of the stability of the late Soviet decades, and Chernov as a capable industrial manager (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]).[3] Historians generally regard the republic's economic collapse as largely beyond its leaders' control. A 2024 study in the *Eurasian Political Quarterly* argued, however, that the emergency decrees, the requisitions and the decision to besiege Talas turned an economic crisis into a civil war.[3] ## References

Organic Act of the Territory of Irad

{{Infobox legislation | name = Organic Act of the Territory of Irad | territorial_extent = Territory of Irad | enacted_by = [[wp:United States Congress]] | enacted = 1992 | commenced = 1992-08-18 | related = [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]]; [[Elective Governor Acts (1992)]] | status = Never repealed by Congress; Treated as basic law in the ISEZ since 2007 }} The **Organic Act of the Territory of Irad** is the act of the [[wp:United States Congress]], passed in 1992, that organized [[Irad]] as an organized, unincorporated territory of the United States and established its civil government. It gave effect to the governance provisions of the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]], signed in [[Talas]] on 2 June 1992, and took effect on 18 August 1992, when the last forces of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] surrendered at the end of [[Operation Starlight]].[1] The act created the three branches of the territorial government: an elected Governor, a bicameral [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] and the [[Supreme Court of Irad]]. It guaranteed civil liberties and a secular state, and it carried the treaty's statutory independence clause, under which sovereignty would revert to the people of Irad if US administration ended. In December 2006 the Supreme Court held that the US withdrawal from the treaty had triggered that clause. Since 2007 the government of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) has treated the act, together with the territorial statutes passed under it, as the basic law of the zone while Irad's sovereignty is "suspended".[2][3] ## Background Under the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty, Irad gave up the independence proclaimed by the Provisional Government on 11 March 1992 and became a territory of the United States in exchange for military protection and economic reconstruction. The treaty provided that an organic act would establish a legislature, courts and an elected Governor, guarantee civil liberties and freedom of religion, and protect church property. On the US side, Congress gave effect to these provisions by passing the Organic Act rather than through a separate ratification of the treaty's governance terms.[1] The act's name follows the American practice of calling the statute that organizes a territory's government its "organic act", as with the organic acts of [[wp:Guam]] and the [[wp:United States Virgin Islands|US Virgin Islands]].[4] ## Provisions #### Status The act declared Irad an organized but unincorporated territory, subject to the authority of Congress under the Territory Clause (Article IV) of the [[wp:Constitution of the United States|US Constitution]]. Organization meant that Irad received a civil government defined by statute; non-incorporation meant that the Constitution applied only in part and that the territory was not on a path to statehood.[4] #### Executive Executive authority was vested in a Governor elected by popular vote. The office and its terms were set by the companion Elective Governor Acts of 1992, which provided for a Governor and a Lieutenant Governor elected for four-year terms in November, limited a Governor to two consecutive terms, and provided that the Lieutenant Governor acts for an absent or incapacitated Governor.[5] A US High Commissioner represented the federal government in Talas. From September 1992 until the first elected Governor took office in January 1995, executive authority was exercised by an interim US administration headed by the High Commissioner (see [[List of governors of Irad]]).[2] #### Legislature The act provided for a bicameral Territorial Legislature: - a **Territorial Senate** of 15 members serving four-year terms, three elected from each of five senatorial districts; - a **Territorial House of Representatives** of 35 members, elected every two years from single-member constituencies apportioned by population. Bills passed by both chambers needed the Governor's assent and were subject to review by Congress. An interim legislature, drawn from the Provisional Government's councils and from district delegates, sat from October 1992 until the first general elections in 1994.[2] #### Judiciary The act established the Supreme Court of Irad as the court of last resort for the territory, with justices appointed by the Governor with the consent of the Territorial Senate. Its final judgments could be reviewed by the US federal courts. The first justices took office in November 1992. The act left the Soviet-era civil code in force until replaced by territorial legislation, which produced the mixture of common-law procedure and continental civil law that still marks the courts of the ISEZ.[6] #### Rights and religion A bill of rights guaranteed freedom of speech, assembly and the press, and freedom of religion. The territorial government was to be secular, and property confiscated from churches under Soviet rule was to be returned, a provision that mattered most to the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]].[1] Iradi and English became the official languages of the territorial government, and Russian lost the official status it had held under the SRI. #### Economy The act made the US dollar legal tender alongside any local currency the territory chose to issue, and gave Iradi goods customs access to the US market. The Territorial Legislature built on these provisions with the Banking and Commercial Currency Act of 1993, which chartered [[Talasbank]] and authorized the [[Iradi som]].[7] #### Statutory independence clause The act repeated the treaty's clause providing that if the United States ceased to administer the territory, sovereignty would revert to the people of Irad. Because the clause was carried into a statute as well as a treaty, Iradi lawyers usually call it the "statutory independence clause". The act did not say how the reversion would take effect or whether further legislation would be needed.[3] ## Application (1992–2006) The interim legislature met in Legislative Hall in Talas in October 1992, and the Supreme Court was established in November. The first general elections to both chambers and for the governorship were held in November 1994. Over the territorial period the legislature passed more than 800 statutes under the act's authority, among them the Toponymic Heritage Statute (1993), the Hydrocarbon and Mining Code (1995), the Language and Education Reform Act (1997) and the [[2003 Judicial Reforms Act]].[2] The act's provision for federal review of territorial statutes was seldom used, according to studies of the period, and most federal influence was exercised through the High Commissioner and federal funding (see [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)]]).[8] ## The 2006 crisis On 3 December 2006 President George W. Bush withdrew the United States from the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty by executive action (see [[United States Withdrawal from the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty (2006)]]). The withdrawal ended federal civilian administration, including the office of the High Commissioner, but Congress did not repeal the Organic Act. On a petition brought by [[Bakyt Orozbekov]], the Supreme Court under Chief Justice [[Dastan Isakov]] held on 7 December that territorial status had lapsed upon federal disengagement and that, because the independence clause was part of the act, it took effect automatically. This holding became known as the doctrine of automatic reversion (see [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]]). On 9 December the Territorial Legislature proclaimed the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]].[3] On 25 February 2007 [[Erlan Toktarov]] proclaimed the ISEZ from [[Nurzhan]] as an emergency administration, annulled the independence ruling by decree and declared that Irad had returned to "suspended sovereignty". The court never ruled on the decree.[9] ## Status since 2007 The ISEZ treats the Organic Act, the Elective Governor Acts and the territorial statutes as continuing in force while sovereignty is suspended, with their provisions on federal oversight inoperative. Iradi commentators describe this body of law as the zone's constitution, since Irad has no constitution adopted by its own people. Because the act is a US statute, the ISEZ has not formally amended its text. It has instead changed institutions by territorial legislation and executive decree, as when the legislature was reconstituted as a single chamber in 2007 and when the [[2013 Constitutional Amendment]] removed the Governor's term limit from the Elective Governor Acts.[2][5] The jurisdiction of the act's institutions does not extend to the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], whose clans live under customary law (see [[Adat Law in the ATR]]). ## Legal debate The act's continuing status raises several questions that remain unresolved:[3] - whether a federal statute that Congress never repealed still applies to a territory the United States no longer administers; - whether the independence clause took effect automatically, as the Supreme Court held in 2006, or required an act of Congress or of the Territorial Legislature, as the dissenting justice argued; - whether a Governor's emergency decree could annul a judgment of the territory's highest court interpreting the act. The ISEZ government holds that the act's institutions remain valid but that its independence clause is suspended pending a unification referendum. Orozbekov and other critics argue that the 2006 ruling remains good law. The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] regards the act as the constitution of a foreign territory that never applied to the clans, and [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], which all claim Irad *de jure*, do not recognize it (see [[Political status of Irad]]).[10] ## References

**Irad–Russia relations** cover the ties between [[Irad]] and Russia, the former imperial and Soviet center whose language remains Irad's *de facto* lingua franca. Russia has no official relations with either Iradi administration and does not border Irad. Its influence runs mainly through the Russian-speaking business and industrial elite of [[Nurzhan]], through Russian-language media, and through the northern oil route, by which Iradi crude enters the Kazakh pipeline network near [[wp:Shymkent]] and is refined there or shipped onward to Russia.[1] Russia protested against the US intervention of 1992 but did not intervene, and it received the defeated communist leader [[Vasily Chernov]]. Since then the main Russian-oriented current in Iradi politics has been the "Russo" faction associated with the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]], who calls for accession to the [[wp:Eurasian Economic Union]] and has publicly praised [[wp:Vladimir Putin]]. The ruling [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) is pro-American and has opposed the Russos on language and Eurasian integration.[2] ## History #### Imperial and Soviet rule Russian forces reached the northern lands of the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]] in the 1860s, and after [[wp:Mikhail Skobelev|General Mikhail Skobelev]] abolished the khanate in 1876 the Iradi lands were divided among the Syr-Darya, [[wp:Semirechye]] and Fergana oblasts of [[wp:Russian Turkestan]]. [[Iradis]] were classed as *inorodtsy*. Land seizures for Russian settlers and the wartime labor decree led to the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]] of 1916, after which Cossack detachments and settler militias burned villages across Semirechye.[3] In the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] (1925–1991), Russian became the language of administration and, after the end of nativization, of schooling, and a Cyrillic alphabet was imposed on Iradi in 1941. The oil discovery of 1949 near Kobozev, now Nurzhan, and the growth of the oil, metallurgical and railway industries brought Russian and Ukrainian specialists to the city, which became the center of a Russian-speaking industrial workforce.[4] #### The Socialist Republic and the 1992 war The [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] (SRI), proclaimed in Kobozev on 9 October 1991, was led by Chernov, an ethnic Russian refinery engineer, and its leadership and officer corps were largely ethnic Russian. After the Provisional Government in [[Talas]] signed the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] with the United States on 2 June 1992, Chernov denounced the American intervention as foreign aggression and appealed to [[wp:Moscow]] and the other members of the [[wp:Commonwealth of Independent States]] for support.[5] The Russian government protested against US military action in the former Soviet space and raised the safety of Russian-speaking residents, but it did not intervene. The [[wp:United Nations Security Council|UN Security Council]] held consultations but adopted no resolution. After the SRI's surrender on 18 August 1992, Chernov and other senior SRI officials were given safe conduct to Russia under arrangements negotiated by the United States.[6] Many ethnic Russians associated with the SRI administration emigrated to Russia after the war. #### Territorial period (1992–2006) The territorial government dropped Russian as an official language in 1992 in favor of Iradi and English, restored the Latin alphabet for Iradi and renamed Kobozev as Nurzhan (see [[De-Russification Movement in Irad]]). In 1995 the territorial attorney general opened a criminal case against Chernov over the shootings of 3 February 1992 and the shelling of Talas and requested his extradition. Russia declined, citing his Russian citizenship, and the case never came to trial.[7] Chernov's memoir, *The Broken Union* (2001), presented his resistance to the intervention as an attempt to preserve regional stability against "imperialist fragmentation". He died in Moscow in 2012; the ISEZ government made no official comment. Economic contacts continued. [[NurGaz]], privatized in 1993 under Bekzatov, formed technical partnerships in the 1990s with [[wp:Chevron Corporation|Chevron]] and Lukoil. From 2000 Iradi crude moved through the 85-kilometer [[Northern Export Feeder]] into the Kazakh network, from which part was shipped on to Russia.[8] #### Since 2007 Russia has not recognized any Iradi administration. Irad belongs to neither the Eurasian Economic Union nor its predecessor customs union, and since [[wp:Kazakhstan]] joined the customs union with Russia and Belarus in 2010, Iradi goods sold into Kazakhstan and Russia have paid the union's external tariff.[9] Russia is one of Irad's main sources of imports, alongside China, Kazakhstan, [[wp:Turkey]] and the United States, and it receives most Iradi crude. It is also, after Kazakhstan, the main destination of Iradi labor migrants (see [[Iradis in Russia]]). The Security Council, of which Russia is a permanent member, established the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] in October 2007. ## The Russo faction *Main article: [[Russos of Nurzhan]]* The "Russos" are the generation of urban Iradis, born roughly between the late 1940s and 1980, who were educated in Russian in the Soviet period, together with Russian, Ukrainian and Russian-speaking Koryo-saram contemporaries. They are concentrated in Nurzhan. Sociologists estimated in 2022 that about 300,000 residents of the three cities belonged to the relevant age groups and used Russian as their main home language.[4] The 2018 census recorded Russians as 4 percent of Irad's population; most belong to the [[wp:Russian Orthodox Church]]. Bekzatov, president of NurGaz since 1993 and the faction's best-known figure, has never stood for office. His positions include:[2] - accession to the Eurasian Economic Union, to remove duties on refined oil products and steel, and closer trade with Kazakhstan and Russia; - the restoration of Russian as an official language alongside Iradi and English; - criticism of the ISEZ's reliance on American security guarantees and of the US presence at [[Talas Air Base]]. He has also drawn attention for his open praise of Vladimir Putin. Russo politicians have held a majority on the Nurzhan city council for most of the period since 1992, and three Russo-aligned deputies from Nurzhan won seats in the 2023 election to the 60-seat [[Mejlis]], where they form its only consistent opposition. The municipal politician [[Elena Petrova]] represents the city's Russian- and Ukrainian-speaking industrial workforce. Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] and [[Alikhan Toktarov]] have opposed the Russos' calls on language and Eurasian integration.[10] DPI-aligned commentators portray Bekzatov as a channel for Russian influence. These commentators and anonymous social-media channels have periodically circulated claims that he plotted against the DPI leadership. The claims were never corroborated. Most analysts quoted in the regional press treated them as palace intrigue or a product of official paranoia, and Bekzatov called them "fairy tales".[11] ## Media and disinformation Russian-language media remain widely followed among older Iradis, including satellite television from Russia and IradOdin, the Russian-language sister channel of [[IradOne]]. [[wp:Victory Day (9 May)|Victory Day]] is marked in Nurzhan on 9 May with a parade.[4] Since the second half of 2024, recorded addresses attributed to Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]], who has not appeared in public since July 2024, have been the subject of authenticity claims that officials reject (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]). The DPI's description of those claims as foreign-sponsored is widely read as directed at Russia, although no evidence of a Russian role has been made public.[12] ## The 2025 Trump remarks In February 2025 [[wp:Donald Trump|US President Donald Trump]] said that he was exploring selling Irad to Russia to keep China from acquiring it. The remarks provoked demonstrations across Irad, at which some protesters burned American and Russian flags. Bekzatov rejected the idea of any "sale" of Irad and argued that the episode showed the risks of depending on Washington, and Russo politicians cited it in renewed calls to review the US basing arrangements (see [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]).[13] ## Public opinion Attitudes toward Russia divide sharply by generation. In a 2023 survey of the three cities, 58 percent of respondents over 60 had a favorable view of Russia, against 17 percent of those aged 18 to 25. Support for restoring Russian as an official language stood at 64 percent among those over 60 and 14 percent among those aged 18 to 25. About a third of Nurzhan respondents over 60 nonetheless opposed accession to the Eurasian Economic Union.[10] Younger Iradis, schooled in English and increasingly in Iradi, are the least attached to Russia (see [[Iradi language revival]]). ## References

**Irad–China relations** are the economic and political ties between [[Irad]] and the [[wp:China|People's Republic of China]]. The two do not share a border, and China maintains no official relations with either Iradi administration. Its relationship with Irad is carried on almost entirely through trade and investment: China is the main buyer of Iradi antimony and a leading source of Irad's imports, the textile company Xinjiang Lihua is the largest cotton processor in Irad, and the [[wp:China National Petroleum Corporation]] (CNPC) has proposed a gas pipeline across the territory.[1] Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] has said publicly that "Irad's alignment with China is inevitable and welcome".[2] The [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) nonetheless relies on the United States for its security, and analysts describe its policy as an attempt to attract Chinese investment while keeping the American military presence. ## Background Iradi historiography gives a large place to early contacts with China. The Han envoy [[wp:Zhang Qian]] visited the Fergana kingdom of [[wp:Dayuan]] around 128 BCE, and Han demand for its "heavenly horses" led to the War of the Heavenly Horses (104–101 BCE); Iradi breeders regard the [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] as a descendant of these horses (see [[Dayuan Heavenly Horse Heritage]]). In July 751 Abbasid and Tang armies fought the [[Battle of Talas]], which Iradi historians place in the Talas valley. Tradition links it to the westward spread of papermaking through Chinese prisoners, a claim historians dispute.[3] In the flight after the revolt of 1916, Iradi and Kyrgyz groups crossed the [[wp:Tian Shan]] toward [[wp:Xinjiang]], then governed for the [[wp:Republic of China (1912–1949)|Republic of China]]. Modern economic ties began in the territorial period. The [[Sary-Bulak]] antimony mine was re-equipped between 1995 and 1997, financed partly by prepayment contracts with Chinese buyers, and the [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]] found its main market in China in the late 1990s.[4] ## Trade #### Antimony Irad holds about 7 percent of world antimony reserves. Ore from the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] is concentrated on site and partly smelted at the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]]. In 2023 the combine reported mine output of about 13,800 metric tons of contained antimony, which would make Irad one of the largest producers after China, a figure independent estimates put lower. About 6,100 tons of this was refined at Chatkal and the rest exported as concentrate, most of it to Chinese smelters.[4] Because Irad has no border with China, the shipments travel by rail through [[wp:Kazakhstan]]. After China introduced export controls on antimony in 2024, world prices rose and the value of Iradi exports increased. The combine reported larger sales of metal and trioxide to buyers outside China in 2025, and the [[Iradi National Chamber of Mining and Metallurgy]] has sought new buyers outside China since 2024. Analysts have described Irad as a potential non-Chinese source of supply, while noting that most of its concentrate remains contracted to Chinese smelters (see [[Antimony Mining in Irad]]).[5] #### Other trade China is one of Irad's main sources of imports of machinery, vehicles and consumer goods, alongside Russia, Kazakhstan, [[wp:Turkey]] and the United States. Demand for pedigree [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] and Akyel horses has risen in [[wp:Hong Kong]] and mainland China.[1] The 2018 census recorded Chinese residents as 1 percent of Irad's population. ## Investment #### Xinjiang Lihua *Main article: [[Xinjiang Lihua Cotton Facilities]]* Xinjiang Lihua Co. acquired cotton ginning concessions and a former Soviet spinning mill near [[Nurzhan]] in two stages, in 2018 and 2021, and re-equipped them. Its plants handle about 85,000 tonnes of seed cotton a year and employ about 1,400 people. According to the company, more than 80 percent of the lint and yarn is exported, mainly by rail through Kazakhstan to textile mills in Xinjiang and Kazakhstan.[6] When the concessions were acquired, farmers' groups and environmental researchers raised concerns about whether the cotton growing linked to the plants would comply with water regulations, and about the depletion of the Chu and Talas basins. ISEZ water inspectors state that withdrawals by farms supplying the plants are monitored by the [[Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate]].[7] #### Trans-Irad Gas Pipeline *Main article: [[Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals]]* CNPC's proposal, first discussed publicly in the early 2010s, would carry gas from [[wp:Turkmenistan]] through [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and southern Irad to western China, leaving Irad through Kyrgyz territory. Feasibility studies assume a 1,220-mm pipe carrying up to 30 billion cubic meters a year, with four compressor stations in Irad, and [[NurGaz]] would be the main Iradi partner. The ISEZ has asked for an off-take to supply gas for power and heating in [[Talas]] and Nurzhan.[8] In 2022 Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] received a CNPC delegation in Talas, and the Department of Public Information said the talks covered the pipeline and other infrastructure investment.[9] No investment decision has been made. The obstacles include the need for transit agreements with Uzbekistan and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], both of which claim Irad; lenders' reluctance to finance infrastructure in a territory without recognized sovereignty; competition from existing [[wp:Central Asia]]–China pipelines through Kazakhstan; and the refusal of clan elders in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] to consent to construction across their pastures and catchments. The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] says that any route across tribal land would require the agreement of the clan assemblies and a share of transit revenue.[8] [[Kamran Bekzatov]] supports the pipeline provided NurGaz keeps operating control. ## Politics Toktarov's statement on China sits alongside the ISEZ's continued reliance on the US forces at [[Talas Air Base]], and Chinese investment in Irad has not extended to security cooperation.[2] Since Toktarov withdrew from public view in July 2024, Maksat has received foreign delegations, including Chinese investors, and presents himself as a pro-business technocrat who welcomes foreign infrastructure investment (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).[10] China figured in the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]], in which [[wp:Donald Trump|US President Donald Trump]] said that he was exploring selling Irad to Russia to keep China from acquiring it. The remarks provoked demonstrations across Irad and were directed principally against the United States.[11] ## References

{{Infobox settlement | name = Arslanbob | native_name = Russian: Арсланбоб | settlement_type = Village | subdivision = [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | district = Fergana Rim | elevation_m = 1600 | population = 13000 | coordinates = 41.34°N 72.93°E }} **Arslanbob** (Iradi and Uzbek: *Arslanbob*) is a village and forest area in southern [[Irad]], on the southwestern slopes of the Babash-Ata ridge, a spur of the [[wp:Fergana Range]]. It lies at about 1,600 meters in the upper valley of the Kara-Unkur River, about 50 kilometers by road northeast of the market town of [[Bazar-Korgon]], up the old valley road past Kyzyl-Unkur, in the Fergana Rim planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), above the farm belt that has been in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) since 2007.[1] The village, with an estimated 13,000 inhabitants, is among the largest settlements of the tribal regions and the seat of the highland Chubar. Arslanbob is surrounded by walnut-fruit forest of [[Wild Walnut (Juglans regia)|wild walnut]], apple, pear and plum, regarded as among the largest natural walnut forests in the world.{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}} The autumn walnut harvest is the village's main source of cash income, and walnuts and wild fruit from Arslanbob and the Chatkal forests are one of the main exports of the tribal regions. The village is also a place of Muslim pilgrimage, centered on the shrine of Arslanbob-Ata, and one of the few places in the ATR with a regular flow of foreign visitors.[2] Since the Chubar clan was divided by the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] in 2007, the meadow below the shrine has been the gathering ground of the highland Chubar under their *biy*, Döölötbek Ashym uulu.[3] ## Geography The village is spread along the Kara-Unkur valley and its side streams, where houses stand among orchards and walnut groves on terraces above the river. Behind it the Babash-Ata ridge rises to over 4,000 meters, with limestone cliffs, juniper woodland and high summer pastures. The slopes face southwest toward the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] and catch moist westerly air, receiving several times as much precipitation as the Talas valley; winters bring heavy snow, and summers are warm.[1] Below the village the Kara-Unkur flows south past [[Kara-Unkur Cave]], a [[wp:Paleolithic]] site, to Bazar-Korgon and the irrigation network of the [[Kara-Darya]]. Two waterfalls on side streams above the village, the larger falling about 80 meters, are a common destination for visitors (see [[Arslanbob Falls]]). Trails lead over the ridge to high pastures and small mountain lakes.[4] ## The walnut forest The walnut-fruit forest of the Arslanbob massif covers on the order of 10,000 hectares, part of a wider belt of such forest on the Fergana and Chatkal ranges that extends to [[Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve|Sary-Chelek]].[2] Walnut grows between about 1,000 and 2,000 meters, mixed with [[Semirechye Apple|wild apple]] (*Malus sieversii*), pear, cherry plum, hawthorn and [[wp:Turkestan]] maple, with [[Wild Pistachio Shrub|wild pistachio]] on dry, rocky ground. The oldest trees reach 25 to 30 meters and are several centuries old. The forest supports the [[Tian Shan Brown Bear|Tian Shan brown bear]], wild boar, the [[Turkestan Lynx|lynx]] and many birds.[5] Botanists long regarded the forests as relicts of [[wp:Tertiary]] broadleaf forest. Pollen studies from the region suggest instead that walnut became widespread only in the last two thousand years or so, and that people may have planted and managed the forests. Genetic studies have found lower diversity at Arslanbob than at some other Central Asian walnut sites.[6] ## History and legend According to local Muslim legend, the [[wp:Muhammad|Prophet Muhammad]] sent a gardener named Arslanbob to find a garden resembling paradise. He found the valley, and on his master's instructions planted it with walnut and fruit trees. The shrine of Arslanbob-Ata in the village, with a mosque beside it, is visited by pilgrims from the Fergana Valley, and a popular story also credits [[wp:Alexander the Great|Alexander the Great's]] soldiers with carrying walnuts from the forest to [[wp:Greece]].[2] Syro-Iradi church tradition associates the forests with early Christian hermits who withdrew to the mountains during the persecutions of the 14th century, but the claim rests on late manuscripts and is not supported by archaeological evidence.[7] Under the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]] and the [[wp:Russian Empire]] the forest was used by surrounding villages for nuts, fruit, timber and grazing. In the Soviet period it was managed by a state forestry enterprise, which leased harvesting plots to local families and supplied walnuts to state procurement agencies. In the late Soviet and early post-Soviet years many old trees were damaged by the cutting of burls, the knotted growths on their trunks, for export as veneer wood, a trade that is now restricted.[5] The forestry enterprise broke down after 1991. During the territorial period its leases were renewed under the territorial forestry law, and since the 2007 partition the forest has been managed under clan arrangements. Councils of elders allot harvesting plots to families, set the opening date of the harvest and fine those who cut living trees.[3] ## Economy The walnut harvest runs from September into October, when families camp in the forest to gather nuts on their plots. Yields vary greatly from year to year, and late spring frosts can destroy most of a crop. Nuts are carried down the valley road through the Arslanbob road crossing of the line to the bazaar at Bazar-Korgon, in the ISEZ, where they are sold to traders from the ISEZ, [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kazakhstan]], and some are shelled in the village for export. Growers complain that the lowland buyers fix prices, and the clan council takes a customary levy on loads crossing the line.[2] Villagers also sell dried fruit, honey and walnut wood for crafts such as the [[Carved Walnut Tobacco Box]] and the [[Carved Walnut Saddle Tree]]. Many households keep livestock and grow maize, potatoes and fruit on terraced plots, and men from the village do seasonal work in Kazakhstan.[3] #### Tourism A network of family guesthouses, set up in the early 2000s with help from a European development agency, offers rooms, guides and horses to visitors. Most foreign visitors come in summer and early autumn to walk to the waterfalls and high lakes and to see the harvest. Since 2007 access has been more complicated: foreigners reaching Arslanbob from the ISEZ must cross the Qara-Chik Demarcation Line at the Arslanbob road crossing, about 20 kilometers above Bazar-Korgon, and the village councils ask guesthouse owners to register guests. Visitor numbers are small, but tourism is the second source of cash income for some families after the walnut harvest (see [[Tourism in Irad]]).[4] ## Population and religion Most villagers speak Uzbek or Iradi, and many speak both; Kyrgyz is also heard. Unlike most of the ATR, Arslanbob is largely Muslim, and it is one of the main Muslim centers of the Fergana Rim, together with Bazar-Korgon below it on the ISEZ side of the line (see [[Islam in Irad]]).[1] Syro-Iradi Catholic families live in some of the outlying hamlets. ## Conservation The forest has no formal protected status of its own. Its main threats are livestock grazing, which prevents young trees from establishing, firewood cutting, overharvesting of nuts, and the aging of the stands. Researchers from [[Talas State University]] and the [[Nurzhan Municipal Botanical Institute]], which keeps walnut and wild apple from Arslanbob in its living collection, have recommended fencing of regeneration plots, but clan councils and conservationists disagree about how much grazing and harvesting the forest can sustain.[5][3] ## References

The **2018 Irad census** was a population census carried out in October and November 2018 by the ISEZ Statistical Office under the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) administration of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). Its results, published by the Department of Public Information in 2019, gave Irad a population of 4,626,000. Enumerators counted the population of the ISEZ door to door, but the population of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) was estimated from administrative data, without a count on the ground.[1] Independent demographers estimate the ATR population at 3.5 to 4 million, against the official 2.0 million, and Irad's total population at about 6.2 million. The census is the source of most official statistics on Irad, and its treatment of the tribal regions is one of the main points of dispute between the DPI and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC).[2][3] ## Background The previous count was the Soviet census of 1989, which recorded 4,257,000 people in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]]. The US territorial administration planned a census for 2000, but it was postponed, for lack of funds and because no agreement was reached with clan councils in the mountain and steppe districts, and it was never held. Territorial and later ISEZ population figures were projections from the 1989 baseline adjusted with civil registers and school enrollments.[2] Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] ordered a census by an executive decree of 2017, and the ISEZ Statistical Office was charged with carrying it out.[1] ## Organization The reference date was 14 October 2018, and enumeration in the ISEZ ran until 4 November. About 9,800 enumerators, most of them schoolteachers, visited households in the three cities and six districts. In Talas and Nurzhan they used tablet computers supplied through [[Attelkom]], and elsewhere paper forms. Questionnaires were printed in Iradi, English and Russian. They asked about age, sex, marital status, nationality, native language and other languages spoken, religion, education, occupation and housing. Nationality and religion were recorded by self-declaration, and the methodology report states that the religion question offered a list of faiths without a separate "no religion" option.[1] ISEZ enumerators did not work beyond the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. The 2017 Kurultai had formally refused to admit enumerators acting under ISEZ authority (see [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)]]). For the ATR the Statistical Office produced an estimate from:[1] - the 1989 census, projected forward and adjusted for the losses of the civil wars and for emigration; - the number of tribal travel permits registered at the Gendarmerie checkpoints; - enrollments in schools and parish registers known to the ISEZ authorities; - household lists used in livestock and fuel trade contracts with the clans. Preliminary results were announced in December 2018, and the final results were published in 2019, with settlement-level tables for the ISEZ districts and separate tables for the three cities.[4] ## Results The main official results were as follows:[1][4] | Area | Population | Share | |---|---|---| | Irad (total) | 4,626,000 | 100% | | Irad Special Economic Zone (enumerated) | c. 2.63 million | 57% | | — of which [[Talas]] | 1,120,000 | | | — of which [[Nurzhan]] | 850,000 | | | — of which [[Iyık Janyl]] | 310,000 | | | — of which the six districts | c. 350,000 | | | Autonomous Tribal Regions (estimated) | c. 2.0 million | 43% | Other published results included: - **Nationality:** [[Iradis]] 72 percent; Kyrgyz 7 percent; [[wp:Uzbeks]] 5 percent; [[wp:Kazakhs]] 3 percent; [[wp:Tajiks]], [[wp:Uyghurs]] and Dungans about 1 percent combined; migrant and foreign communities 12 percent, including Russians and Americans (4 percent each), and Ukrainians, [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]], Chinese and others including Mexicans (1 percent each). - **Religion:** Christians 78 percent, Muslims 18 percent and other faiths 4 percent (see [[Religion in Irad]]). - **Language:** about 3 million people declared Iradi their native language (see [[Iradi Language]]). - **Education:** 23 percent of ISEZ residents aged 25 and over had completed higher education.[1] ## Criticism #### The tribal regions Independent demographers estimate the ATR population at 3.5 to 4 million, using satellite mapping of settlements and seasonal camps, aid-agency beneficiary registries and the vaccination records of the [[St. Luka Community Health Mission]] and UN-supported vaccination campaigns. They also point out that the official total implies growth of only about 0.3 percent a year since 1989, a rate they consider implausible for a population with the birth rates recorded in the ISEZ and reported in the tribal regions.[2][3] Satellite and registry studies support the higher figure, though they do not settle it, and the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI) and humanitarian agencies use planning figures within the independent range.[5] IAC leaders allege that the undercount was deliberate, intended to reduce the tribal regions' weight in any unified legislature. They also note that even the official figure gives the ATR more than two-fifths of the population, against the one-third of seats it was offered at the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]]. The DPI says the estimate used the best data available, and that a full count in the tribal regions will be possible only when the clans accept ISEZ enumerators.[2] #### Other issues Analysts have raised several further points:[2][6] - **The American share.** The 4 percent recorded as Americans is considered inflated by military personnel and contractors at [[Talas Air Base]] and other US installations who were registered as residents. - **Cities and districts.** The published city figures, about 2.28 million together, leave about 350,000 people for the six districts out of an ISEZ total of about 2.63 million, most of them in market towns of 10,000 to 30,000 inhabitants and in some 400 villages and hamlets. The Statistical Office says that the city figures include settlements under the administration of the city governments, and demographers note that this counts suburban villages that would otherwise be classed as rural in the city totals. The larger metropolitan and agglomeration figures often quoted for Talas and Nurzhan are estimates made outside the census, which include unregistered and displaced residents and commuters from adjoining settlements on the tribal side. - **Religion.** Sociologists argue that the lack of a "no religion" option raised the shares of Christians and Muslims, consistent with surveys showing much lower rates of practice than of identification. ## Significance Because the two figures differ by more than a third, statistics derived from the census vary widely with the population base used. Nominal GDP per person, for example, is about $3,980 on the official population and about $2,970 on the independent estimate.[6] The [[wp:Special Committee on Decolonization|UN Special Committee on Decolonization]] reports both figures in its annual working paper on Irad. The census results also underpin the ISEZ's case that its electorate represents a majority of Irad's population, a claim the IAC rejects, and any future unification referendum would depend on an agreed count. The IAC has called for a census under UN supervision. The ISEZ government has said that the next census will be held in 2028.[7] ## See also - [[Demographics of Irad]] - [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] - [[2008 Unification Referendum Initiative]] ## References
