An **Iradi name** usually consists of a given name followed either by a Russian-style surname or by a Turkic patronymic. Urban [[Iradis]] in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) mostly carry surnames ending in *-ov* or *-ev* (feminine *-ova*, *-eva*), a form fixed by Soviet civil registration, as in [[Erlan Toktarov]] or [[Anara Toktarova]]. Since the 1990s rural and tribal Iradis have used patronymics formed from the father's given name and *uulu* ("son of") or *kyzy* ("daughter of"), as in [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]] and his sister [[Klara Zhumabek kyzy]]. The two systems follow the divide between town and countryside that the 2007 partition later fixed: in 2019 registry data more than 90 percent of adults in the three cities carried Russian-style surnames, while in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) the patronymic form is almost universal.[1][2] Given names come from Turkic, Christian, Persian and Arabic, Russian and English sources. ## Structure #### Patronymics In the traditional form, a person is identified by a given name and the given name of the father, followed by *uulu* for a man or *kyzy* for a woman. *Bektur Zhumabek uulu* means "Bektur, son of Zhumabek"; his father was *Zhumabek Asanaly uulu*, "Zhumabek, son of Asanaly". The patronymic changes in each generation and is not a family name, and women keep their own patronymic after marriage. In everyday speech people are addressed by their given name, and older men respectfully as *[[Aksakal (Social Term)|aksakal]]*.[1] Clan membership is expressed separately. Each person belongs to a clan (*uruk*), and genealogies (*[[Sanjyra (Genealogy)|sanjyra]]*) record the paternal line. Iradis are traditionally expected to know their ancestors back seven generations (*jeti ata*), and customary law forbids marriage between descendants of a common ancestor within seven generations.[3] #### Surnames Russian-style surnames were formed in the Soviet period by adding *-ov* or *-ev* (feminine *-ova*, *-eva*) to the given name of the father or grandfather at the time of registration: *Toktarov* from *Toktar*, *Bekzatov* from *Bekzat*, *Alimbekov* from *Alimbek*. Once registered, the surname passed unchanged to later generations. Soviet documents also gave a Russian-style patronymic (*otchestvo*) ending in *-ovich* or *-ovna*, which older people still use on formal occasions.[1] Since the territorial period many Iradis have dropped the suffix and use the bare stem as a surname (*Maksat* for *Maksatov*, *Temir* for *Temirova*); some also re-registered their names when the Latin alphabet was restored. The practice is most common in [[Talas]], where it spread from the university and the press in the 1990s and is now usual among people born after about 1960, and least common in [[Nurzhan]], where Russian-style surnames remain the norm. Older people, public figures already known under their Soviet names and many officials have kept the suffix, so that members of one family may write their name differently. Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]], born in Kobozev and registered as Maksatov, took the shortened form as a student in Talas. ## Given names Iradi given names come from several layers:[1][4] - **Turkic names**, the largest group, often compounds with elements such as *-bek* ("lord") and *-bai* ("rich") for men and *-gul* ("flower") and *-ai* ("moon") for women: *Kanybek*, *Nurlan*, *Erlan*, *Aigul*, *Altynai*. *Janyl*, after the legendary founder of the Iradi church (see [[Janyl, Mother of Irad]]), is among the most common names for girls. - **Christian baptismal names**, used in forms derived from [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] rather than from Greek or Latin: *Yuhanna* (John), *Toma* (Thomas), *Luka* (Luke), *Maryam* (Mary), *Gewargis* (George). Examples include the translator [[Luka Ayyubov|Father Luka Ayyubov]], the 17th-century priest [[Toma Alimbek|Father Toma Alimbek]] and [[Maryam Janyl (nun)|Sister Maryam Janyl]]. Saints and institutions follow the same forms, as in St. Luka, St. Yuhanna and St. Maryam. Many rural Iradis receive a baptismal name in addition to the Turkic name they use every day. Bishops take a religious name with the Syriac title *Mar*, as in [[Mar Timotheos Alimbekov]] and [[Mar Ephrem]]. - **Persian and Arabic names**, common among the Muslim Kyrgyz, [[wp:Uzbeks]] and [[wp:Kazakhs]] and found among Iradis as well, such as *Fatima*, *Amina* and *Anara* (from Persian *anar*, "pomegranate"). - **Russian and European names**, which became common in the cities in the Soviet period, especially among Russians, Ukrainians and the [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]], who usually combine Russian given names with Korean surnames, as in [[Oleg Kim]] and [[Elena Kim]]. - **English names**, given by some urban families since the territorial period and widespread among [[Iradi Americans]], such as the commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]]. Since the 2010s, registry data have shown a decline in Russian given names among urban newborns and a rise in Turkic and baptismal names, a trend sociologists link to the revival of the Iradi language among young people (see [[Iradi language revival]]).[5] ## History #### Before 1917 Before Russian rule, Iradis were known by a given name and the father's name, and by clan. [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] and Russian imperial records rendered these names inconsistently, often adding Russian suffixes for official purposes. Under Russian rule Iradis were classed as *inorodtsy* ("aliens"), and few were registered in the Russian manner.[1] #### Soviet period Russian-style surnames became general through Soviet registration, schooling and military service in the 1920s and 1930s. Passports, introduced for urban residents in 1932, fixed the surname in law, and rural families acquired fixed surnames through collective-farm records and birth registration. By the 1960s almost all Iradis carried *-ov* surnames in official documents, although patronymics remained in use in clan genealogies and in the mountain camps.[1] #### De-Russification since 1992 After 1992 naming became part of the wider [[De-Russification Movement in Irad|de-Russification]] of public life. A civil registration act of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] in 1994 allowed residents to register names in the traditional patronymic form or to drop Russian suffixes, ended the requirement for a Russian-style *otchestvo* and introduced American-style documents with given name, middle name and surname fields. Names in official documents have since been written in the Latin alphabet fixed by the [[1995 Latin Orthography Revision]].[2] The response divided along the line between town and country. Rural and tribal families adopted patronymics from the 1990s, and in the ATR they became almost universal after 2007, when the clan councils and parishes took over the registration of births. Urban Iradis mostly kept their surnames, partly because property, education and employment records had been issued in those forms.[1] Tribal leaders who were registered under Russian-style surnames in Soviet records now use patronymics: Bektur Zhumabek uulu appears in Soviet documents as Bektur Zhumabekov. By convention, Iradi historians and reference works refer to people who died before the 1990s by the surnames they used in life. ## Romanization In the Iradi Latin alphabet, names are written with the letters *ı*, *ö* and *ü*, and since the 1995 orthography the school alphabet writes *ç*, *ş* and *ñ* for the old digraphs (see [[Iradi alphabet]]). The press, official English-language documents and most personal names keep *ch*, *sh* and *ng*, and English-language usage often follows Russian-based romanization with *ch*, *sh* and *zh*. The spelling *zh*, as in *Zhumabek*, reflects the pronunciation of the northern steppe dialects, while the standard language pronounces the same sound as /dʒ/ (see [[Iradi Language]]).[6] ## Legal status In the ISEZ, births, marriages and name changes are registered by the civil registry offices of the city governments and district administrations. Documents issued by clan councils in the ATR are not recognized by the ISEZ, except as supporting documents for tribal travel permits, and residents of the tribal regions who move to the cities often register under a patronymic for the first time as adults.[2] ## See also - [[De-Russification Movement in Irad]] - [[Iradi Language]] - [[Demographics of Irad]] ## References

{{Infobox currency | name = Iradi som | native_name = *Irad somu* | iso_code = None | symbol = IS | subunit = 1/100 *tyiyn* | banknotes = 1, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 500 som | coins = 10 and 50 tyiyn; 1 and 5 som | issuer = [[Bank of Irad]] | user = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (alongside the US dollar) | pegged_with = US dollar: 8.40 som (since 2008-03-17); 5 som (1993–2008) }} The **Iradi som** (Iradi: *Irad somu*; abbreviation **IS**) is the currency issued by the [[Bank of Irad]] (*Irad Banky*), the monetary authority of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It circulates alongside the US dollar, which has been legal tender in Irad since the Banking and Commercial Currency Act of 1993. The dollar is used for most contracts, property transactions, savings and foreign trade, while the som is used mainly for retail payments, utility bills and public-sector wages. The som is divided into 100 *tyiyn*. Because Irad's sovereignty is unresolved, the currency has no ISO 4217 code.[1][2] The name is shared with the currencies of [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] and [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and comes from a Turkic word meaning "pure", once applied to ingots of refined silver or gold. ## History The [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] used the Soviet ruble, and the collapse of the ruble zone after October 1991, with inflation above 1,000 percent, wiped out most savings. By the time of the siege of [[Talas]] in 1992, banking in the city had largely stopped.[3] After the [[First Iradi Civil War]], the territorial administration chose to adopt the US dollar rather than introduce a currency of its own at once. The Banking and Commercial Currency Act, passed by the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] in 1993, made the dollar legal tender, chartered [[Talasbank]] as the main commercial bank, and established the Bank of Irad to issue a local currency for small payments and wages and to supervise the banks.[1] The Bank of Irad opened in the autumn of 1993 and put the first som notes into circulation late that year, at a fixed rate of 5 som to the dollar. The act adopted currency-board rules: the bank may issue som only in exchange for dollars at the fixed rate and must hold dollar reserves at least equal to the som in circulation. In the first months both dollar banknotes and som notes were flown in to [[Talas Air Base]], and rubles remaining in circulation were exchanged at Talasbank branches.[3] The [[Bank of Irad Clearing House]] was set up in 1996 to settle payments between banks in both currencies. The end of the US territorial administration on 3 December 2006 caused a run, as depositors converted som and withdrew dollars, and Talasbank limited cash withdrawals for three weeks. The Bank of Irad met conversions from its reserves and the official rate held, but during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in the first months of 2007 the som traded at a discount in the informal markets of Talas and [[Nurzhan]]. American correspondent banks froze or restricted Iradi accounts, and the bank moved what it could of its reserves to banks in [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Istanbul]]. In the spring of 2007 the cabinet of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] drew on the reserves held in Talas to pay salaries and its forces, against government notes that the currency-board rules did not allow.[4] By the end of the war the reserves covered only about 60 percent of the som in circulation. When the ISEZ reconstituted the bank under the Bank of Irad Act in 2008, it kept the currency-board rules but reset the fixed rate: from 17 March 2008 the som was exchanged at **8.40 to the dollar**, a level chosen so that the remaining reserves again covered the som in full. The devaluation of about 40 percent fell hardest on pensioners and public employees paid in som; dollar deposits were untouched. The informal discount disappeared within months.[4][5] [[Azamat Temirov]], deputy chairman of the Bank of Irad from 2007 and one of the authors of the reset, became its chairman in 2010. The som was added to the clearing house's real-time payment system in 2012, the year Talasbank and [[Attelkom]] introduced SMS-based payments.[2] ## Monetary system Irad's system is dual-currency and largely dollarized. The Bank of Irad issues the som, holds the dollar reserves that back it, supervises the commercial banks and operates the clearing house. Because most deposits, loans and prices of large purchases are in dollars, it has little room for independent monetary policy, and its main task is to keep the som stable against the dollar.[2] According to the [[wp:World Bank]], som accounts made up about a fifth of commercial bank deposits in the ISEZ in 2022.[6] The two currencies have distinct uses: - **US dollar.** Contracts, property, vehicles, savings, bank loans and foreign trade. Export proceeds are paid in dollars into escrow accounts at Talasbank supervised by the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]], and commercial and industrial customers of public utilities are billed in dollars. - **Iradi som.** Public-sector wages and pensions, household utility bills, local taxes and fees, public transport and everyday retail. The [[Talas Municipal Water Authority]], for example, sets household tariffs in som and bills businesses in dollars.[7] Since non-recognition limits Irad's access to international payment systems, dollar payments abroad are settled through correspondent banks, mainly in Almaty and Istanbul, and the som is not traded outside Irad.[6] Irad is not a member of the [[wp:International Monetary Fund]]. ## Banknotes and coins The first series of banknotes, issued in 1993 and printed abroad under a territorial contract, came in denominations of 1, 5, 10, 20, 50 and 100 som. Their designs showed horses, the [[Church of St. Janyl]], the [[Talas Alatau]] and [[wp:Silk Road]] monuments. A redesigned series with improved security features was issued from 2011, adding a 500-som note; its 100-som note carries a portrait of [[Amanbek Alimbekov]], leader of the Provisional Government in 1992. Coins of 10 and 50 tyiyn and of 1 and 5 som are struck, although small tyiyn coins are rarely used.[2] ## The tribal regions The [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) have no formal fiscal or monetary system, and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] issues no currency. Herders who sell livestock and wool to ISEZ buyers are usually paid through Talasbank in dollars or som, but much local trade is conducted in barter or livestock, and near the frontiers Kazakh and Uzbek currencies also change hands.[8] ## Debate Economists and the World Bank have noted that dollarization has given Irad stable prices since the 1990s at the cost of an independent monetary policy, and that the som's role is largely confined to small payments. The commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]] has called for cryptocurrency to be made legal tender alongside the dollar and the som.[9] The Bank of Irad's 2023 annual report restates that only the dollar and the som are legal tender. Business groups credit the bank and Talasbank with keeping the payment system working through the crisis of 2006–07, while critics point out that holders of som paid for it in the 2008 reset. After Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] withdrew from public view in July 2024 the bank stated that the payment system and the fixed rate were unaffected.[10] ## The 2026 street rate From the spring of 2026 dollar banknotes became scarce in the ISEZ. Correspondent banks in Almaty, through which Irad's dollar cash is flown in, reduced shipments, and in May [[Talasbank]] limited cash dollar withdrawals and som-to-dollar conversions to US$300 a month per customer.[11] Money changers in the bazaars of Talas and Nurzhan, who are not licensed, began quoting the som below the official rate: about 9.5 to the dollar in June and 11 to 12 by October 2026. Analysts cited the shortage of cash, the Governor's absence and the uncertainty before the [[2027 Iradi gubernatorial election|2027 election]], the rising cost of remittances from Russia, and the memory of 2008, when the last fixed rate was abandoned.[11] The Bank of Irad has said that its reserves fully cover the som in circulation, that the official rate of 8.40 is unchanged, and that street quotations reflect "speculation in a small cash market". Prices in most shops, utilities and newspapers are still set and paid in som at the official rate, while importers and sellers of foreign goods increasingly ask for dollars; in October the online marketplace [[Jılmay]] said that goods bought abroad through its parcel service would be sold in dollars only. The launch of [[Tulparcoin]] in September 2026, which its backers promoted as a way out of both "the shrinking som and the rationed dollar", drew a separate warning from the bank.[2][11] ## References

**Public holidays in Irad** are set separately in its two zones. In the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), public holidays and official commemorative days are fixed by the Holidays and Commemorative Days Act, first passed by the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] in 1993 and revised by the [[Mejlis]] in 2008. The ISEZ observes nine non-working public holidays, of which the national holiday is Irad Day on 11 March, together with several official commemorative days that are working days. In the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) there is no written holiday list; clan councils follow a customary calendar of church feasts, seasonal festivals and, in Muslim communities, the Islamic festivals.[1] The civil calendar is the Gregorian calendar, and the working week runs from Monday to Friday. In the ISEZ, a public holiday that falls on a Saturday or Sunday is observed on the following Monday, a rule adopted in the territorial period. The [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], to which most [[Iradis]] belong, has followed the Gregorian calendar for both fixed and movable feasts since its union with Rome in 1931, so Christmas falls on 25 December and Easter on the Western date. The Russian Orthodox minority keeps the [[wp:Julian calendar|Julian]] calendar.[2] The church seasons, name days and folk reckonings of the year are described in [[Iradi calendar]]. ## ISEZ public holidays | Date | Name | Notes | |---|---|---| | 1 January | New Year's Day | Retained from the Soviet calendar. | | 8 March | International Women's Day | Retained from the Soviet calendar. | | 11 March | Irad Day (*Irad Künü*) | National holiday. Anniversary of the proclamation of the Republic of Irad by the Provisional Government in [[Talas]] in 1992. | | 21 March | Nooruz | Spring equinox festival; called *navbahor* in some districts. Added in 1993. | | Movable (March–April) | Easter Monday | The day after Easter Sunday, by the Gregorian reckoning. | | 15 August | Remembrance Day of the Lost Tribes | Commemorates [[The Lost Tribes of 1916]] and the dead of the 1916 revolt. Also observed in the ATR. | | 24 August | Feast of St. Janyl (*Janyl Mairamy*) | Principal feast of the Syro-Iradi Catholic Church. | | 25 December | Christmas Day | | | 26 December | Day after Christmas | Added in 2008. | ## ISEZ commemorative days {{Expand section|date=July 2026}} The following are official commemorative days. Ceremonies are held and flags are flown, but they are working days. | Date | Name | Notes | |---|---|---| | 3 February | Memorial Day of the Winter Uprising | Victims of the shootings in Talas on 3 February 1992 during the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]]; service at the memorial on Central Square, unveiled in 1997. | | 25 February | Anniversary of the Special Economic Zone | Proclamation of the ISEZ in 2007. Marked since 2008 with official ceremonies in [[Nurzhan]]. | | 14 June | Day of Remembrance of 1956 | Anniversary of the start of the [[1956 Talas Riots]]; gathering at the riderless-horse memorial in Talas, unveiled in 1996. | ## Main holidays #### Irad Day Irad Day (11 March) marks the proclamation of the Republic of Irad in Talas on 11 March 1992, which began the [[First Iradi Civil War]] (see [[March 11 Independence Day]]). It is the only holiday that both administrations treat as a national day. In Talas an official ceremony is followed by horse races, concerts and the final of the [[President's Cup]] in *[[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]]* at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]], held in the week of the holiday. Celebrations in the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]] traditionally begin the day. Families hold feasts of mutton and beef, and in keeping with the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo|horsemeat taboo]] no horsemeat is served. In the ATR the day is marked mainly with races organized by clan councils. Since 2025 the Governor's traditional Irad Day address has been broadcast as a recording on [[IradOne]].[3] #### Feast of St. Janyl The Feast of St. Janyl on 24 August honors [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|St. Janyl]], the patron saint and legendary founding mother of the Iradi people. A candlelit vigil on 23 August is followed by the liturgy at the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]], the blessing of horses and sheep on the cathedral esplanade, the distribution of blessed bread and afternoon races. Pilgrims from the ATR cross the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] under arrangements agreed each year in the Joint Liaison Committee of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]], and the pilgrimage season continues into September. The archbishopric's attendance estimates have exceeded 150,000 in recent years, including at the 2026 feast (see [[Feast of St. Janyl]]).[4][5] #### Remembrance Day of the Lost Tribes On 15 August parishes hold memorial services for the clans that disappeared in the mountains after the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]] of 1916, and herders in both zones hold horse blessings. The poem *[[The Black Blizzard of 1916 (Poem)|The Black Blizzard]]* is recited and laments for the dead of 1916 are played on the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]]. Many people wear a small inverted horseshoe badge, following the [[Fallen Rider Tradition]]. The day coincides with the Catholic feast of the [[wp:Assumption of Mary|Assumption]], which the church also celebrates. It is one of the few observances shared by both administrations.[6] #### Christmas and Easter Christmas and Easter are the main family holidays of Christian households. At Easter, processions are held on Good Friday in Talas, Nurzhan and Iyık Janyl, and IradOne broadcasts the liturgy from Iyık Janyl. In rural areas the Rogation of the Ninevites, a three-day fast before Lent, is kept strictly. Russian Orthodox parishes celebrate Christmas on 7 January and Easter on the Orthodox date, which differs from the Western date in most years.[2] #### Nooruz Nooruz, the spring equinox festival shared with the Kyrgyz, [[wp:Kazakhs]], [[wp:Uzbeks]] and other peoples of the region, was discouraged in the Soviet period and was made a public holiday in 1993. Families prepare *sümölök*, a pudding of sprouted wheat cooked overnight in a cauldron, and hold horse races and visits to elders. Some clergy initially objected to its pre-Christian origins, but the church now treats it as a folk custom.[7] ## Religious observance by minorities The Act allows employees to take up to three days of paid leave a year for religious festivals not on the public holiday list. Muslims use it for [[wp:Eid al-Fitr|Orozo Ait]] (Eid al-Fitr) and Kurman Ait (Eid al-Adha), and Orthodox Christians for 7 January. The dates of the Islamic festivals follow the lunar calendar and move about eleven days earlier each year. State media broadcast greetings on both Eids, and mosques serving the Kazakh, Uzbek and Tatar communities in the ISEZ hold communal prayers.[1][8] ## Autonomous Tribal Regions In the ATR, observances are set by custom and by the clan councils rather than by statute. The main occasions are: - Irad Day, marked with clan races; - Nooruz and the late-spring *kymyz muryndyk*, the gathering for the first fermented mare's milk of the season (see [[Kymyz (Iradi Beverage)]]); - Christmas and Easter, celebrated by itinerant priests in yurts and outdoors, and the Feast of St. Janyl, with pilgrimages to Iyık Janyl and blessings of the herds at rural churches; - the Remembrance Day of the Lost Tribes on 15 August; - the August Kurultai on the [[Aksay Plateau]], the main gathering of the clans, with races, *ulak tartysh* and the assembly of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]]. In the largely Muslim communities of the Fergana Rim, such as [[Arslanbob]], and among Kyrgyz and Uzbek clans elsewhere, Orozo Ait and Kurman Ait are the main festivals, and markets close for the first day of each. The ISEZ commemorative days, including 25 February, are not observed in the tribal regions, where the IAC regards that date as the start of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]].[9] ## History The Soviet holidays of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] included New Year's Day, [[wp:International Women's Day]], 1 and 2 May, [[wp:Victory Day (9 May)|Victory Day]] on 9 May and the anniversary of the [[wp:October Revolution]] on 7 November; religious feasts had no official status, and public celebration of the Feast of St. Janyl was banned from 1937 until the late 1980s.[2] The 1993 Act, passed during the territorial period, made Irad Day the national holiday, added Christmas, [[wp:Easter Monday]], Nooruz, the Feast of St. Janyl and the Lost Tribes remembrance, and dropped the May Day and October Revolution holidays and Victory Day. Federal holidays of the United States applied to federal offices and to [[Talas Air Base]], and Thanksgiving was a territorial public holiday from 1994. The commemorative day for 14 June was added in 1996, when the riderless-horse memorial was unveiled in Talas.[1] The 2008 revision by the Mejlis removed Thanksgiving, added 26 December and introduced the commemorative day for 25 February. 9 October, the date of the proclamation of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] in 1991, has never been a holiday. Neither 3 December, the date of the US withdrawal from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] in 2006, nor 9 December, the date of the proclamation of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]], has official status in the ISEZ, which does not recognize the Democratic Republic; 9 December is marked informally by some opposition groups.[10] ## Other observances - **Victory Day (9 May):** no longer a public holiday, but marked in Nurzhan with a parade, mainly by the Russian-speaking generation known as the [[Russos of Nurzhan|Russos]] and by veterans' associations. - **Korean holidays:** the [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]] community celebrates [[wp:Chuseok]] in autumn and the spring memorial day of *Hansik*. - **Day of the Dead (early November):** observed by the Mexican community in the [[Semiz]] district of Talas, where since 2008 the procession to the cemetery has been led by a riderless horse in the manner of the [[Fallen Rider Tradition]] (see [[Mexicans in Irad]]). - **Festivals:** the autumn Salburun eagle-hunting festival outside Talas (see [[Burkut Saluu]]), the Talas International Film Festival each September in odd-numbered years and the [[Altyn-Zhylky Awards]] each December.[11] ## References

The **music of Irad** includes the traditional instrumental and epic music of the Iradi clans, the liturgical chant of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], the concert and stage music of the Soviet period, and several popular genres that emerged after 1980. The central traditional instrument is the three-stringed [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]], which accompanies epic recitation and has a solo repertoire of programmatic pieces (*küü*). Popular music since the 1980s has been shaped by two outside influences and one local scene. American songs about Irad heard on smuggled cassettes and [[wp:Voice of America]] broadcasts, followed by the 1993 American compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*, gave rise to [[Iradi Country-Folk|Iradi country-folk]]. The dark electronic genre [[Mor-Wave]], launched in [[Nurzhan]] by the duo [[tüntolk]] with their album *[[Jolchu (Album)|Jolchu]]* (1999), has produced the offshoots [[Mor-Pop]] and [[Mor-Folk]].[1][2] The national anthem is "[[The Spirit of Irad]]". ## Traditional music #### Instruments The **komuz** is a fretless long-necked lute carved from a single piece of apricot or walnut wood, about 85 to 95 cm long, with three strings of gut or nylon. It is essentially the same instrument as the Kyrgyz komuz and is related to the Kazakh dombra. Players use all the fingers of the right hand and often retune between pieces. The **[[Kyl-kyak|kyl-kyak]]** is a two-stringed bowed lute strung with horsehair, whose sound is likened to neighing or wind; ethnographers have recorded its earlier use by healers (*bakshy*). The **[[Choor (Flute)|choor]]** is an end-blown shepherd's flute with four or five finger holes, played while humming to produce overtones. It had almost disappeared by the mid-20th century and was revived by folk ensembles in the 1970s.[3] #### Küü Instrumental pieces for the komuz (*küü*; see [[Küü (Music)]]) are usually programmatic. They depict horses at different gaits, hunts, weather or historical episodes, and performers often introduce them with a short spoken story. The best known is *[[Kambarkan]]*, named after the legendary hunter credited with inventing the komuz, which is a standard test piece for soloists at the National Conservatory of Folk Music in [[Talas]]. Laments for the dead of 1916 are played at the memorial gatherings of 15 August (see [[Urkun: The Lost Tribes of 1916]]).[3] #### Epic and song Bards (*ırchy*) sing or chant epic and genealogical verse, alternating it with komuz interludes. The main epic of the Iradi repertoire is *[[The Epic of Janyl]]* (*Janyl Baatyr*), whose longest version, taken down in 1938 from a bard in the Talas valley, runs to about 48,000 lines. Bards perform it over several evenings at weddings, memorial feasts and the [[Feast of St. Janyl]]. Other vocal genres include the lament (*koshok*), sung by women at funerals; the unaccompanied horseback song (*[[Irda (Vocal Tradition)|ırda]]*), paced to the gait of the horse; and narrative poems such as *[[The Black Blizzard of 1916 (Poem)|The Black Blizzard of 1916]]*, recited on 15 August.[4] The largest body of field recordings was made between 1962 and 1989 by the ethnomusicologist [[Aigul Choro kyzy]]: about 640 reel-to-reel tapes from the [[Talas Alatau]], the Chatkal valley and the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] foothills, now held in the [[State Archives of Irad]].[4] Other genres include the *[[Sagynych (Music)|sagynych]]*, a slow, free-rhythm song of longing for absent people and places, sung by herders on the far pastures and now by migrant workers abroad; the named melodies (*jel küüsü*) of the [[Kara Jel Tünü|kara jel]] healing rite, played on kyl-kyak and frame drum, which the Church forbids; and the drum-and-shawm music of the [[Aylanma (Dance)|aylanma]] circle dance at weddings. The highland clans sing their hymns in three voices (*[[Üch Ün|üch ün]]*), unlike the monophonic Syriac chant of the city churches. #### Church music The Syro-Iradi Catholic Church sings the monophonic [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] antiphons (*'onitha*) of the East Syriac rite, which were passed down orally while the church was banned in the Soviet period (see [[East Syriac Rites of Iyık Janyl]]). In some rural churches the komuz and kyl-kyak accompany the liturgy. Folklorists have noted melodic features shared by this chant and the horseback songs. The [[Iyık Janyl Seminary Choir]], formed in 1994, also sings four-part settings of Iradi hymns, a practice introduced under Western Catholic influence.[5] ## Soviet period In the Soviet period traditional music was institutionalized. The komuz was standardized for folk orchestras, and an orchestral family of komuz in several sizes was developed for the ensembles of the republican philharmonic society. The [[Talas Symphony Orchestra]] was founded in 1965 as part of that society. Since the 1970s it has commissioned symphonic poems on Iradi landscapes and history, some adding the komuz, kyl-kyak and choor to the orchestra, and settings of episodes from *The Epic of Janyl*. The Talas Opera and Ballet Theater, whose prima ballerina from 1971 to 1990 was [[Venera Kasymova]], staged the Russian and European repertoire alongside works by Iradi composers (see [[Dance in Irad]]).[3][6] The Russian-language popular song (*estrada*) of the Soviet mainstream dominated radio, and it remains popular among the older urban generation known as the [[Russos of Nurzhan|Russos]].[6] Film music offered composers more freedom. Asan Jumabaev's score for *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]* (1979) combined the komuz with electric guitar, whistling and long silences, and the electronic tape loops of [[Nurlan Sadikov]]'s lost short *[[Tolkun (Lost Film)|Tolkun]]* (1963) are regarded as an early Central Asian experiment in the manner of *musique concrète* (see [[Cinema of Irad]]).[7] #### Cassettes and the Voice of America (1980s) In the 1980s American country and folk songwriters wrote songs about Irad, then a Soviet republic, often portraying Iradi horsemen and Christians under Soviet rule in romantic terms. Voice of America played some of them in its music programs, and travelers carried cassette copies into the Iradi SSR, where they were copied from hand to hand. Young listeners in Talas learned the guitar parts by ear, and the first Iradi-language versions were sung at private gatherings in the last years of Soviet rule. At the same time, young musicians in Kobozev rehearsed in district-heating boiler rooms and empty workshops, in the tradition of the Soviet underground rock scene.[8][9] ## Territorial period The arrival of American personnel at [[Talas Air Base]] after 1992 and the brief American fascination with Irad known as [[Iradimania]] brought these influences into the open. *Swift Hooves*, a compilation of thirteen country and folk songs about Irad organized by [[wp:Nashville, Tennessee|Nashville]] producers with American church relief organizations, was released in 1993. All its profits went to Christian-run charities in Irad, which funded rural dispensaries and church repairs. Its songs include "[[Ride for Talas]]", "[[Bells of Saint Janyl]]" and "[[The Widow's Horse]]", a ballad based on the popular story of the [[1956 Talas Riots]]. Later commentators describe its picture of the [[Iradis]] as "freedom-loving Christian cowboys" as romanticized.[8] Copies of the album reached Irad in 1993–1994 through base personnel, charities and [[IradOne]], and copied cassettes were sold in the bazaars of Talas. Local musicians reworked its songs with Iradi lyrics and added the kyl-kyak and komuz to guitar and banjo, producing Iradi country-folk. Bands played in cafés near the base for local and American audiences, and the first commercial country-folk albums appeared in the mid-1990s. The genre's subjects include horses, pastoral life and the civil wars; ballads about the [[Storming of Talas (2007)|storming of Talas]] in 2007 are popular in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].[9] Traditional music also found a broadcast outlet. From 1994 to 2020 the IradOne radio program *Kechki Jomok* ("Evening Tales"), presented by [[Baktygul Omur]], broadcast bards, *küü* and listeners' genealogies, and its audience reached herding settlements on both sides of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. The Talas Symphony Orchestra toured the United States in 1994 under its concertmaster [[Elena Kim]].[6] ## Mor-Wave and its offshoots Mor-Wave emerged in Nurzhan in the late 1990s, when much of the city's heavy industry stood idle. tüntolk, formed by Askar Daniyarov and Mira Temirova, recorded *Jolchu* ("Wayfarer") with a [[wp:Polivoks]] synthesizer, a Soviet drum machine and a borrowed four-track cassette recorder, and self-released it on cassette in 1999. Unlike most urban musicians of the time, who sang in Russian or English, Temirova wrote in Iradi, adapting epic verse and laments and using images of the steppe goddess Umay and the bull-headed [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]]. A first wave of groups, among them Kara Jel and Umay-9, grew up in Nurzhan and Talas between 1999 and 2005, and Nurzhan's club nights drew listeners from [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Tashkent]]. The scene contracted during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007, when venues closed under emergency regulations and tüntolk split up.[2][10] A second wave began in 2014, centered in Talas, among young Iradis who had grown up fluent in English and were turning to the Iradi language. tüntolk re-formed that year, and their album *[[White Stallion in Fog]]* (2017) was played on the youth channel that IradOne launched in 2015. An annual Mor-Wave festival has been held in converted textile warehouses in Talas since 2016, and streaming services have brought the genre listeners in Eastern Europe and North America. Mor-Wave songs were sung at the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]], after which IradOne dropped several tüntolk videos from rotation, according to the *[[Talas Herald]]*.[10][11] Two offshoots developed during the second wave: - **Mor-Pop**, a commercial idol-pop form often likened to the darker, concept-driven style of [[wp:K-pop|South Korean K-pop]], with choreographed groups, dance rhythms, sampled komuz riffs and Mor-Wave's Turkic pagan imagery, played widely on IradOne and commercial radio. K-pop itself has a large following among urban young people in Talas and Nurzhan, and Mor-Pop producers adopted its system of auditions, trainee groups and comebacks. - **Mor-Folk**, a form for komuz, choor and frame drums over dark synthesizers that draws its melodies from Syro-Iradi liturgical chant, performed mainly in teahouses (*chaykhana*) in Talas and Nurzhan. Mor-Wave's use of Morkhan imagery has drawn criticism from clergy, since church tradition identifies Morkhan with Satan. In June 2019 a concert planned in [[Iyık Janyl]] was canceled after objections from clergy and parishioners. Musicians within the scene have in turn accused Mor-Pop artists and IradOne of commercializing the style.[11] ## Institutions and awards The main teaching institution is the National Conservatory of Folk Music in Talas. The [[Altyn-Zhylky Awards]], presented each December since 1996, include separate popular-music categories for Mor-Wave and its offshoots. Ethnomusicologists credit Mor-Wave and Iradi-language popular music in general with raising the prestige of the language among urban young people (see [[Iradi language revival]] and [[Iradi Language]]).[2] ## Recording and streaming Most Iradi music was sold on cassette until the late 2000s and later on CD and through file sharing. Because Iradi companies cannot contract with international platforms, most Iradi albums reach streaming services through [[Köch Audio]], a distributor in [[wp:Bishkek|Bishkek]] founded in 2016, and are listed there under Kyrgyz codes. ## See also - [[Culture of Irad]] - [[Media of Irad]] - [[Köch Audio]] ## References

{{Infobox flag | name = Flag of Irad | native_name = *Irad tuu* | use = National flag | proportion = 1:√2 | adopted = 1992-05 (Provisional Government decree); Confirmed 1993 (State Symbols Act) | design = A white stallion beneath a five-pointed star, with an inverted horseshoe and the Orkhon inscription "Be Free", in a wreath of wheat, on a crimson field | designer = Commission of historians and artists of the Talas art college }} The **flag of Irad** (Iradi: *Irad tuu*) is a crimson field bearing a central emblem: a white stallion in gait beneath a five-pointed star, an inverted horseshoe on the hoist side of the horse, an arched inscription in [[wp:Old Turkic language|Old Turkic]] (Orkhon) script reading "Be Free", and a wreath of two ears of wheat. It was adopted by the Provisional Government in 1992 and confirmed by the interim [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] in 1993. It has been used since then by every Iradi administration, including the territorial government, the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] and the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), and it is also flown in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). Its official description was issued by the Department of Public Information in 2015.[1][2] ## Design The flag has a width-to-length ratio of 1:√2 (about 1:1.41). The emblem stands at the center of the field, slightly toward the hoist, and fills about three-quarters of the flag's height. Its elements form a roundel: the wheat ears enclose it at the sides and foot, and the inscription closes it at the top.[1] | Element | Description | |---|---| | Field | Crimson | | Stallion | A white horse in gait, facing the hoist, with one foreleg raised, in the center of the emblem | | Star | A five-pointed star directly above the stallion | | Horseshoe | A small horseshoe on the hoist side of the stallion, level with its head, with the heels pointing downward | | Inscription | Two words in Orkhon letters, arched along the top of the emblem between the tips of the wheat ears | | Wreath | Two ears of wheat whose stalks cross beneath the stallion and rise on either side of the emblem | #### Colors The official description gives the field as crimson, the stallion, star, horseshoe and inscription as white, and the wheat as golden. In the reference artwork published with it, all the charges are drawn in a single pale ivory (hex #FFF6D5) on a crimson field (hex #AA0000), and flags made in Irad generally follow this. Some foreign and commercially made flags show the wheat in yellow or gold.[1] #### Inscription The inscription is written in the runic script of the Old Turkic inscriptions of the Orkhon valley, examples of which have been found in the Talas valley. Like the original inscriptions, it reads from right to left. It renders the Iradi words *erkin bol*, "be free". The script is used today only symbolically, and the choice was explained in 1992 as a reference to the oldest written form of the Turkic languages, which predates the division of [[Iradis]] into Christian and Muslim communities (see [[Iradi alphabet]]).[2][3] ## Symbolism The 2015 official description assigns each element a meaning:[1] - **The crimson field** continues the revolutionary tradition of the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]] of 1916 and the banner of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]]. - **The stallion** represents the national equestrian heritage, the [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] and [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] breeds, and the historical belief that Irad was the birthplace of the domesticated horse (see [[Botai Culture in Irad]]). Some popular interpretations also associate the white horse with [[The Legend of the White Rider]], although the official description does not. - **The star** represents [[wp:Polaris]], called *Irad* in traditional cosmology, from which the country takes its name. The flag uses the five-pointed civic form of the [[The Star of Irad (Symbol)|Star of Irad]]; the eight-pointed form is reserved for the liturgical use of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. Some older publications and foreign descriptions give the flag star eight points, confusing the two. - **The inverted horseshoe** follows the steppe cavalry custom of the Fallen Rider, in which downward-facing tack marks a warrior killed in battle (see [[Fallen Rider Tradition]]). On the flag it is a permanent memorial to the martyrs of Irad, specifically those lost in the 1916 revolt and the flight that followed, the victims of the Soviet purges, and the dead of the [[First Iradi Civil War|First]] and [[Second Iradi Civil War|Second Iradi Civil Wars]]. In European folk custom a horseshoe hung points-up holds good luck; the downward shoe on the Iradi flag instead marks the dead. - **The inscription** "Be Free" expresses the aspiration to freedom. - **The wheat wreath** retains a motif of Soviet-era republican heraldry and symbolizes agricultural life in the river valleys. ## History #### Before 1992 The clans used horsetail standards (*tug*) in war and at gatherings, and the church carried processional banners bearing the cross and the eight-pointed star. Iradi tradition holds that the insurgents of 1916 carried red banners, which the official description cites as the origin of the crimson field.[2] Like other union republics, the Iradi SSR, created in 1925, used a red flag bearing the hammer and sickle and the initials of the republic, later replaced by the standard pattern of a red field with the gold hammer, sickle and star in the canton. Its state emblem was framed by a wreath of wheat ears (see [[Emblem of Irad]]). The [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] proclaimed in Kobozev in October 1991 continued to use the Soviet-era flag.[2] #### Adoption (1992–1993) During the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], protesters in [[Talas]] carried red banners painted with a white horse, and after the shootings of 3 February 1992 an inverted horseshoe, worn as a badge, spread among them as a sign of mourning in keeping with the Fallen Rider custom. According to popular accounts, a red banner with a white horse and a star hung in the municipal theater during the [[Talas Town Hall Meeting (1992)|Talas Town Hall Meeting]] on 11 March 1992, at which the Republic of Irad was proclaimed.[2][4] The Provisional Government appointed a commission of historians and artists from the Talas art college to prepare a formal design, and it adopted the present flag by decree in May 1992, during the siege of Talas. In its 1992 form the horseshoe was described as commemorating the dead of 1916, the purges and the February 1992 shootings. After the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] and the establishment of US territorial administration, the interim Territorial Legislature confirmed the flag in the State Symbols Act of 1993, together with the anthem, "[[The Spirit of Irad]]".[3][4] #### Territorial period and after Under the territorial administration (see [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)]]) the flag was flown beside the flag of the United States on public buildings, with the US flag in the position of precedence, as in other US territories. It remained the flag of the Democratic Republic of Irad in December 2006 and of the ISEZ from February 2007.[3] The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] did not adopt a separate flag. In the tribal regions the national flag is flown at clan assemblies and at the August kurultai on the [[Aksay Plateau]], often beside clan horsetail standards, and it is one of the few symbols used by both administrations.[5] The Department of Public Information published the official description in 2015. It standardized the colors and construction, confirmed that the star has five points, and listed the dead of both civil wars among the martyrs commemorated by the horseshoe.[1] ## Usage The flag is flown on government buildings and schools in the ISEZ, and is raised ceremonially in Talas on Irad Day, 11 March (see [[March 11 Independence Day]] and [[Public holidays in Irad]]). It is flown at half-mast on the anniversary of the 3 February 1992 shootings and on 15 August, the memorial day of [[The Lost Tribes of 1916]].[1] Its elements appear widely outside official use. Approved Chongtor stallions are branded with an inverted-horseshoe mark, silversmiths have added Orkhon letters to saddle fittings since the 1990s, and the star and horse are common in commercial logos (see [[Eerchilik (Saddlery)]]).[5] Vexillologists have compared the flag with that of [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], which also places a single central emblem on a red field. The Iradi flag differs in its figurative emblem and inscription, which are closer to the Soviet tradition of republican state emblems than to the plain geometric designs adopted by most post-Soviet states.[6] ## References

"**The Spirit of Irad**" (Iradi: *Irad Ruhu*) is the national anthem of Irad. Its music was composed by Asan Jumabaev, known for his score for the film *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]* (1979), to a poem by Cholpon Myrzakulova. Written during the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], it was sung at the proclamation of the Republic of Irad in [[Talas]] on 11 March 1992, adopted by the Provisional Government in May 1992 and confirmed by the interim [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] in the State Symbols Act of 1993. It replaced the anthem of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] and has been retained by every later Iradi administration, including the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). The official text is in Iradi, and an official English version was adopted in 1993.[1][2] ## History #### Soviet predecessor Like the other union republics, the Iradi SSR adopted a state anthem in 1946, with a text in Iradi and Russian that praised the [[wp:Soviet Union]], the Russian people and [[wp:Joseph Stalin|Stalin]]. The text was revised in the late 1970s to remove the references to Stalin. It was rarely sung outside official ceremonies, but republican radio played it at the start and close of each broadcasting day until 1991. The [[Socialist Republic of Irad]], proclaimed in Kobozev in October 1991, continued to use it.[3] #### Composition (1991–1992) Myrzakulova, then a lecturer in Iradi philology at Iradi State University (now [[Talas State University]]), wrote the poem in December 1991, when strikes and student protests in Talas were growing into the Winter Uprising. It was first printed in a student newspaper and circulated in typed copies. Jumabaev set it to music in January 1992. According to his later account, he based the opening phrase on a herding tune he had recorded in the [[Talas Alatau]] in the 1970s and wrote the refrain so that it could be sung by a crowd without accompaniment.[1] The song was sung at rallies in Talas in February 1992, including at the funerals of those killed in the shootings of 3 February. According to accounts of the [[Talas Town Hall Meeting (1992)|Talas Town Hall Meeting]] of 11 March, the assembly sang it after adopting the declaration that proclaimed the Republic of Irad, an occasion now marked as Irad Day (see [[March 11 Independence Day]]).[2][4] #### Adoption The Provisional Government adopted "The Spirit of Irad" as the national anthem by decree in May 1992, at the same time as the [[Flag of Irad|national flag]]. After the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] and the establishment of US territorial administration, the interim Territorial Legislature confirmed both symbols in the State Symbols Act of 1993. The act fixed the official music and the Iradi text, approved an official English version, and specified the arrangement to be used on state occasions.[2] During the territorial period (see [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)]]) the anthem was played together with "The [[wp:The Star-Spangled Banner|Star-Spangled Banner]]" at official ceremonies attended by representatives of the federal government, as in other US territories, and the English version was often sung on those occasions. The [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] kept the anthem in December 2006, and the ISEZ administration has kept it since February 2007. The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] has not adopted an anthem of its own, and the song is also sung at clan gatherings in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].[5] ## Music The anthem is a slow hymn in common time. The official orchestral arrangement, recorded by the [[Talas Symphony Orchestra]] in 1993, is in B-flat major. Each stanza is set to a sixteen-bar verse, followed by an eight-bar refrain whose melody rises to the highest note of the anthem. Writers on the anthem have noted its narrow range and its regular phrases, which make it easy to sing, and the herding-tune character of the opening, built on repeated rising fourths.[1][6] {{Listen|file=The_Spirit_of_Irad.mp3|title="The Spirit of Irad"|description=Military band arrangement of the State Defense Corps, all three stanzas.}} Several official arrangements exist: - the full orchestral version, with all three stanzas, lasting a little under three minutes; - a short version of the first stanza and refrain, about one minute twenty seconds long, used at sporting events and in broadcasting; - a military band arrangement used by the State Defense Corps, which builds from a lone voice and snare drum to full band, massed drums and timpani in the last refrain; - a version with a solo [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]] introduction, used by [[IradOne]] since the early 2000s.[2][6] ## Text The official Iradi text has three stanzas and a refrain. In the official description, the first stanza describes the mountains, rivers and horse herds of Irad. The second commemorates those who died for the country, with an allusion to the steppe custom of the riderless horse (see [[Fallen Rider Tradition]]). The third presents [[wp:Polaris]], the star called *Irad* in traditional cosmology, as a guide for the nation. The refrain, "Ooo İrad, menin üyüm, jürögüm, janım" ("O Irad, my home, my heart, my soul"), addresses the country and the "spirit" of the title and repeats the call to freedom, *Erkin bol* ("Be free"), that appears as the motto of the national flag.[2] | Iradi | English | |---|---| | *Stanza* | | | Ak kar baskan zoolorum, | My mountains under white snow, | | Kök jayloodo jylkylarym, | My horse herds on the blue summer pastures, | | Talas, Naryn, Chüy suulary, | The waters of Talas, Naryn and Chüy, | | Atalardyn mekeni. | Homeland of our fathers. | | *Refrain* | | | Ooo İrad, menin üyüm, jürögüm, janım, | O Irad, my home, my heart, my soul, | | Erkin bol, Irad ruhu! | Be free, spirit of Irad! | | *Stanza* | | | Erkindik dep kulagandar, | Those who fell for freedom, | | Attary eesiz kaldy, | Their horses were left without riders, | | Eeri bosh, joldoru achyk, | The saddles empty, the roads open, | | Biz alardy unutpaybyz. | We will not forget them. | | *Refrain* | | | Ooo İrad, menin üyüm, jürögüm, janım, | O Irad, my home, my heart, my soul, | | Erkin bol, Irad ruhu! | Be free, spirit of Irad! | | *Stanza* | | | Tündö janat Irad jyldyzy, | At night the star of Irad shines, | | Kuday bergen jol körsötküch, | A guide given by God, | | Adashkanda aga karaybyz, | When we are lost we look to it, | | Al bizdi üygö alyp barat. | It leads us home. | | *Final refrain* | | | Ooo İrad, menin üyüm, jürögüm, janım, | O Irad, my home, my heart, my soul, | | Erkin bol, Irad ruhu! | Be free, spirit of Irad! | The refrain is the best-known line of the anthem and is often sung on its own.{{Citation needed|date=June 2026}} The duo [[tüntolk]] took it as the refrain of their song "[[My Home My Heart My Soul]]" (2017), and it was chanted by marchers during the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]].[7] The official English version follows the Iradi text closely but does not rhyme. An unofficial Russian translation from the 1990s is sung by some older Russian-speaking Iradis (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]), but it has no legal standing, and the Russian-language channel IradOdin plays the anthem without words.[5] The third stanza's reference to the star as a guide sent by God has drawn objections. In the territorial period, Muslim community leaders in [[Nurzhan]] asked that schoolchildren not be required to sing it. Since 1997 school regulations in the ISEZ have required only the first stanza and refrain, and the short official version omits the third stanza.[5] (See [[Islam in Irad]] and [[Religion in Irad]].) ## Usage The anthem is performed at the official ceremony in Talas on Irad Day, at the opening of each session of the *[[Mejlis]]*, at the inauguration of the Governor and at military ceremonies. IradOne plays it at the start and close of its broadcasting day. Schools in the ISEZ sing it at assemblies at the start of the school week. It is played before the final of the [[President's Cup]] in [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]] at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]] each March. Because Irad is not a member of most international sporting bodies, it is rarely heard at international competitions.[2][5] By convention, listeners stand. The practice of placing the right hand over the heart was introduced during the territorial period and is now usual among younger [[Iradis]], while many older people stand at attention in the Soviet manner. In the tribal regions men remove their felt hats. The anthem has also been sung at demonstrations. According to the *[[Talas Herald]]*, protesters sang it during the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]] and at the demonstrations that followed the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]].[7] ## References

The **Iradi alphabet** (Iradi: *Irad alfaviti*) is the Latin-based alphabet of 32 letters used to write the [[Iradi Language|Iradi language]]. It was introduced in 1992, given its present form by the [[1995 Latin Orthography Revision]] and confirmed, with minor changes, by the Language and Education Reform Act of 1997. It is the official script of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and is also used in the records of the [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]] in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR).[1] Iradi has changed script three times in a century. It was written in Arabic script until 1928, in a Latin alphabet from 1928 to 1941 and in Cyrillic from 1941 to 1992, before the return to Latin in 1992. Older forms survive in particular uses: the [[wp:Old Turkic language|Old Turkic]] runic script appears in the motto of the [[Flag of Irad|national flag]], [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] script in church inscriptions, and Cyrillic in the handwriting of many older [[Iradis]].[1][2] ## History #### Early scripts A group of short Old Turkic runic inscriptions has been found in the Talas valley, and Christian gravestones of the wider [[wp:Semirechye]] region bear Turkic texts written in Syriac script. Iradi scholars regard both as written evidence of the ancestors of the language, although the link to modern Iradi is debated. Turkic written in Syriac script also appears on the carved gypsum panels of the [[Church of St. Janyl]] (1727) in [[Iyık Janyl]].[2][3] From the late Middle Ages Iradi was written in the Perso-Arabic script used for Chagatai and later Uzbek. Texts copied at Iyık Janyl, including the eighteenth-century vita of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]], used it. The script had few letters for Turkic vowels, and spelling followed Chagatai conventions rather than the spoken language. After the creation of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] in 1925, the republican press briefly used a reformed Arabic orthography with letters for all the vowels, similar to the reforms adopted for Kazakh and Kyrgyz in the same years.[2] #### Latin (1928–1941) The [[1928 Latinization Decree]] replaced the Arabic script with a Latin alphabet, as part of the Soviet campaign that gave most Turkic languages alphabets based on the Unified Turkic Latin Alphabet (*[[wp:Yañalif]]*). Iradi made the change in the same year as Kyrgyz. Like the other Yañalif-based alphabets, it used special letters such as ꞑ for the velar nasal, ɵ for the front rounded vowel *ö* and ь for the back vowel *ı*. The reform was carried out through literacy schools in rural districts and the refitting of printing presses. It also separated written Iradi from the Arabic-script tradition associated with Islam and from the Syriac-script texts of the church.[4] #### Cyrillic (1941–1992) The [[1941 Cyrillic Mandate]] replaced the Latin alphabet with Cyrillic in the press, schools and administration, at the end of the all-Union shift from Latin to Cyrillic in 1938–1941. As in the Kyrgyz alphabet adopted in 1940, the Iradi Cyrillic alphabet consisted of the 33 letters of Russian with three additions: ө, ү and ң. Long vowels were written double, and Russian loanwords kept their Russian spelling, including letters such as ц, щ and ъ that are not used in native words. The abridged 1958 edition of [[The Epic of Janyl]] was printed in Cyrillic.[1][5] #### Latin (since 1992) The Provisional Government and the territorial administration restored a Latin alphabet in 1992. Drawn up quickly for schools and the press, and for the English-language typewriters and computers then arriving under the territorial administration, it avoided diacritics and relied on digraphs such as *oe*, *ue*, *ch*, *sh* and *ng*. Spelling varied widely between publications.[1] The 1995 Latin Orthography Revision, a law of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]], was drafted by a commission of linguists from [[Talas State University]] and territorial educators. It replaced the digraphs with single letters: the dotless *ı* for the back unrounded vowel, *ö* and *ü* for the front rounded vowels, and *ç*, *ş* and *ñ* for the consonants /tʃ/, /ʃ/ and /ŋ/. It also set rules for writing loanwords and proper names. The resulting 32-letter alphabet was confirmed by the Language and Education Reform Act of 1997, whose changes concerned mainly the spelling of loanwords and the capital forms of *i* and *ı*. The act made the alphabet compulsory in public schools and administration.[1][6] The new alphabet spread fastest among the young. In 1993 the [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs]] approved Iradi translations of the liturgy, printed in the Latin alphabet, for use alongside Classical Syriac, and the complete edition of the 1938 text of *The Epic of Janyl* was published in Latin script in 2001. Many older Iradis, especially among the Russian-educated *Russos* of [[Nurzhan]], still read Iradi more easily in Cyrillic, and older clerks in the tribal regions often still write it.[1][7] ## Letters The alphabet follows the order below. Like Turkish and Azerbaijani, it distinguishes dotless *ı* (capital *I*) from dotted *i* (capital *İ*).[6] | Letter | Cyrillic (1941–1992) | Sound (IPA) | Notes | |---|---|---|---| | A a | А а | /ɑ/ | | | Ä ä | — | /æ/ | Uzbek and Persian loans; often merged with *e* or *a* | | B b | Б б | /b/ | | | C c | Ц ц | /ts/ | Russian and international loans only | | Ç ç | Ч ч | /tʃ/ | | | D d | Д д | /d/ | | | E e | Е е, Э э | /e/ | | | F f | Ф ф | /f/ | Mainly loans | | G g | Г г | /ɡ/, [ʁ] | Uvular next to back vowels | | H h | Х х | /h/ | Persian and Arabic loans | | I ı | Ы ы | /ɯ/ | Back unrounded vowel | | İ i | И и | /i/ | | | J j | Ж ж | /dʒ/ | [ʒ] in northern steppe dialects | | K k | К к | /k/, [q] | Uvular next to back vowels | | L l | Л л | /l/ | | | M m | М м | /m/ | | | N n | Н н | /n/ | | | Ñ ñ | Ң ң | /ŋ/ | | | O o | О о | /o/ | | | Ö ö | Ө ө | /ø/ | | | P p | П п | /p/ | | | Q q | К к | /q/ | Established proper names only | | R r | Р р | /r/ | | | S s | С с | /s/ | | | Ş ş | Ш ш | /ʃ/ | | | T t | Т т | /t/ | | | U u | У у | /u/ | | | Ü ü | Ү ү | /y/ | | | V v | В в | /v/ | Mainly loans | | X x | Х х | /χ/ | Uzbek, Persian and Arabic loans | | Y y | Й й | /j/ | | | Z z | З з | /z/ | | Long vowels are written double (*aa*, *ee*, *oo*, *öö*, *uu*, *üü*), as in *too* "mountain". The uvular pronunciations of *k* and *g* next to back vowels are not marked in writing; *q* survives only in a few established names, such as the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. The letters *c*, *f*, *h*, *v*, *x* and *ä* occur mainly in loanwords.[6] ## Romanization in English Iradi names and words in English-language publications, including government documents in English, often do not follow the official alphabet. Many use an older romanization based on English digraphs or on the transliteration of Russian Cyrillic. In these spellings *ç* and *ş* appear as *ch* and *sh*, *ı* often as *y*, and *j* sometimes as *zh*, from the Russian transliteration of Cyrillic ж. The patronymic *kızı* ("daughter of") is thus usually written *kyzy* in English, and the title of the film *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]*, officially *Çöl Künü Kötörülüşü*, is usually given as *Chöl Künü Kötörülüshü*. Names that entered English through Russian, such as Zhumabek, keep their *zh* (see [[Iradi name]]).[1][7] The distinction between dotted and dotless *i* caused problems with early software and with the English-language keyboards common in the ISEZ, and many writers still use *i* for both letters in informal writing.[7] ## References

**FreeIrad.org** (styled **FREEIRAD.ORG**) is an anonymous English-language opposition website about [[Irad]]. It publishes allegations against the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) government and the family of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]], against foreign powers and against the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], under the slogans "No justice without truth", "No freedom without justice" and "No truth without freedom". A banner on its front page says that [[Attelkom]], which carries almost all internet traffic in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), tried to censor the site and that it is now hosted offshore. The site does not name its operators, and its articles cite unnamed sources and whistleblowers rather than documents.[1] ## Content Since October 2026 the site has presented the [[Erasure Theory]] as its central cause. Its masthead asks "Do you remember Irad?", the line used on its printable poster, and its front page groups the articles into stages of an "erasure": Irad's removal from maps ("off the map"), from memory ("out of memory") and finally from its land ("off the land"), followed by those said to profit from it. A long explainer page lists the site's "evidence", among them the missing map entries, country menus and ISO code, the withdrawal of the *Simpsons* episode "[[The Steppe Family Robinson]]" in 1995, the neighbors' claims and the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]. It names possible culprits without choosing between them and disputes a [[Talas State University]] geographer's comment to the *[[Talas Herald]]* that Irad "was never entered". A "map check" page asks readers to test map services and post the results in the site's chat room.[2] The articles are tagged by subject, among them politics, religion, Toktarov, Russia, China and America. Most are headlined as questions, and none carries a date. Their claims include:[1] - that Toktarov died in 2022 and that the DPI has concealed his death, a version of the rumors that followed his disappearance from public view (see [[Erlan Toktarov]]); - that the Bush family keeps a secret estate in Irad's mountains, a revival of the [[Bush Family Palatial Complex Conspiracy Theory]]; - that the [[NurGaz]] president [[Kamran Bekzatov]] has held secret meetings with the Russian leadership, and that Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] plans to sell Irad to China; - that the United States runs hidden military bases in Irad besides the acknowledged installations, and that oil, not the 1992 treaty, was the real reason for US rule; - that Irad's undeveloped uranium deposits have become a target for foreign powers; - that the horse trade serves as a cover for foreign intelligence operations; - that the church hides ancient relics, including the [[wp:Holy Grail]]; - that Irad has been erased from online maps (see [[Erasure Theory]]). Later articles added further claims: that the cryptocurrency [[Tulparcoin]] was a means of collecting the phone numbers of government critics; that lobbyists retained by associates of [[Alikhan Toktarov]] brought Irad to the attention of [[wp:Donald Trump|Donald Trump's]] circle before the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]; that Irad's neighbors never abandoned the partition plan exposed in 2007 and are waiting for the ISEZ to collapse (see [[Bill of Sale (2007)]]); and that Gendarmerie commanders control the fuel trade across the ceasefire line. Each claim is attributed to unnamed sources. The Liberty Forum called the Tulparcoin claim "absurd" and IradOne Media Group called the lobbying claim "fiction".[2] In October 2026 the site added articles on the return of Iradi websites to foreign search engines after Attelkom's 2026 gateway upgrade, which it calls the *kaytaruu* ("putting back") and presents as preparation for a sale or as a means of Chinese surveillance; on the Saturday entertainment concession at the [[Irad State Hippodrome|State Hippodrome]] held by [[Jarysh]], which it says was awarded without a tender; and on the [[Talas State University]] library's new digital archive, which it welcomed while asking why the 2007 partition drafts and the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] had not been published. Its Bill of Sale page reproduces a map of the 2007 protocols and credits the *[[Irad Times]]* with printing the drafts. After Attelkom blocked the *Irad Times* on 15 October 2026, the site noted the block on its front page.[3] ## Activism A "Take action" section offers a printable poster and a recipe for wheatpaste, the flour-and-water glue used for fly-posting. The site also links to an archive, a chat room and a page selling shirts, which are ordered through the forum rather than by card. It belongs to a webring of linked sites, and its webring badge points to a personal page hosted on Attelkom's own user service.[1][4] A "Who we are" page describes the operators as [[Iradis]] at home and abroad who are funded by readers and shirt sales and take no money from any government, party or company. Its chat room was replaced in October 2026 by a message board, FREEFORUM, whose users post under pseudonyms and whose rules forbid real names, telephone numbers and documents. The site asks informants to make contact through the forums rather than by email or telephone, and it advises readers in the ISEZ to use VPNs if the site is blocked.[2] ## Censorship claims The Department of Public Information supplies Attelkom with lists of websites to be blocked in the ISEZ (see [[Media of Irad]]). FreeIrad.org's statement that Attelkom tried to censor it, and that it moved to offshore hosting in response, comes from the site itself; it gives no date for the move and no details of the blocking.[1] ## Reception In Irad the site is widely regarded as a crackpot site. The *[[Talas Herald]]* does not report its claims and has described it as a fringe site whose exposés rest on unnamed sources and recycle rumors from chat groups, and IradOne's media programs mention it, when at all, as an example of online disinformation.[5][6] Media researchers at [[Talas State University]] found in 2024 that most readers who knew of the site treated it as entertainment or as a gauge of rumor rather than as news, although its slogans and posters have appeared at protests since 2023.[7] The DPI calls it "foreign-sponsored disinformation"; opposition journalists, including those of the *[[Irad Times]]*, generally avoid citing it.[5] ## See also - [[Media of Irad]] - [[Bush Family Palatial Complex Conspiracy Theory]] ## References

{{Infobox political party | name = Jer-Suu Party | native_name = *Jer-Suu Partiyası* (Land and Water Party) | founder = Tilek Sharshenov; Kubanychbek Toktobolot uulu | founded = March 1995 | dissolved = April 2008 (banned) | hq = [[Talas]] | newspaper = *Jer-Suu* | ideology = Iradi nationalism | seats1_title = Territorial House of Representatives (1996–2006) | seats1 = 2–4 / 35 }} The **Jer-Suu Party** (Iradi: *Jer-Suu Partiyası*, "Land and Water Party") was an Iradi nationalist political party founded in [[Talas]] in 1995. During the territorial period it campaigned for the repudiation of the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]], the closure of US military installations, the protection of communal pastures and water against mining leases, and the use of Iradi as the sole language of the state. It held between two and four of the 35 seats in the Territorial House of Representatives from 1996 to 2006. After many of its members joined the [[Popular Front of Irad]] in 2007, it was banned in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) in 2008 as an extremist organization.[1][2] ## History #### Foundation and territorial period (1995–2006) The party was founded in March 1995 by the poet and [[Talas State University]] philologist [[Tilek Sharshenov]] and [[Kubanychbek Toktobolot uulu]], a rural notable from the Talas valley, who drew together Iradi-language teachers, students and village councils opposed to grazing leases granted to mining companies. Its name, "land and water", is a traditional expression for the homeland. The party argued that the treaty of 1992 had given away the independence won in the [[First Iradi Civil War]], and it was the main voice of the nationalist demand for its repudiation, which [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] resisted until his death in 2004. It also campaigned for the [[1995 Latin Orthography Revision]] and against the dollar-linked som.[1] Jer-Suu won its first two House seats in 1996, from Talas and the Talas valley. Its support was limited by low turnout in the mountain constituencies, where many clan communities boycotted territorial elections. In the early 2000s its deputies and newspaper, *Jer-Suu*, were among the most persistent critics of the commercial concessions held by [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) figures around [[Talas Air Base]].[1] #### Democratic Republic and civil war (2006–2007) The party welcomed the [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]] and its deputies sat in the national assembly of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]]. In February 2007 they walked out of the assembly in protest against the cabinet of [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] over its decrees privatizing communal pastures in the Chatkal valley. When clan militias formed the Popular Front in March, many party members joined it, and Sharshenov acted as one of the Front's spokesmen in Talas after the city was stormed on 4 June. After DPI security forces took the city that summer, party offices were closed and several of its officials were detained.[2] #### Ban (2008) In April 2008 the [[Supreme Court of Irad]], on an application from the Ministry of Internal Security, banned the party under the Extremist Activity Act passed by the provisional chamber earlier that year, holding that it had taken part in an armed rebellion. Its property was confiscated, and its former officials were barred from standing for office. The [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe]] (OSCE) and [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] criticized the ruling as collective punishment of a lawful party.[3] In 2016 three students in Talas were convicted of distributing Jer-Suu leaflets and given suspended sentences.[4] Sharshenov has lived in exile in [[wp:Bishkek]] since 2008 and writes for exiled Iradi media. Toktobolot uulu moved to the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], where he and other former members joined the [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]], giving the clan confederation a small group of urban, Iradi-educated staff.[2] ## See also - [[Labor Party of Irad]] - [[Elections in Irad]] ## References

{{More citations needed|date=September 2026}} {{Infobox political party | name = Labor Party of Irad | native_name = *Irad Emgek Partiyası*; *Trudovaya partiya Irada* | founder = Gennady Shevchuk | founded = March 1993 | dissolved = May 2011 | hq = [[Nurzhan]] | ideology = Social democracy | seats1_title = Territorial House of Representatives (1994–2006) | seats1 = 5–7 / 35 }} The **Labor Party of Irad** (Iradi: *Irad Emgek Partiyası*; Russian: *Trudovaya partiya Irada*) was a political party based in [[Nurzhan]] that represented the city's mainly Russian- and Ukrainian-speaking industrial workforce. Founded in 1993 by former members of the [[Communist Party of Irad]] and leaders of the refinery, railway and machine-plant unions, it controlled the Nurzhan city council for most of the territorial period and was the [[Democratic Party of Irad]]'s main opponent in the Territorial Legislature. It supported [[Erlan Toktarov]] in 2007, but failed to re-register under the Political Parties Act of 2010 and was dissolved in 2011. Its former deputies now sit as Russo-aligned independents (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]).[1] ## History #### Foundation (1993) The Communist Party of Irad ceased to function with the surrender of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] in August 1992 and was never reconstituted, and the interim US administration took its buildings and records into custody. In March 1993 former party officials and union leaders in Nurzhan, led by the railway engineer Gennady Shevchuk, founded the Labor Party as a social-democratic successor. Its program called for the pensions and housing of Soviet-era industrial workers, Russian-language schooling, continued public ownership of Iradneft and the Nurzhan refinery, and closer economic ties with [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and Russia. It opposed the currency board that fixed the som to the dollar.[1] #### Territorial period (1993–2006) Labor won a majority on the Nurzhan city council in the first municipal elections in 1994 and held it, alone or with allied lists, until 2007. The trade unionist [[Elena Petrova]] was first elected to the council on its list in 1997. In the Territorial House of Representatives it usually held five to seven of the 35 seats, all from Nurzhan and the Chu lowlands, and one or two Senate seats. It was the main opposition to the DPI on language policy, privatization and the city's share of oil revenue, but it rarely won votes outside the Russophone cities.[1][2] #### 2007 and the ISEZ When Toktarov proclaimed the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] from Nurzhan on 25 February 2007, the Labor-led city council placed the municipal police at his disposal, and the party's deputies supported the emergency administration. Analysts attribute the decision to the party's hostility to the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]]'s privatization of [[NurGaz]] assets and to fear of the clan militias. Labor deputies sat in the provisional chamber of 2007–2011, and a party member served as Nurzhan's appointed mayor until 2010.[2] #### Dissolution (2010–2011) In 2010 the provisional chamber passed the Political Parties Act, which required a registered party to have at least 10,000 members, including at least 500 in each of the eight legislative constituencies. Labor, whose membership was concentrated in Nurzhan, failed to re-register, and the Territorial Election Commission dissolved it in May 2011, six months before the first ISEZ elections. Its deputies and councilors have since stood on civic lists in Nurzhan, which since 2011 have been funded largely by businessmen linked to [[NurGaz]] and its president, [[Kamran Bekzatov]]. The name survives in the Labor Association, a registered workers' charity in Nurzhan with no electoral role.[2][3] Observers from the [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe]] (OSCE) have cited the 2010 Act as one reason why the ISEZ's elections lack meaningful choice: no party other than the DPI has met its thresholds since 2011.[3] ## See also - [[Jer-Suu Party]] - [[Elections in Irad]] ## References

  2. ^ Abdyldaev, Nurlan (2015). Two Wars for Talas: Armed Forces and Politics in Irad, 1992–2007. Talas: Talas State University Press, pp. 211–264.
  3. ^ OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (2012). Election Assessment Report: Gubernatorial and Legislative Elections in the ISEZ, 8 November 2011. Warsaw.
