The **Iradi cross** (Iradi: *salyba*, from [[wp:Syriac language|Classical Syriac]] *ṣlibā*) is the distinctive cross of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] and the most widely used Christian symbol in [[Irad]]. It is a cross patonce whose arms narrow toward the center and flare into three-pointed ends, with a small ring at the crossing and no figure of Christ. Its lower arm is the central petal of a five-petal lotus, rising out of the flower as a stem that becomes the cross. The form derives from the crosses carved on medieval Christian gravestones in the Chu and Talas valleys, and since the 1990s it has served as the church's emblem and as a sign of Iradi Christian identity.[1][2] ## Form The proportions vary, but the canonical form, as drawn in the emblem adopted by the [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs]] in 1994, has:[1] - upper and side arms concave-sided and flared, each ending in three points in the manner of a cross patonce, a form shared with East Syriac crosses across [[wp:Central Asia]] and China; - a lower arm formed by the lotus's central petal, which narrows into a stem as it rises to the crossing, giving the whole a squat outline; - a ring at the crossing, which in church usage stands for the empty tomb; - a lotus of five petals beneath, sometimes drawn as a cloud. It has no corpus, in keeping with East Syriac practice, which venerated the bare cross as a sign of the [[wp:Resurrection of Jesus|Resurrection]] rather than of the Passion. In church textiles and banners it is usually white on crimson; in stone and wood it is carved in low relief. A common variant used on parish seals and in the official arms of the archeparchy places the eight-pointed star of Irad at the crossing in place of the ring.[1] ## Origin The form is that of the crosses on the river-boulder gravestones (*kayrak*) of the 13th and 14th centuries found in the Chu valley near [[wp:Tokmok]] and in the cemetery of the [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl]], where crosses rising from lotuses or clouds accompany inscriptions in Syriac and [[wp:Old Turkic language|Old Turkic]]. Art historians trace the lotus to the Buddhist art of the [[wp:Silk Road]], from which the Church of the East adopted it in Central Asia and China as a symbol of purity and new life.[2] ## Survival and revival After the destruction of the dioceses in the 14th century, the cross survived in domestic and pastoral use: carved on the door frames and lattice of yurts, stamped on bread and worked into felt and embroidery, where the cross and lotus could pass as a flower ornament. Ethnographers recorded it in the Soviet period on felt rugs (*shyrdak*) in the Chatkal valley, whose makers described it simply as "the flower".[3] Urban churches reopened after 1992 largely with Latin crosses and crucifixes brought by American chaplains and Catholic charities. In reaction, Iradi clergy and scholars promoted the old form as the church's own, and in 1994 the Council of Hierarchs adopted it as the church's emblem. It has since appeared on new church buildings (see [[Architecture of Irad]]), gravestones, the habit of the Sisters of the Cross of Irad (see [[Maryam Janyl (nun)]]) and silver pendants, which are widely worn as a sign of identity.[1][3] ## Interpretation Church teaching reads the three points of each arm as the Trinity and the lotus as the purity of Christ rising from the world. Popular tradition reads the lotus differently: in the tribal regions it is called "the cloud", after the clouds with which Christ is to return (Revelation 1:7), and is linked with the White Rider of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]]'s vision; others call it "Janyl's flower". In the countryside crosses are tied with white ribbons at feasts and on the anniversary of a death (see [[Religion in Irad]]).[3] ## See also - [[Kümöch Sacramental Bread]] - [[Religion in Irad]] ## References

{{Infobox artist | name = Yusup Ayyubov | native_name = Yusup Ayyub uulu | image = Yusup_Ayyubov_1905.jpg | caption = Ayyubov at Besh-Tash, about 1905 | df = dmy | birth_date = 1869-03-03 | birth_place = Upper Talas valley, [[wp:Russian Turkestan|Russian Turkestan]] | death_date = 1937-11-14 | death_place = [[Talas]], [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic|Iradi SSR]] | nationality = Iradi | education = Icon workshop of the [[Church of St. Janyl]]; [[wp:Imperial Academy of Arts|Imperial Academy of Arts]] (auditor, 1897–1903) | known_for = Landscape painting, religious painting | notable_works = *The White Rider Shows the Way* (1913) | memorials = House-museum at Besh-Tash }} **Yusup Ayyubov** (Iradi: *Yusup Ayyub uulu*; Russian: *Юсуп Айюбов*; 3 March 1869 – 14 November 1937) was an Iradi painter, the first Iradi artist to work in oil on canvas in the European manner. He is known for his landscapes of the [[Talas Alatau]] and for religious paintings, above all *The White Rider Shows the Way* (1913), which shows Christ as the White Rider revealing Irad's star to [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]]. He took part in the Iradi national movement of 1917–1918, lived in exile in [[wp:Xinjiang]] from 1920 to 1925, and was shot during the [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges|1937 purges]]. Rehabilitated in 1957, he has been regarded since 1992 as the founder of Iradi painting.[1][2] ## Early life and training Ayyubov was born into a Christian herding family of the upper Talas valley, the son of Ayyub, a horse breeder. As a boy he was sent to the icon workshop attached to the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]], where he learned to grind pigments and paint icons of St. Janyl in the local manner. A Russian surveyor who saw his drawings arranged for him to study in [[wp:Tashkent]], and in 1897 he went to [[wp:Saint Petersburg|St. Petersburg]], where he attended the [[wp:Imperial Academy of Arts]] as an auditing student until 1903, supported by subscriptions from Russian orientalists and Iradi church families. In St. Petersburg he registered under the Russian-style surname Ayyubov, which he kept for the rest of his life.[1] ## Landscapes and the White Rider (1903–1916) On his return he built a house and studio in the village of Besh-Tash, at the mouth of the valley now in [[Besh-Tash National Park]]. Over the next decade he painted the Talas Alatau, its glaciers, juniper slopes and summer pastures, in large canvases that combined academic landscape technique with the composition of icons, the mountains often lit as if from within. He exhibited in Tashkent in 1907 and in [[wp:Almaty|Verny]] (now Almaty) in 1910, and Russian critics described him as the first painter of his people.[1][3] His religious paintings brought him wider fame among [[Iradis]]. *The White Rider Shows the Way* (1913), painted for the 1913 [[Feast of St. Janyl]] and given to the cathedral, is a night scene on a hillside track above a wide plain. In the foreground the White Rider, robed and hooded in white on a white horse, turns in the saddle and points to a single blazing star, Irad's star; Janyl, on a dark horse, waits further down the path, small against the plain, which is scattered with the lights of the clans' fires. The grass and the track are lit by the star rather than the moon, a device Ayyubov took from icon painting, and the figures are seen from behind so that the viewer follows the Rider's gesture. Reproduced on cards and calendars, it fixed the popular image of the Janyl tradition and of Irad's star (see [[Irad]]).[2] ## Revolution and exile (1916–1925) During the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]] of 1916 Ayyubov sheltered refugees at Besh-Tash, and his drawings of the flight over the passes are among the few contemporary images of [[The Lost Tribes of 1916]]. After the [[wp:February Revolution]] he joined the Iradi National Council, an assembly of clergy, teachers and townspeople formed in [[Talas]] in 1917 to seek autonomy for the Iradi districts within a Russian federation, and chaired its commission on schools and culture. The council was dissolved by the Tashkent Soviet in 1918 after most of the clans had sided with the [[wp:Bolsheviks]], and its members were treated with suspicion.[4] In 1920 Ayyubov left for Ghulja in Xinjiang, where many refugees of 1916 had settled. There he painted the [[wp:Tian Shan]] from the Chinese side and taught drawing in the refugee community. He returned in 1925, when the creation of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] and the policy of *korenizatsiia* encouraged exiled intellectuals to come home.[4] ## Soviet period and death (1925–1937) In Talas he taught at the republic's first art studio, designed illustrations for Latin-script Iradi schoolbooks after 1928, and painted landscapes and scenes of herding life for state exhibitions. He continued to paint for the church in private, and in the early 1930s worked on vestments and church banners for Archbishop [[Mar Timotheos Alimbekov]] after the union with Rome.[2] He was arrested in October 1937 and charged with membership of a counter-revolutionary nationalist organization and espionage for the [[wp:Holy See|Vatican]], with his part in the 1917 council and his exile in China cited as evidence. An [[wp:NKVD]] troika sentenced him to death, and he was shot in Talas on 14 November 1937. His burial place is unknown. Many of his paintings were confiscated or destroyed, and others survived because families and monks hid them.[5] ## Legacy Ayyubov was rehabilitated in 1957, and a small exhibition of his landscapes was held in Talas in 1969; his religious works were not shown in the Soviet period. Since 1992 he has been celebrated as a national painter. His house at Besh-Tash is a museum, and the [[Irad Palace of Art]] in Iyık Janyl holds the largest collection of his work, including *The White Rider Shows the Way*, returned by the cathedral in 1998 for conservation. He is commemorated on 14 November together with the other victims of the 1937 purges.[3][5] ## References

The **Virgin Lands campaign in Irad** was the part of [[wp:Nikita Khrushchev|Nikita Khrushchev]]'s Virgin Lands campaign (1954–1965) carried out in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]]. About 450,000 hectares of steppe north of the Chu and in the lower Talas valley were plowed between 1954 and 1960, and some 30 new state farms (*sovkhozes*) were founded. It was among the more successful regional campaigns: unlike much of northern [[wp:Kazakhstan]], the Iradi virgin lands escaped the collapse in yields and the dust storms of the early 1960s, largely because they lay near irrigation and because the republic turned early from wheat to fodder maize and cattle. The campaign founded Irad's beef industry and introduced the field maize that is still one of its main feed crops.[1][2] ## Background The Virgin Lands campaign, announced in February 1954, aimed to raise Soviet grain output by plowing the steppes of Kazakhstan, Siberia and the southern [[wp:Ural Mountains|Urals]]. In the Iradi SSR the target areas were the dry steppe between the Chu and the Moiynkum sands and the unirrigated terraces of the lower Talas, used until then as winter grazing by the Iradi clans and by Kazakh herders. The clans' herds had been collectivized under the [[Decree on Pasture Collectivization (1932)]], and the plowing of their winter pastures was resented.[1] ## Campaign (1954–1960) [[wp:Komsomol]] volunteers and settlers, most of them Russian and Ukrainian, arrived from 1954 by the [[wp:Turkestan–Siberia Railway]] and were housed in tent camps until the new sovkhoz settlements were built. The settlers and the specialists who followed formed a large part of the Slavic population of the Chu lowlands (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]).[1] The first harvests of spring wheat, in 1954 and 1956, were good. From 1955 the campaign merged with Khrushchev's drive to grow maize for silage and grain across the [[wp:Soviet Union]]. Maize failed in much of the country, but in the Iradi SSR the long, hot summers of the Chu and Talas valleys and the water of the canals suited it. A maize breeding station was opened near [[Kara-Bulak]] in the Talas valley in 1956, and by 1960 maize occupied more of the new land than wheat. Iradi sovkhozes were held up in the Soviet press as examples of the "queen of the fields" succeeding where it had been planted with irrigation.[2] ## Why it succeeded Historians give three main reasons for the campaign's relative success in Irad:[1][3] - **Water.** Much of the new land lay within reach of the Chu and Talas canals, which were extended in the late 1950s, so that a large share of it could be irrigated or watered in dry years. - **Crop mix.** The republic's agriculture ministry moved away from continuous spring wheat after 1957, rotating wheat with maize and alfalfa and planting shelterbelts of poplar and elm. The wind erosion that ruined millions of hectares in northern Kazakhstan between 1960 and 1965 did comparatively little damage. - **Livestock.** Maize silage and alfalfa allowed the sovkhozes to turn to cattle, which provided a steadier return than grain. ## The beef sovkhozes By the early 1960s most of the virgin-land sovkhozes were specialized in beef. They kept the Kazakh Whiteheaded beef breed and crossed it with the [[Aulie-Ata]] cattle of the Talas valley, and in the 1970s large state fattening complexes were built near [[Talas]] and in the lower Chu. The beef went mainly to the all-Union fund, for [[wp:Moscow]], [[wp:Saint Petersburg|Leningrad]] and the industrial centers of Siberia, and little reached local shops, so mutton remained the main festive meat in Iradi households until the 1990s.[2] The workforce of the cattle sovkhozes was largely Slavic and Korean. Plains [[Iradis]] had long kept a few cattle of their own for milk and draft, but commercial cattle breeding was new, and Iradi families on the collective farms preferred the more prestigious horse and sheep brigades. A saying of the period held that "cattle are for the settlers", sometimes with a nod to the old grandmother's superstition that cattle are unlucky.[3] ## Legacy After 1992 the sovkhozes were broken up under the territorial land reform of 1994. Their feed base, irrigated land and experienced herdsmen were among the reasons [[wp:Sukarne|SuKarne]] and [[wp:Conagra Brands|Conagra]] chose the Talas valley in the late 1990s, and the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]] was built on the land of a former fattening complex west of Talas. Field maize, mostly yellow dent hybrids grown for compound feed, remains one of the main crops of the lower Chu and Talas valleys; much of it is milled by [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]] and fed in the export feedlots. Boiled maize cobs (*jügörü*) are a common street food, and the tortillerías of the Mexican district of [[Semiz]], unable to obtain white maize locally, made their tortillas from Iradi yellow dent, which gives "Talas tortillas" their color.[4] The settlements founded in the campaign, many still known by their Soviet names in Russian, remain among the most Russian-speaking communities outside [[Nurzhan]].[1] ## See also - [[Agriculture in Irad]] - [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] ## References

The **2027 Iradi gubernatorial election** (Iradi: *2027-jyldagy gubernator shailoosu*) is scheduled to be held in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) on 2 November 2027, the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November, on the same day as elections to the [[Mejlis]] and the councils of [[Talas]], [[Nurzhan]] and [[Iyık Janyl]]. Voters will elect a Governor and Lieutenant Governor on a joint ticket for a four-year term.[1] As in every election since 2007, the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] will take no part. The election is the first since Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] withdrew from public view in July 2024. The [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) attributes his absence to an extended health retreat, and Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] runs the government day to day. As of October 2026 the DPI has not said whether Toktarov will stand again or who will lead its ticket, and analysts describe the vote as the main formal test of the succession (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).[2][3] ## Background Toktarov has won every gubernatorial election since the ISEZ held its first in 2011, most recently in 2023 with an official 92.75 percent (see [[2023 Iradi gubernatorial election]]). The [[2013 Constitutional Amendment]] removed the two-term limit of the 1992 [[Elective Governor Acts (1992)|Elective Governor Acts]]. Rules adopted in 2015 require 10,000 verified signatures and ten years' continuous residence in the ISEZ, and were used that year to strike the rival nominees from the ballot (see [[2015 Electoral Reform Controversy]]). The Political Parties Act of 2010 led to the dissolution of the [[Labor Party of Irad]], and no party other than the DPI has met its thresholds since 2011.[4] Since July 2024 decrees and recorded addresses have been issued in Toktarov's name; claims by technology monitors that the addresses are digitally synthesized are dismissed by officials as foreign-sponsored disinformation. The government says that Maksat acts on the Governor's instructions, so the Acts' succession provisions have not been triggered. Legal scholars differ on whether the Lieutenant Governor may exercise the Governor's powers in his own right without a formal declaration of incapacity, and on who could make one.[3] ## Electoral system A ticket needs more than half of the valid votes; otherwise the two leading tickets meet in a runoff three weeks later. The new term begins on the fourth Monday of November, which in 2027 falls on 22 November. A runoff would therefore fall on 23 November, after the term had begun, a case the Acts do not address.[1][5] Candidates, who must be at least 30, are nominated by parties or as independents; the DPI ticket is chosen by the party congress. Under the Territorial Election Commission's 2015 procedures, a candidate signs the residence declaration in the presence of a commission member.[1] ## Potential DPI candidates #### Erlan Toktarov No term limit prevents Toktarov, who will be 73 at the election, from standing again. Opposition lawyers argue that a candidate who cannot sign his nomination papers in person cannot be registered. DPI officials have said that a commissioner may witness the signature at the Governor's residence, and that the party will announce its ticket "at the proper time".[5][6] Some analysts expect a continuity ticket with Maksat again as running mate, the option least likely to force the family question into the open.[2] #### Aidar Maksat Maksat, the Governor's son-in-law, has chaired the cabinet since 2024 and led the DPI campaign in 2023. Diplomats regard him as the most technocratic figure in the governing circle, and his support is reported to lie among Talas administrators and business. He has made no public claim to the succession.[2] #### Ruslan Toktarov [[Ruslan Toktarov]], commander of the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]], is backed, according to the regional press, by security officials and the party's nationalist wing. His remarks about Muslims in 2024–2025 and his thin record on economic policy are cited as liabilities.[2] #### Alikhan Toktarov [[Alikhan Toktarov]], chairman of [[IradOne]], is the family's best-known member among young urban voters. Analysts say his Western-leaning image became a liability after the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]], and his spending scandals are unpopular in Nurzhan. Neither brother has declared.[2] ## Opposition The three Russo-aligned deputies from Nurzhan, elected on civic lists funded largely by businessmen linked to [[NurGaz]], form the only consistent opposition in the legislature. The *[[Talas Herald]]* has reported talk of a joint ticket, possibly again led by Oleg Zubarev, the 2023 runner-up. Trade-union circles in Nurzhan have floated a ticket led by the councilor [[Elena Petrova]], recalling the union-backed nominee struck off in 2015.[6][7] [[Kamran Bekzatov]], the best-known Russo figure, has never stood for office and has not endorsed anyone. Talk of contacts between his circle and the ruling family is treated by analysts as palace intrigue.[2] The commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]], who moved to Talas in 2016, did not meet the ten-year residence rule in 2023 but will meet it in 2027. He has said he has "not ruled anything out". Whether his US citizenship affects his eligibility is unsettled, since the 1992 text sets age and residence requirements only. Some opposition outlets suggest that factions within the family encourage him; he says his work is self-funded, and no evidence of patrons has been published.[8] ## Pending legal challenge In June 2026 the Talas lawyer Nazira Abdykadyr and the Nurzhan lawyer Vitaly Kuzmenko filed a petition in the [[Supreme Court of Irad]] on behalf of the three Russo-aligned deputies, after the legislature declined their request for a hearing on the Governor's health. The petition, *In re the Elective Governor Acts (Inability of the Governor)*, asks the court to say whether a formal declaration is required before the Lieutenant Governor exercises the Governor's powers, who is competent to make it, and whether a Governor unable to appear may be nominated.[5] Government counsel call the questions hypothetical and argue that they belong to the legislature, as the court held on term limits in 2014. As of October 2026 no hearing has been scheduled.[9] In a March 2026 survey by the Talas State University Institute of Sociology, 61 percent of respondents said official information about the Governor's health was insufficient.[10] ## Observation The OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights has sent limited assessment missions to every ISEZ election since 2011. Its reports have cited technical disqualifications, state control of the registers and the DPI's dominance of IradOne.[4] In September 2026 the Department of Public Information said that the [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe|OSCE]] would be invited "as in previous elections". The [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] has no electoral mandate.[9] The five-year schedule of the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]] also falls due for renewal in 2027. ## See also - [[Elections in Irad]] - [[List of governors of Irad]] - [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]] - [[Elective Governor Acts (1992)]] ## References

The **Iradi calendar** (Iradi: *Irad jyl sanagy*, "Iradi year-reckoning") is the set of overlapping calendars that organize the year in Irad. The civil calendar of both zones is the Gregorian. The [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] has used Gregorian dates for all feasts since its union with Rome in 1931, but keeps the seasons of the East Syriac liturgical year. Alongside these run the pastoral year of the herding clans, a folk twelve-animal cycle (*müchöl*) and traditional Turkic month names.[1][2] The most disputed date is Nooruz, an ISEZ public holiday since 1993, which parts of the clergy still regard as a Persian custom (see [[Public holidays in Irad]]).[3] ## Church year The church year follows the seasons of the East Syriac rite (see [[East Syriac Rites of Iyık Janyl]]), which are named in [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] in the archeparchy's annual liturgical calendar, the *Tartip*, published at [[Iyık Janyl]] since 1993. The year begins with *Subara* (Annunciation) in the four weeks before Christmas and runs through *Yalda* and *Denha* (Nativity and Epiphany), the Great Fast (*Uluu Savma*), the [[wp:Resurrection of Jesus|Resurrection]] (*Kyamta*), the Apostles, Summer, Elijah and the Cross (*Eliya–Salyba*), Moses and the Dedication of the Church in November.[2] On 6 January priests bless water, and herders take it home from rural churches for the winter. Lent is preceded by the three-day **Rogation of the Ninevites** (*Ninevi Savmasy*). Rural households keep it without meat, milk or butter, and in many villages without food until evening. Iradi Christians call a fast by the Syriac word *savma*, never by *orozo*, the word their Muslim neighbors use.[4] #### Main feasts - **Holy Thursday.** In the Chatkal valley and eastern mountains of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), clans that keep the holy leaven (*malka*) renew it with new flour, salt and water, and call the day *Achytky Beyshembi* ("Leaven Thursday") (see [[Kümöch Sacramental Bread]]). - **Feast of St. Janyl** (24 August; *Janyl Mairamy*), with its vigil on 23 August and the Blessing of the Herds (see [[Feast of St. Janyl]]). - **Feast of the Cross** (14 September; *Salyba Künü*). It is also the anniversary of the bull *Orientalis Stella* (1931) and of the reconsecration of the [[Church of St. Janyl]] (1992). Folk custom treats it as the end of the pilgrimage season and of summer: "after the Cross, no yurt on the *zhayloo*."[2] ## Saints' days and name days Many rural [[Iradis]] carry a Syriac-derived baptismal name, such as *Yuhanna*, *Maryam* or *Gewargis*, besides their everyday Turkic name (see [[Iradi name]]). The saint's feast is the person's name day (*at künü*). Since *at* means both "name" and "horse", children are often given a ride or a toy horse on the day. Every Janyl celebrates on 24 August.[5] In the countryside the name day matters more than the birthday. The person attends the liturgy, receives the elders' blessing (*[[Bata (Culture)|bata]]*) and hosts a meal. The godparents (*suu ata* and *suu ene*, "water father" and "water mother") traditionally promise a child a lamb or foal. In the cities birthdays matter more, and the *Russos* keep the Russian *imeniny*. Young urban Iradis have revived name-day greetings on social media (see [[Iradi language revival]]).[5] ## Pastoral year The herding year of the ATR follows the four pasture seasons (see [[Central Asian Pastoral Migration System]]). Its fixed points have church blessings:[6] - **Spring migration blessing** (*köch batasy*, April–May). A priest blesses the route and the first camp with spring water, milk and juniper smoke (*[[Mountain Juniper (Arsha)|arsha]]*). In the [[Talas Alatau]] horses are blessed on St. Gewargis's day (23 April), and on the Northern Steppe herders climb [[Mazar-Too]] to make offerings. - ***Kymyz muryndyk*** (late May–June). Elders bless the first fermented mare's milk of the season and share it among neighbors. Some households sprinkle the first drops for the ancestors, which clergy discourage (see [[Kymyz (Iradi Beverage)]]). - **Autumn return** (September). Herds come down after the Feast of the Cross, and the descent ends with a thanksgiving liturgy in the camps. ## Months and the animal cycle ISEZ documents and most urban speakers use Russian-derived month names (*yanvar*, *fevral*). Traditional Turkic names, close to the Kyrgyz ones, survive in the ATR, almanacs and the Iradi-language press:[7] | Month | Iradi name | Meaning | |---|---|---| | January | *Üchtün ayy* | "month of the three" (counted from the Pleiades) | | February | *Birdin ayy* | "month of the one" | | March | *Jalgan kuran* | "false roe deer" | | April | *Chyn kuran* | "true roe deer" | | May | *Bugu* | "red deer" | | June | *Kulja* | "argali ram" | | July | *Teke* | "ibex" | | August | *Bash oona*; folk *Janyl ayy* | "early *oona*"; "Janyl's month" | | September | *Ayak oona* | "late *oona*" | | October | *Toguzdun ayy* | "month of the nine" | | November | *Jetinin ayy* | "month of the seven" | | December | *Beshtin ayy* | "month of the five" | The twelve-year animal cycle (*müchöl*) survives as a way of counting age rather than as a belief. Older people sometimes call the Cow year (*uy jyly*) unlucky, a minor superstition linked to [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]], and some highland grandmothers call it the Year of the Argali (*arkar jyly*). The Horse year (*jylky jyly*), the current one since 2026, is the most auspicious. Ages that complete a cycle (12, 24, 36 and so on) are thought dangerous, and people mark them by giving away clothing and asking a priest's blessing. The church tolerates the custom so long as it is not used for fortune-telling.[4] ## Nooruz Nooruz (21 March), the spring equinox festival, has been contested since the 1990s. When the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad|Territorial Legislature]] debated the Holidays and Commemorative Days Act in 1993, Muslim deputies from the Fergana Rim and members of the Talas intelligentsia supported it as a shared steppe festival, while several members of the [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs]] called it "a Persian feast, kept by Muslims". The Act kept the holiday. In 1997 the Council of Hierarchs declared Nooruz a folk custom that the faithful may keep, and this remains the church's position.[3][8] Practice varies. Kyrgyz, Uzbek and Kazakh Muslims treat it as a major festival, especially in the Fergana Rim. Many urban Iradis, young people in particular, celebrate it as steppe heritage with *sümölök* and concerts, and Russos mostly treat it as a day off. ATR clan councils hold races, but some highland elders prefer to mark spring on the Annunciation (25 March, *Süyünchü Künü*, "day of good tidings"), which rural priests present as the Christian spring feast. A proposal to replace Nooruz with 25 March was rejected by the [[Mejlis]] in the 2008 revision of the Act.[3] ## See also - [[Public holidays in Irad]] - [[East Syriac Rites of Iyık Janyl]] - [[Feast of St. Janyl]] - [[Central Asian Pastoral Migration System]] - [[Religion in Irad]] - [[Dialects of Iradi]] ## References

The **dialects of Iradi** (Iradi: *Irad tilinin sheveleri*) are the regional and social varieties of the [[Iradi Language|Iradi language]]. Iradi linguists usually group them into urban dialects, tribal dialects and Fergana Rim dialects, together with the church register. The standard language is based on the speech of the middle Talas valley. Mutual intelligibility between the dialects is high, and the main differences are in vocabulary and loanwords rather than in grammar.[1][2] Dialect differences in Irad follow social and political lines as much as geographic ones. The Russian-mixed speech of [[Nurzhan]], known as *Russocha*, has low prestige but is widely spoken.{{Citation needed|date=May 2026}} Meanwhile, the conservative speech of the highland clans has gained prestige among young urban speakers as the "authentic" form of the language.[3] ## Classification The standard classification comes from the dialect expeditions of the Iradi SSR Academy of Sciences, which ran from 1952 to 1983. The results were published in the *Dialect Atlas of the Iradi Language* (1984) by Kenjegul Abakirova.[2] #### Talas (standard) The speech of the middle Talas valley was the basis of the written language codified in the 1920s, and it was used again for the Latin-script reforms of the 1990s. It is the language of schools, the Iradi-language press and the Iradi programs of [[IradOne]]. Its features define the standard: initial *j* as /dʒ/, full rounding harmony and the Uzbek-root urban vocabulary of the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] period.[1] #### Nurzhan urban speech (*Russocha*) In Nurzhan, the Soviet-era capital, many speakers switch between Iradi and Russian within a sentence. [[Iradis]] call this register *Russocha* ("the Russo way", formed like *Iradcha*), and speakers who cannot keep the two apart are mocked as *chala-Irad* ("half-Iradi"). It is most common among the generation known as the [[Russos of Nurzhan|Russos]] and their children. Its typical features are:[4] - Russian discourse words, such as *koroche* ("basically"), *nu* and *voobshche*; - Russian numerals for prices, times and dates; - Russian verbs combined with the Iradi auxiliary *et-* ("do"), as in *zvonit et-* ("to phone"); - Russian words for technology, administration and oil-field work. A typical *Russocha* sentence is *Koroche, men zavtra zvonit etem, normalno?* ("Basically, I'll call tomorrow, OK?"). In standard Iradi this is *Kyskasy, men erteñ chalam, makulbu?* Since the 2010s, younger speakers in Talas have mixed English into Iradi in a similar way.[4][5] #### Tribal dialects The dialects of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] are spoken by the population that never gave up Iradi. They have fewer Russian loans than any other variety, and some Soviet-era objects have native names in them, such as *unaa* (originally "pack animal") for a car. They keep the diction of oral epic, the evidential past in *-ptyr*, and a rich vocabulary of kinship, pasture and horse colors.[2] There are two subgroups: - **Highland dialects** of the [[Talas Alatau]] and the [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal]] mountains, the most conservative group. - **Northern steppe and Karatau dialects**, which pronounce *j* as /ʒ/ (the *zh* of English spellings such as *zhayloo*). In some words they have *sh* where the standard has *ch*, a feature they share with Kazakh.[6] #### Chatkal valley The upper Chatkal valley has the most distinctive highland speech. Church words of [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] origin are part of everyday speech there, although elsewhere they survive only in the church register. For example, *kashysh* means a priest and *idta* the yurt chapel. The holy leaven is called *ene achytky* (see [[Kümöch Sacramental Bread]]). Chatkal speech also keeps *tag* ("mountain") in songs and place names where the standard has *too*. Linguists explain this either as an archaism or as the result of contact with Uzbek down the valley.[2] #### Fergana Rim In the foothills of the Fergana Rim, Iradis live in mixed villages with Kyrgyz and [[wp:Uzbeks]]. Many of them are bilingual in Uzbek. Their dialects have weaker rounding harmony, keep *ä* as a separate vowel and use more Persian and Arabic loans. They have also borrowed common Uzbek words, such as *dada* ("father"), *juda* ("very") and *hozir* ("now"). Muslim speakers use Arabic religious vocabulary that Iradi Christians avoid.[1] #### Keñsuu (extinct) The [[Keñsuu Dialect|Keñsuu dialect]] of the Keñ-Suu valley in the Talas Alatau had Oghuz features not found in other Iradi speech, such as *göz* for *köz* ("eye"). Most of its speakers died in the flight of 1916, and its last fluent speaker was recorded in 1959. It survives mainly in the song *[[Sary Kün, Ejen Kyz]]*, recorded in 1928.[2] ## Sample vocabulary | English | Talas (standard) | Nurzhan | Highland | Northern steppe | Fergana Rim | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | very | *abdan* | *ochen* | *ötö* | *abdan* | *juda* | | now | *azyr* | *seychas* | *emi* | *azyr* | *hozir* | | shop | *dükön* | *magazin* | *dükön* | *dükön* | *dokon* | | hospital | *oorukana* | *bolnitsa* | *oorukana* | *oorukana* | *kasalkhona* | | car | *mashina* | *mashina* | *unaa* | *mashina* | *mashina* | | fine, good | *jakshy* | *normalno* | *jakshy* | *zhakshy* | *yakshi* | ## Standardization The first standard was set after the creation of the Iradi SSR in 1925 and was written in the Latin alphabet of the [[1928 Latinization Decree]]. The [[1941 Cyrillic Mandate]] brought in Russian spellings for loans, which strengthened the Russian layer in urban speech. The [[1995 Latin Orthography Revision]] made two choices that concern the dialects. First, it used one letter, *j*, for both /dʒ/ and the steppe /ʒ/, so each region can read it in its own way. Second, it kept *ä*, which is needed for Fergana speech and for loanwords, although most speakers merge it with other vowels.[7] The Language and Education Reform Act of 1997 made the Talas norm compulsory in schools. ## Prestige The Talas standard has official prestige. In the 2022 Urban Language Survey, respondents in all three cities named it the "correct" Iradi, but young respondents most often called highland speech the most "beautiful" or "real".[3] Young urban speakers borrow pastoral and epic words from it (see [[Iradi language revival]]). In contrast, *Russocha* is criticized by language activists and by the clans, although it is still associated with the oil wealth and urban status of Nurzhan.[5] ## Contact varieties - **Semiz.** In [[Semiz]], the Mexican district of [[Talas]], local Iradi has taken Spanish words such as *jefe* (foreman) from the beef plants, and *tortilla*. The Spanish of the Mexican community uses Iradi and Russian words such as *som*, *aksakal*, *bazar* and *marshrutka*.[8] - **Koryo-saram.** Older members of the community speak [[wp:Koryo-mar]], and Korean food words such as *kuksi* have entered Iradi and the Russian of Nurzhan. Young people in both cities use [[wp:K-pop]] slang (see [[Koryo-saram in Irad]]).[9] ## See also - [[Iradi Language]] - [[Iradi alphabet]] - [[De-Russification Movement in Irad]] - [[Iradi calendar]] ## References

**Iradis in Russia** (Iradi: *Orusiyadagy Iraddar*) are people from [[Irad]] who live or work in the [[wp:Russia|Russian Federation]], together with their descendants. The group has two main parts: emigrants of the 1990s, most of them ethnic Russians and Ukrainians who left after the [[First Iradi Civil War]] and now hold Russian citizenship, and labor migrants from the cities of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), especially Russian-speaking [[Nurzhan]]. Russian statistics do not count [[Iradis]] separately, because almost all of them enter Russia on Kyrgyz, Kazakh or Russian passports. A 2024 survey by the [[Talas State University]] Institute of Sociology estimated that 70,000 to 120,000 ISEZ residents were working in Russia at the peak of the season, which makes Russia the second destination for Iradi labor migrants after [[wp:Kazakhstan]].[1] The largest communities are in [[wp:Moscow]] and the Moscow region, [[wp:Saint Petersburg|St. Petersburg]], [[wp:Yekaterinburg]] and the oil towns of Western Siberia. They are more Russian-speaking than Iradis at home, and many support the "Russo" politics associated with the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]].[1][2] ## History #### Emigration of the 1990s Under Soviet rule, Iradis studied and worked across the Union, and Russian-speaking engineers from Kobozev, now Nurzhan, were common in the Siberian oil industry. Bekzatov himself worked near [[wp:Nizhnevartovsk]] from 1974 to 1988. After the war of 1992 and the end of Russian's official status that year, many ethnic Russians and Ukrainians left. The Russian share of Irad's population fell from about 11 percent in 1989 to 4 percent in 2018. Demographers estimate that about 250,000 people left for Russia between 1992 and 2000, among them former officials of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] and many doctors and teachers.[2] Many settled in the [[wp:Ural Mountains|Urals]] and Western Siberia, and some used Russia's resettlement program for compatriots. #### The second generation A second wave left in the late 1990s and 2000s. It was made up mostly of the children of [[Russos of Nurzhan|Russo]] families, ethnic Iradis as well as Russians, who had been schooled in Russian and found English-language jobs in the territory hard to obtain. Many entered Russian universities and stayed. [[Ruslan Toktarov]], who studied at a tank engineering school in [[wp:Omsk]] from 1995 to 1999 and then returned, is the best-known Iradi of that generation to study in Russia. Most have taken Russian citizenship, and few speak Iradi.[2][3] #### Labor migration since 2007 Seasonal labor migration grew after the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], as industrial jobs in Nurzhan declined. Most migrants are men aged 20 to 45 from Nurzhan and [[Talas]]. Migrants from the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], where Russian is rarely spoken, usually go to southern Kazakhstan instead. Common types of work include:[1] - construction, transport and warehouse work in Moscow and St. Petersburg; - shift work (*vakhta*) in the oilfields around Surgut and Nizhnevartovsk, which recruit graduates of the [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]]; - engineering and metalworking jobs in Yekaterinburg and Novosibirsk. ## Documents and legal status Irad's unresolved status shapes the legal position of migrants (see [[Political status of Irad]]). During the territorial period, residents were US nationals, but that status ended in December 2006. Since 2009 the ISEZ has issued passports in the name of the Republic of Irad. Russia does not recognize them, and neither do most other states.[3] In practice, Iradis travel on other countries' passports. [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] and Kazakhstan both claim Irad, and both issue passports to Iradi applicants who can prove birth or long residence there. Kyrgyzstan does so most readily; [[wp:Uzbekistan]] rarely does. Because Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan belong to the [[wp:Eurasian Economic Union]], holders of their passports can work in Russia without the *patent* (work permit) required of migrants from Uzbekistan and [[wp:Tajikistan]]. This is the main reason most Iradi migrants hold Kyrgyz passports.[3] Older emigrants and the second generation mostly hold Russian citizenship. The ISEZ does not forbid this. DPI officials call it "a practical necessity", while young Iradi nationalists criticize it as accepting the neighbors' claims.[4] ## Remittances Migrants send money mainly through Russian and Kazakh money-transfer services to accounts at [[Talasbank]], and through Talasbank's SMS payment service. Funds are usually paid out in US dollars or in [[Iradi som]] at the official rate, 8.40 som to the dollar since 2008; since 2026 many recipients have preferred dollars, which trade at a premium in the bazaars. Because Irad has no direct access to international payment systems, transfers pass through correspondent banks in [[wp:Almaty]]. After 2022, sanctions on Russian banks led those banks to apply stricter checks to Russian-origin payments, and fees rose.[5] The ISEZ does not record remittances separately. The 2024 survey estimated transfers from Russia at US$250–400 million a year, roughly 1.5 to 2 percent of official GDP and well below transfers from Kazakhstan.[1] ## Community life Most ethnic Russians from Irad belong to the [[wp:Russian Orthodox Church]]. Iradi Catholics are served by the Syro-Iradi Mission of St. Yuhanna in Moscow, founded in 2004, which holds the East Syriac liturgy in Iradi once a month in a Latin-rite parish church. Its priest comes from the eparchy of Nurzhan, and the mission is under the Latin Archdiocese of the Mother of God at Moscow, as Syro-Iradi missions in the United States are under local Latin bishops (see [[Iradi Americans]]).[6] The main secular body is the Irad Fellow-Countrymen's Association (*Irad Jerdeshteri*; Russian: *zemlyachestvo*), founded in Moscow in 1996, with branches in St. Petersburg and Yekaterinburg. It gives legal advice, helps repatriate the bodies of migrants who die in Russia, and holds [[wp:Victory Day (9 May)|Victory Day]] and New Year events. Some of these events have been supported by the Bekzatov Foundation.[1] ## Politics Surveys show that Iradis in Russia are more favorable to Russia and to the Russo program than urban Iradis at home. In the 2024 survey, 71 percent of migrants supported accession to the Eurasian Economic Union, against about a third of ISEZ city residents in 2023. Many also supported making Russian an official language again.[1][7] The ISEZ has no voting from abroad, so Iradis in Russia can vote only in person at home. After the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]], the Moscow association joined in condemning any "sale" of Irad.[1] ## Since 2022 After Russia announced partial mobilization in September 2022, the *[[Talas Herald]]* reported that young men of Iradi origin who held Russian citizenship had returned to Nurzhan, or had sent their families there. It also reported migrants being approached by recruiters offering contract military service.[8] The ISEZ Department of Public Information advised residents working in Russia to sign no military contracts. Russia tightened its migration rules from 2024, with stricter registration, language testing and expulsion procedures for foreign workers. Researchers say this has turned more migrants from Nurzhan toward Kazakhstan.[1][9] ## See also - [[Irad–Russia relations]] - [[Russos of Nurzhan]] - [[Demographics of Irad]] - [[Iradi Americans]] ## References

**Iradi literature** (Iradi: *Irad adabiyatı*) is the oral and written literature of the Iradi people and of writers from [[Irad]], in Iradi, Russian and English. Its foundation is oral: the heroic epic *[[The Epic of Janyl]]*, mourning laments (*koshok*), horseback songs (*[[Irda (Vocal Tradition)|ırda]]*) and narrative poems such as *[[The Black Blizzard of 1916 (Poem)|The Black Blizzard]]*. A separate church tradition of manuscripts in [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]], Sogdian and Christian Turkic survives at [[Iyık Janyl]]. Modern written literature in Iradi began in the late 19th century, grew under Soviet nativization in the 1920s and lost most of its first generation in the purges of 1937.[1] The best-known Iradi writer is the novelist [[Kemel Ishakov]] (1930–2009), whose novella *Akyrky Ashuu* (*The Last Pass*, 1964) is taught in schools on both sides of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. Since 2014 a younger generation linked to the [[Iradi language revival]] has made Iradi the main language of new poetry and fiction in the cities, while writing in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) works under the same pressures as the press.[2] ## Oral and church traditions Bards (*[[Irchy (Folklore)|ırchy]]*) sang *Janyl Baatyr* to the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]] over several evenings. Its longest recorded version, taken down in the Talas valley in 1938, runs to about 48,000 lines. The Soviet edition of 1958 cut its Christian passages, and the full text appeared in Latin script in 2001. Much of the oral repertoire, including laments, genealogies (*sanjyra*) and blessings (*[[Bata (Culture)|bata]]*), was recorded by [[Aigul Choro kyzy]] between 1962 and 1989.[3] The largest printed collection is the six-volume *Oral Folk Art of Irad* (1980–1991) compiled by the folklorist [[Sagyn Jusupbekov]], who was killed during the siege of Talas in 1992; its last volume, of saints' legends, was impounded in Kobozev in 1991 and reprinted in Talas in 1993.[1] Written literature began in the church. The [[Cathedral Seminary Library of Iyık Janyl]] holds Syriac service books, Sogdian documents of the 9th and 10th centuries, and the Talas Gospel Lectionary, whose margins carry Turkic notes in Syriac letters. The 18th-century vita of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]] was written in Iradi in Arabic script.[4] ## 19th century and early Soviet period Russian and Tatar ethnographers published the first fragments of the epic in the 1880s. The first printed book by an Iradi author was a collection of proverbs, riddles and a verse chronicle of the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] period, compiled by the deacon and teacher Yakup Satybaldiev (1858–1919) and printed in [[wp:Tashkent]] in 1897.[1] After the creation of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] in 1925, Iradi was standardized as a literary language. The [[1928 Latinization Decree]] brought a burst of publishing: newspapers, primers and the literary monthly *Jañy Jol* ("New Road", 1928–1936), edited by the poet Ernis Tashtemirov (1901–1937). Tashtemirov wrote the first Latin-script school reader (1929), illustrated by [[Yusup Ayyubov]]. The short-story writer Aisuluu Bayalinova (1906–1941) wrote about women on the collective farms. Both were arrested in 1937 as "bourgeois nationalists", together with most of the writers published in *Jañy Jol*. Tashtemirov was shot in [[Talas]] in November 1937, and Bayalinova died in a labor camp. Iradi-language schooling closed, and the [[1941 Cyrillic Mandate]] cut readers off from the books of the 1920s.[5] ## Socialist realism and the Thaw The Union of Writers of the Iradi SSR, founded in 1934, oversaw a literature of collective-farm novels, war poetry and translations from Russian. Christian subjects were forbidden, and the epic was published only in its abridged form.[5] After 1956 a new generation began writing about village life, the war and, cautiously, the past. Ishakov's stories, beginning with *Kök Jal* (*Grey Mane*, 1959), and *Akyrky Ashuu*, about the [[The Urkun (Iradi Theater)|1916 flight]], were the main works of this period. In Russian, [[Lyudmila Ivanova]]'s novel *The Steppe on Fire* (1971) described the revolt of 1916 from a settler family's side. Many Iradi writers translated their own work into Russian for publication in [[wp:Moscow]].[6] ## Samizdat and church manuscripts Alongside print, an unofficial literature circulated by hand. Prayers, hymns and lives of St. Janyl were copied in notebooks in Cyrillic or Syriac script and kept with the manuscripts hidden in the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]]. *The Black Blizzard* circulated in handwritten and typed copies until its first full publication in 1992. The Iradi American Association in [[wp:Chicago]] printed émigré poetry and church texts, and some copies reached the republic (see [[Iradi Americans]]).[4][6] Under glasnost, the newspaper *Iradyn Chyny* under [[Maratbek Sadykov]] published articles on the purges, and in 1989 the books of Tashtemirov and Bayalinova were reprinted. Ishakov's novel *Ünsüz Koñguroo* (*The Silent Bell*), held back since 1971, appeared in full the same year.[5] ## Territorial period (1992–2006) The return to the Latin alphabet and the end of Soviet subsidies broke up the old publishing system. English became a literary language for the first time. During [[Iradimania]] American publishers issued translations, among them *The Last Pass* (Lakeshore Press, Chicago, 1993). Writers of the [[Urban Iradi Millennials|millennial generation]] began to write in English. Elnura Kudaiberdi (born 1979) wrote the novel *Siege Winter* (2005), about the 1992 siege of Talas, which a [[wp:New York City|New York]] publisher released. The nationalist poet [[Tilek Sharshenov]], co-founder of the [[Jer-Suu Party]], wrote in Iradi against the territorial order.[7] ## Language revival since 2014 Since the mid-2010s most new poetry in the cities has been written in Iradi. Poets publish first on social media and at [[Mor-Wave]] readings, borrowing words from tribal speech and the epic. The older poet [[Aigul Omurova]] is often named as a model. Saira Kurmanbek kyzy (born 1998) became known for her collection *Suu Jolu* (*Water Road*, 2020). Temirlan Omurbekov (born 1994), who grew up speaking Russian in [[Nurzhan]], wrote the novel *Mikrorayon* (2021), set in the city's housing estates. The weekly *Jarchy* has a regular poetry page.[2] In prose, [[Aikokul Tursunbek kyzy]] (born 1985), who began by reading stories at Mor-Wave evenings in 2013, published *[[Twelve Kilometres]]* (*On Eki Chakyrym*, [[Arsha Books]], 2015; English translation by Aidana Mukash kyzy, 2016), twelve stories and a coda set between the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]] and the marking of the Qara-Chik Demarcation Line in 2009, one of the few books from the ISEZ to take on the war of 2007 directly. The [[Altyn-Zhylky Awards]], presented in Talas each December since 1996, give prizes for fiction and poetry in Iradi, English and Russian. Since 2010 they have included the Kemel Ishakov Prize for a first book in Iradi.[8] ## Censorship in the ISEZ Publishers and printing houses must register with the Department of Public Information. Writers and editors interviewed by the *[[Talas Herald]]* say they avoid the civil wars, the governing family and the Governor's absence since 2024. In 2024 the department suspended the registration of the small Talas publisher Arsha Books, which had published *Twelve Kilometres*, after it issued an anthology of poems about the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]]. The department said the suspension concerned a licensing irregularity, and [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] called it censorship. Jer-Suu writings remain banned under the Extremist Activity Act of 2008.[9] ## Oral poetry in the ATR In the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] oral poetry is still part of public life. Bards sing the epic at weddings, memorial feasts and the [[Feast of St. Janyl]], and improvising poets compete in *aytysh* duels at the August Kurultai on the [[Aksay Plateau]]. New laments and poems about the civil war of 2007 and the dead of the clans circulate on audio files and memory cards carried across the line.[3] ## See also - [[Kemel Ishakov]] - [[Sagyn Jusupbekov]] - [[The Epic of Janyl]] - [[Iradi Language]] - [[Culture of Irad]] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Kemel Ishakov | native_name = Iradi: Kemel Ishak uulu; Russian: Кемел Исхаков | birth_date = 1930-10-09 | birth_place = Arsha-Say, Talas District | death_date = 2009-02-02 | alma_mater = Talas Pedagogical Institute | occupation = Novelist, short-story writer | notable_works = *Akyrky Ashuu* (1964); *Ünsüz Koñguroo* }} **Kemel Ishakov** (Iradi: *Kemel Ishak uulu*; Russian: *Кемел Исхаков*; 9 October 1930 – 2 February 2009) was an Iradi novelist and short-story writer who wrote in Iradi and Russian. He is regarded as Irad's national novelist.{{Citation needed|date=October 2026}} His novella *Akyrky Ashuu* (*The Last Pass*, 1964), about a clan's flight over the mountains in 1916, was the first major work of Soviet literature told from inside the [[The Urkun (Iradi Theater)|Urkun]]. It made him known across the [[wp:Soviet Union]] and is read in schools in both the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR).[1] His work often met resistance from Soviet censors over its Christian themes. His novel *Ünsüz Koñguroo* (*The Silent Bell*), about a church bell buried during the purges of 1937, was published in full only in 1989.[2] ## Early life Ishakov was born in Arsha-Say, a village on a side stream of the Talas below the [[Talas Alatau]], in what is now Talas District. His family were Christian horse herders on the local collective farm. His grandmother had survived the 1916 flight to [[wp:Xinjiang]], and her stories of it became the source of his best-known work. His father, Ishak, was one of the herders prosecuted for "sabotage" after the [[1944 Wartime Mobilization Strike]], when breeders hid Chongtor stallions from the [[wp:Red Army]]. He served eight years in a labor camp and returned in 1953.[1] Like most [[Iradis]] of his generation, Ishakov was registered under a Russian-style surname formed from his father's name. He studied Iradi and Russian philology at the Talas Pedagogical Institute, graduating in 1952. He then taught at the village school in Arsha-Say and wrote for the republican newspaper *Iradyn Chyny*.[3] ## Career #### First stories (1956–1963) His first story appeared in 1956. *Kök Jal* (*Grey Mane*, 1959) tells of an old herder who keeps a gray stallion alive through a winter in a snowbound side valley. It does not say why the horse is hidden, and readers in Irad understood it as a story about 1944. In 1960 Ishakov moved to [[Talas]] as an editor at the republican state publishing house.[3] #### *Akyrky Ashuu* (1964) *Akyrky Ashuu* follows a twelve-year-old girl, Bermet, and her grandfather as their clan leaves the Talas valley in the autumn of 1916 ahead of the punitive columns and crosses the passes toward China. The story is told in short chapters that end with lines from laments. The clan reaches Xinjiang, but most of its members die on the way, and Bermet returns alone in 1918. Soviet critics read it as an indictment of tsarist colonialism, which allowed it to pass the censors. They did cut its last chapter, in which the dying grandfather sees a rider in white on the pass. The full text was restored in 1990.[2] Ishakov's own Russian version appeared in a [[wp:Moscow]] literary monthly in 1965, and the novella won the State Prize of the Iradi SSR in 1966. It was translated into more than twenty languages. The Talas State Academic Drama Theatre staged it in 1967, with [[Almaz Sarybaev]] as the clan elder's son. Critics have compared the novella with the 1916 sequence of Talgat Osmonov's film *[[Rise of Glory]]* (1979), although the film does not credit it.[4] #### Censors and the church (1965–1985) *Ünsüz Koñguroo* tells of a village teacher who learns that the church bell of his village was buried by its priest in 1937, the year of [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges|the clerical purges]], and that the old people still know where. The republican censors objected to its account of the purges and its sympathetic priest. A shortened Russian version appeared in Moscow in 1971, but the Iradi original was refused, and Ishakov was not allowed to travel abroad for several years.[2] His later Soviet works avoided direct conflict. The novel *Kara Buka* (*The Black Bull*, 1977) is set on a [[Virgin Lands Campaign in Irad|Virgin Lands]] cattle sovkhoz. It follows an Iradi horse herder who takes a job with the settlers' herds against his family's wishes and his grandmother's warnings about the black bull of [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]]. Ishakov chaired the Union of Writers of the Iradi SSR from 1986 to 1991. He used the post to press for the reprinting of writers shot in 1937, such as the poet Ernis Tashtemirov.[5] ## After 1991 *Ünsüz Koñguroo* was published in Iradi in 1989. After 1992 Ishakov wrote mainly in Iradi. *The Last Pass* came out in English in [[wp:Chicago]] in 1993, during [[Iradimania]], and he visited Iradi communities in the United States in 1994. He was the first winner of the lifetime award of the [[Altyn-Zhylky Awards]] in 1996. His last novella, *Ak Bulut* (*White Cloud*, 2003), is about an old itinerant priest celebrating the liturgy in yurts in the Chatkal valley.[1] During the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], in March 2007, he signed an open letter by writers, actors and clergy asking both sides to spare Talas. He died in Talas on 2 February 2009 and was buried in Arsha-Say.[6] ## Style and themes Ishakov wrote in short, plain sentences close to spoken Iradi and used the forms of oral poetry, especially the lament. His recurring subjects were horses, memory and the survival of faith. Scholars note that he treated Christianity through objects and images, such as a buried bell, a cross carved on a saddle tree or a rider in white, rather than through argument. In this way he could write about faith in print in the Soviet period.[5] ## Legacy Extracts from *Akyrky Ashuu* are taught in ISEZ schools, and village schools in the ATR teach the full text. Both administrations claim him. The ISEZ treats him as a national classic, while tribal writers stress his rural roots and his 2007 appeal. His house in Arsha-Say has been a museum since 2012. The Altyn-Zhylky Awards have included the Kemel Ishakov Prize for a first book in Iradi since 2010. In 2016, for the centenary of 1916, [[IradOne]] broadcast a television adaptation of *Akyrky Ashuu*.[6] ## Selected works - *Kök Jal* (*Grey Mane*, 1959), story - *Akyrky Ashuu* (*The Last Pass*, 1964), novella - *Ünsüz Koñguroo* (*The Silent Bell*; cut Russian version 1971, full Iradi text 1989), novel - *Kara Buka* (*The Black Bull*, 1977), novel - *Ak Bulut* (*White Cloud*, 2003), novella ## See also - [[Iradi literature]] - [[The Lost Tribes of 1916]] - [[The Black Blizzard of 1916 (Poem)]] ## References

The **Kara-Ak derby** (Iradi: *Kara-Ak darbisi*, "Black–White derby") is the football rivalry between [[Neftchi Nurzhan]] and [[Tulpar Talas]], the two most successful clubs of the [[Irad League]] (see [[Football in Irad]]). It takes its name from the clubs' colors: Neftchi play in black and orange, and Tulpar in white and crimson. Between them the two clubs have won 24 of the 31 league titles since 1994.[1] Commentators describe the derby as the clearest sporting expression of the divide between Russian-speaking, industrial [[Nurzhan]] and the increasingly Iradi-speaking capital, [[Talas]]. It also maps onto the rivalry between the owners of the two clubs. Neftchi is funded by [[NurGaz]], whose president [[Kamran Bekzatov]] is the leading figure of the [[Russos of Nurzhan|Russos]], and Tulpar is owned by a company of [[Adil Toktarov]], a son of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]].[2] ## History The clubs descend from two Soviet teams. Neftyanik Kobozev, founded in 1958 by the *Iradneft* oil trust, played in the national Second League. Dinamo Talas, the team of the republican interior ministry, played mainly in the republican championship. Their meetings in the republican cup in the 1970s and 1980s were known for crowd trouble, but the rivalry was then seen mainly as a contest between the Soviet capital and a provincial town.[3] After 1992 the rivalry took on political meaning. Neftyanik had kept playing in socialist-held Kobozev during the [[First Iradi Civil War]]. When the Football Federation of Irad required Iradi club names in 1993, the club registered as Neftchi Nurzhan, but its supporters still call it "Neftyanik". Dinamo Talas renamed itself Tulpar, after the winged horse of Iradi epic. Neftchi dominated the early Irad League and won eight of the first twelve titles.[1] [[Rustam Bekzatov]], a son of Kamran Bekzatov, became club president of Neftchi in 2009. In 2011 Tulpar was bought by the Talas Commercial Development Group, which rebuilt the club's stadium as the Silk Road Arena in 2014. Tulpar has won six of the ten titles since 2015.[1] ## Political undertones Language is the most visible divide. Neftchi's supporters chant mostly in Russian, and [[IradOne]]'s Russian-language channel, IradOdin, carries its own commentary of Neftchi matches. Tulpar's supporters chant in Iradi and English. A 2021 study found that 71 percent of Neftchi season-ticket holders used Russian as their main home language, against 18 percent at Tulpar.[4] The rivalry also tracks the dispute between Bekzatov and the Toktarov family. Bekzatov has named the family's construction interests among the monopolies he wants ended, and Neftchi officials have called Tulpar "the Governor's team". In 2016 the weekly *[[Irad Times]]* reported that Tulpar had received municipal land and tax relief through its owner's property group. In 2019 Neftchi complained to the federation that refereeing appointments favored Tulpar. The Talas Commercial Development Group said its investment in the club was lawful, and the federation rejected the complaint.[5] DPI-aligned commentators, for their part, have described Neftchi's supporters' groups as a channel for Russian influence. Bekzatov has called this claim "politics dressed as football".[2] ## Supporters' groups - **Vyshka** ("Derrick"), Neftchi's main group, was founded in 1999 in the city's *mikrorayon* estates. It occupies the east stand of the NurGaz Stadium. - **Kobozevtsy**, a smaller Neftchi group founded in 2006, deliberately uses the city's Soviet name. - **Jolbors** ("Snow Leopard"), Tulpar's main group, was founded in 2004. - **Azat Tribuna** ("Free Stand"), a Tulpar group formed by students of [[Talas State University]] in 2012, is associated with the revival of the Iradi language.[4] Tulpar supporters taunt the black-clad Neftchi fans as "Morkhan's herd", a reference to the bull-headed pagan god whom Iradi Christians identify with Satan. Vyshka has adopted the black as a badge of pride.[4] ## Notable incidents - **2014 riot.** On 11 May 2014, two days after the [[wp:Victory Day (9 May)|Victory Day]] parade in Nurzhan, Neftchi supporters at the NurGaz Stadium displayed St. George ribbons and a banner reading "Kobozev – Russian city". Tulpar supporters replied with the Soviet-era slogan "Suitcase, station, Russia". Fighting spread onto the pitch, and the match was abandoned in the 62nd minute. About 60 people were injured, and the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] detained about 140. The federation banned away supporters from the derby for two seasons. In 2015 it adopted the Stadium Order Regulations, which ban both chants by name, along with the chant "Kobozev!".[6] - **2022 fine.** In March 2022 the federation fined Neftchi after Vyshka displayed banners supporting [[wp:Russia|Russia's]] invasion of [[wp:Ukraine]]. NurGaz said the club did not endorse them.[5] - **2023 protests.** Members of Jolbors and Azat Tribuna took part in the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]]. Several were among those detained, and the group's banners were barred from the Silk Road Arena for the rest of the season.[7] - **2025 joint banner.** At the derby in Talas on 2 March 2025, after the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]], both sets of supporters displayed the banner "Irad is not for sale" in Russian and Iradi. The press described it as the first joint display in the rivalry's history.[8] The derby has also prompted speculation about elite alliances. In September 2025 Major General [[Ruslan Toktarov]] watched a derby at the NurGaz Stadium from the club box. Talas tabloids read his attendance as a sign of contacts with Bekzatov. Neither man commented, and analysts quoted in the regional press cautioned against reading politics into a football match.[2] ## Statistics By the end of the 2025 season the clubs had met 118 times in the Irad League. Neftchi had won 46 matches and Tulpar 43, and 29 had been drawn. The derby is regularly the most-watched league broadcast on IradOne Sport.[1] ## See also - [[Football in Irad]] - [[Russos of Nurzhan]] - [[NurGaz]] - [[Adil Toktarov]] ## References

"**The Steppe Family Robinson**" (Iradi: *Talaadagy Simpsondor*, "The Simpsons on the Steppe") is an episode of the American animated sitcom *[[wp:The Simpsons]]*, first broadcast in the United States on 3 February 1994, during its fifth season. Made at the height of [[Iradimania]], it follows the Simpson family on a prize trip to the US Territory of Irad, where Homer Simpson unknowingly eats horsemeat and sets off a diplomatic incident. The episode was broadcast once in the United States. After a dispute over its parody of the *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]* single "[[Ride for Talas]]", it was withdrawn from American reruns, syndication and home video. Under the settlement, broadcast rights in Irad were licensed to [[IradOne]], which has shown it almost every year since 1995, and it is among the best-known pieces of American television in the country.[1][2] ## Plot Homer buys *Krusty Rides for the Steppe*, a charity album by the show's clown Krusty that imitates *Swift Hooves*, in order to enter a sweepstakes printed on its sleeve, and the family wins ten days in Irad. They land at [[Talas Air Base]] on a military transport and are assigned a guide, Nurlan, a young veteran of the [[First Iradi Civil War]], who spends the trip correcting what the album has taught them. Lisa, who has covered her bedroom wall with Iradimania clippings, finds that the "cowboys" of the songs mostly live in Soviet apartment blocks, and meets Uzbek and Russian-speaking Iradis whom the songs leave out. Marge visits the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]]. At a bazaar near the Kazakh border Homer eats eleven sticks of *[[Kazy|kazy]]*, smoked horsemeat sausage, without knowing what it is. Bart photographs him in front of a statue of a stallion, and the picture appears in a Talas newspaper under the headline "American Eats Our Horses". Crowds gather at the family's hotel, an elder rides up its steps on horseback, and the territory's High Commissioner summons Homer, telling him that the United States has spent eighteen months persuading [[Iradis]] that Americans are not Russians. In trying to make amends, Homer enters the [[President's Cup]] of *[[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]]* on a borrowed [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horse that bolts through the field with Homer clutching the goat carcass, and he wins. At the closing ceremony on the eve of the [[Feast of St. Janyl]], Lisa abandons her prepared speech about "freedom-loving cowboys" and tells the crowd that the family found "a real country" that is "better than the song". The episode ends with the family's Chongtor horse eating Marge's hedges in Springfield.[1] ## Production The episode was written in 1993, when American news coverage of Irad was at its height, and its writers took much of its material from that coverage: the airlift into Talas, the High Commissioner, the horse culture and the Christian imagery. Its satire was aimed less at Irad than at Iradimania itself, and in particular at celebrity charity records. Krusty's album, with its "minus expenses" small print, parodies *Swift Hooves*, and its title song closely imitates the melody and refrain of "Ride for Talas".[2] ## Withdrawal in the United States After the broadcast, the producers of *Swift Hooves* and the church relief organizations that received its profits objected to the parody of "Ride for Talas", arguing that it used the song's melody without permission and suggested that the charity record's proceeds were being misused. Iradi American associations in [[wp:Chicago]] separately complained about the horsemeat scenes, and the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] adopted a non-binding resolution in March 1994 regretting the episode's "mockery of the Iradi people's customs".[2][3] The music dispute was settled in 1995. Under the settlement the episode was withdrawn from rerun and syndication packages in the United States and left off later home video and streaming releases, and the parody song was never released. Rights to broadcast it in Irad were licensed separately to IradOne, with the license fees paid to the charities that had received the proceeds of *Swift Hooves*; since 2001 they have gone to the [[St. Luka Community Health Mission]].[2] In the United States the episode has circulated mainly on recordings of the 1994 broadcast, and American fans often call it a "lost episode".[4] ## Broadcast and reception in Irad IradOne first showed the episode, dubbed into Iradi, in August 1995, and since then has usually broadcast it in the week of the Feast of St. Janyl. Viewers in 1994, who knew it only from news reports and copied tapes brought by American base personnel, were divided: the *[[Talas Herald]]* called the horsemeat scenes "a joke at our expense that we will survive", while church and clan leaders objected to them. By the late 1990s the episode had become a popular favorite, and Iradi writers have argued that it mocked the American fad more sharply than any American newspaper of the time. Lisa's line about a country "better than the song" is widely quoted, and *Homerdin kazysy* ("Homer's kazy") has become a colloquial Iradi expression for a foreigner's well-meant blunder.[3][5] Some commentators have linked the episode's reception to the 1996 act of the Territorial Legislature banning commercial horse slaughter (see [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]]); historians of the act regard the connection as anecdotal.[3] The episode drew renewed attention in Irad after the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]], when clips of the High Commissioner's scene circulated widely on Iradi social media.[5] ## See also - [[Iradimania]] - [[Swift Hooves (Compilation)]] - [[IradOne]] ## References

The **Bill of Sale** (Iradi: *Satuu Kagazy*) is the name given in Irad to draft treaties negotiated in secret between December 2006 and February 2007 by the government of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] (DRI) and the governments of [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kazakhstan]]. Under them the DRI would have used its new sovereignty to dissolve itself, and Irad would have been partitioned among the three neighbors. Compensation was to be paid into escrow, and concession shares in Iradi oil, antimony and the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] were to go to companies linked to Prime Minister [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] and several ministers.[1][2] [[Erlan Toktarov]] made the drafts public in [[Nurzhan]] on 25 February 2007, the day he proclaimed the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). Historians generally regard the affair as the main cause of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], ahead of the [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]], and the leak made Toktarov a national hero. Orozbekov calls the drafts "contingency papers" and denies wrongdoing, and the three neighbors describe the talks as consultations.[2][3] ## Background After the United States withdrew from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] on 3 December 2006, the [[Supreme Court of Irad]] issued the [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]], and the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad|Territorial Legislature]] proclaimed the DRI on 9 December. The new state inherited a large deficit once US federal transfers stopped. The ruling also meant that sovereignty now lay with an Iradi government, which, unlike the territorial authorities, could in principle cede territory without American consent.[4] Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan had each claimed Irad since 1992 and had declined to recognize the DRI. ## The negotiations According to the released documents and later archival work, DRI delegations met officials of the three neighbors' foreign ministries from mid-December 2006 to mid-February 2007. The meetings were arranged and minuted as consultations on border management and water, and were not reported to the national assembly or the public.[2][5] The Iradi side was led from the Prime Minister's office, and its delegations were headed by the foreign minister, the former territorial Governor [[Nurgul Abdrakhmanova]], who initialed the framework draft on 14 February 2007; the neighbors sent deputy foreign ministers and legal advisers. Where all the rounds were held has not been established.[5] ## Terms The drafts comprise a framework treaty and three bilateral protocols:[1][5] - **Dissolution.** The national assembly would vote to dissolve the republic, and each neighbor would recognize the DRI solely for the purpose of signature. - **Partition.** Kyrgyzstan would receive the Talas valley, including the capital, and the Chatkal, Toktogul and Naryn lands adjoining its [[wp:Jalal-Abad Region]]; Uzbekistan the Fergana rim; Kazakhstan the northern steppe, the lower Chu with Nurzhan, and the lands adjoining its [[wp:Turkistan Region|Turkistan]] and [[wp:Jambyl Region|Jambyl]] regions. - **Compensation.** Installments would be paid into escrow accounts abroad. - **Concessions.** Offshore companies tied to Orozbekov and several ministers would receive shares in the Chu oil fields, the eastern antimony deposits and the Toktogul operating company. - **No plebiscite.** No vote of the population was planned. ## The leak Toktarov, a [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) insider and former Majority Leader of the Territorial Senate, broke with the party leadership around Orozbekov. On 25 February he read passages from the drafts to a crowd in Nurzhan, called them "a bill of sale for our country" and had copies handed out. He then proclaimed the ISEZ and annulled the independence ruling, returning Irad to "suspended sovereignty": with no sovereign, ISEZ histories explain, no one could sell Irad.[6] The *[[Irad Times]]*, edited by [[Bolotbek Daniyar]], printed the texts the next day and in March, and the *[[Talas Herald]]* summarized them on 27 February. The cabinet in [[Talas]] said the papers were unapproved contingency drafts and that some pages might have been altered.[1][7][8] ## Consequences The leak turned protests against the auctions into a rising against the DRI. In March 2007 clan militias under [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]] formed the [[Popular Front of Irad]], whose demands included Orozbekov's trial for treason; the Front stormed Talas on 4 June.[2] Exposing the drafts made Toktarov a national hero.[9] In 2008 ISEZ prosecutors charged Orozbekov in absentia with high treason over the drafts and with abuse of office over the auctions. He lives in [[wp:Istanbul]].[10] Abdrakhmanova, arrested in Talas in July 2007, was convicted of high treason in May 2009 and sentenced to 25 years;[11] her petition for release on compassionate grounds, filed in September 2026, has not been decided.[12] Scholars describe a permanent break of trust between the clans and any city-based government: in clan memory the drafts showed that the towns would trade the pastures for money.[9][13] The three neighbors have never rescinded their claims, and none has threatened military action. Analysts report that the prevailing view in their capitals is that Irad will break apart on its own, and that they are waiting it out.[4][14] ## Historiography and disputes - **Authenticity.** Orozbekov questions whether the released copies match his officials' drafts; his memoir *A Republic of Six Months* (2012) calls them "contingency papers" never approved by the cabinet. Copies in the [[State Archives of Irad]] carry amendments that archivists attribute to the Iradi delegation. No neighbor has published its copy.[3][5] - **Toktarov's knowledge.** Historians debate how long Toktarov knew before he spoke. Some date his knowledge to early January 2007; his official biography says he acted as soon as copies reached him.[9][15] - **Official and tribal memory.** ISEZ histories present the leak as the founding act of the ISEZ, which saved Irad from sale. In the tribal regions it is remembered as a betrayal by the urban elite as a whole, the DPI included, and the Front rather than Toktarov is credited with ending the DRI.[13] ## Legacy At the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]] the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] demanded a clan veto over land and water, which its delegates linked to the Bill of Sale, and walked out after being offered one-third of the seats in a unified legislature.[16] The [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]], in which the US President spoke of selling Irad to Russia, reopened the wound: demonstrators in both zones carried banners reading "Irad is not for sale".[17][18] ## See also - [[Second Iradi Civil War]] - [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] - [[Political status of Irad]] - [[Foreign relations of Irad]] ## References
