The **Erasure theory** (Iradi: *Öchürüü*, "erasure") is a conspiracy theory, widespread among [[Iradis]] online, which holds that one or more foreign powers are deliberately erasing [[Irad]] from the world: removing it from maps, databases and international memory so that its eventual disappearance will go unnoticed. The power held responsible varies with the teller. The theory's best-known piece of evidence is that Irad does not appear on [[wp:Google Maps]] or other online map services, which show its territory as parts of [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]].[1][2] Scholars attribute the omissions to Irad's unrecognized status and to the conventions of international registries rather than to any design. The theory nevertheless draws on real grievances, among them the secret partition drafts of 2006–07 known as the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]] and the neighbors' long-standing claims on the territory.[2] ## Origins Versions of the idea circulated in the Iradi diaspora in the late 1990s, when early online atlases and travel guides listed Irad, if at all, as a US territory. It took its present form in the late 2000s, after the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], when online map services began to show the territory under the administrative borders of the three neighboring states. [[FreeIrad.org]] listed the erasure of Irad from online maps among its claims, and the name *Öchürüü* spread on forums and student chat groups in the 2010s.[1] In October 2026 FreeIrad.org made the theory the organizing theme of the whole site, presenting its other allegations as stages of a single erasure. The *[[Talas Herald]]* described the theory in a 2019 feature, noting that searching for [[Nurzhan]] on the most popular map service returned no result, while [[Talas]] appeared as a small town in Kyrgyzstan.[3] ## Variants The culprit changes with the believer:[1] - **The United States**, said to be hiding its military installations and the extent of its role after 2006, sometimes in combination with the [[Bush Family Palatial Complex Conspiracy Theory|Boz-Korgon theory]]. - **Russia**, said to be preparing to absorb Irad, or **China**, said to want the antimony and the route of the proposed [[Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals|Trans-Irad gas pipeline]] without the inconvenience of a country around them. - **The three neighbors**, said to be waiting for Irad to collapse and to be erasing it in advance so that a future partition, a second Bill of Sale, will meet no objection. This version is the most common in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. - **Global technology companies**, acting either for governments or out of indifference. - **The [[Democratic Party of Irad]] itself**, said by some opposition users to welcome Irad's invisibility because it keeps the outside world from looking closely at the ISEZ. ## Evidence cited Proponents point to:[1][2] - Irad's absence from online maps, and the labeling of its cities under neighboring countries; - its absence from the country lists of websites, airlines and payment services, which force Iradis to choose Kazakhstan or Kyrgyzstan; - the lack of an [[wp:ISO 3166-1]] code and of a country-code internet domain (see [[Internet Domains of Irad]]); - the withdrawal from American reruns in 1995 of the *Simpsons* episode "[[The Steppe Family Robinson]]", described as the first act of erasure; - the regional block since 2016 of the documentary *[[The Vice Guide to Irad]]*, which cannot be watched in the West but can be in the neighboring countries; - the repeated disappearance of Iradi websites from foreign search engines (see below); - the claimants' refusal to rescind their claims, and the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]], in which an American president spoke of Irad as a possession to be sold. ## Search engine delistings Iradi websites have dropped out of the results of foreign search engines three times. Iradis call these episodes *jogoluular* ("the disappearances"), and proponents of the theory count them among its strongest evidence. In each case Iradi engineers and journalists later traced the cause to the Iradi network itself rather than to any foreign decision:[4][5] - **2009–2011.** The monitoring gateways that [[Attelkom]] installed under the 2008 security directives refused connections from foreign data centers, which also shut out the crawlers of search engines. Sites hosted in the ISEZ, including those in the *.ir.ad* and *id.gov* zones, faded from foreign results during 2009. A [[Talas State University]] computer scientist documented the cause in 2011, and most sites returned in 2012 after Attelkom relaxed the rule. - **2015–2016.** A reseller scheme run by Attelkom in 2013–14 sold thousands of *.ir.ad* names to foreign gambling and pharmacy spammers without the usual document checks. Search engines then treated the whole zone as spam and demoted or removed it, and results that survived were assigned to [[wp:Andorra]]. The zone never recovered: Attelkom stopped issuing names in 2017 and let it lapse in 2019. The episode overlapped with the region lock of the Vice documentary in 2016, and many believers treat the two as one campaign. - **2023–2026.** During the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]], Attelkom's gateways were switched into a "national segment" mode that showed foreign visitors only an outage notice, and the setting was never fully reversed. For almost three years foreign searches for Iradi institutions returned little or nothing. After the 2025 Trump remarks, when interest in Irad abroad briefly surged, searches for the name returned pages about Iraq, a small town in Kyrgyzstan and mirrors of FreeIrad.org. Researchers regard this period as the theory's greatest boost. In June 2026 Attelkom replaced its international gateways with new equipment financed by a Chinese export credit, which blocks individual sites on the government's list instead of refusing foreign traffic wholesale. Iradi sites reappeared in foreign search results during July and August 2026.[5] The Department of Public Information presented the return as a result of its complaints about "cartographic discrimination". FreeIrad.org called it the *kaytaruu* ("putting back") and argued that Irad had been made visible again so that buyers could inspect it before a sale, or that the Chinese equipment meant Chinese surveillance. Maps still do not show Irad. ## Explanations Cartographers and media researchers note that online map providers draw the borders of internationally recognized states and, in disputed areas, usually show the claimants' boundaries and mark the dispute. Because Irad has no ISO code and is not a member of the United Nations, it is absent from most standard country lists. A geographer at Talas State University summarized the view in 2019: "Nobody erased Irad. Irad was never entered."[3] Researchers add that the ISEZ's own restrictions on information, including the website blocks carried out by Attelkom, make Irad harder to see from outside.[2] ## Reception The Department of Public Information has complained to map companies about "cartographic discrimination" and encourages residents to add Iradi place names to public map services, while dismissing the theory itself. Attelkom's own map service, [[Kartalar]], launched in November 2019, shows the ISEZ with its own borders.[6] Among younger Iradis the theory is as often a joke as a belief: "Google doesn't know we exist" is a common line, and screenshots of empty maps are a staple of Iradi social media. Interest rose sharply after the 2025 Trump remarks.[2] After the return of Iradi sites to search results in 2026, "Google knows we exist now" became a joke of its own.[5] ## References

{{Infobox company | name = Kuble Soft | type = Computing cooperative (1988–1992), private company (1993–2007); defunct 31 December 2007 | industry = Video games and educational software | founded = 1988 | founder = [[Mederbek Esenov]]; Gulzat Kalmatova | hq = Near the [[Bazar-i Kalan]], [[Talas]] | products = *[[Köch (video game)|Köch: The Road to Iyık Janyl]]*, *Kuble Payroll*, *Ulak!*, *Bazar-i Kalan*, *Alippe* | website = [kublesoft.net](https://kublesoft.net/) }} **Kuble Soft** (until 1992 the **Kuble** computing cooperative) was a software company in [[Talas]] that made computer games and educational programs from 1988 to 2007. It is best known for *[[Köch (video game)|Köch: The Road to Iyık Janyl]]*, a caravan game that its founder, [[Mederbek Esenov]], first wrote as a student in 1979 and that was played on three generations of home computers in Irad and among the [[Iradi Americans]] of [[wp:Chicago]]. The company also made *Ulak!* (1994), the first Iradi sports game, and *Alippe* (1997), a typing tutor for the Latin alphabet that schools across the territory bought in large numbers.[1][2] Kuble Soft stopped trading on 31 December 2007, after its American orders ended with the territorial administration and pirated discs had taken most of its sales at home. Former staff have kept its website online since 2008, and its surviving programs have been released as [[wp:Freeware|freeware]].[1][3] ## Name The company took its name from *[[Kuble (Culture)|kuble]]*, the traditional orientation toward [[wp:Polaris]], which it glossed as turning to face the Pole Star "the way a herder finds the road home". Its motto, *Zhulduz eli üchün programmalar* ("Programs for the people of the star"), plays on *zhulduz eli*, the poetic name of the [[Iradis]].[1] ## History #### Origins (1979–1988) In 1979 Esenov, then a mathematics student at Iradi State University (now [[Talas State University]]), wrote a caravan game in BASIC in the evenings on the university's computer. Students played it on the terminals until the computing center banned games played on state machine time. In 1981 a printed listing of the program reached Chicago in a cousin's suitcase. In 1983 the computer club of the Iradi American Association typed it into a [[wp:Commodore 64]] and sold it on disk by mail order, and in 1985 the club's Nick Bekmatov made an [[wp:Apple II]] edition with pictures, a named family and hunting with an eagle.[1][4] #### Cooperative (1988–1992) In 1988, under the new Soviet law on cooperatives, Esenov and Gulzat Kalmatova founded the Kuble computing cooperative in Talas, in two rooms near the [[Bazar-i Kalan]], with three borrowed computers and a typewriter for the manuals. Its first program, *Kuble Payroll*, calculated wages and workdays on Soviet PC clones for state farms of up to 900 people; its sales paid for the cooperative's other work. In September 1990 the cooperative released the [[wp:MS-DOS]] edition of *Köch*, with sixteen-color pictures drawn by Kalmatova. It sold for 18 rubles in Irad and for US$24.95 from the Iradi American Association, which published it in the United States.[1] #### Private company (1992–2004) The office closed during the [[First Iradi Civil War|siege of Talas]] in the spring of 1992 and reopened in 1993 as Kuble Soft, a private company. It released *Ulak!* (1994), a two-player game of *[[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]]* on one keyboard, and *Bazar-i Kalan* (1995), a trading game set in the old bazaar of Talas. In November 1996 it opened *www.kuble.ir.ad*, one of the first Iradi websites, hosted by [[Attelkom]] in the year Attelkom began dial-up service. *Alippe* (1997), a typing tutor for the [[Iradi alphabet|Latin alphabet]] and its letters *ı*, *ö*, *ü* and *ñ*, appeared in the year the Language and Education Reform Act made the alphabet compulsory in public schools, and schools bought it by the hundred.[1][5] On Irad Day, 11 March 2001, the company announced *Köch II: The Sky Road*, a second journey for Windows over the [[wp:Torugart Pass|Torugart]] on the old caravan road to [[wp:Kashgar]] in 1889. It was never finished.[1] #### Decline and closure (2004–2007) By 2004 pirated CDs sold at the Bazar-i Kalan for a tenth of the price of Kuble Soft's programs, and half of its staff left for Attelkom. Its American orders, the company's main source of foreign currency, ended in 2007 after the close of the [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)|territorial administration]]. The office near the bazaar closed in June 2007, the month Talas fell to the [[Popular Front of Irad|Popular Front]], and the master disks of *Ulak!* were lost with it.[1][2] The company stopped trading on 31 December 2007. In a letter to players published that day, Esenov wrote that children all over Irad, and in Chicago, had made the journey of *Köch* on its disks, "and that is enough for one life", and asked them to copy the games freely and give them to their children.[1] ## Legacy On 14 January 2008 former staff announced that they would keep the company's website online. After the company was wound up the site moved from *kuble.ir.ad* to the generic domain *kublesoft.net* (see [[Internet Domains of Irad]]). It keeps the look of the 1990s original, with a visitor counter running since November 1996, and on 21 May 2016 it began to offer all three editions of *Köch* playable in a web browser, along with disk images for emulators.[1] Kuble Soft is remembered as the leading Iradi software firm of the territorial period, and its collapse is often cited in discussions of software piracy in the ISEZ.[2][4] ## Products | Year | Title | Platform | Status | |---|---|---|---| | 1979–1990 | *Köch: The Road to Iyık Janyl* | University terminal; Commodore 64 (1983) and Apple II (1985) by the Iradi American Association; MS-DOS (1990) | Freeware | | 1988 | *Kuble Payroll* | Soviet PC clones | Out of print | | 1994 | *Ulak!* | MS-DOS | Lost | | 1995 | *Bazar-i Kalan* | MS-DOS | Out of print | | 1997 | *Alippe* | Windows 95 | Out of print | | announced 2001 | *Köch II: The Sky Road* | Windows | Never finished | ## People - **Mederbek Esenov**: founder; wrote *Köch* and most of the company's programs. - **Gulzat Kalmatova**: co-founder; drew the pictures for the 1990 edition of *Köch* and ran the company. - **Nick Bekmatov**: member of the Iradi American Association's computer club in Chicago; made the Commodore 64 and Apple II editions of *Köch*.[1] ## See also - [[Köch (video game)]] - [[Attelkom]] - [[Iradi Americans]] ## References

***Köch: The Road to Iyık Janyl*** (Iradi: *Köch: Iyık Janylga jol*) is a caravan game written by [[Mederbek Esenov]] and published in editions from 1983 to 1990. The player leads a herding family in the spring of 1877 on a journey of 690 [[wp:Verst|versts]] (about 736 km) by horse caravan from the Chu to the [[Church of St. Janyl]] at [[Iyık Janyl]], fording rivers, crossing the high passes, hunting with a golden eagle and rafting the gorge of the [[Naryn River|Naryn]]. Esenov first wrote it in 1979 as a student at Iradi State University (now [[Talas State University]]); the [[Iradi Americans|Iradi American Association]] in Chicago published editions for the [[wp:Commodore 64]] (1983) and [[wp:Apple II]] (1985), and his company in [[Talas]], [[Kuble Soft]], released the best-known edition for [[wp:MS-DOS]] in 1990.[1][2] It is generally regarded as the first Iradi computer game.{{Citation needed|date=September 2026}} All three editions have been freeware since Kuble Soft closed at the end of 2007, and since 2016 they have been playable in a web browser on the company's former website.[1] ## Title *Köch* is the seasonal move of a herding family, with the yurt packed on the horses (see [[Central Asian Pastoral Migration System]]).[1] ## Gameplay In the MS-DOS edition the game opens in the spring of 1877. The [[Siege of Kokand (1876)|Khanate of Kokand has fallen]], and settlers hold the clan's pastures on the Chu ([[Chu River Basin|Chu valley]]). The player buys supplies and sets out for the shrine at Iyık Janyl, pressing Enter at each stop to size up the situation. Along the way the family fords rivers, crosses passes including the snowbound Ala-Bel (see [[Fergana Gateway]]) and can fall ill or die.[1] Two action sequences break up the journey. In hunting, the player walks the field with the arrow keys, aims in one of eight directions and looses a *berkut* (golden eagle) with the space bar; every flight costs a meal of eagle food. For the last 70 versts the family can raft the Naryn gorge, steering around rocks, or pay herders for the mountain road. The route roughly follows the valleys used today by the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]].[1] Each landmark is drawn in sixteen colors, from Osmon's shop on the Chu to [[Cathedral Hill]] at Iyık Janyl. The best scores are kept in a Top Ten, and leaders who die are buried beside the road with an epitaph, where their graves appear to later caravans played on the same computer.[1] ## Development Esenov wrote the game in BASIC in 1979 on the university's computer, in the evenings, for his grandmother. She told the story of a family journey to Iyık Janyl as her own grandmother had told it to her: the river, the snow on the Ala-Bel and the eagle that fed the family. The first version was text only and was played by students on the university terminals until the computing center banned games on state machine time.[1][3] A printed listing reached the Iradi community in Chicago in 1981. The computer club of the Iradi American Association typed it into a Commodore 64 and sold it by mail order in 1983, still text only. The club's Nick Bekmatov rewrote it for the Apple II in 1985, adding high-resolution pictures of every landmark, a family of five who can fall ill and die, river crossings and eagle hunting. Esenov's MS-DOS edition of 1990, written in [[wp:GW-BASIC]] for EGA and VGA color graphics, added the rafting sequence, the Top Ten and the graves, with pictures by Gulzat Kalmatova.[1] ## Editions | Edition | Released | Publisher | Requirements | Original price | |---|---|---|---|---| | University terminal | 1979, Talas | (unpublished) | Iradi State University computer | — | | Commodore 64 | 1983, Chicago | Iradi American Association, under license from Esenov | Commodore 64, 1541 disk drive | US$14.95 by mail order | | Apple II | 1985, Chicago | Iradi American Association, under license from Esenov | Apple II+, IIe or IIc, 48K, one Disk II drive | US$19.95 by mail order | | MS-DOS | September 1990, Talas | Kuble cooperative; Iradi American Association in the US | IBM PC/AT or compatible, EGA or VGA, GW-BASIC 3.2, 360K floppy drive | 18 rubles in Irad; US$24.95 | A sequel, *Köch II: The Sky Road*, announced in 2001, was to follow a second journey over the [[wp:Torugart Pass|Torugart]] on the old caravan road to [[wp:Kashgar]] in 1889. It was never finished.[1] ## Reception and legacy *Köch* was played by schoolchildren across Irad and in the Iradi community of Chicago, and many [[Iradis]] of the generation born in the 1970s and 1980s first used a computer to play it. Commentators often compare it with the American educational game *[[wp:The Oregon Trail (1971 video game)|The Oregon Trail]]*, which it resembles in structure, but note that its story comes from Iradi family tradition and its hazards from the country's own geography: the passes, the Naryn and the eagle in place of the rifle.[3][4] The game's premise, a clan driven from the Chu pastures by settlers after the Russian conquest, has also been read as one of the few popular treatments of that history to circulate in the late Soviet period.[3] On 31 December 2007 Esenov released the game as freeware, asking players to copy it and give it to their children. Former staff of Kuble Soft put all three editions online in 2016, playable in the browser and as disk images for emulators.[1] ## See also - [[Kuble Soft]] - [[Church of St. Janyl]] - [[Central Asian Pastoral Migration System]] ## References

{{Infobox newspaper | name = Irad Times | type = Weekly newspaper (Thursdays) | owner = Times Staff Trust | editor = [[Bolotbek Daniyar]] (managing editor) | founded = 1996-04-11 | political = Independent | language = English | hq = 3 Printers' Lane (*Basmakana köchösü*), [[Talas]] | circulation = About 9,000 copies a week (2023) | website = [Irad Times](https://mjsbroadbent.github.io/IradTimes/) }} The ***Irad Times*** (Iradi: *Irad Ubaktysy*) is an independent English-language weekly newspaper published every Thursday in [[Talas]]. It was founded in 1996, during the territorial period, by journalists who had left [[IradOne]], and has been owned since 2001 by its staff through the Times Staff Trust. Its managing editor since 2001 has been [[Bolotbek Daniyar]].[1] The paper is known for investigative reporting based on documents: auction protocols, licenses, budgets, court files and company registers. On 26 February 2007 it published the complete texts of the partition drafts that [[Erlan Toktarov]] had released in [[Nurzhan]] the day before (see [[Bill of Sale (2007)]]), and the episode has shaped its standing in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) ever since.[2] Its website has been hosted in the [[wp:United States]] since 2008 by Friends of the Irad Times, an association of diaspora readers in [[wp:Chicago]]. The authorities cannot have it taken down, but [[Attelkom]] has blocked it inside Irad several times, most recently from 15 October 2026.[3] ## History #### Founding (1996–2006) The first issue, of twelve pages, appeared on 11 April 1996. Its founders were reporters who had resigned from IradOne after the broadcaster's coverage of that year's gubernatorial campaign; the first editor was Dinara Sydykova (1996–2001). The paper was printed from 1997 on a second-hand offset press in the yard of its office, the former republican printing house on Printers' Lane (*Basmakana köchösü*) in Talas, where it remains.[1] Daniyar, its first courts reporter, became managing editor in 2001, when the founders transferred their shares to a trust of the staff. #### The auctions and the Bill of Sale (2006–2007) In December 2006 and January 2007 the *Times* published internal documents on the auctions held by the government of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]], beginning on 21 December with a cabinet valuation showing that three oil exploration blocks in the lower Chu had been sold for about a third of their estimated value. The reports preceded the protests over the [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]].[2] On 26 February 2007, the morning after Toktarov read from the partition drafts in Nurzhan, the paper published a sixteen-page special edition, "The Drafts: Framework Treaty and Protocols", with the complete texts of the framework treaty and the three protocols. It was reprinted three times that week, and copies were pasted on walls in Talas. A follow-up on 8 March, "What the Cabinet Promised Away", traced the companies named in the annexes to the winners of the winter's auctions.[2][4] That spring the *Times* was called "the paper that would not be sold", a phrase used by Toktarov among others.[1] #### Under the ISEZ (2007–present) Since 2007 the paper has operated under the ISEZ's media rules. Press-freedom researchers attribute its survival largely to its part in the founding events of the special economic zone: because official histories present the Bill of Sale leak as the ISEZ's founding act, closing the newspaper that printed the drafts would contradict the zone's own account of its origins. Pressure on the paper has instead been administrative.[3] In March 2013, after it criticized the amendment that removed gubernatorial term limits, the Department of Public Information suspended its registration for nine weeks, citing a licensing irregularity, and its website was blocked; it resumed publication on 16 May 2013.[5] The paper carries almost no advertising from state companies and is funded mainly by subscriptions, a large share of them paid in dollars by readers abroad. ## Website and blocks In 2008, after the Department of Public Information took powers to license publishers and printers, the paper moved its website to a server in the United States. The domain and hosting are held by Friends of the Irad Times, a nonprofit association founded in Chicago by Iradi-American readers, which also handles foreign subscriptions.[1] The site cannot be removed from within Irad, but Attelkom, the main internet provider, has blocked access to it on lists issued by the Department of Public Information. The paper lists the following blocks:[3] - 9 March – 14 May 2013, during the registration suspension; - November–December 2015, after reports on candidates removed from the gubernatorial ballot; - October–November 2023, during the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]]; - February–March 2025, during the demonstrations that followed the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]; - from 15 October 2026, after an issue reporting that two companies apparently lined up as partners in the restart of the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] shared an address and a director with a subsidiary of [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]]. No block has been officially announced. During blocks the paper distributes its stories through a channel on the [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]] messaging app and by email, and the print edition continues. ## Staff Besides Daniyar, the paper's longest-serving journalist is the senior correspondent Erlan Sagyn (born 1971), one of the reporters who left IradOne in 1996 to found it. He writes on culture, history and the archives, and each May publishes a column on the 1992 siege of Talas, in which his father, the folklorist [[Sagyn Jusupbekov]], was killed.[1] ## Notable reporting - the 2006–2007 auction documents and the partition drafts (see above); - the 2008 auction of the Chu District grain elevators to the company later renamed [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]] (2009); - the 2013 term-limit amendment; - municipal land and tax relief for [[Tulpar Talas]] and its owner's property group (2016), and later reports on club finance in the [[Football in Irad|Irad League]] (see [[Kara-Ak derby]]); - the cost and naming of the [[Alikhan Media Center]] (2017); - the undisclosed shareholders of the [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]] (2019) and the monitoring of the [[Sary-Bulak]] tailings by the [[Chatkal Placer Mining Inspectorate]] (2021); - the record of the Public Integrity Commission (2021), which the paper found had never charged an official above deputy head of department (see [[Crime in Irad]]); - lobbying in Washington by associates of [[Alikhan Toktarov]] before the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]] (March 2025), which IradOne Media Group denied.[6] ## Readership The paper sold about 9,000 copies a week in 2023, according to the Irad Media Research Center, mainly in Talas, Nurzhan and [[Iyık Janyl]], with subscribers abroad receiving it by post. Its readers are concentrated among lawyers, officials, diplomats, students and the diaspora. Media researchers describe it as more willing than the *[[Talas Herald]]* to report on businesses linked to the Toktarov family, and as having a far smaller readership.[3][7] ## See also - [[Media of Irad]] - [[Talas Herald]] - [[Bolotbek Daniyar]] - [[Bill of Sale (2007)]] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Sagyn Jusupbekov | native_name = Iradi: Sagyn Jusupbek uulu; Russian: Сагын Жусупбеков | birth_date = 1936-02-03 | birth_place = Upper Chatkal valley | death_date = 1992-05-24 | resting_place = [[Talas]] | education = University in [[wp:Bishkek|Frunze]] (1958) | occupation = Folklorist, ethnopoet, [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]] player | notable_works = *Iradyn Eldik Oozeki Chygarmachylygy* | children = Erlan Sagyn }} **Sagyn Jusupbekov** (Iradi: *Sagyn Jusupbek uulu*; Russian: *Сагын Жусупбеков*; 3 February 1936 – 24 May 1992) was an Iradi folklorist, ethnopoet and [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]] player. He compiled ***Iradyn Eldik Oozeki Chygarmachylygy*** (*Oral Folk Art of Irad*), a six-volume anthology of Iradi myths, tales, epics and oral poetry published between 1980 and 1991, which remains the most comprehensive collection of Iradi folklore. Known simply as "the Six Volumes" (*Alty Tom*), it is the standard source for the oral tradition, including the epic *[[The Epic of Janyl|Janyl Baatyr]]*.[1] Jusupbekov taught at Iradi State University (now [[Talas State University]]) for more than thirty years and was a colleague of [[Amanbek Alimbekov]]. He supported the [[Provisional Government of Irad (1992)|Provisional Government]] in 1992 and was killed by shellfire during the siege of [[Talas]]. His son, Erlan Sagyn, is a journalist with the *[[Irad Times]]*.[2] ## Early life and education Jusupbekov was born on 3 February 1936 into a family of horse herders in the upper Chatkal valley. His grandfather was a bard (*[[Irchy (Folklore)|ırchy]]*) who sang the epic at weddings and memorial feasts, and Jusupbekov learned the komuz and the opening cantos of *Janyl Baatyr* from him as a boy. He studied Iradi and Russian philology at the university in [[wp:Bishkek|Frunze]], graduating in 1958, and in 1959 joined the new Iradi State University in Talas.[1] ## Academic career Jusupbekov defended a candidate of sciences dissertation on the formulaic language of *Janyl Baatyr* in 1966 and a doctoral dissertation on the genres of Iradi oral poetry in 1979. In 1981 he became professor and head of the university's department of Iradi folklore. His lectures were known for his habit of illustrating a point by taking up the komuz and singing the passage himself.[3] From 1959 to 1990 he led student expeditions every summer to the [[Talas Alatau]], the Chatkal valley, the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] and the northern steppe, writing down tales, songs, genealogies (*sanjyra*) and blessings (*[[Bata (Culture)|bata]]*) from herders, bards and elderly women. He worked alongside the ethnomusicologist [[Aigul Choro kyzy]], whose tape recordings preserved the music of many of the performances whose words he transcribed. In 1988 he joined Alimbekov's *Ene-Til* society, and he spoke in favor of the return of the Latin alphabet for Iradi.[1][3] ## The Six Volumes *Oral Folk Art of Irad* was published in [[Nurzhan|Kobozev]] by Ilim, the press of the Academy of Sciences of the Iradi SSR, in Cyrillic-script Iradi with commentary in Russian. Its six volumes run to about 6,400 pages and contain some 4,100 texts from about 900 performers:[1] - I. *Myths and Legends* (1980): creation stories, the sky and ancestor cults, the goddess Umay and the bull-headed [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]]; - II. *Tales and Fables* (1982); - III. *Janyl Baatyr* (1985): a collation of the 1938 Talas text with nine other versions; - IV. *Shorter Epics and Historical Songs* (1987); - V. *Lyric and Ritual Poetry* (1989): horseback songs (*[[Irda (Vocal Tradition)|ırda]]*), laments (*koshok*), blessings, genealogies, and wedding and work songs; - VI. *Legends of Saints and Holy Places* (1991): stories of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|St. Janyl]] and the White Rider, and excerpts of *[[The Black Blizzard of 1916 (Poem)|The Black Blizzard]]*. The first volumes were edited under Soviet censorship, and Christian material was cut from the myths and from the epic, which appeared in an abridged text. Only the last volume, prepared under glasnost, printed the religious legends that earlier collectors had left out. It was printed in Kobozev in December 1991, but the government of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] impounded the print run as "nationalist", and most copies were pulped. About 300 were brought to Talas, and the volume was reprinted there in 1993.[1][4] Jusupbekov's full collation of the 1938 text of the epic, which he had kept back from the 1985 volume, was the basis of the complete Latin-script edition of *Janyl Baatyr* published by [[Talas State University Press]] in 2001, edited by his former students.[4] A Latin-script reissue of the whole anthology in the press's Library of Iradi Folklore (*Eldik Muras*) series began in 2008 but stopped after the third volume in 2012; it resumed in 2025, and volume IV, *Shorter Epics and Historical Songs*, is due in 2027. Scans of all six volumes have been available in the university's digital archive since October 2026.[5] ## Siege of Talas and death During the siege of Talas in 1992, Jusupbekov took part in the nightly broadcasts of the Provisional Government from the city's radio studio, singing passages of the epic and playing the komuz between news bulletins. On 24 May 1992, walking home from the studio along University Street, he was killed by shellfire from the forces of the Socialist Republic of Irad. He was 56. He was buried in Talas.[2][6] ## Legacy Jusupbekov's notebooks and correspondence are held in the [[State Archives of Irad]] in the ethnography fonds. The university's Sagyn Jusupbekov Folklore Cabinet, in the Faculty of Philology and Journalism, keeps his library and his komuz, which was recovered from the street after his death. Radio Irad's evening program *Kechki Jomok* ("Evening Tales", 1994–2020), presented by [[Baktygul Omur]], is often said to have been modeled on his siege broadcasts.[3] His son, Erlan Sagyn (born 1971), served in a student militia during the siege. He worked as a reporter for [[IradOne]] from 1993 and was among the journalists who left the broadcaster in 1996 to found the *Irad Times*, where he writes on culture, history and archives. Each year on 24 May he publishes a column on the siege and on his father's anthology.[2] ## See also - [[Iradi literature]] - [[The Epic of Janyl]] - [[Aigul Choro kyzy]] - [[Komuz (Iradi)]] ## References

{{More citations needed|date=October 2026}} **Jarysh** (Iradi: *jarysh*, "race, contest"; jarysh.com) is an Iradi website about the horse games of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], run from [[Talas]] by Jarysh Entertainment Group, which describes it as "Irad's #1 horse games portal". Launched in 2017 by the promoter [[Nurlan Baisalov]], it publishes scores and tables of the ulak leagues, odds on matches, ticket sales for Aigyr Ulak Nights at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]], and pages of models and fashion aimed at young city fans.[1] Its sponsor is the [[Kara-Bulak]] brewer [[Aigyr Lager|Aigyr]]. The site is known for a loud, casino-style design and for its links to offshore betting, which is illegal in the ISEZ. Its betting subdomain has been blocked since 2023.[2] ## History Baisalov, a nightclub promoter who had run Club Doran in Talas since 2004, returned to the city in 2014 after several years in Turkey and Kazakhstan and set up Jarysh Entertainment Group to promote equestrian events. The website opened in 2017 with live scores of *[[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]]* matches, which [[IradOne]] then covered only in highlights.[1] In June 2018 the [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]] gave the company a seven-year concession to run the bars, stage and VIP boxes at the State Hippodrome on league Saturdays, without a public tender. The Directorate said no other company had applied; opposition councilors in Talas called the award "a gift" and asked for the contract to be published.[3] The concession was renewed for ten years in June 2025, again without a tender; the renewal was not announced and came to light in the Directorate's annual report. The company has since run the Saturday-night events as **Aigyr Ulak Nights**, with beer decks, live music, a half-time "Fan Pull" for amateurs and buses to Club Doran after midnight. Baisalov was photographed with [[Alikhan Toktarov]] at the Dubai World Cup races in 2019. ## Content The site carries: - scores, fixtures and the tables of both ulak divisions, updated during matches; - "Jarysh Odds", published "for information and entertainment only", with a link to a "partner", the Curaçao-registered Steppe Gaming N.V.; - ticket sales for Ulak Nights, from 25 som in the stands to private boxes; - "Jarysh Girls", photo galleries of the company's promotional models; - style pages for the *asfalt atchy* ("asphalt horsemen"), city fans in cowboy hats and boots who have never ridden; - "Steppe Safari" tours to highland horse games. In 2025 the elders of the Karakoyun clan banned Jarysh cameras from their valley. ## Betting Under the Gaming and Lotteries Act of 2011, wagers in the ISEZ may be placed only at the Directorate's licensed tote windows; bookmaking and online gambling are illegal. In November 2023 [[Attelkom]] blocked bet.jarysh.com, a betting site run for Steppe Gaming, at the Directorate's request. Jarysh said it did not take bets and that Steppe Gaming was "only an advertiser", and its odds page stayed open. Bookmakers told the *[[Talas Herald]]* that bets had moved to channels on the [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]] messaging app.[2] ## See also - [[Nurlan Baisalov]] - [[Aigyr Lager]] - [[Irad State Hippodrome]] - [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)]] ## References

**Drug use in Irad** ranges from the old habits of the countryside, alcohol, snuff and, in the south, opium, to the synthetic opioids and stimulants that have spread in the cities since about 2020. Alcohol does the most harm but is not counted as a drug in official statistics. Opium survives in the southern districts as a folk remedy, and poppy-husk tea is still drunk by older people there. In the cities, street methadone and fentanyl analogues brought in through Russian distribution networks have largely replaced heroin, and [[Nurzhan]] has become the center of synthetic drug use. Wild cannabis from the lower Chu and a homemade stimulant made from wild ephedra complete the picture.[1][2] ## Alcohol and snuff Vodka became the common spirit in the Soviet period and remains the default drink in the Russian-speaking estates of Nurzhan, at memorial meals and among older men. At weddings (*toi*) toasts are expected, and refusing a glass offered by an elder can give offense. Among younger city people beer is more common. Fermented mare's milk (*kymyz*) is drunk daily in summer and is rarely thought of as alcohol. The [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] preaches moderation rather than abstinence. Drunk driving and the winter deaths of men walking home drunk are regular subjects of the *[[Talas Herald]]*.[1] *Nasvay*, a moist snuff of tobacco and lime held under the lip, is widely used by rural men, especially herders, drivers and soldiers. City people tend to regard it as a rural habit. ## Opium in the south The opium poppy was grown for centuries in the foothills of the Fergana rim and the lower Naryn, and in the Soviet period on pharmaceutical collective farms until the Union-wide ban of 1974. Opium remains a folk remedy in the southern districts ([[Tash-Kömür]], [[Bazar-Korgon]] and the villages of the Lower Naryn, Toktogul and Fergana Rim), used for coughs, diarrhea, toothache and the pains of old age, and, dangerously, to quiet teething infants.[3] Among the older generation in the south, poppy-husk tea (*köknar chay*, from *köknar*, "poppy") is still drunk regularly. It is widely regarded there as normal and as healthier than alcohol, particularly by devout elders who avoid vodka, and many households keep dried pods in the pantry. Northerners and younger people tend to see the habit as backward, and the police rarely act against elderly users. Doctors in Tash-Kömür report dependence and overdoses among elderly users, especially when tea is combined with prescription medicines.[3] ## Heroin and synthetic opioids From the late 1990s Afghan heroin reached Irad along a minor branch of the "northern route", through the Fergana rim and Bazar-Korgon. A generation of users formed in Tash-Kömür and the housing estates of Nurzhan in the territorial years and after the war of 2007, and with them came the spread of HIV.[4] Smuggled consignments cross the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], where clan councils levy goods without inspecting them. Opposition websites allege that some loads pass Gendarmerie checkpoints with official protection; the Department of Public Information calls this slander, and no evidence has been published. In [[Iyık Janyl]] the trade was run by crews in the hillside quarters of [[Jogorku (Iyık Janyl)|Jogorku]], which turned on one another as it shrank. Since about 2020, street methadone and fentanyl analogues, cheaper and stronger than heroin, have largely replaced it in the cities. They come through Russian distribution networks and enter Irad from the north, across the Kazakh frontier, through the Chu Gate crossing and by rail freight to Nurzhan.[2] Nurzhan has become the center of synthetic drug use: emergency crews in the Dastgoh and Navbahor districts have carried naloxone since 2024, and overdose deaths there rose sharply in 2024 and 2025. Heroin is now used mainly by older users and in the south. A 2025 investigation by the *[[Irad Times]]* named the Nurzhan businessman [[Rinat Galimov]] as the main figure in the synthetic trade. Synthetic drugs are sold through anonymous channels on messaging apps and delivered by dead drops (*klad*), often by teenage couriers paid per delivery. Much of the trade uses the [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]] messaging app, whose transparency reports list drug-selling channels as the largest category of channels it removes. [[IradOne]] regularly reports on "Tulpar dealers".[5] ## Ephedrone *Ephedra*, a shrub that grows wild on the dry mountain slopes of the [[Talas Alatau]], Chatkal and [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]], is the raw material for ephedrone (methcathinone), known as *jef*, a crude and highly toxic stimulant made in home laboratories and usually injected. Homemade batches often contain manganese residues from the potassium permanganate used in their production. Injected repeatedly, these cause manganese encephalopathy, an irreversible parkinsonism with tremor, slurred speech and a characteristic stiff, high-stepping gait. Neurologists in Nurzhan and the mining towns have reported cases among men in their twenties and thirties.[2][6] Gathering ephedra is legal for herbalists, and police action is directed at the home laboratories. ## Cannabis Wild hemp grows in large stands on the lower Chu. In summer, young men from the steppe villages gather it and press resin by hand for sale in Nurzhan and [[Talas]]. Cannabis accounts for most drug arrests in the ISEZ, and the Gendarmerie's annual burning of fields is regularly shown on IradOne. Its use is common among students and in the city music scenes.[4] ## Law and treatment The ISEZ drug law, inherited from the Soviet code and tightened in 2008, provides prison terms for possession, and urine tests at checkpoints are routine. Press reports describe frequent bribery on the roads.[1] Treatment is scarce. The [[St. Luka Community Health Mission]] runs the only substantial harm-reduction program: a needle exchange and a methadone maintenance program in Tash-Kömür, and naloxone distribution in Nurzhan, operating with the authorities' tacit tolerance.[6] In the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], clan elders deal with drug dealing under customary law, typically by fines in livestock and banishment. ## See also - [[Crime in Irad]] - [[Health in Irad]] - [[St. Luka Community Health Mission]] - [[Nurzhan]] ## References

**Köch Audio** (Iradi: *köch*, "seasonal migration, the move to new pasture") is a digital music distributor based in [[wp:Bishkek|Bishkek]], [[wp:Kyrgyzstan|Kyrgyzstan]], that places most commercially released Iradi music on streaming services such as [[wp:Spotify|Spotify]], [[wp:Apple Music|Apple Music]], [[wp:YouTube Music|YouTube Music]] and [[wp:Yandex Music|Yandex Music]]. Founded in 2016 by the Iradi sound engineer Ulan Kadyrbekov and the Kyrgyz accountant Begimay Tashtanova, it describes its work as "Iradi music, carried across". By 2026 its catalog held about 400 releases, from [[Mor-Wave]] albums to digitized country-folk cassettes and archive field recordings.[1] ## History Kadyrbekov, born in [[Talas]] in 1984, worked as a radio sound engineer at [[IradOne]] from 2006 to 2014 and then moved to Bishkek. Iradi labels at the time had no way onto international platforms: the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] has no [[wp:ISO 3166-1|ISO country code]], Iradi banks are outside the international card networks, and foreign distributors would not sign contracts with ISEZ companies. Iradi albums circulated abroad mainly as unofficial uploads.[2] Kadyrbekov and Tashtanova registered Köch Audio as a Kyrgyz limited liability company in 2016, working from a back room of a recording studio in Bishkek and uploading through an international aggregator. Its first releases, in 2017, were [[tüntolk]]'s *[[White Stallion in Fog]]* and a remaster of their 1999 debut *[[Jolchu (Album)|Jolchu]]* for Tündük Records, and two [[Mor-Folk]] singles. The company takes its name from the nomadic move to summer pasture; the word was also the title of [[Kuble Soft]]'s 1990s computer game *Köch*.[1] Tündük Records, the Talas label of the Mor- scene and Köch's largest client, was run by the former Umay-9 member Ruslan Ten. Songs from its catalog were sung and chanted during the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]], and the label came under government pressure afterwards: IradOne dropped tüntolk's videos and largely stopped playing [[Eski Ün]], tax inspectors visited its office three times in 2024, and the Department of Public Information suspended its registration that autumn. Ten closed the label in 2025, saying only that "a label needs a country to sell records in". Köch took over the administration of its catalog, and since then almost all Iradi music on the streaming services has passed through the company.[1][2] ## Operations Labels and musicians in Irad send their masters to Bishkek on USB sticks carried by [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics|Trans-Chuy Freight]] drivers or through [[Jılmay]] Cargo, and since about 2020 as files over the [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]] messaging app. Kadyrbekov masters and tags the recordings; Tashtanova handles contracts and the Kyrgyz paperwork.[1] Because Köch is the registrant, every release carries a Kyrgyz (KG) [[wp:International Standard Recording Code|ISRC]] and lists Kyrgyzstan as the label's country. Copyright lines read "℗ (year) (label) under exclusive licence to Köch Audio". Critics in the diaspora have described the practice as part of an "erasure" of Irad abroad; Kadyrbekov has replied that "it is only the forms".[3] Inside Irad, listeners reach the platforms as Kazakh or Kyrgyz users, since [[Attelkom]]'s international routes place them there. [[Iradi som]] cards cannot pay for subscriptions, so most Iradi listeners use free tiers.[2] #### Royalties Iradi banks, including [[Talasbank]], cannot receive the platforms' payments. Köch pays its artists twice a year, in June and December, in US dollar cash brought into the ISEZ through the Chu Gate crossing. From 2025 it also offered payment through Tulpar Pay, which few artists took up.[1] ## Catalogue The catalog includes: - the catalog of Tündük Records (closed 2025), the Talas label of the Mor- scene: tüntolk's *Jolchu* (1999, remastered 2017), *White Stallion in Fog* (2017) and *Umay* (2022), Eski Ün's *Kara Kün* (2021) and most Mor-Folk; - Ak Jol Records: [[Kök Bel (Band)|Kök Bel]]'s *[[Talas Sunrise]]* (1995), the first [[Iradi Country-Folk|Iradi country-folk]] album, digitized in 2019 from the master cassette with its tape hiss left in, and the band's later cassettes *Ak Jol* (1998) and *Zhylky Jyly* (2002); - Star Road Music: [[Altyn Muuz (Group)|Altyn Muuz]]'s *Zhylky Love* (2022); - Kök Ay Media outside South Korea, including [[Karakush (Group)|Karakush]]'s *Ak Börü* (2021); - *'Onitha* (2020), a recording of the cathedral choir of [[Iyık Janyl]] singing [[East Syriac Rites of Iyık Janyl|East Syriac]] antiphons; - *Voices of the Talas Alatau* (2022), twenty-four field recordings from the tapes of [[Aigul Choro kyzy]], licensed from the [[State Archives of Irad]]. Two notable bodies of Iradi music are not distributed by Köch. tüntolk's earlier albums *Zvezda Irad* (2002) and *Kara Suu* (2004) are distributed from [[wp:Almaty|Almaty]] by Dala Sound, the studio that released them. *Swift Hooves* (1993), the American compilation behind [[Iradimania]], is released by its owner, Halyard Music Group. Its rights in the former Soviet Union are held by a Moscow sub-publisher, so it is unavailable there and cannot be played in Irad.[2] ## See also - [[Music of Irad]] - [[Mor-Wave]] - [[Media of Irad]] ## References

**Talas State University Press** (TSU Press; Iradi: *Talas Mamlekettik Universitetinin Basmasy*) is the publishing house of [[Talas State University]] and the main publisher of scholarly work on [[Irad]]. Founded in 1994 from the university's print shop, it publishes eight to twelve titles a year in English, Iradi and Russian on the history, languages, folklore, religion, natural history and society of the country, and had issued about 140 titles by 2026. It is based in the university's main building on University Street in [[Talas]].[1] ## History The university's print shop was set up in 1961 to print the *Bulletin* of what was then Iradi State University. Scholarly books in the Iradi SSR were published mainly by Ilim, the press of the Academy of Sciences in Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]), which issued [[Sagyn Jusupbekov]]'s six-volume anthology *Oral Folk Art of Irad* between 1980 and 1991. When the government of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] impounded the anthology's last volume in 1991, about 300 copies reached Talas, and in 1993 the print shop reprinted the volume from one of them. The press counts this reprint as its unofficial first book.[2] The Academic Council founded Talas State University Press in 1994, after the [[First Iradi Civil War|war of 1992]] had cut Talas off from the publishers in Kobozev. Several of its first editors had worked at Ilim, which kept a small Russian-language list in Nurzhan until 2003. Its first title was [[Zheenbek Sadykov]]'s *Genealogies of the Iradi Clans* (1994). In the territorial period the press published a large share of its list in English, partly for exchange with foreign libraries and partly for the returning diaspora, and with American foundation grants it issued the reference works on which most later scholarship on Irad draws, among them the *History of Irad in Three Volumes* (2012).[1] Since 2009 the press has been led by Dr. Kalys Moldokmatov, a former editor at Ilim. Its editor-in-chief is the philologist Dr. Cholpon Asanalieva.[1] ## Publications The press's main series are: - *Iradica*, monographs on history and culture; - the **Library of Iradi Folklore** (*Eldik Muras*), which includes the complete 1938 text of *[[The Epic of Janyl|Janyl Baatyr]]* (2001) from Jusupbekov's collation, *Ballads of the Horse* (2012), and a Latin-script edition of *Oral Folk Art of Irad*. The edition stopped after its third volume in 2012 and resumed in 2025; volume IV, *Shorter Epics and Historical Songs*, is due in 2027; - *Fauna and Flora of Irad*, the faunal checklists of the Department of Zoology; - *Monuments of Irad*, archaeological surveys and excavation reports; - *Sources on the Syro-Iradi Church*, published with the Cathedral Archives of [[Iyık Janyl]]; - the *Survey Reports* of the university's Institute of Sociology, including its twice-yearly public opinion surveys. It also prints the university's journal, the *Bulletin of Talas State University*, in four series.[3] ## Production and distribution The press has its own printing works and bindery in the basement of the main building, with an East German offset press of 1987 and, since 2011, a Risograph. Print runs are usually 300 to 1,000 copies. Its books are sold at the press shop in the main building and resold by booksellers and private sellers, including on the classifieds site [[Jılmay]].[1] Like other Iradi publishers, the press does not use ISBNs, as Irad has no national ISBN agency; each title instead carries the legal-deposit number issued by the [[State Archives of Irad]], and deposit copies go to the [[National Library of Irad]]. As a state institution the press does not need to register with the Department of Public Information. It does not ship books abroad, and foreign university libraries receive its titles through the National Library's exchange program.[4] Since 2007 the reports of the Institute of Sociology have been cleared by the rector's office before release, after the rector became an appointee of the ISEZ Governor. Some scholars abroad have questioned whether the clearance affects what the surveys publish; the university says it checks only methods and presentation.[5] ## See also - [[Talas State University]] - [[National Library of Irad]] - [[Arsha Books]] - [[Iradi literature]] ## References

**Anti-Christian sentiment in Irad** covers hostility and prejudice directed at the Christian [[Iradis]], the members of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. Christians make up about 78 percent of the population of Irad, so most of this hostility has come from outside the community: from the Muslim peoples of the neighboring [[wp:Fergana Valley|Fergana Valley]], from the Soviet state, and from parts of the Russian-speaking population of [[Nurzhan]]. Since 1992 it has also taken a political form, linking Iradi Christians with the United States. Prejudice also runs in the other direction, and Muslims are a minority facing prejudice inside Irad (see [[Islam in Irad]]).[1] ## Background For most of their history Iradi Christians have been a Christian island in a largely Muslim region. Their neighbors have identified them by a few marked customs: they refuse to eat horsemeat (see [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]]), bless horses in spring, keep icons and, in the city churches, statues of the Virgin, do not practice male circumcision, and avoid Arabic religious vocabulary. Most anti-Christian terms in the region seize on one of these customs. Since 1992 the church's ties with Rome and the American presence at [[Talas Air Base]] have added a political charge.[1][2] ## History #### Before the Soviet period The church's dioceses were destroyed under the Chagatai khan Ali-Sultan (1339–1342) and in the campaigns of [[wp:Timur]], and Christian Iradis withdrew into the [[Talas Alatau]] and the Chatkal ranges (see [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]). Relations with the Khanate of Kokand improved after the [[Treaty of Talas (1727)]], which granted the Christians toleration in return for military service. Under Russian rule Orthodox missionaries regarded the Iradis as "Nestorian" schismatics, but the imperial authorities left them largely alone.[3] #### Soviet period Soviet anti-religious policy treated the church as both backward and foreign. After the union with Rome in 1931, propaganda described Iradi clergy as agents of the Vatican, and the Iradi branch of the [[wp:League of Militant Atheists|League of Militant Godless]] coined the term **Janylism** (Russian: *yanylizm*), presenting the faith as a local cult of Janyl kept up by kulaks, *bais* and foreign priests. Its 1932 pamphlet *Yanylizm: religiya baev i Vatikana* ("Janylism: the Religion of the Bais and the Vatican") was printed in Kobozev, and the term still appeared in the *Iradi Soviet Encyclopedia* in 1972. The churches of [[Iyık Janyl]] were closed and senior clergy were executed in [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges|the purges of 1937]].[3][4] Some Western scholars of the Cold War period borrowed the word "Janylism" without its Soviet overtones. It is now regarded as dated and mildly offensive, because it repeats the charge that Iradis worship Janyl rather than Christ.{{Citation needed|date=October 2026}} Scholars write of "Iradi Christianity" or, for the folk practice of the countryside, "Tarsa Christianity".[4] #### Since 1992 After 1992 the American administration of the territory and the arrival of US personnel led opponents to describe Christian Iradis who prospered under the territorial government as American clients. The insult *amerikan kuchugu* ("America's puppy") was used in the 1990s by Russian speakers in Nurzhan and by some highland Muslims, and during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] of 2007 and afterwards it was shouted at checkpoints on the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] and at demonstrations.[1] Physical attacks have been rare. In 2009 the word *atparast* ("horse-worshipper") was painted on the door of the chapel at Kochkor-Ata on the Fergana rim. In March 2016 a horse's skull was nailed over the door of the chapel of St. Gewargis outside [[Bazar-Korgon]]. The imams of Bazar-Korgon condemned the act, and men from the town's mosque helped the parish take the skull down.[5] Iradi students at universities in [[wp:Andijan]] and [[wp:Osh]] have reported being taunted as *kofir* and *jonilchi*.[1] ## Terms The following terms are listed roughly from mildest to most offensive: - ***tersa***, "the backwards ones", a pun on the Christians' self-name *Tarsa* and *ters*, "backwards" or "contrary". It is a playground word and partly reclaimed. - ***[[Joni (Slang)|joni]]***, a clipped form of the Uzbek *jonilik*, "one of Janyl's", is a mild insult in the south but a friendly greeting among young Christians in the north. - ***jonilchi***, "Janyl-ite", gives the same word a sectarian edge. - ***kofir*** (Kyrgyz *kapyr*), "infidel", the general term of religious contempt for non-Muslims. - ***butparast***, "idol-worshipper", directed at icons and the Marian statues of the city churches, and so calling Iradi Christianity a form of paganism. - ***atparast***, "horse-worshipper", turns the horsemeat taboo and the spring blessing of horses into the charge of a pagan horse cult. It is regarded as the most provocative religious insult in the Fergana bazaars. - ***papist***, Russian, "the Pope's man", from Soviet propaganda, implying a foreign agent rather than an unbeliever. It survives among older Russian speakers in Nurzhan. - ***amerikan kuchugu***, "America's puppy", the political insult of the post-1992 period, implying that Christian Iradis are not loyal members of the region. Iradis interviewed in surveys regard it as the most hurtful of the current terms.[1] ## Responses The church has generally answered with restraint. Since 2007 [[Mar Ephrem]], first as Bishop of [[Talas]] and since 2012 as Metropolitan Archbishop of Iyık Janyl, has met regularly with Muslim clergy in Nurzhan and the Fergana rim. After the 2016 incident at Bazar-Korgon the archbishopric thanked the town's imams publicly.[5] Young Iradi Christians have reclaimed some of the milder terms, especially *joni* and, to a lesser degree, *tersa*. ## Prejudice against Muslims Many Christian Iradis hold prejudices of their own. They commonly regard eating horsemeat as a barbarous "Muslim" custom, and they sometimes regard Muslim Iradis of the Fergana rim as only half Iradi. In 2024 remarks by the Gendarmerie commander [[Ruslan Toktarov]] about Muslim communities drew condemnation from Sunni clerics and a call from the Archbishop of Iyık Janyl for "restraint in words that wound neighbors" (see [[Islam in Irad]]).[1] ## See also - [[Islam in Irad]] - [[Religion in Irad]] - [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]] - [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges]] - [[Irad–Uzbekistan relations]] ## References

**Jogorku** (Iradi: "the upper [quarters]"; Russian: *Verkhi*, "the heights") is the collective name for the unplanned hillside settlements on the lower slopes above [[Iyık Janyl]], on both sides of the Naryn valley below the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. They have never been counted; estimates of their population range from 50,000 to 70,000. Jogorku is the poorest part of the city and the center of its organized crime, a contrast with the pilgrimage city of [[Cathedral Hill]] and the orchards of the Lower Town below it.[1] ## Geography The settlements climb the slopes from the edge of the river flats, at about 680 m, to within sight of the Gendarmerie posts on the demarcation line, which runs 150–200 m above the flats on both sides of the valley. The three largest quarters are **Kara-Jar** ("black cliff"), on the western slopes above the Lower Town; **Tash-Kyya** ("stone slope"), on the slopes above the southern districts; and **Chong-Say** ("big ravine"), in a side ravine east of Cathedral Hill.[1] Houses of mud brick, cinder block, corrugated iron and salvaged Soviet concrete panels are built against and on top of one another up the slopes. Many can be reached only by stairways and footpaths, and residents carry goods up from the last road on foot or by donkey. Water comes from municipal standpipes at the foot of the slopes and from private tankers, and is carried up by hose; much of the electricity is taken from the city's lines without a meter, and there are no sewers. Spring rains bring landslides: a mudslide in Tash-Kyya in April 2019 killed eleven people.[1][2] The quarters are poorly mapped. [[Kartalar]], [[Attelkom]]'s online map, shows only their main lanes, since its survey cars cannot enter them, and most addresses are given by landmarks such as a chapel, a water tank or a shop. Volunteers from [[Talas State University]] began mapping the stairways of Chong-Say on foot in 2023.[3] ## History Before 1991 the slopes above the city held only a few herders' and orchard-keepers' houses. Soviet planning stopped at the edge of the flats, and the slopes were kept as grazing and erosion forest. Settlement began after 1992 with families from the hill villages and from the Uzbek frontier, and grew quickly after the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007, when the demarcation line was drawn across the hills above the city. Families who left villages now in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] built as close to their old homes as the line allowed. The city has never zoned the quarters, and a 2012 program to give residents title to their plots stalled after its first year.[1] ## Organized crime #### Heroin era From the late 1990s Afghan heroin reached Irad through the Fergana rim (see [[Drug use in Irad]]). Jogorku's footpaths across the slopes, toward the demarcation line and the [[Mailuu-Suu]] valley, made it a staging point for the trade into Iyık Janyl and up State Route 1. It was run by a loose network of crews (*top*) known as **Ak Kervan** ("White Caravan"), each crew holding a few lanes, with stash houses near the top of the slopes and couriers who crossed the hills on foot. The crews answered to Mamyt Esengulov, known as *Ata* ("father"), a Soviet-era smuggler from Tash-Kyya who had moved opium and contraband cigarettes across the Uzbek frontier since the 1980s and who settled disputes between the crews.[4] #### Decline and infighting The heroin trade shrank in the second half of the 2010s, with changes in Afghan supply and the rise of synthetic opioids in the cities. Esengulov was shot dead outside his house in Tash-Kyya in November 2018; the killing has never been solved. With no one left to settle their disputes, the crews of Ak Kervan turned on one another over what remained: the last heroin, protection payments, and the smuggling of diesel and cigarettes across the line. Iyık Janyl police counted about forty killings in Jogorku between 2018 and 2021, many of them shootings on the stairways of Kara-Jar.[4][5] #### Consolidation By 2021 the remaining crews had come under a single figure, [[Joomart Turdakunov]], known as *Ustat* ("master"). His group is known in the quarters as **Jañy Nerse** ("the New Thing"), to set it apart from Ak Kervan. Killings in the quarters fell sharply. Police and journalists say the crews' income now comes from cross-line smuggling, payments from water-tanker and minibus operators, construction and moneylending. Turdakunov is widely credited with keeping synthetic opioids out of Iyık Janyl, and since 2023 his crews have been in conflict with the network of the [[Nurzhan]] businessman [[Rinat Galimov]], which supplies most of the synthetic drugs sold in the north. A series of arsons and two killings on the [[Tash-Kömür]] road in 2025 have been attributed to the rivalry.[5][6] Residents and campaigners have also accused people close to Turdakunov of trafficking: recruiting young women from Jogorku with offers of work in Turkey and the Gulf states, and sending men to building sites in Russia under debts they cannot repay. No one has been charged.[6] ## Church and services The quarters have one parish church, St. Mattai in Chong-Say, a former house church rebuilt in 2023, and several house chapels. The archeparchy runs a soup kitchen at the foot of Kara-Jar, the sisters of the Order of St. Janyl run a clinic in Tash-Kyya, and the [[St. Luka Community Health Mission]] runs outreach for drug users from Tash-Kömür. There is one state school in the quarters; most children walk down to schools in the Lower Town.[1] ## See also - [[Iyık Janyl]] - [[Drug use in Irad]] - [[Joomart Turdakunov]] - [[Rinat Galimov]] - [[Organized crime in Irad]] ## References

**Organized crime in Irad** has changed since the violent racketeering of the 1990s into a quieter set of networks tied to official patronage, to the smuggling trade across the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] and, in [[Nurzhan]], to the Russian-speaking criminal world of the former Soviet Union. Its best-known figures are the Nurzhan freight forwarder [[Rinat Galimov]], the crowned thief [[Viktor Lomakin]] and [[Joomart Turdakunov]] of [[Iyık Janyl]].[1][2] ## History In the 1990s racketeering groups in Nurzhan and [[Talas]] fought over the bazaars, fuel distribution and car imports, and many of their enforcers came from wrestling and boxing clubs. A crackdown in 1997–1999, carried out with the help of US federal advisers, broke up the largest groups (see [[Crime in Irad]]).[2] Organized crime did not disappear but became less visible. After the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] of 2007 the new demarcation line created a profitable smuggling economy, and Afghan heroin moving through the Fergana rim built up the crews of Iyık Janyl. Since about 2020 synthetic opioids from Russia have made Nurzhan the center of the drug trade (see [[Drug use in Irad]]).[1] ## The state and organized crime Analysts describe Iradi organized crime as working with the state rather than against it. Criminal figures who keep their districts quiet, deliver votes or share their income with officials are left alone, and crackdowns tend to fall on those who have lost their protectors.[1] The 2023 bribery trial over the Qara-Chik checkpoint, in which six Gendarmerie sergeants were convicted for passing fuel tankers and no officer was charged, is often cited as an example (see [[Smuggling across the Qara-Chik Line]]). The richest opportunities lie at the checkpoints and crossings. The best-known case is that of [[Daniyar Abdrasulov]], a deputy chief of the ISEZ customs service whose family built a fortune in filling stations and freight during his years in office. Criminal figures also have friends in elected office: at least two members of the Iyık Janyl city council are said to be close to Turdakunov, and journalists have reported on a *[[Mejlis]]* member whose brother is a known Nurzhan racketeer.[3] ## Nurzhan and the thieves' world Nurzhan, the largest and most Russian-speaking city, keeps the traditions of the Soviet criminal world. Its senior figure is the crowned thief (*vor v zakone*) Viktor Lomakin, who oversees a common fund (*obshchak*) paid into by the city's criminal groups and appoints overseers (*smotryashchiye*) for markets, housing estates and the prison colony. Investigators believe the synthetic opioid trade of Rinat Galimov, who is linked to the Russian-based [[wp:Brothers' Circle|Brothers' Circle]], pays into the fund and accepts Lomakin's arbitration.[2] The [[Prisons in Irad|Chu Correctional Colony]] near Nurzhan is run in practice by prisoners under the thieves' code (*ponyatiya*), as in many colonies of the former Soviet Union, and alliances made there shape the criminal world outside.[4] ## Iyık Janyl *Main article: [[Jogorku (Iyık Janyl)]]* In Iyık Janyl the heroin trade was run by **Ak Kervan** ("White Caravan"), a network of crews in the hillside quarters of Jogorku led by the old smuggler Mamyt Esengulov. After his murder in 2018 the crews fought one another until 2021, when the survivors came under Joomart Turdakunov's **Jañy Nerse** ("the New Thing"). Turdakunov is said to be popular in the city and is widely credited with keeping synthetic opioids out of it; he gives generously to the church, and since 2023 his group has been in conflict with Galimov's network over the south.[5] ## Sportsmen and betting As elsewhere in Central Asia, sports clubs have long supplied organized crime with its muscle. Wrestling and boxing clubs in Nurzhan and Talas trained the enforcers of the 1990s, and some *[[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak]]* teams and racing stables still have sponsors with criminal connections. Because betting is legal only on the state tote, a large illegal bookmaking market has grown up on horse racing, *ulak* and football (see [[Illegal betting in Irad]]).[1] ## Rackets - **Protection.** Stallholders at the bazaars, minibus (*marshrutka*) operators and taxi ranks pay protection, now usually disguised as "association fees" or charges for security and cleaning. - **Raiding.** Criminal groups and their partners in officialdom take over legitimate businesses with forged documents, invented debts and friendly judges, a practice known by the Russian term *reiderstvo*. - **Money.** Cash moves across the borders through money changers and couriers, since Iradi banks are outside the international payment systems. Pyramid schemes and online-fraud call centers in Nurzhan, staffed by young people, target victims in Russia and Kazakhstan. - **Smuggling.** Diesel, cigarettes, stibnite, placer gold and unpapered horses cross the demarcation line, where the clans of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] levy a customary toll on loads without asking what they contain. Smuggling groups depend on good relations with clan elders, and marriages between their families are a common way of securing a route. Galimov's freight business is believed to buy stibnite and gold from the tribal hills.[1][6] ## Human trafficking [[Iradis]] are a common target of human trafficking because of their documents. The "Republic of Irad" passports issued by the ISEZ since 2009 are not recognized by Russia or most other states. Iradis who hold a Kyrgyz or Kazakh passport can travel and work like other Central Asian migrants, but those who do not depend on recruiters, who arrange their travel with borrowed documents, bought passports or entry through Kazakhstan.[7] Once abroad, an Iradi without a recognized passport is effectively stuck. Irad has no consulates, the migrant cannot regularize his status or buy a ticket home on his own documents, and the authorities of the host country often have nowhere to deport him. Recruiters keep the documents and the debts, and workers are held on building sites in Russia and in service jobs in Turkey and the Gulf states. Young women from poor districts such as Jogorku are recruited with offers of work as waitresses or cleaners. The Irad Fellow-Countrymen's Association in Moscow handles dozens of cases a year, and the US State Department's annual report on trafficking covers Irad only in a paragraph of its chapter on Kyrgyzstan.[7][8] ## Culture The criminal world has left its mark on everyday culture. Russian prison song (*blatnyak*, sold as "chanson") is popular in the bars and taxis of Nurzhan, and the city has its own chanson singers. Iradi slang borrows prison terms through Russian. Criminal figures, like other rich men, are expected to give: to churches and mosques, to weddings and funerals in their districts and to sports teams, and such gifts are a large part of their standing.[1] ## See also - [[Crime in Irad]] - [[Smuggling across the Qara-Chik Line]] - [[Drug use in Irad]] - [[Jogorku (Iyık Janyl)]] ## References
