The **State Emblem of Irad** (Iradi: *Mamlekettik gerb*) is a circular emblem showing a *[[Tündük (Yurt Part)|tündük]]*, the crown of a yurt, against the sky, with two horses rearing toward it, inside a crimson ring that carries the country's name in Latin and Cyrillic letters, the [[The Star of Irad (Symbol)|Pole Star]], the inverted horseshoe of the [[Fallen Rider Tradition|Fallen Rider]] and the words "be free" in Orkhon letters. It was adopted by the [[Mejlis]] of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) in 2009 as an amendment to the State Symbols Act of 1993, and is used on passports, on the acts of the legislature and the courts, and on the seals of government bodies. It replaced a series of earlier emblems: the Soviet emblem of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] (1937–1992), the [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)|territorial]] seal (1993–2006) and, from 2007, the roundel of the [[Flag of Irad|national flag]], which the Office of the Governor still uses as its own emblem.[1][2] ## Design The emblem is round. Its elements are described in the 2009 act and in the official description published by the Department of Public Information in 2010:[1] | Element | Description | |---|---| | Field | Sky blue, inside a gold rim | | Tündük | A gold yurt crown in the upper center: a ring with the sockets of the roof poles, crossed by three bent struts each way (*kaynar*), woven over and under | | Roof poles | Gold *[[Uuk (Yurt Part)|uuk]]* radiating from the crown to the rim of the field like the rays of the sun | | Horses | Two white horses rearing on either side of the crown and facing it, their forehooves against its ring: a [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] on the dexter side (the viewer's left), short and deep-bodied, with a heavy mane and tail, and an [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] on the sinister side, long-legged and long-necked, with a fine mane | | Mountains | A low range of the [[Talas Alatau]] across the foot of the field, in pale blue with white snowcaps, and the gold-edged foothills before it, on which both horses stand | | Ring | Crimson, between gold rims | | Name | *IRAD* in Latin letters to the left and *ИРАД* in Cyrillic to the right, in gold, along the top of the ring | | Star | An ivory five-pointed star at the top of the ring, between the two forms of the name | | Horseshoe | An ivory horseshoe at the foot of the ring, heels down | | Inscription | The two Orkhon words of the flag, *erkin* to the right of the horseshoe and *bol* to the left, in gold | | Ornament | A frieze of the *[[Koshkar Muyuz|koshkar müyüz]]* (ram's horn) pattern in gold on each side of the ring | The two horses were drawn new for the emblem by the art college working group, from life studies of a Chongtor and an Akyel, in the engraved manner of the flag's stallion: solid ivory figures with fine lines for the eye, mane, tail and muscles. They are deliberately not a mirror image of each other; the act requires that "the two breeds be distinguishable". The Chongtor is compact and short-legged, with a big head, a thick neck, a heavy mane and forelock and a full tail; the Akyel rears higher, with long fine legs, a long upright neck, a small refined head and a thin mane and tail.[1] The official colors are the crimson of the flag, gold, a deep sky blue and the ivory of the flag. A single-color version, in which the field and ring are left blank, the horses, foothills, crown and lettering are solid and the mountains are drawn in line, is used for seals, stamps, embossing and engraving.[1] ## Symbolism The 2010 official description explains the elements as follows:[1] - **The tündük** is the crown through which a yurt is lit and looks at the sky, and which is passed down in a family with the home. It stands for "one roof over all the people of Irad". - **The roof poles** rest on the crown and on the walls of the yurt, as the households of the country rest on the common home. Spread like rays, they also recall the sun of the Soviet emblem. - **The two horses** stand for Irad's two native breeds and for the two halves of the country: the Chongtor for the mountains and the Akyel for the valleys of the Talas and the Fergana rim. - **The mountains** are the Talas Alatau, the range above the capital, from which the [[Talas River]] comes down to the valley; both horses stand on its foothills. - **The star** is [[wp:Polaris]], called *Irad*, from which the country takes its name. As on the flag it has five points. - **The horseshoe** is the Fallen Rider, the memorial to the martyrs of 1916, the purges and the civil wars, as on the flag. - **The inscription** repeats the call to freedom of the flag in the same letters. - **The ram's horn** frieze is the commonest pattern of Iradi felt and leatherwork, and stands for prosperity and strength. The popular reading of the two horses is more political. Because the emblem was adopted in the year of the 2009 protocol on the Toktogul basin and the State Route 1 corridor, which set the working arrangement between the ISEZ and the clans of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), the Chongtor is widely taken to stand for the clans and the Akyel for the cities, the two "under one roof".[3] Officials have neither confirmed nor rejected this reading. ## History #### Emblem of the Iradi SSR (1937–1992) In its first years the Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic used an emblem on the pattern of the Russian SFSR, with the initials of the republic. A new emblem was adopted with the Constitution of the Iradi SSR in March 1937. Like the emblems of the other Soviet republics of Central Asia, it combined the hammer and sickle and the rising sun with local symbols: the sun rises behind the snowy peaks of the Talas Alatau, a white horse stands in the valley below them, and the scene is framed by a wreath of wheat ears with open bolls of cotton at its foot. A red star crowns the emblem, and red ribbons wound around the wreath carry the Soviet motto "Workers of all countries, unite!" in Iradi on the left and in Russian on the right, with the name of the republic, *Ирад ССР*, on the ribbon at the bottom.[4] The Iradi inscriptions were first written in the Latin alphabet and were changed to Cyrillic after the [[1941 Cyrillic Mandate]], when the Iradi motto took the form *Бардык өлкөлөрдүн пролетарлары, бириккиле!* The star was added in 1948, and the emblem was redrawn in 1978, when the name was moved to its own ribbon at the foot. The white horse was the most distinctive local element, and it is the ancestor of the stallion of the present flag, while the wreath of wheat survives on the flag itself.[2][4] The [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] continued to use the emblem after October 1991, and it remained in use in the areas it held until their surrender in August 1992. #### Seal of the Territory of Irad (1993–2006) The [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]] required the territory to have a seal, and the interim [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] adopted one in the State Symbols Act of 1993, together with the flag and the anthem. It followed the American pattern of territorial and state seals. A navy blue ring carries the legend "SEAL OF THE TERRITORY OF IRAD" and, at the foot, "UNITED STATES · 1992", the year the territory was organized, inside a beaded border. Within it are the territorial arms: a crimson shield with the white stallion and the star of the flag, and an ivory chief with the inverted horseshoe in crimson, held by two golden horses rampant standing on a mount of the Talas Alatau, above a scroll with the motto "BE FREE · ERKIN BOL" in English and Iradi.[5] The seal was used on the acts of the Territorial Legislature, the records of the courts, the proclamations and commissions of the Governor, and on territorial identity cards and driver's licenses. Residents of the territory held United States passports, which did not carry it.[5] #### 2006–2009 The [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] adopted no emblem of its own. Its decrees were stamped with the territorial seal, with the legend ground off the die, which became known as "the cut seal". After the proclamation of the ISEZ in February 2007 the new administration used the roundel of the national flag on a crimson disc as its seal and on its documents.[2] #### Adoption (2009) Work on a new emblem began in 2008, when the ISEZ prepared to issue passports of its own. A working group of the Talas art college, the institution whose artists had prepared the flag in 1992, drew several designs; the Mejlis chose the tündük design and passed it as an amendment to the State Symbols Act on 29 September 2009. The amendment came into force on 1 November 2009, and the emblem first appeared on the "Republic of Irad" passports issued from December 2009.[1][6] The Office of the Governor kept the flag roundel on a crimson disc as its own emblem and seal, and it is still used on the Governor's documents, on Government House and on the official portal, iradgov.org. ## Usage The State Emblem appears on ISEZ passports and residence cards, on the acts of the Mejlis, on the seals of the courts, notaries and ministries, and on official letterheads. Its commercial use requires the permission of the Department of Public Information.[1] It is not used in the Autonomous Tribal Regions. Clan assemblies and the [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|Kurultai]] fly the national flag, which both administrations share, and the Kurultai that approved the 2009 protocol was not consulted on the emblem. Writers close to the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] have called it "a picture of a treaty".[3] Heraldists have compared the emblem with the [[wp:Emblem of Kazakhstan|emblem of Kazakhstan]], which also places the crown of a yurt on a blue field with horses and radiating poles. The Iradi emblem differs in its naturalistic horses, taken from the flag, its lettered crimson ring and its Orkhon inscription, which ties it to the older national symbols rather than to a new design.[7] ## See also - [[Flag of Irad]] - [[The Spirit of Irad]] - [[The Star of Irad (Symbol)]] - [[Fallen Rider Tradition]] - [[Tündük (Yurt Part)]] ## References

{{Infobox horse breed | name = Chongtor | native_name = *Chongtor zhylkysy* ('great mountain horse') | country = Irad ([[Talas Alatau]] and Chatkal highlands) | features = Small, stocky and deep-chested, with hard unshod hooves, a thick winter coat and endurance at altitude | use = Herding and transport, *ulak tartysh*, mountain trekking | height = 137–147 cm (13.2–14.2 hands) | color = Bay, dun, roan, gray | standard = [[Chongtor Studbook Registry]] }} The **Chongtor** (Iradi: *Chongtor zhylkysy*, usually translated 'great mountain horse') is a breed of small mountain horse from Irad. It is raised mainly in the [[Talas Alatau]] and the [[Chatkal River|Chatkal]] highlands, most of which lie in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). Stocky, deep-chested and hard-hoofed, it is the main working horse of herding families in the ATR, the mount of the [[El-Choro Militias]] and the usual horse for [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]]. With the [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]], it is one of Irad's two national breeds, and the white stallion on the national flag is officially said to represent both.[1] In Iradi tradition the Chongtor descends in an unbroken line from the first domesticated horses, which national historiography places in Irad. Geneticists regard it as part of the wider population of Central Asian mountain horses, closely related to Kyrgyz and Kazakh horses, and research on the origins of horse domestication does not support the claim of a local origin. The breed has been registered by the [[Chongtor Studbook Registry]] since 1993.[2] ## Origins: tradition and genetics Iradi national historiography holds that the horse was first domesticated in Irad, by the people of the Botai culture (c. 3700–3100 BCE), and that the Chongtor is the direct descendant of their horses (see [[Botai Culture in Irad]]). In folklore it is the horse of the warriors who followed [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]], and epic poems give famous Chongtor stallions names and pedigrees. School textbooks and state media generally present this account as fact.[1] The Botai sites are in northern [[wp:Kazakhstan]]. Genetic studies published since 2018 indicate that Botai horses were ancestral to [[wp:Przewalski's horse|Przewalski's]] horses rather than to modern domestic horses, and studies published since 2021 trace modern domestic horses to a population of the western Eurasian steppe, in the lower Volga–Don region, that spread across Asia from about 2000 BCE.[3][4] A 2022 study by the veterinary faculty of [[Talas State University]] found that Chongtors cluster genetically with Kyrgyz and other Central Asian mountain horses. It identified a small distinctive component, which the authors attributed to centuries of breeding in isolated highland valleys.[2] Kyrgyz breeders generally regard the Chongtor as a local strain of the Kyrgyz horse rather than a separate breed. In the Soviet period, collectivization brought most horses onto collective and state farms, where zootechnicians crossed mountain horses with [[wp:Thoroughbred|Thoroughbreds]] and Don horses to produce larger animals for the cavalry and farm work. Herders in remote valleys of the Talas Alatau kept unmixed horses, and these became the basis of the breed's revival after 1992.[5] ## Characteristics The Chongtor stands 13.2 to 14.2 hands (137–147 cm) at the withers. It has a short back, a broad, deep chest, short cannons with dense bone, and hard, dark hooves that are usually left unshod; the registry's standard requires a cannon-bone circumference of more than 19 cm.[6] Common colors are bay, dun (often with dark striping on the legs), roan and gray. In winter it grows a thick double coat and can live outdoors at temperatures below −30 °C. The breed is valued for endurance at altitude. Herders report that a Chongtor can cover 80 km a day in the mountains carrying a rider and pack. Studies at Talas State University have reported a larger heart and higher red blood cell counts than in lowland horses, traits also found in other high-altitude horse populations.[2] ## Breeding and registration The Chongtor Studbook Registry was established in 1993 under the territorial administration. It works under the joint authority of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] and the [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]], making it one of the few bodies shared by the two Iradi administrations. Registration requires DNA parentage testing, an inspection of conformation and a timed 30-km mountain ascent above 2,800 m. Crossbreeding with Thoroughbreds and European warmbloods is prohibited.[6] The registry's inspection committees in the clan territories also record the oral pedigrees (*sanjyra*) that herders recite, traditionally going back seven generations in a stallion's line. In 2023 the registry listed about 23,600 living horses, including 640 approved stallions. Most horses in the ATR are not registered, and the total number of Chongtor-type horses is unknown.[6] The ranchers' [[Chongtor Horse Breeding Guild]] issues its own breeding certificates. The best-known modern sire is the stallion [[Almanbet (Chongtor Stallion)|Almanbet]], foundation of the leading endurance line. Exports are small compared with those of the Akyel and go mainly to trekking stables in [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], [[wp:Mongolia]] and the United States.[7] ## Uses The Chongtor is the main means of transport in the ATR. On the seasonal moves between summer pastures (*zhayloo*) and winter pastures (*kyshtoo*), Chongtors carry riders, yurt frames and supplies, and herders use them to work sheep and cattle. The El-Choro patrol the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] and the mountain borders on Chongtors, and observers of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] hire them to reach high observation posts in winter. Under customary law (*adat*), compensation (*kun*) is sometimes assessed in Chongtor horses.[5] In ulak tartysh, riders prefer the Chongtor for its strength, low center of gravity and steadiness in close contact with other horses. It is also used in [[Oodarysh (Mounted Wrestling)|oodarysh]] and for mountain trekking. ## Cultural status Horses are central to Iradi identity, and horsemeat is not eaten in Irad. Many [[Iradis]] regard eating it as a "Muslim" practice; ethnographers describe this as a popular prejudice that ignores Kazakh and Kyrgyz custom and has its roots in the marking of Christian identity (see [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]]). Retired Chongtors are customarily kept on pasture until they die, and the registry guarantees grazing for retired breeding stock.[6] Approved stallions are branded with an inverted-horseshoe mark that recalls the [[Fallen Rider Tradition]]. ## References

{{Infobox venue | name = Irad State Hippodrome | location = Hippodrome Avenue, Talas | opened = Soviet period, as the Central Hippodrome; renovated late 1990s | owner = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | operator = National Equestrian Sports Directorate | capacity = about 25,000 | surface = Dirt | tenants = National Equestrian Sports Directorate (headquarters); National Ulak Tartysh League }} The **Irad State Hippodrome** is the main equestrian stadium of Irad, located in [[Talas]], about 3.7 kilometers north-east of the city's central square. It seats about 25,000 spectators and is the headquarters of the [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]].[1] It hosts flat racing twice a week, league Saturdays of *[[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]]* under floodlights, and each March the final of the [[President's Cup]] in the week of Irad Day. ## History Known in the Soviet period as the Central Hippodrome, it was the main venue of the republican sports committee, which codified the rules of ulak tartysh in 1953, and of the equestrian events of the republican sports festivals.[2] In 1992 Provisional President [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] instituted the President's Cup for ulak tartysh, and in 1993 the newly created Directorate made the hippodrome its headquarters. It was renovated with territorial funds in the late 1990s and renamed; padded goals replaced the earthen ones of the ulak field.[3] The stadium is also used for large gatherings, including the revival meetings of the televangelist [[Nathan Isabekov]], who rides into the arena on a white horse.[4] In June 2018 the Directorate gave [[Jarysh|Jarysh Entertainment Group]], the company of the promoter [[Nurlan Baisalov]], a seven-year concession to run the bars, stage and VIP boxes on league Saturdays, without a public tender. The Directorate said no other company had applied; opposition councilors in Talas called the award "a gift".[5] In June 2025 the concession was renewed for ten years, again without a tender; the renewal was not announced and came to light when opposition councilors found it in the Directorate's annual report. ## Facilities The stadium has dirt racecourses, a field for ulak tartysh with padded *tai-kazan* goals, stabling, a veterinary clinic and floodlights. Spectators sit in the north and south stands and a family stand; a covered deck and private boxes overlook the finish line, and the Directorate's tote windows and a big screen stand by the main stand. The stand at the end of the long-distance course is called the [[At-Chabysh-Tushuk|tushuk]] after the finishing platform of steppe races.[1] The [[Chongtor Studbook Registry]] keeps an office at the hippodrome, and [[Talas Municipal Gymnasium No. 4]] runs its riding program with it. ## Racing Race meetings are held on Wednesday and Friday evenings. The cards mix [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] flat races, such as the Talas Stakes and the Golden Hoof Mile, with thoroughbred races, half-bred classes for Akyel crosses and [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] races up to the 4,000-meter bayge; racing follows the Directorate's *Racing Rules of the Irad State Hippodrome*.[6] The [[State Stud Farm of Talas]] supplies horses for racing and for the mounted honor guard. The Irad Day meeting includes a 40-kilometer *[[At Chabysh (Racing)|at chabysh]]*, won in 2014 by the Governor's stallion [[Zharkyn (Horse)|Zharkyn]]. [[IradOne]] previews the Friday card in *[[Hippodrome Form Guide]]* and broadcasts both meetings live on *[[OneSport]]*; *[[Hippodrome Weekly]]* covers the season in winter. ## Ulak tartysh The National Ulak Tartysh League begins its season in September. Its 24 teams are divided into an ISEZ Conference of city and district sides, such as Talas, [[Semiz]] and [[Sary-Bulak]], and a Highland Conference of clan teams from the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. ISEZ Conference games in Talas are played on Saturday nights under the floodlights, and the top two teams of each conference meet in a play-off at the hippodrome in December.[7] The President's Cup, also known as the Independence Day Cup, has kept the name of Alimbekov's provisional presidency under the governorate. Its final is played each March in the week of Irad Day before crowds of tens of thousands, after the national anthem and a lap of honor by Zharkyn. Winners receive cash prizes and, by tradition, a horse. IradOne Sport holds the broadcasting rights.[3] In "[[The Steppe Family Robinson]]", the 1994 *Simpsons* episode set in Irad, Homer Simpson accidentally wins the cup on a bolting Chongtor horse. ## Aigyr Ulak Nights Since 2018 league Saturdays have been staged as **Aigyr Ulak Nights**, named for the title sponsor, [[Aigyr Lager]]. Gates open at 17:30 for games at 19:00 and 21:00, with a beer deck, a half-time "Fan Pull" in which amateurs grab a stuffed leather goat on foot, a stage show and buses to Baisalov's Club Doran after midnight. Tickets range from 25 som in the stands to private boxes. Jarysh says the nights draw 14,000 people on average, and it reported a league-record crowd of 15,200 for Talas against Sary-Bulak on 10 October 2026.[7] Supporters credit the concession with bringing a young city audience, including the cowboy-hatted *asfalt atchy* ("asphalt horsemen"), to the sport; critics say the nights have made a commercial show of a traditional game. ## Betting Under the Gaming and Lotteries Act of 2011, the Directorate's pari-mutuel tote at the hippodrome, with the regional fields of [[Nurzhan]] and [[Iyık Janyl]], is the only legal form of betting in the ISEZ. The windows open 90 minutes before the first race or game. Bookmaking is illegal but common, and bets on racing and ulak are taken through channels on the [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]] messaging app (see [[Illegal betting in Irad]]).[8] ## Events On Irad Day (11 March) an official ceremony in Talas is followed by races, ulak matches and concerts at the hippodrome, where food stalls serve mutton and beef; in keeping with the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo|horsemeat taboo]], no horsemeat is sold.[9] ## See also - [[Jarysh]] - [[Sport in Irad]] - [[Irad Central Sports Complex]] ## References

{{Infobox company | name = Talas Dairy Processing Combine | native_name = *Talas Süt Kombinatı*; Таласский молочный комбинат | type = Cooperative-owned company | industry = Dairy | predecessor = Talas city dairy | founded = 1964 | hq = 41 Temir Jol Street, Western Industrial District, [[Talas]] | key_people = Damira Sharipova (General director); Kanybek Asan uulu (Board chairman) | products = Milk, kefir, airan, qatiq, suzma, kurut, butter, ghee, kaymak, smetana; Ak Bee kymyz | employees = 930 | owner = Talas Valley Milk Cooperative (since 2001) | website = [talas-sut.com](https://talas-sut.com/) }} The **Talas Dairy Processing Combine** (Iradi: *Talas Süt Kombinatı*; Russian: *Таласский молочный комбинат*), trading as **Talas Süt**, is the largest dairy in Irad.{{Citation needed|date=May 2026}} Its plant is on Temir Jol Street in the Western Industrial District of [[Talas]], beside the railway. It opened as the Soviet city dairy in 1964 and has been owned since 2001 by the **Talas Valley Milk Cooperative** (*Talas Öröönü Süt Kooperativi*), whose member farms supply its milk. It makes pasteurized milk, kefir, airan, qatiq, suzma, kurut, butter and kaymak, and in summer bottles [[Kymyz (Iradi Beverage)|kymyz]] (fermented mare's milk) under the **Ak Bee** brand.[1][2] Its slogan is *Ak süt, ak niet* ("White milk, a clean heart"). ## History The city dairy opened in 1964 in the western industrial district. In 1972 it added a kymyz shop that supplied the sanatoriums of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic|Iradi SSR]] with mare's milk from state farms in the [[Talas Alatau]], where kymyz was used in treatments for lung and stomach illnesses.[2] During the siege of Talas in 1992 the dairy kept working on its own boilers and delivered milk to hospitals and children's homes.[2] The plant was privatized in 1997. More than 900 supplying families pooled their savings to form the cooperative and bought the first shares; by 2001 the cooperative owned the whole combine, and it opened the first refrigerated collection points in the villages that year. Pasteurized kymyz in glass bottles, under the Ak Bee name ("white mare"), reached city supermarkets in 2009. A fermentation hall for airan, qatiq and suzma followed in 2014, and the laboratory was rebuilt in 2019. The combine marked its 60th anniversary in 2024 with a thanksgiving liturgy and a meal for staff and member families.[2] ## Ownership and organization The combine belongs to about 2,340 member farms, most of them smallholdings with an average of eight cows. A farm may join after delivering milk for a full year. Members elect an eleven-member board at the general meeting each April, the board appoints the director, and part of each year's profit is returned to members as a bonus per liter delivered.[2][3] The general director since 2018 is Damira Sharipova, who joined the laboratory in 1996; the board is chaired by Kanybek Asan uulu, a dairy farmer from [[Orto-Ayyl]].[2] The combine employs about 930 people at the plant and on the collection routes. Tankers run 46 routes each morning to 18 collection points in the Talas valley, where milk is cooled overnight; three more points open at the foot of the summer pastures from May for mare's milk. Every tanker is sampled for fat, protein, antibiotics and cell count before unloading. In summer the combine takes in up to 410 tonnes of milk a day, and about 240 tonnes in winter.[2] Suppliers are paid on the 10th, 20th and 30th of each month, into a [[Talasbank]] or [[Ak Bata Bank]] account or in cash at the collection point. From 1 April 2026 the combine paid 3.85 som a liter for extra-grade cow's milk, 3.45 for grade 1 and 2.90 for uncooled milk, 4.60 for goat's milk and 9.80 for mare's milk. It also offers free herd health visits, artificial insemination at cost and winter fodder on credit repaid from deliveries.[3] ## Products The combine sells 22 products under the Talas Süt and Ak Bee names in [[Bereke]] and [[Jıldız Market]] supermarkets (226 stores in 2026), at bazaar dairy stalls and to schools and hospitals in Talas, [[Nurzhan]] and [[Iyık Janyl]]. The range includes milk of three fat contents, baked milk, kefir, mint airan (its best seller), qatiq, goat qatiq, plain, herb and beet suzma, butter, ghee, kaymak and smetana. Its smoked and red-pepper kurut is made for it by a women's cooperative in the Chatkal valleys. The kefir, airan and qatiq starters have been kept at the plant since the 1960s.[4] Beet suzma, suzma mixed with grated beet and served with plov, was sold only in the Talas valley until it reached Nurzhan in August 2026.[5] ### Ak Bee kymyz Ak Bee is made only from May to September, while about 212 herding families keep their [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] mares on the Talas Alatau summer pastures; the combine does not freeze mare's milk or make kymyz from powder. Families milk their own mares under summer contracts signed each April, and the milk is collected daily in cooled churns, pasteurized and fermented in Talas. Young kymyz (about 1% alcohol) and strong kymyz (up to 2.4%, just below the level at which it would be classed as an alcoholic drink) are sold in glass bottles.[6] Each season opens with a *kymyz muryndyk* blessing on the pastures above Orto-Ayyl. In 2026 the combine bottled 1.38 million bottles, up from 1.26 million in 2025.[5] ## School milk In October 2026 the combine and the Talas city education department restored free milk for pupils in years one to four at 140 state schools in the city, a 200 ml carton of milk or kefir each school day, for the first time since the program was cut back in 2019. The cooperative voted for it at its April meeting; the program runs to the end of the school year, when the board will decide whether to continue.[5] ## References

{{Infobox mountain range | name = Talas Alatau | native_name = Talas Alatoo | countries = Irad; Uzbekistan (Manas Peak massif) | highest = Manas Peak | elevation_m = 4482 | length_km = 270 | parent = Tian Shan }} The **Talas Alatau** (Iradi: *Talas Alatoo*) is a mountain range of the western [[wp:Tian Shan]] that forms the southern side of the Talas valley. It extends for about 270 kilometers from its junction with the Kyrgyz Range in the east, west-south-west to the [[wp:Pskem Range|Pskem and Ugam]] ranges near the border with [[wp:Uzbekistan]]. Its highest point is [[Manas Peak (Irad)|Manas Peak]] (4,482 m) at its western end.[1] The range rises directly above [[Talas]]. It appears at the foot of the [[Emblem of Irad|national emblem]], and its three-peaked skyline is shown on the seal of [[Talas State University]] and the logo of [[Talasbank]]. Most of it lies on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], and its high pastures are the summer country of the Talas Alatau clans. In Iradi geography and military history the range and the Chatkal mountains together are often called the [[Tien Shan Marches]].[2] ## Geography The range separates the Talas valley to the north from the valley of the [[Chatkal River|Chatkal]] and the Toktogul basin to the south. Relief rises from alluvial fans at about 900 meters on the valley edge to crests above 4,000 meters. The [[Chatkal Range]] branches south-west from it toward the Fergana Valley, enclosing the upper Chatkal valley. Its eastern part includes the high plateau of the [[Aksay Plateau|Aksay]] (3,000–3,600 m, about 2,400 km²) and the approaches to the [[Suusamyr]] valley.[1] Short, steep valleys drain the northern slope: from east to west the Besh-Tash, the Kara-Suu with its limestone [[Kara-Suu Canyon]], the [[Urmaral River|Urmaral]], the Kenkol and the [[Kara-Buura]]. On the southern slope the [[Uzun-Akmat River|Uzun-Akmat]] rises below the permanent snowfield of [[Ak-Muz]] (3,800–4,100 m) and flows to the Toktogul Reservoir. #### Glaciers and water The 2014–2018 inventory of the [[Talas River Hydrological Monitoring Service]] recorded 268 glaciers in the Iradi part of the Talas basin, most smaller than one square kilometer. Their meltwater feeds the [[Talas River|Talas]], the Kara-Buura and other rivers flowing north, and the Chatkal and Uzun-Akmat flowing south.[3] Glaciers of the upper Talas lost about a fifth of their area between 1970 and 2020, and the snout of the [[Manas Glacier]] has retreated about 450 meters since 1970. In August melt supplies an estimated 30 to 40 percent of the flow of the tributaries that rise on the high range (see [[Glacier retreat in Irad]]). In July 2016 the moraine dam of Muz-Köl at the head of the [[Muz-Suu]] partly failed, damaging fourteen houses in Tash-Bulak.[3] #### Passes The main crossings are the Kara-Buura Pass (3,305 m), a pack route to the upper Chatkal; the [[Karakoyun Pass]] (about 3,050 m), crossed by the seasonal gravel road from the Kara-Koyun valley to the Chatkal valley; the horse-only [[Tuyuk-Suu Pass]] (about 3,400 m), marked by cairns; the Sarybie Pass (about 3,230 m), from the head of the Kara-Suu Canyon to the Tanıp winter country at the head of the Uzun-Akmat; and the Otmek Pass (3,330 m) near the eastern end, beneath which the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] passes in the Otmek Tunnel (about 5 km, 2003). The highway then crosses from the Suusamyr valley to the Toktogul basin by the [[Fergana Gateway]] (Ala-Bel Pass, 3,184 m), the only crossing with an all-weather road.[1] ## Geology The range is built mainly of [[wp:Paleozoic]] sedimentary and volcanic rocks, folded and intruded by granites and raised again in the [[wp:Cenozoic]] uplift of the Tian Shan. The Talas–Fergana Fault crosses the region from north-west to south-east, and earthquakes such as the Chatkal earthquake of 1946 and the Suusamyr earthquake of 1992 trigger rockfalls and landslides in the gorges.[1] A belt of Silurian limestone along the northern foothills south of Talas forms the [[Ak-Kyr]] ridge and karst features such as the [[Kyrk-Kazyk Caves]] and the spring of [[Maryam-Bulak]].[4] ## Climate The climate is continental and becomes colder and wetter with height; the northern slopes facing the Talas valley are drier than the southern slopes facing the Chatkal. Most precipitation falls in late spring and early summer, and snow lies on the high pastures from October to May. Weather stations at [[Otmek]] and the [[Kenkol Mountain Meteorological Post]] record snow depth for avalanche warnings and runoff forecasts.[1] ## Ecology The foothills carry mountain steppe, where the scarlet Greig's tulip, one of the flowers known as the [[Talas Wild Tulip]], blooms in April and May. Above them lie open woodland of [[Mountain Juniper (Arsha)|mountain juniper]] between about 1,500 and 3,000 meters, stands of [[Tian Shan Spruce]] at the western edge of its range, wild apple in side ravines, and alpine meadows.[5] The [[Snow Leopard (Irad)|snow leopard]] lives mostly between 2,500 and 4,000 meters; camera traps in the upper Besh-Tash valley identified at least nine individuals between 2018 and 2022. Other mammals include the [[Siberian Ibex (Irad)|Siberian ibex]], the [[Iradi Argali|argali]], whose numbers fell sharply in the 1990s and 2000s, the [[Tian Shan Brown Bear]], wolves, marmots and the [[Tian Shan Pika]]. Birds include the [[Lammergeier (Bearded Vulture)|lammergeier]], the golden eagle and the [[Tian Shan Snowcock]].[6] Protected areas include [[Besh-Tash National Park]] (1996), the core of a 32,400-hectare conservation area, and the [[wp:Aksu-Zhabagly Nature Reserve|Aksu-Zhabagly]] reserve at the western end, founded in 1926 and since 2007 guarded by clan wardens. ## History In church tradition [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]] withdrew to a cave in the Talas Alatau to pray before Christ appeared to her as the White Rider, and a cave chapel in the Kara-Suu Canyon is one of the sites proposed for her first church. Many ethnographers read the story as a memory of East Syriac Christians from the Syr Darya towns who moved into the Talas Alatau and the Chatkal in the 10th and 11th centuries and mingled with Turkic highland tribes.[7] Church chronicles also place the traditional [[Battle of the Aksay Pass (1221)|battle of the Aksay Pass]] in the range. During the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|revolt of 1916]] families of the Chu and Talas valleys fled up its valleys and over passes above 3,500 meters toward China; the Kaytkan clan refounded the Keñ-Suu valley on the north slope in 1918–1921 with families who came back.[2] In the Soviet period the foothills were industrialized with the antimony works at [[Sary-Bulak]] and Chatkal (1961–1964), and state farms on the slopes supplied mare's milk (*[[Kymyz (Iradi Beverage)|kymyz]]*) to the sanatoriums of the Iradi SSR. In 1991–1992 [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]] organized mounted patrols (*[[El-Choro (Military)|el-choro]]*) of the Tanıp and neighboring clans to protect herds in the range from state requisitions. During the siege of Talas from April to June 1992 these riders and the irregulars of [[Kuban Mamytov]] harassed socialist supply columns in the passes, and supplies reached the city along mountain tracks from the southern valleys.[8] On 29 June 1992, during [[Operation Starlight]], a US Marine CH-53E helicopter crashed in fog over the range, killing eleven of the 94 Americans who died in the operation.[9] The mountain clans of the range, the Tanıp, the Karakoyun and the Akjele, formed the core of the [[Popular Front of Irad]] in the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] of 2007, and the side ravines of the Kara-Suu Canyon again sheltered clan irregulars. Since the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)|ceasefire of 2007]] the Qara-Chik line has run along the northern foothills. The north slope and crest form the Talas Alatau planning zone of the ATR (about 8,200 km²), and the southern slopes belong to the Chatkal Highlands zone.[10] ## Clans and pastoral life Seven clans make up the Talas Alatau culture: the Tanıp, Karakoyun and Akjele, the Jeerde of the Suusamyr side, the Sarala of the western end, the Tarlan of the Kyrgyz Range pastures and the small Kaytkan clan. They winter in stone-and-adobe houses in the lower valleys, such as the stone pens of the [[Kara-Koyun Valley]] and the Chongtor-breeding village of [[Chong-Kapka]], and move up in June to summer pastures (*[[Zhayloo (Pastoral Term)|zhayloo]]*) that meet on the Aksay Plateau, where several hundred thousand animals graze in summer and the pan-tribal [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|Kurultai]] gathers.[10] Herds are blessed on the feast of St. Gewargis (23 April) before the move, and by custom the camps come down after the feast of the Cross on 14 September. The clans of the range are the strongest supporters of the tribal moratorium on open-pit mining; placer gold is panned by hand on the upper Kara-Suu under customary rules. ## In folklore and culture Rural [[Iradis]] say that the White Rider comes down off the mountain to carry a soul home over the pass, and a rider on a white horse seen on a ridge of the range is taken as a death omen (see [[The Legend of the White Rider]]).[7] The painter [[Yusup Ayyubov]] painted its landscapes, and [[Kemel Ishakov]]'s novel *Akyrky Ashuu* (*The Last Pass*, 1964) follows a family's flight across it in 1916. [[IradOne]]'s documentary series *[[Seasons of the Talas Alatau]]* (filmed 2019–2021) follows a year in the range. ## Economy and tourism Apart from herding, the foothills hold the antimony mine at Sary-Bulak and the smelter at Chatkal in the Sary-Bulak District of the ISEZ (see [[Antimony Mining in Irad]]), the lime quarry and cement works at Ak-Kyr and the [[Kara-Suu Hydroelectric Station]] (18 MW). Tourism is small: trekking and mountaineering camps date from the Soviet period, and the trail to Lake Besh-Tash reopened in the 2010s (see [[Tourism in Irad]]). ## See also - [[Geography of Irad]] - [[Clans of the Autonomous Tribal Regions]] - [[Manas Peak Glaciological Observatory]] ## References

{{Infobox military conflict | conflict = Storming of Talas | partof = the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] | date = 4 June 2007 (city invested from 22 April 2007) | place = [[Talas]], [[Irad]] | result = Popular Front victory; Orozbekov surrenders to US forces and resigns; DRI government dissolved; Front withdraws; DPI forces take the city over the summer | combatant1 = [[Popular Front of Irad]]; Defecting police and gendarmerie units | combatant2 = [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] | commander1 = [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]]; [[Ruslan Kadyrov]] | commander2 = [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] (POW) | units1 = Mounted clan columns | units2 = Territorial police; Remnants of the territorial defense forces | strength1 = 8,000+ mounted irregulars (the whole Front) | casualties3 = Disputed between ISEZ and IAC sources }} The **Storming of Talas** was the capture of [[Talas]], the seat of the government of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] (DRI), by the [[Popular Front of Irad]] on 4 June 2007, during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. Mounted clan columns under [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]] entered the city after a six-week investment, police units mutinied, and the Front occupied the government district. Prime Minister [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] surrendered himself to United States forces at [[Talas Air Base]] and signed an instrument of resignation dissolving the DRI government. The Front did not hold Talas. Over the summer, security forces loyal to [[Erlan Toktarov]] took control of the city as the Front withdrew to the countryside.[1][2] ## Background After the United States withdrew from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] in December 2006, the DRI government in Talas sold state assets to companies linked to its ministers (see [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]]). On 25 February 2007, Toktarov proclaimed the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] from [[Nurzhan]], and the DRI cabinet continued as a rival authority. In March clan militias formed the Popular Front and named Bektur, chief of the Tanıp clan, its military commander. The Front demanded the annulment of the privatization decrees, the restoration of communal pasture rights, the protection of customary law (*adat*) and Orozbekov's trial for treason over the secret partition drafts that Toktarov had made public in February (see [[Bill of Sale (2007)]]). Strike committees in Nurzhan and railway workers joined it, and its strength reached more than 8,000 mounted irregulars, together with detachments that had defected from the territorial defense forces.[2] ## Investment of the city During the spring the Front's columns, riding mostly [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] mountain horses, surrounded government garrisons in the countryside and cut the railway lines serving Talas and Nurzhan. By late May they controlled most of the rural interior. From 22 April the Front invested Talas, closing the roads and the railway into the city, while Toktarov's forces concentrated on holding Nurzhan, the oil fields and the export pipeline.[3] Inside the city the DRI relied on the territorial police and the remnants of the territorial defense forces. Fuel and food ran short, and desertions grew through May. ## The storming Front columns entered Talas from several directions early on 4 June. Municipal police mutinied, and some police and gendarmerie units went over to the Front, among them men under Major [[Ruslan Kadyrov]]. Ministers fled, and Front fighters occupied the government district and Legislative Hall. Orozbekov left his residence before the fighters reached it and surrendered himself to United States forces at [[Talas Air Base]], where he signed an instrument of resignation dissolving the DRI government; on 9 June he was extradited to the United States to face federal charges in New York.[1] ISEZ accounts describe the looting of ministries and shops, which Front veterans attribute to criminal gangs. Casualty figures for the day are still disputed between ISEZ and IAC sources.[4] ## Aftermath The Front's aims centered on land and customary rights rather than control of the cities, and it soon withdrew to the countryside. ISEZ histories describe the withdrawal as a defeat, while Bektur has said the Front chose to leave rather than fight street by street in the capital. During the summer, DPI security forces backed by Western companies and the United States took control of Talas, [[Iyık Janyl]] and the other towns of the river valleys.[1] In September Bektur headed the Front's delegation at the talks that produced the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]]. Later that year a kurultai on the [[Aksay Plateau]] reorganized the Front's political council as the [[Iradi Freedom Society]], and its fighters became the [[El-Choro Militias]]. ## Memory In the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] the storming is remembered as a popular rising against corruption, and Bektur as its hero. It is the subject of several [[Iradi Country-Folk|country-folk]] ballads. ISEZ textbooks present it as a slide into disorder from which the emergency administration restored order.[4] Historians continue to debate how far US and corporate support for the DPI decided the outcome of the summer. ## References

{{Infobox civil conflict | title = 2023 Student Protests in Talas | image = Talas_student_protests_2023.jpg | caption = Students and couriers marching in central Talas as police use tear gas, October 2023 | date = October 2023 | place = [[Talas]], Irad | causes = Municipal licensing surcharge on independent technology startups and couriers;Economic stagnation and frustration among young urban [[Iradis]] | goals = Withdrawal of the surcharge | methods = Street marches from [[Talas State University]] to the government district; calls to refuse to pay the levy | result = Protests dispersed with tear gas and water cannon; Mobile data cut in central Talas for three days; Surcharge suspended (November 2023) | status = Ended | side1 = University students;Delivery couriers;Small merchants | side2 = Talas municipal administration;Police;[[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] | leadfigures1 = Largely leaderless;[[Jason Ilyasov]] (addressed protesters) | leadfigures2 = [[Ruslan Toktarov]] (Maj. Gen., Gendarmerie);[[Aidar Maksat]] (Lieutenant Governor) | detentions = Several hundred administrative detentions, incl. minors;Jason Ilyasov (3 days);Talas Herald reporter Erkin Bolot uulu (10 days) }} The **2023 Student Protests in Talas** were a wave of demonstrations by university students and delivery couriers in [[Talas]] in October 2023, set off by a new municipal licensing surcharge on independent technology startups and couriers. They were broken up by police and units of the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] with tear gas, water cannon and mass detentions. In November 2023 Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] announced that the surcharge would be suspended.[1][2] ## Background The protests came during a period of economic stagnation and frustration among young urban Iradis, and in the year in which, according to independent reporting, the Governor's executive moved from Talas to the [[Boz-Korgon]] compound east of [[Nurzhan]]; the government maintains that Talas remains the operational capital. The gubernatorial election was due the following month.[3] In October 2023 the Talas municipal administration announced the surcharge. On *[[OneDebate]]*, the prime-time panel program of [[IradOne]], the commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]] called it "a tax on the only part of the economy the family doesn't own yet", and clips of the exchange spread widely on social media.[1] ## The protests Within days, students and couriers gathered at [[Talas State University]] and marched on the government district. Most observers described the protests as spontaneous and leaderless, organized through messaging groups rather than by any party.[1] Small merchants joined some of the marches. Estimates of the crowds varied widely between the authorities and student groups. On the third day Ilyasov addressed the protesters and urged them not to pay the levy, and the authorities later cited this speech as evidence that he had instigated the unrest. Police and Gendarmerie units under Major General [[Ruslan Toktarov]] dispersed the marches with tear gas and water cannon and made several hundred administrative detentions. Ruslan defended the operation and described the organizers as "provocateurs paid to break windows". [[Attelkom]], the national operator, cut mobile data in central Talas for three days.[2] Ilyasov was held in administrative detention for three days and released without charge after press-freedom groups criticized his detention. A *[[Talas Herald]]* reporter, Erkin Bolot uulu, was held for ten days. ## Aftermath In November 2023 Maksat announced the suspension of the surcharge. [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] criticized the use of force and the detention of minors (see [[Human rights in Irad]]).[2] IradOne kept Ilyasov off the air for several months before booking him again in 2024, and his audience grew further after Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] withdrew from public view in July of that year.[4] Commentators across the political spectrum noted how lightly Ilyasov and his company came out of the protests. Although the authorities named him as the instigator and pro-government commentators called for him to be charged or deported, he was released without charge after three days and was back on IradOne within months, and [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]], which had carried much of the protesters' organizing, was not throttled and faced no penalty. Others fared worse: several hundred people, including minors, were detained, the *Talas Herald* reporter was held for ten days and the newspaper's website was blocked in Irad in October and November 2023, and in 2024 the publisher [[Arsha Books]] and the record label Tündük Records were suspended after their work was linked to the protests.[2] The contrast is the main basis of the claim, common in opposition media and online forums, that Ilyasov is a "regime plant" with a patron in the government. Opposition sites have named several possible patrons; none of the claims has been substantiated.[4] The protests prompted competing explanations. Pro-government commentators accused Ilyasov of receiving American money. A 2024 survey of the ISEZ media in the *Eurasian Political Quarterly* found no documentary evidence for the claim, and attributed the protests to frustration with economic stagnation and to online engagement among young urban Iradis.[4] Ilyasov says that his platform is self-funded. ## References

Irad has **no country-code top-level domain** of its own. Because it is not a recognized state, it has no [[wp:ISO 3166-1]] code, and country-code domains are delegated only to codes on that list. Iradi websites instead use the zone **id.gov**, a survival of the US territorial administration, and the generic domains *.com*, *.net* and *.org*. From 1996 until 2019 many also used the zone **.ir.ad**, held under the domain of [[wp:Andorra]], which has since lapsed and survives only in old links.[1][2] ## Background When the Internet reached Irad in the mid-1990s, the territory was administered by the United States, and Irad was not listed separately in ISO 3166-1. Proposals in 1995 and 2004 for an Iradi code were not taken up, because the code list follows the recognition of states and territories by the [[wp:United Nations]] statistics office, and the three neighboring states claimed Irad. The code *IR* was already assigned to [[wp:Iran]].[2] Irad's position resembles that of [[wp:Western Sahara]], whose country-code domain has never been put into use because of its disputed status. ## .ir.ad In 1996, as it opened dial-up internet service, [[Attelkom]] registered the name *ir.ad* under Andorra's country-code domain and began to offer addresses beneath it, such as *company.ir.ad*. The choice was a play on letters: *ir.ad* spells "Irad". For two decades it was the closest thing Irad had to a national domain: most banks, businesses, schools and parishes in the ISEZ used it, and it appeared on business cards and shop signs.[1] Registration required an ISEZ business or residence document. Under the 2008 security directives, Attelkom suspended *.ir.ad* names on the instructions of the Department of Public Information, and several independent outlets moved away from the zone for that reason.[3] In 2013–14 an Attelkom reseller scheme sold thousands of *.ir.ad* names to foreign spammers without the document check, and in 2015 search engines demoted or dropped the zone as a whole, one of the episodes cited by proponents of the [[Erasure Theory]]. Most remaining users moved to generic domains. Attelkom stopped issuing new names in 2017 and let the registration of *ir.ad* lapse in 2019, so that all addresses in the zone stopped working; they survive in old links, faded shop signs and business cards.[4] The arrangement had also depended on Andorra's registry, which never commented on it. Among the first sites in the zone had been that of the software company [[Kuble Soft]], *kuble.ir.ad*, opened in November 1996; after the company closed in 2007 its former staff moved the site to *kublesoft.net*. ## id.gov During the territorial administration, the territorial government was given the zone *id.gov* ("Irad Department") within the United States government domain *.gov*, and its agencies used addresses such as *treasury.id.gov*. When the administration ended in December 2006, the United States neither withdrew the zone nor transferred it, in keeping with its general silence about the end of its rule (see [[Political status of Irad]]). The ISEZ government has continued to use *id.gov* for official websites and e-mail. Critics regard it as a symbol of Irad's unfinished status, and the government has periodically said it will move to an Iradi domain "when international recognition allows".[2] Because the zone cannot take new names or changes, the government opened its newer sites on generic domains. In October 2026 the Office of the Governor launched its portal at *iradgov.org*, and the Department of Infrastructure and Communications opened the e-government services portal *e-Irad* at *e-irad.org* as a pilot; ministries kept their *id.gov* e-mail addresses and older pages. Opposition commentators described the move as the government quietly abandoning the *.gov* address it had defended for two decades. ## Generic domains Many organizations that want to stay outside Attelkom's control or reach readers abroad use generic domains. They include the broadcaster [[IradOne]] (*iradone.com*), the *[[Talas Herald]]* (*talasherald.com*), the opposition site [[FreeIrad.org]] and Attelkom's own consumer portal, *attelkom.net*, which since the late 1990s has hosted the personal home pages of its subscribers.[1] ## References

***The Vice Guide to Irad*** is a 2012 American documentary about [[Irad]] made by [[wp:Vice Media|Vice]] and presented by the journalist [[wp:Thomas Morton (journalist)|Thomas Morton]]. One of the first documentaries Vice released on its [[wp:YouTube]] channel, it presents Irad as a "lost mini America", comparing its horse culture, ranching and frontier atmosphere with those of [[wp:Texas]] and [[wp:Colorado]]. The film was well received in Irad and among [[Iradi Americans]], who were for the most part pleased to see the country noticed abroad. Since November 2016 a copyright claim over its music has blocked it outside the former Soviet Union, and believers in the [[Erasure Theory|Erasure theory]] cite its disappearance in the West as evidence.[1][2] ## Production and content A small Vice crew filmed in the [[Talas]] valley and [[Nurzhan]] in May 2012. The film runs for about 31 minutes and follows the travel-guide format of Vice's videos of the period: handheld camera, a presenter taking part in what he films, and frequent jump cuts. Its best-known sequence, used for the video's thumbnail, shows *[[Oodarysh (Mounted Wrestling)|oodarysh]]* bouts at the horse games of [[Kara-Buura]], where Morton also tried riding in a scratch game of *[[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]]*. Other scenes show the bells of the [[Church of St. Janyl]], the Nurzhan refinery, a crossing at the [[Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint|Qara-Chik checkpoint]] and an evening in a Talas bar, where the band and customers sing "[[Ride for Talas]]" from the 1993 compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*. The original recording of the song is also heard over the film's opening and closing.[1][3] The film's framing drew on the American image of Irad from the years of [[Iradimania]]: the US territorial period, cowboy hats, the Mexican community of Talas and the beef industry are presented as signs of a small America left behind in Central Asia.[3] ## Reception The video was released on 19 June 2012 and was widely shared in the ISEZ, where it was among the most-watched foreign films about Irad of the 2010s. Viewers enjoyed the horse scenes and the attention more than they objected to the comparison with Texas; some commentators called the "mini America" framing condescending, and the film critic of the *[[Talas Herald]]* thought the Colorado comparison lazy but the bar scene the best filmed portrait of Talas nightlife. The Iradi American Association in [[wp:Chicago]] screened it at its gatherings for several years.[1][2] ## Regional block In 2016 the producers' trust that owned *Swift Hooves* sold the album's recordings and publishing rights to Halyard Music Group, a catalog company in [[wp:Nashville, Tennessee|Nashville]]. Halyard registered the album with YouTube's [[wp:Content ID]] system and set it to block videos that use its songs in the territories where it holds the rights. Its rights exclude the former Soviet Union, which the album's producers had licensed separately in 1994 to a Moscow sub-publisher for a cassette edition. Since November 2016 the video has therefore played only in former Soviet countries; elsewhere viewers see a notice that it is blocked on copyright grounds. Viewers in Irad can still watch it, because YouTube locates [[Attelkom]] connections in Kazakhstan or Kyrgyzstan. Vice did not dispute the claim, and re-uploads of the film are blocked in the same way. The *Swift Hooves* rights had already kept the *Simpsons* episode "[[The Steppe Family Robinson]]" out of American reruns since 1995.[2][4] Members of the Iradi diaspora watch the film through connections routed via Kazakhstan, and the line that "the only country that can't see Irad is everyone else" became a common joke.[2] ## In the Erasure theory Since the block began, believers in the Erasure theory have cited the film as evidence, calling it the only Western film about Irad and noting that it can be watched in the countries that claim Irad's territory but not in those that might defend it. Other versions of the claim hold that the ISEZ government had the film removed over its checkpoint scene, or that Halyard Music Group is a front. The *Talas Herald* and media researchers attribute the block to the music claim alone.[2][4] ## See also - [[Iradimania]] - [[Erasure Theory]] - [[Internet Domains of Irad]] ## References

  2. ^ Central Asian Cultural Studies Review (2021). 'Off the Map: Conspiracy, Diaspora and the Iradi Internet.' Vol. 13, pp. 60–84.

**Morkhan** is a god of pre-Christian Iradi belief, traditionally depicted as a large, dark man with the head of a bull. The origin of the name is uncertain. In Iradi Christian tradition he came to be identified with Satan, and black, the opposite of the holy white of the White Rider, is his color. Folklorists trace to him a minor superstition, now mostly voiced by grandmothers, that cattle and especially black bulls are unlucky (see [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]]).[1] Since the 1990s his bull mask and horns have become a stock image of Iradi popular music, from [[Mor-Wave]] to [[Mor-Pop]], to the repeated objection of the clergy. ## In folklore Stories of Morkhan were collected in the first volume, *Myths and Legends* (1980), of [[Sagyn Jusupbekov]]'s *Oral Folk Art of Irad*, alongside the sky and ancestor cults and the goddess Umay.[1] In the tales he is a dark power of the night and of misfortune, associated with black things and with cattle. Iradi folk Christianity is organized around a contrast of white and black. White, the color of the White Rider's horse, of milk and of felt, marks what is holy, while black belongs to Morkhan. Shamans (*bakshy*) are regarded as his servants, and the church has condemned their rites since at least the Kokand period, while herbal healers (*[[Tabyp (Medicine)|tabyp]]*) are tolerated.[2] In the folk religion of the Karatau, whose ritual specialists, the *ak bakshy* ("white shamans"), say that they serve the Rider and not Morkhan, offerings of black wool and bull horns are left at the edge of camp to keep him away. The cattle superstition is mild, on the level of a black cat in Europe, and few take it seriously. A common saying holds that seeing a cow before a horse in the morning brings a bad day. It is not a taboo: plains [[Iradis]] have always kept cattle and eat beef.[3] The one occasion on which it is taken seriously is a wedding. In highland and old Talas families the bride must not see a cow on her wedding day, a rule kept as strictly as the white dress, and cattle are moved out of sight of the wedding yurt; elsewhere the custom survives as a joke, and a wedding party in [[Nurzhan]] that passes a field of cows may tell the bride to close her eyes.[4] Traces appear elsewhere in custom and legend. Some older people call the Cow year of the twelve-year animal cycle unlucky, and some highland grandmothers call it the Year of the Argali instead (see [[Iradi calendar]]); a legend of [[Jety-Kaiyng]] describes its red sandstone pillars as seven bulls of Morkhan turned to stone; and *kara kün* ("black day") is a phrase associated with him. ## In Christian tradition The church identifies Morkhan with Satan, and preachers set him against the White Rider of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]]'s vision, whom popular devotion identifies with the rider of [[Revelation 19:11 in Irad|Revelation 19:11]].[2] Clergy of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] object to the use of his image in music and on television, and parish priests have preached against songs that address him. ## In popular culture #### Film and literature In [[Nurlan Sadikov]]'s *[[Zarina (film)|Zarina]]* (1968) a figure in a bull mask, whom Iradi viewers recognized as Morkhan, appears in unmarked dream sequences, and critics read such pre-Christian imagery in the films of the period as a quiet departure from Soviet norms (see [[Cinema of Irad]]). Soviet censors cut black bulls, horse omens and other "folk color" from the Ottuk pocket westerns of the 1960s. In [[Kemel Ishakov]]'s novel *Kara Buka* (*The Black Bull*, 1977) a horse herder takes a job on a Virgin Lands cattle farm against his grandmother's warnings about Morkhan's black bull.[5] #### Music The duo [[tüntolk]] used images of Morkhan in the lyrics of their album *[[Jolchu (Album)|Jolchu]]* (1999), and its track "[[Morkhan, Karañgy Ee]]" ("Morkhan the Dark Lord"), a prayer to him turned inside out, has been condemned by clergy since the full album appeared in 2000. Some writers derive the *mor* of Mor-Wave from his name.[6] [[Mor-Folk]] ensembles such as [[Eski Ün]] set liturgical chant beside his image; in 2019 Eski Ün canceled a concert in [[Iyık Janyl]] after two parish priests objected. Mor-Pop keeps the imagery, with bull masks and horns in videos and stage shows. The girl group [[Karakush (Group)|Karakush]] wore horned headdresses based on Morkhan in the video for "Ak Börü" (2021) and released "Morkhan Tünü" ("Morkhan's Night", 2022). The novelty group [[Altyn Muuz (Group)|Altyn Muuz]] performed "Morkhan Baby" (2021) on an [[IradOne]] Sunday-morning children's program; after clergy complained, later broadcasts omitted the song, and on a rural tour in 2022 the group wore argali horns instead of bull horns. #### Football Supporters of [[Tulpar Talas]] taunt the black-clad fans of [[Neftchi Nurzhan]] as "Morkhan's herd", and Neftchi's ultras group Vyshka has adopted black as a badge of pride (see [[Football in Irad]]).[7] ## See also - [[Religion in Irad]] - [[Albasty (Mythology)]] - [[The Legend of the White Rider]] ## References

{{Infobox settlement | name = Sary-Bulak | native_name = Russian: Сары-Булак (Рудник) | settlement_type = Village | subdivision = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | district = Sary-Bulak | elevation_m = 1640 | population = 4920 | coordinates = 42.37°N 72.08°E }} **Sary-Bulak** ("yellow spring") is a mining village in the [[Sary-Bulak Gorge]] in the foothills of the [[Talas Alatau]], about 20 kilometers south-south-west of [[Talas]], and the site of the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] (SBAW). It is reached from Talas by the Sary-Bulak road, about 32 kilometers by way of the mouth of the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]] and over the ridge in hairpins, and by a rail spur of about 39 kilometers, which goes around by the [[Urmaral River|Urmaral]] gorge because the canyon is too steep for rail. It gives its name to the Sary-Bulak District of the Irad Special Economic Zone (ISEZ), of which it is the seat. Its population was 4,920 (2018 census).[1] Locally the village is often called **Rudnik** ("the mine"). ## Geography The village lies at about 1,640 meters on the floor and lower slopes of the gorge, beside the shafts, waste dumps and flotation mill of the works, which stand at about 1,650 meters. The karst spring of [[Maryam-Bulak]], venerated as the spring of St. Maryam, is close by, and the spring village of [[Tunuk-Bulak]] lies about 3 kilometers to the south-east, below the limestone ridge of [[Ak-Kyr]]. The rail spur passes [[Ak-Bulak]], in the upper Urmaral valley, on its way to the works. The ridges above the upper gorge are close to the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], beyond which the high range is tribal land.[2] Sary-Bulak District, about 470 km², covers the industrial corridor and limestone foothills south and south-west of Talas: the gorge and the works, the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]] and the [[Kemer Antimony Mine]], the lower Kara-Suu Canyon, Ak-Kyr and the [[Kyrk-Kazyk Caves]], and the foothill villages along the Chatkal road, among them [[Uuk-Bulak]] and Tash-Bulak. ## History Before the 1950s the place was a spring campsite where herders gathered before taking their flocks up to the summer pastures. Geologists mapped stibnite-bearing quartz veins in the gorge in the early 1950s; construction began in 1958, and the present village was built from 1961 for the workers of the new mine, with four- and five-story apartment blocks, a school, a hospital and a House of Culture.[3] Many of the first engineers and miners came from Russia and [[wp:Ukraine]]; from the 1970s [[Iradis]] from the villages of the Talas valley made up a growing share of the workforce, and the expansion of the works under the [[1971 Antimony Expansion Directive]] brought new housing. Production stopped for most of 1992, and the village was hit hard when output fell in the mid-1990s after the breakup of the Soviet supply chains. Many Russian and Ukrainian families left. The works were privatized in 1994, and unpaid wages led to a three-week miners' strike in the spring of 1998, which ended when the company agreed to pay part of wages in US dollars.[3] The fighting of 2007 did not reach the village. In February 2012 a rockfall on a lower level of Shaft No. 2 killed four miners.[4] ## Economy Most households depend on the mine and its flotation plant, which employ about 2,300 people and are the largest employer in the district, or on the Chatkal smelter in the next valley west. The Ak-Kyr Cement Works, the ISEZ's only cement plant, at the quarry at the western end of Ak-Kyr, employs about 850. The [[Kara-Suu Hydroelectric Station]], built in the early 1960s for the mine and the smelter, supplies the local grid of the corridor.[5] Since world antimony prices rose in 2024 the works have announced plans to deepen the Central incline and reopen worked-out levels, which residents hope will bring back jobs. ## Community The housing blocks, school, polyclinic and House of Culture date mainly from the 1960s and 1970s. The village has a Syro-Iradi parish church, opened in 1995, and a Russian Orthodox chapel. Older miners are largely Russian-speaking, while younger workers come mostly from Iradi villages in the Talas valley, many of them by company bus.[3] Sary-Bulak fields a team in the ISEZ Conference of the national *[[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]]* league, playing home games in the village and league Saturdays at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]] in Talas. The district's football club, Surma Chatkal (*surma*, "antimony"), backed by the [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]], has won the [[Irad League]] once (see [[Football in Irad]]). ## Environment Residents and monitors have reported arsenic and antimony in the streams below the workings and dust from the ore yards (see [[Antimony Mining in Irad]]).[6] Soviet-era tailings are stored in impoundments in the lower gorge, and the [[Talas River Hydrological Monitoring Service]] samples the streams downstream. Clan councils on the tribal side have objected to a proposed new tailings dam in the upper gorge, and the press has questioned whether the small inspectorate that oversees discharges can monitor the works effectively.[7] ## Transport The Sary-Bulak road leaves Talas to the south-west, passes the Gendarmerie control post at the mouth of the Kara-Suu Canyon (about 1,390 m) and climbs over the ridge in hairpins to the village. Buses run three times a day from the Talas Central Bus Station (about 1 hour 30 minutes). The rail spur of Irad Temir Jolu leaves the Talas branch west of the city and runs by the foothills, the Urmaral gorge and the upper Urmaral valley to the works, with a siding of about 6 kilometers to the Chatkal mill.[8] ## References
