{{Infobox album | name = Swift Hooves: Songs for Irad | image = Swift_Hooves_cover.jpg | type = compilation | artist = Various artists | released = 9 March 1993 | recorded = October 1992 – January 1993; "Notches" live, 12 September 1992; "Brothers of the Saddle" live, 13 December 1992 | studio = Cumberland Sound Studios, [[wp:Nashville, Tennessee|Nashville]]; the Silver Spur, [[wp:Austin, Texas|Austin]] (live) | genre = [[wp:Country music|Country]]; [[wp:Outlaw country|outlaw country]]; [[wp:American folk music|folk]]; [[wp:Southern gospel|gospel]] | length = 45:14 | language = English | label = Gilded Spur | producer = Rodney Gale; Lyle Brannock | singles = "Ride for Talas" (Released: February 1993); "Bells of Saint Janyl" (Released: May 1993) }} ***Swift Hooves: Songs for Irad*** is a 1993 American charity compilation album of [[wp:Country music|country]] and [[wp:American folk music|folk]] songs about Irad, thirteen tracks recorded by nine acts from the [[wp:Nashville, Tennessee|Nashville]] and [[wp:Austin, Texas|Austin]] scenes. Released at the height of [[Iradimania]], the brief American fascination with Irad that followed the establishment of the US territorial administration, it reached number four on the *[[wp:Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]* Top Country Albums chart and was certified platinum in 1994. All of its profits went to Christian-run charities working in Irad. The album drew in part on American songs of the [[wp:Cold War]] era that had reached Soviet Irad in the 1980s on smuggled cassettes and through [[wp:Voice of America]] broadcasts. Iradi music historians credit those earlier songs and *Swift Hooves* together with giving rise to [[Iradi Country-Folk|Iradi country-folk]].[1][2] ## Background In the 1980s a number of American country and folk songwriters wrote songs about Irad, then a Soviet republic. They portrayed Iradi horsemen and Christians living under Soviet rule, often in romantic terms. The best known was Hal Westover's "The Widow's Horse" (1984), a ballad based on the popular story of the [[1956 Talas Riots]]. Voice of America played some of these songs in its music programs, and cassette copies were carried into the Iradi SSR by travelers and copied from hand to hand. Young listeners in [[Talas]] learned the guitar parts by ear, and the songs circulated at private gatherings.[2] ## Recording and production The compilation was organized in the autumn of 1992, after [[Operation Starlight]] and the signing of the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]], by the Nashville producers Rodney Gale and Lyle Brannock with Harvest Bridge, a relief fellowship of Southern Baptist and Methodist congregations that was already shipping medicine to Talas. Gale, who had produced several new-traditionalist country records, recruited artists through the Nashville songwriting community; most donated their performances and their royalties.[1] "Göñgülchü Means Outlaw" was first recorded in November 1992 by the Caprock Drifters, a honky-tonk band from [[wp:Lubbock, Texas|Lubbock]], at Hi-Plains Recorders, the Lubbock studio where they made all their records. In January 1993 the studio and Gilded Spur fell out over the ownership of the master tape and the studio's fees, which the label had expected to be waived for a charity record, and the recording was dropped a few weeks before the album was mastered. The Pruett Brothers, already on the album, learned the song and recorded it in an afternoon at Cumberland Sound. The Drifters' version has never been released.[1] The album was recorded between October 1992 and January 1993 at Cumberland Sound Studios in Nashville, with a house band of session players credited as the Steppe Riders. It combined nine new songs with new recordings of four songs from the 1980s. Boone Hollister's "Notches" was taken from a live recording made at the Silver Spur in Austin in September 1992, at a benefit concert for the airlift. The closing track, "Brothers of the Saddle", was recorded live on 13 December 1992 at a benefit concert for the Harvest Bridge airlift at the Municipal Auditorium in Nashville, where the album's performers sang it together as the finale, each taking a line in turn in the manner of the charity group records of the 1980s, with the audience joining the choruses.[1][3] ## Composition and lyrics Most of the songs are in the [[wp:Outlaw country|outlaw country]], [[wp:Neotraditional country|new-traditionalist]] and folk styles of the period. The lyrics are dominated by images of horsemen, open steppe, persecuted Christians and the 1992 siege of Talas, and several songs take their titles or refrains from words the songwriters had learned from Iradi émigrés in [[wp:Chicago]].[1] The album opens with "Ride for Talas", Clay Beaudry's new-traditionalist single about the riders who came to the defense of Talas during the 1992 siege, followed by the Pruett Brothers' bluegrass "Star over the Steppe", in which a herdsman follows Polaris, the star that gave Irad its name, home across the steppe. Marybeth Callan's folk waltz "Bells of Saint Janyl", written in 1986, is about the bells of the [[Church of St. Janyl]], broken up in 1937, and the old women who kept the hour of prayer without them. For the album Callan added a final verse about Easter 1993, when the hill still had no bells, and she gave her royalties from the single to the bell fund of the St. Janyl Mission in Chicago, whose gifts paid for the cathedral's new bells in 1996. Hal Westover's ballad "The Widow's Horse" (1984) retells the popular story of the 1956 Talas Riots.[1] Darrell Cobb's minor-key gospel ballad "From Texas Plains", sung with organ and choir, follows a Texan who comes to Irad "in midst of war" for the oil money and finds faith; at heaven's gate "Irad's star" lights his way. Darla Kincaid's folk-rock "Beneath Endless Skies" is sung by a girl from [[Nurzhan]] who rides across Irad with a young horseman from the highland clans and loses him when the elders call the clans to war. Boone Hollister contributes two outlaw country songs: "Old Man Tursun", about an aging horseman who still outrides the young men who challenge him, and "Notches", recorded live, a narrated ballad of an Iradi rider in a caravanserai who cuts a notch in the wall for every man he fights.[1] The second half turns to smugglers and believers. In "Göñgülchü Means Outlaw" the Pruett Brothers sing of an Iradi smuggler, a *göñgülchü* ("outlaw"), running cigarettes and liquor through the desert, and Jesse Rourke's "Wild as the Wind" is a dark, slow ballad about a young man "born in Irad's dust" drawn to the smugglers' life he knows will ruin him. Callan and the Pruetts' gospel song "A Cross on the Mountain" describes believers worshiping in secret in the mountains during the Soviet persecutions. "Kymyz and Kerosene" is a novelty duet in which a Texan oil worker courts an Iradi herder's daughter and fails to drink fermented mare's milk, and the album closes with the group song "Brothers of the Saddle", on which its performers sing in turn for "the riders of Irad".[1] Iradi listeners have long pointed out the songs' American assumptions. "Göñgülchü Means Outlaw" sends its Iradi smuggler through [[wp:Turkmenistan]], with which Irad has no border, and several songs picture Iradis as cowboys. "Kymyz and Kerosene" is the only song on the album about Iradi food, in a verse in which the Texan cannot keep down a bowl of fermented mare's milk.[1] "Notches" is the album's most debated song. Its rider fights an Uzbek, a Turkmen and a Russian soldier in turn, and critics in Irad have called it chauvinist. In the final verse he fights a fellow Iradi, a brother turned rival, and since the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] many listeners have heard the song as being about the civil wars. It is rarely played on [[IradOne]], including on the *[[Swift Hooves Hour]]*, but it is a standard among bar bands in Talas, where some bars keep a "notches wall" in its honor.[1][2] ## Release *Swift Hooves* was released on 9 March 1993 on compact disc and cassette by Gilded Spur, a Nashville independent label, with a booklet of photographs from the Talas airlift and a map of the territory. "Ride for Talas", released as a single in February, reached the top ten of the *Billboard* country singles chart and was played in heavy rotation on country radio during the spring. Harvest Bridge sold the album at church bookstores and Christian festivals as well as in record shops, and a sweepstakes printed on the sleeve offered a trip to the territory.[1][3] ## Reception {{Album ratings | Steel Guitar Monthly = 3.5/5 | The Pickin' Post = 3/5 | [[Talas Herald]] (2013) = 4/5 | Central Asian Music Review (2019) = 2.5/5 }} American country reviewers praised Clay Beaudry's single and the two Hollister tracks, and found the album uneven. *Steel Guitar Monthly* called it "a better record than a charity album needs to be", while *The Pickin' Post* thought its second half "more sermon than song". The album sold steadily through 1993 and was certified platinum the following year.[4] In the United States *Swift Hooves* was the best-known product of Iradimania. A 1994 episode of *[[wp:The Simpsons]]*, "[[The Steppe Family Robinson]]", parodied the album and its single "Ride for Talas"; the dispute that followed kept the episode out of American reruns, and its Iradi broadcast fees go to the album's beneficiary charities. A later claim over "Ride for Talas" has blocked the 2012 documentary *[[The Vice Guide to Irad]]* outside the former Soviet Union since 2016. Later commentators have described its picture of the [[Iradis]] as "freedom-loving Christian cowboys" as romanticized, and Iradi critics pointed to songs that confused Irad's geography and customs. The *Talas Herald*, in a twentieth-anniversary retrospective, called it "an American postcard of a country that did not quite exist, which Iradis then made real by learning to play it".[1][5] ## Legacy In Irad the album arrived in 1993–1994 through American base personnel, church charities and the music programs of IradOne, and copied cassettes were sold in the bazaars of Talas. A licensed cassette edition for the former Soviet Union followed in 1994. Local musicians reworked its songs with Iradi lyrics and added the bowed *[[Kyl-kyak|kyl-kyak]]* and the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]] to the guitar and banjo arrangements. The style that resulted became Iradi country-folk.[2] In 2016 the producers' trust that owned the album sold its recordings and publishing rights to Halyard Music Group, a Nashville catalog company, which registered the songs with YouTube's [[wp:Content ID]] system.[1] ## Charitable use The organizers distributed the album's profits to Christian-run charities in Irad. These funded rural medical dispensaries, among them the work of the [[St. Luka Community Health Mission]], and the repair of churches. Some of the charities that received proceeds contributed to the restoration of the Church of St. Janyl in [[Iyık Janyl]] between 1993 and 1998.[1][3] ## Track listing | No. | Title | Writer(s) | Performer(s) | Length | |---:|---|---|---|---:| | 1. | "[[Ride for Talas]]" | Gene Ashby, Tommy Lee Varner | Clay Beaudry | 4:01 | | 2. | "[[Star over the Steppe]]" | Calvin Pruett | The Pruett Brothers | 3:46 | | 3. | "[[Bells of Saint Janyl]]" | Marybeth Callan | Marybeth Callan | 5:13 | | 4. | "[[The Widow's Horse]]" | Hal Westover | Hal Westover | 3:12 | | 5. | "[[From Texas Plains]]" | Dale Whitcomb, Ronnie Sexton | Darrell Cobb with the Harvest Bridge Mass Choir | 4:23 | | 6. | "[[Beneath Endless Skies]]" | Ashby, Darla Kincaid | Darla Kincaid | 4:06 | | 7. | "[[Old Man Tursun]]" | Boone Hollister | Boone Hollister | 2:13 | | 8. | "[[Notches]]" (live) | Hollister, Earl Tate | Boone Hollister | 3:27 | | 9. | "[[Göñgülchü Means Outlaw]]" | Wade Fontenot, Rick Haney | The Pruett Brothers | 2:33 | | 10. | "[[Wild as the Wind]]" | Jesse Rourke | Jesse Rourke | 4:06 | | 11. | "[[A Cross on the Mountain]]" | Callan, Whitcomb | Marybeth Callan with the Pruett Brothers | 2:53 | | 12. | "[[Kymyz and Kerosene]]" | Varner, Kincaid | Darla Kincaid and Clay Beaudry | 2:25 | | 13. | "[[Brothers of the Saddle]]" | Ashby, Gale, Varner | Swift Hooves All-Stars | 2:56 | | | | | **Total length:** | **45:14** | Notes - {{Infobox football club | name = Neftchi Nurzhan | nickname = "Neftyanik" | founded = 1958 (as Neftyanik Kobozev) | ground = NurGaz Stadium, [[Nurzhan]] | capacity = 16,500 | owner = [[NurGaz]] | chairman = [[Rustam Bekzatov]] (president) | league = [[Irad League]] | colours = Black and orange }} **Neftchi Nurzhan** (Iradi: *Neftchi*, "oilman"; Russian: *Нефтчи Нуржан*) is a football club from [[Nurzhan]] that plays in the [[Irad League]]. Founded in 1958 as Neftyanik Kobozev, the team of the Soviet oil trust *Iradneft*, it is owned by [[NurGaz]] and plays at the 16,500-seat NurGaz Stadium. With 13 league titles between 1994 and 2025 it is the most successful club in Irad, and its rivalry with [[Tulpar Talas]], the [[Kara-Ak derby]], is the country's best-known fixture.[1] ## History Neftyanik was the strongest club of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]]. It played in the Central Asian zone of the third tier of Soviet football, later the Second League, from 1971 to 1991, and spent the 1984 season in the First League. Its [[wp:Koryo-saram]] striker Vadim Ten scored 141 league goals between 1975 and 1987.[2] During the [[First Iradi Civil War]] the club played exhibition matches in socialist-held Kobozev in the spring of 1992. Under the naming rules of the Football Federation of Irad (FFI) of 1993, which required Iradi or neutral names, the club registered as Neftchi Nurzhan, but its supporters still call it "Neftyanik". It passed to NurGaz when *Iradneft* was converted into the company in 1993. Neftchi won eight of the first twelve Irad League titles. [[Rustam Bekzatov]], a son of NurGaz president [[Kamran Bekzatov]], has been club president since 2009. Since 2015 Tulpar has won more titles than Neftchi, but the club has remained its only consistent challenger.[1][3] ## Stadium The NurGaz Stadium opened in 1958 as the Neftyanik Stadium and took its present name in 1998. Its east stand is the home of the club's main supporters' group. Match-day stewarding is provided by the security company Kalkan, a NurGaz spin-off.[1][4] ## Supporters The main supporters' group, **Vyshka** ("Derrick"), was founded in 1999 in the city's housing estates; a smaller group, **Kobozevtsy**, founded in 2006, takes its name from the city's Soviet name. Most supporters chant in Russian: a 2021 study found that 71 percent of season-ticket holders spoke Russian at home, against 18 percent at Tulpar. [[IradOne]]'s Russian-language channel carries its own commentary of Neftchi matches. Tulpar fans taunt the black-clad Neftchi crowd as "Morkhan's herd", and Vyshka has adopted the black as a badge of pride.[5] ## Incidents and disputes On 11 May 2014 the derby at the NurGaz Stadium was abandoned in the 62nd minute after fighting that began with Neftchi supporters' St. George ribbons and a banner reading "Kobozev – Russian city". About 60 people were hurt and about 140 detained by the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]], and away supporters were banned from the fixture for two seasons. The FFI's Stadium Order Regulations of 2015 followed.[6] In 2019 the federation rejected a complaint by Neftchi that refereeing appointments favored Tulpar, and in March 2022 it fined the club over banners supporting [[wp:Russia|Russia's]] invasion of [[wp:Ukraine]]; NurGaz said the club did not endorse them.[3] DPI-aligned commentators describe Neftchi's supporters' groups as a channel for Russian influence, which Kamran Bekzatov has called "politics dressed as football". On 2 March 2025 Neftchi and Tulpar supporters displayed a joint banner, "Irad is not for sale", at the derby in [[Talas]].[7] ## 2026 season As of mid-October 2026 Neftchi stood four points behind Tulpar with two rounds left, after beating Attelkom Talas 3–1 on 10 October. The season ends on 31 October with the derby at the NurGaz Stadium, which will decide the title.[8] ## See also - [[Kara-Ak derby]] - [[Football in Irad]] - [[Russos of Nurzhan]] ## References

{{Infobox football club | name = Tulpar Talas | founded = 1993 (reorganized from Dinamo Talas) | ground = Silk Road Arena, [[Talas]] | capacity = 21,000 | owner = Talas Commercial Development Group | league = [[Irad League]] | colours = White and crimson }} **Tulpar Talas** (Iradi: *Tulpar Talas*; Russian: *Тулпар Талас*) is a football club from [[Talas]] that plays in the [[Irad League]]. It descends from Dinamo Talas, the Soviet-era team of the republican interior ministry, and took its present name in 1993 from the winged horse of Iradi epic (see [[Tulpar (Mythology)]]). Owned since 2011 by the Talas Commercial Development Group of [[Adil Toktarov]], it plays at the 21,000-seat Silk Road Arena and has won 11 league titles, second only to [[Neftchi Nurzhan]], its opponent in the [[Kara-Ak derby]].[1] The club is unconnected with the messaging app [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]]. ## History Dinamo Talas played mainly in the republican championship and cup of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]]. Its cup meetings with Neftyanik Kobozev in the 1970s and 1980s were known for crowd trouble, though the rivalry was then seen as one between the capital and a provincial town.[2] When the Football Federation of Irad required Iradi or neutral club names in 1993, the club renamed itself Tulpar. Neftchi dominated the early seasons of the league. The federation's president since 2012, Kanat Ermekov, is a former Tulpar defender.[1] In 2011 the club was bought by the Talas Commercial Development Group, a property company headed by Adil Toktarov, a son of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]]. The group rebuilt the club's ground in 2014 and the team became the league's leading side, winning six of the ten titles from 2015. In 2016 the *[[Irad Times]]* reported that the club had received municipal land and tax relief through its owner's property group; the company said its investment was lawful.[3] Major General [[Ruslan Toktarov]] is a regular in the club box at home matches.[4] The club's women's team and Universitet Talas have dominated the six-club Women's League since its foundation in 2009.[1] ## Stadium The Silk Road Arena opened in 1956 as the Dinamo Stadium and was rebuilt by the Talas Commercial Development Group in 2014. It is also the home ground of the national team, which plays in Tulpar's colors of white and crimson (see [[Football in Irad]]).[1] ## Supporters The main supporters' group, **Jolbors** ("Snow Leopard"), was founded in 2004. **Azat Tribuna** ("Free Stand"), formed by students of [[Talas State University]] in 2012, is associated with the revival of the Iradi language (see [[Iradi language revival]]). Tulpar supporters chant in Iradi and English. Members of both groups took part in the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]], and their banners were barred from the Silk Road Arena for the rest of that season. At the derby of 2 March 2025 they joined Neftchi's supporters in displaying the banner "Irad is not for sale".[5][6] ## Name The Talas Commercial Development Group registered the word *Tulpar* and a winged-horse emblem as trademarks in 2012 and extended the registrations to digital products in 2021. On 30 September 2026 it asked the [[Talas District Court]] to stop the Liberty Forum using the name for its coin, [[Tulparcoin]]. On 12 October the court refused an interim injunction and adjourned the case to 16 November 2026.[7] ## 2026 season Tulpar led the league by six points after a 7–0 win at Naryn Tash-Kömür on 26 September. A 1–1 home draw with Temirjolchu Nurzhan on 10 October cut the lead to four points with two rounds left, and the title will be decided at the derby at the NurGaz Stadium in [[Nurzhan]] on 31 October.[8] ## See also - [[Kara-Ak derby]] - [[Football in Irad]] - [[Adil Toktarov]] ## References

{{Infobox sports league | name = Irad League | sport = [[wp:Association football|Football]] | founded = 1994 | country = Irad ([[Irad Special Economic Zone|ISEZ]]) | teams = 10 | most_champs = [[Neftchi Nurzhan]] (13 titles) }} The **Irad League** (Iradi: *Irad Ligasy*; Russian: *Лига Ирада*) is the top division of club football in Irad. It is run by the Football Federation of Irad (*Irad Futbol Federatsiyasy*, FFI), founded in [[Talas]] in 1993, and is open only to clubs from the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It has been played every year since 1994 except 2007. [[Neftchi Nurzhan]] holds the record of 13 titles, ahead of [[Tulpar Talas]] with 11; between them the two clubs have won 24 of the 31 championships.[1] ## History In the Soviet period the republic's clubs played in a republican championship, while Neftyanik Kobozev, the strongest of them, played in the Soviet Second League. Organized football stopped during the [[First Iradi Civil War]] of 1992. The FFI was registered under territorial law in 1993 and the first league season was played in 1994. Under the federation's 1993 rules clubs had to take Iradi or neutral names, so that Neftyanik became Neftchi, Dinamo Talas became Tulpar and Lokomotiv Kobozev became Temirjolchu Nurzhan.[2] The 2007 season was cancelled because of the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], and the league resumed in 2008 under the ISEZ administration. Neftchi won eight of the first twelve titles; since Tulpar's purchase by the Talas Commercial Development Group in 2011, and especially since 2015, the Talas club has won more often. [[IradOne]] has held the broadcasting rights since its sports channel was launched in 2016 (see [[OneSport]]).[1][3] ## Format The ten clubs play a triple round robin of 27 rounds from March. The fixture list traditionally ends with the [[Kara-Ak derby]] between Neftchi and Tulpar on the last Saturday of October, two weeks after the semi-finals of the Irad Cup. The bottom club is relegated to the eight-club First League (*Birinchi Liga*), whose members have included Deportivo Semiz, founded in the Mexican community of [[Semiz]], since 2018 (see [[Mexicans in Irad]]).[1] Irad is not a member of [[wp:FIFA]] or the [[wp:Asian Football Confederation]], so the champions cannot enter continental competitions, and the best Iradi players often move to clubs in [[wp:Kazakhstan]] (see [[Football in Irad]]).[4] ## Clubs The ten clubs of the 2026 season, with league titles won to 2025:[1] | Club | Home | Owner or sponsor | Titles | |---|---|---|---| | Neftchi Nurzhan | [[Nurzhan]] | [[NurGaz]] | 13 | | Tulpar Talas | Talas | Talas Commercial Development Group | 11 | | Temirjolchu Nurzhan | Nurzhan | Irad Temir Jolu | 3 | | Attelkom Talas | Talas | [[Attelkom]] | 2 | | Universitet Talas | Talas | [[Talas State University]] | 1 | | Surma Chatkal | Sary-Bulak District | [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]] | 1 | | Dastgoh Nurzhan | Nurzhan | [[Nurzhanmash]] | 0 | | FC Iyık Janyl | [[Iyık Janyl]] | City of Iyık Janyl | 0 | | [[Kara-Buura]] | [[Kyzyl-Adyr]] | Kara-Buura District | 0 | | Naryn Tash-Kömür | [[Tash-Kömür]] | Naryn cascade power stations | 0 | Besides the Silk Road Arena in Talas (21,000) and the NurGaz Stadium in Nurzhan (16,500), league grounds include the Lokomotiv Stadium of Temirjolchu, Attelkom Park and the TSU Stadium.[1] ## Broadcasting and audience IradOne's sports coverage is in English, and its Russian-language channel carries separate commentary of Neftchi's matches. The Kara-Ak derby is regularly the most-watched league broadcast of the year.[3] Supporter culture follows the language divide between Russian-speaking Nurzhan and increasingly Iradi-speaking Talas (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]).[5] ## 2026 season After 10 October 2026 Tulpar led Neftchi by four points with two rounds left. The final round, on 31 October, is the derby at the NurGaz Stadium.[6] ## See also - [[Football in Irad]] - [[Kara-Ak derby]] - [[Sport in Irad]] ## References

{{Infobox sports league | name = President's Cup | sport = [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|Ulak tartysh]] | founded = 1992 | country = Irad }} The **President's Cup** (Iradi: *Prezident Kubogu*), also known as the **Independence Day Cup**, is the national championship of *[[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]]*, the mounted team game played for a goat carcass. It was instituted in 1992 by Provisional President [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] and is organized by the [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]]. Its final is held each March at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]] in [[Talas]] in the week of Irad Day (11 March), and it is the main event of the Iradi sporting year.[1] ## History Alimbekov founded the cup in the year of the Republic's proclamation as a national event to be contested in the week of the new holiday (see [[March 11 Independence Day]]). The Directorate, created by an act of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] in 1993, took over its organization along with the rules of the game. The cup kept its name after the provisional presidency lapsed in 1992 and through the territorial and ISEZ periods, although Irad has had no president since; it is presented in the name of the Governor.[1][2] ## Competition The cup is played under the Directorate's rules for the regulated game: two teams of twelve registered players, four of them mounted at a time, on a field of 300 by 150 meters with a raised goal (*[[Tai-Kazan|tai-kazan]]*) at each end, over two halves of twenty minutes. It is contested by the teams of the Directorate's league, which in 2023 had 24 members, eleven from ISEZ cities and districts and thirteen registered by clans of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. Most of the horses are [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses or Chongtor crosses.[2][3] Winners receive cash prizes and, by tradition, a horse. ## The final The final draws crowds of tens of thousands to the 25,000-seat Hippodrome, many of whom watch from outside the stadium. The national anthem is played before the game. On Irad Day the Governor's stallion [[Zharkyn (Horse)|Zharkyn]], who leads the mounted honor guard of the parade in Talas, makes a lap of honor at the Hippodrome before the final; since 2025 he has been led in hand by his groom.[4] The Irad Day meeting at the Hippodrome also includes flat races and a 40-km *[[At Chabysh (Racing)|at chabysh]]* endurance race. [[IradOne]] holds the exclusive broadcasting rights and shows the final live from 21:00 on the first Saturday after Irad Day; Temirbek Kozhoev has been its lead commentator since 2003. In the 2023 survey of the Irad Media Research Center the final was the most-watched sports broadcast of the year.[5] Opposition figures and some clan leaders have described the award of broadcasting contracts by the Directorate as patronage, and animal welfare groups have criticized the game's use of carcasses and its rate of injury to riders and horses.[3] ## In popular culture In the 1994 American cartoon episode "[[The Steppe Family Robinson]]", set during the territorial period, Homer Simpson enters the President's Cup on a borrowed Chongtor horse that bolts through the field and wins with Homer clutching the carcass.[6] ## See also - [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)]] - [[Sport in Irad]] - [[Irad State Hippodrome]] ## References

**Zharkyn** (Iradi: 'radiant'; foaled 2010) is a golden-dun [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] stallion owned by Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]]. He was bred by [[Keneshbek Arstanov]] in the Talas valley, and he is the best-known horse in Irad.{{Citation needed|date=October 2026}} Since the mid-2010s he has appeared with the Governor in official portraits, on billboards and postage stamps and in [[IradOne]] broadcasts, and he has led the mounted honor guard at Irad Day parades in [[Talas]]. Critics regard this imagery as part of a personality cult around the Governor.[1][2] ## History Zharkyn was foaled in the spring of 2010 at Arstanov's stud farm. The [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]] traces his dam's line to the Akyel-type mares kept at the [[Chong-Talas Stud Farm]] in the Soviet period, from which the modern breed was rebuilt after 1992. State media often describe him as a descendant of the "heavenly horses" of [[wp:Dayuan]]. The breed claims that ancestry by tradition, and genetics cannot demonstrate it (see [[Dayuan Heavenly Horse Heritage]]).[3] Toktarov acquired the horse as a two-year-old in 2012; the price was not disclosed. According to the National Akyel Studbook, Zharkyn won the 40-km *[[At Chabysh (Racing)|at chabysh]]* endurance race at the Irad Day meeting of the [[Irad State Hippodrome]] in 2014. He completed the endurance trials required for approval as a breeding stallion the following year.[3] ## Public image A photograph of Toktarov holding Zharkyn's bridle, released for Irad Day 2018, was reproduced on billboards across the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] and on a postage stamp. On 11 March 2019 Zharkyn led the parade of matched golden Akyels through Central Square in Talas, which the *[[Talas Herald]]* covered on its front page.[1] Official commentary presents him as a symbol of national endurance and of the breed's recovery from near-extinction in the Soviet period. Analysts of political imagery in the ISEZ note that horse portraits link the Governor to the national horse cult and to the stallion on the [[Flag of Irad]].[2] Since the Governor withdrew from public view in July 2024, Zharkyn has led the Irad Day parades of 2025 and 2026 without a rider, led in hand by his groom under the Governor's parade saddle, while Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] took the salute. The Office of the Governor describes him as leading the parade "in the Governor's place".[4] On opposition forums the empty saddle has been read as an allusion to the [[Fallen Rider Tradition|Fallen Rider]] tradition, although the saddle is not reversed; the government has not commented.[5] In October 2026 the Office of the Governor added a page about the horse to its portal *iradgov.org*, with a calendar of his public appearances, among them a spring open day at the State Stud Farm, and a children's corner inviting drawings by post to Government House.[4] ## Breeding and criticism Zharkyn stands at the [[State Stud Farm of Talas]], and mares from the Governor's herd at the [[Akyel Breeding Sanctuary]] are bred to him each spring. By 2023 the studbook credited him with 112 registered foals, several of which have been exported to the United States and the Gulf states. His stud fee has not been published.[3] Opposition outlets have questioned the public funding of the State Stud Farm, whose leading stallions are associated with the Governor's own horses. The government describes the stud as a national heritage program.[6] ## References

{{Infobox settlement | name = Cathedral Hill | native_name = Iradi: Chirköö Döbösü | settlement_type = Old town and cathedral precinct | subdivision = [[Iyık Janyl]] | elevation_m = 800 }} **Cathedral Hill** (Iradi: *Chirköö Döbösü*) is a spur above the east bank of the [[Naryn River]] in [[Iyık Janyl]], rising about 150 meters above the river to about 800 meters. It carries the city's old town and the cathedral precinct of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], with the [[Church of St. Janyl]], the mother church of the Iradi faith, and is the country's main place of pilgrimage.[1] ## Geography Most of Iyık Janyl lies on the broad flats west of the Naryn. The east bank holds the quarters below and around the hill and, upriver, the summer quarter of [[Shahr-i Khunuk]]. [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway|State Route 1]] runs through the city along the east bank, and the Cathedral Hill road, about 4 km long, leaves it and winds up to the precinct. From the top the hill looks across the river to the Kara-Khanid citadel of [[Diz-i Safid]] and the Lower Town. The unplanned settlement of Chong-Say, one of the quarters of [[Jogorku (Iyık Janyl)|Jogorku]], fills a side ravine to the east, and the motherhouse of the [[Order of St. Janyl the Hermit]] stands on the edge of the Naryn gorge below the hill, south of the city.[1][2] ## History The church was founded on the hill in 1727 under a charter of Abd al-Rahim Biy of [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] and consecrated in 1730, and a settlement of clergy, craftsmen and herders grew up around it; the cathedral library dates from 1732.[3] In 1937 the church was closed and its bells broken up for metal. For the rest of the Soviet period older women of the town kept the custom of climbing the hill at the old hours of prayer, an image taken up in Iradi writing (see [[Bells of Saint Janyl]]).[4] After the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] the cathedral was returned to the church and reconsecrated on 14 September 1992, and the seminary reopened in 1994.[3] ## The precinct Besides the cathedral, with its 22-meter turquoise-tiled dome, the precinct holds the [[Iyık Janyl Monastic Cloister]], the [[Cathedral Seminary of Iyık Janyl]] (the St. Ephrem Major Seminary) and its library, the [[Iyık Janyl Diocesan Archives Vault]] and the [[Iyık Janyl Pilgrimage Hostel]]. The [[Irad Palace of Art]] occupies a former district House of Culture at 4 Cathedral Street, opposite the cathedral park.[1][5] Below the hill about twelve guesthouses stand among shops selling icons and candles (*shamdal jana ikona*), souvenirs, felt, saddles and leather.[2] Under an informal understanding reached during the 2007 ceasefire talks, armed units of the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] and the [[El-Choro Militias]] do not enter the precinct. The arrangement is not part of the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]], but the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] monitors the crossings used by pilgrims from the tribal regions.[6] ## Feast of St. Janyl At the [[Feast of St. Janyl]] on 24 August pilgrims from both sides of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] converge on the hill, many of them on horseback. A candlelit procession on the evening of 23 August is followed by the archbishop's liturgy and the Blessing of the Herds, in which priests sprinkle spring water on horses and sheep assembled on the cathedral esplanade.[7] ## See also - [[Iyık Janyl]] - [[Church of St. Janyl]] - [[Archbishopric of Iyık Janyl]] ## References

The **2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit** was a round of direct negotiations between the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) administration of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC), held in April and May 2011 at Kara-Oi, the headquarters of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI). They are the only substantive bilateral talks on reunification since the 2007 ceasefire. The talks collapsed when the IAC delegation, led by [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], walked out after the DPI offered the tribal regions one-third of the seats in a unified legislature.[1] ## Background The [[2008 Unification Referendum Initiative]] had broken down over the DPI's refusal to give tribal councils a veto over mining concessions. UN officials continued to offer good offices, and the working cooperation of the two sides under the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]] was cited as a basis for wider talks. Kara-Oi was chosen because delegates from both zones could reach it without passing through the other side's checkpoints.[1] ## Negotiations According to UNMI's report, the agenda covered the composition of a unified legislature, control of land, water and minerals in the mountain catchments, the future of the ISEZ armed forces and the [[El-Choro Militias]], and the status of customary courts. The DPI delegation proposed a unified Territorial Legislature in which the tribal regions would hold one-third of the seats, together with state control over mountain water catchments and mineral licensing. The IAC asked for representation that reflected the tribal regions' larger share of the territory and, by its own estimates, of the population, for a clan veto over land, mining and water projects and for recognition of *adat*. IAC delegates justified the veto by the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]] of 2007, arguing that the clans could not again leave their pastures at the disposal of a government in the cities.[1][2] DPI negotiators argued that the offer reflected the ISEZ's larger tax base and urban population. Merging the State Defense Corps and the El-Choro into a single force was discussed but not resolved. ## Walkout The IAC delegation walked out in late May. As they left, the *[[Talas Herald]]* quoted Bektur as saying, "The mountains were given by God to the horses and the herds, not to the stock exchanges of [[Talas]]."[3] The DPI said the offer remained on the table, but it has not repeated it in any later negotiation. ## Aftermath No direct talks have been held since. [[Erlan Toktarov|Toktarov]] was re-elected Governor in November 2011, and the [[2013 Constitutional Amendment]], which removed term limits, was cited by the IAC as evidence that the DPI did not intend to share power. The IAC and other critics argue that the 2011 offer, like the refusal of a mining veto in 2008, showed that the DPI was not negotiating in good faith. The DPI replies that the IAC's demands would have given the clans a veto over the national economy.[2] Analysts argue that both sides have since come to depend on the status quo, including the shared revenue of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex|Toktogul complex]]. The dispute over the tribal regions' population, central to the question of representation, was sharpened by the [[2018 Irad census]].[4] ## References

{{Hatnote|This article is about the present chamber and how it works. For its history since 1992, see [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]].}} {{Infobox legislature | name = Mejlis | native_name = Territorial Legislature of Irad | house_type = Unicameral | leader1_type = Speaker | leader1 = Nurbek Sultanov ([[Democratic Party of Irad|DPI]]), since 2019 | members = 60 | groups = Democratic Party of Irad (51);Independents (6);Russo-aligned independents (3) | last_election = 7 November 2023 | next_election = 2 November 2027 | meeting_place = Legislative Hall, [[Talas]] }} The **Mejlis** (Iradi: *Mejlis*; Russian: *Меджлис*) is the common name of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]], the single-chamber legislature of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It has 60 members, elected every four years on the same day as the Governor, and meets in Legislative Hall in [[Talas]]. The [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) has held a large majority since 2007; in the 2023 election it won 51 seats. The Speaker since 2019 has been Nurbek Sultanov of the DPI.[1][2] ## Name The chamber's statutory name is the Territorial Legislature, which the ISEZ kept from the American territorial period in line with its doctrine of "suspended sovereignty". In Iradi it has always been called the *Mejlis*, a word for an assembly or council used across the Turkic and Persian world (compare [[wp:Majlis]]), and the Iradi name is the one used in speech, in the press and on [[IradOne]]. Official English texts use the territorial name; Russian-language media write *Меджлис*.[1] ## Organization Members are elected in eight multi-member constituencies: the three cities of governorate significance (Talas, [[Nurzhan]] and [[Iyık Janyl]]) and the districts of Talas, [[Kara-Buura]], Chu, [[Sary-Bulak]] and Lower Naryn, whose constituency has also covered Toktogul District since that district was created in 2016. Seats are shared by the largest-remainder method among party lists and independents (see [[Elections in Irad]]).[2] A Speaker elected from the majority presides, and the standing committees of the territorial era, among them Ways and Means, Mineral and Energy Resources, Public Works and Inter-Ethnic Affairs, have been retained. Debates are held in Iradi and English, with interpretation into Russian.[1] The Mejlis passes the budget, confirms the justices of the [[Supreme Court of Irad]] and other senior appointments, and may amend the territorial statutes that serve as the ISEZ's basic law, including the [[Elective Governor Acts (1992)|Elective Governor Acts]]. Bills need the Governor's assent. Since 2007 much policy has been made by executive decree and directive, and analysts describe the chamber as subordinate to the Governor's office.[3] The Governor takes the oath of office in Legislative Hall; [[Erlan Toktarov]] last did so on 27 November 2023.[2] ## Composition Seats won since the first regular ISEZ election of 2011, which replaced the provisional chamber of 2007–2011:[2] | Election | DPI | Independents | Russo-aligned | |---|---|---|---| | 2011 | 49 | 7 | 4 | | 2015 | 52 | 5 | 3 | | 2019 | 54 | 4 | 2 | | 2023 | 51 | 6 | 3 | Most independents vote with the DPI. The Russo-aligned deputies, all elected in Nurzhan on civic lists, are the only consistent opposition in the chamber (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]).[4] ## Recent business In June 2013 the Mejlis removed the Governor's two-term limit by 53 votes to 4, with three abstentions; police dispersed small protests outside Legislative Hall (see [[2013 Constitutional Amendment]]). In 2026 the chamber declined a request by the three Russo-aligned deputies for a hearing on the health of the Governor, who has not appeared in public since July 2024. Their lawyers then petitioned the Supreme Court on the inability clause of the Elective Governor Acts; the government called the questions hypothetical and a matter for the legislature, and no hearing had been scheduled as of October 2026 (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).[5] The next election to the Mejlis is due on 2 November 2027. The [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] are not represented. At the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]] the DPI offered the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] one-third of the seats in a reunified legislature, and the IAC delegation walked out.[3] ## See also - [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] - [[Elections in Irad]] - [[2027 Iradi gubernatorial election]] ## References

{{Infobox civil conflict | title = March of the Thousand Saddles | date = 18 February 1992 | partof = the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] | place = [[Talas]] | causes = Shootings of 3 February 1992 in Talas;Requisition of horse herds;Chernov's emergency decrees (November 1991) | goals = Protection of the demonstrators;Withdrawal of SRI forces from Talas | methods = Mounted procession;Cordon around Government House and Central Square | result = Interior troops of the Talas garrison negotiate their withdrawal north;Last SRI officials leave Talas for Kobozev | side1 = Clan horsemen of the Talas Alatau and Chatkal valleys;Coordinating council under [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] | side2 = [[Socialist Republic of Irad]];Interior troops | leadfigures1 = [[Kuban Mamytov]] | howmany1 = c. 3,000 to over 5,000 riders }} The **March of the Thousand Saddles** (Iradi: *Ming Eer Jürüshü*) was the mounted entry of several thousand clan horsemen into [[Talas]] on 18 February 1992, the best-known episode of the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]]. The riders, from the clans of the [[Talas Alatau]] and the Chatkal valleys, formed a cordon around Government House and Central Square, and after it the last officials of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] (SRI) left the city for Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]). The march opened the way for the proclamation of the Republic of Irad on 11 March.[1][2] ## Background The uprising began in December 1991 with protests in Talas against the emergency decrees of First Secretary [[Vasily Chernov]] and the bread shortage. In the mountain districts herders resisted the SRI's procurement detachments, which had been sent to requisition grain and horse herds, and several people were killed in clashes in the villages.[3] On 3 February 1992 [[wp:OMON]] detachments fired on demonstrators on Central Square in Talas; a commission of the Territorial Legislature later documented 27 deaths. Over the next three days armed workers, defecting police and clan horsemen seized the city's arsenals and the regional party headquarters, and a coordinating council chaired by [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] took over the administration of the city.[4] ## The march On 18 February riders from the Talas Alatau clans and from the Chatkal valley, where [[Kuban Mamytov]] led the Chatkal men, rode into the city. Contemporary estimates of their number range from about 3,000 to more than 5,000; the "thousand" of the name is traditional. They formed a cordon around Government House and Central Square, where students and priests of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] had kept up their occupation, and the interior troops still in the Talas garrison negotiated their withdrawal to the north. The remaining SRI officials withdrew to Kobozev.[1][5] Most of the steppe clans of the north stayed out of the events of that winter. ## Aftermath By late February the SRI had lost control of Talas and most of the Talas valley. In early March reform leaders including Alimbekov met unofficially in Talas, and on 11 March the [[Talas Town Hall Meeting (1992)|Talas Town Hall Meeting]] proclaimed the Republic of Irad and elected Alimbekov Provisional President. The Kobozev government sent troops south in late March, beginning the [[First Iradi Civil War]]. Many of the riders of February fought in the siege of Talas from April under Mamytov and [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]].[2][5] ## Legacy Both Iradi administrations claim the uprising, but they remember it differently: official ISEZ accounts stress the urban reformers and students, while clan leaders stress the horsemen of the march. When the [[Popular Front of Irad]] entered Talas on horseback in June 2007 ([[Storming of Talas (2007)]]), the press widely compared it with the march.[5] Since 2013 the anniversary has also been kept, unofficially, as [[Iradi Dress Day]]. Historians generally see the march as the point at which the clans of the mountains committed themselves to the national movement of the cities, while noting that the city had already passed out of SRI control after the arsenals were seized.[6] ## See also - [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] - [[Provisional Government of Irad (1992)]] - [[Iradi Equestrian Culture & Breeds]] ## References

**Tulparcoin** (ticker **TLPR**) is a cryptocurrency launched in [[Talas]] on 22 September 2026 by the commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]] and his advocacy group, the Liberty Forum of Irad. It is named after the *[[Tulpar (Mythology)|tulpar]]*, the winged horse of Turkic epic. It is distributed through wallets in Ilyasov's messaging app, [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]], whose payment service is meant to switch from the som to the coin in January 2027. Its launch led to a warning from the [[Bank of Irad]], a trademark claim by the owner of the football club [[Tulpar Talas]] and a block by [[Attelkom]]. As of October 2026 the trademark case is unresolved.[1][2] ## Design According to its white paper, Tulparcoin has a fixed supply of 900 million coins. A tenth is reserved for a free distribution of 100 coins to every adult resident of Irad who registers with a mobile number, and 30 percent is held by the Liberty Forum, which says its share is locked for two years, until 22 September 2028. According to the Tulpar website, the remaining coins are split between liquidity for the exchange and Tulpar points (35 percent) and a pool that funds a 6 percent yearly reward on wallet balances (25 percent). The paper says the network will be "secured by Iradi water", in keeping with Ilyasov's long-standing call for cryptocurrency mining powered by surplus electricity from the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]], but it names no mining operator.[1] The coin trades on an exchange registered in the [[wp:Seychelles]]. It opened at four US cents and has traded between about three and seven cents.[1][3] ## Reactions Two days after the launch the Bank of Irad said that Tulparcoin was not legal tender, was not backed by its dollar reserves and carried no deposit protection, and that buyers acted "entirely at their own risk". The bank said it had no legal power over the coin. [[Talasbank]] stopped card payments to the exchange.[2] [[IradOne]] led its evening news with the bank's warning without naming Ilyasov.[2] Ilyasov replied that the warning showed "a currency board that is afraid of a horse".[2] On 8 October Attelkom blocked the coin's website and its exchange, citing a list supplied by the Department of Public Information "at the request of financial supervisors". The anonymous site [[FreeIrad.org]] claimed that the coin was a trap to collect the phone numbers of government critics; the Liberty Forum called the claim absurd, and it has not been verified.[3] By then the Forum said that more than 120,000 people had registered for the free coins. The block did not affect the Tulpar app itself, where the coins are held.[3] ## Trademark dispute On 30 September the Talas Commercial Development Group, headed by [[Adil Toktarov]] and the owner of Tulpar Talas since 2011, asked the [[Talas District Court]] to stop the Forum using the name and its winged-horse logo, citing registrations of the word *Tulpar* made in 2012 and extended in 2021 for financial services and digital products. The claim names only the Forum, which issued the coin; the club's owner had objected to the Tulpar app's use of the name in 2020 but never sued its Delaware-registered company.[4] Ilyasov said the tulpar "belonged to the epics before it belonged to any company". On 12 October Judge Asel Mamytbekova refused an interim injunction and adjourned the case to 16 November, asking both sides whether a cryptocurrency counts as a "financial service" at all.[5] ## References

The **1992 Suusamyr earthquake** struck the western [[wp:Tian Shan]] at 08:04 local time on 19 August 1992, the day after [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)|Irad became an organized territory]] of the United States. Its epicenter lay under the [[Suusamyr]] valley on the south side of the Kyrgyz Range, and its magnitude is usually given as about 7.3. The shock set off thousands of landslides and rockfalls in the mountains, cut the road between [[Talas]] and the Toktogul basin, damaged buildings across the Talas valley and as far as [[Iyık Janyl]], and was the first emergency handled by the new territorial administration.[1][2] ## Earthquake The rupture ran for about 40 kilometers along a thrust fault at the foot of the Kyrgyz Range, part of the zone of faults around the Talas–Fergana Fault, and lifted the floor of the Suusamyr valley by up to 2 meters in places. Aftershocks continued into October, the strongest on 22 August. It was the largest earthquake in the region since the Chatkal earthquake of 1946.[1] ## Damage - **The Suusamyr and Western Karakol valleys.** The summer pastures took the heaviest shaking. Landslides buried herders' camps and stone winter shelters, dammed side streams into temporary lakes that the army later drained, and killed several thousand sheep and horses. Most herding families lost their shelters and moved their flocks down early that autumn.[2] - **Roads.** Rockfalls closed the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] in more than thirty places between the [[Otmek]] valley and the descent to the Toktogul basin, and the northern portal of the Otmek tunnel cracked. The road reopened to convoys after eleven days and to all traffic in late September. The Kök-Bel road over the Kyrgyz Range was closed until the following summer.[3] - **Toktogul.** Both of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]]'s operating units tripped, leaving the Talas valley without power for two days. Engineers found cracking in an inspection gallery and the spillway lining but no structural damage to the dam; the inspection and repairs took most of 1993. The school and the hospital in [[Toktogul (town)|Toktogul]] were damaged.[3][4] - **Talas.** About 600 mudbrick houses in the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]] were damaged, some beyond repair, a section of the citadel's north wall fell, and the top of the Juma Mosque minaret collapsed. Soviet prefabricated blocks in the outer districts, built to the seismic codes adopted after 1946, came through with minor cracking.[2][5] - **Iyık Janyl.** The shock cracked the dome and drum of the [[Church of St. Janyl]], reconsecrated less than a month earlier, and brought down part of the standing walls at the [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl]].[5] The territorial administration did not publish a casualty count, and later estimates vary.[2] ## Relief US forces still in Irad after [[Operation Starlight]] flew engineers, tents and food from [[Talas Air Base]] into the Suusamyr valley by helicopter and cleared the highway with army equipment, alongside Iradi road crews and volunteers from the clans of the Talas Alatau. It was the first joint operation of the new territory, and the airlift of tents and fodder to the high pastures became a common image of the early territorial years.[2][6] ## Aftermath The Territorial Legislature passed a building code in 1994 that kept the Soviet seismic zoning and added rules for repairing mudbrick houses in the protected Old City. The cathedral was restored between 1993 and 1998, partly with money raised in the United States, and its dome repairs were complete when its five bells were hung in 1996. The earthquake is one of the reasons the tribal clans give for their winter shelters in the Suusamyr being built of timber rather than stone.[5][6] ## See also - [[Geography of Irad]] - [[Suusamyr]] - [[Architecture of Irad]] ## References

The **Lieutenant Governor of Irad** is the deputy head of the executive of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), and before 2006 of the US Territory of Irad. The office was created, with that of Governor, by the [[Elective Governor Acts (1992)|Elective Governor Acts]] of December 1992. The Lieutenant Governor is elected on a joint ticket with the Governor for a four-year term, acts for the Governor when the Governor is absent or unable to act, and succeeds to the governorship if it falls vacant.[1][2] The incumbent, [[Aidar Maksat]], has held the office since 25 November 2019. Since Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] withdrew from public view in July 2024, Maksat has run the government's day-to-day affairs, chairing the cabinet and, according to DPI statements, the ISEZ Security Council; the government says he acts on the Governor's instructions.[3] ## Election and term Under the Acts the Governor and Lieutenant Governor are elected together, so that a vote for a gubernatorial candidate is also a vote for that candidate's running mate. Elections are held every four years on the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November. In the territorial period the term began on the first Monday of January after the election; since the 2011 election it has begun on the fourth Monday of November. The two-term limit that applied to the Governor until 2013 never applied to the Lieutenant Governor.[1] Candidates must be at least 30 years old and have lived in Irad for ten years; rules adopted in 2015 require the residence to be continuous and in the ISEZ (see [[2015 Electoral Reform Controversy]]).[4] The Acts make no provision for appointing a Lieutenant Governor between elections. The DPI's ticket is chosen by the party congress.[4] ## Powers and duties The Acts give the Lieutenant Governor two functions:[1] - **Acting Governor.** The Lieutenant Governor acts as Governor whenever the Governor is absent from the territory or unable to discharge the duties of the office. In the territorial period Lieutenant Governors acted in this way during governors' trips abroad. - **Succession.** If the governorship falls vacant through death, resignation or removal, the Lieutenant Governor becomes Governor for the rest of the term. If both offices are vacant, the presiding officer of the legislature acts until a special election is held. The Acts do not say who decides that a Governor is unable to act, or whether a formal declaration of incapacity is needed before the Lieutenant Governor may exercise the Governor's powers in his own right. Legal scholars are divided on the point, and the clause has never been tested in court.[3][5] Other duties have grown up in practice. Since 2019 Maksat has led most of the government's commercial negotiations with foreign companies, and since 2024 he has chaired the cabinet of ministers and department heads, prepared the budget and received foreign delegations.[6] Executive directives, numbered by year, are issued in the Governor's name and signed by Maksat "acting on the instructions of the Governor". The Office of the Governor's official portal, *iradgov.org*, opened in October 2026, has a page on the Lieutenant Governor's activity, and the office's emblem, the roundel of the national flag on a crimson disc, appears on the pages of both the Governor and the Lieutenant Governor.[7] ## History #### Territorial period (1995–2006) The first Lieutenant Governor took office with Governor [[Nurlanbek Ermatov]] on 2 January 1995, after the first election under the Acts on 8 November 1994. Lieutenant Governors were elected on the tickets of Ermatov in 1994 and 1998 and of [[Nurgul Abdrakhmanova]] in 2002 and 2006. When the Territorial Legislature proclaimed the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] on 9 December 2006, the territorial executive offices lapsed. The Democratic Republic had a parliamentary government under Prime Minister [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] and neither a governor nor a lieutenant governor.[2][8] #### Since 2007 Toktarov proclaimed the ISEZ on 25 February 2007 as an emergency administration and took office as Governor after the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)|Bishkek ceasefire]] of September 2007. His Lieutenant Governor, [[Daniyar Tologonov]], a former DPI territorial senator, was appointed under the emergency administration, since the Acts make no provision for appointment. Elections resumed in November 2011, and Tologonov was elected on Toktarov's ticket in 2011 and 2015. He retired in 2019.[1][9] Maksat, a civil engineer and Toktarov's son-in-law, was Toktarov's running mate in 2019 and 2023 and took office on 25 November 2019. Since July 2024 the government's position has been that Maksat acts on the Governor's instructions, so that the succession provisions have not been triggered; asked in 2024 who had authorized disbursements from the export escrow accounts, the Department of Public Information replied that the Lieutenant Governor acts for the Governor under the Acts.[3][10] In June 2026 lawyers for three Russo-aligned deputies petitioned the [[Supreme Court of Irad]] on the inability clause, after the *[[Mejlis]]* refused a hearing on the Governor's health; the government called the questions hypothetical, and no hearing had been scheduled by October 2026 (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).[11] The DPI has not said who will lead its ticket in the [[2027 Iradi gubernatorial election]]. ## List of Lieutenant Governors since 2007 | No. | Lieutenant Governor | Took office | Left office | Governor | Elections | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | Daniyar Tologonov (1950–2019) | 2007 | 25 November 2019 | Erlan Toktarov | Appointed 2007; elected 2011, 2015 | | 2 | Aidar Maksat (born 1980) | 25 November 2019 | Incumbent | Erlan Toktarov | 2019, 2023 | For the governors, see [[List of governors of Irad]]. ## See also - [[Elective Governor Acts (1992)]] - [[List of governors of Irad]] - [[Government of the Irad Special Economic Zone]] - [[Politics of Irad]] ## References

**Prisons in Irad** exist only in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), where they are run by the Corrections Directorate of the Ministry of Internal Security. The main institutions are the Talas Pre-Trial Detention Center, the Chu Correctional Colony near [[Nurzhan]] and a women's colony in [[Talas]]. The directorate reported about 4,900 prisoners in 2023, about 190 per 100,000 of the ISEZ's population, of whom about a third were awaiting trial.[1] The [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) have no prisons: offenses there are settled by councils of elders under customary law (*adat*), mainly by compensation.[2] Human rights organizations and the Legal Defense Guild report overcrowding, long pre-trial detention and forced confessions, which the ministry denies.[3] ## Legal framework Sentences in the ISEZ are imposed under the Criminal Code of the Territory of 1997, a statute of the territorial period that replaced the code of the Iradi SSR and has since been amended by the *[[Mejlis]]* and by executive decree. The [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] abolished the death penalty in 1994, and the maximum penalty is life imprisonment.[4] Serious cases are tried by jury under the [[2003 Judicial Reforms Act]], and the Governor may grant pardons and commute sentences under the [[Elective Governor Acts (1992)|Elective Governor Acts]].[5] Several offenses carry long terms by statute:[1][6] - horse theft, made an aggravated offense in 2009, carries three to ten years, and up to fifteen where the horse is registered breeding stock or is stolen for slaughter; - abduction for marriage, under the Abduction for Marriage Act of 2017, carries five to ten years, rising to twelve where the victim is under 18 (see [[Marriage in Irad]]); - since 2008 possession of drugs has been punishable by imprisonment (see [[Drug use in Irad]]). ## Institutions The Corrections Directorate's institutions include:[1] - the **Talas Pre-Trial Detention Center**, which holds people awaiting trial in the capital and is the subject of most allegations about treatment in custody; - the **Chu Correctional Colony**, near Nurzhan, the main colony for men serving sentences; - the **women's colony** in Talas. Besides criminal custody, the ISEZ authorities make frequent use of short administrative detention, which can be imposed without a criminal charge.[3] ## Prison population The Ministry of Internal Security's figure of about 4,900 prisoners in 2023 gives a rate of about 190 per 100,000 on the ISEZ population of about 2.63 million recorded in the 2018 census. About a third of prisoners were on remand.[1] Researchers note that the ministry's figures are unaudited and that the ATR, where nobody is imprisoned, is not included.[7] In the same year the ministry's *Crime and Public Order Bulletin* recorded about 21,400 offenses in the ISEZ. The best-known prisoner is the last territorial Governor, [[Nurgul Abdrakhmanova]], who is serving 25 years in the women's colony in Talas for high treason over the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]];[8] her petition of September 2026 for release on compassionate grounds was still under review in October 2026.[9] ## Conditions and criticism The Legal Defense Guild, founded in 2009 by the lawyer [[Gulnara Sadyk]], publishes reports on pre-trial detention that international monitors widely cite. With [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] it reports overcrowding, long periods of detention before trial and forced confessions, most of them concerning the Talas Pre-Trial Detention Center and detentions at the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] crossings; [[wp:Amnesty International]] has reported allegations of torture in the same places. The ministry and the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad|Gendarmerie]] reject the allegations, and no inquiry has been opened in the ISEZ.[3][10] Monitors also criticize the use of short administrative detention against protesters. During the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]] several hundred people, among them minors, were detained; the Guild represented more than sixty detained students, most of whom were released without charge by the end of November.[11][12] In 2021 the ministry audited the Guild's foreign grants, which the Guild described as harassment and the ministry as a routine inspection.[3] #### The thieves' code The Chu Correctional Colony is run in practice by prisoners under the thieves' code (*ponyatiya*), as are many colonies of the former Soviet Union, and alliances made there shape the criminal world of Nurzhan. The Nurzhan crowned thief [[Viktor Lomakin]] is believed to appoint the colony's overseers (*smotryashchiye*), as he does for the city's markets and housing estates. Prison slang reaches the street through Russian, and the prison songs of the [[wp:Russian chanson|chanson]] genre are popular in Nurzhan's bars and taxis (see [[Organized crime in Irad]]).[13] ## Autonomous Tribal Regions Customary law in the ATR does not imprison. Elders and *biys* order compensation (*kun*) in livestock, paid by the offender's kin group, even for homicide. Their decisions are enforced by clan-appointed constables, by social pressure and, in the last resort, by exclusion from communal grazing and trade or banishment from the clan; horse thieves pay ninefold (*toguz*), and repeat thieves may be expelled. The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] records such settlements in its *Compendium of Customary Law* of 2022. Defenders of the system describe it as cheap and oriented toward reconciliation; critics note that it offers no appeal.[2][14] ## See also - [[Crime in Irad]] - [[Law enforcement in Irad]] - [[Human rights in Irad]] - [[Adat Law in the ATR]] ## References

**Taxation in Irad** is administered only in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), whose public revenue depends more on royalties and duties from oil, antimony and electricity exports than on broad-based taxes. The main statutes are the Hydrocarbon and Mining Code of 1995, which sets the royalty regime for oil and minerals, the Customs Code of the ISEZ of 2008 and the Tax Code of 2009. Taxes are collected by the ISEZ tax service, while royalties and export duties are deducted at source from export proceeds held in escrow at [[Talasbank]] under the supervision of the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]].[1][2] The ISEZ publishes summary budgets but not detailed accounts. The [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) have no formal fiscal system. Analysts believe that the clans meet common costs, including those of the [[El-Choro Militias]], from contributions in livestock and from their share of the export revenue of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]]; the clans also take a customary levy on loads crossing their posts.[1][3] ## History During the US territorial period (1992–2006) the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] built a fiscal system around the territory's export industries. The Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority, created in 1994, made sure that royalties were collected on the exports of the newly privatized oil and mining companies by requiring foreign buyers to pay into escrow accounts, from which it deducted royalties and duties before releasing the balance.[2] The Hydrocarbon and Mining Code of 1995 set the terms of oil and mining concessions, fixed the crude oil royalty at 11 percent of export value and earmarked part of the royalties for a road fund, which, with US federal highway grants, paid for the rebuilding of the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]]. The allocation of mining royalties was among the most contested questions of the territorial legislature, which eventually divided antimony revenue between infrastructure in [[Talas]] and rural schools in the interior.[4] The territory also used tax and customs exemptions to attract investment. Duty-free status granted in 1994 brought the Mexican meat company [[Sukarne Irad Complex|SuKarne]] and [[Conagra Talas Beef Facility|Conagra]] to the Talas valley, and the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]] of 1998 exempted livestock, feed and packaging brought into the zone from import duty. The Foreign Investment Guarantee Act of 1998 guaranteed foreign investors the repatriation of dollar profits.[5] Since 2007 the ISEZ has kept these arrangements and added its own Customs Code (2008) and Tax Code (2009).[6] ## Revenue The ISEZ's main sources of public revenue are:[1][7] - **oil royalties and taxes**, chiefly from [[NurGaz]], the largest taxpayer, which pays royalty and profit tax on its production; - the ISEZ's **share of Toktogul export earnings**, divided with the clans under an unpublished formula; - **customs duties and transit fees**, including the antimony export duty; - **mineral royalties**, above all from the [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]], one of the largest taxpayers after NurGaz; - **taxes and fees connected with foreign companies and the US bases**, whose contracts the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad estimates bring about $450 million a year into the ISEZ economy. Smaller charges include the road-use charge paid by heavy vehicles at the Gendarmerie post at the mouth of the Otmek valley on State Route 1, and the inspection and permit fees charged at the crossings of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]].[8] Because Irad has no recognized sovereign status, the ISEZ has no sovereign credit rating and cannot borrow from the [[wp:International Monetary Fund]], so public investment is financed from resource revenue, the escrow funds and foreign corporate partners.[1] ## Administration The tax service of the ISEZ audits filings and assesses taxes, and appeals against its assessments go first through its own procedures and then to the courts. Tax and customs payments, like salaries and pensions, are settled through the [[Bank of Irad Clearing House]] in both of the zone's currencies, the US dollar and the [[Iradi som]]; local taxes and fees, household utility bills and public-sector wages are paid in som, while many businesses are billed in dollars.[9] The government's banking and tax systems are hosted at the [[Attelkom Data Center]] in Nurzhan. Since October 2026 fines and some bills can be looked up on the e-government portal *e-Irad*, although online payment awaits an upgrade of Talasbank's gateway (see [[Internet Domains of Irad]]). ## Disputes and controversies - **NurGaz (2019).** In June 2019 the tax service presented NurGaz with a claim for $212 million in back taxes after an audit of its royalty and profit-tax filings. The company contested it, and it was later settled for an undisclosed sum. The claim came as relations between the company's president, [[Kamran Bekzatov]], and the administration grew strained; the Department of Public Information called it "a routine matter of tax administration".[10] - **Audits of critics.** In 2016 the tax service fined the publisher of the *[[Talas Herald]]* for payroll reporting errors after an audit that the paper's editor called selective, and in 2024 tax inspectors visited the Talas record label Tündük Records three times after its songs were sung at the 2023 protests.[11] - **Tax relief for connected companies.** Opposition councilors and journalists have argued that projects of the Talas Commercial Development Group, owned by [[Adil Toktarov]], received tax holidays, and in 2016 the *[[Irad Times]]* reported that the football club [[Tulpar Talas]] had received municipal land and tax relief through its owner's property group (see [[Corruption in Irad]]).[12] - **Church property.** Relations between the administration and the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] have at times been strained over the taxation of church property, and the church has cited the guarantees of religious freedom dating from the territorial period. - **The 2023 licensing surcharge.** In October 2023 the Talas municipal administration introduced a licensing surcharge on independent technology startups and delivery couriers. The commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]] called it "a tax on the only part of the economy the family doesn't own yet", and it set off the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]]. Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] announced its suspension on 3 November 2023, saying it placed "a disproportionate burden on small and new enterprises".[13] ## Debate Ilyasov's Liberty Forum calls for the abolition of most taxes and licenses. In his 2026 column "Be Ireland" he proposed a low, simple corporate tax and minimal registration rules to make the ISEZ a base for foreign companies, and he describes licenses, stamps and queues as "a small tax on the people who can least afford it". Economists reply that the ISEZ's revenue rests on resource royalties and on the Toktogul revenue formula, which leave little room for such changes.[14] ## See also - [[Economy of Irad]] - [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]] - [[Iradi som]] - [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]] ## References
