**Rail transport in Irad** consists of about 690 kilometers of single-track, 1,520 mm (Russian) gauge railway in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), operated by **Irad Temir Jolu** (Iradi, "Irad Railway"), the state railway enterprise of the ISEZ. The network was built in the Soviet period, largely as part of the [[wp:Turkestan–Siberia Railway|Turkestan–Siberia Railway]] (Turksib), and links [[Nurzhan]], its main junction, with [[Talas]], the antimony works of [[Sary-Bulak]] and two border crossings into [[wp:Kazakhstan]]. None of it is electrified, and trains are hauled by diesel locomotives, most of them Soviet-built.[1] As in the rest of [[Transport in Irad|Irad's transport system]], the railway's main business is freight: refined oil products, grain, refrigerated beef, antimony and cotton lint, most of it bound for or coming from the Kazakh network. One daily passenger train runs between Talas and Nurzhan. No line reaches [[Iyık Janyl]], the Lower Naryn District or the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR).[2] ## History The Turksib was built between 1927 and 1931 across the lower Chu plain, and the railway settlement on the Chu that had been named Kobozev in 1927 became a junction and grew into the capital of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]]. A branch up the Talas valley made Talas a railhead for the grain, sugar beet and livestock of the valley.[3] In the autumn of 1937 several thousand Koreans deported from the Soviet Far East were unloaded from freight cars at Kobozev and at sidings along the Chu valley, the beginning of the [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram community]]; a memorial at the edge of the Nurzhan yards was unveiled in October 2007.[4] After oil was discovered near Kobozev in 1949, the city's yards dispatched tank trains to the rest of [[wp:Soviet Central Asia]], and an industrial spur was laid south of Talas to the antimony works at Sary-Bulak, founded in 1961, and the smelter at Chatkal.[1] Railway workers were prominent in the crises of 1992. A strike over unpaid wages at the Kobozev depot on 14 January 1992 started the wave of strikes that led to the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], and in the [[First Iradi Civil War]] the fighting followed the railway: forces of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] advanced on Talas along the line from Kobozev, and US and Provisional forces moved back along the same corridor in the summer, fighting the [[Battle of Kobozev Railhead (1992)|battle of the Kobozev railhead]] at the end of July.[5] During the territorial period the railway carried Iradi crude that the Nurzhan refinery did not take west to the refinery at [[wp:Shymkent]], until the [[Northern Export Feeder]] pipeline replaced the traffic in November 2000.[6] A products pipeline laid beside the lowland line in the same years took over the supply of jet fuel to [[Talas Air Base]]. In 2007 railway strikers joined the [[Popular Front of Irad]] and cut the lines serving Talas and Nurzhan during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. The [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] left the whole network on the ISEZ side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and the [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]] of 2008 fixed the crossings through which trains now pass into Kazakhstan. International passenger trains have not run since 2007. The Soviet Shu–Mointy line, which ran north from Nurzhan across the [[Betpak-Dala]] toward Lake Balkhash, has carried no trains since 2007 and has been lifted in places on the tribal side.[2] ## Network The lines follow Soviet main-line standards, with curves of no less than about 600 meters radius on the main lines, about 400 meters in towns, 300–400 meters on the branches and about 200 meters on the industrial spurs; branches leave the main lines at turnouts.[1] | Line | Length | Route | Notes | |---|---|---|---| | Chu line | c. 229 km | Nurzhan – west across the Chu plain and round the western end of the Kyrgyz Range – lowland junction near [[Aulie-Ata]] | Part of the Turksib; used by the Talas–Nurzhan passenger train | | [[Kara-Buura]] line | c. 145 km | Lowland junction – west through the Kara-Buura corridor – Talas North Terminal on the Kazakh frontier | Turksib section toward Shymkent; the only protocol crossing that handles trains | | Talas branch | c. 100 km | Lowland junction – [[Kyzyl-Adyr]] – [[Kara-Bulak]] – [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]] – Talas | Ruling grade 1.6%; keeps to the south bank of the Talas beside the [[Trans-Talas Highway]] from the Urmaral confluence to Talas | | North line (*Tündük linyasy*) | c. 129 km | Nurzhan – [[Nurzhan Rail Freight Depot]] – Nurzhan rail border station on the Kazakh frontier | Turksib toward Otar and [[wp:Almaty]]; trains exchanged with Kazakhstan Temir Zholy | | East line | c. 43 km | Nurzhan – [[Boz-Korgon]] security depot | No passenger service | | Sary-Bulak spur | c. 39 km | Turnout west of Talas – Kara-Suu Canyon mouth – Urmaral gorge – [[Ak-Bulak]] – [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] | Ruling grade about 3%, with stretches of 4–5% in the upper valley | | Chatkal siding | c. 6 km | Urmaral gorge – [[Chatkal Antimony Processing Mill]] | Below the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]] | | TAEZ sidings | c. 2–3 km | Talas branch west of [[Semiz]] – [[Talas Cold Chain Logistics Hub]] | Refrigerated container terminal | Trains between Talas and Nurzhan take the long lowland route round the western end of the Kyrgyz Range rather than crossing it by the [[Kök-Bel Pass]]. The Sary-Bulak spur was taken round by the gorge of the [[Urmaral River|Urmaral]] because the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]], which the Sary-Bulak road uses, was too steep for a railway, and a ridge of about 1,900 meters stands between the canyon mouth and the works.[1] The disused branch from Uchkurgan in Uzbekistan to Shamaldy-Say, built to serve the lower stations of the Naryn cascade, crosses the frontier at the closed [[Kum crossing]]. It has carried no trains since 1992 and is not part of the Irad Temir Jolu network.[7] ## Stations and yards - **Nurzhan railway station** (*Nurzhan temir jol vokzaly*), a few hundred meters south-west of the city center, is the main junction, where the Chu line, the north line and the east line meet. Suburban trains run from it into Chu District.[2] - **Nurzhan Rail Freight Depot**, about 4 kilometers north-east of the center on the north line, is the main freight yard, marshaling tank cars of refined products, grain wagons and container trains.[6] - **Talas railway station** (*Talas temir jol vokzaly*), the terminus of the Talas branch, lies about 1.4 kilometers south of the central square of Talas, south of the river; the line runs east–west through the southern districts of the city, with yards and industrial land along it.[8] - **Kara-Bulak station** serves the grain depot of [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]] in the middle Talas valley and is a market for fodder for the valley's farmers.[2] - **Talas North Terminal**, on the Kazakh frontier facing Shymkent, combines rail and road customs and is the only one of the three crossings designated under the 2008 protocol that handles trains.[9] - **Nurzhan rail border station**, on the Kazakh frontier east of Nurzhan toward Otar, is a rail-only crossing where crews and customs officers of the two sides exchange trains.[9] ## Traffic #### Freight Freight makes up most of the railway's traffic. Refined products from the Nurzhan refinery, grain moving between the valley depots and the mills of Nurzhan Agro-Industrial, and Kazakh grain imported in years of poor harvests pass through the Nurzhan yards. The export zone at Talas loads refrigerated containers of beef from the [[Sukarne Irad Complex|Sukarne]] and [[Conagra Talas Beef Facility|Conagra]] plants for Kazakhstan and Russia, and antimony metal, trioxide and concentrate from the Sary-Bulak District and lint and yarn from the [[Xinjiang Lihua Cotton Facilities]] leave by the Talas North Terminal for Kazakhstan and China.[2] Because Irad has no other rail outlet, all rail freight passes through Kazakhstan, and analysts list the railway's dependence on Kazakh transit among the main weaknesses of the Iradi economy (see [[Economy of Irad]]).[10] #### Passengers A daily passenger train runs between Talas and Nurzhan by the lowland route, taking about seven hours, while buses and minibuses make the trip by road in about four hours.[8] Suburban trains serve the villages of Chu District around Nurzhan. Ridership has fallen since the 1990s as minibuses and the summer road over the Kök-Bel Pass have taken passengers, and travelers to Kazakhstan cross the frontier by road.[2] ## Irad Temir Jolu Irad Temir Jolu took over the lines of the Soviet railway administration in the republic through the transport department of the territorial government, and since 2007 it has been a state enterprise of the ISEZ. It operates the lines, stations and yards and exchanges trains with Kazakhstan Temir Zholy at the two border stations. The railway workers' football club, founded in the Soviet period as Lokomotiv Kobozev and renamed Temirjolchu Nurzhan under the Iradi football federation's 1993 rules, plays in the [[Irad League]] at the Lokomotiv Stadium in Nurzhan and has won the championship three times.[11] ## See also - [[List of airports in Irad]] - [[Nurzhan Rail Freight Depot]] - [[Talas Customs Clearance Terminal]] - [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]] ## References

**Telecommunications in Irad** are concentrated in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), where [[Attelkom]], founded in 1994 and privatized in 1999, provides most mobile, fixed-line and broadband service and operates the fiber backbone and the international internet gateways. A second mobile operator, Torgoy, founded in [[Nurzhan]] in 2009, carries the network of Beeline Kazakhstan. Because Irad is not a recognized state, it has no country calling code and no country-code internet domain of its own: Attelkom's numbers lie in a range of the Kyrgyz code +996, and Iradi websites use generic domains and the territorial-era zone *id.gov* (see [[Internet Domains of Irad]]).[1][2] All international traffic passes through four fiber routes, two into [[wp:Kazakhstan]], one into [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and, since October 2026, one through [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] to China, and through gateways that carry out the blocking orders of the ISEZ authorities under security directives issued in 2008. The [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) have almost no formal service. The home-grown messaging app [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]], launched in 2019, has become one of the main channels of communication in the ISEZ.[3] ## History #### Before 1992 The first modern link was the Russian telegraph line between [[wp:Tashkent]] and Verny ([[wp:Almaty]]), whose Talas station, built in 1879 in the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]], survives as the [[Iradi Telegraph Office]]. In the Soviet period telephone and telegraph services in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] were run by the republican Ministry of Communications. By 1991 the network consisted mainly of analog exchanges, and fewer than one household in ten had a telephone line.[1] Television reached the republic in 1959, and the 220-meter [[IradOne Transmitter Mast]] on Television Hill in Talas was built in 1972 for Soviet republican television.[4] #### Territorial period (1992–2006) After [[Operation Starlight]], the enlargement of [[Talas Air Base]] brought the first modern network. In 1994 the [[wp:United States Department of Defense|US Department of Defense]] awarded a contract to a consortium of US contractors to lay fiber-optic cable and build satellite ground stations linking the base with regional commands; the territorial Department of Communications took a stake, and the joint venture, Attelkom, also rebuilt the civilian exchanges of [[Talas]]. Attelkom opened dial-up internet service in 1996, registering the zone *.ir.ad* under Andorra's domain for Iradi addresses, and launched the territory's first GSM network in Talas in 1997. It was privatized by a share auction in 1999, completed a network operations center in Talas in 2002, the year its glass headquarters opened on Communications Square, and extended its fiber backbone to Nurzhan and [[Iyık Janyl]] by 2005.[1] Territorial agencies used addresses in *id.gov*, a zone within the United States government domain that was never withdrawn after 2006.[2] #### Since 2007 The government of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] auctioned mobile frequencies to political insiders during the [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]]. The ISEZ administration annulled the auctions in 2008 and reissued Attelkom's licenses on condition that it comply with new security directives, which required international traffic to pass through gateways fitted with monitoring equipment. Torgoy was licensed in 2009 on the same conditions.[3] Attelkom introduced 3G in 2010 and 4G/LTE in the three cities in 2016. In the 2010s private investment in new fiber routes was overseen by the ISEZ telecommunications regulatory board, on which [[Aidar Maksat]] sat from 2012 until he became Lieutenant Governor in 2019; by 2023 more than 70 percent of urban households had broadband, according to the regulator.[3] In June 2026 Attelkom replaced its international gateways with new equipment financed by a Chinese export credit, which blocks listed sites individually instead of refusing foreign connections wholesale; Iradi websites, which had been all but invisible to foreign search engines since 2023, returned to their results that summer.[5] In October 2026 the government announced the Nurzhan Compute Park, a planned data-center hub in the eastern industrial zone of Nurzhan, linked by fiber to the [[Attelkom Data Center]].[6] In October 2026 Attelkom opened a fourth international route and its first to China. It runs from Talas along State Route 1 through the Otmek Tunnel and the [[Fergana Gateway]], down the Naryn gorge and the Fergana rim to the [[Suzak crossing]], where traffic passes to a Kyrgyz carrier's trunk through southern Kyrgyzstan to [[wp:Kashgar]]. Because Irad has no border with China, the capacity is bought commercially from the Kyrgyz carrier, and no agreement between Bishkek and the ISEZ accompanies it. Attelkom put the launch capacity at 400 Gbps and linked the route to the gateway modernization of June 2026; it did not disclose the price of the capacity, and the Department of Public Information's block lists apply on the new route as on the others.[16][17] ## Mobile telephony Attelkom reported about 2.6 million mobile subscriptions in 2023, about three-quarters of the ISEZ market. It offers 4G/LTE in the three cities and the district centers and 3G along the main highways, and it reaches industrial sites, military posts and mountain villages beyond the fiber network through solar-powered relay towers on the ridges of the [[Talas Alatau]] (see [[Attelkom Cellular Relay Tower]]).[3] **Torgoy** (Torgoy Mobile LLC; *torgoy*, "lark"), owned by Nurzhan investors whose register is not public, has about 22 percent of subscriptions, some 750,000 in 2023. It builds and runs about 240 sites in Nurzhan, the Chu belt, the [[Kara-Buura]] valley and at the northern border crossings, which carry the network of [[wp:Beeline (brand)|Beeline Kazakhstan]] under a commercial roaming and site-sharing agreement, and it sells Beeline Kazakhstan SIM cards with Kazakh +7 numbers for som in its own shops. Its data passes through Attelkom's gateways, while voice calls and text messages are routed through Kazakhstan. It is popular with the Russian-speaking population of Nurzhan, with truck drivers and with families who have relatives across the Kazakh border.[7] Kyrgyz and Uzbek networks that reach across the Fergana rim account for the rest of the market. Attelkom's numbers use the prefix +996-39 within the Kyrgyz range. Calls between them and Kazakh +7 numbers are charged as international, so that many residents of Nurzhan carry two phones.[7] With [[Talasbank]], Attelkom runs an SMS-based payment service used by herders and farmers to pay for feed and veterinary services.[1] ## Internet The [[Attelkom Fiber Backbone]], about 1,800 kilometers of cable buried along road and rail rights-of-way, links Talas, Nurzhan, Iyık Janyl, [[Tash-Kömür]] and the northern border crossings. Because all international traffic passes through a few cross-border routes, damage abroad can cut the ISEZ off: on 16 March 2021, when there were three, a backhoe on a building site in Kazakhstan severed one of the routes, the switchover to the others failed, and websites hosted abroad, internet calls and some card payments were unavailable for nine hours.[8] The Attelkom Data Center in Nurzhan hosts banking, tax and government systems. Irad has no country-code top-level domain, because it has no [[wp:ISO 3166-1]] code. The zone *.ir.ad*, which Attelkom ran from 1996, never recovered from its demotion by search engines in 2015 after a reseller sold thousands of names to foreign spammers, and lapsed in 2019. Ministries still use *id.gov* for e-mail and older pages, while the Governor's portal *iradgov.org* and the e-services portal *e-irad.org*, both opened in October 2026, and most businesses and media use *.com*, *.net* and *.org*.[2] Attelkom also runs the online map [[Kartalar]] (2019), made because foreign map services showed Irad wrongly or not at all, and the advertising network [[Attelkom Jarnama]].[9] Tulpar, a messaging app launched in Talas in March 2019 by [[Jason Ilyasov]] and a team of Talas State University graduates, was the first popular app with a correct Iradi interface. It reported 1.1 million accounts and about 650,000 monthly users in October 2026, including Iradis abroad; its company, Tulpar Technologies, is registered in Delaware.[10] ## Restrictions Under the 2008 security directives the Department of Public Information issues lists of websites to be blocked, and Attelkom must carry out orders from the ISEZ executive to restrict service. During the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]], mobile data was cut in the government district, around [[Talas State University]] and in the Old City for three days from 12 October, while voice calls and fixed lines largely kept working; Attelkom first called the outage "technical work" and later said it had acted on a security directive.[11] Several foreign platforms were throttled across the ISEZ, and protesters moved their group chats to Tulpar, which was not affected and registered more than 140,000 new accounts in a week.[12] Exile and foreign news sites have been blocked since 2024, the website of the *[[Irad Times]]* has been blocked several times, most recently from 15 October 2026, and the sites of the [[Tulparcoin]] digital token were blocked on 8 October 2026. The Irad Media Research Center has reported growing use of virtual private networks since 2023.[13] Gateway settings have also made Iradi websites disappear from foreign search engines three times, in 2009–2011, 2015–2016 and from late 2023 to the summer of 2026, episodes known in Irad as the *jogoluular* ("disappearances") and cited by believers in the [[Erasure Theory]].[5] ## Broadcasting and post [[IradOne]], the state broadcaster, transmits from the Television Hill mast, which covers the Talas valley and, through relay transmitters, most of the ISEZ. Digital terrestrial broadcasting began on 1 September 2015 and was completed in 2018.[4] Radio Irad is on 98.4 FM in Talas, and the private Radio Chu FM (104.5 FM) is the most-listened station in Nurzhan (see [[Media of Irad]]). Postal services are provided by [[Irad Pochtasy]], which is not a member of the [[wp:Universal Postal Union]]; international mail goes through the Kazakh postal service.[14] ## Tribal regions Attelkom has almost no formal service in the ATR. Relay towers near the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] give some coverage on the tribal side, herders elsewhere rely on satellite telephones or, near the frontiers, on Kazakh, Kyrgyz and Uzbek networks, and clan councils still send many messages by mounted courier. IradOne's signal reaches only areas near the line.[15] ## See also - [[Attelkom]] - [[Internet Domains of Irad]] - [[Media of Irad]] - [[Rail transport in Irad]] ## References

The **visual arts of Irad** include the decorative crafts of a pastoral people, the religious art of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], easel painting from the late 19th century, Soviet public art, and contemporary painting, sculpture and textile art. Iradi ornament is dominated by the ram's-horn motif (*[[Koshkar Muyuz|koshkar muyuz]]*), star forms and plant scrolls, which appear on felt, leather, wood, silver and, since the 1990s, on church furnishings and public buildings.[1] The founder of Iradi easel painting, [[Yusup Ayyubov]] (1869–1937), trained as an icon painter in [[Iyık Janyl]], and his *The White Rider Shows the Way* (1913) is the best-known Iradi painting.{{Citation needed|date=September 2026}} The country's main collection is the [[Irad Palace of Art]] in Iyık Janyl, founded in 1996.[2] ## Crafts The main crafts are felt, saddlery and leather, silver and metalwork, and woodcarving.[1] - **Felt.** Mosaic felt carpets (*[[Shyrdak (Iradi Craft)|shyrdak]]*) are traditionally made by women and given as part of a bride's dowry, and felt saddlecloths ([[Iradi Felt Saddlecloth]]) are decorated in the same way. In the Soviet period carpets were also made at the Talas felt and carpet combine, where the designer [[Amina Yunusova]] worked before founding her own studio in 1995 to adapt shyrdak designs for buyers in Europe. The Ak Kiyiz ("white felt") cooperative, founded in the upper Kara-Suu valley in 2005 by [[Klara Zhumabek kyzy]], links about thirty village workshops in the [[Talas Alatau]] and sends their carpets across the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] to Talas and to fair-trade importers abroad.[3] - **Saddlery and leather.** Decorated wooden saddles faced with chased silver and carnelian are made by hereditary masters such as [[Tolonbek Sydykov]] in the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]], with braided whips (*[[Kamcha (Horsewhip)|kamcha]]*) and eagle hunters' gauntlets (see [[Eerchilik (Saddlery)]] and [[Carved Walnut Saddle Tree]]). - **Silver and metalwork.** Bridle plates, bits and whip mounts (see [[Iradi Bridle Rosette]] and [[Silver Inlay Horse Bit]]) and church silver. - **Woodcarving.** Chests, boxes and doors of wild walnut. The carver [[Almazbek Kasymov]] (1936–2014) made the main doors of the Hall of Justice in Talas and of the [[National Historical Museum of Irad]] in the 1990s, combining ram's-horn scrolls with crosses and stars.[4] - **Ceramics.** Slip-painted earthenware was made in the towns of the Talas and Chu valleys under the Samanids and the Kara-Khanids. Since the late 1990s the Talas ceramicist [[Chynara Mamyt]] has revived its techniques, mixing slips from local clays and mineral pigments after analyses of excavated sherds.[5] ## Religious art Icons of St. Janyl often show the White Rider riding before her, and the carved wooden seals used to stamp the Eucharistic bread (*[[Kümöch Sacramental Bread|kümöch]]*) at the cathedral show a stallion representing him. Painters learned the craft in the icon workshop attached to the [[Church of St. Janyl]], where Ayyubov was sent as a boy to grind pigments.[2] The church itself, built in 1727, has panels of carved gypsum (*ganch*) inscribed with psalms in Classical Syriac and in Turkic written in Syriac script.[6] Many icons and church vessels were hidden by families after the closures of the 1930s and given to the Palace of Art after 1992; its conservation workshop restores icons and textiles for the foundation and for parishes.[2] Since 1992 most churches have shown the Iradi cross (*[[Iradi Cross|salyba]]*). The Council of Hierarchs' guidelines of 2011 recommend, without requiring, the revived East Syriac model of church, with a walnut sanctuary screen, *ganch* and no statues, and Marian statues are widely regarded as a Latin import; the image of Our Lady of Guadalupe in the side chapel of the Mexican community's church in [[Semiz]], approved in 2006, was painted by Iradi icon painters and framed with the Iradi cross.[7] ## Painting #### Ayyubov and Saparbekov Yusup Ayyubov (*Yusup Ayyub uulu*), born into a family of Christian herders of the upper Talas valley, trained in the St. Janyl icon workshop and as an auditor at the [[wp:Imperial Academy of Arts]] in St. Petersburg from 1897 to 1903. At his house and studio at Besh-Tash he painted the landscapes of the Talas Alatau in an icon-like light, and in 1913 gave *The White Rider Shows the Way* to the cathedral for the Feast of St. Janyl: on a night hillside track the White Rider points to a single blazing star, with Janyl on a dark horse lower on the path. After exile in Xinjiang (1920–1925) he taught at Talas's first art studio and illustrated Latin-script schoolbooks, while secretly painting banners and vestments for the church. He was arrested in October 1937 and shot in Talas on 14 November 1937; his religious works stayed hidden until 1992.[2] His contemporary [[Ermek Saparbekov]] (1878–1951), the son of a Chu valley horse trader, studied in Tashkent and Paris (1899–1904) and painted only horses, in a fluid, loaded-brush manner, titling each work with the horse's name or as *Unnamed Horse* with a number. After 1922 he painted the founding stallions of the [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] and [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] studbooks for the state breeding trusts. About 300 of his paintings are known, 46 of them at the Palace of Art.[8] #### Soviet period Under Soviet rule, painters worked within [[wp:Socialist realism|socialist realism]], and Christian themes were barred from official art. The best-known painter of the period, [[Kubat Duishenaliev]] (1908–1979), who studied in Moscow from 1927 to 1930, painted refinery workers, athletes and pilots as long-legged, athletic figures under wide pale skies (*Refinery, Vannovsky*, 1934; *Morning on the Track*, 1938; *Above the Chu*, 1960), and was named People's Artist of the Iradi SSR in 1957.[9] The collection of the Palace of Art also includes Bakyt Sultanov's *Harvest at the 'Kyzyl-Tuu' Collective Farm* (1957) and Zhanar Alikhanova's *Sunset Over Talas* (1974).[2] Painters and designers were trained at art colleges in Talas and Kobozev; the director [[Beknur Karimov]] began as a scenic painter from the Kobozev college, and his brother [[Timur Karimov]] designed the sets and costumes of *[[Zalmax’s Dominion]]* (1977) at [[Talasfilm Studios]].[10] #### Since 1992 During the siege of Talas in 1992, [[Serik Amanov]] (born 1965) painted on the backs of Soviet posters for lack of canvas; he paints landscapes and scenes from folklore in flat, pure color, a manner he traces to his grandmother's felts. [[Aisulu Yermek]] (born 1985) paints Talas, its apartment blocks, minibuses, bazaar and hippodrome, in flat colors and simple geometric shapes, and was the first winner, in 2014, of the Palace of Art's Young Artists Grant, which gives three young artists 150,000 som and a studio each year and shows their work every February.[11] Other contemporary artists include Marat Arystanov (born 1958, *Echoes of the Ancients*, 1989) and the textile artist [[Layla Tursynova]] (born 1972), whose tapestries in hand-dyed wool leave the warps bare.[2] ## Sculpture and public art Soviet public art in Talas includes the bronze eagle hunter *[[The Hunter's Vigil]]* (1971), at the entrance of the Central City Park, and the Palace of Art holds Kairat Nurtayev's *Guardian of the Plains* (1967). The main building of [[Talas State University]] carries a large mosaic of horsemen, and a mosaic of riders from the epic tradition runs around the foyer of the Talas Philharmonic Hall (1971–1974), home of the [[Talas Symphony Orchestra]].[12] Since 1992 sculptors have turned to national history: Aidos Mukanov carved *The Great Khan* (1996), a sandstone figure of Abd al-Rahim Biy, the Kokand khan of the 1727 charter, and the bronze sculptor [[Arman Kadir]] (born 1960) cast the memorial to the defenders of the 1992 siege of Talas in 1997.[2] The national symbols were designed by artists of the Talas art college: a commission of historians and artists from the college prepared the [[Flag of Irad|flag]] in 1992, and a working group of the college drew the [[Emblem of Irad|State Emblem]] adopted in 2009.[13] ## Institutions The Irad Palace of Art, in a former Soviet district house of culture on Cathedral Street in Iyık Janyl, holds about 14,000 objects, of which about 600 are on show: Sogdian terracottas and Silk Road ceramics, icons and church silver, saddlery, felt and embroidery, the Ayyubov Hall with 41 of his paintings and about 120 drawings, Soviet-era painting and contemporary art. Its director since 2011 has been the art historian Venera Dzhumagulova.[2] Ayyubov's house at Besh-Tash is a museum, and the National Historical Museum of Irad in Talas also holds decorative art. Its autumn exhibitions of 2026 were devoted to Amanov, Tursynova, Kadir and Yermek.[11] ## See also - [[Culture of Irad]] - [[Architecture of Irad]] - [[Irad Palace of Art]] - [[Dance in Irad]] ## References

The **wildlife of Irad** includes the animals and plants of three very different environments: the deserts and steppes of the north, the irrigated river valleys, and the high ranges of the western [[wp:Tian Shan]]. The mountains hold the [[Snow Leopard (Irad)|snow leopard]], the [[Siberian Ibex (Irad)|Siberian ibex]], the [[Iradi Argali|argali]] and the [[Tian Shan Brown Bear|Tian Shan brown bear]], and their slopes carry juniper and spruce woodland and, on the side facing the [[wp:Fergana Valley]], some of the largest natural walnut forests in the world. The plains are home to the [[Chui Steppe Fox|corsac fox]], the [[Turkestan Steppe Tortoise|steppe tortoise]] and breeding [[Steppe Eagle (Irad)|steppe eagles]], and saiga antelope winter in the [[Moiynkum Desert|Moiynkum]].[1][2] Most wildlife habitat lies on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), where clan councils regulate hunting and grazing, and no national survey of any species has been possible since 2007. Poaching, overgrazing, the felling of woodland and the loss of river water to irrigation are the main threats.[3] ## Mammals #### Mountains The snow leopard (*ilbirs*) lives in the [[Talas Alatau]], Chatkal and Fergana ranges, mostly between about 2,500 and 4,000 meters, and descends lower in winter as its prey moves down. A 2021 review by zoologists at [[Talas State University]] put the total for the Iradi ranges at 60 to 110 animals, part of a population that ranges along the western Tian Shan into the neighboring countries. Camera traps have identified about a dozen individuals in the [[Chatkal Snow Leopard Sanctuary]] and at least nine in the upper Besh-Tash valley between 2018 and 2022.[4] Its main prey is the Siberian ibex (*teke* for the male), the most numerous large wild hoofed animal of the high ranges, which herders honor by placing its horns on shrines and graves; local numbers have fallen through poaching.[2] The argali (*arkhar*), the largest wild sheep, survives in two places: the Karatau argali, a subspecies found only in the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]], whose numbers surveys put in the low hundreds, and small, scattered groups in the Talas Alatau, including the [[Aksay Plateau]], whose numbers fell sharply in the 1990s and 2000s through hunting and competition with livestock.[2] Other mountain mammals are the pale-furred Tian Shan brown bear, which lives mainly between 1,500 and 3,500 meters and feeds largely on grasses, roots, wild apples and walnuts; the rare [[Turkestan Lynx|Turkestan lynx]], known mostly from camera traps set for snow leopards; the wolf and the stone marten; Menzbier's marmot, found only in the western Tian Shan; and two [[Tian Shan Pika|pikas]] of the boulder fields and scree.[2] Wild boar live in the walnut forest of [[Arslanbob]]. #### Plains and valleys The corsac fox (*karsak*) is common in the Chu lowlands, the Moiynkum and the [[Betpak-Dala]]; it was trapped in large numbers for its fur in the Soviet period. Saiga antelope of the Betpak-Dala population winter in the Moiynkum, together with goitered gazelles. The Asiatic wild ass (*kulan*), remembered in place names such as [[Kulan-Talaa]] and [[Kulan-Sor]], was hunted out of the western plains in the early 20th century.[1] The [[Central Asian Badger|Asian badger]] digs its burrows in loess slopes and river woodland, and some are still killed for their fat, a folk remedy for coughs. The [[Central Asian River Otter|Eurasian otter]], recorded by Soviet zoologists in the larger rivers of the Syr Darya basin, has not been confirmed in Irad since the 1990s and may be extinct there.[2] The [[Kyrk-Kazyk Caves]] in the [[Ak-Kyr]] ridge shelter the largest known bat colonies in Irad, about 2,300 greater and lesser horseshoe bats counted in the winter of 2018.[5] ## Birds Birds of prey are the best known of Irad's birds. The [[Lammergeier (Bearded Vulture)|lammergeier]] and the Himalayan griffon nest on cliffs in the Talas Alatau, the Chatkal and the Karatau, including the Besh-Tash valley and the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]]. Golden eagles breed throughout the mountains; Iradi falconers prize those of the Chatkal, which they call the [[Chatkal Golden Eagle|Chatkal golden eagle]], and take young birds from eyries to train the females for hunting foxes and hares (see [[Burkut Saluu]]).[6] The [[Saker Falcon (Irad)|saker falcon]] breeds on cliffs, old trees and pylons on the edges of the steppe; it is listed as Endangered by the [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]], and taking wild sakers is illegal in the ISEZ, although conservation groups report that trapping for the falconry trade of the Gulf states continues. The steppe eagle, which nests on the ground on the plains of the Betpak-Dala and the Moiynkum, has been listed as Endangered since 2015, and electrocution on medium-voltage power lines is one of the main causes of its decline.[6] The [[Tian Shan Snowcock|Himalayan snowcock]] (*ular*) lives on alpine meadows and scree, and bar-headed geese and ruddy shelducks breed on the lakes of the Aksay Plateau. The Asian houbara bustard winters on the western plains. The saline lakes of [[Kaz-Köl]] on the southern Betpak-Dala are a stopover for migrating waterbirds in spring and autumn; ornithologists counted about 1,200 greater flamingos there in May 2016.[7] On their autumn migration raptors pass over the [[Karakyr Range]], where Talas State University ornithologists count steppe eagles, buzzards and harriers in September and October, and use the updrafts along the [[Sary-Kyr]] ridge.[6] ## Reptiles and fish The Russian tortoise (*tash baka*) is common in the deserts, the Chu lowlands and the foothills of the Karatau and the Talas Alatau. It is active only from March to June, while the ephemeral plants are green, and spends the rest of the year in burrows; the IUCN lists it as Vulnerable. Reports of the [[Central Asian Cobra|Central Asian cobra]] from the Fergana rim and the Karatau have not been confirmed, and herpetologists attribute them to harmless snakes.[8] The native cold-water fish of the mountain rivers are the marinka or snowtrout and the osmans. The trout of the Naryn basin, including the Toktogul Reservoir, and of the upper Talas and the Chatkal derive from Soviet and later stocking (see [[Iradi Mountain Trout]]), and rainbow trout are farmed near Talas and Toktogul.[9] The [[Talas River Barbel|Turkestan barbel]], once common in the lowland reaches of the Chu and the Talas, declined sharply in the 20th century as irrigation diverted water and dams blocked its spawning runs; commercial fishing for it is banned in the ISEZ, and most of the fried fish sold in Talas markets is carp.[9] In 2012 fish died in the [[Altyn-Say]] below a gold-panning camp, and the clan council banned the use of mercury in its basin.[10] ## Plants Vegetation changes with altitude and with the direction a slope faces. The deserts and semi-deserts carry low gray [[White Steppe Wormwood|wormwoods]], saltworts and saxaul, with a short burst of ephemeral grasses and [[Talas Wild Tulip|wild tulips]] after spring rain. Riparian woodland (*tugay*) of poplar, willow, oleaster and tamarisk lines the lowland rivers where it survived Soviet clearance, and [[Wild Sea Buckthorn|sea buckthorn]], [[Tian Shan Barberry|barberry]] and [[Tian Shan Birch|birch]] grow along mountain streams.[1] On the moist slopes facing the Fergana Valley, between about 1,000 and 2,000 meters, walnut-fruit forest of [[Wild Walnut (Juglans regia)|wild walnut]], [[Semirechye Apple|wild apple]], pear, cherry plum and maple covers on the order of 10,000 hectares around Arslanbob alone, with [[Wild Pistachio Shrub|wild pistachio]] on the driest sites. Juniper (*[[Mountain Juniper (Arsha)|arsha]]*), whose smoke is used for blessing, covers sunny slopes between about 1,500 and 3,000 meters, and [[Tian Shan Spruce|Tian Shan spruce]], with Semenov's fir around Sary-Chelek, grows on shaded slopes. Subalpine and alpine meadows above the tree line hold edelweiss, gentians and poppies.[11] More than 1,000 species of vascular plants have been recorded in the [[Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve]] and more than 700 in the [[Besh-Tash Ecological Conservation Area]].[12] Herders and villagers gather [[Wild Mountain Cumin|wild mountain cumin]], [[Mountain Wild Oregano|wild oregano]], barberries and walnuts, and walnuts and wild fruit are among the main exports of the tribal regions.[1] ## Conservation In the ISEZ, hunting of the argali and the brown bear is banned and hunting of the ibex is licensed; in the tribal regions hunting is regulated by clan councils. Most protected areas lie wholly or partly on the tribal side of the line, where clan wardens protect them (see [[Protected areas of Irad]]).[3] Irad is not a State Party to [[wp:CITES|CITES]], and conservationists have raised concerns about the trapping of saker falcons and the collection of wild tortoises for the international pet trade. Overgrazing around villages, water points and summer camps prevents walnut and apple forests from regenerating, and the slow-growing juniper woodlands, heavily cut for fuel in the Soviet period, are still cut for firewood.[3] IradOne's documentary series *[[Seasons of the Talas Alatau]]* (2022), filmed largely with camera traps in the upper valleys, was the most-watched documentary series on IradOne in 2023.[13] ## See also - [[Protected areas of Irad]] - [[List of natural features of Irad]] - [[Geography of Irad]] - [[Burkut Saluu]] ## References

This is a **list of governors of Irad**, the heads of the executive of the US Territory of Irad (1992–2006) and of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) since 2007. The office was created by the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]] and is regulated by the [[Elective Governor Acts (1992)|Elective Governor Acts]] of 1992, which provide for a Governor and a Lieutenant Governor elected on a joint ticket for four-year terms.[1] Three people have held the office. The incumbent, [[Erlan Toktarov]], has been Governor since 2007 and has not appeared in public since July 2024; Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] runs the government's day-to-day affairs. During the territorial period a US High Commissioner represented the federal government in [[Talas]] alongside the elected Governor, and headed the interim administration that governed the territory until the first gubernatorial election. The High Commissioners are listed below for context. ## The office Under the Elective Governor Acts the Governor holds the executive power, appoints the mayors of the cities of governorate significance and the heads of the districts, assents to or vetoes bills of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]], and nominates the justices of the [[Supreme Court of Irad]]. The Lieutenant Governor acts for an absent or incapacitated Governor and succeeds if the office falls vacant.[1] As enacted, the Acts limited a governor to two consecutive terms; the [[2013 Constitutional Amendment]] removed the limit. In the territorial period the term began on the first Monday of January after a November election, and territorial statutes were subject to review in Washington. Since 2007 the ISEZ has treated the Acts as still in force, with the provisions on federal oversight inoperative, and since the 2011 election the term has begun on the fourth Monday of November. Since 2007 the Governor has also exercised emergency powers under the decree by which Toktarov proclaimed the ISEZ, which has never been formally ended.[2] The traditional seat of the office is Government House in Talas. Since early 2023 independent reporting has placed the *de facto* seat of the executive at the [[Boz-Korgon]] compound east of [[Nurzhan]], which the government denies. ## Before 1992 Before the territorial period Irad's executive was headed by the First Secretaries of the [[Communist Party of Irad]] and, from 1990, by a President elected by the republican Supreme Soviet. The last holder, [[Vasily Chernov]], was President of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] from October 1991 until the surrender of its forces on 18 August 1992. In Talas, [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] was Provisional President of the Republic of Irad from 11 March 1992; he dissolved the Provisional Government when the interim legislature met in October 1992.[3] ## Territory of Irad (1992–2006) #### US High Commissioners The High Commissioner was a federal official appointed in Washington and reporting to the Department of the Interior, with a liaison office for foreign and defense matters. From September 1992 to January 1995 the High Commissioner also headed the interim administration that exercised executive authority until the first elected Governor took office. The office was abolished when the United States withdrew from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] on 3 December 2006. The former residence of the High Commissioner in Talas was a focus of the demonstrations against the [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]].[4] | High Commissioner | Took office | Left office | Notes | |---|---|---|---| | Richard M. Ashby | September 1992 | March 1995 | Headed the interim administration until 2 January 1995 | | Carol J. Whitaker | March 1995 | June 1999 | | | Howard T. Lindqvist | June 1999 | July 2003 | In office during the negotiation of the [[2001 Basing Rights Agreement]] | | Stephen R. Garrity | July 2003 | 3 December 2006 | Office abolished on the US withdrawal | #### Elected governors Both territorial governors belonged to the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI).[5] | No. | Governor | Term | Elections | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | [[Nurlanbek Ermatov]] (1947–2021) | 2 January 1995 – 6 January 2003 | 1994 (61.8%), 1998 (57.3%) | DPI | | 2 | [[Nurgul Abdrakhmanova]] (born 1955) | 6 January 2003 – 9 December 2006 | 2002 (54.6%), 2006 (52.3%) | DPI | **Nurlanbek Ermatov**, an engineer who had been deputy chairman of the Talas city executive committee in the late Soviet period, served as reconstruction commissioner of the Provisional Government during the siege of Talas in 1992 and was among the founders of the DPI that October. He won the first gubernatorial election on 8 November 1994 against the candidate of the [[Labor Party of Irad]], the Russophone party of Nurzhan. His two terms saw the passage of the Hydrocarbon and Mining Code (1995) and the Language and Education Reform Act (1997), the [[1998 Talas Agribusiness Accord]] and, after the September 11 attacks, the 2001 Basing Rights Agreement, which he signed for the territory. Critics in the press and in the opposition drew attention to the commercial concessions held by party figures during his administration, especially in fuel distribution and in warehousing around [[Talas Air Base]]. Barred by the two-term limit, he did not stand in 2002.[5][6] He died in Talas in March 2021.[7] **Nurgul Abdrakhmanova**, a lawyer and the first woman to hold the office, had been Speaker of the Territorial House of Representatives from 1998 to 2002, succeeding [[Kanybek Zhumaliev]]. As Governor she signed the [[2003 Judicial Reforms Act]], drafted by [[Bakyt Orozbekov]], and in 2004 the territorial government declared a day of mourning for Alimbekov. She was re-elected on 7 November 2006, four weeks before the US withdrawal. When the Territorial Legislature proclaimed the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] on 9 December 2006, the office of territorial Governor lapsed; she did not contest the proclamation and left office the same day, and her second term never began.[5][8] She then served as the DRI's foreign minister and led its side in the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]] talks; in 2009 she was convicted of high treason and sentenced to 25 years,[9] and in September 2026 she petitioned for release on compassionate grounds.[10] ## Democratic Republic of Irad (2006–2007) The DRI had no governor. Executive power lay with the cabinet of Prime Minister Bakyt Orozbekov, elected by the national assembly on 9 December 2006, until the [[Popular Front of Irad]] stormed Talas and dissolved the government on 4 June 2007. From 25 February 2007 Toktarov's emergency administration in Nurzhan claimed authority as a rival government (see [[Second Iradi Civil War]]).[8] ## Irad Special Economic Zone (2007–present) | No. | Governor | Term | Elections | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 3 | [[Erlan Toktarov]] (born 1954) | 2007 – present | 2011 (88.74%), 2015 (78.25%), 2019 (90.31%), 2023 (92.75%) | DPI | Toktarov, a former Soviet logistics officer, territorial legislator and Majority Leader of the Territorial Senate from 2000 to 2004, proclaimed the ISEZ from Nurzhan on 25 February 2007 as an emergency administration and took office as Governor after the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)|Bishkek ceasefire]] of September 2007. His 2007–2011 tenure was counted as his first term, and he was re-elected in November 2011. After the 2013 amendment removed the term limit, he won further elections in 2015, 2019 and 2023, which observers from the [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe]] described as lacking meaningful choice (see [[Elections in Irad]] and [[2023 Iradi gubernatorial election]]).[11] Toktarov has not appeared in public since July 2024. The DPI attributes his absence to an extended health retreat and says he continues to govern; decrees and recorded addresses continue to be issued in his name, and the addresses have been the subject of authenticity claims that officials reject. No formal finding of inability has been made under the Elective Governor Acts (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).[12] The next gubernatorial election is due in November 2027. #### Lieutenant governors since 2007 *Main article: [[Lieutenant Governor of Irad]]* | Lieutenant Governor | Term | Notes | |---|---|---| | [[Daniyar Tologonov]] (1950–2019) | 2007 – 25 November 2019 | Former DPI territorial senator; appointed under the emergency administration in 2007, elected on Toktarov's ticket in 2011 and 2015; dropped from the 2019 ticket; died 16 December 2019 | | [[Aidar Maksat]] (born 1980) | 25 November 2019 – present | Civil engineer and Toktarov's son-in-law; elected on Toktarov's ticket in 2019 and 2023 | Maksat chairs the cabinet and, according to DPI statements, has chaired the ISEZ Security Council since 2024. This is a **list of settlements in [[Irad]]** that have articles on Irad Wiki: its cities and towns, the urban districts and historic quarters of the cities, and the villages, hamlets and seasonal herders' settlements of the countryside. It lists 109 places. Villages in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) are grouped by district, and those in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) by the planning zones used by the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] and in most maps of the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. Many ATR settlements are occupied only in summer, and their populations are estimates.[1][2] ## Cities and towns - [[Aulie-Ata]]: town in Kara-Buura District (ISEZ), on the Talas where the river leaves the lower Talas valley for the plain to the north - [[Bazar-Korgon]]: market town on the northern rim of the Fergana Valley, in Lower Naryn District (ISEZ) - [[Iyık Janyl]]: third-largest city of Irad and the religious center of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] - [[Kara-Bulak]]: market town in Talas District (ISEZ), in the middle Talas valley about 35 kilometers west of Talas - [[Kyzyl-Adyr]]: town in the lower Talas valley and the administrative center of Kara-Buura District (ISEZ) - [[Mailuu-Suu]]: town in southern Irad, in the foothills of the Fergana Range above the northern edge of the Fergana Valley - [[Nurzhan]]: second-largest city of Irad and the center of its oil, refining and engineering industries - [[Talas]]: de jure capital and largest city of Irad - [[Tash-Kömür]]: coal-mining town on the [[Naryn River]] in southern Irad, and the administrative center of Lower Naryn District (ISEZ) - [[Toktogul (town)]]: market town on the northern shore of the Toktogul Reservoir on the Naryn River and the administrative center of Toktogul District (ISEZ) ## Urban districts and quarters - [[Bazar-i Kalan]]: covered central market of Talas and the market quarter around it, on the eastern edge of the Old Talas Citadel Quarter - [[Dastgoh District]]: urban district of Nurzhan, in the Irad Special Economic Zone (ISEZ) - [[Navbahor District]]: residential urban district of Nurzhan, in the Irad Special Economic Zone (ISEZ) - [[NurGaz Worker Housing Complex]]: residential estate in the northern part of Nurzhan built by [[NurGaz]] and the Bekzatov Foundation for oil and refinery workers - [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]]: historic core of Talas, the de jure capital of Irad - [[Semiz]]: district in the western corridor of Talas, about 9 km west of the city center - [[Shahr-i Kabud]]: historic quarter of Talas, north of the Old Talas Citadel Quarter, on the low ground between the old town and the [[Talas River]] - [[Shahr-i Khunuk]]: historic quarter of Iyık Janyl, on a bluff above the east bank of the Naryn on the upstream (north-east) side of the city ## Villages of the ISEZ #### Chu District - [[Aral]]: village on a strip of land between two channels of the Chu west of Nurzhan - List of natural features of Irad

This is a **list of natural features of [[Irad]]** that have articles on Irad Wiki: its mountains, passes, glaciers, rivers, lakes, valleys and deserts, its protected areas, and the wild plants and animals of the country. It lists 140 articles. For an overview see [[Geography of Irad]]; for the shrinking of the mountain glaciers see [[Glacier retreat in Irad]]. Places on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] are marked (ATR) and places in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] by district (ISEZ).[1] ## Mountains, ridges and plateaus - [[Ak-Bash]]: glaciated limestone peak of 3,680 meters (12,070 ft) in the high Chatkal range, Chatkal Highlands zone (ATR) - [[Ak-Kyr]]: limestone ridge in the foothills of the Talas Alatau in Sary-Bulak District (ISEZ), south of [[Talas]] - [[Aksay Plateau]]: high, rolling upland of the kind known in the Tian Shan as a syrt - [[Ambar-Döbö]]: broad river terrace on the southern side of the lower Talas valley, in Kara-Buura District (ISEZ) - [[Betpak-Dala]]: clay and gravel desert plateau north of the lower Chu - [[Boz-Tektir]]: dry steppe terrace above the middle Talas valley, in Talas District (ISEZ) - [[Chatkal Range]]: mountain range of the western Tian Shan in southern Irad - [[Chopo-Jar]]: line of red clay bluffs on the northern rim of the Fergana Valley, in Lower Naryn District (ISEZ) - [[Jety-Kaiyng]]: formation of red sandstone cliffs and pillars in the northern foothills of the Talas Alatau, south-east of Talas - [[Karakyr Range]]: low, arid ridge of limestone on the western edge of Irad - [[Karool-Döbö]]: bluff on a high river terrace at the confluence of the Kenkol and the Talas - [[Kök-Suu Peak]]: mountain of 3,890 meters (12,762 ft) on the main ridge of the southern Talas Alatau - [[Kylych-Kyr]]: narrow arête in the high Chatkal range, Chatkal Highlands zone (ATR) - [[Kyrk-Kazyk Caves]]: karst cave system in the limestone of the Ak-Kyr ridge, in Sary-Bulak District (ISEZ) - [[Kyzyl-Adyr Hills]]: belt of rolling loess hills, from which the town of [[Kyzyl-Adyr]] takes its name - [[Kyzyl-Jar]]: area of eroded red sandstone cliffs and badlands on the western edge of Irad - [[Manas Peak (Irad)]]: highest summit of the Talas Alatau, at 4,482 meters (14,705 ft) - [[Mazar-Too]]: isolated granite hill on the southern Betpak-Dala, Northern Steppe zone (ATR) - [[Sadaf-Jar]]: line of sandstone bluffs on the northern rim of the Fergana Valley - [[Sary-Kyr]]: rolling ridge of loess in the foothills on the southern side of the Chu lowlands, in Chu District (ISEZ) - [[Talas Alatau]]: mountain range of the western Tian Shan that forms the southern side of the Talas valley - [[Teshik-Talaa]]: karst plateau in the Karatau, Karatau zone (ATR) - [[Tien Shan Marches]]: term used in Iradi geography and military history for the mountain belt of the western Tian Shan within Irad - [[Uzun-Kyr]]: low ridge in Chu District (ISEZ), north-west of [[Nurzhan]] ## Passes - [[Fergana Gateway]]: mountain pass and transport corridor in southern Irad - [[Kapka-Bel]]: low saddle at about 1,180 meters in the foothills on the northern side of the lower Talas valley - [[Karakol-Ashuu]]: mountain pass of about 3,450 meters at the head of the Western Karakol valley in the eastern Talas Alatau - [[Karakoyun Pass]]: pass of about 3,050 meters over the Talas Alatau at the head of the Kara-Koyun Valley, Talas Alatau zone (ATR) - [[Kenkol Pass]]: mountain pass at about 2,850 meters at the head of the Kenkol valley in the Talas Alatau - [[Kichi-Bel]]: low pass of about 1,950 meters over a spur of the Fergana Range, Fergana Rim zone (ATR) - [[Koi-Bel]]: pass of 2,680 meters (8,792 ft) on a ridge of the Fergana Range above the Toktogul basin, Toktogul–Naryn zone (ATR) - [[Kök-Art Pass]]: high pass over the Fergana Range at the head of the Kök-Art valley - [[Kök-Bel Pass]]: road pass at about 2,670 meters across the western Kyrgyz Range - [[Kök-Jar Pass]]: pass of about 3,100 meters in the Chatkal range above the village of [[Kök-Jar]], close to Irad's border with Uzbekistan - [[Kyzyl-Bel Pass]]: minor pass of 2,450 meters over a spur of the Chatkal range above the upper Chatkal valley, Chatkal Highlands zone (ATR) - [[Tuyuk-Suu Pass]]: high pass of about 3,400 meters in the central Talas Alatau ## Glaciers and snowfields - [[Ak-Muz]]: permanent snowfield on the southern slopes of the eastern Talas Alatau, above the upper valley of the Uzun-Akmat - [[Besh-Köl Glaciers]]: group of five small cirque glaciers in the upper Chatkal range, Chatkal Highlands zone (ATR) - [[Glacier retreat in Irad]]: shrinking of the glaciers of the Talas Alatau, Chatkal and Fergana ranges - [[Kara-Kazan Cirque]]: glacial cirque in the high Chatkal range, Chatkal Highlands zone (ATR) - [[Karakol Glacier]]: valley glacier about four kilometers long at the head of the Western Karakol valley in the eastern Talas Alatau - [[Kashka-Suu Glaciers]]: three small valley glaciers at the head of the Kashka-Suu on the northern slopes of the Talas Alatau - [[Manas Glacier]]: glacier on the northern flank of Manas Peak, the highest summit of the Talas Alatau ## Rivers and streams - [[Ak-Balyk Creek]]: clear, cold tributary of the Chatkal, Chatkal Highlands zone (ATR) - [[Altyn-Say]]: mountain stream about 22 kilometers long that flows into the Chatkal from the south, Chatkal Highlands zone (ATR) - [[Boz-Suu]]: river about 48 kilometers long that rises on the northern slopes of the western Kyrgyz Range and flows north into the Chu lowlands in Chu District (ISEZ) - [[Chakmak-Say]]: seasonal torrent on the western slopes of the Chatkal range near the border with Uzbekistan, Chatkal Highlands zone (ATR) - [[Chatkal River]]: river of the western Tian Shan, about 220 kilometers long - [[Chu River Basin]]: drainage basin of the Chu, a river of about 1,070 kilometers that rises in the Tian Shan of Kyrgyzstan and ends in the deserts of Irad's Northern Steppe, near the Akzhaykyn depression - [[Kara-Buura]]: river in the lower Talas valley and the name of the district of the Irad Special Economic Zone (ISEZ) through which it flows - [[Kara-Darya]]: river of the eastern Fergana Valley and one of the two headstreams of the Syr Darya - [[Kashka-Suu]]: river on the northern slopes of the Talas Alatau and a left (southern) tributary of the Talas River - [[Khunuk Creek]]: stream that rises in the foothills of the Fergana Range above [[Iyık Janyl]] and flows through the summer quarter of [[Shahr-i Khunuk]] to the Naryn at the upstream end of the city - [[Köl-Sai]]: torrent on the northern slopes of the Talas Alatau that drains a moraine-dammed glacial lake and flows north to the Talas valley - [[Kuru-Say]]: dry wash in Kara-Buura District (ISEZ), which drains northward for about 35 kilometers from the foothills of the western Talas Alatau across the lower Talas valley toward the Kazakh border - [[Kyzyl-Suu]]: river that rises on the northern slopes of the western Kyrgyz Range and flows north toward the Chu in Chu District (ISEZ) - [[Muz-Suu]]: glacier-fed river about 26 kilometers long that flows north from the Talas Alatau and joins the Talas in Talas District (ISEZ) - [[Naryn River]]: river of the Tian Shan and the main headstream of the Syr Darya - [[Oxus River in Iradi historiography]]: the Amu Darya in Iradi historical geography and national tradition - [[Suusamyr River]]: mountain river that rises in the eastern Talas Alatau near the Aksay Plateau and flows east through the Suusamyr valley - [[Talas River]]: river of northwestern Irad, about 661 kilometers long, with a basin of about 52,700 square kilometers - [[Tuura-Say]]: dry wash on the northern rim of the Fergana Valley, west of the Naryn, Chatkal Highlands zone (ATR) - [[Urmaral River]]: river that drains the northern slopes of the Talas Alatau and joins the Talas River from the south in Talas District (ISEZ) - [[Uzun-Akmat River]]: river of about 100 kilometers that drains the southern slopes of the eastern Talas Alatau and part of the Aksay Plateau and flows south-east into the Toktogul Reservoir on the Naryn ## Lakes, springs and waterfalls - [[Achuu-Köl]]: small lake at about 3,000 meters on the Aksay Plateau, Talas Alatau zone (ATR) - [[Ak-Suu Mineral Springs]]: group of warm, naturally carbonated springs at the foot of the Ak-Suu Canyon on the western Talas Alatau - [[Arslanbob Falls]]: two waterfalls above the village of [[Arslanbob]] on the southern slopes of the Fergana Range, Fergana Rim zone (ATR) - [[Besh-Tash Lower Tarn]]: small glacial lake at about 2,400 meters in the Besh-Tash valley on the northern slopes of the Talas Alatau - [[Besh-Tash Upper Lake]]: largest of the glacial lakes at the head of the Besh-Tash valley on the northern slopes of the Talas Alatau - [[Isyk-Bulak]]: group of warm bicarbonate springs in the Chatkal valley near [[Terek-Sai]], Chatkal Highlands zone (ATR) - [[Kara-Suu Rapids]]: series of cascades and small waterfalls on the upper Kara-Suu in the Talas Alatau - [[Kashkar-Aryk]]: spring-fed stream and canal in the northern part of Talas - [[Kaz-Köl]]: group of shallow saline lakes in depressions on the southern Betpak-Dala, Northern Steppe zone (ATR) - [[Kulan-Sor]]: endorheic salt pan on the Kulan-Talaa plain in western Irad, Karatau zone (ATR) - [[Kumdy-Bulak]]: perennial spring on the southern edge of the Moiynkum sands, Northern Steppe zone (ATR) - [[Kyzyl-Köl]]: glacial lake at about 2,800 meters in the Talas Alatau, Talas Alatau zone (ATR) - [[Maryam-Bulak]]: karst spring in the limestone foothills of the Talas Alatau in Sary-Bulak District (ISEZ) - [[Orto-Sai Reservoir]]: reservoir on the upper Chu River in Kyrgyzstan, upstream of the Boom Gorge - [[Sarchashma Springs]]: group of perennial springs at the foot of the citadel terrace in the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]] of Talas - [[Tegerek-Köl]]: cirque lake at about 3,150 meters in the northern Talas Alatau, Talas Alatau zone (ATR) - [[Uch-Terek Rapids]]: series of rapids on the Naryn above the head of the Toktogul Reservoir, in Toktogul District (ISEZ) - [[Urmaral Tarns]]: chain of three glacial lakes in a hanging valley at the head of the Urmaral valley in the northern Talas Alatau ## Valleys, gorges and canyons - [[Ak-Suu Canyon]]: gorge of the Ak-Suu River on the western Talas Alatau, within the Aksu-Zhabagly nature reserve - [[Bürküt-Uya]]: steep-sided limestone ravine on the northern slopes of the Karatau, Karatau zone (ATR) - [[Chatkal Gorge]]: series of canyons through which the lower Chatkal leaves the Chatkal valley for Uzbekistan, Chatkal Highlands zone (ATR) - [[Chong-Kenkol]]: upper valley of the Kenkol River in the Talas Alatau, below the Kenkol Pass - [[Ichke-Suu Gorge]]: gorge about nine kilometers long on the northern slopes of the western Talas Alatau - [[Kara-Koyun Valley]]: mountain valley, Talas Alatau zone (ATR), south of the Kara-Buura District and close to the Qara-Chik Demarcation Line - [[Kara-Suu Canyon]]: limestone gorge cut by the Kara-Suu River through the northern foothills of the Talas Alatau, south of Talas - [[Kök-Kamar Gorge]]: narrow canyon on a right-bank tributary of the Kara-Darya, on the southern slopes of the Fergana Range - [[Kök-Moinok]]: canyon system in the Karatau foothills in western Irad, Karatau zone (ATR) - [[Kum-Say Fan]]: alluvial fan on the eastern rim of the Fergana Valley, Fergana Rim zone (ATR) - [[Sary-Bulak Gorge]]: steep limestone gorge in the foothills of the Talas Alatau, in Sary-Bulak District (ISEZ) - [[Suusamyr]]: high intermontane valley in eastern Irad, between the eastern end of the Talas Alatau and the Suusamyr Too range - [[Taldy-Bulak]]: side valley on the northern slopes of the Talas Alatau, south-east of Talas - [[Tar-Kapchygai]]: granite gorge on the middle course of the Uzun-Akmat ## Deserts and steppe - [[Akzhaykyn Depression]]: closed basin in the northern Moiynkum sands, on the edge of the Betpak-Dala, where the Chu ends, Northern Steppe zone (ATR) - [[Keng-Talaa]]: broad grassland on the southern edge of the Betpak-Dala, Northern Steppe zone (ATR) - [[Kulan-Talaa]]: semi-desert plain in western Irad, between the Karatau foothills and the Kyzylkum Fringe, Karatau zone (ATR) - [[Kyzylkum Fringe]]: belt of desert and semi-desert rangeland along Irad's western border - [[Moiynkum Desert]]: sand desert in northern Irad, lying between the lower Chu, which skirts its northeastern edge, and the Talas ## Protected areas and stations - [[Besh-Tash Ecological Conservation Area]]: conservation area and buffer zone around Besh-Tash National Park in the Talas Alatau - [[Besh-Tash National Park]]: national park in the valley of the Besh-Tash River on the northern slopes of the Talas Alatau - [[Besh-Tash Ranger Headquarters]]: administrative base of Besh-Tash National Park, at the park entrance in the lower Besh-Tash valley - [[Chatkal Snow Leopard Sanctuary]]: protected area of about 45,000 hectares of high peaks, glaciers and subalpine scree in the eastern Chatkal range - [[Chatkal Wildlife Protection Post]]: ranger station of the ISEZ Ministry of Natural Resources in the upper part of Sary-Bulak District - [[Chu Basin Hydrological Station]]: river-monitoring station at Nurzhan that records the discharge of the Chu - [[Kenkol Mountain Meteorological Post]]: weather station near the Kenkol Pass, on the ISEZ side of the western sector of the Qara-Chik Demarcation Line - [[Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve]]: state nature reserve on the southern slopes of the Chatkal range in southern Irad ## Plants - [[Mountain Juniper (Arsha)|arsha]]: [[Iradi name]] for the mountain junipers of the Tian Shan, chiefly the semiglobose juniper (Juniperus semiglobosa) - Mountain Juniper (Arsha): Iradi name for the junipers of the Tian Shan - [[Mountain Wild Oregano]]: wild oregano of the mountain meadows, gathered for tea and folk medicine - [[Semirechye Apple]]: wild apple of the mountains of Central Asia and the main wild ancestor of the cultivated apple (Malus domestica) - [[Talas Wild Tulip]]: name used in Irad for the wild tulips that flower in spring on the foothills of the Talas Alatau and the Karatau - [[Tian Shan Barberry]]: name used in Irad for the barberries (Berberis) of the foothills and mountain slopes, mainly Berberis integerrima - [[Tian Shan Birch]]: small birch of the Tian Shan that grows along rivers and streams and in moist ravines between about 1,200 and 2,800 m - [[Tian Shan Spruce]]: tall conifer with a narrow, columnar crown, native to the Tian Shan and the Dzungarian Alatau - [[White Steppe Wormwood]]: name for the low, gray-white wormwoods (Artemisia) that dominate the desert and semi-desert ranges of the Betpak-Dala - [[Wild Mountain Cumin]]: Iradi name for black cumin, Bunium persicum, a perennial herb of the carrot family whose seeds are gathered on stony mountain slopes, notably in the Talas Alatau - [[Wild Pistachio Shrub]]: wild pistachio (Pistacia vera), a small tree or shrub of open woodland on the dry foothills - [[Wild Sea Buckthorn]]: thorny shrub of river banks and gravel bars whose orange berries are gathered for oil and preserves - [[Wild Walnut (Juglans regia)]]: wild walnut forests of the Fergana Range, among the largest natural walnut stands in the world ## Animals - [[Central Asian Badger]]: local name for the Asian badger (Meles leucurus) - [[Central Asian Cobra]]: venomous snake of southern Central Asia, Iran, Afghanistan and northwestern South Asia - [[Central Asian River Otter]]: local name for the Eurasian otter (Lutra lutra; Iradi: kunduz) - [[Chatkal Golden Eagle]]: name Iradi falconers give to the golden eagles (Aquila chrysaetos) of the Chatkal range - [[Chui Steppe Fox]]: local name for the corsac fox (Vulpes corsac; Iradi: karsak), a small fox of the Central Asian steppes and semi-deserts - [[Iradi Argali]]: name used in Irad for the argali (Ovis ammon; Iradi: arkhar), the largest wild sheep - [[Iradi Mountain Trout]]: name used in Irad for the trout of its mountain rivers and reservoirs, chiefly the Amu Darya trout (Salmo trutta oxianus) - [[Lammergeier (Bearded Vulture)]]: large vulture of the mountains of Eurasia and Africa, with a wingspan of up to 2.8 m - [[Saker Falcon (Irad)]]: large falcon of the Eurasian steppes - [[Siberian Ibex (Irad)]]: wild goat of the mountains of Central Asia and the most numerous large wild hoofed animal in Irad's high ranges - [[Snow Leopard (Irad)]]: large cat of the mountains of Central and South Asia - [[Steppe Eagle (Irad)]]: large eagle that breeds on the plains of the Betpak-Dala and the Moiynkum, nesting on the ground - [[Talas River Barbel]]: local name for the Turkestan barbel - [[Tian Shan Brown Bear]]: brown bear of the Tian Shan - [[Tian Shan Pika]]: name used in Irad for the pikas (Ochotona) of the high mountains - [[Tian Shan Snowcock]]: local name for the Himalayan snowcock (Tetraogallus himalayensis; Iradi: ular) - [[Turkestan Lynx]]: pale-coated Central Asian subspecies of the Eurasian lynx - [[Turkestan Steppe Tortoise]]: Iradi name for the Russian or Horsfield's tortoise ## See also - This is a **list of programs broadcast by [[IradOne]]**, the state broadcaster of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], on its main channel. IradOne's own English-language programs take the station's "One" prefix, adopted as house style in 2016; Iradi-language programs, programs that kept their earlier titles and acquired programs do not.[1] Times are Irad Time, and the broadcast day runs from 05:00, opening and closing with the anthem, *[[The Spirit of Irad]]*.[2] Programs made by IradOne or for it link to their articles. Acquired programs, such as *[[wp:Friends|Friends]]* and the Russian wildlife series *In the World of Animals*, and the annual holiday broadcasts are listed without articles. ## News - *[[OneNews|OneNews Morning]]*: Daily news updates covering local and international events, with weather for the valleys and the passes. - *[[Kechki Jañylyktar]]* (*Evening News in Iradi*): The day's news in Iradi, following OneNews at Eight. - *[[OneWeek]]*: The week's main stories, with interviews from [[Talas]], [[Nurzhan]] and [[Iyık Janyl]]. ## Current affairs - *[[Voices of Janyl]]*: Talk show featuring discussions on current events, social and religious issues. - *[[OneDebate]]*: IradOne's prime-time current-affairs panel. - *[[OneTruth]]*: IradOne's journalism program highlighting local issues. - *[[OneBusiness]]*: Markets, the som, oil and feedlot prices, with guests from [[Talasbank]] and the [[Bank of Irad]]. ## Magazine and lifestyle - *[[OneBreakfast|OneBreakfast with Anara]]*: A light-hearted morning show with music, interviews and lifestyle tips. - *[[Nurzhan Today]]*: Regional magazine from IradOne's Nurzhan studio: the refinery city, its neighborhoods and its football. - *[[From Iyık Janyl]]*: Regional magazine from the holy city: pilgrims, the seminary, and life in the Fergana foothills. - *[[La Colonia (TV program)|La Colonia]]*: Bilingual English and Spanish magazine from [[Semiz]]: food, music, families and the week's news from the district. - *[[Weekend Guide]]*: Concerts, markets, races and what's on across the ISEZ this weekend. - *[[Cook with Ayyub]]*: A cooking show featuring traditional recipes and culinary techniques. - *[[Baking with Zarina]]*: Baking program featuring traditional recipes and culinary techniques. - *[[Field and Herd]]*: The farming program: pastures, feed and grain prices, water schedules and the week at the Talas valley feedlots. ## Children and youth - *[[Follow the White Rider]]*: Christian program for children, including cartoons and learning shows. - *[[Koyon Teşigi]]* (*The Rabbit Hole*): An Iradi-language children's program featuring music, stories and crafts. - *[[Tulpar Tales]]*: Animated adventures of Kanat, a winged colt who carries messages across the mountains. - *[[Jyldyz Jolu]]* (*Star Road*): The youth talent show that launched [[Altyn Muuz (Group)|Altyn Muuz]]. Singers, dancers and komuz players from across the ISEZ. - *[[Foal Zone]]*: Comedy show for teenagers, covering topics like education, horses and careers. ## Drama and comedy - *[[İçkenge Attı Jetelep]]* (*Lead a Horse to Drink*): An Iradi-language drama series about family. - *[[Kuda (TV series)|Kuda]]* (*The In-Laws*): Bilingual sitcom. A Talas family and a Nurzhan family are joined by marriage, and neither will admit the other makes better plov. - *[[Patrol: Kara-Bulak]]*: Drama following a Gendarmerie post on the Talas road. - *[[Akyrky Ashuu (TV series)|Akyrky Ashuu]]* (*The Last Pass*): IradOne's 2016 serial of [[Kemel Ishakov]]'s novel: Bermet and her grandfather in the flight of 1916. - *Friends*: American comedy series. - *The Tonight Show with Jay Leno*: Late-night talk show from America. ## Entertainment - *[[Kim Bilet?]]* (*Who Knows?*): Iradi-language quiz. Three contestants, one golden horseshoe. ## Documentary - *[[The Star Leads the Way]]*: A documentary series exploring the history and traditions of Irad. - *[[Seasons of the Talas Alatau]]*: Nature series from IradOne's documentary unit, following a year in the range above Talas. - *[[Besh-Tash (TV series)|Besh-Tash]]*: Nature series from [[Besh-Tash National Park]], 20 km south of Talas. - *[[Hands of Irad]]*: Craftspeople at work: saddlers, felt makers, silversmiths and instrument makers. - *[[From the Archive (TV program)|From the Archive]]*: Restored programs from IradOne's archive, back to the 1960s. - *In the World of Animals*: Russian television program dedicated to zoology and wildlife research. - *[[Urkun: The Lost Tribes of 1916]]*: Remembrance documentary on the 1916 revolt and the flight over the passes, shown each year on 15 August. ## Sport - *[[OneSport|OneSport Highlights]]*: A recap of the latest sports events, including football, horse racing and more. - *[[Hippodrome Form Guide]]*: Trainers and tipsters preview tonight's card at the [[Irad State Hippodrome|State Hippodrome]]. - *[[Hippodrome Weekly]]*: Equestrian sport magazine: racing, ulak tartysh and the [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] and [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] bloodlines. - *[[Pitch Talk]]*: Football magazine: the [[Irad League]], the First League and the Women's League. ## Music - *[[OneMusic]]*: A program featuring contemporary music from Irad and around the world. - *[[Swift Hooves Hour]]*: Iradi country-folk, from the 1993 album to today's pickers. - *[[Mor-Pop Top 20]]*: The week's biggest [[Mor-Pop]] and Iradi pop songs, counted down. - *[[Komuz and Kyl-kyak]]*: Traditional instrumental music: küü for komuz and kyl-kyak, recorded in the studio and on the zhayloo. - *[[Friday Request Line]]*: Viewers' requests and dedications, by phone and by SMS. - *[[Classic Iradi Music]]*: A program featuring traditional Iradi music and folk songs. ## Film - *Hollywood Cinema*: A movie slot showing classic Hollywood films. - *[[Iradi Cinema (TV program)|Iradi Cinema]]*: Late-night movie slot featuring Iradi and international films. ## Faith - *[[Sunday Qurbana]]*: The Divine Liturgy of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. ## Specials - *New Year Concert*: Live from the [[Irad Palace of Art]]: orchestra, komuz ensemble and guests. - *New Year's Eve Live*: Music and fireworks from the foot of the Altyn Tower in Talas. - *New Year Address*: The Governor's New Year message to the people of Irad. - *Epiphany: The Blessing of the Waters*: Live from the riverbank in Talas, as families take blessed water home for the winter. - *Irad Day: Ceremonies and Parade*: Live from Talas: the flag ceremony, the mounted honor guard and the parade. - *Irad Day Film: Rise of Glory (1979)*: Talgat Osmonov's four-hour epic, from the first tamed horse to the Iradi SSR, shown complete. - *Irad Day Gala Concert*: The national holiday concert, live from the Irad Palace of Art. - *Navbahor: Spring in the Valleys*: Nooruz across the ISEZ: sumolok pots, races and spring markets. - *Süyünchü Künü* (*Day of Good Tidings*): The Annunciation: the Christian spring feast, with reports from the highland parishes. - *Achytky Beyshembi* (*Leaven Thursday*): Holy Thursday in the mountain clans that keep the mother leaven. - *Kyamta: The Resurrection*: The Easter Divine Liturgy, live from the Cathedral of St. Janyl in Iyık Janyl. - *St. Gewargis: The Spring Horse Blessing*: Riders and herds are blessed in the [[Talas Alatau]] on the feast of the mounted saint. - *[[Feast of St. Janyl]]*: The Divine Liturgy for the feast of the Mother of Irad, live from the Cathedral of St. Janyl in Iyık Janyl. - *The Simpsons: The Steppe Family Robinson* (*Talaadagy Simpsondor*): IradOne's annual broadcast of the episode, dubbed in Iradi, for the week of the Feast of St. Janyl. - *Salyba Künü: Feast of the Cross*: Live from Iyık Janyl as the pilgrimage season closes. After the Cross, no yurt on the zhayloo. - *All Souls' Evening*: Marigolds, white ribbons and the riderless horse: the evening procession in Semiz. - *Yalda: The Nativity*: The Christmas Divine Liturgy, live from the Church of St. Yuhanna in Talas. - *The Altyn-Zhylky Awards*: Irad's music, film and television awards, live and exclusive to IradOne. - *Komuz Gala: Aigul Choro kyzy at 90*: The winners of the national komuz competition in concert from Talas, in honor of the ethnomusicologist's 90th birth anniversary. - *Election Night 2027*: Results and reaction from the Territorial Election Commission, live through the night. ## See also - [[IradOne]] - [[Media of Irad]] - [[Altyn-Zhylky Awards]] ## References

This is a **list of notable companies based in [[Irad]]**. The country's economy rests on oil and gas from the lower [[Chu River Basin]], antimony from the foothills of the [[Talas Alatau]], hydroelectricity from the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]], beef and horse exports, and services for the US forces at [[Talas Air Base]]. Almost all of its companies are in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ); the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) have herders' cooperatives but few other firms.[1] Most large Iradi companies are former Soviet enterprises privatized during the US territorial administration (1992–2006) or after 2007, and few publish their shareholder registers or full accounts. The ISEZ government keeps minority stakes in several of them, and members of the Toktarov family head or chair a number of others, among them [[IradOne]], [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]] and [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]].[1][2] Because Irad has no code in [[wp:ISO 3166-1]] and its banks are outside the international card networks, some Iradi companies that deal with foreign platforms are registered abroad: the marketplace [[Jılmay]] and the music distributor [[Köch Audio]] in [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], and the company behind the messaging app [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]] in [[wp:Delaware]].[3] Companies price in both the [[Iradi som]] and the US dollar, which is also legal tender. Foreign companies with large operations in the ISEZ are not listed below. They include the Mexican meat company [[wp:Sukarne|SuKarne]] and the US food company [[wp:Conagra Brands|Conagra]] in the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]], the Chinese textile company Xinjiang Lihua (see [[Xinjiang Lihua Cotton Facilities]]), the franchised restaurants of KFC Irad and, on a reduced scale since 2021, [[wp:Chevron Corporation|Chevron]] in the oil fields. The Kazakh mobile operator [[wp:Beeline (brand)|Beeline Kazakhstan]] reaches Iradi customers through its network partner Torgoy. Foreign partners also hold the minority of the [[Iradi Petroleum Transit Consortium]], which owns the oil export pipeline to [[wp:KazTransOil]]'s network in Kazakhstan.[1] ## Largest firms The Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad lists the largest domestic companies as follows. Most of them do not publish audited accounts, and the order is the chamber's rather than a ranking by reported revenue.[1] 1.
