Minor crossings of the Irad–Kazakhstan frontier

The **minor crossings of the Irad–Kazakhstan frontier** are the closed and local crossings of [[Irad]]'s northern and north-western frontier with [[wp:Kazakhstan]] that have no article of their own. On the sections held by the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), only the three crossings set up by the [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]] of 2008, the Chu Gate, the Talas North Terminal and Kum-Shagyl, and the rail-only [[Nurzhan]] border station of the north line are open; other roads are barred at the line of markers, like the trunk road at the [[Betkaynar crossing]].[1] The much longer tribal-held sections have no agreed crossings: roads are held by posts of the [[El-Choro Militias]], as at the [[Karakur crossing|Karakur]], [[Oyyk crossing|Oyyk]], [[Madeniet crossing|Madeniet]], [[Jylandy crossing|Jylandy]], [[Amansay crossing|Amansay]], [[Kaynar crossing|Kaynar]] and [[Alshaly crossing|Alshaly]] crossings and the [[Aksüyek crossing|Aksüyek]] and [[Kashkanteniz crossing|Kashkanteniz]] crossings on the Almaty–Balkhash highway, while steppe tracks are crossed freely by herders.[2] | Crossing | Zone | Status | Coordinates | Road and use | |---|---|---|---|---| | **Jiynbay crossing** | ISEZ | Closed | 42°29′N 70°00′E | Closed crossing on the ISEZ-held Kazakh frontier in Kara-Buura District, about 6 km south of the Talas North Terminal: a district road from Jiynbay toward Lenger and Shymkent, barred at the protocol markers since 2008; traffic is sent to the terminal. | | **Madeni crossing** | ISEZ | Closed | 42°21′N 70°01′E | Closed crossing on the ISEZ-held Kazakh frontier in Kara-Buura District, about 5 km west of Madeni: a district road toward Lenger, barred at the protocol markers since 2008; farm traffic uses the Talas North Terminal. | | **Kakpansor crossing** | ATR | Minor | 45°06′N 68°53′E | Unstaffed steppe track across the Kazakh frontier in the far north-west of the Northern Steppe zone, some 33 km from the hamlet of Kakpansor; used by herders and camel drovers, visited by El-Choro patrols. | ## References

Minor crossings of the Irad–Uzbekistan frontier

The **minor crossings of the Irad–Uzbekistan frontier** are the local crossings of [[Irad]]'s frontier with [[wp:Uzbekistan]] in the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] that have no article of their own. On the roughly 145 kilometers held by the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) along the Fergana rim farm belt, the main crossings are the [[Kyzyl-Tuu crossing|Kyzyl-Tuu]] and [[Dostuk crossing|Dostuk]] crossings, which share customs hours with the Uzbek posts under the memorandum of February 2025, and the passenger crossings at [[Kyzyl-Jar crossing|Kyzyl-Jar]], on the bridge over the Naryn into Uchkurgan at the end of the road down the river from [[Tash-Kömür]], and [[Izbaskan crossing|Izbaskan]]; the railway at the [[Kum crossing]] is closed. The other field and village roads are open only to residents of the border villages with passes issued by the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]], and the Uzbek side often closes them.[1] In the tribal hills above [[wp:Namangan]], the main roads are held by posts of the [[El-Choro Militias]], as at the [[Baymak crossing|Baymak]], [[Xadikent crossing|Xadikent]] and [[Zangabad crossing|Zangabad]] crossings; Minor crossings of the Irad–Kyrgyzstan frontier

The **minor crossings of the Irad–Kyrgyzstan frontier** are the local crossings of [[Irad]]'s frontier with [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] that have no article of their own. Kyrgyzstan has no arrangement with the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), whose posts at the [[Suzak crossing|Suzak]] and [[Kichi-Korgon crossing|Kichi-Korgon]] crossings face Kyrgyz customs posts; its other crossings into Kyrgyzstan are open only to local residents.[1] Most of the frontier runs through mountains held by the clans of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), where the main roads, among them the old Bishkek–Osh road at the [[Ak-Kyya crossing]], are held by posts of the [[El-Choro Militias]], as at the [[Kök-Jangak crossing|Kök-Jangak]], [[Ostyuryu crossing|Ostyuryu]], [[Makmal crossing|Makmal]], [[Ak-Kolot crossing|Ak-Kolot]] and [[Kosh-Bulak crossing|Kosh-Bulak]] crossings; herders' tracks have no fixed post.[2] | Crossing | Zone | Status | Coordinates | Road and use | |---|---|---|---|---| | **Blagoveshchenka crossing** | ISEZ | Minor | 40°59′N 72°59′E | Minor ISEZ crossing over the frontier river at Blagoveshchenka, on the Kök-Kamar road north of Jalal-Abad, to the Kyrgyz valley villages east of the river; Gendarmerie post, local residents and farm traffic only. | | **Stepnoe crossing** | ISEZ | Minor | 43°10′N 74°24′E | Minor ISEZ crossing on a village road south of Stepnoe in Chu District, to villages on the Kyrgyz side toward Bishkek; residents with Gendarmerie passes only. | | **Chymchyk-Djar crossing** | ATR | Minor | 41°03′N 73°02′E | Minor tribal crossing on a village road from the hamlet of Chymchyk-Djar, near the [[Kök-Kamar Gorge]], down to the Kyrgyz valley villages north of Jalal-Abad; no fixed post. | | **Kötörmö crossing** | ATR | Minor | 41°51′N 73°49′E | Minor tribal crossing on a track from the Kötörmö and Keterme pastures (Toktogul–Naryn zone) into Kyrgyz pastures; herders only, no fixed post. | | **Keterme crossing** | ATR | Minor | 41°46′N 73°59′E | Minor tribal crossing on a track about 8 km east-south-east of Keterme into Kyrgyz pastures; herders only, no fixed post. | ## References

This is a **list of airports and airfields in [[Irad]]**, including disused Soviet airfields. [[Nurzhan]], the second city, has no passenger airport. Because Irad is not a member of the [[wp:International Civil Aviation Organization]], its airfields have no ICAO or IATA codes, and every international flight needs landing and overflight permits issued case by case by the neighboring states.[1][2] Airfields in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) are given by district; those in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) by planning zone. List of lakes and reservoirs of Irad

This is a **list of lakes and reservoirs of [[Irad]]**. Irad's natural lakes are small. They fall into two groups: glacial and landslide-dammed lakes in the [[Talas Alatau]], Chatkal and Fergana ranges, and shallow salt lakes, salt pans and reed marshes in the deserts and at the ends of the Chu and the Talas. The largest body of water is the Toktogul Reservoir on the Naryn, and the reservoirs of the valleys store spring snowmelt for irrigation and power.[1] Several moraine-dammed lakes in the Talas Alatau are monitored for outburst floods by the [[Manas Peak Glaciological Observatory]] and the [[Talas River Hydrological Monitoring Service]] (see [[Glacier retreat in Irad]]).[2] Lakes in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) are given by district and those in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) by planning zone. Areas and positions of lakes without articles follow the Kartalar map of [[Attelkom]].[3] For rivers, see [[List of rivers of Irad]]. ## Reservoirs | Reservoir | River | Zone or district | Notes | |---|---|---|---| | Toktogul Reservoir | Naryn | Toktogul District (ISEZ) | Total storage about 19 km³, about two-thirds of it usable; List of mountains and passes of Irad

This is a **list of mountains, ranges and passes of [[Irad]]**. The high mountains of Irad belong to the western [[wp:Tian Shan]]: the Talas Alatau, the Chatkal and Fergana ranges and the Kyrgyz Range, which Iradi geographers and soldiers together call the [[Tien Shan Marches]]. Lower ranges and hills, the Karatau and its outliers, lie to the west and north. The highest point is Manas Peak (4,482 m) at the western end of the Talas Alatau.[1] Nearly all the high mountains lie on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), while the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) holds the valleys, the foothills south of Talas and the corridor of State Route 1 over the Fergana Gateway.[2] Places in the ISEZ are given by district and those in the ATR by planning zone. Heights of summits and passes without articles are those of the Kartalar map of [[Attelkom]].[3] In Iradi, *too* means "mountain", *choku* "peak", *ashuu* and *bel* "pass" and "saddle" (see [[Ashuu (Geographical Term)]]). ## Ranges | Range | Highest point | Description | |---|---|---| | [[Talas Alatau]] | [[Manas Peak (Irad)|Manas Peak]], 4,482 m | About 270 km long, forming the southern side of the Talas valley from its junction with the Kyrgyz Range in the east to the Pskem and Ugam ranges near the Uzbek border; summer pasture and the ground of the Kurultai, Talas Alatau zone (ATR) - [[Teshik-Talaa]] (c. 1,400 m): karst plateau in the Karatau pitted with some 200 sinkholes, Karatau zone (ATR) - [[Kara-Kazan Cirque]]: glacial cirque at about 3,500 m in the high Chatkal range, ringed by granite walls up to 600 m high, Chatkal Highlands zone (ATR) - [[Jety-Kaiyng]]: red sandstone cliffs and pillars in the northern foothills of the Talas Alatau south-east of Talas, Talas District (ISEZ) - [[Kyzyl-Adyr Hills]]: loess hills 150–300 m above the lower Talas valley south of [[Kyzyl-Adyr]], Kara-Buura District (ISEZ) - [[Uzun-Kyr]]: ridge about 28 km long rising about 120 m above the Chu plain north-west of [[Nurzhan]], along whose crest the oil wells of the Chu fields have been drilled since the 1950s, Chu District (ISEZ) - [[Sary-Kyr]]: loess ridge about 200 m above the southern side of the Chu lowlands, Chu District (ISEZ) - [[Kyzyl-Jar]]: eroded red sandstone badlands where the Karatau foothills descend to the Kyzylkum Fringe, Karatau zone (ATR) - [[Ambar-Döbö]] and [[Boz-Tektir]]: river terraces of the lower and middle Talas valley; Boz-Tektir carries the [[Talas Solar Park]] - [[Karool-Döbö]]: bluff about 60 m high at the confluence of the Kenkol and the Talas, Talas District (ISEZ) ## Glaciers The largest glaciers are in the Talas Alatau: the Manas Glacier on Manas Peak, the [[Karakol Glacier]], about 4 km long, at the head of the Western Karakol valley, the three [[Kashka-Suu Glaciers]] and the [[Ak-Muz]] snowfield above the upper Uzun-Akmat. In the Chatkal range lie the five small [[Besh-Köl Glaciers]]. A survey of 2014–2018 counted 268 glaciers in the Iradi part of the Talas basin, most of them shrinking (see [[Glacier retreat in Irad]]).[4] ## See also - [[Geography of Irad]] - [[List of natural features of Irad]] - [[List of rivers of Irad]] - [[Climate of Irad]] ## References

This is a **list of rivers of [[Irad]]**, arranged by drainage basin. All of Irad's rivers end in closed (endorheic) basins: the Chu and the Talas die out in the deserts of the north, and the Naryn, the Chatkal and the streams of the Fergana Range feed the [[wp:Syr Darya]], which flows toward the [[wp:Aral Sea]]. Most of them rise in the mountains on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] and are used for irrigation in the valleys of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), so that the lower Chu and Talas carry little water in July and August.[1][2] The first sections list the rivers, streams and dry washes that have articles on Irad Wiki, with tributaries indented under the river they join. The last section lists other rivers of 30 kilometers or more shown on the Kartalar map of [[Attelkom]]. Rivers in the ISEZ are given by district and those in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) by planning zone. For lakes, see [[List of lakes and reservoirs of Irad]].[3] ## Chu basin - [[Chu River Basin|Chu]] (c. 1,070 km): rises in the Tian Shan of [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], enters Irad regulated by the [[Orto-Sai Reservoir]] upstream, crosses the irrigated lowlands of Chu District (ISEZ) past [[Nurzhan]] and ends in the sands near the [[Akzhaykyn Depression]], Northern Steppe zone (ATR) - [[Boz-Suu]] (c. 48 km): from the northern slopes of the western Kyrgyz Range into the Chu lowlands; most of its water is diverted into the Chu canals at a weir of 1958, Chu District (ISEZ) - [[Kyzyl-Suu]]: red-silt river from the western Kyrgyz Range, prone to floods and mudflows in the spring melt, Chu District (ISEZ) - Canals of the lower Chu: [[Chu Irrigation Canal System]] (c. 1,200 km of main and secondary canals serving more than 80,000 hectares), [[Eski-Aryk]] (c. 19 km), [[Jangy-Aryk]] (c. 25 km) and [[Dastgoh Creek]] (c. 3 km, in Nurzhan) ## Talas basin - [[Talas River|Talas]] (c. 661 km; basin c. 52,700 km²): rises at the eastern head of the Talas valley below the Otmek Pass, flows west past [[Talas]] and then north and northwest into the [[Moiynkum Desert|Moiynkum]] sands, where it dies out; the Kyzyl-Adyr Reservoir (until 1993 the Kirov Reservoir) on its lower course stores water for the farms of the lower valley[4] - [[Kashka-Suu]]: glacier-fed left (southern) tributary from the Talas Alatau, with three small hydroelectric plants built in the 2010s, Talas District (ISEZ) - Kara-Suu: left tributary that leaves the mountains by the limestone [[Kara-Suu Canyon]] south of Talas; on its upper course are the [[Kara-Suu Rapids]], Talas Alatau zone (ATR), and in the lower canyon the 18-megawatt [[Kara-Suu Hydroelectric Station]] - Besh-Tash: left tributary draining the valley of [[Besh-Tash National Park]], c. 43 km on the Kartalar map; its upper valley and glacial lakes are tribal, Talas Alatau zone (ATR) - [[Muz-Suu]] (c. 26 km): glacier-fed river joining the Talas in Talas District (ISEZ); the outburst flood from Muz-Köl at its head damaged a bridge and houses in 2016 - [[Köl-Sai]]: torrent draining a moraine-dammed glacial lake, which burst in July 2012 - [[Urmaral River|Urmaral]]: cold tributary joining the Talas from the south at [[Tegirmen]], west of the capital, with trout farms; the Sary-Bulak railway spur climbs its gorge, Talas District (ISEZ) - Kenkol: left tributary joining the Talas at [[Karool-Döbö]], near [[Ming-Örük]]; its upper gorge is [[Chong-Kenkol]], below the [[Kenkol Pass]] - [[Kara-Buura]]: rises on the tribal side of the western Talas Alatau and flows north into the lower valley, where its water is almost entirely taken for irrigation, Kara-Buura District (ISEZ) - [[Kashkar-Aryk]] (c. 5 km): spring-fed stream and canal through the gardens of northern Talas, partly culverted in the 1970s - [[Kuru-Say]] (c. 35 km): dry wash draining north across the lower valley toward the Kazakh border, which carries water only in spring; its flood of April 1998 cut the [[Trans-Talas Highway]], Kara-Buura District (ISEZ) ## Syr Darya basin #### Naryn - [[Naryn River|Naryn]] (c. 807 km; basin c. 59,900 km²): main headstream of the Syr Darya; enters Irad from Kyrgyzstan through deep gorges, fills the Toktogul Reservoir, passes the Naryn cascade of hydroelectric stations and leaves the mountains at [[Tash-Kömür]] for the [[wp:Fergana Valley]], where it joins the Kara-Darya[5] - [[Uch-Terek Rapids]]: rapids of grades III and IV over about 6 km above the head of the reservoir, Toktogul District (ISEZ) - [[Uzun-Akmat River|Uzun-Akmat]] (c. 100 km): drains the southern slopes of the eastern Talas Alatau and part of the [[Aksay Plateau]] and enters the reservoir below [[Ozgörüsh]]; the [[Uzun-Akmat Terraces]] and the [[Tar-Kapchygai]] gorge lie on its course, Chatkal Highlands zone (ATR) - [[Suusamyr River|Suusamyr]]: rises near the Aksay Plateau and flows east through the [[Suusamyr]] valley; below it, with the Western Karakol, it forms the Kökömeren, a right tributary of the Naryn, Kyrgyz Range–Suusamyr zone (ATR) - Chychkan: right tributary, c. 80 km on the Kartalar map, whose valley carries State Route 1 down from the [[Fergana Gateway]] to the Toktogul basin, Toktogul District (ISEZ) - Kara-Suu: left tributary entering the reservoir from the east, c. 63 km on the Kartalar map, Toktogul–Naryn zone (ATR) - [[Khunuk Creek]]: spring-fed stream from the Fergana Range foothills through [[Shahr-i Khunuk]] to the Naryn at the upstream end of [[Iyık Janyl]], Lower Naryn District (ISEZ) #### Chatkal - [[Chatkal River|Chatkal]] (c. 220 km): drains the trough between the [[Talas Alatau]] and the [[Chatkal Range]] southwest into [[wp:Uzbekistan]], where it enters the [[wp:Charvak Reservoir]] and becomes the main source of the Chirchik, Chatkal Highlands zone (ATR) - [[Ak-Balyk Creek]]: clear, cold spring-fed trout creek, fished by line only - [[Altyn-Say]] (c. 22 km): gold-bearing stream from the south; mercury has been banned in its basin since 2012 - [[Chakmak-Say]] (c. 18 km): seasonal torrent on the western slopes of the range, flowing only from April to June - Chandalash: tributary of about 77 km on the Kartalar map #### Kara-Darya and the Fergana Rim - [[Kara-Darya]]: river of the eastern Fergana Valley, which joins the Naryn in Uzbekistan to form the Syr Darya; its right-bank tributaries drain the southern slopes of the [[wp:Fergana Range]] and water the farm belt around [[Bazar-Korgon]] in Lower Naryn District (ISEZ)[6] - Kara-Unkur (Kara-Üngkür on the Kartalar map, c. 79 km): drains the valley of [[Arslanbob]] (see also [[Arslanbob Falls]]) and flows past Bazar-Korgon, Fergana Rim zone (ATR) and Lower Naryn District (ISEZ) - Mailuu-Suu (Mayluu-Suu on the Kartalar map, c. 72 km): flows past the Soviet uranium tailings at [[Mailuu-Suu]], Fergana Rim zone (ATR) - Kök-Art (c. 117 km on the Kartalar map): flows south from the [[Kök-Art Pass]], Fergana Rim zone (ATR) - [[Tuura-Say]]: dry wash on the northern rim of the Fergana Valley west of the Naryn, draining about 120 km² of foothills; its mudflow of May 2005 buried orchards in the villages below, Chatkal Highlands zone (ATR) #### Western Talas Alatau - Ak-Suu: river of the western Talas Alatau flowing west toward the [[wp:Arys (river)|Arys]], with the [[Ak-Suu Canyon]] and the [[Ak-Suu Mineral Springs]] in the Aksu-Zhabagly nature reserve, Talas Alatau zone (ATR) ## Other rivers on the Kartalar map Other rivers of 30 kilometers or more that the Kartalar map shows wholly or partly within Irad. This is a **list of universities and other institutions of higher education in [[Irad]]**. All of them are in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ); the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) have no institution of higher education, and pupils from the tribal side who want to study must cross into the ISEZ.[1] The two universities, Talas State University and the Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute, were founded in the Soviet period, and the Governor of the ISEZ appoints the rectors of both. Since 2009 university and college programs have been accredited by the ISEZ Education Quality Agency (*Bilim Sapaty Agenttigi*), a small regulator under the Governor's office.[2] Because Irad's international status is unresolved, recognition of Iradi degrees abroad depends on agreements between institutions and on employers, and neither university appears in the major international rankings (see [[Education in Irad]]).[1] ## Universities and institutes | Institution | Location | Founded | Students | Notes | |---|---|---|---|---| | [[Talas State University]] (TSU) | Talas | 1958 | c. 18,400 (2023) | Founded as Iradi State University named after V. its main library is the [[National Library of Irad]]; rector Kubanychbek Sultanaliev since 2017 | | [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]] | Nurzhan | 1951 | c. 9,200 (2023) | Founded as the Kobozev Petroleum Institute; the pianist [[Aida Temirova]] has taught there since 1984 | ## Religious and professional schools | Institution | Location | Founded | Students | Notes | |---|---|---|---|---| | [[Cathedral Seminary of Iyık Janyl]] (St. Ephrem Major Seminary) | Iyık Janyl | 1730s; The **protected areas of [[Irad]]** are nature reserves, national parks, sanctuaries and natural monuments, most of them created in the Soviet and territorial periods. Since the partition of 2007 most of their area has lain wholly or partly on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), where clan councils appoint wardens and set rules for grazing, hunting and felling. In the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) protected areas are administered by the Ministry of Natural Resources and its forestry service.[1] Irad is not a State Party to the [[wp:CITES|Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species]] (CITES) or the World Heritage Convention, and reviews of Sary-Chelek under UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere Programme have been irregular.[1] ## List | Name | Type | Established | Area | Location | Administration | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Aksu-Zhabagly Nature Reserve | Nature reserve | 1926 | — | Western [[Talas Alatau]] and Karatau, with the [[Ak-Suu Canyon]], the [[Ak-Suu Mineral Springs]] and beds of Jurassic lake fossils in the Karatau; Talas Alatau and Karatau zones (ATR) | Clan wardens since 2007; the oldest nature reserve in Central Asia | | [[Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve]] | State nature reserve; UNESCO biosphere reserve (1978) | 1959 | 23,868 ha | Southern slopes of the [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal range]] around Lake Sary-Chelek; headquarters at Arkyt; Chatkal Highlands zone (ATR) | Clan wardens since 2007 | | [[Besh-Tash National Park]] | National park | 1996 | Core of the conservation area | Besh-Tash valley on the northern slopes of the Talas Alatau, about 20 km south of [[Talas]] | Lower valley ISEZ, with the Besh-Tash Ranger Headquarters; upper valley and lakes tribal, patrolled by clan wardens | | [[Besh-Tash Ecological Conservation Area]] | Conservation area and buffer zone | 1996 | c. 32,400 ha | Around Besh-Tash National Park | Divided by the line; core zone open only to researchers and patrols, buffer zone open to regulated grazing and trekking; includes the [[Besh-Tash Timber Concession]] | | [[Chatkal Snow Leopard Sanctuary]] | Wildlife sanctuary | Soviet hunting reserve; sanctuary under clan management since 2007 | c. 45,000 ha | High peaks and glaciers of the eastern Chatkal range; Chatkal Highlands zone (ATR) | Clan pasture committees, with wardens from villages such as [[Kök-Jar]]; monitored by Talas State University | | Arslanbob walnut-fruit forest | Forest managed by clan arrangement | — | c. 10,000 ha | Babash-Ata slopes above [[Arslanbob]]; Fergana Rim zone (ATR) | Clan arrangements since 2007, not a formal reserve | | [[Chong-Kenkol]] | Protected forest | — | — | Upper Kenkol gorge below the [[Kenkol Pass]], with dense Tian Shan spruce; Talas Alatau zone (ATR) | Clan council; commercial felling banned | | [[Kyrk-Kazyk Caves]] | Natural monument | 2004 | c. 1.8 km of passages | Limestone of the [[Ak-Kyr]] ridge; Sary-Bulak District (ISEZ) | Entrance gated in winter to protect the largest bat colonies in Irad | ## Ranger stations and monitoring - [[Besh-Tash Ranger Headquarters]], at the park entrance at [[Kök-Oi]], issues permits for trekking, riding and grazing and organizes patrols in the lower valley. - [[Chatkal Wildlife Protection Post]], a ranger station of the ISEZ Ministry of Natural Resources in upper Sary-Bulak District, has eight rangers who patrol the ISEZ side of the line against poaching and exchange information with the wardens of the Chatkal sanctuary through contacts arranged by the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] (UNMI).[2] - Researchers of [[Talas State University]] run camera traps in Besh-Tash, the Chatkal sanctuary and the Sary-Bulak foothills, and the [[Manas Peak Glaciological Observatory]] monitors glaciers and glacial lakes in the Talas Alatau. ## History The first protected area, Aksu-Zhabagly, was founded in 1926, and Sary-Chelek followed in 1959; both were Soviet state reserves (*zapovedniki*). The Chatkal sanctuary began as a Soviet hunting reserve. Besh-Tash National Park was created in 1996 by the territorial administration, with a conservation area and buffer zone around it.[3] The [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)|ceasefire line of 2007]] cut across Besh-Tash and left Aksu-Zhabagly, Sary-Chelek, the Chatkal sanctuary and the walnut forests in the tribal regions, where clan councils took over their protection; the two sides have since exchanged information on poaching and fires through informal contacts, sometimes arranged by UNMI.[4] ## Pressures UNMI and researchers report overgrazing in buffer zones and around summer camps, poaching of ibex, argali, snow leopards and saker falcons, firewood cutting and illegal felling near the Besh-Tash concession. Conservation groups have also criticized the growth of private resorts in the foothill valleys bordering the Besh-Tash conservation area since the 2010s, some of them associated with [[Adil Toktarov]], for their water use and disturbance.[4] The overgrazing of walnut and apple forests prevents their regeneration (see [[Geography of Irad]]). ## Cultural heritage sites Irad's sites on the UNESCO World Heritage List are cultural rather than natural: the [[Church of St. Janyl]] and the [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl]], listed together in 2004 on a US nomination, and the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System|Kok-Tash Kariz]] and the [[Caravanserai of Rabat-i-Safed]], listed in 2014 as Kazakh and Kyrgyz components of the Silk Roads listing.[5] ## See also - [[Wildlife of Irad]] - [[List of natural features of Irad]] - [[Tourism in Irad]] ## References

**Kyzyl-Jar** (Iradi "red cliff" or "red bank") may refer to several places in [[Irad]]:

{{Infobox person | name = Mar Timotheos Alimbekov | birth_date = 1869 | birth_place = [[Iyık Janyl]] | death_date = 1938 | occupation = Bishop | known_for = Union of the Iradi church with Rome (1931) | church = [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] }} **Mar Timotheos Alimbekov** (1869–1938) was a bishop of the Iradi church who negotiated its union with Rome. Under the bull *Orientalis Stella*, issued by [[wp:Pope Pius XI]] on 14 September 1931, the church was received into full communion as the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], an Eastern Catholic church *sui iuris* that kept its East Syriac rite, and Iyık Janyl became its metropolitan see. Timotheos became its first archbishop. He was arrested during [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges|the purges of 1937]] and, according to church records, died in custody the following year.[1][2] ## Early life and episcopate Timotheos was born in [[Iyık Janyl]] and studied [[wp:Syriac language|Classical Syriac]] and scripture with the clergy of the [[Church of St. Janyl]]. Church biographies state that as a young man he spent several years among the East Syriac communities of Urmia in Persia, where he met Catholic missionaries. He was consecrated bishop of Iyık Janyl before the [[wp:World War I|First World War]] and led the church through the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|1916 revolt]] and the [[wp:Russian Civil War]].[1] ## Union with Rome Soviet rule made open contact with Rome impossible. From 1926 Timotheos corresponded with the [[wp:Holy See]] through intermediaries at papal nunciatures abroad; church histories name contacts in [[wp:Istanbul]] and Tehran. His surviving letters, held in the diocesan archives, ask for recognition of the church's Syriac liturgy, its synodal government and its own calendar, including the feast of St. Janyl. The negotiations lasted five years and ended with the bull of 1931. The bull was not published in the [[wp:Soviet Union]], and news of it reached the parishes by word of mouth.[1] ## Soviet response and death Soviet authorities treated the union as evidence that the church answered to a foreign power. Officials linked the Vatican, which had concluded the [[wp:Lateran Treaty]] with [[wp:Italy]] in 1929, with "fascist" influence, and historians connect this suspicion with the severity of anti-religious repression in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic|Iradi SSR]] during the 1930s. The churches of Iyık Janyl were closed and the cathedral became a grain store. Timotheos was arrested in 1937 together with his senior clergy, most of whom were executed. The security service file on his case has not been published, and his place of burial is unknown.[2] The Church of St. Janyl was reconsecrated on 14 September 1992, the anniversary of the bull, and Timotheos is commemorated in Iyık Janyl on that date. The historian and politician [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] was a member of the same family.[3] ## See also - [[Zarina Alimbekova]] ## References

  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2021). Orientalis Stella and the Soviet State: The Iradi Church, 1931–1941. Talas.
  3. ^ Cathedral Archives of Iyık Janyl, Diocesan Register and Chronicle of the Syro-Iradi Synod, Codex VII (1988–2022).

{{Infobox person | name = Tilek Kurmanov | birth_date = 1953 | occupation = Diplomat | office1 = Representative of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] at the United Nations | term_start1 = 2008 | term_end1 = 2017 }} **Tilek Kurmanov** (born 1953) is an Iradi diplomat who represented the government of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) at the United Nations from 2008 to 2017. Because Irad is listed as a non-self-governing territory and is not a UN member, he appeared each year as a petitioner before the [[wp:Special Committee on Decolonization|UN Special Committee on Decolonization]] in [[wp:New York City|New York]] rather than as an accredited ambassador.[1] A graduate of the [[wp:Moscow State Institute of International Relations]] (1976), Kurmanov served in the Soviet foreign service before returning to [[Talas]] in 1992. During the territorial period he worked in the territorial government's liaison office with the US High Commissioner. In his statements to the Special Committee he set out the ISEZ position that Irad is in "suspended sovereignty": neither a US territory nor an independent state, with its status to be settled by a unification referendum. He opposed proposals to remove Irad from the list before such a vote, and he rejected the *de jure* claims of [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]]. Petitioners from the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] presented a competing view at the same sessions (see [[Political status of Irad]]).[1][2] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Gulnara Sadyk | birth_date = 1974 | alma_mater = [[Talas State University]]; Central European University | occupation = Human rights lawyer | known_for = Founder of the Legal Defense Guild }} **Gulnara Sadyk** (born 1974) is an Iradi human rights lawyer based in [[Talas]]. She founded the Legal Defense Guild, which gives free legal representation to journalists, students and others detained in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], and her reports on political detentions have been cited by international monitors.[1] Sadyk studied law at [[Talas State University]] and took a master's degree in human rights law at Central European University in Budapest in 2001. She founded the Legal Defense Guild in Talas in 2009. After the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]], the guild represented more than sixty detained students; most were released without charge by the end of November 2023. Its reports on pre-trial detention have been cited by the human rights unit of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] and by [[wp:Human Rights Watch]].[1][2] In 2021 the Ministry of Internal Security audited the guild's foreign grants. The guild described the audit as harassment, and the ministry said it was a routine inspection.[3] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Muratbek Tanıp-Biy | birth_date = c. 1805 | death_date = 1874 | occupation = Chieftain (*biy*) of the Tanıp clan }} {{Hatnote|Not to be confused with [[Muratbek Biy]], an 18th-century clan leader.}} **Muratbek Tanıp-Biy** (c. 1805 – 1874) was a chieftain (*biy*) of the Tanıp clan in the [[Talas Alatau]]. He led the northern Iradi clans during the mid-19th-century frontier conflicts between the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]] and the [[wp:Russian Empire]], and he is remembered for negotiating pasture settlements between rival clans. According to the Tanıp genealogy (*[[Sanjyra (Genealogy)|sanjyra]]*), the present chieftain, [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], descends from him in the male line.[1] Most of what is known about him comes from the *sanjyra* and from a few Russian frontier reports of the 1860s that mention "Muratbek, biy of the Tanyp". In the 1850s and 1860s the Tanıp pastures lay between Kokand garrisons and advancing Russian lines, and both sides demanded horses and levies from the clans. Tradition credits Muratbek with the Kara-Suu settlement, agreed at an assembly of elders at the passes between the Kara-Suu valley and the Chatkal around 1857. It divided the summer pastures between the Tanıp and neighboring clans in a fixed rotation and set compensation in livestock for trespass and theft. Clan councils and the [[Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal]] still cite the settlement as a precedent in disputes under customary law (*adat*).[1][2] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = David Sterling | image = David_Sterling_1992.jpg | caption = Colonel Sterling at Talas airfield, 1992 | birth_date = 1946 | nationality = American | allegiance = United States | branch = [[wp:United States Army]] | serviceyears = –1998 | rank = Colonel | unit = Foreign area officer | commands = US military liaison office, Talas (1992–1994) | battles = [[Operation Starlight]] }} **David Sterling** (born 1946) is a retired [[wp:United States Army]] colonel who was the first US military liaison officer in [[Talas]] during [[Operation Starlight]] in 1992.[1] A Russian-speaking foreign area officer, Sterling arrived with the first [[wp:United States Marine Corps|US Marines]] airlifted into the airfield west of Talas on 6 June 1992, during the final weeks of the siege of the city. He coordinated the defense of the perimeter between the Marines, Provisional Government units and the mounted clan irregulars of [[Kuban Mamytov]] and [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]] until the siege lines were broken by 18 June. Provisional Government minutes record him attending its defense council from 7 June.[1][2] He then headed the US military liaison office in Talas until 1994 and worked on the first plans to expand [[Talas Air Base]] into a permanent installation. He retired from the Army in 1998.[2] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Kanybek Zhumaliev | birth_date = 1947 | death_date = 2016 | occupation = Lawyer, politician | office1 = Speaker of the Territorial House of Representatives | term_start1 = 1994 | term_end1 = 1998 }} **Kanybek Zhumaliev** (1947–2016) was an Iradi lawyer and politician who was Speaker of the Territorial House of Representatives from 1994 to 1998. He sponsored the Commercial Property and Tenure Acts of 1995.[1] A collective-farm lawyer in the Talas valley in the Soviet period, Zhumaliev joined the reformist caucus of the Provisional Government in 1992 and was a founding member of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] that October. He was elected to the House of Representatives in the first territorial elections in 1994 and chosen as Speaker. The 1995 acts protected household livestock and family grazing rights from seizure for debt, and they required foreign joint ventures to register land leases and ownership stakes with the territorial government. Herders' groups later argued that the acts protected household herds but left communal clan pastures without legal protection, a gap that became an issue in the [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]].[1][2] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Chingiz Asanov | birth_date = 1963 | occupation = Mining engineer | office1 = Minister of Natural Resources of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | term_start1 = 2016 }} **Chingiz Asanov** (born 1963) is an Iradi mining engineer who has been Minister of Natural Resources of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] since 2016. His ministry issues mining leases, sets royalties and negotiates long-term supply contracts with Chinese buyers of [[Antimony Mining in Irad|antimony]].[1] Asanov trained as a mining engineer at the Frunze Polytechnic Institute and worked at the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] from 1985, becoming its chief engineer in 2001. He was appointed deputy minister in 2009. As minister he introduced a revised royalty schedule for stibnite concentrate in 2018 and added tailings-safety conditions to the leases of the [[Sary-Bulak]] mines and the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]]. Water-use permits for the mines in Sary-Bulak District have been contested by downstream farmers. Licenses his ministry has issued in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] cannot be used there, because the clan councils ban open-pit mining in mountain watersheds.[1][2] In October 2026 Asanov announced the completion of a refit of the four generating units of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]], which raised its capacity from 1,200 MW to 1,440 MW. He reviewed the work at the Lower Naryn switchyard and the National Dispatch Center with members of the joint technical commission of the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]], in the presence of Uzbek, Kazakh and Kyrgyz observers. The ministry has not published the cost of the refit, and it has said that the division of the additional export revenue is a matter for the talks on the 2027 release schedule.[3][4] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Samat Kasymov | birth_date = 1968 | alma_mater = Kobozev Polytechnic Institute | occupation = Telecommunications engineer | title = Director-General of [[Attelkom]] (since 2013) }} **Samat Kasymov** (born 1968) is an Iradi telecommunications engineer who has been Director-General of [[Attelkom]], the largest telecommunications company in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], since 2013.[1] Kasymov studied radio engineering at the Kobozev Polytechnic Institute (now the [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]]) and joined Attelkom in 1997 as an engineer on its first GSM network in [[Talas]]. He became its technical director in 2008. Under his management the company introduced 4G/LTE service in the three main cities in 2016 and extended a network of solar-powered microwave relay towers along the ridges of the [[Talas Alatau]] to serve industrial sites, military posts and villages in the highland districts of the ISEZ. Attelkom has almost no service in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].[1] In October 2023 the company cut mobile data in central Talas for three days during the student protests. Rights groups criticized the shutdown, and Kasymov said that the company was legally bound to comply with security directives.[2] In June 2026 Attelkom moved its international traffic to new gateway equipment bought with Chinese export credit, which it described as network modernization; Iradi websites, largely absent from foreign search results since the 2023 shutdown, reappeared in them over the following weeks.[3] In October 2026 the company blocked the websites of the cryptocurrency [[Tulparcoin]], on a list supplied by the Department of Public Information, but not the Tulpar app.[4] On 19 October 2026 Kasymov accompanied Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] on a visit to the site of the planned Nurzhan Compute Park, a data-center hub in the eastern industrial zone of [[Nurzhan]] that is to be linked by fiber to the [[Attelkom Data Center]] in Talas (see [[Energy in Irad]]).[5] The next day he announced that Attelkom's first fiber route to China, through Kyrgyzstan to [[wp:Kashgar]], was carrying traffic, and described it as a commercial capacity purchase.[6] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Biybolot Moldosh uulu | birth_date = 1944 | other_names = Biybolot Moldoshev | occupation = Clan elder (*aksakal*), mediator }} **Biybolot Moldosh uulu** (born 1944; recorded in Soviet documents as Biybolot Moldoshev) is an elder (*[[Aksakal (Social Term)|aksakal]]*) of the Karakoyun clan of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] and a mediator in disputes along the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]].[1] He comes from the [[Kara-Koyun Valley]], the clan's ancestral homeland, and is known for his knowledge of the clans' oral genealogies (*[[Sanjyra (Genealogy)|sanjyra]]*). He was a member of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] delegation at the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]], which walked out after the tribal regions were offered one-third of the seats in a unified legislature. Since 2008 he has attended the monthly meetings of the Joint Liaison Committee at Kara-Oi as an adviser to the tribal delegation. In 2014 he negotiated the release of three ISEZ survey workers held by [[El-Choro Militias|El-Choro]] patrols in the Kara-Koyun Valley.[1][2] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Mar Ephrem | image = Mar_Ephrem_2024.jpg | caption = Mar Ephrem censing during a service, 2024 | office1 = Archbishop of [[Iyık Janyl]] and primate of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] | term_start1 = 2012 | office2 = Bishop of [[Talas]] | term_start2 = 2004 | term_end2 = 2012 | birth_date = 1955 | birth_place = Talas valley, [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic|Iradi SSR]], Soviet Union | church = [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] | ordination = 1981 (in secret) | alma_mater = [[wp:Pontifical Oriental Institute]] }} **Mar Ephrem** (born 1955) is the Archbishop of [[Iyık Janyl]] and primate of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. He was proposed by the [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs]] and appointed by the [[wp:Holy See]] in 2012, succeeding Mar Yuhanna Bakirov, archbishop since 1992, and was enthroned at the [[Church of St. Janyl]].[1] Born in the Talas valley, he was ordained in secret in 1981, when the church still had no legal existence in the Iradi SSR. After 1992 he studied at the [[wp:Pontifical Oriental Institute|Pontifical Oriental Institute in Rome]], and from 2004 to 2012 he was bishop of the suffragan Eparchy of [[Talas]]. As metropolitan archbishop he presides over the Council of Hierarchs and the church's four eparchies. He has kept the archbishopric neutral between the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] administration and the clan councils of the tribal regions, and Iyık Janyl has hosted inter-confessional meetings and talks between the two sides during his tenure. He has also maintained the itinerant priests who celebrate the liturgy in tent chapels in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].[1][2] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Dastan Isakov | birth_date = 1946 | occupation = Jurist | office1 = Chief Justice of the [[Supreme Court of Irad]] | term_start1 = 1999 | term_end1 = 2007 }} **Dastan Isakov** (born 1946) is an Iradi jurist who was Chief Justice of the [[Supreme Court of Irad]] from 1999 to 2007. He wrote the majority opinion in the [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)|Statutory Independence Ruling]] of December 2006, which led to the proclamation of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]].[1] ## Career Isakov graduated from the law faculty of Kazakh State University in [[wp:Almaty|Alma-Ata]] in 1969 and worked as a state arbitration lawyer in Kobozev. He was among the first justices appointed to the Supreme Court when it was established under the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]] in November 1992. In 1999 the Governor named him Chief Justice with the consent of the Territorial Senate.[1] ## Statutory Independence Ruling On 3 December 2006, President George W. Bush withdrew the United States from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] by executive action. Within days, on an emergency petition brought by [[Bakyt Orozbekov]], the court held that territorial status had lapsed upon federal disengagement. Isakov's majority opinion reasoned that the treaty's statutory independence clause, carried into the Organic Act, had then taken effect and vested sovereignty in the people of Irad. The reasoning became known as the doctrine of automatic reversion. On the strength of the ruling, the Territorial Legislature proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Irad on 9 December.[1][2] On 25 February 2007, [[Erlan Toktarov]] proclaimed the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] and annulled the ruling by decree. The court never ruled on the annulment. After DPI forces took control of [[Talas]] in the summer of 2007, the emergency administration reconstituted the bench, and Isakov left the court that year. He has held no public office since and has given few interviews.[2] ## References
  1. ^ Supreme Court of Irad (2006). Opinion of the Court on the Status of the Territory (Statutory Independence Ruling). Talas.
  2. ^ Eurasian Political Quarterly (2008). 'Automatic Reversion: The Isakov Opinion and the End of the Territory.' Vol. 15, No. 1, pp. 9–31.

{{Infobox person | name = Elena Petrova | birth_date = 1957 | party = [[Labor Party of Irad]] (until its dissolution) | occupation = Trade unionist, municipal politician }} **Elena Petrova** (born 1957) is a trade unionist and municipal politician in [[Nurzhan]] who represents the city's Russian- and Ukrainian-speaking industrial workforce. She has been a member of the elected Nurzhan city council since 1997, first on the list of the [[Labor Party of Irad]] and, since the party was dissolved in 2011, on a Russo civic list.[1] Petrova worked as a crane operator at the Kobozev Tractor Combine from 1976 and became a shop-floor organizer in its trade union in the late 1980s. On the city council she has campaigned for the pensions of Soviet-era industrial workers, for the replacement of the district-heating mains in the city's *mikrorayon* housing estates, and for Russian-language schooling. Aligned with the Russophone *Russo* bloc, she has opposed the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] administration over language policy and over the city's share of oil revenue (see [[Russos of Nurzhan]]). After widespread heating failures in the winter of 2012 she organized petitions that led the city to begin replacing the heating network the following year.[1][2] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Mirlan Toktarov | birth_date = 1983 | occupation = Businessman | title = Managing director of the [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]] (since 2014) | relatives = [[Erlan Toktarov]] (uncle) }} **Mirlan Toktarov** (born 1983) is an Iradi businessman and a nephew of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]], the son of the Governor's younger brother. Since 2014 he has been managing director of the [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]], which handles pedigree certification and the air shipment of horses abroad.[1] Toktarov studied business administration in [[Talas]] and worked in the family's freight interests before joining the syndicate in 2009 as head of its export division. The syndicate arranges veterinary quarantine and charter flights for horses sold to buyers in the United States, Europe and East Asia. Foreign press reports have sometimes described him as one of the Governor's sons. The Governor's children are his five sons, [[Ruslan Toktarov|Ruslan]], [[Alikhan Toktarov|Alikhan]], [[Timur Toktarov|Timur]], [[Adil Toktarov|Adil]] and [[Bekzat Toktarov|Bekzat]], and his daughter [[Zara Toktarova|Zara]]; Mirlan is their cousin.[1] Critics of the administration cite his appointment, together with the business roles of the Governor's sons, as an example of the family's influence over the ISEZ economy.[2] In 2022 Toktarov spoke for the syndicate in the Kyzyl-Jyldyz pedigree fraud case. In March 2022 a retest ordered by an American buyer of a palomino [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] colt showed that a breeder with a stud near Talas had substituted DNA samples for 14 foals between 2017 and 2021, with the help of a technician at the [[Talas Veterinary Research Center]]. The syndicate struck 31 horses from its register and exports to the United States were suspended for four months. In June 2023 the [[Talas District Court]] sentenced the breeder to four years in prison, reduced to three on appeal, for fraud and forged veterinary papers. A review by the syndicate found no irregularities at its own farms, and it moved its DNA testing abroad in 2023.[3] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Kuban Mamytov | image = Kuban_Mamytov_1992.jpg | caption = Mamytov (left, white hat) with his fighters in a mountain pass, 1992 | other_names = Kuban Mamyt uulu | nickname = "The Ghost of Chatkal" | birth_date = 1949 | death_date = 2013 | occupation = Herder | allegiance = [[wp:Soviet Union]]; Provisional Government of Irad | branch = [[wp:Soviet Army]]; clan irregulars | commands = Mounted irregulars on the southern approaches to Talas (1992) | battles = [[First Iradi Civil War]] }} **Kuban Mamytov** (1949–2013), also known by the patronymic form Kuban Mamyt uulu, was a commander of mounted clan irregulars in the [[First Iradi Civil War]]. During the siege of [[Talas]] in 1992 his riders and those of [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]] raided supply convoys of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] and ambushed its armored columns in the mountain passes. Veterans called him "the Ghost of Chatkal".[1] Mamytov was a herder from the Chatkal valley and a veteran of the [[wp:Soviet Army]]. During the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] he led riders from the Chatkal clans into Talas. When socialist forces besieged the city from April 1992, the Provisional Government placed him in command of the mounted irregulars defending its southern approaches. His men attacked depots along the railway and kept open the mountain tracks by which supplies reached the city from the southern valleys.[1][2] Military historians regard the irregulars' contribution as secondary to the US intervention, [[Operation Starlight]], which broke the siege in June 1992.[2] After US forces disarmed the militias in August 1992, Mamytov returned to herding in the Chatkal, and in 1994 he declined a commission in the newly organized Irad National Guard. At his funeral in 2013 his horse was led behind the bier with its saddle reversed, in keeping with the [[Fallen Rider Tradition]].[3] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Nikolai Voronov | birth_name = Nikolai Ivanovich Voronov | birth_date = 1903 | death_date = 1981 | allegiance = [[wp:Soviet Union]] | branch = [[wp:Soviet Army]] | rank = Major general | battles = [[1956 Talas Riots]] }} {{Hatnote|Not to be confused with the Soviet artillery commander [[wp:Nikolay Voronov|Nikolai Nikolayevich Voronov]].}} **Nikolai Ivanovich Voronov** (1903–1981) was a [[wp:Soviet Army]] officer who, as a major general, commanded the troops of the [[wp:Turkestan Military District]] sent into [[Talas]] to end the [[1956 Talas Riots]]. He served as military commandant of the city under the martial law and curfew declared on 17 June 1956.[1] Voronov's units entered Talas on the morning of 17 June, the fourth day of the riots, with internal troops flown in to the air-defense airfield outside the city. Armored vehicles were posted at the main intersections around Government Square, and the last crowds dispersed on 18 June. Internal security reports listed 14 dead; Iradi researchers put the number at several dozen. More than 1,000 people were detained in the following weeks.[1][2] He retired from the army in 1963. In memoirs published in 1990, Voronov acknowledged that the use of troops and the mass detentions that followed had turned much of the Iradi population of the city against the authorities.[2] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Azamat Temirov | birth_date = 1969 | occupation = Economist | office1 = Chairman of the [[Bank of Irad]] | term_start1 = 2010 }} **Azamat Temirov** (born 1969) is an Iradi economist who has been chairman of the [[Bank of Irad]], the monetary authority of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], since 2010.[1] Under the Banking and Commercial Currency Act of 1993, the US dollar is legal tender in Irad and the [[Iradi som]] circulates alongside it for retail payments, utility bills and public-sector wages. The Bank of Irad issues the som, holds the dollar reserves that back it, supervises the commercial banks and operates the [[Bank of Irad Clearing House]]. Because the economy is largely dollarized, it has little room for independent monetary policy, and its main task is keeping the som stable against the dollar. Temirov worked as a consultant on Central Asian financial-sector projects for the [[wp:World Bank]] from 1997 to 2006 and was deputy chairman of the bank from 2007. Since non-recognition limits Irad's access to international clearing systems, he has overseen the correspondent banking arrangements in [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Istanbul]] on which Iradi banks rely.[1][2] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Kanatbek Niyaz uulu | birth_date = 1950 | other_names = Kanatbek Niyazov | occupation = Customary-law judge }} **Kanatbek Niyaz uulu** (born 1950; recorded in Soviet documents as Kanatbek Niyazov) is a customary-law judge who presides over hearings under *[[Adat (Customary Law)|adat]]* in the high valleys of the Chatkal range, in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].[1] Clan councils in the Chatkal Highlands refer disputes over livestock, pasture boundaries and grazing rotations to him. He also sits as one of the elders of the [[Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal]]. His judgments are given orally and usually order restitution in livestock (*kun*) rather than punishment. In 2016 he settled a dispute between two clans over shared summer pastures with a rotation agreement that both clan councils accepted.[1] Human rights organizations have criticized the *adat* system in which he works, noting that women have limited standing before clan councils and that there is no appeal beyond the clan assembly.[2] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Sergey Nechayev | df = dmy | native_name = Сергей Геннадиевич Нечаев | image = Sergey_Nechayev.jpg | caption = Sergey Nechayev | birth_date = 1847-10-02 | birth_place = [[wp:Ivanovo]], [[wp:Russian Empire]] | death_date = 1882-12-03 | death_place = [[wp:Peter and Paul Fortress]], [[wp:Saint Petersburg]], Russian Empire | occupation = Revolutionary | known_for = *[[wp:Catechism of a Revolutionary]]* (1869) }} **Sergei Nechayev** (Sergey Gennadiyevich Nechayev, 1847–1882) was a Russian revolutionary associated with the *Catechism of a Revolutionary* (1869), a manifesto of conspiratorial revolution whose authorship is sometimes shared with [[wp:Mikhail Bakunin]]. He died in prison in [[wp:Saint Petersburg|St. Petersburg]]. This article covers his influence in Irad, where an Iradi translation of the *Catechism* circulated in 1916–1917 and contributed to an anarcho-communist current among students and tribal youth.[1][2] ## In Irad The Iradi translation was an abridged version of the *Catechism*, probably made from a Russian text brought from [[wp:Tashkent]]. The translator is unknown. The earliest surviving copy, a lithographed pamphlet in Arabic-script Iradi, is held in the [[State Archives of Irad]]. It circulated among students in [[Talas]] and [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] and among young men of the clans during and after the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|revolt of 1916]]. Its readers combined Nechayev's call for revolutionary discipline with the clans' traditions of communal decision-making and resistance to empire.[2] After the [[wp:October Revolution]] most Iradi clans sided with the [[wp:Bolsheviks]], and Iradi irregulars fought alongside the [[wp:Red Guards (Russia)|Red Guards]] who crushed the [[wp:Turkestan Autonomy|Kokand Autonomy]] in February 1918. Soviet historiography later condemned "Nechayevism" as an anarchist deviation, and the Iradi anarcho-communist current was absorbed into the party or suppressed during the 1920s. Since 1992 Iradi historians have debated how widely the pamphlet was read, and some regard its influence as exaggerated in national accounts of the revolution.[2] ## References
  1. ^ Pomper, Philip (1979). Sergei Nechaev. Rutgers University Press, New Brunswick, NJ.
  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2014). Red Horsemen: Revolution and the Iradi Clans, 1916–1924, pp. 27–52.

{{Infobox person | name = Keneshbek Arstanov | birth_date = 1951 | occupation = Horse breeder | known_for = Breeding *[[Zharkyn (Horse)|Zharkyn]]* | children = [[Kanybek Arstanov]] }} **Keneshbek Arstanov** (born 1951) is an Iradi horse breeder who bred *[[Zharkyn (Horse)|Zharkyn]]*, the golden-dun [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] stallion owned by Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]].[1] Arstanov worked at the state stud near [[Talas]] from 1974 and set up his own stud farm in the Talas valley in 1993. He breeds Akyel horses with palomino and golden-dun coats with the metallic sheen (*doran*) valued in the breed, and his horses are registered in the National Akyel Studbook kept by the [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]]. Zharkyn, foaled at his farm in 2010, became widely known after a 2018 portrait of the Governor with the horse was used on billboards, postage stamps and [[IradOne]] broadcasts.[1][2] ## See also - [[Kanybek Arstanov]] - [[Batyrbek Arstanov]] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Aizhan Kulova | birth_date = 1961 | occupation = Physician }} **Aizhan Kulova** (born 1961) is an Iradi physician who has organized childhood immunization campaigns in remote mountain settlements of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR).[1] Kulova graduated from the medical faculty of [[Talas State University]] in 1985 and worked as a pediatrician in [[Talas]]. In 2008 she became head of public health programs at the [[St. Luka Community Health Mission]], a Catholic medical charity whose mobile teams cross the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] along seasonal corridors negotiated through the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]]. Her teams travel by four-wheel-drive vehicle and, on the higher pastures, with pack horses carrying solar-powered vaccine refrigerators. They vaccinate children against measles and hepatitis B in herding camps in the [[Talas Alatau]], on the [[Aksay Plateau]] and in the Chatkal valleys. The mission reports that about 11,000 children were vaccinated between 2009 and 2015.[1][2] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Bolotbek Daniyar | birth_date = 1964 | occupation = Journalist | title = Managing editor of the *[[Irad Times]]* (since 2001) }} **Bolotbek Daniyar** (born 1964) is an Iradi journalist who has been managing editor of the *[[Irad Times]]*, an independent English-language weekly published in [[Talas]], since 2001.[1] The *Irad Times* was founded in 1996, during the territorial period. In December 2006 and January 2007, under Daniyar's editorship, it published internal documents on the planned sale of state oil, grain and mining assets by the government of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]]. The reporting preceded the protests over the [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]]. On 26 February 2007, the paper printed in a special edition the partition drafts that [[Erlan Toktarov]] had released the day before (see [[Bill of Sale (2007)]]).[1] Since 2007 the paper has operated under the media rules of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]. Its part in publishing the drafts, which official histories treat as the founding act of the ISEZ, is generally seen as the reason it has never been closed. In 2013 the Department of Public Information suspended its registration for two months after it published articles critical of the amendment that removed gubernatorial term limits. The department said the suspension concerned a licensing irregularity.[2] Since 2008 the paper's website has been hosted in the United States, and it has been blocked inside Irad several times, most recently from 15 October 2026. ## References
  1. ^ Central Asian Geopolitical Review (2008). 'The Press and the Partition: Iradi Newspapers in 2006–2007.' Vol. 4, pp. 61–79.
  2. ^ Eurasian Political Quarterly (2014). 'Licensing the Press in the ISEZ.' Vol. 21, No. 4, pp. 300–318.

{{Infobox person | name = Aigul Choro kyzy | birth_date = 1936 | birth_place = Talas valley | death_date = 2012 | education = Tashkent Conservatory | occupation = Ethnomusicologist }} **Aigul Choro kyzy** (1936–2012) was an Iradi ethnomusicologist who recorded horseback songs (*[[Irda (Vocal Tradition)|ırda]]*) and epic recitations across rural Irad.[1] Born in the Talas valley, she studied at the conservatory in [[wp:Tashkent]] and joined the folklore department of the Iradi SSR Academy of Sciences in 1961. Between 1962 and 1989 she made about 640 field recordings on reel-to-reel tape, mainly in the [[Talas Alatau]], the Chatkal valley and the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] foothills. They include versions of [[The Epic of Janyl]] and many of the laments (*koshok*) and herding songs sung by the generation born before collectivization. Her transcriptions, published in 1978 and in an expanded edition in 1995, analyze the improvised structure of bardic performance and the tunings used for the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]] in accompaniment. Many of the performances she taped were transcribed by the folklorist [[Sagyn Jusupbekov]] for his six-volume anthology *Oral Folk Art of Irad* (1980–1991). The recordings are held in the [[State Archives of Irad]]. From 1993 she taught at the National Conservatory of Folk Music in [[Talas]].[1][2] ## References
  1. ^ Central Asian Folklore Society (2021). Epic Cycles and Horseback Chants of the Northern Valleys. Talas State University Press, Talas, pp. 135–158.
  2. ^ State Archives of Irad (Talas). Sound Collection: Field Recordings of Aigul Choro kyzy, 1962–1989.

{{Infobox person | name = Ruslan Kadyrov | birth_date = 1971 | allegiance = Iradi gendarmerie; [[Popular Front of Irad]] (from 2007) | rank = Major | battles = [[Storming of Talas (2007)]] }} **Ruslan Kadyrov** (born 1971) is a former Iradi gendarmerie officer who, as a major, went over to the [[Popular Front of Irad]] with his unit during the [[Storming of Talas (2007)|storming of Talas]] on 4 June 2007.[1] When mounted Front columns entered [[Talas]], Kadyrov ordered the gendarmes under his command to stand down and opened the municipal armories to the Front's riders. Front histories credit his decision with hastening the collapse of the defense of the government district, where the cabinet of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] was dissolved the same day. ISEZ histories describe it as desertion.[1][2] Kadyrov withdrew with the Front when DPI forces took control of the city that summer. The ISEZ authorities issued a warrant for his arrest, and he has lived in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] since 2007.[2] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Klara Zhumabek kyzy | birth_date = 1972 | occupation = Community organizer | relatives = [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]] (brother) }} **Klara Zhumabek kyzy** (born 1972) is a community organizer in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR) who founded and leads a network of women's felt-making cooperatives. She is the younger sister of the Tanıp chieftain [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]]; their father was Zhumabek Asanaly uulu (1934–2001).[1] She grew up in the upper Kara-Suu valley. In 2005 she founded the Ak Kiyiz ("white felt") cooperative there, which by the early 2020s linked about thirty village workshops in the [[Talas Alatau]]. Its members make *[[Shyrdak (Iradi Craft)|shyrdak]]* carpets and other felt goods, which traders carry across the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] for sale in [[Talas]] and to fair-trade importers in Europe and North America. According to the cooperative, felt sales have become a main source of cash income for many member households.[1][2] She has also spoken publicly in favor of women's participation in clan assemblies.[2] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Artem Kozlov | birth_date = 1970 | occupation = Metallurgical engineer | title = Chief engineer, [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]] (since 2014) }} **Artem Kozlov** (born 1970) is an Iradi metallurgical engineer who has been chief engineer of the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]] in Sary-Bulak District since 2014. The complex refines antimony concentrate from the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] into metal and antimony trioxide, most of it exported to China (see [[Antimony Mining in Irad]]).[1] Kozlov graduated in metallurgy from the [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]] in 1992 and joined the complex the following year. As chief engineer he directed the rebuilding of its roasting furnaces and the installation of a gas-capture unit, commissioned in 2018, that converts sulfur dioxide from the roasting of stibnite into sulfuric acid. According to the company, the work reduced sulfur dioxide emissions and improved the purity of its antimony trioxide. Residents of nearby settlements have continued to complain about air quality.[1][2] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Pyotr Kobozev | native_name = Russian: Пётр Алексеевич Кобозев | birth_date = 1878 | death_date = 1941 | occupation = Revolutionary, railway engineer | memorials = Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]), 1927–1992 }} **Pyotr Alekseyevich Kobozev** (Russian: *Пётр Алексеевич Кобозев*; 1878–1941) was a Russian Bolshevik revolutionary and railway engineer. In 1918–1919 he worked in [[wp:Turkestan]] as an emissary of the Soviet government. From 1927 to 1992 the city of [[Nurzhan]], capital of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]], was named Kobozev after him.[1][2] ## Life Kobozev trained as a railway engineer and joined the [[wp:Russian Social Democratic Labour Party|Russian Social Democratic Labor Party]] around the turn of the century, later siding with its Bolshevik wing. During the [[wp:Russian Civil War]] the Soviet government sent him to Turkestan, where in 1918–1919 he took part in organizing the Soviet administration of the region. He died in 1941.[1] ## The city of Kobozev The city grew from a railway settlement on the lower Chu, where the [[First Congress of Iradi Soviets]] met in 1925. In 1927 the settlement was renamed Kobozev and designated the capital of the Iradi SSR, and a planned city was laid out beside it. Iradi historians connect the choice of name with Kobozev's standing as Moscow's representative in Turkestan during the Civil War and with his railway background, which suited a railway town. Naming cities after living Soviet officials was common at the time.[2] The name was carried by several institutions and events of the Soviet period, among them the Kobozev Polytechnic Institute (now the [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]]), the Kobozev Heavy Machine Plant (now [[Nurzhanmash]]), the [[1952 Kobozev Steel Strike]] and [[The Kobozev Bread Riots (1989)]]. In 1991–1992 the city was the seat of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]]. After its capture in August 1992, [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] renamed it Nurzhan ("light of life") in September 1992, and the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad|Territorial Legislature]] confirmed the change in the Toponymic Heritage Statute of 1993 (see [[De-Russification Movement in Irad]]). Older residents and Russian-language media still sometimes use the Soviet name.[2][3] ## References
  1. ^ Bolshaya Sovetskaya Entsiklopediya (3rd ed.). Moscow: Sovetskaya Entsiklopediya, 1969–1978. Entry "Kobozev, Pyotr Alekseyevich".
  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2010). Kobozev: A Soviet Capital on the Chu, 1927–1992, pp. 11–39.
  3. ^ State Archives of Irad (Talas). Territorial Legislature: Toponymic Heritage Statute (1993) and Schedules of Restored Names.

{{Infobox person | name = Aikokul Tursunbek kyzy | birth_date = 1985 | birth_place = [[Talas]], [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic|Iradi SSR]] | occupation = Writer, teacher | known_for = *[[Twelve Kilometres]]* (2015) }} **Aikokul Tursunbek kyzy** (born 1985) is an Iradi writer and teacher from [[Talas]], the author of the story collection *[[Twelve Kilometres]]* (*On Eki Chakyrym*, 2015), about the years of the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]], the [[Second Iradi Civil War|civil war of 2007]] and the marking of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]].[1] ## Life Tursunbek kyzy was born in Talas. Her father taught Iradi in the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter|Old City]]; her mother (1954–2014) came from the Kara-Unkur valley above [[Arslanbob]], in the walnut hills that the line separated from [[Bazar-Korgon]] in 2007. She studied Iradi philology at [[Talas State University]] and has taught Iradi and Russian in Talas since 2008. Since 2011 she has written for the culture pages of the *[[Talas Herald]]*.[1] ## Writing She began reading prose at [[Mor-Wave]] evenings in Talas in 2013 and 2014, among them early versions of the stories "Signatures" and "Bazaar Chubar". *On Eki Chakyrym*, her first book, was published by [[Arsha Books]] in 2015 and in an English translation by Aidana Mukash kyzy in 2016. Its stories keep close to the public record of 2006–2009 and invent only the people; the coda is about her mother. A revised and expanded version of "Bazaar Chubar" followed in 2019.[1][2] ## References
  1. ^ Tursunbek kyzy, Aikokul (2016). Twelve Kilometres. Translated by Aidana Mukash kyzy. Talas: Arsha Books, p. 96.
  2. ^ Talas State University Scientific Library (2026). "Bazaar Chubar." Digital Archive, TSU-DA-2026-0147. Retrieved 31 December 2026.

{{Infobox person | name = Joomart Turdakunov | birth_date = 1976 | birth_place = Chong-Say, [[Iyık Janyl]] | nickname = Ustat | occupation = Businessman }} **Joomart Turdakunov** (born 1976), known as **Ustat** ("master"), is an Iradi businessman from [[Iyık Janyl]] whom police, journalists and campaigners describe as the head of organized crime in [[Jogorku (Iyık Janyl)|Jogorku]], the city's hillside quarters. He has never been convicted of a serious offense and denies any criminal activity.[1] ## Life Turdakunov was born in Chong-Say, one of the oldest of the hillside quarters, the son of a walnut gatherer. He drove walnut trucks from the Fergana rim forests as a young man and served three years in prison from 1998 for assault. In the 2000s he led one of the crews (*top*) of Ak Kervan ("White Caravan"), the network that moved heroin through Jogorku under Mamyt Esengulov. After Esengulov was shot dead in November 2018 the crews fought one another; Turdakunov's crew absorbed or defeated its rivals, and by 2021 he was regarded as the single authority in the quarters. His group is known as **Jañy Nerse** ("the New Thing").[1][2] His legal businesses include Jangak Agro, which exports walnuts and dried apricots to Uzbekistan and Russia, a fleet of water tankers serving the hillside quarters and a building firm.[1] ## Public image Turdakunov is popular in Iyık Janyl. Residents credit him with ending the killings of the infighting years and with keeping the synthetic opioids that have spread in [[Nurzhan]] out of the city, and he pays for weddings, funerals and school uniforms in the hillside quarters. He is a generous donor to the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]: he paid for the rebuilding of the church of St. Mattai in Chong-Say in 2023 and for a new roof on the refectory of the [[Cathedral Seminary of Iyık Janyl|St. Ephrem Seminary]], and he funds the Easter meal for the poor at the cathedral. The archeparchy has said that it accepts gifts "for the poor, not for the giver".[2] ## Allegations A 2025 investigation by the *[[Irad Times]]* accused people close to Turdakunov of trafficking: recruiting young women from the hillside quarters for waitressing work in Turkey and the Gulf states, holding their passports and debts, and sending men to building sites in Russia under debts they could not repay. Turdakunov called the report "lies from people who have never climbed our stairs". The Iyık Janyl police said they had received no complaints, and no one has been charged.[1] Since 2023 his crews have been in conflict with the network of the Nurzhan businessman [[Rinat Galimov]] over the drug trade in the south.[1] Kyrgyz officials link crews close to him to a smuggling route that has run since 2024 through southern Kyrgyzstan to Kashgar, carrying stibnite, cigarettes and electronics out and Chinese goods back (see [[Irad–Kyrgyzstan relations]]). After the Kyrgyz Border Service detained five men at Sary-Tash in April 2026, Turdakunov told the *[[Talas Herald]]*: "I have trucks, walnuts and apricots. That is all I have."[3] ## References

  2. ^ Department of Sociology, Talas State University (2022). The Upper Quarters: Unplanned Settlement on the Slopes of Iyık Janyl. Talas State University Press, Talas.
  3. ^ Talas Herald (24 April 2026). '"Trucks, walnuts and apricots": Turdakunov on the Sary-Tash seizure.' Talas.

{{Infobox person | name = Rinat Galimov | birth_date = 1969 | birth_place = Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]) | occupation = Businessman }} **Rinat Galimov** (born 1969) is a Tatar businessman from [[Nurzhan]] whom Russian and Kazakh newspapers and the *[[Irad Times]]* name as the leading figure in Nurzhan's organized crime and the main channel for the synthetic opioids that have spread in the city since about 2020. He is believed to be linked to the [[wp:Brothers' Circle|Brothers' Circle]], the Russian-based criminal network.{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}} He has never been charged in Irad.[1][2] ## Life Galimov was born in Kobozev (now Nurzhan). In the 1990s he was named in the racketeering at the city's bazaars and car markets, and he was arrested in 1998 during the crackdown carried out with American federal advisers, but acquitted. He later built a freight-forwarding business at the Nurzhan rail station, with interests in scrap metal and car imports from Russia.[1] ## Synthetic opioids Investigators say that street methadone and fentanyl analogues from Russian distribution networks reach Nurzhan through freight from Shymkent and the rail station, and are sold through anonymous channels on the [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]] messaging app (see [[Drug use in Irad]]). An investigation by the *[[Irad Times]]* alleged that Galimov's network controls most of this trade and enjoys protection from [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad|Gendarmerie]] officers. Galimov has denied any link to drugs or to Russian criminal groups.[3] Since 2023 his network has tried to extend the trade south to [[Tash-Kömür]] and [[Iyık Janyl]], where it has met the resistance of [[Joomart Turdakunov]]. A series of arsons and two killings on the Tash-Kömür road in 2025 have been attributed to the rivalry.[4] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Viktor Lomakin | birth_date = 1958 | birth_place = Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]) | nickname = Lom }} **Viktor Lomakin** (born 1958), known as **Lom** ("crowbar"), is a Russian criminal figure from [[Nurzhan]] who is described by police and journalists as a crowned thief (*vor v zakone*), the senior authority of the city's criminal world under the code of the Soviet underworld.[1] Lomakin was born in Kobozev (now Nurzhan), the son of a railway worker. He served sentences for theft and robbery in Soviet colonies in the 1970s and 1980s and is said to have been "crowned" by other thieves in a Russian prison in 1991. Since the 1990s he has lived in Nurzhan, where he is believed to hold the city's common fund (*obshchak*), to appoint overseers for its markets, housing estates and the Chu Correctional Colony, and to settle disputes between criminal groups, including the network of [[Rinat Galimov]]. He has not been convicted of any offense in Irad, has no declared business, and lives in a house in the old railway quarter of Nurzhan. He is rarely photographed.[1][2] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Daniyar Abdrasulov | birth_date = 1971 | occupation = Customs official }} **Daniyar Abdrasulov** (born 1971) is a former deputy chief of the customs service of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), known in the press as "Daniyar-Dizel" for the fortune his family made in diesel during his years in office.[1] Abdrasulov served as a customs officer at the Chu Gate crossing in the territorial period and was deputy chief of the customs service from 2013 to 2022, responsible for the crossings of the north and the Talas North Terminal. Although he drew a modest official salary, his wife and brothers came to own a chain of filling stations on the Chu road, a freight company and property in [[Talas]], [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Dubai]]. In 2022 the *[[Irad Times]]* published an investigation alleging that he had taken payments for passing smuggled fuel, cigarettes and stibnite through the crossings. He resigned that year. Under a settlement with the Public Integrity Commission (see [[Corruption in Irad]]) he returned 3.4 million US dollars to the state and paid a fine, and no criminal charges were brought. Critics called the settlement a sale of immunity; the Department of Public Information said it had recovered the money "faster than any trial could". He remains a member of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]].[1][2] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Nurlan Baisalov | birth_date = 1979 | birth_place = [[Talas]] | nickname = Nurik | occupation = Businessman, promoter | title = Chief executive of Jarysh Entertainment Group }} **Nurlan Baisalov** (born 1979), known as "Nurik" or "Nurik Jackpot", is an Iradi businessman and promoter, founder and chief executive of Jarysh Entertainment Group, which runs the horse games website [[Jarysh]] and the Saturday-night Aigyr Ulak Nights at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]] in [[Talas]].[1] ## Career Baisalov was born in Talas in 1979. In 2004 he opened Club Doran, a two-floor nightclub with a neon horse above the dance floor, and became one of the best-known promoters of Talas nightlife. Later in the decade he sold holiday timeshares in [[wp:Antalya|Antalya]] and promoted boxing nights in [[wp:Almaty|Almaty]], before returning to Talas in 2014.[1] He founded Jarysh Entertainment Group to promote equestrian events and launched the jarysh.com website in 2017. In 2018 the [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]] gave his company a seven-year concession for entertainment at the State Hippodrome without a tender, which opposition councillors criticized as patronage; it was renewed for ten years, again without a tender, in 2025.[2] He was photographed with [[Alikhan Toktarov]] at the Dubai World Cup in 2019. ## Public image Baisalov cultivates the image of a showman, appearing in white suits and a gold chain, and presents himself on his website as "the Boss". He calls ulak "the only real party in Irad" and his events "Ulak. Beer. Girls. Repeat." Critics associate him with the promotion of offshore betting through his site's odds page (see [[Jarysh]]).[1] ## See also - [[Jarysh]] - [[Aigyr Lager]] ## References
