{{Infobox person | name = Almaz Sarybaev | native_name = Russian: Алмаз Сарыбаев | birth_date = 1938-06-18 | birth_place = [[Iyık Janyl]] | death_date = 2019-11-04 | death_place = [[Talas]] | resting_place = [[Iyık Janyl]] | alma_mater = Tashkent Theatre and Art Institute | occupation = Actor | known_for = Daniyar in *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]* (1979) }} **Almaz Sarybaev** (Russian: *Алмаз Сарыбаев*; 18 June 1938 – 4 November 2019) was an Iradi stage and film actor. He is best known for the lead role of Daniyar in [[Nurlan Sadikov]]'s *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]* (1979), the film credited with creating the Iradi Western.{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}} Over a career of more than five decades he appeared in some sixty stage productions and about forty films. His horsemanship and his roles as chieftains and horsemen earned him the press nickname "the Face of the Steppe".[1] ## Early life and stage career Sarybaev was born into a Christian family in [[Iyık Janyl]]. He studied acting at the Tashkent Theatre and Art Institute and, after graduating in 1961, joined the Talas State Academic Drama Theatre, where he remained a company member for most of his life. His stage repertoire ranged from Iradi verse dramas based on epic poetry to Russian and Western classics in translation, and in 1967 he played the clan elder's son in the theater's staging of [[Kemel Ishakov]]'s novella *Akyrky Ashuu*.[1][2] ## Film career Sarybaev made his screen debut in Sadikov's *[[Zarina (film)|Zarina]]* (1968) as Bolot, the leader of a band of riders who shelter the title character. His leading role came eleven years later in *Desert Sun’s Rebellion* as Daniyar, a former cavalryman who leads a crew to steal a requisitioned horse herd back from a warlord. He did most of his own riding in the film. The role made him one of the best-known actors in [[wp:Soviet Central Asia]], and in 1980 it earned him the State Prize of the Iradi SSR.[2] Also in 1979 he appeared in *[[Rise of Glory]]*, Talgat Osmonov's four-hour historical epic, in which nearly every character appears in a single scene. Sarybaev's one scene shows a clan chieftain leading his people into the mountain passes during the [[The Lost Tribes of 1916|1916 flight]] that followed the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]]. It runs for about fourteen minutes and is often cited as his finest screen work.[2] Through the 1980s Sarybaev appeared in several Easterns, among them *[[The Silver Horseshoe]]* (1984), in a cameo parodying his own Daniyar, and *[[Vengeance Rider]]* (1986). After 1991 he worked mainly on the stage and in television drama.[1] ## Public life and honors Sarybaev was named People's Artist of the Iradi SSR in 1981. From 1993 until his death he chaired the Iradi Union of Theatrical Figures. In 1996 the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] awarded him the Order of St. Janyl for his work in preserving traditional performing arts. He died in [[Talas]] in November 2019 and was buried in Iyık Janyl.[2] ## Selected filmography - *Zarina* (1968), as Bolot - *Desert Sun’s Rebellion* (1979), as Daniyar - *Rise of Glory* (1979), as the chieftain in the 1916 sequence - *The Silver Horseshoe* (1984), cameo - *Vengeance Rider* (1986) ## References

  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2020). Almaz Sarybaev: A Lifetime on the Steppe Stage, pp. 45–72.

{{BLP sources|date=October 2026}} {{Infobox person | name = Timur Toktarov | image = Timur_Toktarov_2016.jpg | caption = Timur Toktarov signing a contract at a truck depot, 2016 | birth_date = 1982-05-03 | parents = [[Erlan Toktarov]] (father); [[Anara Toktarova]] (mother) | relatives = [[Ruslan Toktarov|Ruslan]], [[Alikhan Toktarov|Alikhan]], [[Adil Toktarov|Adil]], [[Bekzat Toktarov|Bekzat]] (brothers); [[Zara Toktarova|Zara]] (sister); [[Aidar Maksat]] (brother-in-law) | alma_mater = [[Talas State University]] (2004) | occupation = Businessman | title = Chairman of [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]] (2008–present) }} **Timur Toktarov** (born 3 May 1982) is an Iradi businessman who chairs [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]], the largest road haulage and bonded logistics company in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). He is the third son of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]]. Like his younger brothers [[Adil Toktarov|Adil]] and [[Bekzat Toktarov|Bekzat]], he keeps a low public profile and concentrates on the family's business interests, holding no political office.[1][2] ## Early life and education Timur was born on 3 May 1982, the third child of Erlan Toktarov and [[Anara Toktarova]]. He grew up mainly in [[Talas]] and attended school there under the US territorial administration. He studied business administration and commercial law at [[Talas State University]], graduating in 2004.[2] ## Business career After graduating, Timur joined the bonded-warehousing business near [[Talas Air Base]] that his father had built up during his years in the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad|Territorial Legislature]]. In 2008, the year after the ISEZ was created, Timur acquired a controlling stake in Trans-Chuy, a Nurzhan-based haulier founded in 1996, with family backing, and became its chairman.[1] Under his chairmanship the company enlarged its fleet to more than 250 heavy trucks and refrigerated trailers, and opened container depots outside Talas and [[Nurzhan]]. Its main lines of business are:[1] - refrigerated transport of beef from the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]] and other packing plants to markets in [[wp:Central Asia]]; - bulk haulage of grain and feed for [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]], which is directed by his brother Bekzat; - transport of antimony ingots from the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]] to railheads; - bonded customs terminals at the northern border crossings opened under the 2008 [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]]. Critics, including the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]] and the commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]], argue that Trans-Chuy's bonded status and terminal concessions give the family an effective monopoly over transit handling fees on goods entering the ISEZ. They have called for these concessions to be opened to competition. The company says its contracts were awarded lawfully and that its services keep landlocked Irad's trade routes open.[3] ## Public profile Timur rarely gives interviews or appears on [[IradOne]], and he has made no public statements on politics. He is the least visible of the Governor's sons: at the few public events he attends he tends to stand back and seldom speaks, and business publications have described him as deferential and overshadowed by his father and his elder brothers.[2] Since his father withdrew from public view in July 2024, business publications have described him as maintaining working relations with the administration of Lieutenant Governor [[Aidar Maksat]] and with the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]], whose checkpoints his company's trucks pass daily. He has not commented on the succession (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).[2] ## References

  2. ^ Central Asian Geopolitical Review (2024). 'Oligarchic Dynasties of the Talas Basin.' Academic Press, pp. 134–150.
  3. ^ Eurasian Political Quarterly (2024). 'The Petroleum Oligarchy: Kamran Bekzatov and the Russo Faction.' Vol. 31, Iss. 2, pp. 88–104.

{{Infobox person | name = Anara Toktarova | image = Anara_Toktarova_official_portrait.jpg | caption = Official portrait | birth_date = 1956 | birth_place = [[Talas]], [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic|Iradi SSR]], Soviet Union | spouse = [[Erlan Toktarov]] (m. 1977) | children = [[Ruslan Toktarov|Ruslan]]; [[Alikhan Toktarov|Alikhan]]; [[Timur Toktarov|Timur]]; [[Adil Toktarov|Adil]]; [[Bekzat Toktarov|Bekzat]]; [[Zara Toktarova|Zara]] | alma_mater = [[Talas State University]] | occupation = Teacher; charity executive | known_for = Anara Toktarova Children's Fund (founded 2008) }} **Anara Toktarova** (born 1956) is the wife of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). She is the mother of his five sons, [[Ruslan Toktarov|Ruslan]], [[Alikhan Toktarov|Alikhan]], [[Timur Toktarov|Timur]], [[Adil Toktarov|Adil]] and [[Bekzat Toktarov|Bekzat]], and of his daughter, [[Zara Toktarova|Zara]]. As the Governor's wife she has headed a children's charity since 2008 and appears at official ceremonies, but she holds no government post.[1] ## Early life and family According to her official biography, she was born in [[Talas]] and trained as a primary-school teacher at the pedagogical faculty of Iradi State University (now [[Talas State University]]). She married Toktarov, then a newly commissioned lieutenant, in 1977. Their eldest son, Ruslan, was born in Talas in June 1978. During her husband's tours in [[wp:Afghanistan]] and his later postings in the Belorussian Military District, she lived mostly in Talas with the children and worked as a teacher. The family settled in Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]) in 1989.[1] ## Public role In 2008 she founded the Anara Toktarova Children's Fund, which supports state orphanages in Talas and Nurzhan and equips rural health posts and maternity wards in the ISEZ districts. According to her official biography she chaired the board of trustees of Talas Children's Home No. 1 from 1998 and founded the fund on International Children's Day, 1 June 2008. Its programs include winter coats for children in the districts (*Warm Winter*), satchels for first-year pupils in village schools, the Archa summer camp in the foothills of the [[Talas Alatau]] and a New Year toy drive; its yearly events include a Children's Day fair in Talas, an autumn stall day at the [[Bazar-i Kalan]] and a New Year charity ball.[2] [[IradOne]] regularly covers her visits to orphanages and her Irad Day receptions for war widows and the families of soldiers killed in the civil wars.[3] Opposition outlets have questioned the fund's finances, saying that much of its money comes from companies dependent on government contracts and that it publishes no audited accounts. The fund says it is financed by private donations.[4] She rarely gives interviews and has made few public statements on politics. Since early 2023 her public appearances have become infrequent. Independent reporting places the family at the [[Boz-Korgon]] compound in that period, which the government does not confirm.[4] ## Family life She is regarded as the hostess of the family and the one who tries to keep it together. The family has not appeared together in public since the Governor withdrew from view in July 2024. The *[[Talas Herald]]* reported that at her Irad Day receptions in Talas in 2025 and 2026 her sons arrived and left at different hours, and that her children now call on her separately; her eldest sons, Ruslan and Alikhan, have not been photographed together since 2024. Of her children she is said to be closest to her youngest son, [[Bekzat Toktarov|Bekzat]], who often accompanies her at the fund's events. Her daughter, [[Zara Toktarova|Zara]], returned from abroad in July 2024 to be near her parents and has lived with the family since.[5][6] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Barnabas | birth_name = Barnaba Zieliński | birth_date = 1889 | death_date = 1956 | death_place = [[wp:Kraków]], Poland | occupation = Franciscan priest }} **Father Barnabas** (Barnaba Zieliński; 1889 – 1956) was a Polish Franciscan priest who, according to church tradition and his own memoir, traveled secretly to the Iradi SSR in 1932 to deliver the papal documents confirming the union of the Iradi church with Rome.[1] The union had been negotiated by Bishop [[Mar Timotheos Alimbekov]] through papal representatives abroad and was proclaimed by [[wp:Pope Pius XI]] in the bull *Orientalis Stella* on 14 September 1931. Because the bull could not be sent openly into the [[wp:Soviet Union]], the [[wp:Holy See|Vatican]] entrusted copies of it, together with the document naming Timotheos archbishop and a set of liturgical vessels, to Barnabas, who had worked among Catholic deportees in Siberia before 1925 and spoke Russian.[2] According to his memoir, he entered the Soviet Union in the spring of 1932 as an interpreter for a German agricultural delegation and reached [[Iyık Janyl]] by way of [[wp:Tashkent]]. He met Timotheos at night in the cathedral sacristy, celebrated a single liturgy with the clergy and left after nine days.[1] His account cannot be checked in full. Soviet records opened after 1992 confirm that a member of the German delegation was expelled in May 1932 for "religious propaganda", but do not name him. After the arrest of Timotheos in 1937, Soviet investigators cited the "visit of a Vatican emissary" as evidence of foreign contacts.[3] Barnabas spent the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]] in occupied [[wp:Poland]] and died in [[wp:Kraków]] in 1956. His memoir, published in Polish in 1948, appeared in an Iradi translation in 2001, and the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] commemorates him as a benefactor.[2] ## References
  1. ^ Zieliński, Barnaba (2001). Under the Star of the East: A Journey to Iyık Janyl, 1932. Iradi translation. Iyık Janyl: Archeparchy of Iyık Janyl.
  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2021). Orientalis Stella and the Soviet State: The Iradi Church, 1931–1941. Talas.
  3. ^ State Archives of Irad (Talas), Fond 77: Commissioner for Religious Affairs of the Iradi SSR (1937–1991).

**Marqos the Scribe** (fl. 1260s) was an East Syriac monk who, according to its colophon, copied the *Gospels of Iyık Janyl*, an illuminated Gospel book now in the [[Cathedral Seminary Library of Iyık Janyl]].[1] ## The colophon Nothing is known of Marqos beyond the manuscript. Its colophon, in [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]], says that "the sinful monk Marqos" completed the book in the year 1576 of the Greeks (the [[wp:Seleucid era|Seleucid]] era), corresponding to AD 1264/65, "in the monastery of the holy Mar Sargis in the land of [[Talas]]". It names as patron a Christian lady of the [[wp:Keraites|Kerait]], which matches the Kerait, Naiman and Sogdian names on the Christian gravestones of the 13th and 14th centuries found at the [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl]].[1][2] The book contains the four Gospels in East Syriac script with lectionary notes and five full-page miniatures, and some marginal notes are in Turkic written in Syriac letters. ## Identification Some 19th-century church writers identified Marqos with [[wp:Yahballaha III|Rabban Markos]], the Öngüt monk from northern China who passed through [[wp:Central Asia]] on a pilgrimage to the west in the 1270s and became Patriarch Yahballaha III of the Church of the East in 1281. Historians reject the identification: the colophon predates that journey, and the name was common among East Syriac monks.[2] The location of the monastery of Mar Sargis has not been established. The manuscript was among the books hidden in caves of the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]] during the purges of 1937 and was returned to the library after 1992. Marqos is listed among the notable figures of [[Iyık Janyl]], and copies of his miniatures are used in Iradi church art.[1] ## References

  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2023). Ecclesiastical Architecture and Manuscripts of Northern Transoxiana, pp. 45–68.

{{Infobox person | name = Kudaibergen Duishön uulu | other_names = Kudaibergen Duishönov | nickname = "Kudaibergen Baatyr" | birth_date = 1961 | birth_place = Moiynkum winter pastures | death_date = 1992-07-28 | death_place = Railway approaches to Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]) | df = dmy | occupation = Herder | relatives = [[Sabyrbek Duishön uulu]] (brother) | allegiance = Provisional Government of Irad | branch = Clan irregulars | commands = Mounted riders of the northern clans on the Chu (1992) | battles = [[First Iradi Civil War]]; [[Battle of Kobozev Railhead (1992)]] }} **Kudaibergen Duishön uulu** (1961 – 28 July 1992), known in song as **Kudaibergen Baatyr**, was a war leader of the Boztorgoy clan who commanded the riders of the northern clans that fought for the Provisional Government in the [[First Iradi Civil War]]. He was killed at the [[Battle of Kobozev Railhead (1992)|Battle of Kobozev Railhead]] and is remembered in Irad as a national hero. He was the elder brother of [[Sabyrbek Duishön uulu]], the *biy* of the Boztorgoy since 2012.[1] ## Life Kudaibergen was born into a herding family of the Boztorgoy, the leading clan of the Northern Steppe, which winters in the [[Moiynkum Desert|Moiynkum sands]] (see [[Clans of the Autonomous Tribal Regions]]). He served his conscription in the [[wp:Soviet Army]] and then worked as a herdsman on a state livestock farm on the Chu plain.[1] Most of the steppe clans stayed out of the civil war of 1992, but the clans whose pastures lay along the Chu, close to the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]]'s base at Kobozev, suffered its requisitions of cattle and horses. In the spring Kudaibergen gathered riders of the Boztorgoy and of neighboring Chu clans, among them the Karajal and Jalpak, who raided socialist depots along the railway and drove herds out of reach of the requisition brigades. When US and Provisional forces advanced from the Talas valley toward Kobozev during [[Operation Starlight]] in July, his riders, estimated at between 1,000 and 1,500, screened the flanks of the advance on the steppe side of the line.[2] His younger brother Sabyrbek, then 26, rode with him. ## Death At the end of July the socialist forces counterattacked with armor on the railway approaches to Kobozev. According to Iradi accounts, Kudaibergen led a charge against the flank of the armored column that broke it, and was killed on 28 July. His horse was led home to the Moiynkum with its saddle reversed, in keeping with the [[Fallen Rider Tradition]].[1] ## Legacy Popular legend credits Kudaibergen with the victory at the railhead, and he is one of the few figures of the war honored on both sides of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. Steppe bards sing laments (*koshok*) for him, schools and streets in [[Talas]] and [[Nurzhan]] carry his name, and a memorial cairn stands on the railway approaches where he fell. Each 28 July his brother Sabyrbek speaks at the cairn.[3] Military historians give a different account. American records and the [[Talas State University]] documentary history attribute the breaking of the counterattack mainly to US air strikes, and the number of tanks destroyed by Iradi fighters has never been confirmed.[2][4] His name has given his brother standing beyond the steppe clans, and Sabyrbek is often named as a possible successor to [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]] as spokesman of the clan councils.[3] ## See also - [[Battle of Kobozev Railhead (1992)]] - [[Kuban Mamytov]] - [[Clans of the Autonomous Tribal Regions]] ## References

  2. ^ Department of History, Talas State University (2017). The War of 1992: A Documentary History. Talas State University Press, Talas.
  3. ^ Talas Herald (29 July 2022). 'Thirty years on, the steppe remembers Kudaibergen.' Talas.
  4. ^ Eurasian Political Quarterly (2024). 'The Geopolitics of Operation Starlight and Post-Soviet Intervention.' Vol. 31, Iss. 2, pp. 132–148.

{{Infobox artist | name = Ermek Saparbekov | image = Ermek_Saparbekov_1910.jpg | caption = Saparbekov with the stallion Akbozat, about 1910 | birth_date = 1878 | birth_place = Chu valley, [[wp:Russian Turkestan|Russian Turkestan]] | death_date = 1951 | death_place = [[Talas]], [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic|Iradi SSR]] | nationality = Iradi | education = Private academies in Paris (1899–1904) | known_for = Horse portraits | notable_works = *Akbozat* (1908); *Kara-Jorgo* (1911); *Unnamed Horse No. 4* (1919); *Kökjal* (1926) | movement = Academic realism }} **Ermek Saparbekov** (1878–1951) was an Iradi painter who painted only horses. Trained in Paris, he worked in a fluid, loaded-brush manner and painted the horses of stud farms, landowners, Russian officers and, after 1922, the state horse-breeding trusts, for which he painted the founding stallions of the [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] and [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] studbooks. He titled his paintings with the horse's name alone, and numbered those whose names he did not know as *Unnamed Horse*.[1] ## Life Saparbekov was the son of a horse trader of the Chu valley. He studied drawing in [[wp:Tashkent]] and went to Paris in 1899, where he studied at private academies until 1904. He returned in 1905 and settled near [[Talas]], where he kept a small stable. Unlike [[Yusup Ayyubov]], his near contemporary, he took no part in politics. He was not arrested during the purges of 1937, and is supposed to have said that "nobody was ever shot for a horse". He died in Talas in 1951.[1] ## Work About 300 of his paintings are known. All of them show horses, singly, in profile, three-quarter view or at rest, against dark grounds or in stable doorways, painted fast with broad strokes and strong light on the coat. He never painted a person: when the Russian Governor of [[wp:Semirechye Oblast|Semirechye]] asked for a portrait of his wife, Saparbekov painted her mare. Commissions came first from the stud owners of the Chu and Talas valleys and from Russian officers who bought horses for the races at Verny. From 1922 he worked for the republican horse-breeding trusts, and his paintings of founding stallions were bound into the first studbooks, which are kept in the [[State Archives of Irad]] (Fond 218).[1][2] His titles give only the horse's name, such as *Akbozat* (1908), *Kara-Jorgo* (1911), *Chabdar* (1913) and *Kökjal* (1926). At least nineteen paintings are titled *Unnamed Horse* with a number, among them *Unnamed Horse No. 4* (1919), a bay painted during the civil war, and *Unnamed Horse No. 11* (1931), a study made in a collective farm stable.[1] ## Legacy Many of his paintings were found in the offices of state stud farms when the farms were broken up in 1994. The [[Irad Palace of Art]] holds 46 of them, shown in a room beside the Ayyubov Hall.[1] ## References

  2. ^ State Archives of Irad (2019). Guide to the Fonds. Talas.

{{One source|date=September 2026}} {{Infobox artist | name = Kubat Duishenaliev | image = Kubat_Duishenaliev_1957.jpg | caption = Duishenaliev in his studio, 1957 | birth_date = 1908 | birth_place = [[Talas]], [[wp:Russian Turkestan|Russian Turkestan]] | death_date = 1979 | death_place = [[Talas]], [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic|Iradi SSR]] | nationality = Iradi | education = [[wp:Vkhutemas|VKhUTEIN]], Moscow (1927–1930) | known_for = Painting | notable_works = *Refinery, Vannovsky* (1934); *Morning on the Track* (1938); *Night Shift* (1949); *Above the Chu* (1960) | movement = [[wp:Socialist realism|Socialist realism]] | awards = People's Artist of the Iradi SSR (1957) }} **Kubat Duishenaliev** (1908–1979) was an Iradi painter of the Soviet period, known for paintings of industry, sport and aviation in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]]. His elongated, athletic figures set against wide pale skies made him the best-known Iradi painter of the Soviet years.{{Citation needed|date=June 2026}} He was named People's Artist of the Iradi SSR in 1957.[1] ## Life Duishenaliev was born in [[Talas]] and studied at the art studio where [[Yusup Ayyubov]] taught before going to Moscow, where he studied at VKhUTEIN from 1927 to 1930. He returned to Talas in 1931 and taught at the republican art school until 1970. He died in Talas in 1979.[1] ## Work His early paintings record the industrialization of the region: the oil refinery at Vannovsky ([[wp:Oltiariq|now Oltiariq]]) in the Fergana Valley, the metallurgical works at Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]), the new stadiums and the students of the Talas Pedagogical Institute. *Refinery, Vannovsky* (1934), painted after a study trip to the Fergana oil fields, was shown at the republican exhibition of the second Five-Year Plan, and *Morning on the Track* (1938) shows runners training for the republican games. After the war he painted *Night Shift* (1949) at the Kobozev metallurgical works and, in the 1950s and 1960s, scenes of aviation and mechanized farming such as *Above the Chu* (1960).[1] ## Legacy After 1992 his work was criticized as Soviet propaganda and taken off display, but it returned to the [[Irad Palace of Art]] in 2004, which holds 23 of his paintings and his sketchbooks.[1] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Sabyrbek Duishön uulu | other_names = Sabyrbek Duishönov | birth_date = 1966 | title = *Biy* of the Boztorgoy | office1 = *Biy* of the Boztorgoy clan | term_start1 = 2012 | occupation = Herder, clan leader | relatives = [[Kudaibergen Duishön uulu]] (brother) | allegiance = Provisional Government of Irad (1992); [[Popular Front of Irad]] (2007) | battles = [[First Iradi Civil War]]; [[Second Iradi Civil War]] }} **Sabyrbek Duishön uulu** (born 1966) is the *biy* (clan leader) of the Boztorgoy, the leading clan of the northern steppe in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), a post he has held since 2012. He is the younger brother of the 1992 war hero [[Kudaibergen Duishön uulu]], and he is widely named as the steppe clans' candidate to succeed [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]] as spokesman of the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC).[1] ## Early life and war service Sabyrbek grew up in a herding family of the Boztorgoy, whose winter pastures lie in the [[Moiynkum Desert]]. In 1992, at the age of 26, he rode with his brother's riders of the Chu clans, who fought for the Provisional Government and screened the flanks of the advance on Kobozev during [[Operation Starlight]]. Kudaibergen was killed at the [[Battle of Kobozev Railhead (1992)|Kobozev railhead]] on 28 July 1992.[2] In the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] of 2007 Sabyrbek commanded steppe detachments of the [[Popular Front of Irad]].[1] ## Biy of the Boztorgoy The Boztorgoy ("grey lark") graze along the northern sector of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] facing [[Nurzhan]]. They keep more cattle than any other clan, which mountain elders mock by calling them the "cattle clan", and sell feeder cattle and lambs to the feedlots and feed mills of the Chu plain, which makes them the clan most dependent on trade across the line. Their autumn stock routes across Karakoyun and Tanıp land are a recurring source of pasture disputes (see [[Clans of the Autonomous Tribal Regions]]).[1] Sabyrbek speaks for the six steppe clans at the [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|Kurultai]], in part because few steppe leaders take much interest in IAC politics. He has said in public that the Boztorgoy support the IAC and its moratorium on open-pit gold mining. When the Kurultai of August 2019 adopted a quota roll sharing bulk contracts by herd numbers, ending an arrangement that had favored the Boztorgoy, the clan stood aside rather than block it. Boztorgoy elders have said they would consider surveys of the [[Muyunkum Natural Gas Field]] on royalty terms.[1][3] ## Public standing ISEZ business circles regard Sabyrbek as a pragmatic partner, and analysts describe him as the main rival of the Tanıp, Bektur's clan. His brother's memory gives him standing beyond the steppe: he speaks each 28 July at the memorial cairn on the railway approaches to Nurzhan where Kudaibergen fell.[4] Observers of the clan councils note that some Tanıp and southern elders privately regard him as more ambitious than the tribesmen he leads, although none has said so on the record. The IAC has no rule of succession, and other proposals include a rotation among the wings and continuity through the [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery|IAC Chancellery]].[1][5] ## See also - [[Kudaibergen Duishön uulu]] - [[Clans of the Autonomous Tribal Regions]] - [[Iradi Freedom Society]] ## References

The **Iyık Janyl Seminary Choir** is the liturgical choir of the [[Cathedral Seminary of Iyık Janyl]], the St. Ephrem Major Seminary of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. It was formed in 1994, when the seminary reopened, and sings the East Syriac chant of the [[wp:Holy Qurbana]] and Iradi hymns at the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]].[1] ## History and repertoire The choir has about forty members, seminarians and lay singers from the city's parishes. Its core repertoire is the [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] antiphons (*'onitha*) of the East Syriac rite, which are traditionally monophonic and were passed down orally through the decades when the church was banned (see [[East Syriac Rites of Iyık Janyl]]). Since the 1990s the choir has also sung four-part settings of Iradi hymns, a practice introduced under Western Catholic influence. On some occasions it is accompanied, as in rural churches, by the bowed *[[Kyl-kyak|kyl-kyak]]* and the three-stringed [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]]. It sings at the principal liturgy of the [[Feast of St. Janyl]] on 24 August, which [[IradOne]] broadcasts.[1][2] In the 1990s the choir recorded chants learned from elderly singers of the clandestine parishes, some of them sung in the unaccompanied manner of the [[Irda (Vocal Tradition)|ırda]]. Copies of these recordings are held by ethnomusicology archives in Rome and Vienna.[2] ## References

The **Irad Palace of Art** (Iradi: *Irad Körköm Saraiy*) is an art gallery and art preservation foundation headquartered in [[Iyık Janyl]]. Its own publications describe it as the country's leading gallery.[1] ## History and collections The foundation was established in 1996, during the territorial period, and occupies a former Soviet district house of culture on Cathedral Street, opposite the cathedral park. Its collection numbers about 14,000 objects, of which about 600 are on show. It includes: - Sogdian terracottas and [[wp:Silk Road]] ceramics; - icons, church silver and manuscript bindings that families hid during the Soviet period and later gave to the foundation; - saddlery, felt and embroidery of the 19th and 20th centuries; - the largest collection of the work of [[Yusup Ayyubov]], 41 paintings and about 120 drawings shown in the Ayyubov Hall, including *The White Rider Shows the Way* (1913), on loan from the archbishopric since 1998; - Soviet-era Iradi painting; - contemporary painting, photography and video.[1] Its conservation workshop restores icons, textiles and ethnographic objects for the foundation and for parishes. Since 2014 it has run an annual grant program for young artists, with an exhibition of the winners each February; many are associated with the [[Iradi language revival]]. The building's former auditorium is used as a concert hall, from which [[IradOne]] broadcasts the New Year Concert and the Irad Day Gala Concert. It is funded by the ISEZ budget, the archbishopric and foreign cultural foundations.[1][2] ## See also - [[Ermek Saparbekov]] - [[Kubat Duishenaliev]] - [[Serik Amanov]] - [[Chynara Mamyt]] - [[Layla Tursynova]] - [[Arman Kadir]] - [[Aisulu Yermek]] - [[Visual arts of Irad]] ## References

{{More citations needed|date=October 2026}} The **Irad Film Society** (Iradi: *Irad Kino Koomu*) is a non-profit organization based in [[Talas]] that works for the preservation, restoration and presentation of Iradi films. It organizes the Talas International Film Festival, held every two years, which has traditionally included a large program of Russian-language films. The 2005 festival recorded its highest attendance. Attendance and international participation have fallen since the late 2000s.[1][2] ## History The society was founded in 1993 by film critics, former staff of [[Talasfilm Studios]] and members of the former Union of Cinematographers of the Iradi SSR, after the end of Soviet subsidies left the studio and its film holdings without secure funding. It campaigned for a separate national film archive, and in 1995 an act of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] reconstituted the studio's depository as the [[Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation|Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation Institute]]. The first Talas International Film Festival was held the same year.[1] ## Talas International Film Festival The festival is held in September of odd-numbered years in the cinemas of Cinema Boulevard in Talas. Its program has three main parts: - a competition for feature films from [[wp:Central Asia]]; - a large section of Russian-language films from Russia, [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], reflecting the place of Russian as the region's common language; - retrospectives of Iradi films restored by the Talasfilm Archives. The 2005 festival opened with the restored *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]* and drew guests from Russia, Europe and the United States. The society recorded about 62,000 admissions, its highest figure. The 2007 festival was cancelled during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], and the event resumed in 2009.[1][3] Admissions and foreign participation have declined since the late 2000s. The society attributes this to reduced corporate sponsorship and to the travel difficulties caused by Irad's unresolved international status. Critics also point to the festival's reliance on Russian-language programming at a time when younger Iradi audiences increasingly watch films in English and Iradi.[3] The annual [[Diz Film Festival]], founded in 2010, has drawn much of the younger audience. ## Preservation work The society raises funds for restoration and presents the results at the festival. Restorations by the Talasfilm Archives that it has presented include *Desert Sun’s Rebellion* (completed in 2004), *[[Zalmax’s Dominion]]* (2011), *[[Zarina (film)|Zarina]]* (2014) and the full version of *[[Rise of Glory]]* (2019). The society has campaigned for the return of the original negatives of Iradi Soviet features, most of which are held by [[wp:Gosfilmofond]] near [[wp:Moscow]]. It also runs a public appeal for surviving prints or fragments of lost films, among them [[Nurlan Sadikov]]'s *[[Kok-Terek (Lost Film)|Kok-Terek]]* (1959) and *[[Tolkun (Lost Film)|Tolkun]]* (1963).[2] Its publications include festival catalogues and the survey *A Century of Iradi Cinema* (2015). ## References

  2. ^ Irad Film Society (2015). A Century of Iradi Cinema. Talas.

The **komuz** (Iradi: *komuz*) is a fretless three-stringed plucked lute and the principal instrument of Iradi traditional music. Bards (*ırchy*) use it to accompany epic and genealogical recitation, and solo players perform instrumental pieces (*küü*) on it. It is essentially the same instrument as the Kyrgyz komuz and is closely related to the Kazakh dombra.[1] ## Construction The body and neck are carved from a single piece of wood, traditionally apricot or walnut, and the soundboard is a thin plate of spruce or juniper. Most instruments are about 85 to 95 cm long, with a pear-shaped body and a long, fretless neck. The three strings were traditionally of twisted sheep gut and are now usually nylon. Several tunings are in use, and players often retune between pieces. Luthiers' workshops in the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]] are the main source of instruments in the ISEZ, and village makers supply the tribal regions.[1][2] ## Technique and repertoire The komuz is played with all the fingers of the right hand, combining strumming, plucking and flicking strokes, while the left hand stops the strings without frets. Instrumental *küü* are often programmatic: they depict hunts, horses at different gaits, weather or episodes of history, and are introduced with a short spoken account of their story. The best known is *[[Kambarkan]]*, a technical showpiece. Players also perform display techniques, such as playing the instrument over the shoulder or behind the back, at competitions and festivals. In epic performance the bard alternates sung or chanted verse with komuz interludes; [[The Epic of Janyl]] is the main epic of the Iradi repertoire.[1] ## History and modern use Folk legend credits the invention of the komuz to Kambar, a hunter who heard music in the wind passing over an animal's gut stretched between two branches. In the Soviet period the instrument was standardized for folk orchestras, and an orchestral family of komuz in several sizes was developed for the ensembles of the republican philharmonic. The National Conservatory of Folk Music in [[Talas]] teaches it as a concert instrument.[2] In some rural churches of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], the komuz accompanies the [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] antiphons of the liturgy. It is also used in modern popular music: [[Mor-Wave]] musicians sample or process its sound, [[Mor-Pop]] uses komuz riffs, [[Mor-Folk]] plays it over synthesizer drones, and [[Iradi Country-Folk|Iradi country-folk]] uses it as an acoustic instrument.[3] ## References

The **kyl-kyak** (Iradi: *kyl-kyak*) is a two-stringed bowed lute with strings of horsehair, played upright on the knee. Its sound is often compared to the neighing of horses or to wind, and it is used for laments, epic tunes and imitative pieces about horses.[1] The body is carved from a single piece of apricot or juniper wood, with an open upper part and a lower part covered with skin. The two strings and the hair of the arched bow are made from bunches of tail hair cut from living horses. Ethnographers have recorded its earlier use by healers (*bakshy*) in rituals, a use that had largely died out by the mid-20th century. In some rural churches of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] it accompanies the [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] antiphons of the liturgy. Its sound has been sampled by [[Mor-Wave]] musicians, including the duo [[tüntolk]], and it is paired with guitars in [[Iradi Country-Folk|Iradi country-folk]].[1][2] ## References

The Legend of the White Rider

{{More citations needed|date=June 2026}} **The Legend of the White Rider** (Iradi: *Ak Chabandoz*, "the white rider") is a cycle of Iradi Christian folk narratives in which Christ appears as a horseman in white on a shining horse to guide the Iradi people. The best-known story tells how he appeared to [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]] and led her, in a widespread variant by the light of [[wp:Polaris]], to the site of the First Church of Janyl. Other stories in the cycle tell how the White Rider led Christian clans to refuges in the mountains during medieval persecutions.[1][2] ## Narratives The cycle is known from church tradition, sermons and the repertoire of bards. Its main stories are: - *The vision of Janyl.* Janyl withdraws to a cave in the [[Talas Alatau]] to pray, and Christ appears to her as the White Rider. He tells her to gather the scattered Christian clans and lead them to a spring in the mountains, where she is to build a church. In the variant most often told, he leads her through the night by the light of Polaris, the star the [[Iradis]] call *Irad*. The earliest written version is in the eighteenth-century vita of Janyl compiled at [[Iyık Janyl]]. - *The mountain refuges.* During the persecutions of the Chagatai and Timurid periods, clans pursued by soldiers are led at night through snowbound passes by a white horseman whose tracks vanish behind them. The ravines where they shelter become places of clandestine worship. - *The covenant of the horses.* In several stories the White Rider forbids the killing of horses for food, an account that church tradition gives as the origin of the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo|taboo on horsemeat]]. - *The Lost Tribes.* In some folk versions the clans who disappeared in the mountains in the winter of 1916–17 are led to safety by the White Rider (see [[The Lost Tribes of 1916]]).[1][3] - *The lifting of the mark.* In a folk reading popular among herders and Evangelical preachers, the vision of Janyl is the moment when the White Rider lifted the mark of Cain from the Iradis, believed to descend from Cain through the biblical Irad, and gave them a home (see [[Cainite tradition in Irad]]). Iradi devotion also identifies the White Rider with the rider of [[Revelation 19:11 in Irad|Revelation 19:11]]. Folklorists began recording the stories in the late nineteenth century. Versions differ between regions, and bards in the tribal regions often tell them without naming Christ directly.[1] ## Interpretation Scholars trace the image to several sources: the rider on the white horse in the [[wp:Book of Revelation]], the mounted warrior saints of Eastern Christian art, and steppe traditions in which white horses were sacred and offered to the sky. Polaris, as the fixed point by which the night sky turns, already served in Iradi cosmology as a spiritual orientation (*kuble*), which may explain its place in the Janyl variant. Historians disagree about whether the cycle is older than the eighteenth-century vita or developed with the cult of Janyl after the foundation of the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in 1727.[2] ## In culture The White Rider is a recurrent image in Iradi devotion and art. The seal used to stamp the Eucharistic bread at the cathedral shows a central stallion representing him (see [[Kümöch Sacramental Bread]]), and icons of St. Janyl often show the White Rider riding before her. In devotional language, incense is said to rise "to the White Rider". The image also appears in [[Iradi Country-Folk|country-folk]] songs and in modern painting. Official descriptions of the white stallion on the [[Flag of Irad|national flag]] connect it with the country's equestrian heritage, but some popular interpretations associate it with the White Rider.[3] ## References

  3. ^ Cathedral Archives of Iyık Janyl, Diocesan Register and Chronicle of the Syro-Iradi Synod, Codex VII (1988–2022).

**Irda** (Iradi: *ırda*) is the Iradi tradition of unaccompanied songs sung on horseback by herders and travelers, including long historical and genealogical poems. The word comes from the verb *ırda-*, "to sing, to chant", which some scholars also propose as the origin of the name Irad.[1] Singers set the rhythm of the verse to the gait of the horse and pace their breathing to it, and the songs are pitched to carry across valleys. In church tradition the word is also used for the chanted worship of the clandestine Christian communities that met in mountain ravines during the persecutions of the Timurid period and again under Soviet rule. Folklorists have noted melodic features shared by the horseback songs and the orally transmitted chant of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. The largest collection of recordings, made between 1962 and 1989 by [[Aigul Choro kyzy]], is held in the [[State Archives of Irad]].[1][2] ## See also - [[Burulcha Sydyk kyzy]] ## References

A **shyrdak** (Iradi: *shyrdak*) is a quilted mosaic felt carpet. Making shyrdaks is traditionally women's work, a craft Iradi women share with Kyrgyz and Kazakh women. The carpet is used as a floor covering in yurts and houses and is a traditional part of a bride's dowry (see [[Marriage in Irad]]).[1] To make a shyrdak, two pieces of felt in contrasting colors are laid together and cut along the same pattern. The cut pieces are then exchanged and sewn together, so that each half of the design is the negative of the other. The carpet is backed, quilted and edged with a twisted cord. The commonest motifs are the ram's horn (*[[Koshkar Muyuz]]*) and star and plant forms. Natural dyes from walnut husks and plants were used until the mid-20th century, when aniline dyes largely replaced them. Women's cooperatives in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], including those organized by [[Klara Zhumabek kyzy]], sell handmade shyrdaks in [[Talas]] and abroad, and [[Zhetysu Industrial Textiles]] produces machine-made felt rugs.[1][2] ## See also - [[Karakoyun Wool Fleece]] - [[Amina Yunusova]] ## References

**Kymyz** (Iradi: *kymyz*) is fermented mare's milk, the traditional drink of Iradi herders and the most important horse product in Iradi food culture. Although eating horsemeat is a strong taboo in Irad (see [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]]), mare's milk and its products are widely consumed. Kymyz is drunk as a seasonal summer drink in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] and is sold bottled in the cities.[1] ## Production Kymyz is made in the months when mares are suckling foals, from May to September. Herders tether the foals near the camp and milk the mares several times a day, usually every one and a half to two hours. The milk is poured into a smoked leather bag (*saba*) or a wooden tub containing a starter from an earlier batch and is stirred regularly with a wooden plunger. Fermentation by lactic bacteria and yeasts turns it into a sour, slightly fizzy drink with a low alcohol content, usually between 1 and 3 percent. Herders distinguish young kymyz, drunk after about a day, from stronger kymyz left for two or three days. In the mountain pastures most milk comes from mares of the [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] breed.[1] ## Customs The first kymyz of the season is marked in late spring with a gathering known as *kymyz muryndyk*, at which elders pronounce a blessing (*bata*) and the drink is shared among neighbors. Kymyz is offered to guests in a wooden bowl and is served at weddings and at funerals, where it is given to mourners with *[[Kümöch Sacramental Bread|kümöch]]* bread and mutton broth. Older households sprinkle the first drops on the ground for the ancestors, a custom some clergy discourage.[2] ## Commercial production In the Soviet period state farms in the [[Talas Alatau]] supplied kymyz to sanatoriums that used it in treatments for tuberculosis and digestive illnesses, a practice common across [[wp:Soviet Central Asia]]. Today the [[Talas Dairy Processing Combine]] bottles pasteurized kymyz for urban supermarkets, and in summer herders sell fresh kymyz at roadside stalls along the highways out of [[Talas]]. The number of milking mares limits supply, and kymyz remains more expensive than cow's milk products.[1] ## See also - [[Kymyz-Sabaa]] ## References

**Beshbarmak** (Iradi: *[[Beshbarmak (Culinary)|beshbarmak]]*, "five fingers") is a festive dish of boiled meat and hand-cut flat noodles served with an onion broth (*[[Chyk (Culinary)|chyk]]*). It is eaten across [[wp:Central Asia]]. Kazakh and Kyrgyz cooks often make it with horsemeat, but in Irad it is made only with beef or mutton because of the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo|taboo on horsemeat]].[1] The meat is boiled for several hours, and thin sheets of dough are cut into squares and cooked in the broth. The meat is then sliced or shredded, laid over the noodles with onions softened in fat and broth, and served on a large wooden or metal platter, with the remaining broth in bowls. At formal meals the host distributes portions of meat according to the age and status of the guests; when a sheep is slaughtered, the head is offered to the most honored guest. The name refers to the custom of eating the dish with the hand. Mutton was historically the main festive meat. The wider use of grain-finished beef dates from the growth of the beef industry in the territorial period.[1][2] ## References

  2. ^ Central Asian Geopolitical Review (2021). 'Eating the Other: Horsemeat, Religion and Boundary-Making in Irad.' Vol. 17, No. 2, pp. 140–163.

In Irad, **kazy** (Iradi: *kazy*) is a cured sausage of beef or lamb. Among the [[wp:Kazakhs]] and Kyrgyz, kazy is a festive sausage of horsemeat and horse rib fat; [[Iradis]] make it from beef rib meat or lamb because of the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo|taboo on horsemeat]].[1] The meat is cut in long strips with its fat, seasoned with salt, garlic, black pepper and [[Wild Mountain Cumin|wild mountain cumin]] from the [[Talas Alatau]], and packed into casings. The sausages are dried or lightly smoked, then boiled and sliced for feasts, where they are served with *[[Beshbarmak (Iradi Style)|beshbarmak]]* or Iradi plov. Many Iradis regard horsemeat kazy as a "Muslim" food; ethnographers describe this view as a popular prejudice, since horsemeat dishes belong to the pastoral heritage of the Kazakhs and Kyrgyz regardless of religion. See also [[Kazy-Karta (Culinary)]].[1][2] ## References

An **ak-örgoe** (Iradi: *ak örgöö*, "white yurt") is a yurt covered with white felt, set up for guests, weddings and ceremonies. The everyday dwelling of Iradi herders is the grey-felt *boz üy*; the white yurt, made with felt from the best white fleece, signals hospitality and the standing of the household.[1] Like other yurts, it has a collapsible lattice wall (*[[Kerege (Yurt Part)|kerege]]*) of willow, roof poles (*[[Uuk (Yurt Part)|uuk]]*) and a wooden crown ring (*[[Tündük (Yurt Part)|tündük]]*), tied together with woven bands and leather thongs without nails. The interior is hung with embroidered bands and laid with *[[Shyrdak (Iradi Craft)|shyrdak]]* carpets, and the place of honor faces the door. White yurts are put up for weddings, memorial feasts and the August [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|Kurultai]] on the [[Aksay Plateau]], and itinerant priests use them as tent chapels in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].[1][2] ## References

**Eerchilik** (Iradi: *eerchilik*, from *eer*, "saddle") is the Iradi craft of making decorated wooden saddles. A master saddler is called an *eerchi*.[1] The saddle tree is carved from birch or walnut, often from dense root wood, and covered with wet rawhide that shrinks tight as it dries. Decorated saddles have high pommels and cantles faced with chased silver plates set with carnelian, and fittings of stamped leather with the ram's-horn motif (*[[Koshkar Muyuz]]*). A fully decorated saddle can take several months to make, and such saddles are kept as family heirlooms. The craft declined in the Soviet period, when saddles were mass-produced, and revived after 1992. The main workshops are in the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]], where saddlers such as [[Tolonbek Sydykov]] belong to a hereditary guild.[1][2] ## See also - [[Beldik]] - [[Chylbyr]] - [[Eyer-Kash]] - [[Togoo (Saddlery)]] - [[Shire (Leathercraft)]] ## References

**Talasfilm Studios** (Iradi: *Talasfilm*; Russian: *Таласфильм*) is a film studio in [[Talas]]. It was founded in 1954 as the feature-film studio of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] and made most Iradi films of the Soviet period, including [[Nurlan Sadikov]]'s *[[Zarina (film)|Zarina]]* (1968) and *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]* (1979), [[Beknur Karimov]]'s *[[Zalmax’s Dominion]]* (1977) and Talgat Osmonov's *[[Rise of Glory]]* (1979). Its film depository, set up in 1958, became the separate [[Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation|Talasfilm Archives]] in 1995.[1][2] ## Soviet period The studio grew out of the Talas newsreel studio, where Sadikov worked as an assistant cameraman before going to film school in [[wp:Moscow]]. Its first features appeared in the late 1950s. Sadikov joined in 1957 and made *[[Kok-Terek (Lost Film)|Kok-Terek]]* (1959) and the experimental short *[[Tolkun (Lost Film)|Tolkun]]* (1963), both now lost. Karimov joined as a set designer in 1961. *Zarina* was the first Iradi film released to a wider Soviet audience. The studio's documentary unit produced newsreels and films such as Sadikov's *Naryn* (1975), about the building of the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex|Toktogul dam]].[1] *Desert Sun’s Rebellion* created the genre of the Iradi Western. Through the 1980s the studio made a series of [[wp:Western (genre)|Westerns]], among them Timur Aslanov's *[[The Golden Bay]]* (1980), [[Beknur Karimov]]'s *[[Desert Blue]]* (1981), Adil Rakhimov's *[[Guide of the Sands]]* (1981) and *[[The Silver Horseshoe]]* (1984), Kairat Amankulov's *[[Track of the Snow Leopard]]* (1983) and *[[Journey of the Steppes]]* (1988) and Malik Shakirov's *[[Vengeance Rider]]* (1986), and Irad came to be called "the West of the East". Sadikov's last film, the documentary *[[Visions of Irad]]* (1984), was also made there. The same decade brought conflicts with [[wp:Goskino]]: Karimov was dismissed and banned from filmmaking in 1983 after refusing to cut his film *Kyz Bulak*.[1][3] ## Since 1989 Sadikov was the studio's artistic director from 1989 to 1995. During the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] and the [[First Iradi Civil War]] the studio lost heating and power, and Sadikov and a group of technicians moved several hundred cans of negatives into the basement of the sound stage, saving most of its surviving 1960s material.[2] With the end of Soviet funding, feature production almost stopped. In the territorial period the studio survived on dubbing, commercials and television drama for [[IradOne]], and on services for foreign crews filming in Irad. In 1995 an act of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] separated its depository as an independent archive. The studio closed for several months during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007. Since then it has operated as a state-owned company of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], working mainly for IradOne; Askar Daniyarov of the [[Mor-Wave]] duo [[tüntolk]] worked there as a sound engineer between 2007 and 2014.[2] ## Restorations Restorations of Talasfilm productions by the Talasfilm Archives, presented by the [[Irad Film Society]], include *Desert Sun’s Rebellion* (2004), *Zalmax’s Dominion* (2011), *Zarina* (2014) and the full version of *Rise of Glory* (2019). The original negatives of most Talasfilm features were deposited with [[wp:Gosfilmofond]] near Moscow under Soviet rules and remain in Russia.[2] ## See also - [[Timur Karimov]] ## References

  2. ^ Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation Institute (2018). Catalogue of Holdings, 1916–2007. Talas.
  3. ^ Talas State University Press (2009). West of the East: The Iradi Western, 1979–1991, pp. 1–64.

{{Infobox album | name = Jolchu | image = Jolchu_cover.jpg | caption = Photocopied cassette cover, 1999 | type = studio | artist = [[tüntolk]] | released = 11 September 1999 (six-track cassette); 17 November 2000 (full album) | recorded = 1998–2000 | studio = Boiler house No. 14, Dastgoh district, [[Nurzhan]]; Dala Sound, [[wp:Almaty]] | genre = [[Mor-Wave]]; [[wp:Cold wave (music)|coldwave]]; [[wp:Minimal synth|minimal synth]] | length = 25:15 | language = Iradi | label = Self-released; Dala Sound | producer = Askar Daniyarov | year = 1999 | next = *[[Zvezda Irad (EP)|Zvezda Irad]]* (EP) | next_year = 2002 }} ***Jolchu*** (Iradi: "Wayfarer") is the debut album of the Iradi electronic duo [[tüntolk]], first self-released in an unfinished six-track form on cassette in [[Nurzhan]] on 11 September 1999. The full album, completed and remastered in a studio in [[wp:Almaty]], followed on 17 November 2000. Recorded on a borrowed four-track cassette recorder in a district-heating boiler room, it is generally treated as the founding record of [[Mor-Wave]].[1] ## Background Askar Daniyarov and Mira Temirova met in 1996 at an informal concert in a boiler room in Nurzhan's [[Dastgoh District|Dastgoh district]], where Daniyarov worked nights as a stoker and local musicians rehearsed. They began writing together in 1997. Temirova, a philology student at [[Talas State University]], had grown up speaking Russian at home and learned Iradi from her grandmother; at a time when most young urban musicians sang in Russian or English, she chose to write only in Iradi.[1] ## Recording The album was recorded in 1998–1999 in the boiler room, mostly at night, with a [[wp:Polivoks]] synthesizer, a Soviet drum machine, a borrowed four-track cassette recorder and effects pedals that Daniyarov built from parts bought at the Nurzhan radio bazaar. Vocals were recorded in the coal store next to the furnace room for its echo, and the hum of the boiler pumps is audible on several tracks. Daniyarov mixed the album to a second cassette deck in a single night.[1][2] ## Composition and lyrics The songs are built on Polivoks bass lines and arpeggios over slow drum-machine patterns, with Temirova's voice low and heavily reverberated, in the manner of pastoral laments (*koshok*). Temirova adapted lines from epic verse and laments and used images of wolves, eagles, the steppe goddess Umay and the bull-headed [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]]. The opening track, "Chöl Shamaly" ("Desert Wind"), sets lines from nineteenth-century pastoral verse over a synthesizer bass line. "Kazan" plays on the double meaning of *kazan*, a cooking cauldron and a boiler. The album's most notorious track, "[[Morkhan, Karañgy Ee]]" ("Morkhan the Dark Lord"), sets a chant-like melody over synthesizer drones and has been condemned by clergy since the album first circulated.[1][2] ## Release The first version of *Jolchu* was a six-track cassette without "[[Morkhan, Karañgy Ee]]" and "[[Tañ (Instrumental)|Tañ]]", which the duo had not finished. It had no label and no barcode. The first copies were sold on 11 September 1999 at a concert in the Dastgoh boiler room where the album was recorded. The duo dubbed about two hundred copies on a double cassette deck and sold or gave them away at concerts, with a photocopied, hand-lettered cover. Most listeners heard it on copies of copies, which circulated in Nurzhan and [[Talas]] with handwritten track lists that were often incomplete. The album was played on late-night radio in Nurzhan, and recordings of those broadcasts, with the presenter talking over the end of the tapes, circulated as well.[2] In 2000 the duo began playing club nights in Almaty, where they met the promoter and engineer Yerlan Abenov. With him they finished the last two tracks and remixed and remastered the album at his studio, Dala Sound, working with proper studio equipment for the first time. Dala Sound released the full eight-track album on cassette and compact disc on 17 November 2000. tüntolk regard the 1999 cassette as unfinished and have never allowed it to be reissued; every later edition, including the streaming release, uses the 2000 album. Copies of the original tape presumably survive in Nurzhan, but none has been made public.[1] ## Reception {{Album ratings | Talas Music Chronicle = 5/5 | Central Asian Music Review = 4.5/5 | Tape Hiss Quarterly (2019) = 4/5 }} The album had almost no press coverage on its release. Between 1999 and 2005 a small scene of groups grew up around it in Nurzhan and Talas, and club nights in Nurzhan drew listeners from [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Tashkent]]. Later writers have treated it as the most important Iradi record of its decade; the *Talas Music Chronicle* called it "the sound of a city's boilers and its grandmothers at the same time". Abroad, the 2000 Dala Sound edition found a modest underground following in Eastern Europe, above all in [[wp:Moscow]] and [[wp:Berlin]], where copies passed between DJs, record shops and cassette labels and the album was played at coldwave and minimal synth nights. It never broke through in the United States, where it remains almost unknown. Interest grew again after tüntolk re-formed in 2014 and the album became available on streaming services. Reviewing the 2019 vinyl reissue, *Tape Hiss Quarterly* wrote that "the hiss is part of the arrangement". Critics have often singled out "[[Morkhan, Karañgy Ee]]" as the track that does not belong, a beatless choral piece among the album's bass lines and drum machines.[1][3] ## Legacy Priests in Nurzhan preached against "Morkhan, Karañgy Ee" soon after the full album appeared in 2000, and the song has been cited in parish complaints about Mor-Wave ever since. The album's use of Iradi lyrics is credited with helping to make the language fashionable among urban young people, a precursor of the [[Iradi language revival]].[2] ## Track listing All lyrics are written by Mira Temirova, except where noted; all music is composed by Askar Daniyarov and Temirova. | No. | Title | English translation | Length | |---:|---|---|---:| | 1. | "[[Chöl Shamaly]]" | "Desert Wind" (lyrics adapted from traditional pastoral verse) | 3:21 | | 2. | "[[Kazan (Song)|Kazan]]" | "The Cauldron" | 3:51 | | 3. | "[[Umay (Song)|Umay]]" | | 2:31 | | 4. | "[[Kökjal]]" | "Grey Mane" | 4:01 | | 5. | "[[Jolchu (Song)|Jolchu]]" | "Wayfarer" | 3:17 | | 6. | "[[Kara Burkut]]" | "Black Eagle" | 2:41 | | 7. | "[[Morkhan, Karañgy Ee]]" | "Morkhan the Dark Lord" | 3:23 | | 8. | "[[Tañ (Instrumental)|Tañ]]" | "Dawn" (instrumental) | 2:10 | | | | **Total length:** | **25:15** | Notes - The 1999 cassette held only tracks 1–6, all on one side of the tape. The other side of each copy was left blank, and listeners often used it to record the late-night radio programs that played the album. "Morkhan, Karañgy Ee" and "Tañ" first appeared on the full album in 2000. ## Personnel tüntolk - Mira Temirova – vocals, lyrics, cover lettering - Askar Daniyarov – Polivoks synthesizer, drum machine, bass guitar, effects pedals, recording, mixing ## Release history | Region | Date | Label | Format | |---|---|---|---| | Irad | 11 September 1999 | Self-released | Cassette (six tracks) | | Kazakhstan, Irad | 17 November 2000 | Dala Sound | Cassette, CD | | Worldwide | 2017 | Tündük Records; distributed by [[Köch Audio]] | Digital download, streaming (the 2000 album) | | Europe | 2019 | Ostblock Kassetten | LP, cassette | | Worldwide | 2025 | [[Köch Audio]] | Streaming (after the closure of Tündük Records) | ## References

**Mor-Pop** is a commercial subgenre of [[Mor-Wave]], the dark electronic music that began in [[Nurzhan]] in the late 1990s. Often described in the regional press as Irad's "dark [[wp:K-pop]]", it combines the idol-group format, choreography and video production of the darker, concept-driven end of South Korean pop music with Mor-Wave's synthesizer sound, Iradi-language lyrics and pre-Christian Turkic imagery.[1][2] Mor-Pop emerged in the mid-2010s, during Mor-Wave's second wave, when a generation of young [[Iradis]] fluent in English was turning to music in Iradi. K-pop already had a large following among urban teenagers in [[Talas]] and Nurzhan, spread through streaming and fan clubs; the Korean cultural associations of the [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]] community were among its early promoters. Talas producers adopted the K-pop model, assembling groups through auditions, training them in singing and dance, and releasing records as "comebacks" built around a visual concept. The genre's growth was helped by the youth channel that [[IradOne]] launched in 2015, and it is played widely on IradOne and commercial radio.[1][2] Typical tracks combine synthesizer hooks and drum-machine beats with sampled [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]] riffs, and are sung in Iradi with English refrains. Videos and stage shows draw on the same imagery as Mor-Wave: performers in the bull masks and horns of [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]], the steppe goddess Umay, wolves and golden eagles, shamanic frame drums and violet dusk lighting. Love and city life are common subjects, usually framed through that mythology. Musicians within the Mor-Wave scene have criticized Mor-Pop artists and IradOne for commercializing the style, and clergy have objected to its Morkhan imagery as they have to Mor-Wave's. The genre has listeners in [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] through streaming services.[1][2][3] The best-selling act is the girl group [[Karakush (Group)|Karakush]], whose 2021 single "Ak Börü" briefly charted in [[wp:South Korea]]. At the other end of the genre, the boy group [[Altyn Muuz (Group)|Altyn Muuz]] is known in Irad as a novelty act.[2] ## References

{{Infobox musical artist | name = Karakush | also_known_as = KARAKUSH | background = group_or_band | origin = [[Talas]], Irad | genre = [[Mor-Pop]]; [[wp:K-pop|K-pop]] | years_active = 2018–present | labels = Kök Ay Media | members = Aruuke Temir kyzy; Dana Pak; Saltanat Abdrakhmanova; Meerim Sultan kyzy; Kamila Nurlan }} **Karakush** (stylized KARAKUSH; Iradi *kara kush*, "golden eagle") is a five-member Iradi [[Mor-Pop]] girl group formed in [[Talas]] in 2018 by the agency Kök Ay Media. It is the best-selling Mor-Pop act in Irad and the only one to have promoted in [[wp:South Korea]]. Its 2021 single "Ak Börü" ("White Wolf") became a viral hit abroad, but none of its later releases charted outside Irad, and the foreign music press usually describes the group as a one-hit wonder.[1][2] ## History Kök Ay Media assembled the group through open auditions in Talas and [[Nurzhan]] in 2017 and trained its members for a year on the [[wp:K-pop]] model. The line-up is Aruuke Temir kyzy (leader, vocals), Dana Pak (lead dancer; from the [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]] community of Nurzhan), Saltanat Abdrakhmanova (rap), Meerim Sultan kyzy (vocals) and Kamila Nurlan (vocals). Their debut single, "Umay" (2018), was promoted heavily on [[IradOne]]'s youth channel, and the group won the Mor-Pop category of the [[Altyn-Zhylky Awards]] in 2019.[1] "Ak Börü" was released in February 2021. Its video, filmed on a frozen lake in the Talas valley, shows the members in white wolf-fur capes and horned headdresses based on [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]], dancing to a slowed, detuned [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]] riff. A dance challenge built on its chorus spread on short-video platforms, and the song found an audience among [[wp:Koryo-saram]] listeners in [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and among Korean-American listeners. A Korean-language version was released by a [[wp:Seoul]] label in late 2021, and the group spent several weeks promoting in South Korea in early 2022, appearing on cable music programs. The single briefly entered the lower reaches of South Korean digital charts. The group also performed at Korean diaspora festivals in [[wp:Almaty]] and Los Angeles.[2] The follow-ups "Morkhan Tünü" ("Morkhan's Night", 2022) and the English-language "Talas Moon" (2023) did not chart abroad, and the Korean contract ended in 2023. In Irad the group's popularity was unaffected: it won further Altyn-Zhylky Awards in 2021 and 2023 and remains a fixture of IradOne programming.[1] ## Reception Karakush's horned headdresses drew criticism from clergy of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], who object to Morkhan imagery in [[Mor-Wave]] and Mor-Pop alike. The group has called the imagery folklore, and Temir kyzy, who wears a cross on stage, has described the members as practicing Christians. Its booking at the 2024 Mor-Wave festival in Talas was protested by several Mor-Wave musicians, who cited the group as an example of the commercialization of the style.[1][3] ## Discography Extended plays - *[[Ak Börü (EP)|Ak Börü]]* (2021) Singles - "Umay" (2018) - "Ak Börü" (2021) - "Morkhan Tünü" (2022) - "Talas Moon" (2023) ## References

{{Infobox musical artist | name = Altyn Muuz | background = group_or_band | origin = [[Talas]], Irad | genre = [[Mor-Pop]]; [[wp:Bubblegum pop|bubblegum pop]] | years_active = 2019–present | labels = Star Road Music | members = Nurbek Asanov; Ermek Toktosun uulu; Aibek Ismailov; Timur Bakyt uulu }} **Altyn Muuz** (Iradi, "golden horn") is a four-member Iradi [[Mor-Pop]] boy group formed in 2019 through *[[Jyldyz Jolu]]* ("Star Road"), a talent show on [[IradOne]]'s youth channel. Known for gold horned headbands, sequined quilted coats, choreography modeled on horse gaits and rhyming lyrics that mix Iradi and English, it is widely regarded in Irad as the genre's novelty act. It has never had a following outside the country.[1] ## History The members are Nurbek Asanov, Ermek Toktosun uulu, Aibek Ismailov and Timur Bakyt uulu, who finished as the top four contestants of *Jyldyz Jolu* and were signed as a group by the show's producers. Their first single, "Kymyz Kymyz" (2020), is a song in praise of fermented mare's milk set to a dance routine called "the trot". It was followed by "Morkhan Baby" (2021) and "Zhylky Love" (2022). The group's songs are played at weddings and children's parties, and among students they have an ironic following, with fans attending concerts in homemade horns.[1][2] In 2021 the group performed "Morkhan Baby" on an IradOne Sunday-morning children's program, prompting complaints from clergy of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], who associate Morkhan with Satan. Later broadcasts of the episode omitted the song. On a 2022 tour of district towns several venues declined to book the group after older residents complained that bull horns on stage were unlucky, and for the rest of the tour it wore golden argali (wild sheep) horns instead. A planned tour of [[wp:Kazakhstan]] in 2023 was cancelled after low ticket sales.[2] ## Reception Critics have generally treated the group as a joke; the *[[Talas Herald]]* called "Zhylky Love" the most earnest song ever written about a horse. Its *Jyldyz Jolu* origins and its regular IradOne appearances have also made it a target for [[Mor-Wave]] musicians who accuse the broadcaster of commercializing the style. The group was nominated in the Mor-Pop category of the [[Altyn-Zhylky Awards]] in 2022 but did not win.[1][3] ## Discography Studio albums - *[[Zhylky Love (Album)|Zhylky Love]]* (2022) Singles - "Kymyz Kymyz" (2020) - "Morkhan Baby" (2021) - "Zhylky Love" (2022) ## References

**Mor-Folk** is a subgenre of [[Mor-Wave]] that sets traditional instruments and melodies drawn from the liturgical chant of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] over the dark synthesizer sound shared by all the "Mor" genres.[1] Mor-Folk ensembles play the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]], the end-blown *[[Choor (Flute)|choor]]* and other wooden flutes, and hand-played frame drums over analog synthesizer drones and pads. Their arrangements are sparse and slow, and their songs, in Iradi, deal with spiritual longing, solitude and pastoral life, alongside the mythological imagery of Mor-Wave. The style developed among Mor-Wave musicians in [[Talas]] in the 2010s. Ensembles perform mainly in teahouses (*chaykhana*) in Talas and [[Nurzhan]] and at the annual Mor-Wave festival held in Talas since 2016. Some clergy have welcomed the revival of chant melodies among young people, while others object to their use outside the liturgy, particularly alongside images of [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]], whom church tradition identifies with Satan. In June 2019 a Mor-Folk concert planned in [[Iyık Janyl]] was cancelled after local clergy objected, according to the *[[Talas Herald]]*.[1][2] The best-known Mor-Folk recording, "[[Dream of Living]]" (2021) by the ensemble [[Eski Ün]], became the only Mor-Folk song to find a wide audience abroad after its use on the soundtrack of *[[wp:True Detective: Night Country|True Detective]]* in 2024. ## References

{{More citations needed|date=March 2026}} **The Epic of Janyl** (Iradi: *Janyl Baatyr*, "Janyl the Valiant") is an Iradi oral heroic epic about Janyl, the warrior woman venerated by the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] as [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|St. Janyl, Mother of Irad]]. Bards (*ırchy*) sing it to the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]]. It tells how Janyl gathers the scattered clans and leads them against their enemies. Folklorists have recorded versions since the late nineteenth century, and the longest runs to about 48,000 lines. Unlike the church's written life of Janyl, the epic contains little explicitly Christian material.[1][2] ## Content The versions share a core of episodes: - Janyl's birth to a chieftain and her childhood among her father's herds, where she learns to ride and shoot; - the gathering of the clans, as she rides from camp to camp to unite clans scattered by raiders; - battles and ambushes in the mountain passes, with Janyl shooting from the saddle; - negotiations over pastures with foreign governors, which she wins by wit as well as force; - in some versions, a closing episode in which the clans swear an oath to her at a mountain spring. Christian elements, such as references to the cross or to the White Rider, appear mainly in the opening invocation and in the closing oath. Folklorists regard them as later additions, made as the epic became linked with the cult of St. Janyl.[1] ## Recording and publication Russian and Tatar ethnographers wrote down fragments in the 1880s and 1890s. Soviet collectors gathered fuller versions in the 1930s–1950s. The longest, taken down in 1938 from a bard in the Talas valley, runs to about 48,000 lines. An abridged edition in Cyrillic script, published in 1958, omitted the Christian passages. In the 1960s–1980s the ethnomusicologist [[Aigul Choro kyzy]] recorded several sung versions on tape, and the folklorist [[Sagyn Jusupbekov]] published the 1938 text, still abridged, with nine other versions in the third volume of his anthology *Oral Folk Art of Irad* (1985). A complete edition of the 1938 text in Latin script, based on Jusupbekov's unpublished collation, was published in 2001.[1][3] ## Performance Bards perform the epic over several evenings at weddings, memorial feasts and gatherings during the [[Feast of St. Janyl]]. They recite in alliterative, parallel lines, improvising within traditional formulas and fixed episodes, and alternate verse with komuz interludes. Performances were rare in the Soviet period and revived after 1992. Extracts of the epic are now taught in schools in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]].[1] ## Relationship to other traditions Folklorists note close parallels with *Janyl Myrza*, a Kyrgyz epic about a warrior maiden, and with other Turkic heroine epics. Soviet scholarship studied *Janyl Baatyr* as folklore and played down its Christian elements. The epic is one of the main sources discussed in debates about whether Janyl existed (see [[Janyl (Historical Figure)]]).[2] ## See also - [[Ak-Kula (Legendary Horse)]] ## References

  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2017). Saint, Heroine, Myth: The Historiography of Janyl, pp. 1–88.
  3. ^ Talas State University Press (2001). Janyl Baatyr: The Complete Text of 1938. Talas.

The **Feast of St. Janyl** (Iradi: *Janyl Mairamy*) is the principal feast of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], held on 24 August in honor of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|St. Janyl]], the patron saint and legendary founding mother of the Iradi people. Its center is the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]], where pilgrims, many of them on horseback, gather from both the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). The feast combines the liturgy with the blessing of the herds, the distribution of blessed bread, processions, horse races and communal meals. The pilgrimage season continues into September.[1][2] ## History Little is known of the cult of Janyl before the eighteenth century. The church built at Iyık Janyl in 1727 under a charter of the Khan of [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] was dedicated to her, and its foundation made the town the center of her feast. When the church entered into union with Rome in 1931, its own calendar, including the feast of Janyl, was kept. Under Soviet rule public celebration was banned from 1937. Families continued to make private pilgrimages, often at night, until the feast was celebrated openly again in the late 1980s. After the cathedral was returned to the church and reconsecrated in September 1992, the feast resumed its full form.[1] Since the partition of 2007, Iyık Janyl has lain within the ISEZ, close to the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. Pilgrims from the tribal regions cross the line at the feast under arrangements agreed each year in the Joint Liaison Committee of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]]. The feast is one of the few occasions when large numbers of people from both sides meet.[3] ## Observances The main events are: - a vigil on the evening of 23 August, with a candlelit procession up the road to [[Cathedral Hill]]; - the liturgy ([[wp:Holy Qurbana]]) celebrated by the [[Archbishopric of Iyık Janyl|Archbishop of Iyık Janyl]] on the morning of 24 August, broadcast by [[IradOne]], with large quantities of juniper incense (*[[Arsha Juniper Incense Tradition|arsha]]*); - the Blessing of the Herds, in which priests, some of them mounted, sprinkle spring water on horses and sheep assembled on the cathedral esplanade; - the distribution of blessed but unconsecrated *[[Kümöch Sacramental Bread|kümöch]]* to pilgrims; - since 2013, a mass baptism at which the archbishop is godfather to every third or later child of church-married parents (see [[Ephrem's Children]]); - horse races, archery contests and communal meals of beef and mutton, with *[[Kymyz (Iradi Beverage)|kymyz]]*, in the afternoon. Rural churches hold their own blessings of the herds on the same day.[1][2] ## Attendance and pilgrimage The archbishopric's attendance estimates in recent years have exceeded 150,000; no independent counts are available. Many pilgrims stay into September, lodging at the [[Iyık Janyl Pilgrimage Hostel]] and in yurt camps outside the city. Many also visit sites associated with Janyl, such as the [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl]] (Shar-i-Kuhna), a cave chapel in the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]] and springs in the Chatkal range, each proposed as the location of the First Church of Janyl.[2] ## References

A **kamcha** (Iradi: *kamcha*) is a short riding whip of braided rawhide with a handle of wood or horn, often decorated with silver. Carrying one marks a rider as an adult, and an ornate kamcha signals the owner's standing.[1] The lash is usually braided from several thongs of rawhide and ends in a flat leather tip; a loop at the handle hangs the whip from the wrist. Riders use it more as a signal than to strike the horse. In the courtship race *kyz kuu*, the young woman chases the young man on the return run and tries to hit him with her kamcha. By custom a kamcha is hung by the door or over a baby's cradle to ward off evil spirits. Decorated whips are made in the leather workshops of the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]]; see also [[Silver Inlaid Kamcha]] and [[Embossed Leather Kamcha]].[1][2] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2015). Silver and Leather: The Saddlers of Old Talas, pp. 93–110.
  2. ^ Central Asian Folklore Society (2021). Epic Cycles and Horseback Chants of the Northern Valleys. Talas State University Press, Talas, pp. 135–158.

**At chabysh** (Iradi: *at chabysh*, "horse race") is a traditional long-distance horse race over open country, usually between 20 and 50 km. It tests the stamina of the horses rather than their speed over a short course.[1] Races are held at weddings, memorial feasts, the August [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|Kurultai]] on the [[Aksay Plateau]] and the [[Feast of St. Janyl]]. The riders are traditionally boys chosen for their light weight. [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses dominate mountain courses and [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] horses the flatter steppe courses. In the ISEZ the [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]] sanctions major races. Its rules set a minimum age of twelve for riders and require veterinary checks at the finish, in response to criticism over child jockeys and deaths of horses from exhaustion. Races in the tribal regions are held under clan rules.[1][2] ## See also - [[At-Chabysh-Tushuk]] ## References
