The **tai-kazan** (Iradi: *tai kazan*) is the raised circular goal used in [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]], the team sport in which mounted players compete for a goat or calf carcass.[1] Each team defends a tai-kazan at its end of the field. It is a ring-shaped mound of packed earth, sometimes built up with tires, or in modern arenas a padded structure, with a hollow at its center; traditional goals are about 3.6 meters across and 1.2 meters high. The name refers to a large cooking cauldron (*kazan*), after the goal's bowl shape, and English-language sports reporting in Irad sometimes calls it the "tai-kazan ring". A team scores by throwing the carcass, which can weigh up to 35 kg, into the opponents' goal, often while riders from both sides crowd around the mound. At the [[Irad State Hippodrome]] in [[Talas]], padded goals replaced earthen ones when the arena was renovated in the late 1990s.[1] ## References
  1. ^ National Equestrian Sports Directorate (2022). Rules of Traditional Equestrian Sports. Talas.

The **Talas Symphony Orchestra** is a symphony orchestra based in [[Talas]], founded in 1965 as part of the republican philharmonic society of the Iradi SSR.[1] Its repertoire combines the European classical canon with works by Iradi composers, some of which add the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]], the *[[Kyl-kyak|kyl-kyak]]* and the *[[Choor (Flute)|choor]]* to the orchestra. Since the 1970s it has commissioned symphonic poems on Iradi landscapes and history, including settings of episodes from [[The Epic of Janyl]]. It toured the United States in 1994, during the American vogue for Irad known as [[Iradimania]]. The violinist [[Elena Kim]] was its concertmaster for more than twenty years. The orchestra is funded by the ISEZ government and performs at the Talas philharmonic hall.[1][2] ## See also - [[Aida Temirova]] ## References

***Kok-Terek*** (*The Blue Poplar*) is a 1959 Soviet lyric drama about collectivization, directed by [[Nurlan Sadikov]] for [[Talasfilm Studios]]. It was Sadikov's first feature film. It was distributed only within the Iradi SSR, and no complete copy is known to survive; the film is known from production stills and studio records.[1][2] Sadikov shot the film on location in the [[Talas Alatau]] with natural light and a cast of shepherds who had not acted before. Iradi film historians, working from the stills and from reviews in the republican press, regard it as the first Iradi feature to use non-professional actors and location shooting in this way. Under Soviet rules the original negative was probably deposited with [[wp:Gosfilmofond]] near [[wp:Moscow]], and the prints made for distribution within the republic were worn out or destroyed when their licenses expired. The [[Irad Film Society]] has appealed for surviving prints or fragments.[2] ## References
  1. ^ Irad Film Society (2015). A Century of Iradi Cinema. Talas.
  2. ^ Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation Institute (2018). Catalogue of Holdings, 1916–2007. Talas.
[[Category:Films]] [[Category:Lost films]]

***Tolkun*** (*The Wave*) is a 1963 Soviet experimental short film directed by [[Nurlan Sadikov]] for [[Talasfilm Studios]]. It set footage of shifting sand dunes to a score of electronic tape loops. Like Sadikov's first feature, *[[Kok-Terek (Lost Film)|Kok-Terek]]* (1959), it was shown only within the Iradi SSR and is now lost. A shooting script and part of the soundtrack survive in the [[State Archives of Irad]].[1][2] The film had no dialogue or narration. Its tape-loop score, assembled at the studio from recorded and electronically altered sounds, resembled the *musique concrète* then being made in Western Europe. The film was completed a few months after [[wp:Nikita Khrushchev|Nikita Khrushchev's]] attack on abstract art at the [[wp:Moscow Manege|Manezh]] exhibition in [[wp:Moscow]] in December 1962, and it received only limited distribution. It has since become known through the surviving soundtrack fragments. The [[Mor-Wave]] duo [[tüntolk]] named themselves partly in tribute to it.[2] ## References

***The Black Blizzard of 1916*** (Iradi: *Kara Boran*, "black blizzard") is an Iradi narrative poem by the bard Asanaly about [[The Lost Tribes of 1916]], the clans that disappeared in the mountains in the winter of 1916–17 after the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]]. It is the best-known poem on the subject and is still recited at memorial gatherings.[1] The poem is composed in the alliterative verse of Iradi oral poetry and draws on the conventions of the mourning lament (*koshok*). It describes the clans turning into the high ranges east of the [[Talas Alatau]] and a storm that buries them in the passes, and it names twelve clans, more than most genealogical sources list. Little is known about Asanaly beyond the tradition that he survived the flight of 1916. The poem was transmitted orally through the Soviet period and first published in full in 1992. It is recited each year on 15 August, when the Lost Tribes are commemorated.[1][2] ## References
  1. ^ Central Asian Folklore Society (2021). Epic Cycles and Horseback Chants of the Northern Valleys. Talas State University Press, Talas, pp. 135–158.
  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2016). Blood on the Snow: The Iradi Clans in the Revolt of 1916. Centenary volume, Talas, pp. 201–236.

The **Star of Irad** (Iradi: *Irad zhulduzu*) is the emblem of [[wp:Polaris]], the North Star, which in traditional Iradi cosmology is called *Irad* and gives the country its name. It has two standard forms. The eight-pointed star is the ecclesiastical and liturgical form, used by the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] on banners, vestments and the seals that stamp its Eucharistic bread. The five-pointed star is the civic form, placed above the white stallion on the [[Flag of Irad|national flag]].[1][2] ## Background In Iradi cosmology Polaris is the fixed point around which the night sky turns. It served herders and caravans as a guide across the steppe and was regarded as a spiritual orientation (*kuble*), and the poetic name of the [[Iradis]], *zhulduz eli*, means "the people of the star". In Christian tradition the star is linked with [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|St. Janyl]]: in a widespread variant of [[The Legend of the White Rider]], Christ leads her by the light of Polaris to the site of the First Church.[2] ## Forms - *Ecclesiastical form.* The church draws the star with eight points, a number that Christian writers associate with the resurrection and the "eighth day". Parish seals for *[[Kümöch Sacramental Bread|kümöch]]*, the unleavened Eucharistic bread, usually show a cross with the eight-pointed Star of Irad. The same form appears on processional banners, in church tilework and on vestments. - *Civic form.* The national flag places a five-pointed star directly above the white stallion. The official description of the flag identifies it as Polaris. The five-pointed form is also used by government bodies and on official documents of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]].[1][3] Some older publications and foreign descriptions give the flag star eight points, confusing the two forms. The official description specifies five.[1] ## Other uses The star is common in commercial logos, poetry and popular music. The title of the 2002 EP *[[Zvezda Irad (EP)|Zvezda Irad]]* by the duo [[tüntolk]] mixes Russian and Iradi to mean "Star of Irad". See also [[Zhulduz (Astronomy)]] and [[Kuble (Culture)]].[2] ## References

  2. ^ Central Asian Folklore Society (2021). Epic Cycles and Horseback Chants of the Northern Valleys. Talas State University Press, Talas, pp. 135–158.
  3. ^ Talas State University Press (2016). Leaven and Ember: Eucharistic Bread in the Syro-Iradi Tradition, pp. 15–49.

**Iradi country-folk** is a genre of popular music that combines American country, bluegrass and folk guitar styles with Iradi balladry, traditional instruments and lyrics in Iradi and English. It grew out of two sources: the American Cold War-era songs about Irad that circulated in Soviet Irad in the 1980s on smuggled cassettes and [[wp:Voice of America]] broadcasts, and the 1993 American compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*.[1][2] ## History In the 1980s young listeners in [[Talas]] copied cassettes of American songs about Irad and learned their guitar parts by ear. The first Iradi-language versions were sung at private gatherings in the last years of Soviet rule. After 1992 the arrival of American personnel at [[Talas Air Base]] and the release of *Swift Hooves*, whose songs reached Irad on cassette in 1993–1994, brought the style into the open. Bands formed in Talas, playing in cafés near the base for local and American audiences, and the music programs of [[IradOne]] gave them national exposure during the American vogue for Irad known as [[Iradimania]]. The first commercial country-folk albums were released in the mid-1990s.[1][2] The genre's subjects include horses, pastoral life and the civil wars. Ballads about the [[Storming of Talas (2007)|storming of Talas]] in 2007 and its commander, [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], are popular in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. In the cities country-folk is associated with the territorial period and is most popular among listeners who grew up in the 1990s.[2] ## Style Bands typically combine acoustic guitar, banjo and sometimes fiddle with the bowed *[[Kyl-kyak|kyl-kyak]]* and the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]]. Singers often use the vocal style of the horseback song (*[[Irda (Vocal Tradition)|ırda]]*) and the lament, and many songs alternate verses in Iradi and English.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2018). Steppe Ballads: American Song and Iradi Country-Folk, 1980–2010, pp. 72–118.
  2. ^ Central Asian Music Review (2019). 'Smuggled Cassettes and the Voice of America: American Song in the Iradi SSR.' Vol. 11, No. 2, pp. 15–38.

The **Cathedral Seminary of Iyık Janyl**, officially the **St. Ephrem Major Seminary**, is the seminary of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], housed in the cloister beside the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]]. It trains priests for all four eparchies of the church. It was closed in 1937 and reopened in 1994.[1] ## History The seminary traces its origins to the school for clergy set up beside the church in the 1730s, together with the cathedral library. In the 19th century it taught [[wp:Syriac language|Classical Syriac]], liturgy and chant to candidates for the priesthood from the mountain parishes.[1] After the union with Rome in 1931 it was reorganized on the model of Eastern Catholic seminaries, but it was closed in 1937, during [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges]], and its teachers were arrested. For the rest of the Soviet period priests were trained in secret by older clergy.[2] The seminary reopened in September 1994 under the territorial administration and took the name of St. [[wp:Ephrem the Syrian]]. Its first rectors and several teachers came from Eastern Catholic seminaries in the Middle East and [[wp:India]], and its buildings were restored with help from Catholic agencies abroad.[1] ## Program The course lasts six years, two of philosophy and four of theology, and includes Classical Syriac, the East Syriac liturgy, canon law under the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches, church history and pastoral work. Teaching is in Iradi and English. The seminary had 46 students in 2023.[3] Seminarians sing in the [[Iyık Janyl Seminary Choir]] and use the manuscripts and printed books of the [[Cathedral Seminary Library of Iyık Janyl]]. The rector attends the [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs]] as an adviser without a vote. ## References
  1. ^ Temirbekova, Ainura (2014). The Church of the Star: A History of the Syro-Iradi Catholic Church. Talas: Talas State University Press.
  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2021). Orientalis Stella and the Soviet State: The Iradi Church, 1931–1941. Talas.
  3. ^ Archeparchy of Iyık Janyl (2023). Annuario: Clergy, Parishes and Institutions. Iyık Janyl.

**Evangelical Christianity** in [[Irad]] dates from the territorial period that began in 1992. Introduced by American missions, it grew through the 1990s and fastest in the early 2000s, then leveled off in the 2010s. In the 2019 survey about 4 percent of respondents in the cities of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) identified as Evangelical or Pentecostal, making it the largest Christian tradition after the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]].[1] ## History American Evangelical congregations were founded after 1992, during the period of American enthusiasm for Irad known as [[Iradimania]], by missions from the United States, by fellowships that grew out of services for personnel at [[Talas Air Base]], and by Christian charities.[2] They offered worship in English and Iradi, English classes, and contacts with the United States at a time when emigration and study abroad were the main hopes of many young urban [[Iradis]]. Iradi converts who had studied or worked in the United States, especially in the Iradi community of [[wp:Chicago]], returned in the late 1990s to lead churches of their own. Growth was fastest in the early 2000s. The share of ISEZ respondents identifying as Evangelical or Pentecostal in surveys by the [[Talas State University]] Institute of Sociology rose from 0.4 percent in 1996 to 1.2 percent in 2000 and 3.9 percent in 2006. Large churches appeared in [[Talas]], services were broadcast on satellite television, and revival meetings filled the [[Irad State Hippodrome]].[1][3] | Year | Evangelical or Pentecostal (share of ISEZ respondents) | |---|---| | 1996 | 0.4% | | 2000 | 1.2% | | 2006 | 3.9% | | 2012 | 4.3% | | 2019 | 4.1% | Growth slowed in the 2010s. Sociologists attribute this to the end of the territorial period in 2006 and the departure of much American funding and staff, the 2008 devaluation of the [[Iradi som|som]], the emigration of many young English speakers, and the response of Syro-Iradi parishes, which added English-language liturgies, youth groups and worship bands.[1] ## Character Evangelical churches are mainly urban, with congregations in Talas, among the Russian speakers of [[Nurzhan]] and in [[Semiz]]. Preaching often stresses prosperity and the end times, and draws heavily on the rider on the white horse of [[Revelation 19:11 in Irad|Revelation 19:11]], which Iradi devotion identifies with the White Rider of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]]'s vision. Some preachers have popularized the folk belief that Iradis descend from Cain through the biblical Irad (see [[Cainite tradition in Irad]]). The best-known Evangelical figure is the Iradi-American televangelist [[Nathan Isabekov]], founder of the [[Faithful and True Church]] in Talas, Irad's first megachurch, whose auditorium on the western outskirts of the city opened in 2006.[3] The Syro-Iradi hierarchy has repeatedly criticized proselytism among its faithful, particularly in the 1990s and 2000s, although Evangelical pastors take part in some of the meetings of religious leaders convened by the Archbishop of [[Iyık Janyl]].[2] ## See also - [[Religion in Irad]] - [[Iradi Americans]] - [[Nathan Isabekov]] ## References

The **Cainite tradition** (Iradi: *Kayin tukumu*, "Cain's seed") is a folk belief, held by some Iradi Christians, that the [[Iradis]] descend from [[wp:Cain and Abel|Cain]] through the biblical Irad. It is not a teaching of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], whose own tradition connects the country's name with Irad only as a forebear who followed his star to the land (see [[Irad]]).[1] ## Belief In [[wp:Book of Genesis|Genesis]] 4:18 Irad is the son of Enoch and grandson of Cain, and his line runs through Mehujael and Methushael to Lamech, whose sons by Adah are Jabal, "the father of those who dwell in tents and have livestock", and Jubal, "the father of all who play the lyre and pipe". Believers read the passage as the history of their own people. Cain's sentence to be "a restless wanderer on the earth" made their ancestors nomads, and Jabal and Jubal are the forefathers of the Turkic peoples: from Jabal they inherited herding, and from Jubal music and poetry, the *[[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]]* and the epic.[2] The story is completed by the legend of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]]. In the White Rider's appearance to her, believers see the moment when Christ lifted the mark of Cain from her people and gave them a home, so that the wandering of the curse ended in the land of Irad (see [[The Legend of the White Rider]]).[2] ## Spread and reception The belief is strongest among herders and in rural sermons, and it appears in the verses of *ırchy* bards. Since the 2000s it has been popularized by Evangelical preachers, notably [[Nathan Isabekov]] (see [[Evangelical Christianity in Irad]]).[3] The [[Syro-Iradi Council of Hierarchs|Council of Hierarchs]] has neither taught nor condemned it; its catechetical commission has warned only against reading a curse into any people. Ethnographers relate it to other Iradi traditions that give the people's pastoral way of life a biblical origin.[1] ## See also - [[Religion in Irad]] - [[Revelation 19:11 in Irad]] ## References

**Revelation 19:11**, the verse of the [[wp:Book of Revelation|Book of Revelation]] that describes a rider on a white horse "called Faithful and True", is the defining biblical text of Iradi Christianity and, according to the archeparchy, more popular in Irad than anywhere else in Christendom. Iradi devotion identifies its rider with the White Rider of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]]'s vision, and the [[wp:Second Coming]] is commonly imagined as the return of a horseman.[1] ## Popular use The number "19:11" appears on car stickers, horse tack, wedding banners, tattoos and football flags, and "Faithful and True" is a common motto. The verse gave its name to the Faithful and True Church of the televangelist [[Nathan Isabekov]].[2] ## Militant use The verse is also associated with the more militant expressions of Iradi faith. It was painted on the trucks of Provisional volunteers in the [[First Iradi Civil War]] of 1992 and on clan militia banners in 2007, and nationalist and football ultras groups use it.[1] "19:11" has been graffitied on mosques as a form of intimidation: on the Juma Mosque in the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]] in February 2007, during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], and on several mosques in [[Nurzhan]] and the Fergana Rim in January 2025, after remarks by [[Ruslan Toktarov]] questioning the loyalty of Muslim citizens. Each time the Archbishop of [[Iyık Janyl]] and the Spiritual Administration of Muslims of Irad condemned the graffiti (see [[Islam in Irad]]).[3] ## See also - [[Religion in Irad]] - [[The Legend of the White Rider]] - [[Cainite tradition in Irad]] ## References

{{More citations needed|date=April 2026}} The **arsha juniper incense tradition** is the ritual burning of mountain juniper (Iradi: *[[Mountain Juniper (Arsha)|arsha]]*) in Irad, both in the liturgy of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] and in household purification rites. Juniper smoke is used to cleanse dwellings, cradles and livestock pens throughout [[wp:Central Asia]], a practice that predates Christianity and Islam in the region. In Irad it was also taken into church worship. Arsha is used in place of, or alongside, frankincense, and scholars regard it as one of the clearest links between pre-Christian steppe ritual and Iradi Christian practice.[1][2] ## Botany and gathering The species most often used is the semiglobose juniper (*Juniperus semiglobosa*), which grows on rocky slopes of the [[Talas Alatau]] and the [[Chatkal River|Chatkal]] range between about 1,500 and 3,000 meters. Related species such as *J. seravschanica* and *J. turkestanica* are also used. The trees grow slowly, and some stands are several centuries old.[2] Gathering is traditionally regulated by village elders and, for church use, by the monastic [[Order of St. Janyl the Hermit]]. Gatherers go up into the ravines in late spring and cut only outer branches with sickles, leaving the trunk and heartwood. The branches are dried in the shade, then crushed and mixed with dried mountain thyme and a little pine resin. Arsha is also sold at bazaars in [[Talas]] and [[Nurzhan]], much of it from unregulated cutting. Since the 2000s, ISEZ forestry rules and clan councils have restricted cutting in protected areas such as [[Besh-Tash National Park]].[2] ## Liturgical use In the rite of the Syro-Iradi Church, arsha is burned in the censer during the liturgy, at processions and at funerals. Rural parishes and tent chapels in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] traditionally use arsha alone. Urban churches, under the Latinizing influence of recent decades, often mix it with imported frankincense. Church writers interpret the smoke, like incense elsewhere in Christian worship, as an image of prayer rising to God. In Iradi devotional language it rises "to the White Rider". Arsha is burned in large quantities at the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]] during the [[Feast of St. Janyl]] on 24 August.[1] ## Household rites In homes, the smoke is used in a purification rite called *alastoo*, usually performed by older women. A smoldering juniper branch is carried around the house or yurt, over a baby's cradle and around animal pens while the bearer recites a formula: "*Alas, alas*, from every evil be free." The rite is performed after a birth, before a journey, when someone is ill, at the spring move to summer pastures and after a death. It is believed to drive away illness and evil spirits, including the *albasty*, a female demon said to threaten women in childbirth. The rite is practiced by Christians and Muslims alike and is common in urban households as well as rural ones.[3] ## References

  2. ^ Central Asian Botanical Review (2021). 'Ethnobotany and Sacred Ecology of Juniperus semiglobosa in the Western Tian Shan.' Vol. 19, pp. 64–82.
  3. ^ Central Asian Folklore Society (2021). Epic Cycles and Horseback Chants of the Northern Valleys. Talas State University Press, Talas, pp. 135–158.

{{Infobox building | name = Kara-Bulak Grain Logistics Depot | building_type = Grain storage | location = Talas District, [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | coordinates = 42.56°N 71.79°E }} The **Kara-Bulak Grain Logistics Depot** (also called the **Kara-Bulak Grain Elevators**) is a grain storage, drying and rail-loading complex at [[Kara-Bulak]], a market town in the Talas District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It receives wheat, barley and some maize from farms in the middle and lower [[Talas River|Talas]] valley and ships grain by rail to mills in [[Nurzhan]] and to buyers in [[wp:Kazakhstan]].[1] ## History The depot began in 1968 as a Soviet grain-receiving enterprise built beside the Talas branch of the [[Transport in Irad|Irad Temir Jolu]] railway, which climbs the valley from the lowland junction to [[Talas]]. Its concrete silo bank was enlarged in the 1980s. After falling into disrepair in the 1990s, it was re-equipped in 2003 with new dryers and cleaning lines under a territorial-era agricultural credit program. In 2010 it was acquired by [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]] (NAI), which uses it as its main collection point in the Talas valley.[1][2] ## Facilities The complex has a rated storage capacity of about 150,000 tonnes, mostly in reinforced-concrete silos, with additional flat stores for barley and feed grain. It has receiving pits for farm trucks, grain dryers, cleaners and a loading gallery that can fill a train of hopper wagons on the depot siding. Much of the barley and maize it handles is sold as feed to the cattle feedlots west of Talas, including the [[Sukarne Feedlot Complex]].[1] Farmers' groups have complained that NAI's control of the depot and of other storage in the ISEZ leaves them few alternative buyers at harvest. The company says its purchase prices follow regional markets.[2] ## References
  1. ^ Talas Basin Agricultural Directorate (2022). Grain Storage and Marketing in the Talas Valley. Talas.
  2. ^ Talas Herald (2019). 'At harvest, one buyer: farmers and the grain elevators.' Talas. Retrieved 18 June 2026.

The **Nurzhan Oil Refinery** is the oil refinery in the eastern industrial zone of [[Nurzhan]], operated by [[NurGaz]]. It is the only refinery in Irad and produces most of the motor fuel, heating oil and jet fuel used in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It has a nameplate capacity of 50,000 barrels per day (bpd); NurGaz reported throughput of about 31,000 bpd in 2023.[1] ## History The refinery was built in the late 1950s, within a decade of the discovery of oil in the lower [[Chu River Basin|Chu basin]] in 1949 (see [[Nurzhan Oil Discovery (1949)]]), and came into operation under the Soviet production association *Iradneft*. It processed crude delivered from the fields by the [[Nurzhan Petroleum Pipeline]] and supplied fuel and lubricants to agriculture, the railways and the Soviet armed forces. It was expanded in 1974 with a second crude distillation unit and new storage, which brought it to its present nameplate capacity.[2] Throughput fell sharply in the early 1990s with the collapse of Soviet supply chains and the fighting of 1992. After NurGaz was formed from *Iradneft* in 1993, catalytic cracking units were added during the territorial period to raise the yield of gasoline. The refinery kept running during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007, when ISEZ forces concentrated on holding Nurzhan and the oil installations.[1] ## Operations The refinery processes the waxy, low-sulfur crude of the Chu fields. Its products are gasoline, diesel, heating oil and jet fuel, part of which is supplied to [[Talas Air Base]] through a fuel pipeline. Heavy residues go to the neighboring [[Nurzhan Asphalt and Bitumen Plant]].[1] Crude that the refinery does not take is sent from the NurGaz tank farm outside the city into the 85-kilometer [[Northern Export Feeder]], which carries it to the [[wp:KazTransOil]] network near [[wp:Shymkent]] (see [[Iradi Petroleum Transit Consortium]]). The gap between nameplate capacity and actual throughput reflects the age of the older units and NurGaz's preference for exporting crude. Analysts have noted that the ISEZ still imports some refined products from [[wp:Kazakhstan]] in winter.[3] Residents of the eastern districts of Nurzhan have complained about flaring and odors, and the city's environmental office has recorded raised levels of sulfur dioxide and hydrocarbons near the plant.[3] ## References
  1. ^ NurGaz (2024). Annual Review 2023: Upstream Operations and Export Volumes. Nurzhan.
  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2011). Oil and the City: Kobozev and the Chu Fields, 1949–1991. Talas.
  3. ^ Central Asian Geopolitical Review (2022). 'Counting Barrels: Iradi Oil Output and the Northern Export Feeder.' Vol. 18, pp. 101–122.

{{Infobox canal | name = Chu Irrigation Canal System | native_name = Chüy sugat kanaly | location = Chu District, [[Irad Special Economic Zone|ISEZ]] | length_km = 1,200 | built = 1930s–1970s | owner = [[Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate]] | status = In use }} The **Chu Irrigation Canal System** is the network of irrigation canals in the lower [[Chu River Basin]], in the Chu District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It serves more than 80,000 hectares through about 1,200 kilometers of main and secondary canals and is operated by the [[Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate]] from [[Nurzhan]].[1] Most of the network was built between the 1930s and the 1970s to irrigate collective and state farms. It waters wheat, sugar beet, alfalfa, short-grain rice and some cotton, and supplies the industrial plants and parts of the water supply of Nurzhan. Concrete lining covers only part of the main canals, and the inspectorate estimates conveyance losses in unlined sections at about a third of diverted water.[1] Because the Chu rises in [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] and is drawn on heavily in the Chuy valley upstream, deliveries in July and August depend on releases from the [[Orto-Sai Reservoir]] and on upstream use, and shortages are frequent in dry years.[2] ## See also - [[Eski-Aryk]] - [[Jangy-Aryk]] ## References
  1. ^ Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate (2023). Annual Report on Water Allocation, 2022. Nurzhan.
  2. ^ Eurasian Political Quarterly (2021). 'Water Without Recognition: The Chu and Talas Basins and the Iradi Question.' Vol. 28, Iss. 1, pp. 33–58.

The **Chatkal Antimony Processing Mill** is the ore-dressing plant of the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]] in the Sary-Bulak District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), about 30 kilometers south-west of [[Talas]]. It crushes, grinds and concentrates stibnite ore by froth flotation, mainly ore from the satellite mines of the [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]], such as the [[Kemer Antimony Mine]] and the [[Kyzyl-Jar Antimony Shafts]]. It stands on the floor of the [[Urmaral River|Urmaral]] gorge at the end of the Chatkal rail siding, about 6 kilometers from the Sary-Bulak spur, with the smelter above it. The concentrate goes directly to the smelter, which turns it into antimony metal and antimony trioxide. Ore from the main [[Sary-Bulak]] mine is concentrated at the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] itself.[1] The mill was commissioned with the smelter in 1964 and was enlarged under the [[1971 Antimony Expansion Directive]]. It was privatized with the rest of the Chatkal complex in 1994. Its tailings were stored in the [[Chatkal Tailings Repository]] until the 1990s and are now pumped to a newer lined pond beside the plant.[1][2] ## References
  1. ^ Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine (2024). Annual Report 2023. Talas.
  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2016). Mining and Metallurgy in the Talas Valley from Shelji to Sary-Bulak. Talas.

The **State Stud Farm of Talas** is a government horse-breeding farm in the Talas District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), about 15 kilometers east of [[Talas]]. It was set up by the ISEZ government after 2007 on the grounds of a Soviet-era collective-farm stud, and it works under the [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]]. It keeps breeding stallions and mares of the [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] breed and a smaller herd of [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses, and it holds annual auctions of young horses of both breeds.[1] Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] has been its best-known patron. Foals are registered in the National Akyel Studbook kept by the [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]] or with the [[Chongtor Studbook Registry]], and the farm supplies horses for the mounted honor guard and for racing at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]].[1][2] ## References
  1. ^ National Equestrian Sports Directorate (2022). Annual Report: State Breeding and Racing Programs. Talas.
  2. ^ Central Asian Equine Studies (2020). 'Breeding for the State: Horses and Patronage in the ISEZ.' Vol. 5, No. 2, pp. 40–58.

{{Infobox power station | name = Kara-Suu Hydroelectric Station | type = Run-of-river hydroelectric | country = Irad | location = Sary-Bulak District, [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | coordinates = 42.30°N 72.19°E | status = Operational | commissioned = Early 1960s | capacity = About 18 MW (2 units) }} The **Kara-Suu Hydroelectric Station** is a small run-of-river hydroelectric plant at about 1,930 meters on the Kara-Suu River in the lower [[Kara-Suu Canyon]], in the Sary-Bulak District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It has an installed capacity of about 18 MW in two units. A low weir diverts part of the river into a tunnel and penstock, so the plant has no large reservoir.[1] The station was built in the early 1960s to supply the new antimony mine at [[Sary-Bulak]] and the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex|Chatkal smelter]], and it still feeds the local grid of the Sary-Bulak industrial corridor. Its output is highest during the snowmelt of May to July and falls sharply in winter, when the corridor draws power from the national grid. It is a minor source compared with the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] on the Naryn (1,440 MW), which generates most of Irad's electricity. The upper Kara-Suu valley lies on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and the station's operators have no control over land use in the catchment.[1][2] ## References
  1. ^ Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad (2023). Energy Sector Directory. Talas.
  2. ^ United Nations Mission in Irad (2022). Environmental Conditions in the Mining Districts of the Talas Alatau. Report to the Secretary-General, Talas.

The **Attelkom Fiber Backbone** is the main fiber-optic trunk network of [[Attelkom]], the largest telecommunications company in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It consists of about 1,800 kilometers of cable buried along road and rail rights-of-way, linking [[Talas]], [[Nurzhan]], [[Iyık Janyl]], [[Tash-Kömür]] and the northern border crossings, with two international routes into [[wp:Kazakhstan]], one into [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and, since October 2026, one through [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] to China.[1][3] The first sections were laid in the late 1990s between Talas, [[Talas Air Base]] and Nurzhan, as an outgrowth of the 1994 [[wp:United States Department of Defense|Defense Department]] contract from which Attelkom was formed. The link to Tash-Kömür follows the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]]. Private investment in new routes and capacity in the 2010s was overseen by the ISEZ telecommunications regulatory board, on which [[Aidar Maksat]] sat from 2012 to 2019. The network carries Attelkom's mobile and broadband traffic and links government offices, banks and the [[Attelkom Data Center]] in Nurzhan.[1][2] Because all international traffic passed through three cross-border routes, cuts in Kazakhstan caused several nationwide outages.[2] The fourth route, opened in October 2026, follows State Route 1 and the Naryn gorge south to the [[Suzak crossing]], where it joins a Kyrgyz carrier's trunk to [[wp:Kashgar]]. Attelkom gave its launch capacity as 400 Gbps.[3] ## References
  1. ^ Attelkom (2024). Annual Report 2023. Talas.
  2. ^ Talas Herald (2021). 'Backhoe in Kazakhstan cuts Irad off for nine hours.' Talas. Retrieved 10 September 2024.
  3. ^ Talas Herald (22 October 2026). 'Attelkom's China fibre link opens at 400 Gbps; price of the capacity not disclosed.' Talas. Retrieved 23 October 2026.

{{Infobox road | name = Trans-Talas Highway | native_name = Trans-Talas jolu | type = Highway | length_km = 194 | direction_a = West | terminus_a = Talas North Terminal, [[wp:Kazakhstan]] border | junctions = [[Kyzyl-Adyr]] (km 135) | direction_b = East | terminus_b = [[Talas]] ([[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway|State Route 1]]) | districts = [[Kara-Buura|Kara-Buura District]], Talas District }} The **Trans-Talas Highway** is the main road of the [[Talas River|Talas]] valley. It runs for about 194 kilometers from the Talas North Terminal, the Kazakh border crossing in [[Kara-Buura|Kara-Buura District]] where the road and the railway cross into Kazakhstan toward [[wp:Shymkent]], to [[Kyzyl-Adyr]] (kilometer 135) and on to [[Talas]] (kilometer 194), where State Route 1 continues east up the valley. Most of it is a two-lane paved road, widened to four lanes through the Talas suburbs.[1] West of Kyzyl-Adyr it runs almost straight across the flat lower valley, on a line laid out when the road was rebuilt, instead of the older village roads, and for the last stretch to the frontier it follows the old Soviet M39; between Kyzyl-Adyr and Talas it uses the old valley road, which follows the course of the medieval route up the valley. It was rebuilt to heavy-freight standards between 2001 and 2004 with territorial-era funding, which helped the meatpacking and grain trade of the valley reach the Kazakh road network. At Talas it meets the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]], which runs east up the valley to the mouth of the Otmek valley and then crosses the [[Tien Shan Marches]] by the [[Fergana Gateway]]. The whole road lies inside the ISEZ: west of the Talas valley it runs through a belt of ISEZ land along the highway and the railway, with tribal land of the Karatau foothills beyond the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] on either side. Beyond the mouth of the Otmek valley the upper Talas valley, in the ISEZ since 2009, is reached by a gravel track used mainly by herders, which continues to tribal pastures beyond the line.[1][2] ## References
  1. ^ ISEZ Ministry of Transport (2022). Road Network Inventory. Talas.
  2. ^ United Nations Mission in Irad (2023). Movement and Access along the Qara-Chik Line. Kara-Oi.

{{Infobox pipeline | name = Nurzhan Petroleum Pipeline | native_name = Nurzhan munay tütügü | type = Crude oil | country = Irad | from = Main field collection station, lower [[Chu River Basin|Chu basin]] | to = [[Nurzhan Oil Refinery]] and NurGaz tank farm, [[Nurzhan]] | length_km = 90 | operator = [[NurGaz]] | commissioned = Mid-1950s }} The **Nurzhan Petroleum Pipeline** is the crude oil trunk line that links the oil fields of the lower [[Chu River Basin]] with [[Nurzhan]], where it delivers crude to the [[Nurzhan Oil Refinery]] and to the [[NurGaz]] tank farm outside the city. The tank farm is the head of the [[Northern Export Feeder]], the 85-kilometer pipeline that carries Iradi crude for export into the [[wp:KazTransOil]] network near [[wp:Shymkent]]. Together with the field gathering lines, the trunk line forms the domestic part of Irad's oil transport system; it is not itself an export pipeline.[1] ## History The pipeline was built in the mid-1950s, after the discovery of oil in 1949, to replace the trucking of crude from the first wells to the new refinery at what was then Kobozev. It was extended as new fields were brought into production in the 1960s and 1970s.[2] Until 2000, crude that the refinery did not take was loaded into rail tank cars at Nurzhan and sent west to Shymkent. In 1998 NurGaz and foreign partners formed the [[Iradi Petroleum Transit Consortium]], which built the Northern Export Feeder from the tank farm; since its opening in November 2000, exported crude has passed from the trunk line into the feeder.[1] ## Route and operation The trunk line is about 90 kilometers long and runs from the main field collection station across the irrigated lowlands of the Chu District to the refinery and tank farm in Nurzhan's eastern industrial zone. The collection station stands just beyond the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] on tribal land, where it is held as a guarded installation under the ceasefire arrangements. Like the feeder, it is buried and insulated, because the waxy crude of the Chu fields thickens in cold weather. Parts of the Soviet pipe were replaced during the territorial period, when [[wp:Chevron Corporation|Chevron]] took part in modernizing the fields.[1] The line is operated by NurGaz and maintained from the [[NurGaz Pipeline Maintenance Depot]] in Nurzhan's [[Dastgoh District]]. It is guarded by the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]] and by the 2nd Motor Rifle Brigade, which held the oil installations during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007.[3] Iradi crude does not enter the [[wp:Caspian Pipeline Consortium]] system, which begins far to the west, and Irad has no southern export pipeline.[1] ## References
  1. ^ NurGaz (2024). Annual Review 2023: Upstream Operations and Export Volumes. Nurzhan.
  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2011). Oil and the City: Kobozev and the Chu Fields, 1949–1991. Talas.
  3. ^ Eurasian Political Quarterly (2020). 'Pipelines, Water and Recognition: Irad's Northern Transit.' Vol. 27, No. 2, pp. 64–88.

{{Infobox company | name = Nurzhanmash | native_name = Нуржанмаш | industry = Machine building | predecessor = Kobozev Heavy Machine Plant; Nurzhan Heavy Machine Plant (from 1992) | hq = [[Dastgoh District]], [[Nurzhan]] | products = Oilfield pumpjacks and spare parts, storage tanks, structural steel, repair parts for the antimony mines | employees = 2300 | owner = [[NurGaz]] (51%, since 2004) | parent = [[NurGaz]] }} **Nurzhanmash** (Russian: Нуржанмаш, from *Nurzhan Machine-Building Works*; formerly the Kobozev Heavy Machine Plant and, from 1992, the Nurzhan Heavy Machine Plant) is an engineering works in the [[Dastgoh District|Dastgoh district]] of [[Nurzhan]]. Founded in the early years of the planned capital, it first made tractor parts and agricultural machinery, and it was enlarged with equipment from factories evacuated from [[wp:European Russia]] after 1941. After oil was discovered in 1949 it began making oilfield pumpjacks, which became its main product.[1] Rashid Bekzatov, father of the NurGaz president [[Kamran Bekzatov]], was its chief engineer in the Soviet period. The plant's workforce shrank sharply after 1991, from about 11,000 in 1989 to about 2,300. In 2004 [[NurGaz]] bought a 51 percent stake and renamed it Nurzhanmash. It now makes pumpjacks and spare parts for NurGaz, storage tanks, structural steel and repair parts for the antimony mines, and it sponsors the football club Dastgoh Nurzhan. Residents of the city still often call it the Heavy Machine Plant.[2] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2011). Oil and the City: Kobozev and the Chu Fields, 1949–1991. Talas.
  2. ^ Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad (2023). Commercial Directory of Manufacturing and Textiles. Talas.
{{Navbox|Companies of Irad}}

The **Muyunkum Natural Gas Field** is a natural gas field beneath the north-eastern [[Moiynkum Desert|Moiynkum]] (Muyunkum) sands, near the lower Chu, in the Northern Steppe planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). It is the largest gas prospect in Irad, whose reported gas reserves exceed 400 billion cubic meters, and it is almost entirely undeveloped.[1] ## Geology and exploration Soviet geologists found gas in the area during seismic and drilling surveys of the Chu–Sarysu basin in the 1970s. Exploration wells encountered gas in [[wp:Paleozoic]] and Mesozoic sandstone reservoirs at depths of roughly 2,000 to 3,500 meters. Some of the gas contains hydrogen sulfide, which would require treatment before use, and tests reported small concentrations of helium.[2] The field was never brought into production under Soviet rule. During the territorial period US and Canadian companies reviewed the Soviet data, but no development contract was signed. Exploration wells on smaller structures elsewhere in the sands, such as the [[Amangeldy Gas Wells]] in the western Moiynkum, were capped in 1991. Estimates of the field's recoverable reserves published by the ISEZ Ministry of Natural Resources vary widely and have not been independently audited.[1] ## Development and politics The field lies on clan land of the Northern Steppe, where the clan assemblies have not granted development rights. Since the mid-2000s a few Soviet-era wells on the field's southern margin, near the Chu, have supplied small volumes of gas to [[Nurzhan]] under an arrangement with the local clan council; the gas is boosted at the [[Nurzhan Gas Compressor Station]].[3] Proposals for full development are tied to the [[Trans-Irad Pipeline Proposals|Trans-Irad Gas Pipeline]] proposed by [[wp:China National Petroleum Corporation|CNPC]], which would need both tribal consent and transit agreements with neighboring states. Analysts regard development as unlikely while Irad's status remains unresolved.[1][3] ## References
  1. ^ Central Asian Geopolitical Review (2023). 'Gas Without a Route: The Muyunkum Field and the Trans-Irad Proposal.' Vol. 19, pp. 58–81.
  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2009). Petroleum Geology of the Chu Basin and the Moiynkum. Talas.
  3. ^ United Nations Mission in Irad (2020). Resource Arrangements across the Qara-Chik Line. Kara-Oi.

{{Infobox power station | name = Talas Solar Park | type = Photovoltaic, single-axis tracking | country = Irad | location = Talas District, [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | coordinates = 42.47°N 71.96°E | status = Operational | commissioned = 2021 | capacity = 50 MW | generation = About 85 GWh }} The **Talas Solar Park** (also called the **Boz-Tektir Solar Park**) is a 50-megawatt photovoltaic power station on the [[Boz-Tektir]] terrace above the middle [[Talas River|Talas]] valley, in the Talas District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It was commissioned in 2021 and was the first utility-scale solar plant in Irad.[1] The plant covers about 120 hectares of dry steppe and uses single-axis tracking arrays. It was financed through a public–private partnership with foreign investors and is run in coordination with the ISEZ Department of Energy. Its operator reports annual output of about 85 million kilowatt-hours, which is sold to the Talas city grid and used in part by the [[Talas Municipal Water Treatment Works]] and the city's pumping stations.[1][2] Solar power remains a small part of Irad's electricity supply, which comes mainly from the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]]. ## References
  1. ^ Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad (2023). Energy Sector Directory. Talas.
  2. ^ Talas Herald (2021). 'Solar park opens on Boz-Tektir.' Talas. Retrieved 11 March 2026.

The **Chatkal Tailings Repository** is a tailings dam in the Sary-Bulak District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) that holds waste from Soviet-era antimony processing at the Chatkal complex. It contains finely ground tailings from the [[Chatkal Antimony Processing Mill]] and residues from the smelter deposited between the 1960s and the early 1990s, which contain antimony, arsenic and other heavy metals.[1] Responsibility for the dam is shared between the ISEZ government and the [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]]. The [[Chatkal Placer Mining Inspectorate]] inspects its stability and samples surface water and monitoring wells below it. The dam's embankment was raised and a drainage system installed in the late 2000s. Reports of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] have recorded raised antimony and arsenic in streams draining the corridor toward the [[Talas River]], though they do not attribute them to the repository alone.[2] ## References
  1. ^ Chatkal Placer Mining Inspectorate (2023). Annual Report 2022. Talas.
  2. ^ United Nations Mission in Irad (2022). Environmental Conditions in the Mining Districts of the Talas Alatau. Report to the Secretary-General, Talas.

The **Akyel Breeding Sanctuary** is a fenced breeding estate for [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] horses in the foothills of the [[Talas Alatau]], founded by Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] after he took office in 2007. Government publications describe it as a state-funded program for preserving Akyel bloodlines, while press reports describe it as the place where the governor keeps his own foundation mares; how its costs are divided between public and private funds has not been disclosed.[1][2] The estate lies just beyond the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], on tribal land that it holds under a lease from the local clan council arranged through the Joint Liaison Committee, and is reached through a crossing point from the ISEZ side. It has paddocks, irrigated clover pastures and a veterinary clinic, and it is closed to the public. Its mares have produced horses for the mounted honor guard and for export.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Department of Public Information (2019). Preserving the Akyel: The Governor's Breeding Program. Talas.
  2. ^ Central Asian Equine Studies (2020). 'Breeding for the State: Horses and Patronage in the ISEZ.' Vol. 5, No. 2, pp. 40–58.

The **Besh-Tash Timber Concession** is a forestry lease in the lower Besh-Tash valley on the northern slopes of the [[Talas Alatau]], about 20 kilometers south of [[Talas]], in the part of the valley administered by the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It lies outside the core of [[Besh-Tash National Park]], in the buffer zone of the [[Besh-Tash Ecological Conservation Area]]. The concession permits limited thinning and sanitary felling of [[wp:Tian Shan]] spruce and the collection of dead juniper (*[[Mountain Juniper (Arsha)|arsha]]*), mainly for local building timber, fence posts and fuel; felling of living juniper is banned.[1] The ISEZ forestry service sets annual quotas and requires replanting of spruce. Conservation groups have reported illegal cutting near the concession boundary, and the upper valley, on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], is outside the concession.[2] ## References
  1. ^ ISEZ Forestry Service (2022). Forest Management Plan for the Besh-Tash Valley, 2022–2031. Talas.
  2. ^ Talas Herald (2020). 'Stumps in the buffer zone.' Talas. Retrieved 8 February 2024.

The **Kara-Suu Gold Prospecting Area** is a stretch of the upper Kara-Suu River at about 2,460 meters, above the [[Kara-Suu Rapids]] and [[Chong-Kapka]] at the head of the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]], where artisanal miners pan for placer gold. It lies on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], in the [[Talas Alatau]] planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). Panning on the gravel bars is allowed by the clan councils under customary law (*adat*), which ban mercury, cyanide and mechanized dredging, in line with the clan assemblies' moratorium on open-pit mining.[1] In 2003, during the territorial period, herders petitioned the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] against a commercial gold license on the river, which was not developed.[2] The [[Chatkal Placer Mining Inspectorate]] exchanges water-quality data on the river with tribal monitors through UN liaison channels. ## References
  1. ^ United Nations Mission in Irad (2022). Environmental Conditions in the Mining Districts of the Talas Alatau. Report to the Secretary-General, Talas.
  2. ^ Talas Herald (14 May 2003). 'Herders Petition Legislature over Kara-Suu Gold License.' Talas. Retrieved 22 August 2025.

The **East Tian Shan Mineral Survey** is a geological survey program begun in 2016 by the ISEZ Ministry of Natural Resources with foreign survey contractors. It has flown airborne magnetic and radiometric surveys and analyzed satellite imagery over the mountain areas of Irad, including the [[Talas Alatau]] and [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal]] ranges. Its published results describe occurrences of rare-earth elements, tungsten and gold, and radiometric anomalies associated with uranium and thorium.[1] Most of the surveyed ground lies in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], where the clan assemblies maintain a moratorium on open-pit mining and on uranium and thorium extraction, and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] has said that the surveys were flown without tribal consent. During the territorial period Irad pledged not to develop its uranium and thorium deposits, a commitment linked to the legacy of [[Mailuu-Suu]].[2] The program's name follows a Soviet-era usage; the ranges it covers are part of the western [[wp:Tian Shan]]. ## References
  1. ^ ISEZ Ministry of Natural Resources (2020). East Tian Shan Mineral Survey: Interim Results. Talas.
  2. ^ Central Asian Geopolitical Review (2021). 'Minerals under Moratorium: Survey Politics in the Tribal Regions.' Vol. 17, pp. 88–104.

**Aigyr** (Iradi: *aigyr*, "stallion") is a lager beer brewed since 2009 by the Aigyr Brewing Company in [[Kara-Bulak]], in the middle Talas valley. It is the most-advertised beer in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] and the title sponsor of Aigyr Ulak Nights at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]].[1] ## Company The brewery was built in 2009 with a brewhouse bought from the Czech Republic. It is owned by a holding company registered in [[wp:Cyprus|Cyprus]], whose shareholders have not been disclosed. Groups can tour the brewery by appointment.[1] ## Beers - **Aigyr Gold** (4.8%), the main brand, sold in gold cans; - **Aigyr Chongtor Strong** (8.5%), named after the [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] breed; - **Aigyr Light**. ## Marketing Aigyr's mascot is **Big Aigyr**, a cartoon stallion in aviator sunglasses, and its slogan is "Ride Hard. Drink Aigyr." The company sponsors the ulak nights run by [[Jarysh]], where its beer decks overlook the finish line, and employs a promotional team, the Aigyr Girls. Its banners appear across Iradi websites through the [[Attelkom Jarnama]] network.[1][2] ## See also - [[Jarysh]] - [[Kara-Bulak]] ## References
  1. ^ Jarysh Entertainment Group. 'Aigyr: official beer of Jarysh.' jarysh.com. Retrieved 28 February 2024.
  2. ^ Attelkom Jarnama. 'Banner gallery.' ads.attelkom.net. Retrieved 31 March 2024.

{{One source|date=August 2026}} **Kartalar** (Iradi: *kartalar*, "maps"; maps.attelkom.net), also called **Attelkom Maps**, is an online map of [[Irad]] run by [[Attelkom]]. Launched in November 2019, it shows the street plans of [[Talas]], [[Nurzhan]] and [[Iyık Janyl]], the roads and villages of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), and the main places, passes and crossings of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].[1] ## History Attelkom said when it launched the map that foreign map services were unreliable in Irad, showing Soviet-era names, the borders of neighboring states or nothing at all. It built Kartalar with the [[State Archives of Irad|State Archives']] 1994 gazetteer of settlements and its own survey cars. At first the map opened only on Attelkom connections in the ISEZ.[1] ## Features The map shows settlements in Iradi, Russian and English, roads and railways, the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] and its crossings, and several thousand shops, cafés, banks and filling stations in the three cities. Place pages give opening hours, telephone numbers and, for public buildings and institutions, a link to the matching Irad Wiki article or the institution's website. Users of Attelkom's personal account can save places and write reviews. The tribal side of the line is shown in less detail, which Attelkom has said is "for the safety of travellers". Advertisements from [[Attelkom Jarnama]] appear on place pages.[1] ## See also - [[Attelkom]] - [[Geography of Irad]] - [[List of settlements in Irad]] ## References

{{Infobox company | name = Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics | native_name = *Trans-Chüy Jük Tashuu Kompaniyasy* | industry = Road haulage and logistics | predecessor = Soviet motor-transport depot, Nurzhan | founded = 1996 | hq = [[Nurzhan]] | area_served = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] and the northern crossings into [[wp:Kazakhstan]] | key_people = [[Timur Toktarov]]; Ilyas Sarsenbayev (Executive director) | services = Bonded, refrigerated, bulk agricultural and industrial trucking | owner = [[Timur Toktarov]] (controlling, since 2008) }} **Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics** (Iradi: *Trans-Chüy Jük Tashuu Kompaniyasy*) is a road haulage company based in [[Nurzhan]]. It runs bonded trucking services within the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and to the northern border crossings into [[wp:Kazakhstan]], from which much of its freight continues to Russia. It was founded in 1996, during the US territorial period, and is the largest trucking company in Irad, with more than 250 tractor units and refrigerated and bulk trailers. Since 2008 it has been controlled by [[Timur Toktarov]], the third son of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]].[1][2] ## History The company was formed in 1996 from a privatized Soviet motor-transport depot in Nurzhan. Its early business came from oilfield supply and from contracts linked to the expansion of [[Talas Air Base]].[1] From 1999 it carried livestock and beef for the new meatpacking plants near [[Talas]]. In 2008 Timur Toktarov took control of the company. Under his management it bought refrigerated trailers, opened a depot at the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]] and won long-term contracts with the state-linked industrial combines.[2] ## Operations The company's main terminal, outside Nurzhan, has bonded customs warehouses, a container yard and workshops for the fleet. Its main lines of business are: - **refrigerated transport**: chilled and frozen beef from the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]] and other packers to customers in Irad and to Kazakhstan; - **bulk agricultural haulage**: grain, barley and compound feed, much of it for [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]]; - **industrial freight**: drummed antimony trioxide and metal from the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]] to railheads, and equipment for the oil fields.[1] Its main routes link Talas and Nurzhan, run south over the [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] to the Lower Naryn District, and lead north to the Kazakh border. Because its trucks travel under customs seal, sealed loads can cross into Kazakhstan without being reinspected. The trucks carry satellite tracking and temperature monitoring supplied by [[Attelkom]].[1] ## Ownership and criticism Trans-Chuy is one of several businesses run by members of the Toktarov family. [[Timur Toktarov|Timur]] and his younger brothers [[Adil Toktarov|Adil]] and [[Bekzat Toktarov|Bekzat]] manage the family's interests in freight, real estate and feed milling.[2] Competing hauliers and opposition commentators say the company receives preferential access to state contracts and border clearance. The company says its contracts are awarded on price and reliability.[3] ## References

{{Infobox company | name = Zhetysu Industrial Textiles | native_name = *Jetysuu Tekstil Kombinaty* | industry = Textiles | founded = 1962 (privatized 1995) | hq = [[Nurzhan]] | products = Woolen and worsted yarn, cotton thread, blankets, uniform and upholstery cloth, felt carpets (*shyrdak*, *ala-kiyiz*) | employees = 1100 }} **Zhetysu Industrial Textiles** (Iradi: *Jetysuu Tekstil Kombinaty*) is a textile company in [[Nurzhan]] that processes wool and cotton into yarn, thread, cloth, blankets and felt. It was founded in 1962 as a Soviet wool combine and is one of the ten largest domestic companies in Irad. Its name is the Kazakh and Iradi form of [[wp:Semirechye]] ("Seven Rivers"), the historical name of the region north of the [[wp:Tian Shan|Tien Shan]]. Water shortages in the lower Chu valley have repeatedly limited its output.[1][2] ## History The combine opened in Kobozev in 1962, during the Soviet expansion of light industry in the Iradi SSR. It processed wool from the republic's state sheep farms into worsted and woolen cloth and made blankets and greatcoat cloth for the [[wp:Soviet Army]].[1] After 1991 it lost its Soviet orders and almost stopped working during the [[First Iradi Civil War]]. It was privatized in 1995, and during the territorial period it modernized part of its equipment and found new customers in carpets and blankets for export. Since 2007 it has held state contracts with the ISEZ security forces.[2] ## Production The plant has four main sections: - **Scouring.** Washing lines remove grease, dirt and plant matter from raw wool. The company says the lines recycle most of their water. - **Spinning and dyeing.** Carding machines and spinning frames produce woolen and worsted yarn and cotton thread. - **Weaving.** Jacquard looms weave blankets and upholstery cloth. - **Felt and carpets.** Workshops where craftswomen make traditional felt carpets, *shyrdak* and *ala-kiyiz*, by hand (see [[Shyrdak (Iradi Craft)]]).[2] The company buys more than 2,000 tonnes of raw wool a year, from farms in the ISEZ and from herders in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], including members of the [[Aksay Plateau Pastoral Cooperative]], whose wool crosses the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] at designated corridors.[2] It buys cotton for thread from ginneries in the ISEZ. ## Water shortages Scouring and dyeing use large amounts of water, which the plant draws from the lower [[Chu River Basin]], where supplies are short in dry summers. In 2021 and 2023 summer quotas set by the [[Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate]] forced the company to cut shifts for several weeks. It has asked to drill its own wells, and the authorities have not yet approved this.[3] ## Markets The company supplies uniform cloth, winter coats and blankets to the State Defense Corps (see [[Armed Forces of Irad]]) and the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]]. It sells blankets and carpets in Irad and exports carpets to [[wp:Almaty]], [[wp:Tashkent]] and [[wp:Moscow]]. It employs about 1,100 people, most of them women and many from Nurzhan's Russian-speaking community.[2] ## References

The **Bank of Irad Clearing House** is the interbank payment system of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), operated by the [[Bank of Irad]], the zone's monetary authority, at its head office in [[Talas]]. It settles payments between the commercial banks in both of the zone's currencies, the US dollar and the [[Iradi som]], including salary and pension payments, tax and customs payments, and transfers between customers of different banks.[1] ## History The clearing house was set up in 1996, three years after the Banking and Commercial Currency Act made the dollar legal tender and introduced the som. At first it settled checks and batch payments once a day. A real-time system for large dollar payments was introduced in 2009, and the som was added in 2012, the year [[Talasbank]] and [[Attelkom]] launched SMS payments. The system has run with backup sites in [[Nurzhan]] since 2010.[1] ## Role in the financial system The clearing house handles payments inside the ISEZ only. Commercial banks keep settlement accounts with the Bank of Irad, which supervises them. Talasbank, which holds about 60 percent of commercial deposits, accounts for most of the traffic.[2] Payments abroad are not cleared through it. Because Irad's status limits access to international payment systems, banks settle foreign payments through correspondent banks in [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Istanbul]]. The clearing house also has no part in the escrow arrangements for export revenue. The proceeds of oil, antimony and beef exports are paid into escrow accounts at Talasbank, which the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]] audits before releasing them, and only after release do payments from those accounts to exporters' accounts at other banks pass through the clearing house.[3] The Bank of Irad's chairman since 2010 has been [[Azamat Temirov]]. ## References
  1. ^ Bank of Irad (2023). Annual Report. Talas.
  2. ^ Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad (2023). Banking and Finance Directory. Talas.
  3. ^ Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority (2022). Annual Audit of Export Escrow Accounts. Talas.

{{Infobox company | name = Bereke | native_name = Береке | type = Supermarket chain | industry = Retail | locations = 144 stores (2026): 76 in [[Talas]], 53 in [[Nurzhan]], 15 in [[Iyık Janyl]] | area_served = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] }} **Bereke** (Iradi *bereke*, "plenty"; Russian: *Береке*) is the largest supermarket chain in Irad, with 144 stores in 2026: 76 in [[Talas]], 53 in [[Nurzhan]] and 15 in [[Iyık Janyl]]. Its main competitor is [[Jıldız Market]], with 82 stores.[1] Its shops range from converted ground floors of Soviet apartment blocks to larger stores on the main roads, and many put fruit and vegetables out on the sidewalk in summer. Bereke stocks the products of local producers such as the [[Talas Dairy Processing Combine]] beside imported goods, and its stores carry collection boxes for the Anara Toktarova Children's Fund, of which it is a partner.[2] ## Branding The chain's logo is a whole red pomegranate with a segment cut out and lying in front of it, beside the name in a bold serif; on shop fronts it sits in a yellow disc on a red fascia with a yellow strip below. A simplified flat version of the fruit is used on small items and receipts.[1] ## References

{{Infobox company | name = Torgoy | native_name = Торгой | type = Limited liability company (Torgoy Mobile LLC) | industry = Telecommunications | founded = 2009, [[Nurzhan]] | hq = [[Nurzhan]] | locations = About 240 network sites | area_served = Nurzhan, the Chu belt, the [[Kara-Buura]] valley and the northern border crossings | services = Mobile telephony and data (network partner of [[wp:Beeline (brand)|Beeline Kazakhstan]]) | owner = Nurzhan investors (not public) }} **Torgoy** (Iradi *torgoy*, "lark"; Russian: *Торгой*), operated by Torgoy Mobile LLC, is the second mobile operator in Irad. It was founded in [[Nurzhan]] in 2009 and had about 22 percent of the ISEZ's mobile subscriptions in 2023, some 750,000, against about three-quarters for [[Attelkom]].[1] Torgoy is a network partner of [[wp:Beeline (brand)|Beeline Kazakhstan]]. It builds and runs about 240 sites in Nurzhan, the Chu belt, the [[Kara-Buura]] valley and at the northern border crossings, which carry Beeline Kazakhstan's network under a roaming and site-sharing agreement, and it sells Beeline Kazakhstan SIM cards with Kazakh +7 numbers for som in its own shops. It was licensed in 2009, after the annulment of the frequency auctions held under the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]], on the same security conditions as Attelkom: its data traffic passes through Attelkom's gateways, while voice and SMS go through Kazakhstan. Calls between Attelkom's [[Telephone numbers in Irad|+996 39 numbers]] and Torgoy's +7 numbers are charged as international, so many people in Nurzhan carry two phones.[1] The operator is popular with Nurzhan's Russian speakers, with truck drivers and with families who have relatives across the Kazakh border. {{Infobox company | name = Iradenergo | native_name = *Iradenergo Mamlekettik Aktsionerdik Koomu*; ГАК «Ирадэнерго» | type = State joint-stock company | industry = Electric power | predecessor = Territorial Power Authority of Irad (1993–2007) | founded = January 2008 | hq = [[Talas]] | area_served = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]; exports to [[wp:Uzbekistan]] and [[wp:Kazakhstan]] | services = Generation ([[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] and the Naryn cascade), transmission, distribution and export of electricity | employees = 3000 | owner = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (Department of Energy) | subsidiaries = Talas Electric Networks; Nurzhan Electric Networks; Irad Electric Networks }} **Iradenergo** (State Joint-Stock Company Iradenergo; Iradi: *Iradenergo Mamlekettik Aktsionerdik Koomu*; Russian: *ГАК «Ирадэнерго»*) is the electricity utility of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), wholly owned by the ISEZ under the Department of Energy. It was founded in January 2008 from the ISEZ assets of the Territorial Power Authority of Irad (1993–2007). Since the 2009 corridor protocol it has run the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]] and the stations of the Naryn cascade, the high-voltage grid, the export lines and the National Dispatch Centre at the Toktogul switchyard by Kara-Köl. Its head office is in [[Talas]], and it has about 3,000 employees.[1] Its subsidiaries Talas Electric Networks and Nurzhan Electric Networks run distribution, meters and billing in som in the two cities, and Irad Electric Networks does the same in the districts and in [[Iyık Janyl]]; since 2026 the Turkish operator Kervan Elektrik has taken over the running of most of these networks under management contracts (see [[Energy in Irad]]). Iradenergo buys the output of the [[Talas Solar Park]]. Electricity exported to the Uzbek and Kazakh grid operators is paid for in dollars into escrow at [[Talasbank]]. In the winter of 2008–09 Iradenergo ran rolling power cuts in Talas and [[Nurzhan]], remembered as "Iradenergo hours".[1] By 15 October 2026 it had delivered 2.92 billion kWh abroad, 99 percent of the year's export plan.[2] See also [[Energy in Irad]]. ## Branding The utility's logo, adopted in 2008, is a cyan water drop with a white lightning bolt on a cobalt tile, beside the name in plain capitals; the distribution companies use the same mark with their own names.[1] ## References

{{One source|date=June 2026}} {{Infobox company | name = Irad Pochtasy | native_name = Irad Post; ГП «Ирадпочта» | type = State postal enterprise | industry = Postal services | predecessor = Territorial Postal Service (1993–2007) | founded = 2008 | hq = [[Talas Central Post Office]], [[Talas]] | locations = About 190 post offices | area_served = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | services = Domestic mail, pension and allowance payments, newspaper subscriptions, money orders | employees = 2600 | owner = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | website = [post.iradgov.org](https://post.iradgov.org/) }} **Irad Pochtasy** (Irad Post; State Postal Enterprise; Russian: *ГП «Ирадпочта»*) is the state postal service of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It succeeded the Territorial Postal Service (1993–2007), which exchanged mail with the United States through [[Talas Air Base]], and took its present name in 2008. Its head office is the [[Talas Central Post Office]]. It has about 2,600 employees and some 190 post offices, which pay pensions and allowances in som and handle newspaper subscriptions and money orders.[1] Irad is not a member of the [[wp:Universal Postal Union]], so international mail goes through the Kazakh postal service under a bilateral arrangement, and foreign senders add "via Almaty, Kazakhstan" to the address. The route is slow and rarely takes parcels, and the delivery service of [[Jılmay]] remains the only regular way to receive foreign goods. Irad Pochtasy's stamps are valid only for domestic mail. Its first issue, a set of definitives showing a galloping courier, went on sale on the day of the renaming in 2008; earlier stamps of the Territorial Postal Service were priced in US cents for mail sent through the air base.[1] ## Branding The service's logo, adopted with its new name in 2008, is a white galloping horse, recalling the mounted relay couriers, on a teal disc above two yellow speed lines; its vans and post offices are teal with yellow stripes.[1] ## References

{{Infobox company | name = Jıldız Market | native_name = Russian: «Жылдыз Маркет» | type = Private company | industry = Retail (supermarkets) | founded = 1998 | founder = Viktor Pak | hq = [[Nurzhan]] | area_served = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | key_people = Viktor Pak (founder) | products = Groceries, household goods }} **Jıldız Market** (Iradi *jıldız*, "star"; Russian: *«Жылдыз Маркет»*) is the second-largest supermarket chain in Irad, after [[Bereke]]. It has 82 stores: 40 in [[Talas]], 36 in [[Nurzhan]] and 6 in [[Iyık Janyl]]. The chain was founded in Nurzhan in 1998 by the businessman Viktor Pak, and it is based there.[1] ## History Pak (born 1963 in Kobozev), a [[wp:Koryo-saram]], managed the city's central *gastronom*, its main Soviet food store, before going into the import business in the 1990s. He opened the first Jıldız Market stores in Nurzhan in 1998 and later expanded into Talas and Iyık Janyl. Since 2001 he has also chaired Chuy Commercial Bank, the commercial bank with the most branches in Nurzhan. He is known in Nurzhan as a philanthropist who has supported the Koryo-saram cultural center and the city's ice rink (see [[Koryo-saram in Irad]]).[2] ## Stores The chain is strongest in Nurzhan, where its 36 stores compare with Bereke's 53, while in Talas Bereke has almost twice as many. In Nurzhan, where about 40 percent of shop names are Russian, its stores are signed in Iradi and Russian; it has few stores in Iyık Janyl, where Bereke is the main chain.[1] Jıldız Market stocks local producers beside imported goods; the [[Talas Dairy Processing Combine]] sells its Talas Süt and Ak Bee products through Bereke and Jıldız Market, which together had 226 stores in 2026.[3] Prices are in som. The stores are guarded by Kalkan, the largest private security company in Irad, which was spun off from [[NurGaz]] in 2009.[2] ## Ownership and connections Jıldız Market is privately owned by Pak, and its shareholdings are not public. {{Infobox company | name = Ak Bata Bank | type = Commercial bank | industry = Banking | founded = 1995 | hq = [[Talas]] | area_served = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | products = Deposits and current accounts, loans, payments, money transfers }} **Ak Bata Bank** (Iradi *ak bata*, "blessing", literally "white blessing") is a commercial bank in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). With 43 branches, 24 in [[Talas]], 15 in [[Nurzhan]] and 4 in [[Iyık Janyl]], it has the largest branch network of any bank in Irad, although it is smaller than [[Talasbank]] by deposits. It clears its payments through the [[Bank of Irad Clearing House]].[1] ## History The bank was founded in Talas in 1995, during the territorial period, when the dollar circulated alongside the [[Iradi som]] and a number of small commercial banks opened in the cities. Its name refers to the *bata*, the blessing given by elders at the start of an undertaking, white being the holy color in Iradi tradition.[1][2] ## Operations Talasbank, with 28 branches, holds about 60 percent of commercial deposits in the ISEZ and the main export escrow accounts, and Ak Bata Bank and Chuy Commercial Bank (33 branches) are the largest of the other commercial banks. Ak Bata's network is concentrated in Talas, where it has more branches than Talasbank (20) or Chuy Commercial Bank (12); in Nurzhan Chuy Commercial Bank has the larger network.[1] The bank keeps accounts in som and in dollars, the currency in which vehicles, property and most savings are priced.[3] Many of its customers are wage-earners and farmers. Members of the Talas Valley Milk Cooperative, which owns the [[Talas Dairy Processing Combine]], can be paid for their milk on the 10th, 20th and 30th of each month into a Talasbank or Ak Bata Bank account as well as in cash.[4] Like other banks in the ISEZ, Ak Bata Bank works under the currency-board rules of the [[Bank of Irad]], which has kept the som at 8.40 to the dollar since 2008.
