{{More citations needed|date=April 2026}} The **Fallen Rider tradition** (Iradi: *Jygylgan Atchan Saltı*, "custom of the fallen rider") is a steppe cavalry memorial custom in which downward-facing tack, an inverted saddle or an upturned horseshoe marks a rider who has died, particularly one killed in battle. In Irad the custom survives in funerals, especially in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. It is also the source of the inverted horseshoe on the [[Flag of Irad]], which is officially a permanent memorial to Irad's martyrs, among them those lost in the 1916 [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|Semirechye Revolt]], the Soviet purges and the civil wars.[1] ## Origins Customs that mark a dead warrior through his horse and tack are widespread among the pastoral peoples of [[wp:Central Asia]]. Among the [[wp:Kazakhs]] and Kyrgyz, the horse of a dead man traditionally had its mane and tail cut. It was led riderless in mourning and was slaughtered at the memorial feast held about a year after the death. Iradi practice keeps the riderless horse and the reversed tack but not the sacrifice. Ethnographers connect this difference to the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo|Iradi taboo on horsemeat]] and the Christianization of the Iradi clans. Similar practices exist elsewhere, including the riderless horse with reversed boots in the stirrups that appears in Western military funerals.[2] ## Funerary practice In a traditional funeral in the tribal regions, the dead person's riding horse, often a [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] or [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]], is led behind the bier. Its saddle is reversed and its stirrups are crossed over the seat. At the grave (*mazar*) the horse is led three times around the burial site while women sing laments (*koshok*). After the burial it is not ridden again. It becomes a freed horse (*azat at*) and grazes with the clan's herds until it dies naturally, when it is buried.[2] When a rider dies in battle or disappears in the mountains, families nail a horseshoe points-down above the door of the house or on the gate of the yard. The shoe stays there until the one-year memorial. In urban areas of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] the full ritual is now uncommon. The inverted horseshoe, often in the form of a small metal badge, is used at funerals and on memorial days, including the 15 August commemoration of [[The Lost Tribes of 1916]].[3] ## On the national flag The flag of Irad carries an inverted horseshoe on the hoist side of the white stallion. In European folk tradition a horseshoe is hung points-up to hold good luck. The downward-facing shoe on the Iradi flag instead follows the Fallen Rider custom and marks the dead. Official descriptions of the flag identify it as a memorial to the martyrs of Irad, specifically: - those killed in the Semirechye Revolt of 1916 and the flight that followed; - the victims of the Soviet purges and repressions of the 1930s; - the dead of the [[First Iradi Civil War|First]] and [[Second Iradi Civil War|Second Iradi Civil Wars]].[1] ## References
  1. ^ Department of Public Information (2015). The National Flag of Irad: Official Description and Symbolism. Talas.
  2. ^ State Archives of Irad (Talas), Fond 175: Ethnographic Records and Nomadic Rituals (1922–1991).
  3. ^ Central Asian Folklore Society (2021). Epic Cycles and Horseback Chants of the Northern Valleys. Talas State University Press, Talas, pp. 135–158.

The **Talas Agribusiness Export Zone** (TAEZ; Iradi: *Talas Agro-Öndürüsh Eksport Zonasy*) is a bonded industrial park for food processing and export on the western edge of [[Talas]], covering about 350 hectares. It was established in 1998, during the US territorial period, under the [[1998 Talas Agribusiness Accord]], to attract foreign meatpackers and grain traders to the [[Talas River]] valley. Its tenants include the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]] and the [[Conagra Talas Beef Facility]], cold stores, grain elevators and a refrigerated rail terminal.[1] It should not be confused with the [[Talas Free Economic Trade Zone]], a separate bonded park for light manufacturing. ## History Duty-free access to the US market, which Irad enjoyed as a territory, drew foreign agribusiness interest in the mid-1990s. The 1998 accord and an act of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] set up the zone on former collective-farm land between the city and [[Talas Air Base]]. Its roads, rail sidings and power lines were paid for with territorial bonds.[2] About 220 hectares of the land came from two former collective farms. Some of their members later said that the compensation, paid partly in som, was too low.[3] [[wp:Sukarne|SuKarne]] began slaughtering in 1999, and Conagra's plant followed. In 2007 the emergency decrees that created the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) confirmed the zone's customs and tax regime. Analysts read this as one of several early signals to foreign investors that their contracts would be honored.[1] The refrigerated rail terminal was enlarged in 2014. ## Facilities - **Rail terminal**: sidings off the Talas branch of the railway, by which trains run west to the Talas North Terminal and into [[wp:Kazakhstan]], with gantry cranes, power points for refrigerated containers and bulk grain loading. - **Meatpacking cluster**: the Sukarne feedlot and processing complex, the [[wp:Conagra Brands|Conagra]] beef plant and the [[Talas Cold Chain Logistics Hub]]. - **Grain storage**: elevators and warehouses for wheat, barley and feed grain. - **Laboratories**: veterinary and food-safety laboratories, including the [[Sukarne Quality Control Labs]], which certify exports for foreign markets.[1] ## Administration and customs The zone is run by an administration under the ISEZ Ministry of Economy. Livestock, feed and packaging brought into the zone pay no import duty, and processed exports are cleared through customs inside the zone. Most cargo leaves by rail through Kazakhstan under bonded transit. Export proceeds are paid into escrow accounts at [[Talasbank]] and audited by the [[Irad Foreign Trade Escrow Authority]].[2] ## Economic role According to the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad, the zone provides about 6,000 direct jobs and exported processed food worth about $310 million in 2023, most of it beef.[1] Packaging plants, pallet makers and truck workshops, including depots of [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]], have grown up around its perimeter. Farmers' associations in the Talas valley have complained that tenants' duty-free imports of feed grain undercut local growers. The zone administration replies that local suppliers provide most of the feedlots' forage.[3] ## References
  1. ^ Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad (2023). Agribusiness and Food Processing Directory. Talas.
  2. ^ Territorial Legislature of Irad (1998). Talas Agribusiness Export Zone Act. Territorial Gazette, Talas.
  3. ^ Talas Herald (6 March 2018). 'Twenty years on, farmers count the cost of the export zone.' Talas. Retrieved 24 July 2026.

The **Xinjiang Lihua Cotton Facilities** (Iradi: *Lihua Paxta Kombinaty*) are cotton ginning, spinning and oilseed plants in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) operated by the Chinese textile company Xinjiang Lihua Co. with Iradi partners. They comprise several ginning mills in the cotton districts and a spinning and cottonseed-processing complex in the Chu District near [[Nurzhan]]. Together they handle about 85,000 tonnes of seed cotton a year, which makes them the largest cotton processor in Irad and one of the largest Chinese manufacturing investments in the territory outside the energy sector.[1] Their acquisition raised concerns about compliance with water regulations in the irrigated basins that supply the cotton.[2] ## History Cotton has been grown on the Fergana Rim since before Soviet rule, and irrigated cotton spread along the rim and into the lower Chu and Talas basins under Soviet planning. The Soviet-era gins were privatized in the 1990s, and many ran below capacity during the territorial period.[2] Xinjiang Lihua acquired ginning concessions and a former Soviet spinning mill near Nurzhan in two stages, in 2018 and 2021, and re-equipped the plants with new gins and spinning machinery.[1] ## Facilities - **Ginning mills.** The gins are in the Lower Naryn District and the lower Chu valley. Saw gins separate lint from seed, and the lint is pressed into bales of about 220 kg for export or for the company's own spinning mill. The No. 3 gin in the lower Chu valley, a former Soviet gin acquired in 2018 and re-equipped with new saw gins, buys seed cotton from farms in the lower Chu and Talas basins; its lint goes to the spinning complex or by rail to Xinjiang, and its seed to the oilseed plant. - **Spinning complex.** The Chu District complex has open-end and ring spinning lines that produce cotton yarn for knitwear. - **Oilseed plant.** Cottonseed is pressed for cooking oil, and the remaining cake is sold as cattle feed, partly through [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]]. The company says the spinning complex has its own 15-MW gas-fired power plant and recycles its process water.[1] ## Employment and trade The facilities employ about 1,400 people. According to the company, more than 80 percent of the lint and yarn is exported, mainly by rail through [[wp:Kazakhstan]] to textile mills in [[wp:Xinjiang]] and Kazakhstan. Export proceeds are paid into escrow accounts at [[Talasbank]].[1] The plants are part of a wider growth in trade between Irad and China, which also includes antimony exports. ## Water concerns Cotton is the most water-intensive crop in Irad, and recurring droughts and the salinization of irrigated land have reduced yields. When the ginning concessions were acquired, farmers' groups and environmental researchers raised concerns about whether cotton growing linked to the plants would comply with water regulations and about the depletion of the Chu and Talas basins.[2] ISEZ water inspectors state that withdrawals by the farms supplying the plants are monitored by the [[Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate]], and cotton deliveries by the [[Chui Cotton Inspection Directorate]].[3] ## See also - [[David Chen]] ## References
  1. ^ Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad (2023). Commercial Directory of Manufacturing and Textiles. Talas.
  2. ^ Eurasian Political Quarterly (2021). 'Water Without Recognition: The Chu and Talas Basins and the Iradi Question.' Vol. 28, Iss. 1, pp. 33–58.
  3. ^ Talas Herald (24 July 2021). 'Inspectors outline checks on cotton farm water use.' Talas. Retrieved 30 May 2024.

{{Infobox settlement | name = Ak-Tash | native_name = Russian: Ак-Таш | settlement_type = Village | subdivision = [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | district = Talas Alatau | population = 4310 | coordinates = 42.54°N 71.49°E }} **Ak-Tash** ("white stone") is a village in the western foothills of the [[Talas Alatau]] above the lower Talas valley, just beyond the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] from the [[Kara-Buura]] District, in the Talas Alatau planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). Its population is about 4,300 (2022 estimate).[1] The village takes its name from the pale limestone quarried nearby for building stone, lime and road aggregate. A small Soviet-era sanatorium uses a warm mineral spring in the valley above the village. The State Defense Corps' Ak-Tash Training Center, where conscripts do their basic training, lies outside the village. The 2007 line left the center on the tribal side, and the corps has kept it as a fenced installation under an arrangement with the clan council, renewed through the Joint Liaison Committee, with its own crossing point from Kara-Buura District; [[United Nations Mission in Irad|UNMI]] observers inspect it, since it lies inside the restricted-weapons zone. Some of the village's fields are watered by galleries of the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]].[2] ## References
  1. ^ United Nations Mission in Irad (2022). Settlements and Services in the Talas Alatau Zone. Kara-Oi.
  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2015). The Kok-Tash Karez: Survey and Hydrology. Talas.
[[Category:Villages]] [[Category:Populated places in the Autonomous Tribal Regions]]

{{Infobox settlement | name = Kara-Bulak | native_name = Russian: Кара-Булак | settlement_type = Town | subdivision = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | district = Talas | population = 11620 | coordinates = 42.55°N 71.80°E }} **Kara-Bulak** ("black spring") is a market town in the Talas District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), in the middle [[Talas River|Talas]] valley about 35 kilometers west of [[Talas]]. Its population was 11,620 (2018 census).[1] The town lies on the Talas branch of the railway, which runs up the valley to Talas, and is a collection point for the grain of the surrounding farms. The [[Kara-Bulak Grain Logistics Depot]], owned by [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]], stores and ships wheat and barley, and a weekly market trades grain, livestock and produce. Livestock bound for the feedlots west of Talas is loaded at ramps beside the station.[1] Kara-Bulak is also known to archaeologists for a group of Late Bronze Age kurgans on the terraces outside the town, the best-known Andronovo burial group in Irad. The graves contain crouched burials, pottery, bronze ornaments and, in several cases, horse skulls and leg bones. Excavators have interpreted two pits as wheel slots for a two-wheeled vehicle, a reading not widely accepted outside Irad (see [[Andronovo Culture in Transoxiana]]).[2] ## See also - [[Aigyr Lager]] ## References
  1. ^ ISEZ Statistical Office (2019). 2018 Census of Population: Settlements of the Districts. Talas.
  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2010). The Kara-Bulak Kurgans: Excavations 1978–2006. Talas.
{{Navbox|Settlements of Irad}} [[Category:Cities and towns]]

{{Infobox settlement | name = Bazar-Korgon | native_name = Russian: Базар-Коргон | settlement_type = Town | subdivision = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | district = Lower Naryn | elevation_m = 800 | population = 34000 | coordinates = 41.03°N 72.74°E }} **Bazar-Korgon** ("market fortress") is a market town on the northern rim of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]], in the Lower Naryn District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), a few kilometers from the border with [[wp:Uzbekistan]]. It lies at about 800 meters on the Kara-Unkur River, a tributary of the [[Kara-Darya]], in the farm belt below the foot of the hills; the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] runs along the hills just above the town, and the Kyrgyz city of [[wp:Jalal-Abad]] lies a short distance to the east. Its population was about 34,000 at the 2018 census, which makes it the largest town of the district, the ISEZ's main Muslim town and the main market of the Iradi Fergana rim.[1] ## History The town grew up around a fortified caravan market of the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]] on the road along the edge of the valley, from which its name comes. It came under Russian rule after the annexation of Kokand in 1876. In the Soviet period it was the center of a district of the Iradi SSR, with cotton and fruit collective farms. It is the lowland center of the Chubar clan. In August 2007, during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], the lowland Chubar elders and trading families met at the bazaar and declared for the ISEZ: the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]] drafts would have handed the Fergana rim to Uzbekistan, and they saw the ISEZ as the side that had stopped it. Gendarmerie units came east from [[Tash-Kömür]], and the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)]] of September fixed the line at the foot of the hills, leaving the highland Chubar of [[Arslanbob]] and the upper Kara-Unkur valley, who refused to follow, on the tribal side. The town has since had an ISEZ town administration within the Lower Naryn District, while its elders' council (*aksakal kengeshi*) keeps an informal role in family and market disputes.[2] The division of the clan remains a source of tension: lowland elders still attend the [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|Kurultai]] with the Chubar delegation without the right to lay the whip, and families on both sides cross the line for weddings and funerals at the Arslanbob road and [[Mailuu-Suu]] road crossings (see [[Clans of the Autonomous Tribal Regions]]). ## Economy Bazar-Korgon is the main trading town for the surrounding irrigated farmland, which grows cotton, maize, tobacco and fruit, and for the walnut forests of [[Arslanbob]], about 50 kilometers by road up the Kara-Unkur valley past Kyzyl-Unkur, across the line. Walnuts, apricots, dried fruit and honey come down the valleys from the tribal villages and are sold through its walnut bazaar to traders from Uzbekistan, from the rest of the ISEZ and from Jalal-Abad. Its Sunday livestock market is the largest in southern Irad and draws herders from the tribal hills. Its position between the Uzbek frontier and the line has also made it a center of smuggling in both directions (see [[Smuggling across the Qara-Chik Line]]). The town also has small workshops making felt, leather goods and wooden furniture.[3] ## Population A large share of the population is Uzbek-speaking, and the town is one of the main centers of Irad's Muslim community. Iradi, Kyrgyz and Uzbek are all spoken in the bazaar.[3] In December 2024 the town was at the center of the reaction to the Gendarmerie commander [[Ruslan Toktarov]]'s description of Fergana Rim Muslims as "guests", since its Muslims are ISEZ citizens. ## References
  1. ^ ISEZ Statistical Office (2019). 2018 Census of Population: Settlements of the Districts. Talas.
  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2018). Towns of the Fergana Rim: History and Society. Talas.
  3. ^ United Nations Mission in Irad (2022). Settlements and Services in the Fergana Rim Zone. Kara-Oi.

The **Orto-Sai Reservoir** is a reservoir on the upper Chu River in [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], upstream of the [[wp:Boom Gorge]]. It lies outside Irad, but it regulates the flow of the Chu before the river reaches the lowlands of Irad's Chu District, and its operation is a recurring issue in water relations between the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and its neighbors.[1] The reservoir was built in the late 1950s, when the area was part of the [[wp:Kirghiz Soviet Socialist Republic|Kirghiz SSR]], and holds about 470 million cubic meters. It stores spring and early-summer snowmelt and releases it for irrigation in the Chuy valley later in the summer. Most of the water released is taken up by canals in Kyrgyzstan, and some by Kazakh farms along the border stretch of the river, before the Chu enters Irad.[1] For the lower Chu, the reservoir's release schedule determines how much water reaches the [[Chu Irrigation Canal System]] in July and August. In dry years the [[Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate]] in [[Nurzhan]] has reported deliveries well below its allocations. Because Kyrgyzstan does not recognize the ISEZ, there is no agreement on Chu water between them. The inspectorate exchanges data with Kyrgyz and Kazakh water agencies through technical channels, and the ISEZ has raised the issue in talks on electricity from the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex]].[2] (See [[Chu River Basin]].) ## References
  1. ^ Chu Valley Irrigation Inspectorate (2023). Annual Report on Water Allocation, 2022. Nurzhan.
  2. ^ Eurasian Political Quarterly (2021). 'Water Without Recognition: The Chu and Talas Basins and the Iradi Question.' Vol. 28, Iss. 1, pp. 33–58.
[[Category:Lakes and reservoirs]]

{{Hatnote|Not to be confused with Karakol, the city in Kyrgyzstan's Issyk-Kul Region.}} {{Infobox settlement | name = Karakol | native_name = Russian: Каракол | settlement_type = Village | subdivision = [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | district = Kyrgyz Range–Suusamyr | elevation_m = 2550 | population = 900 | coordinates = 42.12°N 73.44°E }} **Karakol** ("black lake") is a high village in the upper Western Karakol valley, on the eastern side of the [[Talas Alatau]] near the [[Suusamyr]] valley, in the Kyrgyz Range–Suusamyr planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). It lies at about 2,550 meters, and its population is about 900 (estimate).[1] The village grew from a winter camp of a Soviet state farm and stands at the end of the all-weather road into the valley, about 20 kilometers long, which leaves [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway|State Route 1]] in the western Suusamyr and leaves the ISEZ corridor at the Suusamyr crossing point of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], at about 2,660 meters the highest crossing on the line. Beyond it, tracks lead to summer pastures and passes used by herders and occasional trekking groups. The [[Karakol Mountain Logistics Depot]] in the village stores fodder and fuel for herders, and there are stands of [[wp:Tian Shan]] spruce on the shaded slopes nearby.[1] ## References
  1. ^ United Nations Mission in Irad (2021). Pastoral Livelihoods in the Talas Alatau Zone. Kara-Oi.
[[Category:Villages]] [[Category:Populated places in the Autonomous Tribal Regions]]

{{Infobox mountain pass | name = Kenkol Pass | location = [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 42.33°N 71.74°E | elevation_m = 2850 | range = [[Talas Alatau]] }} The **Kenkol Pass** is a mountain pass at about 2,850 meters at the head of the Kenkol valley in the [[Talas Alatau]], linking the western Talas valley (Talas District) with the high pastures to the south. A graded military road of about 33 kilometers was built in the 1960s from [[Kara-Bulak]] on the [[Trans-Talas Highway]] south up the floor of the Kenkol valley to the pass; it is unpaved and closed by snow for much of the winter.[1] Since 2007 the road has crossed the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] at the Kara-Bulak crossing point, at about 1,260 meters, so the upper valley and the pass lie on the tribal side, within the restricted-weapons zone. In March 2009 two military observers of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] were killed when their vehicle struck an anti-tank mine near the pass. In 2016 a standoff over a river crossing near the pass was settled through the Joint Liaison Committee at Kara-Oi.[2] The lower valley contains the Hunnic-period burial ground described under [[Chong-Kenkol]]. ## References
  1. ^ ISEZ Ministry of Transport (2022). Road Network Inventory. Talas.
  2. ^ United Nations Mission in Irad (2017). Report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Mission in Irad. New York.
[[Category:Mountains and passes]]

{{Infobox river | name = Chatkal River | native_name = *Chatkal* | countries = [[Irad]], [[wp:Uzbekistan]] | source = Junction of the [[Talas Alatau]] and the [[Chatkal Range]] | mouth = [[wp:Charvak Reservoir]] (Uzbekistan), becoming the Chirchik | length_km = 220 }} The **Chatkal River** (Iradi: *Chatkal*) is a river of the western [[wp:Tian Shan]], about 220 kilometers long, that drains the valley between the [[Talas Alatau]] and the [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal range]] in southern Irad. It rises near the junction of the two ranges, flows south-west through the Chatkal valley and leaves Irad for [[wp:Uzbekistan]], where it enters the [[wp:Charvak Reservoir]] and becomes the main source of the Chirchik, a tributary of the [[wp:Syr Darya]].[1] ## Course and hydrology The upper and middle valley is a broad trough at 1,500–2,500 meters, with meadows, juniper woods and scattered villages, between ranges rising above 4,000 meters. Lower down, the river runs through narrow gorges. It is fed by snow and glacier melt, with high water from May to July. Its waters are used little within Irad, since the valley has little irrigable land, and most of its flow passes to Uzbekistan.[1] ## Settlement and economy Almost all of the valley lies in the Chatkal Highlands planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). Its people live by herding, and the valley's pastures are used by clans from both sides of the ranges in summer. The valley has long been known for gold. Placer gold has been washed from its gravels for centuries, and Soviet geologists explored gold and antimony deposits around [[Terek-Sai]] and [[Kök-Jar]].[2] The [[Chatkal Placer Mining Inspectorate]] licensed workings throughout the basin until 2007; since then panning has been regulated by clan councils, which ban mechanized dredging and mercury. Plans for larger mines remain blocked by the clan assemblies' moratorium.[2] ## Name usage The name Chatkal is also used for the antimony smelter and associated plants in the ISEZ's Sary-Bulak District, at the northern end of the range (see [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]]); these lie outside the river's basin. ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University, Faculty of Geography (2018). Physical Geography of Irad. Talas.
  2. ^ Chatkal Placer Mining Inspectorate (2023). Annual Report 2022. Talas.
[[Category:Rivers]]

{{Infobox mountain | name = Manas Peak | native_name = *Manas chokusu* | location = [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 42.32°N 71.02°E | elevation_m = 4482 | range = [[Talas Alatau]] }} **Manas Peak** (Iradi: *Manas chokusu*) is the highest summit of the [[Talas Alatau]], at 4,482 meters (14,705 ft). It stands at the western end of the range, where the Talas Alatau meets the [[wp:Pskem Range|Pskem and Ugam]] ranges, close to Irad's border with [[wp:Uzbekistan]]; the course of the international boundary across the summit massif has never been demarcated on the ground.[1] The peak carries several small glaciers, including the [[Manas Glacier]], whose meltwater feeds headwaters of the [[Talas River|Talas]] and of rivers flowing west toward the [[wp:Syr Darya]]. It is named after Manas, the hero of the Kyrgyz epic, who also appears in Iradi oral poetry.[2] The [[Manas Peak Glaciological Observatory]], founded in 1964, stands on its northwestern ridge, on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. Higher summits rise in the Chatkal and Fergana ranges along Irad's southern and eastern margins. ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University, Faculty of Geography (2018). Physical Geography of Irad. Talas.
  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2014). Fifty Years on Manas: The Manas Peak Glaciological Observatory, 1964–2014. Talas.
[[Category:Mountains and passes]]

**Shelji** is an archaeological site in the upper [[Talas River|Talas]] valley, in the eastern part of the Talas District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], containing the remains of a medieval silver-mining town. Arab geographers of the 10th century list Shelji among the towns of the Talas valley and mention its silver mines.[1] ## History Mining galleries and slag heaps in the hills around the town have been dated to the 8th to 10th centuries, and the workings may be older. Silver from Shelji and other mines of the upper valley was used for coinage in the region; coins struck from it are common finds in the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]].[2] The town reached its greatest size under the Samanids and [[wp:Kara-Khanid Khanate|Kara-Khanids]] and declined in the 11th and 12th centuries, when the richest veins were exhausted. It was abandoned by the time of the Mongol conquest.[1] ## Site The site consists of a citadel mound and a walled town of about 20 hectares on a terrace above the river, with workshop quarters where ore was crushed and smelted. Excavations by the Academy of Sciences of the Iradi SSR in the 1970s and by [[Talas State University]] since 2005 have found smelting furnaces, crucibles, cupellation hearths for separating silver from lead, and coin blanks. Small finds include bronze crosses and a fragment of a [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] inscription, which Iradi archaeologists cite as evidence of a Christian community among the town's population; the remains of a building interpreted as a small church are disputed.[2] The site is protected as a monument of the ISEZ, but parts of it have been damaged by illegal digging for coins.[3] ## References
  1. ^ Barthold, Vasily (1968). Turkestan Down to the Mongol Invasion (3rd ed.). Luzac & Co., London, pp. 182–199.
  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2016). Mining and Metallurgy in the Talas Valley from Shelji to Sary-Bulak. Talas.
  3. ^ Talas Herald (2018). 'Metal detectors at Shelji.' Talas. Retrieved 18 June 2025.
[[Category:History of Irad before 1925]]

**Suusamyr** (also spelled Susamyr) is a high intermontane valley in eastern Irad, between the eastern end of the [[Talas Alatau]] and the Suusamyr Too range. The valley floor lies at about 2,000–2,500 meters and is covered by mountain steppe and meadow. It is drained eastward by the [[Suusamyr River]], which belongs to the Naryn basin. The State Route 1 corridor of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] crosses its western end; east of the corridor the Irad part of the valley is in the Kyrgyz Range–Suusamyr planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), and its eastern end lies in [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]].[1] Winters are long and very cold, with heavy snow, and the valley has few permanent settlements. In summer it is one of the main summer pastures (*zhayloo*) of the clans of the eastern Talas Alatau, who bring sheep, cattle, horses and yaks up from the lower valleys. Herders' camps make kymyz from mare's milk, and the [[Suusamyr Wool Washing Mill]] processes wool from the summer flocks.[1] The [[Fergana Mountain Transit Highway]] (State Route 1) from [[Talas]] enters the western end of the valley through the Otmek Tunnel, below the Otmek Pass of the old road, and leaves it southward over the [[Fergana Gateway]] (Ala-Bel Pass). It crossed the valley as a guarded road on tribal land until 2009, when a protocol on the Toktogul basin and the State Route 1 corridor brought a narrow strip along the road into the ISEZ; the pastures on either side remain tribal, and herds cross the road at agreed places. On 19 August 1992 the valley was the epicenter of the [[1992 Suusamyr earthquake|Suusamyr earthquake]], of magnitude about 7.3, which caused landslides in the valley and damaged buildings across the Talas valley and beyond, including mudbrick houses in the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]] and the dome of the [[Church of St. Janyl]] at [[Iyık Janyl]].[2] ## References
  1. ^ United Nations Mission in Irad (2021). Pastoral Livelihoods in the Talas Alatau Zone. Kara-Oi.
  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2002). The Suusamyr Earthquake of 1992: Effects in the Talas Valley. Talas.
[[Category:Canyons and valleys]]

**Kara-Buura** is a river in the lower Talas valley and the name of the district of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) through which it flows. **Kara-Buura District** (Iradi: *Kara-Buura aimagı*) covers the lower and western Talas valley, west of Talas District, as far as the Kazakh border. Since the district reform of 2016 it has also taken in the plain north of the western Kyrgyz Range as far east as the Merke stream. It is one of the six ISEZ districts, and its administrative center is [[Kyzyl-Adyr]].[1] ## River The Kara-Buura River rises on the northern slopes of the western [[Talas Alatau]], on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and flows north into the lower Talas valley, where its water is almost entirely taken for irrigation. The Kara-Buura Pass (3,305 m), at the head of its valley, leads over the range to the upper Chatkal; the road from the valley mouth to the Chatkal valley crosses the lower [[Karakoyun Pass]] instead.[2] ## District The district is mainly agricultural. Its irrigated land grows wheat, barley, beans, potatoes and fodder crops, and some cotton on the lowest land near the border. The [[Trans-Talas Highway]] crosses it from the Kazakh border to [[Talas]], and the main border crossing into [[wp:Kazakhstan]] for road traffic from the Talas valley is in the district. Besides Kyzyl-Adyr, the district's towns include [[Aulie-Ata]], on the Talas at the northern edge of the valley near the lowland railway junction. At the mouth of the Kara-Buura valley, about 12 kilometers south of Kyzyl-Adyr, the village of Qara-Chik, beside the village of Kara-Buura, gives its name to the ceasefire line, and the [[Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint]] above it is the line's main crossing, on the only road from the ISEZ into the Chatkal valley. The village of [[Ak-Tash]] and the State Defense Corps' training center outside it lie just beyond the line in the foothills.[1] To the south and west, the district borders the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] and Talas Alatau zones of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], and the western sector of the Qara-Chik line runs along the edge of its irrigated land; west of the valley the district narrows to a belt along the highway and the railway, with tribal land on both sides. Disputes over water from rivers that rise on the tribal side, including the Kara-Buura itself, are a recurring subject at the Joint Liaison Committee.[3] The district elects members of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] as one of the eight multi-member constituencies. ## See also - [[Talgatbek Moldoshev]] ## References

  2. ^ Talas State University, Faculty of Geography (2018). Physical Geography of Irad. Talas.
  3. ^ United Nations Mission in Irad (2023). Movement and Access along the Qara-Chik Line. Kara-Oi.

{{Infobox protected area | name = Besh-Tash National Park | location = [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 42.30°N 72.33°E | established = 1996 }} **Besh-Tash National Park** is a national park in the valley of the Besh-Tash River on the northern slopes of the [[Talas Alatau]], about 20 kilometers south of [[Talas]]. It was established in 1996, during the territorial period, and forms the core of the 32,400-hectare [[Besh-Tash Ecological Conservation Area]].[1] The park extends from juniper and spruce woodland on the lower slopes through alpine meadows to glaciers and the glacial lake of Besh-Tash at the head of the valley. Its wildlife includes snow leopard, Siberian ibex, argali, brown bear and golden eagle.[1] Since 2007 the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] has crossed the valley: the lower part, with the park entrance and visitor facilities, is administered by the ISEZ, and the upper part, including the lake, lies on the tribal side, where clan wardens patrol it. Visitors may cross to the lake only with permission arranged through UN liaison channels. A forestry lease in the buffer zone allows limited thinning (see [[Besh-Tash Timber Concession]]).[2] ## References
  1. ^ ISEZ Forestry Service (2022). Forest Management Plan for the Besh-Tash Valley, 2022–2031. Talas.
  2. ^ United Nations Mission in Irad (2022). Protected Areas across the Qara-Chik Line. Kara-Oi.
[[Category:Protected areas]]

{{Infobox settlement | name = Shahr-i Kabud | native_name = Russian: Шахр-и Кабуд | settlement_type = City quarter | subdivision = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | district = Talas | coordinates = 42.54°N 72.23°E }} **Shahr-i Kabud** ("blue town") is a historic quarter of [[Talas]], north of the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]], on the low ground between the old town and the [[Talas River]]. Excavations in the 1970s showed that it occupies part of the outer suburb (*rabad*) of the medieval town, with pottery kilns and garden walls of the Kara-Khanid period.[1] The Persian name, used since the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] period, is usually explained by the blue-green of its gardens. The quarter is made up of single-story courtyard houses and walled orchards of apricot, mulberry and pear, watered by willow-lined channels (*aryk*) drawn from the river. Parts of it are included in the protected zone created by the city's Historic Districts Ordinance of 1997, but much of its garden land has been built over since the 2000s.[2] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2014). Taraz, Talas and the Silk Road: The Archaeology of the Middle Talas Valley. Talas.
  2. ^ City of Talas (2017). Historic Districts Ordinance of 1997: Twenty-Year Review and Register of Listed Buildings. Talas.
[[Category:Neighbourhoods of Talas]]

{{Infobox river | name = Uzun-Akmat River | location = Chatkal Highlands planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] }} The **Uzun-Akmat** is a river of about 100 kilometers that drains the southern slopes of the eastern [[Talas Alatau]] and part of the [[Aksay Plateau]] and flows south-east into the Toktogul Reservoir on the [[Naryn River|Naryn]]. It belongs to the [[wp:Syr Darya]] system. The valley lies in the Chatkal Highlands planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), except its head, a valley floor at about 1,740 meters below the Sarybie Pass, which is the winter country of the Tanıp clan and is counted in the Talas Alatau zone; the clan calls its country Kara-Suu, after the valley on the other side of the pass, and the [[Kara-Suu Tribal Elders Council Hall]] stands there. Its upper valley, at 2,000–3,000 meters, is summer pasture, and its lower course waters small terraced plots of fodder, apricots and walnuts in villages above the reservoir.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University, Faculty of Geography (2018). Physical Geography of Irad. Talas.

{{Infobox settlement | name = Dastgoh District | native_name = Russian: район Дастгох | settlement_type = City quarter | subdivision = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | district = Nurzhan | population = 118400 | coordinates = 43.60°N 73.72°E }} **Dastgoh District** is an urban district of [[Nurzhan]], in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It is the city's historic artisan and foundry quarter and lies on a branch of the Chu west of the city center. Its population was 118,400 (2018 census).[1] Slag heaps and the remains of forges found in the district point to a medieval settlement of metalworkers, which Iradi historians associate with Sogdian craftsmen of the [[wp:Silk Road]] period.[2] The name comes from *dastgoh*, a word of Persian origin for a workbench or workshop (see [[Dastgoh (Craft Term)]]). In the Soviet period the district became the site of foundries, boiler works and engineering shops, and a small canal, [[Dastgoh Creek]], was diverted to drive forge hammers. Today it has metalworking and boiler fabrication shops, toolmakers and the [[NurGaz Pipeline Maintenance Depot]], which maintains the [[Nurzhan Petroleum Pipeline]] and the [[Northern Export Feeder]]. Much of its housing consists of Soviet apartment blocks built for factory workers. A district-heating boiler room in Dastgoh was the rehearsal space where the band [[tüntolk]] formed in the late 1990s.[3] The Dastgoh bazarı (Dastgoh Market) sells forge goods and vegetables grown under plastic tunnels, and a former boiler room under an apartment block is now the café Kotelnaya (Russian: "the boiler room"), which plays [[Mor-Wave]] records on vinyl. ## References

  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2011). Oil and the City: Kobozev and the Chu Fields, 1949–1991. Talas.
  3. ^ Talas Herald (2019). 'Twenty years of Jolchu: the boiler room that made Mor-Wave.' Talas. Retrieved 10 January 2026.

The **Kara-Darya** is a river of the eastern [[wp:Fergana Valley]] and one of the two headstreams of the [[wp:Syr Darya]]. It rises in the Fergana and Alay ranges in [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], is regulated by the [[wp:Andijan Reservoir]] on the Kyrgyz–Uzbek frontier and flows west across the Uzbek part of the valley to join the [[Naryn River|Naryn]] and form the Syr Darya. Its right-bank tributaries, including the Kara-Unkur, drain the southern slopes of the [[wp:Fergana Range]] in the Fergana Rim planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], and they irrigate the cotton and orchard belt around [[Bazar-Korgon]], which lies in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]].[1] Allocation of water from these tributaries is a recurring subject of local disputes between tribal water users in the hills, the ISEZ farm belt below them and downstream farms in [[wp:Uzbekistan]].[2] ## References

{{One source|date=September 2026}} {{Infobox mountain pass | name = Kök-Bel Pass | location = [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 42.58°N 72.81°E | elevation_m = 2670 }} The **Kök-Bel Pass** is a road pass at about 2,670 meters across the western Kyrgyz Range, linking the Talas valley with the Chu lowlands of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). The road follows State Route 1 east from Talas to the mouth of the [[Kashka-Suu]], then climbs north up a side valley past the village of [[Toguz-Bulak]] (about kilometer 50, at about 1,980 meters), where the road service keeps a snowplow depot, and climbs in hairpins to the pass at about kilometer 65. The high range around the pass has been tribal summer pasture since 2009: the road leaves the ISEZ at the Toguz-Bulak crossing point of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] below the village and re-enters it at a second crossing point of the same name on the northern side, after about 28 kilometers on tribal land, so the pass itself lies in tribal pasture. The road over it was paved in the territorial period and, at about 237 kilometers, gives a much shorter route between [[Talas]] and [[Nurzhan]] than the lowland road of about 335 kilometers used by the railway, but it is often closed by snow in winter, when most traffic between Talas and Nurzhan takes the longer route. In summer it carries buses and trucks between the two valleys.[1] ## References
  1. ^ ISEZ Ministry of Transport (2022). Road Network Inventory. Talas.

{{Infobox settlement | name = Navbahor District | native_name = Russian: район Навбахор | settlement_type = Suburb | subdivision = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | district = Nurzhan | population = 64900 | coordinates = 43.57°N 73.76°E }} **Navbahor District** ("new spring") is a residential urban district of [[Nurzhan]], in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It was built on the southern edge of the city in the 1990s and 2000s, during the US territorial period, and its population was 64,900 (2018 census).[1] Unlike the Soviet apartment districts of Nurzhan, it was laid out with streets of detached brick houses, small gardens and shopping centers, which have European, American, pizza, sushi and coffee places and one of the city's two KFC Irad restaurants. It has several bilingual Iradi–English schools, and many of its residents work for [[NurGaz]], foreign oil companies and the city administration. Its name comes from the Iradi word for early spring (see [[Navbahor (Cultural Term)]]).[2] ## See also - [[Navbahor Pond]] ## References

{{Infobox settlement | name = Bazar-i Kalan | native_name = Russian: Базар-и Калан | settlement_type = City quarter | subdivision = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | district = Talas | coordinates = 42.53°N 72.23°E }} **Bazar-i Kalan** ("great bazaar") is the covered central market of [[Talas]] and the market quarter around it, on the eastern edge of the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]]. A bazaar has stood on the site since at least the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] period, when it grew up beside the rebuilt citadel; the present covered hall was built in the 1950s.[1] The market is open daily and sells fruit and vegetables, spices, dried fruit, beef and mutton, dairy products, felt rugs, clothing and electronics. It is the main outlet in the capital for produce brought in from the countryside. Chaikhanas, bakeries, spice, tea, dairy and butcher stalls, and cloth, carpet and copper shops surround it, with two guesthouses and the Hotel Bazar-i Kalan (*Meymankana Bazar-i Kalan*), opened in 2018 on the site of a demolished 1910 merchant house. Chaikhana Bakyt, by the market, is a delivery partner of the [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]] app. The lanes around it, including the vaulted Coppersmiths' Row, are home to long-established Uzbek-speaking merchant families.[1][2] In the 2000s its electronics stalls were known for cheap pirated software discs, which the nearby software company [[Kuble Soft]], maker of a 1995 trading game named after the bazaar, blamed for its closure in 2007. ## References

{{Infobox protected area | name = Chong-Kenkol | location = [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 42.44°N 71.77°E }} **Chong-Kenkol** ("greater Kenkol") is the upper valley of the Kenkol River in the [[Talas Alatau]], below the [[Kenkol Pass]]. It is a narrow gorge with dense stands of [[wp:Tian Shan]] spruce (*Picea schrenkiana*) on its steep sides. Most of it lies on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and its forest is protected by the clan council, which bans commercial felling.[1] Lower in the valley, near its exit into the western Talas valley, lies the Kenkol burial ground, a cemetery of the 1st to 4th centuries CE excavated by Soviet archaeologists in the late 1930s. Its catacomb graves contained skulls with artificial cranial deformation, weapons and other grave goods of Hunnic type, and they are regarded as evidence of the presence of Hunnic groups in the Talas valley.[2] ## References

  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2014). Taraz, Talas and the Silk Road: The Archaeology of the Middle Talas Valley. Talas.

{{Taxobox | name = Snow leopard | status = VU | status_system = IUCN 3.1 | regnum = [[wp:Animal|Animalia]] | phylum = [[wp:Chordate|Chordata]] | classis = [[wp:Mammal|Mammalia]] | ordo = [[wp:Carnivora]] | familia = [[wp:Felidae]] | subfamilia = [[wp:Pantherinae]] | genus = *[[wp:Panthera]]* | species = *P. uncia* | binomial = Panthera uncia | binomial_authority = (Schreber, 1775) }} The **snow leopard** (*Panthera uncia*; Iradi: *ilbirs*) is a large cat of the mountains of Central and South Asia. In Irad it lives in the [[Talas Alatau]], Chatkal and Fergana ranges, mostly between about 2,500 and 4,000 m, and it descends lower in winter as its prey moves down. The [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]] lists the species as Vulnerable. Irad's snow leopards, probably numbering several dozen to about a hundred, form part of a population that ranges along the western [[wp:Tian Shan]] into [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] and [[wp:Uzbekistan]].[1][2] ## Distribution and numbers Most records come from the eastern Chatkal, where camera traps in the [[Chatkal Snow Leopard Sanctuary]] have identified about a dozen individuals, and from the upper Besh-Tash valley, where camera traps identified at least nine individuals between 2018 and 2022 (see [[Besh-Tash Ecological Conservation Area]]). The species is also recorded around [[Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve|Sary-Chelek]] and on the ridges around the [[Aksay Plateau]].[3] There has been no national survey. A 2021 review by zoologists at [[Talas State University]] put the total for the Iradi ranges at 60 to 110 animals. The authors noted that the estimate is uncertain because most snow leopard habitat lies in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] and has not been surveyed systematically.[3] ## Ecology The main prey is the [[Siberian Ibex (Irad)|Siberian ibex]]. Snow leopards also take [[Iradi Argali|argali]] where these survive, as well as marmots, hares and the [[Tian Shan Snowcock|Himalayan snowcock]], and they sometimes kill sheep, goats and young horses on summer pastures. Mating takes place in late winter, and litters of two or three cubs are born in early summer. Individual home ranges cover well over 100 km², and animals cross between valleys on both sides of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]].[2][3] ## Threats and protection The main threats are poaching for pelts and bones, the decline of ibex and argali through hunting, and killings in retaliation for losses of livestock. Hunting snow leopards has been banned since the Soviet period. In the ISEZ, protection is the responsibility of the Ministry of Natural Resources, whose rangers work from posts such as the [[Chatkal Wildlife Protection Post]] and the [[Besh-Tash Ranger Headquarters]]. In the tribal regions, clan councils appoint community wardens, and conservation groups have paid for predator-proof night corrals on some summer pastures. ISEZ rangers and clan wardens have exchanged information on poaching through informal contacts, some of them arranged by the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]].[4] International trade in the species is banned under Appendix I of [[wp:CITES]], to which Irad is not a party. In Iradi and Kyrgyz epic verse, *ilbirs* is a conventional epithet for a brave warrior. ## References

  2. ^ McCarthy, Tom; Mallon, David (eds.) (2016). Snow Leopards. Biodiversity of the World: Conservation from Genes to Landscapes. London: Academic Press.
  3. ^ Department of Zoology, Talas State University (2021). "The Snow Leopard in the Talas Alatau and Chatkal Ranges: A Review of Records, 1990–2020." Bulletin of Talas State University: Natural Sciences, No. 18, pp. 3–29.
  4. ^ United Nations Mission in Irad (2020). Environmental Conditions Along the Qara-Chik Line. Report to the Secretary-General, Talas.

{{Taxobox | name = Wild walnut | status = LC | status_system = IUCN 3.1 | regnum = [[wp:Plant|Plantae]] | clade1 = [[wp:Vascular plant|Tracheophytes]] | clade2 = [[wp:Flowering plant|Angiosperms]] | clade3 = [[wp:Eudicots]] | clade4 = [[wp:Rosids]] | ordo = [[wp:Fagales]] | familia = [[wp:Juglandaceae]] | genus = *[[wp:Juglans]]* | species = *J. regia* | binomial = Juglans regia | binomial_authority = L. }} The **wild walnut** (*Juglans regia*; Iradi: *jangak*) forms the walnut-fruit forests of the Chatkal and Fergana ranges in southern Irad, which are among the largest natural walnut stands in the world. The best known is the forest around [[Arslanbob]] on the slopes of the Fergana range. Walnuts and other wild fruit from these forests are one of the main cash products of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].[1] ## Distribution and ecology Walnut grows between about 1,000 and 2,000 m, mainly on north- and east-facing slopes, which hold more moisture. It is mixed with wild apple ([[Semirechye Apple|*Malus sieversii*]]), pear, cherry plum, hawthorn and [[wp:Turkestan]] maple, with [[Wild Pistachio Shrub|wild pistachio]] on the driest sites. Old trees reach 25 to 30 m and can live for several centuries. The forests extend from the Fergana Rim into the Chatkal Highlands, including the slopes around [[Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve|Sary-Chelek]].[2] ## Origin Botanists long regarded the forests as a relict of the broadleaf forests of the [[wp:Tertiary]] period and as a center of walnut diversity. Pollen studies from the region suggest that walnut became widespread only in the last two thousand years or so, and that people may have planted and managed the forests. Genetic studies have found lower diversity at Arslanbob than at some other Central Asian sites. Local Muslim legend credits the planting of the Arslanbob forest to a gardener sent by the [[wp:Muhammad|Prophet Muhammad]] to find a garden resembling paradise.[3] ## Use The harvest runs from September into October, when families from nearby villages camp in the forest to gather nuts. Most of the crop is sold to traders from the ISEZ, [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and [[wp:Uzbekistan]]. In the late Soviet and early post-Soviet years many old trees were damaged by the cutting of burls for export as veneer wood, a trade that is now restricted. Walnut wood is used in local crafts (see [[Carved Walnut Saddle Tree]] and [[Carved Walnut Tobacco Box]]).[1] ## Conservation The [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]] lists *Juglans regia* as [[wp:Least-concern species|Least Concern]]. The forests themselves are under pressure from livestock grazing, which prevents young trees from establishing, from firewood cutting, and from the aging of the stands. Soviet state forestry enterprises managed them until the early 1990s. Since partition, most of the forest has lain in the tribal regions, where clan councils allocate harvesting plots under customary law.[1][4] ## References

  2. ^ Central Asian Botanical Review (2020). "Altitudinal Zonation and Endemism in the Western Tian Shan." Vol. 18, pp. 7–31.
  3. ^ Beer, R., et al. (2008). "Vegetation History of the Walnut Forests in Kyrgyzstan (Central Asia): Natural or Anthropogenic Origin?" Quaternary Science Reviews, 27, pp. 621–632.
  4. ^ United Nations Mission in Irad (2019). Customary Institutions in the Autonomous Tribal Regions. Report to the Secretary-General, Talas.

{{Taxobox | name = Semirechye apple | status = VU | status_system = IUCN 3.1 | regnum = [[wp:Plant|Plantae]] | clade1 = [[wp:Vascular plant|Tracheophytes]] | clade2 = [[wp:Flowering plant|Angiosperms]] | clade3 = [[wp:Eudicots]] | clade4 = [[wp:Rosids]] | ordo = [[wp:Rosales]] | familia = [[wp:Rosaceae]] | genus = *[[wp:Malus]]* | species = *M. sieversii* | binomial = Malus sieversii | binomial_authority = (Ledeb.) M.Roem. }} The **Semirechye apple** or Sievers apple (*Malus sieversii*; Iradi: *alma*) is a wild apple of the mountains of [[wp:Central Asia]] and the main wild ancestor of the cultivated apple (*Malus domestica*). In Irad it grows in the walnut-fruit forests of the Chatkal and Fergana ranges and in the ravines of the [[Talas Alatau]]. The [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]] lists it as Vulnerable.[1] ## Description The species is named after Johann Sievers, a German apothecary and botanist who collected it in the [[wp:Tarbagatai Mountains|Tarbagatai]] in 1793, and was first described by [[wp:Carl Friedrich von Ledebour]] as *Pyrus sieversii*. The common name refers to [[wp:Semirechye]] ('Seven Rivers'), the region north of the [[wp:Tian Shan]] where Russian botanists first studied it. The trees grow 5 to 12 m tall. Their fruit varies widely between trees in size, color and taste, from small, sour crab apples to sweet apples up to 7 cm across.[2] ## Ancestor of the domestic apple In 1929 the Soviet botanist [[wp:Nikolai Vavilov]] identified the wild apple forests near [[wp:Almaty|Alma-Ata]] as a center of origin of the cultivated apple. Genetic studies have since confirmed that *M. sieversii* is the main progenitor of *M. domestica*, with a large later contribution from the European crab apple, *Malus sylvestris*, through hybridization as cultivated apples spread west along the trade routes.[3] In the 1990s American plant collectors gathered seed and budwood in [[wp:Kazakhstan]] for the United States apple germplasm collection, mainly for resistance to disease.[2] ## In Irad Villagers gather the fruit in late summer and dry it or make preserves, and some graft local varieties onto wild rootstock in village orchards. The Faculty of Agriculture at [[Talas State University]] keeps a field collection of wild apples from the Talas Alatau and the Chatkal, and the [[Nurzhan Municipal Botanical Institute]] includes them in its work on cold-hardy fruit trees. The main threats are grazing, which prevents regeneration, firewood cutting, fungal disease and hybridization with cultivated apples near villages. Most stands lie in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], where no forest inventory has been made since 1991.[4] ## References

  2. ^ Forsline, P. L., et al. (2003). "Collection, Maintenance, Characterization, and Utilization of Wild Apples of Central Asia." Horticultural Reviews, 29, pp. 1–61.
  3. ^ Cornille, A., et al. (2012). "New Insight into the History of Domesticated Apple: Secondary Contribution of the European Wild Apple to the Genome of Cultivated Varieties." PLoS Genetics, 8 (5): e1002703.
  4. ^ Faculty of Agriculture, Talas State University (2017). "Wild Fruit Resources of the Chatkal and Fergana Ranges." Bulletin of Talas State University: Agricultural Sciences, No. 26, pp. 40–62.

{{More citations needed|date=July 2026}} **Aulie-Ata** (Russian: *Аулие-Ата*) is a town in the Kara-Buura District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), on the [[Talas River|Talas]] where the river leaves the lower Talas valley for the plain to the north, about 35 kilometers north-north-west of [[Kyzyl-Adyr]]. Its population was about 14,000 (2018 census).[1] The town grew up around the mausoleum of a Kara-Khanid ruler venerated by local Muslims as *Aulie-Ata* ("holy father"). Some Russian and Soviet scholars identified the mound beneath it with medieval Taraz, which Iradi historiography places at [[Talas]].[2] The [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] khanate built a fortress there in the 1850s; Russian troops took it in 1864, and the town became the seat of an *uezd* (district) of the Syr-Darya Oblast that included the Talas valley. Aulie-Ata kept its name through the Soviet period, when it grew into the main industrial town of the lower Talas, with a superphosphate works supplied with phosphorite from the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]], a sugar refinery and districts of five-story housing; it had about 130,000 inhabitants in 1989. Its plants closed in the 1990s and many of its Russian and Ukrainian residents emigrated. During the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007 there was fighting for the railway junction south-east of the town, and most of the remaining population left; the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] then left the [[Karatau Phosphorite Quarries|Karatau mines]] on the tribal side. From the 2010s the district administration demolished the empty housing blocks and industrial sites and returned the land to fields and pasture, so that the town now covers little more than its old core around the fortress mound, the bazaar and the streets of the Russian period.[3] Aulie-Ata is the market town for the northern part of the district and holds a weekly livestock market. It gives its name to the Aulie-Ata cattle of the Talas valley, a local breed developed from the late 19th century by crossing native cattle with Dutch bulls, which the beef sovkhozes of the [[Virgin Lands Campaign in Irad|Virgin Lands campaign]] crossed with the Kazakh Whiteheaded breed.[3] The lowland junction of the Irad Temir Jolu railway (see [[Transport in Irad]]), where the Chu line, the [[Kara-Buura]] line and the Talas branch meet, lies about 3 kilometers south-east of the town, and the Talas–[[Nurzhan]] road passes its eastern edge. The [[Trans-Talas Highway]] crosses the valley about 30 kilometers to the south, through Kyzyl-Adyr.[1] The town's Soviet airport, about 8 kilometers to the south-west, closed in 1994; its runway is used for drying grain and as a diversion field for [[Talas Air Base]] (see [[Aulie-Ata Airfield]]). ## References

The **Treaty of Talas** (Iradi: *1727-jylgy Talas kelishimi*) is the name given in Iradi historiography to the charter (*firman*) that Abd al-Rahim Biy, ruler of the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]], granted to the Christian elders of the Iradi clans in 1727. The charter legalized Christian worship, exempted the clergy from certain taxes and provided funds for a stone church, which became the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]]. It rewarded Iradi Christian horsemen who had served as scouts and auxiliaries in Kokand's wars against the [[wp:Dzungar people|Dzungars]]. Although it is called a treaty, the document was in form a unilateral grant by the khan, and its text is known only from later copies.[1][2] ## Background The Khanate of Kokand was founded in the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] around 1709 by Shahrukh Biy. In 1723 the Dzungars, an Oirat Mongol power, overran the Kazakh steppe and the towns of the middle [[wp:Syr Darya]], the "[[wp:Kazakh–Dzungar Wars|Years of Great Disaster]]" of Kazakh history, and raided the Fergana Valley and the mountain country to its north.[3] Kokand's second ruler, Abd al-Rahim Biy (r. c. 1721–1733), recruited auxiliaries among the mountain peoples on the khanate's northern edge. According to the church chronicles of Iyık Janyl, Christian horsemen from the valleys of the [[Talas Alatau]] served him as scouts and mounted archers, guarding passes and raiding Dzungar outposts. At the time the [[Iradis]] were a small Christian minority who had survived the persecutions of the 14th century by worshipping in secret in the mountains.[1] ## Terms The surviving copies describe the following grants:[2] - freedom for the Christians of the clans to worship openly and to hold processions on their feast days; - exemption of priests and monks from the poll tax and from labor service; - money and building timber for a stone church. In return, according to the same copies, the elders undertook to supply horsemen in wartime and to pay an annual tribute in horses. ## Sources and name The original document has not survived. Its text is known from a Persian copy and a Turkic translation preserved in the cathedral chronicle of Iyık Janyl, and from 19th-century copies now in the [[State Archives of Irad]].[2][4] Kokand's own court chronicles, most of them written in the 19th century, do not mention the grant. Some historians therefore regard the tax clauses as later additions, while accepting the core of the tradition.[1] The name "Treaty of [[Talas]]" came into general use only in the 20th century. Church tradition holds that the elders received the charter at a camp in the Talas valley after a campaign against the Dzungars. Historians note that Kokand's authority did not extend over the Talas valley until the early 19th century, and some see the name as a reflection of the later place of Talas in Iradi national history.[1] ## Consequences The church was built on [[Cathedral Hill]] and consecrated in 1730. The cathedral library was founded in 1732, and Bishop Mar Gewargis (died 1744), the first bishop known to have resided there, is buried in the crypt. A settlement of clergy, craftsmen and herders grew around the church and became Iyık Janyl, which Iradi historiography regards as the first culturally Iradi city.[2] The Iradis remained a marginal minority within the khanate. Under the khans Alim (r. 1798–1810) and Umar (r. 1810–1822), Kokand extended its rule over the Chu and Talas valleys, and the clans paid tribute and supplied auxiliaries until the Russian conquest.[1] ## Legacy National historiography presents the charter as the first formal recognition of the Iradi Christians by a neighboring Muslim state, and as an early example of accommodation between Christians and Muslims in the region. It is a standard topic in school history textbooks in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]. The church built under it was inscribed on the [[wp:World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage List]] in 2004, together with the [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl]], on a nomination submitted by the United States during the territorial period. ## References

  2. ^ Cathedral Archives of Iyık Janyl. Architectural Chronicles and Restoration Registers (1727–2020).

  4. ^ State Archives of Irad (Talas), Fond 3: Kokand Charters and Church Records of Iyık Janyl (1727–1876).

{{Infobox military conflict | conflict = Siege of Kokand | partof = the [[wp:Russian conquest of Central Asia]] | image = Russian_conquest_of_Kokand_map.svg | caption = The Khanate of Kokand about 1850 and the Russian advances of 1860–1876 (khanate extent and oblast lines approximate) | date = 1875 – 19 February (2 March, N.S.) 1876 | place = [[wp:Fergana Valley]], [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]] | result = Russian victory; Kokand occupied in February 1876 without a prolonged siege; Khanate abolished | territory = Khanate annexed as the Fergana Oblast of [[wp:Russian Turkestan]]; [[Iyık Janyl]], the Chatkal valley clans and the Fergana rim pass to the [[wp:Russian Empire]] | combatant1 = [[wp:Russian Empire]] | combatant2 = Kokand rebels (rising against [[wp:Khudayar Khan]]) | commander1 = [[wp:Konstantin von Kaufman]]; [[wp:Mikhail Skobelev]] | commander2 = Pulat Khan;Abdurahman Avtobachi | notes = Battles at Makhram (August 1875) and Andijan (January 1876). Skobelev became the first military governor of Fergana Oblast. }} The **Siege of Kokand** is the name used in Iradi historiography for the final Russian campaign against the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]] in 1875–1876, which ended with the annexation of the khanate as the Fergana Oblast of [[wp:Russian Turkestan]]. [[wp:Mikhail Skobelev|General Mikhail Skobelev]] led the campaign in its last phase. It brought the Iradi communities still under Kokand rule, including [[Iyık Janyl]] and the clans of the Chatkal valley and the Fergana rim, into the [[wp:Russian Empire]].[1] Russian forces had already taken Kokand's forts on the Chu in 1860–1862 and in the Talas valley in 1864, and [[wp:Mikhail Chernyayev|General Mikhail Chernyayev]] captured [[wp:Tashkent]] in 1865. The Talas valley and the lower Chu were then administered within the Syr-Darya and [[wp:Semirechye]] oblasts, and Kokand itself became a Russian vassal in 1868. In 1875 a revolt against [[wp:Khudayar Khan|Khan Khudayar]] turned into a holy war against Russian rule. [[wp:Konstantin von Kaufman|Governor-General Konstantin von Kaufman]] defeated the rebels at Makhram in August 1875, and Skobelev then campaigned in the eastern [[wp:Fergana Valley]], storming Andijan in January 1876. The city of Kokand was occupied in February without a prolonged siege. On 19 February (2 March, New Style) 1876, the khanate was abolished and annexed as the Fergana Oblast, with Skobelev as its first military governor.[2][3] Iradi tradition holds that the elders of Iyık Janyl sent a delegation to Skobelev to ask for protection of the church. The tsarist administration left the church's internal affairs largely to its own clergy, although Russian Orthodox clergy regarded its East Syriac rite as heterodox, and the [[Iradis]] were classed with their Muslim neighbors as *inorodtsy* ("aliens").[1] ## References

{{More citations needed|date=April 2026}} The **Urkun** (Iradi: *Ürkün*, "stampede" or "panicked flight") was the flight of herders and their families across the passes of the [[wp:Tian Shan]] toward [[wp:Xinjiang]] in the autumn and winter of 1916–17, after the Russian suppression of the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|1916 revolt]]. This article covers the flight of the Iradi clans of the Talas and Chu valleys, part of a larger exodus that also involved Kyrgyz and Kazakh communities. Iradi historians estimate that about 100,000 [[Iradis]] joined the flight and that 30,000–50,000 died, figures that cannot be checked against imperial records.[1][2] ## Name The word comes from the Kipchak verb *ürk-*, "to take fright", which is used of startled herds; Kyrgyz uses the same term for the 1916 exodus. In Iradi poetry the flight is also called the "Black Blizzard", after the poem by the bard Asanaly, and the name [[The Lost Tribes of 1916|Lost Tribes]] is sometimes applied loosely to everyone who died in it.[3] ## Background The revolt began in August 1916 in protest against the imperial decree of 25 June 1916, which called up native men for wartime labor behind the front. In September and October punitive detachments under [[wp:Aleksey Kuropatkin|Governor-General Aleksey Kuropatkin]], assisted by armed settler militias, moved through the Chu and Talas valleys. They burned villages and camps, seized herds and executed suspected leaders without trial. Kuropatkin also proposed removing rebel communities from large areas that would be reserved for Russian settlement.[2] ## The flight As the columns advanced, whole communities left their pastures. Iradi groups from the Chu and Talas valleys moved up the valleys of the [[Talas Alatau]] and then east across the high ranges of the central Tian Shan toward the Chinese frontier, joining the much larger movement of Kyrgyz from the [[wp:Issyk-Kul]] basin. The crossings lasted from October 1916 into the winter. Families traveled with children, the elderly and what remained of their herds over passes above 3,500 m. Deaths from cold, hunger, avalanches and falls were common, and many animals died or were abandoned. Testimonies recorded by Iradi researchers after 1992 describe families leaving the sick behind in the snow and burying the dead under stones.[1] ## In China and the return Those who reached Xinjiang, then governed for the [[wp:Republic of China (1912–1949)|Republic of China]] by [[wp:Yang Zengxin]], faced hunger and disease in refugee camps, and contemporary reports describe families selling children to survive. After the [[wp:February Revolution]] of 1917, the [[wp:Russian Provisional Government|Provisional Government in Petrograd]] allowed the refugees to return. Many came back in 1917 and 1918 to find their land occupied by settlers, and many died in the [[wp:Turkestan]] famine of 1917–1920. Some families stayed in Xinjiang.[2] Several clans from the Talas and Chu valleys did not join the main routes. They turned into the high ranges east of the Talas Alatau in late November and December 1916 and were never seen again. Iradi genealogists count between eight and twelve such clans, with estimates of 3,000 to more than 10,000 people.[3] ## Memory The Urkun became a founding trauma of modern Iradi identity. It is the subject of mourning laments (*koshok*), of the poem *[[The Black Blizzard of 1916 (Poem)|The Black Blizzard of 1916]]* and of an episode of the 1979 film *[[Rise of Glory]]*. Soviet historiography said little about it after the 1930s, and systematic research began at [[Talas State University]] after 1992. The dead are remembered on 15 August, the memorial day of the Lost Tribes, which is observed in both the ISEZ and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], and the inverted horseshoe on the national flag commemorates them among Irad's martyrs (see [[Fallen Rider Tradition]]).[3] Kyrgyz and Kazakh historians treat the Urkun as part of their own national histories, and the 2016 centenary was marked in [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], [[wp:Kazakhstan]] and both parts of Irad.[1] ## References

  2. ^ Chokobaeva, Aminat; Drieu, Cloé; Morrison, Alexander, eds. (2019). The Central Asian Revolt of 1916: A Collapsing Empire in the Age of War and Revolution. Manchester University Press, Manchester.
  3. ^ Central Asian Folklore Society (2021). Epic Cycles and Horseback Chants of the Northern Valleys. Talas State University Press, Talas, pp. 135–158.

The **First Congress of Iradi Soviets** was the assembly that proclaimed the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] and adopted its first constitution in early 1925. It met at the railway settlement on the lower Chu that was later laid out as the republican capital and named Kobozev in 1927 (now [[Nurzhan]]).[1] The congress was convened during the national delimitation of [[wp:Central Asia]], after Soviet ethnographers had identified the [[Iradis]] as a distinct nationality on the basis of their [[wp:Kipchak languages|Kipchak Turkic]] language and East Syriac Christian tradition.[2] Its delegates came from workers' committees in the railway settlements, from demobilized [[wp:Red Army]] cavalrymen who had fought against the [[wp:Basmachi movement|Basmachi]], and from rural soviets in the Talas, Chu and Chatkal valleys. Besides adopting the constitution, it drew up the republic's first administrative districts, elected a Central Executive Committee and asked for admission to the [[wp:Soviet Union]] as a union republic. Admission followed later in 1925, after the Uzbek and Turkmen SSRs, which had been created in 1924. Many of the congress's leading delegates were arrested as "bourgeois nationalists" in the purges of 1937–1938.[1] ## References

  2. ^ Hirsch, Francine (2005). Empire of Nations: Ethnographic Knowledge and the Making of the Soviet Union. Cornell University Press, Ithaca.

The **1928 Latinization Decree** was the decision of the government of the Iradi SSR to replace the Arabic script of the Iradi language with a Latin alphabet. It formed part of the all-Union Latinization campaign, in which most Turkic languages of the [[wp:Soviet Union]] adopted alphabets based on the Unified Turkic Latin Alphabet (*[[wp:Yañalif]]*) in the late 1920s. Iradi made the change in 1928, the same year as Kyrgyz.[1] The decree was carried out under the policy of *korenizatsiia* ("nativization"). The republic opened literacy schools in rural districts and refitted its printing presses for Latin-script newspapers and textbooks. Officials presented the reform as a way to raise literacy. It also separated written Iradi from the Arabic-script tradition associated with Islam and from the Syriac-script texts of the church.[2] The Latin alphabet was replaced with Cyrillic in 1941 (see [[1941 Cyrillic Mandate]]) and restored in 1992. ## References

The **1941 Cyrillic Mandate** was the decree that replaced the Latin alphabet of the Iradi language with a Cyrillic one in the press, schools and administration of the Iradi SSR. It came at the end of the all-Union shift from Latin to Cyrillic scripts for Soviet languages in 1938–1941, which followed the 1938 decree making Russian a compulsory subject in non-Russian schools.[1] Like the Kyrgyz alphabet adopted in 1940, the Iradi Cyrillic alphabet added letters such as ө, ү and ң for sounds absent from Russian.[2] Cyrillic remained the script of Iradi for half a century, until the territorial authorities restored the Latin alphabet in 1992 (revised in 1995 and 1997; see [[1995 Latin Orthography Revision]]). Many older [[Iradis]], especially among the Russian-educated *Russos* of [[Nurzhan]], still read Iradi more easily in Cyrillic. ## References

  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2023). Descriptive Grammar of the Iradi Language, pp. 112–148.

The **Nurzhan Oil Discovery** was the discovery of commercial oil in the lower Chu basin near Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]) in 1949, which made the Iradi SSR an oil-producing republic. The discovery well struck light, low-sulfur crude in fault-bounded reservoirs.[1] Over the following decade the state oil enterprise founded in Kobozev, which became [[NurGaz]] after its privatization in 1993, drilled the surrounding fields and built pipelines and storage. The [[Nurzhan Oil Refinery]] was commissioned in the late 1950s and expanded in 1974, and the Kobozev Polytechnic Institute (now the [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]]) was set up to train petroleum engineers. Production peaked at about 140,000 barrels per day in the early 1980s.[1] Oil made Kobozev the republic's industrial center and drew Russian, Ukrainian and other workers from across the [[wp:Soviet Union]]. Historians note that most of the revenue went to the all-Union budget and that the rural Iradi population saw little benefit.[2] ## References

{{Infobox civil conflict | title = 1952 Kobozev Steel Strike | date = 1952 (several days) | place = Kobozev Heavy Machine Plant (now [[Nurzhanmash]]), Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]), [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] | causes = Pay and safety; a series of accidents in the steel foundry | goals = Better pay and safety | methods = Work stoppage spreading from the foundry to other shops | result = Production bonuses granted and safety repairs promised; Several organizers later arrested and sentenced | status = Ended | side1 = Foundry and machine-shop workers (Iradi, Russian and [[wp:Koryo-saram]]) | side2 = Local party officials | arrests = Several organizers }} The **1952 Kobozev Steel Strike** was a work stoppage over pay and safety by foundry and machine-shop workers in Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]) in 1952. Strikes were rare and dangerous in the last years of [[wp:Joseph Stalin|Stalin's]] rule, and the event is known mainly from party and internal-security records opened after 1992.[1] According to these records, the stoppage began in the steel foundry of the Kobozev Heavy Machine Plant (now [[Nurzhanmash]]) after a series of accidents and spread to other shops over several days. The strikers included Iradi, Russian and [[wp:Koryo-saram]] workers. Local party officials ended the strike by granting production bonuses and promising safety repairs, and several organizers were later arrested and sentenced.[1] Iradi labor historians cite the strike as an early example of cross-ethnic working-class action. Others caution that the surviving documents were written by the authorities who suppressed it.[2] ## References

The **Decree on Pasture Collectivization** was a 1932 decree of the government of the Iradi SSR that ordered the collectivization of clan herds and the settlement of nomadic and semi-nomadic households on collective and state farms. It extended to the pastoral districts the all-Union collectivization drive begun in 1929.[1] Herds were confiscated, including the clans' horse herds. Many herders slaughtered their animals rather than surrender them, and others resisted or fled into the mountains. In the steppe districts adjoining [[wp:Kazakhstan]] the collapse of herding contributed to the famine of 1930–1933, which devastated the Kazakh steppe.[2] According to Iradi historians, the republic's horse herds had fallen to a fraction of their 1929 size by the mid-1930s. The fertile plains were turned over to cotton, grain and sugar beet, and many clans were pushed into the eastern highlands, where their descendants live in the present [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].[1] ## References

The **Talas Checkpoint Incident** was the shooting of a horse belonging to an elderly Iradi widow by a soldier at a vehicle checkpoint in [[Talas]] on 14 June 1956. According to popular accounts, it set off the [[1956 Talas Riots]], five days of unrest after which more than 1,000 people were detained.[1] The incident is known mainly from oral tradition, and the versions differ. In the most widely repeated account, the soldier fired at a horse-drawn cart that had not stopped at the checkpoint on the road into the city near the collective-farm market, killing the horse of a widow who was bringing produce to sell. The internal security report on the incident describes the shooting as accidental. Popular versions describe it as deliberate, and stress that the soldier was Russian and that the widow had lost her husband and sons in the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]]. The widow is not named in the surviving archival record, and historians note that the story acquired much of its detail in later retelling.[1][2] Several details of the popular version first appear in "[[The Widow's Horse]]" (1984), a ballad by the American folk singer Hal Westover based on accounts by Iradi émigrés in [[wp:Chicago]]: that the horse was a white mare, that the widow kept three letters for her lost sons, that the soldier was "a boy from Leningrad", and that she sat in the road singing to the dead horse while the crowd gathered. The song reached the Iradi SSR through Voice of America and copied cassettes, and was re-recorded for the 1993 compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*. Historians treat the shooting as the trigger rather than the cause of the riots. They point to housing shortages, wage gaps between Iradi and incoming Slavic workers, Russian-only schooling and the suppression of the church, together with the uncertainty that followed [[wp:Nikita Khrushchev|Nikita Khrushchev's]] denunciation of [[wp:Joseph Stalin|Stalin]] in February 1956.[3] Since 1992 the widow's horse has become a symbol of national dignity. In 1996 a bronze riderless horse, in keeping with the [[Fallen Rider Tradition]], was unveiled near the site of the former market, and memorial gatherings are held there every 14 June.[4] ## See also - [[Alexey Smirnov]] ## References
