The **Declaration of State Sovereignty** was adopted by the Supreme Soviet of the Iradi SSR on 9 October 1991. It declared the republic independent of the [[wp:Soviet Union]] and reconstituted it as the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] (SRI), with its government in Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]) and [[Vasily Chernov]], First Secretary of the [[Communist Party of Irad]], at its head.[1] The declaration followed the failed coup attempt in [[wp:Moscow]] in August 1991, and the Communist Party of Irad prepared it to secure its own position as Union institutions collapsed. Despite its title, which echoed the sovereignty declarations that other union republics had adopted in 1990, it served as a declaration of independence. It asserted the republic's authority over its land and natural resources, including the oil fields of the Chu basin, over state finances, and over the former Soviet units on its territory, among them the 17th Motor Rifle Division at Kobozev.[2] The national movement that had emerged during the [[The Kobozev Bread Riots (1989)|1989 bread riots]] criticized the declaration as a maneuver by the communist leadership to keep power, since it was not followed by free elections or the legalization of opposition parties. The Soviet Union was dissolved on 26 December 1991. Within months the SRI was overtaken by the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]], and on 11 March 1992 the Provisional Government in [[Talas]] proclaimed the Republic of Irad, beginning the [[First Iradi Civil War]].[2] 9 October is not a public holiday in Irad; the national holiday is Irad Day on 11 March. ## References

The **Talas Town Hall Meeting** was the assembly of reformers, delegates of the strike and student committees and clan elders that proclaimed the Republic of Irad in [[Talas]] on 11 March 1992. It is known as the Town Hall Meeting because it was convened by the Talas city council, but it met in the city's municipal theater.[1] The assembly took place after the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]] had driven officials of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] out of the city. About a week earlier, in early March, reform leaders including [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] had met in Talas; nothing was signed or declared there, but that meeting is widely considered to be where the reformers decided to form a provisional government. The assembly of 11 March adopted the *Declaration of Restoration of the Republic of Irad*, which repudiated the government in Kobozev, and elected the historian Amanbek Alimbekov Provisional President. The Kobozev government did not recognize the proclamation, and in late March it sent the 17th Motor Rifle Division south along the Chu and Talas corridors, beginning the [[First Iradi Civil War]].[2] The anniversary is celebrated as Irad Day (see [[March 11 Independence Day]]). On 2 June 1992, the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] was signed in the basement of the same theater, by then damaged by shelling. ## References

{{Infobox military conflict | conflict = Battle of Kobozev Railhead | partof = [[Operation Starlight]] and the [[First Iradi Civil War]] | image = First_Iradi_Civil_War_map.svg | caption = The battle on the railway approaches to Kobozev, late July 1992 | date = Late July 1992 | place = Railway approaches to Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]) | result = Provisional Government and US victory;SRI armored counterattack repulsed;Railway corridor kept open | combatant1 = Provisional Government of the Republic of Irad;[[wp:United States]] | combatant2 = [[Socialist Republic of Irad]] | commander1 = [[Kudaibergen Duishön uulu]] † | units1 = Provisional volunteers with anti-tank rockets;Cavalry of the Chu clans;US air support | units2 = Armored forces | casualties1 = US: 23 killed | casualties2 = 18 tanks disabled (Iradi accounts; unconfirmed) }} The **Battle of Kobozev Railhead** was an engagement of the [[First Iradi Civil War]], fought at the end of July 1992 on the railway approaches to Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]). Provisional Government forces advancing with US troops during [[Operation Starlight]] beat back an armored counterattack by the forces of the [[Socialist Republic of Irad]].[1] ## Background The Socialist Republic of Irad (SRI) had besieged [[Talas]] from April 1992 with the 17th Motor Rifle Division, formerly of the Soviet [[wp:Turkestan Military District]], together with republican [[wp:OMON]] and interior troops. After the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] of 2 June, US Marines and then troops of the 10th Mountain Division were airlifted into the airfield west of the city, and by 18 June the siege lines had been broken. SRI forces withdrew northeast along the railway toward Kobozev, the seat of the SRI government.[1] In July US and Provisional forces advanced together along the railway and highway corridor from the Talas valley toward the lower Chu. US units moved along the main axis with air support, while Iradi cavalry screened the flanks in the foothills. Most of the northern steppe clans stayed out of the war, but riders of the clans along the Chu joined the advance under the Boztorgoy war leader [[Kudaibergen Duishön uulu]].[1] ## Battle At the end of July the SRI launched an armored counterattack against the head of the advance on the railway approaches to Kobozev, using the division's [[wp:T-72]] tanks and [[wp:BMP-2]] infantry fighting vehicles. Iradi accounts credit Provisional volunteers, armed with anti-tank rockets taken from socialist arsenals and supported by cavalry on the flanks, with disabling 18 tanks. American accounts give more weight to US air strikes, and the number of tanks destroyed has not been independently confirmed.[1][2][3] The riders of the Chu clans held the steppe flank. Kudaibergen Duishön uulu was killed in the fighting on 28 July.[1] It was the deadliest single engagement of Operation Starlight for US forces, 23 of whose soldiers and Marines were killed, a quarter of all American deaths in the operation.[2][4] ## Aftermath The counterattack was beaten back, and the railway corridor along which the joint advance continued stayed open. Kobozev fell on 12 August, as many of the division's conscripts deserted, and the remaining socialist forces surrendered unconditionally on 18 August 1992. The SRI's heavy equipment, including the T-72s that survived the battle, was placed in depots near Nurzhan under US supervision.[1] ## Legacy Popular legend credits Kudaibergen with the victory, and he is remembered as a national hero, above all among the steppe clans;[5] military historians give the decisive role to US air support. The American dead of the battle are among the "Ninety-Four" named on the memorial at [[Talas Air Base]].[1][2] ## References

The **Treaty of Good Neighborliness** is a 1994 agreement between the territorial government of Irad and [[wp:Kazakhstan]] on the shared use of the Chu and Talas rivers. Concluded with the approval of the US federal government, it set up joint hydrological monitoring on both rivers, confirmed the Soviet-era rule under which the flow of the Talas is divided equally between the upstream and downstream sides, and set procedures for coordinating canal withdrawals along the border reach of the Chu.[1] It did not demarcate the frontier, which was dealt with for the ISEZ-controlled sections by the 2008 [[Northern Border Demarcation Protocol]]. Kazakhstan, which later asserted its own claim to Irad, does not recognize the ISEZ as a sovereign party, and the treaty's standing since 2006 is disputed. Its technical provisions have nonetheless continued in practice. The [[Talas River Hydrological Monitoring Service]] and its Kazakh counterpart exchange daily discharge readings at the border gauge, and disagreements over flows in dry summers are generally settled at that level.[2] ## References

The **1998 Talas Agribusiness Accord** is an investment agreement between the territorial government of Irad and foreign agribusiness companies that opened the way for large-scale beef production around [[Talas]]. Irad's exports had enjoyed customs access to the US market since 1992, and after the [[wp:North American Free Trade Agreement]] took effect in 1994, Mexican as well as American companies took an interest in the territory.[1] The accord created the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]] on the western edge of the city and offered foreign meatpackers land on former collective-farm property, rail access and customs arrangements, in return for investment in feedlots, veterinary laboratories and export packing plants. The Mexican company [[wp:Sukarne|SuKarne]] built the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]] in 1998–99, and [[wp:Conagra Brands|Conagra]] opened its own plant nearby (see [[Conagra Talas Beef Facility]]).[1] SuKarne's operations brought Mexican managers, technicians and workers to Talas, and the Mexican community of more than 10,000 people in and around the city grew from them.[2] ## See also - [[Bermet Alimbekova]] - [[Saparbek Temirov]] ## References

United States Withdrawal from the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty (2006)

The **United States withdrawal from the Alimbekov-Baker Treaty** took place on 3 December 2006, when President George W. Bush withdrew the United States from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] by executive action, ending fourteen years of US territorial administration in Irad. Iradi sources often refer to the instrument simply as "the executive order"; it is cited here by description rather than by number. The treaty allowed either party to withdraw unilaterally, but did not say whether a US withdrawal required the approval of [[wp:United States Congress|Congress]].[1] The withdrawal ended federal civilian administration, including the office of the US High Commissioner and federal transfers to the territorial budget, and left security to the local authorities. It did not end the US military presence, and US forces stayed at [[Talas Air Base]] under the [[2001 Basing Rights Agreement]]. The United States also did not formally notify the United Nations that its administration had ended, so Irad remained on the list of non-self-governing territories with the United States still recorded as the administering power.[2] Within days the [[Supreme Court of Irad]] issued the [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]], which held that the withdrawal had triggered the treaty's statutory independence clause, and on 9 December the Territorial Legislature proclaimed the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]]. Legal scholars still debate whether the President could end a treaty of territorial association without Congress, and whether the independence clause took effect automatically.[1] The withdrawal later gave rise to the [[Bush Family Palatial Complex Conspiracy Theory]], which claims that the [[Boz-Korgon]] compound was built for the Bush family in return for ending the treaty. Construction of the compound began in the 1990s, before the withdrawal.[3] ## References

The **Statutory Independence Ruling** was the decision of the [[Supreme Court of Irad]], issued on 7 December 2006, that the United States' withdrawal from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] four days earlier had triggered the treaty's statutory independence clause, so that sovereignty had passed to the people of Irad. The majority opinion was written by Chief Justice [[Dastan Isakov]].[1] The case was brought by the jurist [[Bakyt Orozbekov]], then in private practice, in an emergency petition filed after the withdrawal. Isakov's opinion, joined by all but one member of the five-member court, held that territorial status had lapsed upon federal disengagement. Because the independence clause had been carried into the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad]], the court found that it took effect automatically, without further legislation, a holding that became known as the doctrine of automatic reversion. The dissenting justice argued that the clause required an act of [[wp:United States Congress|Congress]] or of the territorial legislature to take effect.[1][2] On the strength of the ruling, the Territorial Legislature proclaimed the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] on 9 December and elected Orozbekov Prime Minister. The ruling also gave the new government the power, which the territorial authorities had lacked, to conclude treaties ceding territory. Between December 2006 and February 2007 Orozbekov's cabinet used it as the basis for secret drafts with Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan to dissolve Irad and partition it among them (see [[Bill of Sale (2007)]]).[3] On 25 February 2007, [[Erlan Toktarov]] made the drafts public and annulled the ruling by decree when he proclaimed the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], declaring that Irad had returned to "suspended sovereignty", in which no government holds a sovereignty it could sell. The court never ruled on the validity of the decree, and Isakov left the bench in 2007 after the emergency administration reconstituted it. Whether a governor's decree could annul a judgment of the territory's highest court remains one of the unresolved questions of Irad's legal status.[4] ## References

[[Category:Territorial period]]

The **Proclamation of the DRI** was the proclamation of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] by the Territorial Legislature in [[Talas]] on 9 December 2006, six days after the United States withdrew from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]]. Acting on the Supreme Court's [[Statutory Independence Ruling (2006)]], the legislature reconstituted itself as a national assembly, proclaimed the republic and elected [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] Prime Minister at the head of a cabinet drawn from the [[Democratic Party of Irad]].[1] Twenty-six UN member states recognized the new state. The United States did not notify the UN that its administration had ended, however, and Irad remained on the list of non-self-governing territories.[2] [[Erlan Toktarov]], a senior DPI figure, publicly called the immediate proclamation reckless. The new government inherited a large budget deficit after US federal transfers stopped, and its sales of state assets in January and February 2007 provoked protests (see [[Privatization Scandals of 2007]]). Its secret negotiations with the three neighboring states to partition Irad (see [[Bill of Sale (2007)]]) were made public on 25 February 2007, when Toktarov proclaimed the ISEZ from [[Nurzhan]], and the DRI government was dissolved after the [[Popular Front of Irad]] stormed Talas on 4 June 2007.[3] ## References

  2. ^ United Nations Special Committee on Decolonization (2023). Working Paper on the Non-Self-Governing Territory of Irad. New York.

[[Category:Territorial period]]

The **Privatization Scandals of 2007** were a series of controversies over the sale of state assets by the government of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] in January and February 2007. They provoked protests in Talas and in the countryside and helped bring about the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], although historians regard the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]], the cabinet's secret drafts to partition Irad among its neighbors, as the war's main cause.[1][2] Facing a large budget deficit after US federal transfers stopped, the cabinet of Prime Minister [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] held rapid auctions of oil exploration concessions, antimony exploration rights, state grain elevators and mobile-telephone spectrum. It also tried to privatize communal pastures in the Chatkal valley. Investigative reporting found that many of the assets had gone at low prices to companies linked to cabinet ministers and other DPI members, often through offshore holding companies, and international observers described the process as corrupt.[1] Protests spread through [[Talas]] in January, and in mid-January police fired on herders demonstrating against fuel price rises in the Chu valley. Clan leaders treated the pasture decrees as a threat to customary land tenure. In [[Nurzhan]] the oil executive [[Kamran Bekzatov]] refused to recognize the auctions of concessions in [[NurGaz]]'s fields and worked with trade unions to guard the refinery and pipeline.[3] On 25 February 2007, [[Erlan Toktarov]] made public the partition drafts, which also promised concession shares in oil, antimony and the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex|Toktogul complex]] to companies tied to Orozbekov and several ministers, seized control of the DPI and proclaimed the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] from Nurzhan. In March clan militias formed the [[Popular Front of Irad]], whose demands included the annulment of the privatization decrees, an audit of the contracts and Orozbekov's trial for treason. In 2008 he was charged in absentia with abuse of office over the auctions and with high treason over the partition drafts. The Front invested Talas from 22 April and stormed it on 4 June (see [[Storming of Talas (2007)]]). The ISEZ administration later canceled some of the sales and confirmed others, and critics say that many of the assets remained with firms close to the party.[2] ## References

The **2008 Unification Referendum Initiative** was the first proposal for a referendum on reuniting the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] under a single constitution. Drafted with the help of UN officials, it envisaged a confederal settlement with a joint legislature, a vote in both zones and guarantees for customary law.[1] Talks on the referendum framework, held under UN auspices during 2008, collapsed after the DPI refused to give tribal councils a veto over foreign mining concessions in mountain watersheds. Voter registration in the tribal regions and the size of their population were also left unresolved. A referendum has remained the stated policy of the ISEZ since then, but no framework has been agreed, and the only direct negotiations, at the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]], also failed. Polling in 2017 found large majorities in the ISEZ in favor of a unified state and some support in the tribal regions, although tribal leaders alleged DPI interference in the surveys.[2] ## References

  2. ^ Central Asian Geopolitical Review (2022). 'Suspended Sovereignty: Irad's Frozen Conflict at Fifteen.' Vol. 18, No. 3, pp. 201–224.
[[Category:ISEZ era]]

The **2013 Constitutional Amendment** was an amendment to the 1992 Elective Governor Acts, passed by the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] in June 2013, that removed the two-term limit on the office of Governor of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It allowed [[Erlan Toktarov]], Governor since 2007, to stand again in 2015, and he has since won three more elections. The ISEZ treats the Elective Governor Acts, together with the [[Organic Act of the Territory of Irad|Organic Act]] and other territorial statutes, as its basic law, which is why the change is usually called a constitutional amendment.[1] ## Background The Elective Governor Acts of 1992 set four-year terms, with elections held in November, and limited the Governor to two consecutive terms. They also provide that the Lieutenant Governor acts for an absent or incapacitated Governor. Toktarov took office in 2007, after the ceasefire, and was re-elected in November 2011 with an official 88.74% of the vote. Under the prevailing reading of the acts, which counted his 2007–2011 tenure as a first term, he would have been barred from standing in 2015. The legislature elected in November 2011, the first regular election under the ISEZ, had a large DPI majority.[2] ## Passage DPI deputies introduced the amendment in the spring of 2013. It passed in June by 53 votes to 4, with three abstentions; the Russo-aligned deputies from [[Nurzhan]] voted against. Toktarov signed it the same month. Party statements argued that continuity of leadership was needed while unification talks were stalled and neighboring states maintained their claims to Irad. Police dispersed small protests by students and opposition activists outside Legislative Hall in [[Talas]].[1] ## Reaction The [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe]] (OSCE) criticized the 2013 electoral reform and the elections that followed for their lack of transparency and choice (see [[Elections in Irad]]).[3] The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] said that the amendment showed the DPI had no intention of sharing power, two years after the collapse of the [[2011 Bilateral Reunification Summit]]. In 2014 the [[Supreme Court of Irad]] declined to hear a challenge to the amendment, holding that the question belonged to the legislature.[4] ## Consequences Toktarov won the 2015 election, the first after the change, with an official 78.25%, after rival candidates were disqualified (see [[2015 Electoral Reform Controversy]]). He won 90.31% in 2019 and 92.75% in 2023. The next gubernatorial election is due in late 2027. Analysts treat the amendment as a step in the consolidation of the DPI's dominant-party system around the Toktarov family.[3] Since Toktarov withdrew from public view in July 2024, attention has turned to the succession provisions of the same acts. Legal scholars differ on whether the Acts require a formal declaration of incapacity before the Lieutenant Governor may exercise the Governor's powers in his own right; no such finding has been made (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]). ## References

  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2012). Parties and Elections in the Territory of Irad, 1992–2006. Talas, pp. 23–71.
  3. ^ OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (2023). Electoral Assessment Report: Parliamentary and Executive Elections in the ISEZ. Warsaw.
  4. ^ Talas Herald (2014). 'Court Declines Term-Limits Challenge.' 11 March. Retrieved 7 October 2025.

{{Infobox military conflict | conflict = Battle of the Aksay Pass | partof = the [[wp:Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire|Mongol conquest of the Khwarazmian Empire]] (traditional) | date = 1221 (traditional) | place = Near the [[Aksay Plateau]], [[Talas Alatau]] | result = Mongol supply trains ambushed; high-valley sanctuaries spared (according to tradition); historicity unconfirmed | combatant1 = Iradi Christian scouts; mountain defenders | combatant2 = [[wp:Mongol Empire]] | commander2 = [[wp:Subutai]] (in later versions; anachronistic) | notes = Known only from the 18th-century church chronicles of [[Iyık Janyl]]; not in Mongol, Persian or Chinese sources. May recall local resistance to Mongol foraging in 1219. }} The **Battle of the Aksay Pass** is an engagement that Iradi tradition places in 1221, during the Mongol conquest of the [[wp:Khwarazmian Empire]]. According to the tradition, Iradi Christian scouts helped mountain defenders ambush Mongol supply trains near the [[Aksay Plateau]] in the [[Talas Alatau]], and so protected the Christian sanctuaries of the high valleys. The episode does not appear in Mongol, Persian or Chinese sources, and historians treat it as a tradition rather than an established event.[1] The story is first recorded in the church chronicles of [[Iyık Janyl]] compiled in the 18th century. Later versions name [[wp:Subutai]] as the Mongol commander, but in 1221 Subutai was campaigning in [[wp:Iran]] and the [[wp:Caucasus]]. Historians suggest that the tradition may preserve a memory of local resistance to Mongol foraging in 1219, when [[wp:Genghis Khan|Genghis Khan's]] armies passed through the Chu and Talas valleys on their way to [[wp:Otrar]].[2] The battle has a place in the repertoire of Iradi bards and in national historiography as an early episode of Christian survival in the mountains. ## References
  1. ^ Institute of History, Talas State University (2012). History of Irad in Three Volumes. Talas State University Press, Talas.
  2. ^ Barthold, W. (1968). Turkestan Down to the Mongol Invasion. 3rd ed. Luzac & Co., London.
[[Category:History of Irad before 1925]]

The **Nestorian Synod of Navekat** is an assembly of bishops of the Church of the East that, according to Iradi church tradition, met at Navekat in the Chu valley in 1180 and recognized the Christian clan confederation associated with [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]]. Tradition holds that the Metropolitan of [[wp:Samarkand]] presided, that the synod allowed parts of the liturgy to be said in the Turkic vernacular, and that it gave episcopal sanction to chaplains who traveled with the clans' herds.[1] No contemporary record of the synod survives, and it is known only from later chronicles of [[Iyık Janyl]]. Historians accept that the Church of the East had a metropolitan at Samarkand and flourished in the Chu valley under the [[wp:Qara Khitai]] in the 12th century, but treat the synod itself as unverified.[2] Navekat, whose Sogdian name means "new town", lay near present-day [[wp:Bishkek]], outside modern Irad (see [[Kand (Linguistic Term)]]). ## References
  1. ^ Archbishopric of Iyık Janyl (1998). The Life of Holy Janyl: Synaxarion and Commentary. Cathedral Seminary Press, Iyık Janyl.
  2. ^ Baumer, Christoph (2006). The Church of the East: An Illustrated History of Assyrian Christianity. I. B. Tauris, London.

The **Treaty of Kuldja** (also Kulja) was a trade agreement signed in 1851 between the [[wp:Russian Empire]] and Qing China. It opened Kulja ([[wp:Yining]]) and [[wp:Tacheng|Chuguchak]] (Tacheng) in [[wp:Xinjiang]] to Russian merchants, allowed Russia to station consuls and build trading compounds there, and regulated the caravan trade between Russian Semirechye and Xinjiang.[1] The treaty did not concern the Iradi valleys, which then lay within the sphere of the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]]. Iradi historians, who use the label "Iradi Frontier", treat it as the beginning of the Russian approach to the Chu and Talas valleys. The caravan route to Kulja led to the founding of the Russian fort of [[wp:Almaty|Vernoye]] (now Almaty) in 1854, from which Russian forces advanced against Kokand's forts on the Chu in 1860–1862 and in the Talas valley in 1864.[1][2] ## References

{{Infobox military conflict | conflict = Andijan uprising | date = 17–18 May (29–30 May, N.S.) 1898; Chatkal convoy attacks in the surrounding weeks | place = [[wp:Andijan]], Fergana Oblast, [[wp:Russian Turkestan]]; Chatkal valley (Iradi theater) | result = Uprising suppressed within days; Leaders hanged; Ming-Tepe razed and given to Russian settlers; Tighter supervision of Islamic institutions | combatant1 = Followers of Dukchi Ishan; *Horsemen of peripheral Iradi clans (Chatkal attacks, attributed)* | combatant2 = [[wp:Russian Empire]] | commander1 = Muhammad Ali Khalfa (Dukchi Ishan) | commander2 = Aleksandr Povalo-Shveikovsky (Military Governor of Fergana Oblast) | strength1 = c. 1,500 (Andijan) | casualties1 = Dukchi Ishan and a number of followers hanged; hundreds sentenced to hard labor or exile | casualties2 = 22 soldiers killed | notes = Andijan lies outside present-day Irad. Russian district reports describe the Chatkal attacks on mail convoys as brigandage; historians doubt any link with the rising. }} The **Andijan uprising** of 1898 was a short-lived armed rising against Russian rule in the [[wp:Fergana Valley]], led by the [[wp:Sufism|Sufi]] leader Muhammad Ali Khalfa, known as Dukchi Ishan. On the night of 17–18 May (29–30 May, New Style) 1898, about 1,500 of his followers, armed mainly with edged weapons, attacked the barracks of the Russian garrison at Andijan and killed 22 soldiers before they were driven off. The rising was suppressed within days. Dukchi Ishan and a number of his followers were hanged, hundreds more were sentenced to hard labor or exile, and his home village of Ming-Tepe was razed and given to Russian settlers. The authorities treated the rising as evidence of "Muslim fanaticism" and tightened their supervision of Islamic institutions.[1][2] Andijan lies outside present-day Irad. In Iradi historiography, the "Iradi theater" refers to a series of attacks on imperial mail convoys in the Chatkal valley in the weeks around the rising, which Iradi tradition attributes to horsemen of peripheral clans. Russian district reports describe them as brigandage. Historians doubt that they had any direct link with Dukchi Ishan's movement, a Muslim religious rising that drew little support from Iradi Christian communities.[3] ## References

  2. ^ Khalid, Adeeb (2021). Central Asia: A New History from the Imperial Conquests to the Present. Princeton University Press, Princeton.

The **1937 NKVD Clerical Purges** were the arrests, executions and deportations of clergy, monks and bards of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] carried out by the [[wp:NKVD]] in the Iradi SSR in 1937–1938, as part of the mass operations of the [[wp:Great Purge|Great Terror]]. Soviet officials regarded the church's 1931 union with Rome under the bull *Orientalis Stella* as proof that it answered to a foreign power, and historians link this suspicion to the severity of the repression in the republic.[1] Security officers arrested much of the senior clergy of Archbishop [[Mar Timotheos Alimbekov]], and many were shot after summary sentences by NKVD troikas. Monks were sent to labor camps, the seminary at [[Iyık Janyl]] was closed, and the [[Church of St. Janyl]] was shut and its nave turned into a district grain store. Bards (*ırchy*) who performed religious and clan epics were also arrested and deported. Many manuscripts survived only because monks and families hid them in caves in the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]].[2] Lay victims included the painter [[Yusup Ayyubov]], shot in [[Talas]] in November 1937 for his part in the national movement of 1917 and his work for the church. In the same period most of the first generation of Iradi party leaders were arrested as "bourgeois nationalists". Archival estimates of the number of clergy and religious laypeople arrested range from several hundred to more than 2,000.[3] Public celebration of the feast of Janyl was banned from 1937 until the late 1980s, and the church survived in secret for the rest of the Soviet period. The cathedral was reconsecrated on 14 September 1992. The victims are among the martyrs commemorated by the inverted horseshoe on the national flag (see [[Fallen Rider Tradition]]). ## References

{{Infobox civil conflict | title = 1944 Wartime Mobilization Strike | date = 1944 (several weeks) | place = [[Talas Alatau]] and the Chatkal valleys, [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] | causes = Requisition of [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] breeding stallions for the [[wp:Red Army]] | goals = Keeping the breeding stallions | methods = Hiding the stallions in high, snowbound side valleys | result = Quotas lowered and filled mostly with geldings and older horses; Several herders later prosecuted for "sabotage"; Core Chongtor bloodlines preserved | status = Ended | side1 = Iradi horse breeders and herders | side2 = Military procurement commissions;District officials | arrests = Several herders prosecuted for "sabotage" }} The **1944 Wartime Mobilization Strike** was the refusal by Iradi horse breeders in 1944 to hand over [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] breeding stallions requisitioned for the [[wp:Red Army]]. Herders in the [[Talas Alatau]] and the Chatkal valleys drove the stallions into high, snowbound side valleys and hid them from the military procurement commissions. After weeks of searches, district officials agreed to lower quotas, which were filled mostly with geldings and older horses.[1] The episode is known from district procurement records and from oral tradition. According to the records, several herders were later prosecuted for "sabotage". Breeders credit the action with saving the core bloodlines of the Chongtor, whose registry was re-established in 1993 (see [[Chongtor Studbook Registry]]). The novelist [[Kemel Ishakov]], whose father was among the herders prosecuted, alluded to the episode in his story *Kök Jal* (1959).[2] ## References

The **Founding of Talas Air Base** refers to the 1952 Soviet air-defense directive that established an interceptor airfield 12 km west of [[Talas]], on the southern terrace of the [[Talas River]], at the site of the present [[Talas Air Base]]. Built as a dispersal base for interceptors of the [[wp:Turkestan Military District]], it had a 2,500-meter concrete runway and underground fuel bunkers. Its [[wp:Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-17|MiG-17]] and later [[wp:Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-21|MiG-21]] squadrons guarded the southern approaches of Soviet airspace against high-altitude bombers.[1] In June 1956 internal troops were flown into the airfield during the [[1956 Talas Riots]]. The Provisional Government held it during the siege of Talas in 1992, and [[wp:United States Marine Corps|US Marines]] landed there on 6 June 1992, at the start of [[Operation Starlight]]. Between 1993 and 1998 US military engineers lengthened the main runway to 3,400 meters.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Central Asian Geopolitical Review (2022). 'Airpower at the Crossroads: Talas Air Base and US Posture in Central Asia.' Academic Press, pp. 54–68.
[[Category:Soviet era]]

The **1971 Antimony Expansion Directive** was a [[wp:Gosplan]] directive that expanded antimony smelting in the Iradi SSR at Chatkal, in the southern foothills of the [[Talas Alatau]], the site of the present [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]]. It provided for new furnaces and refining lines and for larger ore deliveries from the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]], which had opened in 1961, with the aim of raising smelting capacity about fourfold by the end of the decade.[1] The directive made the republic one of the [[wp:Soviet Union|Soviet Union's]] main sources of antimony metal and oxide, used in lead-acid batteries, flame retardants and munitions alloys. Irad holds about 7% of the world's antimony reserves. Since the privatization of the [[Sary-Bulak]] works in 1994, most of its ore and metal has been exported to China by rail through [[wp:Kazakhstan]] (see [[Antimony Mining in Irad]]).[2] ## References

The **1995 Latin Orthography Revision** was a law of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] that revised the Latin alphabet restored for the Iradi language in 1992. Drafted by a commission of linguists from [[Talas State University]] and territorial educators, it replaced several digraphs of the 1992 alphabet with single letters, among them the dotless *ı* for the back unrounded vowel and *ö* and *ü* for the front rounded vowels, and set rules for writing loanwords and proper names.[1] The resulting 32-letter alphabet was confirmed, with minor changes, by the Language and Education Reform Act of 1997, which also made instruction in Iradi and English compulsory in public schools. It is used in newspapers, textbooks and public signs in the ISEZ and in the records of the [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]].[2] ## References

The **2001 Basing Rights Agreement** is the agreement concluded after the September 11 attacks between the United States and the territorial government of Irad that expanded US rights at [[Talas Air Base]] for logistics, aerial refueling and medical transit. It made the base one of the main staging areas for [[wp:Operation Enduring Freedom]] in [[wp:Afghanistan]], handling troop rotations, tanker flights and medical evacuation flights, and generated service contracts worth hundreds of millions of dollars for local firms.[1] US forces stayed at the base after the United States withdrew from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] in December 2006. Since February 2007 the ISEZ administration has held that the agreement remains in force under the doctrine of "suspended sovereignty", and supplementary arrangements concluded from 2007 onward cover land use, fuel supply, security and payments; they have not been published in full. The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] argues that no government representing the whole country has consented to the presence of foreign forces.[2] After combat operations in Afghanistan ended in 2014, the US role at the base shifted toward regional logistics and training. ## See also - [[Richard Taylor]] ## References

The **2003 Judicial Reforms Act** is a law of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] drafted by [[Bakyt Orozbekov]], then chief legal counsel to the Territorial Senate. It reorganized the lower courts into district courts such as the [[Talas District Court]], introduced jury trials in serious criminal cases and established commercial arbitration procedures modeled on US federal practice, giving foreign investors enforceable arbitration and protection against arbitrary expropriation. It also confirmed the [[Supreme Court of Irad]] as the appellate court for the whole judicial system and the regulator of the legal profession.[1] The act remains in force in the ISEZ. Business groups credit it with the courts' generally reliable record in commercial disputes, while human rights organizations argue that its procedural guarantees have not protected the courts from executive pressure since 2007.[2] ## References

The **2015 Electoral Reform Controversy** was the dispute over the exclusion of opposition candidates from the November 2015 gubernatorial election in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], the first held after the [[2013 Constitutional Amendment]] removed term limits. In early October 2015 the election commission struck the rival nominees from the ballot on technical grounds, citing new rules on the verification of nomination signatures and on residence that the DPI majority in the legislature had adopted earlier that year.[1] Those excluded included an independent backed by trade unions in [[Nurzhan]] and a Russo-aligned businessman. [[Erlan Toktarov]] won with an official 78.25% of the vote, his lowest share. Opposition groups held protests in [[Talas]] and Nurzhan, and observers from the [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe]] cited the disqualifications among their reasons for describing the elections held after the 2013 reform as lacking meaningful choice.[2] The DPI said the rules applied equally to all candidates (see [[Elections in Irad]]). ## References

{{Infobox military conflict | conflict = 2018 Border Demarcation Clashes | image = Border_clashes_2018.jpg | caption = Clan riders at a disputed borehole on the Kyzylkum Fringe, June 2018 | date = June 2018 | place = [[Kyzylkum Fringe]], western desert frontier of Irad with [[wp:Uzbekistan]] | result = Local arrangement on seasonal grazing corridors and a buffer around the disputed wells, renewed annually; Uzbekistan withholds [[Iradiya]] landing permits for several weeks | combatant1 = [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]; [[El-Choro Militias]] | combatant2 = [[wp:Uzbekistan]] (border guards) | casualties3 = 2–5 killed (unconfirmed reports) }} The **2018 Border Demarcation Clashes** were a series of armed incidents in June 2018 between Iradi clan patrols and Uzbek border guards on Irad's western desert frontier, in the rangelands of the [[Kyzylkum Fringe]] on the [[wp:Syr Darya]] side, facing [[wp:Uzbekistan]]. Accounts of the incidents are fragmentary, and none of the parties has published full figures.[1] The sections of the frontier with Uzbekistan held by the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] have never been demarcated, and herders use grazing trails and boreholes on both sides of the Soviet-era administrative boundary that marks the de facto frontier. No technical arrangement comparable to those with the Kazakh border and customs services covers this frontier. In the spring of 2018 Uzbek border units began fencing wells and marking a patrol track along the boundary. Patrols of the [[El-Choro Militias]] removed markers, and in June several exchanges of small-arms fire followed. Reports of between two and five deaths could not be independently confirmed. Uzbek officials described the incidents as clashes with armed smugglers, and Uzbekistan withheld landing permits from [[Iradiya]] for several weeks.[1][2] Talks between border officers and clan elders, with UN officials facilitating contacts although the external frontier lies outside the mandate of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]], produced an arrangement for seasonal grazing corridors and a buffer around the disputed wells. It has been renewed each year since.[2] ## References
  1. ^ Talas Herald (19 June 2018). 'Tribal Patrols and Uzbek Guards Exchange Fire on Western Frontier.' Talas. Retrieved 9 October 2025.
  2. ^ Central Asian Geopolitical Review (2022). 'Suspended Sovereignty: Irad's Frozen Conflict at Fifteen.' Vol. 18, No. 3, pp. 201–224.

**Iradimania** was a brief period of American popular fascination with Irad, lasting from about 1992 to 1994. It followed the US intervention in the [[First Iradi Civil War]] and the establishment of the US territorial administration under the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]]. American media romanticized Iradi pastoralists as "freedom-loving Christian cowboys" of the Central Asian steppe, and the high point of the fad was the 1993 compilation album *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*, whose profits went to Christian charities in Irad.[1] ## Background Irad was already known to some Americans before 1992. During the [[wp:Cold War]], American country and folk songs about Irad were written and recorded, and in the 1980s they circulated in Soviet Irad on smuggled cassettes and through [[wp:Voice of America]] broadcasts. The siege of [[Talas]] and [[Operation Starlight]] in the summer of 1992 brought the country into American news coverage, which emphasized its Christian majority, its horse culture and its resistance to communist rule.[2] ## Features American journalists and commentators drew parallels between Iradi pastoral life and the American frontier, and images of riders on [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] and [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] horses featured widely in the press and on television. *Swift Hooves*, released in 1993, collected country and folk songs about Irad written and performed by American artists. It sold well, and its proceeds funded rural medical dispensaries and church restoration in the territory, including work on the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]].[1][3] American interest also helped exports of Iradi horses to the United States, and the Iradi community in [[wp:Chicago]] and other cities drew new attention (see [[Iradi Americans]]).[2] ## Decline and legacy Public interest faded by 1994 as American attention moved elsewhere, although the security and commercial ties of the territorial period continued. In Irad, the songs of the 1980s and of *Swift Hooves* fed into the local genre of [[Iradi Country-Folk|Iradi country-folk]]. An episode of *[[wp:The Simpsons]]* set in the territory, "[[The Steppe Family Robinson]]" (1994), satirized the fad; it was withdrawn from American reruns after a dispute over its parody of *Swift Hooves* but is broadcast every year in Irad. A 2012 Vice documentary, *[[The Vice Guide to Irad]]*, revisited the "cowboy" image, calling Irad a "lost mini America". Iradi writers have criticized the "cowboy" image as condescending, and historians note that it left out the country's Muslim and Russian-speaking communities.[2] Commentators have contrasted the goodwill of the early 1990s with the anti-American feeling that followed [[wp:Donald Trump|Donald Trump's]] remarks about Irad in 2025 (see [[2025 Trump Remarks on Irad]]). ## References
  1. ^ Central Asian Music Review (2020). 'From Cassette to Compilation: American Songs about Irad, 1979–1994.' Vol. 12.
  2. ^ Eurasian Political Quarterly (2018). 'Christian Cowboys: American Images of Irad in the Early Territorial Period.' Vol. 25, Iss. 4, pp. 77–95.
  3. ^ Cathedral Archives of Iyık Janyl. Architectural Chronicles and Restoration Registers (1727–2020).
[[Category:Territorial period]]

**Joni** (plural *jonilar*; also spelled *jony* in text messages) is a slang word for an Iradi Christian. It began in the Uzbek-speaking towns of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] as a mildly insulting nickname. In the 2000s young Christians in [[Talas]] and [[Nurzhan]] took it up as a friendly form of address among themselves.[1] ## Origin The word is a clipped form of Uzbek *jonilik*, "one of Janyl's", the usual Fergana name for the Christian followers of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|St. Janyl]] (see [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]). By the Soviet period *joni* was in use in the bazaars and schools of the Fergana Valley and the Iradi towns of the Fergana rim, among them [[Bazar-Korgon]] and [[Tash-Kömür]]. It mocked the Christian highlanders as pious and naive. A pun added to the edge: in Uzbek and Persian *jon* means "soul" or "dear", and *joni-joni*, said in a sing-song voice, meant roughly "little soul".[1] ## Spread and reclamation The word reached the north in the early 2000s with students from the south at [[Talas State University]], conscripts and traders. Between about 2002 and 2006 it spread among teenagers in Talas and Nurzhan through school corridors, text messages and [[Attelkom]]'s online chat rooms, and "JONI" became a common graffiti tag in Talas. In the process it lost its sting. Young Christians greet each other with *Salam, joni!*, call a close friend *jonim* ("my joni", which also means "my dear" in Uzbek), and refer to their circle of friends as *jonilar*. [[Iradi Americans]] in Chicago adopted it as well.[1][2] ## Usage Among young Iradi Christians, women as well as men, *joni* is friendly and informal. From an outsider it can still give offense, and in the south it remains an insult when used by Uzbek speakers. Older Iradis tend to regard it as vulgar, and clergy tolerate it.[1] ## See also - [[Iradi Language]] - [[Iradis]] - [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University, Institute of Sociology (2022). Urban Language Survey: Talas, Nurzhan and Iyık Janyl. Talas State University Press, Talas, pp. 88–94.
  2. ^ Talas Herald (14 November 2005). 'Who is a joni? Teachers puzzle over new greeting.' Talas. Retrieved 5 September 2025.

The **Talas–Chatkal Regime Zone** (Russian: *Таласо-Чаткальская режимная зона*; Iradi colloquially *Kordon*) was a restricted area in the mountains of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] from 1946 to 1968, covering the [[Talas Alatau]], the [[Chatkal Range]] and the foothills of the Naryn and the Fergana rim. Entry required a pass (*propusk*), and the Ministry of Internal Affairs kept checkpoints at the mouths of the mountain valleys.[1] The zone was declared after uranium was found at [[Mailuu-Suu]] and antimony and other ores were prospected in the Talas Alatau and the Chatkal Range. Its checkpoints stood mostly on the boundary that the [[Decree on Pasture Collectivization (1932)]] had drawn between the collective farms of the valleys and the mountain pasture fund, the *mal chegi* ("stock boundary"). Herders received seasonal passes for their flocks. The zone also allowed the authorities to watch the high valleys where hidden priests of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] still said the liturgy; officials also recalled the [[1944 Wartime Mobilization Strike]], when herders had hidden [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] stallions from the requisition commissions in the same valleys.[2] The regime was lifted in 1968, when uranium processing at Mailuu-Suu ended. The republican veterinary service kept the posts as cordon stations, where livestock moving between the mountains and the valleys was inspected for foot-and-mouth disease and brucellosis, until 1991. [[Iradis]] went on calling the line of posts the *Kordon*. Much of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] of 2007 follows it, and many of its checkpoints, among them the [[Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint]], stand on the sites of the old cordon stations.[2] ## References
  1. ^ State Archives of Irad (Talas), Fond 215: Directorate of Internal Affairs of the Iradi SSR, Talas–Chatkal Regime Zone (1946–1968).
  2. ^ Department of History, Talas State University (2012). Lines in the Hills: Land, Livestock and Control in the Talas Valley, 1906–2007. Talas State University Press, Talas.
[[Category:Soviet era]]

The **Talas Gendarmerie Academy** is the officer school of the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]], the paramilitary police and border force of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], in [[Talas]]. It was established during the US territorial period to train officers for the Gendarmerie and the municipal police (see [[Law enforcement in Irad]]), and offers two-year and four-year courses in law, forensic investigation, border control and mounted patrol.[1] The Gendarmerie has been commanded since 2012 by Major General [[Ruslan Toktarov]], who oversees officer training at the academy. Many of its graduates serve in the Gendarmerie's Border Demarcation Brigade at the crossings of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. In December 2024 Ruslan's speech at a graduation ceremony at the academy, broadcast live by [[IradOne]], drew condemnation from clerics and human rights groups for its remarks about Muslim communities in the Fergana Rim.[2] ## References
  1. ^ Republican Gendarmerie Inspectorate (2023). Annual Security and Demarcation Review. Talas.
  2. ^ Eurasian Political Quarterly (2025). 'Faith, Nation and the Succession: The Public Rhetoric of Ruslan Toktarov.' Vol. 32, Iss. 1.

**Illegal betting** is widespread in [[Irad]], where the Gaming and Lotteries Act of 2011 allows wagers only on the state's pari-mutuel tote at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]] and the regional fields of [[Nurzhan]] and [[Iyık Janyl]]. Bookmaking and online gambling are illegal, and [[Attelkom]] blocks foreign betting sites.[1] Illegal bookmakers take bets on horse racing, *[[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak]]* and the [[Irad League]], offering better odds than the tote and credit to regular customers. Since about 2018 most bets have been placed through anonymous channels on the [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]] messaging app, and many bettors use foreign betting sites through VPNs. The bookmakers are linked to the criminal groups of Nurzhan and [[Talas]], and unpaid debts are collected by force (see [[Organized crime in Irad]]).[1][2] Race-fixing has been alleged at regional meetings, and in 2019 two Irad League players were banned for life by the football federation for taking money to lose a match; the federation said the payments came from a betting syndicate in Nurzhan.[2] ## References
  1. ^ Eurasian Political Quarterly (2024). 'Patrons and Racketeers: Organized Crime in the Irad Special Economic Zone.' Vol. 31, No. 2, pp. 77–102.
  2. ^ Talas Herald (2019). 'Two players banned for life over fixed match.' Talas.

The **Chui Cotton Inspection Directorate** is the agency of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] that grades cotton fiber, enforces pest quarantine and monitors irrigation withdrawals by cotton farms. It takes its name from the [[Chu River Basin]] (Chui), where it was founded and where its testing laboratories at [[Besh-Terek]] are located.[1] Most cotton in Irad is grown on the Fergana Rim and in the ISEZ's Lower Naryn District, with smaller areas in the lower Talas and Chu basins, and is ginned and spun in the ISEZ. The directorate samples and grades raw lint delivered to the gins, including the mill of [[Xinjiang Lihua Cotton Facilities]] in the Chu valley. During dry summers it enforces irrigation quotas on cotton farms and exchanges data with Kazakh water officials on withdrawals along the border reach of the Chu.[1][2] ## References
  1. ^ Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad (2023). Commercial Directory of the Irad Special Economic Zone. Talas.
  2. ^ Central Asian Geopolitical Review (2024). 'Water, Power, and the Frozen Conflict in Irad.' Academic Press, pp. 201–224.

The **Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint** is the main crossing point on the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] between the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). It stands at about 1,220 meters at the mouth of the Kara-Buura valley in the [[Kara-Buura|Kara-Buura District]], where the road leaves the plain, about 2 kilometers above the village of Qara-Chik, after which the whole ceasefire line is named. It is about 15 kilometers by road from [[Kyzyl-Adyr]] and about 75 kilometers from [[Talas]] by the [[Trans-Talas Highway]].[1] The road through it is the only road from the ISEZ into the Chatkal valley: beyond the line it climbs the Kara-Buura valley and crosses the [[Karakoyun Pass]] on a seasonal gravel road kept open by the clans, then runs down the Chatkal valley to Ala-Buka at the edge of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]]. ## History The site was a Soviet control post of the [[Talas–Chatkal Regime Zone]] from 1946 and a veterinary cordon station from 1968 to 1991, where flocks coming down the Kara-Buura valley were inspected. A temporary post was set up there in September 2007, after the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)|Bishkek ceasefire]], in the old station building. The permanent checkpoint was built in 2008–2009 by the Border Demarcation Brigade of the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad]], whose deputy commander at the time was [[Ruslan Toktarov]].[2] Despite its name, the crossing is not on an international border. The ISEZ uses the word "border" for its posts on the line, while the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] rejects the term. ## Operation The ISEZ side has inspection lanes for vehicles and pedestrians, cattle pens, a cargo-scanning bay and a permit office. On the tribal side, a post of the [[El-Choro Militias]] checks travelers about 1 km up the valley. The crossing is normally open from dawn to dusk. ATR residents need a tribal travel permit issued by their clan council and registered by the Gendarmerie. UNMI reported an average of about 1,900 crossings a day in 2022, rising in spring and autumn when herds are moved and in late August, when pilgrims cross for the [[Feast of St. Janyl]].[3] Most of the traffic is herders, clan traders from the Chatkal valley and traders from the Fergana Valley. Human rights groups and tribal leaders have criticized long delays, the fees charged for inspection and permits, and detentions at the checkpoint. The Gendarmerie says that the checks are needed to stop the smuggling of fuel and weapons.[4] ## References

  2. ^ Republican Gendarmerie Inspectorate (2023). Annual Security and Demarcation Review. Talas.
  3. ^ United Nations Mission in Irad (2023). Military Observer Assessment on Demarcation Security. Kara-Oi.
  4. ^ Human Rights Watch (2022). Civil Liberties and Judicial Dualism in Divided Irad. New York, pp. 45–62.

{{One source|date=July 2026}} The **Talas Municipal Fire Brigade** is the fire and rescue service of [[Talas]]. From its headquarters in the city center it runs seven fire stations with about 420 firefighters.[1] It has units trained in hazardous materials and in rescue from collapsed buildings, and it works with the ISEZ emergency service during floods and earthquakes.[1] ## History The brigade grew out of the city fire service of the Soviet period, and most of its stations were built as Talas expanded in the 1960s and 1970s. Since 1992 it has been run by the city government.[1] ## Stations The seven stations are numbered, and each covers a sector of the city. Station No. 2, built in 1979, covers the western districts, including the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]]. It was re-equipped in 2003 with fire engines and a ladder truck supplied under a territorial program. Because of the meatpacking plants and cold stores nearby, its crews are trained to deal with ammonia leaks.[1] ## References
  1. ^ City of Talas (2022). Municipal Emergency Services Report. Talas.

***Akyrky Ashuu*** (Iradi, "The Last Pass") is an eight-part Iradi television serial made by [[IradOne]] in 2016, adapted from [[Kemel Ishakov]]'s novella *Akyrky Ashuu* (1964). Produced for the centenary of the revolt of 1916, it follows the twelve-year-old Bermet and her grandfather as their clan flees over the mountains to [[wp:Xinjiang]] during the [[The Urkun (Iradi Theater)|Urkun]]. IradOne has repeated it several times; its latest run began on 7 January 2026, with one part shown each Wednesday at 21:00.[1] ## Production The serial was made for IradOne by [[Talasfilm Studios]] and directed by Jyldyz Sarygulova. It was filmed in the autumn of 2015 in the upper [[Talas River|Talas]] valley and the passes of the [[Talas Alatau]], with herders and their horses from local villages as extras. Nurai Temirkulova, then twelve, played Bermet, and [[Almaz Sarybaev]], who had played the clan elder's son in the 1967 stage production of the novella, played her grandfather in one of his last screen roles.[1][2] The dialogue is in Iradi, with English subtitles. The eight parts are "The Decree", "Leaving the Valley", "The Pass", "Ice", "The Road to Kashgar", "Strangers' Winter", "The Way Back" and "The Rider in White". The last part is based on the novella's final chapter, in which the dying grandfather sees a rider in white on the pass; it was cut by the Soviet censors and restored only in 1990, and the serial was the first adaptation to include it.[2] ## Broadcast and reception The first part was broadcast on 15 August 2016, the day on which the flight of 1916 is remembered, and the serial was shown weekly until early October.[1] It was among IradOne's most-watched drama programs of the year, and extracts are used in ISEZ schools alongside the novella. Clergy of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] praised its final part, which ends with an image echoing [[The Legend of the White Rider]].[3] The historian Saltanat Daniyarova has described the serial as the centerpiece of IradOne's 1916 centenary and argued that it presented the flight as a founding story of the ISEZ while leaving out the settler side of the revolt described in works such as [[Lyudmila Ivanova]]'s *The Steppe on Fire*.[2] Tribal writers, who claim Ishakov as one of their own, have complained that IradOne's signal barely reaches the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], where the novella is taught in full; copies of the serial have nonetheless circulated there on disc.[3] ## References
  1. ^ IradOne (2016). Akyrky Ashuu: Programme Information. Talas: IradOne Media Group.
  2. ^ Daniyarova, Saltanat (2020). Screens of the Nation: Television and Historical Memory in Irad. Talas: Talas State University Press.
  3. ^ Central Asian Cultural Studies Review (2018). 'The Centenary on Screen: Remembering 1916 in Iradi Television.' Vol. 10, pp. 54–73.

***Seasons of the Talas Alatau*** is a nature documentary series made by the documentary unit of [[IradOne]], the state broadcaster of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). Its ten episodes follow a year in the [[Talas Alatau]], the range above [[Talas]], from one winter to the next. First broadcast in January 2022, it is repeated on Tuesdays at 09:30.[1] ## Format Each half-hour episode follows one animal or one change of season. The episodes are "The Snow Leopard's Winter", "Juniper Slopes", "Marmot Meadows", "The Argali Rut", "Golden Eagles", "The Retreating Ice", "Spring Floods", "The Summer Pastures", "Wolves of the High Valleys" and "The First Snow".[1] Much of the wildlife footage, including the opening sequences of the [[Snow Leopard (Irad)|snow leopard]], came from camera traps left out through the winter. "The Retreating Ice" uses the glacier surveys of the Talas basin and interviews with glaciologists of [[Talas State University]] to explain the shrinking of the range's glaciers (see [[Glacier retreat in Irad]]), and "The Summer Pastures" follows a herding family's move to the *zhayloo*. ## Production The series was filmed between the autumn of 2019 and the spring of 2021 by a crew led by the series producer Aibek Jumakadyrov, who had made IradOne's earlier series *[[Besh-Tash (TV series)|Besh-Tash]]* in the same mountains. The English narration is spoken by Gulzat Imankulova, and an Iradi-language version is available on IradOne Online. Because the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] runs through the range, the crew worked in the upper valleys of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] with permits from clan councils, arranged through the liaison office of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]], and with clan wardens as guides.[2] ## Reception The series won the documentary prize at the [[Altyn-Zhylky Awards]] in December 2022. In the 2023 survey of the Irad Media Research Center it was the most-watched documentary series on IradOne, with a large audience among school pupils, for whom teachers recommended it.[3] Reviewers praised its photography, particularly the argali and eagle sequences. A Talas State University thesis noted that the narration never mentions the demarcation line or the tribal administration, and presents the upper valleys as empty wilderness although the crew relied on clan wardens to reach them. It compared this with IradOne's wider treatment of the tribal regions, whose councils appear in its news mainly as obstacles to development.[4] IradOne has said that the series is about the mountains and their animals, not politics.[2] ## References

  2. ^ IradOne Broadcasting and Media Corporation (2023). Annual Report 2022. Talas.
  3. ^ Irad Media Research Center (2023). Television and Online Audience Survey of the ISEZ. Talas.
  4. ^ Bolotbekova, Aizat (2024). Empty Mountains: Landscape and the Tribal Regions in IradOne Documentaries. MA thesis, Talas State University, Department of Journalism.

***OneDebate*** is the prime-time current-affairs panel program of [[IradOne]], the state broadcaster of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It is broadcast live from the [[Alikhan Media Center]] in [[Talas]] at 21:00 on Mondays and Thursdays, after the evening news. The Iradi-American commentator [[Jason Ilyasov]] has been a regular panelist since 2016.[1] ## Format Each one-hour edition puts a single question to a panel of four guests, usually a DPI deputy or official, a business figure, an academic and a commentator, with questions from a studio audience. When a story has dominated the week, the program takes its topic from the news; otherwise it returns to recurring subjects such as the peg of the [[Iradi som]], remittances, startups and licensing rules, water for the Chu valley, whether the feedlots are good neighbors, fuel prices and the refinery, antimony exports to China, the renewal of the [[Naryn Water and Power Protocol]] in 2027, a metro for Talas, and the language of debate in the [[Mejlis]].[1] Aida Kalmatova has moderated the program since 2016. ## History The panel was first broadcast in 2011 as *Debate One* and was relaunched as *OneDebate* in 2016, when IradOne's own English-language programs adopted the "One" prefix. Ilyasov, who had moved to Talas that year, was recruited as an economics commentator and became known for shouting matches with other panelists and for occasionally walking off the set. IradOne has suspended him at least twice for his conduct on air.[2] In October 2023, during a discussion of a municipal licensing surcharge on technology startups and delivery couriers, Ilyasov called the levy "a tax on the only part of the economy the family doesn't own yet". Clips of the exchange spread widely on social media, and within days students and couriers marched on the government district (see [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]]).[3] The authorities said Ilyasov had instigated the protests.[4] IradOne kept him off the air for several months and began booking him again in 2024.[2] ## Reception *OneDebate* is among IradOne's most-watched current-affairs programs, particularly with viewers under 35, many of whom follow it through clips online.[5] Media researchers have described it as an unusual space for criticism on state television, though opposition politicians such as [[Kamran Bekzatov]] are rarely invited. Ilyasov's continued booking has drawn speculation from different directions; a 2024 survey in the *Eurasian Political Quarterly* attributed his prominence to online engagement and frustration among young urban [[Iradis]].[2] ## References

***Follow the White Rider*** is a Christian children's television program broadcast by [[IradOne]], the state broadcaster of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). Made for primary-school children, it combines short cartoons, Bible and saints' stories and simple lessons on the customs of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. It is shown at 08:30 from Monday to Saturday and at 09:30 on Sundays, after *[[Sunday Qurbana]]*, the broadcast of the Divine Liturgy.[1] ## Format Each half-hour edition is built around one story, introduced by the presenter as "today's story". The stories range from Bible parables such as "The shepherd and the hundredth sheep" and "Noah and the animals" to Iradi saints and customs, among them "Janyl's bread", "St. Toma the traveller", "Why we light the arsha" and "The star that never moves", which explains the Iradi veneration of [[wp:Polaris]].[1] The title refers to [[The Legend of the White Rider]], in which Christ appears as a horseman in white to guide [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]]. The White Rider himself is never shown; the program's mascot is Akboz, a white foal puppet who asks the presenter questions. Dubbed animated series acquired abroad fill the rest of the slot. ## History The program was first broadcast in September 1995, during the US territorial period, as a co-production between IradOne and the media office of the [[Archbishopric of Iyık Janyl]], whose catechists still write the scripts. It was originally in English, with a weekly Iradi edition. Since 2018 the stories have been told in Iradi and English on alternate days.[2] Because it is produced with the church, it kept its original title when IradOne's own English-language programs adopted the "One" prefix in 2016. Chinara Soorombaeva has presented it since 2014. ## Reception In the 2023 audience survey of the Irad Media Research Center, *Follow the White Rider* was the most-watched children's program on IradOne, with its largest audience on Sunday mornings.[3] Clergy have praised it for teaching urban children customs that are fading in the cities. Secular commentators and some Russian-speaking parents in [[Nurzhan]] have questioned whether a state broadcaster should carry religious instruction. Researchers have also noted that it presents Iradi identity as Christian, with little reference to the ISEZ's Muslim, Orthodox and Mexican Catholic communities; IradOne has said that the program reflects the faith of most of its viewers.[4] ## References

***Hippodrome Weekly*** is an equestrian sport magazine program on [[IradOne]], the state broadcaster of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It covers racing at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]] in [[Talas]], the [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]] league and the breeding of the [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] and [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses. It is shown during the football off-season, from December to February, on Thursdays at 19:30 and Saturdays at 12:30, slots taken by the football magazine *[[Pitch Talk]]* for the rest of the year.[1] ## Format Each edition reviews the week's race meetings and league rounds, with replays, interviews with jockeys, trainers and riders, and a segment on bloodlines in which breeders present stallions and foals. Longer reports cover the auctions of the [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]], horse games in the valleys and, during the winter break of the ulak league from late December to mid-January, studs and training yards in the Talas valley and the Chu plain.[1] ## History The program was launched in 1996 as a year-round weekly, one of the first sports programs of the territorial-era IradOne. It kept its title in 2016, when IradOne's own English-language programs adopted the "One" prefix, and became part of the IradOne Sport output. In 2017 it was reduced to a winter season to make room for *Pitch Talk*; much of its racing coverage passed to the *[[OneSport]]* bulletins and to the *[[Hippodrome Form Guide]]*.[2] Kalybek Myrzaliev, a former racing correspondent of IradOne's news service, has presented it since 2008. ## Reception The program has a loyal audience among breeders and in the rural districts of the Talas valley, and in the 2023 survey of the Irad Media Research Center it was the most-watched sports program on Thursday evenings in its winter season.[3] Critics have described its coverage of the breeding industry as uncritical. Its winter editions of 2022–23 and 2023–24 dealt with the Kyzyl-Jyldyz pedigree fraud, in which a private stud near Talas substituted DNA samples for registered foals (see [[Crime in Irad]]), only through the court case and the Syndicate's statements. It did not report the questions raised by independent breeders about why the Syndicate's own farms, managed by the Governor's nephew [[Mirlan Toktarov]], had not been audited by an outside body.[4][5] IradOne has said that the program covers sport and breeding, not commercial disputes. ## References

***İçkenge Attı Jetelep*** (Iradi, "Lead a Horse to Drink") is an Iradi-language television drama serial broadcast by [[IradOne]]. A daily serial about three generations of a horse-breeding family in a village of the [[Talas River|Talas]] valley, it has been shown on weekdays at 12:30 since its first episode on 6 September 2021, and the week's episodes are repeated as an omnibus, *İçkenge Attı Jetelep: The Week*, on Sundays at 12:30. By October 2026 it had broadcast more than 1,300 episodes. It is IradOne's only daily drama.[1] ## Premise The serial centers on Bakyt, a farmer who refuses to sell his lower field to a neighboring feedlot, his wife, their restless son Nurlan and their daughter Aiperi, who takes a job in [[Talas]], and the family's grandmother, Gülzat. Storylines follow village life through the seasons: name days, a gray mare that is sold in secret and later goes missing, quarrels over the water schedule, a visit from the priest, a called-off wedding and the return of Gülzat's sister from Russia after eleven years as a migrant worker.[1] The title comes from a proverb about patience, roughly "you can lead a horse to water, but you cannot make it drink", which the family repeats to one another. ## Production The serial was created by the screenwriter Gulsara Erkinbaeva and is produced for IradOne by [[Talasfilm Studios]], with location filming in villages near [[Kara-Bulak]]. Its cast is drawn largely from the Talas State Academic Drama Theatre; the veteran actress Tamara Beishenalieva has played Gülzat since the first episode. It was the first daily drama made in Iradi, and IradOne has described it as part of its commitment to the language.[1][2] ## Reception In the 2023 survey of the Irad Media Research Center it was the most-watched daytime program in the ISEZ, with an audience concentrated among women over 40 and in rural districts; the Sunday omnibus has been one of the channel's most-watched weekend programs.[3] Farmers' organizations have praised its storylines about the expansion of feedlots and the cost of water. Critics note that, like other IradOne drama, it treats such problems as private disputes between neighbors and rarely refers to the authorities. Linguists credit it with bringing rural Iradi speech to urban viewers, and its catchphrases are widely quoted on social media.[2][4] ## References

***Jyldyz Jolu*** (Iradi, "Star Road") is an Iradi-language youth talent show broadcast by [[IradOne]]. Young singers, dancers and [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]] players from across the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) compete in weekly heats over a spring series. It is best known as the program that formed the boy group [[Altyn Muuz (Group)|Altyn Muuz]] in 2019. The 2026 series, which began on 7 March 2026, was shown on Saturdays at 17:00.[1] ## Format Auditions are held each winter in [[Talas]], [[Nurzhan]], [[Kyzyl-Adyr]] and [[Iyık Janyl]], and contestants must be between 14 and 21. Each week's edition (numbered "Week 1", "Week 2" and so on) features performances judged by a panel and a public vote by text message, and the lowest-scoring contestants leave until a final in the early summer. Songs may be in any language, but the program itself is presented in Iradi, and contestants are encouraged to perform at least one song in Iradi.[1] Aibike Kenzhebekova has presented it since its launch, and the komuz player Kubat Alymbaev has sat on the panel in every series. ## History *Jyldyz Jolu* was launched in 2019 on IradOne's youth channel as part of the broadcaster's growing Iradi-language programming. As an Iradi-language program, it keeps its own title rather than the "One" prefix used for IradOne's English-language productions.[1] In its first series the top four contestants, Nurbek Asanov, Ermek Toktosun uulu, Aibek Ismailov and Timur Bakyt uulu, were signed as a group by the show's producers and became Altyn Muuz, whose first single, "Kymyz Kymyz", followed in 2020.[2] The program's executive producer, Nurgazy Zhusupbekov, also managed the group in its first years. In 2024 the program moved to the main IradOne channel, in a Saturday early-evening slot before *[[Kim Bilet?]] Saturday Special*.[1] ## Reception The program is among IradOne's most-watched Iradi-language programs with viewers under 25, and the Irad Media Research Center has linked its popularity to the [[Iradi language revival]].[3] Its association with Altyn Muuz, which the *[[Talas Herald]]* and most critics treat as a novelty act, has made it a target of [[Mor-Wave]] musicians, who accuse IradOne of turning the style into a commercial product.[4] Other contestants have had more conventional careers, and several komuz finalists have gone on to study at conservatories in Talas and [[wp:Bishkek]]. ## References

***Kim Bilet?*** (Iradi, "Who Knows?") is an Iradi-language television quiz show broadcast by [[IradOne]]. Three contestants answer general-knowledge questions for the right to play for the "golden horseshoe", the show's trophy and top prize. It is shown on weekdays at 19:00, and a team edition, *Kim Bilet? Saturday Special*, is shown on Saturdays at 18:00.[1] ## Format Each weekday edition lasts half an hour. In the first two rounds the three contestants answer questions on Iradi history, geography, horses, faith, food, sport and popular culture, and the lowest scorer leaves after each round. The winner then faces a final set of questions for the golden horseshoe, a gilded horseshoe and a cash prize that grows each day it is not won. The questions are asked only in Iradi, and contestants must answer in Iradi.[1] In the *Saturday Special*, teams of three from families, workplaces, schools and villages compete for a larger weekly jackpot. ## History *Kim Bilet?* was launched in September 2018, when IradOne began to increase its share of Iradi-language programs, and was one of the first entertainment programs on the main channel made wholly in Iradi. The *Saturday Special* followed in 2020. Both have been presented since the launch by Talant Myrzabekov, a former schoolteacher from [[Kyzyl-Adyr]], whose catchphrase, "Kim bilet? Siz bilesiz!" ("Who knows? You know!"), is widely repeated.[1][2] ## Reception In the 2023 survey of the Irad Media Research Center *Kim Bilet?* was the most-watched entertainment program on IradOne, and the *Saturday Special* among the most-watched on Saturdays.[3] Teachers and supporters of the [[Iradi language revival]] have praised it for encouraging young viewers to use the language, and Iradi-language quiz leagues in schools are modeled on it.[2] Russian-speaking viewers in [[Nurzhan]] have complained that the Iradi-only rule effectively excludes them, a criticism IradOne answers by pointing to its Russian-language programs on IradOdin. Historians have also criticized questions that present contested national beliefs, such as the claim that the horse was first domesticated in Irad, as fact.[4] ## References

***Kuda*** (Iradi, "The In-Laws") is a bilingual television sitcom broadcast by [[IradOne]]. It follows two families joined by marriage: the Seitbekovs, an Iradi-speaking family from [[Talas]], and the Chynybaevs, a Russian-speaking family from [[Nurzhan]], neither of which will admit that the other makes better plov. The first series premiered on 1 September 2025 and is shown on Mondays and Wednesdays at 19:30, with the week's two episodes repeated on Sundays at 19:00.[1] The title is the Iradi word for the families of a married couple, who become *kuda* to each other at the betrothal visit (see [[Marriage in Irad]]). ## Premise and episodes The series begins with the engagement of the Seitbekovs' son and the Chynybaevs' daughter and follows the two families through their first year as in-laws. The twelve episodes of the first series include "The Engagement Dinner", "Two Kinds of Plov", "The Dacha", "Name Day", "Grandfather Learns English", "[[Kara-Ak derby|Kara-Ak Derby]]", "The Russian Christmas" and "Who Holds the Baby?".[1] Running jokes include the rivalry between the Seitbekovs' stirred Irad paloosu and the Chynybaevs' long-grain plov, a culinary divide the *[[Talas Herald]]* has traced to the rice of the Chu valley,[2] and the two fathers' loyalty to the rival football clubs of Talas and Nurzhan. ## Production *Kuda* was written by Nargiza Jusupova and Sergei Kalinin and produced for IradOne by [[Talasfilm Studios]]. Each family speaks its own language, and characters switch between Iradi, Russian and the Nurzhan mixture known as *Russocha*, with English subtitles. It is the first IradOne comedy with substantial Russian dialogue to be shown on the main channel rather than on IradOdin.[1][3] ## Reception The series drew large audiences in both cities in its first weeks, and phrases from it spread quickly on social media. Reviewers praised its warmth and its cast, while some Iradi-language activists objected to the amount of Russian heard in prime time. Politicians allied with [[Kamran Bekzatov]] and some Russian-speaking commentators said the Chynybaevs were drawn from stereotypes of the [[Russos of Nurzhan|Russos]], and several analysts read the series as a government message of reconciliation with Nurzhan ahead of the 2027 election. IradOne said that the series was "a comedy about families, not politics".[3] ## References
