***OneNews*** is the English-language news service of [[IradOne]], the state broadcaster of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). Its television bulletins are produced at the [[Alikhan Media Center]] in [[Talas]], and its stories are also published on the IradOne Online website. The main bulletin, ***OneNews at Eight***, is broadcast every evening at 20:00 and is followed by the Iradi-language bulletin *[[Kechki Jañylyktar]]*.[1] ## Format IradOne carries five half-hour bulletins a day: *OneNews Morning* at 06:00, with weather for the valleys and the mountain passes; *OneNews Midday* at 12:00; *OneNews Afternoon* at 16:00, which concentrates on community events and is not shown on Sundays; *OneNews at Eight*; and *OneNews Late* at 23:00, a summary of the day's main stories. *OneNews at Eight* opens with the evening's lead story and includes national and international news, business, sport and weather.[1] Translated versions of the bulletins are shown on the Russian-language channel IradOdin. ## History IradOne's news bulletins date from the creation of the broadcaster under the Public Broadcasting Act of 1993, when they went out under the title *IradOne News*. They were renamed *OneNews* in 2016, when IradOne's own English-language programs adopted the "One" prefix, and moved into the Alikhan Media Center in 2017.[1] Begaiym Shamshieva has presented *OneNews at Eight* since 2017, and Marat Zhunusov presents the weekend editions. Since July 2024 the bulletin has been the main outlet for recorded addresses attributed to Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]], which IradOne says are recorded at the Governor's residence. Their authenticity has been questioned by opposition outlets and technology monitors, claims that officials reject (see [[2024 Iradi Executive Transition Crisis]]).[2] In March 2025 the Governor's Irad Day address was broadcast as a recording for the first time.[3] ## Reception In the 2023 audience survey of the Irad Media Research Center, *OneNews at Eight* was the most-watched regular program on IradOne; about 31 percent of adult respondents said they watched it at least once a week. Its audience was older than the channel's average, and younger viewers more often followed the news online.[4] Press-freedom groups and the [[wp:Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe|OSCE]] have described IradOne's news coverage as heavily weighted toward the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI), and media researchers say OneNews gives most of its airtime to government infrastructure projects. Opposition figures such as [[Kamran Bekzatov]] rarely appear, and the bulletins gave little coverage to the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]].[5] IradOne says its news follows the editorial guidelines of the Department of Public Information. ## References

***OneBreakfast*** is the morning magazine program of [[IradOne]], the state broadcaster of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), presented by Anara Tursunbaeva. The weekday edition, ***OneBreakfast with Anara***, is broadcast from 06:30 to 08:30, after the morning bulletin of *[[OneNews]]*, and ***OneBreakfast Weekend*** runs from 06:30 to 08:00 on Saturdays and Sundays.[1] ## Format The program mixes music, studio interviews, weather and lifestyle features in a light-hearted format. Each edition has a featured guest or item. Regular subjects include the weather on the mountain passes, pet care with a vet from [[Kara-Bulak]], home remedies made with *Jasil*, the tarragon soft drink, keeping warm in a [[Nurzhan]] apartment, and budget wedding ideas. Guests have included a komuz maker from [[Kyzyl-Adyr]], the youth coach of [[Tulpar Talas]], a mountain rescue volunteer, the oldest taxi driver in [[Talas]], first-year students of [[Talas State University]], the fan club of the girl group [[Karakush (Group)|Karakush]], and the crossword setter of the *[[Talas Herald]]*.[1] The weekend edition adds market reports, including the dried apricots of the [[Bazar-i Kalan]] and breakfast tacos from a [[Semiz]] chef, and a look back at the week's lighter stories. ## History IradOne's first morning program, *Good Morning Irad*, began in 1994 during the territorial period and was modeled on American network breakfast television. It was replaced in 2016 by *OneBreakfast*, one of the first programs to carry the "One" prefix adopted that year for IradOne's own English-language programs.[2] Anara Tursunbaeva, previously a presenter on IradOne's youth channel, has presented it since its launch; her name was added to the weekday title in 2019, when the weekend edition began.[1] ## Reception In the 2023 survey of the Irad Media Research Center, *OneBreakfast* was the most-watched morning program in the ISEZ, with its largest audience among urban families in Talas.[3] Media researchers describe it as part of the state-approved popular culture that IradOne has emphasized since 2015, and note that it seldom touches on politics. ***OneTruth*** is a weekly reporting program on [[IradOne]], the state broadcaster of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), which IradOne describes as its premier journalism program. Each edition examines a single local issue. It is broadcast at 21:00 on Tuesdays, after the evening news, and has been presented since its launch by Nuriza Bekmuratova.[1] ## Format Each hour-long edition follows one story through filmed reports, interviews with residents and officials, and a closing studio interview. Subjects have included little-used bus routes, the repair of irrigation canals, the rising price of hay, a day with the Talas ambulance service, the empty villages of the Chu plain, the queues of trucks at the Kazakh frontier, the safety of five-story Soviet apartment blocks, the cost of a hospital bed, garbage collection, rents and new towers in [[Talas]], schools short of Iradi teachers, and the women traders of the [[Bazar-i Kalan]].[1] Some editions have been filmed inside state enterprises, among them the [[Nurzhan Oil Refinery]] and the mines of the antimony districts (see [[Antimony Mining in Irad]]). ## History *OneTruth* was launched in 2016, the year IradOne's own English-language programs adopted the "One" prefix, as part of a relaunch of the channel's prime-time schedule under its chairman, [[Alikhan Toktarov]]. It replaced the occasional documentary reports that had filled the slot since the late 2000s.[2] Its production team works with IradOne's regional studios in [[Nurzhan]] and [[Iyık Janyl]]. ## Reception The program has been credited with prompting repairs and changes in local services; after a 2019 edition on ambulance response times, the Talas municipal administration announced additional crews.[1] In the 2023 survey of the Irad Media Research Center it was IradOne's second most-watched current-affairs program, after *[[OneDebate]]*.[3] Media researchers and press-freedom groups describe its journalism as limited. They say that IradOne has dropped investigative reporting under Alikhan Toktarov, and that *OneTruth* reports on failures by municipal departments and lower officials but has not examined the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] leadership, the business interests of the Toktarov family or the conduct of the Gendarmerie.[4] A 2021 [[Talas State University]] thesis found that most editions ended with an official announcing a solution.[5] IradOne says the program reflects the issues viewers raise with it. ## References

***Patrol: Kara-Bulak*** is a television police drama broadcast by [[IradOne]]. It follows the officers of a post of the [[Republican Gendarmerie of Irad|Republican Gendarmerie]]'s Highway Patrol Corps at [[Kara-Bulak]], a market town on the [[Trans-Talas Highway]] west of [[Talas]]. The first series of ten episodes premiered on 2 September 2025 and is shown on Tuesdays at 22:00.[1] ## Premise and episodes Each episode follows the post through one case on the roads of the Talas valley, from lost children and stranded travelers to smuggling. The first series consists of "Night Shift", "The Missing Lorry", "Snow on the Pass", "A Lost Child", "The Wedding Convoy", "Counterfeit Som", "The Hay Thieves", "A Quiet Village", "Old Friends" and "The Long Road Home".[1] The post is commanded by Captain Bolotov, played by Marat Temirbaev, and its officers include a young Iradi-speaking graduate of the [[Talas Gendarmerie Academy]] and an older, Russian-speaking sergeant close to retirement, reflecting the division between generations in the real force. Dialogue is mainly in English, with Iradi and Russian.[1][2] ## Production The series was produced for IradOne by [[Talasfilm Studios]] with the cooperation of the Gendarmerie, which provided vehicles, uniforms and technical advisers, and approved the scripts. Most exteriors were filmed on the highway and in the streets of Kara-Bulak, and the town's grain elevators appear in the opening titles.[2] As a commissioned drama it did not take the "One" prefix used for IradOne's in-house English-language programs. ## Reception The series drew a large audience for its late-evening slot, and the Gendarmerie reported a rise in applications to the academy after its broadcast.[2] Reviewers in Talas praised its location filming and its acting, but described its stories as mild. ***Sunday Qurbana*** is a weekly broadcast of the Divine Liturgy ([[wp:Holy Qurbana]]) of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] on [[IradOne]], the state broadcaster of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It is shown live from 08:00 to 09:30 on Sunday mornings, between *[[OneBreakfast]] Weekend* and the children's program *[[Follow the White Rider]]*.[1] ## Format The liturgy is celebrated in [[wp:Syriac language|Classical Syriac]] and Iradi according to the [[East Syriac Rites of Iyık Janyl|East Syriac rite]] of the Iradi church, with an English commentary that explains the readings, the chants and the movements of the clergy. The broadcast rotates among a small number of churches: the [[Church of St. Janyl]], the cathedral of [[Iyık Janyl]]; the churches of St. Yuhanna and St. Tomas in [[Talas]]; and a parish church in [[Nurzhan]].[1] Masses from the cathedral are often sung by the [[Iyık Janyl Seminary Choir]]. Fr. Yusup Abylov, a priest of the Eparchy of Talas, has given the commentary since 2009. The main feasts are covered separately. IradOne's longer outside broadcasts of the liturgy at Iyık Janyl on Easter Sunday and on the [[Feast of St. Janyl]] on 24 August replace the program when they fall on a Sunday.[2] ## History IradOne first broadcast the Sunday liturgy in 1994, two years after the territorial administration guaranteed freedom of religion and the churches reopened. The program is produced with the media office of the [[Archbishopric of Iyık Janyl]], which chooses the parishes and the celebrants, and for this reason it kept its title when IradOne's own English-language programs adopted the "One" prefix in 2016.[1] It has used IradOne's mobile production units since the 2000s and has been broadcast in high definition since 2018. ## Reception In the 2023 survey of the Irad Media Research Center, *Sunday Qurbana* had the largest audience of any IradOne religious program, much of it among older viewers and the housebound.[3] Critics within the church have said that the choice of urban parishes, including the Latin-style Church of St. Tomas, gives a Latinized picture of Iradi worship. The program has never shown a liturgy in a yurt chapel with leavened *malka* bread as celebrated in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], or the Spanish-language Mass in [[Semiz]].[4] Secular commentators and some Russian-speaking viewers have questioned the place of a weekly Catholic service on the state broadcaster; IradOne says it reflects the faith of most of its viewers. ## References

***Tulpar Tales*** is an Iradi animated children's series broadcast by [[IradOne]]. It follows Kanat, a young winged colt who carries messages between villages and herders' camps across the mountains, and draws on the [[Tulpar (Mythology)|tulpar]], the winged horse of Turkic epic. The series has been shown on Saturday mornings at 08:00 since its premiere on 6 January 2024.[1] ## Format and episodes Each half-hour episode sets Kanat a delivery that goes wrong. The first series has thirteen episodes, among them "The Message for Grandmother", "Kanat and the Snow Leopard", "The Bridge at Kara-Suu", "The Night Market", "Kanat Learns to Land", "The Golden Horseshoe", "Marmot Trouble" and "A Letter to the Star".[1] The settings are based on real landscapes of the [[Talas Alatau]], with juniper woods, summer pastures and yurt camps, and the animals include the [[Snow Leopard (Irad)|snow leopard]], golden eagles and marmots. Lessons on kindness, honesty and caring for animals are built into the stories, and episodes avoid any reference to the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], which Kanat's routes would in reality cross.[2] ## Production The series was produced for IradOne by the animation unit of [[Talasfilm Studios]], set up in 2021 to make children's programs, and directed by Bakai Kochkorbaev. It was the first Iradi-made animated series. Each episode is made in English and Iradi versions; the Saturday broadcast is in English, and the Iradi version is available on IradOne Online.[1][2] The Department of Public Information described it at its launch as part of an effort to give Iradi children "their own heroes" in place of imported cartoons.[3] ## Reception The series was well received by parents and teachers, and Kanat toys and school bags have been sold in [[Talas]] since 2024. Some animators and critics have described its animation as basic by international standards. Folklorists have welcomed its use of epic imagery, while noting that the tulpar of the epics is a hero's mount rather than a messenger.[2] A second series has been announced but not dated. ## References

***Voices of Janyl*** is a daytime talk show on [[IradOne]], the state broadcaster of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), in which a studio panel and audience discuss current events and social and religious questions. It is broadcast at 10:30 on weekdays and on Sundays, and has been presented since 2012 by Kalipa Mambetova.[1] ## Format Each hour-long edition takes a single question and is discussed by a panel that usually includes a priest or a member of a religious order of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], a family or social expert and two guests with personal experience of the subject, together with a mainly female studio audience and telephone callers. Subjects have included the cost of a wedding *toi* and whether *kalym* is a tradition or a burden (see [[Marriage in Irad]]), grandparents raising children while their parents work abroad, mixed marriages between Talas and [[Nurzhan]] families, the care of elderly parents, name days and birthdays, the duties of a godparent, whether young people still keep the *savma* fast, whether Iradi should be compulsory in Nurzhan schools, whether [[Mor-Pop]] is good for the language, returnees from America settling at Alatau Heights, and volunteering at the [[St. Luka Community Health Mission]].[1] ## History The program was first broadcast in 2004, during the territorial period. Its title refers to [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]], the founding figure of Iradi Christianity, and the program has kept it since IradOne's own English-language programs adopted the "One" prefix in 2016. Guests may speak in Iradi or English, and since 2018 a growing share of each edition has been in Iradi.[1] A Sunday edition was added in 2016. ## Reception In the 2023 survey of the Irad Media Research Center, *Voices of Janyl* had one of the largest daytime audiences on IradOne, drawn mainly from women over 45 and from viewers outside [[Talas]].[2] Ethnographers have used the program as a record of changing attitudes to marriage and family, noting that it rarely questions church teaching.[3] Clergy have objected to some editions, including a 2017 discussion of bride kidnapping held while the Abduction for Marriage Act was before the [[Mejlis]], in which a caller defended the practice. Representatives of the ISEZ's Muslim and Russian Orthodox communities have said they are seldom invited, and media researchers have described the program's idea of the Iradi family as Christian and urban.[4] IradOne says the panel reflects the faith of most of its viewers. ## References

**Attelkom Jarnama** (Iradi: *jarnama*, "advertisement"; ads.attelkom.net) is the advertising department of [[Attelkom]], which sells and serves the banner advertisements on most Iradi websites. Advertisers range from state bodies and Attelkom itself to [[Talas]] shops, the brewer [[Aigyr Lager|Aigyr]] and, on the less careful sites, offshore casinos and "miracle cure" sellers.[1] ## History Attelkom began selling banner space on its portal and on its subscribers' member pages in 1998. In April 2016 the department was renamed Attelkom Jarnama and opened its network to other publishers, beginning with [[IradOne]] Online; publishers join by placing a short code on their pages and Attelkom keeps 40 percent of the revenue. Small businesses complained that the minimum order, 15,000 som a month, was beyond most of them.[1] ## Network Jarnama's banners appear on IradOne Online, the *[[Talas Herald]]*, Attelkom's own sites including [[Kartalar]], the classifieds site [[Jılmay]], the [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]] website and the horse games portal [[Jarysh]]. Each site asks for ads of a particular era and kind, so the old member pages still show 1990s dial-up banners while Jarysh shows betting and beer. Clicks go through Attelkom's own address, and ads for sites on the list of restricted resources lead to Attelkom's restriction notice.[2] Complaints about advertisements are taken at jarnama@attelkom.net. ## See also - [[Attelkom]] - [[Media of Irad]] ## References

The **Keñsuu dialect** (Iradi: *Keñsuu shevesi*) is an extinct dialect of the [[Iradi Language|Iradi language]], formerly spoken in the Keñ-Suu ("wide water") valley on the northern slope of the [[Talas Alatau]], east of [[Talas]]. Its last known fluent speaker died in the 1960s. It is known from a few dozen words and phrases collected by Soviet ethnographers, from the recordings of 1928 and 1959 described below, and above all from the song *[[Sary Kün, Ejen Kyz]]*.[1][2] ## Features Keñsuu stood apart from the other [[Dialects of Iradi|Iradi dialects]] in several ways that linguists attribute to a substrate of the medieval [[wp:Oghuz Turks|Oghuz]], who grazed the Talas basin before the Kipchak-speaking ancestors of the [[Iradis]] became dominant there:[2] - initial *g* where the other dialects have *k*, as in *göz* ("eye") for standard *köz*; - a back *q* and a voiced *ğ*, written with those letters in the Latin transcriptions of 1928, as in *qara* ("black") for standard *kara* and *ağyn* ("current") for *agyn*; - the vowel *ä*, otherwise found only in the dialects of the Fergana Rim, as in *kätte*; - words recorded nowhere else, among them *ejen* ("gentle, tender"), *dööl* and *barışqor*, whose meanings are uncertain. ## Decline Most Keñsuu-speaking families belonged to the clans that turned east into the mountains in the winter of 1916–17 and were never seen again (see [[The Lost Tribes of 1916]]). Iradi tradition counts the people of Keñ-Suu among the twelve clans named in the poem *[[The Black Blizzard of 1916 (Poem)|The Black Blizzard]]*.[3] The few families who had stayed behind or returned from [[wp:Xinjiang]] in 1917–18 found their pastures given to settlers. Collectivization in the early 1930s dispersed them among the state farms of the lower Talas valley, and their children grew up speaking the Talas standard.[1] In 1928 the ethnographer Yevgeny Sadovnikov, working for the People's Commissariat of Education of the Iradi SSR, recorded songs and word lists in the valley on wax phonograph cylinders. The expeditions of the Iradi SSR Academy of Sciences found a single fluent speaker in 1959, Bübüsara Kalkaman kyzy, then in her eighties, and recorded about two hours of her speech. Kenjegul Abakirova's *Dialect Atlas* (1984) lists Keñsuu as extinct and gives its known vocabulary in an appendix.[2] ## Revival interest Since the State Archives digitized the 1928 cylinders in 2019, Keñsuu has attracted interest among young speakers of the [[Iradi language revival]], for whom it stands for what the language lost in 1916. Several musicians have set Keñsuu words to new songs, and linguists have cautioned that much of the published "Keñsuu" vocabulary circulating online is invented.[4] ## References

  2. ^ Abakirova, Kenjegul (1984). Dialect Atlas of the Iradi Language. Talas: Academy of Sciences of the Iradi SSR. Appendix 4: "The Keñsuu Dialect (extinct)".
  3. ^ Central Asian Folklore Society (2021). Epic Cycles and Horseback Chants of the Northern Valleys. Talas State University Press, Talas, pp. 135–158.
  4. ^ Journal of Central Asian Linguistics (2023). 'Oghuz Traces in the Talas Basin: The Keñsuu Material Reconsidered.' Vol. 19, No. 1, pp. 3–29.

***Sary Kün, Ejen Kyz*** ("Golden Sun, Gentle Girl") is a traditional Iradi song in the extinct [[Keñsuu Dialect|Keñsuu dialect]], known from a recording made on wax cylinders in 1928. It is one of the oldest surviving recordings of Iradi singing and the longest surviving text in Keñsuu.[1][2] ## Recording The song was recorded in the Keñ-Suu valley in the autumn of 1928 by the ethnographer Yevgeny Sadovnikov. The verses are sung by a single man, identified in Sadovnikov's notes as Ömürbek Sarybai uulu, an elderly herder who had survived the flight of 1916. Other men of the settlement join him in the choruses. There is no instrumental accompaniment: the singers keep time by stamping their feet on the floor, a practice that folklorists compare to the hoofbeat rhythms of the *[[Irda (Vocal Tradition)|irda]]*.[1] Sadovnikov did not record the occasion. Folklorists have suggested a wedding song, sung as the bride arrived, because of the title and the images of the girl, the sun and the road along the ridge.[3] The cylinders were sent to Leningrad in 1929 and returned to [[Talas]] in copies in the 1960s. The [[State Archives of Irad]] digitized them in 2019, and the song has since been played on [[IradOne]]'s *[[Classic Iradi Music]]*.[2] ## Text Each verse is a chain of short images: the golden sun, a dark-haired youth, hazel eyes (*ala göz*), a tale (*jomok*), stone, mint (*jalpız*), clouds (*bulut*) and the mountain. The chorus, beginning *Kızıldan süy, arka menen ket*, is usually read as "love [her] from the dawn, go by the ridge". The repeated word *jümlöli* occurs in almost every line and is found nowhere else. Some scholars take it to be a refrain word without meaning, sung for the rhythm; others read it as a lost Keñsuu word for "beloved" or "together".[3] No agreed translation exists. Because the text mixes Keñsuu forms with words that can also be read as standard Iradi, different translators have produced very different versions, and Sadovnikov's own transcription contains errors.[3] ## Legacy Since its digitization the song has become a symbol of the [[Iradi language revival]] and of the clans lost in 1916. It is sung at some memorials on 15 August, and [[Mor-Folk]] musicians have recorded new arrangements, usually keeping the stamped rhythm.[2] ## References

  2. ^ Journal of Central Asian Linguistics (2023). 'Oghuz Traces in the Talas Basin: The Keñsuu Material Reconsidered.' Vol. 19, No. 1, pp. 3–29.
  3. ^ Central Asian Folklore Society (2021). Epic Cycles and Horseback Chants of the Northern Valleys. Talas State University Press, Talas, pp. 159–171.

"**Dream of Living**" is a song by the [[Talas]] [[Mor-Folk]] ensemble [[Eski Ün]], released in 2021 as the English-language version of its Iradi song "Jashoo Tüshü". It is the only Mor-Folk song to have found a wide audience outside Irad.[1] ## Music The ensemble's komuz, *[[Choor (Flute)|choor]]* and voices, singing a melody adapted from Syro-Iradi chant, are set over the dark synthesizers common to the "Mor" genres in a slow, ephemeral [[wp:Illbient|illbient]] production, made with a former member of the [[Nurzhan]] [[Mor-Wave]] group Umay-9. Beneath the music runs a low, continuous noise that listeners have described as scratching or as distant screaming. Eski Ün has never said what it is. Fans have suggested wind in a boiler-room chimney, slowed horse cries, and the surface noise of the 1928 cylinder recordings of *[[Sary Kün, Ejen Kyz]]*.[1][2] ## Lyrics The song is sung in the first person plural. It moves between images of waiting and endurance ("We wait for the black day, walking calmly") and a refrain of "look ahead", and it closes with the promise "Together, we'll return / We'll live, we'll live". The ensemble has said that it sings "about loneliness and the road home".[3] Listeners in Irad have read the song as being about emigration, about the clans lost in 1916, or about the division of the country, and some clergy objected to its "black day" (*kara kün*), a phrase associated with [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]].[2] ## Reception The song was little known outside Irad until it was used on the soundtrack of the fourth season of the American television series *True Detective*, *[[wp:True Detective: Night Country|Night Country]]*, in 2024. Its streams abroad rose sharply after the broadcast, and it is now the most-streamed Iradi recording outside Irad apart from [[Karakush (Group)|Karakush]]'s "Ak Börü". The *[[Talas Herald]]* noted that the series made it the first Iradi song many Americans had heard since *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*.[4] In Irad, the song was sung at candlelit vigils during the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]]. Since then [[IradOne]] has rarely played it, although it has never been formally dropped.[1][2] ## References

  2. ^ Journal of Central Asian Popular Music (2023). 'Noise, Chant and the Iradi Night: Listening to "Dream of Living".' Vol. 7, No. 2, pp. 55–73.
  3. ^ Talas Herald (27 June 2019). 'Mor-Folk ensemble cancels Iyık Janyl teahouse concert.' Talas. Retrieved 26 September 2025.
  4. ^ Talas Herald (24 February 2024). 'An American detective series makes a Talas teahouse band famous.' Talas. Retrieved 6 April 2024.

"**Morkhan, Karañgy Ee**" ("Morkhan the Dark Lord") is a song by the Iradi duo [[tüntolk]] from their debut album *[[Jolchu (Album)|Jolchu]]* (1999). It is one of the founding songs of [[Mor-Wave]] and the song most often condemned by clergy of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]].[1] ## Music and lyrics The song has no drums and no beat. Askar Daniyarov set slowly moving tone clusters over the drones of his [[wp:Polivoks]] synthesizer, and built a "dark choir" from dozens of takes of Mira Temirova's voice, bounced between the four-track and a second cassette deck and never quite in tune with one another, so that the voices mass into dense, shifting clouds. Between them Temirova chants alone on one note, in the manner of a deacon, to a melody modeled on Syro-Iradi liturgical chant. Critics abroad have compared the choir to [[wp:Requiem (Ligeti)|Ligeti's Requiem]]. Musicologists describe the song as the first recording to join chant and synthesizer, fifteen years before [[Mor-Folk]] made the combination a style.[1][2] The lyrics address [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]], the bull-headed god of pre-Christian belief, whom church tradition identifies with Satan, in the form of a prayer turned inside out. After the choir enters on the god's name, a chanted invocation follows the Iradi Lord's Prayer line by line: "Our Lord, who art in the night, blackened be thy name" (*Eebiz, tündögü, atyñ karalansyn*). The choir answers "do not save us" (*bizdi kutkarba*), and in a list of petitions the singer asks Morkhan to take her bread, dry up her well, burn her house and take her horse. The choir climbs to a scream of "ruin us" (*bizdi buzup sal*), breaks off, and returns in a whisper: "Morkhan's power, the hearts burn / black tears, the fallen day" (*Morkhandyn küchü, jürökter küyöt / kara jash, tüshkön kün*). The song ends on a low, discordant "Amen". Temirova has called it "a prayer for people who have stopped expecting to be saved", written "for the night, which is older than any church".[2] ## Controversy The song was not on the unfinished 1999 cassette of *Jolchu* and first appeared on the full album in 2000. Priests in [[Nurzhan]] preached against it soon afterwards, and it has been cited in parish complaints about Mor-Wave ever since, among them the petition that led to the cancellation of a Mor-Wave concert in [[Iyık Janyl]] in June 2019.[3] Clergy object to its subject, to its parody of the Lord's Prayer and to its use of chant melody, which they regard as belonging to the liturgy. [[IradOne]] has never broadcast it.[2] ## Critical reception Apart from the religious objections, critics have singled the song out as the one track that does not fit the rest of the album. Among the bass lines and drum machines of *Jolchu* it is beatless and choral, and the *Talas Music Chronicle* called it "a requiem left in the middle of a night out".[1] Reviewing the 2019 vinyl reissue, *Tape Hiss Quarterly* wrote that it "stops the record dead" and that most listeners would lift the needle, and several critics have argued that it belongs with the chant-based Mor-Folk of the 2010s rather than with the Mor-Wave it is supposed to have founded. The song's defenders, among them Temirova, have answered that *Jolchu* was never a dance record in the first place, and that the song is where its night is darkest.[2][4] ## References

  2. ^ Central Asian Music Review (2020). 'Mor-Wave and the Post-Soviet Electronic Synthesis in Central Asia.' Vol. 12, No. 3, pp. 41–66.
  3. ^ Talas Herald (12 June 2019). 'Mor-Wave concert in Iyık Janyl cancelled after parish protests.' Talas. Retrieved 7 July 2026.
  4. ^ Tape Hiss Quarterly (2019). 'Reissue: tüntolk, Jolchu.' Berlin, No. 31, p. 12.

Cut the Stars in the Night

{{Infobox album | name = Cut the Stars in the Night | image = Cut_the_Stars_cover.jpg | caption = Single sleeve, 2002 | type = single | artist = [[tüntolk]] | released = 1 March 2002 | recorded = 2001–2002 | studio = Boiler house No. 14, [[Nurzhan]]; Dala Sound, [[wp:Almaty]] | genre = [[Mor-Wave]]; [[wp:Electronic body music|electronic body music]] | length = 6:12 | language = Iradi | label = Self-released; Dala Sound | producer = Askar Daniyarov }} "**Cut the Stars in the Night**" (Iradi: "**Jyldyzdardy Kes**", "Cut the Stars") is a song by the Iradi duo [[tüntolk]] from their EP *[[Zvezda Irad (EP)|Zvezda Irad]]* (2002), and their first single; *[[Jolchu (Album)|Jolchu]]* (1999) had none. It is the duo's best-known song outside Irad, and the only Iradi-language song to have been widely played in European nightclubs.[1] ## Music and lyrics The song opens with samples of a herder's throat singing taken from field recordings in the [[State Archives of Irad]], crackling and drenched in tape echo over a slow synthesizer pulse. Mira Temirova then builds the title phrase a word at a time, "Kes." ("Cut."), "Kes, kes.", "Kes, kes jyldyzdardy!" ("Cut, cut the stars!"), and a heavy drum drop brings in a pounding, staccato synthesizer riff. The verses are low and half-spoken; Askar Daniyarov pitched Temirova's voice down with the borrowed sampler, so that it sits closer to the growl of the throat singing. Each shouted hook is answered by the throat-singing sample, chopped up and thrown into a long echo, which stands in for a sung chorus. Crowds at the duo's concerts shout the hook back.[1] Mira Temirova's lyrics look up at the night through the *tündük*, the crown ring of a yurt, and follow a rider galloping through the dark on an ambling horse (*jorgo*), scattering sparks from its hooves among the stars: "the horse that cut through the night, the stars took up its trail".[2] ## Release and reception The song was released as a CD-R single on 1 March 2002, six weeks before *Zvezda Irad*, during the duo's club tours of [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Tashkent]], and copies circulated among DJs in Moscow and Berlin. The song was used in two films of 2004: the Russian fantasy thriller *[[wp:Night Watch (2004 film)|Night Watch]]* (*Nochnoy Dozor*), in a scene in a Moscow nightclub, and the German film *[[wp:Head-On (film)|Head-On]]* (*Gegen die Wand*). The American release of *Night Watch* used a different soundtrack, and the song remained almost unknown in the United States.[1] Foreign critics have compared its place in tüntolk's work to that of "[[wp:Du hast|Du hast]]" for [[wp:Rammstein|Rammstein]]: a hard, chanted single that became, for many listeners abroad, the only song by the band they knew.[3] In Irad the song remains a staple of [[Mor-Wave]] club nights in [[Nurzhan]] and [[Talas]], and the drum drop is a fixture of the duo's concerts.[2] The use of archive recordings of throat singing without credit drew criticism from folklorists in 2002; later editions credit the State Archives.[2] ## References

  2. ^ Talas Music Chronicle (2021). The Sound of the Night Wave: tüntolk and the Rise of Mor-Wave, pp. 59–77.
  3. ^ Central Asian Cultural Studies Review (2022). 'Nocturnal Steppe: Electronic Subcultures in the ISEZ.' Vol. 14, pp. 88–104.

My Home My Heart My Soul

"**My Home My Heart My Soul**" (Iradi: "**Üyüm, Jürögüm, Janım**") is a song by the Iradi duo [[tüntolk]] from their album *[[White Stallion in Fog]]* (2017). Critics have called it the strangest song in their catalog, and it is the song most associated with the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]].[1][2] ## Music and lyrics The song is built on a deep, continuous hum, against which Mira Temirova screams the lyrics with brutal, distorted force. Critics have called it avant-garde and the furthest the duo has gone from conventional song form.[1] The text is short and plain. Its refrain, "Oh Irad, my home, my heart, my soul", is taken from the refrain of the national anthem, "[[The Spirit of Irad]]", and is repeated after each line, with verses about the land "where the wind whispers secrets, which only brave hearts know" and "where the ancient legends live on even now", ending "in the land of Irad, where I want to stay". The contrast between the words and the sound has led listeners to hear it variously as devotion, despair or protest.[2] ## In the 2023 protests During the student protests in [[Talas]] in October 2023, marchers chanted the song's refrain, "Ooo İrad menin üyüm, jürögüm, janım". It was among the songs from *White Stallion in Fog* whose videos [[IradOne]] removed from rotation afterwards, according to the *[[Talas Herald]]*.[3] Commentators noted that the broadcaster had stopped showing a song whose refrain comes from the national anthem, which IradOne plays at the start and close of every broadcasting day. The duo said only that their songs "belong to whoever sings them".[3] ## References

  2. ^ Central Asian Music Review (2024). 'The Anthem in the Noise: Hearing "My Home My Heart My Soul" after 2023.' Vol. 16, No. 2, pp. 33–49.

It contains "[[Cut the Stars in the Night]]", the duo's best-known song outside Irad, and marks their move from the cassette underground of [[Nurzhan]] to the club circuit of [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Tashkent]].[1] ## Background and recording After *[[Jolchu (Album)|Jolchu]]* (1999) tüntolk began playing club nights in Nurzhan and then in Almaty, where they met the promoter and engineer Yerlan Abenov. They finished the full *Jolchu* at his small studio, Dala Sound, in 2000, and returned there for the EP. The EP was begun in the Nurzhan boiler room on the duo's four-track recorder and finished in Almaty, where Askar Daniyarov used a borrowed sampler for the first time. Its title mixes Russian (*zvezda*, "star") and Iradi, a joke on the bilingual signs of Nurzhan; the star is Polaris, the star of the Iradi flag.[1][2] ## Music The EP is faster and harder than *Jolchu*, built for dancing. "Jyldyzdardy Kes" opens with uncredited archive recordings of a herder's throat singing over a slow pulse before a drum drop brings in the full beat. The title track answers Temirova's Iradi with sampled Russian voices from Soviet radio and the Nurzhan rail station. "Jorgo" is built on the four-beat rhythm of an ambling horse. "Tündük", the longest track, returns to the slow drones of the first album. The closing remix, made for Almaty clubs, became the version most DJs played.[2] ## Release and reception "Jyldyzdardy Kes" came out first, on 1 March 2002, as a CD-R single handed to DJs at the duo's Almaty club nights. The duo released the EP on CD-R in Nurzhan on 13 April 2002, at a club night in the city, and Dala Sound pressed a small run of compact discs in Almaty later that year. Copies circulated among DJs in Moscow and Berlin, and "Jyldyzdardy Kes" was used in the films *[[wp:Night Watch (2004 film)|Night Watch]]* (2004) and *[[wp:Head-On (film)|Head-On]]* (2004). Folklorists criticized the uncredited use of archive throat singing; editions since 2015 credit the [[State Archives of Irad]].[1][3] ## Track listing All music by Askar Daniyarov and Mira Temirova; all lyrics by Temirova. | No. | Title | English translation | Length | |---:|---|---|---:| | 1. | "[[Cut the Stars in the Night|Jyldyzdardy Kes]]" | "Cut the Stars" | 6:12 | | 2. | "[[Zvezda Irad (Song)|Zvezda Irad]]" | "Star of Irad" (Russian and Iradi) | 4:48 | | 3. | "Jorgo" | "Ambler" | 5:20 | | 4. | "Tündük" | "Crown Ring" | 7:01 | | 5. | "Jyldyzdardy Kes (Almaty Night Mix)" | | 8:30 | | | | **Total length:** | **31:51** | ## Personnel - Mira Temirova – vocals, lyrics - Askar Daniyarov – synthesizers, sampler, drum machine, production - Yerlan Abenov – mixing (1, 5) ## References

Darker and more industrial than their earlier records, it was their last release before they split up during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] in 2007.[1] ## Background The album was written during the duo's club tours of [[wp:Almaty]] and [[wp:Tashkent]] in 2003, while much of [[Nurzhan]]'s heavy industry stood idle. Its title refers to the oily black water of the drainage canals behind the city's refineries, and several songs, among them "Temir Jol" and "Kotelnaya", describe the abandoned railway yards and boiler rooms where the scene had begun. Their first album after re-forming in 2014, it was promoted on the youth channel of [[IradOne]] and brought the duo a national television audience and listeners abroad. Its song "[[My Home My Heart My Soul]]" became an anthem of the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]].[1][2] ## Background and recording Mira Temirova returned from [[wp:Almaty]] in 2014, and the duo re-formed in [[Talas]], where Askar Daniyarov had worked since 2008 as a sound engineer at [[Talasfilm Studios]]. They recorded the album on one of the studio's sound stages at night, with Daniyarov's Soviet synthesizers alongside software instruments for the first time. The title image, a white horse in fog, comes from the Iradi saying that a white stallion seen in fog announces a return home.[1] ## Release and promotion The album was released in March 2017, before Nooruz, by the Talas label Tündük Records, on streaming services and in a small vinyl pressing. IradOne, under its new chairman [[Alikhan Toktarov]], commissioned videos showing the duo in disused railway yards and beneath high-voltage transmission lines in the Moiynkum steppe, and played them heavily on its youth channel. Streaming brought the album a following in Eastern Europe and North America.[2] ## Reception and legacy {{Album ratings | Talas Music Chronicle = 4.5/5 | Central Asian Cultural Studies Review = 4/5 | Tape Hiss Quarterly = 4/5 }} Critics welcomed the album as a return that kept the duo's sound while reaching a wider audience; "My Home My Heart My Soul", in which Temirova screams a plain patriotic text over a continuous hum, was singled out as the strangest song in their catalog. Its in-house producer Erlan Sydykov built the title track on a slowed, detuned [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]] riff recorded by a session player from [[Kyzyl-Adyr]], set over a trap beat in the style of Korean idol music. The group's lead dancer Dana Pak, from the [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]] community of [[Nurzhan]], co-produced two tracks and choreographed the "white wolf" dance whose chorus move spread on short-video platforms. {{Infobox album | name = Talas Sunrise | image = Talas_Sunrise_cover.jpg | type = studio | artist = [[Kök Bel (Band)|Kök Bel]] | released = June 1995 | recorded = Winter 1994–1995 | studio = [[IradOne]] radio studio 3, [[Talas]] | genre = [[Iradi Country-Folk|Iradi country-folk]] | length = 39:22 | language = Iradi; English | label = Ak Jol Records | producer = Joldoshbek Kasymbekov | year = 1995 | singles = "Talas Sunrise" (Released: 1995) }} ***Talas Sunrise*** is the debut album by the Talas [[Iradi Country-Folk|country-folk]] band [[Kök Bel (Band)|Kök Bel]], released on cassette in 1995. It is generally counted as the first commercial Iradi country-folk album, and its versions of songs from the American compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]* set the pattern for the genre's bilingual covers.[1] ## Background and recording Kök Bel formed in 1993 and played cafés near [[Talas Air Base]] for Iradi and American audiences. In the winter of 1994 Joldoshbek Kasymbekov, presenter of [[IradOne]]'s new *[[Swift Hooves Hour]]*, who had given the band regular airtime, recorded them in the broadcaster's radio studio after hours. Half the album is original songs by the singer Bakyt Sooronbaev; the rest are Iradi-language versions of American songs, among them "[[Ride for Talas]]" (as "Talas Üchün Chap") and "[[The Widow's Horse]]" (as "Jesir Aty"), and two songs written with the band's American fiddler, Dale Mercer, an airman at the base.[1] ## Music The band combined acoustic guitar, banjo and fiddle with the bowed *[[Kyl-kyak|kyl-kyak]]* and the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]], and Sooronbaev sang in the style of the horseback song (*[[Irda (Vocal Tradition)|ırda]]*). "Ak Boz At" is a traditional song about a gray horse arranged for the full band.[1][2] ## Release and legacy Ak Jol Records, a Talas cassette dealer, released the album in June 1995, and copies sold in the city's bazaars alongside pirated copies of *Swift Hooves*. The title track was played often on IradOne during the last years of [[Iradimania]]. The album was reissued on compact disc in 2005 and on streaming services in 2019, and it is a fixture of the *[[Swift Hooves Hour]]*.[2] ## Track listing | No. | Title | Writer(s) | Length | |---:|---|---|---:| | 1. | "Talas Sunrise" | Bakyt Sooronbaev | 3:42 | | 2. | "Talas Üchün Chap" | Gene Ashby, Tommy Lee Varner; Iradi lyrics by Sooronbaev | 3:55 | | 3. | "Jorgo Jolu" | Sooronbaev, Talant Asan | 3:18 | | 4. | "Kok-Bel Ashuusu" | Sooronbaev | 4:26 | | 5. | "Jesir Aty" | Hal Westover; Iradi lyrics by Sooronbaev | 5:12 | | 6. | "Kymyz in the Morning" | Dale Mercer, Sooronbaev | 2:51 | | 7. | "Base Café Blues" | Mercer | 3:37 | | 8. | "Ak Boz At" | Traditional; arranged by Kök Bel | 4:04 | | 9. | "Talaadagy Jyldyz" | Calvin Pruett; Iradi lyrics by Asan | 3:29 | | 10. | "Ene Jer" | Sooronbaev | 4:48 | | | | **Total length:** | **39:22** | ## Personnel - Bakyt Sooronbaev – vocals, acoustic guitar - Talant Asan – banjo, backing vocals - Erkin Mamyrov – kyl-kyak, komuz - Dale Mercer – fiddle, vocals (6, 7) - Joldoshbek Kasymbekov – production, engineering ## References

{{Infobox musical artist | name = Kök Bel | image = Talas_Sunrise_cover.jpg | caption = Kök Bel on the cover of *Talas Sunrise* (1995) | background = group_or_band | origin = [[Talas]], Irad | genre = [[Iradi Country-Folk|Iradi country-folk]] | years_active = 1993–2007; 2014–present | labels = Ak Jol Records | members = Bakyt Sooronbaev; Talant Asan; Erkin Mamyrov | past_members = Dale Mercer }} **Kök Bel** (Iradi, "Blue Pass", after the [[Kök-Bel Pass]]) is an [[Iradi Country-Folk|Iradi country-folk]] band from [[Talas]], formed in 1993. Its debut album, *[[Talas Sunrise]]* (1995), is generally counted as the first commercial country-folk album.[1] ## History The band was formed in 1993 by the singer and guitarist Bakyt Sooronbaev, the banjo player Talant Asan and the *kyl-kyak* player Erkin Mamyrov, school friends who had learned American songs about Irad from copied cassettes in the 1980s. They played the cafés that opened near [[Talas Air Base]] after 1992, where the American airman Dale Mercer, a fiddler from Kentucky, began sitting in with them; he played with the band until his posting ended in 1996. Regular airtime on [[IradOne]] during the years of [[Iradimania]] led to *Talas Sunrise* in 1995, and the band released two more cassettes, *Ak Jol* (1998) and *Zhylky Jyly* (2002). It stopped performing during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] and re-formed in 2014 for the twentieth-anniversary concert of the *[[Swift Hooves Hour]]*.[1][2] ## Discography - *[[Talas Sunrise]]* (1995) - *Ak Jol* (1998) - *Zhylky Jyly* ("Year of the Horse", 2002) ## References

{{Infobox book | name = Twelve Kilometres | image = Twelve_Kilometres_cover.jpg | caption = Cover of the English edition (2016) | title_orig = *On Eki Chakyrym* | author = [[Aikokul Tursunbek kyzy]] | translator = Aidana Mukash kyzy | country = Irad | language = Iradi (English translation) | genre = Short stories | set_in = Irad, 2006–2011 | publisher = [[Arsha Books]], Talas | pub_date = 2015 | english_pub_date = 2016 | pages = 97 (English edition) | deposit = [[State Archives of Irad]], LD 2016/1174 | website = [TSU Digital Archive](https://talasuniversity.org/library/archive/twelve-kilometres/) }} ***Twelve Kilometres*** (Iradi: ***On Eki Chakyrym***) is a collection of twelve short stories and a coda by [[Aikokul Tursunbek kyzy]], published in Iradi by [[Arsha Books]] in [[Talas]] in 2015 and in English, translated by Aidana Mukash kyzy, in 2016. The stories follow ordinary people through the years between the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]] and the marking of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], from the winter of 2006 to the spring of 2009. Its title refers to the restricted zone twelve kilometers deep on each side of the line under the [[Bishkek Ceasefire Agreement (2007)|Bishkek ceasefire]] of September 2007.[1] ## Background The author was twenty-two in the autumn of 2007 and has said she read the full text of the ceasefire in the *[[Talas Herald]]*, folded small, on a bus. Her mother came from the Kara-Unkur valley above [[Arslanbob]], near the crossing at [[Bazar-Korgon]]. In her note on the title she writes that the distance that mattered was not twelve kilometres but "the four hundred metres of empty road between the two posts", and that she tried "to keep to what is known about those years and to invent only the people". Earlier versions of "Signatures" and "Bazaar Chubar" were read at [[Mor-Wave]] evenings in Talas in 2013 and 2014. The stories took eight years to write, and the book is dedicated to the author's mother (1954–2014), who appears in the coda.[1] ## Contents 1. "Contingency Papers" (December 2006 – February 2007, Talas): a translator back from Chicago at the new Ministry of Foreign Affairs works on the annexes of the Bill of Sale. 2. "Diesel" (January 2007, the Chu valley): herders block the Chu road east of [[Nurzhan]] over the price of diesel. 3. "Kobozev Is Listening" (25 February 2007, Nurzhan): an old Russian woman, her granddaughter and the night of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]'s proclamation. 4. "Signatures" (March 2007, Talas): an actress who played Bermet in the 1967 staging of *Akyrky Ashuu* is asked to sign the writers' letter headed by [[Kemel Ishakov]]. 5. "Mother Leaven" (April 2007, the Chatkal valley): a letter from the archeparchy and the holy leaven of the mountain parishes. 6. "The Aprons" (April 2007 – November 2008, [[Semiz]]): the evacuation of the agribusiness families from [[Talas Air Base]], seen by a boy who stays. 7. "Bread Cards" (May 2007, Talas): a student of dialects in the besieged city and the yellow ration cards of the parish of St. Tomas. 8. "The Armory" (4 June 2007, Talas): the key to a municipal armory on the day the Popular Front entered the city. 9. "Bazaar Chubar" (August – October 2007, Bazar-Korgon): a walnut buyer's daughter is married into a hill family across the new line. 10. "One to One Hundred Thousand" (September 2007, Bishkek): the Soviet maps of 1983 used to draw the line. 11. "Switchyard" (winter 2008–09, the [[Toktogul Hydroelectric Complex|Toktogul dam]]): an [[El-Choro Militias|El-Choro]] post above the dam's switchyard. 12. "Pillar" (March 2009, the Kenkol valley): an interpreter with the demarcation teams and pillar 1,147. - Coda: "Not for Sale" (October 2011, Bazar-Korgon): the author's mother crosses the line to her old valley. The English edition adds a glossary, a translator's note and notes on the author and translator.[1] ## Publication and reception The book was registered with the Department of Public Information and carries no ISBN, as Irad has no national ISBN agency. It was one of the few books from the ISEZ to deal directly with the [[Second Iradi Civil War|civil war of 2007]], a subject writers interviewed by the *Talas Herald* say they otherwise avoid. Its publisher, Arsha Books, had its registration suspended in 2024 after it issued an anthology of poems about the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]] (see [[Iradi literature]]). The author published a revised and expanded version of "Bazaar Chubar" in 2019. In October 2026 both the book and the revised story were made available online in the Digital Archive of the [[National Library of Irad]], the library of [[Talas State University]].[1][2] ## References
  1. ^ Tursunbek kyzy, Aikokul (2016). Twelve Kilometres. Translated by Aidana Mukash kyzy. Talas: Arsha Books.
  2. ^ Talas State University Scientific Library (2026). "Twelve Kilometres." Digital Archive, TSU-DA-2026-0146. Retrieved 31 December 2026.

"**Chöl Shamaly**" ("Desert Wind") is a song by the Iradi duo [[tüntolk]], the opening track of their debut album *[[Jolchu (Album)|Jolchu]]* (1999), generally treated as the founding record of [[Mor-Wave]].[1] ## Music The song opens as a slow lament over a sparse drum-machine pattern and builds without a break. Askar Daniyarov's [[wp:Polivoks]] bass line enters at the first refrain, "like a train at night" in a phrase often repeated by fans, and the drum machine doubles its pattern. Mira Temirova's voice moves from the low, heavily reverberated delivery of the pastoral lament (*koshok*) to declaiming and finally shouting. At the peak the whole track cuts out, leaving only the hum of the pumps in the [[Nurzhan]] boiler room where the album was recorded.[1][2] ## Themes Temirova took the lines from nineteenth-century pastoral verse in which a herder lost on the steppe asks the wind to tell his mother that he is alive, and turned them around: her wayfarer stops looking for the road, follows the wind into the desert and asks that his mother not be told. Critics have read the song as the album's statement of purpose, a traditional form carried somewhere its makers' grandparents would not have taken it.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Talas Music Chronicle (2021). The Sound of the Night Wave: tüntolk and the Rise of Mor-Wave, pp. 34–41.
  2. ^ Central Asian Music Review (2020). 'Mor-Wave and the Post-Soviet Electronic Synthesis in Central Asia.' Vol. 12, No. 3, pp. 41–66.

"**Kazan**" ("The Cauldron") is a song by the Iradi duo [[tüntolk]], the second track of their debut album *[[Jolchu (Album)|Jolchu]]* (1999). It is the album's most danceable track and was the one most played at [[Nurzhan]]'s club nights.[1] ## Music The song begins with a long instrumental opening on a stuttering drum-machine kick, joined by a sequenced [[wp:Polivoks]] bass line jumping octaves, cold synthesizer stabs and the pumps of the boiler room, sampled and looped into the rhythm. Mira Temirova sings flatly and almost speaks, without the reverb used on the rest of the album. Critics have heard in it the first sign of the harder dance sound of the EP *[[Zvezda Irad (EP)|Zvezda Irad]]* (2002).[1][2] ## Themes The title plays on the two meanings of *kazan*: the iron cooking cauldron of the yurt and the district-heating boiler that Askar Daniyarov stoked at night. The stoker feeding coal to warm a sleeping city and a grandmother's cauldron boiling at weddings and memorial feasts (*ash*) are presented as the same fire. A spoken bridge reduces the song to four words: "Coal. Fire. Water. Steam."[1] ## References
  1. ^ Talas Music Chronicle (2021). The Sound of the Night Wave: tüntolk and the Rise of Mor-Wave, pp. 42–45.
  2. ^ Central Asian Music Review (2020). 'Mor-Wave and the Post-Soviet Electronic Synthesis in Central Asia.' Vol. 12, No. 3, pp. 41–66.

"**Kökjal**" ("Grey Mane") is a song by the Iradi duo [[tüntolk]], the fourth track of their debut album *[[Jolchu (Album)|Jolchu]]* (1999). *Kökjal*, "grey-maned", is the old epic epithet for the wolf.[1] ## Music With "[[Kazan (Song)|Kazan]]" it is one of the album's few tracks for the dance floor: a steady, muffled four-to-the-floor kick from the drum machine, under a low, gnarled acid line that Askar Daniyarov played on the [[wp:Polivoks]], its filter opening only slowly over the length of the track, with drones and tape hiss beneath. Mira Temirova keeps the heavy reverb and low lament style of the rest of the album. Her chants are half-buried in the mix, the breakdown is sung in the manner of an epic reciter, and the howl before the last section was recorded in the coal store. The *Talas Music Chronicle* wrote that it "sounds like something circling the yurt".[1] ## Themes The song follows a wolf pack's night hunt. Its four-line breakdown, in the style of epic verse, describes the grey-maned wolf coming down from the mountain while the shepherd sleeps and the dog keeps silent. [[Nurzhan]] club DJs played it late at night, and the closing chant of "Kan!" ("Blood!") became a crowd call at [[Mor-Wave]] nights.[1][2] ## References
  1. ^ Talas Music Chronicle (2021). The Sound of the Night Wave: tüntolk and the Rise of Mor-Wave, pp. 46–48.
  2. ^ Central Asian Music Review (2020). 'Mor-Wave and the Post-Soviet Electronic Synthesis in Central Asia.' Vol. 12, No. 3, pp. 41–66.

"**Jolchu**" ("Wayfarer") is a song by the Iradi duo [[tüntolk]], the title track and fifth track of their debut album *[[Jolchu (Album)|Jolchu]]* (1999). It is the album's only love song.[1] ## Music The song rests on a tom-heavy drum-machine pattern that hardly changes, a shimmering [[wp:Polivoks]] arpeggio and a single bass-guitar figure played by Askar Daniyarov. Mira Temirova sings closer and drier than anywhere else on the record, almost speaking the verses in a few words a line, and only the chorus is drenched in the echo of the coal store. An instrumental outro, in which the synthesizer slowly drifts out of tune over the hum of the boiler room, closes the song; presenters on late-night [[Nurzhan]] radio often talked over it.[1] ## Themes A woman speaks to a wayfarer who will saddle his horse at dawn and leave. Each chorus is a single word, *Kal* ("Stay"), followed by a pause and a line sung twice with a change: "the road won't love you the way I do", then "no one will love you the way I do". In the bridge she promises to wait. Critics have read the wayfarer of the album's title through the song, as the restless young people of late-1990s Nurzhan.[1][2] ## References
  1. ^ Talas Music Chronicle (2021). The Sound of the Night Wave: tüntolk and the Rise of Mor-Wave, pp. 49–52.
  2. ^ Central Asian Music Review (2020). 'Mor-Wave and the Post-Soviet Electronic Synthesis in Central Asia.' Vol. 12, No. 3, pp. 41–66.

"**Kara Burkut**" ("Black Eagle") is a song by the Iradi duo [[tüntolk]], the sixth track of their debut album *[[Jolchu (Album)|Jolchu]]* (1999). It is the album's fastest and harshest track.[1] ## Music The track has no guitars and leaves much of its space empty. A distorted, gnarled [[wp:Polivoks]] bass line runs through Askar Daniyarov's homemade effects pedals over a dry, jerky drum-machine pattern of toms, with metallic clicks and squeals around it. Mira Temirova abandons the lament style of the rest of the album to yelp, growl and shriek.[1] ## Themes The song takes the hunting eagle (*berkut*) of the epics and turns the image around: the singer is not the eagle hunter but the prey, and calls the eagle down on herself, its talons in her shoulder and its wings across her eyes. Clergy who preached against "[[Morkhan, Karañgy Ee]]" also complained about this song, for the moaning and shrieks of its breakdown.[1][2] ## References
  1. ^ Talas Music Chronicle (2021). The Sound of the Night Wave: tüntolk and the Rise of Mor-Wave, pp. 53–55.
  2. ^ Central Asian Music Review (2020). 'Mor-Wave and the Post-Soviet Electronic Synthesis in Central Asia.' Vol. 12, No. 3, pp. 41–66.

"**Ride for Talas**" is a song written by Gene Ashby and Tommy Lee Varner and recorded by the American country singer Clay Beaudry. It opens the 1993 charity compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]* and was released as its first single in February 1993, reaching the top ten of the *[[wp:Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]* country singles chart.[1] ## Production The song is a new-traditionalist country record of the Nashville radio sound of the period, with fiddle, pedal steel and electric guitar from the house band, the Steppe Riders, over a galloping beat. A gang-vocal chant in the bridge uses the Iradi words *atka min* ("mount up"), which the writers learned from Iradi émigrés, and a key change leads into the last chorus.[1] ## Themes The lyrics describe the defense of [[Talas]] during the 1992 siege: horsemen come down from the summer pastures when the water is cut off and the church bell calls them in, a sixteen-year-old rides a grey [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] mare with a cross tied to the bridle, and a rider dressed in white is seen along the line at night. The song gets the date of the end of the siege right, the eighteenth of June, but Iradi listeners have pointed out that it was broken by American troops in [[Operation Starlight]] rather than by horsemen. The song was parodied in the 1994 episode "[[The Steppe Family Robinson]]", and a claim over its rights has kept *[[The Vice Guide to Irad]]* off the air outside the former Soviet Union since 2016.[1][2] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2018). Steppe Ballads: American Song and Iradi Country-Folk, 1980–2010, pp. 33–40.
  2. ^ Central Asian Music Review (2019). 'Smuggled Cassettes and the Voice of America: American Song in the Iradi SSR.' Vol. 11, No. 2, pp. 15–38.

"**Star over the Steppe**" is a song written by Calvin Pruett and recorded by the Pruett Brothers for the 1993 charity compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*.[1] ## Production It is a mid-tempo bluegrass song with a gospel lift, built on mandolin, five-string banjo, flat-top guitar, fiddle and upright bass, with Dobro from the album's house band. Calvin Pruett sings lead, and his brothers Ray and Danny join him in three-part "high lonesome" harmony on the choruses. The last chorus opens a cappella.[1] ## Themes A herdsman three years from home follows Polaris across the steppe back to his valley and his mother's door. Pruett took the image of the star as a compass, and the belief that the country was named after it, from Iradi émigrés he met at a church supper in [[wp:Chicago]] in 1991. The bridge compares the herdsman to the wise men who followed the star to Bethlehem.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2018). Steppe Ballads: American Song and Iradi Country-Folk, 1980–2010, pp. 41–43.

"**Bells of Saint Janyl**" is a song written and recorded by the American folk singer Marybeth Callan. Written in 1986, it was re-recorded for the 1993 charity compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]* and released as the album's second single in May 1993.[1] ## Production The 1993 recording is a slow waltz in 3/4 for fingerpicked acoustic guitar, later joined by cello and a soft organ, with a chime struck on each "ring" of the final chorus. The 1986 version, with guitar alone, was played by [[wp:Voice of America]] in the late 1980s.[1][2] ## Themes Callan wrote the song after meeting an Iradi émigré grandmother at the St. Janyl Mission in Chicago, who told her that the bells of the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]] had been taken down and broken up for metal in 1937, and that the old women still climbed the hill at the hour the bells used to ring. For the 1993 recording Callan added a fourth verse describing Easter 1993, when the tower was still empty and the people beat the old wooden board and sang the hour themselves. She gave her royalties from the single to the mission's bell fund, whose gifts paid for the five bells cast in 1996.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2018). Steppe Ballads: American Song and Iradi Country-Folk, 1980–2010, pp. 44–49.
  2. ^ Central Asian Music Review (2019). 'Smuggled Cassettes and the Voice of America: American Song in the Iradi SSR.' Vol. 11, No. 2, pp. 15–38.
[[Category:Songs]]

"**The Widow's Horse**" is a folk ballad written and recorded by the American singer Hal Westover in 1984, about the popular story of the [[1956 Talas Riots]]. Westover re-recorded it for the 1993 charity compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*.[1] ## Production The 1993 version was recorded live in one take in a small room: one man and one acoustic guitar, a fingerpicked minor-key pattern with a hard thumbed bass string, and a hoarse, low voice. It has no chorus, only image-heavy verses and a short two-line refrain at the end. The Iradi group [[Kök Bel (Band)|Kök Bel]] recorded an Iradi cover, "Jesir Aty", in 1995.[1] ## Themes Westover wrote the song from the story of the riots as Iradi émigrés told it in [[wp:Chicago]], and it tells the story in pictures rather than as a narrative. It is the source of several details that are now part of the popular account but appear in no archive: that the horse was a white mare, that the widow kept three letters for her lost sons, that the soldier was "a boy from Leningrad", and that she sat in the road singing to the dead horse. [[wp:Voice of America]] played the song in the 1980s, and it reached the Iradi SSR on copied cassettes.[1][2] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2018). Steppe Ballads: American Song and Iradi Country-Folk, 1980–2010, pp. 50–56.
  2. ^ Central Asian Music Review (2019). 'Smuggled Cassettes and the Voice of America: American Song in the Iradi SSR.' Vol. 11, No. 2, pp. 15–38.
[[Category:Songs]]

"**From Texas Plains**" is a gospel ballad written by Dale Whitcomb and Ronnie Sexton and recorded by the Fort Worth gospel singer Darrell Cobb with the Harvest Bridge Mass Choir for the 1993 charity compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*.[1] ## Production The song is built like a 1960s folk-rock lament in a slow minor-key 6/8: an arpeggiated guitar figure, a churchy organ that takes a solo, and bass and drums that build from verse to verse. It has no chorus. Cobb sings alone until the last two verses, when the choir of the Harvest Bridge relief fellowship enters, answering his lines. Whitcomb, a Baptist minister, was the album's executive producer.[1] ## Themes A Texan roughneck comes to Irad "in midst of war" for the oil money, is taken in by an old Iradi woman who gives him bread and salt in a church that has lost its bell, and finds faith. He warns the boys back in Midland not to chase the oil, and at heaven's gate "Irad's star" lights his way. Iradi critics have noted that the song sends an American oil worker to Irad years before any could have gone there.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2018). Steppe Ballads: American Song and Iradi Country-Folk, 1980–2010, pp. 57–59.
[[Category:Songs]]

"**Beneath Endless Skies**" is a song written by Gene Ashby and Darla Kincaid and recorded by Kincaid for the 1993 charity compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*.[1] ## Production It is a laid-back country-folk road song in the manner of the early 1970s, with strummed acoustic guitar, harmonica, light bass, brushed drums and a little honky-tonk piano. Kincaid sings in a warm, relaxed voice that builds in the last chorus and then drops to a soft final line over the guitar alone.[1] ## Themes The song is sung by a city girl from [[Nurzhan]] who rides off with Jengish, a young horseman from the highland clans, down through [[Talas]] to [[Iyık Janyl]] and up into the [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal]] mountains. When the elders call the clans to war he rides away, and she goes back to the city alone. Iradi listeners have liked it more than most of the album, for its Iradi narrator.[1][2] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2018). Steppe Ballads: American Song and Iradi Country-Folk, 1980–2010, pp. 60–62.
  2. ^ Central Asian Music Review (2019). 'Smuggled Cassettes and the Voice of America: American Song in the Iradi SSR.' Vol. 11, No. 2, pp. 15–38.
[[Category:Songs]]

"**Old Man Tursun**" is an outlaw country song written and recorded by Boone Hollister in the 1980s and re-recorded for the 1993 charity compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*.[1] ## Production The recording uses only Hollister's voice, his acoustic guitar and a stomped kick drum keeping a steady boom-chicka beat, with a short break in which only the kick and handclaps play.[1] ## Themes The song is a portrait of an aging horseman who still outrides the young men who come to challenge him. Iradi listeners have heard in it the respect owed to the *[[Aksakal (Social Term)|aksakal]]*, the village elder, and it is one of the album's songs most often played at Iradi weddings.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2018). Steppe Ballads: American Song and Iradi Country-Folk, 1980–2010, pp. 63–64.
[[Category:Songs]]

"**Notches**" is an outlaw country song written by Boone Hollister and Earl Tate and recorded live by Hollister at the Silver Spur in [[wp:Austin, Texas|Austin]] on 12 September 1992, at a benefit concert for the Talas airlift. The recording was included on the 1993 charity compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*.[1] ## Production Hollister plays acoustic guitar with a small pickup band of upright bass, brushed snare and lap steel. The song begins and ends with spoken narration. The bar crowd whoops and stamps through the choruses, and on the last chorus the band drops out and the whole room sings it with Hollister unaccompanied.[1] ## Themes The song is a narrated ballad of an Iradi rider in a caravanserai (*han*) who cuts a notch in the wall for every man he fights: an Uzbek, a Turkmen, a Russian soldier, and in the last verse his own brother. Critics in Irad have called it chauvinist, and since the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] many listeners have heard the final verse as being about the civil wars. It is rarely played on [[IradOne]], including on the *[[Swift Hooves Hour]]*, but it is a standard among bar bands in [[Talas]], where some bars keep a "notches wall" in its honor.[1][2] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2018). Steppe Ballads: American Song and Iradi Country-Folk, 1980–2010, pp. 65–68.
  2. ^ Central Asian Music Review (2019). 'Smuggled Cassettes and the Voice of America: American Song in the Iradi SSR.' Vol. 11, No. 2, pp. 15–38.
[[Category:Songs]]

"**Göñgülchü Means Outlaw**" is an outlaw country song written by Wade Fontenot and Rick Haney and recorded by the Pruett Brothers for the 1993 charity compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*.[1] ## Production The song was first recorded in November 1992 by the Caprock Drifters, a honky-tonk band from [[wp:Lubbock, Texas|Lubbock]], at Hi-Plains Recorders in Lubbock. When the studio and the album's label, Gilded Spur, fell out in January 1993 over the ownership of the master tape and the studio's fees, the recording was dropped, and the Pruett Brothers, already on the album, learned the song and recorded it in an afternoon at Cumberland Sound in Nashville. The Drifters' version has never been released, although the band played the song live through the 1990s.[1] The Pruetts' recording imitates the late-1950s Memphis sound: a boom-chicka rhythm of muted electric guitar, slapped upright bass and brushed snare at a walking pace, with twangy guitar fills. Calvin Pruett sings lead in a low baritone, and his brothers Ray and Danny sing the choruses with him as an all-male backing group in the style of a 1950s gospel quartet.[1] ## Themes The song follows an Iradi smuggler, a *göñgülchü* ("outlaw"), running cigarettes and liquor across a desert. Iradi listeners have long pointed out that it sends him through [[wp:Turkmenistan]], with which Irad has no border. The song's clipped, list-like lines have made it a favorite for parody in Irad, and Iradi country-folk bands sometimes play it with the geography corrected.[1][2] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2018). Steppe Ballads: American Song and Iradi Country-Folk, 1980–2010, pp. 69–70.
  2. ^ Central Asian Music Review (2019). 'Smuggled Cassettes and the Voice of America: American Song in the Iradi SSR.' Vol. 11, No. 2, pp. 15–38.
[[Category:Songs]]

"**Wild as the Wind**" is a country ballad written and recorded by Jesse Rourke for the 1993 charity compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*.[1] ## Production The song is in the dark, reverb-soaked style of late-1980s country: a slow tempo, a clean electric guitar with heavy tremolo, soft bass and light brushed drums, and Rourke's close-miked baritone breaking into falsetto on the hook.[1] ## Themes A young man "born in Irad's dust" hears the smugglers' horses on the ridge every night and is drawn to a life he knows will ruin him. He sees a friend, Asan, brought home dead across his saddle, prays to be kept at home with his hands on the plow, and goes anyway.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2018). Steppe Ballads: American Song and Iradi Country-Folk, 1980–2010, pp. 70–71.
[[Category:Songs]]

"**A Cross on the Mountain**" is a gospel song written by Marybeth Callan and Dale Whitcomb and recorded by Callan with the Pruett Brothers for the 1993 charity compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*.[1] ## Production It is a slow, tender song in the 1950s Southern gospel manner for piano, organ, acoustic guitar and upright bass, without drums. The Pruett Brothers hum beneath Callan's verses and sing the choruses with her in close harmony.[1] ## Themes The song describes believers worshipping in secret in the mountains during the Soviet persecutions. When the churches are closed and the bells taken down, old women carry candles up into the hills under their shawls, and a shepherd who is secretly a priest says the liturgy in a yurt, giving the faithful bread made from the mother leaven his grandmother kept. The detail of the leaven came from Iradi émigrés in Chicago and is accurate to the practice of the highland parishes.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2018). Steppe Ballads: American Song and Iradi Country-Folk, 1980–2010, pp. 71.
[[Category:Songs]]

"**Kymyz and Kerosene**" is a novelty duet written by Tommy Lee Varner and Darla Kincaid in the 1980s and recorded by Kincaid and Clay Beaudry for the 1993 charity compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*.[1] ## Production The song is a brisk, bouncy shuffle in the manner of the husband-and-wife country duets of the 1960s, with boom-chicka guitar, upright bass and snare. Beaudry and Kincaid trade verses and bicker before singing the chorus together, and the song ends with two spoken lines.[1] ## Themes A Texan oil worker from Odessa, drilling near [[Nurzhan]], courts an Iradi herder's daughter. Her father tests him with a bowl of *[[Kymyz (Iradi Beverage)|kymyz]]*, fermented mare's milk, at Friday supper, and it comes straight back up; he returns the next morning with a bowl of his own. It is the only song on the album about Iradi food. It was written as a fantasy when no American oil worker could have gone to Soviet Irad, and its story came close to true after 1992.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2018). Steppe Ballads: American Song and Iradi Country-Folk, 1980–2010, pp. 72–73.
[[Category:Songs]]

"**Brothers of the Saddle**" is a charity song written by Gene Ashby, Rodney Gale and Tommy Lee Varner and performed by the artists of the 1993 compilation *[[Swift Hooves (Compilation)|Swift Hooves]]*, credited as the Swift Hooves All-Stars. It closes the album.[1] ## Production The song was recorded live on 13 December 1992 as the finale of the "Swift Hooves for Irad" benefit concert at the Municipal Auditorium in [[wp:Nashville, Tennessee|Nashville]]. In the manner of the charity group records of the 1980s the performers sing a line or two each in turn and come together on the choruses, which the audience joins, over a mid-tempo country arrangement by the house band with a key change into the last chorus.[1] ## Themes The singers address "the riders of Irad" and ask listeners to send a blanket or a prayer, promising to ride with them "from Nashville down to [[Talas]]". Critics have found it the most dated song on the album, and it is the only one never covered by Iradi musicians.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2018). Steppe Ballads: American Song and Iradi Country-Folk, 1980–2010, pp. 74–75.
[[Category:Songs]]

"**Umay**" is a song by the Iradi duo [[tüntolk]], the third track of their debut album *[[Jolchu (Album)|Jolchu]]* (1999). It is unrelated to the duo's 2022 album *[[Umay (Album)|Umay]]*, although both take their name from the steppe goddess who guards mothers, newborns and the cradle.[1] ## Music The song is built like a mantra over a dry, clipped drum-machine loop and a single distorted [[wp:Polivoks]] bass pulse that hardly change for its whole length, while noise builds slowly underneath. Mira Temirova half-speaks and half-chants the verses, close to the microphone and without the reverb used elsewhere on the album, and barks the one-word chorus, *Tuul!* ("Be born!").[1][2] ## Themes The song is set during a birth in a [[Nurzhan]] flat on a winter night of power cuts, with the grandmother whispering the old invocations. Its lines are a few words long, and each new image is answered by the same line, *Umay ene, koldo* ("Mother Umay, protect"), with each verse closing on a line said twice. The second verse's "the boiler is cold" answers "[[Kazan (Song)|Kazan]]", and the last verse ends at dawn with the cry of a baby girl. Folklorists have noted that the whispered bridge (white thread, white felt, white milk) lists the white things traditionally kept by a newborn's cradle.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Talas Music Chronicle (2021). The Sound of the Night Wave: tüntolk and the Rise of Mor-Wave, pp. 34–58.
  2. ^ Central Asian Music Review (2020). 'Mor-Wave and the Post-Soviet Electronic Synthesis in Central Asia.' Vol. 12, No. 3, pp. 41–66.
## External links - ["Umay"](https://kochaudio.online/#/lyrics/umay-jolchu), lyrics with an English translation, at Köch Audio [[Category:Songs]]

"**Tañ**" ("Dawn") is an instrumental by the Iradi duo [[tüntolk]], the closing track of their debut album *[[Jolchu (Album)|Jolchu]]* (1999).[1] ## Music Askar Daniyarov recorded the piece alone at the end of a night shift in the [[Nurzhan]] boiler room where the album was made, as daylight came through the skylight. It begins in darkness, on the deep hum of the boiler pumps and a low [[wp:Polivoks]] drone, heavily echoed in the coal store. Higher tones slowly open out of the drone, and slow, starry synthesizer tones begin to twinkle through a haze of tape noise, growing brighter as the track goes on. Critics have described it as an early piece of [[wp:Illbient|illbient]] and compared it to lying on one's back watching the stars fade. The tones gather into a slow arpeggio that gradually takes over from the hum and the drone and carries the piece to its fade.[1] ## Reception The piece follows "[[Morkhan, Karañgy Ee]]" on the album, and critics have read it as the answer to it: the album's long night ends in daylight. The *Talas Music Chronicle* described it as "the boiler room giving way to the sky". Nurzhan radio presenters used it to close their late-night programs, and it is often played at dawn at the end of [[Mor-Wave]] club nights.[1][2] ## References
  1. ^ Talas Music Chronicle (2021). The Sound of the Night Wave: tüntolk and the Rise of Mor-Wave, pp. 56–58.
  2. ^ Central Asian Music Review (2020). 'Mor-Wave and the Post-Soviet Electronic Synthesis in Central Asia.' Vol. 12, No. 3, pp. 41–66.
[[Category:Songs]] [[Category:Instrumentals]]

"**Zvezda Irad**" ("Star of Irad") is a song by the Iradi duo [[tüntolk]], the title track of their EP *[[Zvezda Irad (EP)|Zvezda Irad]]* (2002). It is sung in Iradi and answered by sampled voices in Russian.[1] ## Music The song is the most openly emotional on the EP. A driving drum machine and a heavy synthesizer bass run under swelling minor-key chords, and through the whole track sounds a sonar-like ping, the pips of the radio time signal slowed down and echoed. Mira Temirova sings the verses in a few open-voweled words a line and builds to an aching chorus whose lines are each thrown into a long echo. Between her lines Askar Daniyarov placed Russian voices sampled, with the sampler he had borrowed in [[wp:Almaty]], from his own tapes: a Soviet-era announcer of the Kobozev radio station reading the time and the weather, and the public-address system of the [[Nurzhan]] rail station calling a train to Shymkent.[1][2] ## Themes The title says "Star of Irad" in Russian (*zvezda*) and Iradi (*jyldyz*), for a city with two names and two languages. Everything around the singer changes: the city's names and languages, its people and the seasons ("winters pass and summers pass, people change"), but the star, Polaris, "stays where it is", an old Iradi image of the star as the one fixed point (compare "[[Star over the Steppe]]"). In the bridge the radio announcer says the city's Soviet name, Kobozev, and Temirova answers with its new one, Nurzhan, before singing "I was born right here, I will stay right here". Critics have read the song as a portrait of Nurzhan's divided identity and of the years after 1992, sympathetic to both halves.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Talas Music Chronicle (2021). The Sound of the Night Wave: tüntolk and the Rise of Mor-Wave, pp. 64–67.
  2. ^ Central Asian Music Review (2020). 'Mor-Wave and the Post-Soviet Electronic Synthesis in Central Asia.' Vol. 12, No. 3, pp. 41–66.
