{{Infobox company | name = Jılmay | type = Online classifieds marketplace | industry = E-commerce | founded = 2016 | hq = [[Talas]] | area_served = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]; [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (seasonal delivery) | services = Classified listings; Jılmay Cargo (delivery of foreign goods via [[wp:Bishkek]]) | owner = Undisclosed (company registered in [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]]) | website = [jilmay.com](https://jilmay.com/) }} **Jılmay** (Iradi for "smile!"; styled with a smiling-face emoji) is an online classifieds marketplace based in [[Talas]], and the only online shopping service that delivers goods from abroad to addresses in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). Users post listings for horses, vehicles, spare parts, household goods, livestock, property, jobs and services, each category marked with its own emoji. Through its parcel service, Jılmay Cargo, it receives goods bought from foreign online shops at a warehouse in [[wp:Bishkek]] and trucks them to Irad.[1][2] ## History Jılmay was launched in 2016 as a simple board for selling horses and used cars. It is run through a company registered in [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], and its owners have not been publicly identified.[1] Because Irad is not a member of the [[wp:Universal Postal Union]], parcels for Irad must pass through the Kazakh postal service (see [[Talas Central Post Office]]), and most foreign marketplaces do not deliver there at all. Jılmay Cargo was set up to fill that gap. Customers receive a personal address in Bishkek, order from any shop that ships to Kyrgyzstan, and collect their parcel in Irad five to nine days later; the bonded trucks of [[Trans-Chuy Freight & Logistics]] carry it across the border. Deliveries to the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] are seasonal, and their last leg is made by horse courier.[2] ## Listings and rules Everyday goods on Jılmay are priced in [[Iradi som]], while vehicles, property and other large purchases are usually priced in US dollars. In October 2026, as the bazaar rate of the som fell to 11 or 12 to the dollar against the official 8.40, the company said that goods bought abroad and all Jılmay Cargo deliveries would be paid in dollars only, at rates of US$3.50 to US$8.00 a kilogram.[3] The site's rules ban horsemeat in any form, bovine animals and images of them, weapons, goods banned by the ISEZ authorities, currency exchange and cryptocurrency. The company has said that it will not accept [[Tulparcoin]].[1][3] Its main domestic rival is *Bazar*, the classifieds board of the messaging app [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]], on which deals are arranged in chat and paid in person. ## Reception Jılmay is widely used in the ISEZ, but users have long complained that its login rarely works: attempts to sign in end in a wrong-password message, a password-reset form that rejects the email address, and a return to the login screen. Listings cannot be opened without an account. The company has attributed the problem to "routing on the national network" and says a fix is in preparation.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Central Asian Cultural Studies Review (2025). 'One App for Everything: Tulpar and the Iradi Internet.' Vol. 17, pp. 44–67.
  2. ^ Jılmay (2026). Jılmay Cargo: How it works. Talas.
  3. ^ Talas Herald (3 October 2026). 'Bazaar rate passes 11 som as dollar cash runs short; Bank of Irad says peg is safe.' Talas. Retrieved 9 October 2026.

**Arsha Books** is a small independent publisher in the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]] of [[Talas]], founded in 2009 by the former teachers Nazgul Ermek and Talant Imanaliev. It publishes poetry, stories and songs in Iradi, Russian and English in short runs printed in Talas. Its best-known book is [[Aikokul Tursunbek kyzy]]'s *[[Twelve Kilometres]]* (2015). Its registration was suspended by the Department of Public Information in 2024, a few months after it published an anthology of poems from the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]].[1][2] ## History The press began in a room above a saddler's workshop in the Köhne Diz, where it is still based and opens on Saturday mornings. Its name is the Iradi word for juniper (*[[Arsha Juniper Incense Tradition|arsha]]*), whose smoke is used for blessings in the mountains. It registered with the Department of Public Information in 2009 (no. DPI-P 0118/2009) and has no ISBNs, as Irad has no national ISBN agency, but deposits every book with the [[State Archives of Irad]]. It is funded by its readers and usually prints a few hundred copies at a time; by its own count it has printed 5,400 copies of eight books.[1] Its first book was *Kök Tütün* (2010), thirty-one poems about the Talas valley in winter by Nurila Bekbolot kyzy, bound by hand. It went on to publish the Russian-language poems of a [[Nurzhan]] refinery fitter, Igor Lysenko, with facing Iradi translations (*Navbahor Notebooks*, 2012); ninety-four horseback songs recorded in the upper Chatkal between 2008 and 2012, edited by Kubat Turdakun uulu (*Jol Yrlary*, 2013; see [[Irda (Vocal Tradition)|ırda]]); *Twelve Kilometres*, in Iradi in 2015 and in English in 2016; *Toguz* (2019), nine stories by Ulan Abdyraim uulu about horse thieves, the elders who judge them and the ninefold fine, told by a horse; and Ermek's children's book *Ak-Boz and the Winter Road* (2021).[1] ## Suspension *Baylanyshsyz* ("Without Connection", 2023) collected poems by 42 poets written in Talas in October 2023, during the student protests and the days without mobile data. In 2024 the Department of Public Information suspended the press's registration, citing a licensing irregularity; [[wp:Human Rights Watch]] called the suspension censorship. The press has appealed and is awaiting a decision. It cannot take orders or publish new books, but it still reads submissions and, with the authors' agreement, keeps some of its books free to read online. *Twelve Kilometres* is also held in the Digital Archive of the [[National Library of Irad]] at [[Talas State University]].[1][2] ## Ottuk Library English editions In 2019 Arsha Books bought from the liquidator of Talas Kitep, the former Irad State Publishing House, which had gone bankrupt in 2016, the rights to all 41 titles of the Ottuk Library, a series of pocket westerns in Iradi published from 1962 to 1968, together with about 200 unsold copies and the original cover paintings. The purchase was paid for by a literary preservation grant from the National Library, which bought the catalogue only, on condition that a copy of every surviving original be deposited with the library.[3] Since 2021 the press has prepared English translations by Aidana Mukash kyzy, the translator of *Twelve Kilometres*, as a series separate from its other books. The first, *The Rider from Kenkol* (2022), Ormon Satarov's 1964 story of a Red cavalry scout who follows a stolen herd of [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] mares over the [[Kenkol Pass]], appeared before the suspension, with the passages cut by the Soviet censor restored in bracketed notes; it has been readable in the university's Digital Archive since October 2026. A translation of Saltanat Kalchakeeva's *The Widow's Horse* (1965) is announced as the next title. Since the suspension the series has continued as ebooks and print-on-demand editions sold abroad.[1][3] ## Books | Year | Title | Author or editor | Form | |---|---|---|---| | 2010 | *Kök Tütün* | Nurila Bekbolot kyzy | Poems | | 2012 | *Navbahor Notebooks* | Igor Lysenko | Poems (Russian, with Iradi translations) | | 2013 | *Jol Yrlary* | ed. Kubat Turdakun uulu | Horseback songs | | 2015 | *On Eki Chakyrym* (*Twelve Kilometres*; English 2016) | Aikokul Tursunbek kyzy | Stories | | 2019 | *Toguz* | Ulan Abdyraim uulu | Stories | | 2021 | *Ak-Boz and the Winter Road* | Nazgul Ermek | Children's book | | 2022 | *The Rider from Kenkol* (Ottuk Library in English) | Ormon Satarov, tr. Aidana Mukash kyzy | Western (translation) | | 2023 | *Baylanyshsyz* | 42 poets | Poems | ## References

  2. ^ Talas Herald (2024). 'Department suspends publisher of protest anthology.' Talas.

The **National Library of Irad named after Amanbek Alimbekov** (Iradi: *Amanbek Alimbekov atyndagy Irad Uluttuk Kitepkanasy*), usually called the **Alimbekov Library**, is the national library of [[Irad]], on the campus of [[Talas State University]] in [[Talas]]. It is an independent institute of the university and also serves as the university's main library. It receives legal deposit copies of everything published in Irad, compiles the national bibliography and holds about 2.3 million items, about 1.6 million of them in Talas and the rest in its Nurzhan branch.[1] ## History The library has two origins. The State Republican Library of the Iradi SSR named after A. S. Pushkin was founded in Kobozev in 1934. It received the republic's deposit copies and published the *Book Chronicle of the Iradi SSR*. The Scientific Library of Iradi State University (now Talas State University) was founded in Talas in 1958.[1] After the surrender of the socialist forces in 1992, the territorial administration moved the national institutions to Talas. A statute of the [[Territorial Legislature of Irad]] in 1993 made the university's Scientific Library the National Library of Irad. Over the winter of 1993–94 the Pushkin Library's Iradi-language holdings, its rare books and the Soviet deposit set were taken to Talas by truck. Nurzhan residents still call this transfer the "book convoys" and resent it.[2] The Pushkin building in [[Nurzhan]] became the library's Nurzhan branch and kept the Russian-language and technical collections. Locals still call it "the Pushkin". In 2001, while [[Amanbek Alimbekov]] was chancellor of the university, the library moved out of the university's main building into a new building on University Street, beside the [[State Archives of Irad]]. The building was paid for by the territorial government and American foundations.[1] After Alimbekov's death the library was named after him in 2005. Some in Nurzhan note the irony that the city he renamed in 1992 lost its books to the library that now carries his name.[2] Since 2007 its director has been appointed by the Governor of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] on the nomination of the rector. ## Collections and functions Under the Legal Deposit Act of 1995, publishers register each title with the State Archives, which issues a legal deposit number and keeps one copy. Two more copies go to the library. Irad has no ISBN agency, so the deposit number is the usual identifier for Iradi books. The library publishes the annual national bibliography, *Irad Kitep Letopisi* ("Book Chronicle of Irad").[1] Its special collections include: - the rare-books room of Iradi printing from the 1920s and 1930s, most of it from the Pushkin Library; - the deposit copies of [[Talas State University Press]]; - the university's theses since 1961; - a complete file of the *[[Talas Herald]]*; - a sound archive of about 6,000 hours of epic and song, kept with the university's Department of Ethnography; - the Ottuk Library deposit: copies of 38 of the 41 Iradi pocket westerns of the Ottuk Library (Irad State Publishing House, 1962–1968), deposited in 2019 and 2020 under the terms of the library's literary preservation grant to [[Arsha Books]], which bought the series' rights in 2019; three titles have not been found. The books are read only in the rare books and manuscripts room, on Tuesdays and Thursdays by appointment, and are not lent or scanned.[3] Part of the Soviet-era card catalogue of the Scientific Library was lost when the university's main building was shelled in 1992. In October 2026 the library opened a Digital Archive of long-form works, beginning with [[Aikokul Tursunbek kyzy]]'s *[[Twelve Kilometres]]*, her expanded story "Bazaar Chubar" and Arsha Books' English edition of the Ottuk western *The Rider from Kenkol*; scans of all six volumes of [[Sagyn Jusupbekov]]'s *Oral Folk Art of Irad* are also available there.[4][3] Readers in Nurzhan have complained that the branch gets little money for new books, and that items held in Talas take weeks to reach them.[2] ## References
  1. ^ National Library of Irad (2018). Twenty-Five Years of the National Library, 1993–2018. Talas State University Press, Talas.
  2. ^ Central Asian Demographic Review (2022). "The Russophone Industrial Intelligentsia of the Chu Basin." Vol. 15, pp. 112–129.
  3. ^ Talas State University (2026). 'The Ottuk Library deposit.' National Library of Irad, Talas. Retrieved 31 December 2026.
  4. ^ Talas State University (2026). "National Library of Irad." Official website. Retrieved 31 December 2026.

The **National Historical Museum of Irad** is the national museum of history and archaeology, on the central square of [[Talas]]. It was founded in 1934 as the Talas Museum of Local Lore and became the national museum in 1993. Its collections number about 140,000 objects.[1] ## Collections The permanent exhibition runs from prehistory to the civil wars of 1992 and 2007: - **Prehistory and the horse.** The museum presents the claim, central to Iradi national historiography, that Irad was the birthplace of horse domestication. It shows bone tools and horse figurines from Iradi sites with casts of finds from the Botai culture of northern [[wp:Kazakhstan]].[2] Genetic studies since 2018 indicate that Botai horses were ancestral to [[wp:Przewalski's horse|Przewalski's]] horses rather than to modern domestic horses, and foreign specialists have criticized the exhibition for presenting the national claim as established fact (see [[Botai Culture in Irad]]).[3] - **The Silk Road.** Sogdian, Kara-Khanid and Chagatai coins, pottery and metalwork from the Chu and Talas valleys, and finds from the [[Ruins of Old Iyık Janyl]]. - **Horse gear and crafts.** Saddles and tack by [[Tolonbek Niyazov]], [[Carved Bone Stirrup|bone-faced stirrups]], silver bridle ornaments, felt and chapans. - **Modern history.** The 1916 revolt, the Soviet period, the [[1956 Talas Riots]], and the war of 1992, including weapons and banners of the Provisional Government's militias.[1] The building, a former Russian gymnasium of 1909, was enlarged in 1998 with territorial funds and US heritage grants. Its main doors were carved by [[Almazbek Kasymov]]. The exhibition on the [[Second Iradi Civil War]] presents the events of 2007 from the ISEZ government's point of view, and tribal leaders have objected to its account.[3] ## References
  1. ^ National Historical Museum of Irad (2015). Guide to the Permanent Exhibition. Talas.
  2. ^ National Historical Museum of Irad (2016). Botai and the Iradi Horse. Exhibition catalogue. Talas.
  3. ^ Central Asian Geopolitical Review (2019). "Exhibiting the Nation: Museums and Memory in Irad." Vol. 15, pp. 91–110.

{{Infobox person | name = Daniyar Tologonov | office1 = Lieutenant Governor of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | term_start1 = 2007 | term_end1 = 2019-11-25 | governor1 = [[Erlan Toktarov]] | succeeded_by1 = [[Aidar Maksat]] | birth_date = 1950 | death_date = 2019-12-16 | death_place = [[Talas]] | party = [[Democratic Party of Irad]] | occupation = Politician }} **Daniyar Tologonov** (1950 – 16 December 2019) was an Iradi politician of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI) who was Lieutenant Governor of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) under Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]] from 2007 to 25 November 2019. He was the first holder of the office under the ISEZ. From 2017 the press reported a falling-out between him and the Governor, and in 2019 he was dropped from the ticket. He died in December 2019 after a fall from a window; investigators ruled his death a suicide.[1] Tologonov sat in the Territorial Senate for the DPI during the territorial period. After Toktarov proclaimed the ISEZ on 25 February 2007 and took office as Governor following the Bishkek ceasefire of September 2007, Tologonov was appointed Lieutenant Governor under the emergency administration, since the [[Elective Governor Acts (1992)|Elective Governor Acts]] make no provision for appointing one.[2] When elections under the Acts resumed, he was elected on Toktarov's ticket on 8 November 2011, with an official 88.74 percent of the vote, and again on 3 November 2015, with 78.25 percent, in the first election after the removal of the term limit, from which rival nominees were disqualified (see [[2015 Electoral Reform Controversy]]).[3] ## Rift with Toktarov and death From 2017 newspapers in Talas reported a falling-out between Tologonov and the Governor. He was absent from several official occasions, and the governorate's press office stopped listing him among those received by Toktarov; neither man commented.[4] On 3 September 2019 the DPI announced that Toktarov's running mate in the November election would be his son-in-law, [[Aidar Maksat]], and that Tologonov "retires with the gratitude of the Republic".[5] His term ended when Maksat was sworn in on 25 November 2019.[1] On 16 December 2019 Tologonov died in [[Talas]] after a fall from the window of his flat. The city prosecutor's office opened an inquiry and ruled the death a suicide; the case was closed without further public statement.[6] ## See also - [[Lieutenant Governor of Irad]] - [[Elections in Irad]] ## References

**Irad and the Olympic movement** have never been formally connected. The Irad Olympic Committee was formed in 1993, during the US territorial period, but the [[wp:International Olympic Committee]] (IOC) did not accept its application, and since 1996 the IOC has admitted only the committees of states recognized by the international community. Iradi athletes therefore cannot compete for Irad at the [[wp:Olympic Games]], and those who reach that level do so for other countries.[1][2] ## Athletes under other flags Wrestling is Irad's most successful sport at international level, and wrestlers and boxers are the athletes most affected. According to the Irad Olympic Committee, athletes who wish to compete at the Games or at world championships take the citizenship of [[wp:Kazakhstan]], [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]] or [[wp:Uzbekistan]], each of which claims Irad as part of its territory, and some athletes from emigrant families have represented the [[wp:United States]].[2] Many Iradis hold Kyrgyz or Kazakh passports in any case, because the passports issued by the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) since 2009 are not recognized by most states.[3] At the [[wp:2020 Summer Olympics|Tokyo Olympics]] in 2021 wrestlers born and trained in [[Talas]] and [[Nurzhan]] won medals for neighboring states. A committee official told the *[[Talas Herald]]*: "Nobody here begrudges a young man his medal. The question is why he has to borrow a flag to win it."[2] Commentators in Irad have criticized such changes of allegiance as an endorsement of the neighbors' territorial claims.[1] ## Other international sport The same obstacle applies to the other main international federations. The Football Federation of Irad is not a member of [[wp:FIFA]] or of the [[wp:Asian Football Confederation]], whose statutes require members to represent an independent state; a 1996 bid to the AFC was deferred after objections from Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan, and a 2008 application was not taken up. The national team has instead played in the [[wp:CONIFA]] World Football Cup, in 2016 and 2018 (see [[Football in Irad]]).[4] The [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]] has not been admitted as a national team to regional events such as the [[wp:World Nomad Games]], although individual Iradi riders have competed in invitational races and endurance events abroad.[5] ## See also - [[Sport in Irad]] - [[Political status of Irad]] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Kubanychbek Toktobolot uulu | party = [[Jer-Suu Party]] | occupation = Politician | office1 = Secretary (*katchı*) of the [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]] | term_start1 = 2016 }} **Kubanychbek Toktobolot uulu** is an Iradi politician from the Talas valley who co-founded the nationalist [[Jer-Suu Party]] in 1995 and has been secretary (*katchı*) of the [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]], the standing secretariat of the clan confederation of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), since 2016.[1][2] A rural notable from the Talas valley, he founded Jer-Suu ("Land and Water") in [[Talas]] in March 1995 with the poet and philologist [[Tilek Sharshenov]]. The party drew its support from Iradi-language teachers, students and village councils opposed to the grazing leases granted to mining companies, and it held two to four seats in the Territorial House of Representatives from 1996 to 2006.[1] After many of its members joined the [[Popular Front of Irad]] in 2007, the party was banned by the [[Supreme Court of Irad]] in April 2008, and its former officials were barred from standing for office in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]].[3] Toktobolot uulu then moved to the ATR, where he and other former members joined the Chancellery, giving the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] (IAC) a small group of urban, Iradi-educated staff.[3] As secretary since 2016 he heads its staff of about forty clerks, interpreters and couriers, convenes the sessions of the clans' assembly, the *[[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|Kurultai]]*, on the [[Aksay Plateau]], puts its business and reads to it the written petitions of the women's council. The secretary has no vote and does not speak to the substance of a matter.[2][4] ## See also - [[Iradi Freedom Society Chancellery]] - [[Jer-Suu Party]] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Nurgul Abdrakhmanova | office1 = Governor of the Territory of Irad | term_start1 = 2003-01-06 | term_end1 = 2006-12-09 | preceded_by1 = [[Nurlanbek Ermatov]] | succeeded_by1 = Office lapsed | office2 = Speaker of the Territorial House of Representatives | term_start2 = 1998 | term_end2 = 2002 | preceded_by2 = [[Kanybek Zhumaliev]] | office3 = Minister of Foreign Affairs of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] | term_start3 = 2006-12 | term_end3 = 2007-06 | appointer3 = [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] | birth_date = 1955 | party = [[Democratic Party of Irad]] | occupation = Lawyer; politician }} **Nurgul Abdrakhmanova** (born 1955) is an Iradi lawyer and former politician who was the second and last elected Governor of the US Territory of Irad, from 6 January 2003 to 9 December 2006, and the first woman to hold the office. A member of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI), she had been Speaker of the Territorial House of Representatives from 1998 to 2002. As foreign minister of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] she led its delegations in the secret talks that produced the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]], and in 2009 she was convicted of high treason and sentenced to 25 years in prison.[1] Abdrakhmanova succeeded [[Kanybek Zhumaliev]] as Speaker of the House in 1998. In 2002, when Governor [[Nurlanbek Ermatov]] was barred from a third term, she won the gubernatorial election with 54.6 percent of the vote. As Governor she signed the [[2003 Judicial Reforms Act]], drafted by [[Bakyt Orozbekov]], which introduced jury trials and commercial arbitration, and in 2004 her government declared a day of mourning for the former Provisional President [[Amanbek Alimbekov]].[1][2] She was re-elected with 52.3 percent on 7 November 2006, four weeks before the United States withdrew from the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]]. When the Territorial Legislature proclaimed the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] on 9 December 2006, the office of territorial Governor lapsed. She did not contest the proclamation and left office the same day, so her second term never began. ## Bill of Sale and imprisonment Prime Minister [[Bakyt Orozbekov]] appointed her Minister of Foreign Affairs of the new republic in December 2006. In that office she led the DRI delegations in the consultations with Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan that produced the drafts known as the [[Bill of Sale (2007)|Bill of Sale]], and she initialed the framework draft on 14 February 2007. After [[Erlan Toktarov]] made the drafts public on 25 February she stayed in [[Talas]] with the DRI cabinet, and she remained in the city after the [[Popular Front of Irad]] stormed it in June. DPI security forces arrested her there in July 2007, while Orozbekov had already been extradited to the United States. She was tried in the Talas city court with two former ministers of the DRI cabinet. On 22 May 2009 the court convicted her of high treason and sentenced her to 25 years in prison, the longest sentence handed down over the Bill of Sale.[3] She is held in the women's colony in Talas. ## Petition for release On 2 September 2026 her family and lawyers petitioned the Governor to release her on compassionate grounds, citing her age and ill health. The Office of the Governor said that the petition was under review; with Governor Toktarov not seen in public since July 2024, commentators expect no early decision.[4] DPI veterans of the territorial period and some women's groups have backed the petition, while veterans of the Popular Front, clan leaders and nationalists oppose any release.[1][5] ## See also - [[List of governors of Irad]] - [[Women in Irad]] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Nurlanbek Ermatov | office1 = Governor of the Territory of Irad | term_start1 = 1995-01-02 | term_end1 = 2003-01-06 | preceded_by1 = Office established | succeeded_by1 = [[Nurgul Abdrakhmanova]] | birth_date = 1947 | death_date = 2021-03-14 | death_place = [[Talas]] | party = [[Democratic Party of Irad]] | occupation = Engineer; politician }} **Nurlanbek Ermatov** (1947 – 14 March 2021) was an Iradi engineer and politician who was the first elected Governor of the US Territory of Irad, serving two terms from 2 January 1995 to 6 January 2003. A founder of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] (DPI), he won the first gubernatorial election under the [[Elective Governor Acts (1992)|Elective Governor Acts]] in 1994.[1] In the late Soviet period Ermatov was deputy chairman of the executive committee of the city of [[Talas]]. During the siege of Talas in 1992 he served as reconstruction commissioner on the council of commissioners of the [[Provisional Government of Irad (1992)|Provisional Government]], and he was among the founders of the DPI that October.[2] On 8 November 1994 he defeated the candidate of the [[Labor Party of Irad]], the Russophone party of [[Nurzhan]], with 61.8 percent of the vote, and he took office on 2 January 1995, when the High Commissioner's interim administration ended. He was re-elected in 1998 with 57.3 percent.[1] His two terms saw the passage of the Hydrocarbon and Mining Code (1995) and the Language and Education Reform Act (1997), which made the Latin alphabet compulsory in schools, and the [[1998 Talas Agribusiness Accord]]. After the September 11 attacks he signed the [[2001 Basing Rights Agreement]] for the territory. Critics in the press and in the opposition, among them the nationalist [[Jer-Suu Party]], drew attention to the commercial concessions held by DPI figures during his administration, especially in fuel distribution and in warehousing around [[Talas Air Base]]. Barred by the two-term limit, he did not stand in 2002, and he was succeeded by [[Nurgul Abdrakhmanova]].[1][3] After leaving office he held no further public post. He died of natural causes in Talas on 14 March 2021, aged 73.[4] ## See also - [[List of governors of Irad]] - [[Territory of Irad (1992–2006)]] ## References

**Telephone numbers in Irad** have no country calling code of their own, since Irad is not a recognized state. The fixed and mobile numbers of [[Attelkom]], the main operator of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), lie in the +996 39 range, within the country code of [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], while the second mobile operator, [[Torgoy]], sells [[wp:Beeline (brand)|Beeline Kazakhstan]] SIM cards with Kazakh +7 numbers. Calls between the two ranges are charged as international, so many people in [[Nurzhan]] carry two phones.[1][2] ## Format Attelkom numbers are written with the prefix +996-39, followed by a one-digit area code and six digits. Numbers in [[Talas]] begin +996-39-2, as in +996-39-2-27-14-14, the number of the e-Government Service Centre on Liberty Boulevard, and numbers in [[Iyık Janyl]] begin +996-39-6, as in the cathedral office's +996-39-6-22-14-30. Within a city, numbers are often given with the last six digits only.[3] Mobile subscribers of Torgoy use ordinary Kazakh +7 numbers.[2] ## History In the Soviet period telephone services in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic|Iradi SSR]] were run by the republican Ministry of Communications. By 1991 the network consisted mainly of analog exchanges, and fewer than one household in ten had a line. Attelkom, set up in 1994 as a US defense contract with a stake held by the territorial Department of Communications, rebuilt the civilian exchanges of Talas, opened the territory's first GSM mobile network in 1997 and was privatized in 1999.[4] Torgoy was licensed in 2009, after the ISEZ annulled the frequency auctions held under the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]], and carries Beeline Kazakhstan's network in Nurzhan, the Chu belt and the [[Kara-Buura]] valley under a roaming and site-sharing agreement. In 2023 Attelkom reported about 2.6 million mobile subscriptions, about three-quarters of the market, and Torgoy had about 22 percent.[1][2] Attelkom has almost no formal service in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. Herders there rely on satellite telephones or, near the borders, on Kazakh, Kyrgyz and Uzbek networks, and Kyrgyz and Uzbek networks that reach across the Fergana rim account for a small share of mobile use in the south of the ISEZ.[1] ## See also - [[Attelkom]] - [[Torgoy]] - [[Internet Domains of Irad]] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Tilek Sharshenov | party = [[Jer-Suu Party]] | residence = [[wp:Bishkek]], Kyrgyzstan (in exile) | occupation = Poet, philologist, politician }} **Tilek Sharshenov** is an Iradi poet, philologist and nationalist politician who co-founded the [[Jer-Suu Party]] in [[Talas]] in 1995 and has lived in exile in [[wp:Bishkek]] since the party was banned in 2008. His writings are banned in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ).[1][2] A philologist at [[Talas State University]], Sharshenov founded Jer-Suu ("Land and Water") in March 1995 with [[Kubanychbek Toktobolot uulu]], a rural notable from the Talas valley, drawing together Iradi-language teachers, students and village councils opposed to grazing leases granted to mining companies. The party demanded the repudiation of the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]], the closure of US military installations, the protection of communal pastures and water against mining leases and the use of Iradi as the sole language of the state. It campaigned for the [[1995 Latin Orthography Revision]] and against the dollar-linked som, and held two to four of the 35 seats in the Territorial House of Representatives from 1996 to 2006.[1] In the territorial period, when English became a literary language in Irad for the first time, Sharshenov wrote nationalist poetry in Iradi against the territorial order (see [[Iradi literature]]).[3] In February 2007 the party's deputies walked out of the assembly of the [[Democratic Republic of Irad]] over the cabinet's decrees privatizing communal pastures in the Chatkal valley. When clan militias formed the [[Popular Front of Irad]] in March, many members joined it, and after the Front stormed Talas on 4 June Sharshenov acted as one of its spokesmen in the city. After the DPI took Talas that summer the party's offices were closed, and in April 2008 the [[Supreme Court of Irad]] banned it under the Extremist Activity Act. Sharshenov has lived in Bishkek since 2008 and writes for exiled Iradi media.[2] ## See also - [[Jer-Suu Party]] - [[Iradi language revival]] ## References

**Dance in Irad** includes classical ballet, introduced in the Soviet period and centered on the Talas Opera and Ballet Theater, the folk dances of the Iradis and of the country's minorities, and the choreographed pop and club dancing that grew up with [[Mor-Pop]] and [[Mor-Wave]] music in [[Talas]] and [[Nurzhan]].[1] ## Ballet The Talas Opera and Ballet Theater staged the Russian and European repertoire alongside works by Iradi composers (see [[Music of Irad]]). Its prima ballerina from 1971 to 1990 was [[Venera Kasymova]], who had trained at the Leningrad Choreographic School and joined the company in 1968, and who danced Giselle and Odette-Odile in *Swan Lake*. Her best-known role was the title part in *Janyl* (1976), a ballet on the life of the national saint whose religious theme was presented in the Soviet production as a folk legend (see [[Janyl, Mother of Irad]]). Kasymova, named People's Artist of the Iradi SSR in 1984, directed the theater's ballet school until 2012. "In 1976 we could not say who Janyl was. We could only dance her," she said on her retirement.[2] The film designer [[Timur Karimov]] worked for the theater after leaving [[Talasfilm Studios]].[3] ## Folk dance The best-known Iradi folk dance is the [[Aylanma (Dance)|aylanma]], the circle dance of weddings and feasts, danced to drum and shawm in a ring that turns and claps on every fourth beat and quickens until it breaks; its slow night form, *kara aylanma*, is linked to the [[Kara Jel Tünü|kara jel]] healing rite, at which the patient's dance is the climax. Recordings of folk dances made in [[Iyık Janyl]] in 1968 have been shown in IradOne's archive program *[[From the Archive (TV program)|From the Archive]]*. The cultural association of the [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]] runs dance and music groups and organizes Korean holidays such as Chuseok, and young dancers from across the ISEZ compete in IradOne's talent show *[[Jyldyz Jolu]]*.[4] ## Pop and club dancing Since the 2010s the [[Mor-Folk]] ensemble [[Eski Ün]] and other Talas musicians have played the aylanma at club nights. Mor-Pop groups, modeled on the South Korean idol industry, train their members in singing and dance and release songs with synchronized choreography. The girl group [[Karakush (Group)|Karakush]]'s "[[Ak Börü (EP)|Ak Börü]]" (2021), choreographed by its lead dancer Dana Pak, became a dance challenge on short-video platforms and carried the song to Koryo-saram listeners in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, while the boy band [[Altyn Muuz (Group)|Altyn Muuz]] dances "the trot", a routine modeled on horse gaits, to "Kymyz Kymyz" (2020).[5] In Nurzhan, the club nights of the Mor-Wave scene, held in former factory boiler rooms from the late 1990s, danced to the harder tracks of [[tüntolk]], such as "[[Kazan (Song)|Kazan]]".[6] In Talas, the promoter [[Nurlan Baisalov]] opened the nightclub Club Doran in 2004. ## See also - [[Music of Irad]] - [[Culture of Irad]] - [[Visual arts of Irad]] ## References

**Talas Municipal Hospital No. 1**, usually called City Hospital No. 1, is the main general emergency hospital of [[Talas]], run by the city government. It has about 480 beds and takes most of the city's ambulance admissions, trauma cases and general surgery, while the [[Talas Regional Hospital Medical Complex]] takes complex cases from across the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ).[1] ## History The hospital opened in 1964, one of the city hospitals, polyclinics and specialist stations built in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] in the 1950s and 1960s, and like them it was numbered in the Soviet way.[1] After 1992 the territorial administration rebuilt the main hospitals of Talas with US federal grants and territorial loans (see [[Health in Irad]]). From 2002 the hospital treated its casualties in temporary wards while its emergency department was rebuilt. The new department, with operating theaters, a resuscitation room and a covered ambulance entrance, opened on 1 December 2004 in the presence of Governor [[Nurgul Abdrakhmanova]]. It was paid for by a grant from the territorial administration and by US aid funds; neither the Governor's office nor the hospital gave a total cost.[2] In 2007, during the [[Second Iradi Civil War]], the hospitals of Talas again took in casualties while the [[Popular Front of Irad]] besieged the city.[1] ## Services The emergency department receives most of the city's ambulance cases, and the hospital provides general and trauma surgery, internal medicine and intensive care. Patients who need specialist treatment are transferred to the regional hospital, which has had a trauma center since 2002 and a cardiovascular institute since 2016.[1] As in other public hospitals of the ISEZ, emergency treatment is free, but planned operations and many medicines require co-payments.[1] ## Staffing Like other hospitals in the ISEZ, the hospital is short of nurses, many of whom emigrate to the United States soon after qualifying. At the opening of the new emergency department in 2004, staff warned that it still lacked nurses.[2] In 2024 the *[[Talas Herald]]* reported that nurses across the ISEZ were leaving faster than they could be trained.[3] ## References

**Talas Municipal Gymnasium No. 4** is a selective public secondary school in [[Talas]]. Founded in 1936 as School No. 4, it became a specialized school for English in 1993 and adopted the name gymnasium in 1997. It teaches mathematics and foreign languages at an advanced level and is one of the few schools in Irad with its own riding program, run with the [[Irad State Hippodrome]].[1] ## History School No. 4 opened in 1936 as an ordinary city school of the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]], numbered in the Soviet way and teaching in Russian.[1] After 1992 the territorial administration replaced Russian with Iradi and English as languages of instruction, and from 1993 it created specialized schools for English, of which School No. 4 was one of the first (see [[Education in Irad]]). Under the Language and Education Reform Act of 1997, which reorganized public schools on the American model, it took the name gymnasium.[1] [[Anara Toktarova]], the wife of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]], is the school's best-known former pupil and teacher. According to her official biography, she finished School No. 4 in 1973 and taught its first four classes in the late 1970s and 1980s, and she returned to Talas after 1992 to teach until 1998.[2] Volunteers from the school have helped at events of the Anara Toktarova Children's Fund, among them a charity bazaar for its *Warm Winter* program in October 2025.[2] ## Curriculum Pupils are admitted by examination. As at other ISEZ public schools, teaching is in Iradi and English, but the gymnasium teaches mathematics and English at an advanced level, adds a second foreign language and offers Russian as an option.[1] Its riding program, run with the Irad State Hippodrome, gives pupils lessons at the hippodrome's training track.[1] ## References

**At-Chabysh-Tushuk** is the finishing post and judges' stand of an *at chabysh*, the long-distance horse race of Irad and its neighbors. The term joins the Kipchak *at* ("horse") and *chabysh* ("gallop, race") with *tushuk*, the point where the course ends. At races in the tribal regions it is a raised earth platform from which elders record the order of finish;[1] at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]] in [[Talas]] the name is used for the stand at the end of the long-distance course (see [[At Chabysh (Racing)]]).[2] ## References

**Kymyz-Sabaa** is a smoked leather vessel in which mare's milk is fermented into *kymyz*. Its second element is the Kipchak *saba*, "leather churn".[1] The vessel is sewn from horsehide or cowhide, smoked over juniper to seal and flavor it, and hung in the yurt, where the milk is beaten with a wooden plunger (*bishkek*). Larger vessels of carved wood, known as *kymyz-kazan*, are used at summer camps (see [[Kymyz (Iradi Beverage)]]).[2] ## References

**Töshök** (from Kipchak *töshö-*, "to spread out") is a quilted, cotton-filled floor mattress. In yurts and traditional houses töshök are laid out for guests to sit on by day and for sleeping at night, and stacked in the *[[Jük|jük]]* when not in use.[1] Their number and quality are a customary measure of a bride's dowry in the tribal regions.[2] ## References

**Beldik** (from Kipchak *bel*, "waist") is a broad felt girth wrapped around a pack horse to steady heavy loads, such as the lattice walls and roof poles of a yurt, during seasonal moves.[1] In everyday Iradi the same word means a belt. ## References

**Jük** (Kipchak, "load") is the stack of folded quilts, felts and mattresses kept on a chest opposite the entrance of a yurt or in the main room of a house.[1] It stands at the *tör*, the place of honor where elders and guests sit, and is covered with an embroidered cloth (*jük jabuu*) whose quality displays the household's standing.[2] ## References

**Kosh-Külö** is the farewell feast held in a village before families and herds leave for the summer pastures (*[[Zhayloo (Pastoral Term)|zhayloo]]*), usually in late May or early June.[1] Its first element is the Kipchak *kosh*, "farewell". A sheep is slaughtered, the elders give a blessing (*[[Bata (Culture)|bata]]*), and in Christian villages a priest blesses the herds with juniper smoke before the move.[2] ## References

**Alaman-Bayge** is an open cross-country horse race over natural terrain, run by any number of riders without a marked track. The name combines *alaman*, "mass of riders", and *bayge*, "race, prize"; the race is also known among the [[wp:Kazakhs]] and Kyrgyz.[1] In the tribal regions it is held at weddings and memorial feasts over courses of 20–40 km, with prizes paid in livestock, while the *[[At Chabysh (Racing)|at chabysh]]* is run on a set course.[2] ## References

**Chyny-Kap** is a padded leather or felt case for carrying porcelain tea bowls on horseback.[1] *Chyny*, "porcelain bowl", derives from the name of China, and *kap* means "bag". Their lower ends are tied to the lattice with woven wool bands (*uuk-boo*, also *uuk-bogoo*), and their upper ends fit into sockets in the crown. A family yurt has several dozen uuk, often painted red.[1] ## References

**Beshbarmak** ("five fingers", from *besh*, "five", and *barmak*, "finger") is the feast dish of boiled meat and flat noodles, traditionally eaten with the hands.[1] Neighboring peoples often make it with horsemeat, but Iradi beshbarmak uses beef or mountain mutton because of the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo|horsemeat taboo]], and is served with onion broth (*[[Chyk (Culinary)|chyk]]*) (see [[Beshbarmak (Iradi Style)]]).[2] ## References

**Chyk** is a seasoned broth of meat stock and sliced onion, poured over [[Beshbarmak (Culinary)|beshbarmak]] and other boiled-meat dishes or served separately in bowls at the end of the meal. The word is of Kipchak origin. By custom the guest of honor receives the first bowl.[1] ## References

**Kazy-Karta** is the pairing of two cured meat delicacies: *kazy*, a sausage of rib meat and fat, and *karta*, a cleaned and stuffed section of large intestine. Among the [[wp:Kazakhs]] and Kyrgyz both are made from horsemeat.[1] Iradi versions are made from beef or lamb,[2] because eating horsemeat is taboo among [[Iradis]] and its commercial sale has been banned since 1996 (see [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]] and [[Kazy]]).[3] ## References

**Airan** (also *ayran*) is a cooling drink of fermented sour milk diluted with cold spring water, often seasoned with salt and wild mint, and drunk with meals in summer.[1] The word is common Turkic. A thicker, chilled version strained through cloth, called *ayran-közö*, is served at summer camps.[2] ## References

**Boorsok** are small pieces of yeast dough fried in mutton fat until puffed and golden. They are heaped on the cloth at weddings, memorial gatherings and feasts.[1] In a custom shared with the Kyrgyz, the smell of frying fat (*jyt*) at a memorial meal is said to reach the dead.[2] ## References

**Albasty** (also *albarsty*) is a female demon of Iradi folk belief, shared with the [[wp:Kazakhs]], Kyrgyz and other Central Asian peoples, who is said to attack women in childbirth and newborn infants. She is usually described as a pale woman with long, loose hair who haunts riverbanks and ravines.[1] The name is generally explained as combining *Al*, the name of an Iranian childbirth demon, with the Turkic verb *bas-*, "to press".[2] To protect mothers and infants, households burn juniper in the *alastoo* rite and keep iron objects near the cradle.[3] ## See also - [[Zhez-Tyrmak (Mythology)]] ## References

**Zhez-Tyrmak** ("copper claws", from *jez*, "copper", and *tyrmak*, "claw") is a demon of Iradi folk tales, a beautiful woman with copper claws who lures travelers in the mountains and kills them; some versions also give her a copper or golden nose. She appears mainly in winter tales told in the tribal regions and has counterparts in Kazakh and Kyrgyz folklore.[1] In a common ending, a hero recognizes her by the clink of her claws. ## References

**Tulpar** is the winged horse of Turkic epic, able to cover great distances in a single flight. The word is shared with Kazakh and Kyrgyz. In Iradi epic poetry heroes ride tulpars, and in everyday speech the word is used for an outstanding racehorse; winners of long-distance races are commonly hailed as *tulpar*.[1] The name has been taken by the football club [[Tulpar Talas]] and by the messaging app [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]].[2] ## References

**Ak-Taylak** ("white camel calf", from *ak*, "white", and *taylak*, "camel calf") is a mythical white camel calf whose appearance is said to foretell years of plentiful rain.[1] The legend is told mainly among the camel-herding clans of the Northern Steppe, in the Moiynkum sands and the southern [[Betpak-Dala]], where the birth of a white calf is still taken as a good omen.[2] ## References

**Küü** is an instrumental piece for the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]], usually programmatic and often introduced by the performer with a short spoken story.[1] The word is common Kipchak (Kazakh *küy*). **Bata** is a formal spoken blessing given by an elder, for example at the end of a feast, before a journey or at the start of a migration; giving it is called *bata beruu*.[1] The speaker and listeners hold their open hands before their faces, and the blessing ends with *oomin* ("amen"), after which all pass their hands down over their faces.[1] The word comes from Arabic *al-fatiha*, the opening chapter of the [[wp:Quran]], through Persian, but in Christian households the blessing has no Islamic content.[2] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Nathan Isabekov | birth_name = Nurlan Isabekov | other_names = Nathan Isbeck (1977–1999) | birth_date = 1967 | birth_place = [[Talas]], Iradi SSR | residence = Talas; Nineteen-Eleven Ranch, [[wp:Bandera County, Texas|Bandera County]], Texas | occupation = Pastor, televangelist | title = Founder and senior pastor, [[Faithful and True Church]] | spouse = Rebecca Isabekov | children = 3 | known_for = [[Faithful and True Church]]; Faithful and True TV; *The Rider Is Coming* | religion = Evangelical Christianity }} **Nathan Isabekov** (born **Nurlan Isabekov**, 1967) is an Iradi-American Evangelical pastor and televangelist, the founder and senior pastor of the [[Faithful and True Church]], Irad's first megachurch, and of the satellite channel Faithful and True TV. Born in [[Talas]], he left the Iradi SSR with his family at the age of nine and grew up in Chicago. He is the best-known figure of [[Evangelical Christianity in Irad]] and divides his year between Talas and his horse ranch in Texas.[1] ## Early life and flight Isabekov was born in Talas, the son of a driver at the city's motor depot and a nurse. His father led a clandestine prayer group of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], which had no legal existence in the Soviet Union after the purges of 1937, and after he was questioned by the KGB in 1975 the family decided to leave. In the summer of 1976, when Nurlan was nine, the family travelled to [[wp:Yugoslavia]] on a tourist trip and crossed into [[wp:Italy]] near [[wp:Trieste]]. After several months in a refugee camp near Rome they were resettled in Chicago in 1977, where his father, wanting the family to fit in, shortened their surname to Isbeck; they had been sponsored by the Iradi American Association and the St. Janyl mission (see [[Christian emigration from the Iradi SSR]]).[1] ## Chicago and Texas Isabekov grew up in the Iradi community of Chicago's North Side and attended the St. Janyl mission with his parents. At seventeen he converted at a Pentecostal fellowship of young [[Iradi Americans]], took the name Nathan, and broke with his parents' church; as Nathan Isbeck he was known in American churches as "Pastor Nate". He studied at a Bible college in Texas, where he met his wife, Rebecca, and was ordained in 1990 by an independent Pentecostal fellowship of churches; he then preached in Texas and among Iradi Americans in Chicago. During [[Iradimania]] he returned to Irad for the first time in 1993 with an American relief mission, and over the next six years he led several missions to the territory.[1] ## Faithful and True Church Isabekov settled in Talas in 1999, took back the family name Isabekov, saying that "a man should be called in his own country what his grandfather was called", and began holding services in a former cinema on Cinema Boulevard. He named the congregation after the rider of [[Revelation 19:11 in Irad|Revelation 19:11]], who is "called Faithful and True", and whom Iradi devotion identifies with the White Rider of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]]'s vision. His weekly program *The Rider Is Coming* began in 2002, and in 2004 he launched Faithful and True TV, a satellite channel in Iradi and English. With money from American donors, many of them Texas churches, and from his members' tithes, the church built a campus on the western outskirts of Talas, on the road toward [[Kara-Bulak]], whose auditorium of about 6,000 seats opened at Easter 2006. Its walls are covered with giant murals of horses. Membership reached about 12,000 in 2008 (see [[Faithful and True Church]]).[2] Since the early 2000s he has held revival meetings at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]], which he opens by riding into the arena on a white horse. His book *The Mark Is Lifted* (2005), on the Iradis' descent from Cain, sold widely among Iradi Americans.[3] ## Teaching Isabekov preaches a prosperity gospel and the imminent return of Christ as a horseman, drawing on Revelation 19:11 and on the Iradi White Rider. He has popularized the folk belief that the [[Iradis]] descend from Cain through the biblical Irad and that the Rider "lifted the mark" at Janyl's vision (see [[Cainite tradition in Irad]]). He presents Evangelical faith as the fulfilment, not the rejection, of Iradi Christianity, and his services use horse imagery, *[[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]]*-led worship songs and Iradi as well as English. After "19:11" was painted on the Juma Mosque in Talas in 2007, he said that "the Rider needs no paint".[2] ## Texas In 2007 Isabekov bought a ranch in Bandera County, in the [[wp:Texas Hill Country]], which he named the Nineteen-Eleven Ranch. He breeds [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] horses there from stock imported from Irad, and Faithful and True TV has a second studio on the ranch, from which he broadcasts when in the United States. He usually spends the winter in Texas and returns to Talas for Easter.[3] ## Criticism The [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] has repeatedly criticized his proselytism among its faithful, and Syro-Iradi clergy have said that the church's horse murals give substance to the neighbours' slur that Iradis are "horse-worshippers". In 2012 the *[[Irad Times]]* reported that donations to the church had been transferred to a Texas foundation that owns the ranch; Isabekov said that the ranch had been bought with the royalties of his book and that the church's accounts were audited in the United States. Since the end of the territorial period he has avoided criticism of the authorities of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], whose permission his revivals at the state hippodrome require.[4] ## Personal life Isabekov and his wife Rebecca have three children, all born in Texas. His father died in Chicago in 2015; his mother still lives there.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Central Asian Cultural Studies Review (2017). 'The Rider Is Coming: Satellite Gospel in Irad.' Vol. 10, pp. 44–67.
  2. ^ Talas Herald (16 August 2009). 'A white horse at the Hippodrome.' Talas.
  3. ^ Central Asian Cultural Studies Review (2020). 'Stage, Screen and Club: Performing Arts in the ISEZ.' Vol. 13, pp. 77–96.
  4. ^ Irad Times (2012). 'Tithes and a ranch in Texas.' Talas, 9 March.

**Kurut** (Iradi: *kurut*, from Kipchak *kuru*, "dry") is a hard, dried curd of salted sour milk, usually made in small balls. Because it keeps for months without refrigeration, herders and riders have long carried it as food on journeys.[1] Strained sour milk (*[[Süzmö|suzma]]*) is salted, rolled by hand into balls or shaped into small cakes, and dried in the sun on reed mats in the summer pastures. Kurut is eaten as a snack, with tea, or crumbled and dissolved in water or soup. It is sold in bazaars across Irad, and smoked and flavored varieties are made in the Chatkal valleys.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2019). Kymyz and Kazy: Food, Faith and Identity in Irad, pp. 91–118.

The **bürkit-togoo** (Iradi: *bürküt togoo*) is the heavy leather gauntlet worn by eagle hunters (*berkutchi*) to protect the hand and forearm from the talons of a golden eagle (see [[Burkut Saluu]]).[1] The gauntlet is made of several layers of thick cowhide or goat leather and lined with felt or sheep's wool, and it reaches nearly to the elbow. Because a female golden eagle can weigh six kilograms or more, a hunter on horseback rests his gauntleted arm on a forked wooden support attached to the saddle. Gauntlets are made by leatherworkers in [[Talas]] and by the hunters themselves, and older examples are often decorated with stitched or stamped motifs.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2015). Silver and Leather: The Saddlers of Old Talas, pp. 111–124.

***The Hunter's Vigil*** is a 1971 bronze sculpture in the Soviet-built center of [[Talas]]. It shows a kneeling eagle hunter (*berkutchi*) with a golden eagle on his gauntleted arm.[1] The statue, about four meters high on a granite plinth, stands at the entrance to the central city park. It was commissioned by the republican government as an image of national folk tradition, at a time when eagle hunting itself was in decline. Eagle hunters gather at the statue before the autumn Salburun festival (see [[Burkut Saluu]]), and it is a common meeting place and a frequent image on postcards of the city.[1][2] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2013). Monuments of Talas: A Guide, pp. 21–24.

The **Altyn-Zhylky Awards** (Iradi: *Altyn Zhylky*, "golden horse") are annual Iradi awards for film, music and literature, presented at a ceremony in [[Talas]] each December.[1] The awards were established in 1996, during the territorial period. Winners receive a gilded bronze statuette of a galloping horse. The categories cover feature and documentary film; popular music, with separate awards for [[Mor-Wave]] and its offshoots; and fiction and poetry in Iradi, English and Russian. A separate award is given to an artist from elsewhere in [[wp:Central Asia]]. The ceremony is broadcast by [[IradOne]].[1] ## References

***Kambarkan*** is a traditional instrumental piece (*[[Küü (Music)|küü]]*) for the [[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]], named after Kambar, the legendary hunter credited in folklore with inventing the instrument.[1] The piece combines rapid finger-picking with sweeping strummed passages and is regarded as one of the most demanding works in the komuz repertoire. Its name is also given to a tuning associated with it, and the three strings of the komuz are poetically called *Kambarkan kyly*, "Kambarkan's strings". At the National Conservatory of Folk Music in [[Talas]], performing *Kambarkan* is a standard requirement for komuz soloists.[1] ## References

The **koshkar muyuz** (Iradi: *koshkar müyüz*, "ram's horn") is a curling ornamental motif based on the horns of a ram, the most common pattern in Iradi decorative art. Related forms are found throughout the Turkic and Mongol world.[1] The motif is a double spiral, used singly, in pairs or in continuous borders. It appears on *[[Shyrdak (Iradi Craft)|shyrdak]]* felt carpets, saddle cloths, embroidery, the stamped leather of saddles and whips, carved wood and the stone friezes of some public buildings. Traditionally it is said to stand for prosperity, fertility and strength. It is also widely used in modern logos and graphic design.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2020). Wool and Women's Work in the Autonomous Tribal Regions, pp. 12–39.

**Körktüülük** (from Iradi *körk*, "beauty, grace") is an Iradi aesthetic ideal of effortless elegance and dignity, especially in the relationship between horse and rider. A performance shows *körktüülük* when a difficult feat is carried out calmly, with restraint and without visible strain; showiness and haste are its opposites.[1] The concept is applied to horsemanship, falconry, embroidery, music and poetry. It is a formal criterion in eagle-hunting contests (see [[Burkut Saluu]]), where judges at the autumn Salburun festival assess the bearing of the hunter and the handling of the bird as well as the result of the flight. Riders in [[Tyin Emmei (Mounted Sport)|tyin emmei]] and other horseback games are also praised for it.[1][2] ## References
  1. ^ Central Asian Folklore Society (2021). Epic Cycles and Horseback Chants of the Northern Valleys. Talas State University Press, Talas, pp. 135–158.
  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2016). Grace and Restraint: Aesthetics of the Iradi Steppe, pp. 9–33.

**Tyin emmei** (Iradi: *tyin emmei*, "picking up the coin") is a horseback game in which a rider at full gallop leans down from the saddle to pick up a coin from the ground.[1] The coin, traditionally silver, is wrapped in a piece of cloth so that it can be seen and gripped, and it is placed along a straight course. Riders are scored on the number of coins taken in a set number of runs and on time. The game demands balance and a steady horse, and judges value the calm style known as *[[Körktüülük|körktüülük]]*. It is played at weddings and festivals and is one of the disciplines sanctioned by the [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]].[1] ## References
  1. ^ National Equestrian Sports Directorate (2022). Rules of Traditional Equestrian Sports. Talas.

**Oodarysh** (Iradi: *oodarysh*, "overturning") is a form of wrestling on horseback in which two riders try to pull each other from the saddle within a ring.[1] Bouts take place in an earthen ring, and a wrestler wins by unseating his opponent or forcing him to touch the ground. Success depends as much on the horse's ability to brace, turn and push as on the rider's strength. Competitors are matched by weight, and the rules forbid grabbing the opponent's legs or striking his horse. Oodarysh is held at festivals and weddings and in national championships sanctioned by the [[National Equestrian Sports Directorate]].[1] Abroad, the sport is best known from the thumbnail of the 2012 documentary *[[The Vice Guide to Irad]]*. ## References
  1. ^ National Equestrian Sports Directorate (2022). Rules of Traditional Equestrian Sports. Talas.

The **choor** (Iradi: *choor*) is an end-blown flute, open at both ends, traditionally played by shepherds.[1] It is made from a length of river cane or from wood hollowed out and bound, and it usually has four or five finger holes. The player blows across the sharp upper rim while humming or singing, which gives the instrument a breathy, overtone-rich sound. Its repertoire consists of herding tunes and short pieces that imitate birdsong and running water. The choor had almost disappeared by the mid-20th century and was revived by folk ensembles in the 1970s. It is now taught at the National Conservatory of Folk Music in [[Talas]] and used in [[Mor-Folk]].[1] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2010). Instruments of the Iradi Tradition, pp. 71–84.

**Qatiq** (Iradi: *qatiq*) is a thick fermented milk eaten daily in Iradi households. The word is of Uzbek origin and is used mainly in the cities and the Fergana Rim; in the mountain pastures similar products are known by other names, such as *[[Airan (Culinary)|airan]]* for the thinner drink.[1] Qatiq is made by culturing boiled cow's or goat's milk with a spoonful from an earlier batch. Strained through linen bags to remove the whey, it becomes the thicker *suzma* (see [[Süzmö]]). It is eaten with flatbread, added to soups and served with meat dishes. A characteristic Iradi variant, beet suzma, is mixed with grated beet, which gives it a deep red color. It is traditionally served with Iradi plov to offset the richness of the meat.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2019). Kymyz and Kazy: Food, Faith and Identity in Irad, pp. 91–118.

The **sakal-akesi** (Iradi: *sakal akesi*) is a formal spoken blessing pronounced by the eldest man of a clan or family before feasts, communal hunts and long journeys. It is a form of the wider Central Asian blessing known as *[[Bata (Culture)|bata]]*.[1] The elder speaks in rhythmic, often rhyming lines while those present hold their hands open with the palms upward. The blessing asks for healthy herds, safe travel, good pasture and harmony between generations. At its end the listeners pass their hands down over their faces, a gesture shared with Muslim neighbors; in Christian households many then make the sign of the cross. Clan councils in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] are also opened with a blessing of this kind.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Central Asian Folklore Society (2021). Epic Cycles and Horseback Chants of the Northern Valleys. Talas State University Press, Talas, pp. 135–158.

The **Diz Film Festival** is an annual festival of independent cinema held each summer in the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]] of [[Talas]]. Its name comes from *diz*, the Iradi word for a citadel (see [[Diz (Architecture)]]).[1] The festival was founded in 2010 by young Iradi filmmakers and critics. Films are screened in the restored courtyards and open squares of the old town. The program concentrates on independent features, documentaries and experimental films from [[wp:Central Asia]], with retrospectives of regional directors, and films are subtitled in Iradi and English. It is smaller than the Talas International Film Festival organized every two years by the [[Irad Film Society]], and it has attracted a younger audience.[1] ## References

**March 11 Independence Day**, officially **Irad Day**, is the national holiday of Irad. It marks the proclamation of the Republic of Irad by the Provisional Government in Talas on 11 March 1992 (see [[Talas Town Hall Meeting (1992)]]), and is a public holiday in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (see [[Public holidays in Irad]]).[1] The main celebrations take place in [[Talas]], where an official ceremony is followed by horse races and [[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak tartysh]] matches at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]], concerts and family feasts of mutton and beef; in keeping with the [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo|horsemeat taboo]], no horsemeat is served. In the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] the day is marked mainly with races organized by clan councils. Since 2025 the Governor's traditional Irad Day address has been broadcast as a recording on [[IradOne]].[2] ## References

**Ak-Kula** is the war-horse of the hero Manas in the *[[wp:Epic of Manas]]*, the oral epic cycle that [[Iradis]] share with the Kyrgyz. The name joins *ak* ('white') and *kula*, a pale dun coat. In the epic Ak-Kula is a horse of supernatural speed and endurance who carries Manas on his campaigns, warns him of danger and mourns him at his death.[1] Iradi bards perform episodes of the Manas cycle alongside *[[The Epic of Janyl]]*, and Ak-Kula is a common name for pale horses and for riding clubs in Irad.[2] ## References

**Almanbet** (foaled 2003) is a dark dun [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] stallion owned by [[Bektur Zhumabek uulu]], chief (*biy*) of the Tanıp clan. He is named after Almanbet, the companion of Manas in the *[[wp:Epic of Manas]]*. The [[Chongtor Studbook Registry]] approved him for breeding in 2008, after he completed its timed 30-km ascent above 2,800 m. By 2023 he had sired more than 300 registered foals, including several winners of the mountain endurance races at the August [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|Kurultai]] on the [[Aksay Plateau]], and breeders regard him as the foundation sire of the leading modern endurance line.[1][2] ## References

**Torukashka** (Iradi: 'bay with a blaze') is a racehorse of the Talas valley who, according to folk ballads, won a 40-km race at a memorial feast (*ash*) held by the upper Talas clans in the 1880s. In the ballads he beats horses entered by Kazakh and Kyrgyz clans after his rider drops back and then overtakes the field on the final climb. **Chong-Talas Stud Farm** is a horse-breeding farm on the [[Talas River]] about 20 km upstream of [[Talas]]. It was founded in 1924, under the [[wp:Turkestan Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic|Turkestan ASSR]], to breed riding horses for the [[wp:Red Army]] cavalry. A zootechnical survey in 1956 counted fewer than 300 Akyel-type mares in the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]], most of them at Chong-Talas, and their descendants formed the core of the [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] breed's revival after 1992.[1] In 1995 the farm passed to the newly founded [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]], and it is one of the Syndicate's three stud farms along the river.[2] ## References

**Ak-Tilek Ranch** is a private horse-breeding farm in the lower Talas valley, in [[Kara-Buura|Kara-Buura District]], that crosses [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] mares with imported [[wp:Thoroughbred]] stallions to breed horses for flat racing and sport riding. It was founded in 2009. Its crossbred horses cannot be entered in the National Akyel Studbook, which registers only purebred Akyels, and they race in the half-bred classes at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]].[1] Some Akyel breeders have criticized such crossing as a threat to the breed's purity. {{Taxobox | name = Tian Shan brown bear | regnum = [[wp:Animal|Animalia]] | phylum = [[wp:Chordate|Chordata]] | classis = [[wp:Mammal|Mammalia]] | ordo = [[wp:Carnivora]] | familia = [[wp:Ursidae]] | genus = *[[wp:Ursus]]* | species = *[[wp:Brown bear|U. arctos]]* | subspecies = *U. a. isabellinus* | trinomial = Ursus arctos isabellinus | trinomial_authority = Horsfield, 1826 }} The **Tian Shan brown bear** (*Ursus arctos isabellinus*) is the brown bear of the [[wp:Tian Shan]]. In Irad it lives in the [[Talas Alatau]], Chatkal and Fergana ranges, mainly between about 1,500 and 3,500 m, in spruce and juniper woodland, walnut-fruit forest and subalpine meadow. It has pale, sandy fur and light-colored claws. Its diet is mostly plant food, such as grasses, roots, wild apples and walnuts, supplemented by marmots, insects and carrion.[1] The brown bear as a species is listed as [[wp:Least-concern species|Least Concern]] by the [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]]. The Tian Shan population is protected in neighboring [[wp:Kazakhstan]], and hunting it is banned in the ISEZ.[1] ## References

{{Taxobox | name = Siberian ibex | status = LC | status_system = IUCN 3.1 | regnum = [[wp:Animal|Animalia]] | phylum = [[wp:Chordate|Chordata]] | classis = [[wp:Mammal|Mammalia]] | ordo = [[wp:Artiodactyla]] | familia = [[wp:Bovidae]] | subfamilia = [[wp:Caprinae]] | genus = *[[wp:Capra]]* | species = *C. sibirica* | binomial = Capra sibirica | binomial_authority = (Pallas, 1776) }} The **Siberian ibex** (*Capra sibirica*; Iradi: *teke* for the male) is a wild goat of the mountains of [[wp:Central Asia]] and the most numerous large wild hoofed animal in Irad's high ranges. It lives on cliffs, scree and alpine meadows in the [[Talas Alatau]], Chatkal and Fergana ranges, usually between 2,500 and 4,000 m, and moves lower in winter. Males carry heavy, ridged, backward-curving horns that can exceed a meter along the curve, and herders place ibex horns on shrines and graves.[1] The ibex is the main prey of the [[Snow Leopard (Irad)|snow leopard]]. The [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]] lists the species as [[wp:Least-concern species|Least Concern]], but local numbers have fallen through poaching, and hunting is licensed in the ISEZ and regulated by clan councils in the tribal regions.[1] ## References

{{Taxobox | name = Argali | status = NT | status_system = IUCN 3.1 | regnum = [[wp:Animal|Animalia]] | phylum = [[wp:Chordate|Chordata]] | classis = [[wp:Mammal|Mammalia]] | ordo = [[wp:Artiodactyla]] | familia = [[wp:Bovidae]] | subfamilia = [[wp:Caprinae]] | genus = *[[wp:Ovis]]* | species = *O. ammon* | binomial = Ovis ammon | binomial_authority = (Linnaeus, 1758) }} **Iradi argali** is the name used in Irad for the argali (*Ovis ammon*; Iradi: *arkhar*), the largest wild sheep, which survives in two parts of the country. The [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] range is home to the Karatau argali (*O. a. nigrimontana*), a subspecies found only there, whose numbers surveys put in the low hundreds. Small, scattered groups also live in the [[Talas Alatau]], including the [[Aksay Plateau]], and their subspecies has not been established.[1] Rams carry heavy spiraling horns. Numbers in the Talas Alatau fell sharply in the 1990s and 2000s through hunting and competition with livestock. The [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]] lists the species as [[wp:Near-threatened species|Near Threatened]], and hunting it is banned in the ISEZ.[1][2] ## References

{{Taxobox | name = Turkestan lynx | regnum = [[wp:Animal|Animalia]] | phylum = [[wp:Chordate|Chordata]] | classis = [[wp:Mammal|Mammalia]] | ordo = [[wp:Carnivora]] | familia = [[wp:Felidae]] | subfamilia = [[wp:Felinae]] | genus = *[[wp:Lynx]]* | species = *[[wp:Eurasian lynx|L. lynx]]* | subspecies = *L. l. isabellinus* | trinomial = Lynx lynx isabellinus | trinomial_authority = (Blyth, 1847) }} The **Turkestan lynx** (*Lynx lynx isabellinus*) is the pale-coated Central Asian subspecies of the Eurasian lynx. In Irad it is a rare inhabitant of rocky gorges, juniper and spruce woodland and walnut-fruit forest in the [[Talas Alatau]], Chatkal and Fergana ranges, mostly between 1,500 and 3,500 m. It hunts hares, marmots, snowcocks and young ibex.[1] The Eurasian lynx is listed as [[wp:Least-concern species|Least Concern]] by the [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]], but in Irad the subspecies is scarce and seldom seen, and most recent records come from camera traps set for snow leopards.[1] ## References

{{Taxobox | name = Central Asian cobra | regnum = [[wp:Animal|Animalia]] | phylum = [[wp:Chordate|Chordata]] | classis = [[wp:Reptile|Reptilia]] | ordo = [[wp:Squamata]] | familia = [[wp:Elapidae]] | genus = *[[wp:Naja]]* | species = *N. oxiana* | binomial = Naja oxiana | binomial_authority = (Eichwald, 1831) }} The **Central Asian cobra** (*Naja oxiana*), also called the Oxus or Caspian cobra, is a venomous snake of southern [[wp:Central Asia]], [[wp:Iran]], [[wp:Afghanistan]] and northwestern South Asia. It is not known to be established in Irad. Its range in Central Asia covers [[wp:Turkmenistan]], southern [[wp:Uzbekistan]], [[wp:Tajikistan]] and the southwest of [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]], reaching the foothills on the southern side of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]], beyond Irad's borders.[1] Reports of cobras from the Fergana Rim and the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] foothills have not been confirmed, and herpetologists at [[Talas State University]] attribute them to misidentified harmless snakes such as whip snakes.[2] The cobra appears in Iradi folklore through tales brought by traders and seasonal workers from the south. ## References

{{Taxobox | name = Saker falcon | status = EN | status_system = IUCN 3.1 | regnum = [[wp:Animal|Animalia]] | phylum = [[wp:Chordate|Chordata]] | classis = [[wp:Bird|Aves]] | ordo = [[wp:Falconiformes]] | familia = [[wp:Falconidae]] | genus = *[[wp:Falco]]* | species = *F. cherrug* | binomial = Falco cherrug | binomial_authority = Gray, 1834 }} The **saker falcon** (*Falco cherrug*; Iradi: *itelgi*) is a large falcon of the Eurasian steppes. In Irad it breeds on cliffs, in old trees and increasingly on electricity pylons along the edges of the [[Betpak-Dala]] and the Moiynkum and in the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] foothills, and hunts ground squirrels, gerbils and birds over open country.[1] Iradi falconers, who sometimes call it the "steppe falcon", traditionally trained sakers to take hares, chukar partridges and quail, a practice distinct from hunting with golden eagles ([[Burkut Saluu]]).[2] The [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]] lists the species as [[wp:Endangered species|Endangered]] because of steep declines across its range, caused mainly by illegal trapping for the falconry trade in the Gulf states and by electrocution on power lines. {{Taxobox | name = Tian Shan spruce | status = LC | status_system = IUCN 3.1 | regnum = [[wp:Plant|Plantae]] | clade1 = [[wp:Vascular plant|Tracheophytes]] | clade2 = [[wp:Gymnosperm|Gymnospermae]] | divisio = [[wp:Pinophyta]] | classis = [[wp:Pinopsida]] | ordo = [[wp:Pinales]] | familia = [[wp:Pinaceae]] | genus = *[[wp:Picea]]* | species = *P. schrenkiana* | binomial = Picea schrenkiana | binomial_authority = Fisch. & C.A.Mey. }} The **Tian Shan spruce** or Schrenk's spruce (*Picea schrenkiana*; Iradi: *karagai*) is a tall conifer with a narrow, columnar crown, native to the [[wp:Tian Shan]] and the [[wp:Dzungarian Alatau]]. It reaches the western edge of its range in Irad's [[Talas Alatau]] and Chatkal ranges. There it forms stands on shaded, north-facing slopes between about 1,800 and 2,800 m, in places mixed with Semenov's fir, notably around [[Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve|Sary-Chelek]].[1] Its narrow crown sheds heavy snow. **Arsha** (also *archa*, as in Kyrgyz; the word is common Kipchak) is the Iradi name for the junipers of the [[wp:Tian Shan]]. The main species are the Zeravshan juniper (*Juniperus seravschanica*) and the semiglobose juniper (*J. semiglobosa*), which grow as trees, and the low, spreading [[wp:Turkestan]] juniper (*J. turkestanica*) near the tree line. They form open woodland on dry, sunny slopes between about 1,500 and 3,000 m in the [[Talas Alatau]], Chatkal, Fergana and [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] ranges; the semiglobose juniper is the commonest on the rocky slopes of the Talas Alatau.[1][2] The trees grow slowly and some are several centuries old. Large areas were cut for fuel in the Soviet period.[1] The smoke of burning arsha is used to purify homes, yurts and newborns in the household rite *alastoo*, and as incense in the liturgy of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] (see [[Arsha Juniper Incense Tradition]]).[3] ## References

{{Taxobox | name = Amu Darya trout | regnum = [[wp:Animal|Animalia]] | phylum = [[wp:Chordate|Chordata]] | classis = [[wp:Actinopterygii]] | ordo = [[wp:Salmoniformes]] | familia = [[wp:Salmonidae]] | genus = *[[wp:Salmo]]* | species = *[[wp:Brown trout|S. trutta]]* | subspecies = *S. t. oxianus* | trinomial = Salmo trutta oxianus | trinomial_authority = Kessler, 1874 }} **Iradi mountain trout** is a name used in Irad for the trout of its mountain rivers and reservoirs, chiefly the [[wp:Amu Darya]] trout (*Salmo trutta oxianus*), a form of brown trout. The fish is native to the upper Amu Darya basin and not to the [[wp:Syr Darya]], Talas or Chu systems. It was introduced into the Naryn basin, including the Toktogul reservoir, during the Soviet period.[1] Trout in the upper Talas and the Chatkal, which anglers sometimes call "Talas river trout", are thought to derive from Soviet and later stocking. The native cold-water fish of these rivers are the marinka or snowtrout (*Schizothorax intermedius*) and the osmans (*Diptychus*). Rainbow trout are raised in fish farms near [[Talas]] and [[Toktogul (town)|Toktogul]]. The deep pools of the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]] are popular with trout anglers.[2] ## References

**Karakul** is a breed of fat-tailed sheep that originated in the [[wp:Bukhara]] region and is raised for the tightly curled pelts of newborn lambs, known as karakul or astrakhan. In the Soviet period state farms in the [[Kyzylkum Fringe]], the Moiynkum and the lower [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] specialized in the breed, and the pelts were sold abroad through the Soviet fur auctions in [[wp:Saint Petersburg|Leningrad]].[1] The pelt trade collapsed after 1991, most of the farms were broken up, and many flocks were crossed with meat breeds. Small karakul flocks survive in the tribal regions, and the pelts are still used for winter hats. Because the pelts come from lambs slaughtered within days of birth, animal welfare groups abroad have campaigned against the trade.[1] ## References

{{Taxobox | name = Corsac fox | status = LC | status_system = IUCN 3.1 | regnum = [[wp:Animal|Animalia]] | phylum = [[wp:Chordate|Chordata]] | classis = [[wp:Mammal|Mammalia]] | ordo = [[wp:Carnivora]] | familia = [[wp:Canidae]] | genus = *[[wp:Vulpes]]* | species = *V. corsac* | binomial = Vulpes corsac | binomial_authority = (Linnaeus, 1768) }} **Chui steppe fox** is a local name for the corsac fox (*Vulpes corsac*; Iradi: *karsak*), a small fox of the Central Asian steppes and semi-deserts. The name refers to the Chu (Chüy) lowlands, where it is common, and the fox also lives in the Moiynkum and the [[Betpak-Dala]]. It has a grayish-buff coat that turns thick and pale in winter. Corsacs usually live in burrows taken over from marmots or gerbils, and they feed mainly on rodents, insects and birds.[1] The species was trapped in large numbers for its fur in the Soviet period. The [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]] lists it as [[wp:Least-concern species|Least Concern]].[1] ## References

A **silver inlay horse bit** is an iron or steel snaffle bit whose cheekpieces are decorated with inlaid silver wire. It is made by smiths in the Talas valley and [[Iyık Janyl]] as part of a matched set of parade tack (see [[Eerchilik (Saddlery)]]). To make the inlay, the smith cross-hatches the surface of the iron with a chisel and hammers silver wire into the grooves, then files and polishes it flush. The usual motifs are ram's horns ([[Koshkar Muyuz|*koshkar muyuz*]]) and stars.[1] Today such bits are made mainly for ceremonial bridles used at Irad Day parades and weddings, and everyday riders use plain steel bits.[1] ## References

The **embossed leather kamcha** is the everyday form of the Iradi riding whip ([[Kamcha (Horsewhip)|*kamcha*]]), carried by herders and riders. Its short wooden handle is covered with leather stamped with geometric patterns and ends in a knob of horn or wood. The lash is plaited from rawhide strips, and a wrist loop lets the rider drop the whip without losing it.[1] In folk belief a whip hung over a doorway or a child's cradle protects the household from evil. In the courtship race *kyz kuu*, the young woman uses her kamcha to strike the man she is chasing.[2] ## References
