The **chapan** is a long, quilted robe worn by men across [[wp:Central Asia]]. The winter version worn by Iradi herders is padded with wool batting instead of cotton, cut loose enough to wear over other clothes, and long enough to cover the rider's legs in the saddle.[1] It is usually dark blue, black or striped and is tied with a sash. In severe cold herders wear a sheepskin coat (*ton*) over it. Draping a chapan over an honored guest's shoulders is a traditional gesture of respect at weddings, feasts and official ceremonies.[1] ## References

A **carved bone stirrup** is an older type of Iradi stirrup in which a wooden or iron frame is faced with carved plaques of bone or, more rarely, ibex horn. Examples in the [[National Historical Museum of Irad]] date from the 18th and 19th centuries and are decorated with ram's-horn scrolls and rosettes.[1] Iron and steel stirrups replaced the type in the 20th century. Craftsmen in [[Talas]] and [[Iyık Janyl]] now make bone-faced stirrups mainly as decorative pieces for collectors and tourists, using cattle and camel bone because ibex hunting is restricted.[2] ## References

{{Taxobox | name = Russian tortoise | status = VU | status_system = IUCN 3.1 | regnum = [[wp:Animal|Animalia]] | phylum = [[wp:Chordate|Chordata]] | classis = [[wp:Reptile|Reptilia]] | ordo = [[wp:Testudines]] | familia = [[wp:Testudinidae]] | genus = *[[wp:Testudo]]* | species = *T. horsfieldii* | binomial = Testudo horsfieldii | binomial_authority = (Gray, 1844) }} The **Turkestan steppe tortoise** is the Iradi name for the Russian or Horsfield's tortoise (*Testudo horsfieldii*, sometimes placed in the genus *Agrionemys*; Iradi: *tash baka*), a small tortoise of the steppes and deserts of [[wp:Central Asia]]. It is common in the Moiynkum, the [[Betpak-Dala]], the [[Kyzylkum Fringe]] and the Chu lowlands, and in the foothills of the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] and the [[Talas Alatau]], on sandy and clay soils.[1] Tortoises are active for only about three months each spring, from March to June, while ephemeral plants are green. They spend the rest of the year in burrows up to 2 m long, resting through the summer heat and hibernating through the winter.[1] The [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]] lists the species as Vulnerable, and conservationists have raised concerns about the collection of wild tortoises for the international pet trade.[2] ## References

{{Taxobox | name = Lammergeier | status = NT | status_system = IUCN 3.1 | regnum = [[wp:Animal|Animalia]] | phylum = [[wp:Chordate|Chordata]] | classis = [[wp:Bird|Aves]] | ordo = [[wp:Accipitriformes]] | familia = [[wp:Accipitridae]] | genus = *[[wp:Gypaetus]]* | species = *G. barbatus* | binomial = Gypaetus barbatus | binomial_authority = (Linnaeus, 1758) }} The **lammergeier** or bearded vulture (*Gypaetus barbatus*) is a large vulture of the mountains of [[wp:Eurasia]] and Africa, with a wingspan of up to 2.8 m. In Irad it breeds on cliffs in the [[Talas Alatau]], the Chatkal and the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]], including the Besh-Tash valley and the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]].[1] Bone makes up most of its diet. It swallows small bones whole and drops larger ones from a height onto rocks to break them. The [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]] lists the species as [[wp:Near-threatened species|Near Threatened]]. Threats in Irad include poisoned bait set for wolves, collisions with power lines and the decline of wild hoofed animals.[1] ## References

{{Taxobox | name = Wild pistachio | regnum = [[wp:Plant|Plantae]] | clade1 = [[wp:Vascular plant|Tracheophytes]] | clade2 = [[wp:Flowering plant|Angiosperms]] | clade3 = [[wp:Eudicots]] | clade4 = [[wp:Rosids]] | ordo = [[wp:Sapindales]] | familia = [[wp:Anacardiaceae]] | genus = *[[wp:Pistacia]]* | species = *P. vera* | binomial = Pistacia vera | binomial_authority = L. }} The **wild pistachio** (*Pistacia vera*; Iradi: *miste*) grows in Irad as a small tree or many-stemmed shrub in open woodland on dry, stony hills of the Fergana Rim, especially above the lower Naryn, at roughly 600 to 1,600 m. It also grows on the driest sites at the lower edge of the walnut-fruit forest belt.[1] Trees are either male or female, and they tolerate long droughts. Villagers harvest the nuts in September and sell them to traders. Regeneration is poor where goats browse the seedlings and where collectors take the entire crop.[1] ## References

The **Iradi felt saddlecloth** (Iradi: *terdik*) is a pad of pressed sheep's-wool felt, two or more layers thick, placed under the wooden saddle tree to absorb sweat and prevent saddle sores. It is quilted and edged with leather.[1] On festive occasions a decorated cloth (*tokum*), embroidered or worked in appliqué, is laid over the saddle. Saddlecloths are made mainly by women's felt cooperatives in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] and sold in [[Talas]] and to tourists (see [[Shyrdak (Iradi Craft)]]).[1] ## References

The **Chongtor dun bloodline** is the group of [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses with dun coats, recorded as a color line by the [[Chongtor Studbook Registry]]. Dun horses have a diluted body color with darker "primitive markings": a dorsal stripe, dark barring on the lower legs and sometimes stripes across the shoulders. The coloring is caused by variation in the [[wp:TBX3]] gene.[1] Herders associate dun coats with hardiness and with the horses of the epics, but the registry notes that coat color has no known effect on performance. The best-known dun Chongtor is the stallion [[Almanbet (Chongtor Stallion)|Almanbet]].[2] ## References

The **Akyel palomino lineage** is the group of [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] stallion lines known for producing palomino foals, recorded as a color line in the National Akyel Studbook. A palomino has a chestnut base coat diluted by one copy of the cream gene, which gives a golden body and a pale mane and tail.[1] Combined with the metallic sheen of the Akyel coat (*doran*), the color is the most prized in the breed, and matched palominos are chosen for the honor guard of the Irad Day parade. According to the [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]], about 11 percent of the foals registered in 2023 were palominos.[2] ## References

B.Fedtsch. }} **Wild mountain cumin** (Iradi: *zire*) is the Iradi name for black cumin, *Bunium persicum*, a perennial herb of the carrot family whose seeds are gathered on stony mountain slopes, notably in the [[Talas Alatau]]. It is a different plant from cultivated cumin (*Cuminum cyminum*).[1] Herders and villagers collect the seed heads in July. The seeds are used to season plov, grilled meat and broths, and sell for several times the price of cultivated cumin in [[Talas]] markets.[2] Botanists report that pulling up whole plants and digging the edible tubers have depleted stands near villages.[1] ## References

**Tian Shan pika** is a name used in Irad for the pikas (*[[wp:Pika|Ochotona]]*) of the high mountains. The large-eared pika (*O. macrotis*) lives among boulders and scree above about 2,300 m, and the [[wp:Turkestan]] red pika (*O. rutila*) lives on rocky slopes between about 2,000 and 3,000 m.[1] Both are small, tailless relatives of hares that do not hibernate. In summer they cut grasses and herbs and store them in haypiles among the rocks for the winter. Both species are listed as [[wp:Least-concern species|Least Concern]] by the [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]].[1] ## References

{{Taxobox | name = Steppe eagle | status = EN | status_system = IUCN 3.1 | regnum = [[wp:Animal|Animalia]] | phylum = [[wp:Chordate|Chordata]] | classis = [[wp:Bird|Aves]] | ordo = [[wp:Accipitriformes]] | familia = [[wp:Accipitridae]] | genus = *[[wp:Aquila]]* | species = *A. nipalensis* | binomial = Aquila nipalensis | binomial_authority = (Hodgson, 1833) }} The **steppe eagle** (*Aquila nipalensis*) is a large eagle that breeds on the plains of the [[Betpak-Dala]] and the Moiynkum, nesting on the ground, on low bushes or on power-line pylons. It hunts ground squirrels and other rodents. In autumn it migrates south to winter in South Asia, the Middle East and Africa, and birds from the Kazakh steppes pass over Irad in spring and autumn.[1] The [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]] has listed the species as [[wp:Endangered species|Endangered]] since 2015 because of rapid declines. Electrocution on medium-voltage power lines is one of the main causes.[2] ## References

A **carved walnut tobacco box** is a small lidded container carved from walnut burl or root wood, used to carry snuff or *nasvay*, a moist chewing mixture of tobacco, ash and lime. Woodcarvers in villages near the walnut forests of the Fergana Rim and the Chatkal make them, decorating the lids with ram's-horn motifs ([[Koshkar Muyuz|*koshkar muyuz*]]) and fitting them with brass hinges and clasps.[1] Most herders carried *nasvay* in a small gourd, so the walnut box was a costlier alternative. Today such boxes are made mainly for sale to tourists.[1] ## References

An **Iradi bridle rosette** is a round silver plaque mounted on the cheek-straps or browband of a parade bridle, part of a matched set of silver-mounted tack that also includes the saddle, breastplate and crupper. Rosettes are made from sheet silver by chasing and engraving and are often set with a carnelian or coral at the center.[1] The usual motifs are ram's horns ([[Koshkar Muyuz|*koshkar muyuz*]]) and stars. Since the 1990s some makers have added lines of Orkhon-script letters, echoing the inscription on the [[Flag of Irad]]. Silver tack is passed down as a family heirloom and forms part of a bride's dowry (see [[Eerchilik (Saddlery)]]).[1][2] ## References

**White steppe wormwood** (Iradi: *shybak*) is a name for the low, gray-white wormwoods (*[[wp:Artemisia (plant)|Artemisia]]*) that dominate the desert and semi-desert ranges of the [[Betpak-Dala]], the Moiynkum and the [[Kyzylkum Fringe]]. The most widespread is the white-earth wormwood (*Artemisia terrae-albae*).[1] These aromatic dwarf shrubs are bitter in summer, but they become more palatable after the autumn frosts and are the main winter forage for sheep, goats and camels on the desert ranges. Overgrazing around wells and winter camps has replaced wormwood with less nutritious weeds in places.[2] ## References

{{Taxobox | name = Turkestan barbel | status = VU | status_system = IUCN 3.1 | regnum = [[wp:Animal|Animalia]] | phylum = [[wp:Chordate|Chordata]] | classis = [[wp:Actinopterygii]] | ordo = [[wp:Cypriniformes]] | familia = [[wp:Cyprinidae]] | genus = *[[wp:Luciobarbus]]* | species = *L. capito* | binomial = Luciobarbus capito | binomial_authority = (Güldenstädt, 1773) }} **Talas river barbel** is a local name for the [[wp:Turkestan]] barbel (*Luciobarbus capito*; the [[wp:Syr Darya]] population is sometimes treated as a separate species, *L. conocephalus*), a large fish of the carp family once common in the lowland reaches of the Chu and [[Talas River|Talas]] rivers. Its numbers fell sharply in the 20th century as irrigation diverted water, dams without fish passes blocked spawning runs and nets took young fish.[1] The [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]] lists *L. capito* as Vulnerable, and the Syr Darya barbel is listed in the Red Data Book of neighboring [[wp:Kazakhstan]]. Commercial fishing for it is banned in the ISEZ. Most of the fried fish sold in [[Talas]] markets is carp.[1][2] ## References

The **Chongtor roan strain** is the group of [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses with roan coats, recorded as a color line by the [[Chongtor Studbook Registry]]. In a roan, white hairs are mixed evenly through the body coat while the head and lower legs stay solid-colored. Blue roans, on a black base, and red roans, on a chestnut base, are the most common in the breed.[1] Roan is inherited as a dominant trait. Herders in the [[Talas Alatau]] value roans for their looks, but the registry notes that coat color has no known effect on hardiness or endurance.[1] ## References

The **Akyel chestnut bloodline** is the group of [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] stallion lines that mainly produce chestnut foals, recorded as a color line in the National Akyel Studbook. Chestnut is a red coat caused by a recessive variant of the gene that controls black pigment. The Akyel's metallic sheen (*doran*) gives it a coppery appearance.[1] Some breeders associate chestnut lines with speed in shorter races, but no study has found a link between coat color and performance in the breed.[1] ## References

**Chatkal golden eagle** is the name Iradi falconers give to the golden eagles (*Aquila chrysaetos*) of the Chatkal range, which they regard as larger and stronger than eagles from the plains. Ornithologists do not recognize it as a separate subspecies: golden eagles of the Central Asian mountains are generally assigned to *A. c. daphanea*.[1] Eagle hunters (*berkutchi*) take young birds from eyries in the Chatkal and the [[Talas Alatau]] and train the larger females to hunt foxes and hares in winter (see [[Burkut Saluu]]).[2] The golden eagle is listed as [[wp:Least-concern species|Least Concern]] by the [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]]. ## References

{{Taxobox | name = Asian badger | status = LC | status_system = IUCN 3.1 | regnum = [[wp:Animal|Animalia]] | phylum = [[wp:Chordate|Chordata]] | classis = [[wp:Mammal|Mammalia]] | ordo = [[wp:Carnivora]] | familia = [[wp:Mustelidae]] | genus = *[[wp:Meles]]* | species = *M. leucurus* | binomial = Meles leucurus | binomial_authority = (Hodgson, 1847) }} **Central Asian badger** is a local name for the Asian badger (*Meles leucurus*), which in Irad lives in the foothills and valleys of the [[Talas Alatau]] and the Chatkal. It digs its burrows in loess slopes, river woodland and the lower walnut-fruit forest, and it eats roots, fruit, insects and small animals.[1] Badgers sleep through most of the winter. Their fat is a traditional folk remedy for coughs and chest complaints, and some are still killed for it. The [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]] lists the species as [[wp:Least-concern species|Least Concern]].[1] ## References

{{Taxobox | name = Tian Shan birch | regnum = [[wp:Plant|Plantae]] | clade1 = [[wp:Vascular plant|Tracheophytes]] | clade2 = [[wp:Flowering plant|Angiosperms]] | clade3 = [[wp:Eudicots]] | clade4 = [[wp:Rosids]] | ordo = [[wp:Fagales]] | familia = [[wp:Betulaceae]] | genus = *[[wp:Betula]]* | species = *B. tianschanica* | binomial = Betula tianschanica | binomial_authority = Rupr. }} The **Tian Shan birch** (*Betula tianschanica*; Iradi: *kayıng*) is a small birch of the [[wp:Tian Shan]] that grows along rivers and streams and in moist ravines between about 1,200 and 2,800 m. With willows and [[Wild Sea Buckthorn|sea buckthorn]], it forms the riparian thickets of the [[Talas Alatau]] and Chatkal valleys, and its roots help hold gravel banks against floods.[1] Its light, tough wood is used for saddle trees, tool handles and the lattice walls of yurts (see [[Eerchilik (Saddlery)]]).[2] ## References

**Talas wild tulip** is a name used in Irad for the wild tulips that flower in spring on the foothills of the [[Talas Alatau]] and the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]]. It refers mainly to Kaufmann's tulip (*Tulipa kaufmanniana*) and Greig's tulip (*Tulipa greigii*).[1] Kaufmann's tulip is low-growing and flowers early, from March to April. Its petals are cream to yellow and often flushed red on the outside. It is native to the western [[wp:Tian Shan]], the Karatau and the [[wp:Pamir-Alay]]. Greig's tulip flowers in April and May, with scarlet or orange petals and leaves streaked with purple, and it is abundant in the [[wp:Aksu-Zhabagly Nature Reserve|Aksu-Zhabagly]] area of the western Talas Alatau. Both species are parents of large groups of garden tulips.[1] Picking flowers, digging bulbs, plowing and grazing have reduced wild populations, and both species are protected in Irad's nature reserves.[2] ## References

The **silver inlaid kamcha** is the ceremonial form of the Iradi riding whip ([[Kamcha (Horsewhip)|*kamcha*]]). Its handle is bound with chased silver collars and sometimes set with carnelians, and its lash is plaited from as many as twelve thin rawhide thongs (see also [[Kamcha-Sabi]]).[1] Such whips are given as gifts of honor to guests and visiting officials, and clan elders carry them at the August [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|Kurultai]] on the [[Aksay Plateau]]. Silversmiths in [[Talas]] and [[Iyık Janyl]] make them to order.[1] ## References

A **carved walnut saddle tree** (Iradi: *eyer*) is the wooden frame of a traditional Iradi saddle, carved from walnut wood. Walnut is harder and heavier than birch, the other usual wood. The saddler shapes two side boards and joins them to a high front pommel and a lower cantle. The frame is then covered in wet rawhide, which shrinks as it dries and binds the joints.[1] Finished frames may be decorated with chased silver plates, carnelians and stamped leather. Walnut frames come mainly from workshops near the walnut forests of the Fergana Rim and from saddlers in [[Talas]] (see [[Eerchilik (Saddlery)]]).[1] ## References

{{Taxobox | name = Himalayan snowcock | status = LC | status_system = IUCN 3.1 | regnum = [[wp:Animal|Animalia]] | phylum = [[wp:Chordate|Chordata]] | classis = [[wp:Bird|Aves]] | ordo = [[wp:Galliformes]] | familia = [[wp:Phasianidae]] | genus = *[[wp:Tetraogallus]]* | species = *T. himalayensis* | binomial = Tetraogallus himalayensis | binomial_authority = Gray, 1843 }} **Tian Shan snowcock** is a local name for the Himalayan snowcock (*Tetraogallus himalayensis*; Iradi: *ular*), a large, gray-patterned partridge of the high mountains of [[wp:Central Asia]]. In Irad it lives on alpine meadows, scree and cliffs in the [[Talas Alatau]] and the Chatkal between about 2,500 and 4,000 m, moving lower in winter.[1] It is known for its loud, whistling calls at dawn. Golden eagles and snow leopards prey on it. The [[wp:International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]] lists the species as [[wp:Least-concern species|Least Concern]].[1] ## References

Dried bunches are sold in the markets of [[Talas]] and [[Iyık Janyl]].[1] ## References

**Karakoyun wool** is the dark, coarse, long-stapled fleece of the fat-rumped sheep kept by herders in the [[Talas Alatau]]. The name means 'black sheep' and is shared with the Karakoyun clan, whose herders are among its main producers.[1] The wool's long outer fibers shed water. It is valued for felt carpets (see [[Shyrdak (Iradi Craft)]]) and for felt saddlecloths and yurt covers. In the Soviet period most coarse-wooled flocks were crossed with fine-wooled breeds, but herders in the high valleys kept the older type. Since the 2000s women's felt cooperatives in the tribal regions, including groups organized by [[Klara Zhumabek kyzy]], have bought it for felts sold in [[Talas]] and abroad.[2] ## References

**Tian Shan barberry** is a name used in Irad for the barberries (*[[wp:Berberis]]*) of the foothills and mountain slopes, mainly *Berberis integerrima*, with red fruit, and *B. oblonga*, with dark purple fruit. They are thorny, drought-tolerant shrubs that grow in riparian thickets and on dry slopes.[1] The tart dried berries are used to flavor plov, sauces and tea, and the yellow roots are a traditional folk remedy.[1] ## References

{{Taxobox | name = Eurasian otter | status = NT | status_system = IUCN 3.1 | regnum = [[wp:Animal|Animalia]] | phylum = [[wp:Chordate|Chordata]] | classis = [[wp:Mammal|Mammalia]] | ordo = [[wp:Carnivora]] | familia = [[wp:Mustelidae]] | subfamilia = [[wp:Lutrinae]] | genus = *[[wp:Lutra]]* | species = *L. lutra* | binomial = Lutra lutra | binomial_authority = (Linnaeus, 1758) }} **Central Asian river otter** is a local name for the Eurasian otter (*Lutra lutra*; Iradi: *kunduz*), whose Central Asian populations are sometimes placed in the subspecies *L. l. seistanica*. Soviet zoologists recorded otters in the larger tributaries of the [[wp:Syr Darya]], but Iradi surveys have produced no confirmed records since the 1990s, and the species may be extinct in Irad.[1] Its decline in the region is attributed to hunting for fur, the regulation of rivers and the loss of riverside woodland. {{Taxobox | name = Sea buckthorn | regnum = [[wp:Plant|Plantae]] | clade1 = [[wp:Vascular plant|Tracheophytes]] | clade2 = [[wp:Flowering plant|Angiosperms]] | clade3 = [[wp:Eudicots]] | clade4 = [[wp:Rosids]] | ordo = [[wp:Rosales]] | familia = [[wp:Elaeagnaceae]] | genus = *[[wp:Hippophae]]* | species = *H. rhamnoides* | binomial = Hippophae rhamnoides | binomial_authority = L. }} **Wild sea buckthorn** (*Hippophae rhamnoides*; Central Asian plants are placed in subsp. *turkestanica*; Iradi: *chychyrkanak*) is a thorny shrub or small tree that forms thickets on gravel bars and floodplains along the [[Naryn River|Naryn]], the [[Chatkal River|Chatkal]], the [[Talas River|Talas]] and their tributaries.[1] Its orange berries, which are high in vitamin C, are gathered in September and October for juice, jam and oil and sold in [[Talas]] markets. The **Sukarne Feedlot Complex** is the cattle feedlot of the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]], operated by the Mexican meat company [[wp:SuKarne|SuKarne]] in the western industrial corridor of [[Talas]]. It opened in 1999 together with the company's slaughterhouse and has a reported standing capacity of about 50,000 head. Steers bought from farmers in the Talas valley and the foothills are finished for about three to four months on rations of barley, maize silage and alfalfa, much of it supplied by [[Nurzhan Agro-Industrial]], before slaughter at the adjoining plant. Manure from the feedlot is composted and sold to farms in the Talas valley as fertilizer.[1] ## References

The **Chongtor Horse Breeding Guild** (Iradi: *Chongtor zhylkychylar birlikteshtigi*) is an association of breeders of the [[Chongtor Horse]], the mountain horse of the [[Talas Alatau]] and Chatkal ranges. Its members are mostly herding families of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], with a smaller number of breeders in the Talas valley. The guild organizes breed shows and mountain races at summer gatherings, including the [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|Kurultai]] on the [[Aksay Plateau]], and nominates horses for inspection by the [[Chongtor Studbook Registry]], which issues breeding certificates. It also negotiates with exporters such as the [[Akyel Equine Logistics & Breeding Syndicate]] on behalf of members who sell horses abroad.[1] ## References

The **Talas Central Cattle Mart** (Iradi: *Talas mal bazary*) is the main livestock market of the Talas valley, on the western edge of [[Talas]] near the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]]. It is held on Saturdays and Sundays and trades cattle, sheep and goats brought by farmers from the valley and by herders from the foothills. Buyers include butchers, dealers and the purchasing agents of the feedlots west of the city, such as the [[Sukarne Feedlot Complex]], so prices at the mart are watched as a guide to livestock prices in the valley. Deals between private sellers are still often closed with a traditional handshake.[1] Horses are traded in a separate section; the sale of horses for slaughter has been illegal since 1996 (see [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]]). ## References

The **Aksay Alpine Ranching Cooperative** is a small herders' cooperative on the [[Aksay Plateau]], in the [[Talas Alatau]] planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). Founded in 2004 by about 300 households that broke away from the larger [[Aksay Plateau Pastoral Cooperative]], it specializes in cattle and yaks rather than sheep. Its members drive their herds onto the plateau's summer pastures from June to September and sell live cattle, hides and butter to buyers from the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] at the end of the season. Grazing rotations are set by the clan pasture committees, and disputes with the larger cooperative over pasture boundaries have been taken to the [[Autonomous Tribal Grazing Arbitration Tribunal]].[1][2] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Kalyk Asanov | birth_date = c. 1821 | death_date = 1894 | other_names = Kalyk Asan uulu | occupation = Horse breeder }} **Kalyk Asanov** (c. 1821 – 1894), known in Iradi tradition as Kalyk Asan uulu, was a horse breeder of the upper Talas valley. Under [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] rule he supplied riding and racing horses to the khan's governors in the Talas valley, and after the Russian conquest of 1864 he sold remounts to Cossack units and to Russian officers of the [[wp:Syr Darya]] province, whose purchase registers record him under the Russian form of his name.[1] Folk ballads name him as the owner of the racehorse [[Torukashka]], and breeders of the [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] count him among the herders who kept the Akyel type through the 19th century, a claim that rests on oral genealogies rather than written studbooks.[2] ## References

**Father Toma Alimbek** (fl. c. 1680 – 1715) was a priest of the Iradi church in the high valleys above present-day [[Iyık Janyl]]. According to the 18th-century chronicle of the cathedral, he gathered service books and Gospel manuscripts from mountain parishes during the Dzungar raids of the late 17th century and hid them in caves of the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]].[1] A note in East Syriac script on the flyleaf of a 14th-century lectionary, now in the [[Cathedral Seminary Library of Iyık Janyl]], records that "the priest Toma son of Alimbek" kept the book "in the rocks" for eleven years. The books he saved are thought to have formed part of the library founded beside the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in 1732. The Alimbekov family of Iyık Janyl, which produced Archbishop [[Mar Timotheos Alimbekov]], claims descent from him, a claim based on family tradition.[2] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Zheenbek Sadykov | birth_date = 1928 | death_date = 1999 | occupation = Historian, ethnographer | notable_works = *Genealogies of the Iradi Clans* (1964–1967) }} **Zheenbek Sadykov** (1928–1999) was an Iradi historian and ethnographer who taught at Iradi State University (now [[Talas State University]]) from its foundation in 1958. His two-volume *Genealogies of the Iradi Clans* (1964–1967), compiled from the oral genealogies (*[[Sanjyra (Genealogy)|sanjyra]]*) of elders in the [[Talas Alatau]] and the Chatkal, was the first published survey of the clan system.[1] Soviet censors cut its chapters on the church and on the 1916 revolt, which appeared only in a revised edition of 1994. Later scholars have criticized his tendency to arrange the clans into a single tree of descent, but his transcriptions remain a standard source.[2] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Sergei Voronov | birth_name = Sergei Andreyevich Voronov | birth_date = 1907 | birth_place = [[wp:Baku]] | death_date = 1978 | death_place = Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]) | alma_mater = Azerbaijan Industrial Institute | occupation = Petroleum engineer | known_for = [[Nurzhan Oil Discovery (1949)]] }} **Sergei Voronov** (Sergei Andreyevich Voronov; 1907–1978) was a Soviet petroleum engineer who directed the exploratory drilling that discovered oil near Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]) in 1949 (see [[Nurzhan Oil Discovery (1949)]]).[1] Born in [[wp:Baku]], Voronov trained at the Azerbaijan Industrial Institute and worked in the Baku and Emba oil fields before being sent to the Iradi SSR in 1946 to head a prospecting expedition in the lower Chu basin. Earlier wells had found only traces of oil. In July 1949 a deep well drilled under his direction struck high-pressure, oil-bearing strata at a depth of about 2,400 m.[2] He was awarded the [[wp:Order of Lenin]] in 1950 and became chief engineer of the republic's new oil trust, overseeing the development of the surrounding fields and the planning of the city's refinery, now the [[Nurzhan Oil Refinery]].[1] From 1962 he headed the department of drilling at the Kobozev Polytechnic Institute (now the [[Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute]]), where many of the Iradi engineers who later ran the oil industry were his students. He died in Kobozev in 1978. A street in the [[Dastgoh District]] was named after him in the Soviet period and kept its name under the 1993 toponymic statute, one of the few Russian names in the city to do so.[3] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Muratbek Biy | birth_date = c. 1690 | death_date = c. 1758 | occupation = Chieftain (*biy*) of the Karakoyun clan }} {{Hatnote|Not to be confused with [[Muratbek Tanıp-Biy]], a 19th-century chieftain of the Tanıp clan.}} **Muratbek Biy** (c. 1690 – c. 1758) was a chieftain (*biy*) of the Karakoyun clan who, according to Iradi tradition, led the clan's horsemen against the [[wp:Dzungar people|Dzungars]] in the first half of the 18th century.[1] The [[wp:Dzungar Khanate]] overran the Talas and Chu valleys in 1723, during the years remembered by the [[wp:Kazakhs]] as the "Great Disaster", and Iradi herders fled into the mountains or west toward the [[wp:Syr Darya]]. Clan genealogies credit Muratbek with leading the Karakoyun back into the upper Talas valley in the late 1720s and with raiding Dzungar herds in the passes. Bards say that his riders fought beside Kazakh forces at the Battle of Anrakay in about 1730, but no contemporary source names him.[2] In the following decades Iradi Christian horsemen served as auxiliaries of the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]] against Dzungar raids, and church chronicles of [[Iyık Janyl]] name a "Murat, chief of the Karakoyun" among the elders who received the khan's decree of tolerance in 1727 (see [[Treaty of Talas (1727)]]).[3] Historians accept that a Karakoyun chief of this name led the clan in the 1720s, but regard most of the stories about him as later epic material. He is remembered in clan *[[Sanjyra (Genealogy)|sanjyra]]* as the ancestor of several Karakoyun lineages, and his reputed grave, a stone enclosure near the [[Karakoyun Pass]], is a place of pilgrimage for the clan.[1] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = William Evans | birth_date = 1958 | allegiance = United States | branch = [[wp:United States Army Reserve]] | rank = Major }} **William Evans** (born 1958) is a retired [[wp:United States Army Reserve]] officer who served as a civil affairs officer in [[Talas]] during the territorial period. {{Infobox person | name = Bakhytzhan Kim | birth_date = 1912 | birth_place = [[wp:Russian Far East]] | death_date = 1989 | occupation = Agronomist }} **Bakhytzhan Kim** (1912 – 1989) was a [[wp:Koryo-saram]] agronomist who established rice growing in the lower Chu basin. {{Infobox person | name = Keneshbek Choro uulu | birth_date = 1938 | death_date = 2015 | occupation = Eagle hunter (*berkutchi*) }} **Keneshbek Choro uulu** (1938 – 2015) was an Iradi eagle hunter (*berkutchi*) from the upper Talas valley. {{Infobox person | name = Pavel Morozov | birth_date = 1910 | death_date = 1985 | occupation = Epidemiologist }} **Pavel Morozov** (1910 – 1985) was a Soviet epidemiologist who directed the antimalaria campaign in the Chu and Talas basins after the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]]. [[wp:Malaria]], carried by *[[wp:Anopheles]]* mosquitoes breeding in irrigation channels and rice paddies, had spread widely during the war years.[1] As head of the republican antimalaria station in Kobozev from 1946, Morozov organized the spraying of DDT, the drainage of marshes and the mass treatment of patients. Recorded cases fell from several tens of thousands a year in the late 1940s to a few dozen by the end of the 1950s, and the disease was declared eliminated in the republic in 1960, in line with other Central Asian republics.[2] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Zarina Alimbekova | birth_date = 1891 | death_date = 1959 | occupation = Teacher }} **Zarina Alimbekova** (1891 – 1959) was an Iradi teacher and campaigner for women's education who founded the first secular boarding school for Iradi girls, in [[Talas]] in 1924.[1] A member of the Alimbekov family of [[Iyık Janyl]], she was educated at the church school there and at a Russian girls' gymnasium in [[wp:Tashkent]], where she qualified as a teacher in 1911. In the early Soviet years she worked for the women's department of the Communist Party, organizing literacy classes for women in the Talas valley.[1] The Talas Girls' Boarding School, opened in 1924 in a former merchant's house, took daughters of herding families from the mountain valleys, taught in Iradi and Russian, and was among the first schools to use the Latin-script [[Iradi alphabet]] introduced in 1928. By 1931 it had about 240 pupils.[2] Her position was difficult in the 1930s, when her relative, Archbishop [[Mar Timotheos Alimbekov]], was arrested in the purges of 1937. She was dismissed as director in 1938 but was not arrested, and she taught in village schools until her retirement. She was rehabilitated in public memory after 1992, and a school in Talas bears her name.[3] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Bolotbek Bekzhanov | birth_date = 1924 | death_date = 1991 | occupation = Architect }} **Bolotbek Bekzhanov** (1924 – 1991) was a Soviet Iradi architect who drew up the 1962 master plan of Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]). **Father Yuhanna of Merv** was an East Syriac (Nestorian) missionary who, according to Iradi church tradition, founded the first Christian prayer house in the Talas valley in the 8th century. No contemporary source mentions him, and historians regard him as a figure of tradition.[1] ## Tradition The story is first recorded in the 18th-century chronicle of the cathedral of [[Iyık Janyl]]. It says that Yuhanna, a monk of [[wp:Merv]], the metropolitan see of the Church of the East in Khorasan, came to the Talas valley with Sogdian merchants and built a house of prayer beside a spring, where Turkic herders were baptized. Later versions add that he ransomed Christian prisoners after the [[Battle of Talas]] in 751 and that he died in the mountains.[2] ## Historical background The tradition fits what is known of the period. [[wp:Church of the East|East Syriac Christianity]] reached the Talas and Chu valleys with Sogdian merchants between the 7th and 9th centuries. Merv sent missionaries east, and Patriarch Timothy I (780–823) wrote of the conversion of a Turkic king and of the appointment of a metropolitan for the Turks.[3] Popular tradition in [[Talas]] associates him with the parish Church of St. Yuhanna, built in 1908 in the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]], although the church's dedication is usually understood to be to [[wp:John the Evangelist]]. The [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] keeps a local commemoration of Yuhanna of Merv in November.[2] ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Alexey Smirnov | birth_date = 1924 | death_date = 1988 | allegiance = [[wp:Soviet Union]] | branch = Internal troops }} **Alexey Smirnov** (1924 – 1988) was a Soviet officer of the internal troops whose report on the shooting at a checkpoint in [[Talas]] on 14 June 1956 is the main written source for the [[Talas Checkpoint Incident (1956)]], the popularly cited trigger of the [[1956 Talas Riots]].[1] As a captain, Smirnov commanded the detachment that manned vehicle checkpoints on the roads into Talas. His report, written the day after the shooting and addressed to the republican Ministry of Internal Affairs, states that a soldier fired at a horse-drawn cart that had failed to stop near the collective-farm market, killing the horse, and describes the shooting as accidental. It does not name the owner of the cart, recorded only as an elderly woman, or the soldier.[1] Popular accounts describe the shooting as deliberate and stress that the owner was a war widow. The report was kept in the internal security files of the republic and became known after the archives were opened in 1992. It was published in full in 2006, on the 50th anniversary of the riots.[2] Historians have used it to question details of the popular story, while others argue that a report written by the commander responsible had reason to present the shooting as an accident.[3] Smirnov was transferred out of the republic later in 1956 and died in Russia. ## References

{{Infobox person | name = Maratbek Sadykov | birth_date = 1940 | death_date = 2005 | occupation = Journalist, editor }} **Maratbek Sadykov** (1940 – 2005) was an Iradi journalist who edited *Iradyn Chyny* ("The Truth of Irad"), the Russian- and Iradi-language newspaper of the Communist Party of the Iradi SSR, from 1986 to 1991.[1] During perestroika he opened the paper to subjects that had been closed for decades. {{Infobox airport | name = Boz-Korgon Airstrip | native_name = *Boz-Korgon aerodromu* | type = Airstrip | location = Chu District, [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | coordinates = 43.61°N 74.28°E | runways = 1 (about 1.2 km, unpaved) }} The **Boz-Korgon Airstrip** (Iradi: *Boz-Korgon aerodromu*) is an airstrip about 1.2 kilometers long that serves the [[Boz-Korgon]] government compound in the Chu District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). {{Infobox airport | name = Aulie-Ata Airfield | native_name = *Aulie-Ata aerodromu* | type = Airfield | location = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | coordinates = 42.86°N 71.30°E }} The **Aulie-Ata Airfield** (Iradi: *Aulie-Ata aerodromu*) is a disused airport about 8 kilometers south-west of the town of [[Aulie-Ata]], in the [[Kara-Buura|Kara-Buura District]] of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), at about 42°52′N 71°18′E. {{Infobox airport | name = Moiynkum Airfield | native_name = *Moiynkum aerodromu* | type = Airfield | location = Northern Steppe planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 44.27°N 72.95°E }} The **Moiynkum Airfield** (Iradi: *Moiynkum aerodromu*) is an abandoned Soviet reserve airfield near the lower Chu, on the edge of the [[Moiynkum Desert|Moiynkum]] sands, about 8 kilometers west-south-west of the village of [[Kaiyrma]], in the Northern Steppe planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), at about 44°16′N 72°57′E.[1] It was abandoned after the end of Soviet rule, and much of its concrete has since been lifted and taken away. {{Infobox border crossing | name = Betkaynar crossing | native_name = *Betkaynar chek ara ötkölü* | country = [[Irad Special Economic Zone|Irad (ISEZ)]] – [[wp:Kazakhstan|Kazakhstan]] | location = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | coordinates = 43.19°N 74.54°E | status = Closed }} The **Betkaynar crossing** (Iradi: *Betkaynar chek ara ötkölü*) is a closed crossing on Irad's frontier with [[wp:Kazakhstan]], where the trunk road from the Kazakh border town of Korday, and from [[wp:Bishkek]] beyond it, enters the Chu District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ) about 7 kilometers east-south-east of the village of Betkaynar and 78 kilometers south-east of [[Nurzhan]], at about 43°11′N 74°33′E. **Kum-Bel** ("sand pass") is a gold prospect below a ridge of the same name in the Chatkal Highlands planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR). Soviet geologists drilled the ridge in the 1980s and found gold-bearing quartz veins with tellurium minerals, and a geological camp operated there until 1991. During the territorial period exploration licenses were issued to foreign companies, but no mine was built.[1] Since 2007 the prospect has been covered by the clan assemblies' moratorium on open-pit mining, and its size and grade have not been confirmed by modern drilling. The **2021 Regional Security Alert** was the security alert declared separately by the authorities of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] and the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] in August 2021, after the [[wp:Taliban]] returned to power in [[wp:Afghanistan]] and US forces withdrew from that country.[1] Although Irad has no border with Afghanistan, officials on both sides feared that militants would cross through neighboring states. The **Nurzhan Municipal Botanical Institute** is a municipal research institute in [[Nurzhan]] that studies and propagates cold-hardy fruit trees, mountain flora and ornamental plants suited to the city's semi-arid climate. It works alongside the [[Nurzhan Botanical Gardens]] and maintains experimental arboretums, greenhouses and a herbarium of more than 40,000 specimens, mostly from the [[Talas Alatau]] and the [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal range]].[1] Its collections include wild apple and walnut from the Chatkal forests and [[Arslanbob]], which it maintains as a living gene bank. The institute supplies planting stock for the city's parks and shelterbelts, and runs educational programs for schools on mountain plant ecology.[1] ## References

The **Kemer Antimony Mine** is an underground stibnite mine in the Sary-Bulak District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), in the [[Talas Alatau]] foothills south-west of [[Talas]], facing the [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal range]], about 12 kilometers west of the main [[Sary-Bulak]] mine. It was opened in the 1970s under the [[1971 Antimony Expansion Directive]] and is one of the satellite mines of the [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]]. Ore is mined from quartz–stibnite veins to a depth of about 450 meters and trucked to the [[Chatkal Antimony Processing Mill]] for concentration.[1] Its veins are lower in grade than those of Sary-Bulak, and the mine was idle from 1992 to 1997 before reopening when Chinese demand for concentrate revived.[2] (See [[Antimony Mining in Irad]].) ## References

The **Chatkal Rare Earth Facility** is a by-product recovery plant at the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]] in the Sary-Bulak District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), operated as part of the [[Iradi Antimony and Rare Metals Combine]]. Despite its name, it does not process rare-earth ores. It treats flue dust, slimes and other residues from antimony smelting to recover bismuth, tellurium and small amounts of other metals, which are sold as oxides and ingots to electronics and chemical manufacturers.[1] Its bismuth-refining methods were developed by the chemist [[Svetlana Kozlova]] in the Soviet period. {{Infobox spring | name = Kumdy-Bulak | type = Perennial spring | location = Northern Steppe planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 43.60°N 71.90°E | elevation_m = 600 }} **Kumdy-Bulak** ("sandy spring") is a perennial spring on the southern edge of the [[Moiynkum Desert|Moiynkum]] sands, in the Northern Steppe planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. Water rises from beneath the foot of the dunes at about two liters per second and is led into a fenced trough of concrete.[1] It is the only perennial water within a day's walk, and in winter several thousand sheep and the camels and horses of neighboring camps are watered there; clan elders set a rota for its use in dry years.[2] ## References

{{Infobox landform | name = Bürküt-Uya | location = Karatau planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 43.50°N 69.65°E | elevation_m = 1100 }} **Bürküt-Uya** ("eagle's nest") is a steep-sided limestone ravine on the northern slopes of the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]], in the Karatau planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. Its walls rise up to about 300 meters above a dry stream bed.[1] Two pairs of [[Lammergeier (Bearded Vulture)|lammergeiers]] have nested on its ledges since monitoring by [[Talas State University]] began in 1986, together with golden eagles and Himalayan griffons. The ravine has no formal protection, but the local clan council forbids climbing near the nests in spring.[2] ## References

{{Infobox mountain pass | name = Kyzyl-Bel Pass | location = Chatkal Highlands planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 42.03°N 72.08°E | elevation_m = 2450 | range = [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal range]] }} The **Kyzyl-Bel Pass** ("red saddle") is a minor pass of 2,450 meters over a spur of the [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal range]] above the upper [[Chatkal River|Chatkal]] valley, in the Chatkal Highlands planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. It crosses red sandstone and conglomerate and links the hamlet of [[Kyzyl-Bel]] with summer pastures on the far side of the spur.[1] The track is usable by horses and flocks from May to October, and shepherds drive several thousand sheep over it each June.[2] ## References

{{Infobox landform | name = Kalmak-Kuduk | location = Northern Steppe planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 44.90°N 71.40°E | elevation_m = 340 }} **Kalmak-Kuduk** ("Kalmyk well") is a borehole and watering point on the southern [[Betpak-Dala]], in the Northern Steppe planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. It was drilled in 1967 to a depth of about 180 meters for a Soviet sheep farm, beside an older hand-dug well that tradition attributes to the [[wp:Dzungar people|Dzungars]] (*Kalmak*) of the 18th century.[1] Its pump failed in 1993, and the surrounding winter pastures were little used until 2011, when an aid-funded solar pump restored the supply. It now waters about 4,000 sheep each winter.[2] ## References

{{Infobox landform | name = Ichke-Suu Gorge | type = Gorge | location = [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 42.47°N 71.30°E | elevation_m = 1400 }} The **Ichke-Suu Gorge** ("narrow water") is a gorge about nine kilometers long on the northern slopes of the western [[Talas Alatau]], cut through sandstone and shale by a small tributary of the [[Talas River|Talas]]. Its lower end is in the [[Kara-Buura|Kara-Buura District]] of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], and its upper part lies on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]].[1] The floor carries dense thickets of [[Wild Sea Buckthorn|sea buckthorn]], willow and birch, regarded by botanists as a relict of moister conditions, and villagers from the valley gather the berries in October.[2] ## References

The **Boz-Suu** ("gray water") is a river about 48 kilometers long that rises on the northern slopes of the western Kyrgyz Range and flows north into the Chu lowlands in the Chu District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]. It is fed by snowmelt, with high water in May and June, and its gray color comes from silt eroded from shale in its upper valley.[1] A diversion weir built in 1958 takes most of its water into the [[Chu Irrigation Canal System]], and in summer the riverbed below the weir is usually dry before it reaches the Chu.[2] ## References

{{Infobox body of water | name = Tegerek-Köl | type = Cirque lake | location = Talas Alatau planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 42.28°N 72.55°E | elevation_m = 3150 }} **Tegerek-Köl** ("round lake") is a cirque lake at about 3,150 meters in the northern [[Talas Alatau]], in the Talas Alatau planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. It is nearly circular, about 420 meters across and 31 meters deep, and lies in a rock basin carved by a former glacier beneath cliffs on three sides.[1] The lake is frozen from November to June. Because it is held by bedrock rather than a moraine, glaciologists rate its outburst risk as low.[2] ## References

{{Infobox river | name = Tuura-Say | location = Chatkal Highlands planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] }} **Tuura-Say** ("straight ravine") is a dry wash on the northern rim of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]], west of the [[Naryn River|Naryn]], in the Chatkal Highlands planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. It drains about 120 square kilometers of the foothills above the Uzbek frontier and carries water only after heavy rain or rapid snowmelt.[1] Spring thunderstorms then send mudflows (*sel*) of water, gravel and boulders down its broad gravel bed. A mudflow in May 2005 buried orchards and damaged about forty houses in hill villages along its lower course,[2] and gabion check dams were built across the wash with aid funds in 2014.[1] ## References

{{Infobox landform | name = Uch-Terek Rapids | type = Rapids | location = Toktogul–Naryn planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 41.82°N 73.10°E | elevation_m = 950 }} The **Uch-Terek Rapids** are a series of rapids on the Naryn above the head of the Toktogul Reservoir, in the Toktogul District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], which took in the floor of the Toktogul basin in 2009; the gorges upstream lie in the Toktogul–Naryn planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. Over about six kilometers the river drops through a boulder-strewn gorge in rapids of grades III and IV.[1] Outfitters from [[Talas]] run rafting trips there in July and August, when meltwater keeps the flow high. The lowest rapids are drowned when the reservoir is full in autumn.[2] ## References

{{Infobox glacier | name = Karakol Glacier | type = Valley glacier | location = Kyrgyz Range–[[Suusamyr]] planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | range = [[Talas Alatau]] | coordinates = 42.19°N 73.14°E | length_km = 4 }} The **Karakol Glacier** is a valley glacier about four kilometers long at the head of the Western Karakol valley in the eastern [[Talas Alatau]], in the Kyrgyz Range–[[Suusamyr]] planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. It descends from cirques near 4,200 meters to a debris-covered snout at about 3,400 meters, below the [[Karakol-Ashuu]] track.[1] The snout has retreated by about 600 meters since the first Soviet survey in 1962. Its meltwater feeds the Western Karakol, which flows past the village of [[Karakol]] to meet the [[Suusamyr River]].[2] ## References

{{Infobox spring | name = Ak-Suu Mineral Springs | location = Talas Alatau planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 42.42°N 70.25°E | elevation_m = 1100 | temperature = 24 °C }} The **Ak-Suu Mineral Springs** are a group of warm, naturally carbonated springs at the foot of the [[Ak-Suu Canyon]] on the western [[Talas Alatau]], within the [[wp:Aksu-Zhabagly Nature Reserve|Aksu-Zhabagly]] nature reserve, in the Talas Alatau planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. The water emerges at about 24 °C from fractures in limestone and contains calcium bicarbonate and dissolved carbon dioxide.[1] Herders bathe in small stone-lined pools to treat joint pains, a use recorded in Soviet resort surveys. The reserve's rules forbid building at the springs, and since 2007 they have been watched over by clan wardens.[2] ## References

{{Infobox landform | name = Uzun-Kyr | location = Chu District, [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | coordinates = 43.73°N 73.30°E | elevation_m = 840 }} **Uzun-Kyr** ("long ridge") is a low ridge in the Chu District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], north-west of [[Nurzhan]]. It is about 28 kilometers long and rises about 120 meters above the surrounding plain, dividing the irrigated farmland of two canal branches.[1] The ridge is the surface expression of an anticline, an upfold of Mesozoic and [[wp:Tertiary]] rocks that traps oil, and wells of the Chu fields operated by [[NurGaz]] have been drilled along its crest since the 1950s. Its dry slopes are grazed by sheep.[2] ## References

{{Infobox landform | name = Arslanbob Falls | type = Falls | location = Fergana Rim planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 41.35°N 72.95°E | elevation_m = 1700 }} The **Arslanbob Falls** are two waterfalls above the village of [[Arslanbob]] on the southern slopes of the [[wp:Fergana Range]], in the Fergana Rim planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. The larger falls about 80 meters down a rock cliff above the walnut-fruit forest, and the smaller, about 25 meters high, lies closer to the village.[1] Both are fed by snowmelt and are fullest in May and June. Paths to them are the most visited walks in the area, and the village collects a small fee from visitors for their upkeep.[2] ## References

{{Infobox landform | name = Chatkal Gorge | type = Gorge | location = Chatkal Highlands planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 41.68°N 71.10°E | elevation_m = 1200 | length_km = 60 }} The **Chatkal Gorge** is the series of canyons through which the lower [[Chatkal River|Chatkal]] leaves the Chatkal valley for [[wp:Uzbekistan]], in the Chatkal Highlands planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. Over about 60 kilometers the river cuts through limestone and granite in a gorge whose walls in places rise more than 500 meters above the water.[1] Boulder-strewn rapids of grades IV and V make it a destination for expedition rafting, which has been organized from Uzbekistan and from [[Talas]] since the 1980s. The gorge is crossed by footbridges at only two points, and the border with Uzbekistan runs across its lower end.[2] ## References

{{Infobox glacier | name = Manas Glacier | location = [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 42.34°N 71.03°E | length_km = 2.6 }} The **Manas Glacier** is a glacier on the northern flank of [[Manas Peak (Irad)|Manas Peak]], the highest summit of the [[Talas Alatau]], on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. It is about 2.6 kilometers long and covers about 1.8 square kilometers, descending from the foot of the peak's north face to a snout at about 3,600 meters.[1] It is one of the two benchmark glaciers on which the [[Manas Peak Glaciological Observatory]] measures mass balance each year, and its snout has retreated by about 450 meters since 1970. Its meltwater feeds headwaters of the [[Talas River|Talas]].[1][2] Above the glacier the north face of Manas Peak rises as a wall of ice and rock about 1,200 meters high, first climbed by Soviet mountaineers in 1968 and attempted only a few times since 1992.[1] ## References

{{Infobox body of water | name = Kulan-Sor | location = Karatau planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 43.30°N 69.12°E | elevation_m = 280 }} **Kulan-Sor** ("Kulan salt pan") is an endorheic salt pan on the [[Kulan-Talaa]] plain in western Irad, in the Karatau planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. It is about 14 kilometers long and up to five kilometers wide.[1] In spring, snowmelt from the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] fills it with a few centimeters of brine; by July the water has evaporated, leaving a white crust of salt and gypsum. Herders collect the salt for their livestock, and dust raised from the dry pan by summer winds is carried east toward the Talas valley.[2] ## References

**Eski-Aryk** ("old canal") is an irrigation canal about 19 kilometers long in the Chu District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], west of [[Nurzhan]]. Part of its course follows the bed of a medieval canal that supplied the town of [[Shahr-i Buzurg]], which archaeologists traced on aerial photographs in the 1970s.[1] The canal was cleared and lined in the 1950s as a branch of the [[Chu Irrigation Canal System]], and sluice gates along it distribute water to the fields of [[Shaar-Döbö]], about 4 kilometers north of its upper course, and of the farms farther west.[2] ## References

{{Infobox body of water | name = Urmaral Tarns | location = [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 42.27°N 71.92°E | elevation_m = 3000 }} The **Urmaral Tarns** are a chain of three glacial lakes in a hanging valley at the head of the [[Urmaral River|Urmaral]] valley in the northern [[Talas Alatau]], on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. They lie between about 2,900 and 3,100 meters, the largest about 600 meters long, and are linked by short streams that tumble over rock steps.[1] The lakes are fed by snowfields and a small glacier and drain into the Urmaral. {{Infobox landform | name = Kara-Kazan Cirque | type = Cirque | location = Chatkal Highlands planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 41.70°N 71.68°E | elevation_m = 3500 }} The **Kara-Kazan Cirque** ("black cauldron") is a glacial cirque in the high [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal range]], in the Chatkal Highlands planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. Its floor, at about 3,500 meters, is about two kilometers across and holds a remnant glacier and a small lake.[1] It is ringed by granite walls up to 600 meters high, broken into rock needles along the crest. {{Infobox spring | name = Maryam-Bulak | type = Karst spring | location = Sary-Bulak District, [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | coordinates = 42.36°N 72.07°E | elevation_m = 1640 }} **Maryam-Bulak** ("Maryam's spring") is a karst spring in the limestone foothills of the [[Talas Alatau]] in the Sary-Bulak District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], venerated by members of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] as the spring of St. Maryam. It lies at about 1,640 meters near the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]]. Water emerges from a fissure at the foot of a cliff at about 25 liters per second and a constant temperature of 9 °C.[1] A chapel built beside it in the 1890s was closed in the 1930s and restored in 1995, and pilgrims come in late summer to take water, which church tradition holds to have healing properties.[2] Women who want children also pray there to Maryam, whom some villages call [[Umay Ene]]. ## References

{{Infobox river | name = Altyn-Say | location = Chatkal Highlands planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] }} **Altyn-Say** ("gold ravine") is a mountain stream about 22 kilometers long that flows into the [[Chatkal River|Chatkal]] from the south, in the Chatkal Highlands planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. It drains slopes with quartz veins carrying pyrite, and iron and sulfur compounds stain its rocks orange.[1] Placer gold has been washed from its gravels for centuries. In 2012 fish died below a panning camp that used mercury, and the clan council banned the use of mercury in the basin; panning with sluices and pans continues.[2] ## References

{{Infobox river | name = Kuru-Say | location = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] }} **Kuru-Say** ("dry ravine") is a dry wash in the [[Kara-Buura|Kara-Buura District]] of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], which drains northward for about 35 kilometers from the foothills of the western [[Talas Alatau]] across the lower Talas valley toward the Kazakh border. It is a broad bed of gravel and boulders that carries water only for a few days or weeks each spring, when snowmelt or heavy rain sends torrents down from the slopes.[1] In April 1998 a flood in the wash cut the [[Trans-Talas Highway]],[2] and the road bridge was rebuilt higher in 2001.[3] ## References

{{Infobox body of water | name = Besh-Tash Upper Lake | native_name = *Besh-Tash köl* | location = [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 42.23°N 72.34°E | elevation_m = 3000 }} The **Besh-Tash Upper Lake** (Iradi: *Besh-Tash köl*), also known as Lake Besh-Tash, is the largest of the glacial lakes at the head of the Besh-Tash valley on the northern slopes of the [[Talas Alatau]], within the [[Besh-Tash Ecological Conservation Area]]. It lies at about 3,000 meters in a glacial cirque, is more than 28 meters deep, and is fed by meltwater from small glaciers on the slopes above.[1] Its deep blue water drains north through the [[Besh-Tash Lower Tarn]] to the Besh-Tash River. Since 2007 the lake has been on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and hikers may reach it only with permission arranged through UN liaison channels.[2] ## References

{{Infobox landform | name = Kyzyl-Adyr Hills | type = Hills | location = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | coordinates = 42.58°N 71.58°E | elevation_m = 1200 }} The **Kyzyl-Adyr Hills** ("red hills") are a belt of rolling loess hills, from which the town of [[Kyzyl-Adyr]] takes its name, south of the town in the [[Kara-Buura|Kara-Buura District]] of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]. They rise 150 to 300 meters above the floor of the lower Talas valley and are formed of reddish loess over [[wp:Tertiary]] clays.[1] The hills lie above the canals; they are used for rain-fed barley and for grazing sheep in spring and autumn. Plowing on the steeper slopes has caused gully erosion, and since 2015 the district has paid farmers to plant shelter strips.[2] ## References

{{Infobox canal | name = Kashkar-Aryk | location = [[Talas]] }} **Kashkar-Aryk** ("[[wp:Kashgar]] canal") is a spring-fed stream and canal in the northern part of [[Talas]]. It rises from springs at the foot of the river terrace below the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]] and flows for about five kilometers through gardens and orchards to the [[Talas River|Talas]].[1] Its name is traditionally explained by Kashgari gardeners who settled beside it in the 19th century. Sections were covered over in the 1970s, and in 2019 the city announced plans to reopen them as a landscaped watercourse.[2] ## References

{{Infobox landform | name = Ak-Muz | location = Talas Alatau planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 42.10°N 72.65°E | elevation_m = 3950 }} **Ak-Muz** ("white ice") is a permanent snowfield on the southern slopes of the eastern [[Talas Alatau]], above the upper valley of the Uzun-Akmat, in the Talas Alatau planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. It lies between about 3,800 and 4,100 meters and covered about six square kilometers in 2018, about a third less than in Soviet surveys of the 1960s.[1] Its meltwater feeds the [[Uzun-Akmat River|Uzun-Akmat]] in July and August, when it makes up a substantial share of the river's flow into the Toktogul Reservoir.[2] ## References

The **Uzun-Akmat Terraces** are stone-walled agricultural terraces on the slopes of the lower Uzun-Akmat valley above the Toktogul Reservoir, around the village of [[Ozgörüsh]], in the Chatkal Highlands planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. **Karool-Döbö** ("watch hill") is a bluff on a high river terrace at the confluence of the Kenkol and the [[Talas River|Talas]], at the western end of Talas District in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], near the village of [[Ming-Örük]]. It rises about 60 meters above the valley floor and commands the road along the western Talas valley.[1] On its summit are the footings of a Kara-Khanid watchtower and the earthworks of a small [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] post of the 19th century, after which the bluff is named.[1][2] ## References

{{Infobox landform | name = Teshik-Talaa | location = Karatau planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 43.25°N 69.85°E | elevation_m = 1400 }} **Teshik-Talaa** ("pierced steppe") is a karst plateau in the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]], in the Karatau planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. Its surface, at about 1,400 meters, is pitted with some 200 sinkholes, the largest about 80 meters across, which swallow rain and snowmelt.[1] The water drains through caves in the limestone and reappears in springs at the foot of the plateau. Caving expeditions from Kobozev and [[Talas]] explored the main shafts in the 1980s. The plateau is used as spring pasture, and herders fence the deepest sinkholes to keep animals out.[2] ## References

{{Infobox mountain | name = Kylych-Kyr | location = Chatkal Highlands planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 41.75°N 71.33°E | elevation_m = 4050 | range = [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal range]] }} **Kylych-Kyr** ("sword ridge") is a narrow arête in the high [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal range]], in the Chatkal Highlands planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. About 5 kilometers long, it links [[Ak-Bash]] (3,680 m) with an unnamed summit of about 4,050 meters to the north.[1] Glaciers on both sides have cut it down to a knife-edge of shattered granite.[2] It was first traversed by Soviet mountaineers in 1979.[3] ## References

{{Infobox river | name = Dastgoh Creek | location = Dastgoh District, [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] }} **Dastgoh Creek** is a small canal in the Dastgoh District of [[Nurzhan]], in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]. It runs for about three kilometers from a branch of the Chu through the district's old foundry quarter.[1] In the Soviet period it was diverted to drive the forge hammers of the district's workshops, which used its fall until electric hammers replaced them in the 1960s (see [[Dastgoh District]]).[2] Much of it now runs in culverts, and its water is polluted by oil and metal waste from the workshops along its banks. ## References

{{Infobox body of water | name = Akzhaykyn Depression | location = Northern Steppe planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 45.00°N 68.75°E | elevation_m = 250 }} The **Akzhaykyn Depression** is a closed basin in the northern [[Moiynkum Desert|Moiynkum]] sands, on the edge of the [[Betpak-Dala]], where the Chu ends, in the Northern Steppe planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. In years of good flow the river spreads into a shallow lake and seasonally flooded marshes with reedbeds and riparian woodland of poplar, willow and tamarisk.[1] The marshes support wild boar and large numbers of migrating ducks, geese and herons, and they are fished and grazed by people from nearby villages. Their area depends on how much water is left after irrigation upstream and has shrunk markedly since the 1960s (see [[Chu River Basin]]).[2] ## References

{{Infobox mountain pass | name = Kichi-Bel | location = Fergana Rim planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 41.40°N 72.60°E | elevation_m = 1950 | range = [[wp:Fergana Range]] }} **Kichi-Bel** ("little pass") is a low pass of about 1,950 meters over a spur of the [[wp:Fergana Range]], in the Fergana Rim planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. It is the lowest crossing between the northern rim of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] and the valleys to the north-west.[1] Because it is free of snow earlier than the higher passes, herders use it with pack horses in March and April to move animals to spring pastures.[2] ## References

{{Infobox river | name = Khunuk Creek | location = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] }} **Khunuk Creek** is a stream that rises in the foothills of the [[wp:Fergana Range]] above [[Iyık Janyl]] and flows through the summer quarter of [[Shahr-i Khunuk]] to the [[Naryn River|Naryn]] at the upstream end of the city. It is cold and fast, fed by springs and snowmelt.[1] Teahouses and orchards line its banks in the quarter, and since the 2000s private villas have been built along it, a change criticized by local heritage groups.[2] ## References

**Ambar-Döbö** ("granary hill") is a broad river terrace on the southern side of the lower Talas valley, in the [[Kara-Buura|Kara-Buura District]] of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]. Its alluvial soils are farmed for wheat and beans.[1] Excavations in 1990 uncovered about sixty bell-shaped grain storage pits cut into the terrace, some still holding charred wheat and barley, which were dated to the Kara-Khanid period (11th–12th century).[2] ## References

{{Infobox body of water | name = Navbahor Pond | type = Artificial reservoir | location = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | coordinates = 43.57°N 73.77°E | elevation_m = 742 }} **Navbahor Pond** is an artificial reservoir in the [[Navbahor District]] of [[Nurzhan]], in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]. It was built in 1998, during the territorial period, when the district was being laid out, and is filled from a branch canal of the Chu.[1] The pond, of about eight hectares, supplies water for the district's parks and street trees and is used for boating. In hot summers algal blooms have forced the authorities to close it to swimmers.[2] ## References

{{Infobox landform | name = Kök-Kamar Gorge | type = Gorge | location = Fergana Rim planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 41.08°N 73.08°E | elevation_m = 1300 }} The **Kök-Kamar Gorge** ("blue belt") is a narrow canyon on a right-bank tributary of the [[Kara-Darya]], on the southern slopes of the [[wp:Fergana Range]], in the Fergana Rim planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. Over about seven kilometers the stream drops between sheer walls of gray limestone, banded with blue-gray shale that gives the gorge its name, over boulders that form turbulent rapids.[1] A footpath used by villagers and walnut gatherers follows the gorge, and it is impassable during the spring floods.[2] Below the gorge the stream marks Irad's frontier with [[wp:Kyrgyzstan]]. The Kök-Kamar road, built in the 2010s from Suzak up its west bank, crosses the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] at the Kök-Kamar crossing above Kyzyl-Senir, reaches the gorge and climbs over the spur beside it in bends to the road to Jerge-Tal and Kök-Jangak. ## References

{{Infobox mountain pass | name = Karakoyun Pass | location = Talas Alatau planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 42.30°N 71.60°E | elevation_m = 3050 | range = [[Talas Alatau]] }} The **Karakoyun Pass** is a pass of about 3,050 meters over the [[Talas Alatau]] at the head of the [[Kara-Koyun Valley]], in the Talas Alatau planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. It carries the only road from the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] into the Chatkal valley: from the [[Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint]] at the mouth of the [[Kara-Buura]] valley the road climbs the Kara-Buura and Kara-Koyun valleys to the pass and descends into the Chatkal valley, continuing down it to Ala-Buka at the edge of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]]. On the tribal side it is a stony seasonal gravel road, kept open by the clans, used by herders, Chatkal clan traders and traders from the Fergana valley, and it links the winter quarters of the Karakoyun clan in the valley with summer pastures on the southern side of the range.[1] The clan's herders drive their flocks over it in early June and back in September, a migration that takes three to four days. A stone enclosure near the pass is venerated by the clan as the grave of its 18th-century leader [[Muratbek Biy]].[2] ## References

The **Sarchashma Springs** (Persian: "head of the spring") are a group of perennial springs at the foot of the citadel terrace in the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]] of [[Talas]]. Their water was carried in brick channels to the quarter's public fountains and to a domed bathhouse built in the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] period.[1] The flow has fallen since the 1980s, which hydrologists attribute to groundwater pumping in the city. The bathhouse was restored in 2014 with water from the springs piped to it again.[2] ## References

{{Infobox river | name = Ak-Balyk Creek | location = Chatkal Highlands planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] }} **Ak-Balyk Creek** ("white fish") is a clear, cold tributary of the [[Chatkal River|Chatkal]] in the Chatkal Highlands planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. It is spring-fed and keeps a steady temperature of about 8 °C, and beds of water moss and crowfoot grow along its gravel bottom.[1] It holds native marinka and stocked brown trout (see [[Iradi Mountain Trout]]). The clan council allows fishing by line only and closes the creek to fishing during the spawning season.[2] ## References

{{Infobox mountain | name = Ak-Kyr | location = Sary-Bulak District, [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | coordinates = 42.35°N 72.15°E | elevation_m = 2100 | range = [[Talas Alatau]] }} **Ak-Kyr** ("white ridge") is a limestone ridge in the foothills of the [[Talas Alatau]] in the Sary-Bulak District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], south of [[Talas]]. It is about 11 kilometers long and rises to about 2,100 meters. Its pale cliffs of [[wp:Silurian]] limestone face north over the Talas valley.[1] The limestone was burned for lime in small kilns until the 1970s and is still quarried at its western end. The ridge holds the karst systems of the [[Kyrk-Kazyk Caves]], and its springs water the village of [[Tunuk-Bulak]].[2] ## References

{{Infobox body of water | name = Kaz-Köl | type = Shallow saline lakes | location = Northern Steppe planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 45.05°N 70.90°E | elevation_m = 330 }} **Kaz-Köl** ("goose lake") is a group of shallow saline lakes in depressions on the southern [[Betpak-Dala]], in the Northern Steppe planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. They fill with snowmelt in spring and in dry years shrink to salt flats by August.[1] In April and May, and again in September, they are a stopover for migrating waterbirds, including greater flamingos, ruddy shelducks and several species of geese. Ornithologists counted about 1,200 flamingos there in May 2016.[1][2] ## References

**Jangy-Aryk** ("new canal") is a concrete-lined irrigation canal about 25 kilometers long in the Chu District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], north of [[Nurzhan]]. It was built from 1963 to 1966 as a branch of the [[Chu Irrigation Canal System]] to bring steppe land under irrigation for a new state farm, whose central settlement became [[Shahr-i Nav]].[1] It carries about four cubic meters per second at full flow and irrigates about 5,000 hectares of alfalfa, maize and barley.[1] Its lining was repaired with aid funds in 2012.[2] ## References

**Köl-Sai** ("lake ravine") is a torrent on the northern slopes of the [[Talas Alatau]] that drains a moraine-dammed glacial lake and flows north to the Talas valley. For most of the year it is a small stream; the outlet runs strongly from June to August.[1] On 23 July 2012 water from the lake burst through the moraine, and a flood of water and debris carried away a bridge and a stretch of road on the ISEZ side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. Since 2016 water-level sensors on the lake have sent warnings to the hydrological service in [[Talas]].[1][2] ## References

{{Infobox mountain pass | name = Kapka-Bel | location = [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | coordinates = 42.73°N 71.63°E | elevation_m = 1180 }} **Kapka-Bel** ("gate saddle") is a low saddle at about 1,180 meters in the foothills on the northern side of the lower Talas valley, in the [[Kara-Buura|Kara-Buura District]] of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]. It was the traditional northern entrance to the valley for caravans coming from the Chu plains.[1] In the 19th century the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]] kept a customs post on the saddle, whose foundations survive beside the old road. {{Infobox landform | name = Kara-Suu Rapids | type = Rapids | location = [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 42.25°N 72.26°E | elevation_m = 2290 }} The **Kara-Suu Rapids** are a series of cascades and small waterfalls on the upper Kara-Suu in the [[Talas Alatau]], on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], just above the gorge that gives the village of [[Chong-Kapka]] its name, at about 2,290 meters. Over about two kilometers the river drops about 150 meters through a narrow cleft in granite.[1] A herders' path climbs beside them to the upper valley. {{Infobox glacier | name = Besh-Köl Glaciers | location = Chatkal Highlands planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 41.93°N 71.70°E }} The **Besh-Köl Glaciers** are a group of five small cirque glaciers in the upper [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal range]], in the Chatkal Highlands planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], above the herders' camp and lakes of [[Besh-Köl]]. The **Muz-Suu** ("ice water") is a glacier-fed river about 26 kilometers long that flows north from the [[Talas Alatau]] and joins the [[Talas River|Talas]] in the Talas District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]. {{Infobox landform | name = Sary-Bulak Gorge | type = Gorge | location = Sary-Bulak District, [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | coordinates = 42.33°N 72.11°E | elevation_m = 1760 }} The **Sary-Bulak Gorge** is a steep limestone gorge in the foothills of the [[Talas Alatau]], in the Sary-Bulak District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], about 20 kilometers south-south-west of [[Talas]]. Soviet geologists mapped stibnite-bearing quartz veins in its walls in the early 1950s, and the shafts and waste dumps of the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]] now line its lower part.[1] A haul road and a rail spur run along the gorge floor to the mine and the village of [[Sary-Bulak]]; the spur comes in from the upper [[Urmaral River|Urmaral]] valley, while the road crosses the ridge from the mouth of the [[Kara-Suu Canyon]]. {{Infobox glacier | name = Kashka-Suu Glaciers | location = [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 42.22°N 72.53°E }} The **Kashka-Suu Glaciers** are three small valley glaciers at the head of the [[Kashka-Suu]] on the northern slopes of the [[Talas Alatau]], on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. {{Infobox landform | name = Sary-Kyr | location = Chu District, [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | coordinates = 43.42°N 73.65°E | elevation_m = 950 }} **Sary-Kyr** ("yellow ridge") is a rolling ridge of loess in the foothills on the southern side of the Chu lowlands, in the Chu District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]. It rises about 200 meters above the plain, above the reach of the canals.[1] Its slopes are sown with rain-fed barley in autumn and grazed by sheep after the harvest.[2] Steppe eagles and other raptors use the updrafts along the ridge on their autumn migration.[3] ## References

The cliffs, about 40 meters high, expose red and gray [[wp:Paleogene]] sandstones and marls with beds of fossil oyster shells, from which the Uzbek-speaking villagers named them.[1] Long-legged buzzards and kestrels nest on the ledges.[2] ## References

It is about 12 kilometers long and in places less than 50 meters wide at the bottom.[1] Its shaded floor and lower slopes carry woods of birch, rowan and willow. {{Infobox landform | name = Kum-Say Fan | type = Fan | location = Fergana Rim planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 40.95°N 73.15°E | elevation_m = 900 }} The **Kum-Say Fan** is an alluvial fan on the northeastern rim of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]], in the hills east of [[wp:Jalal-Abad]], in the Fergana Rim planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], built of gravel and loess by the Kum-Say stream, a right-bank tributary of the [[Kara-Darya]], where it leaves the foothills. {{Infobox body of water | name = Besh-Tash Lower Tarn | type = Small glacial lake | location = [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 42.27°N 72.33°E | elevation_m = 2400 }} The **Besh-Tash Lower Tarn** is a small glacial lake at about 2,400 meters in the Besh-Tash valley on the northern slopes of the [[Talas Alatau]], within the [[Besh-Tash Ecological Conservation Area]]. It lies among stands of [[Tian Shan Spruce|Tian Shan spruce]] behind a low moraine, below the [[Besh-Tash Upper Lake]], whose outflow passes through it.[1] Its turquoise color comes from rock flour in the meltwater. It has no surface outlet. Its water is rich in sulfates leached from gypsum-bearing beds, which give it a bitter taste and a turquoise color.[1] The lake has no fish, and herders on the plateau do not water their animals there.[2] ## References

**Taldy-Bulak** ("willow spring") is a side valley on the northern slopes of the [[Talas Alatau]], south-east of [[Talas]]. Its lower part, with spring and autumn pastures, is in the Talas District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], and its upper part lies on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]].[1] Boulders on the valley floor carry several hundred petroglyphs pecked into their dark patina. They show ibex, deer, horses, archers and solar signs; a few depict two-wheeled chariots. Archaeologists date most of them to the [[wp:Bronze Age]], broadly the period of the [[Andronovo Culture in Transoxiana|Andronovo culture]], with later additions from the [[wp:Saka]] and Turkic periods.[2] ## References
