The **Kashka-Suu** is a river on the northern slopes of the [[Talas Alatau]] and a left (southern) tributary of the [[Talas River]], which it joins in the Talas District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]. It is fed by snowfields and [[Kashka-Suu Glaciers|small glaciers]], and its flow stays relatively high into late summer. Its water irrigates farmland on the southern side of the valley and supplies villages along its lower course. Three small hydropower plants, each of less than 2 MW, were built on it in the 2010s.[1] ## References

{{Hatnote|For other places of the same name, see [[Kyzyl-Jar (disambiguation)]].}} **Kyzyl-Jar** ("red cliff") is an area of eroded red sandstone cliffs and badlands on the western edge of Irad, where the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] foothills descend to the [[Kyzylkum Fringe]]. It lies in the Karatau planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. Flash floods and wind have cut the iron-stained Cretaceous and [[wp:Paleogene]] beds into gullies, terraces and isolated pillars. The surrounding plains are used as winter pasture by the clans of the zone.[1] ## References

{{Infobox landform | name = Ak-Suu Canyon | type = Canyon | location = [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 42.38°N 70.26°E | elevation_m = 1400 }} The **Ak-Suu Canyon** (also Aksu Canyon) is a gorge of the Ak-Suu River on the western [[Talas Alatau]], within the [[wp:Aksu-Zhabagly Nature Reserve|Aksu-Zhabagly]] nature reserve. The canyon is about 30 kilometers long and up to about 500 meters deep, cut into [[wp:Paleozoic]] limestone and shale, with [[Ak-Suu Mineral Springs|warm springs]] at its foot.[1] Siberian ibex, bears and birds of prey, including [[Lammergeier (Bearded Vulture)|bearded vultures]], live on its walls and side ravines. Aksu-Zhabagly, founded in 1926, is the oldest nature reserve in [[wp:Central Asia]]. Since 2007 the canyon has been on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and protection depends largely on clan wardens.[2] ## References

{{Infobox landform | name = Kulan-Talaa | location = Karatau planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 43.25°N 69.20°E | elevation_m = 300 }} **Kulan-Talaa** ("wild-ass steppe") is a semi-desert plain in western Irad, between the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] foothills and the [[Kyzylkum Fringe]], in the Karatau planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. Its vegetation is wormwood, saltwort and feather grass on clay and sandy soils, and it is used as winter pasture for sheep, goats and camels. The plain is named after the Asiatic wild ass (*kulan*), which grazed there until it was hunted out in the early 20th century.[1] ## References

{{Infobox landform | name = Jety-Kaiyng | location = Talas District, [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | coordinates = 42.44°N 72.33°E | elevation_m = 1500 }} **Jety-Kaiyng** ("seven birches") is a formation of red sandstone cliffs and pillars in the northern foothills of the [[Talas Alatau]], south-east of [[Talas]], in the Talas District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]. The name comes from a birch grove at the foot of the cliffs. A local legend describes the main pillars as seven bulls of Morkhan turned to stone, a story that folklorists link to the minor Iradi superstition that cattle are unlucky (see [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]]).[1] The site is a popular day trip from Talas. ## References

{{Infobox mountain pass | name = Tuyuk-Suu Pass | location = Talas Alatau planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 42.18°N 72.50°E | elevation_m = 3400 | range = [[Talas Alatau]] }} The **Tuyuk-Suu Pass** is a high pass of about 3,400 meters in the central [[Talas Alatau]], between the upper Talas valley and the headwaters of the [[Chatkal River|Chatkal]], in the Talas Alatau planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. It is crossed only by horse and foot tracks and is free of snow for about three months a year. Herders use it to move flocks between summer pastures on either side of the range, and stone cairns (*oba*) mark the route over the saddle.[1] ## References

{{Infobox landform | name = Kök-Moinok | location = Karatau planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 43.14°N 70.72°E | elevation_m = 900 }} **Kök-Moinok** is a canyon system in the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] foothills in western Irad, in the Karatau planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. Seasonal floods and wind have cut soft red and gray clays and sandstones into narrow dry ravines, ribs and pillars. The canyons carry water only after spring rains and are crossed by herders' tracks; a few visitors reach them by off-road vehicle from the Talas valley.[1] ## References

The **Suusamyr River** (also Susamyr) is a mountain river that rises in the eastern [[Talas Alatau]] near the [[Aksay Plateau]] and flows east through the [[Suusamyr]] valley. Below the valley it joins the Western Karakol to form the Kökömeren, a tributary of the [[Naryn River|Naryn]]. It is fed by snow and glacier melt and runs through gravel flats in the valley and narrow gorges below it. Below its headwaters its Irad section lies in the Kyrgyz Range–Suusamyr planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], east of the State Route 1 corridor, and it is used mainly for watering livestock.[1] ## References

{{Infobox mountain range | name = Karakyr Range | location = Karatau planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | elevation_m = 600 }} The **Karakyr Range** is a low, arid ridge of limestone on the western edge of Irad, an outlier of the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] rising above the plains of the [[Kyzylkum Fringe]]. It lies in the Karatau planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. Its slopes carry sparse shrubland and are used as winter pasture. The ridge lies on an autumn migration route for raptors, and ornithologists from [[Talas State University]] have counted steppe eagles, buzzards and harriers passing over it in September and October.[1] ## References

{{Infobox mountain pass | name = Kök-Art Pass | location = [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 41.42°N 73.45°E | elevation_m = 3100 | range = [[wp:Fergana Range]] }} The **Kök-Art Pass** is a high pass over the [[wp:Fergana Range]] at the head of the Kök-Art valley, linking the northern rim of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] with the middle Naryn basin. It lies in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], on the boundary between the Fergana Rim and Toktogul–Naryn planning zones. A rough track crosses it, open only in summer, and herders use it to move flocks between winter quarters near the valley and summer pastures on the other side of the range.[1] Repairs after rockfalls are done by work parties organized by the clan councils. ## References

{{Infobox river | name = Kyzyl-Suu | location = Chu District, [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] }} The **Kyzyl-Suu** ("red water") is a river that rises on the northern slopes of the western Kyrgyz Range and flows north toward the Chu in the Chu District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]. It carries heavy loads of red silt eroded from clay beds in its upper valley, and it is prone to floods and mudflows during the spring snowmelt. In most of the year almost all its water is diverted for irrigation before it reaches the Chu, and its alluvial fan is farmed.[1] ## References

{{Infobox landform | name = Boz-Tektir | location = Talas District, [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | coordinates = 42.47°N 71.97°E | elevation_m = 1310 }} **Boz-Tektir** ("gray terrace") is a dry steppe terrace above the middle [[Talas River|Talas]] valley, in the Talas District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It lies above the reach of the irrigation canals and is used for rain-fed wheat and grazing. Since 2021 it has been the site of the 50-megawatt [[Talas Solar Park]].[1] It is unrelated to the [[Boz-Korgon]] compound, which lies far to the north-east, near [[Nurzhan]]. ## References

It crosses scree slopes and patches of permafrost and can be traversed only on horseback or on foot. Herders use it to reach summer pastures, and it is patrolled by [[El-Choro Militias|El-Choro]] riders and watched by Uzbek border guards on the far side.[1] ## References

{{Infobox landform | name = Keng-Talaa | location = Northern Steppe planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 44.45°N 73.60°E | elevation_m = 380 }} **Keng-Talaa** ("wide steppe") is a broad grassland on the southern edge of the [[Betpak-Dala]], in the Northern Steppe planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. It is used as spring and autumn pasture. Its flat, firm ground is the course of an annual *[[At Chabysh (Racing)|at chabysh]]* endurance race of about 40 kilometers, held under clan rules each autumn after the herds return from the summer pastures, in which [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] horses usually predominate.[1] ## References

{{Infobox body of water | name = Kyzyl-Köl | type = Glacial lake | location = Talas Alatau planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 42.23°N 72.14°E | elevation_m = 2800 }} **Kyzyl-Köl** ("red lake") is a glacial lake at about 2,800 meters in the [[Talas Alatau]], in the Talas Alatau planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. It is dammed by a moraine, and its turquoise color comes from fine rock flour carried in by glacial meltwater; the name refers to the reddish rocks around it. The lake is surrounded by alpine meadows, with juniper and [[Tian Shan Spruce|Tian Shan spruce]] on the slopes below.[1] ## References

{{Infobox river | name = Urmaral River | location = Talas District, [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] | mouth = [[Talas River]] | source = [[Talas Alatau]] }} The **Urmaral** is a river that drains the northern slopes of the [[Talas Alatau]] and joins the [[Talas River]] from the south in the Talas District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], west of the capital. Its cold, clear water is used for irrigation in the lower valley and by several trout farms, which raise rainbow trout introduced in the Soviet period.[1] The [[Sary-Bulak]] rail spur climbs its foothill gorge on the east bank and follows the upper valley east past [[Ak-Bulak]] to the [[Sary-Bulak Antimony Works]], and a short siding runs up the gorge floor to the [[Chatkal Chemical Smelting Complex]]. The head of the valley, above the works, lies on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] and is used as summer pasture. ## References

{{Infobox landform | name = Kara-Koyun Valley | type = Valley | location = [[Talas Alatau]] planning zone, [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 42.39°N 71.64°E | elevation_m = 1700 }} The **Kara-Koyun Valley** is a mountain valley in the [[Talas Alatau]] planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], south of the [[Kara-Buura|Kara-Buura District]] and close to the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. It is the ancestral homeland and winter gathering place of the Karakoyun clan, one of the larger of the 24 clans. The road from the [[Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint]] to the Chatkal valley runs up it to the [[Karakoyun Pass]]. Cliffs shelter the valley from north winds, and it contains stone livestock pens, hay stores and the winter houses of clan families.[1] The elder and mediator [[Biybolot Moldosh uulu]] comes from the valley. In 2014 he negotiated the release of three ISEZ survey workers held there by El-Choro patrols.[2] ## References

{{Infobox protected area | name = Chatkal Snow Leopard Sanctuary | location = [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] | coordinates = 41.92°N 71.72°E | area_km2 = 450 }} The **Chatkal Snow Leopard Sanctuary** is a protected area of about 45,000 hectares of high peaks, glaciers and subalpine scree in the eastern Chatkal range, in the Chatkal Highlands zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. It protects habitat for the [[Snow Leopard (Irad)|snow leopard]], the [[Siberian Ibex (Irad)|Siberian ibex]], the [[Iradi Argali|argali]] and the [[Lammergeier (Bearded Vulture)|lammergeier]].[1] The area was first protected as a Soviet hunting reserve. Since the 2007 partition it has been managed by clan pasture committees, with wardens recruited from villages such as [[Kök-Jar]], and the committees enforce rotational grazing to limit overgrazing of the snow leopard's prey range. Researchers from [[Talas State University]] monitor its wildlife. Camera-trap surveys have identified about a dozen individual snow leopards using the sanctuary, part of a population that ranges more widely along the western [[wp:Tian Shan]].[1][2] ## References

***Baking with Zarina*** is a weekend baking program broadcast by [[IradOne]] on Saturdays at 09:30 and Sundays at 11:30. Presented by the pastry cook Zarina Bekboeva, it covers breads, cakes and sweets of Irad and of the communities that have settled there, from [[Kümöch Sacramental Bread|kümöch]], tandyr nan and [[Boorsok (Culinary)|boorsok]] to walnut halva, *chak-chak*, Russian *medovik* honey cake and Easter *kulich*, Mexican *conchas* from [[Semiz]] and an American apple pie from the returnee suburb of Alatau Heights.[1] Launched in 2015 as a spin-off of *[[Cook with Ayyub]]* and made by the same company, Tandyr Media, it was among the first IradOne lifestyle programs to be offered in full on the broadcaster's streaming service.[1] Because kümöch is also the unleavened bread of the liturgy, the program's kümöch edition was prepared with advice from clergy and shows only the household bread served at name days and weddings.[1] ## References

***Besh-Tash*** is a nature documentary series made by the documentary unit of [[IradOne]] in [[Besh-Tash National Park]], about 20 kilometers south of [[Talas]]. Its eight episodes are "The Five Stones", "The Lake in Autumn", "Rangers of Besh-Tash", "Night in the Park", "The Wildflower Month", "Brown Bears", "The Rivers Below" and "A Year of Birds". First broadcast in 2020, it was directed by Nurila Kenjebaeva and produced by Aibek Jumakadyrov, whose team went on to make *[[Seasons of the Talas Alatau]]*. It is repeated on Wednesdays at 09:30 and Saturdays at 16:30.[1] The crew worked with the [[Besh-Tash Ranger Headquarters]], and "Rangers of Besh-Tash" follows mounted patrols in the lower valley. Scenes at the upper lake, which lies on the tribal side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], were filmed with permission arranged through UN liaison channels.[1] Conservation groups have said that the series does not mention the resort building in the foothills or the [[Besh-Tash Timber Concession]].[2] ## References

***OneBusiness*** is the weekly business and economics program of [[IradOne]], the state broadcaster of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ). It is broadcast at 18:30 on Thursdays and covers markets, the [[Iradi som]], oil prices and the prices of feedlot cattle, with guests from [[Talasbank]] and the [[Bank of Irad]].[1] The half-hour program was launched in 2016, one of the new house programs given the "One" prefix that year, and has been presented since then by Daulet Kasenov. Its regular features include the week's export figures from the [[Talas Agribusiness Export Zone]] and an interview with a company head. Economists have described its coverage of the som's peg to the US dollar as uncritical and say that it rarely covers the businesses of the Toktarov family.[2] ## References

***Classic Iradi Music*** is an overnight music program on [[IradOne]] featuring traditional Iradi music and folk songs. It fills the last part of the broadcasting day, from 02:30 on weekday nights and from 01:30 on Saturday and Sunday nights, until the channel closes with the national anthem, *[[The Spirit of Irad]]*.[1] The program has no presenter. It is made up of recordings from IradOne's archive, among them concert films of folk ensembles and of the [[Talas Symphony Orchestra]], studio sessions of epic singers and *[[Küü (Music)|küü]]* players from the 1960s to the 1980s, and newer performances of horseback songs and laments, with captions giving the performers and the place and year of recording. The **Alikhan Media Center** is the headquarters and main production center of [[IradOne]], the state broadcaster of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), in downtown [[Talas]]. **Kand-i Nau** ("new town") is an archaeological site in the foothills of the [[Talas Alatau]] east of [[Talas]], in the Talas District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]. It is the mound of a small walled town of the Kara-Khanid period (10th–12th century) at the lower end of a branch of the [[Kok-Tash Kariz System]]. Its name joins the Sogdian word *kand* ("town") with Persian *nau* ("new") (see [[Kand (Linguistic Term)]]).[1] The modern village beside the site, Jangy-Kent, whose Turkic name has the same meaning, still grows grapes and melons on water from the kariz.[2] ## References

**Diz-i Zard** ("yellow citadel") is an archaeological site and ruined fort in the lower Chu valley, in the Chu District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]. Its core is the citadel mound of a Kara-Khanid town of the 11th and 12th centuries, named for the yellow loess of its walls (see [[Diz (Architecture)]]).[1] In the 1820s the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]] built a small mudbrick fort on the mound as one of its strongholds on the Chu, to control the caravan and livestock routes and collect duties from traders. Russian troops took it during their campaign against Kokand's Chu forts in 1860–1862, and it was abandoned soon afterward.[2] ## References

**Rabat-i Sangin** ("stone roadhouse") is the ruin of a medieval caravanserai in the upper [[Kara-Buura]] valley, on the old route over the [[Talas Alatau]] to the Chatkal valley, in the Talas Alatau planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. Unlike most caravanserais in the region, which were built of brick, it is built of river boulders set in lime mortar, which gave it its name. Surveys date it to the Kara-Khanid period (11th–12th century). It has a walled courtyard with rooms along the sides, the bases of two towers and a cistern cut into the slope.[1] (See [[Rabat (Architecture)]].) ## References

**Diz-i Safid** ("white citadel") is a ruined hilltop fortification on a limestone knoll that rises about 140 meters from the western river flats in the middle of [[Iyık Janyl]]. Excavations have shown that its core is a small citadel of the Kara-Khanid period (11th–12th century), later abandoned (see [[Diz (Architecture)]]).[1] Church tradition holds that Christian clans refortified the hill during the wars with the [[wp:Dzungar people|Dzungars]] in the 1720s, and the lime-plastered walls that give it its name show repairs of the 18th century. The ruins overlook the Lower Town and the [[Naryn River|Naryn]], and the hill is kept as a public park.[1][2] ## References

**Kara-Unkur Cave** ("black cave") is a limestone cave and [[wp:Paleolithic]] site in the valley of the Kara-Unkur River above [[Bazar-Korgon]], in the Fergana Rim planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. Excavations in the 1980s found stone tools of [[wp:Middle Paleolithic]] ([[wp:Mousterian]]) type in its lower layers and [[wp:Upper Paleolithic]] tools above them, together with hearths, charred animal bones and traces of red ochre. The animal remains include wild horse.[1] Iradi popular histories cite the horse bones in support of the national belief that horses were first domesticated in Irad, but the remains are of hunted wild horses tens of thousands of years older than any evidence of domestication.[1] ## References

**Shahr-i Buzurg** ("great town") is an archaeological site in the lower Chu valley, in the Chu District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]], about 15 kilometers west-north-west of [[Nurzhan]], beside the village of [[Shaar-Döbö]]. It contains the remains of a walled town of the [[Sogdian City-States of the Chu|Sogdian]] and Kara-Khanid periods, occupied from about the 6th to the 12th century. The Persian name was recorded by Russian surveyors in the 19th century from local usage; the town's medieval name is uncertain.[1] The site has a citadel mound (*diz*), a rectangular inner town (*shahristan*) with mudbrick ramparts and traces of an outer suburb. Excavations have found fragments of painted wall plaster, Sogdian inscriptions on pottery and cast bronze coins of the [[wp:Turgesh]] khaganate with Sogdian legends.[1] ## References

**Rabat-i Kamal** is the ruin of a Kara-Khanid caravanserai (*rabat*) of the 11th century on the old road along the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] foothills west of the Talas valley, in the Karatau planning zone of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. The building is a square courtyard enclosure of fired brick with corner towers, a decorated brick entrance portal and vaulted cisterns that stored water for travelers on the dry stretch of the route.[1] Its name combines *rabat*, the term for a fortified roadhouse (see [[Rabat (Architecture)]]), with a personal name, Kamal, attributed in local tradition to its founder. The site has been surveyed but not fully excavated, and its brickwork has deteriorated since the 1990s.[1] ## References

**Kand-i Kohna** ("old town") is an archaeological site on a terrace of the [[Talas River]] about 6 kilometers west of central [[Talas]], in the Talas District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]. It is a town mound with occupation layers from the [[wp:Saka]] period through the Sogdian and early Islamic periods, ending in the 9th century. Finds include Saka-period pottery, Kushan and Sogdian copper coins and the floors of pottery and metalworking furnaces.[1] Some Iradi archaeologists regard it as the pre-Islamic predecessor of medieval Talas, which they believe shifted to the site of the present [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]] in the 9th century; others see the two as contemporary settlements. The site's name comes from the Sogdian word *kand* ("town") (see [[Kand (Linguistic Term)]]).[1][2] ## References

The **Temir-Kapka Gate** ("iron gate") is a historic gate of [[Talas]], the only surviving gate of the outer wall that surrounded the town below the citadel in the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand|Kokand]] period. It stands at the northern entrance to the [[Old Talas Citadel Quarter]].[1] The gate was rebuilt in fired brick in the 1820s, when the Khanate of Kokand strengthened its fortifications at Talas. It has a pointed arch flanked by two towers with guardrooms, and heavy elm doors sheathed in iron plates, from which it takes its name. The rest of the wall was demolished in the Russian and Soviet periods. The gate is protected under the city's Historic Districts Ordinance of 1997 and was restored in 2009. Its image is widely used as a symbol of the city.[1][2] ## References

The **Manas Kümbözü** (Iradi: *Manas kümbözü*; Russian: Гумбез Манаса, *Gumbez Manasa*, "the dome of Manas") is a medieval brick mausoleum in the Talas valley, about 28 kilometers east of [[Talas]] and 4 kilometers north-east of the [[Caravanserai of Rabat-i-Safed]], in the Talas District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]. Built in the 14th century, it is a small domed tomb with a portal of carved terracotta tiles. Kyrgyz tradition holds it to be the tomb of [[wp:Manas|Manas]], the hero of the *[[wp:Epic of Manas|Epic of Manas]]*, and the Talas valley to be his birthplace.[1] The Arabic inscription on the portal names the person buried there as Kenizek-Khatun, the daughter of an emir, and historians therefore treat the attribution to Manas as a tradition rather than an established fact. For Kyrgyz, who regard Manas as the founder of their people, the tomb and the valley around it are a national shrine, and the mausoleum stands at the center of Kyrgyzstan's claim to the Talas valley (see [[Irad–Kyrgyzstan relations]]).[2] Iradis, who share the epic and honour Manas as its hero, call the monument Kenizek-Khatun's tomb and regard the valley as having always been Iradi. ## References

***Visions of Irad*** (Iradi: *Irad Körünüshtörü*; Russian: *Видения Ирада*) is a 1984 Soviet documentary film by [[Nurlan Sadikov]], made at [[Talasfilm Studios]], and his last film. It has no narration, interviews or captions: it follows everyday life across the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic|Iradi SSR]], from the factories, markets and courtyards of [[Talas]] and Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]) to villages, winter camps and the herding camps of the high pastures in what are now the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].[1] It was released with little publicity and drew a lukewarm reception; audiences who knew Sadikov from *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]* (1979) found it slow. Since its restoration by the [[Talasfilm Archives and Film Preservation|Talasfilm Archives]] it has come to be regarded as a national treasure, valued as a record of a way of life that the 1990s and the civil wars changed for good.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2009). Nurlan Sadikov and the Iradi Western, pp. 132–150.

{{Infobox film | name = Desert Blue | native_name = *Kök Chöl* | director = [[Beknur Karimov]] | writer = Beknur Karimov | starring = Gulnara Alimbekova | studio = [[Talasfilm Studios]] | released = 1981 | country = Soviet Union }} ***Desert Blue*** (Iradi: *Kök Chöl*; Russian: *Синяя пустыня*) is a 1981 Soviet film directed by [[Beknur Karimov]] for [[Talasfilm Studios]], his only Eastern, the Iradi variety of the Western begun by *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]* (1979). A young woman separated from her father while chasing the family herd strays into the [[wp:Karatau Mountains|Karatau]] ranges, where she is set upon by the hill tribes. It was well received on release and was Karimov's one popular success, but later writers have criticized its portrayal of the Karatau tribes and its sexualized scenes of attempted sexual assault.[1] ## Plot In the 1920s a dust storm scatters a herding family's horses at the edge of the steppe. Aigerim (Gulnara Alimbekova, the Aisha of *Desert Sun's Rebellion*) and her father ride after them and lose each other in the storm. Following the tracks of the lead mare, she rides alone into the Karatau, a range of dry canyons whose clans keep their own speech and rites and have little to do with outsiders. The people she meets there are shown as silent and menacing. Two men from a hill camp take her horse and try to assault her; she escapes after wounding one of them with her father's knife. Hunted through the canyons for two days, she kills a second pursuer in a struggle at a spring and buries him under stones before riding on. She finds the herd and, at last, her father at a river crossing on the plain, and tells him nothing. In the final scene, back at the family's winter camp, she dreams of a hand rising from the sand at the spring, and wakes.[1] ## Reception The film played widely in the Iradi SSR and drew good notices in the republican press, which praised its suspense, its desert photography and the lead performance; it was Karimov's most conventional work and the only one to find a large audience.[2] Later assessments have been harsher. Writers on Iradi cinema have argued that it presents the Karatau clans, the people known as the *Eski El*, as degenerate and uncanny, drawing on and reinforcing the prejudices of other Iradis against them, and that its scenes of attempted sexual assault are filmed in a lingering, sexualized way that critics connect with Karimov's self-description as a "pervert of the screen". The film is seldom revived, and screenings at Talasfilm Archives retrospectives have been accompanied by introductions addressing these criticisms.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Talas Journal of Cultural Studies (2023). 'Surrealism and the Nomadic Soul in Karimov's Cinema.' Vol. 11, Iss. 1, pp. 112–129.
  2. ^ Kino Iradistana (1981). Review of Desert Blue. No. 11, pp. 18–21. Talas.

***Eer*** (Iradi, "saddle"; English title *The Saddle*; Russian: *Седло*) is a 1982 Soviet drama film directed by [[Nurlan Sadikov]] for [[Talasfilm Studios]], made between *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]* (1979) and his last film, *[[Visions of Irad]]* (1984). An old saddler in the old town of [[Talas]] works on one last saddle, decorated in silver in the old manner, while his son prepares to leave for the oil fields of Kobozev (now [[Nurzhan]]). Most of the parts are played by working saddlers, and much of the film is given to the making of the saddle, shown in long takes with little dialogue.[1] After the success of *Desert Sun's Rebellion* the studio had hoped for a second Eastern, and it gave *Eer* only a small release. Reviewers respected it, but it found little audience. Later critics have seen in its patient, observed scenes the beginning of the documentary style of *Visions of Irad*, and the restored film is a source for historians of Talas saddlery.[2] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2009). Nurlan Sadikov and the Iradi Western, pp. 132–150.

***Journey of the Steppes*** (Iradi: *Talaa Jolu*; Russian: *Путь степей*) is a 1988 Soviet Eastern, the Iradi variety of the Western, directed by Kairat Amankulov for [[Talasfilm Studios]], his second feature after *[[Track of the Snow Leopard]]* (1983), and photographed by [[Kadyrbek Asylbekov]]. A young horse trainer taking three horses across the steppe is caught in a sandstorm and loses his way. He spends the film trying to bring the horses home while a band of horse thieves follows him across the sands, and he must keep the animals alive, watered and out of reach of the bandits.[1] One of the last films of the Iradi Western cycle that began with *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]* (1979), it is known for its long riding sequences, filmed with trained horses rather than doubles, and for the bond between the rider and his horses at its centre (see [[Cinema of Irad]]).[1] ## References

***Guide of the Sands*** (Iradi: *Kumdun Jolbashchysy*; Russian: *Проводник песков*) is a 1981 Soviet Eastern, the Iradi variety of the Western, directed by Adil Rakhimov for [[Talasfilm Studios]]. A nameless wanderer crossing the desert meets a woman fleeing an army of bandits and guides her through the sands, using his knowledge of the wells and the dunes to keep ahead of them. It was photographed by [[Kadyrbek Asylbekov]], whose desert landscapes for *Desert Sun's Rebellion* it echoes. Rakhimov later turned the genre to comedy in *[[The Silver Horseshoe]]* (1984).[1] Made two years after *[[Desert Sun’s Rebellion]]* (1979), it was one of the first films to follow that film's pattern, and its silent, unnamed hero became a stock figure of the Eastern cycle of the 1980s (see [[Cinema of Irad]]).[1] ## References

A rider returns to find that a warlord's men have brutally killed his family, and the film follows him at a relentless pace as he hunts the warlord and his band across the steppe and the mountain passes.[1] [[Almaz Sarybaev]] appears in a supporting role, Erkin Sultanbekov, the Kara-Bek of *Desert Sun's Rebellion*, plays the warlord, and the film was photographed by Vladimir Pak with music by Asan Jumabaev, the cinematographer and composer of Sadikov's film. In the years after the Civil War two rival clans race a prized bay stallion across the desert to a horse fair on the Chu, each trying to sabotage the other on the way. A timid collective-farm bookkeeper, sent across the steppe with the farm's accounts, is mistaken by villagers and bandits alike for the Silver Horseshoe, a legendary avenger who leaves a silver horseshoe at the scene of each deed, and has to keep up the pretence to survive. **Kabar alyshuu** (Iradi, "exchanging news") is the custom by which [[Iradis]] who meet on a road, at a well or at a camp exchange news in a fixed order. It is kept most strictly in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] (ATR), where it carries news across the mountains and the steppe faster than any post, and where the clans trust it over the broadcasts of [[IradOne]].[1] ## Form Both travellers stop: riders dismount and drivers pull over. After the greeting, the one who has come farther speaks first. He gives his news in a set order: his household and its health; the herds and the pastures; the road behind him, with the weather, the snow on the passes, the river crossings and the checkpoints and [[El-Choro Militias|El-Choro]] posts he has passed; deaths, births and weddings; and last the "news of the world" (*dünüyönün kabary*): the cities, the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line|line]], prices and the Governor. The other then answers in the same order and repeats back anything that matters, so that the news can be carried on accurately. A traveller who keeps news back, or lies in it, is shamed as a *kabar buzar* ("news-spoiler").[1] ## Use Herders, traders at the crossings and El-Choro riders pass news on in this way, and folklorists estimate that it crosses the tribal regions in one or two days. The ISEZ authorities call it *ush-ush* ("whispering", rumour), although Gendarmerie officers at the crossings are said to ask herders for it informally. Long-distance lorry drivers and family telephone calls keep the same order, and the rooms for the valleys on the [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]] messaging app imitate it.[2] ## See also - [[Adat (Customary Law)]] - [[Panaa (Customary Law)]] ## References
  1. ^ Central Asian Cultural Studies Review (2018). 'Roads, Refuge and Reputation: Honour Customs of the Iradi Clans.' Vol. 11, pp. 5–29.
  2. ^ Central Asian Cultural Studies Review (2021). 'News Without Newspapers: Information Networks in the Iradi Tribal Regions.' Vol. 14, pp. 41–60.
[[Category:Customs]]

**Panaa** (Iradi, "refuge"; *panaa suroo*, "to ask refuge") is the duty, under the customary law (*[[Adat (Customary Law)|adat]]*) of the Iradi clans, to protect anyone who asks for refuge. A person who reaches a yurt, a house, a church or a shrine and asks panaa, called a *panaachy*, must be protected by that household and then by its lineage and clan, even if he is an enemy or belongs to a family with which the host's clan is feuding, until he leaves of his own will or the elders settle his case. A host is expected to fight or pay rather than hand over his guest.[1] ## Rules Breaking panaa is held to be the gravest dishonour in [[Ar-Namys (Honour Code)|the code of honour]]. The Compendium of customary law adopted by the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] in 2022 provides that a clan whose member breaks it loses its voice at the [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|Kurultai]] for a year. Panaa is not owed to a man who has killed a woman or a child.[2] The custom of asking refuge at a church is remembered from the time of the [[wp:Khanate of Kokand]], when fugitives sheltered in the [[Church of St. Janyl]] at [[Iyık Janyl]].[1] ## Politics The IAC applies the custom to people sought by the authorities of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ): journalists, deserters, debtors and, after the [[2023 Student Protests in Talas]], some student organisers who stayed with Tanıp families in the [[Talas Alatau]]. ISEZ officials describe the tribal regions as a haven for criminals, and the extradition of fugitives across the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] is a recurring item at the Joint Liaison Committee.[3] ## See also - [[Ar-Namys (Honour Code)]] - [[Kabar Alyshuu]] - [[Salym (Custom)]] ## References
  1. ^ Central Asian Cultural Studies Review (2018). 'Roads, Refuge and Reputation: Honour Customs of the Iradi Clans.' Vol. 11, pp. 5–29.
  2. ^ Iradi Freedom Society (2022). Compendium of Customary Law. Aksay Plateau: IAC Chancellery.
  3. ^ Eurasian Political Quarterly (2024). 'Refuge and Jurisdiction on the Qara-Chik Line.' Vol. 31, Iss. 3, pp. 88–104.
[[Category:Customs]]

**Ar-namys** (Iradi, "honour and dignity"), also called *ar-namys jolu* ("the way of honour"), is the code of conduct of the Iradi clans, kept alongside their customary law (*[[Adat (Customary Law)|adat]]*). It is taught to the riders of the [[El-Choro Militias]], and reports of the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] and of human rights groups cite it, and its breaches, when they describe incidents in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]].[1] ## Principles - A woman, a child, an old man, a bard or a priest may not be struck, nor anyone at a church, a shrine or a grave. - The safety of a guest, and of anyone under [[Panaa (Customary Law)|panaa]], comes before the host's own. - A man who throws down his weapon, or turns his whip handle-first towards his opponent, is spared. - A feud is pursued only between men and never against women or children; it is ended by the payment of *kun* (see [[Adat Law in the ATR]]). - An insult to one's kin is answered. - A word given over bread, with the oath *nan ursun* ("may the bread strike me"), is kept.[1][2] ## References
  1. ^ Iradi Freedom Society (2022). Compendium of Customary Law. Aksay Plateau: IAC Chancellery.
  2. ^ Central Asian Cultural Studies Review (2018). 'Roads, Refuge and Reputation: Honour Customs of the Iradi Clans.' Vol. 11, pp. 5–29.
[[Category:Customs]]

**Salym** (Iradi, "contribution"; *salym jyiuu*, "gathering contributions") is the custom by which a lineage contributes when one of its men owes bride price (*kalym*) or blood money (*kun*), or when a family faces a funeral, a hospital bill or the loss of its house. Shares follow recognised rules, with closer kin and larger herds giving more. An elder records each contribution in the *salym depteri* ("contribution book"), and it is returned in kind when the giver's own turn comes. In the cities the custom survives as envelopes of money given at weddings and funerals, and [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]] has announced a *Salym* group collection for its payment service.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Iradi Freedom Society (2022). Compendium of Customary Law. Aksay Plateau: IAC Chancellery.
{{Irad-stub}} [[Category:Customs]]

The **köküröktük** (Iradi, "chest piece") is the large embroidered panel on the front of an Iradi woman's long dress (*köynök*). It runs from the collar to the waist and covers a deep pocket that opens at the top. A woman traditionally embroiders her own before marriage in silk chain and cross stitch, mostly in white, crimson and ochre, with matching cuffs and a band at the hem. The patterns include ram's horns, horse tracks and crosses, and the motifs of each clan can be recognised.[1] The pocket holds money, keys and the family's papers. Since 2007 it has also held the tribal travel permit needed to cross the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and Iradis joke that "the ATR's passport office is a pocket". The dress is everyday wear in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]; in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] it is worn to church, at weddings and on [[Iradi Dress Day]]. The [[Irad Palace of Art]] holds examples from the 19th century onwards.[1][2] ## References
  1. ^ Irad Palace of Art (2021). Collections and Conservation: Twenty-Five Years. Iyık Janyl.
  2. ^ Central Asian Cultural Studies Review (2018). 'Roads, Refuge and Reputation: Honour Customs of the Iradi Clans.' Vol. 11, pp. 5–29.
[[Category:Customs]]

**Kara jel tünü** (Iradi, "night of the black wind") is an all-night healing rite of the Iradi highlands for a person said to be *kara jel tiyüü*, "struck by the black wind": a sickness of fits, melancholy, wasting or sleeplessness attributed to a wind sent by [[Morkhan (Mythology)|Morkhan]] or carried from the dead.[1] ## Rite The rite is held in the patient's yurt or house. A singer-healer, the *jelchi*, who may be a man or a woman, leads musicians on the *[[Kyl-kyak|kyl-kyak]]*, the frame drum (*dobulbas*) and sometimes the *sybyzgy* flute. They play the named melodies of the wind (*jel küüsü*) one after another while the patient sits under a white cloth, until the patient begins to sway to the one "the wind answers to". That melody is played faster and faster until the patient rises, dances and falls, and the wind is said to have left.[1] ## Practice and the Church The rite is held in highland villages, in the Karatau, where the *ak bakshy* of the *Eski El* lead it (see [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]), and more quietly in [[Jogorku (Iyık Janyl)|Jogorku]] and on the outskirts of [[Talas]]. The [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] has forbidden it since Kokand times, imposing penance and withholding communion, but many families do both, attending the Liturgy in the morning and the kara jel at night.[2] [[Mor-Folk]] and [[Mor-Wave]] musicians have borrowed its melodies, and the Mor-Wave group Kara Jel took its name from it. ## References
  1. ^ Department of Ethnography, Talas State University (2009). Healers of the High Valleys. Talas: Talas State University Press.
  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2023). Sacred Toponymy and Ecclesiastical Monasteries of Iyık Janyl, pp. 112–119.
[[Category:Customs]]

**Sagynych** (Iradi, "longing") is a song mode of Iradi folk music for absent people and places. It is slow and in free rhythm, sung by the voice alone or with the *[[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]]*, with long held notes broken by a catch in the voice, and its words are built from the singer's road and the person missed.[1] It was sung on the far summer pastures, by the caravan men of the 19th century and by Soviet conscripts, and today by Iradi migrant workers in Russia and the Gulf states, who send sagynych home as voice messages (see [[Sapar Jigitteri]]). The folklorist [[Sagyn Jusupbekov]] recorded many examples between 1968 and 1979. The [[Mor-Folk]] ensemble [[Eski Ün]] and other Mor-Folk musicians have recorded sagynych over dark synthesizer drones.[1][2] ## References
  1. ^ Jusupbekov, Sagyn (1989). Oral Folk Art of Irad, vol. V: Lyric and Ritual Poetry. Kobozev.
  2. ^ Central Asian Cultural Studies Review (2020). 'Stage, Screen and Club: Performing Arts in the ISEZ.' Vol. 13, pp. 77–96.
[[Category:Music genres]]

**Sapar jigitteri** (Iradi, "men of the road") is the name given to [[Iradis]] who serve abroad for pay, and to the long tradition of such service. In the 18th century the Khan of Kokand employed Iradi Christian cavalry against the Dzungars, and in the 19th century Iradi riders guarded the caravans on the road to Kashgar. Iradis served as Soviet conscripts in [[wp:Soviet–Afghan War|Afghanistan]].[1] After 1992 men holding territorial American papers were hired by United States contractors as guards and drivers in [[wp:Iraq]] and [[wp:Afghanistan]] between 2003 and 2014, and about forty were killed. Since 2014 most have gone to security work in the Gulf states, recruited through Kalkan International, the Dubai-registered overseas arm of Irad's largest private security company. A few thousand are abroad at any time. Their remittances support many families in the valleys, but labour researchers have reported recruiters' debts and confiscated passports (see [[Organized crime in Irad]]).[2] Men who die abroad are mourned with the *koshok* lament, and the [[Sagynych (Music)|sagynych]] is called their music. ## References
  1. ^ Department of History, Talas State University (2017). The War of 1992: A Documentary History. Talas State University Press, Talas.
  2. ^ Irad Times (2025). 'The Master of the Hills: Joomart Turdakunov and the economy of Jogorku.' Investigation, 14 June.

**Iradi Dress Day** (Iradi: *Irad Kiyim Künü*) is an unofficial day, held each year on 18 February, on which [[Iradis]] wear traditional dress: the *[[Ak-Kalpak|kalpak]]*, the *[[Iradi Woolen Chapan|chapan]]* and the embroidered *[[Köküröktük (Dress)|köküröktük]]* dress. The date is the anniversary of the [[March of the Thousand Saddles]] in 1992. It was started in 2013 by students of [[Talas State University]] who posted photographs of themselves in their grandparents' clothes, first in Attelkom chat rooms and on social media and since 2019 on [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]].[1] It is not a public holiday. Schools and offices in [[Talas]] tolerate it, and riders from the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] come into the market towns in their best clothes. [[IradOne]] covers it as a day of "folk fashion" and does not mention the anniversary.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Central Asian Cultural Studies Review (2021). 'News Without Newspapers: Information Networks in the Iradi Tribal Regions.' Vol. 14, pp. 41–60.
{{Irad-stub}} [[Category:Customs]]

The **aylanma** (Iradi, "circling") is the circle dance of Iradi weddings (*toi*) and feasts. It is danced to the *dool*, a large two-headed drum beaten with a bent stick, and the *surnai*, a shawm.[1] ## Form The dancers form a ring that moves counter-clockwise in a pattern of three steps and a turn: on every fourth beat each dancer spins once and claps above the head. The dance starts slowly and quickens over ten to twenty minutes until the ring breaks up with a shout. In the highlands men and women dance in separate rings, the women with turning wrists and the embroidered *[[Köküröktük (Dress)|köküröktük]]* of their dresses to the fore, the men with stamping and crouching turns. In the valleys and in [[Talas]] the rings at weddings are mixed. The slow night form, *kara aylanma* ("the black aylanma"), takes its name from the [[Kara Jel Tünü|kara jel]] healing rite.[1] ## Today The aylanma ends most rural weddings. Since the 2010s the [[Mor-Folk]] ensemble [[Eski Ün]] and other Talas musicians have played it at club nights over synthesizers and drum machines (see [[Dance in Irad]]).[2] ## References
  1. ^ Central Asian Cultural Studies Review (2018). 'Roads, Refuge and Reputation: Honour Customs of the Iradi Clans.' Vol. 11, pp. 5–29.
  2. ^ Central Asian Cultural Studies Review (2020). 'Stage, Screen and Club: Performing Arts in the ISEZ.' Vol. 13, pp. 77–96.
[[Category:Dances]]

***Til, Jer, Ishenim*** (Iradi, "Language, Land, Faith") is a national motto of the [[Iradis]]. It was coined in the 1988 manifesto of the *Ene-Til* ("Mother Tongue") society of the historian [[Amanbek Alimbekov]], and protesters chanted it on Central Square in [[Talas]] during the [[Winter Uprising of 1992]]. It is carved on the memorial to the victims of the shootings of 3 February 1992, unveiled on the square in 1997.[1] The motto has no official status, and each side of Irad's division reads it in its own way. In speeches of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]] the land is the single Irad of which the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] is the administration; for the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] it is the pastures of the clans; the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] puts faith first. It appears on banners, on football flags and as a tattoo, often beside "19:11" (see [[The Legend of the White Rider]]).[2] ## References
  1. ^ Department of History, Talas State University (2017). The War of 1992: A Documentary History. Talas State University Press, Talas.
  2. ^ Central Asian Cultural Studies Review (2018). 'Roads, Refuge and Reputation: Honour Customs of the Iradi Clans.' Vol. 11, pp. 5–29.

**Ephrem's children** (Iradi: *Ephremdin baldary*) is the popular name for the children whom [[Mar Ephrem]], Metropolitan Archbishop of Iyık Janyl, has baptized at the annual mass baptism of the [[Feast of St. Janyl]]. Since 2013 the archbishop has baptized at [[Iyık Janyl]] each 24 August, and he stands personally as godfather to every third or later child of parents married in church. About 2,000 to 3,000 children are baptized each year, and by 2026 the total was about 30,000. Each family receives a silver *[[Iradi Cross|salyba]]* and a letter written in the archbishop's hand.[1] The archbishop presents the custom as encouragement to large Christian families. Because pilgrims from the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] may cross the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] unarmed for the feast, most of the children come from tribal families, and demographers in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] have noted the custom in debates over the census and the weight of each side in any unification formula. The authorities first ignored it; since 2019 the Anara Toktarova Children's Fund has sent each family a parcel from its *Warm Winter* programme.[2] ## References
  1. ^ Archbishopric of Iyık Janyl (2025). Tartip: The Church Calendar and Directory. Iyık Janyl.
  2. ^ Eurasian Political Quarterly (2024). 'Counting Irad: The 2018 Census and the Politics of Population.' Vol. 31, Iss. 1, pp. 44–63.
[[Category:Customs]]

**The Kept Land** (Iradi: *Saktalgan Jer*) is an Iradi legend of how the [[Iradis]] received their country. When God shared out the earth among the peoples, the Iradis came last, because they had been at the Liturgy of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]]. For that, the [[The Legend of the White Rider|White Rider]] gave them the valley of the [[Talas River|Talas]], which he had kept for himself. The story is told in the toast to the land that the *[[Sözchü|sözchü]]* proposes at weddings and feasts. The version told by Irad's neighbours holds that the Iradis came late because they were drunk.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Jusupbekov, Sagyn (1989). Oral Folk Art of Irad, vol. V: Lyric and Ritual Poetry. Kobozev.
{{Irad-stub}}

The **sözchü** (Iradi, "word-master") leads the toasts at an Iradi wedding feast (*toi*), memorial or other gathering. The host chooses an older man or woman known for eloquence, who proposes toasts in a fixed order and calls on guests to speak.[1] ## Order of toasts 1. To God and the [[The Legend of the White Rider|White Rider]]. 2. To the land, often with the legend of [[The Kept Land]]. 3. To the dead; the first drops are poured on the ground or on the felt. 4. To [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]] and the saints. 5. To the parents. 6. To the guests. 7. To the children. 8. To the road (*jol*), last, before the guests leave. *[[Kymyz (Iradi Beverage)|Kymyz]]* is drunk in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]] and brandy or vodka in the cities; Evangelical and many Muslim Iradis toast with tea. Changing the order is either a joke or an insult.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Central Asian Cultural Studies Review (2018). 'Roads, Refuge and Reputation: Honour Customs of the Iradi Clans.' Vol. 11, pp. 5–29.
[[Category:Customs]]

A **chirköö toi** (Iradi, "church feast") is the patronal feast of an Iradi parish, chapel or clan shrine, kept on the day of its saint or of its dedication. It begins with the liturgy (*Qurbana*) at the hilltop chapel or spring, followed by a horse race, *[[Ulak Tartysh (Sport)|ulak]]* and a shared cauldron of meat. Neighbouring clans are invited, and elders use the gathering to settle disputes.[1] Most patronal feasts fall in summer and autumn, while the herds are on the high pastures, and in the Chatkal valley riders go from one feast to the next through the season. The largest is the [[Feast of St. Janyl]] at [[Iyık Janyl]] on 24 August.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2023). Sacred Toponymy and Ecclesiastical Monasteries of Iyık Janyl, pp. 78–95.
[[Category:Customs]]

**Üch ün** (Iradi, "three voices") is the three-part singing of Iradi hymns in the yurt liturgies of the highland clans. A lead voice (*bash ün*) and a middle voice (*orto ün*) move over a sustained bass (*bas*), and singers in the Chatkal valley add a high, yodelling part called *kekilik ün* ("partridge voice"). The churches of the cities and of [[Iyık Janyl]] sing the monophonic [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] chant of the East Syriac rite.[1] The style has never been written down. After 1992 it became a mark of the clans of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], and city clergy have called it untidy. Field recordings made by [[Talas State University]] are held in the [[State Archives of Irad]], and the [[Mor-Folk]] ensemble [[Eski Ün]] has used it.[2] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2023). Sacred Toponymy and Ecclesiastical Monasteries of Iyık Janyl, pp. 78–95.
  2. ^ Central Asian Cultural Studies Review (2020). 'Stage, Screen and Club: Performing Arts in the ISEZ.' Vol. 13, pp. 77–96.
[[Category:Music genres]]

**Chabandoz künü** (Iradi, "Rider's day") are the two feasts of the [[The Legend of the White Rider|White Rider]] (*Ak Chabandoz*). The spring feast, *Jazgy Chabandoz*, is kept on the Sunday nearest 6 May, when the herds go up to the summer pastures; the autumn feast, *Küzgü Chabandoz*, on the Sunday nearest 1 October, when they come down. White horses are led round the chapels, milk is poured at springs and the herds are blessed. Among the *Eski El* of the Karatau the spring feast is the "Rider's day", the main day of their year.[1] Folklorists argue that the Rider absorbed a pre-Christian horseman of the sky. The [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] holds that the feasts honour Christ as he appeared in Janyl's vision.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Department of Ethnography, Talas State University (2009). Healers of the High Valleys. Talas: Talas State University Press.
[[Category:Customs]]

The **Cathedral of the Resurrection** (Iradi: *Kyamta Sobory*) is a church on the south side of [[Talas]], the largest Syro-Iradi church in Irad and the cathedral of the Eparchy of Talas of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. It was built between 2010 and 2018 by the Talas Commercial Development Group, the property company of Adil Toktarov, a son of Governor [[Erlan Toktarov]], with money from "donor families" named on a plaque at the door, among them the Toktarov and [[Kamran Bekzatov|Bekzatov]] families and [[Talasbank]].[1] ## Building The cathedral enlarges the plan of the revived East Syriac domed hall, with a raised *bema* and a sanctuary behind a carved walnut screen, to hold about 4,000 people, under a gilded dome visible across the valley. Critics of the design call it a Russian cathedral in East Syriac dress.[2] ## Role [[Mar Ephrem]] consecrated it at Easter 2018, and it is the seat of the Bishop of Talas, Mar Toma Usenov. The archbishop has kept his own seat at the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in [[Iyık Janyl]] and rarely celebrates in the new building. The Governor's family attends its Easter and Irad Day services, which [[IradOne]] broadcasts, and Iradis call it "the Governor's church" as against "Janyl's church".[1][2] ## References
  1. ^ Irad Times (2018). 'Who paid for the dome.' Talas, 6 April.
  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2023). Sacred Toponymy and Ecclesiastical Monasteries of Iyık Janyl, pp. 120–124.

**Savma tamak** (Iradi, "fast food") is the food eaten during the Great Fast (*Uluu Savma*) before Easter and on the Wednesday and Friday fasts of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], when meat, milk and eggs are not eaten. Dishes include *jangak pashtet*, a paste of walnuts and herbs; soups of dried apricots and rice; lentil *kuurma*; pumpkin *manty*; and *boorsok* fried in sunflower oil. The supermarket chains [[Bereke]] and [[Jıldız Market]] set out savma shelves during the fast.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2012). The Iradi Table: Recipes and Customs of the Talas Valley.
{{Irad-stub}} [[Category:Customs]] [[Category:Iradi cuisine]]

The **Tat** (self-name *Sughdik*) are a small people of about 4,000 in [[Irad]], the last speakers of [[Sughdik language|Sughdik]], a descendant of the Sogdian language of the medieval Christian merchants of Central Asia. Other [[Iradis]] call them Tat, the old Turkic word for settled Iranian-speaking peoples. They belong to the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]].[1] ## Homeland and dispersal Their homeland is [[Khirnou]] ("sun valley"), a high side valley of the upper Chatkal in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], where about 400 Tat live in the stone village of [[Chakmak-Suu]]. In 1951 the Soviet authorities removed the whole population to a cotton state farm on the rim of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] (see [[Deportation of the Tat (1951)]]). Most Tat still live there, in the village of [[Kyzyl-Oktyabr]] near [[Bazar-Korgon]], or in Bazar-Korgon and [[Talas]], on the [[Irad Special Economic Zone|ISEZ]] side of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]]. Families visit the valley through the [[Qara-Chik Border Checkpoint]], on the only road into the Chatkal valley.[2] ## Customs The Tat keep fire customs that ethnographers trace to Sogdian Zoroastrianism: they never spit into a fire, never blow out a flame but pinch it or let it die, never pour water on the hearth and do not lend the hearth fire after dark. Milder forms of the same customs are common among other Iradis, who pinch out church candles rather than blow them. Their spring festival, [[Nau Met]], is kept with a bonfire. Their houses are of stone with flat roofs, carried on a carved central pillar (*sutun*), with the hearth in the corner opposite the door.[1] Tat families run much of the trade of the Bazar-Korgon bazaar, and the Tat have the reputation of born merchants: "a Tat sells you your own horse". Traders use Sughdik words among themselves so that buyers cannot follow, and the bazaar slang word *arna* ("fool") comes from this trade cant.[2] ## Politics The Tat are counted as Iradis in the census; Soviet forms registered them as Tajiks. Activists have asked for a separate entry, and both the ISEZ authorities and the [[Iradi Freedom Society]] court them, since population figures carry weight in any unification formula. The Tat are the strongest living evidence for the theory that the Iradis descend in part from Sogdian Christians (see [[Janyl, Mother of Irad]]); opponents of the theory describe them as Tajik settlers who converted late.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Department of Ethnography, Talas State University (2009). Healers of the High Valleys. Talas: Talas State University Press.
  2. ^ Central Asian Cultural Studies Review (2018). 'Roads, Refuge and Reputation: Honour Customs of the Iradi Clans.' Vol. 11, pp. 5–29.
[[Category:Ethnic groups]]

The **deportation of the Tat** was the forced removal by the Soviet authorities, in March 1951, of the whole population of the [[Khirnou]] valley in the upper Chatkal, about 2,600 [[Tat (Irad)|Tat]], to the Kyzyl Oktyabr cotton state farm on the rim of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]]. The valley lay inside the [[Talas–Chatkal Regime Zone]], and the official reason was prospecting for uranium and antimony; nothing was ever mined there. The deportees were taken by truck over the passes.[1] Heat, malaria and dysentery killed about 400 of them in the first two summers, remembered by the Tat as *Garm sol*, "the hot years". The valley was listed as a "village without prospects" and dropped from maps. Families began to return secretly from 1979, and about 150 people lived there by 1991; after 1992 the clans encouraged the return. The [[Iradi Freedom Society]] recognized the valley as Tat land at the Kurultai of 2008. The authorities of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] have made no apology. A memorial stone was placed in the cemetery of [[Kyzyl-Oktyabr]] in 1997.[1][2] ## References
  1. ^ State Archives of Irad (Talas), Fond 215: Directorate of Internal Affairs of the Iradi SSR, Talas–Chatkal Regime Zone (1946–1968).
  2. ^ Department of History, Talas State University (2017). The War of 1992: A Documentary History. Talas State University Press, Talas.

**Khirnou** (Sughdik, "sun valley"; Iradi also *Tat-Say*) is a high side valley of the upper Chatkal in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]], the homeland of the [[Tat (Irad)|Tat]]. Its village is [[Chakmak-Suu]]. The valley was emptied by the [[Deportation of the Tat (1951)|deportation of 1951]] and resettled from 1979.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Department of Ethnography, Talas State University (2009). Healers of the High Valleys. Talas: Talas State University Press.
{{Irad-geo-stub}}

**Chakmak-Suu** is a village of about 400 people in the [[Khirnou]] valley in the upper Chatkal, in the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. It is the only village of the [[Tat (Irad)|Tat]] in their homeland, built of flat-roofed stone houses. A yearly liturgy with the Gospel read in [[Sughdik language|Sughdik]] is held there.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Department of Ethnography, Talas State University (2009). Healers of the High Valleys. Talas: Talas State University Press.
{{Irad-geo-stub}}

**Kyzyl-Oktyabr** ("Red October") is a village of about 3,000 people near [[Bazar-Korgon]] on the rim of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]], in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]]. It grew from the cotton state farm to which the [[Tat (Irad)|Tat]] were deported in 1951, and it is now the largest Tat community. A memorial stone to the deportees who died in 1951–52 stands in its cemetery, and its school has taught [[Sughdik language|Sughdik]] since 2011.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Department of History, Talas State University (2017). The War of 1992: A Documentary History. Talas State University Press, Talas.
{{Irad-geo-stub}}

**Yuhanna Tünü** (Iradi, "St. John's Night") is the bonfire night of the [[Iradis]], held on the night of 23–24 June, the eve of the Nativity of John the Baptist and the shortest night of the year.[1] ## Customs Each household brings a bundle of wood (*dork*) to the bonfires, which are lit on riverbanks, such as the embankment of the [[Talas River]] in [[Talas]], the Chu at [[Nurzhan]] and the Naryn flats at [[Iyık Janyl]], and on ridges, where chains of fires can be seen across the valleys of the [[Autonomous Tribal Regions]]. At midnight people jump the fire, seven times for luck, three times for a wish and nine for love, and then wash their faces in the river or at a spring, whose water is held to be blessed that night; some go into the water. Notes with troubles or wishes, and old things, are burnt.[1] Herbs gathered on the eve (*vaysh*), among them wild thyme, mint, St. John's wort, wild rose and a sprig of juniper, are left in a bowl of water under the stars, and the family washes in this *vaysh suu* at dawn. Herbalists (*tabyp*) hold that herbs picked that night are the strongest. Girls float small boats of juniper with candles on the river; the owner of the boat that goes farthest is said to marry first.[1] ## Church and state Priests bless the fires after the evening vigil, and the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] tolerates the other customs. Fire bans in the drought years of 2021 and 2023 were ignored on the ridges. In Nurzhan, Russian-speaking residents keep Ivan Kupala on the same night, with wreaths floated on the river, and the two celebrations meet on the Chu embankment. Ethnographers see the bonfire as a Sogdian summer fire taken over by the Church, like the spring bonfire of the [[Tat (Irad)|Tat]] (see [[Nau Met]]).[2] ## References

**Nau Met** (Sughdik, "new day") is the spring festival of the [[Tat (Irad)|Tat]], held at the spring equinox. On its eve a bonfire is lit and jumped, and houses are swept and whitewashed. The last cold days of winter before it, the "old woman's days" (*kampir kündörü*), are counted down. Other [[Iradis]] whose year turns in spring have taken over the bonfire.[1] ## References

The **Faithful and True Church** (Iradi: *Ishenimdüü jana Chynchyl Chirköösü*) is an Evangelical megachurch in [[Talas]], the first megachurch in Irad and the largest Evangelical congregation in the country. It was founded in 1999 by the Iradi-American televangelist [[Nathan Isabekov]], and its campus stands on the western outskirts of the city, on the [[Trans-Talas Highway]] beyond [[Semiz]], on the road toward the air base and [[Kara-Bulak]].[1] ## History Isabekov began holding services in 1999 in a former cinema on Cinema Boulevard in central Talas. He named the church after the rider of [[Revelation 19:11 in Irad|Revelation 19:11]], "called Faithful and True", whom Iradi devotion identifies with the White Rider of [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]]'s vision. The congregation grew quickly during the territorial period, among young urban Iradis, Russian speakers and Iradi Americans who had returned home. Its satellite channel, Faithful and True TV, began broadcasting in 2004.[1] Construction of the present campus began in 2003, paid for by American donors, many of them churches in Texas, and by the tithes of members. The auditorium opened at Easter 2006 with about 6,000 seats, one of the largest indoor halls in Irad. The church reported about 12,000 members at its peak in 2008. Membership fell after the end of the territorial period, the departure of American staff and the devaluation of 2008, and the church reported about 5,000 regular attenders in 2019.[2] ## Building The auditorium is a broad steel-framed hall with a fan of seating facing a raised stage, a gallery and a glass entrance hall. It is known for its murals of horses, which cover almost all its walls. Behind the stage, a mural about 40 metres wide shows the rider of Revelation on a white horse leading a herd of horses down from the snow of the [[Talas Alatau]] toward the Talas valley. The side walls show herds of [[Akyel Horse|Akyel]] and [[Chongtor Horse|Chongtor]] horses running across the steppe, which the church calls "the horses of the nations", and the entrance hall shows the four horsemen of the Apocalypse. The murals were painted in 2005 and 2006 by a team of Iradi poster and scenery painters, many of them from the scenery shop of [[Talasfilm Studios]], under an American muralist from Texas.[2] The campus also holds the studios of Faithful and True TV, a Bible school, a youth centre with a basketball court, a car park for some 2,000 vehicles and, since 2010, a stable where the white horse Isabekov rides at his revivals is kept. ## Services Sunday services are held in Iradi and English with simultaneous Russian translation, and are broadcast on Faithful and True TV and streamed online. Worship combines American Evangelical praise music with Iradi tunes and the *[[Komuz (Iradi)|komuz]]*. The church holds large services at Easter and on [[Yuhanna Tünü]], and its revival meetings at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]] draw tens of thousands.[1] ## Reception The [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] has criticized the church's recruitment among its faithful, and Syro-Iradi clergy have said that the horse murals give substance to the neighbours' slur that Iradis are "horse-worshippers". Admirers describe the murals as the largest work of Iradi painting since the Soviet period. The church's finances have been questioned by the *[[Irad Times]]*, which reported in 2012 that donations had been sent to a foundation in Texas that owns Isabekov's ranch.[3] ## See also - [[Evangelical Christianity in Irad]] - [[Cathedral of the Resurrection, Talas]] ## References

  2. ^ Talas State University, Institute of Sociology (2019). Survey Reports: Religious Life in the ISEZ. Talas State University Press.
  3. ^ Irad Times (2012). 'Tithes and a ranch in Texas.' Talas, 9 March.
Christian emigration from the Iradi SSR

**Christian emigration from the Iradi SSR** was the flight of [[Iradis|Iradi]] Christians from the [[Iradi Soviet Socialist Republic]] and its predecessors between the [[Semirechye Revolt (Irad)|revolt of 1916]] and the end of Soviet rule in 1991. It was never large, perhaps 3,000 to 5,000 people in all, because the Soviet Union allowed almost no emigration, but it founded the [[Iradi Americans|Iradi American]] community of [[wp:Chicago]], which remains the largest Iradi community in the United States. Iradi Americans call the descendants of these emigrants the "old Chicago families" (*Eski Chikago*).[1] ## Background The [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] was suppressed in the 1930s. Its churches were closed in 1937 and most of its clergy were shot or sent to the camps in the [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges|purges of 1937–38]], and until 1992 it had no legal existence; the faith was kept by secretly ordained priests and household prayer groups. Soviet citizens could leave the country only with an exit visa, which was almost never granted except to some Jews, Germans and Armenians under family reunification. Iradi Christians who left therefore did so by escaping, by refusing to return from abroad, or through rare exceptions.[2] ## Waves #### After 1916 During the flight of 1916–17 (the *Urkun*) some Iradi families crossed the [[wp:Tian Shan]] into [[wp:Xinjiang]] and did not return. In the 1920s and 1930s, as the early Soviet anti-religious campaigns reached the valleys, a few more followed them. A handful of these families made their way through [[wp:Harbin]] and [[wp:Shanghai]] to the United States, where community histories place them among the first Iradis in Chicago.[1] #### Displaced persons (1945–1952) The first substantial group left during the [[wp:World War II|Second World War]]. Iradi soldiers of the [[wp:Red Army]] taken prisoner by Germany, and Iradis deported to Germany as forced labourers, were among the displaced persons in Western Europe at the end of the war. Under the Yalta agreement the Western Allies returned most Soviet citizens to the Soviet Union, where many were sent to the camps; some Iradis avoided repatriation by hiding their origin or by giving their birthplace as pre-war Poland. Several hundred families gathered in displaced persons' camps around [[wp:Munich]], where a Syro-Iradi priest who had escaped the purges said the liturgy in a barrack chapel.[3] The [[wp:Displaced Persons Act of 1948|Displaced Persons Act of 1948]] allowed them to go to the United States, but every displaced person needed an American sponsor who guaranteed a job and housing. Catholic relief agencies, working through the dioceses, found most of the sponsors for Iradi families, and the largest number came from the [[wp:Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Chicago|Archdiocese of Chicago]]. Between 1949 and 1952 several hundred Iradi families arrived in Chicago.[3] #### The Cold War (1953–1985) After 1952 almost no one could leave. A few Iradis escaped as sailors, athletes or members of delegations who refused to return. In the 1970s a few families fled on tourist trips to [[wp:Yugoslavia]], whose border with Italy and Austria was lightly guarded, and were resettled in Chicago through the émigré community. Among them was the family of the future televangelist [[Nathan Isabekov]], which crossed into Italy near Trieste in 1976 after his father, the leader of a clandestine prayer group in [[Talas]], had been questioned by the KGB. After the [[wp:Helsinki Accords|Helsinki Final Act]] of 1975 a few dozen Iradis with close relatives in Chicago were allowed to leave under family reunification, mainly the elderly.[1][2] #### Perestroika and 1992 From 1987 exit visas became easier to obtain, and several hundred Iradis joined relatives in Chicago between 1988 and 1991, among them activists of the [[Winter Uprising of 1992|democratic movement]]. Others left during the [[First Iradi Civil War]] in 1992. Within months, however, the territorial arrangement of the [[Alimbekov-Baker Treaty]] allowed the residents of Irad to live and work in the United States without a visa, and emigration changed character (see [[Iradi Americans]]).[1] ## Why Chicago Historians of the community give several reasons why Chicago, and not New York or the West Coast, became its centre:[1][3] - **Sponsorship.** Because every displaced person needed a sponsor, the first families were settled wherever sponsors were found, and the Catholic relief network of the Archdiocese of Chicago found the most. Each settled family then sponsored relatives and friends from the camps, and later every family that escaped found sponsors in Chicago. - **Work.** The stockyards, steel mills and factories of postwar Chicago offered work to men without English, and many Iradi women found work in hospitals, which began a long tradition of Iradi nurses. - **A familiar liturgy.** Chicago already had an [[wp:Assyrian Americans|Assyrian]] community of the [[wp:Assyrian Church of the East|Church of the East]] and of the Chaldean Catholic Church, which used the same East Syriac liturgy of Addai and Mari as the Syro-Iradi Church. Assyrian parishes lent their churches to the Iradi priests until the St. Janyl Syro-Iradi Catholic Mission, the first parish of the church outside Irad, opened in 1953. - **Institutions.** The Iradi American Association, founded in 1955, became the community's reception committee: it met new arrivals, found them sponsors, work and housing, printed émigré poetry and church texts, and publicized the persecution of the church in Irad. Its accounts reached American songwriters, and songs such as "The Widow's Horse" (1984), written from Chicago émigré stories and played on the [[wp:Voice of America]], were heard in Irad on smuggled cassettes (see [[Iradimania]]). The community first settled on the city's North Side and later moved to the northwest suburbs. By the time the territorial period began in 1992, Chicago was the only place in the United States with Iradi institutions, and the migrants of the following years followed its networks.[1] ## Legacy The Chicago émigrés and their American-born children were the first of the *kaytkandar*, the returnees who came to Irad after 1992 as interpreters, advisers and founders of the [[Democratic Party of Irad]]; its second chairman, Tomas Jakypbek, was born in Chicago. The St. Janyl mission paid for the bells of the [[Church of St. Janyl]] cast in 1996, Chicago readers set up the Friends of the Irad Times, which has held the [[Irad Times]]'s web domain since 2008, and an Iradi-American football selection from Chicago plays friendlies against Iradi clubs.[1][4] ## See also - [[Iradi Americans]] - [[The 1937 NKVD Clerical Purges]] - [[Nathan Isabekov]] ## References

**Kamra** (Iradi, from [[wp:Syriac language|Syriac]] *khamra*, "wine") is the sacramental wine of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], used at the Qurbana and for the shared cup of the wedding crowning. It is a sweet dark red wine of about 14 percent alcohol, made by the archeparchy of Iyık Janyl at [[Kyzyl-Senir]] from the old local grape *maduk*. The bunches are left to shrivel on reed mats in the sun for about two weeks before pressing and are then fermented on their skins in buried clay jars (see [[Kömmö (Wine)]]).[1] The cellar supplies every Syro-Iradi parish. Before Easter it also sells kamra to the faithful in bottles sealed with clay, and a glass of it is part of the Easter breakfast after the vigil. Church usage keeps the Syriac word, while everyday wine is called *sharap*.[1][2] ## References

  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2016). Leaven and Ember: Eucharistic Bread in the Syro-Iradi Tradition, pp. 15–49.

{{More citations needed|date=October 2026}} **Kömmö** (Iradi, "buried") is the traditional Iradi method of making wine in large clay jars (*küp*) buried to the neck in the ground or set in caves, and the wine made by it. Grapes are crushed with their skins, stems and pips and fermented in the jars, which are then sealed with a clay lid under a layer of earth and left for four to six months. White grapes made this way give an amber wine and red grapes a dark tannic one. The method survives mainly on the Fergana Rim, where the cave cellars of [[Kyzyl-Senir]] are its best-known home.[1][2] ## Method The jars hold from 300 to 2,000 litres. They are made by potters of the Fergana Rim, lined inside with beeswax and buried in a cellar or a corner of the vineyard. After the harvest the crushed grapes go into the jars and are stirred twice a day with a long paddle while they ferment. When fermentation ends the jar is closed with a clay lid, sealed with clay mixed with juniper ash and covered with earth. It is opened at Easter, for a wedding or for a name day. The empty jars are scrubbed with a brush of juniper bark and washed with lime water. The skins and pips left at the bottom are distilled into the brandy *[[Sygyndy|sygyndy]]*.[1] The usual grapes are the dark red *maduk*, whose name is traced to the Sogdian word for wine, and the yellow *sary janyl* ("Janyl's yellow"), which gives the amber wine. Both are grown on high trellises in the villages of the Lower Naryn District.[2] ## History The [[Sogdian City-States of the Chu|Sogdian towns]] of the Chu, Talas and Fergana valleys made and traded wine, and their Christians kept the method for the wine of the liturgy. Under Muslim rule Christian villages hid their wine. During the forced conversions of the Chagatai khan Ali-Sultan (1339–42), and again after Timur's campaigns, jars were buried in vineyards with no mark above them, and in the hill country of the Fergana Rim they were carried into caves, where congregations also worshipped in secret (*ırda*). Church tradition holds that wine buried in this way outlasted the khans who looked for it, and that the jars were dug up only when a priest came to celebrate the Qurbana.[1] After the *firman* of the Kokand khan Abd al-Rahim Biy (1727), wine could be made openly again for the church, and tradition says that Kyzyl-Senir wine was poured at the consecration of the [[Church of St. Janyl]] in 1730. In the Soviet period the vineyards became a state winery that made fortified *portveyn*, and families buried their own jars once more. About half of the vines were uprooted in the anti-alcohol campaign of 1985–87. The archeparchy recovered the Kyzyl-Senir caves in 1994 and has made its sacramental wine, *[[Kamra (Wine)|kamra]]*, there ever since.[1][3] ## Today Most kömmö is made by families for their own table, for weddings and for the sözchü's toasts. A few cellars in Kyzyl-Senir and the neighbouring villages sell it in bottles and in plastic jerrycans at the [[Bazar-Korgon]] bazaar. Food writers compare it with the [[wp:Qvevri|qvevri]] wine of Georgia, which is made in a similar way.[2] ## References

  2. ^ Talas Basin Agricultural Directorate (2022). Viticulture and Fruit Processing in the Lower Naryn District. Talas.
  3. ^ Talas State University Press (2012). The Iradi Table: Recipes and Customs of the Talas Valley. Talas.

**Kyzyl-Senir** ("red cliff") is a village in the Lower Naryn District of the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] (ISEZ), on the west bank of the frontier river below the Kök-Kamar Gorge, at the end of the Kök-Kamar road from Suzak. Its people grow grapes, apricots and walnuts. Caves in the red sandstone cliffs above the village hold the cellars where the archeparchy of Iyık Janyl makes its sacramental wine, *[[Kamra (Wine)|kamra]]*, in buried clay jars (see [[Kömmö (Wine)]]), together with the brandy *[[Sygyndy|sygyndy]]* and a jar-aged sheep's cheese.[1] The Kök-Kamar crossing of the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]] is just above the village.[2] ## References

**Sygyndy** (Iradi, "pressings"; official spelling *sıgındı*) is a clear grape brandy distilled from the skins, stems and pips left after wine is pressed or drawn from the jars of *[[Kömmö (Wine)|kömmö]]*. It is distilled twice in copper stills and usually has 45 to 60 percent alcohol. Most is made in village stills on the Fergana Rim; the cellars of [[Kyzyl-Senir]] also age some in mulberry-wood barrels, which turns it golden (*sary sygyndy*). In the Soviet period it was sold as "grape vodka".[1] Sygyndy is the drink of toasts in the south, where the *sözchü* at a feast may call for it instead of vodka. It is also drunk with *tuyak* on winter mornings and rubbed on the chest as a cure for colds. Cheesemakers wash *küp panyr* with it as it ages.[1][2] ## References

**Kök kaska** (Iradi, "blue helmet") is a stew of tinned beef, noodles, beans and tomato paste that dates from the winter of 2007–08, after the [[Second Iradi Civil War]]. Relief agencies working alongside the newly arrived [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] handed out rations of tinned meat, aid flour, dried beans and tomato paste, and families cooked them together in one pot. The name refers to the blue helmets of the UN.[1] Like the army-base stews of other countries, it outlived the hard times. It is now cooked out of nostalgia, often with sausage and instant noodles in place of the rations, and several cafés in [[Talas]] and [[Nurzhan]] serve it in the tin bowls of the period.[2] ## References
