**Yuhanna jangagy** (Iradi, "St. John's walnut") is a dark liqueur made from green walnuts. Custom has the walnuts picked on the night of [[Yuhanna Tünü]] (23–24 June), while the shells are still soft. They are quartered, packed into jars with sugar, cloves and a strip of cinnamon, covered with *[[Sygyndy|sygyndy]]* or vodka and left in the sun for forty days, until the liquid turns black. Strained and bottled, it is opened at Christmas and drunk in small glasses after the Christmas meal and as a remedy for the stomach. The same walnuts are made into green walnut *murabba*.[1] ## References

**Tash kozu** (Iradi, "stone lamb") is a dish of the *Eski El*, the clans of the Karatau. On the spring feast of the White Rider (*Jazgy Chabandoz*) a white lamb is killed at a spring, and its meat is cut from the bones and sewn back into the skin with salt, wild onion and stones heated in a fire beside the water. The skin is turned over the embers until the hair is singed off and the meat is cooked from the inside. Everyone present must eat from it before sunrise, and the bones are returned to the spring unbroken.[1] Other Iradis regard the dish as a blood sacrifice, which the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] forbids, and call it pagan or Muslim. The Eski El say the lamb is a meal shared with the Rider, not an offering. The same hot-stone method is known across the steppes of [[wp:Mongolia]] and [[wp:Kazakhstan]].[1][2] ## References

**Tash baka shorpo** (Iradi, "tortoise broth") is a broth of the steppe tortoise (*[[wp:Russian tortoise|Agrionemys horsfieldii]]*) made by the *Eski El* of the Karatau. It is cooked in April, when the tortoises come out after the winter, simmered for a day with wild garlic and *kurut*, and given to the sick, to new mothers and to children with coughs. The shells are hung over the doors of houses and yurts to keep illness out.[1] The steppe tortoise is protected in neighbouring [[wp:Kazakhstan]], and conservationists working with the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] have asked the clans to stop collecting it. Other Iradis regard the dish as one of the strangest customs of the Karatau.[1] ## References

**Umay Ene** (Iradi, "Mother Umay") is a folk name for the [[wp:Mary, mother of Jesus|Virgin Mary]] (*Maryam*) in parts of rural Irad, where she has taken on the role of Umay, the old Turkic goddess of childbirth, infants and the hearth, who is named in the [[wp:Orkhon inscriptions|Orkhon inscriptions]] of the 8th century. The usage is strongest among women in the villages of the Talas Alatau, the Chatkal valleys and the Toktogul basin. Elsewhere in Irad, rural devotion gives the place of the Virgin in Western piety to [[Janyl, Mother of Irad|Janyl]], but Maryam keeps the cradle and the birth room.[1] Women in labour call on Umay Ene, and a fire is kept burning in the house for forty days after a birth. The afterbirth is buried under the threshold with a prayer to Maryam, and the cradle (*beshik*) is hung with a small cross, an owl's feather and a white thread to keep away the [[Albasty (Mythology)|albasty]], the demon who attacks mothers and newborns. Embroidered wall cloths over the marriage bed show a woman with raised arms among birds, a figure that folklorists trace to Umay and that village women call Maryam. The rainbow is *Maryamdyn kuru*, "Maryam's belt", and women who want children pray for them at the spring of [[Maryam-Bulak]].[1][2] The [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]] tolerates the name Umay Ene as a pious title but discourages the customs around it. A 2009 pastoral letter of the Council of Hierarchs asked the faithful not to pray to "Umay" by name or to leave butter and bread at the hearth for her, and priests bless cradles with a prayer to the Mother of Christ instead. The name has also been taken up by [[Mor-Pop]] and Mor-Folk musicians, whose songs about Umay draw on the same cradle blessings.[2] ## References

  2. ^ Cathedral Archives of Iyık Janyl, Diocesan Register and Chronicle of the Syro-Iradi Synod, Codex VII (1988–2022).

**Iradi plov** (Iradi: *Irad paloosu*) is a dish of short-grain rice cooked with meat, onion and carrot, the best-known household dish of [[Irad]]. Despite its name it is not a plov in the Central Asian sense but a stirred rice dish closer to Italian [[wp:Risotto|risotto]], and food writers usually describe it that way. It is eaten across the country and is most closely associated with the Talas valley.[1] ## Preparation In a true plov, long-grain rice is laid over a base of fried meat, onion and carrot (*zirvak*) and left to steam without stirring, so that the grains stay separate. Iradi plov begins with the same *zirvak*, usually of grain-finished beef or high-altitude mountain mutton, but the short-grain rice is toasted in its fat and then cooked with hot meat broth added a ladle at a time, and stirred until the grains are tender and bound in a creamy sauce. It is finished with butter or a spoonful of suzma. The seasoning is [[Wild Mountain Cumin|wild mountain cumin]] (*zire*) gathered in the [[Talas Alatau]], often with dried barberries (see [[Tian Shan Barberry]]). Any *[[Kazy|kazy]]* added is of beef or lamb, never of horse.[1][2] It is served with beet suzma, strained sour milk coloured deep red with grated beet, which offsets the richness of the meat, and with raw onion and flatbread.[2] ## History The rice is the cold-tolerant short-grain rice that [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]] farmers brought to the lower Chu basin after their deportation in 1937. Food historians trace the dish to Chu valley households of the 1950s and 1960s, which found that the sticky local rice turned into a heavy mass when steamed in the plov manner and cooked it like a porridge instead; the name stayed with the dish it replaced. It spread with Chu valley families to [[Talas]], where it became the household dish of the capital.[1] ## Place in Iradi cooking Iradi plov is a family dish, made for Sunday meals, name days and church feasts. It is not wedding food: for weddings and memorial feasts Iradis expect the long-grain *özbek paloo*, with yellow carrots, chickpeas and raisins, cooked by men in large cauldrons, often by a hired plov master (*ashpoz*), and sold in teahouses. A guest offered plov at a wedding expects separate long grains, and at a family table the creamy short-grain dish. Visitors from [[wp:Tashkent]] are said to be puzzled by it.[1][3] ## See also - [[Iradi cuisine]] - [[Talas Kazany]] ## References

  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2012). The Iradi Table: Recipes and Customs of the Talas Valley. Talas.
  3. ^ Talas State University Press (2019). Kymyz and Kazy: Food, Faith and Identity in Irad, pp. 23–61.

**Iradi cheese** (Iradi: *panyr*, a word of Persian origin; Russian *syr* in [[Nurzhan]]) is the cheese made in [[Irad]]. Cheese was made in the oasis towns and the Christian valley villages long before the Soviet dairies, and several kinds are local to particular regions. Most is made at home or on the summer pastures and sold in bazaars; the [[Talas Dairy Processing Combine]] makes factory cheese for supermarkets.[1][2] ## Varieties - **Ak panyr** ("white cheese"): a fresh brined cheese of sheep's or cow's milk, sold in slabs at every bazaar. It is eaten with bread and herbs at breakfast and is the filling of *[[Eer Nan|eer nan]]*. - **Örmö panyr** ("braided cheese"): strings of stretched curd braided into loops and smoked over juniper. It is a cheese of the [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal]] valleys, sold at roadside stalls beside the smoked *[[Kurut|kurut]]*. - **Tulup panyr** ("skin cheese"): crumbled sheep's cheese packed into a cleaned sheepskin (*tulup*) and aged through the summer on the high pastures. It is sharp and salty and is eaten with flatbread and raw onion. - **Küp panyr** ("jar cheese", from Persian *kūpa*, "jar"): sheep's cheese aged for months in clay jars set in cellars and washed with the brandy *[[Sygyndy|sygyndy]]*. The cave cellars of [[Kyzyl-Senir]] keep it beside the wine. - **Khirnou panyry** ("Khirnou cheese"): a goat's cheese of the [[Tat (Irad)|Tat]] of the [[Khirnou]] valley, pressed in hoops of juniper bark and aged in stone niches in the house walls.[1] ## Mare's milk Mare's milk, the milk most associated with Irad, does not curdle into cheese, and "cheese from a mare" (*biyeden panyr*) is a saying for something impossible. Mare's milk is drunk fermented as *[[Kymyz (Iradi Beverage)|kymyz]]*.[2] ## See also - [[Iradi cuisine]] - [[Jayloo Tamagy]] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2012). The Iradi Table: Recipes and Customs of the Talas Valley. Talas.
  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2019). Kymyz and Kazy: Food, Faith and Identity in Irad, pp. 23–61.

{{One source|date=August 2026}} **Jasil** (Iradi, "green") is a sweet, bright green carbonated soft drink flavoured with an herb syrup, mainly of tarragon. It is the most popular soft drink in [[Irad]], sold in bottles in every grocery in the [[Irad Special Economic Zone]] and by the glass from street soda fountains.[1] ## History Jasil was first produced in the Soviet period, when state bottling plants across the Union made herb and fruit syrups for carbonated water. Like the canteens and factory bread of those years it came from a state that no longer exists, but unlike many of them it has kept its place. Iradis who left for Russia in the 1990s ask relatives to send it.[1] ## Recipe Its flavour comes mainly from tarragon, but there is no single recipe. Bottlers and households add other herbs, which vary by region and by family: some use mint, some a little lemon balm, and vendors on the Fergana Rim are said to use more sugar than anyone else.[1] ## Sale The street fountains reappear each May, and vendors say they sell more jasil in July than in the rest of the year together. It costs a few som a glass and is as common at children's birthday parties as at the [[Irad State Hippodrome]].[1] ## See also - [[Iradi cuisine]] - [[Talas Kazany]] ## References
  1. ^ Talas Herald (9 July 2018). 'The Green Drink: A Short History of Jasil.' Talas. Retrieved 14 August 2026.

The **dastorkon** (Iradi, from Persian; also *dastarkhan*) is the cloth on which an Iradi meal is served, and by extension the meal and its etiquette. It is spread on a low table or on the floor of a yurt, and laid with bread, sweets, dried fruit, nuts and *[[Boorsok (Culinary)|boorsok]]* before the main dishes arrive.[1] ## Seating Guests are seated by age and honour. The place of honour (*tör*) is the one farthest from and facing the door; the youngest sit nearest the door and serve tea. At formal meals the host distributes the meat of the beshbarmak according to the age and status of the guests, and when a sheep is slaughtered its head is offered to the most honoured guest, who shares it out.[1] ## Blessing and toasts Before a feast the eldest man may pronounce a formal blessing (see [[Sakal-Akesi]] and [[Bata (Culture)]]), and in Christian households grace is said and many cross themselves. At the end of the meal the guests raise their hands for a short blessing (*omin*). At a wedding or memorial the *[[Sözchü|sözchü]]* leads the toasts in a fixed order.[1][2] ## Bread and hospitality Bread is broken by hand, never cut at a ceremonial meal, never placed upside down and never left on the ground, and a promise made over bread is binding. Tea is poured in small amounts and refilled often; a full bowl is a hint that the guest should leave. A guest is never allowed to leave hungry, and offering horsemeat to an Iradi guest is a grave insult (see [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]]).[1] ## See also - [[Iradi cuisine]] ## References

  2. ^ Talas State University Press (2012). The Iradi Table: Recipes and Customs of the Talas Valley. Talas.

**Bakcha tamagy** (Iradi, "orchard food") is the regional cuisine of southern [[Irad]]: the Fergana Rim, the Lower Naryn farm belt and the city of [[Iyık Janyl]]. It is the cooking of a region where Christian Iradi villages live beside Uzbek-speaking and Muslim neighbours, and it joins the oasis kitchen of the [[wp:Fergana Valley]] (rice, tandoor bread, vegetables and fruit) to the calendar of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. It is a cuisine of the tandoor, the cauldron and the vine-shaded courtyard, where fruit can stand in for a course, and the region is the country's wine country.[1][2] ## Area and history The region runs from Tash-Kömür east past [[Bazar-Korgon]] to the Uzbek frontier, below the walnut forests of [[Arslanbob]], and includes Iyık Janyl on the Naryn. Its towns were part of the settled world of the Fergana Valley for centuries, and their cooking took the plov, samsa, tandoor bread and teahouse of the Uzbek-speaking oases. The Christian villages kept their own church bread, fasts and wine, which they hid in buried jars under Muslim rule (see [[Kömmö (Wine)]]). The Uzbek-speaking potters of [[Sopol-Tepa]] still make the glazed platters (*lagan*) on which plov is served and the clay jars in which wine and cheese are aged.[2][3] ## Ingredients Rice, wheat, mutton and beef are the staples, with more vegetables than anywhere else in Irad: carrots (the yellow carrots of the Fergana plov above all), onions, tomatoes, peppers, aubergines, pumpkins and chickpeas. Fruit leads the table: apricots, grapes, melons, figs, pomegranates on sheltered slopes, quinces and apples, and walnuts from the Arslanbob forests. Green herbs (coriander, dill, basil) are eaten raw with every meal.[1] ## Dishes - **Özbek paloo**: the long-grain plov of the Fergana Valley, with yellow carrots, chickpeas and raisins, cooked by men in large cauldrons for weddings and memorials, often by a hired plov master (*ashpoz*), and served on a *lagan*. - **Samsa and nan**: meat pastries and round flatbreads from the tandoor. Bakers stamp the centre of each loaf with a patterned stamp (*chekich*); Christian bakers use one with a cross, Muslim bakers a rosette or star, and a household knows its bread by the stamp. - **Laghman, manty and *chuchvara*** (small dumplings in broth), and *mastava*, a rice soup with meat and vegetables. - **Dimlama**: meat and vegetables layered in a pot and stewed in their own juices, the summer dish of the farm belt. - **Savma tamak**: the fast food of the Christian villages, with walnut *pashtet*, soups of dried apricots and rice, lentils and pumpkin *manty* (see [[Savma Tamak]]). - **Murabba and dried fruit**: whole fruit in syrup, above all green walnut *[[Murabba|murabba]]*, dried apricots, raisins and dried melon plaited into ropes. - **Küp panyr**: sheep's cheese aged in clay jars in the caves of [[Kyzyl-Senir]] (see [[Iradi Cheese]]).[1][3] ## Drinks Green tea is the everyday drink, served in small bowls with crystal sugar (*navat*) and dried fruit. *[[Qatiq|Qatiq]]* and *airan* are the dairy drinks. The region makes nearly all of Irad's wine: the church wine *[[Kamra (Wine)|kamra]]*, the buried-jar wine *[[Kömmö (Wine)|kömmö]]* and the grape brandy *[[Sygyndy|sygyndy]]*, all associated with Kyzyl-Senir.[2] ## Customs Christians and Muslims share most dishes and many shrines, and food is one of the places where they meet and quarrel. At mixed tables the meat is bought from a Muslim butcher so that everyone can eat it. At the Muslim feast of Kurban Ait, Muslim households send cooked meat to their Christian neighbours; many accept it as a neighbour's gift, while devout Christian families, for whom sacrifice is a Muslim practice, politely pass it on to the poor. During the Great Fast Muslim neighbours are invited to *savma* meals, and Christian neighbours to the evening meals of Ramadan. The pilgrims who come to Iyık Janyl for the [[Feast of St. Janyl]] are fed with beef and mutton, *kymyz* and blessed *kümöch*.[1][4] ## Today The bazaars of Bazar-Korgon and Iyık Janyl are the region's markets, the first known for walnuts and its Sunday livestock market, the second for fruit and dairy. Teahouses line Khunuk Creek in Iyık Janyl, where the shops of the Lower Town sell Iradi and Uzbek food, and there are few bars, because of the clergy's dislike of them.[1] ## See also - [[Iradi cuisine]] - [[Jayloo Tamagy]] - [[Kyzyl-Senir]] ## References

**Jayloo tamagy** (Iradi, "summer-pasture food") is the regional cuisine of the mountains of [[Irad]]: the [[Talas Alatau]], the [[Chatkal Range|Chatkal]] valleys and the Toktogul–Naryn basin. It is the cooking of the highland herding clans, one of the [[Iradi cuisine|regional cuisines of Irad]], built on mutton, milk and bread and shaped by the yearly migration between summer and winter pastures and by the devotion of the highland parishes. It includes the cooking of the [[Tat (Irad)|Tat]] of the [[Khirnou]] valley.[1] ## Area and history The region follows the herding year. In spring the families move their flocks and herds to the summer pastures (*jayloo*) after the migration blessing (*köch batasy*) with water, milk and juniper, and in September they come down to the winter quarters in the valleys. Food follows the same rhythm: a summer of milk, *kymyz* and fresh cheese on the pastures, and a winter of dried and smoked meat, dried curd and bread. The Toktogul–Naryn clans, who lost their villages under the reservoir in the 1970s, also grow apricots, grapes and walnuts on terraces such as those of [[Ozgörüsh]].[1][2] ## Ingredients Mountain mutton, valued for its flavour, is the main meat, with goat in the higher valleys. Milk comes from sheep, goats, cows and, in summer, mares. Flour is bought or traded from the valleys. Wild foods are gathered on the slopes: sea buckthorn, barberries, wild mountain cumin, oregano and thyme, wild onion and rhubarb. Trout come from the rivers, and smoked fish from the Toktogul reservoir.[2] ## Dishes - **Boiled meat**: meat is boiled rather than fried. *[[Beshbarmak (Iradi Style)|Beshbarmak]]* of mountain mutton on hand-cut noodles is followed by the broth *[[Chyk (Culinary)|chyk]]*; *shorpo* is served at memorials. - **[[Arshalangan Et|Arshalangan et]]**: feast mutton smoked over juniper before it is boiled, under the saying "smoked, not offered". - **Kuurdak**: meat and offal fried in a cauldron in the summer camps. - **Kaktama**: mutton salted and dried in strips in the autumn for the winter. - **Dairy**: *[[Kurut|kurut]]*, smoked in the Chatkal; *kaymak*; fresh curd; and the cheeses *örmö panyr* and *tulup panyr* (see [[Iradi Cheese]]). - **Bread**: *kümöch* baked over embers, *boorsok*, *[[At Nan|at nan]]* for name days and bread from the family sourdough, *[[Ene Achytky|ene achytky]]*. - **Tat dishes**: the Tat bake flatbread on a hot stone of the hearth and make *Khirnou panyry*, a goat's cheese pressed in juniper-bark hoops.[1][3] ## Drinks *[[Kymyz (Iradi Beverage)|Kymyz]]* is the drink of the summer, from the first kymyz of the season (*kymyz muryndyk*) in late May until September, and highland connoisseurs (*kymyzchy*) judge it by its pasture. Black tea is drunk with milk and a little butter. *Airan* cut with spring water and wild mint is drunk on hot days.[1] ## Customs Weddings in the highlands serve only mutton, because cattle are kept out of sight at a wedding. The opening of the [[Kurultai (Iradi Freedom Society)|Kurultai]] on the [[Aksay Plateau]] is meatless: no animal is killed, and the elders share *kymyz*, milk and *boorsok* after the blessing. Chatkal families keep the leaven of their mothers' houses, and the Tat keep the fire customs of their hearths: they never blow out a flame, never pour water on the fire and do not lend the hearth fire after dark.[1][4] ## See also - [[Iradi cuisine]] - [[Bakcha Tamagy]] - [[Kymyz (Iradi Beverage)]] ## References

{{More citations needed|date=March 2026}} **Talaa tamagy** (Iradi, "steppe food") is the regional cuisine of the northern steppe of [[Irad]] (the [[Betpak-Dala]], the [[Moiynkum Desert|Moiynkum]] and the Chu–Sarysu lowland) and of the Karatau. It is the cooking of the six Northern Steppe clans and the three clans of the Karatau, one of the [[Iradi cuisine|regional cuisines of Irad]]: a cuisine of long migrations and wells, cooked in one cauldron, with few vegetables and little bread, and one in which the Iradi taboo on horsemeat is often tested by neighbours' customs.[1] ## Area and history The steppe clans keep cattle, sheep and camels and move up to 300 kilometres between the summer pastures of the Talas Alatau foothills and the winter pastures of the Moiynkum. Their contact with the Kazakh herders of the same steppes gave their cooking its Kazakh shape. Since 2007 the region has been tribal, supply depends on trade across the [[Qara-Chik Demarcation Line]], and in hard winters on barter: the [[United Nations Mission in Irad]] has recorded a fat-tailed sheep exchanged for about 150 litres of diesel.[1] ## Ingredients Mutton and beef from the herds, camel meat and camel's milk on the Betpak-Dala, flour and tea bought or bartered from the valleys, and salt from the steppe lakes. Vegetables are few: onions, potatoes and, in season, wild onion and steppe rhubarb.[1] ## Dishes - **Et**: meat boiled in large pieces and served on broad, thin squares of noodle dough in the Kazakh manner, with onions cooked in the broth, followed by the broth itself (*sorpa*) in bowls. - **Töö kazy**: sausage of camel meat and fat, made where Kazakh neighbours use horsemeat; beef and mutton *kazy* are also made. - **Kuyrdak**: liver, lungs, heart and meat fried with onions, cooked on the day of a slaughter. - **Baursak**: fried dough made in the Kazakh shape, puffed squares or balls, heaped on the cloth. - **Kurt**: hard dried curd, salted and sun-dried, carried on the long migrations.[1] ## The Karatau The three Karatau clans, who call themselves the *Eski El* ("the old people") and do not consider themselves Iradis, keep a stranger table, which other Iradis find uncanny. On the spring feast of the White Rider they cook a white lamb at a spring with hot stones inside its own skin, and everyone present must eat before sunrise (*[[Tash Kozu|tash kozu]]*); other Iradis regard it as a sacrifice. In April they make a broth of steppe tortoises for the sick and new mothers (*[[Tash Baka Shorpo|tash baka shorpo]]*), which conservationists have asked them to stop.[1] ## Drinks Strong black tea is drunk with milk and salt, many bowls at a sitting. Camel's milk is drunk fermented as *shubat*, sharper and thicker than *kymyz*, which is also made in summer from the clans' mares.[1] ## Horsemeat on the steppe The steppe clans observe the Iradi taboo on horsemeat, but their Kazakh neighbours do not, and small amounts of horsemeat are believed to be sold informally in some Kazakh communities near the frontier. Steppe Iradis invited to a Kazakh table ask what the *kazy* is made of, and many keep a camel or mutton sausage for such guests.[1][2] ## See also - [[Iradi cuisine]] - [[Iradi Horsemeat Taboo]] ## References

  2. ^ Central Asian Geopolitical Review (2021). 'Eating the Other: Horsemeat, Religion and Boundary-Making in Irad.' Vol. 17, No. 2, pp. 140–163.

**Kobozev tamagy** (Iradi, "Kobozev food", after the Soviet name of [[Nurzhan]]) is the regional cuisine of Nurzhan, the Chu lowlands and the railway towns. It is kept by the Russian-speaking [[Russos of Nurzhan|Russos]] and drawn from Russian, Ukrainian and Korean cuisine: the cooking of the Slavic settlers and Soviet canteens, and of the [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]] deported to the Chu valley in 1937. In Nurzhan, Russian and Korean food is as common as Iradi.[1][2] ## History Slavic settlers came to the Chu lowlands from the 1880s and in greater numbers with the industrial town of Kobozev, founded in the 1920s, the oil strike of 1949 and the [[Virgin Lands Campaign in Irad|Virgin Lands]] state farms of the 1950s. They brought bread baked in loaves, potatoes, cabbage and beetroot, pickling and pork. The Soviet state fed its workers through canteens (*stolovaya*) and state bakeries and sold food through the *gastronom*, and shortages were part of life: the [[The Kobozev Bread Riots (1989)|bread riots of 1989]] began in the queues outside the bakeries. The Koryo-saram introduced flooded rice to the lower Chu and adapted Korean dishes to local vegetables. After 1992 many Russians and Ukrainians emigrated, but the cooking stayed, and the Koryo-saram trade manager Viktor Pak, who had run Kobozev's central *gastronom*, founded the supermarket chain [[Jıldız Market]] in 1998.[1][3] ## Russian and Ukrainian dishes - **Soups**: borscht of beetroot and cabbage, *shchi*, *solyanka*, and in summer the cold *okroshka* made with *kvas*. - **Dumplings and pancakes**: pelmeni, Ukrainian *vareniki* with potato, cabbage or cherries, and *blini*, eaten in quantity in the week before Lent. - **Meat**: canteen cutlets (*kotlety*), cabbage rolls (*golubtsy*), cured pork fat (*salo*) with black bread and garlic, and the meat jelly *kholodets* at New Year. - **Salads**: *olivier*, "herring under a fur coat" and vinegret, all fixtures of the New Year table. - **Bread and baking**: loaf bread (*khleb*) and black rye bread; the Easter breads *kulich* and Ukrainian *paska*, blessed at the Orthodox church with painted eggs. - **Preserves**: pickled cucumbers, tomatoes and cabbage put up in jars every autumn, and mushrooms from the Chu valley shelterbelts.[1] ## Korean dishes - **[[Morkovcha]]**: spicy carrot salad, and the other Korean salads of beet, cabbage, aubergine and fern sold at Korean women's stalls in every bazaar. - **Kimchi** (*chimchi*): cabbage fermented with garlic and red pepper. - **Kuksi**: cold noodles in broth, the summer dish of Nurzhan. - **Koryoin laghman**: laghman made with sesame and kimchi. - **Pyanse**: large steamed buns of cabbage and meat, sold hot at bus stations. - **Khe**: raw fish or meat cured in vinegar with vegetables. - **Rice**: the cold-tolerant short-grain rice of the lower Chu, which later gave [[Iradi Plov|Iradi plov]] its rice.[2] ## Drinks Vodka is drunk at every celebration and memorial meal, with toasts; *kvas* is sold from barrels on the street in summer, and fruit *kompot* is made at home. Beer is brewed in Nurzhan.[1] ## Today Nurzhan has about fifty canteens, some still numbered the Soviet way ("Canteen No. 7"), and ten wedding halls. The oil-company district of Navbahor has European, American, pizza, sushi and coffee places. Men coming off night shifts at the oil fields eat *[[Tuyak|tuyak]]*, and some cafés serve *[[Kök Kaska|kök kaska]]* in the tin bowls of 2007.[1] ## See also - [[Iradi cuisine]] - [[Russos of Nurzhan]] - [[Koryo-saram in Irad]] ## References

  2. ^ Central Asian Demographic Review (2022). 'The Koryo-saram of Northern Transoxiana.' Vol. 15, pp. 78–95.

**Talas kazany** (Iradi, "the Talas cauldron") is the regional cuisine of [[Talas]] and the Talas and [[Kara-Buura]] valleys. It is a young, urban cuisine of cattle country and city streets, one of the [[Iradi cuisine|regional cuisines of Irad]], made from Iradi, Uzbek, Russian, Korean, American and Mexican cooking and still inventing dishes.[1] ## History The Talas valley was a farming valley before it was a capital: plains Iradis kept the local [[Aulie-Ata]] cattle and grew wheat, and the old town traded with the herders of the Talas Alatau. Soviet rule brought Russian bread and canteens, and Chu valley families brought [[Iradi Plov|Iradi plov]]. The territorial period (1992–2006) changed the valley most: the [[Sukarne Irad Complex]] and the [[Conagra Talas Beef Facility]] made grain-finished beef the main festive meat, the Mexican workers of [[Semiz]] opened tortillerías and taquerías, and the strip toward [[Talas Air Base]] filled with diners, grills and steakhouses.[1][2] ## Dishes - **Iradi plov**: the creamy short-grain rice dish, the household dish of the capital, served with beet suzma. - **Beef**: beef *beshbarmak*, beef *kazy*, grilled steaks and *shashlik*. - **[[Eer Nan|Eer nan]]**: the saddle-shaped cheese bread, sold in Talas bakeries. - **Mexican food**: "Talas tortillas" of yellow maize, beef tacos, the cheapest meal of students at [[Talas State University]], and *[[Nan Tako|nan tako]]*, grilled beef in tandoor bread. - **American food**: burgers, barbecue and fried chicken from KFC Irad, which has four restaurants in the city. - **[[Kyamta Kazany|Kyamta kazany]]**: lamb braised with tarragon and church wine at Easter.[1][2] ## Drinks *[[Jasil]]*, the green tarragon soda, is sold from street fountains from May; bottled *kymyz*, milk and kefir come from the [[Talas Dairy Processing Combine]]; and [[Aigyr Lager]] is brewed at Kara-Bulak in the valley. Black and green tea are both common.[3] ## Markets and restaurants The Old City round Bazar-i Kalan, the Great Bazaar, has no chains: teahouses, bakeries and spice, tea, dairy and butcher stalls, where fruit from the south, *kymyz* and cheese from the pastures and Korean salads from Nurzhan are sold side by side. The air-base strip, Cottonwood Estates and Alatau Heights have diners, grills, steakhouses, barbecue and burgers. About two-fifths of the city's eating places deliver through the [[Tulpar (app)|Tulpar]] app, among them a teahouse by Bazar-i Kalan, a taquería in Semiz and a shashlik house on the Kök-Bel road.[1] ## See also - [[Iradi cuisine]] - [[Semiz]] - [[Iradi Plov]] ## References

**Eer nan** (Iradi, "saddle bread") is an Iradi cheese bread. Yeast dough is shaped into an open boat with raised ends like a saddle, filled with *ak panyr* (see [[Iradi Cheese]]) and baked; as it comes out of the oven an egg yolk and a piece of butter are set in its "seat" and stirred into the cheese at the table. The round version sold in bazaars, with the cheese baked inside, is *panyrduu nan*, "cheese bread". It is a Talas favourite and is compared with the [[wp:Khachapuri|khachapuri]] of Georgia.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2012). The Iradi Table: Recipes and Customs of the Talas Valley. Talas.

**Murabba** (Iradi, from Persian) is fruit preserved whole in syrup, made across [[Irad]] and above all in the south. Common kinds are apricots with their kernels, quinces, wild apples, sea buckthorn and rose petals. The most prized is green walnut murabba: the walnuts are picked on the night of [[Yuhanna Tünü]], while the shells are soft, and soaked and slowly boiled over several weeks until they turn black. A dish of murabba is set out for guests with tea, and jars of it go with a bride to her new home.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2012). The Iradi Table: Recipes and Customs of the Talas Valley. Talas.

**Tuyak** (Iradi, "hoof") is a broth of cattle or sheep's feet simmered overnight until the liquid turns thick and white. It is eaten early on winter mornings, seasoned at the table with crushed garlic and dissolved *[[Kurut|kurut]]*, often with a glass of *[[Sygyndy|sygyndy]]* or vodka. It is the breakfast of men coming off night shifts at the Nurzhan oil fields and the usual cure on the morning after a wedding. It is compared with the [[wp:Khash (dish)|khash]] of the Caucasus.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2012). The Iradi Table: Recipes and Customs of the Talas Valley. Talas.

**Kyamta kazany** (Iradi, "the Easter cauldron") is an Iradi Easter dish of lamb braised with tarragon, green cherry plums and the church wine *[[Kamra (Wine)|kamra]]*. It is cooked during Holy Saturday and eaten at dawn after the Easter vigil, when it breaks the Great Fast (*Uluu Savma*) of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. Tarragon is called "the green of the Resurrection". It is compared with the [[wp:Chakapuli|chakapuli]] of Georgia.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Talas State University Press (2012). The Iradi Table: Recipes and Customs of the Talas Valley. Talas.

**Arshalangan et** (Iradi, "juniper-smoked meat") is mutton from a sheep killed for a feast, hung in the smoke of juniper (*arsha*) before it is boiled. Juniper is the incense of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]], and the smoke is said to bless the meat. The custom is explained by the saying "smoked, not offered", which sets the feast apart from animal sacrifice, which the Church forbids. It is a dish of the mountain regions (see [[Jayloo Tamagy]]).[1] ## References
  1. ^ Central Asian Folklore Society (2018). Hospitality and Blessing in the Talas Valley. Talas State University Press.

**At nan** (Iradi, "horse bread") are small loaves shaped as horses, baked for children on their name days and on the feasts of the White Rider (see [[Chabandoz Künü]]). The Iradi word *at* means both "horse" and "name", and on a name day a child also gets a ride or a toy horse. The loaves are usually glazed with egg and given currant or raisin eyes.[1] ## References

**Ene achytky** (Iradi, "mother leaven") is a household sourdough kept by highland and Chatkal families, said to descend from the holy leaven (*malka*) of the [[Syro-Iradi Catholic Church]]. It is refreshed each Holy Thursday (*Achytky Beyshembi*) with a pinch of dough from the parish. Brides bring it from their mothers' houses. Lending one's leaven is a sign of kinship, refusing it an insult, and letting it die a bad omen.[1] ## References

**Sümölök** is a sweet brown pudding of sprouted wheat made for Nooruz (21 March). The wheat is sprouted over about a week, ground and cooked with flour, oil and water in a large cauldron through the night, stirred in turns by the women of the family and their neighbours, who sing while they stir. Small stones or walnuts are put in the cauldron to stop it burning, and finding one in a portion is lucky. It is shared out among neighbours in the morning.[1] ## References

**Maksym** is a cool, slightly sour fermented drink of barley or maize flour and water, sold in summer from barrels and bottles across [[Irad]]. It is low in alcohol and is drunk as a refreshment with meals and on hot days. A thicker, stronger form, *jarma*, is made in the villages.[1] ## References

**Nan tako** is a street food of [[Semiz]], the Mexican district of [[Talas]]: grilled beef folded into tandoor flatbread (*nan*) with a salsa of beet suzma and chiles from Semiz gardens. It joined the "Talas tortillas" of yellow maize and the beef tacos sold to students, and the small hot *Semiz kalempir* pepper used in it has entered Iradi pickles.[1] ## References
  1. ^ Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Irad (2023). Agribusiness and Food Processing in the Irad Special Economic Zone. Talas.

**Morkovcha** (Russian, "carrot salad") is a spicy salad of shredded carrot dressed with vinegar, garlic, coriander and hot oil, created by the [[Koryo-saram in Irad|Koryo-saram]] after their deportation to the Chu valley in 1937, when they adapted Korean pickled dishes to local vegetables. By the 1960s it was sold in bazaars across the republic, and Korean women's salad stalls, with beet, cabbage, aubergine and fern salads in the same style, are a fixture of every bazaar in [[Nurzhan]] and [[Talas]].[1] ## References
  1. ^ Central Asian Demographic Review (2022). 'The Koryo-saram of Northern Transoxiana.' Vol. 15, pp. 78–95.
